en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Analysis of the Vinaya (First Part)
The Introduction to the Composition (Ka):
Manifested from the sky of the Solar Dynasty;
I pay homage to the Buddha, who possesses great wisdom,
whose halo of radiance is like a rainbow,
and who has dried up the evil nature of defilements with the water of the Dhamma.
(Kha) Its stream of words is clear and deep,
garlanded with the infinite waves of various methods.
I pay homage to the Dhamma, that great flowing river, which is a school of immortal fish consisting of the aggregates of virtue and the rest.
(Ga)
The sun of virtue, garlanded with the conch of ascetic practices;
with contentment as its water, tranquility as its soil, and the mind as its essence;
having the duty of striving and the heart of higher consciousness;
I pay homage to the Saṅgha, which is like the great ocean.
(Gha) Those sons of the King of Sages who possess the qualities of the lineage;
To those who, preserving [the tradition] until this very day,
have brought forth a stainless commentary—
to those ancient teachers, I pay homage.
(Ṅa) He who bore a name equal to that of the General of the Dhamma;
he was like a lamp for the island of Sri Lanka.
The great general Mahāyatinda brought me to growth within the teaching of the Conqueror.
(ca)
By whom this commentary was made upon the *Aṭṭhakathā* named *Samantapāsādikā*,
as well as upon the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā*;
And the science of astrology from other teachers as well;
(six) by one who establishes the concord of the Nikāyas;
I pay homage to that venerable one, a worthy recipient of reverence, who was honored with offerings by King Parakkantibhuja, the sovereign of Laṅkā.
Thus did I obtain this [vision] while paying homage to the Triple Gem,
which is worthy of veneration by those who themselves should be venerated.
By the power of that accumulation of merit which has become abundant,
may all obstacles be destroyed. (Jha)
He who was highly praised even by the teacher Buddhaghosa,
who is himself well-praised by the wise—
he who is named the teacher Buddhadatta—
The great poet, a beacon for the lineage of the Elders,
composed this work entitled *Vinayavinicchaya*. (Ña)
This excellent and beneficial treatise,
which provides proficiency in the methods of discipline for those who seek it,
was formerly a Sinhalese commentary on this work.
(Ṭa) Because it does not accomplish the welfare of the monks in all the islands without exception, that [is not the true Dhamma].
Therefore, one who is a refuge of compassion and desires the welfare of ascetics everywhere [should act accordingly].
(Ṭha)
By the Elder Sumaṅgala, the most excellent,
who dwells in the forest, who knows the method, and who possesses the virtuous aspiration for excellence, [this was composed] with due care.
He was entreated by one who desires its long continuance,
through the power of his virtuous qualities. (Ḍa)
Of the Dhamma taught by the Lord of Dhamma,
[this work was composed] by the Elder Buddhamitta,
who shone like a lamp in the land of Coḷa and was elevated by such virtues as faith.
(Ḍha) Likewise, by the Elder named Mahākassapa,
who was full of reverence for the training rules;
By Kudiṭṭhimattebhavidāraka,
who was honored by the King of Coḷa, and by Siha.
(Ṇa)
By that faithful lay follower (upāsaka) named Dhammakitti— so called because he was praised for his virtue—
who was adorned with various qualities such as moral discipline (sīla) and the like;
Here, by a wise person who desires the true Dhamma—
by one endowed with faith and possessed of wisdom— [through] moderation;
By Maṅgalyavaṃsa of great renown,
by Vāṇijabhānu who was entreated [to do so],
and by Varañña, the source of virtuous qualities.
Therefore, having set forth that Pali language,
relying upon the instruction of the ancient teachers;
Having abandoned the fault of the attainments of other schools,
and having avoided an excessively prolix method, [I shall provide] a concise [treatment]. (Da)
Revealing the meaning not yet expressed and without overstepping the sequence of the text,
I shall comment upon the essence of that meaning.
Having extracted the essence even from other books,
for those people who desire its long endurance;
May the virtuous listen well to this concise commentary being composed by me upon the stainless teaching that brings about welfare.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Book.

As this teacher commences this treatise on the Vinaya—which brings about the accumulation of qualities such as vast and stainless faith and wisdom; which is the sole cause for the welfare of all beings;

and which constitutes the very root of the Jina’s Dispensation’s endurance—he first, at the commencement of the work, sets forth [the following]: the homage to the Triple Gem, the title of the work, the subject matter, the function, the purpose, the causal motive, the author, and the extent.
To demonstrate this, he said, “Having paid homage,” and so forth. In that context, the Three Jewels (Ratanattaya) are defined as follows:
“That which is honored and of great value, incomparable and rare to behold, and enjoyed by extraordinary beings—therefore it is called a ‘jewel’ (ratana).”
The specific nature of each has been pointed out as follows:
"The Buddha is omniscient wisdom; the Dhamma is the nine supramundane states;
and the Sangha consists of those established in the paths and fruits—this is the Triple Gem."

The Triple Gem—which has its various manifestations fully analyzed, which wards off the suffering of all states of existence, and which is the sole refuge within the three realms—is the object of homage.
What is called "homage" (paṇāmo) is the volition (cetanā) that brings about the act of paying homage. That [volition] is threefold:

bodily homage, verbal homage, and mental homage. Among these, bodily homage is a physical action consisting of such acts as joining the palms in reverence, preceded by the recollection of the virtues of the Triple Gem.

Volition that originates bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). What is called "verbal salutation" (*vacīpaṇāma*) is likewise volition that originates verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), proceeding by way of an act of praise whose nature is the manifestation of various specific qualities.

What is called "mental salutation" (*manopaṇāma*) is volition that, without originating either of the two intimations, accomplishes through the mere recollection of qualities a state of the mental continuum being inclined toward, leaning toward, and bent toward [the object], characterized by the flow of reverence and great respect.
First, the purpose of this homage to the Triple Gem is to accomplish the intended goal.

For an act of homage rendered to the Triple Gem—which is worthy of such homage due to its possession of preeminent qualities—by virtue of its nature as a distinguished merit, wards off the net of calamities brought about by non-meritorious karma;
for such karma acts as an obstacle, an affliction, and a torment to the attainment of one’s desired ends.

By providing support for the meritorious deed that has the attainment of one’s own fortune as its cause, and by increasing the lifespan, happiness, strength, and so forth within the continuum of its ripening,
it becomes the cause for the long-term persistence [of the teaching] and the basis for the accomplishment of the intended treatise. Furthermore, for the listeners,
it serves as the means for the undertaking preceded by homage to those worthy of veneration, and for the sequence of learning, memorizing, and so on, free from obstacles.

It is for the purpose of establishing the means for understanding the treatise. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of generating reverence for the treatise in those listeners who already know the Teacher, by causing them to recollect the specific qualities of the Blessed One as they truly are and thereby engendering faith;
and for those who do not know the Teacher, it is for the purpose of generating reverence for the Teacher—the source of the treatise—by means of the treatise’s well-expounded nature.
Primarily for the benefit of those who hear it, teachers place at the beginning of their compositions verses that express praise and homage.

Otherwise, since the intended purpose would be accomplished even without such placement—merely by means of physical and mental prostration—what need would there be for this which merely causes weightiness to the book? This is the summary here.
In detail, however, the purpose of the salutation should be understood according to the method shown in the *Sāratthadīpanī* and other such works.

The statement of the title is for the sake of ease of conventional usage. The statement of the subject matter—that which is to be presented by the treatise as a whole—is for the purpose of showing the essential nature of the treatise that is to be undertaken.
[The mention of] what is known, blameless, meaningful, easy to perform, and undertaken...
For those who are critical observers consider that only a well-constructed treatise (*pakaraṇa*) is worthy of being undertaken.

The demonstration of the manner of composition is for the purpose of inspiring the audience; for listeners are inspired to hear a treatise that has been composed in a manner that is orderly, unconfused, and so forth.
Furthermore, the statement of the purpose is for the purpose of inciting the audience to study the treatise.
For if the purpose were not stated, those engaged in recitation would remain unaware of its purpose.

The statement of the cause [of composition] is for the sake of generating respect for the work among like-minded people; for it is only when a work arises from a praiseworthy cause that like-minded people conceive respect for it.
The statement regarding the author is intended so that there may be reverence for the work through reverence for the person.
The statement regarding the extent is for the purpose of encouraging those who are negligent in recitation and other duties;

for when they hear the extent of the work, they become encouraged, thinking, "This is but a small amount; we shall complete it before long," and thus they apply themselves to recitation and the rest. By the word "etc. (*ādi*),...

The exhortation to listen attentively (*sakkacca-savaṇa-niyojana*) is included [here] for the purpose of producing the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*suta-maya-ñāṇa*), which is the root cause of all success.
For one who listens without attention, since there is no hearing, there is also an absence of the knowledge consisting of what has been heard that is caused by it.
Thus, even when a person with a distracted mind is told of all forms of success, they say: "I have not heard it; [tell it] again..."
"It should be spoken," he says.
Therein, first, in the initial verse, by the word "having paid homage" (*vanditvā*), the threefold prostration is shown without distinction.
But specifically, by these four terms—"the best," "without a counterpart," "that which brings about the end of existence," and "free from defilement"—[it is shown].
It should be understood that with the words "pada" [and "sirasa"] the verbal salutation (*vacīpaṇāma*) is shown; by the word "sirasā," the physical salutation (*kāyappaṇāma*) is shown;
and by these three words—"Buddhaṃ, Dhammaṃ, Gaṇañca"—the Triple Gem, which serves as the object of the act of salutation, is indicated.
By the phrase "Vinayassa vinicchayaṃ," the designation is shown through a compound (*aluttasamāsa*) consisting of the name "Vinayavinicchaya."

By way of demonstration. Furthermore, the subject matter (*abhidheyya*)—which is to be presented by this entire treatise as the cause for the occurrence of words through its conformity to the literal meaning—is also shown by that very same [term].

By the phrases “in brief” (*samāsena*) and “unconfused, uncluttered, with a sequence of sweet meanings and words,” the manner of composition (*karaṇappakāra*) is demonstrated. And by the phrase “for the sake of welfare” (*hitatthāya*), [it is shown that it] produces proficiency.

The purpose [of this work] is indicated by such phrases as "in the procedures of the Vinaya" and "for those crossing to the further shore. By the words "of the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs," the external object is shown.
As for the internal object, however, it is compassion directed toward the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs who constitute that external object;
since this is understood from the very commencement of the Master’s treatise, it is not stated separately. "I shall explain"—this is the promise to undertake the task.
The pure agent expressed as "I," which is obtained through this state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), is shown in a general sense.
However, specifically at the conclusion of the treatise:
"It was composed by Buddhadatta, the wise one of pure mind;..."
“By one who desires the long endurance of the Great Sage’s Dispensation”—
with this verse, and by Tambapaṇṇiya, the supreme expounder, skilled in the methods and procedures of the Tipiṭaka,
the one who causes the lotus-forest of the hearts of the most excellent poets to blossom, the bull among eminent poets, who utters sweet words that bring supreme delight...
And by this statement, “This *Vinayavinicchaya* was composed by Buddhadatta of Uragapura,” as well as by later and more eminent poets who praised his virtues in such words as,

“Even after Buddhadatta has passed away, there are still poets like me,” one should understand that the venerable teacher Buddhadatta possessed highly extolled qualities. Furthermore, because he is the author of the *Hetu*, it is in that very same work—
The Great Elder Buddhasīha, who has completed his studies under the urging of Pakaraṇaññāṇa,
says: "The exposition of the Vinaya as spoken by Buddhasīha..."
This [work] has been composed for the monks, dedicated to my co-resident, Buddhasīha.
“For the benefit [of others], in brief.
Thus it was shown.
Furthermore, because the *Uttarapakaraṇa* has the Elder Saṅghapāla as its author, he too—
“Patience, gentleness, virtue, wisdom, faith, compassion, and the like—
those qualities are firmly established in him, just as jewels are in the ocean. By him,
who is endowed with discipline and proper conduct, [this should be performed] carefully and with reverence.”
He was requested by the Elder Saṅghapāla, whose mind was steadfast,
who desired that the Vinaya of the Great Sage endure for a very long time,
and who sought proficiency for the monks in the discernment of the Vinaya:
“I performed this supreme [deed], named Uttara.
Thus it is shown. Not only these two great elders were the causal agents; rather, in the Mahāvaṃsa and other texts, it is said:
“Like that of the Buddha, profound...”
They declared him by his name as “Buddhaghosa,” for he was like a Buddha upon the surface of the earth.

In this manner, the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa, the author of the commentaries on the Tipiṭaka-pāriyatti, whose virtues have been extolled above, should be understood as the "efficient cause" by way of oral tradition.

How so? It is said that when the venerable teacher Buddhadatta was traveling from the island of Laṅkā to Jambudīpa—his own ancestral land—he encountered the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa, who was surrounded by residents of Jambudīpa who were devoted to the practice of the path and endowed with the qualities of skill and proficiency.
Having translated the Sinhalese *Aṭṭhakathā* composed by the most eminent of the Great Theras,
and seeing [the author] on the way to the island of Laṅkā in order to write a commentary on the Tipiṭaka scriptures in the vernacular tongue common to all people,
he examined him through conversation; [he saw him] as one who, with a jewel-treasure-like wisdom and virtue surpassing the whole world, was like a revealer of hidden treasures.

Perceiving that he desired to compose a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) for it—much like one who, though extremely poor, has attained great satisfaction—he promised him in person, saying, "Please send us the commentary you have written up to the intended limit, and we shall write its treatise (*pakaraṇa*).
And being requested by him, "It is well; it should be done thus," [he set about] the Abhidhamma commentary.
It is said that he composed the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, the *Vinayaṭṭhakathā* together with its commentary (*sauttara*), and the *Vinayavinicchaya-pakaraṇa*;
thus one should not be envious. By the word "in brief" (*samāsena*), the extent [of the work] is shown in a general sense, because that general extent is understood even within the detailed extent.
Specifically, however, it is twofold: the extent of the sections (*pariccheda*) and the extent of the text (*gantha*). Therein:
In this treatise, "delimitation" (pariccheda) refers to the measure [of the subject matter] expressed by way of conventional terminology.

That is to say: the discourse on the *pārājika* offenses, the discourse on the *saṅghādisesa* offenses, the discourse on the *aniyata* offenses, the discourse on the *nissaggiya* offenses, the discourse on the *pācittiya* offenses, the discourse on the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses, and the discourse on the *sekhiya* training rules—thus the discourse on the *bhikkhu-vibhaṅga* is sevenfold; from among those, the discourse on the *aniyata* offenses...
Excluding likewise the sixfold exposition on the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, as well as the twentyfold exposition on the Khandhakas beginning with the Mahākhandhaka and ending with the Bhikkhunīkhandhaka,
along with the exposition on formal acts (kamma), the exposition on the failure of formal acts, the miscellaneous determinations, and the method for the development of meditation subjects—
these constitute the thirty-seven sections of exposition in the Vinaya-vinicchaya.
And in the *Uttarapakaraṇa*, according to the method stated [therein], there is: sevenfold discourse on the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga*; sixfold discourse on the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga*;

immediately following that, discourse on failure (*vipatti*); discourse on the conditions for legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-paccaya*); discourse on questions concerning the *Khandhakas*; discourse on the headings of the origins (*samuṭṭhāna-sīsaka*);

discourse on the origins of offenses (*āpatti-samuṭṭhāna*); discourse on the method of single-increment (*ekuttara-naya*); discourse on the breaking of perspiration (*sedamocana*); and discourse on the introduction and other matters of the two *Vibhaṅgas*.
There are thirty-six sections of discourse: the discourse on all the marks [of a Great Man] and the discourse on the enumeration of the retinue.
However, it is stated without doubt that there are "thirty-eight sections of discourse";
this includes sixteen sections by taking the twelvefold and fifteenfold methods—which were not shown in the single-incremental method—and thus accounts for a slight deficiency or excess in the count.
It should be understood that this was stated on the grounds that [the number] does not exist.
In both cases, the extent of the sections of the discourse is seventy-threefold. Without doubt, the resolution regarding the statement "seventy-fivefold" follows the same method already explained.
As for the extent of the text, however, it consists of four thousand and eighty gāthās, with an additional fifty gāthās in the latter portion.
There are nine hundred sections (gantha). Therefore it is said at the conclusion of the *Uttara*:
“Four thousand and nineteen verses— This should be known as the extent Of the Vinaya’s exposition.”
"Indeed, there are nine hundred and fifty-plus verses;
this is the count for the *Uttara* [section] according to the *anuṭṭhubha* meter.
Thus, the two treatises—the *Vinayavinicchaya* and the *Uttara*—consist of five thousand and thirty verses.
And here, "the exposition of the Vinaya" (*vinayavinicchaya*) refers to the treatise that compiles the expositions found in both the *Vibhaṅgas* and the *Khandhaka*.
Following that, the treatise that compiles the meaning of the *Parivāra* is called the "Uttara. For this very reason, he will say:
"The essence of the Vinaya, its exposition, which has been composed by me..."
"Now I shall compose for it [this work] which is the most supreme among all things supreme.

Why is it designated by the name *Uttara* (The Supreme)? Although it should have been included as such within the *Parivāra*, which stands as a "Supreme Answer" (*pañhuttara*) to questions, [the author], having shown merely the discussion of the *Pārājika* rules in that manner, says:
"From here on, setting aside [the formal structure], there is merely the asking of questions."

Having said, "The determination of the meaning occurs precisely through the method of answering," they speak in that way because, after setting aside the question, only the subsequent portion is shown from that point onward.
However, by the words "Therefore, the means of training" and so forth, he urges the audience to listen attentively; for [the goal] is dependent upon attentive listening.
For this is the collective meaning here: that all mundane and supramundane attainments are indeed [the goal].

However, as for the individual meaning—since it is easier to understand when the word-arrangement (*padayojanā*) is presented first and then explained according to the sequence of the application of the meaning—it is for this reason that we shall provide the commentary on the meaning after first establishing the word-arrangement in that manner.
The construction is as follows: "Having bowed my head to the Buddha, who is supreme and peerless; to the Dhamma, which brings about the cessation of existence; and to the stainless Saṅgha;
I shall, being composed, speak in brief the exposition of the Vinaya for the benefit of both the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs.
In this context, "supreme" (*seṭṭha*) means that while all these [three jewels] are praised, this one is praised to the highest degree among them; thus, it is "supreme. Likewise...

For that Blessed One was endowed with the attainment of unsurpassed qualities such as the jhānas, which served as the cause for his thorough knowledge and discernment of his own status as the eldest and most excellent, when he said to the Brahmin of Verañjā, “I am indeed, O Brahmin, the eldest and most excellent in the world. Thus:
“You alone are the Fully Awakened One; you are the unsurpassed Teacher.”
In this world with its devas, there is no one who is your equal.
You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher, you are the Sage who has overcome Māra.
Having cut off all latent tendencies, you have crossed over and brought this generation across.
You have transcended the acquisitions; your taints are shattered.
You are a lion, free from clinging, having abandoned fear and terror.
O Great Hero of great wisdom, you blaze with spiritual power and glory.
“I pay homage at the feet of the One who has transcended all enmity and fear, the Visionary.
By such various modes as these, he is the most highly praised and lauded by the world including the devas; thus, “the most excellent, the most praised” is the meaning.

“Without a counterpart” (*appaṭipuggala*): there is no counterpart to him, whether superior or equal; thus he is “without a counterpart. For, by way of his qualities, in the infinite and immeasurable world-systems, there exists no person superior to him or even equal to him.
“I have no teacher; there is none equal to me;
in this world with its devas, there is no rival to me.
Thus, by himself, he has declared his own state of being unrivaled and free from error. Therefore, the meaning is that he is unrivaled and supreme over the entire world.
"Buddha" means one who has awakened (*buddha*) to the entire circle of the knowable (*ñeyya-maṇḍala*), which is infinite, immeasurable, and without remainder;

by this, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*) is shown—the sovereign of the sublime Dharma (*Saddhamma-vara-cakkavattī*), adorned with the splendor and majesty of the Dharma-body and the Form-body, perfected through the power of the accumulations of merit and knowledge gathered over many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons.
Alternatively, [he is so called] because he has himself realized the Four Truths through the ripening of the perfections (*pāramitā*) accumulated by him.

He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened by means of self-born knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) which abandons the defilements (*kilesa*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) without remainder. As it is said:
"That which was to be directly known has been directly known; that which was to be developed has been developed;
that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me. Therefore, O Brahmin, I am the Buddha."

The detailed explanation of this term, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Niddesa* and other texts, beginning with: "He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the people.

Regarding its grammatical derivation (*saddasiddhi*) for those following the Buddhist tradition (*sāsanika*), from the verbal root *budh* used in the sense of "understanding," when the suffix *ta* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *ta* occurs in the meanings of state (*bhāva*) and object (*kamma*)," and subsequently the suffix *tā* is applied according to the Kaccāyana sutta: "after *budh*, *gam*, etc., the suffix *tā* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattar*)."
It should be understood from the rule prescribing the *ta*-suffix in the active voice (*kattari*).

However, since even roots meaning "to awaken" (*bodhana*) among worldly [roots] are stated to have the sense of "going" (*gamana*), it should be understood by applying the *ta*-suffix in the active voice according to the sutta beginning with "those having the sense of going" (*gatyattha*) and "intransitive" (*akammaka*).
Alternatively, because roots have multiple meanings, this root *budha* is functioning here in the senses of "awakening" (*jāgaraṇa*) and "blooming" (*vikasana*).

Regarding the term *akammaka* (intransitive): as in the examples "the man has awakened" (*pabuddho puriso*) and "the lotus has awakened" (*pabuddhaṃ padumaṃ*), one who has awakened—opening the eyes of wisdom by the departure of the sleep of ignorance—is called *buddho*.

Alternatively, [it means] "blossomed through qualities. Thus, by the word *buddha*, established in its active sense, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, whose feet are like jewels of passion for the unique crest-jewels of the three realms, is called *Buddho*. In this [context]...
In the *Pakkhepi-gatyatthādi-sutta*, the formulation of the suffixes should be understood as occurring through the inclusion of the term "intransitive" (*akammaka*).

Alternatively, since transitive roots become intransitive when there is no desire to express the object, the application [of the suffix] to the root *budh* in the sense of "awakening" in the agentive case is established, as in examples such as "the fruit ripened by itself" (*phalaṃ sayameva pakkaṃ*). Now...

Alternatively, just as the designation "blue" is applied to cloth and other objects through their connection with the quality of blueness, so too, by adopting the word *buddha* in its sense as a state (*bhāvasādhana*), the Blessed One is designated as "Buddha" due to his connection with the qualities of a Buddha.
Thus, the meaning is: "that Blessed One who is spoken of by means of the word *buddha*, which is established in these various ways, [is] that King of Dhamma."
The two phrases “the Best” (*seṭṭha*) and “the Peerless One” (*appaṭipuggala*) are qualifiers of the term “Buddha.

Here, by means of these three words—“Buddha,” “Best,” and “Peerless One”—one should understand, according to the method [of interpretation], numerous Sutta passages such as “Thus indeed is the Blessed One:
the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” and “The Blessed One, the Sakyan Sage, the Foremost among speakers, who has accomplished what was to be done among men.”

It demonstrates, in its entirety, the perfectly pure collection of the Buddha’s qualities, which is comprised of the threefold sets of: the near and far causes and fruits shown by way of their distant and proximate origins; the benefit to sentient beings; the basis;

and the extraction of the world from the phenomena and objects [of existence]. Indeed, this very demonstration of the method (*naya*) is the means for showing the Buddha’s qualities without remainder;
otherwise, it would be impossible to describe the immeasurable qualities of the Buddha through a mere commentary on the path.
For who indeed would be able to reach its limit? As it is said:
"Even a Buddha, speaking the praises of a Buddha, without uttering anything else, might do so for an eon."
“An eon might pass away in its long duration,
yet the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.
Thus, by means of these three phrases, which constitute a hymn of praise enumerating his qualities without remainder, [the phrase] “having paid homage” refers to prostration.

It should be understood that because it has been stated thus, by means of this half-stanza, the act of homage—consisting in praise and prostration—is shown with reference to the first object of veneration, known as the Buddha-ratana.
Immediately following that, in order to show the prostration to the Dhamma-ratana, he said: "the Dhamma that brings about the cessation of existence. Herein...
By the term *bhava*, two types of existence are stated: *kamma-bhava* (existence as action) and *upapatti-bhava* (existence as rebirth).
Therein, *kamma-bhava* is called "existence" because from it the fruit comes into being (*bhavati etasmā phalam*).

However, *upapatti-bhava*—consisting of the resultant aggregates and the kamma-produced matter—is conditioned by the *kamma-bhava* characterized as wholesome or unwholesome volition, which is joined with cooperative causes such as ignorance, craving, clinging, and formations.

That which comes into being according to its respective conditions is called "existence" (*bhava*). Furthermore, it is ninefold by way of: sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), perception-existence (*saññībhava*), non-perception-existence (*asaññībhava*), neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence (*nevasaññīnāsaññībhava*), one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), and five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).
Thus, among these nine types of existence, even the tenfold phenomena—while sustaining the personal continuum—[cease] in the Nibbāna-element without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

Because it effects the non-relinking [of consciousness] and thereby brings about the absence of existence (*bhava*) within the realms of becoming, it is called "the maker of the absence of existence" (*bhavābhāvakara*).
The meaning is that it brings about the state of non-occurrence by uprooting the cause of the continuous succession of successive births.
It is called "Dhamma" because it supports (*dhāreti*) itself and supports those who uphold themselves, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery or into *saṃsāra*.

Thus, it is tenfold: the nine supramundane states consisting of the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna; and the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti), which is the means for realizing those [supramundane states] and is divided into the eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma aggregates—also known by the name of the "Ninefold Teaching" (navanga-sāsana).
That too is twofold: the Dhamma in the ultimate sense (nippariyāya-dhamma) and the Dhamma in the conventional sense (pariyāya-dhamma).
Therein, the Dhamma in the ultimate sense refers to the five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), which are the primary causes for rebirth in the lower realms or within *saṃsāra*.

The state of the path (maggadhamma) is so called by way of severing the ten fetters (saṃyojana) pertaining to the lower realm, and the state of Nibbāna (nibbānadhamma) is so called because it serves as the sign for the accomplishment of that function;
thus, since these five kinds [of states]—taken non-figuratively—bear the personal continuum (puggalasantāna), they are called "non-figurative states" (nippariyāyadhamma).
However, the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are so called because they proceed in accordance with the path through the abandonment and subsiding [of defilements].

And since the *pariyatti* (the scriptures) is the fundamental cause for the attainment of the Path and Nibbāna, all fivefold aspects are indeed called the "Dhamma by way of the method" (*pariyāyadhamma*). Up to this point,
[we have discussed] that which was spoken in such Suttantas as "The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One," and "The stainless,

griefless fading away of lust," as well as that which is praised in their respective commentaries and other works, and which— by means of the recollection of the Refuges— is the cause for obtaining the attainment of heaven and liberation.
It should be understood that because the quality of the jewel of the Dhamma has been indicated by way of its entirety,
and because bowing is shown by the word "having paid homage" (*vanditvā*), the act of homage— consisting in praise and prostration— is thereby demonstrated toward the second object of veneration,
which is designated as the jewel of the Dhamma.
Immediately following that, it is said, "The host free from blemish," in order to demonstrate the act of venerating the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Here, "blemish" (*aṅgaṇa*) refers to lust, hatred, and delusion as stated.

One who has gone forth (*niggata*) from those blemishes of lust and so on—by way of liberation through the abandonment of those very factors (*tadaṅga-vimutti*), suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*), subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), and final escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*)—is "free from blemish" (*niraṅgaṇa*). That which is free from blemish is "the blemish-free one" (*taṃ niraṅgaṇaṃ*). [This is further qualified] by the noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*), namely: virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
It is called a "group" (*gaṇa*) because it is reckoned by its multitude of virtues; that [group].

Up to this point, [the Sangha] has been described by various scriptural passages such as, "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well," and "They say that what is given where yields great fruit:
among the four pure pairs of persons. And in their respective commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), etc.,...
And by the word "having paid homage" (*vanditvā*), because it expresses both praise (*thuti*)—
which has the nature of proclaiming the various kinds of priceless qualities of the Jewel of the Saṅgha, such as its stainless, incomparable, all-pervading, and graceful virtue—

and because it expresses prostration (*paṇāma*) of the aforementioned specific forms, it constitutes praise and prostration directed toward the third object of veneration, known as the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
It should be understood that "veneration" (vandanā) is thus demonstrated. "With the head" (sirasā) means with the crown of the head, which brings forth self-confidence and reverence.
"Having venerated" (vanditvā) means having bowed down or having praised.
Thus, having shown in the first verse the veneration consisting of praise and bowing toward the Triple Gem worthy of veneration—

Immediately following that, by means of the verse which sets forth the purpose for which [the teaching] is to be demonstrated and so forth, although the term "bhikkhū" refers to the eight types of noble persons (ariyapuggala) together with the virtuous worldlings (kalyāṇaputhujjana)—on the grounds that they "see fear in the cycle of existence" (saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhati)—nevertheless, in the Pāḷi it is explained as:
"One who wears a torn robe is a bhikkhu; one whose nature is to beg is a bhikkhu," and so on.

Having shown other etymological derivations by way of extracting the meaning of the word *bhikkhu*, in order to show that it is intended specifically for one who is worthy of being restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*, it was stated:

"One who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) through a formal act (*kamma*) consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) by a harmonious Saṅgha—one that is irreversible and fit for the occasion—this is the 'bhikkhu' intended in this context. Thus, those who desire training and abide within the Dispensation [are meant].
"Son of good family" (*kulaputta*) refers here to those [laymen] and to the monks (*bhikkhu*). "And of the nuns" (*bhikkhunīnañca*):
by this, daughters of good family who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the formal act (*kamma*) consisting of eight proclamations in both Saṅghas are indicated.

Those who have received ordination in only one [Saṅgha] are also included under the general term. And "those ordained in one [Saṅgha]" refers to those who, having been ordained in the Bhikkhunī-Saṅgha, [are subsequently ordained] in the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha...
They do not attain [it]. Here, the nun who has attained the state of a nun through the transformation of gender (liṅgaparivattanena) is intended;
[the term refers] to those nuns.
"For the sake of welfare" means for the purpose of producing all forms of excellence; it leads (hinoti) or proceeds toward the accomplishment of the desired fruit.
"It proceeds as benefit" (*pavattati hitaṃ*): this refers to the causes for health and so forth, such as the "ambrosial medicine" (*amatosadha*) and the like.

Here, however, it refers to the guarding of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, which is the cause for the attainment of the success of heaven and liberation; [the work is] "for that purpose.
He by whom the path of discernment is "well-placed" (*sammā āhita*) and set in motion (*pavattita*) through concentration (*samāhita*) is called "Samāhita," the author of this treatise.

It has been demonstrated. Alternatively, because his mind is properly placed (*sammā-āhita*), established, and set in motion regarding the discernment of the Vinaya, he is called "one whose mind is concentrated" (*samāhitacitto*);
though one should say *samāhitacitto*, it is expressed as *samāhito* by eliding the latter member of the compound.

By this qualification, [the author] indicates within himself the cause for the arising of a concentrated mind, which is appropriate for engaging in the discernment of the meaning of the most profound and difficult-to-cross Vinaya Piṭaka. His own...
Concentration, which is the proximate cause of knowledge, has been shown; the meaning is: "having become concentrated by means of that concentration.

"I shall explain" means I shall explain in a specific manner, by which manner those who practice today—possessing dull mindfulness, intelligence, and energy—may easily grasp and retain the even more profound exposition of the meaning of the Vinaya Piṭaka when the determination of the Vinaya has been stated.
The meaning is: "I shall speak in such a specific manner that they are able [to understand]. "By way of summary" (*samāsena*) means:

*samāsanaṃ* is contraction or abbreviation, which is *samāsa*; by means of that [summary], it is for the benefit of those who prefer brevity, those of the *ugghāṭitaññū* type, those who have performed their preliminary duties, those of superior knowledge, those who fear prolixity, those of dull intellect whose grasping and retention are weak, and so forth—by means of a method that is not overly extensive.
The meaning is as follows: "Of the Vinaya" means of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
For it is said: "Because of its various and distinct methods, and because of the disciplining of body and speech;"

It is called "Vinaya" by virtue of the specific meanings declared by those who are experts in the meaning of the Vinaya: "This is the Vinaya; this is not the Vinaya. For that [Dhamma] whose essential nature has been thus demonstrated as "Vinaya,"...

This is the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya*, a treatise so named because it is an exposition (*vibhajana*) that has received the name "detailed analysis" (*vinicchaya*)—meaning it is specifically or in various ways accumulated (*ciyati*) and analyzed (*vibhajīyati*) for the purpose of removing misconduct.

It is the supreme among the *Vinayapiṭaka*, its virtues having been extolled by the compilers of the Council, such as Mahākassapa and others, who said: "This indeed is the life-span of the Dispensation. *Vinicchaya*: [The term] is derived from the sense of being specifically (*visesena*) or in various ways (*vividhena vā ākārena*) accumulated (*cīyati*) and analyzed (*vibhajīyati*) by way of removing wrong practice;
thus it is called an "analysis" (*vinicchaya*). It is stated to be the treatise known as the *Vinayavinicchaya*.
The term “*vinayassavinicchaya*” is a compound formed without elision (*aluttasamāsa*), as in examples such as “*Devānaṃpiyatisso*” and “*kaṇṭhekāḷo*.
Having thus shown one part of the author’s motive, purpose, the subject matter, the title, and the type of work through the second verse, he says “*anākulaṃ*,” etc.,
in order to demonstrate the type of work and other details by way of indicating the reason for listening attentively.

In this context, "unconfused" (*anākula*) means that there is no confusion—either through word, meaning, or exposition—such as contradiction between what precedes and what follows, or a state of being mixed;
thus it is "unconfused. The connection is: "Understand from me as I speak that unconfused exposition of the Vinaya.
"Unmixed" (*asaṃkiṇṇa*) means not blended with the tenets of other schools.

“Madhuratthapadakkama” means the sequence of words (*padānaṃ kamo*), the order of words, or the progression of words; the meaning is the pronunciation of sounds. That which possesses both a sweet meaning (*madhuro attho*) and a sequential arrangement of words (*padakkamo*) is called “Madhuratthapadakkama.
As it is said: “The seven verses whose meanings have been proclaimed in a sweet manner—by means of these, the wise revel as if with honey, like those who subsist on honey.”

By virtue of these characteristics of both words and meanings, it is called *madhur-attha-padakkama* because it is adorned with the ornament of sweetness (*mādhuriya-alaṅkāra*), which is another name for the sevenfold arrangement of words (*padāsattā*).
Regarding *paṭubhāvakara*: that which goes, proceeds, or understands is *paṭu*, meaning one possessed of wisdom (*paññavā*).

The state of being *paṭu* is *paṭubhāva*; it is the wisdom that serves as the cause for the manifestation of words. That which produces or generates this *paṭubhāva*, this specific excellence of wisdom, is *paṭubhāvakara*; thus, it means "that which generates a specific excellence of wisdom."

The meaning is as follows: the construction is "this is the exposition of the Vinaya. "Supreme" means most excellent. "The sequence of the Vinaya" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka and its meaning; the sense is that it produces proficiency in the sequence of occurrences. Thus, having encouraged the audience by pointing out the virtues of the work through the third verse, [he now proceeds] with the fourth verse beginning with "apāram": ... [text continues] ... In this way, the Blessed One has shown the purpose for undertaking this treatise. Now, the venerable Ānanda, who was present at the time of the recitation, wishing to show his gratitude to the Blessed One for this great favor, spoke these verses: *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo paṭhamo.* [The commentary continues: "One who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore," "one who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore"—to such a person, the foremost master of the Vinaya gives this boat.

This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo dutiyo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the second master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo tatiyo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the third master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo catuttho.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the fourth master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo pañcamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the fifth master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo chaṭṭho.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the sixth master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo sattamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the seventh master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo aṭṭhamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the eighth master of the Vinaya gives this boat.

This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo navamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the ninth master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo dasamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the tenth master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo ekādasamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the eleventh master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who knows the path leading to the further shore of Nibbāna, and he has given this boat of the Vinaya to those who wish to cross over. *Apāraṃ pāraṃ gantukāmo, Pāraṃ apāraṃ taritum icchati yo; Tassa imaṃ nāvaṃ dadāti, Vinayadharo dvādasamo.* To one who desires to go from the hither shore to the further shore, and who wishes to cross from the further shore to the hither shore, the twelfth master of the Vinaya gives this boat. This is said because the Blessed One, the Teacher,

Having depicted both this treatise and its source, the Vinaya Piṭaka, as an ocean and a ship respectively, he inspires his audience by proclaiming the excellence of the treatise through a poetic ornament (*rūpālaṅkāra*) consisting of a concealed simile (*tirobhūtopameyyopamāna*). In this context, "apāra" means that which has no further shore;
thus, it refers to the ocean of the Vinaya. For indeed, during the arising of previous Buddhas, [the Buddha] gained confidence in the Dispensation (*sāsana*) and [studied] the Vinaya Piṭaka...

It is called "the shoreless" (*apāra*) because it is difficult for persons who have not performed their duties—by way of grasping, retaining, practicing, and actualizing—to reach its limits in terms of the Dhamma, its meaning, its terminology, and its inspired eloquence.
"For those who descend" (*otarantānaṃ*) means for those who plunge into it by way of recitation, hearing, retention, and so forth.

It is [called] "the essence" (*sāra*) because it elucidates the essence of virtue known as the restraint of the *pātimokkha*, which is the root of the preliminary practice—the equipment for the Noble Path—that serves as the very essence for attaining Nibbāna.
The essence. "The ocean of the Vinaya" means the ocean known as the Vinaya Piṭaka. For the Vinaya is like an ocean because of its extreme depth and vastness;
it is an ocean because it is not within the scope even of the Dhamma General (Sāriputta) and others, owing to their knowledge of the proper time for the proclamation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
It is the "ocean of the Vinaya" because it is both the Vinaya and an ocean, due to its possession of qualities that are bottomless and shoreless. That [ocean].
The meaning is: "the Vinaya Piṭaka is like the ocean.

Although the second verse mentions "of the monks and nuns," because it is connected with the phrase "for their welfare" and because it is remote due to being separated by intervening sentences, that [phrase] is not taken here;
rather, this is for the purpose of showing the specific qualification of the agent who is fit to plunge into the ocean of the Vinaya and to practice for its sake.
It should be understood that the words "of the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs" are stated again [at the end]. "Nāvābhūta" means one who has become like a boat; the meaning is:
that which stands in the place of a boat, resembling a great ship. "Manorama" means that by which or in which the mind delights;
the meaning is: it is delightful to the virtuous who are devoted to recitation and intent upon practice.

Having thus inspired the audience by briefly describing the virtues of this treatise, he now says, beginning with “Therefore, the means of training,” in order to enjoin them to listen with careful attention.
Therein, “therefore” (*tasmā*) means because it is adorned with the various priceless ornaments of qualities such as the aforementioned lack of confusion;
the sense is: for that reason. “The means of training” (*vinayanūpāya*) refers to the leading (*nayana*) of body and speech in various ways, or according to specific methods.
*Taming* (*damana*) is the turning away from what should not be done and the directing toward what should be done; *guiding* (*vinaya*) is the same.
It is called a *means* (*upāya*) because by approaching it, that fruit arises in the future; thus, it is the cause. The means for guiding is the "means of guidance" (*vinayanūpāya*).
This refers to the removal of inappropriate physical and verbal agitation among the well-behaved monks and nuns who desire training and are indifferent to body and life.
It is meant that [the work] has become the cause.
Having thus far stated the qualifying epithets such as "unconfused" (*anākula*) by way of elucidating the qualities of non-confusion and so forth—
which serve as the causes for the engagement of the wise in this treatise intended to be composed by oneself— one now [states the object] regarding attentive hearing and comprehension.

In order to show what is to be qualified, he said, "the exposition of the Vinaya. Here, in the second verse, the phrase "the exposition of the Vinaya" was stated by way of showing the object of the action "I shall speak"; even if that were brought here and connected, it would constitute a remote connection.
Therefore, without bringing that over, [he uses the phrase] for the purpose of indicating the object of this action, "understand," as follows:
Because it is stated as “the determination of the Vinaya,” one should understand that there is no fault of redundancy here.
Regarding the phrase “with an undistracted mind”: here, *vikkhitta* (distracted) means cast or sent toward various objects;

it is a mind that is unsettled and overwhelmed by restlessness, doubt, and so forth, and is thus unconcentrated (*asamāhita*). *Avikkhitta* (undistracted) is the opposite of that: a wholesome mind that is concentrated (*samāhita*).

The meaning is: with a concentrated mind—that is, a mind that has not fallen into distraction by way of engaging with various objects without the activity of hearing this supreme treatise, and so forth.
And by saying, “Listen attentively... understand it,” [the Teacher] implies through his own words:
“This Dhamma is for one who is undistracted; this Dhamma is not for one who is distracted,” because one who is distracted lacks the status of an heir to the teachings.
This is an instruction for practicing correctly the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), which constitutes the subject matter of this own work.
Regarding the phrase "vadato me" (when I speak), there is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*) here: "and out of respect. In that context, the meaning is as follows:

"out of respect when I am speaking," and "for the reasons already stated. Because there is no distinction between the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) and the locative case (*bhummavacana*) in the word "me," the genitive form "me" [is understood] as "in me" (*mayi*).

This meaning was stated because the purpose is possible. And the intention is that, because this treatise is endowed with qualities such as being free from confusion, you should listen with a concentrated mind out of reverence for me, the speaker. Or, "Nibodhatha" (understand) means: understand thoroughly by way of the meaning of the sentence, the meaning of the words, the intended meaning, and the literal sense;
having heard it carefully, awaken to and discern the *Vinayavinicchaya* (the Determination of the Discipline). This is the meaning.

The intention is: "Produce the knowledge consisting of what is heard (*suta-mayañāṇa*), which serves as the basis for the knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintā-maya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), by means of its subject matter, the treatise (*pakaraṇa*).
The commentary on the introduction to the book is finished.
The *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga*.
The Discussion on the Pārājikas:
Commentary on the First Pārājika. 6.
Thus, having shown the homage to the Triple Gem and so forth with these five verses, [the author now proceeds] to the determination as promised.

To demonstrate this, he said, "In three ways," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "in three ways" and so on, he shows the analysis (*vinicchaya*) of the first *pārājika* training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"In three ways" is connected with the phrase "in three kinds of ways," meaning by way of the three types of passages: the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth.
"Even as much as a sesame seed" is connected with the phrase "the sexual organ (*aṅgajāta*"); it is called a "passage" because it is the exit door for feces and urine.

And it is connected with the term "aloka-āsaya" (the non-luminous receptacle) in reference to those parts of the body designated as "paths" (maggā), by virtue of their being the gateways for the entry and exit of food,
drink, bile, phlegm, and so forth. Although one might say, "In the paths, there is the volition of indulgence even to the extent of a sesame seed in three [types]," the inclusion of the word *vidha*—
which denotes manner— in the expression "threefold" (*tividhe*) serves to group them according to their common nature into three aggregates, thereby presenting them by way of their classification.
The thirtyfold path has been shown.

To wit: in order to show the seven beings who serve as the basis for the paths beginning with the subject matter of the *pārājika* offenses, there are the human females, non-human females, and animal females mentioned in the Canon by way of the passage beginning, “three kinds of women: a human female, a non-human female, and an animal female.”
There are nine paths by way of each of the three types of hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) as they have been shown;

furthermore, there are six paths consisting of two paths each for the three types of eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*)—namely, those with the mouth-path, the anus-path, and both—and likewise three paths for the three types of men; thus, there are thirty kinds in total.
"Sevanacetanā" (the volition of practicing) is an analysis of the compound meaning "one who has the volition regarding the practice of sexual intercourse.

The sense is: "one who is endowed with a volition associated with lust for sexual intercourse. "In a moist place" (*allokāse*) means in a moist area not touched by natural wind on any one of the thirty paths;
by this, he indicates that there is no external *pārājika* field [of action]. Regarding the qualification...

Because the second verse requires a specific qualification, one should bring forward the two words from that verse, “he who is under training,” and construe them thus: “He who has the intention to engage [in sexual intercourse] is a bhikkhu under training.

That which is born in the limb, the body, is the *aṅgajāta*; it is the male organ. Even though the remaining parts of the body also exist in that manner [as being born from the body], [the term refers specifically to this].
It is stated thus by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhivasena*). "Entering" means performing the bodily action consisting of the union of the couple (*dvaya-dvaya-samāpatti*).

"Defeated" means that, having been deprived of the happiness of attaining the rare worldly and supramundane qualities—which are obtainable through the attainment of the rare opportune moment—one has been brought to defeat by the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*); such is the meaning.

This is the application here: when a bhikkhu who possesses training and has the intention to engage in sexual intercourse inserts his organ even as much as a sesame seed into the three kinds of paths or the non-local space [of the mouth], he is defeated (*pārājika*).

Up to this point, it should be understood that the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) proclaimed by the Blessed One—“Whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, should engage in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training and without disclosing his weakness, even with an animal, he is defeated and no longer in communion”—is thus included.

7. Having thus shown the *pārājika* offense rooted in one’s own initiative (*attūpakkama*) by means of this verse, he now says “insertion,” etc., in order to show the *pārājika* offense rooted in the initiative of another (*paropakkama*), which occurs in the manner described as:
“enemies of the bhikkhu bring a human woman to the presence of the bhikkhu and cause her to sit down upon his organ with her anus.
Therein, “insertion” refers to [the act] by the enemies of the bhikkhu...
Having brought any one of the objects such as a human woman who is heedless regarding the Sutta [training rules], he causes it to enter any one of the aforementioned paths;
thus, it describes the entry into the path that is possible when causing the monk’s organ to sit upon it.
The construction is: "that trainee who consents to the entry. Herein, "he consents to the entry, he tolerates it... [and so on].

Based on the commentary’s statement, "At that moment he arouses a mind of enjoyment," the meaning is that one who, while inserting [the member] from the tip down to the base, arouses a mind of gratification, passes away from the teaching at that very instant.
The same application should be made for the other locations mentioned, such as "having entered" (paviṭṭha) and so forth.
"Having entered" refers to the moment of entry; by the terms "having entered" and so on, the moment characterized by each respective action is indicated.
It should be understood. For that very reason, the accusative case is used here to express immediate connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

Regarding the word "standing" (*ṭhita*), since the commentary’s statement "at the time of emission of semen" refers to a period entirely devoid of activity, the time of emission itself should also be included.
Therefore, according to the method stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, [the offense applies] from the moment one has entered until the commencement of withdrawal.
The time of remaining [within] should also be understood as "occurring. "Extraction" (*uddharaṇa*) means the time of bringing out.
*Vā* signifies an alternative; *api* signifies a conjunction. By the word *vā*, it indicates that the positions presented as alternatives possess equal weight.
Thus, by these two [terms], in the Pāḷi text [the cases] beginning with "If he consents to the entering" and "He consents to what has entered" [are established].
This shows that a *pārājika* offense is incurred by consenting to even a single moment, such as the entry [of the organ], which is obtainable through the method already described.
"One who trains" (*sasikkho*) means one who conducts himself together with the training; the meaning is "one whose training has not been renounced.
"Consenting" (*sādiyanto*) means establishing the intention for sexual intercourse. "That monk"—excluding his own initiative (*kiriyam*).
"Without. "Fallen" means that one is not exempt from the charge on the pretext of saying, "This was done by my adversaries, not by me";
for if there is a mind of approval, the intention is that one has indeed fallen from the Teaching.
And here, "with the training" refers to the wording of the training rule: "without having renounced the training and without having manifested weakness."

It has been demonstrated by way of showing the meaning. Its analysis in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) and its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) should be understood in brief as follows: the renunciation of the training occurs through the recognition of the mind, the field, the time, the application, and the person;
it does not occur in the absence of these. For the renunciation of the training occurs only with a mind that desires to fall away from the state of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
It occurs through the mind, not for one who speaks out of sport or in jest. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of the mind, not by the mere absence of that [intention].
Likewise: “I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dhamma; I renounce the Saṅgha;
the training; the Vinaya; the Pātimokkha; the recitation; the preceptor; the teacher; the co-resident; the pupil; one who shares the same preceptor;”
Of these twenty-two: the fourteen beginning with the Buddha, who were addressed thus, "I renounce my fellow teacher and my companion in the holy life";

and the eight beginning with the householder, who were addressed thus, "Regard me as a householder, a lay follower (upāsaka), a monastery attendant (ārāmika), a novice (sāmaṇera), a member of another sect (titthiya), a disciple of another sect (titthiyasāvaka), one who is not an ascetic (assamaṇa), or one who is not a son of the Sakyans (asakyaputtiya). Of these [twenty-two].

Regarding the field of training, for anyone who wishes to say anything at all concerning those [fields] by means of any synonymous term, there is a renunciation of the training whenever they speak anything;
it does not occur when one renounces the training after merely taking the name of a particular tree or the like.
Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of the field, and not in the absence of that [field].
In this context, there is the statement in the present tense, namely “I renounce” (*paccakkhāmī*) and “hold me [in mind]” (*maṃ dhārehi*); and there are those statements expressed as verbs—
such as “Enough for me of the Buddha,” “What need have I of the Buddha,” “I have no use for the Buddha,” and “I am well-liberated from the Buddha”—
which, without specifying a particular time, are joined with the preceding fourteen phrases.
The four phrases beginning with “Enough for me” constitute a renunciation by way of those very synonyms;

it is not a renunciation for one who utters past, future, or hypothetical expressions such as “He has renounced,” “He will renounce,” “Do you remember me? “Will you remember me? or “What if I were to renounce? and so forth.
Thus, the renunciation occurs both by way of the present time and by way of a time not specifically designated, but not by way of their absence.
Furthermore, the application (payoga) is twofold: physical and verbal.

Therein, by making a vocal utterance in any language whatsoever according to the method beginning with "I renounce the Buddha," the renunciation occurs through verbal application alone; it does not occur through the writing of letters.
or making a physical effort such as showing hand gestures and so forth—in this way, the renunciation occurs through verbal application alone, not in the absence of it.
Furthermore, the person is twofold: he who renounces and he to whom one renounces. Among these, he who renounces...
Thus, provided that he is not one who is insane, deranged, or afflicted by pain;

and provided that the person to whom he renounces the training is of human birth, is not one who is insane or otherwise disqualified, and is present before him at the time of the renunciation of the training—
for the announcement made to one who is not present, whether by messenger or by letter, is not valid— then, in this manner, for the aforementioned [person]:
The renunciation occurs by way of a specific person, not through their mere absence.

Furthermore, the act of making known is twofold: determined and undetermined. In this regard, it refers to one who, having made a determination, says, "I inform this person" or "I inform these people.
If those people, upon hearing the words as they would normally hear them from humans in the world, at the moment of mental advertence—
If, immediately after those words, they know by any means whatsoever that "this person is dissatisfied" or "he aspires to the state of a householder"—
that is, they recognize his state of having renounced the training— the training is indeed renounced. However, if later on,
after considering "What was said by him?", they come to know, or others know, [of his intention], it is not yet renounced.

There is training. However, for one who announces it without specifying [the person], if anyone belonging to the human race understands the meaning of the words in the manner described, the training is indeed renounced.
Thus, renunciation occurs by way of such understanding, not merely by the absence of that [understanding].
But he who renounces it even in jest has not renounced the training at all.
Thus, one who has not renounced the training by virtue of these aforementioned factors, such as the mind and so forth, is called "one still under training" (*sasikkha*). 8–10.
To refute the pretext of wicked monks who claim, "Now, there is no fault in striking one who is already struck because there is no striking of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*"), [the text says]:
"The enemies of the monks [approach] a human woman for the sake of a monk..."

Having brought [the woman] near, they sit down with the male organ inserted into the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth—whether there is a covering or no covering—thus summarizing the meaning of the sections on "covering" (*santhatavāra*) as stated in the Pāḷi, he says: "With a covering" (*santhatena*), and so forth.
Therein, "with a covering" means covered by leather, cloth, a double-layered pad, and so on. By the word "inserting," the section on covering...
By stating that "perception based on another's initiative" is a characteristic, he shows that it should also be applied to one's own initiative;
its connection is with the term "defeated," which will be explained later. By the phrase "in the same way," he refers to the manner of "entering" and so forth.
To the question, "When is one who enters in this way defeated? he says, "by means of what is appropriated," and so on. Here, "by what is appropriated" (upādinnena) means by craving and views.
It is called "clung-to" (*upādinna*) because it has been taken up and grasped by means of a deed that has come to fruition as one's own result.
By this term, he shows the physical sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*) located at the place where there is contact with one's own genitals, with the physical basis and the person, and with the Path.

By this very same term, the non-deficient physical sensitivity located in the genitals, the skin-covering, and the pustules and so forth are also to be understood. "The 'clung-to' is the body-faculty."
This is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. By way of its opposite, "unappropriated" refers to items such as cloth that conceal it.
The construction is as follows: when the field of defeat (*pārājika-khetta*) is touched by what is appropriated against what is appropriated or unappropriated;
or when the field of defeat is touched by what is unappropriated against what is appropriated or unappropriated. And here, the words end in instrumental case endings.
“By the genitals” refers to the qualifiers of this [term].

Having thus far demonstrated the *pārājika* offense within the sphere of a *pārājika* when there is self-aggression (*attūpakkama*) by way of the fourfold set regarding the spread (*santhata*), he now says “If,” etc., in order to demonstrate it even in the case of aggression by another (*parūpakkama*).
“In this context” means among these four alternatives. Within the sphere of a *pārājika*.
In the phrase *paviṭṭhe tu*, the word *tu* (but/then) includes the triad of moments: entering, staying, and emerging.

Because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are always connected, when the word *taṃ* is employed as in "so" (*so*), the word *yaṃ* as in "who" (*yo*) must also be supplied; and by implication, the particle *api* has the sense of inclusion.
This is the construction of the meaning here: [the robe] having been brought by the enemies of the bhikkhu... to the bhikkhu.

If one consents— meaning, if one is not startled like someone entering the mouth of a snake, but is instead overcome by the thirst of sensual lust— at the moment when the penis has entered the *pārājika* field (defined as any one of the three paths belonging to a woman or similar being who has been made to sit upon the private parts),
or at any of the moments included by the word "or" (*tu*), such as the moments of entry, remaining, or withdrawal; if, that is to say, one consents...

The construction is: "If he consents, that monk too is defeated. By this phrase "if he consents," which contains a qualifying condition, it is indicated that there is no offense if he does not consent.
By the phrase "in the case of a defeat (pārājika) zone," it is implied that for one who transgresses in another place where [the rule] is delimited, [the offense is] in this very [category].

In order to show the other offenses that arise in the case of a *vikappa* (substitution), he says "in the field" (*khette*), and so forth. The word "here" (*ettha*) should be brought forward and connected [to this].

Although "in the field" is a general designation, because it was specified below as "the field of a *pārājika* offense," and because the *thullaccaya* and other offenses are being prescribed above, by the force of implication (*sāmatthiya*)—characterized by the impossibility of it being otherwise—it follows that [this refers to] the field of the *thullaccaya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses.

This meaning is established. By the method beginning with the words "in the ear-holes, nostrils, and so forth," it is meant that these refer to the fields of serious offenses (*thullaccaya*) and wrongdoings (*dukkaṭa*) occurring in a living body, which will be explained later.

Since it is impossible to say regarding these two fields that "there is no offense for one who causes a mat or similar object to enter another mat or similar object, or for one who endures the contact of what is appropriated (*upādinna*) with what is appropriated," all the alternatives stated for the field of defeat (*pārājika*) [apply here].

Those applying this here should apply it in this way: when one engages with the sexual organ in the case of a grave offense (thullaccaya)—whether the area is covered or uncovered, whether the organ is covered or uncovered—then if there is contact with what is appropriated (upādinna) or what is not appropriated (anupādinna), or likewise with what is not appropriated [on the part of the other], a grave offense is to be designated for him.
Thus, in the case of an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), when the area is covered...
"...or... pe ... when struck, a *dukkaṭa* offense is to be assigned to him"—this is how it should be connected.
Here, in all three fields, by the term "clung-to" (*upādinna*), the non-material faculties of the body and the genitals, as well as the skin, calluses, and pustules arising thereon, are included;
however, in the field of *dukkaṭa*, other parts such as the fingers and so forth are also included. In all three fields, by the term "not clung-to" (*anupādinna*)...

Clothing and other items that conceal the private parts (*aṅgajāta*) and so forth are included; however, in the case of the field of a *dukkaṭa* offense, the objects are those where the physical faculties have perished, such as skin, calluses, warts, body hair, and so on.

These are non-appropriated (*anupādinnaka*). Furthermore, for one who inserts [the organ] into any part—whether the private parts themselves or another appropriated limb—into any of the three fields, there is only a *dukkaṭa*.

Up to this point, regarding a living body, according to whether it is covered or uncovered, within each of the three fields—the *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa* fields—there are three types [of offenses].
Having demonstrated, as far as applicable, the offenses of *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa* that may arise for one who indulges with the two types of signs—
namely, those that are prepared and those that are unprepared— when there is an assault by another and he consents, [the author] now states,
"But for those who indulge in such a manner with a dead body, there is no fault," in order to ward off any pretext for wicked monks.
In order to show the three offenses that may occur in the three fields as they were described and presented in the Pāḷi, he said, “If [the person] is dead,” and so forth.
Therein, for the word “dead” (*mate*), the syntactical connection should be made by supplying the words “on the body of a human female, etc.
By this, the physical basis (*nissaya*) for the signs shown by the phrase “if it is not decomposed,” and so forth, is demonstrated. [This refers to] the mere sign (*nimittamattaṃ*).

As in the verse that will be spoken in the manner beginning with "having set aside" (*sesetvā*), even when the entire body has been eaten, the very state of the sign (*nimitta*)—whether it exists or does not exist—is the criterion for the existence or non-existence of the offense.

Thus, by the word "unconsumed" (*akkhāyite*), one should qualify the word "dead" (*mate*) without distinction, having supplied the word "sign" (*nimitte*) and qualified it by that [word "unconsumed"]. Alternatively, [it should be understood] by the phrase "the mere sign" (*nimittamattaṃ*) and so forth.
The word "in the sign" (*nimitte*) from the verse about to be recited should be brought forward and connected [to this].
"When it has not been told at all" means when the sign that constitutes the basis for a *pārājika* offense has not been declared in any way whatsoever.

"And when the majority has been told" means when, after some small portion has been consumed, the sign remains in abundance. "Of which three-quarters... [refers to] when three out of four parts [of the sign] remain.
They say that what has been consumed is called the "predominant sign" (*yebhuyyakkhāyita-nimitta*).

Regarding sexual intercourse (*methuna*): it is "sexual" because it belongs to a pair (*mithuna*) who have attained a state of similarity through the obsession of lust (*rāga-pariyuṭṭhāna*); even though there is no such attainment of similarity through the obsession of lust in the case of dead women and so forth, transgression with them is still called "sexual" by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).
“Defeated by a *pārājika* offense” means having incurred defeat. For this term *pārājika* applies to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the offense (*āpatti*), and the person (*puggala*).

Regarding the training rule, it is said: “It is impossible, Ānanda, it cannot happen that the Tathāgata would abolish a *pārājika* training rule laid down for his disciples on account of the Vajjis or the Vajjiputtakas. Thus, in reference to the training rule...
It should be understood as occurring in relation to [the offense]. In the passage, “Bhikkhu, you have fallen into an offense of defeat (pārājika),” it occurs in relation to the offense (*āpatti*).
In the passage, “We are not defeated; he who was carried off is the one who is defeated,” it occurs in relation to the person (*puggala*).

However, regarding such passages as “One should accuse another with a matter of defeat,” they say that it occurs in relation to the matter (*dhamma*). For in those cases, the term “matter” (*dhamma*) refers in some instances to the offense, and in others...
Only the training rule (sikkhāpada) is intended here; therefore, it should not be mentioned separately.
