In this context, the training rule "defeats" (parājeti) whoever transgresses it, and for that reason it is called "an offense entailing defeat" (pārājika).
On the other hand, the offense "defeats" whoever commits it, and for that reason it is called "a defeat" (pārājikā). As for the person...

He has been defeated and has fallen into defeat; therefore, he is called "one who has undergone defeat" (pārājika). Regarding the offenses among the training rules (sikkhāpada), the word *pārājika* is derived from the agentive sense as "one who defeats" (*parājeti*), thus "one who has undergone defeat";
however, it should be understood that in reference to the person, it is derived from the objective sense as "one who is defeated" (*parājīyati*).
By the word "man" (*nara*), only the monk previously mentioned is intended. Thus, a general designation is restricted to a specific case.
12. *Yebhuyyakkhāyita* means having eaten until only one of four portions remains. *Upaḍḍhakkhāyita* means having eaten until half remains.
A grave offense is a *thullaccaya*; that which is committed as such is an "offense," thus it is a *thullaccayāpatti*.
Here, the term *thullaccaya* refers to offenses such as *pācittiya*, and not to *pārājika* or *saṅghādisesa*.
It should be seen. "In the rest" means in the remaining parts, such as the armpits and so forth. For it is said in the Commentary:
"In the rest of the body, in the armpits and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is called *dukkaṭa* because it is badly done (*duṭṭhu kataṃ*).
Since the word *dukkaṭa* is invariably neuter, it functions as an adjective qualifying the feminine noun *āpatti* by matching its gender.
"Even when [the body] appears with only a mere sign remaining": here, this means even when the entire body has been devoured, leaving behind one or another of the three signs.
The word "even" (*pi*) indicates a contrast, implying "how much more so in other cases.
Whether that sign is not visible at all or is mostly visible—among the three signs described in these two ways—if sexual intercourse occurs with respect to any one of those signs...

The intention is that even by using [the robe], there is a defeat, which constitutes an offense of expiation (pārājika). Regarding the phrase "even by using" (*sevatopi*), the particle *pi* here expresses inclusion;

therefore, it implies that it is not only the cases mentioned previously that apply. The various alternatives such as "santhatā" and so forth should also be applied here according to the method already stated.
14. Regarding the phrase "when the state of being bloated and so forth has been reached": here, "when the body has become bloated, swollen, discolored blue, and swarming with flies..."

Because of the commentary’s statement: “When [the body] is infested with swarms of worms and is impossible even to approach due to the state of the old corpse oozing from the nine openings, then one abandons both the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense;
in such a body, regardless of where one makes an effort, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense,” it follows that in all cases, including all permutations such as being unexposed and so forth...
It should be understood that the fields for *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa* offenses have been included here.

Furthermore, it is said "dukkaṭa" to show that even there, a transgression does not constitute a non-offense (*anāpatti*). Regarding the phrase "khāyitakkhāyita" and so forth, it should be construed as follows:
all these instances of "khāyitakkhāyita" (chewed and chewed) and the rest are to be understood as referring only to dead bodies, not to those that are living.

15. Regarding the question "How [is it] while living?", he says: "But having cut," and so forth. Therein, "from the inclusion of the wound" (*vaṇasaṅkhepato*) means from the grouping together of the wound.
"In that" (*tasmiṃ*) refers to that place where the sign (*nimitta*) situated [there] was torn out.
Here, however, the second word *pana* (but/however) illuminates a specific meaning not explicitly shown here but understood according to the method found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Even if the sign (*nimitta*) has completely disappeared and even the skin and hide are gone, if the shape of the sign is still discernible and penetration occurs,
it is indeed a *pārājika* offense"— according to this ruling stated regarding what is lifeless,
so too in the case of what is living, if only the skin and hide have been entirely torn away, yet the shape of the sign is discernible and capable of being penetrated...
It is said that this clarifies the meaning understood as: "For one who indulges therein, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

16. The connection is "from that sign" (*tato nimittato*). Regarding the word *patitāyaṃ*: it means "in that which has fallen," or this very reading [is accepted]. "From the sign" (*nimittato*) means from the location of the sign;
the connection is "in that piece of flesh which has fallen. Or, it refers to that which has fallen after being cut or sliced.

The meaning is: "in those [parts], in the sign or in the piece of flesh. The construction is: "one should designate a *dukkaṭa* offense for one who makes an effort with the passion of sexual intercourse.
Regarding the verse beginning with "Even if it is the size of a fingernail or the back of a hand," the commentary beginning with "having cut" should be brought forward and connected.

In the word "satī" (being), the phrase "in what remains" (*avasiṭṭhe*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text. In the word "jīvamāne" (living), the phrase "in the body" (*sarīre*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text. [Thus, it means] "in a living body."

The construction is as follows: having cut and sliced [the flesh], when the mark has been torn away and even a piece of flesh the size of a fingernail or a tendon remains, one who engages in sexual intercourse is "defeated" (parājita).
Regarding the verse beginning with "Ear-hole and eye," the word "while living" (jīvamāne) must be supplied and connected; [this refers to] "in the body."

This is the remainder of the text. Since horses, oxen, buffaloes, and so forth will be mentioned [later] in the phrase beginning with “of horses, oxen, buffaloes, etc.,” by way of elimination (pārisesato), it follows that “of humans” is understood.
The construction is: “it enters into the ears... or into wounds on the living bodies of humans.

“In the sheath” means inside the urinary passage. “In wounds” means in wounds made by knives and the like. “The member” refers to even a portion of the sexual organ as small as a sesame seed. “With lust” means with the lust for sexual intercourse.
19. "In the remaining parts of the body" (*avasesasarīrasmiṃ*) means in those areas of the body excluding the aforementioned bodily parts such as the ear-cavities and so forth.

Therefore he said, "in the armpits, thighs, and so on. "Armpit" (*upakaccha*) refers to the area between the base of the arms. "Thighs and so on" (*ūrukādisu*) refers to the thighs, the middle of the thighs, and so forth.
By the word "and so on" (*ādi*), he includes the remaining parts of the body not explicitly mentioned. The term "genital organ" (*aṅgajātaṃ*) should be brought forward and connected [to this].
“Having inserted”: this is understood through the force of the context; it means having inserted the male organ even to the extent of a sesame seed.

“While practicing with oiliness due to lust for sexual intercourse”: the meaning is, while transgressing out of lust for sexual intercourse. The description stated by the passage beginning with “by means of a cloth” (santhatena) and so forth should also be applied here.
20. Regarding "horses, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the cow-eared ox, the ox-less [animal], and others are included.
Horses and the rest are indeed well known. Because of the upcoming term "of those that are dead," the phrase "of those that are living" is obtained by implication. They "frequent" it;

because the phrase "through the passion for sexual intercourse" (*methunarāgassa*) follows, one who inserts even as much as a sesame seed into the region of the genitals out of passion for sexual intercourse incurs a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
The word *phuseti* (touches) is the connection [to the following]. And here, the reading should be: *“of female camels, she-asses, and female donkeys;

of horses, cows, buffaloes, and so forth.”* For if this is the case, then by means of the word *ādi* (and so forth), which expresses the sense of "manner" as indicated at the end of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), all beings—including those not explicitly mentioned such as those who commit a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), those who have violated a nun, and those with a rotten nose or a rotten mouth—are included.
This is because [the word *ādi*] is indicated at the end of the first line as: *“of horses, cows, buffaloes, and so forth.”*
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of female camels and female donkeys as well; therefore, their separate mention would be purposeless. 21. The connection is:

"for one who engages [in intercourse] in such a manner, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "All animals" (*sabbatiracchānaṃ*): they move horizontally (*tiriyaṃ*) and grow (*añcanti*), thus they are "animals" (*tiracchā*);
all those who are animals are "all animals," and [the phrase refers to] those all animals. "In such a manner" (*tathā*).
Because this refers to [the rules] beginning with "fat [is for the purpose of] lust for sexual intercourse," it is stated that for one who, out of lust for sexual intercourse,
inserts even a sesame-seed-sized portion of the genitals into the eyes or other parts of any animal, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Here too,
since it is impossible to claim that there is no fault when using substitutes such as a cloth covering, that point must also be applied.

22. Having thus shown the offenses incurred regarding the living bodies of animals, he says "of them" (*tesam*) and so forth in order to show the offenses that may arise even regarding their dead bodies.

They say that by the word "of them," both humans and animals are included. Regarding the dead and living bodies of humans, within the spheres of the *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa* [offenses]:

Because three types of offenses have already been shown, and because there would be no purpose in mentioning them again, one should connect this [phrase] with "all animals that follow" (*anuvattamānasabbatiracchāna*), meaning "of all those belonging to the animal realm. Regarding "in all bodies":

when the three kinds of fields—namely, fresh corpses that have not yet reached the state of bloatedness and so forth, whether they are spread out or not—are present, it is by the power of sensual desire for sexual intercourse (*methunarāga*).
The phrase "there may be a threefold offense for one who engages [in it]" is to be construed with the following words.

Regarding the "threefold field": in the case of the human body, according to the method already stated, there is the field of defeat (*pārājika*) consisting of the three paths—namely, the categories of "mostly decomposed" (*yebhuyyakkhāyita*) and "half-decomposed" (*upaḍḍhakkhāyita*)—as well as the same [field] consisting of the three paths in the case of a corpse that has been mostly decomposed or half-decomposed.

In the field of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) consisting of the three parts of the body—namely, the ear-cavity, the right nostril, the eye-socket, and the opening of the urinary passage—which is classified as "unexposed," "mostly exposed," or "half-exposed";

and in that same field consisting of the ear-cavity, the right nostril, the eye-socket, and the opening of the urinary passage, which is classified as "unexposed," "mostly exposed," "half-exposed," or "mostly exposed";
and in what is known as the rest of the body, which is classified as "unexposed," "mostly exposed," "half-exposed," or "mostly exposed."
"In all three kinds of fields" means in the three types of fields. "If existing" means while it is present.

The meaning is that if one indulges [in sexual intercourse] under the influence of lust for sexual union—whether the field is covered or uncovered—there would be a threefold offense corresponding to the circumstances, designated as *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, or *dukkaṭa*.

And when the body has reached the state of bloatedness and so forth, for one who engages in sexual intercourse with any part of the three paths—as described in the section on "lying down" and other permutations—with lust for sexual union, the offense of *dukkaṭa* that must be incurred is to be understood according to the method stated for human bodies:
namely, that it is a *dukkaṭa* in every case where the body has reached the state of bloatedness and so forth. This applies even in the case of an animal body.
In order to show the specific distinction, it was stated, "in their moist bodies," and so forth; thus, the *dukkaṭa* offense should be understood according to the method previously explained.
As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "But in the case of putrid corpses, there is a *dukkaṭa* everywhere, precisely according to the method previously explained.
23. The construction is "of one who touches externally. The "sign" (*nimitta*) is the urinary organ. Although it is stated generally as "of a woman,"...

Since the term "female animal" (*tiracchānagatitthiyā*) will be mentioned in the fourth verse, by the method of elimination (*pārisesato*), this [present verse] refers only to human and non-human females;

thus, there is the inclusion of non-human females here as well. Since the word "female" (*itthiyā*) is carried over from the immediately preceding verse, there might also be the inclusion of non-human females there too.
Therefore, having excluded that as well, [the offense of] *saṅghādisesa* for bodily contact [is established].
In order to show that the female human being alone is the basis [of the offense], it should be understood that the additional word "of a woman" (*itthiyā*) stated therein serves as an indicator.

Furthermore, because the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* states in general terms, "If one touches the female organ with the mouth out of lust for sexual intercourse, it is a *thullaccaya*," and because the *Dhammakkhandhaka* states, "Monks, the private parts must not be touched with a lustful mind... [the meaning is established].

"Whoever should touch [her], there is an offense of thullaccaya"—because of this general statement, and because even in the case of a living woman who has not yet reached the state of bloatedness (uddhumātaka) and so forth, if there exists a sign that is either unmanifested or mostly manifested, it constitutes the basis for a pārājika offense;

therefore, in that case as well, touching her externally results in a thullaccaya. Thus, this matter also applies without making a distinction between whether she is dead or alive, simply by saying "of a woman."
This should be understood by this very general term. 24.
"By the sign" means by one's own private parts. "By the mouth" means by the natural mouth. "The sign of a woman" refers to the private parts of a living human female.
Furthermore, because in the cases for training regarding bodily contact, the case of a dead female is [included] within the case of a living female...
Regarding one who touches with lustful intent for physical contact a dead woman’s body, it has been stated: “There is no offense of *saṅghādisesa* for the monk;
there is an offense of *thullaccaya*. Therefore, a dead human female must not be taken [for sexual purposes].

Likewise, in the case of the *yakkha* story, regarding him whose body was touched by a *yakkhinī* with lustful intent for physical contact, it has been stated: “There is no offense of *saṅghādisesa* for the monk...”
Because it has been stated, "there is an offense of *thullaccaya*," and because it will be stated later in the second *saṅghādisesa*:

"In the case of a paṇḍaka, a female spirit (*yakkhinī*), or a female petal spirit (*petī*), there may be a *thullaccaya* for him," a non-human female (*amanussitthī*) must not be included here either. Therefore, it is said:
"the genitals of a living human female. This is because, when there is a desire to insert [the organ] inside, sexual contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) through lust cannot occur.

By the phrase “through lust for physical contact,” the desire to touch externally is indicated; thus, the meaning of “externally” (bahī) is obtained even without the explicit mention of the word “externally.
“Heavy” means an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
25. The construction is: “likewise for one who touches externally”; this means for one who touches only on the outside without inserting [the organ] inside.
[It] exists. "By lust for both" means by lust for bodily contact or by lust for sexual intercourse. "Of a man too" means even of a living man.
The word "too" (pi) indicates that the offense does not apply only to one who touches the sign of a woman in the manner already described, but rather applies to a man as well.
"The sign" refers specifically to the female organ. "Of a living man"—this is the distinction.

If one asks, "From where is this obtained? It is obtained from this statement in the Aṭṭhakathā: "If, out of lust for bodily contact or lust for sexual intercourse, one touches organ to organ without inserting it into the vaginal canal of a living man, it is a *dukkaṭa*. 26.
The group-of-six bhikkhus, out of lust for sexual intercourse, mounted the backs of cows that were crossing the Aciravatī River.
Regarding the phrase "they touched organ with organ," in this context he says "by means of a sign" and so forth to show the method established in the rule:
"Monks, one should not touch an organ with a mind of lust; whoever should touch it, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
Here too, because the word "likewise" (tathā) follows from the previous [rule], the word "externally" (bahī) is understood. [This refers to] by means of one's own organ, [touching] a female animal.
The construction is as follows: for one who touches outside [the garment] out of lust for sexual intercourse, there is a *thullaccaya* offense.

Regarding the phrase "out of lust for sexual intercourse" (*methunarāgato*), he says "by way of lust for bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsaggarāgena*) and so forth in order to show the meaning excluded by that term.
Here too, by the force of the expression "by way of lust for bodily contact," touching outside [the garment] is to be understood. "Of the sign" (*nimittassā*)...
“Of the urinary passage. *Chupana* means touching. 28.
Regarding *tamāvaṭṭakate*: here the word division is *taṃ āvaṭṭakate*. *Āvaṭṭakate* means when it is open.

Because the word “in the mouth” (*mukhe*) is a relative term, and because no other correlate has been specified, it refers specifically to the ear—the correlate that follows the sequence of what was previously mentioned.
And because of the force of the preceding verse, although the connection is understood to apply specifically to "the mouth of a female animal" (*tiracchānagatitthiyā*),
nevertheless, by means of this verse, it refers to the case of the severed head shown in the Vinaya account:
"A certain bhikkhu, having gone to a charnel ground and seen a severed head, inserted his organ— which was not touching— into the mouth which had been turned upward."
Because it is included [in the category of humans], one might think that only the mouth of a human being should be understood [as the location].

However, since it would be impossible to say that insertion in such a manner into the mouths of animals or non-humans (*amanussa*) is faultless, this [definition] must be taken as an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) for the mouths of all those capable of causing a *pārājika* offense.
That is the "male organ" (*aṅgajāta*). Regarding the phrase "having turned it there":

The construction is as follows: for one who, having placed [the object] in the mouth of those capable of committing a *pārājika* offense, removes it without letting it touch anywhere else, or lifts it out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Alternatively, having construed "in the mouth" with "turned upside down like an animal," the inclusion of other cases should be understood by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*).

29. “Tathā” means “having made it occupy space”; this refers back to the manner previously described. “With four sides” is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the direct object (*sahatthe karaṇavacana*).

Because the word “passehi” (with sides) is a relative term, the word “of the sign” (*nimittassa*) is understood by implication. Because the word “itthiyā” (of a woman) is a general term, the phrase “of all” (*sabbassa*) is supplied as a textual ellipsis.
It is in the singular number because it denotes a genus (*jātivācakattā*). “With four... [The sentence continues:]... [of sides].
Although there is no mention of the related term "pass the lower surface" in these [texts], because this section concerns the offense of sexual intercourse (methunapārājika),
and because this exposition— which is included at the end of the commentary on the fourfold rules for rugs—
is concluded with the following verse: "And just as it has been stated regarding the female sex organ, so should the characteristic be understood in all cases."

Because the extended application (*atidesa*) of the determination of the characteristic (*nimitta-vinicchaya*) has been made, the term "of the characteristic" (*nimittassa*) is obtained by implication (*sāmatthiyena*).
This very [term] is to be understood as the locus (*ādhāra*) for the word "having inserted" (*pavesetvā*). The term "the male organ" (*aṅgajāta*) follows [from the previous context].
Thus, having completed the sentence: "Just as, having inserted the male organ into a mouth that has been turned [downward], and having made it enter into space..."
The meaning should be stated by applying [the following]: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who extracts [it];

likewise, there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who, having inserted the male organ into the female organ—defined as the urinary passage—of any woman, extracts it while keeping the four sides together with the lower surface, making the four sides and the lower surface not touch but remain in the air."
30. *Uppāṭitoṭṭhamaṃsesu*: the analysis is "those whose lip-flesh has been torn away. Regarding those teeth:

"or with teeth protruding outward" means with teeth that have come out from the natural position of the lip-flesh. "Of one who makes an effort" means of one who touches [the organ] with the *aṅgajāta*.
31. *Aṭṭhisaṅghaṭṭanaṃ katvā*: having made contact with the bones that depend upon the sign and the flesh. He seeks.
On a path made of a collection of bones. "Possessed of two kinds of lust" means either through lust for sexual intercourse or through lust for bodily contact.
"Of one who makes an effort" means of one who inserts the genitals and moves them.
"Of one who embraces" means of one who clings to [the other]. Regarding "taking the hand" and so forth, "hand" refers to that part starting from the wrist.
"Down to the fingertips. Grasping the hand and what is connected to it is "grasping by the hand" (*hatthaggāha*).
Touching the remainder of the body and what is connected to it is "touching" (*parāmāsa*).
However, it is stated without doubt that "grasping with the hand the body of a woman or what is connected to her is grasping by the hand"; this is not [the view] of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
It is settled. Therefore, since it has been handed down in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) precisely according to the method already stated, that alone should be accepted as the essential point.
As for the "touching," what was said there—"the touching of the body with the hand and of what is connected to it"—that too is not tenable;
for even one who touches by means of any remaining part of the body incurs only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding "kissing and so forth":
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one includes seizing by the hair and so forth. By the phrase "this method," it extends the application (atidissati) of this meaning:
"For a woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for seizing the hand and so forth out of lust for sexual intercourse.
33. Among other animals—whether human or non-human—at the lower limit of which the act constitutes an offense involving defeat (pārājika) for sexual intercourse, [the same rule applies].

In order to show the sentient beings, he says "footless," and so forth. This term "in the category of sentient beings" should be qualified by these specific attributes: "footless, two-footed, four-footed. [The phrase] is: "in the footless category of sentient beings.

"Serpents" refers, among land-dwellers, from the highest limit including the elephant-swallowing pythons (*ajagara*) down to the lowest limit, which includes snakes (*nāga*). "Fish" refers, among aquatic creatures, to the uppermost limit.
Regarding the fish: starting from the *timirapiṅgala* and others that are five hundred *yojanas* long, down to the lowest limit, there are the *pāṭhīna*, *pāvusa*, and other such fish.
Regarding the bipeds among the class of beings: starting from the upper limit, the *garuḷa* (supernatural bird), down to the lowest limit, there are the pigeons (*kapota*) and their kind.
Some say "pigeons" refers to the *pārāvata* (doves). Regarding the quadrupeds among the class of beings: starting from the upper limit, the *godhā*...
"Starting from the elephant down to the lizard"—these are the sentient beings. "Down" means by way of the lower limit.
"The basis for a *pārājika* offense" refers to the bases for the *pārājika* offense regarding sexual intercourse; this is the remainder of the text. 34.
"Desire to engage in" is the craving (*taṇhā*) for engaging in sexual intercourse; the mind associated with that [craving] is what is termed sexual lust (*methunarāga*).

The mind desiring to engage in sexual intercourse. "Searches for" means in one of the passages, such as the urinary passage and so forth. "Insertion" means the entry of his own penis into the passage. Regarding the term *antimavatthu*:
it is "final" (*antima*) because it occurs at the end or destruction of the going-forth or of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha;

a person who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense is called "final" (*antima*). Because that basis is the cause for the state of being final, the *pārājika* offense is called the "final basis" (*antimavatthu*).
That very [offense] is the "first-and-last matter" because it was taught at the beginning of the four *pārājikas*;
thus, it refers to the first *pārājika* of that first-and-last matter.
35. "Adjacent" (*sāmanta*) means existing near an offense; they exist prior to and in proximity to a *pārājika* offense.
The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "but for the remaining three," this refers to the three remaining *pārājika* offenses, such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth.

The connection is: "A grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is declared to be the vicinity. How is it declared? In the second [offense], it is said: "If he causes it to quiver, there is an offense of a grave nature (*thullaccaya*)," and:
"If he digs a pit aiming at a human being, and [the person] falls and experiences painful sensation..."
In the third [case], it was stated: "If he understands, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*; if he does not understand, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.

And here, regarding the fourth *pārājika*, the nature of the offense of *thullaccaya* as being an offense bordering upon [the full offense] applies to one who [claims] a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
When one converses with another, as long as that person does not understand, there is the possibility of an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) due to the act of conversing;
and when that person has understood the matter thus conversed about, there is the possibility of an offense involving defeat (pārājika).
This latter case should be understood as being already included by the rule: "When spoken to one who does not understand, it is a serious transgression."
36. Regarding "one who does not know": this refers to one who, having seen the male organ become rigid due to wind, commits an offense according to his own desire while approaching women;
or, as stated, it refers to one who does not know that an act is being performed by others, like a bhikkhu who has fallen asleep during the day in a great forest.
By the phrase "just so," it draws in the statement: "it should be understood that there is no offense."
"Relishing" means: when those who are adversaries of the bhikkhus overcome him and commit transgressions, or cause them to be committed;
and when, like one who has entered the mouth of a snake, he does not endure it out of terror;

and when, like a bhikkhu who has gone for his midday rest in the great forest, even though he recognizes the attack of another, he does not endure it out of terror as if his body were being consumed by a blazing fire—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase “of one who does not know,” the word *api* (also/even) should be supplied here.

Because it was the very first thing to appear in the Buddha’s teaching—which is as stainless as the waters of the ocean of milk—it is both the beginning (*ādi*) and the action consisting of transgression (*kamma*); thus, it is *ādikamma*.
One who possesses this is an *ādikammī*. In this context, the monk Sudinna is to be understood as the *ādikammī*. This applies to what follows as well.
The meaning of these terms in every place where they occur should be understood according to this very method.
Furthermore, the seventeenfold common analysis—beginning with the introduction (*nidāna*) and so forth—will be made clear here in brief, and in detail below in all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
Therefore, it should be understood that it is not shown here.

37–38. *Vinaye* means in the Vinaya Piṭaka. *Anayūpame*: the term *naya* (method) refers to that which leads (*neti*) one to the perfection of virtue, the perfection of concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;
it is restraint (*saṃvara*), defined as non-transgression through the doors of body and speech. Its opposite is non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), which is called "misfortune" (*anaya*).

The cessation (*uparama*) or turning away from that [misfortune] occurs therein; thus it is *anayūpama*. It is the Vinaya; therefore, [the phrase means] "in that Vinaya which is the cessation of misfortune."

Therefore, it means "supreme" (*parama*) in the sense of being most excellent (*ukkaṭṭha*). Alternatively, it should be understood as "supreme" in the sense of the cessation or turning back of misfortune (*anaya*).
Or again, it should be understood thus: "The glory (*mā-sāsana-sirī*) of the Dispensation is supreme (*parā*) here; thus it is 'supreme' (*paramo*)," namely, the Vinaya.
Because of the statement, "The Vinaya is called the life-span of the Dispensation," the meaning is that it is endowed with the attainment of the most excellent Dispensation.

"Sujana" means a beautiful person (*sujana*); it refers to a son of noble family who desires training, who shines through the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), and whose character is dear.
"His eyes" is connected to "he disciplines those resembling eyes. Because they are not led astray and because they are supreme, they are the eyes of the noble son of noble family, resembling eyes.
"Bringing happiness" (*sukhānayane*) means that he brings the happiness distinguished as mundane and supramundane.
"Bringing happiness" refers to that [path]. And this is an adjective qualifying the word "bringing. If one asks: for what purpose is this adjective used?
It should be understood that it is intended to show the specific distinction possible here from the natural eye, which is taken as the basis of the simile.
If one asks: what is that distinction? The natural eye is a supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for defilements such as lust and hatred.

Having sacrificed, it becomes a condition for suffering both in this present life and in future lives. However, this method of discipline (vinaya-nayana) does not result in such a state for this clansman;
rather, it is taught for the purpose of showing this distinction: that it becomes a condition exclusively for the happiness of bringing about liberation.

Just as, by practicing without transgressing the discipline, there arises—rooted in the restraint of virtue accomplished through such practice—a sequence beginning with non-regret and culminating in parinibbāna without remainder...
It is said that he brings about both mundane and supramundane happiness that arises by way of the attainment of its fruit; this is what is meant by "in the Vinaya.

Regarding the phrase "delighting in striving" (*padhānarato*), there is the word *api* ("even") as a textual supplement. The meaning is: even though he delights in the application of striving toward the Vinaya, or even though he exerts himself in the Vinaya through means such as recitation, hearing, and reflection.
Alternatively, according to the statement "Dispassion (*virāga*) is the best of states," the "striving" (*padhāna*) is Nibbāna.
"Delighting in that" means finding pleasure therein. "In the Sāramata" means in that which is considered the essence (*sāra*).

Alternatively, it is called the "Sāramata" Vinaya adjudication because the essence—that is, the core meaning free from chaff—is the teacherly tradition (*ācariyamata*) of the Mahāvihāravāsins; [it refers] to that. "Here" means in this Vinaya adjudication.
"Delighting" means being utterly devoted. Regarding the phrase "not delighting," the negative particle (*na*) is connected with the final word, "delights" (*ramate*).
The connection is: "But he who, having applied himself, does not delight.

Among the elder, junior, and middle-ranking monks and nuns, that person who does not delight—that is, does not sport—by means of constant turning over [the teachings], hearing, recollecting, and reflecting, even if that person delights in striving regarding the Vinaya, by means of studying, hearing, and so forth within the Vinaya Piṭaka...
This shows that even one who is already proficient becomes more so; it does not mean that proficiency does not exist at all.
The intention is that those who desire proficiency in the Vinaya Piṭaka must first apply themselves with diligence to this very work.
To demonstrate this same point along with the successive benefits and purposes, he says "Imaṃ" (this), and so forth. "Imaṃ" refers to what is about to be mentioned.
The connection is with the word “understood” (*avedī*) in the phrase *vinayavinicchayaṃ*. “Whoever” (*yo*) is an elliptical addition to the text.

Whoever—a son of good family endowed with mindfulness, clear comprehension, and faith—rightly understood (*sammā avedi*) and knew this *Vinayavinicchaya*. To the question “Of what nature [is it]? he says: “The elucidation of welfare” (*hitavibhāvanaṃ*).

Since it is the fundamental means for achieving mundane and supramundane success, virtue (*sīla*) is here called “welfare” (*hita*); it elucidates and makes manifest that, thus the analysis (*viggaha*) is: “the elucidation of welfare” (*hitavibhāvana*).

Because it is said: “Being established in virtue... unravel the tangle,” the Pātimokkha restraint of virtue is the foremost among the fourfold purities of virtue, which serve as the root for the attainment of all mundane and supramundane qualities.

This is because they serve as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the eight kinds of concentration—both with and without the higher knowledges (abhiññā), including the form and formless realms—which in turn are the proximate causes for supramundane knowledge that unravels the tangle of all defilements.
This is due to its function of elucidating those virtues.
This exposition of the Vinaya is called the "Illuminator of Welfare" (*Hitavibhāvana*).
Regarding the term *bhāvana*: it is called *bhāvana* because it is cultivated (*bhāviyati*) and repeatedly established in the mind; thus, it is said to be "that which is to be cultivated.
Because it illuminates welfare, it is said that those who desire welfare should repeatedly dwell upon it in their minds. Such being its nature—
*Vinayavinicchayaṃ*: "Rasa" (taste/flavor) is that which arises from what is excellent (*sura*), is tasted, or is relished;

it refers to the flavor of the Dhamma, the flavor of the meaning, the flavor of compassion and so forth, and the flavor of liberation. That whose flavor is beautiful (*sobhana*) is *surasa*. Thus, it is the *vinayavinicchaya* (the determination of the Vinaya), which is *surasa*.
*Bhavaṃ* means "bhavantaṃ" (the venerable one); it is said to be "peaceful" (*santa*). Being *surasa*, it has become *surasa* (*surasaṃ bhūtaṃ*).

Meaning (*attha*). What is meant? It refers to the thirty-five ornaments of meaning (*atthālaṅkāra*)—such as *sabhāvākhyāna*, *upamā*, *rūpaka*, *dīpaka*, *āvutti*, and so forth—as well as the excellence of the aesthetic flavor of words (*saddarasa*), which consists of the ten qualities of the life-force of sound (*saddajīvitaguṇa*) described by poets as "cohesion (*silesa*), clarity (*pasāda*), evenness (*samatā*), sweetness (*madhurata*), delicacy (*sukhumālatā*), lucidity of meaning (*atthabyatti*), loftiness (*udāratā*), vigor (*oja*), luster (*kānti*), and concentration (*samādhi*). In these [ornaments],...

It is said that this *Vinayavinicchaya* is "flavorful" (*surasa*) because it is endowed with the excellence of meaning—comprising figures of speech such as *padhāna* (predominance) and *alaṅkāra* (ornamentation)—which are expressed through descriptions of appropriate natures and so forth; and because it is joined with the flavors of compassion (*karuṇā-rasa*), the marvelous (*abbhuta-rasa*), the wonderful (*santara-rasa*), and others, as far as possible.
Alternatively, it is because the virtue of restraint by the *Pātimokkha*, which is primarily enjoined by this treatise, invariably leads to concentration (*samādhi*).
It should be understood that because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for concentration and wisdom, and because wisdom leads to Nibbāna,
this Vinaya-vinicchaya— acting as the fundamental cause— gradually bestows the excellence of the flavor of the nectar-fruit of Nibbāna,
and thus it is said to have become "delicious" through the form of supreme satisfaction and the flavor of the liberation of steadfastness (*dhitivimutti*). Herein, they arise...

That which is called "pleasure" is both bodily and mental; it is called "sambhava" (origin) because it arises from this. It is the Vinaya-vinicchaya (the determination of the Vinaya), which serves as the root cause for bodily and mental pleasure.

According to the method already stated, it is the source of the mental pleasure produced by the great festival of the excellence of the essence of the aforementioned flavors, and likewise the source of the bodily pleasure that has that [mental pleasure] as its originating condition and support.
This is the meaning. To this extent, the reason for the correct understanding of this *Vinayavinicchaya* has been demonstrated.
If one asks, "What becomes of that clansman who thus fully comprehends this *Vinayavinicchaya*, which is a mine of jewels of manifold virtues?"—he becomes equal to Pāli and Upāli.
Regarding the term "Pāli": because he protects the Dispensation (*sāsana*), he is called a "guardian" (*pāla*); thus, the Vinaya is referred to as "Pāli."
For it is said: “The Vinaya is the life-span of the Dispensation. Because he possessed that [Vinaya], he was called Pālī;

and because he maintained the Dispensation—known as the formulation of the Vinaya—which constitutes the very life of the threefold Dispensation by way of study, practice, and realization, he was known by the name Pālī. As it is said:
“This is the foremost, monks, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are masters of the Vinaya, namely Upāli.”

It is said that he is equal to the Great Elder Upāli, who—sitting in the midst of the fourfold assembly—had his lotus-like face opened by the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Supreme Wheel-Turner of the True Dhamma;
who was proclaimed as one of the "Foremost Ones" (etadagga); and who specifically received the name "Pālī" because of his quality of protecting the [Vinaya] tradition.
If it is asked, "In what domain does he become impartial? It is in the Dispensation (sāsana). "Dispensation" refers to the threefold Dispensation as previously described;

therein, specifically, to the Dispensation of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana), which maintains both practice and realization and is like a circular mandala encompassing the entire range of stationary and moving objects;
and even within that, to a specific portion of the scripture known as the Vinaya Piṭaka, since the present context concerns the discourse on the Vinaya.
The meaning is "he becomes equal.

In what kind of dispensation? In the "dispensation that is the prey of Māra" (*mārabalisāsane*). The "prey of Māra" (*mārabali*) is the domain of Māra; his dispensation is a "dispensation that is the prey of Māra," which is harmful, and in that [dispensation].
Among the five Māras, such as the aggregates (*khandha*), it refers to the defilement-Māra (*kilesamāra*), which originates from the primary passion for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and so forth.

Because it was spoken in the manner beginning with, "Whosoever monk... [is found] not in communion," for the purpose of causing the relinquishing of objects such as tangible things—the supports for the bodies of women known as *balis* (sacrificial offerings) and so forth—by way of their being sense-fields (*gocara*), it is a "teaching that destroys the army of Māra.
Thus, the meaning is: it is the Teaching known as the Vinaya-proclamation, which is the name of the instruction that destroys the army of Māra.

Alternatively, since it will be explained in the commentary on the water-element passage—“With a hook, or with a net, or with a hand, or with a fish-basket”—the word *baḷisa* refers to the fish-killing barb.
That which casts away, or avoids, the hook of Māra is called *mārabaḷisāsana*.

In that regard, because it is said, “The snare of Māra is all-encompassing,” [it refers to] the fish known as the worldlings (*puthujjana*), who are slaves to the defilements and are tossed about in the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
The intention is as follows: in the Teaching known as the Vinaya formulation, one abandons— by means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*),

abandonment through transcendence (*vītikkamappahāna*), and so forth— the great hook of defilements such as sensual lust, which is baited with the five strands of sensual pleasure consisting of the forms, sounds, and so forth of women,
designated as "fishhooks," and cast into the great net of Māra for the purpose of capturing [beings].

And herein, O Sāramati, he who does not delight in this discernment of the Vinaya—that person, being one who has not reached ruin, becomes clever, even more clever, and most excellent in the Vinaya—which is supreme, the highest, the means for bringing happiness to the virtuous, a guide, and comparable to the eye—and who delights and rejoices in it, being intent on exertion and applying himself to its study and so forth. What [is there to say]? [He becomes exceedingly proficient.]
It is not so. Therefore, for the sake of proficiency in the Vinaya, one should apply oneself with diligence precisely here;
thus should the thematic interpretation of the meaning, together with its underlying intention, be understood in brief.

Alternatively, that person who delights in—and is devoted to—the fourfold supreme effort (*sammappadhāna*), which is the primary [virtue], and who, O Sāramati, finds delight here in this discernment of the Vinaya, from that [delight]...
Therefore, the construction is as follows: he is proficient and skilled in the Vinaya, which leads to the ultimate end of misfortune and brings happiness to virtuous people.

He who has known—that is, understood—this Vinayavinicchaya, which reveals welfare, illuminates welfare, is to be cultivated, is to be practiced, originates from the Sugata, is itself sweet, is a true source of sweetness, and has happiness as its cause.
That person, while the teaching—which brings about the abandonment of Māra’s domain—is being proclaimed within the teaching that lies within Māra’s snare;

or rather, while the threefold teaching of the Victor (Jina) is being proclaimed, specifically within the scriptural teaching (pariyatti-sāsana) which serves as the foundation for both practice and realization;
and even there, within a portion of the scriptural teaching known as the Vinaya-paññatti, which is like the very lifeblood of the entire dispensation.

The construction is as follows: because Upāli was established by the Lord as the foremost among those who have mastered the Vinaya, and because the Vinaya-piṭaka—designated as "pāla" (protector)—is more highly praised than other branches of learning since it is the very root for protecting the Dispensation, he is equal to the Great Elder Upāli.
Thus [ends] the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the first *pārājika* discussion in the *Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The commentary on the second *pārājika* discussion.
39. Now, in order to show the second determination of the *pārājika* offense, he says: “Taking,” and so forth. Herein, the phrase “with a thieving mind” (*theyyacittena*) is an elliptical addition.
That [phrase] must be construed with all the words ending in the singular accusative case; the connection is: “one who takes with a thieving mind is defeated.
Having laid claim to another’s property, such as a monastery and so forth, and having defeated the owner, with a thieving mind—
It is said that one who takes [the property] incurs a *dukkaṭa* for the prior effort made toward that end, and having incurred a *thullaccaya* by causing doubt in the owner,
he— by relinquishing his responsibility both for the other and for himself— becomes a non-heir to the attainment of the morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha and is thus defeated.

The terms “tathā,” “api,” and “parājito” should be combined with “theyyacittena” (with a thieving mind) and then joined with each of the four phrases beginning with “haranto” (while taking). The construction is: even one who takes [the object] with a thieving mind is likewise defeated.
This refers to one who, while taking another’s property such as the head [of a corpse], commits a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) upon the touching of the object with a thieving mind.

The meaning is that even one who, having committed a *thullaccaya* offense by shaking [the object], performs an action such as pulling it from the head to the shoulder, is likewise defeated (*parājita*).
The construction is: "even one who takes away with a mind of theft is likewise defeated. This, however, is the meaning here—by others...

With reference to concealment and so forth, even one who, when pressed with the words "Give me back my goods" regarding property deposited with him, speaks falsely—saying "I did not take it," and so on—and then takes it with a thieving mind, incurs a *thullaccaya* offense for causing doubt in the other person;
yet, by thus abandoning the matter, he is defeated (*parājita*). This refers to having denied and rejected [the charge] by saying, "I did not take it," and so forth.
One who is "taking away" is called "carrying off.
The construction is: even one who disturbs the deportment with a thieving mind is likewise defeated.

Furthermore, having stopped someone—such as another person who is carrying goods—who is taking those goods while saying, "I shall take them along with that merchandise," by means of a thieving mind, [and then] toward the direction desired by oneself...

The meaning is that even by disturbing his natural posture, having incurred a *thullaccaya* offense with the lifting of the first foot, he is likewise defeated (*parājita*) upon crossing the limit of the second step. The construction is:
"Even one who causes [the object] to move from its place with a mind of theft is likewise defeated. Regarding goods situated on dry land and so forth, with a mind of theft...

Even when one moves [the object] from its place with the desire to steal it, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* for all the preliminary efforts—beginning with the second search and ending with the touching—and a *thullaccaya* for the act of moving it;
furthermore, by moving it even as much as a hair’s breadth from its place, one is defeated (*parājita*) in exactly the same manner as will be explained below. This is the meaning.

If it is asked: "In this way, why is the sixth phrase not included among the six phrases found in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*)—namely, 'should take up,' 'should carry off,' 'should steal,' 'should disturb the deportment,' 'should displace from its place,' and 'should pass the appointment'—when the first five phrases are included?
It is because this verse was not spoken to show that specific word-analysis.

Now, with reference to the analysis of those terms, and wishing to show the twenty-five ways of bringing about forfeiture (*nissaggiyāvahāra*) as stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), [the author] spoke [these verses] with the intent of showing the five groups of five that constitute its parts; therefore, it should be understood that the sixth term is not mentioned here.
Alternatively, [it is omitted] because of the term "bringing about forfeiture" (*nissaggiyāvahāra*) which will appear in the third group of five to be discussed.

Since it is included within the "formulation of the taking away" (*parikappāvahāra*) in the fifth pentad, it should be understood that the sixth category was not included here in order to show, without confusion, the two sets of fivefold objects (*pañcaka-bhaṇḍa*). 40.
When the matter of this *pārājika* offense of taking what is not given has arisen, regarding the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) to be made, there are twenty-five modes of taking away (*avahāra*).

There are constituent factors, and these are specified as fivefold sets: the fivefold set of various articles, the fivefold set of a single article, the fivefold set of taking with one’s own hand, the fivefold set of prior preparation, and the fivefold set of theft by carrying away.

Among these, this verse begins with the words “In that regard” (*tatthā*) in order to include ten types of theft within the two divisions of the fivefold set of various articles, and thereby to show the remaining three fivefold sets. In that context:
"In that" (*tattha*) means in this verse. "Not [taking] various and single articles" (*nānekabhaṇḍānaṃ*): the analysis of the compound is "those which have various [and] one article.
One should understand there to be five types of various articles by way of animate and inanimate articles, and five types of single articles by way of animate articles alone.
"Of those which have five as their measure" (*pañcaparimāṇā yesaṃ te pañcakā, tesaṃ*): "of those. "Theft" (*avahārā*): [the taking away].
"Appropriations" means acts of theft; this is what is meant. "These" refers to those beginning with "one who takes," as specified in the immediately preceding verse.
One who "cultivates"—that is, develops—the distinction or discernment within the continuum of practice is a "discerner" (*vibhāvī*), namely one who upholds the Vinaya; by such a discerner.
"To be understood" refers to animate objects belonging to others, such as monasteries and the like, or [inanimate things] such as slaves, peacocks, and so forth.

The five modes of taking—beginning with the aforementioned forms of receiving and ending with the removal from its place—which are committed solely to steal a mere conscious object, proceed by having as their objects either various articles or a single article as previously described;

thus, there are ten modes of theft, namely the "fivefold case of various articles" and the "fivefold case of a single article. This is because they assist in the determination of the matter for one who has fallen into [an offense], according to the Vinaya master.
The meaning is: "it should be known as it truly is.

41. Having thus shown two sets of five regarding the five groups of five articles among the twenty-five acts of taking that ought to be explained, he now says "sāhatthā" and so forth in order to show the remaining three groups of five. Therein, "sāhatthā" means:
*Sāhattha* means "by one's own hand," produced by it, or related to it; thus, it refers to a theft committed by the thief with his own hand—this is the meaning.
*Āṇattika ceva* means "and that which is produced by command";
it is a theft accomplished by commanding anyone, such as saying to a thief, "Take this particular article. *Nissaggo* means... [the remainder of the sentence is not provided in the source text].
*Nissajjana* means relinquishing; it is the taking away, or the act of dropping goods outside after standing in a customs station or in a designated place—this is what is meant. *Atthasādhaka*:
he accomplishes the matter (attha) defined as an offense of defeat (*pārājika*), thus he is an "accomplisher of the matter"; and that is the taking away.
When one commands another to steal unilaterally, without violating the threefold instruction— either by commanding generally,
"Steal the property of so-and-so," or by specifying any one of the particular details such as the specific object to be stolen, the time of taking, the place of taking, or the manner of taking—
or when one commands the theft of any item worth a quarter [of a kahāpaṇa], such as oil for drinking, sandals, or other such things;

"Application such as throwing down [an object] from an oil-vessel or similar items"—this and other such applications are called "theft accomplishing the purpose," because they establish the matter designated as a *pārājika* offense even prior to the actual completion of the act.
"And the relinquishing of the burden" (*dhuranikkhepana*) means the laying down of the burden; that too is theft, regarding things belonging to others.
Regarding the application of effort toward gardens and the like, as well as regarding goods and so forth deposited [as collateral],
there is the "transaction of laying down the burden," which consists of the thief’s lack of enthusiasm for returning the property to the owner— whether at any time or in any manner— with the thought,
"I shall take it whenever and however I please. Thus, this laying down of the burden is of the aforementioned kind.

The "tetrad beginning with 'with one's own hand'" (*sāhatthādicatukka*) and the collection of the five types of theft constitute the "pentad"; this pentad beginning with 'with one's own hand' is called the "hand-pentad" (*sāhatthapañcaka*).
It should be understood that the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is indicated by elision (*lutta*).

42. Regarding the phrase "and the prior and simultaneous applications" (*pubbasahapayogā ca*), the word "application" (*payoga*) should be construed individually with both "prior" (*pubba*) and "simultaneous" (*saha*).
“Because of the commentarial statement, ‘The preliminary effort is to be understood by way of the command,’ for one who takes [the goods] without violating the sequence of the command,
the act of commanding— ‘Steal such-and-such a person’s goods named so-and-so’— is called the preliminary effort of the theft.
The employment of body or speech in giving the command is the ‘effort’ (payoga), because it precedes the taking of the goods by the one commanded.”

It should be understood that "the preliminary act" (*pubbapayoga*) means the act of taking (*avahāra*) itself, as it consists of both the prior effort and the actual act. Regarding the statement in the Commentary,

"It should be understood as a simultaneous act (*sahapayoga*) by way of causing displacement from one's place," since this is an illustrative expression (*upalakkhaṇapada*), it should be understood that the simultaneous act of taking consists of both causing displacement from one's place and entering another's territory, such as crossing over a boundary-stake (*khīla*).

“Agreement and taking” (*saṃvidāharaṇa*) refers both to the act of taking another’s property with a thieving mind after having made an agreement— many having come together and agreed, “We shall steal such-and-such goods”—
and to the act of taking by all together, or by one acting on behalf of all with their consent, or by one alone. It also includes cases where, having first joined together in a group,
even if one person subsequently acts alone with a thieving mind, [the offense is established] from the very first step.
Or, when a value equal to a *pāda* has been taken, it should be understood that for all [the participants], it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

"Concerted theft" (*saṃvidāharaṇa*) means stealing after having made an agreement and consulted together. The derivation of the word should be understood according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*).
"Concerted theft" (*saṃvidāharaṇa*) is a synonym for "concerted taking" (*saṃvidāvahāra*). "Many people, having made an agreement, one person steals the goods..."

Because of the statement, “The offense for all is a *pārājika*,” it should be understood that when those who have made a mutual appointment converse with one another, if even one among them takes hold of a foot or something equivalent to a foot with a thieving mind, a *pārājika* offense occurs for all those who made the appointment.
“Making an appointment” (*saṅketakamma*) means an agreement (*saṅketa*) consisting of a determination of time, such as the forenoon; the act performed by means of that is “making an appointment.”
“Taking away” refers to making a secret signal (*saṅketakamma*). However, if one has set a specific time such as before a meal and says,
“At this time, steal such-and-such an article,” and the person steals that very article at that very time,
it should be understood in brief that for the one who made the signal, there is a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of the signal.
"By sign" (*nemitta*) means that scratching the eyes or similar acts are called "signs" because they serve as the cause for taking another's goods;
what is produced by that is "by sign. "Taking" (*avahāra*) refers to the act of theft.

When one who has been commanded—"When I have scratched my eye or raised my eyebrow, steal such-and-such a good"—sees that sign and, without violating the stated condition, steals the very good specified; [that constitutes the offense].
If it is taken, the one who made the sign commits a *pārājika* offense at the very moment the sign was made.
If it is taken by violating the stated rule, the one who made the sign is released, and the *pārājika* offense belongs to the thief alone.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has the preliminary effort as its beginning" is *pubbapayogādi*; and that which is both *pubbapayogādi* and the pentad (*pañcaka*) is the full compound.
43. *Theyya*, *pasayha*, *parikappa*, *paṭicchanna*, and *kusa*—these are *theyyapasayhaparikappapaṭicchannakusā*.
Those acts of taking away (*avahāra*) for which these are the preceding qualifying terms are called *theyya...kusādikā avahārā*.

By this it is meant: "the act of taking by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*) and so forth, up to "the act of taking by means of *kusa*. In that context, *theyyāvahāra*: *theno* refers to a thief; his... [text continues].
"Bhāva" means theft (*theyya*); here, the elision of the letter "na" should be understood according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*).

Therefore, "taking by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*) refers to both taking by way of breaking into walls and so forth while remaining unseen, and taking after deceiving others with false measures, counterfeit coins, and the like.

"Taking by force" (*pasayhāvahāra*) means taking after having overcome or subdued [the owner]; it includes seizing property from owners by overpowering them, as village plunderers do, as well as seizing fixed taxes or extra levies by overpowering them, as royal officials and the like do.
Stealing by imagining—that is, stealing after having mentally delimited and imagined items such as cloth—is twofold: by way of imagining the goods and by way of imagining the space.

Regarding that, when one enters a dark place where goods have been deposited and takes the boxes or other containers in which items such as thread have been placed, [the thought occurs]: "If I take the cloths, but not the threads..."

Lifting [an object] after having made a mental reservation in such a manner as "I shall take it," is called the offense of *bhaṇḍaparikappāvahāra* (theft by mental reservation), because it is preceded by a mental reservation regarding the object.

Having entered a monastery garden, a courtyard, or similar places, and seeing an alluring object, one mentally reserves some location—such as the interior of a room, the floor of a palace, the top of a story, a veranda, a courtyard, a wall, a gate, or a watchtower—and thinks:
"If he sees me within this space, I will show him that I have taken it, as if I were looking at it."
If one does not [take it], but rather thinks, "I shall take it," and having taken it and gone, there is the transgression of exceeding the designated place;
because this is preceded by the delimitation of space, it should be understood in brief as the "offense consisting of the delimitation of space.
The theft of goods concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth is "concealed theft" (*paṭicchannāvahāra*). By those playing in gardens and such places...
Or, having seen any kind of goods such as ornaments that have been left behind after being removed by people attending the Saṅgha,
one stands there thinking, "They might come back and take them," and conceals it with grass,

leaves, dust, sand, and so forth; then, after searching for the owners and finding none, when those who had expectations have departed, the subsequent taking with a thieving mind is likewise [an offense].

"Concealed taking" (*paṭicchannāvahāra*) is said to be the act of pressing down on merchandise in mud and so forth with the fingers or other parts of the hand while intending to steal, causing it to sink, and then passing over the spot where it was touched by the lower part with the upper part.
"Grass-taking" (*kusāvahāra*) means taking by means of grass; it refers to shifting [the goods] by means of grass with the intent to steal, according to the value of the portion belonging to another.

The meaning is: "the taking of [a portion] that is either large or equal. Furthermore, when the Saṅgha’s robes are being distributed by means of casting lots (*kusapātana*), whichever monk—desiring to misappropriate another’s portion—takes from his own portion [something] equal to, greater than, or less than his own share, worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas in value... [he commits an offense].

If one who wishes to cause a *kus*a slip to fall into another’s portion lifts it up, there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*) at the moment of lifting it nor at the moment it falls into the other’s portion;
however, if while removing the *kus*a written in the other’s name from that person’s portion he shifts it even by the breadth of a hair, he becomes defeated.
If he first removes the *kus*a from the other’s portion, [he becomes defeated].
At the moment of pulling out [the grass] from one's own portion, at the moment of throwing it down, and at the moment of writing one’s own name, one does not incur a *pārājika* offense.
However, at the moment of throwing it into another’s portion, if even a hair’s breadth [of the grass] has been released from the hand, one becomes *pārājika*.
If both [monks] have concealed the two pieces of *kusa* grass and all the monks have departed, each taking his own respective portion, then in whichever [portion]...
He hid the *kusa* grass. When its owner arrived and asked, "Why is my *kusa* not to be seen?", the thief said,
"My *kusa* is also not to be seen," and showing his own portion as if it belonged to the other,
whether they quarreled or not, once he had taken it and departed, if the other were to unearth that [other] portion, at the very moment it is unearthed—
He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. If another person says, "I will not give my portion to you;

you must take it after searching out your own portion," and having been told this, he takes the other's portion even though he knows it does not belong to him, at the very moment it is taken, he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. If the other person, out of fear of a dispute, says, "What..."
Thinking, "Let there be no dispute," one might say, "Whether the bowl be mine or yours, you take the choice portion";
since this is considered "taken after it has been given," it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense.
If, however, being told, "Take whichever you prefer," one—out of fear of a dispute—sets aside the choice portion that is one's own and takes the inferior portion...

The thief departed; because he took what remained after the search was finished, he is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense. In this way, the determination regarding the taking of what is stolen (*kusāvahāra*) should be understood.

This is a summary of the twenty-five types of theft herein; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
44. Having thus far demonstrated twenty-five types of theft that must be learned in the form of the constituent parts of the analysis of the *pārājika* offense of taking what is not given,
now, as the analysis of taking what is not given is reached, the following is commenced with the words "In regard to the object,
time, value, and place," etc., in order to show the five points that must first be examined before hastily charging someone with an offense.
In this context, "the object" (*vatthu*) refers to the stolen goods. What is meant?
Even when the thief says, "I have stolen such-and-such an object," one must investigate whether that object has an owner or not.
If it has an owner, one must determine at the time of the theft whether they had an attachment (*sālaya*) to it or were detached (*nirālaya*). At the time of their attachment...
If that taken article, after being appraised, is worth one *māsaka* or less than a *māsaka*, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
if it is worth more than a *māsaka* or less than five *māsakas*, it is a *thullaccaya*; if it is worth five *māsakas* or more than five *māsakas*, it must be dealt with as a *pārājika*.
If it was taken when the owners were absent from their home, there is no *pārājika*. [Regarding] the owners of the goods...
However, when having goods brought back, either those goods or something of equal value must be returned.
"Time" refers to the time of the theft. These goods sometimes have a high value and sometimes a low value;
therefore, by those who are determining the value of the stolen goods, it should be determined in a way that corresponds to the time at which they were stolen.
It is meant that the determination of the time must be made.
"Value" refers to the value of the goods stolen. Furthermore, the value of goods is not always the same;
new goods are of high value, whereas old ones are of equal or lesser value. Therefore, at the time of the theft, [the value] of the goods—
The intention is that the value must be determined by fixing it according to whether it is in a new state or an old state.
"And the place" refers to the location where the goods were brought from.

In this context, since the same goods may be of low value at the place of origin but high value elsewhere, those who determine the offenses corresponding to the value must first fix the value of the goods as they were transported.
The intention is that, having fixed the location of the theft for the purpose of determining the value, one should impose corresponding offenses based on the value at that location.
"Use" (*paribhoga*) means the use made by others of the stolen goods prior to the act of theft. And here, for whom...
It is said that because the value of any article may decrease through its use, one must ask the owner of the article;
even if that article is new, once it has been used by anyone in any manner whatsoever, its value must be determined after such depreciation has been accounted for.

By this method and others like it, he says, "A wise person should render a decision only after having understood these five points," in order to show that the adjudication must be made precisely after investigating these five bases.
45. Having thus far demonstrated the twenty-five modes of taking and the five considerations of the place regarding the analysis of the components of the offense of taking what is not given,
[the author], now desiring to show that there is no escape for one who takes any kind of property belonging to another—
wherever it may be situated and by whatever means— for the purpose of closing off even a slight opening for future wicked bhikkhus, says:
Thus it was said by the Tathāgata:
"That which stands upon the earth, that which stands upon dry land,
and furthermore, that which stands in the sky."
One who has gone to the upper story, one who has gone to the water,
and one who is on a boat as a means of transport;
those carrying a burden, Rāma, and one staying in a monastery.
A field, a site, and likewise a village, the king’s property, water,
a tooth-stick, and a forest tree.
Haraṇaka, panidhi,
and suṅkaghātaka; pāṇaka,
apada, and dvipada.
Four-footed and many-footed,
the prowler and the protector;
and also the taking by agreement.
“The thirty excellent headings (mātikā) are: ‘The act of convention’ and ‘The sign.

Having thus set them forth, desiring to show the analysis according to the sequence in which they appear in the word-commentary (padabhājana) and the method transmitted in their respective commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), he first states, beginning with “or the second pond,” in order to show the analysis regarding the meaning of the ground (bhūmaṭṭha).
In this context, the connection is that for one who seeks [the treasure] with a thieving mind, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

This applies to all subsequent cases as well. When one desires to extract a great hoard covered by tree creepers that have grown up, bricks, stones, and so forth, and thinks, "I cannot do this alone," one seeks another companion with a thieving mind from the place where one was lying.
The meaning is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all activities such as rising [from one's seat] and so forth.
A spade (kudāla) is for the purpose of digging the earth, or a basket (piṭaka) is for the purpose of removing soil; "any vessel" refers to these two.
If the handle of this spade is missing, and one cuts a handle from a tree for the sake of a handle, or if it is not a spade and one [seeks] iron filings for the purpose of making a spade...
It should be understood that for one who digs unallowable earth for the purpose of extraction, or cuts leaves for the purpose of making a back-rest,
or cuts creepers for the purpose of weaving a basket— whether in both cases or even when lying falsely during the search—
the offense is both *dukkaṭa* and *pācittiya*; whereas in other instances of such activity, it is only *dukkaṭa*.

The meaning is that for one who, having sought a companion and found or not found one, goes toward the place where the treasure is located, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step.

Furthermore, because the phrase "with a thieving mind" (*theyyacitto*) is stated in the *Pāḷi* in the passage beginning "or seeks a second [companion] with a thieving mind," whereas here the expression "with a thieving mind" (*theyyacittena*) is used, [the intention is]: "Having obtained this treasure, I shall perform an offering to the Buddha."

It should be understood that there is no offense when there is the occurrence of a wholesome state of mind in such a manner as, "I will prepare [food] for myself" or "I will provide a meal for the Saṅgha.

Regarding the phrase "from the preliminary effort": the meaning is that it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) because it constitutes the preliminary application for taking what is not given, specifically in the preliminary efforts such as the second search and so forth.

There are eight kinds of *dukkaṭa*: *pubbapayoga-dukkaṭa* (offense of preliminary effort), *sahapayoga-dukkaṭa* (offense of simultaneous effort), *anāmāsa-dukkaṭa* (offense of improper contact), *durupaciṇṇa-dukkaṭa* (offense of misconduct), *vinaya-dukkaṭa* (offense against the discipline), *ñāta-dukkaṭa* (recognized offense), *ñatti-dukkaṭa* (offense of formal motion), and *paṭissava-dukkaṭa* (offense of assent). Regarding these, [it is said]:
"If one, with a thieving mind, seeks out a second spade or a basket, or goes [to fetch them], there is an offense..."
Regarding the statement, "of a *dukkaṭa*," this refers to what is called the preliminary *dukkaṭa*. Here, in the place where there is a *pācittiya*, there is a *pācittiya*;

in the other preliminary acts, there is a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the statement, "If one cuts wood or a creeper growing there, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*," this refers to the *sahapayoga-dukkaṭa* (simultaneous *dukkaṭa*).
Here, because the act is accompanied by the taking of what is not given, there is a *pācittiya* in the case [of the object]; elsewhere...

"And it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing)"—this is the distinction here. Regarding the ten treasures such as pearls and gems, the seven grains such as rice, and all items including weapons and goods:
the *dukkaṭa* incurred by the reason of touching them is the "touching *dukkaṭa*" (*anāmāsana-dukkaṭa*).

For one who touches only the fruit of trees such as the plantain, coconut, and jackfruit, the *dukkaṭa* stated is the "badly performed *dukkaṭa*" (*durupaciṇṇa-dukkaṭa*). "Upaciṇṇa" means approaching; it means grasping.
The meaning is as follows: that which is badly performed is "durupaciṇṇaṃ"; the wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in what is badly performed is "durupaciṇṇadukkaṭaṃ.
At the time of wandering for alms, if dust has fallen into the bowl, to receive alms without first receiving the bowl or without washing it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense;
this is a *vinayadukkaṭa*, meaning a *dukkaṭa* prescribed in the Vinaya. Although there are other *dukkaṭa* offenses as well...

Although these [terms] are indeed prescribed in the Vinaya, nevertheless, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), this very thing is so called, just as peacocks and other birds are designated by the sounds "morā" and so forth.
What is stated as, "Having heard it, they do not speak; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," is called the "wrong-doing of what is known.
Among the eleven formal admonitions (*samanubhāsanā*), what is stated as, "There is a wrong-doing by means of the motion (*ñatti*)," is the "wrong-doing of the motion. "Monks, for that monk..."
When it is said, "The first [rainy-season] is not recognized, and there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for making a formal promise," this refers to what is called the *dukkaṭa* of promising.
Among these eight types of *dukkaṭa*, the *dukkaṭa* to be incurred here is called the *dukkaṭa* of preliminary action (*pubbapayoga-dukkaṭa*).

Therefore, he said "from the preliminary action" (*pubbayogato*); however, for the sake of the meter in the verse, the prefix was omitted, and it is read as "from the preliminary application" (*pubbapayogato*).
It should be understood that it is stated [in the text] as "from the preliminary practice" (*pubbayogato*).
And here, although there are many *dukkaṭa* offenses not included among these [specific] *dukkaṭas*— namely,

the *dukkaṭas* concerning sleeping during the day and so forth found in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*, as well as many *dukkaṭas* found in the *Khandhaka*— nevertheless, they should all be subsumed under *vinaya-dukkaṭa* itself.
For it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that "the wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) prescribed in the Vinaya is 'Vinaya-wrong-doing'.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the inclusion of only the "dust-covered wrong-doing" under the term "Vinaya-wrong-doing" is merely illustrative.
Otherwise, the numerical limit of "eight wrong-doings" would be rendered meaningless; thus, [the rule applies] even to the wrong-doings and so forth from previous applications.

Although [these offenses] are to be included within the *vinayadukkaṭa* itself, their separate mention should be understood as being for the purpose of showing a few examples while grouping the others together—just as the eight types of verses, such as the *geyya* and *gāthā*, are shown separately even though they are included within the *sutta* division. 46.
Regarding the phrase "wood grown there" (*tatthajātakaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ vā*): this refers to wood, whether fresh or dry, that has grown upon a long-deposited heap of refuse (*nidhūpa*) in that place.
Or a creeper, or such a climbing vine. This is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), since grasses and the like, as well as small shrubs, are to be included.
"In both cases" means on both the moist and the dry; this is what is meant.

He shows the reason why, for one cutting down moist trees and so forth, there is not a *pācittiya* offense but merely a *dukkaṭa*: "because of the simultaneous application" (*sahapayogato*). [This is] by way of taking away (*avahārena*).
It is stated that because it is a simultaneous application (*sahita-payoga*), even in a case where a *pācittiya* offense would otherwise apply, there is only a *dukkaṭa*.

One who says, "Because it is a simultaneous application, there is a *dukkaṭa* in both cases," demonstrates the distinction between the prior application shown in the first verse and this simultaneous application shown here. 47.
"Earth" (*pathaviṃ*) means either allowable or unallowable earth. Because of the simultaneous application of one who digs unallowable earth...
It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding the word *byūhati*: it refers to one who makes a heap of soil on one side.

Although the verbal root *ūh-* arises in the sense of "thinking" (*vitakka*), according to the commentary’s statement, “*viyūhati* means he makes a heap on one side,” it should be understood that because roots have multiple meanings, here—by virtue of the prefix *vi-*—it functions in the sense of making a heap.
[He takes] the soil that has become a heap with a spade...
For one who lifts or removes [the treasure] with the hand or with a basket, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each instance of the action;
it should be understood that the word "or" (vā) here includes by way of a collective sense what has not been explicitly stated—that is, even when the dust itself blows away.
"Touching" means touching the treasure-jar with the hand. "Or" (vā) is used in the sense of inclusion. "Wrong-doing" (dukkaṭa) refers to an ill-performed action.
