“Dukkaṭa” (wrong-doing) refers to that which is committed by failing to follow what was spoken by the Teacher, through having stumbled or erred.
And this has been stated in the Parivāra: “Listen now to the truth regarding what is called ‘dukkaṭa’:
That which is transgressed, missed, and stumbled over—this is dukkaṭa.”
It is called *dukkaṭa* because it is badly or deformedly done (*duṭṭhu virūpaṃ kataṃ kiriyā*).
This has also been stated in the *Parivāra*: "Whatever evil a person does, whether openly or in secret, they declare it to be 'dukkaṭa'; therefore it is so called."
Thus, regarding the five offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) involving concomitant action— namely, the dukkaṭa of cutting,
the dukkaṭa of digging, the dukkaṭa of piling up, the dukkaṭa of removing, and the dukkaṭa of touching—

as presented in the two verses beginning with “*tatthajātakaṃ*,” the offenses of wrong-doing incurred through each preceding action are extinguished upon reaching the subsequent wrong-doing at the conclusion of each respective action.
If, having fallen into a state of shamefulness, one desists, one becomes pure after confessing the respective *dukkaṭa* offense.
It is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that for one who causes [the organ] to quiver without having abandoned the burden, the *thullaccaya* is incurred and the *dukkaṭa* of touching is pacified.
According to the reading of the *Pāḷi*, however, there is a pacification of each preceding offense: "for the motion (*ñatti*), a *dukkaṭa*."

Since it is stated in the Pāḷi, "By two formal proclamations (kammavācā), the grave offenses (thullaccaya) are pacified," it should be understood that this [pacification] occurs only through the proclamation itself.
Furthermore, following the method of this sutta as explained in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā,
one must reach the conclusion that the measure for the pacification of an offense applies here in this training rule (sikkhāpada) on taking what is not given as well.
48. “If he makes it quiver, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*. If he causes it to move from its place, there is an offense of *pārājika*. Thus it was said.
Regarding the *pārājika* for causing movement from its place and the *thullaccaya* which is a neighboring offense to that, these must be explained by way of making known the breaking of the place;
therefore, to demonstrate this now, he said “*mukhepāsan*” and so forth. Therein, “in the mouth” means in the opening of the jar-mouth.
“Having inserted the snare” means having cast the binding snare. “Upon a stump” refers to an iron stump or a *khadira* wood stump.
The connection is: “The variation in the positions of the bindings is to be understood according to the bindings.
49. Now he shows the variation in positions with the words beginning “two,” etc. By the phrase “upon one stump,” [he indicates] in two directions.
Alternatively, having dug stakes in three or four directions, the distinction of locations that arises through counting the bound stakes is characterized.
"Valayaṃ...pe...katāya vā dve ṭhānāni" (a ring... or when made, two locations) is the construction; "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction, and [the distinction] is characterized.
50. Having thus shown the distinction of locations, he now says in order to show the offenses that must be incurred by way of location:
“Of one who is pulling up,” and so forth. *Saṅkhalin* means a rope or cord.
A *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is so called because among the offenses that must be confessed in the presence of another person, it is both grave (*thulla*) and an offense (*accaya*).
For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*: “That which is called a *thullaccaya*...”
Listen to that as it truly is:
he who confesses it in the presence of another,
and he who accepts that confession.
“There is no transgression equal to this;
therefore it is called thus.

And here, although one should say *thūlaccaya* (grave offense), [the term *accaya* is used] in such passages as: “In the future life there is a happy destination, yet that has a bitter fruit,” and so forth.
Just as there is a doubling of the letter *la*, it should be understood that in a conjunct, the vowel *ū* becomes short.

After that, following the "breaking of the chain" (*saṅkhalikabheda*), "he moves from his place" means he displaces [the object] even by the measure of a hair-tip from its standing position. And here, in the Commentary on the Vinaya (Nāvaṭṭhakathā), it says:
"If he moves it upwards, downwards, or across, even by the measure of a hair-tip, it is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)."
According to the method already stated, there are six locations: the four directions described as "across," plus above and below.

When a cauldron is being moved toward one of these directions, if—by means of shaking—it does not exceed even a hair’s breadth of the space touched by the side facing the opposite direction while standing on the other side, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

It should be understood that when [the object] has been moved from its place, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense because of having caused it to be displaced from its location. It is with reference to this very point that it was said:
"If he causes it to be moved from its place, he is fallen. This same method applies even in the case of moving a treasure-jar that is devoid of movement. 51.
Having thus shown the method for first cutting the bond and subsequently taking hold of the jar, now [he explains] first...
Having removed the pot, he says "first," etc., in order to show the method for the subsequent removal of the bond. That method refers back to that same point:
"In the first lifting there is a *thullaccaya*; in the second lifting there is a *pārājika*. 52. *Valaya*:
the ring inserted at the base of the chain fastened to the pot. Rubbing it at the base...
The construction is: "it moves it hither and thither. "Rubbing" means causing contact. "Moves it hither and thither" means it causes it to shift from this side to that side.
Regarding "protects," there is a textual ellipsis here of "the bhikkhu's virtue"; what is meant is that he does not fall into a *pārājika* offense.
"Therein" means in that root. "Making it go to the sky" means without letting the root touch anything on any side.
"Making it as if it were in the sky. "Defeated" means that one has incurred defeat because of having committed an offense involving expulsion from one's status.
53. "Grown on the top of a water-jar" is the construction. The meaning is: because it was planted a long time ago, it stands entwining the water-jar with its roots.
"Cutting down a tree grown nearby" is the construction. And here, "wood grown there..."
In the verse beginning with "or," an offense is stated for one who cuts down trees, creepers, and so forth standing on the ground above a hidden treasure;

however, by this [present] verse, it should be understood that there is no fault of tautology, because it refers to taking hold of a living tree, a stump, or the like—the root of which remains entwined with the treasure after the ground has been dug and descended into. [The term used is] "atatthajaṃ."

By this, he states the absence of simultaneous application. By this very [statement], he illustrates that the wood, bamboo, and so forth mentioned in the preceding verse—which are connected to a treasure—are the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense as described, whereas if they are in close proximity [to the treasure], they are the basis for a *pācittiya* offense.
54. Now, having thus searched and seen the vessel containing the treasure, without moving it from its place of location, [one may take] what is inside.
To show the legal determination regarding one who takes even a small amount of merchandise, he said: "That which has gone inside the jar," and so forth.
Therein, "he moves it" means he moves it by way of piling it up or otherwise, in order to place it in his own vessel once it has been put inside the cask.
Or, "he shifts it" means he shifts it as if removing those things standing above in order to take what is standing below. Alternatively, "shifting it" means...

"Making twofold the words of the commentary" means that one makes a heap here and there in order to place them within one's own vessel, as the meaning stated in the *gaṇṭhipada* (knot-word) should be understood. "Right there" means right inside the pot.
"Carrying away" means taking away. "Cuts a handful" means, having placed it into one's own vessel, to take hold of it.
Being unable to reach inside the jar with his hand, he delimits the goods within the jar with his fist so that they remain unbundled;
taking what is in the jar with his fist, he delimits it so that what is in the jar and what is in the fist are not mixed,
[taking] either what is worth one *pāda* or more than one *pāda*.
Or it is said that he takes [it]. The construction is: "or he cuts it after having placed it in his own vessel.
The meaning is that he demarcates it so that, having been placed in his own vessel, it is not mixed with what is in the jar;
provided that the goods, having been placed in his own vessel and being unmixed with what is in the jar, amount to five māsakas or more than five māsakas.
"Or it is worth [a certain amount]" means it is stated that it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
"Or a necklace" (*hāraṃ vā*) means a pearl necklace. "Or an anklet" (*pāmaṅgaṃ vā*) means a string of anklets made of gold or silver.

"Threaded on a string" (*suttāruḷhaṃ*) means that which is mounted upon a string is "threaded on a string"; thus, both the string and what is threaded on the string are referred to as "threaded on a string."
The *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member of a group with similar parts) should be understood here.

Based on the commentary’s statement, “This is a designation for both that which is strung on a thread and that which consists of thread,” one should include various garlands made by stringing together gold, silver, coral, and other gems without the first type of string, as well as articles made of thread. “Standing in a jar” means:
This is the remainder of the recitation. "Causes to tremble" means to move [the object] with a mind of theft, out of a desire to seize it.

"According to the basis" means that there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) corresponding to the transgression; this is the intended meaning. "Causes to move from its place" means to cause it to pass even by the breadth of a hair from the position where it stood.
"Fallen" means one who has fallen away from the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; this is the sense.

In the case of a pot that is not yet full, when one moves even a hair’s breadth of goods from here and there within it to another spot inside the same pot, or makes them occupy space right there within it,
this is similar to the cases of "making it enter one's own vessel" or "cutting off a handful," and thus constitutes an offense under that rule.
"Is she one who has committed a *pārājika* offense when she values [the object] by the quarter?"—this is the definitive conclusion in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

If, having placed a corner on the bottom of the vessel, she gradually fills the entire interior of the vessel with that very [object] and places a single corner at the rim, then for a necklace or similar item thus placed, the entire vessel constitutes the "place"; therefore, for one who lifts it straight up after grasping a corner...
Furthermore, for one who makes even a hair’s breadth of the edge of the bowl enter the space beyond the surface of the bowl;

or for one who, having rubbed it against the rim and pulled it back, exhausts the entire interior of the bowl and then, with the tip placed on the rim, allows the other tip to pass even a hair’s breadth beyond the point of contact;
or for one who covers half the interior of the bowl with cloth or similar materials—these are [offenses].
It is stated that for one who, having filled [a vessel] with something, places it upon another object such as a necklace or a thread, the "place" (ṭhāna) is precisely that location where it remains;
therefore, even for one who moves it away by a mere hair's breadth from there, a *pārājika* offense occurs.
57. Regarding "ghee and so forth": this refers to any liquid substance such as ghee contained within a vessel. "Pādapūraṇa" (filling the foot/verse-quarter) refers to the verse-quarter (*pāda*).

“Fills” (*pūreti*) means filling out the line; the meaning is "worth a penny for the verse. The connection is: "while drinking, there is defeat" (*pivato parājaya*). If one asks "When?"—the construction is:
"at the mere act of drinking with a single effort, [there is] filling out the line. There is an elliptical supplement to the text: "without [it] having reached the mouth.
In that context, "with a single effort" means by the act of drinking after drawing it in as a continuous whole, without laying down the burden (i.e., without pausing).
Regarding the phrase “without [the liquid] being in the mouth”: if the foot [of the vessel] is filled by that which has gone into the throat, it is said that it has entered within the throat.
If it is filled by that which has gone into the mouth, it is said that the mouth-located [liquid] is separated from the vessel-located [liquid] while the lips are closed.

For one who drinks by drawing [the liquid] up with a bamboo tube or a reed, it is filled by that which has gone into the tube; the tube-located [liquid] is [separated] from the vessel-located [liquid].
"Having separated [the grain] at the tip of the stalk with a finger covered [by the hand]"—this is what is meant.

The intention is that this should be understood according to the method explained in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), following the principle stated as: "he makes it enter his own vessel, or he cuts a handful."
Regarding the statement, “There is defeat (pārājika) upon merely drinking with a single act of application,” this should be understood as follows:

if the value of the ghee or other substances is such that they alone constitute the full measure, then there is defeat even when the connection is severed by a single instance—whether it be a single mouthful of ghee or the like, or when the connection is severed by the substance being poured from its vessel into one’s own vessel after the pot has been tilted;
likewise, there is defeat even when the connection is severed once the substance has entered the pot.

58. Regarding the statement, “There is no defeat for one who drinks again and again after having laid down the burden,” it is stated by implication that there is defeat for one who drinks again and again without having laid down the burden.

It should be understood that defeat occurs for one who, without laying down the burden, takes [the liquor] repeatedly with the mouth or with bags and the like, drinking even as much as is required merely to fill the feet.
59–60. “If he throws it with a thieving mind” is the connection. “Any kind of goods” refers to goods such as oil-vessels, fine linen garments, pieces of leather, and so forth.
“In the oil-pot belonging to another” is understood; that is the deposited goods. “Certainly” means unconditionally.
“It is destroyed at that very moment” is the connection. “At that very moment” (tāvade) means at that precise instant. In what [circumstance]?
He says, "As soon as it is released from the hand," meaning that because of the prior application [of effort], it occurs even before the oil has reached the state of being drunk;
this is the intended sense. "Is destroyed" means it reaches the destruction of virtue (*sīlavināsa*). "Having drawn out" means having expelled. "Drips" means causes to flow.
They also read "sāḷeti," which has the same meaning. The root is *sāḷa* in the sense of hearing. "In the same way" refers to one who has a mind of theft (*theyyacitta*).
"‘It will perish’—he pulls it away; for one who acts thus with a thieving mind, it is said that he incurs a *pārājika* offense.

(61) “*Taṃ*” refers to that article of property, such as clothing, which was first placed in an empty vessel with a thieving mind—namely, a foot-measure of oil for drinking, knowing it to be oil intended for pouring.
By the restrictive phrase “*uddharanto vā*,” [it is implied that the offense occurs at the moment of lifting].
“The defeat [is incurred] upon merely drinking” thus rejects the opinion of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. “Dhaṃsito” means “overthrown from the wish-fulfilling tree of the Dispensation”;

the intention is that he has fallen into a *pārājika* offense. The word “thus” (*tathā*) should be brought forward and connected with the phrase “with a thieving mind” for the purpose of drawing it in.
By this, [it refers to] placing cloth or the like in an empty vessel for the sake of concealment by one with a pure mind.
It is demonstrated that there is no fault for one who, having set it down, does not look at it again, but later removes it with a pure mind after it has been soaked in oil. 62.
"Right there" means in the very place where it stood. "Breaking [it]" refers to a monk who, like one burning grass, does not move it from its position.
For one who breaks [a vessel] by striking it with a stone or some other object, without the intention of causing it to fall from its place;
and they also say, "for one who breaks it through the power of spells or medicinal herbs. "Of one who discards" means:
even for one who does not wish to discard it, the meaning is that he pours sand or water into full jars of oil and so forth out of negligence while emptying them. "A watercourse toward a jar..."

They say: "Having done so, he causes it to sink. Even though there is an intention to displace it from its place, because of the absence of a thieving mind (*theyyacitta*), there is no offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*);
rather, the determination is that it is an offense requiring the payment of the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). "Causing it to burn" means causing it to burn by throwing firewood [upon it].
"Making it unfit for use" means making it unfit for use by pouring excrement, urine, and so forth upon it.

“Dukkaṭa”: this is stated because, regarding these four instances beginning with breaking [the boundary], only a *dukkaṭa* offense is mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*). This concludes the commentary on the section concerning what is situated on the ground. 63.
Now, in order to show the determination regarding what is situated on dry land (*thalaṭṭha*), he says “placed,” and so forth. Therein, “having spread out” means:
"Having spread out. Here, the word *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned;

by this, it includes that which was not explicitly stated—that the determination regarding grain and so forth heaped up on dry land can be understood according to the determination already stated for a *nimikumbhi* (a small jar). "Spreading out and so forth" means spreading out covers and so forth.
"Of one who is removing after having wrapped [it]" refers to the method of gathering together a palm-leaf mat (*kilañja*).

For one who rolls up, gathers together, and picks up [the robe]. "When released from the place" means: when, having gradually gathered it together, even a hair's breadth has been released from the place where it was standing.
"Ruination" means: fallen away from the Dispensation (sāsana). 64.
Having thus shown the determination regarding the gathering and taking up of cloth and so forth that were spread out and placed there, [he now speaks] concerning the horizontal direction...
To show the legal determination regarding pulling [the robe], he said: “By the near edge,” and so forth. The particle *pi* (also) and *vā* (or) serve to include another mode of action.

Even when pulling straight [toward oneself], that is, when one pulls straight toward one of the four directions a cloth or similar object that has been spread out and placed there, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
When? Even here, it is when the space touched by the near edge has been passed beyond from the far edge.

The construction is: “an offense involving defeat” (*pārājika*). Taking the space touched by one’s own edge, the place where one stands after having pulled [something] toward oneself, delimited by the direction in which one is situated, is [the measurement].
“From the opposite edge” means by means of the opposite edge; the suffix *-to* is used in the sense of the instrumental case.

What is called “dry land” (*thala*) includes concealed and unconcealed ground, palaces, mountain plateaus, and so forth; grain and other goods situated thereon are said to be “situated on dry land. In all these cases, the detailed analysis should be understood according to the method already stated.
Commentary on the Land Portion (Thalaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā). 65–6.
Regarding "delimitations" (pariccheda), these refer to spatial delimitations. The rest is easily understood. 67–8.
"Gone into the air" (khegata) means having gone into space. "His" (assa) refers to the peacock. "It" (taṃ) refers to the peacock.

69. "Places" (*ṭhāna*) refers to the six kinds of places as previously defined. "Of that" (*tassa*) is to be construed with "he makes the peacock tremble. Alternatively, "of that" (*tassa*) refers to the monk, for whom a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) has been declared. 70.
Without catching it with his hand, by means of such methods as throwing a clod of earth, he frightens the peacock and causes it to move from its standing place.
"Its own places" (*attano ṭhānā*) refers to the sixfold places belonging to the peacock. "His own place" (*sayaṃ ṭhānā*) refers to the monk’s own place.
What is meant is "the state of being a recluse" (*samaṇabhāva*).
Now, in order to clarify the "dislodging from one's position" (*ṭhānācāvana*) indicated by the phrase "if he should dislodge me from my place," [the author] says "the touched space," and so forth.
"He hides in the hand" means he sits upon the palm of the outstretched hand.
75. "Having flown up" means having leaped into the air. 76.
"Clinging to the limbs" means clinging to the parts of the body such as the shoulders and so forth. "On the foot" refers to his own first raised foot; [then] on the second foot. 77.
"Of the two feet" means of the two feet. "Of the mass" refers to the mass of the body as it touches the ground.
78. "Then, from the earth" means from a portion of earth established by three parts; it is not [an offense] from the first part, because there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) there;

nor from the second part, because there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) there; but it is stated that from the third part, even if one causes it to move even as much as a hair’s breadth from its place, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
To this extent:
"If one removes a peacock standing in a cage together with the cage, it is a *pārājika*.

But if the foot [of the bird] is not worth [the full amount], then in all cases it must be determined according to the value. If, with a thieving mind, [one takes] a peacock wandering within the enclosure on foot..."

If, while carrying it out from the interior, he passes beyond the boundary of the door, it is a *pārājika*. For the enclosure (*vaja*) is like the interior space for a beast of burden standing within that enclosure;

thus, his position [within the enclosure] is analogous to the interior space. However, if he takes hold of it with his hand and makes it enter the space even while still within the interior space, it is likewise a *pārājika*.
Even if it is moving within the village, if he causes it to pass beyond the boundary of the village, it is a *pārājika*.

But if he himself goes out and, while [the bird] is wandering in the vicinity of a village or the vicinity of a dwelling, frightens it with a stick or a clod of earth with a thieving intent and sends it toward the forest;
or if the peacock flies up and perches on a roof or the top of a covering within the village or within the dwelling—[in these cases], he protects [the bird].
However, if it flies up or goes toward the forest, [he does not protect it].

Or, even if there is no intention such as, “I will seize it after leading it into the forest,” if the bird has risen even a hair’s breadth from the ground, or at the moment of the second step [of the hunter], it is a *pārājika* offense.
Why? Because for one leaving a village, the very place where it was standing is considered its "place.

Thus, the determination found in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) should be understood as the defining characteristic. This same determination should be applied to birds belonging to others, such as the *kapiñjara* and so forth.
79. He causes [the object] to fall into the bowl held in the hand of a bhikkhu standing at the gate for alms.

Of him who has the intent to steal. 80. "Without picking up" means: without having picked up with the hand the gold or other [valuables] fallen into the bowl; because it is understood that a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) occurs at the moment of the first step, it is not explicitly stated.

81. "In the hand" means on the palm of the hand. "On the cloth" means on the robe. "On the head" means on the crown of the head. Or, the word *vā* is used according to the requirements of the meter (*gāthā-chanda*).
The shortening of the vowel *ā* [to *a*]. "Falling" means having fallen. "That" refers to that piece of gold or the like being cut.
If one seizes with the hand that which is moving through the air or falling, the place where it remains while held in the hand is indeed the "place";
for one who moves it even by the breadth of a hair from there, there is a *pārājika* offense. Likewise, for one who, having thus seized it, departs with the intention to steal...
Regarding the second removal of the foot: this same principle applies even when [the robe] has fallen onto items such as a cloth.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning space. 82.
Regarding "on beds, chairs, and so forth": here, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), items similar to beds and chairs that are situated in the air, such as canopies and the like, are included.
He embraces. "Tangible" (*āmāsam*) refers to things such as clothing that may be touched with the hand or the body.
"Intangible" (*anāmāsam*) refers to things such as gold that are not to be touched in that way. "Of one who touches" means of one who grasps with the hands or other limbs.

By the term "dukkaṭa," it is implied that there is a *thullaccaya* for causing movement and a *pārājika* for moving [the object] from its place, according to the method explained below regarding items situated on dry land.

It is indicated that this can be understood by analogy. As for the delimitation of location (*ṭhānapariccheda*), it is defined by the four legs of a bed and so forth when one is lifting [the object] up;

or, for one who takes hold of it exactly where it stands—such as a stiff cloth smeared with oil that touches the four leg-heads of a bed but does not touch its middle—it is defined by the four leg-heads of that cloth; or, in the case of pillars...
It should be understood by way of the [measuring] lines for one who stands having touched [the ground].
83. "In the bamboo" (*vaṃse*) means in the robe-bamboo; by this, the tree-sticks, rods, cords, and so forth, placed there for the purpose of laying out the robes, are indicated.
"From within" (*orato*) means from the direction facing where one is standing oneself. "The length" (*bhogaṃ*) refers to the robe once it has been gathered together.
The middle portion is established by folding [the robe]. "The edge" means that which has been made into one side after folding, or the edge of both [layers].
"Having placed it on the far side" means having placed it beyond the bamboo [frame].

84. "The space touched by the robe" means the place touched by the robe. "Of that" refers to the robe placed in such a manner. The connection is: "That entire bamboo frame does not constitute the location. It is considered [to be] finished.
85–6. “Or by the near side” (*orimantena*) is connected with “having touched that space.

Having taken hold of the robe-material with a thieving mind and pulling it toward oneself, when one has touched the robe on the robe-pole in the direction where one is standing, and one causes the other side—the limit of the place where it stands—to be passed by the [other] side (*itarena*), that is the point of severance (*cuti*).
By the other side (*itarena*), meaning by the far side (*pārimantena*), [this refers to] the robe in the direction of the wall.

The construction is as follows: for one who causes that space touched by the other [robe]—which extends to the limit of the space touched [by the robe]—to pass beyond its near limit, there is a "falling away" (*cuti*).
"By the other" means by the far limit, having touched the robe-pole on the wall-side with the edge of the robe placed there.
"Touched" refers to the space occupied by the robe-pole. "By the near limit" means by the portion of the robe placed after touching the robe-pole in the direction where one is standing oneself.
"Atikkāmayato" means for one who passes beyond even by the measure of a hair’s tip.
Having thus shown the possible alternative regarding the drawing out along the long edge, he now says "with the right side," etc., to show the method of passing beyond along the horizontal edge.
"Punāti" means "or else. [The area] touched by the right side [is touched] by the left side.
The construction is: "for one who causes [the robe] to pass beyond, there is death (defeat). The meaning is:

for one standing facing the robe in order to take it away, if he causes the area where the robe is situated—which was touched by the edge of the robe on his own right side—to be passed beyond by means of the edge on the left side, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
Or, the construction is: "there is death (defeat) for one who causes the place touched by the left edge to be passed beyond by the other. By the left edge...
“The place touched” means the area where the robe is situated, touched by the edge of the robe on the left side of one standing facing the robe.
The meaning is that for one who passes beyond it with the edge of the robe on the other side—the right side—there is death (the end of life) as a *pārājika* offense.
87. “From the bamboo” means from the area of the bamboo pole upon which the robe stands after being touched by the robe. In some places, it is said to be “even the breadth of a hair-tip.”

They write [the word] in the manuscript as *ukkhitto*; that should not be accepted. Because it stands in grammatical apposition with the locative singular *ukkhitte*, its being in the nominative singular is not appropriate.
The reading *kesaggammatte ukkhitte* is seen in some places, and that is authoritative.
88. The construction is: "while releasing [it], he incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. Whether he causes it to touch the robe-pole or does not cause it to touch it...
The meaning is that one who, with a thieving mind, desires to take a robe placed there after being tied with a rope, incurs a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) while loosening the bond.
"When released" means as soon as it is released. The intention is that he becomes one defeated (*pārājika*) because of having moved from his place.
89. Regarding "having wrapped": here, by implication, the word "bamboo pole" (*vaṃsa*) is understood. Having wrapped the bamboo pole for the robes...
The connection is as follows: for a monk who unfastens a robe that was placed right there, this same method applies.
"Unfastening" means undoing it. "This same method applies" refers by extension to the stated method: "For one unfastening it, there is a *thullaccaya*;
once unfastened, it is a *pārājika* offense. The connection is also: "for one cutting a bangle, this same method applies. [Regarding] "for a monk..."
And it should be connected by bringing in the phrase, "a robe placed on a bamboo pole.

Having been placed upon the robe-stand, once the circle of the robe has been cut so that it falls from its position, for the monk who cuts it in that manner, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for the act of cutting, and a *pārājika* (defeat) when it is severed;
this is the meaning. This same method applies to one who is unfastening it as well; here too, the term "circle" (*valaya*) refers to the same thing.

These words, beginning with "of a bhikkhu," should be construed together with this [phrase]. Regarding a robe placed in the robe-storage (cīvaravaṃsa), even for one who is releasing a fastening-ring, the *thullaccaya* and *pārājika* offenses are exactly as previously stated.
Here, by the first word "api" (also/even), the two aforementioned modes are combined; by the other word "api," there is a combination of what was not explicitly mentioned.
Because there is no specific difference in meaning, it includes the unstated sense; by this, it encompasses the two modes: "either he makes it go into the air, or he takes it out.

Thus, even for one who—like a chain or a bracelet placed as a treasure at the foot of a tree—does not let the robe-bracelet touch any part of the robe-rod, but makes it go into the air, [the offense occurs] at the tip of the robe-rod.
It includes these very cases, stating that for one who carries [the robe] outside, the *thullaccaya* and *pārājika* offenses are to be understood in the same manner as previously described:
“Whether one cuts the cord, or releases it, or makes the cord hang in the air, or carries it out”—
without performing even one of these four alternatives, having rubbed the robe-cord against the robe-stand, from here...

And when one moves the circle of the robe, the entire robe-pole remains in its place; thus, it should be understood that "there is no removal from its place" is shown by way of the opposite of what was stated [previously]. 90.
Regarding the phrase "for when it has been placed," one should supply the particle *hi* (for/indeed) which indicates a well-known fact, and connect it as "just as in the case of the robe."
Having brought in the particle *tu* which indicates a specific meaning, it should be construed as "of that which has been placed.

Alternatively, because particles have multiple meanings, the word *hi* may be construed in its original position to indicate a specific meaning, and the word *tu* to indicate well-known fact (*pasiddhi*).
The construction is: "The decision (*vinicchaya*) is to be understood. [This refers to] a robe placed on a robe-stand after having been spread out either lengthwise or crosswise.
As for the detailed exposition (*vinicchaya*), it has been stated by summarizing it as the exposition on robes established in the *Cīvaravaṃsa*.
The meaning is that it should be understood according to the method stated in the three verses beginning with: "If [the robe] is on this side... pe ... it would be a *pārājika* offense.
(91) "With a carrying-sling" (*sikkāya*) means in a hanging support. "Whatever goods" (*yaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ*) is the connection. "Having placed inside" (*pakkhipitvā*) means having set it down.

"Laggitaṃ hoti" means it is hanging down. Regarding the alternative reading, "being taken from the sling or having fallen," the displacement from its place should be understood by way of its contact with the sling.
In the second alternative, if there were a point of contact between the sling and the wall-side of the binding-place, the displacement from its place should be understood by way of that [contact].
92–3. Regarding the phrase "a spear, etc.," by the word "etc.," long objects such as a *bhindivāla* (a type of javelin) are to be understood.
Deer horns or spikes fixed in a wall in a row like wooden pegs or posts are called *nāgadanta* (elephant-tusk hooks).
"At the tip" means at the point of the spear-blade; "at the thick part" means at the base of the spear-head. "Dragging along" means dragging it straight forward.

"Phuṭṭhokāsaṃ" (the touched space) refers to the place touched by each individual peg; the connection is that for one who passes beyond [that space], there may be defeat by even the measure of a hair-tip (*kesaggamatta*).
The meaning is that for one who leaves behind the places where [the pegs] were set and passes beyond even the measure of a hair-tip, it is a *pārājika*.
It should be understood that "defeat" occurs by means of the hair-tip as the intervening cause (*hetu*); [this applies to] even the measure of a hair-tip.
The meaning is that it constitutes a *pārājika* offense because it is the cause of taking away.

Having thus shown the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) regarding drawing [the organ] out lengthwise and lifting it up, he said, "Facing toward a wall," etc., in order to show the legal determination regarding drawing it across and leading it away. He draws it... himself.
It draws [the object] toward the place where it stands. "The space touched by the near side" (*orimantaphuṭṭhokāsaṃ*) means the space touched by the near side;

the meaning is: the space touched by the staff of the spear in one's own direction. Here, although the genitive case would have been expected due to its connection with the action of reaching, the accusative case is used.
This is because the use of the accusative case is seen in the Māgadhī dialect when employed with verbal roots that take an object.
Some say that the accusative case ending occurs only when [the word] expresses the object; this is consistent with the grammatical rules of Kaccāyana. As for the term *itarantaccaya*:

"a transgression (*accaya*) committed by means of the other limit (*itaranta*)"—this is a compound with the middle term elided (*majjhepadalopa*); the meaning is "committed in a transgression to be performed by means of the further limit (*pārimanta*).
The construction is "fallen away by means of the hair-tip" (*kesaggena cuto*), and the meaning is exactly as previously stated.
“Pushing from the other side” means pushing after having placed it on the other side; the meaning is, pressing it toward the surface of the wall.

“In the same way” refers to pulling [the hair] back with the words “fallen by the tip of the hair. And the application of this method is that it applies even when a spear or similar object is placed [therein].
The meaning is that this very same method of determination must be stated by means of the passage beginning with “by the tip of the hair.”

96. When that bhikkhu shakes the fruit of a palmyra tree, the offense becomes a *pārājika* at the moment the fruit is released from its stalk—that fruit by which the value of five māsakas is reached. This is the construction [of the rule]. 97.
"He cuts the cluster of the palmyra" means he cuts the stalk-base (*kaṇṇikā*) of the palmyra fruit.

Regarding the phrase "by the mere cutting of that by which the value is reached, there would be a *pārājika* for him," the method explained below should also be applied here. [This refers to] the palmyra cluster (*tālapiṇḍi*).
If it has gone into the air, the root of the stalk itself is the location.
If it is standing supported by a leaf-stalk or a leaf, then including the roots of the stalk along with the locations where it stands, one should understand the breaking of the location;

through the displacement from that location, it should be regarded as a *pārājika* offense. This is the same method: "When the object is fulfilled, once it is released from its bond, there is a *pārājika* offense for him."
"Could it be so?"—the method is exactly as stated above. In all these instances, prior to the actual transgression of a *pārājika*, there is a *thullaccaya* for the immediate preliminary application;

for the simultaneous application, there is a *dukkaṭa* in the place where a *pācittiya* would otherwise apply; and for the preliminary application even before that, there is both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa* in the place where a *pācittiya* would apply.
This is because the subsequent applications, such as seeking a companion for the journey and so forth, are preceded by the act of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
And the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) must be understood by those who are not confused.

This concludes the commentary on the section concerning "standing in the air" (vehāsaṭṭha). 98. The connection is: "one goes to a place where there is water. [The phrase] "in shallow water" refers to going step by step.

The construction is: "For one who is walking, for every step taken, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to prior application. However, regarding "deep [water]," the phrase "for one walking by foot-steps, there is an offense of wrong-doing" is extended by analogy (*atidiśati*) as previously stated. Regarding "walking," this means crossing;

for one crossing without moving the hand, it is according to the count of foot-steps, and for one making effort with the hand, the term "by foot-step" is made a figurative designation (*upalakkhaṇa*).
The offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are to be understood by counting each hand-movement and each foot-step. Therefore it is said in the Commentary:
"For one who exerts effort with hands or feet in deep [water], there is a wrong-doing for every exertion, according to the number of hand-movements or foot-steps."
"Submerging and so forth": here, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), submerging is included. Here too, because the word "likewise" (tathā) is carried over, the meaning should be understood as follows:
for every instance of the action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

This means that even when diving in and out of water to grasp a jar placed [there], whether by hand alone, by foot alone, or by both hand and foot, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, it was said in the Commentary:
“The same principle applies to diving and surfacing for the purpose of seizing a pot.

From the statement in this verse, “there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one going to a place where treasure is kept,” it is understood through the method of contrast (vyatireka) that there is no offense for one who, while going there, flees out of fear upon seeing a water-snake or a fierce fish, because his going was not for that specific purpose. Herein...

In all applications beginning with the second search, where there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), one should understand that it is an offense of expiation together with an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);

in the remaining applications, it is a pure offense of wrong-doing; in the case of simultaneous application, [there is] an offense of wrong-doing for touching what is not permitted to touch, an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya) for causing it to move, and an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for moving it from its place—just as was stated regarding the treasure-pot. Thus it can be understood.
It should be understood that [the word] "not stated" is used. In that regard, the division of positions is fivefold;
here, because it is possible to press down and let it settle, it becomes sixfold when including the downward direction—this is the distinction between them.

99. Regarding the phrase "among the flowers of the Jātaka": this refers to the *uppala* (blue lotus) and other flowers growing in that water; the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

The phrase "with which flower" is to be determined [by context]. Regarding the word "cutting," one should not take the meaning according to the present tense (*vattamānakāla*), but rather take the meaning according to the past tense (*bhūta*) as "one who has cut.

When this is so understood, until the cessation of the final application, because it entails a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), and because the statement of a *pārājika* offense would contradict the basis (*vatthu*) for this very last flower—[therefore, the offense is established].

In order to show that there is no *pārājika* offense even when only the bark on the side of the flowering stalk is removed at the time of blossoming—and because the method to be stated immediately following the phrase "one stalk...
protects" would otherwise be contradictory—it was written here to demonstrate this specific legal analysis:
"When the substance [of the flower] is fulfilled in a particular flower, at the mere cutting of that [stalk], there is a *pārājika*."

Because it contradicts the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and because one must not take the present tense but rather the past tense, it should be understood that [the term] is stated as being in the past by using the designation "present" for what is near the present—just as in the answer to the question "When did Devadatta come? which is "Here I am coming; do not strike me as I am coming."

100. Regarding the phrase “of the *uppalajāti* [lotus]”: since this is stated by way of contrast with the phrase “of the *padumajāti* [lotus],” it should be understood that the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*—namely, “but when the stalk of those belonging to the *padumajāti* is cut, even though the internal fiber (*sutta*) is not cut, it protects [the flower]”—is included here.
Or, in the phrase “on one side of the single stalk,” although it should have been said “on one side of the stalk,” it was stated thus for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.
It should be understood that this has been stated. "From there" means from the stalk.
Since the determination regarding flowers tied in bundles will be explained later, the phrase "having been cut and set aside" should be taken as referring to flowers that are not tied in bundles.
"In the manner previously stated" means according to the determination stated regarding flowers grown in that very place. "By which..."

The distinction here in the application [of the rule] is that it is not stated, "It is fulfilled by the flower when it has been cut," but rather, "It is a *pārājika* offense as soon as it has been taken.
102. "Bhārabaddhāni" (bound for carrying) is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*majjhapadalopī-samāsa*), meaning "those bound together to form a load.

"Flowers" refers to blue lotuses and other such blossoms worth one-quarter of a *paṇa*. "In six ways" means: because they can be made to sink in water, there are four directions including the downward direction;...

"Directions" (*disā*) refers to these six directions; the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "In some way or other" (*kenaci ākārena*) indicates that which is to be selected.

Because it is the most effective instrument for causing displacement from one's position, the instrumental case is used where the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) applies. "He perishes" (*nassati*):

by causing flowers worth a quarter of a *pāda* to be displaced from their place, he incurs a *pārājika* offense and thus perishes—that is, he is deprived of the foundation for all mundane and supramundane qualities.
The meaning is that by destroying the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, one dies through the death of one's own excellence.
103. "A cluster of flowers" refers to a bouquet of blue lotuses and other flowers worth a quarter of a coin (*pāda*). "Having stirred the water" means having stirred it so that waves arise.
"The places where the flowers stand" refers to the locations where the flowers are situated. "He displaces" means [he displaces] the cluster.
He carries it away even by a hair’s breadth. In some manuscripts, the reading “he moves the flower from its place” (*pupphaṃ ṭhānā cāveti*) is seen;
however, because only the cluster of flowers is being grasped, the former [reading] alone should be accepted.
104. The construction is joined with the elided portion of the text: “I shall take what has gone there. He imagines: “What has gone there...”
“I shall take it,” thinking thus, he demarcates the spot and speculates.
“He guards” means that even if there is a displacement from that spot, that mental construct protects the monk from an offense involving defeat (pārājika). “The place where it has gone”:
the analysis is “that place which has been reached and arrived at by the cluster of flowers. By the word “removing,” one should connect it with “the cluster of flowers.”
“*Katāṭṭhānā*” is also a reading; the connection is: “removing [the flowers] from the places where they were placed.

Having stirred the water and raised waves, he removes the cluster of flowers that has reached the place demarcated on the surface of the water by the impact of the waves, from the spot where it stood, without moving it even as much as a hair’s breadth—that is the meaning.
This word “*ṭhānā*,” namely, [is used in the sense of] “*bhaṭṭho*” (fallen from).

This is to be connected [with the following]. "He is called *bhaṭṭho*" means that he is said to have "fallen" from the place where the sprouts of all the jewels of virtue—comprising the morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha—are produced by him having undertaken and guarded them.
Regarding the phrase "from the burning, having risen up," the word "of the flower" is understood here by implication; [it refers to] from the surface of the burning [flower].
The entire body of water is the location for the flower that has risen up;
having extended the flower-stalk from the surface of the mud up to the surface of the water, it stands covering all the water—this is what is meant by "the location.
"Having pulled up" means having dragged the tip of the flower and pressed it upward. "From there" means from that mass of water which constitutes the location of the flower. "Straight" means upright.
"Having done so. "Uddharato" means while pulling it out.
"Nāḷante" means at the tip of the root of the stalk from which the flower has been pulled out. "Jalato" means from the surface of the water. The remaining portion of the text should be construed as:

"muttamatte kesaggamattaṃ dūraṃ katvā," meaning "having moved [the stalk] a distance of even a hair's breadth from the water. This applies to both the first and third quarters [of the verse]: "jalato."

It should be understood that although the statement is repeated twice, there is no fault of tautology (*punarutta-dosa*), because it is spoken by way of the *addha-yamaka* (half-parallelism) ornament despite the lack of difference in meaning.
Furthermore, it should be connected as "in the mere release" and "in the non-release," or it should be understood as being stated in both places due to the distinction between the two meanings.
The connection is with the phrase "in that [place] at the end of the tube."
107. Regarding that which has been uprooted after being named: even for that which is uprooted together with its stalk, this same analysis applies.
Here, however, the "shaking from its place" (*ṭhānācāvana*) should be understood as the act of moving all flowers, leaves, and stalks from their original location, starting from the root.
Thus, for one who uproots flowers and so forth, there is an offense for the disturbance of the habitat of living beings (*bhūtagāma-vikopana*). In this context...
It should be understood that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the concurrent application [of the factors].

(108–9) Because of the mention of implements for catching fish, such as hooks and the like, and because the determination regarding dead and live fish in water will be explained later, the word "fish" (macche) here refers to live fish.
Alternatively, it may be taken in the sense of an elliptical inclusion (samuccaya) by way of illustration.
Or, by the word "or" (vā), it should be understood that fishing hooks and other such implements for catching fish are also included.

"Vatthu" means the foot. "In that [foot]" refers to the fish. "Uddhaṭo" means merely lifted up; thus, "in that [fish]" refers to one who has been merely lifted up from the water, having been removed even by as much as a hair's breadth from the water—this is what is meant.
110. Why was it stated, taking the entire body of water as the "place" rather than restricting the "place" to where the fish actually reside—as one might do with flowers?
To this he says: "For it is the place of those born in the water," and so forth. Those "born in the water" (*salilajā*) are, by the context of the work, understood to be fish alone.
Words acquire specific meanings through factors such as the meaning of the context, other words in proximity, and so on.
"They say. *Hi* is used in the sense of what is well-known. *Kevalaṃ* is used as a restriction; it means "only water.
By this, external water is excluded. Since the entire place is nothing but water, therefore, by releasing water from its watery state, one becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
This construction should be understood as a relationship between cause and that which possesses the cause (*hetu-hetumantabhāva*). One defeats (*parājeti*) that which has been reached (*āpannaṃ*).
One who has committed a *pārājika* offense; because this [offense] belongs to him, he is called a *pārājika*, that is, a person.
111. *Nīra* means water. That which is born in water—*vārija*—is understood here, by the context, to be a fish.
By this very same principle, it should be understood that a fish leaping into the air is implied, as are turtles and other such creatures that have emerged onto dry land for the sake of feeding.
The determination regarding their seizure should be understood according to the method explained in the *Ākāsaṭṭha* and *Thalaṭṭha* discourses.

"One should designate [the offense] by the value of the goods" means that one should declare the offenses of *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, or *pārājika* in accordance with the monetary value of the goods constituting the object of the offense. 112. "In a pond" (*taḷāke*) means in a lake;
by this term, reservoirs such as tanks (*vāpi*), lotus ponds (*pokkharaṇī*), and pools (*sobbha*) are included. "In a river" (*nadiyā*)...
"By the term *ninnagā* (river), ravines and the like are included. *Ninneti* means in a pit. Regarding the phrase "that which is called fish-poison":

here the word *nāma* (called) is used in the sense of a designation (*saññā*). One should understand this as referring to the *madanaphala* fruit and so forth, which bear the name "fish-poison. *Gate* means when the fisherman who threw the poison has departed. 114.
*Sāmikesu* means when the owners of the fish, having applied the poison, have departed. *Āharantesu* means when they are causing [the fish] to be brought back. *Bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ* means..."
The analysis of the compound is "the goods (*bhaṇḍa*) and that which is to be given. The meaning is that either the article taken by oneself or goods of equivalent value must be returned.
115. *Macche* means dead fish. *Sese* means other than dead fish. 116.
"When dead [fish] have been taken"—this is understood from the context; furthermore, this locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). There is no offense.
"They say" means they say there is no offense for the transgression of taking what is not given; however, for the offense of killing, it remains a *pācittiya*.
And this legal analysis is to be understood in the case of unguarded and unprotected reservoirs and the like that have no owner.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of water.
117. Here, "boat" should be understood as anything fit for crossing water—even a single vessel, or even a raft made of a single load of dye, bamboo, or reeds—based on the statement:
"A boat is that by which one crosses. "Goods belonging to a boat" refers to any property whatsoever, whether bound to a sense-faculty (animate) or not bound to a sense-faculty (inanimate).
By the phrase "having carried it away, I will take it," the meaning of "with a thieving mind" is established.
He makes it known. "At every step" refers to one who goes for the purpose of a second search and so forth, while lifting up the foot.

"Faults" means offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). These were spoken by the Blessed One in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*) thus: "If, with a thieving mind, thinking ‘I will steal goods not left behind,’ he either searches for a second [person] or goes, there is an offense of wrong-doing. By this, the wrong-doings of preliminary effort and simultaneous effort are indicated.
It should be understood that the *thullaccaya* for causing to tremble and the *pārājika* for moving from one's place are shown by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*). 118.
Regarding "in a violent current" (*caṇḍasote*): this refers to a flow of water moving with great force.
By the term "violent current," the fact that [the place] does not remain stable by its own nature in the absence of a binding is indicated; thus, it defines the "place" as being "only the binding."
It should be understood that the reason is shown. Because it was moored in a violent current, it is said that "binding" alone is considered the single factor;
thus, "therein" means in that binding. "The wise" refers to those who uphold the Vinaya.
By the phrase, "The mooring of the boat remains firm in still water," the delimitation of the sixfold factors is [established].
This shows the reason for the possibility [of the offense]. The connection is: "For one who drags the boat, it is a *pārājika*.
Again, asking "What does he do?", he says: "Touched by a single part," and so forth. The connection here is: "For one who causes that boat to pass beyond [the boundary].

In this case as well, the meaning should be construed according to the past tense (*bhūtavatasa*) as "for one who has dragged" and "for one who has caused to pass beyond. Whatever is to be said regarding this [is as follows]:
That is exactly according to the method explained below.

Having thus shown the determination regarding the dragging toward the four sides, [the author] now says "likewise," etc., in order to show the determination regarding lifting up and sinking down above and below.
"Likewise" means that it drags [the offense] into "his *pārājika*. In what?
He says, “Even as much as a hair’s breadth above,” and so forth. “Below the bottom of the boat” (*adhonāvātalam*) means below the bottom of the boat;
this is to be connected with the phrase “released even as much as a hair’s breadth of water from above. The construction is:
“even as much as a hair’s breadth touched by that [water] was released from the rim of the mouth. “By that” refers to the water touched by the bottom of the boat.
It should be understood that even if one releases [the boat] by so much as a hair’s breadth while the mouth-stopper is still in place. 122.

However, regarding a boat that has been moored on the bank and placed in still water, its "place" and its "mooring" are considered to be twofold: the location where it stands and the means of binding it;
such is the construction of the text. 123. The construction is: "If one releases the mooring first—that is, initially—there is a *thullaccaya* offense. "By some means" means...
“By any means whatsoever among the six methods previously described, such as ‘in front or behind’ and so forth”—this is the meaning. He causes the boat to move from its place.

“Having first moved it from its place” means having first moved the boat from the spot where it was stationed by means of one of the six modes previously described, beginning with “in front or behind. And this same method applies to the boat.
The meaning is that this same principle should be applied here: first, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) when it moves from its place of rest;

subsequently, there is a *pārājika* (defeat) upon the release of the bond. In this context, there are two locations—the boat tied to the bank and placed in still water, which constitutes the bond and the place of rest—and if one first releases it from the bond, it is a *thullaccaya*. Afterwards, [when it reaches] the shore...

If one causes [the woman] to move from her place by means of any one of the [specified] modes, it is a *pārājika*. Having first caused her to move from her place, the same principle applies even to the subsequent loosening of her bonds;

this is the determination stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary). It should be understood that the *dukkaṭa* and *thullaccaya* offenses regarding touching and shaking were not mentioned here because they can be understood through the method already explained below in the section on the water-pot (*kumbhi*). The same applies to what follows.
125. "Having hauled up" means having brought [the boat] from the water onto dry land. "Having overturned" means having turned it face downwards. The construction is:
"the place touched by the rim of the hull of the boat standing on dry land is the location. The word "hi" indicates a distinction;
by it, he illuminates the specific difference between the boat situated in the water and the boat situated on dry land as described.
126. Here, since sinking downwards is not possible, he says “is to be known,” etc., to show the displacement from its place by means of the other five modes [of movement] excluding that.
“From anywhere whatsoever” means: crossing over even as much as a hair’s breadth toward any direction whatsoever—by way of the four horizontal directions and the upward direction.
127. “Even when turned upside down” (*ukkujjitāya*) means even when placed with its opening facing upwards. “Of the *ghaṭikās*” refers to pieces of wood.

By the word “likewise” (*tathā*), he extends by analogy the method already stated in the passage beginning with “the delimitation of the location is to be known. That [method] applies to a ship that has been turned upside down and placed on the ground.
However, for a ship placed upon *ghaṭikās*—that is, fixed upon elephant-tooth pegs—the determination explained for spears placed on *nāgadantas* (elephant-tooth pegs) applies.
128. “Theyyā” (by theft) is a qualification for the phrase “while rowing. “In a ford” means in water near a landing-place. “With an oar” means with a paddle.
“With a rudder” means with a wooden board used as a rudder. “While rowing” means while propelling.
The reading “taṃ pājetī” (he rows that) is also seen; the meaning is that defeat belongs to him who rows that boat.
129–30. *Chatta* means a sunshade (*ātapavāraṇa*). *Paṇāmetvā* means having spread it out so that it catches the wind.

*Ussāpetvā va cīvaraṃ* means having raised the robe upward; the shortening of the vowel in *va* is due to the requirements of the meter (*gāthāchanda*). *Laṅkārasadisaṃ* means resembling a spread-out cloth.
*Samīraṇaṃ* means the breeze (*māluta*). *Na doso tassa vijjatīti*: no fault is found in him.
This was stated with reference to a boat being carried away by a wind that arrives later, while one is acting in this manner at a time when the wind is not yet present.
However, it should be understood that if one acts in this way while the wind is actually blowing, there is indeed an offense.
131–2. The connection is "approached by oneself. A landing place near a village is a "village landing" (*gāmatittha*). "That" refers to the boat.
“Places” (*ṭhāna*) refers to the spots where one stands at a village ford after having traveled by means of a parasol, a robe, or the wind caught by them.
“Without moving” (*acāletvā*) means not even causing it to tremble; by this, he shows the absence of a *thullaccaya* offense.

There is also the reading “without making move” (*acāvayitvā*), which means not shifting it even by the breadth of a hair from its standing place; by this, he shows the absence of a *pārājika* offense. “Having purchased” (*kiṇitvā*)...
"Having sold by means of the root [text]" (*mūlena vikkiṇitvā*). And as for "she goes herself," here the word *ca* (and) is used to include an additional point.
Likewise, she goes while being fanned with a parasol held over her or with a robe raised above her, or while being carried along by the wind.
"He causes her to move from her place" means that, having turned her toward the direction he desires, he causes her to move from her place of travel by means of striking her with a whip.
Commentary on the *Nāva-aṭṭhakathā*. 133–4.

It is called a *yāna* because one goes by means of it (*yāti etena*). It is called a *ratha* because it causes delight (*ramayati*). Or else, it is called a *vayha* because it carries (*vahati*), is carried (*vuyhati*), or is carried by means of it (*vahanti etena*).
Regarding the phrase "having covered [it] like a canopy above, with a tiled roof, or entirely enclosed," this is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

A cart (*sakaṭa*) made in the manner described is called a *vayha*. A *sandamānikā* is a specific type of vehicle made according to the method explained in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), which states:
"A *sandamānikā* is one constructed with crossbeams made of gold, silver, and so forth on both sides, in the manner of the wings of a Garuḍa.
Regarding the phrase "in the application of causing displacement from a place" (*ṭhānā cāvanayogasmim*), it means in the application of causing displacement from a place.

135–6. Since those who declare a *pārājika* offense based on the non-transgression from ten places must first know the classification of the places, [the author], after showing that, speaks the words beginning with “of a vehicle yoked with two” (*yānassa dukayuttassa*) in order to show the classification of the offenses. “Yoked with two” (*dukayuttassa*) means:
of which there is a pair (*duka*)—a pair of oxen (*goyuga*)—yoked; the analysis (*viggaha*) is either “yoked in which” (*yutte yasmiṃ*) or “in which. “Ten places” refers to the two...
The meaning is: one should speak of ten places by way of these ten points of support—namely, the eight feet of the oxen and the two wheels.
By this same method, the principle for the classification of places in vehicles such as those yoked with four [oxen] and so forth has been demonstrated, up to eighteen [places].
"Of one driving a vehicle" means of one sending forth a vehicle such as a cart and so forth. "'At the pole' means near the yoke."
This is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathā*. It means "near the place where [the ox] is bound together with the yoke at the pole.

Furthermore, "dhura" is a name for the yoke itself. From the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, "having abandoned the dhura" and "having placed the dhura," the place of attachment associated with it is also called "dhura.
However, in this context, it is like the word "Ganges," which refers to the vicinity of the Ganges.
The status of the yoke being in use is obtained at the place near the yoke where the driver is seated.
The construction is: "One should designate a *thullaccaya* for him when the oxen lift their feet.

And this is stated with reference to a time when the oxen are not going against the grain (are moving in the normal direction). To illuminate the specific distinction that occurs during the time they are going against the grain, [the text says] "but a *thullaccaya*" in this context.

By the word "but" (*tu*), the commentary states: "If, however, the oxen, realizing 'this is not our master,' abandon the yoke and stand still or struggle while being pulled, [the precept] is still protected.
But for one who again straightens the oxen, puts the yoke back on them, yokes them firmly, and drives them on by piercing them with a goad—according to the method already described, for those..."
It should be understood that the specific qualification stated as "a grave offense (thullaccaya) by lifting [the wheel]" is included here.
Regarding the phrase "of the wheels," the emphatic particle *hi* in this context indicates:

"Even if one wheel has become stuck in the mud on a muddy road, and the oxen, while turning it, cause the second wheel to roll along, because one [wheel] remains stationary, there is as yet no theft. When the oxen..."
However, it should be understood that the specific distinction stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*— namely, that for one who, having straightened it again, is driving [the cart] while the wheel is stationary,
the offense of *pārājika* occurs once the space touched by the tip of a hair has been transgressed—

is thus demonstrated. Having shown the determination regarding a suitable vehicle (*yuttayāna*) up to this point, he now says [the following] to show the determination regarding an unsuitable vehicle (*ayuttayāna*).

“Of one that is unyoked,” and so forth. The construction is as follows: for that [cart] which stands supported by the pole (*dhura*), even though it is unyoked, there are exactly three places by way of the supporting wheels. Therein, “of one that is unyoked” means of one not yet harnessed to oxen.
“By the pole” means by the region near the place where the pole was yoked according to the method already stated; [and] “by the front of the cart” (*sakaṭasīsa*).
It has been said. Regarding "the prop" (*upatthambhani*): it refers to that which stands above the prop for the front of a cart.

It is called a "prop" (*upatthambhanī*) because it supports the yoke (*dhura*). The pair of poles provided for the purpose of supporting the rear part of the cart is called the "rear prop" (*pacchimopatthambhanī*); the prop provided for the front part is the "front prop" (*purimopatthambhanī*).
This is the distinction regarding the "supporting" [factors]. Here, the first supporting factor is intended.
As for the statement, "There are only three instances by way of the wheels of the supporting factors," this was said with reference to the supporting factor that has not been adjusted;
however, by way of the one that has been adjusted, it should be stated that there are "four."
By the word “likewise” (*tathā*), it draws in the phrase “only three places”; the meaning is that there are three places by way of the two wooden wheels.
By the word “of wood” (*dārūnaṃ*) expressed in the plural, it should be understood that this includes a heap of wood, as well as even a single log or a single plank.
By the phrase “on the ground also, with the yoke itself, and likewise for that which is placed,” there are only three [places].
The term *ṭhānāni* (bases) is extended by analogy. Here, there are three bases according to the locations where the primary wheels are established.

Furthermore, it is possible to effect a conjunction by applying the particle *ca*—from the phrase "and of that which has been placed above"—also to the phrase "of that which has been placed on the ground.
In this context, by means of the redundant particle *ca*, [the text implies] what is stated in the Commentary: "But as for that which is improper..."
It is supported by one prop at the front and two props at the rear;

thus, there are five locations based on those three props and the wheels. If the prop at the front is fixed to the lower part, there are six locations—this summarizes the determination as it has been stated.
Regarding the phrase "whether from the front or from behind," the word "having dragged" (*kaḍḍhitvā*) is to be supplied as a textual ellipsis.

By the particle *api*, it includes what was not explicitly stated, namely "having lifted up" (*ukkhipitvā*). The construction is as follows: "he who, having dragged [the object] from the front, displaces it from its place; or he who, having dragged it from behind, displaces it from its place;
or he who, having lifted it up, displaces it from its place. By the word "three" (*tiṇṇaṃ*), these three [types of persons] are included.
“Of them” is understood through the force of the context; it means “of those three persons. To the question “When what happens?
he says: “But a grave offense... [etc. ...defeat. The phrase “from his position” should also be connected with this term “grave offense.
Because the particle *tu* is employed for the purpose of indicating a distinction, when there is displacement from a position that is not yet complete, there is a grave offense of causing agitation.
It should be understood that when the removal from one’s place is performed without remainder, the offense of *pārājika* for "removal from one's place" (*ṭhānācāvana*) is stated.

140. "With the two ends of the axle" means with both ends of the axle. According to the rule, "In the case of expressing a genus, the plural is used for a single entity," the plural form is appropriate for a singular meaning. [The word] "of the vehicle" (*yānassa*) is an adjective qualifying the term "standing" (*ṭhitassa*).

The qualification is obtained through the force of the context. Because it is stated, "There are two places," just as the yoke of a cart does not touch the ground, only a vehicle that has been placed upon two higher wooden beams—such as those of a scale—and upon which two axle-ends have been mounted, is understood here.
141. "Dragging" means rubbing against the wooden supports of the two axle-ends and moving back and forth.
"Dragging. "Lifting up" means raising [the axle] from its upright position. "Beyond the space touched" means when it exceeds by even a hair's breadth the space that was touched.
"Of another" means other than the type previously described; that is, of any vehicle such as a chariot and so forth. 142.
"Of the four axles" refers to the four pins that fasten the axles. From the place where the two ends of the axle are inserted into the wheels...
The four pins driven into the two inner sides of the cart-poles like two fingers for the purpose of blocking the axle are called *akkhudhi*.
"Of the pole" (*dhurassa*) means of the front tip of the chariot situated near the place where the yoke is fastened; that is the vehicle.
By the word "or" (*vā*), other actions are indicated: either pulling it by seizing it on the side, or lifting it up by seizing it in the middle.
He adjusts it. Regarding the word "having taken," the phrase "while pulling" is to be supplied as a textual supplement.

"Displaces from its place" means that while pulling it by the poles, he causes it to pass even by the width of a hair beyond the spot touched by the tip of the pole raised toward his own direction, using the other end of the pole as the limit.
By the expression "or by the poles," which indicates a state of danger, the existence of vehicles without poles is also implied. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*...
“Furthermore, if there are no protruding parts, the arms are made level and pierced in the middle so that the ends of the axle-pins are inserted;
it stands touching the entire ground surrounding the lower surface.
In this case, a *pārājika* offense should be understood to occur by way of exceeding the point touched in any of the four directions or above. This is the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) as stated.
He includes [them] by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*).
143. "Not facing" means not with the face toward it. "There might be only one place" means that the single spot touched by the navel becomes the "place";
this is the meaning. The reading "ekam assa siyā ṭhānan" is seen in manuscripts; therefore, the former reading alone [is correct].
"More beautiful. Regarding the phrase "even the circumference" (*paricchedopi*), here the particle *pi* indicates a specific distinction; the meaning is "but the circumference.
"In five ways" means that from the center of the hub (*nābhi*) to the edge of the four sides, and upwards as well, it has a fivefold manner of being displaced from its position.
"Two places" refers to the two locations touched by the rim (*nemī*) and the hub. "Of it" means of the wheel.

Regarding those two points: this same analysis (*vinicchaya*) stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) concerning a wheel placed without leaning against a wall or similar support is also presented by this reading.
145. "Unprotected" means not having security arranged by the owner. "Having let down" means having driven out the oxen.

The intention is that it is permissible and there is no offense of defeat (*pārājika*). However, if the owner causes [the wheel] to be brought back, there is the obligation to pay for the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).

Commentary on the Exposition of the Vehicles (Yānaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā). 146. Regarding the Exposition of the Burden (Bhāraṭṭhakathā): The burden is fourfold according to the bodily parts known by the names head, shoulder, hip, and waist.
In this context, for the sake of avoiding confusion regarding the burden of the head and so forth, the delimitation of the head and other parts should be understood.
First, regarding the head: from the front of the neck to the back of the neck, in some there is a curl at the edge of the hair;
in others, curls of hair grow descending on both sides of the neck, which are called "ear-lobes" (*kaṇṇacūḷikā*), as well as the lower part thereof—this is the lower limit.
Above that is the head. The weight situated within this interval is called the "head-weight."
The shoulder is that portion situated between the two sides, starting from the ears and the occipital protuberances below, from the temples above,
from the hollow of the neck and the nape of the neck below, and from the middle of the back and the center of the chest at the seat of the heart above;
the weight carried within this space is called "shoulder-load."

From the curve of the middle of the back and from the hollow of the heart downwards as far as the tips of the toenails—this is the division of the waist (*kaṭipariccheda*). The weight situated all around the body within this interval is called the "waist-weight" (*kaṭibhāra*).

From the collarbone (*kappara*) downwards as far as the tips of the fingernails—this is the division of the hanging parts (*olambakapariccheda*). The weight situated within this interval is called the "hanging-weight" (*olambaka*). It is called "weight" (*bhāra*) because it bears (*bharati*); or else, it is called "weight" because one bears by means of it or in it.
Thus, the aforementioned members beginning with the head are [the parts of] the weight.
[They] are so called. "It stands upon a burden" means *bhāraṭṭha*; thus, the goods placed upon the head and so forth are so called.

According to the commentarial statement, "The burden itself is the *bhāraṭṭha*," the word *bhāra*—established in the sense of the object (*kamma*) as that which is to be borne (*bharīyati*)—refers specifically to the goods.

147. "Only on the head" means precisely on the head as it has been defined. "He shakes it" means he shakes it here and there without throwing it down. "There may be a grave offense" means there would be a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for shaking it.
148. "Aggregates" (*khandhā*) refers to the aggregate exactly as it has been delimited. "Removed" (*oropite*) means discarded.

Regarding the phrase "from the head," there is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*) of the word "above" (*uddham*); the meaning is "above the head as it was delimited. "Even by the measure of a hair-tip" (*kesaggamattampi*) means having made even a hair-tip's distance [the limit].
The word "even" (*pi*) indicates that this is the case even at such a slight distance, let alone further than that. "While releasing" (*mocento*) means not touching with the tip of a hair.

"Taking away. Here too, by the word "api" (also/even), one refers back to what was stated previously: that it is not only for one who lowers the bundle that there is a *pārājika* offense, but rather, even for one who releases it, there is defeat.

Furthermore, regarding a double burden such as a shoulder-bag (*pasibbaka*) and so forth, because it rests in two places—on the head and on the back—it constitutes a *pārājika* offense through taking it away from those two locations; and that...
“It is to be understood that [the phrase] ‘releasing from the head’ already includes this by way of a single part.

149–50.
