Having thus shown the determination regarding the burden of the head, and although the determinations regarding the burden of the aggregates (*khandhabhāra*) and so forth must be shown next in the order of enumeration, [the author] shows the determination regarding the burden of the hanging ornament (*olambakabhāra*) mentioned at the end, [thereby covering] the burdens at the beginning and the end.
In order to extend the analysis to the remaining cases by following the stated method, he says "the burden," and so forth.

"With a pure mind" means one who has no intent to steal for reasons such as breakfast; however, for one who places a burden already in hand on the ground or relinquishes it with an intent to steal, it is a *pārājika* offense at the mere moment it leaves the hand—it should be understood that this is what is indicated by this [term].
"By the method stated here" means according to what was said regarding the head-load and the shoulder-sling load.

"In the other loads as well" refers to the trunk-load and so forth. "The determination should be understood by one of wise judgment" means that when someone with a thieving mind touches any object worth a *pāda* coin—be it a place already delimited or otherwise—with the intention, "I shall take it," [the offense is determined].

The meaning is that this should be understood as the legal decision (*vinicchaya*): there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who makes it shake without moving it from its place; there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for one who makes it move from its place by shaking it;
and there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) for one who moves it from its place either by exceeding the delimited area or by lifting it upward.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning "the burden" (*bhāra*).
151–3. Now, in order to show the determination regarding the monastery grounds (*ārāma*), he says "an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*), and so forth.
"A monastery ground" (*ārāma*) refers to any one of the two types of grounds: a flower garden such as that of the *campaka* tree, or a fruit orchard such as that of the mango tree.

The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that wherein those desiring flowers and the like take delight"; thus it is "a monastery ground. When used in conjunction with the prefix *abhi*, it takes the accusative case. "By assailing" (*abhiyuñjato*) means by bringing [the grounds] under the power of another.

This should be connected as follows: for one who, knowing [the object belongs to another], makes a legal claim that "it is mine" and, with a thieving mind, applies himself to seeking a second companion and so forth in order to establish a partnership, the Buddha has declared a *dukkaṭa* offense;

the meaning is that because it is a preliminary effort toward taking what is not given, the Blessed One has stated that there is a *dukkaṭa* according to the counting of concurrent efforts. "Practicing the Dhamma" means making a legal claim.
If one defeats the actual owner, the construction is that one is defeated by the teaching itself.

"Of him" means of the owner of the goods. "To one who generates doubt" means to the thief who gives rise to uncertainty, thinking, "By engaging in a legal dispute with this man, shall I obtain what belongs to me, or not? Even he who, while practicing the Dhamma himself...
The construction is: "He commits an offense of expiation (pārājika), and for him there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
When he casts off the responsibility toward the owner, thinking, "This man is stubborn and harsh; he might even create an obstacle to my holy life;
enough now with this monastery for me," and when the responsibility toward the owner has been cast off, [thinking] of himself, "I will not give it."
The construction is: "and in the laying down of the burden. Thus, when both have laid down the burden, it is a *pārājika* offense. "Of him" refers to the one making the accusation.
Regarding the phrase "and of all false witnesses," it should be understood that the word "and" (*ca*) is indicated by elision.
Even though they know the thief is ownerless, those who say anything at all for the sake of acting under his influence are false witnesses; [the offense applies] to all such monks as well.
The meaning is that it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the monastery (*ārāma*). 154.

In the commentary on the section concerning the dwelling (*vihāra*), because "dwelling" is used as a characteristic term, one should understand it to include both "a cell (*pariveṇa*)" and "a residence (*āvāsa*)."
“Belonging to the Saṅgha” means belonging to the Saṅgha because it was given to the monks for the sake of the fourfold Saṅgha.

“Anything whatsoever” means whether small or large. There is also a syntactical connection with the remainder of the text: “For one who, having seized it, brings a legal charge in order to take it, the offense of *pārājika* is not established.
He shows the reason: “Because there is no laying down of the burden by anyone,” that is, by everyone.
The meaning is: because it is impossible for there to be a relinquishment of responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*) regarding the Saṅgha of the four quarters.

By using the qualifying term "belonging to the Saṅgha" (*saṅghika*) instead of merely saying "monastery" (*vihāra*), it is stated that the offense is a *pārājika* for one who takes back a monastery or similar property given to a group—such as those of the Dīgha-bhāṇaka lineage—or to a single individual, after having previously relinquished their responsibility.

The detailed explanation here should be understood as being the same as that for the monastery (*ārāma*). It should be understood that the explanation regarding goods situated therein (*tatraṭṭhabhaṇḍa*)—namely those situated on the ground, on dry land, in the air, or in space—has not been stated here because it can be known through the method already described.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of what is situated in a monastery (*vihāra*).
155–6. "The heads in the field" refers to the stalks (*vallī*). "Having reaped them" means having done so in such a way that the mere grain comes into one's hand.
"With a sickle" means with a blade. "Having gathered" means having cut. In all these verbal expressions, the phrase "the heads of rice and so forth" is to be supplied.
When one takes the heads of rice and so forth after having reaped them, whichever seed is taken therein—
The construction is as follows: when the object is fulfilled and that [person] is released from bondage, there is a *pārājika* offense for him.

For one who takes it by pulling it out with a sickle, the construction is: "when the head [of the stalk] is grasped... there is [an offense]. For one who takes it by cutting it with a hand-sickle, the construction is:
"when it is grasped in the fist... there is [an offense]. "Seed" refers to the fruit of rice and so forth. "The object is fulfilled" means it reaches the value of one *pāda*. "In the fist" means...
"A handful of heads" or "a handful of seeds. "Released from bondage" means released from the place of confinement. "Or a staff" refers to a staff of grain sufficient to fill a vessel.
The connection is: "if it is unbroken, it protects. "Or its bark" means the outer skin on one side of that staff;
the connection remains: "if it is unbroken, it protects. By the inclusion of the word "or," [the alternative is indicated].
The term "vāka" mentioned here includes what is found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "Vāka" refers to that which is on the outside, whether on a staff or on bark.
Here too, the construction is: "even the bark, when unpeeled, protects.

"Or even a rice stalk" refers to the stalks of wild rice, kudrūsa grass, and so forth, which grow from the heads of harvested grain such as *śāli* rice; it is called the "sheath of bark. "Long" means long.
This is what it means. With the phrase “or not having emerged,” there is a connection to the word “staff. The word “from that” (*tato*) is an ellipsis.
The meaning is: from that long rice stalk, the seed-bearing tip-staff is completely severed, and even by the width of a hair-tip, it has not emerged outside the severed end.
“He protects” means he protects that bhikkhu from the corresponding offenses of *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, or *pārājika*.
It protects. The meaning is: "If, having been released, one does not guard [it].
And this has been stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā): "The stalk of rice is long; as long as the tip of the rice grain has not emerged from within the stalk, it continues to protect.
Even when the tip has emerged by the measure of a hair's breadth from the lower surface of the stalk..."
"He should be dealt with according to the value of the goods. Likewise, by this very same legal decision (*vinicchaya*), the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) indicates such rulings as:
"Even when the roots of a handful of rice stalks sufficient to fill a container have been cut, if they remain entangled together with uncut rice tips, it is protected [from the offense];
but when the entanglement is untied and separated, the aforementioned offenses such as *pārājika* occur. This and other such rulings should be understood.
158. “Having crushed” means having crushed the tips of the rice grains. “Having winnowed” means having blown away the husks and such.

The construction is: “He imagines, ‘I will take the essence from this. “From this” means from the tip of the rice grain. “I will take the essence” means I will take the essential portion. The construction is: “If he imagines [this].
“He guards” means [he guards] with a sickle [the amount] sufficient for the purpose of the plot.

The meaning is that even if one has taken [the grain] by carrying it away, cutting it with the hand, or displacing it from its place, one is protected from an offense as long as the intention (parikappa) has not been finalized. 159.
"Even in threshing" means even in threshing the heads of rice. "Even in uprooting" means even in removing the straw. "Even in winnowing" means...
Even in the removal of refuse such as husks and the like, there is no fault; thus, by virtue of the value [of the object], offenses such as *pārājika* do not occur.
However, a *dukkaṭa* offense still exists due to the preliminary effort (*sahapayoga*). "One's own...

defeat" means that after having performed everything according to the manner first imagined for oneself, as soon as one has placed it in one's own vessel to take the valuable portion, the aforementioned *pārājika* and other offenses occur.
160. To this extent, the four types of "field-placed" goods—namely, those stated as "field-placed means the goods are deposited in a field in four ways:
on the ground, on dry land, in the air, or suspended in the sky"—are similar to what was previously mentioned.
Having set those aside, and having shown the determination regarding "grown there" (*tatthajāta*) and so forth as they appear in the Pāḷi, [the author] now...

Regarding the term "field" (*khetta*), which is defined as "wherein grain or vegetables grow," the author says "knowing," etc., in order to show the legal determination even in the case of such a field.
"Knowing" means knowing that it belongs to another. "Stake" (*khīla*) refers to either a driven wedge or another stake made of stone and so forth.
"Transfers" (*saṅkāmeti*) means that the owners transfer the land under the control of another in such a way that they themselves perceive it [as done].
Or otherwise, the meaning is that with a thieving mind, one buries even a spot as small as a hair’s tip so that what belongs to oneself becomes as if it were not one's own property.
Regarding when that constitutes a *pārājika* offense for him, he says: "When the owners have relinquished their responsibility."

The word “hoti” (there is) is the remainder of the text. Because the qualification “or of one’s own” is included by the particle *tu*, the meaning is that there is a *pārājika* offense both when the owner relinquishes his responsibility—which is defined as being free from attachment—and when one relinquishes one’s own responsibility by thinking, “I will not give it to the owner.
“Thus declared” means it was spoken and determined in this way: “even a mere hair’s breadth.”
162. "But which" means: but which ground. Regarding those two boundary-poles (*khīla*):

"First, a grave offense (*thullaccaya*)" means that when the first boundary-pole has been moved, that monk incurs a grave offense. "In the second" means: when the second boundary-pole has been moved, there is a defeat (*parājika*);
such is the construction. And this is the determination regarding the two boundary-poles that mark the limit in a place where [the site] is to be taken up by many boundary-poles.

This is what is meant by that very [statement]. However, the distinction here is that a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs when one drives in the remaining stakes without the two end stakes, as well as in all other applications for those same purposes.
163–4. The connection is: "desiring to make known, 'This belongs to me. Regarding land belonging to another, the state of being dependent on another—

"Having known [the value]," means with a thieving mind, desiring to take possession of even a hair's breadth of space, one measures it with a rope or a staff, thinking, "This much space is mine," and intends to make it known to another—this is the meaning.
"By which two modes of action" means by either of the two modes of action: the final drawing out of the rope or the throwing down of the staff.
In the phrase "tesu" (among them), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

Here, although the word "or" (*vā*)—which has the sense of an alternative—should be construed with "a staff" (*yaṭṭhiṃ vā*) as well as with "rope" (*rajjuṃ*) or "a well" (*vāpī*), the particle "pi" (also) is stated as an additional expression for the purpose of including what was not explicitly mentioned;
for by it, the determination regarding those who possess noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsika*), which was not stated here, is made known.

As determined in the *Uttara-rajjuyaṭṭhi-vinicchaya*, when one— possessing a thieving mind and desiring to seize even as much as a hair’s breadth of land belonging to another— plants a fence post, constructs a fence by means of branches,
sets up a boundary marker, builds a wall, or increases the earth and clay [of the enclosure], these constitute preliminary acts (*pubbapayoga*).

It should be understood that this exposition also includes the determination that, in the case of an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya), there is both expiation and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the simultaneous application;
an offense of only wrong-doing for the two subsequent applications; a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the first application; and an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for the final application.
Commentary on the Section on Land (Khettaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā). 165. Regarding the terms "one who stands on cloth" (*vatthaṭṭha*) and so forth:

here, because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that "cloth means the site of a monastery (*ārāmavatthu*) or the site of a vihāra (*vihāravatthu*"), this refers both to ground prepared and set aside for constructing flower gardens and the like, as well as to previously established monasteries.

When there is destruction, a vacant site, a monastery that is being constructed, or a site where a monastery has fallen into ruin—when it exists with such distinctions, whether it be a plantation or a monastery, it is called a "site" (*vatthu*). Thus, there are two kinds of sites.
Regarding "goods stored on a site" (*vatthuṭṭhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ*), goods are deposited on a site in four ways: [stored] on the ground (*bhūmaṭṭhaṃ*), etc.

Because of the statement, “standing on land, standing in the air, or standing in the sky,” this twofold category—namely, the fourfold goods and [the aforementioned two]—should be understood as being shown by the term “vatthaṭṭhassa.

This is formed by compounding “vatthu” and “vatthuṭṭha” into “vatthu-vatthuṭṭha” according to the rule of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining one member of a group that shares a common form), and then changing the vowel *u* to *a*. Thus, it refers to the two kinds of objects already mentioned.

"Of goods placed on cloth" means this. Regarding "placed in a field," the compound here is to be understood in the same way as before; that is, it should be taken as "in a field and in what is placed in a field.
The same method applies to the designations "placed on a boat" and so forth. Regarding "and in what is placed in a village":
when it is said, "Goods placed in a village (gāmaṭṭha) are those placed in a village in four ways: placed on the ground... [etc. ...or placed in the air," [the same analysis applies].
The meaning is: "even in the case of the four kinds of village property.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning property located in villages. 166.
In the commentary on property located in the forest, the connection of the phrases beginning with "grass" is with the phrase "grown there."

“Grown there” means: because of the statement, “What is called ‘forest’ is that which is claimed as property by people,” anything belonging to humans grown there must not be taken against the will of the owners; thus, the meaning is that it has arisen in a forest where protection is required.
“Or grass” means: that which has been gathered and set aside by others, or that which one may gather oneself, and which is fit for roofing a house.
"Grass" or "leaf" means such things as palm leaves and other foliage suitable for roofing a house. "Creeper" means such things as rattan creepers and the like.

As for that which is long and has reached a great tree or a shrub by piercing through it or by winding around it—even if its base is cut, it does not constitute an act of theft, nor does it if its tip is cut.
But when it has been cut at both the top and the root, then it constitutes an act of theft (*avahāra*).
However, if it remains wrapped [around the tree], the moment it is released from the tree after being unwrapped constitutes an act of theft; this is the distinction here.
Furthermore, the remaining goods such as bark, shoots, and so forth, which have not been relinquished by the owner, are included by implication through this very same definition.

It should be understood. "Or even a piece of wood" means a log of timber. Regarding the phrase "it must be made to be paid according to the value of the goods," here the meaning should be taken as "it must be caused to be paid" by way of the sense of a cause that is included within [the term].
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "it must be made to be paid according to the value of the goods.

If, among the goods such as grass and so forth that have been stolen, the value is one *māsaka* or less than a *māsaka*, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If it is more than a *māsaka* but less than five *māsakas*...
If it is worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, it is a *thullaccaya*. If it is worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, it is a *pārājika*.
The meaning is that if one has not committed a *pārājika*, one should be made to undergo the *dukkaṭa* for touching and the *thullaccaya* for causing movement. "Taking" means stealing. 167–74.
Now, in order to show the legal determination regarding the wood of trees mentioned as "or even timber," he says "in the case of high value," and so forth.
"Of great value" means being worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas.
"Is lost" means that one who possesses the intent to steal incurs a *pārājika* offense even at the mere moment of cutting it. The word "even" (*pi*) is used for emphasis.
By the phrase "anyone at all," the meaning is that even if it has been carried some distance, whether it be fresh or old, once it has been cut and set aside, it must certainly not be taken.
“Root” is merely an illustration. Based on the commentary’s statement, “It is cut at both the top and the root,” it should be understood as having cut both the root and the top.
“Addhagata” means that which is worn out, decayed, fallen off, and stripped of bark; it is said to have existed for a long time.
“Lakkhaṇa” refers to a mark made by cutting the bark on the trunk of a tree in order to identify one's own property.
“Enveloped on all sides” (*challiyonaddha*) means having been covered all around by newly grown bark until it has become invisible.
Regarding the phrase “and inhabited” (*ajjhāvuttha*), the word “house” (*geha*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text. The construction is:
“both the house that was built and the one that was inhabited. Having given the price to the owners of the forest and having purchased the trees, that house was built from felled timber.
The meaning is "that which has been used. Regarding the phrase "perishing," there is also the textual supplement "the remaining timber.
Having built that house, [the timber] remains and perishes, being worn away by various factors such as rain and heat;
thus it is said, "the timber is ruined. The connection is: "there is no fault whatsoever for one who takes it. Regarding the phrase "the owners have no home," for one who takes it, there is no...

The meaning is that there is no offense. If one asks what the reason is: it is because the owners of the forest took the timber and gave it to others, and they had discarded it without any further attachment; this is the reason here.
For it is said in the Commentary: "When trees have been cut down for the sake of houses and such, and those [structures] have been built and inhabited..."
There are also pieces of wood in the forest that are destroyed by rain and sun;
having seen such things as these, it is permissible to take them, thinking, "They have been discarded. Why? Because the owners of the forest have no authority over them.
Those who gave the gift to the forest owners and had [the wood] cut down are the ones with authority, and they have discarded them; there, one is without attachment.
"has been born. Even so, it should be understood that when the owners later cause [the goods] to be brought back, there is an obligation to pay restitution for the property (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
"And whoever" refers to the monk who, while entering the property of the forest-owners, takes hold of trees with the thought, "I will give them upon leaving," without having given anything;
and whoever, having reached the place of protection where the forest-guardians are seated—
They guard the forest; having reached that place, "thinking" is understood by implication as "he might pass over [it]," because it requires another action.

Therefore, in the phrase "having applied the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and so forth to the mind," the word "and so forth" (ādi), in the sense of "manner," includes wholesome types of thought (vitakka). Or, while thinking of something else, having reached the place of guarding—

The meaning should be stated by connecting [the phrase] "should overstep. In that context, "thinking of something else" (*aññaṃ cintento*) or "being occupied with something else" (*aññaṃ vihito*) includes the aforementioned types of thought.
Regarding the word *assa*, because it is used in the genitive case as the agent in connection with the gerundive (*deyya*), the meaning is "by him.

In the phrase "and whoever" (*yo cā*), by the particle *ca* used in the sense of an unstated inclusion (*avuttasamuccaya*), [it refers to one who,] at the time of entering the forest, according to the method already described...
If one enters the forest without paying the fee, takes firewood, and then departs— thinking, "I will give it if the forest guards ask for it"—
and goes away without giving it because they did not ask; or if, having arrived there while the guards are playing,
sleeping, or gone outside, one stands there [waiting] for the guards...
It should be understood that even one who departs after searching but not finding [the goods], and likewise one who returns there and—
having given what must be given from his own hand by the officials appointed there, or having shown himself honor, or having persuaded the guards,
or having requested leave from the guards and being granted leave by them— departs, is included because these cases are similar to what has been stated thus far.
"Boars" refers to wild pigs (*sūkara*). "Tigers" refers to leopards (*byaggha*). "Bears" refers to hyenas (*accha*). "Jackals" refers to black lions (*kāḷasīha*).

By the word "etcetera," predatory animals such as leopards, elephants, and lions are included. These very boars and others, because they move near what is undesirable—leading to death and other such misfortunes—through their coming together, approach the vicinity of the undesirable;
thus they are called "calamities" (*upaddava*). At the time when [the forest] has come to a place requiring protection...
This means "due to dangers such as wild boars and the like. "With the desire for liberation" means with the intention for release (*mokkha*).

By the phrase "just so," the very meaning already implied by the force of the preceding verse—namely, that one enters without giving the gift to be given at the time of entry, thinking "I will give it when leaving," and having entered, takes wood and reaches the place of protection—is here demonstrated.
"That place" means that location for guarding. "He passes beyond it" means that he passes by while fleeing, having become fearful due to the mere failure to perceive, "This is that place";
however, the construction is that he becomes liable to pay the fine (bhaṇḍadeyya).
Regarding the phrase "from the toll-house," it should be understood here too that the word *pi* is indicated as being elided; thus, it means "also from the place where the toll is collected."
*Attha*: *Suṅkaghāta* means the mere seizing by theft of the king’s share that ought to be given as toll (*suṅka*).

Alternatively, the analysis (*viggaha*) is: it is called *suṅkaghāta* because toll is destroyed (*haññati*) therein. The specific nature of *suṅkaghāta* will be made clear later. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of the gravity of that *suṅkaghāta*.
"That" (*taṃ*) refers to that place of toll-destruction. "Going without entering" (*anokkamma gacchato*) means not having entered [the toll-house].

For one who is walking away, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) has been declared: "If he evades the toll, there is an offense of wrong-doing. "This" refers to the aforementioned place of protection.

"For one carrying it away with a thieving mind" means for one who, having carried it away with a thieving mind, goes a long distance. The connection is: "Even for one going through the air, an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) has not been declared by the Teacher.
But is it not said: "However, for one carrying it away with a thieving mind, even if going through the air, it is indeed an offense entailing expulsion"?
Apart from the statement found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in the *Vibhaṅga* on the summary heading (*mātikā*) "forest-dwelling" (*araññaṭṭha*) in the *Pāḷi*, it says:
"If, with a mind intent on theft, one touches wood, a creeper, or grass growing there, valued at five māsakas or more than five māsakas, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one makes it move, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*). If one moves it from its place, there is an offense of [saṅghādisesa]."
Regarding the phrase "of a *pārājika* offense," since this is a general statement, one might ask:

although there is no separate mention of a *pārājika* offense for one who avoids a place of guard—just as in the case of the statement regarding the evasion of customs duty, "If one evades customs duty, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)"—why did [the author] say "by the Teacher" instead of saying "in the commentary"?
It is said in reply: by the commentator of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it was stated exactly thus...

He spoke because it had been so stated. But why did the commentator, even though he was familiar with the wording of the Canon, point out a *pārājika* offense that was not mentioned in the Canon itself by saying, "We shall not promulgate what has not been promulgated; we shall not abolish what has been promulgated"?
Herein, the reason is that the method [of the decision] spoken by the Blessed One when questioned by the monks is found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
One who knows that this same method has been demonstrated in the *Samantapāsādikā* should understand that it was stated here as "by the Teacher" by this very teacher as well.

Alternatively, having stated, "If one avoids the toll, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," the omission [of further detail] in the determination regarding the place of protection [is to be understood].
There are three possibilities: that it may be because the subject matter as previously described has not been seen; or that this [subject] might thus be blameless;
or that it might be easily understood according to what has been stated. Among these, the first possibility is merely a flawed hypothesis, as it contradicts the state of omniscience.
The second possibility is unacceptable, for it is logically untenable that this, which is blameworthy according to worldly standards, should be blameless.
The third alternative is appropriate by way of exclusion.

If it is asked: "In that context, what is meant by 'according to what was stated,' and how is the ease of understanding for this [third case] explained according to that?"—it is because in the description of forest locations presented first, it was stated in general terms:
"If she causes her to move from that place, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika)."
This has been stated, but not the avoidance of a place of watchfulness with a thieving mind. And as for the statement:

"When departing, for one who goes without giving according to the previously imagined rule—thinking, 'I will go after giving the price'—there is indeed the offense of anticipation (parikappāvahāra)," and:
"But departing from that place which was abandoned in whatever manner it was imagined is called 'removal from the spot' (ṭhānācāvana)."
It is not stated separately that "it becomes a *pārājika* offense by that very fact" (*hoteva*) and "by [the phrase] 'he causes her to move from her place,
there is an offense of *pārājika*', the meaning is already understood. However,
because avoiding a toll-station is of the same nature as avoiding a place, even though it is such by its own nature, this is like a hypothetical place.
To explain that even if one bypasses a place designated as a royal toll-station— which is distinct from the places yet to be described— even though it is a merely imagined location,

it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who goes by avoiding it with a thieving mind, just like one who takes his own bowl with a thieving mind, and not a state of defeat (*pārājika*),
[the text says]: "If he evades the toll, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
It must be concluded that because the Master of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya), who understood the Blessed One’s intention, stated "it is indeed a pārājika," this teacher also said,
"The Teacher did not point out it as a pārājika," merely to demonstrate the very manner in which it was stated in the commentary.
This is how the matter should be understood.
Therefore, because it is extremely grave—being sufficient for a *pārājika* offense—even for one who proceeds after having avoided [the object] from afar with a mind of theft by thus circumventing it;
therefore. "In this" (*ettha*) means in this place of guarding the forest.

The phrase "by way of distinction" (*visesena*) should be connected as the reason for the statement "one must be heedful. And [the phrase] "with a mind endowed with mindfulness" (*satisampannacetasā*).

“Of amiable character” (*piyasīlena*) is an epithet for the “monk” (*bhikkhu*). Since a monk who is unwilling to train is not a fit vessel for this instruction, [the author] said “of amiable character” in order to exclude him.

Furthermore, since one of amiable character who lacks mindfulness cannot maintain recollection in situations requiring alertness and is thus not a fit vessel for this [instruction], [the author] said “with a mind endowed with mindfulness” (*satisampannacetasā*) in order to exclude him.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Forest-Dweller (Araññaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā). 175–6. "In a time when water is difficult to obtain" (*toyadullabhakāle*): that in which water is scarce is "a time when water is difficult to obtain";

that which is both such a time and a period is "a time when water is difficult to obtain," and it is in that [time]. "Or having turned [the vessel]" (*āvajjetvā vā*): or having tilted the water-vessel.
"Or having placed it inside" means having put one's own vessel into that [other vessel]. "Or having made a hole" means having made a hole in the water-vessel by scratching it or similar means;
this is to be connected with what will be stated later: "for one who takes [it], he shall be declared guilty according to the value of the goods.
"In that manner" means just as there is a *pārājika* offense for one who steals water that has been protected and guarded in a vessel during a time when water is scarce.
It was stated in that very same manner. "In a reservoir" means in a reservoir belonging to another that is guarded.

"In a pond" means in a similar natural lake. In this way, it should be understood that ponds and so forth which are guarded by others are included either by these specific terms or by the word "or" (*vā*) used as a collective for what has not been explicitly mentioned.
"For one who takes after having inserted his own vessel" is a qualifying phrase.

Regarding water contained in a vessel, as in the case of oil here, it should be understood that for one who drinks by drawing it out with the mouth or with bamboo tubes and so forth with a thieving mind, the classification of the offense is according to the specific basis [of the act]. 177.
"Boundary" refers to the embankment or enclosure of tanks and the like. "Cutting" means removing the earth and such materials with spades and other tools.
For one who acts in two ways. By the word *tu*, which clarifies a specific meaning, [it refers to]: having broken the boundary and weakened it;
or having himself entered the water to stir up waves for the purpose of breaking it;
or having caused cows, buffaloes, other people, or playing children to enter; or having frightened those who have entered of their own accord.
If one cuts down, causes to be cut down, fells, or causes to be felled a tree standing in water, thereby agitating the water,

then even though the boundary is severed by the waves rising from that [disturbance], it is considered severed by that very act. In the same way, when cattle, buffalo, and so forth ascend the boundary—
whether by themselves or by causing others to ascend— even if the boundary is severed by their hooves, [the offense occurs] regarding the drainage of water and so forth.
"Having closed it oneself or having had it closed, or having bound a low place along the boundary of a pond oneself or having had it bound,
or having prevented water from being led out from the path for the excess water to flow away, or having caused water to enter from the outside,
one fills it; even if the boundary is broken by a flood, it is considered broken by that very act"— such is the specific detail found in the Aṭṭhakathā.
He includes [this]. "Because it was preceded by taking what is not given" means because it was a preliminary act for taking what is not given.

"Even together with a living plant" means even together with a living plant (*bhūtagāma*). By the word "even" (*api*), he includes the digging of the earth. While cutting a boundary, one cuts the grass and such growing there;
together with the *pācittiya* offense regarding living plants, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense. [This applies to] earth that has grown [there].
"He cuts" means that he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) together with the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for digging the earth;

this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "it must be made," there is a textual supplement here: "by the value of the goods, according to the offense. It should be understood as "it must be made to be done" by way of the sense of the causal suffix contained within [the word].
One who cuts while standing inside [the boundary] does so by means of the outer limit; one who cuts while standing outside does so by means of the inner limit.
The construction is as follows: "Standing in both places and cutting [the boundary] from the middle, one should be dealt with according to an offense equal in value to the goods.

This, however, is the meaning here: having stood within the enclosure and cut the boundary so that the water has gone outside, one should be dealt with according to the specific offense incurred—whether it be a *dukkaṭa*, a *thullaccaya*, or a *pārājika*—according to the value of the water that has exited.
Standing outside and cutting through the boundary, at the very moment the water entering the inner pond is displaced from its standing place,

one is to be dealt with according to the offense based on the value of the water that has flowed out. Sometimes standing inside and sometimes standing outside, while cutting through the boundary by placing it in the middle,
once the standing place in the middle has been cut through, at the moment the water is drawn out, [one is to be dealt with] according to the value of the water drawn out.
"He is to be dealt with according to the value of the offense.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of Water (Udakaṭṭhakathā). 179–80.
"By turn" means that by turns, the novices [bring] whatever tooth-sticks from the forest for the sake of the Saṅgha.
The construction of the meaning is as follows: if, after bringing [the tooth-sticks], they also bring some for the teachers,
then until they have cut those tooth-sticks to the proper length and assigned them to both the Saṅgha and the teachers,
because they were brought from the forest, all that tooth-stick— whether for the Saṅgha or for their respective teachers— belongs to those very novice monks who brought the tooth-sticks.
181. Therefore, because it belongs to those very novices themselves; thus, the connection is:
"that tooth-stick brought from the forest, and the tooth-stick which is heavy property belonging to the Saṅgha.
What is meant is: the tooth-stick that has arisen on land belonging to the Saṅgha, and which has become heavy property because it is protected and guarded by the Saṅgha.

Regarding the phrase "and for one who takes": by the addition of the word "and" (*ca*), that which was not explicitly mentioned here but is found in the commentary—the tooth-sticks belonging to a group, an individual, or a householder, whether grown in a monastery or a garden, or cut or uncut, or protected and guarded—is included.
Thus, it is illustrated that for one who takes those with the intent to steal, the offenses must be declared according to the value of the tooth-sticks once they have been carried away.
182. By those novice monks who were tooth-stick carriers. "Delivered" means presented to the Great Sangha. 183.

To show the reason why there is no offense of theft even for one who takes [the tooth-sticks] with a thieving mind starting from the time they have become property of the Sangha, he says: "Because of the lack of protection," and so forth.
In that context, "because of the lack of protection" refers to the fact that although the tooth-sticks have been obtained as the property of the Sangha, they are not guarded or protected.
Because there is an absence of protection provided by the Saṅgha as if it were [their own].

"Because it must be distributed according to seniority" means that even though it belongs to the Saṅgha, it cannot be distributed like fruits, flowers, and so forth—which are to be distributed according to seniority without overstepping the proper order.
And "because it is common to all" means because it is shared in common by all those who are included within the Saṅgha.
"This is the tooth-stick entrusted to the Saṅgha. "As if it were another" means as if it were another tooth-stick belonging to a group or an individual that has been guarded and protected.

Thus, although the reason for the absence of theft when one takes [the item] by stealth has been established, since it is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for one who takes their own requisites with a thieving mind, one who takes in such a manner incurs wrong-doing.
It should be understood that he is not released [from the offense]. However, the proper procedure (*vatta*) must be known:

when taking a tooth-stick belonging to the Saṅgha, one who enters the meditation hall or similar quarters and returns late should count the days spent outside and take a tooth-stick of the corresponding length.
When traveling on a journey, one should go after placing one or two tooth-sticks in one's bag.
"Living right there, one should take the tooth-stick that is to be chewed each day.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the tooth-stick. 184.
Regarding the phrase "or gives fire," etc., the word "tree" is understood from the context, because it will be stated later that "the tree is destroyed."

And as for the tree: because it is stated in the Canon that "a 'forest-lord' (vanappati) is a tree that is possessed by people and fit for their use," and according to the method explained in the Commentary, one must understand this to refer specifically to trees such as mangoes, breadfruit, and jackfruit—those belonging to humans, fit for human use, and which are indeed guarded and protected.
"Or gives fire" means he kindles a fire by means of theft.
Or: "He strikes a tree all around with a weapon" means that, while cutting the bark of the tree with a weapon such as an axe or a hatchet, he shows a trench all around it.
Or: "He strikes poison called *maṇḍūkakaṇṭaka* into the tree" means that, desiring to destroy the tree by stealth, he introduces the poison named *maṇḍūkakaṇṭaka* into the tree.
"By whatever means" (yena vā tena vā) means by any method whatsoever, whether that which has been mentioned or that which has not been mentioned. "The tree perishes" (vinassati):
having given fire to it, it is consumed; like a heap of grain or a jar of oil, it will perish right where it stands, even without being moved from its place.
The phrase "it burns" (ḍayhati) is said with reference to the act of "giving fire. "It perishes" (vinassati) refers to the remaining applications, such as pricking it with frog-thorns and so forth.
It should be understood as being spoken with intentional meaning (*sandhāya vutta*): "If one cuts with a thieving mind, for every blow there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
when one blow has not yet reached [the target], there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*); when that blow has reached it, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
This is because the offense entailing defeat is established through the displacement from its place. Here, the phrase "in the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathāya*) is to be supplied.
However, as for the *pārājika* offense that has come down in the recitation (*pāṭhāgata*), it is also indicated by way of exclusion (*pārisesato*).

Since neither the word expressive of it nor a summarizing statement exists here, the detailed exposition (*vinicchaya*) found there is not mentioned here either, even though it is authoritative. This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Forest-dweller (*Vanappatikathāvaṇṇanā*).

186–7. Regarding the explanation of "stolen goods" (*haraṇaka*) as stated [in the Vinaya]: "Stolen goods means another person's goods that are being carried away. If one touches them with a thieving intent, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one makes them move, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*). If one causes them to be removed from their place, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).

In this passage, regarding the phrase "if one causes them to be removed from their place, there is an offense entailing defeat," the term "place" (*ṭhāna*) refers to the various locations such as the head, etc., which were previously mentioned.
In order to show the determination as it appears in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), he says: "for one who takes [it] after having cut and having untied.

Because actions (*kriyā*) have objects, the word "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text. "Having cut" refers to necklaces and the like; "having untied" refers to earrings and the like.
Regarding the phrase "at the mere moment of being untied from the head, etc.," the words "in the ornament" are used here for the purpose of specifying that very same object.
It should be understood according to the singular case ending of the word *bhūmī*. Regarding "pulling toward" (*ākaḍḍhana*) and "pulling away" (*vikaḍḍhana*):

here, taking "pulling toward" (*ākaḍḍhana*) to mean pulling in the direction of oneself, it is the drawing [something] near to oneself; taking "pulling away" (*vikaḍḍhana*) to mean pulling in the opposite direction, it is the drawing [something] away from that.
188–9. *Valayanti*: that which reaches the hand, being curved or smooth. *Kaṭakampi*: even a bracelet;

this refers to that which has been fashioned by joining together many curves, whether or not bubbles and such [flaws] were shown during its making. *Aggabāhuṃ*: the upper arm, starting from the elbow.
*Aparāparaṃ cāreti*: he moves it here and there. Alternatively, the reading is *sāreti*, which has the same meaning. That...
"A bracelet or a bangle. "He makes it go into space" means he makes it go into space so that it does not touch his hand from any direction whatsoever.

Regarding the case where one makes a bracelet go into space without touching it from any direction at the foot of a tree into which the treasure-bracelet has been inserted, there is a *pārājika* offense.
Why is it said here, "he guards it"? He says: "Because [the object] is animate," and so forth.
“*Idaṃ*” refers to bracelets and anklets.
By the phrase “a cloth worn,” even a robe (*cīvara*) is included. “Of another” means of the owner of the cloth. “Another” also refers to the owner of the cloth.
“That” refers to the cloth one is wearing oneself that is being snatched away by a thief. Out of shame, [one acts] suddenly...
“He does not let go” means that out of shame he does not relinquish it very quickly.

191. The construction is: “Even a thief drags it away; another person also drags it away. That “other person” is someone other than the thief; the meaning is the owner of the cloth. “Of the other” means of the owner of the cloth. 192.

Regarding the reading “he should cause it to be moved from its place,” by the word *ṭhāna* (place), it is meant that it is to be taken away from the head or other places included therein; thus, it is called “the taking away” (*haraṇaka*).

Having shown that there is a *pārājika* offense by causing the removal of merchandise such as ornaments already mentioned, [the author] now states that for one who carries away that same merchandise along with the thief, the "removal from its place" (*ṭhānācāvana*)—by taking it away from the location where the thief was standing—is also included within the phrase "he should cause it to be removed from its place" (*ṭhānā cāveyya*).
To show the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) regarding this as well, he says: "The thief together with the merchandise," and so forth. [This refers to] the merchandise.
*Sa-bhaṇḍahārakaṃ*: "One who carries goods" (*bhaṇḍahāraka*) refers to a thief, a robber, or the like;

"together with him" means together with those living beings—men, women, and so forth—who are going along having taken ornaments, clothing, and other such items. *Bhaṇḍaṃ*: because these are being carried away by them, it refers to the goods consisting of clothing, jewelry, and so forth.

*Nentassa*: the word-division is "nento assa" (of one who is leading away). *Nento*: having caused [the victim] to move from the place where they stood, [leading them] toward the direction desired by oneself.
"Causing [the thief] to go. The construction is to be supplied with the phrase: "When his first foot has passed, he incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.

"Of him" (*assa*) refers to this thief who carries away the goods. When the first foot has passed—that is, when the thief has gone toward the direction intended by the thief from the direction where one must first go oneself—having incurred the *thullaccaya* offense, the construction is:
"When the second [foot] has passed, he would be fallen (*cuto*)."
193. If one with the intention to steal, having threatened [the owner], causes another's property to fall from their hand, the construction of the sentence is as follows:
at the very moment the property is released from the other's hand, for the one who caused it to fall by means of the threat, there is defeat (parājaya).
"At the very moment the property is released" means at the instant even a hair’s breadth of the property has been released from the hand.
194. *Athāpi* means *atha vā* (or else). Regarding the phrase *parikappetvā pātāpeti vā* (“or causes it to be thrown down after having made a supposition”), the construction is as follows:

if one causes it to be thrown down after making a supposition—either by threatening with the thought, “I will take whatever pleases me,” or by specifying, “If it is of such a kind, I will take it”—it is a *dukkaṭa*.
It is stated that for the thief who has thus caused the goods to be thrown down, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the act of touching (*āmasana*) them.
195. "Yathāvatthu" means in accordance with the value of the goods; the intention is that there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
"Even when discarded" means even when the goods, being carried away by himself out of fear and terror after he has been recognized as a thief, are abandoned.
He said, "There is no fault," meaning that one should not consider it a *pārājika* (defeat) because the moving from that place was caused by the thief himself. "Stay, stay! [is the command].
The intention is that when it has been stated [that the object was discarded], the discarding occurred without his command, and thus there is no offense for him in that regard.
However, for one who speaks in such a manner, there is indeed an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) because it constitutes a preliminary act of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
196. "That" refers to that discarded article. "In its recovery" means in the recovery of that discarded article.
It is a *pārājika* offense. To the question of when it becomes a *pārājika*, he says: "when the owner has departed with attachment.
By contrast, he shows that there is no fault for one who takes what has been abandoned and left without an owner, provided there is no intention to steal.
(197) To show the manner in which there is no *pārājika* offense even for one taking [an object] while the owner still possesses attachment, he says: "for one who takes."
In the preceding verse, the word "that" (taṃ) is carried over here.

"Taking it with the perception that it is one's own" means taking that object—which was abandoned out of fear upon hearing the words "Stop! Stop!"—with the perception that it belongs to oneself. "In the taking" means on account of the taking with the perception of ownership;
because of taking the goods with the perception of ownership for one's own sake, the monk incurs the offense of theft (avahāra).
The intention is that he "guards. Therefore, it says: "But he guards [the object] upon taking it. The construction is: "but there is an obligation to pay for the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it extends the application of the phrase "he guards upon taking it.
198–9. "Having laid down the burden" means: "What use have I for this goods? It is better to protect my life alone."
Having become homeless. Therefore he said: "Frightened, one flees from thieves. Here, "from thieves" (*corā*) is used in the ablative case to express the cause.

Regarding the phrase "taking," there is an ellipsis of the word "that" (*taṃ*); thus the meaning is "that goods which were abandoned in that manner. "An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of taking away":
even though the object itself is blameless, an offense of wrong-doing occurs by virtue of the intent to steal; in the absence of the intent to steal, there is no offense of wrong-doing either.
"It does not exist" is what is meant. Regarding the term "āharāpente," the locative case is used here to indicate a characteristic state (*bhāvalakkhaṇa*);
the meaning is: "while that owner of the goods is having [the items] brought back.

As for why there is defeat (*parājika*) both for taking an object abandoned by one who has no attachment and for one who does not pay the value of the goods, he says "tassā" and so forth. "In others" refers to the other commentaries, such as the *Mahāpaccarī*.
Commentary on the Story of the Thief (Haraṇaka-kathā-vaṇṇanā). 201.
Regarding the story of the deposit (*upanidhi*), the construction is: "He utters a conscious lie (*sampajāna-musāvāda*) saying, 'I will not take it.
This refers to a commodity that was entrusted in private by someone with the words, "Please store this my property and return it to me," which is later [refused] by the owner.
When it was said, "Give me that goods," he spoke a conscious lie (*sampajānamusāvāda*) in order to avoid giving them up, saying, "I will not take them.
This is the meaning. Regarding the statement "I take them" (*gaṇhāmi*), he had already taken them; for this is an expression of the past used in the present tense.

As for the question, "Why is a *dukkaṭa* offense mentioned in the scope of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) 'In the case of a conscious lie, there is a *pācittiya*'?," he replies: "Because it is preceded by taking what is not given," and so forth.

In this context, "having taken stealing as a preliminary act" means that stealing serves as a precursor by way of being an associated preliminary effort (*sahapayoga*), not by way of being a prior preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga*).
For there is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the place of an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for a prior preliminary effort of stealing. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"Because it is a preliminary effort of stealing."
202. *Etassa* means "in the vicinity of this. *Kiṃ nu dassati* means "will he perhaps give? *Vimatuppāde* is the locative case used for the cause (the reason for the arising of doubt).
*Tassa* refers to that monk in whose presence the item was deposited. 203. *Tasmiṃ* refers to that monk in whose presence it was deposited.
*Dāne nirussāhe* means when the owner of the goods deposited with him lacks the inclination toward giving—that is, when he has abandoned his responsibility, thinking, "I will not give this now."
The intended meaning is "whoever. For this very reason, he said: "upon the laying down of the burden by both. "The other" refers to the owner of the goods.
"Burden" refers to the effort [thinking], "I shall take it by whatever means possible. "Lays down" means he should lay it down.

Regarding the phrase "or desiring to take it with the mind," there is a textual supplement here: "whoever of her... The word *ca* is used in the sense of the particle *api*. "Whoever" refers to the thief.

The construction is: even for that thief who, though mentally unwilling to give, says with his mouth, "I will give. Alternatively, in the phrase "being unwilling to give," there is an ellipsis of the word "having been" (*hutvā*).
This is the stated meaning. The word "even" (*eva*) connects with the term "defeat" (*parājaya*). The construction is:
even for one who, being mentally unwilling to give, says with his mouth, "I will give," there is indeed defeat when the owner relinquishes his responsibility.
Commentary on the Story of the Deposit (Upanidhikathāvaṇṇanā).

205. Regarding "a customs house": as for the phrase "a customs house is that which has been established by the king on a mountain ridge, at a river crossing, or at the gate of a village," which appears in the Canon;
and regarding the commentary passage: "They collect the tax from there... they cause it to disappear."
“Nirutta” refers to a place such as a mountain range that has been designated by kings or other local lords with the instruction:

“From this point onward, when goods are being transported, such-and-such a portion must be taken as the royal share. “Outside” (bahī) means outside the boundary established for the purpose of collecting taxes.
“Drops [the goods]” (pātetī): here, the phrase “with a thieving mind” is understood from the context. “Worthy of the king” (rājārahaṃ)...

The word "goods" (*bhaṇḍa*) is the remainder of the text. From whatever source of goods, if a portion worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas must be given to the owner—such as a king or others—the meaning is that one with a thieving mind throws such goods so that they fall outside.
Regarding the phrase "it certainly falls," here too the word "that" (*taṃ*) is the remainder of the text, and [the word] "goods" (*bhaṇḍa*) [is the remainder].
This is obtained from the treatise (*pakaraṇa*). Just as that stolen goods, once thrown, falls entirely outside; so it is with that article of property as soon as it is released from the hand.
Regarding the phrase "it certainly falls," he says "that [article] on the tree," etc., in order to show the contrast (*byatireka*).
The construction is: "that article of property, which was thrown out for the purpose of stealing, having been struck back. There is also the reading "even when tossed by the wind."
It should be accepted. Or, "blown by the wind" (*vātakkhitto*) should be understood as a grammatical change of gender (*liṅgavipallāso*).

207. "Afterwards" means having waited for a short while at the place where it fell; by this, he shows that even with merely a short delay, the act accomplished through effort is indeed completed, and thus the cause for a *pārājika* offense is fully established. Therefore he said, "there may be a *pārājika*. 208.
By the words "having stood," etc., [he shows that] even if one does not wait long at the place where it fell, but departs, then even elsewhere than the external place where it fell—

By the phrase "having delayed," he shows that the application of casting outside has been successfully performed and is indeed accomplished, thereby demonstrating the establishment of the cause for a *pārājika* offense.

For this very reason, he says, "defeat. By the phrase "not remaining," and so forth, he shows the futility of the application due to not delaying anywhere at all. For this very reason, he says, "he protects."
209. This is the statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*. 210.
"Or he rolls it himself" means that, standing inside [the boundary], he himself rolls a place lower than the outside boundary with his hand, his foot, or a staff.
"Without stopping" means as soon as it has begun to roll, without stopping anywhere inside. "While it is rolling" means...
"Moving forward": "Gone" means that even by the distance of a hair’s breadth outside the boundary, there has been the mere act of crossing beyond the boundary.
211. The construction is: "If that article, having stopped and stopped while inside, goes outside. The meaning is:
if it goes outside the boundary after having repeatedly stopped within the boundary. "He protects" means [he protects] by the very first turning back from the movement while within the boundary.

The intention is this: because the momentum of that monk’s effort has ceased, and because no further cause for its cessation can be found beyond that point, and because he himself has already departed, that object which has not yet reached the boundary protects the monk who instigated it from the offense.
"Placed with a pure mind" means: "When it is placed in this way, it will roll along and go."
Without the intention to steal, but with the thought, "I will simply set it aside," if one places the object by letting it roll down toward a lower spot outside the boundary, it is permissible.

"It is permissible" means it is permissible because no offense has been committed. This refers to a case where the goods themselves, having become inclined toward a lower spot, roll and go beyond the boundary on their own.
"Permissible" means it is permissible due to the non-commission of an offense.

212. "Going" refers to those who go by themselves, without the instigation of a thief. "That" refers to the merchandise subject to duty, consisting of more than five māsakas or at least five māsakas, which is due to the king.

The construction is: "Even when it has been removed, there is no offense. This is because the mere intention to steal is not a constituent factor of the offense, and because there is an absence of bodily or vocal instigation such as that of a driver or the like;
for [the case of] a vehicle or similar object where the goods are placed, [the thief acts] by himself.
The meaning is that because [the thief] has reached the outside boundary and because the goods themselves have gone with him, there is no offense of theft for the monk.
213. "Without an effort" means without the thief’s own exertion. Regarding the statement "there is no theft," the reasoning here is exactly as previously stated. 214.
"A jewel" refers to a precious gem worth a quarter [of a kahāpaṇa] that must be paid as toll; by this qualifying term, whatever else [is similar] is implied.
The goods have indeed been collected. "It may be an offense of defeat (pārājika)" means that the vehicle has been won by oneself; this is the intended meaning.
"In crossing the boundary" means in crossing the designated place where customs duties are collected.
215. "Approved" means authorized by kings [with the decree]: "From such-and-such an amount of goods, such-and-such an amount shall be taken. "The rest is a mere matter of talk" means...
“Having reached a customs station, if one searches for goods but does not find them while the customs officers are sleeping, playing, or absent, there is no offense;
one must pay the value of the goods. Such is the method of the discourse on legal decisions (*vinicchaya-kathā*).

The phrase “similar to the discourse on forest-dwellers” means it is identical to the aforementioned discourse on forest-dwellers, beginning with the words “And he who, having reached a guard post,” and so forth.
“Having placed the meditation subject in mind,
If one were to go thinking of it while distracted by other things, One would arrive at the toll-house.”
"It is indeed a gift for the treasury," and so on;
it is exactly as stated in that manner. The intention is that, because its meaning has already been covered, it will not be examined here.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Customs Duties Collector.

216. Regarding the statement “a living being (*pāṇo*) is said to be a human being,” both from the canonical text (*pāḷi*) and from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) which says, “there is no theft for one who carries off even a free person (*bhujissa*),” it is intended that only a human being who is another’s slave is meant.

To demonstrate this very point, he says “born inside,” and so forth. One born from the womb of a female slave in the house of a male slave is called “born inside” (*antojāta*); or [one acquired] by means of wealth.
"A slave bought for wealth" means one purchased with money. "Or given by someone" means one who has been made a slave and given away by anyone, such as a maternal uncle or an elder.

The term "slave" (*dāsa*) should be connected to each [of the preceding categories]. "Or a slave brought as a captive" (*karamarānīta*) means a so-called slave brought from another territory after plundering it, taken into slavery. For one who carries [such a person] away, there is defeat (*parājaya*).

In this context, the intended meaning is as follows: for touching [the object] with the thought, "I shall steal it by theft," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for causing it to move, one incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya);
and when one causes it to pass even by the breadth of a hair from the place where it was situated, it becomes an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
217. "A free person" (bhujissa) means any human being who is not a slave. "A human being" (mānusa) means a sentient being of human birth. "Deposited" (āṭhapita) means placed down as a pledge.
218. "Among those born in the house and so forth"—that is, among any of the slaves. "Desiring to escape" means desiring to cause [him] to flee, or desiring to drive him out.
Alternatively, the meaning may be understood as: having lifted that slave up with both arms, [thinking], "This one desires to escape.
"With both arms" means with both hands. "From the place where he stands" (*taṃ-ṭhitaṭṭhānato*): his standing place is *taṃ-ṭhitaṭṭhāna*; from that, *tato taṃ-ṭhitaṭṭhānato*.
This was stated in order to show that the meaning "a place where one stands by means of one's own body" should not be accepted.
"He moves something" means he causes even as much as a hair-tip to reach another location than that. In the phrase "or with the arms," the word *vā* (or) refers to a subsequent alternative method;
it should be construed as "or he moves [it]."
219. "Having threatened" (*tajjetvā*) means having intimidated by means of words that cause fear, or by a pretext, or by a gesture;
the connection is with the phrase "of him who leads [her] away. Regarding the phrase "step-by-step" (*padavārato*), the construction is:

"there are offenses such as *thullaccaya* connected with each step. The meaning is: there is an offense of *thullaccaya* connected with the first step, and there is an offense of *pārājika* connected with the second step.
220. "In the case of hands, etc."—by the word "etc.," hair, clothing, and so forth are included. "Him" refers to the slave.

"Even while dragging" means even while pulling. "Defeat" (pārājika): because the phrase "per step" is understood to follow, the meaning is that there is a *thullaccaya* in the first step, and when the second step is exceeded, it is a *pārājika*. This is the method: "Per step, there are *thullaccaya*s and so forth."
The method of explanation is as stated: "There are offenses. 221. *Vegasā* means "with speed";
it is said that by the thief's words, one proceeds with a forceful momentum of movement devoid of any specific action to be performed. By this, he shows the reason for the state of non-offense.

222. *Saṇikaṃ* means "slowly," i.e., with a sluggish pace. *Vadati* means he speaks such words as "Go! Depart! Flee! and so forth. *Sopi ca* refers to the one who was addressed in this way while traveling at a slow pace.
223. "Having fled" means having gone away, abandoning her husband. "Another place" means a location other than that which is under the control of her husband;
it may be a market town (*sāpaṇa*) or a village situated along a trade route (*vīthisannivesa*). "From there" means from the village or similar place where she entered after fleeing.
"Him" refers to that slave who entered [the place] after fleeing.

Commentary on the Discussion of Poisonous Snakes (Pāṇakathāvaṇṇanā). 224. “By theft” means with a mind of theft. “A snake-basket” means a box for a snake’s bedding. “As it was” refers to a grave offense (thullaccaya). “From its place” means from the location where the snake-box was situated. “Moving it” means when it has moved even by the measure of a hair’s breadth.
225. “A basket” means a snake-box. “Having opened” means having uncovered it. “From the bottom of the basket” means from the inner floor of the box. “At the tail” means at the end of the tail.
226. *Ghaṃsitvā* means having caused [the snake] to touch the side of the basket. *Sappakaraṇḍassa mukhavaṭṭito* means from the opening of the mouth of the snake-basket.

The construction is: "at the mere mention of its tail. 227. *Nāmato* means by name; it is said that he spoke the name. *Pakkosantassa* means of one who is calling out. *Tassa* refers to the caller. 228.

*Tathā* means having opened the basket. The construction is: "of one who, making the sounds of frogs and mice, calls out by name. By the word *vā*, [the author] includes such acts as scattering parched grain and striking with arrows.
229. "They look into the opening of a snake’s basket. And likewise for one who acts [in this way]:
that is, for one who calls out after making the perception of a frog, or the perception of a mouse, or by scattering parched grain, or by snapping his fingers, or by calling out the name.
"By whatever means" means by whichever method has been mentioned, or by any other.

230. "He does not call" means that having applied [the rule] according to the method already stated, he does not call by name. "Of him" refers to the monk who has opened the mouth of his basket. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning those without feet (*apadaka*).
231. "In an elephant" (*hatthin*): this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.

232. *Sālāyan* means in an elephant stable (*hatthisālā*). A "site" (*vatthu*) is that wherein one dwells; it refers to a royal palace. "Within that" means within the site, i.e., within the royal residence.
"In the courtyard" (*aṅgaṇe*) means in the inner royal courtyard. The word "also" (*pi*) includes "within the city," even though it was not explicitly mentioned.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in "and the site" (*vatthu ca*), he combines the courtyard. "The entire courtyard is the place."
This is said with reference to a courtyard area suitable for elephants to roam; "the entire hall" (sakalasālā) should be understood [in this sense]. 233. Regarding the phrase "of one not bound":
this is stated in relation to the aforementioned hall, royal residence, and courtyard. For an elephant that is not bound, the entire hall and so forth constitute its domain;
the meaning is that if it exceeds those limits, there is a displacement from its proper place. The particle *hi* is used here for emphasis.
In the phrase “baddhassa hi,” the meaning should be understood as a qualification; that is to say, “but of one who is bound.

Furthermore, “of one who is bound” means of one who is present within a hall or similar structure. “And the place where he stands” refers to the place where he stands in the hall or similar structure, meaning the spot trodden upon by his four feet.
“And the binding” refers to the collar on the neck or the fetters on the two hind legs.

Or, in both cases, there is the place of binding. "Therefore" means because six or five places are obtained—namely, the place where it stands and the binding itself; therefore. "Of those places. Regarding "should have [it] made":

here, by implication, the word "offense" (*āpatti*) is understood. "Taking" refers to one who takes it by theft from an elephant stable or similar location. "Should have [it] made" refers to the touching.
It is a *dukkaṭa* offense; by counting the number of places where [the elephant] is moved, there are *thullaccaya* offenses for each of the preceding places until the final place.
At the final place, even if it moves the distance of a single hair’s breadth, one commits a *pārājika* offense—this is the meaning.

234. "The standing place" refers to the area covered by the four feet when stepped upon; this is stated with reference to an unbound elephant. Regarding a bound elephant, the determination is the same as that which was stated for those bound in stables and so forth, and thus it is not repeated here as its meaning has already been established.
235. "One place" means merely the place where he was lying. "In that" refers to the elephant. "His" refers to the bhikkhu. Regarding horses, buffaloes, and so forth—both bipeds and multi-peds.
236. "This same method is to be understood; there is nothing further to be said"—this is the construction. In this context, "turaṅgā" means horses. "Mahisā" means buffaloes.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is an inclusion of quadrupeds such as cows, camels, donkeys, and so on. "There is nothing further to be said" means...
The various locations for unbound beds, saddles, and so forth—such as the royal palace, the arena, or outside the city—are not mentioned because they are similar to what has already been stated.
However, regarding a horse that has been bound and set down: if it is bound at the four feet, there are eight locations according to the number of bindings and the hooves;
if it is also bound at the mouth, there are nine locations; if it is bound only at the mouth, [there is one location].

"Five places" refers to the classification of places: first, the classification of places consisting of the four feet together with the points where they were bound when [animals] such as deer and pigs were tied and stationed upon four-footed grounds;
second, the classification of places obtainable in the same manner when cattle and buffaloes are tied; and third, the classification of places when [animals] are made to enter locations such as pits.
In the case of one who calls out after removing or not removing wooden pegs at the doors, or after mentioning or not mentioning a name;
or of one who entices by showing branches, broken twigs, grass, and so forth, whether having called out or not;
or of one who departs under threat—the specific distinctions applicable to the case of the snake-basket should be understood here as well, in all instances and variations of the situation.
In many peripheral cases there is a grave offense (thullaccaya), and in the central case it is a defeat (pārājika), similar to what has been stated;

since this entire analysis is already understood by the phrase "the same method applies," and because there is no specific distinction to be made regarding anything not brought forward, it is said: "there is nothing further to be said."

“Bipeds” refers to humans—as stated in the Canon: “Bipeds are those born with feathered wings”—as well as beings such as peacocks and others with feathered wings, bats and others with leathery wings, and bees and others with membranous wings.
“Many-footed” means those many-footed beings mentioned in the Canon: “Many-footed are the scorpions, centipedes, and *uccāliṅga* insects. This is the meaning.
To this extent, having shown twenty-five of the thirty-two analytical matrices (mātikā) mentioned in the word-commentary for the purpose of burning away even a trace of opportunity for evil monks,
[the author] first presents the discourse on the triad of matrices— namely, the act of appointment,
the making of a sign, and the making of a gesture— which serve as the preliminary equipment for the analysis of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) in the remaining five matrices.
Standing at the point of viewing the twenty-five modes of theft:
"Prior agreement, as well as mutual consultation;
making a signal, giving a hint, and the five beginning with prior preparation."

"By this [term] it is included": having set that aside, regarding the two discourses on "the spy" (*ocarako*) and "the guard of the privy" (*oṇirakkho*), because the discourse on the spy involves the application of an instruction (*āṇatti*), and because the displacement from one's place being performed by the guard of the privy occurs either through physical action (*sāhatthika*) or through an instruction, it too is included in the pentad of physical actions under the phrase "both physical and instructional.
(*Sāhatthāṇattiko ceva*) Thus it is said in the Pentad on Physical Action.

It should be understood that those two [cases] were not mentioned because they were already included in the first [category], and because they are included in the commentaries on the *Thalaṭṭha* and *Vehāsa* offenses.
In this context, the person who steals goods and then points them out is called an "ocāraka" (a scout), as stated in the Canon: "An ocāraka is one who, having scouted the goods, reports them."
It should be understood as follows: "He spies" (*ocarati*) means he is a spy (*ocarako*); what is meant is that having gone here and there, he enters within.

Regarding the statement in the Canon, "One called a 'guardian of the deposit' (*oṇirakkho*) is one who guards goods brought [to him]," this "guardian of the deposit" should be understood as the protector of another's goods placed with him for a short time.
He guards what has been deposited (*oṇitaṃ*), thus he is a guardian of the deposit (*oṇirakkho*); he is one by whom [the goods] have been deposited by another.

When one says, "Venerable sir, please look after this goods brought to your dwelling for a moment while I go and perform such-and-such a task," and the other protects it, that is the designation for this.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of two, three, or four verses.

237. By way of the phrase, “For one who takes what is not given in five ways, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika),” etc., [the author] speaks the words beginning with “of others” in order to include the five factors as they appear in the Pāḷi.
Therein, by the phrase “wealth belonging to others,” the fact that it belongs to another person is indicated;
by the phrase “having recognized it as belonging to others,” the awareness of its state of being dependent on another is indicated.
By the term "valuable," the fact that it is worth one *pāda* or more than one *pāda* is indicated; by the term "with a thieving mind," the state of having a thieving intention is indicated;
and by the term "removes from its place," the possession of one of the twenty-five modes of theft is indicated.
Thus, the inclusion of these five factors should be understood here.

238. Having thus summarized the determination of the thirty matrices (*mātikā*), he now states "there is no offense" (*anāpatti*) and so forth, in order to collect the section on non-offenses as it appears in the Canon (*pāḷi*) according to the method beginning with:

"There is no offense for one who perceives [it as his own] when taking by trust, when taking for a limited time, when taking what belongs to the departed, when taking what belongs to animals, or when perceiving it as refuse-rags (*paṃsukūla*). Therein, "for one who perceives" (*sasaññissa*) means even that which belongs to another...
“*Sasantakan*” (one’s own property): the phrase “there is no offense for one who takes it with the perception that it is [his] own” should be applied in all instances.
When the owners see what has been taken in this manner and ask for it back, if he does not give it, there is a *pārājika* offense due to both parties abandoning their responsibility.
Regarding “*tiracchānapariggaha*” (the possession of animals): this refers to an object possessed by animals. For even if it be a male or female *nāga*, *garuḷa*, *māṇavaka*, or *māṇavikā*...
It is stated that there is no offense if people sit with their stalls set out for trade and a monk takes what belongs to them with a thieving mind.
