Furthermore, there is no fault in preventing wild animals such as lions, tigers, leopards, and the like from eating their prey first, so that after releasing it, they might injure themselves; rather, one should prevent them from eating even a little.
There is no fault. It is permissible to cause animals such as those in an army or other wild creatures to release whatever forage they have seized. For this is said in the Commentary:
“It is permissible to seize [the food] even from an army or similar group after causing them to drop it while they are carrying away their provisions.

In the same way, it should be understood that it is permissible to cause frogs and other creatures seized by the *dhamma-nidēḍḍubha* and other predators to be released for the sake of protecting their lives.

"Taking on loan": for one who takes something on loan with the intention, "I will return it," if the owner of the goods—whether an individual or a group—should give permission, saying, "You may take it yourselves," it is permissible. If they do not give permission, he should not take it; it must be returned.
If he does not return it, there is a *pārājika* offense through the relinquishing of responsibility by both parties. However, as for what belongs to the Saṅgha, it must simply be restored.
"It is permissible," so it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
Regarding "receiving on trust": "Monks, I allow you to receive on trust from one endowed with five qualities:
he is a kinsman, he is a friend, he has been spoken to [with confidence], he is living, and he is pleased when the gift is taken."

The determination regarding the taking of property belonging to one endowed with five factors on the basis of trust, as it appears in the Pāli, should be understood from the commentary on the aforementioned Sutta.
As it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "In that context, 'a person seen' (*sandiṭṭha*) means a mere acquaintance;
'a person befriended' (*sambhatta*) means a firm friend; 'a person addressed' (*ālapita*) means [one who says], 'My property...'"
When told, "Take whatever you wish; there is no need for permission when taking," [the meaning is:
"He lives" means that even while lying on his back in a state of inactivity, he does not reach the point where the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is cut off.
And "he is delighted when it is taken" means that his mind becomes joyful when it is taken; by one who knows that such a person will be "delighted when it is taken," [one may take it].
It is permissible to take [the goods]. These five factors have been stated by way of taking them entirely; however, taking on trust succeeds through three factors:
one who is seen, who is living, and who is pleased when the goods are taken; one who is a friend, who is living, and who is pleased when the goods are taken;
and one who has spoken [with him], who is living, and who is pleased when the goods are taken.
However, if someone who is still living is not pleased when [the goods] are taken, then even what was taken by way of a trust from his property must be returned.
When returning it, first, the wealth of the deceased should be given to those who have authority over that wealth, whether they be householders or renunciants.
If he is displeased, the property belonging to him should be given back to him alone. But as for one who, right from the beginning...
Having expressed approval either by speech, saying, "You have done well in taking what belongs to me," or even by a mere thought, one may not later, for any reason, demand it back when angry.
Furthermore, even one who is unwilling to give, but consents in his mind and says nothing, may likewise not demand it back again. Whoever...
However, if it is said, "I have taken or used what belongs to you," and he replies, "Whether it was taken or used,
I have set it aside for some purpose; it is proper that it be restored to its original state," then this person is permitted to have it returned.

Regarding "belonging to the departed" (*petapariggaha*): in this context, those born in the realm of the departed (*pettivisaya*), those who have died and been reborn in that very same state of existence, and the gods of the Four Great Kings and above are called "departed.
The meaning is that there is no offense for one who takes what belongs to them.
For even if Sakka, the king of the gods, were sitting with his market-stalls spread out, and a monk possessed of the divine eye [were to see it]...
Knowing this, it is permissible to snatch and take even a garment worth a hundred thousand coins while the owner is still crying out.
What need is there to mention that there is no fault for one who takes smooth cloth and such from trees and other places for the purpose of worshipping the deities?

There is also no offense for one who takes it with the perception that it is refuse-rag cloth (*paṃsukūla*). Even if it has been taken in that manner, if it belongs to an owner, [one must return it] to the owner.
"It should be given when they cause it to be brought" is to be understood as an indicative mark (*upalakkhaṇa*).

239. "In this regard" refers to the adjudication of the second *pārājika*. By the particle *ca*, in the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated, it encompasses the adjudications of the remaining training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
"It should be stated" means it should be explained at the conclusion, as in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* and other such works. "The adjudication apart from the text" (*pāḷimuttavinicchaya*)—
The analysis concerning origins and so forth, which was not included in the text of each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*), was established by the Elder Upāli and others.

240. "By the single stain of defeat" means that [defilement] has been defeated through the abandonment by eradication, together with its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), by means of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*), which has as its proximate cause the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) produced by the perfections (*pāramitā*) accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of incalculable eons.
By him by whom the various stains of the defilements, such as lust and the rest, have been conquered—he is "one by whom the manifold stains have been conquered.
By that one who has conquered the manifold stains, the second *pārājika* was spoken; and the meaning of this second *pārājika* has been stated by me in brief.
For who indeed is capable of stating its meaning in its entirety, through an excessively detailed method? This is the construction [of the sentence]. Herein—
The word *ca* has the sense of including the first *pārājika*. The word *hi* is used for emphasis;
it indicates that there is no one at all—other than a Tathāgata—who is capable of explaining its meaning in its entirety.
Thus [ends] the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the discussion of the second *pārājika* in the *Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the third *pārājika*.
241–2. Having thus shown the second *pārājika*, which is crowded with such extremely subtle principles, he now says “a human being,” etc., in order to show the third *pārājika*.
Therein, “human being” (*manussajāti*): it is called a “birth” (*jāti*) because it is born; it is the rebirth-linking of the form and formless realms.
One who is born among humans is a “human-born” (*manussajāti*); what is meant is one who possesses a human body, a human being. That is the “human being.”
And here, "among humans" means among those persons designated as humans because of the predominance of wholesome and unwholesome mind.

By the method stated in the word-commentary— "the first consciousness that arises in the mother's womb"— this refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness arising for the first time in the mother's womb,
as well as the triad of aggregates consisting of feeling, perception, and mental formations associated with it, and the [material] phenomena co-nascent with them.
“Just as a drop of ghee-cream, unmixed and clear,

when poured into sesame oil that has been spoken of as having the appearance of color and then shaken after being poured in and lifted out— this is what is called ‘kalala. Thus it was said regarding the fine threads of the birth-hair, when they have been dipped into clear sesame oil or ghee-cream and then shaken.

The thirty material phenomena (rūpa) consisting of the *kalala*—measured by the size of a hanging drop—at the stage of those possessing sex organs (*sabhāvaka*), by way of the decads of body, sex, and base;
and the twenty material phenomena at the stage of those lacking sex organs (*abhāvaka*), by way of the decads of body and base:

this linking of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-paṭisandhi*) is what is understood here as "birth" (*jāti*). By the other word "of whom" (*yassa*), [it is indicated that] "until the time of death, within this interval, this..."

By the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)—"a human being"—the term "being" (*satta*) is understood as the continuum of existence beginning from the first *bhavaṅga* consciousness up to the end of the *bhavaṅga* consciousness proximate to the death-consciousness.
By this, he shows that the human being, from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) onwards, constitutes the basis for an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
"Knowing" means knowing, "This is a being. "Whoever should deprive of life" refers to whichever bhikkhu should separate [the being] from the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
"Should deprive [him] of life" means that one would cut off and obstruct his life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). Therefore, it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"To deprive of life means to cut off and obstruct the life-faculty.
And that life-faculty is twofold, by way of being material (*rūpa*) and immaterial (*arūpa*). Among these, the immaterial life-faculty, because it is without physical form (*aviggaha*),...

It is not an object for intentional effort (*upakkama*). However, because its existence is dependent upon the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*), and because it is cut off at the very same moment that the latter is cut off by the severance of that faculty, both [the past and future] should be included here in a general sense. Yet, the past and future must not be included here, because they do not exist.

Only the present, which is fit to be an object of intentional effort, should be included; and that is threefold, according to the divisions of the moment (*khaṇa*), the continuity (*santati*), and the duration (*addhā*).
In this context, a state that is included within the three moments by way of arising, presence, and dissolution is called "momentary present.

Because it is subject to destruction through its own inherent nature (*sarasabhaṅga*), it does not possess a destruction that is brought about by an external effort or that involves a process of disintegration.
It is like the disappearance of darkness for one who has entered a chamber after standing in the sun, or like the coolness for one who has entered a room after being in the heat.

The continuity of material phenomena produced by a dissimilar temperature, as well as that which exists between the removal of cold and heat, is called "present by way of continuity" (*santati-paccuppanna*).
The continuity of the aggregates occurring in the interval between rebirth-linking and death is called "present by way of duration" (*addhā-paccuppanna*).
In these two cases, there is an occurrence through external intervention; by virtue of that, life is cut off because it becomes a condition for the cessation of the continuity.
The two types of present [phenomena] belonging to the continuity-period (santati-addhā) cease prematurely through the force of an intervention before reaching their predetermined time limit;

therefore, it should be understood that both the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) of the continuity-period and the immaterial life-faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya) which ceases along with its cessation are included here under the term "life" (jīvita).
It is with reference to this very point that the word-commentary (padabhājana) states: "He disrupts the continuity."

Because the state of being a living being (*pāṇa*) constitutes the state of an offense (*āpatti*), it is from this standpoint that the *Aṭṭhakathā* presents the analysis of the living being, the taking of life, the taker of life, and the application of the means of taking life.

Therein, "living being" (*pāṇa*) is, in conventional usage, a sentient being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) that is being cut off, which is expressed by the term "from life" (*jīvitā*).
"Taking of life" (*pāṇātipāta*) is the volition of killing, and that is expressed by the term "should deprive."
The person who takes life is indicated by the word "whoever" (*yo*). As for the application of taking life, it has been stated:
"The Great Seer has described six applications of taking life."
According to this method, because the classification will be explained right here, it should be understood according to that very method to be explained.
The construction is: "He should lay down his weapon against him. "Assa" means "against one who belongs to the human race.

There is an ellipsis of the word "hatthapāse" (within arm's reach). "Arm's reach" means "in close proximity. "Assa" is used in the genitive case to express proximity. "Satthaṃ" (weapon) refers here to the means of taking life.

Those things possessing handles, such as swords and so forth, as well as those lacking handles, such as clubs, spears, javelins, and maces, should be understood by way of illustration through their common characteristic of being instruments.
It is called *sattha* because it cuts (*sasati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*). For this very reason, it is said in the word-commentary:
"Whether it be a sword, or a spear, or a javelin, or a mace, or a stone, or a weapon, or poison, or a rope."
Here, items such as a saw, a knife, or a dagger, which were mentioned previously, are included by the term "weapon" (*sattha*).

"Should place near" means that he should set them down in its vicinity with that very intention, so that it may obtain [the object] for the sake of enjoyment, or so that it may seize it at the desired moment for its own destruction; by this, the method involving stationary objects is demonstrated.
The construction is: "he might speak of the virtue in death. The meaning is that he praises the virtue in death for the sake of death.
This is because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "He shows the disadvantage in living and speaks of the virtue in death.
Thus, by such means as "What is the use of this wretched, miserable life for you, since you do not obtain to eat choice foods? and so forth, [he speaks] for the sake of death.
And speaking in dispraise of life, [he says]: "You, O lay follower, have done what is wholesome and not done what is evil;

death is better for you than life. Having passed away from here, you will dwell in the excellent Nandana grove, resounding with the songs of various birds, filled with rows of noble trees adorned with most fragrant flowers, frequented by throngs of celestial nymphs who move and speak with most delightful grace, and where you will be surrounded by a host of apsarases."

By such means as "you shall wander [in saṃsāra]," while demonstrating the benefits of death for the sake of dying, it is said: "one might speak of the virtue in death. The construction is: "one might teach the means to death.
With the very intention of death, [one might say]: "Take up a weapon, or eat poison..."

"He might die by hanging himself with a rope"—thus he would explain such means of death as those mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) under "taking one's own life," as well as even that which was not mentioned, such as falling into ravines, hells, or precipices. The word-division is "hoti ayam pi";
the particle *api* (also/even) conjoins the two things previously mentioned. It is like a rock split in two, which cannot be joined back together.

"He is one who should be known" (*so ñeyyo*) means that he should be understood as being unable to maintain himself in his present existence due to the two teachings of the Blessed One— the practice (*paṭipatti*) and the penetration (*paṭivedha*)— which are like a stone split in two.
(243) By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "stable and so forth," the two types of application consisting of science (*vijjāmaya*) and supernormal power (*iddhimaya*) are included.
244. *Tattha* means among those six modes of action (*payoga*). *Sahattha* means one’s own hand; that which is produced by it is *sāhatthika*, the mode of action.

Here, the mention of the "hand" is illustrative (*upalakkhaṇa*); therefore, a murderous act accomplished by means of one's own limbs and members, such as the hands and so forth, should be understood as *sāhatthika*.

245. “Having struck him thus, kill him”—this instruction given by one person to another to a bhikkhu is the method known as the *āṇattika* (the method of command). This is the construction. Regarding the term *āṇattiko nayo*: it is simply a command (*āṇatti*) that is *āṇattika*. It is called a *naya* because it leads (*neti*) or sets in motion;
this is a name for the application (*payoga*). 246. “At a distance” means standing at a distance. Regarding the phrase “with something connected to the body”:

here, a part of the body such as the hand is called “the body,” using the name of the whole for its parts, just as one says, “the village is burned. That which is connected to the body, such as a bow and so forth, is what is called “connected.”

Just as "Devadatta" is [abbreviated] as "Datta" by eliding the first member of the compound; the word *vā* is indicated as being elided, meaning "either by means of the body or by means of something connected to the body," which connects with the phrase "the hurling of arrows and so forth. *Vidhānaṃ* means method (*vidhi*), that is, application (*payoga*).
247. "By means of an immovable device" means by means of a device that is immovable, not subject to shifting. "A pit" (*opāta*) is so called because beings fall into it.
"Ādi" (etcetera) refers to things such as the preparation of antidotes and medicines; "opātādayo" (ditches, etc. refers to those [things], and "opātādividhānaṃ" (the preparation of ditches, etc.
refers to the act of digging ditches and so forth. 248.

"Vijjāya" means by means of the science (*vijjā*) known as the death-spells found in the *Atharvaveda*. "Jappanaṃ" means repeating the words again and again in such a way that another person does not hear them.

249. The construction is as follows: "That psychic power (*iddhi*) born of the ripening of karma (*kamma-vipāka*) which is capable of killing is called 'the application consisting of psychic power' (*iddhimaya-payoga*).

It is born from the ripening of karma, hence it is "born of the ripening of karma. This psychic power is described in many ways in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), such as: "the psychic power of the *nāgas*, the psychic power of the *supaṇṇas*, the psychic power of the *yakkhas*," and so forth. Among these, regarding those whose venom has been seen, tasted, or touched:
The supernormal power (*iddhi*) of nāgas should be understood by seeing them, biting, and touching, as well as in their causing harm to others.

The same applies to the rest. "Supernormal power" (*iddhi*) itself is what is meant by "consisting of supernormal power" (*iddhimaya*); however, the application of supernormal power consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*) should not be taken here. For this has been stated in the Commentary:
"Some, however, say that even by means of supernormal power consisting of meditation one can cause harm to others. Together with the causing of harm to others..."
And they maintain that the destruction of supernormal power (*iddhi*) is like the breaking of a water-jar thrown from atop a burning house; however, that is merely their own wish.
Why? Because it does not accord with the categories of wholesome feeling, thought, and the limited triad (*parittattika*), and so forth.
How so? For this so-called supernormal power consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*) is composed of the fourth jhāna and is wholesome within the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*).

And [the remaining factors] are both indeterminate and unwholesome; killing living beings is unwholesome. In the triad of feeling, [the remaining factors] are associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, whereas killing living beings is associated with painful feeling.
In the triad of applied thought, [the remaining factors] are without applied and sustained thought, whereas killing living beings is with applied and sustained thought.
In the triad of limited states, [the remaining factors] are exalted, whereas killing living beings is indeed limited.”
250. *Tattha* means among those six kinds of applications (*payoga*). *Uddeso pi*: "Uddesa" is the act of pointing out;

thus it is said that an application accompanied by that [act] is also called "uddesa," just as in the expression "pierce with a spear. And because it must be stated in this way, it should be understood that the term "anuddesa" (non-pointing-out) is itself an indicator for its opposite.
Here, each one is both an "uddesa" and an "anuddesa"; however, their distinction is as follows:

The construction is: "it is explained as being twofold. Because each one of these six applications is twofold due to the performance of the act of designating (*uddissa*) or not designating (*anuddissa*), their twelvefold division is shown both in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) and in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The intention [of the author] is: "I shall now demonstrate the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) therein."

251. *Bahūsu pi*: among many people. *Tena kammena*: by that action, namely, the action consisting of the giving of a blow. *Bajjhati*: it is bound; the meaning is that it is bound by the fetter of karma, having set aside other karmas in order to lead [the being] to the states of misery (*apāya*).
252. *Pahāre pi*: even upon a blow. *Dehino*: of a person possessing a body (a human being). *Tassa*: of him who has been struck. 253. *Pahaṭamattam vā*: at the very moment of being struck. *Pacchā*:
afterwards, either immediately due to that condition or at a later time. In both cases...
"And by whom it is thought" means even when it is thought by either of two people. "The killer" is the murderer.
"At the mere striking" indicates—by means of the word *matta* (mere)—that at the very moment that blow capable of causing death is received, and thus even prior to death.
And among the many blows given for the purpose of death and for other purposes, [the offense occurs] by means of the blow given specifically for the purpose of death.

Whenever one dies, the offense of *pārājika* occurs at the very moment the blow is delivered. It is stated that if one should die through the force of a blow given with the intention of not causing death, there is no offense.

254. "Two modes of action" (*payoga*) refers to two modes: those performed by one's own hand and those by command, which are further divided into the categories of directed (*uddissa*) and undirected (*anuddissa*) actions.
255. *Karaṇassa* means of the action. *Viseso* means diversity. *Āṇattiniyāmakā* means those which determine and establish the command;

thus they are "command-determiners. 256. *Tattha* means among those six modes of command-determination. By the word *ādi* ("etcetera") in the phrase *yobbanādi*, specific states such as youth, stability, dullness, playfulness, old age, and so forth, are included.

257. What is that weapon (*sattha*) which is indicated in the matrix (*mātikā*)? *Sattamāraṇaṃ*: it is called *sattamāraṇaṃ* because beings are killed by means of it; it refers to instruments of slaughter such as the sword and so forth.
258. "Piercing" (*vijjhana*) means piercing with arrows and the like. "Splitting" (*bhedana*) means dividing into two parts with saws and the like.
"Cutting" (*chedana*) means dividing into two parts with swords and the like. "Beating" (*tāḷana*) means striking with clubs and the like.

"Of such kinds as these" (*evamādividha*) means of such types as these. "Many" (*aneka*) means numerous varieties. The meaning is that the distinction of the instrument is the distinction of the action.

259–60. Regarding the statement “Having struck [him] from the front, kill him,” which was spoken by the commander, the construction is: “by that person thus commanded, [he was] killed from behind,” and so forth.
In this context, “the object-instruction is a misdirection” means that the misdirection regarding the object is shown by the passage beginning with “that which [was said] ‘kill him’...

from there. The misdirection regarding the instruction is shown by the passage beginning with “from the front... having been killed. The “root-person” (mūlaṭṭha) is the commander. The “root” (mūla) is—
For the issuing of an order is in accordance with the prior action; thus, "standing there" refers to the one who is at the root [of the act].

Having shown by this that there is no offense for the sender in the case of a misunderstanding (*visaṅketa*), he says "the object," etc., to show that when there is no failure in the communication (*saṅketa*), both incur a *pārājika* offense. When the person is killed without having missed that object, for both... [etc.]
"Uttered," "as commanded," and "having killed"... [etc.]... the construction is "uttered. "When the matter has been killed" is obtained by implication (*sāmatthiyā*).

"Of both" refers to the one who commands and the one who is commanded. "At the proper time" means without exceeding the moment of the command by the commander and the moment of the killing by the one commanded.
Bondage is *bandha*; bondage through karma is *kammabandha*. Now...
It is called *bandha* (bond) because one is bound by it; thus, karma itself is the bond, which is *kammabandha*. 264. *Visaṅketo na* means there is no discrepancy;
the meaning is that for both [the past and future], the bond of karma alone constitutes the delimitation according to their respective times.

265. *Sabbaso* means in all divisions of time; alternatively, it is connected as "it should be understood in every way. *Sabbaso* means in every manner. *Vibhāvinā* means by the wise person (*paṇḍita*); for he is so called because he makes the meaning manifest (*vibhāveti*).
“‘Standing in this village’—this was said for the purpose of identifying that [person], not to establish a restriction regarding the location at the moment of death;
therefore, even after saying ‘standing anywhere,’ he stated, ‘there is no ambiguity regarding him. ‘His’ refers to the commander.
Alternatively, the reading is ‘tattha,’ meaning ‘in that command. ‘Kill the enemy standing in the village itself’—this is with emphasis.”

If one who has been commanded kills someone standing in the forest—having been told with a restrictive qualification, "Kill the enemy standing in the forest itself"—the construction is that he kills someone standing in the village.

Some manuscripts write, "By a bhikkhu, with a restrictive [qualification]," but not taking that, the reading "In the forest, or with a restrictive [qualification]" alone should be accepted. *Visaṅketa* means that the convention, namely the rule of the command, has departed from it.
269. *Sabbadesūsu* means in all places, such as villages, forest clearings, courtyards, houses, and so forth.

*Bhedato* means from diversity. 270. Regarding the phrase *“But kill with a weapon,”* the construction is: when someone is commanded by anyone [to kill], there is no discrepancy in the offense if he kills with whatever weapon [is used]. 271–2.
In the phrase *“For by this sword...”* here, the particle *hi* is for the purpose of completing the meter (*padapūraṇe*). If one is told, “You shall kill with this sword,” [and he uses] another...

The construction is as follows: if one kills with a sword, or if, being told, "Kill this enemy with this edge of the sword," he kills that enemy with the other edge, or kills him with the hilt (*tharu*), or kills him with the point (*tuṇḍa*), then even though he has killed him in such a way, it is indeed a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).
"With the hilt" means with the pommel of the sword. "With the point" means with the tip of the sword. "Or a breach of the agreement" [is the phrase].
This is a statement for the purpose of showing that there is no *pārājika* offense simply because of a failure in the agreement (*saṅketa*).

273. "In all types of weapons" means here in the general category of all striking instruments, such as those not specifically mentioned—namely, the *karapālikā* (a type of knife), the *churikā* (a small sword), and so forth. "Specifically" means by way of distinction.
274. "By another" means by the monk. "He" refers to the one who was commanded. "If he kills him while he is sitting, there is no breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*)"—this is the meaning.
Because it was not stated with such restriction as "Kill him only while he is walking," there is no confusion for one who kills him even when he is sitting,

thinking "it is that very same person. Since speaking without a restriction is said to cause one to perceive [the person] as such, the intention is that it does not determine the posture (iriyāpatha).

275–6. Having shown the absence of a convention when there is no restriction, he now says “only while sitting,” etc., to show the lack of convention regarding different postures when there is a restriction.
If one is told, “Kill him only while he is sitting,” and kills him while he is walking, it should be known as a breach of convention.
If one is told, “Kill him only while he is walking,” and kills him while he is sitting, it is a breach of convention.
"Should be known" is the connection [of the sentence]. It is with reference to this very sequence of connections that he says "in due order.
277. "Having pierced" means having pierced with arrows and so forth.
278. "Having cut" means having cut with swords and so forth. "Again, that" refers to the application.
279. *Karaṇesu* means in specific actions such as piercing and so forth. 280–1.

Having thus far shown the exposition of the determiner of the command (*āṇatti-niyāmaka*), he now says “long,” etc., in order to show the possible ambiguity (*visaṅketa*) that may also occur by way of gender, such as the long [vowel] and so on:
“‘Kill the long one... and so on, up to ‘the thick one,’ he commands without having specified.”

According to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), even without the word "only" (*eva-kāra*), if someone is commanded with the unrestricted instruction, "Kill the long one," and that person who was thus commanded kills anyone of that kind, there is no discrepancy in the agreement (*visaṅketa*);

the construction is that for both there is defeat (*parājaya*). In this same way, the construction should be applied individually to all the terms such as "the short one" (*rassa*) and so forth. The phrase "without restricting" (*aniyametvā*) refers to the absence of a discrepancy in the agreement.
This is the demonstration of the cause. The particle *eva* is a rhetorical ornament. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it refers to the application of the act of commanding.

Because it is stated that "there is defeat for both," the term "anyone else of such a kind" indicates, by way of this expression, any human being other than the commander who possesses the aforementioned characteristics at the specified moment.
If the commander, having given the command, kills himself, the commander dies having incurred an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); as for the one commanded...

It is a *pārājika*. When an order has been given by the commander specifically for himself, if the one commanded kills another such person without knowing [the specific identity], the commander is released because the location was not specified; the other is bound by the deed.
However, if he gives the order after specifying the location, saying, "Kill such a person sitting in such-and-such a night-quarters or day-quarters," [then both are involved].

In that regard, if another person is killed by the one who gave the order, there is a *pārājika* offense for both. If he is killed outside of that [designated] area, the karmic consequence falls upon the killer alone.

If the one who gave the order gives the command specifically targeting himself, and the other kills him right there, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the one who gave the order, and a *pārājika* offense for the one who carried out the command.
If he kills him elsewhere, the original perpetrator is released from the offense. If, not knowing [the identity], he kills another...
Whether he kills him there or elsewhere, the murderer incurs a *pārājika* offense, while the one who instigated it is released.
In the case of an act constituting an immediate transgression (*ānantariya*), it should be applied together with that immediate transgression. 282.
If someone digs a pit intending for a certain person, then for that person digging the pit in such a manner—
"An offense called *dukkaṭa* occurs"—this is an instance of *ajjhāhāra-yojanā* (interpolated construction).
This construction is of two kinds: *yathāruta-yojanā* (literal construction) and *ajjhāhāra-yojanā*. Therein, the construction of the words as they actually appear in the text is *yathāruta-yojanā*;

the construction of the words as they appear in the text together with interpolated words for the purpose of filling a deficiency is to be understood as *ajjhāhāra-yojanā*. For example: "And the pit while digging."
The reading is seen in the manuscripts. It has been stated without doubt that the reading “khaṇantassa tathopātaṃ” is superior.
And it has also been stated: “‘Āvāṭa’ is a synonym for ‘opāta’. Furthermore: “With reference to some person...”
"And whoever digs a trench—
while he is digging it in that manner,
there is for him an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

The reading is more excellent. For one who digs up earth that has already been formed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the counting of the preliminary effort (*payoga*), because it constitutes an act leading to defeat (*pārājika*).
283. *Tattha* means in that pit. *Tassa* refers to the human being who has fallen. *Dukkhassuppattiyā* means for the sake of the arising of suffering.
*Tassa* refers to that monk by whom the pit was dug. If, having fallen, he dies...
The construction is: "In that opinion, there is a *pārājika* offense for that bhikkhu.
(284) "In another" means: in one other than that for which the pit was dug. "Indiscriminate" (*anuddissaka*) is an adverbial modifier;
the meaning is "having made it indiscriminate. If it is a qualifier of the pit, the word-division is "an indiscriminate pit" (*anuddissako opāto*).
In expressions such as “aggamakkhāyati,” one should understand that the vowel *a* takes the place of the vowel *o*, and the letter *m* is inserted;
the meaning is that a non-specific pit has been dug.
If a non-specific pit is dug with the thought, “Let whoever falls here die,” then however many [beings] fall into it...
The construction is: "If they die, he incurs as many faults as there are [victims]. By the phrase "whosoever," one's own mother and father are included.
"Faults" refers to the faults of karmic bondage; however, the *pārājika* offense is only one. "His" refers to the person by whom the indiscriminate pit was dug.
Regarding the phrase "if dead in the case of an immediate (*ānantariya*) deed," there is an ellipsis of the word "having fallen therein," which is the governing topic; [this applies] to an *arahant*.
The meaning is: having fallen upon his mother and father, they have died and passed away.

Regarding the term *ānantariyaka*, here the suffix *-ka* should be understood as expressing either the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), or as denoting something contemptible (*kucchite*), or as forming a technical designation (*saññāyaṃ*).

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it is indicated that within this compound word *ānantariyavatthusmiṃ*, both the constituent part *vatthusmiṃ* and [the phrase] "having died after falling thereupon" (*tattha patitvā mate*) [are implied].
And this implies the following: the construction is that when one falls into the matter of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) or similar, and dies there, the grave offenses and so forth occur.

It is stated that if non-human beings such as *yakkhas* die after falling into that pit, or if one dies during the infliction of suffering upon the object of a *pārājika* offense, it is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*); if a human being dies, it is a *pārājika*; and if an animal dies, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

287. Regarding "two instances of taking life": because there are two intentions, there are two acts of taking life; by one [intent] there is a *pārājika* offense, and by the other there is merely the binding of karma. Regarding "only one when destroying one by one": in the case of the death of either the mother or the child, there is only one act of taking life. 288.

"If one pursued by thieves falls into this pit and dies, it is said that the *pārājika* offense belongs to the pit-digger alone"—this is the construction of the sentence. The word "it is said" (*kira*) indicates a lack of conviction regarding the oral tradition.
289–90. "Enemies other than the monk" refers to persons who are enemies. In that context, if one causes a human being to fall into that pit...
If they kill [the victim] there; or if the enemies, having themselves carried out a person who has fallen there, kill him outside;

or if those spontaneously born humans (*opapātika*), having been reborn in that pit, were to die while unable to emerge from it—in all these aforementioned cases, the application of the rule is that the loser is the one who dug the pit. Having been reborn...

*Hi*: here, *hi* is for the purpose of completing the meter (*padapūraṇa*). Wherever the meaning of particles (*nipāta*) is not explicitly shown, it should be understood there as being merely for the completion of the meter.

291. *Yakkhādayo* ("yakkhas, etc."): by the word "etc.," the inclusion of animals (*tiracchāna*) is intended. *Vatthuvasā* ("by way of the basis"): by way of the yakkhas and animals who constitute the basis (*vatthu*) for the grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) and the offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*). *Thullaccayādayo* ("grave offenses, etc."): by the word "etc.," the inclusion of the offenses of expiation is intended.
293. "This method" refers to the method stated as "there is no offense.

294–5. "They are bound" means if they are inevitably bound. "Therein" means in that snare. By the phrase "the moment it is released from the hand," he illustrates that the action accomplishes its purpose.
296. However, the construction is to be understood thus: there is no offense declared when one binds someone other than the one for whose sake the snare was set.
"297. Or 'in vain' means without a root. 'Only for the one who has the root-status' means only for the one who caused the construction.
'Bondage of karma' refers to the taking of life. It is called a 'bond' (bandha) because one is bound by it; thus, 'karma-bond' is simply karma that acts as a bond.

Although only the offense of *pārājika* should have been mentioned, since [the act] continues until [the death], the *pārājika* applies by way of the first among the beings who die while bound therein; as for the remainder..."

Because it arises from the mass of unwholesome states known as the destruction of life, he says "the bondage of kamma" in order to include all of that and show both together by way of their commonality. 298.
"If the one who caught it straightens the snare or goes past it..."
Having seen [the fault], he makes a fence and inserts it in front; or he places a more rigid crossbar;

or he ties a stronger rope for the crossbar; or he hammers in a firmer post. To include the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he said: "or even when the crossbar slips out.
Here, by the word "even" (*pi*), which has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*samuccaya*), [the cases] beginning with "he adjusts it" are included.
“*Bandhati* (binds)” indicates that the application [of the action] is shown as ending with the act of binding.

In the phrase “or firmly (*thiraṃ vāpi*),” the particle *api* should be understood as including the action mentioned in the commentary as remaining unstated—namely, “he strikes a stump”—since it serves as an alternative option for both meanings.
“*Evaṃ* (thus)” means when this is the case; that is, even by one who has obtained the snare, when such a distinction has been made regarding the snare.
This has been stated. "Of both" means of both the one who made the trap and the one who, having now obtained it, maintains it.
(299–300) "Who" refers to either the maker of the trap or the one who obtained the trap.
"Having caused to be disgorged" means having opened [the mouth], that is, having acted in such a way that living beings are not caught there. "And therein" refers to when it has been restored again.
And as for "by the side": who is liberated? He by whom it was obtained. 301–2. Regarding "having guarded":
the construction is that liberation does not exist because of guarding. The suffix *-tvā* should be understood here in the sense of a cause, as in such expressions as "fear arises upon seeing a lion.
As for "another... does not liberate him," the word *na ca* here means "not at all."
"Having destroyed it completely" means having destroyed it by cutting and so forth, in such a way that no instrument for the destruction of any living being remains.
"That stake for the snare"—who is liberated? The maker of the snare.
"Of one who impales on a stake" means of one who drives in a stake. "Of one who fixes" means of one who establishes it.
304. Regarding the term *asañcicca* (“unintentionally”), the phrase *“by means of an exertion performed”* (*katena payogena*) is to be supplied as a textual supplement;

it is connected with the words *“even if [the person] has died, there is no offense.”* The meaning is that if one has not thought, “By this means I shall kill this person,” and has not made an effort toward that end, but rather acts with a mind intent on something else, then even if another dies through an exertion performed by someone else, there is no offense—just as in the cases concerning the throwing of a pestle and so forth.

It is said that if one perceives this being as merely "a being" and, being devoid of the conceptualization associated with the volition that initiates the transgression—thinking, "By this means I shall kill this one"—there is no *pārājika* offense even if the person dies through an effort undertaken for some other purpose. Regarding the phrase "of one who does not know":
there is no offense even if another dies through one's effort when one does not know, "By this [means] this person will die."
It is stated that, as in the case of the incident involving alms-food containing poison, there is no offense even if a person dies when one acts without knowing "this is the cause.

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it draws in the phrase "there is no offense" (*anāpatti*). The meaning is that there is no offense even if another person dies through an attempt made by one whose mind is not intent on death—that is, a mind accompanied by a desire for non-death—as in the cases concerning those who have gone forth in old age and so forth. Those such as the insane (*ummattaka*) are exactly as they were described in their own nature.

305. By the phrase “In the human being’s hand,” the state of being human is shown as a constituent factor. By the phrase “If his mind is associated with death,” the state of having a mind associated with death is shown.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā*, titled *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the discussion of the third *pārājika* is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the fourth *pārājika*, §§306–7:
Having thus shown the determination of the third *pārājika* by a method that is neither too concise nor too detailed, [the author now] presents the determination of the fourth *pārājika*.
To demonstrate this, he said, "Asantaṃ" (what is non-existent), and so forth. Therein, by supplying the words through the force of the context— namely,

supplying "attani" (in oneself) in relation to "asantaṃ," "uttarimanussadhammaṃ" (superhuman states) in relation to "jhānādibhedaṃ" (the various kinds of jhāna, etc.), and "yo bhikkhu" (whatever monk) in relation to "samudācareyya" (should speak)—
it should be construed according to the method beginning with "attani asantaṃ."
"Not existing in oneself" means not being present because it has not been produced within one's own continuity (saṃtāna) in that particular personal existence (attabhāva).
"Having made it dependent on oneself" means having made it referable to oneself, having made it as if it were existing in oneself, and having brought it near to oneself.

"And having resolved upon existence while it is occurring" means having mentally resolved upon—that is, having conjectured—the existence that is occurring from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) onwards.

"Having set aside" means having excluded. "And having set aside figurative expressions" means excluding the indirect discourse that will be stated in the manner beginning with, "The bhikkhu who dwells here in this monastery.

"And having set aside overweening pride" means excluding the overweening pride consisting in the thought, "I have attained a state superior to that of ordinary men," which is characterized by the perception of what has not been seen as seen, and so forth.

"Jhānādibhedaṃ" means that which has jhānas and so forth as its divisions or distinctions; it refers to the specific qualities such as jhāna mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "the state surpassing human phenomena (*uttarimanussadhamma*)," namely:

jhāna, liberation (*vimokkha*), concentration (*samādhi*), attainment (*samāpatti*), knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), development of the path (*maggabhāvanā*), realization of the fruit (*phalasacchikiriyā*), the abandoning of defilements (*kilesappahāna*), freedom from hindrances (*vinīvaraṇatā*), and delight in empty dwellings (*suññāgāre abhirati*).

The meaning is as follows: Regarding the phrase “a state beyond human condition” (*uttarimanussadhamma*), it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that it is “the state of those who have transcended humans, namely both meditators and noble ones (*ariya*).
Because it has been attained by both those who have gained meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and by the eight types of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), it is reckoned as a state belonging to them;
thus it is called a “state beyond human condition.”
The phrase "whatever monk should address with body or speech one who stands within the range of communication" (*viññattipathe*) should be supplied and connected [to the rest of the rule].
"Standing within the range of communication" means standing within a distance of twelve *hattha*s;
it refers to anyone whatsoever—whether woman or man, layperson or one gone forth—as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
“By body” means by means of the body, such as by way of hand gestures (*hatthamuddā*) and so forth.
Since it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that “the renunciation of training does not descend upon a hand gesture;

this reporting of what is untrue does descend even upon a hand gesture,” here both bodily movements such as hand gestures and the touching of limbs and members must be understood by the term “by body.”
"By speech" means by whatever expression whatsoever that can be understood by one standing within earshot.
"A monk" means one who is fully ordained—whether an elder, a novice, or one of middle standing.
"Should address" means he should speak in any manner among the various forms of speech such as, "I am entering the first jhāna," and so forth. "Regarding that matter" means by that...
Regarding the meaning of the stated sentence: "Only when known" means precisely when it is known.

Whether spoken with reference to a woman or a man—or indeed anyone whatsoever—or whether spoken without such reference, as soon as the words are uttered, if any human being standing within earshot understands the aforementioned types of meanings (such as "this person is an attainer of the first jhāna"), it is only then [that the offense is incurred].
Having supplied the word "so" (he), it should be connected as: "He, moreover, is incapable of growth.

A person who speaks thus, having established himself in conduct based on desire and making qualities that do not exist in himself appear as if they were present, is unworthy of attaining the wisdom known as *buddhi* within the Dispensation—that is, the mundane and supramundane qualities obtainable at higher and higher stages by being firmly established in virtue.

The meaning is as follows. To the question "In what way?", he says: "Just as... [etc. ...in the state of having grown. This connects with the word "just as" (yathā), and the sense is completed by "so too" (tathā). The meaning is:
just as a palmyra tree cut at the top is incapable of growing again, so too one who has committed a *pārājika* offense is to be regarded in exactly that same way.

Now, in order to show the classification of offenses that can occur through the sense of contrast (*byatireka*) in these two statements—"one who knows is incapable" and "without the designation of another"—he says: "Even while non-existent," and so forth.
“Immediately after” means right after the words such as, “I am attaining the first jhāna.
“He” refers to another person who stands within twelve cubits and hears that speech.

“And knows” means that if he knows it without long delay, according to the manner of the statement made by him—such as, “This one is an attainer of the first jhāna”—without deviating from the actual meaning; this is the sense. However, as for the one who...
Even one who does not know the actual nature of the jhānas and so forth— either because he has not attained them himself,

or because he has not become familiar with them through study, questioning, and the like— might, simply because he has previously heard such expressions as "jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment," say,
when the words "I shall enter the first jhāna" are spoken: "So this man is entering jhāna..."
If he knows even this much meaning—that [the other] enters [into attainment]—then he too should be understood as "knowing," for that is what is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

The word *hi* (for/indeed) is used here for emphasis. For when only that much has been known by him as stated by himself, that wicked person, who proclaims qualities he does not possess, even though he has climbed this great tree of the nectar of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) which is endowed with the excellence of the fruits, has failed to enjoy those fruits.
It is said that one who has offended and fallen is called "dead. It should be understood that there is no fault of tautology here,

because although this same point was stated previously by way of the phrase "non-existent" (*asanta*) and so forth, it is stated again as a restatement (*anuvāda*) in order to demonstrate the meaning of its contrapositive (*byatireka*).

Now, in order to show the meaning of the contrapositive (byatireka), he says: “If not... it does not happen. If the one to whom he reports does not know, then for that speaker of falsehood who reveals non-existent qualities, [the offense follows].
To show the classification of offenses possible according to the presence or absence of the contrapositive meaning indicated by the phrase “and without using another pretext,” he says:
“Whosoever... and so forth. The construction is: “Whosoever monk dwells here in this monastery, yours.”

"Revealed" (*dīpita*) means when one's own intention has been made manifest. "And he knows" means that whoever hears the words spoken in such a manner knows them immediately upon hearing the speech, either thinking, "By this indirect designation (*aññāpadesa*), he reveals his attainment of jhāna," or "This person is an attainer of jhāna.
"His" refers to that bhikkhu who spoke those words; "that" refers to the speech uttered by him.

The meaning is that it is only a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), not a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). It should be understood that the manner of speaking— describing one's own non-existent qualities as if they were real, as if one were describing the conduct of someone else to the donors who built one’s own dwelling—
is expressed by way of the meaning of this verse.

And here, by the word "and" (*ca*) used in the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avuttasamuccaya*), it should be understood that the remaining modes of exposition (*pariyāyavāra*) included in the Pāḷi are also comprised.
Likewise, in the phrase "one who has attained jhāna," because the mention of "jhāna" implies the liberation (*vimokkha*) and so forth,
one who has heard the discourse concerning the tenfold superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) beginning with jhāna would, at that moment—

It should be understood that by this verse the meaning is already shown: when the matter is known, a *thullaccaya* offense is incurred through speaking in a figurative manner; and when it is not known, or is known only after a long time, a *dukkaṭa* offense is incurred. 310.
"This" refers to the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) consisting of the various types such as *jhāna* mentioned above. "By overestimation" means [thinking], "I have attained it."

“Thus arisen conceit” means excessive conceit; it is said with reference to one who speaks with conceit that has arisen firmly, thinking, “This Dhamma has been attained by me. “The method of non-offense has been stated” means that the absence of an offense is “non-offense” (anāpatti);
taking this very [absence] as the method—that is, as that which is to be understood—it is said, “there is no offense. “By overweening conceit” (adhimānena) thus—

The meaning is that it was said by the Blessed One. It is stated that there is no offense for one who, out of overestimation (*adhimāna*), says things such as "I am an attainer of the first jhāna" while thinking, "I have realized the Dhamma.

If one asks, "To whom does this overestimation belong, and to whom does it not belong?"—it does not belong to the Noble Ones (*ariya*) because of their reviewing of the path (*magga-paccavekkhaṇa*) and so forth.

It does not arise in one who is immoral because of his lack of enthusiasm for attaining noble qualities, despite having experienced joy through the five kinds of reflection due to having crossed over doubt.
Nor does it arise in one who is virtuous but lacks application to the meditation subject, being intent on the pleasures of sleep and so forth, because he has abandoned his commitment to development.
It arises, however, in one who is firmly established in perfectly pure accomplishment of virtue and is devoted to the development of serenity (*samatha*).

It arises either in one who has attained the form or formless attainments, or in one devoted to insight who has acquired the knowledge of the arising and passing away of defilements. It should be understood that by means of the development of serenity and insight, it prevents the manifestation of defilements from occurring;
instead of allowing them to become factors of distinction, it renders them factors of stagnation and establishes them as such.
“*Panā*” has the sense of the particle *api*. By the word “*eva*,” he refers back to [the phrase] “the method for non-offense (*anāpatti-naya*) has been stated.
“*Avattukāmassā*” (of one not wishing to speak) and the expression found in the Canon “*anullapanādhippāyassā*” (of one whose intention is not to misrepresent) do not have different meanings.

The construction is: “it is said thus, ‘of one not wishing to speak. [This applies to] one who, out of hypocrisy and being motivated by evil desires, says, “I am an attainer of the jhānas and so forth.”

The meaning is that the intention (*ajjhāsayo*) is called "the purpose of boasting"; thus, it is stated by the Blessed One that there is likewise no offense for one who explains something else to fellow celibate practitioners when such was not the case. The construction is: "It is stated even for a beginner.

The meaning of "there is no offense for a beginner" (*anāpatti ādikammikassa*) is that the state of being without offense is also stated by the Blessed One for a beginner. In this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), [this applies].

The monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River are the originators of this rule. By the word *tathā* (likewise), used here in the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated, those who are insane, deranged, or afflicted by pain—though not mentioned here—are included.

"Possessed of evil desires" (*pāpicchā*) means: having an evil, base desire (*icchā*) characterized by a longing for the acquisition of requisites, which serves as a cause for being held in esteem; that is, a longing motivated by the desire to be regarded by people [with the thought], "In this way, people will hold me in high regard," on account of such things as attaining the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
And the state of being endowed [with it]. "Of that" means of that superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) which was proclaimed, distinguished by the various divisions such as jhāna and so forth.
"The state of non-existence" means the state of being non-existent due to its not having been produced within one's own continuum during the present birth.
"And the reporting to a human being" refers to a person of human birth who understands the meaning of the words spoken at that very moment.

“‘He attained the first jhāna’”—thus, by way of such a method, there is the announcement made while standing within earshot. And there is the announcement by means of another’s statement (*aññāpadesa*). The connection is:
“and the announcement by means of another’s statement,” such as by way of the method: “The monk who dwells in your monastery attained the first jhāna.
And there is the direct announcement, without the mediation of another’s statement. That itself is knowledge (*tad-eva ñāṇaṃ*); that very moment is the knowledge (*tadā eva ñāṇaṃ*).
"Without delay" means knowing [the offense] at the very moment it was spoken. "In this" refers to this fourth *pārājika* offense. "The wise" refers to those who uphold the Vinaya.
(312) "In the first, the second, and the third"—that is, in the aforementioned three *pārājikas*, excluding the *pārājika* concerning the human form (*manussaviggaha*).
"No alternative exists" means that no figurative expression (*pariyāyavacana*) is found for the path of a *pārājika* offense. "But not the others."
This should also be applied here; however, the meaning is that for the others, no such method exists in the third *pārājika*.
It is stated that for one who speaks by way of indirect methods—such as "one should praise death," or "O man, what use have you for this?

and so forth, or "he who dies in this manner obtains wealth" and so forth—it is indeed a *pārājika*. An injunction (*āṇatti*) is the application of an injunction that serves as the cause for a *pārājika*.
"But not the others" means that in the first and fourth *pārājikas*, the instruction (*āṇatti*) that constitutes the cause for a *pārājika* offense is not obtained.
313. "The beginning" refers to the first *pārājika*. "Single origin" means having a single cause. It is called an "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) because an offense arises from it;
it is the cause, such as the body and so forth. That [cause] is sixfold: body, speech, body and speech, body and mind, [mind and speech, and mind and body].
[There are] speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind. We shall explain their analysis later, in the very place where it has come down.
Herein, this is "one origination": because one body-and-mind is its origination, it is so called. Therefore he said: "Two factors, from body and mind.
The word "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*) is to be supplied [to the phrase]. By whichever origination the first *pārājika* offense [is committed],...

The cause is that which is reckoned as its origination. "Two factors" (duvaṅga) means that which has two factors or parts—the body, reckoned as the organ of generation, and the mind of sexual intercourse;
the meaning is that it possesses the nature of both, just as one speaks of "the fourfold jhāna having two factors.
"The rest" refers to the remaining three pārājikas. "Threefold origination" means body and mind.

"By speech, mind, body, speech, and mind" means that these have three origins—namely, three origins—taken collectively. "Of those" refers to those three origins. "Factors" (aṅgāni) means constituent parts. [The seven are:
body, mind, speech, mind, body, speech, and mind; what is meant is that they possess that respective nature.
314. The first *pārājika* has the nature of volition associated with a mind intent on engaging in sexual intercourse. The construction is: "It is declared to be accompanied by pleasure or equanimity.

The meaning is that when there is a cause for joy, such as the attainment of a desirable object, it is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); when that is absent, it is stated to be associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*).

"Third, painful feeling": the meaning is that the third *pārājika* involving human beings is associated with painful feeling because its essential nature is volition (*cetanā*) conjoined with a mind of aversion (*dosa*).
"Second": the second *pārājika*, characterized by the volition of taking what is not given, is associated with joy (*somanassa*) in one who takes another's property through theft out of greed;
however, for one overcome by anger, it occurs after having plundered or caused it to be plundered.
For one who takes [it] with grief, it is associated with mental pain (*domanassa*); for one who takes it with joy, it is associated with happiness (*somanassa*);

and for one who takes it with indifference, as if desiring neither to take it nor not to take it, it is associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*). Thus he said, "It is declared to have three types of feeling.
And "the fourth" refers to the fourth *pārājika*, characterized by the volition of falsely claiming superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

For one who is already quite satisfied with the desire for esteem or the hope for requisites, when they say, "I attain the first jhāna," and so forth, by way of proclaiming their own attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), it is associated with joy (*somanassa*).
When speaking with a mind obstructed toward other persons due to a preoccupation with quarreling, it is associated with grief (*domanassa*). [This occurs] through the non-attainment of requisites...
Because it is impossible for one who speaks with indifference to endure the suffering of hunger and so forth, it is associated with equanimity;
thus he said, "three feelings are declared.
(315) Regarding "eight consciousnesses," the construction is that eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed are obtained; they are obtained.
"Meaning" (attha) means they are associated with the first *pārājika* by way of the nature of volition (*cetanā*). The same applies to the subsequent cases.

"Two" refers to the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*). "Ten types of consciousness" refers to the eight accompanied by greed (*lobha*) and the two associated with aversion.
"Are obtained" means they are obtained by way of association.
316. Therefore: because it is associated with the aforementioned states of mind, for that reason [it is so called].

It is an "action" (*kiriyā*) because it is to be accomplished by means of an act. It is "liberation through perception" (*saññāvimokkha*) because there is liberation from it through the absence of the perception of transgression.
It is "worldly-reprehensible" (*lokavajja*) because it is shown—that is, made manifest—as something to be avoided by the world due to its unwholesome nature.

317. “In the case of an offense itself” (*āpattiyaṃyeva*): by the word “itself” (*eva*), he shows that it is not a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). “This procedure” (*idaṃ vidhānaṃ*): this refers to the aforementioned procedure, beginning with the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth. “By one who is discerning” (*vibhāvinā*): by one possessing wisdom who is a bearer of the Vinaya. 318–9. “And with a supple back” (*mudupiṭṭhi ca*):
having shown the manner of bending like a creeper and moving about to dance, [he means] one whose back is soft and pliable.
“And pendulous” (*lambī*): endowed with a long, hanging organ (*aṅgajāta*). “Pendulous” (*lamba*): that which hangs down; [here] the organ.
He who has that [disease] is a "lambī" (one with a protruding member).

These two, because they are capable of violating [the precept] by inserting their own genitals into their own mouths or anus when afflicted by the fever of sensual desire, are avoided as being similar to those who have committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Mukhaggāhī" means grasping with the mouth; one who has this is a "mukhaggāhī," referring to one who [inserts] another's genitals into his own mouth.
The meaning is "taking [it] with the mouth. A "sitter" is one who sits upon another's organ with his own anus.
These two are excluded because they destroy the virtue of their co-residents; since they are similar to those who have committed a *pārājika* offense, they are unfit to live with others.
By the common characteristic of being "unfit for communal life" (*asaṃvāsa*), the term "of them" includes all four who have committed a *pārājika*. "Of them..."

"Because of the commonality between the path and the practice of the path, it should be understood as being 'conformable' (anulomika) only for one who has committed the first *pārājika* offense"—thus it was stated without doubt.

By this, it is understood that the status of being a "conformable *pārājika*" is also stated for the four cases of those who have not committed an offense, such as those with a supple back and so forth.
However, in the *Samantapāsādikā*:

“Furthermore, they say there are four *anuloma*-pārājikas by way of these four: one who is ‘lambī’ (pendulous), one who has a ‘mudupiṭṭhika’ (smooth back), one who takes another’s sexual organ into his mouth, and one who sits down upon another’s sexual organ.
For these are called ‘the practice of sexual intercourse’ (*methunadhamma*) because they are the dhamma of two who have attained a state of similarity through passion.”
And because it is stated [in the *Sāratthadīpanī*], both in that [text] and in its commentary: “Therefore, since they are to be committed merely by the entry of the organ into the path—

even without having engaged in the act of sexual intercourse— in this manner, they are called ‘conformable offenses entailing expulsion’ (*anuloma-pārājika*) as they conform to the offense of sexual misconduct entailing expulsion.”
"One whose organ hangs down due to its extreme length is called *lambī*. To that extent, he is not defeated (*pārājika*);
however, when, oppressed by lack of lust, he inserts his own organ into his own mouth or anus, then he becomes defeated.
One who has a soft back is called *mudupiṭṭhiko*, meaning one who has a back made soft through preparatory treatment."
He is endowed [with these qualities]. When he, being oppressed by lack of desire for sexual intercourse, inserts his own organ into his own mouth, he is then defeated (pārājika).

"He takes another’s organ with his mouth" means: one who, being oppressed by lack of desire for sexual intercourse, takes the organ of another person—whether they are asleep or heedless—with his own mouth. "He sits upon another’s organ" means...
One who, oppressed by lack of sexual desire, sees another’s genitals being functional and sits upon them with his own anus,
meaning he inserts his own anus into that [genital organ]. Although the four beginning with Lambī are included under the first *pārājika*,
it is because both [parties] are characterized by the method known as the obsession of lust (*rāgapariyuṭṭhāna*).
“They do not engage in sexual intercourse; therefore, they are stated separately.
Because this has been said, it should be understood that only those who have committed an offense are “defeated” (pārājika).
Regarding the phrase “and four for the bhikkhunīs,” the words “not shared” (asādhāraṇāni) are to be supplied as the remainder of the text; [these four] are not shared with the bhikkhus.

The four *pārājika* offenses specific to bhikkhunīs alone are: [the offense of] exposing the thighs, concealing a fault, following one who has been suspended, and the eight grounds [of defeat]. The phrase "those corresponding to them" (*tesaṃ anulomikā*) should be supplied and connected as follows:
a bhikkhunī who has herself left the order (*vibbhantā*) corresponds to those four *pārājikas*.

This is the construction [of the sentence]. Having become subject to the mind [of others], a bhikkhunī who—having herself put on even the robe she was wearing in the manner of a woman’s undergarment, and having taken pleasure in a householder’s dress—falls away from the Dispensation at the very moment it is donned, is what is meant by "a bhikkhunī.

By acting in this way, because they have entered the state of a householder, they are not fit to live in community with these four [classes of ordained persons] due to their commonality of status as householders. Thus it is said of these four.
They have become concordant with the *pārājika* offenses.

"In that way" means that just as these [offenses] shown by him are *pārājika* because they entail exclusion from the community (*asaṃvāsa*) and incapacity for the state of a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*), so too are the eleven persons incapable [of ordination].
The eleven incapable ones are: the matricide, the patricide, and so forth.

The eleven are: the murderer of an arahant, the schismatic of the Saṅgha, the shedder of blood [from a Tathāgata’s body], a paṇḍaka, an animal, one with both sexual organs, one living in communion by theft, a defiler of nuns, and one who has gone over to another sect.
The intention is that all these twenty-four persons are to be understood when taken together.

320. The construction is as follows: these twenty-four persons who have committed a *pārājika* offense are said to be incapable of the state of a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*) here [in this world], just like one whose head has been cut off.

321. To show the reason for the incapacity of these eleven [types of persons], he says, "And the paṇḍaka," and so forth. "And the paṇḍaka" refers to the *āsitta-paṇḍaka*, the *ussūya-paṇḍaka*, the *pakkha-paṇḍaka*, the *opakkamika-paṇḍaka*, and the *napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*.
The five kinds of *paṇḍaka* have been mentioned. Regarding "animal" (*tiracchāna*): it is called "animal" because it moves or goes horizontally (*tiriyaṃ añchati*);

thus, it includes the nagas, supaṇṇas, and all other animal-born beings. It should be understood that all non-human beings, such as *yakkhas* and so forth, are also included here within the category of animals. And "the hermaphrodite" (*ubhatobyañjana*) refers to one who possesses the characteristics (*byañjana*) that produce both female and male traits.

One whose secondary sexual characteristics (*byañjana*), such as the breasts and so forth, have arisen from both [sets]—this is the etymological derivation (*nirutta*) for a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*).
There are two types of hermaphrodites: the female hermaphrodite and the male hermaphrodite. Regarding "one who has failed in the basis" (*vatthuvipanna*):

the "basis" (*vatthu*) is that wherein the state of being a monk resides because it has been cultivated through that very state; it is the fitness of persons for the state of being a monk. Furthermore, that consists in being endowed with the qualities free from all defects mentioned in the *Pabbajjā-kkhandhaka*.
Those who have failed due to the presence of neuterhood (*paṇḍaka*) and so forth should be understood as "those whose basis has failed. The word *hi* indicates a reason;
because their basis has failed, it is therefore said that they are incapable of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) in this present existence.

By the expression "those with non-causal rebirth-linking" (*ahetupaṭisandhika*), he states that these individuals are possessed of the obstruction of karmic result (*vipākāvaraṇa*); by this, [he shows] their incapacity for the attainment of the Path.
It should be understood that the state of being excluded has been shown.

322. "The five who face immediate retribution" refers to those such as matricides and so forth, who—due to being possessed by the obstruction of karma—fall away from the attainment of heaven and liberation and are destined for rebirth in the states of misery immediately after death;
these are the five who face immediate retribution. And "one who lives in communion through theft" [is also included].

There are three kinds of one who dwells in communion through theft: one who dwells in communion by means of a mark, one who dwells in communion by means of co-residence, and one who dwells in communion by means of both.
Furthermore, there is the "corrupter of nuns," so called because, having engaged in sexual intercourse with a regular nun, he corrupts her due to that corruption;

thus he is called a "corrupter of nuns" (*bhikkhunīdūsaka*). And there is the "one who has gone over to another sect," meaning one who has adopted the views and the dress of the non-Buddhist sectarians (*titthiya*).

Having consented and taken him, he entered among them. Thus, the construction is: "But these eight [types of persons] are lost through their actions. "Iti" (thus) is stated because it has this meaning; "these" (*ime*) is what is meant.

The connection is "these [are] those" (*te ime*). The meaning is: "These eight, having become unworthy of the state of a bhikkhu in this present existence due to such actions as matricide and so forth, are lost.
Up to this point, the eleven who are incapable (*abhabba*) have been discussed.
The reason for incapacity has been shown. 323.

The construction is as follows: "By following and pursuing this essential exposition of the *pārājika* rules which has been stated by me, the rest of the exposition can be understood in its entirety by one who is wise and learned.
324. [This is said] by one who desires the ultimate method (*paramatthanaya*) within the *Vinayapiṭaka*, which is endowed with various supreme methods that produce proficiency.
The construction is: "This should be constantly mastered. In that context, "by various" means by many different kinds.

"By methods" (*nayehi*) refers to those called "methods" because they are led (*nīyanti*) or recited according to the stated sequence; these include methods such as the "wheel-turning" (*cakkapeyyāla*) and others. "The method of the ultimate meaning" (*paramatthanaya*):
it is the "ultimate meaning" (*paramattha*) because it is both supreme (*parama*) and an object (*attha*), or because it is the meaning that must be specifically determined as supreme.
The "ultimate method" (*paramatthanaya*) is that which must be led by the intellect of those seeking a formal determination (*vinicchaya*);
it is called the "ultimate method" because the means of determination is led by means of it.
"Desiring that ultimate method" means desiring—seeking—the formal determination or its means within the Vinaya Piṭaka; the sense is "wishing for it. "This should be mastered" means...
Word-division: the letter *ma* arises from a phonetic sandhi (*āgama-sandhi*), and there is a substitution of the vowel *a* for the vowel *o*.

"It should be mastered" means it should be recited, heard, reflected upon, and retained; this is what is stated. This refers to the *vinaya-vinicchaya* (the determination of the Vinaya). Thus, [ends] the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī* (The Elucidation of the Essence of the Meaning of the Vinaya).
The commentary on the discussion of the fourth *pārājika* in the *Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the *saṅghādisesa* offenses.

325. Having thus shown the exposition of the Pārājika section adorned with various methods, he now says “the desire to release,” etc., in order to show the exposition of the Thirteen-section (terasa-kaṇḍa) which was recited immediately following it.
One who desires to release is "desirous of releasing" (mocetukāmo); the state of that is "the desire to release" (mocetukāmatā);
the consciousness associated with that is "consciousness desirous of releasing" (mocetukāmatā-citta). Herein, "the desire to release" (mocetukāmatā) [is explained as follows].
Among these eleven types of lust, that which is called "the relish of emission" refers to the lust pertaining to the emission of semen, which is the fundamental cause of this *saṅghādisesa* offense.

The eleven types of lust are: "the relish of emission," "the relish of the process of emitting," "the relish of having emitted," "the relish of sexual intercourse," "the relish of physical contact,"...

The gratification of scratching, the gratification of seeing, the gratification of sitting, the gratification of speaking, affection based on the household, and the pleasure of the forest-thicket—these are what have been mentioned.

Here, "liberation" (mocana) refers to the liberation of the element of generation; the feeling associated with lust for that object, for the sake of that liberation, is called the "gratification of liberation.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "The gratification of liberating is the 'gratification of liberation'. While being liberated...

The gratification (*assāda*) is the gratification of emission; when the element of origination (*sambhava-dhātu*) is being emitted, the feeling associated with lust for that is called the "gratification of emission.
In this same manner, the sequence of meanings should be understood for the remaining terms beginning with the gratification of what has been emitted and ending with the gratification of speech.
By these nine terms, under the heading of gratification, lust—which accompanies them—is demonstrated according to the analogy of a bamboo staff. As it has been said:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “Lust is spoken of under the heading of the gratification associated with the nine terms.

Regarding the phrase “affection based on the household” (*gehassitapema*): here, the mother and others are called “the household” (*geha*) by way of a metaphorical expression for the container and its contents.
Just as in such expressions as “the beds are shouting,” lust—which is a synonym for affection—referring to that which is dependent upon them, is called “affection based on the household.”
