Thus it is said. By this phrase, the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of lust is demonstrated. "Gathering from the forest" (*vanabhaṅgiya*) refers to whatever fruits, flowers, and so forth are brought back after being plucked from the forest.

In this context, however, it refers to those possessed by lust who, for the sake of removing the suffering of separation from women, place their minds bound by lust in their stead and experience them through seeing and touching.
“Vanabhaṅgiya” (the breaking of the forest) refers to things such as betel-leaf together with the garlands worn by those [women] from whom it is to be taken.
By this, lust whose objective domain consists of desired objects is demonstrated by way of the things dependent upon them. As it is said in the Commentary:
“By one word, lust is stated in its own form; by another word, it is stated by way of its object. For the ‘breaking of the forest’ is [a metaphor for] lust.”
"It is the basis, not lust alone.

By using the word "mind" instead of saying merely "the desire to release," he shows a specific state of mind associated with lust that originates the bodily intimation which effects the transgression. That which is originated by that mind...
He shows by the term "effort" (*vāyāma*) the transgression known as intimation (*viññatti*). "Effort" refers to the energy (*vīriya*) associated with that consciousness.

Here, however, it should be understood that the transgression itself is expressed by means of a word denoting the energy that is its specific cause, according to the principle of designating the cause by the name of the effect—as in the cases of "phlegm-sugar" (*semho guḷo*) and so forth.
[The other types of misconduct are] striking internal or external objects, and shaking the hips in the air.
The meaning is that "effort" (vāyāmo) has the sense of the emission of semen (sukkamocana). The emission of semen is *sukkamocana*.

And here, regarding the word "of semen" (*sukkassa*), [it refers to] the ten types of semen mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "Semen is blue, yellow, red, white, the color of buttermilk, the color of water, the color of oil, the color of milk, the color of curd, and the color of ghee."

The meaning is: "of one of the ten kinds of semen," which is divided in many ways according to the different dispositions of bile and so forth among beings, or according to the division of the four primary elements beginning with the earth element, or the six bodily constituents beginning with lymph, blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow.
"Emission" (*mocana*) is a synonym for "discharge" (*vissaṭṭhi*); the meaning is emission from its natural place of location.
As it is said in the *Padabhājana*: "‘Emission’ (vissaṭṭhi) is called the causing of displacement from its place. Here, some say:
"Place" (*ṭhāna*) means the base of the urinary organ, known as the opening of the bladder. Others say: "The hips. Still others say: "The entire body.
Among these three statements, because the third position is praised in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, [it follows that] hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth...
Excluding the places devoid of flesh, as well as urine, feces, saliva, snot, and the stiff, dry skin,

the remainder of the entire body should be understood as the location of the physical sensitivity (kāyappasāda), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and the element of cohesion (sambhava-dhātu), just as [these are present] in unbound bile.
What is meant by the term “sukkamocana” (ejaculation)? It means that one ejaculates with any one of the ten kinds of intentions included in the following:

for the sake of health, for the sake of pleasure, for the sake of medicine, for the sake of giving, for the sake of merit, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of heaven, for the sake of seed, for the sake of experimentation, or for the sake of sport;
and while being possessed of such an intention, [one does so] when there is an obstruction caused by lust...
At one of the five times mentioned— namely, during an obstruction caused by feces,
an obstruction caused by urine, an obstruction caused by wind, or an obstruction caused by being bitten by a high-legged insect— he emits [the semen] by means of one of the four methods mentioned—
namely, while shaking his hips in space, whether toward internal form, external form, or both internal and external form— due to the aforementioned demon of lust.

In brief, it should be understood that if, being devoid of self-control, one emits even as much as a small fly could drink from any of the ten types of secretions arising from the aforementioned locations— as previously described—
[it constitutes an offense]. And here, "creeping insects" (uccāliṅga-pāṇaka) refers to hairy creatures whose genitals become functional when their hair is moistened.
"Except in a dream" (*aññatra supinantā*): "Dream-end" (*supinanta*) means a dream itself;
because it occurs in a context where the ablative case is expected, it carries the sense of the instrumental case, thus meaning "except by means of a dream.

What is called a "dream" (*supina*) arises either through the disturbance of the bodily humors such as wind (*vāta*), or through objects previously experienced such as the form of a woman, or through the power of desirable or undesirable deities, [resulting in] a matter to be obtained through merit or a matter to be reached through demerit.

Among the four causes mentioned—“or it occurs by way of a preliminary sign”—it is stated that the emission of semen occurring from an object seen in a dream during the monkey-sleep is an emission outside the [proper] sphere (*avisaya-sukkavissaṭṭhi*).
It is a *saṅghādisesa* offense precisely because of its nature as a *saṅghādisesa*. For a clansman who, having committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense, desires to emerge from it...

Because it is said, "The Saṅgha is to be sought at the beginning for the purpose of granting probation (parivāsa), in the middle—either with or without a formal sending back to the beginning (mūlāya-paṭikassana)—for the purpose of granting the trial period (mānatta), and at the end for the purpose of rehabilitation (abbhāna); thus, 'the Saṅgha is desired at the beginning and at the remainder,' it is called a *saṅghādisesa*";
therefore, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* regarding the emission of semen.
This is the meaning. As it is said in the word-commentary: “The Saṅgha alone grants probation for that offense, sends back to the beginning, grants the trial period, or rehabilitates;
neither a group nor a single individual does so. Therefore it is called a ‘Saṅghādisesa.
It is the name, the designation, and the synonym for that very class of offenses; for that reason also it is called ‘Saṅghādisesa.’”
And here, the discussion regarding the *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth will be clarified at the very place where it occurs at the conclusion of the *saṅghādisesa* rules.

Having thus far demonstrated the offense rooted in self-exertion as found in the original training rule (*mūlasikkhāpada*), he now says "by another," etc., in order to demonstrate that one may also incur this *saṅghādisesa* offense through the exertion of another. "Having caused [another] to exert" means...
Having caused the grasping or the rubbing of the genitals. 327.

"Intentionally" means having intended and resolved, thinking, "I will make an effort; I will release [the semen]. "While making an effort" means while rubbing against any one of the three internal bases, such as the internal form (the penis) and so forth.
"Specified" means: "He intends and makes an effort, but does not emit..."
The intention is that this was stated by the Blessed One in the word-commentary (padabhājana): “there is an offense of thullaccaya.

In this verse, by the phrase “of one who makes an effort upon his own *aṅgajāta*,” the meaning of “one who strikes his own *aṅgajāta* against an internal form, or an external form, or an internal-and-external form” is expressed.

Because it is absent without the friction of the genitals, even though it is not being grasped, when there is the emission of semen by shaking the hips in the air, it is included under the general term "effort" (*vāyāma*) in the first *saṅghādisesa* rule; therefore, setting that aside, [the text says]:
"Now at that time, a certain monk, intending emission, was shaking his hips in the air..."

“Unclean matter was emitted... [and so on] ... unclean matter was not emitted. He felt remorse... [and so on] ... there is no offense for the bhikkhu regarding the *saṅghādisesa*, but there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Since this was stated in the case of the story concerning the shaking of the legs in the air, he said “intentionally,” etc., in order to include the *thullaccaya* in cases where there is no emission.
Therein, “intentionally” (*sañcicca*) means having known and recognized: “I shall make an effort; I will emit it. “Of one who makes an effort” (*upakkamantassa*).
To distinguish that [action] from its general category, he said, "even by shaking in the air"; it should be understood as "shaking the hips. If one asks how this is obtained:

it is obtained through the power of the proximity of the word "in the air" (ākāse), which accompanies the expression "one who shakes the hips" (kaṭiṃ kampentassa) within the passage of the subject matter to be included in this discourse, namely, "of one shaking the hips in the air."
Because words reveal specific meanings through the proximity of other words within a semantic context (*atthappakaraṇa*).
329. "A bladder" (*vatthi*) means a urinary bladder; the meaning is "the bladder for urine.

"Having filled it for play" means having firmly grasped a urinary bladder and filled it out of a desire to play, like a village boy; as it is said regarding the bladder and its contents: [text follows].
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says: “Those bhikkhus, having gripped their penises firmly and filling them again and again, discharged urine like village boys.

Why was it stated in general terms that “it is not allowable”? Because, according to the method explained in that specific case, for one who discharges [semen] by gripping firmly, filling again and again, and emitting with the intention of emission, once the semen has been emitted, the intention of emission [remains].
Because the factors of "he intends," "he makes an effort," and "there is emission" are fulfilled, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa*;
because a *thullaccaya* occurs when there is no emission, he speaks in order to include both cases. 330.
Regarding the matter of gazing: "Monks, one who is lustful must not gaze at the private parts of a woman."
Regarding the statement in the Pāḷi, “Whoever should gaze [upon her], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” because it is stated in general terms as “of a woman,” he says, “of three.
However, “of three women” refers to three women by way of being human, non-human, or animal.
Because it is specified as “the organ of generation,” “the sign” refers specifically to the urinary tract.
It is said that the meaning is: "the birth canal," whether it be covered or uncovered by even a hundred cloths. Therefore, the Commentary says:

"Even if she is clothed in a hundred cloths, for one who stands in front or behind and gazes intently, thinking, 'The sign is in this spot,' there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). [This applies even] to village girls who are unclothed..."
"But what need is there to say anything more for one who is closely contemplating the sign? Regarding the phrase "in front," the word "standing" (*ṭhatvā*) is to be supplied as a textual ellipsis.
331. The connection is: "for each [instance], seeing one [object], there is one *dukkaṭa*.

From the statement "by a single act of application (*payoga*), there is one *dukkaṭa*," it follows by way of contrast that by multiple acts of application there are multiple *dukkaṭas*. As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
"Looking here and there again and again, and contemplating [the object] repeatedly, for every such act there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Because this commentary states "here and there," in the phrase "opening and closing [the eyes]," the sense is obtained as: "not looking at various things, but looking only at that [object]."
332. The construction is: "It is declared that there is no offense for one whose intention is to cause emission when emission has occurred.

This means that for one who, without the intention to cause emission, applies medicinal ointment to the genitals with a pure mind for the purpose of making medicine, or for one who voids feces, urine, and so forth with a purely clean mind—even if emission occurs—there is no offense.
This is stated by the passage beginning: "There is no offense if it occurs in a dream, or for one who does not intend emission," and so on.
The meaning is that it has already been stated in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*) according to this method.

In this reading, even though the phrase "one who does not make an effort" (*anupakkamantassa*) is not explicitly mentioned, it is because of the statements preceding this passage: "He intends but does not make an effort;
[if] emission occurs, there is no offense," and "He neither intends nor makes an effort; [if] emission occurs, there is no offense."
He states the reason for including that [case] with the words: “And it is declared that there is no offense even in one who is liberated from [the urge] without approaching.

This refers to when one—being oppressed by a longing for liberation, thinking “O, may I be released!”—or even in the absence of a mind preceded by such oppression from a longing for liberation, being merely afflicted by a thought of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*), [commits an offense] through the act of contact with such internal or external objects.
The meaning is that, according to the aforementioned textual passage, there is no offense even if semen is emitted while one is not performing an intentional act—
whether by means of shaking the hips in the air, or by the power of such a thought, or by the power of sensual thoughts.
Regarding the statement, "When it is emitted in a dream, no offense is declared," the meaning is "in a dream" (*supine*), because the sense of the word *anta* (end) is absent here.

The meaning is that there is no offense for one who engages in sexual intercourse while lying on his back, or who enters into physical contact with women, even when semen is emitted, because it is not within the scope [of the rule];
this is indicated in the Pāḷi by the statement: “There is no offense for a bhikkhu in a dream.
Standing upon this point, the Aṭṭhakathā states: “But if, in a dream, there arises a volition of enjoyment and it becomes an object for him...”
"One must remain motionless. One must not play with the sign (the genitals) using the hand.

However, it is permissible to take hold of it with the hollowed palm and go to a water source for the purpose of cleaning it in order to protect the saffron-colored robe-cloth," because it has been stated thus;
therefore, like a hen guarding her eggs, like a yak guarding its tail-hair, and like a man guarding his one eye, [one must guard the organ] even at the cost of one's body and life.

This is the instruction here: a son of good family who wishes to abandon worldly concern, who desires to guard his virtue, who desires to train himself, and who desires to fulfill the practice leading to Nibbāna, should practice with diligence after understanding from the Commentary the intention of the Tathāgata when he said, "Except in a dream. This is the exhortation.
Commentary on the Discussion of Emission of Semen: 333.
"A human female" means a female belonging to the human species. Regarding the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"A woman (*mātugāma*) is a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, not a female animal; this includes even a girl born on that very day, let alone one who is older."
Because it has been stated [as such], it is understood that "a living human woman" refers even to one who exists as a girl born on that very day. One might ask:
"How is this specific distinction—that 'human female' means a *living* human female—obtained from the general term 'human female'?
It is obtained through the method of elimination (*pārisesato*), because in the Vinaya source (the *Vinītavatthu*), touching the body of a dead woman is said to constitute a *thullaccaya* offense.
"Touching" (*āmasanta*) means touching in one of various ways, such as by grasping the hand, grasping the braid of hair, or touching any other limb or member of the body;
this is the meaning because it is stated [in the Vinaya] as "touching with the hand, or grasping the braid of hair, or touching any particular limb.
"Lust for bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsaggarāgo*) is the lust that arises when there is physical contact or mingling with the body of a woman through one's own body. This is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
"Belonging to this" means *saṅghādisesa*; what is meant is that one has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense of bodily contact.

334. The construction is as follows: for a monk who, out of lust for bodily contact, touches even so much as a single hair on a woman with a hair from his own body, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*. In this context, "there are *saṅghādisesas* according to the number of hairs."

Because the opinion of the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* is that [the offense] does not exist by way of counting parts, but exists by way of counting individual hairs, and because the opinion of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* is established as being "it does not exist by counting parts,
but exists by counting individual hairs," then in the case of bedding belonging to the Saṅgha that has not been covered by anything such as a coverlet,
even if there are many hairs touched, it is not according to the count of the hairs themselves, but rather [it is considered a single offense] for each hair touched.
There is one offense for a single act; there are as many offenses as there are acts—this is the conclusion regarding multiple acts.
335. "A woman" means a human female. "Touched" means having come into physical contact with a part of the body such as the hand.

"With the intention of indulgence" means having exerted oneself by moving one's own body out of a lustful desire for bodily contact—this is the meaning. "An offense entailing suspension" (saṅghādisesa).
In this context, the suffix is a *taddhita* derivative used in its own sense (*sakatthe*). However, the reading “saṅghādisesitā” is more elegant;

its meaning is the state of being a *saṅghādisesa*, that is, the existence or the fact of being present. Since the existence—consisting in the actual presence—of the offense of *saṅghādisesa* serves as the ground for the application of the word *saṅghādisesī* to a person (in the sense of the suffix *ī*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*) is obtained by virtue of that meaning.
As they say: "When a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, suffixes such as -tta and so forth are used to denote that [quality].
(336) Regarding the phrase "having grasped with one hand," the words "through lust for bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsaggarāgena*) should be supplied and connected here.
"A human woman" (*manussitthiṃ*) is an elliptical insertion (*ajjhāhāra*). "That human woman. In the phrase "here and there" (*tattha tattha*), it refers to various parts of that woman.
Regarding "a limb of the body": the phrase "a single offense" is stated because the hand previously taken has not been relinquished.
However, by way of contrast, it is understood that for one who releases the taken hand and touches again and again, there is an offense according to the number of applications (*payoga*). 337.
Without grasping with one hand, [moving] from the head down to the foot, or from the foot up to the head, the hand [is moved] across the body...
The construction is: for one who touches that woman even for a single day without releasing her, there is one offense.
Here too, by way of contrast, it follows that for one who touches her after having released her, there are multiple offenses according to the number of applications. 338.
If there were to be an offense based on the counting of five fingers taken together, then [there would be an offense] for the body of a single woman...
For one who touches with a mind of lust, since there is no body apart from the thirty-two parts, there ought to be an offense according to the count of those thirty-two parts;
however, because that [separate body] does not exist, he said, "It cannot be [an offense] by way of parts," in order to show that this too does not occur.
340–1. Even for a woman who is doubtful, if she touches a woman’s body with her own body, there is a thullaccaya for her.
It may be that for a woman who perceives another as a *paṇḍaka* (a eunuch or impotent person), there is a *thullaccaya* offense when she touches the body of that woman with her own body.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), men and animals are included. For a woman who perceives another woman as such, there is a *thullaccaya* offense when she touches what is connected to the body of that woman with her own body.
[Likewise] for one who perceives a *paṇḍaka* as a *paṇḍaka*, [there is an offense] when she touches herself...
For one who touches the body of a paṇḍaka with his own body, there may be a thullaccaya offense.
The construction is as follows: for one who touches the body of a yakkhinī or a petī with his own body, perceiving her to be a yakkhinī or a petī, there may be a thullaccaya offense.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā: "By the mention of the *paṇḍaka*, the *ubhatobyañjanaka* (hermaphrodite) is also included. [And] "even for one who is doubtful about a woman..."

One should not construe [the text] thus: "Even for one who perceives [the person] as a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) and so forth, if he touches the body-connected part of a woman with his own body, there would be a *thullaccaya* offense" for him.
Why? Because if it were construed in that way, a *dukkaṭa* would have been stated in the Pāḷi, rather than a *thullaccaya*, which would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭhappasaṅga*).
This is because the case is included within the method presented in the Vinaya source: "There is a *dukkaṭa* in bodily contact with a female animal."

By that same method, it should be understood that all the offenses of *dukkaṭa* mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) regarding the three cases of physical contact—namely, when one perceives a paṇḍaka as a woman or has doubt, and so forth;

when one perceives a male animal or has doubt regarding a male animal, and so forth; and when one perceives a paṇḍaka or has doubt, and so forth—all these are to be characterized as applicable to the three types of persons and the objects such as seats and so on.

342. The construction is as follows: for a bhikkhu who touches with his own body, which is attached [to clothing], the body of a woman which is attached [to clothing], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Here, the word *pi* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for the aforementioned *dukkaṭa*s. Furthermore, by the word *ca*, which has the sense of a conjunction for what is not yet mentioned, [it is said]:
"He touches with a relinquished [article] the body; he touches with a relinquished [article] that which is attached to the body..."

“He touches it. If he touches what is subject to forfeiture with what is subject to forfeiture, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); thus should the inclusion of the *dukkaṭa* offenses mentioned in the Canon be understood.
343–4. Not only the female body and so forth mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) are untouchable;

following the cases in the Vinaya, there are also female effigies such as dolls made of wood or clay, and—following the section on forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vāra*)—non-body parts such as clothing and ornaments previously used by women.

Following the method explained in the Vibhaṅga, Khandhaka, and other sections, he says "of women," and so forth, in order to include the offense incurred by one who touches any remaining object described in the commentaries that is not itself subject to defilement (*anāmāsavatthu*).
Regarding the phrase "the female form of women," this refers to instances such as "the woman’s wealth of a woman" and "those with faith, whose ultimate resort is faith."
This is stated according to worldly convention. The construction is: "the female form made of wood, metal, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes female forms made of clay or dough from the lower limit [of permissible materials].
Having accepted everything except that which is given by anyone as being composed of all kinds of jewels, one should break the female form and [use] requisites suitable for a recluse.
It is permissible to have it made, or to apply it to something that is not to be used without having first touched it.

By the term "cloth" (*vattha*), both the lower garment (*nivāsana*) and the upper robe (*pārupana*) are included in a general sense. Furthermore, even if this has been set aside for a woman to use, it remains *anāmāsa* (untouchable);
however, it is permissible to accept and take it once it has been given for the purpose of robes. This is the minimum limit.
This includes even a tuft of grass or a leaf-ring for a finger, provided it is merely an ornament.

Furthermore, in this context, items such as ivory needles used for threading hair or arranging curls—which are allowable articles—may be accepted when given for the purpose of requisites suitable for a recluse.
Likewise, fruit grown there may be eaten; that is, jackfruit, coconut, and other fruits found on trees may be consumed by people.

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "the same principle applies even when [fruit] has been heaped by humans," the phrase "that which has been heaped" (*rāsikata*) should be understood as an illustrative term (*upalakkhaṇa*) meaning that such fruit is not to be touched (*anāmāsa*).

It is permissible to pick fruit fallen from a tree in the forest with the intention, "I will give this to one who is not fully ordained. This is because the phrase "mung beans, etc., grown there" (*muggādiṃ tatthajātakaṃ*) is also an illustrative term.
Even when one is walking away, it should be taken up. Regarding the term "muggādi" (mung beans, etc.), the word "aparaṇṇaṃ" (other grains) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
"All grains" refers to the seven types of grain mentioned: "rice, paddy, barley, millet, rye, and excellent wheat.
One walking by way of a field should proceed without touching the rice ears with the hand. If the path is narrow...
It is permissible; even when grain touches the body, there is no fault because it is on the path.

If one is unable to go by stepping aside when grain is spread out on a road or in a courtyard, it is allowable to go thinking, "I will go along this path," based on the commentary’s statement that "one should go having determined it to be a path. If, however, a seat is prepared on top of the grain in a family home...
"It has been given; it is permissible to sit," so it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
"When grain is scattered in the dining hall, one should not walk over it, but having prepared a seat to one side, one may sit.
If people offer a seat by placing it on top of that grain, it is permissible to sit," because this is stated in the Commentary, [one may sit] there oneself...
It is not permitted to sit after having prepared a seat. 345. The connection is:
"all [instruments] beginning with the *dhamana* and the conch, as well as the fivefold musical ensemble. A *dhamana*-conch is a conch that produces sound.
By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), flutes, horns, drums, and so forth are included. The "fivefold musical ensemble" (*pañcaṅgaturiya*) consists of the *ātata*... [and so on].
The fivefold musical ensemble consists of the *ātata*, the *vitata*, the *ātatavitata*, the *ghana*, and the *susira*.
Among these, *ātata* refers to single-surfaced instruments, such as drums covered with leather, which are stretched and bound on one side.
*Vitata* refers to double-surfaced instruments, which are stretched and bound on both sides. *Ātatavitata* refers to those that are [stretched] on both sides...
"Enveloped on all sides from the middle": "solid" (*ghana*) refers to a drum (*tāḷa*); the inclusion here also encompasses the bell, the small gong, and so forth.
"Hollow" (*susira*) refers to the flute and the like.

Here, according to the method stated in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, there are the kettle-drum (*bheri*) and its bowl, as well as the skin of the kettle-drum, and the lute (*vīṇā*) and the skin of the lute-bowl.

"And the staff is not to be touched. Regarding this, the *Mahāpaccarī* states: "Having performed worship, one should sweep the remaining areas—such as the courtyard of the cetiya—without moving the drums placed there.
When discarding rubbish, it should be gathered like refuse and set aside in one place.
Among musical instruments, whatever is being given to oneself should be exchanged [for something else].

One should consent to accept allowable requisites. A trough or a basin may be taken for the purpose of setting aside tooth-sticks, and leather may be taken for the purpose of making sheaths for knives.
And as for "all kinds of gems," these are: pearl, gem, beryl, conch, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and so forth.
And all gems are called "masāragalla. In this context, all pearls—whether pierced or unpierced, such as those from the ocean and so forth—are untouchable (*anāmāsa*).
It is not permitted to take them even for the purpose of their value as merchandise.

Even down to the *jātiphalika* (cinnamon-stone), every kind of gem distinguished by color such as blue, yellow, and so on, is untouchable when polished and pierced. One that remains in its natural state, unpierced and unpolished, [is likewise untouchable].
It is stated that it is permissible to accept items such as jewels and cloth for the purpose of providing the raw materials [for robes]. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, this is prohibited.
Only glass beads (*kācamaṇi*) made by melting [the material] are permitted. The determination regarding *veḷuriya* (cat’s-eye) is exactly the same as for jewels (*maṇi*).
The conch shell used for blowing (*dhamanasaṅkha*) is included among musical instruments in the verse beginning with “all conch shells used for blowing,” etc. [An object] inlaid with gems...
A conch shell is not to be touched (*anāmāsa*). A water-conch, whether washed or unwashed, is to be touched.
However, other types of conch shells are permitted to be kept for the purpose of medicinal ointments and the like, or as the base material for items such as alms bowls.
A stone ground smooth with gold, having the color of a mung bean, is not to be touched. Other stones are permitted to be kept for minor tasks such as sharpening tools.

Because it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that “coral, whether washed or unwashed, pierced or unpierced, is in every respect untouchable (*anāmāsa*), and one must not even consent to it,” one must neither take nor touch images of coral or shrines,
nor the round [ornaments] made in the shape of lotuses and so forth that are to be inserted at the base and the tip of the needles to be placed inside books.
Starting from the seed, silver and gold—whether worked or unworked—are entirely untouchable and must not be accepted.
By this [rule], he will state that images and the like made of these, as well as base metals (*ārakūṭaloha*), are untouchable.

Because the non-acceptance of worked and unworked gold and silver is what has come down in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) here, [the Buddha] spoke regarding the Golden Cetiya brought by the Northern Prince after having it constructed.

"It is not allowable" means that it was rejected by Mahāpaduma Thera; therefore, anything such as a golden image, a cetiya, a book-cover, a gem-lotus, or a round ornament must not be accepted at all, nor should they be touched. However, it is allowable to use furniture or requisites made from these materials.
It is also allowable to maintain a Dhamma-maṇḍapa built with them. As for a gem of red color:
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that a *masāragalla* gem is entirely *anāmāsa* (untouchable) and must not be accepted. 346. Regarding "all weapons and implements":

all weaponry and equipment, such as swords and the like, when offered for the purpose of obtaining basic requisites like bowls and other allowable items, must not be accepted because they are improper for a merchant;
if one is given [something] saying, "Take this," one should break it [before accepting].
It is permissible to accept [an object] by having it cut into pieces with the thought, "I shall have it made into allowable requisites such as a razor.

Upon seeing a sword or similar item fallen on a battlefield or on a road, it is permissible to break it with a stone and take it with the thought, "I shall have it made into allowable articles such as a razor.
A spear, javelin, or similar weapon should be taken for the purpose of having it made into allowable requisites by removing the shaft from the point.
The string is like a bow. By the letter *ca*, one includes items such as hooks and spears that were not mentioned in this verse, along with their accessories.
A "bow-handle" (*dhanudaṇḍaka*) is a bow-handle devoid of a string.

If these implements for harming others, such as weapons and the like, have been placed in a place within the monastery that is to be swept, one should sweep it without moving them, provided that after informing the owners, they do not take them back.

"And a net" means a net such as a fish-net, a bird-net, and so forth. When a net is being given for the purpose of covering a parasol, or when there is a need to bind it to the top of a throne, a cetiya, or similar objects, it should be accepted for that purpose.

A "shield" (saravāraṇa) refers to a wooden shield or similar object used to ward off arrows discharged by others for the purpose of piercing oneself; since it serves as a cause for destruction or obstruction, it is for the sake of the value of the goods.
It is permissible to eat it. Having removed the handful [of food], it is permissible to take whatever one desires, such as a tooth-stick, a stand for the tooth-stick, or a board.
347. Regarding the term *cetiya*: here, the phrase "golden cetiya" is understood because it was mentioned immediately after "golden images and so forth.
Furthermore, the mention of "gold" is illustrative; thus, those made of silver should also be included. *Ārakūṭaka* means gold-colored.
He states a specific type of metal: “Not to be touched” (*anāmāsa*) is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) for the phrase “or not having accepted.
348. The connection is “all that is played upon. “To have covered” means to bind with leather, thongs, or strings.
“To have caused to be covered” means to have it done in that same way by others. “To have caused to be played” means to have it played by others. “To play” means to play it oneself.
“Vāditam” means that which is to be played, just as “kāritam” [is used for] “karaṇīyam”; the meaning is musical instruments worthy of being played.
And this is the object of the action such as covering and so forth.

“Upahāraṃ karissāma” means “we shall perform worship. This is for the purpose of obtaining permission. “Vattabbā” is to be construed as: “they are to be addressed; they are those who should be spoken to.”

"By a woman who is a *dhuttī*" means by a loose woman of depraved conduct. "While being touched by her own [hand]" means while the monk is being touched by the woman herself, without his own exertion.
"Without moving the body" means without moving one's own body for the purpose of experiencing the contact with her body. "Perceiving the touch" means experiencing the touch.
Regarding the term *asañcicca* (unintentionally), there is a textual supplement here: *“phusane”* (in touching). This means:

without having intended, thinking, “By this means I shall touch her. What is meant? It refers to one who, without thinking, “By this means—such as by means of a bowl, a vessel, or the like—I shall experience the physical contact of her body,” causes [a woman] to take hold of her own hand while it contains a bowl, a ladle, a tray, a leaf-cup, medicine, or similar items.

It is stated that there is no offense in cases such as touching with the hand. As for the phrase "through lack of mindfulness," this is not mentioned separately here because it is already included by the preceding [term].
The meaning is: one who touches while extending the hands, feet, and so forth, without being aware of the act of touching the female body, being distracted and having failed to establish mindfulness.
"Without knowing" means: when one touches a girl who has the appearance of a child, not knowing her to be "a woman," because of some business;
and "one whose intention is liberation" means: "If one whose intention is liberation makes an effort with the body and perceives contact, there is no offense.
If one whose intention is liberation makes an effort with the body and does not perceive contact, there is no offense. One whose intention is liberation..."
"If one does not exert oneself with the body but discerns contact, there is no offense.

If one intends liberation, does not exert oneself with the body, and does not discern contact, there is no offense"—this refers to the four types of persons who possess the intention for liberation, as stated.
This is to be connected with the phrase "there is no offense."
Among these, the first person is one who, when being overwhelmed by a woman through methods such as embracing and so forth, desires to remove her from his own body and,
wishing to release himself, employs hand-waving, or repelling with the fist and so on,
or uses methods such as striking her. [The second is one who], upon seeing a woman coming to overwhelm him, employs every method such as the manner of striking and so forth.
The second [type] is one who, having shown himself and terrified her, does not allow his body to be touched.

The third is one who, thinking "she will flee of her own accord" because she considers him "one who desires no pleasure" when he is embraced after being overwhelmed by a woman, and knowing that "non-friction itself is the means of escape," remains motionless while experiencing the contact.
[The fourth is one who remains motionless] as she comes to overwhelm him...

One who, upon seeing a woman, does not make a physical movement to frighten her as a second [offender] would, but remains motionless while thinking, "I will cause her to fall when she has not yet arrived," or "I will strike her and frighten her," is to be understood as the fourth.
Regarding the phrase "by the first," there is a textual supplement here: "by a pārājika offense"; thus, it is meant that [the offense] originates from both body and mind.
Here, "mind" refers to a mind associated with lust for physical contact, or a mind associated with the desire to discharge semen.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of physical contact. 353–4.
Regarding "delight in lewd speech": it is called *duṭṭhulla* because it goes toward (*ulati*) a state that is bad (*duṭṭhu*) or vile (*kucchita*). It is lewd...
And that speech which is extremely indecent is "indecent speech," namely speech connected with sexual intercourse via the anus or the urinary passage;
as it is said: "Indecent speech means speech connected with sexual intercourse via the anus or the urinary passage.
The gratification derived from indecent speech is "the gratification of indecent speech"; it is associated with the consciousness that originates the vocal intimation proceeding in such a manner.
Volition (*cetanā*); the lust associated with that is here called “delighting in lewd speech” by way of association.
The meaning is: “by means of that lust associated with delighting in lewd speech. By this, the cause for the “shining forth” (*obhāsantassa*) which is about to be mentioned is shown.
The construction is: “a monk who perceives a woman as a woman. Regarding “perceives a woman as a woman”: “a woman (*mātugāmo*) is a human female.”

The meaning is: a monk who perceives as a woman a human female—of the specific type described in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "neither a *yakkhī*, nor a *petī*, nor an animal, but one who is conscious and capable of understanding what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, and what is grave and not grave"—who knows what is well-spoken and ill-spoken.
[The term] "of a woman" is used here in connection with the phrase "of two paths."
This should be applied according to the Sāmiva method; the meaning is: "the anus and the urinary passage of a woman of the aforementioned appearance.
And "by way of praise and blame" means: "to speak praise is to extol, laud, and commend the two passages;
to speak blame is to revile, disparage, and censure the two passages," according to the method stated in the Niddesa.
It means "with reference to both paths," by way of praising and censuring.
"Soliciting sexual intercourse and so forth" refers to *methunayācanādayo*; by means of those [acts] such as soliciting sexual intercourse—namely, by way of what is stated in the enumeration:
"he solicits, he entreats, he asks, he inquires back, he explains, he instructs, and he even reviles."
This has been stated. By these two [terms], the "shining forth" (*obhāsana*) mentioned in the phrase "of one shining forth" (*obhāsantassa*) is demonstrated.
"Of one shining forth" means of one who is indicating or making manifest; this is the meaning. By the word "intelligent" (*viññuṃ*), the object of the act of shining forth is expressed.

That which is to be qualified by this—namely, "a human woman"—is obtained from the context, specifically an intelligent person whose form corresponds to that found in the textual analysis (*padabhājana*) as it has been shown.
"Capable woman" means a human female; "even by means of a hand-gesture" indicates the lower limit for illumination.

When there is a relish for indecent speech, it refers to a human female who—whether by way of requesting sexual intercourse or otherwise—knows the difference between the foul and the non-foul regarding the anus or the urinary passage, as defined by the lower limit.
The meaning is that one might also speak by means of hand gestures.
In these two verses, for a monk who, out of delight in indecent speech, perceives a woman as a woman and makes a proposal to her—
even if only by hand gesture— by way of praising the two paths, it would be a grave offense.
There is one sentence; likewise, by connecting the phrases "by way of disparaging two paths" and "by [means of] soliciting sexual intercourse and so forth," there are two sentences.
Thus, by way of such connections, there are three sentences.
Among them, for one who speaks words of praise and so forth included under the term "words of praise" in the first sentence, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
There is no *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who speaks merely for the purpose of praise, saying, "You were endowed with the female characteristic and the beautiful characteristic.
However, there is an offense for one who says, "Such is your anus and such is your urethra—so beautiful and well-proportioned;
indeed, you were endowed with such a female characteristic and such a beautiful characteristic."
The two terms “vaṇṇeti” (praises) and “pasaṃsati” (extols) are synonyms for the term “thometi” (honors).
In the second sentence, among the triad beginning with “khuṃsana” (reviling) which is included under the term “avaṇṇa” (disparagement), “khuṃsana” means piercing with harsh words that are like goads.
As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: “‘Khuṃseti’ means he strikes with the goad of speech. [The phrase] “patujjatena” means...
“Goad” (*patoda*) refers to the piercing and driving stick used to urge on horses and other animals as they move. “Contempt” (*vambhana*) means disparagement.
Disparagement means causing one to fall away from their virtues; as it is said: “He contemns means he disparages. “Reproach” (*garahā*) means the attribution of faults;
as it is said: “He reproaches means he assigns blame. This speech is connected with such censures as *khumsanā* and the like.
When speaking by applying any one of these three phrases among those about to be mentioned— “You are a *sikharaṇī*,” “You are a *sambhinnā*,” or “You are a *ubhatobyañjanā*”—
it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the speaker alone, not for the other. In the third statement,
even for one who performs a request or the like that is subsumed under the expressions of requesting sexual intercourse and so forth, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

“Begging” means that by joining each individual phrase—such as “Give me,” “It is right for you to give me,” and so forth—with the phrase regarding sexual intercourse, such as “Give me the practice of sexual intercourse,” it constitutes precisely one who is begging for sexual intercourse. [Examples include:
“When will your mother be pleased? When will your father be pleased? When will the deities be pleased?”
In the description of the words of supplication beginning with, “When will there be for you a good day, a good lunar mansion, and a good moment?
each individual word is connected with the phrase stated at the very end, “When shall I obtain sexual intercourse with you?”—thus it pertains only to one who is supplicating for sexual intercourse.

Furthermore, in the statements describing the questions, such as, “How do you give to your husband? How do you give to a paramour? it pertains only to one who asks while connecting either of those phrases with the term “sexual intercourse.”

This applies specifically to one who asks a question after having combined and distinguished one of the statements from the "counter-question" (*paṭipucchā*) or "instruction" (*niddesa*) formulas with the term "sexual intercourse" (*methunadhamma*), such as: "In this way, it seems, you give to your husband; in this way, you give to your lover.

When a woman is asked, "How does she become dear to her husband while giving? the same principle applies to the words of instruction and exhortation given to her: "Give in this way; by giving in this way, she will be dear and pleasing to her husband."

355. Regarding the eleven categories mentioned in the *Akkosaniddesa*— namely, "you are signless," "you are a mere sign," "you are bloodless," "you are constantly bleeding," "you are always clad in rags," "you are oozing," "you are a *sikharaṇī*," "you are a female eunuch," "you are a man-like woman," "you are a *sambhinnā*," and "you are a hermaphrodite"—
the three terms "you are a *sikharaṇī*," "you are a *sambhinnā*," and "you are a hermaphrodite" [are explained] individually.
Regarding the phrase "causing an offense": together with the three previously mentioned terms—*vaccamagga*, *passāvamagga*, and *methunadhamma*—there are six terms in total.

Since each of these six terms individually causes an offense, the eight subsequent terms beginning with *animitta* are to be combined with the term *methunadhamma* according to the method [of the text], such as:
"You are without signs; give me sexual intercourse," and so forth.
It should be understood that these are indeed stated as causes for an offense. Regarding the phrase "by means of soliciting sexual intercourse,
etc.," although the eleven abusive terms included under the word "etc."— such as "you are without genitals" and so forth— are also included therein,
he said "you are a *sikharaṇī*" and so on to indicate that three specific terms, being solely causes for an offense, must be categorized separately as more serious.
Regarding the phrase *sikharaṇīsī*: here the word-division is *sikharaṇī asi*. The word *asi* (“you are”) should be construed with each [epithet].
The particle *tu* indicates a distinction, signifying that even a single abusive expression constitutes an offense. The construction is: “even by a single abusive word.
*Sikharaṇīsī* means you are one whose flesh of the anus has protruded. *Sambhinnāsī* means one whose passages for feces and urine have become mixed together.
“Those with both sexual characteristics” (*ubhatobyañjanā*) means those endowed with both female and male characteristics.
It is called a “characteristic” (*byañjana*) because it makes manifest (*byañjeti*) that “this is a woman” or “this is a man”; these are the urinary organs.
Regarding the phrase “of one who hears,” the term “a woman who is a human being of discernment” is understood here by virtue of the governing context; by this, the basis for the abuse is shown.
The meaning is: for a human woman who hears what is said and knows what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense due to abusive speech occurring within her range. 356.
The construction is: "For one who repeatedly makes a proposal, there may be heavy [offenses] according to the count of the words. Here, "one..."

The word “woman” (*itthi*) must be supplied [from the previous context]. The construction is as follows: even for one who illuminates many [things] with a single utterance, there would be a heavy offense according to the number of women.
Here too, the phrase “even though they are women” (*itthiyopi*) is applicable.
357. Regarding the phrase “if she does not admit it”: here, [it refers to] a human woman whom they hear [speaking], by way of praising or disparaging two paths.
"‘It shines forth; if she does not acknowledge it’—this should be construed by taking what is obtained through the force of the context.
The meaning is: if, immediately after her own speech, she does not recognize it as a grave matter (duṭṭhulla) by way of its significance. ‘Of him’ means of that monk who spoke the grave matter.
Also, in the case of speaking while referring to [the area] above the knees or below the collarbone..."
“For him there may be a *thullaccaya* offense”—this is the construction. Regarding the phrase “in speaking”: it refers to the description of the qualities (*vaṇṇa*) and so forth of two paths.

Some also write “of one who speaks” (*bhaṇato*), meaning “for one who is speaking,” or “on account of speaking. This suffix *-anta* is used in the sense of a cause, as in the word “unawakened” (*asambudha*) and others.
“Above the knees” (*ubbhajāṇuṃ*) means above the knee. “Below the collarbone” (*akkhekaṃ*) means below the collarbone.
358. *Ubbhakkhakaṃ* means above the collarbone (*akkhaka*). *Adhojāṇumaṇḍalaṃ* means below the kneecaps (*jāṇumaṇḍala*). *Uddisanti* means pointing out;
they write it as "pointing out [the area] above the collarbone or likewise below the kneecaps," and that reading is excellent.

The connection is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in describing the color and so forth. This is understood from the governing context of "for a woman who is a human being capable of understanding."
Regarding the statement that "there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in describing the color and so forth of what is connected to the body," the same principle applies here as well.
The anus and the urinary tract are the domain of a Saṅghādisesa offense; the area below the collarbone and above the kneecaps is the domain of a Thullaccaya offense;
and the area above the collarbone and below the kneecaps is the domain of a Dukkaṭa offense. Among these three domains, both the collarbone and the kneecaps [are included].
Wherein is that which serves as the boundary for both the *thullaccaya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses included?
It is included within the field of *dukkaṭa* itself. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The collarbone and the kneecaps, however, are included in this very field of *dukkaṭa*."
359. Regarding the description of the appearance and other qualities of the two paths among paṇḍakas, yakkhis, and petīs: for one who speaks thus, there is a thullaccaya offense.

This should be connected with the words that follow according to their respective contexts. In the phrase "among paṇḍakas, etc.," the word "etc. includes yakkhis and petīs. 360. The method beginning with "above the collarbone...
and so forth—this method should be connected with the phrase "among paṇḍakas, etc. This method [indicates] that it is merely a dukkaṭa offense.
The method has been stated thus: "It happens. "In all cases" means in all fields, by way of the fields of *saṅghādisesa*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa*.
361. The construction is: "There is no offense even for one who utters a hint (*obhāsa*) while having the welfare [of others] as his primary concern.

Or, for one who speaks the words "you are without signs," etc., having made the explanation of the meaning of such phrases as "you are without signs" to women his primary concern, or [for one who speaks] with women...
The meaning is that there is no offense for those who are reciting [the texts] together with the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The construction is: "There is no offense for one who, having placed the Dhamma foremost, speaks from a mere illumination.

Or, for one who is teaching the canonical Dhamma (*pāḷidhamma*), or who—having placed their recitation foremost while they are listening—speaks anything to a woman, whether she be a female renunciant or otherwise, regarding such passages as "you are signless" (*animittāsi*) and so forth.
“Non-offense” means: having kept in mind the instruction, that is, having kept in mind the instruction: “Now you are without marks... [etc. ... you are a hermaphrodite;
now you should practice heedfulness, so that in the future you will not become like this again.
(362) “Of those who are insane, etc. refers to two types of insanity—namely, insanity due to bile and insanity due to a *yakṣa*—and those included by the word “etcetera.”
It is stated that there is no offense for this first offender, the Elder Udāyī. "This training rule has three origins:
it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. It is an action; it is liberated by perception;
it involves consciousness; it is a worldly transgression; it is bodily action and verbal action; and it is an unwholesome state of mind."
He shows the miscellaneous determinations stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* with the words: "The origins and so forth... are equal.

Because it is not completed by taking what is not given through feeling, he says: "Feeling here is considered twofold"; the meaning is that it is considered twofold by way of pleasant and neutral feeling.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of improper speech.

363. Regarding "service for the sake of sensual pleasure" (*kāmapāricariyā*): it means service by means of sensual pleasure, which is designated as the act of sexual intercourse; the sense is "service through the act of sexual intercourse.
Alternatively, "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) refers to those things desired or longed for;

the sense is "longed for by way of lust for sexual intercourse. It is "sensual pleasure and that service," hence *kāmapāricariyā*; thus it should also be understood as "of that service for the sake of sensual pleasure."
The meaning is: "with a mind of lust for sexual intercourse, she aspired to serve [him]. This connects with the phrase "speaking in praise":
"Sister, this is the foremost of services—that one should serve someone like me, who is virtuous, of good character, and living the holy life, with this kind of service.
Thus he spoke of the quality and the benefit of his own service through the act of sexual intercourse.
"Speaking" means it is said [thus]. "At that very moment" means at the very moment of speaking.
"If she knows" means if she who was spoken to understands immediately upon hearing the words. 364.
"If that human woman does not know, there is a thullaccaya for him"—this is the connection. [This applies] among yakkhinīs, petīs, and devīs.

The construction is as follows: when [the women] know [he is a man], and when he speaks in praise of serving his own desires to a paṇḍaka whom he knows [to be one], that bhikkhu incurs a thullaccaya offense.

Regarding the word "the rest": when he speaks in praise of serving his own desires within the domain of male animals or to non-human beings such as yakkhas whom he does not know [to be such], that offense is a dukkaṭa; this is the construction.

365. "By robes and so forth" means by robes, almsfood, and the rest. "By objects of sensual desire" (*vatthukāma*) refers to the conditions known as *vatthu* because they serve as the basis for craving, and as *kāma* because they are desired;

thus, they are designated as "objects of sensual desire. 366. "Lust itself is lustfulness" (*rāgatā*). Alternatively, the reading is "lustfulness" (*rāgitā*): one who has lust is a "lustful one" (*rāgī*); the state of being such is lustfulness.
The meaning is that lust consists in the pursuit of one's own sensual desires. "Radiance" (*obhāsa*) refers to the praising of the virtues of one's own pursuit of sensual desires. By that—
"By lust" means by the lust for the service of one's own desires. "At that moment" means at the moment of speaking.
"Understanding" means that which understands the meaning of those words spoken by him who praises the service of his own desires with reference to a human woman; this is what is meant. 367.
"The five factors" are: being a human woman, the perception of her as such, being lustful regarding the service, the manifestation of that lust, and...

"At that moment, one understands": this means that here, in this training rule concerning the service of one's own desires (*attakāmapāricariyā*), there are five factors, which are the five grounds for an offense (*āpatti*).
"Of this" refers to the training rule concerning the service of one's own desires. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the service of one's own desires.
368. Regarding the phrase “paṭiggaṇhāti” (accepts) and so forth: because of the capacity for the threefold action of undertaking, it is to be applied three times.
Since the words “yo bhikkhu” (whatever monk) and “garu hoti” (it is serious) possess the capacity [to indicate the subject], the word “tassa” (for him) is understood.
Thus, together with these three types [of offenses], it means: “Whatever monk accepts a man’s message, investigates it, and reports it back, for him...”
"Is heavy," this constitutes one sentence. Likewise, by connecting it with "or even for a woman," this also constitutes one sentence;
thus, two sentences are appropriate for this verse.
Here, first of all, for the sake of understanding both the sequence of the message and the sequence of the construction, [one should consider] "of women" and "of wives."
The classification and the nature [of these] are explained: among them, women are of ten kinds. As it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):

"Ten kinds of women: one protected by her mother, one protected by her father, one protected by both parents, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by the Dhamma, one who has guardians, and one who is subject to punishment. And wives are also of ten kinds.
They exist. As it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): “Ten kinds of wives:

one purchased with wealth, one who lives by her own will, one who lives on her earnings, one who shares the water-pot, one whose head-cloth has been removed, a slave-wife, a wife who is a laborer, one captured under a banner, and a momentary wife.
The classification of these and their specific characteristics should be understood briefly as follows:
One who does not cohabit with men is "protected by her mother" (*māturakkhitā*). As it is said:

"Protected by her mother means that the mother protects her, guards her, exercises authority over her, and keeps her under her control. The same principle applies to those protected by their father (*piturakkhitā*) and the others.
In this context, she is protected by those born into the very same lineage (*gotra*), such as the Koṇḍañña clan, in which she herself was born.
“Protected by family” (*gottarakkhitā*): as it is said, “one protected by family means one who is protected by those of the same clan,” and so forth.
“Protected by Dhamma” (*dhammarakkhitā*): she is protected by those who have gone forth under the same Teacher or by those included in the same monastic group;

as it is said, “one protected by Dhamma means one who is protected by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma,” and so forth. “One with a guardian” (*sārakkhā*) means one who has been taken in marriage even while in the womb.
The expression used in the Canon is: "She belongs to me," even in the case of one who is merely adorned with a garland of flowers.
"With a penalty" (*saparidaṇḍā*) means: "A penalty has been set by certain people, saying, 'Whoever approaches such-and-such a woman, for him there is such-and-such a penalty.
This is a summary of the characteristics of the ten types of women. Among these ten, regarding those who are "with a protector" (*sārakkha*) and "with a penalty" (*saparidaṇḍā*):
Sexual misconduct occurs when one serves two men; for others, it does not. These ten women are also not to be approached by those who observe the five precepts (*pañcasīla*).
Among the ten types of wives, because it is said that "one bought with wealth" means she is kept after being purchased with money, she is considered a wife.
One who is taken after giving wealth, whether little or much, is called "bought with wealth" (*dhanakkītā*).
One who is accepted by a man according to his own desire—because it is said, "She who dwells by consent (*chandavāsinī*) is one whom the lover makes dwell with him"—is called "dwelling by consent.

One who is made to dwell [with him] after being given property—because it is said, "She who dwells for the sake of property (*bhogavāsinī*) is one whom he makes dwell after giving property"—[refers to] household requisites such as the mortar, pestle, and so forth.
A woman from the countryside who becomes a wife after being purchased is called a *bhogavāsinī*.

A poor woman who becomes a wife after receiving merely a lower garment (*nivāsana*) or an upper garment (*pārupana*) is called a *paṭavāsinī*, because it is said that "one who dwells by giving a cloth is a *paṭavāsinī*.
One who is called an *odapattakinī* is so named because "she dwells after touching a water-bowl."

Because it is said, "Be united and inseparable like this water," a woman who has been led to the state of wife by lowering her hand into a single bowl of water together with a man is called [a *mātugāma*]. Because it is said,

"One whose head-cloth is removed (*obhaṭacumbaṭā*) means she dwells having taken off the head-cloth (*cumbaṭa*)," one who has been led to the state of wife after removing the head-cloth from her head is [called so].

A woman such as a wood-gatherer who has had her nose-ring removed is called "one whose nose-stopper has been taken off. A female slave and wife is so called because it is stated: "she is both a female slave and a wife";
having been made a wife and lived with him, she is called "his very own female slave and wife. A female laborer and wife is so called because it is stated:
"she is both a female laborer and a wife"; [this refers to one] regardless of whether she was previously a primary wife.
Having been made to perform household duties, she was brought to the state of being a wife; once the work was done, she was called "a wife who is also a laborer.

Because it is said, "One 'brought by the banner' is one brought as a prisoner of war," she was brought back after having gone with a great army that had raised its banners and plundered a foreign territory, and having been captured, she was brought to the state of being a wife.

A woman is called "one carried by the flag" (*dhajāhaṭā*). Because it is said, "One called 'momentary' (*muhuttikā*) is termed 'instantaneous'," a woman taken for the purpose of cohabitation for a short time is called "momentary.
This is the summary of the ten types of wives. Among the ten women mentioned above, the intended meaning is for any one of them to be placed in the position of any one of the ten wives.
He accepts the message given by a man—such as, "Go, venerable sir, tell so-and-so who is protected by her mother:

'May you, it is said, become the wife of so-and-so for a price,'" and so forth—either by making a verbal response such as, "Very well, lay follower," and so forth, or by means of nodding the head and the like; thus it is said: "He accepts the message from the man."
In this context, because the term "of a man" (*purisassa*) is used as an illustration, one should understand it to include the mother, father,
and so forth of the man mentioned in the Canon by way of such phrases as "the man’s mother sends a bhikkhu. "He investigates" means that he reports the message thus received to either his own mother,
father, or another relative, ensuring that he does not at all fail her.

The meaning is as follows. Here too, because the word "investigates" (*vīmaṃsati*) is used as an illustration, one should also understand it to mean "causes [someone] to investigate," since it is stated:
"If, having caused the pupil to investigate, he receives [the message] himself, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*. Regarding "he reports back":
having heard the message thus brought back, whether that woman has accepted it or not, out of shame...

It is said that he reports back on that occurrence and explains it to her while she remains silent. Here too, because the term "reports back" (*paccāharati*) is used as an indicative characteristic (*upalakkhaṇa*), one must understand it to include "causes to report back," since it is stated:
"If he accepts [the matter], investigates it, and causes the pupil to report back, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*."

“Or by a woman”—having connected this with the second sentence thus taken up, the meaning should be explained in exactly the same way. Regarding that, the sequence of the message should be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi text beginning with:
“A mother-guarded woman sends a messenger [to a monk], saying: ‘Go, venerable sir, tell so-and-so:
“I am the wife of so-and-so, purchased for a price,”’” and so forth. Here too, [the phrase] “she causes to be examined”...
And this [phrase] "he causes to be brought back" should be understood according to the method already stated.
By this same principle, after stating the names of ten women individually, the sequence of sending a message for the sake of one among ten wives should be applied.
Here too, because the phrase "or even by a woman" is an inclusive indication (*upalakkhaṇa*), [it includes cases such as: "The mother of a woman protected by her mother sends a monk, saying: 'Go...'"
"Venerable sir, speak thus: 'Let such-and-such a woman be the wife of such-and-such a man, purchased with wealth,'" and so forth;
according to this canonical formula, the sequence of messages between the woman and her mother, father, and others should be applied.

370. "That occurrence": on account of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*), that is, for the purpose of conveying messages. "Is not released": the meaning is that one is not released from the *saṅghādisesa* offense incurred by the reason of acting as a go-between by receiving messages between a woman and a man.
371. “Aññaṃ vā” means one or another among those protected by mother, father, and so forth.

They write “bhāsato,” but because that contradicts the word “pesito,” one should discard that and adopt the reading “bhāsati,” or else supply the missing words [to read “pesito bhāsati”]. It has been stated without doubt:
“The construction is ‘yo aññaṃ bhāsati ce, tassa bhāsato’” (if he speaks of another, it is for him who speaks). “Mātarā rakkhitaṃ... [and so on].

Our preference is that the construction is more appropriate as follows: "If one who has been sent [with the message], 'Go, speak to a woman,' speaks to one protected by her father or another, there is a breach of the agreement (visaṅketa)";
and "If, having been sent by a mother... [etc. ... with the words, 'Go, speak,' one speaks to one protected by her father or another, there is a breach of the agreement. This is our view.
372. Regarding "by means of receiving and so forth": *paṭiggaṇhanatā* is simply the state of receiving. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), examination and bringing back [the message] are included.
Regarding *sañcaritte*: it means in the act of acting as a go-between. Regarding *samāpanne*: when [the messenger] has gone.
Regarding *garukāpattiṃ ādiseti*: here the word "to her" (*tassā*) is to be supplied. *Ādiseti* means she should speak.
373. Regarding the statement, "By two [factors], a thullaccaya is said": here it should be understood that when one has engaged in matchmaking through two by two factors, a thullaccaya is said.
"If she accepts [the proposal], investigates, but does not bring back a reply, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If she accepts, does not investigate, but brings back a reply, there is an offense of thullaccaya. If she does not accept, but investigates..."
"He brings back [the message], there is an offense of *thullaccaya*": the meaning is that an offense of *thullaccaya* is stated for each pair of factors.

"In the case of eunuchs, etc. means among eunuchs, yakṣas, and so forth. The construction is: "When one has engaged in matchmaking (*sañcaritta*) even with three factors, an offense of *thullaccaya* is stated.
"By only one" means by only one factor. "In all cases" refers to all women, such as those protected by their mothers, and in the context of the formal legal procedure (*vinītavatthu*).
Now at that time, a certain man directed a certain bhikkhu, saying: “Go, venerable sir, and investigate such-and-such a woman.
Having gone, he asked people, “Where is such-and-such a woman?
They replied, “She is asleep, venerable sir”… [and so on] …“She is dead, venerable sir. “She has gone out, venerable sir. “She is not a woman, venerable sir. “She is a paṇḍaka-woman, venerable sir.”

He felt remorse. “There is no offense, monk, for a *saṅghādisesa*; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)”—thus it is stated in the five [categories] beginning with the Sutta. 374. “There is no offense when it is made known”:
this refers to what must be done at a shrine (*cetiyādi*) on behalf of a woman by a man, or by a man [on behalf of another].
The meaning is that there is no offense for one who, having received a message from a woman, has investigated it, returned, and reported it;
for this is stated in the Canon: "There is no offense if he goes on account of the Saṅgha, or a shrine, or a sick person, or if he is insane, or a first-time offender."
375. *Tathā tassā* means "of that woman" who belongs to the human species. *Nanālaṃvacanīyā*:
she is not one who can be spoken to with the words "this is mine," nor can she be spoken to without apprehension regarding restraint or favor; thus she is *alaṃvacanīyā*.

She is ownerless (*assāmikā*), for she cannot be claimed by anyone as "this is mine," nor can she be spoken to with words of restraint or favor without apprehension. She is not one who can be spoken to [with such claims].
"She is not 'not fit to be spoken to'" (*nālaṃvacanīyā*) means she has a husband; for since he is able to act in that manner toward her, she is "not fit to be spoken to.
"Not not fit to be spoken to" (*nanālaṃvacanīyā*) means she is indeed "fit to be spoken to" (*alaṃvacanīyā*), as expressed by the word *alaṃvacanīyā* itself.
Since two negations convey the original meaning, the state of being "not not fit to be spoken to" is "not-unfit-to-be-spoken-to-ness" (*nanālaṃvacanīyatā*).

By "without attachment," it is meant that she is beyond reproach and has no owner. Alternatively, "alaṃvacanīyā" (one who need not be spoken to) should be understood as meaning that she is not one who can be spoken to by a monk on account of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*).
In the phrase "by way of receiving and so forth," the particle *ca* is indicated as being elided.
Therefore, it is by way of the three factors consisting of receiving, investigating, and returning [the message].

And because it was previously stated that one who has been previously instructed is not "one with whom one may speak," this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is connected to five factors (*aṅga*) which are the causes for an offense, by way of those two aforementioned factors. 376.
This is the training rule on matchmaking (*sañcaritta*). Alternatively, through a change of gender, this is a *saṅghādisesa*.
It should be understood thus: it has six origins because it arises from body, from speech, from body and speech, from body and mind, from speech and mind, or from body, speech, and mind.
For that very reason, it is stated to be "without mind. Indeed, that which originates from a combination [of factors] is "without mind" [in the sense that no single factor is present].
To show which mind is absent such that it is called "without mind" even when other minds are present, he said: "the state of being 'enough' to be spoken."
“Or,” and so forth. Due to the requirements of the metrical composition (gāthā), the short vowel is used; it should be understood as “the state of being one to whom [the offense] is to be spoken.

The meaning is: the state of being dependent upon that person who sends the message. Or, regarding “not knowing the designation”: the connection is that for one who does not know the designation known as the training rule on acting as a go-between (sañcaritta-sikkhāpada), it is declared to be unintentional (acittaka).
377. "Sāsana" means a message from a woman or a man.
"By means of a bodily gesture" means by a bodily movement such as shaking the head. "Having received" means having accepted it.

"Approaching that person" means approaching the woman or man to whom the message was received and who is to be told [the matter]. "Having investigated" means having concluded that business. "Of one who conveys" means...

"For one who brings back [the robe]" means: "It may be from the body" (*kāyato siyā*)—the meaning is that because the receiving and so forth are performed by the body alone without vocal expression, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa* offense solely through bodily origination. 378.
"Having heard the words of a woman"—this is the construction. "As he was sitting" (*yathā nisinno va*) means: in the very place where he was habitually seated.

"Seated. Regarding that statement: "To one who has come to that very place" means that without leaving the seat where he was seated when he received the woman's message, [he speaks] to the man who has come to his own sitting place; here, the words "having announced" (*ārocetvā*) are to be supplied as a textual ellipsis.
Again, the phrase "to her who is announcing" refers to that same woman who had come to that very place.

This should be applied to a woman in the same way. The meaning is: for a woman who, having been given a message and having gone [to the messenger], returns to that very place and conveys it by means of bodily action alone—without words—immediately after she has become known [to the recipient].
This is stated with reference to the reception of a message from a woman and so forth.

Alternatively, the application may also be made by way of receiving a message from a man and so forth: having heard a man’s words while sitting as one was, and having reported those words to a woman, one then reports them back to that same man who has returned to that very place.
And here, the phrase "to one who has returned to that very place" is an illustration; for [the offense occurs] even by merely accepting the verbal message of the instruction.

Whether one has gone away for another task, or has spoken at a place seen according to one’s own wish, and then reports it again at that very same place where it was seen, its status as an origination (samuṭṭhāna) should be understood by the words alone. 379. As for “Enough... [etc.

...for one who does not know,” the reason for the absence of mental intent (acittaka) has already been stated; why then is it said again, “An offense of formal designation (paṇṇatti) for one who does not know”?
If it is asked, "Why was it said [thus]?"—it should be understood that it was said in order to indicate that there is no separate cause for either of those two.
"The method for him" (*naṃ vidhiṃ*) refers to the procedure consisting of receiving the teaching, bringing it back, announcing it, and returning from the announcement.

"Even for an Arahant" (*arahatopi*) means even for one whose taints are destroyed; the word "even" (*api*), used in the sense of esteem, indicates that this applies all the more so for those who are still in training (*sekkha*) and for worldlings (*puthujjana*).
380. "Having known" means having known either the state of being one who need not be addressed, or the designation, or both.
"In that way" should be construed with the phrase "by one acting through body and speech. "With those possessing mind" means with those possessing mind as previously described.
"By those very same" refers to those very things, namely the body and so forth; there is also a reading, "by those three."

Commentary on the Discussion of Acting as a Matchmaker (Sañcaritta-kathāvaṇṇanā). 381–2. Regarding the phrase "only when [the requisites] have been personally requested": here, the words "by means of requisites" (*upakaraṇehi*) are to be supplied. The meaning is:

"only by means of those requisites which have been obtained after one has personally requested them in such a manner as 'Give me a man,' and so forth. As it is said: "What is called 'requesting' (*saññācikā*) is that which is done by oneself..."
“Having asked for a man, or even something that makes one a man, or a cow, or a cart, or an axe, or a spear, or a hatchet, or a hoe, or a pick.
Here, by the word *eva* (even), it excludes what has not been asked for. By this, it is indicated that [the dwelling] is ownerless.
By the term “hut” (*kuṭikā*), it is meant that a hut is either plastered on the inside, or plastered on the outside, or plastered both inside and outside.

Because it is stated as “or,” starting from the ground, having covered the walls and the roof, and having left space for the plastering of the doors, windows, and so forth, it is called *ullitta* by virtue of being plastered on the inside;
or it is called *avalitta* by virtue of being plastered on the outside; or it is called *ullittāvalitta* by virtue of being plastered both on the inside and on the outside.
Or it is said that they are "making a hut.

"Exceeding the measure" means that because they exceed the stated dimensions for length and breadth—namely, "in this case, the measure is twelve spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and seven spans across"—they are called "exceeding the measure.
And herein, having penetrated the three characteristics and uprooted the three roots of defilement, [one understands] all phenomena as existing within the three periods of time...

Having thus determined that the Sugata’s span—the measure of a finger of the Blessed One, the Dharma King, who is the sole refuge for the three worlds—is three fingers more than the finger of an average man;
that one *vidatthi* becomes three *vidatthis*, and one *ratana* becomes three *ratanas*;
