thus, the Sugata’s span is one and a half *ratanas* in measure according to the carpenter’s *ratana*.

It is so. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “The ‘span of the Sugata’ (sugatavidatthi) is now equal to three spans of a medium-sized man, or one and a half cubits (*hattha*) by the carpenter’s measure.
Therefore, twelve spans of the Sugata amount to eighteen cubits by the carpenter’s measure. “Twelve spans of the Sugata in length... [and so forth].
Because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "by the outer measurement," [the area] is eighteen cubits in extent from the outer edge,
excluding the final layer of plaster and including the limit of the husk-mud or the great mud;
and because it is stated in the word-commentary as "seven spans across by the inner measurement," it is ten cubits plus twelve finger-breadths in width by the inner measurement.

"The measurement of the hut" must be grasped. It should be understood briefly that the phrase "exceeding the measurement" is said in order to show that even a hut exceeding the established measurement by as much as a hair's breadth—whether in length, in width, or in both—is a factor for an offense.

"Designated for oneself": it is called *uddesa* because it is to be designated; this hut has oneself as its designation, thus it is "designated for oneself" (*attuddesā*). That [hut] is what is "designated for oneself."

Because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that “*attuddesaṃ* means for one’s own benefit,” the meaning is: “having designated [the dwelling] to oneself, thinking, ‘This shall be for my residence.

As for the phrase “by one doing it,” this should be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakkhaṇa*), since the agent who employs another must also be included according to the method stated in the word-commentary: “‘By one doing it’ means either by one doing it himself or by one having it done.”

"In that same way" means: just as there is an offense for one who builds a hut exceeding the [prescribed] measure when it possesses such characteristics as being ownerless and so forth, so too there is an offense for one who builds a hut even if its site has not been formally designated (*adesitavatthu*), provided it possesses those very same characteristics.
By this, it is shown that the "undesignated site" (*adesitavatthu*) is a primary factor for an offense independently, just like the "improper measure" (*appamāṇika*). He dwells.

"Herein" (*ettha*) means the site, the ground; that which has no such site declared for it is "one whose site is undeclared" (*adesitavatthukā*); [this refers to] a hut (*kuṭi*), and that [hut] is one whose site is undeclared.

What is meant? That monk who intends to build a hut, having cleared the site for the hut and had it leveled, should approach the Saṅgha, pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, sit down in a squatting posture, and with palms joined...
Having taken hold [of the site] and said three times, "Venerable sirs, I wish to build a hut by means of solicitation for myself, without an owner; therefore, Venerable sirs,
I request the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the hut," he should, together with him,
go with either two experienced and competent bhikkhus authorized by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma), or with those authorized by the Saṅgha.
Having gone to the site for the hut and observed it, those who see that there is either construction activity,
or a lack of sufficient space, or both, should prevent him by saying, "Do not build here. If, however, it is free from construction activity and has sufficient space,
then after returning and informing the Saṅgha, the monk who is building the hut should approach the Saṅgha in the manner previously described.
Having prostrated at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, sat down in the kneeling posture (ukkhuṭika), and raised his joined palms in reverential salutation, he should say three times:
"Venerable sirs, I desire to build a hut by means of solicitation for myself, without an owner; therefore, Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha to designate the site for the hut.
Once this has been requested, with the consent of the elders, a competent and capable bhikkhu shall perform the formal act consisting of one motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma).
Because there is no plot of land for a hut that has been formally handed over after being designated through the formal ritual (*kammavācā*), it is one where the site has not been designated.

For one who, by means of requisites requested by himself, builds or causes to be built such a hut as described above—characterized by the aforementioned modes such as being ownerless—it is said that two *saṅghādisesa* offenses occur:
"if he does not have monks designate the site, or if he exceeds the [prescribed] measurement."

The meaning is that because it is joined with the word *vā* (or), which indicates equal force (*tulyabalatā*), there are two *saṅghādisesa* offenses due to being accompanied by both aforementioned factors.

As it is said: "If a monk builds a hut whose site has not been approved, which exceeds the proper measure, but which is free from danger and has a space for walking around, there is an offense of two *saṅghādisesas*"; and: "A monk builds a hut..."
Because it is stated: "If a hut has an unassigned site, no danger of injury, and an open space around it, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa)," and also:

"If a monk builds a hut that exceeds the prescribed dimensions, but has no danger of injury and an open space around it, there is an offense entailing suspension," it follows that if one of these two factors is lacking, there is only one offense entailing suspension. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if one [factor] is deficient":
She will say, "It may be a serious offense for one alone.
Regarding the phrase "in cases such as *sārambha*": here, the word *sārambha* is a synonym for "with danger" (*sa-upaddava*). As it is said in the Commentary:

"*Sārambham anārambhan ti saupaddavam anupaddavan*" ("'With provocation' and 'without provocation' mean 'with danger' and 'without danger'"). In this context, [the passage] reads: "*Setam chāgam ārabhetha yajamāno*" ("The sacrificer should slaughter a white goat").

Since the word *ārambha*—preceded by the prefix *ā*—is seen to have the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsa*) just as it does in the sense of "exertion" (*payoga*), the term *ārambha* functions as an agent-noun denoting injurious beings such as ants and the like; thus, a place associated with them is called *sārambha*.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Word-Commentary (*padabhājana*): "*Sārambha* means a nest of ants, or [a nest] of termites..."
“...or it is the lair of rats, or snakes, or scorpions, or centipedes, or elephants, or horses, or lions, or tigers...
By the word “etcetera,” the lack of space for circumambulation is included. “With space for circumambulation” means that it is possible for one who is properly equipped [to walk around].
"‘To be able to circumambulate with a cart, or to be able to circumambulate all around with a ladder— this is what is called “having a space for access.
Contrary to the characteristics stated [in that definition], if one places one wheel at the edge of the water where the rim of the well is and places the other wheel outside,
thereby enclosing the hut, then for a yoked cart or a ladder being brought in to be looked upon...
It should be understood as "without a path" because it is impossible for those covering the hut to go beyond it by means of a ladder.
If it is endowed with these two factors—namely, the commencement (*sārambha*) and the lack of a path as described, then there are two *dukkaṭa* offenses.
As it is said: "A monk builds a hut on a site that has been designated, of the proper measure, involving destruction [of vegetation], and lacking a path."
“There is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*. But if it is one [offense], there is only one. As it is said:

“If a monk builds a hut on a site that has been designated, which is of the proper measure, where harm is being done, and which lacks space for walking around, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. If a monk builds a hut on a site that has been designated, which is of the proper measure, where no harm is being done, and which lacks space for walking around, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. This is [the case].
This too should be understood as being included under the general category of "wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding contentiousness and so forth.

It is called "one-faulted" because one of its factors—either the measurement or the fact that it has been formally proposed—is defective. The meaning of the terms *saṅghādisesa* and so on, whose meanings were explained previously, should be understood in the same manner already stated. "That" refers to the hut possessing the characteristics as previously described.
383. Now, regarding the origin (*aṭṭuppatti*) of this training rule: "They dwelt with much requesting and much entreating..."
In order to briefly show the determination of what is allowable and what is not allowable as it appears in the commentary on the Pāli passage beginning with, “Give a man!
Give one who performs manly tasks,” he says “A man,” and so forth. “For the sake of assistance in work” means for the state of being an assistant in some task;
that is to say, for the purpose of performing work. [The thought is: “It is necessary to obtain a man in order to perform such-and-such a task.”
The meaning is that it is permissible to ask for [them]. As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "It is permissible to ask, 'Give me a man,' for the purpose of performing work.
"By way of cutting off the root" means by way of severing the root consisting of dependence upon the owners;
what is meant is: by way of making them dependent upon oneself.
384. *Avajjanti* means "faultless," that is, free from blame. For hunters, fishermen, and the like, their own work is called "blameworthy work" (*vajjakamma*).

Therefore, when one asks a hunter or similar person for manual labor, one should not say in general terms, "Give us your manual labor," or "Manual labor must be given," but rather, "The work called so-and-so must be given."

One must request [the work] having specified [the task]. However, whether they are hunters or others, if they have no other occupation, it is permissible to have them perform the work according to one's wish even without requesting it.

To demonstrate that the request for manual labor is entirely allowable, it is said that when someone was building a great palace after requesting various craftsmen and specifically requesting manual labor, he realized he had no other option.
Since it is stated in detail in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "when others are performing [work], the wages must be given,
and it is permissible to accept them when they are being given," one who does not neglect the welfare of those engaged in wholesome deeds should request [payment] through a proper,

suitable, and allowable procedure. For those who are unable to perform the requested work themselves, if wages for manual labor are being given to those who are doing it, [one may accept them] after having the work performed.
Having pointed out the laborer, [the gift] should be caused to be given. Thus, in order to show the reason found in the Aṭṭhakathā regarding the blameless nature of such a request, he said:
“Even manual labor,” and so forth. The word *pi* (even/also) is used for emphasis or as a verse-filler. The word *hi* (for/because) indicates a reason.
Because this manual labor is not a [material] object [of giving], therefore manual labor is indeed blameless; however, it is permissible to request it.
385. Regarding "relatives and so forth": this refers to when one has been invited by relatives. "Setting aside" means excluding. "To one who asks for a bull on loan":
this refers to one who asks for a bull from a stranger who has not invited him, not for a temporary period, but solely for the purpose of doing work.

"In those cases too": the construction is that it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) to ask for a bull on loan even from relatives and others if it results in the permanent loss of the animal. "It is permissible in all cases according to the method of lending on loan."

According to the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, from the time of the formal act of offering until the time of the actual performance of the work, it is permissible to request [the loan] from all—whether they are relatives or strangers, or whether they have invited one or not.
Whether one has requested it thus or not, if it is taken, it must be returned to the owners after being protected and well-cared for.
If the ox is lost or a horn is broken, and the owners do not accept [the compensation], the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) must be paid.

386. Regarding the word *demāti* here, the phrase “of you” (*tumhākan*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. However, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: “But when it is said, ‘We give it to the monastery,’ one should say, ‘Inform the monastery attendants so that they may look after it.
Since the determination regarding carts is the same as the determination regarding oxen, he did not repeat it; rather, he spoke only to show the distinction, saying: “A cart... is permissible.”
The phrase “when it is said, ‘We give it to you’” should be brought forward and connected [to the previous statement]. As it is said in the Commentary:
“When it is said, ‘We give it only to you,’ it is permissible to accept what is called a wooden utensil. 387.
Regarding the phrase “in the case of axes and so forth,” here the word “and so forth” (ādi) includes a chisel. This method is to be understood.

This is the remainder of the recitation. The formal analysis (vinicchaya) states: "One should not request [an item] from an unrelated person who has not invited one, treating it as a temporary loan like a bullock for a cart;
nor should one request it from an unrelated person who has not invited one by way of cutting off the very root; rather, it should be requested as a temporary loan.
Furthermore, the specific analysis (visesavinicchaya) stating "the cart... is permissible" should also be understood to apply to tools such as axes and the like. This is the method.
Meaning: "Not inhabited" (*anajjhāvutthaka*) means not claimed as "mine" by anyone.
Because of the commentary’s statement, "Indeed, it is only in a place that is guarded and protected that the term 'request' (*viññatti*) is used," it is said to mean "not guarded and not protected.
Having also stated the determination regarding creepers and so forth in the commentary, [it says]: "But as for anything that is 'not inhabited,' one may have it brought..."

Because it is stated, “it is allowable,” the word “all” here should be understood to include both the oxen and so forth mentioned previously, as well as the creepers and so forth that will be mentioned later.
By this, it is shown that the previous decision concerns the domain of what has been guarded and protected.

Regarding the phrase “it is also allowable to have it carried away,” the word “also” (api) indicates that it goes without saying that it is allowable if someone has already carried it away and given it.
388. Regarding the phrase "creepers, etc.," the word "etc. includes rattan, muñja grass, and clay.

Here, "grass" refers to thatching grass for houses, excluding muñja and pabbaja grass. "Sufficient for heavy goods" means [the creepers] possess the characteristics described by the rule beginning with "even a creeper half an arm's length," which qualify them as being sufficient for heavy goods.
By the restrictive particle "only" in the phrase "belonging only to others," it is indicated that they must not be [creepers] over which one does not have proprietary rights (anajjhāvutthaka).
"Dukkaṭa" indicates [the offense] by way of contrast.

"In the requisites" means in the three requisites consisting of robes, almsfood, and lodgings. By the word "eva," it indicates that requesting is permissible regarding the fourth requisite, which consists of the requisite for the sick.
"Requesting" (viññatti) means [asking for] a desired requisite, such as saying, "Bring it," or "Give it."
Having stated the name, there is the request. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "It is not permissible in every respect.
To show that this has a restrictive sense, because it is stated as "and it is not permissible," the meaning should be understood as "it is not permissible at all.
Because they are not obtained through intimation (*viññatti*), immediately after [the discussion on] requisites, from among the three conditions mentioned together, [the following]...
In order to show the specific distinction found only in the third condition, it was stated: "In the third, indirect speech (*parikathā*), hinting (*obhāsa*), and signs (*nimitta*) are obtained.
Consequently, it follows that in the remaining two [conditions], indirect speech and the others are not obtained.

Since it is established by the word *ca* (and) in the sense of conjunction that the triad beginning with indirect speech is obtained even in the unstated fourth condition, the word *eva* (only) in the phrase "in the three only" [is used].

Since it has been permitted by way of negative implication (*byatirekamukhena*) that even *viññatti* (intimation) is allowed, it is established that in the fourth requisite—medicine for the sick—parikathā (indirect hinting), obhāsa (manifestation), nimitta-kamma (signaling), and *viññatti* are all permissible.
Up to this point, it should be understood that it has been stated that all four, beginning with parikathā, are permissible for the fourth requisite;
for the third requisite, the remaining three are permissible except for *viññatti*; and for the first two requisites, none of them is permissible.

Regarding the preliminary talk on the requisite of lodgings (*senāsanapaccaya*): after observing a suitable location for constructing a Uposatha hall or similar facilities, one speaks in the hearing of lay devotees (*upāsaka*), saying, "In this very place, it would be fitting to build such a lodging," or "It is appropriate," or "It is suitable.
This is called a *parikathā*. [For example: "Lay devotees, where do you reside?"
When he asked, "In a mansion, venerable sir? and it was replied, "But for monks, lay followers, a mansion is not permitted," the discourse that proceeded in this manner is called *obhāsa*.

While the lay followers were looking on, having stretched a cord upon the ground, divided the site, and driven in stakes, when they asked, "What is this, venerable sir? [the reply] beginning with, "Lay followers, we shall build a dwelling here," and so forth, is called *obhāsa*.
"Talk" means talk on worldly matters. Regarding the requisite of medicine, it should be understood accordingly in this same manner.
All of this has been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
(390–3) Now, in order to show the offense for a monk who builds a hut, he says "not pointed out," and so forth. That [passage] is of plain meaning.

"Nibsenta-sā" means while sharpening [an axe] by striking it against a stone. "Together with the *pācittiya*" means together with the *pācittiya* offense stated as "there is a *pācittiya* for the destruction of vegetation.
"An offense" refers to the *pācittiya* and the *dukkaṭa* in the place of the *pācittiya*, and elsewhere, the *dukkaṭa* of the mere act (*suddha-payoga*).

"But which" means which hut. Regarding the phrase "in the first and second," here the instrumental plural "by heaps" (*piṇḍehi*) must be construed by changing its case-ending to the locative singular "on the heap" (*piṇḍe*), and the word "placed" (*nikkhitte*) must be supplied;
the locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic of the state, meaning "when it has been placed."
394. The word-division is “sace aññassa. “Vippakataṃ” means commenced but not finished.
“Anāpatti” (no offense) is said with reference to the absence of a *saṅghādisesa* offense that would otherwise have to be incurred once [the act] is finished.

For by the mere preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga*), there are also *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses, which must nevertheless be confessed. By the word “tathā,” it draws in the phrase “anāpatti”; thus, regarding the *saṅghādisesa* offense—
By this, it is shown that in the prior stage, one must confess the *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa* offenses incurred due to non-existence.
"That hut" refers to that hut which has been left unfinished.
"Another," such as a dining hall and so forth. "In the same way" indicates there is no offense.

396. By the word “karoto” (by one who does), “kārāpayato” (by one who causes to be done) is also understood. By both [terms], he shows the cause for the phrase “kriyato” (by one who acts). By the word “appamāṇikaṃ” (immeasurable), he shows a factor of the *saṅghādisesa* offense.

397. “Taṃ” (that) refers back to what was thus called “appamāṇikaṃ. “Kriyākriyato” (by way of acting and not acting) is said with reference to both the building of the hut and the non-performance of the assignment of the site.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the construction of a hut (*kuṭikārasikkhāpada*).
398. "Without having pointed out the site" is the connection [of the phrase].

According to the method set forth in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)—namely, "that monk who is building a monastery, having cleared the site for the monastery, should approach the Saṅgha"—the monk who is having the monastery built, after clearing the site for the monastery and having it made level, should approach the Saṅgha and [address] the elder monks...
Having prostrated at his feet, sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture, and extended his joined palms, he requested three times:
"Venerable sir, I wish to build a large dwelling for myself, with a patron. Therefore, Venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the dwelling.
Once this has been granted, the elder monks, having been appointed by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), [should proceed].

Or, having led monks there and shown them the site of the monastery after it has been prepared, just as when inspecting the site for a hut, those monks who have gone there should inspect it and examine whether it is free from harm and the like;
once they have ascertained that it is free from harm and possesses a path of circumambulation, they should return and report it to the Saṅgha.
Then, he [the applicant] should again approach the Saṅgha, pay homage at the feet of the elder monks, and...
Having sat in the squatting posture and raised his joined palms, he should request three times, saying: "Venerable sirs, I wish to build a large dwelling for myself, with a patron;
therefore, Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha to designate a site for the dwelling.

After he has thus requested, the site for the dwelling should be designated by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*); it is [an offense] if this is not done in that manner.
This has been stated. Here, the details regarding "hostility" (*sārambha*) and so forth should be understood according to the method explained in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"Large" (*mahallaka*): it is called "large" because it possesses a magnitude greater than that of a hut built by personal solicitation (*saññācika-kuṭi*) due to its having an owner;
or alternatively, because it is permissible to build it even by exceeding the prescribed measurements after having had the site designated, it is thus large by way of its measurement as well.

"Mahallaka" means "possessed of greatness," according to the method explained in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Vihāra" means a lodging of the kind described in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as:
"A vihāra is either plastered on the inside, or plastered on the outside, or plastered both inside and outside. The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"they dwell in this. The specific characteristics of being plastered on the inside and so forth are exactly as stated in the preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The construction is: "whoever should make that monastery. "Should make or should cause to be made" is according to the method already stated previously.

"For the purpose of his own residence" means depending upon his own dwelling; by this, it is understood through contrast (*vyatireka*) that there is no offense if one builds for the purpose of another's residence.
Regarding the term "grave," because the site was not caused to be prepared, the three alternatives previously mentioned—namely, that "there is only one *saṅghādisesa* offense"—apply here as well.
It should not be accepted. And this will be stated: "Because of the measure... [etc. ...the nature of a *saṅghādisesa* offense. 399.

Regarding the absence of origination through action (*kriyāsamuṭṭhāna*): it should be understood that there is an absence of origination through action here because an offense is impossible even when the measure is exceeded.

Regarding the phrase "because of the characteristic of action...": here, by way of contrast, the state of not being originated through action is permitted due to the fact that no object has been formally declared.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Mahallaka Vihāra. 401–3.

“Among those” refers to the twenty-four *pārājika* offenses. “Nineteen are appropriate for a monk” means that four—beginning with the *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika* (offense involving sitting above the knees)—are specifically prescribed for nuns;
together with the nun who has defrocked in accordance with those [rules], they constitute nineteen.
Apart from the five *pārājika* offenses, the remaining nineteen *pārājikas* are not suitable for a monk.

If it is argued that the statement here—“nineteen”—contradicts the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) of this training rule, which says, “by means of one or another of the four *pārājika* states,” there is no contradiction. Why? Because the word-commentary...
That which proceeds by taking only what has come down in the recitation of the Pātimokkha should be understood as not being in conflict with this [present work],
for the latter proceeds by taking the Buddha’s approval and the opinion of those teachers who have propagated the study of the Vinaya. Regarding the teacher [Buddhaghosa],

because the act of "causing one to fall away from the holy life" (brahmacariyā cāveyya) mentioned in the context of all pārājikas is the absolute means for the violation [of the rule], he [treats] the group of five pārājikas that are specifically applicable and favorable for bhikkhunīs.
It includes everything except for the remainder; therefore, in the *Gaṇṭhipadavivaraṇa* of the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "Regarding 'one of the four':

this is said by taking what appears specifically in the recitation of the Pātimokkha; even for one who does not proclaim [the offense] by means of any other of the remaining [categories], there is a *saṅghādisesa*.
Consequently, because it proceeds by grasping the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) in the reading "he should proclaim" (*anuddhaṃseyya*), [it is so stated].
The opinion of these teachers should be accepted as authoritative. Since it will be stated later, "by one among them," the word "which" (*yāni*) is understood here by implication after "nineteen.
The construction is: "by one [of them] without foundation. "Without foundation" means being devoid of the bases for accusation, such as seeing and so forth, on the part of the accuser.
"Groundless" refers to a *pārājika* offense. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"That *pārājika* which has not been seen, heard, or suspected regarding the person being accused by the accuser—this is called 'groundless' (*amūlaka*) due to the absence of these roots, namely seeing, hearing, and suspicion.
And herein, "seen" means seen either with the fleshly eye or with the divine eye.
"Seen" means: what is heard through the natural ear or the divine ear is called "heard.
What is suspected by the mind is called "suspected. That is threefold, by way of the seen, the heard, and the suspected.
In that regard, having seen a monk engaging in some improper conduct with a woman in a suitable and secluded place, [one might suspect him].
Grasping otherwise and thinking, "Has he perhaps committed an offense?"—this grasping is called "suspicion based on what has been seen.

When a monk is hidden by a wall and a woman hears his voice, yet, not knowing whether another intelligent man is present there, she thinks, "Has he perhaps committed an offense?"—this grasping is called "suspicion based on what has been heard. At the edge of the monastery...
Having spent the day with young women and men and then departing,
a bhikkhu— observing the scattered flowers at the place where they had gone and smelling the odor of meat and liquor— examined the matter, thinking, "Whose deed is this? Then,
smelling the body odor of a bhikkhu who was yellowish-brown and who had offered garlands and perfumes at a cetiya, he felt a doubt as to whether that might indeed be his deed.
"Based on what has been seen or suspected" means: since there is an absence of such a basis consisting of what was seen, heard, or suspected, it is "on account of a groundless *pārājika* offense";
this is the summary here, while the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. "Accuses" means:
he himself accuses by means of such words as "you have fallen into a *pārājika* offense," and so forth; however, the act of causing another to accuse will be explained later.

"Having become one whose intention is to cause a fall" means having become possessed of a mind that has arisen with the desire to cause another to fall away from this holy life, thinking, "Perhaps I might cause him to fall from this holy life.
"Whether pure or impure" is a description of the action (kamma) of the act of accusing mentioned by the word "accuses";
"another bhikkhu" is the remainder [of the phrase], referring to one who has not committed a *pārājika* offense.

"Or another nun who has committed [an offense]"—this is the meaning. "He" refers to the monk mentioned in the matrix (mātikā). The phrase "corrupt, with hatred, displeased" must be supplied here; the meaning is:
that monk who, being himself corrupted by the arisen stain of hatred, corrupts another, and is thus deprived of rapture, bliss, and so forth.
This is to be connected with the word "her" (tassā) which will be mentioned later.
The word division is *kate okāsamhi*. Because the sense of the causal suffix (*hetvattha*) is contained within the reading *okāsaṃ kārāpetvā*, it is a synonym for *kate* and *kārite*;
the meaning is: "Make room for me, for I wish to speak to you," having thus caused room to be made.
The word division is *akate okāse*; the meaning is exactly as stated previously. [This refers to] the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
[He is] together with the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) because he did not have the space prepared.
404–5. "Koṇṭha" means you are a rogue. "Jeṭṭhabbatika" means you are one devoted to the vow of Queen Kālī.
It is said that Queen Kālī was the elder sister of Queen Sirī; therefore, one who observes her vow is called a "jeṭṭhabbatika. Having undertaken that vow...
Smearing soot over his entire body and clutching crow feathers in his fist, he had Queen Kālī painted on a wooden board;
having bound it to the tip of a bamboo pole, he entered a cesspool filled with foul things such as leftover water and filth, wandering about and proclaiming, "You are immoral!
You are devoid of virtue! You are bereft of moral conduct!"

Because of your immorality and your base disposition, you are one of evil nature and vile character. Because you have entered within through putrid action—the failure of virtue—you are "putrid within.
Because you have been soaked by the constant flow of defilements such as lust through the six sense-doors, you are "leaking.
The rest here is of plain meaning. Regarding the phrase "pointing out what is grave," it refers to both "when permission has been granted" and likewise "when no permission has been granted."
And this should be connected by bringing in the phrase: “together with an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The same applies to what follows.
“Face-to-face” means in the presence of the one who has been accused; the sense is that he is not far away. “By hand-sign” means by means of fingers, hands, and so forth.
That which was spoken by way of a hand-sign is referred to as such. “The other” refers to the one being accused, whom you have charged. “A bhikkhu” refers to the bhikkhu who is the accuser.
407. “Standing face-to-face” means standing near the one who has been accused.
Regarding the phrase “of the one accusing,” this should be connected as an accusative case, because it follows the word “kamma” (the formal act). The same applies to subsequent instances.
“By anyone” means by some other person. “Of that accuser”: the repetition of the word “accusing” is for the purpose of restriction.

408. "He too" refers to the other person who incites [the act] by causing [the instruction] to be learned; thus, it includes both the instigator and the one who incites. "Of those two" means of both the instigator and the one who incites. 409.
One who carries a written leaf or a message to the stated place is called a "messenger" (*dūta*);

since such a person is included under the phrase "having sent a leaf or a message," although they need not be mentioned separately, the word "messenger" here refers to a dispatched messenger (*nissaṭṭhadūta*).
A monk who has been sent forth after being given only the essential matter— without being given a written note, or without being given an instruction such as "Speak thus and so," or "Examine him"—

is to be understood here as a "sent messenger" (*nissaṭṭhadūta*). Alternatively, it refers to a monk who has been sent forth after being made to learn how to examine [the person], or even without being made to learn that.
It should be accepted like a messenger. By the term "letter," one should accept a letter sent in the hand of anyone—whether ordained or unordained—in which a formal charge has been written.
By the term "message," one should accept a message sent by saying, "He has committed a *pārājika* offense," and so forth.
These three [methods] are so called because they are carried out by others while one remains seated at a distance.

Regarding the phrase “codāpentassa”: one should bring the word “another” (paraṃ) and connect it [to the verb]. In this context, there is no requirement for obtaining formal permission (okāsakārāpana). 410.

“Tathā” means that just as [the offense is incurred] when formal permission has been obtained or not obtained in the presence of another regarding a groundless *pārājika*, so too it is with groundless *saṅghādisesas*;
this is what is meant. By the addition of the locative case in the phrase “vutte sammukhā pare,” it is indicated that the action occurs in the presence of another.

It should be connected as follows: "He accuses or causes another to accuse" is what is meant. Regarding the offense of *pācittiya*: it should be understood that when the opportunity has been granted, it is a *pācittiya* alone;

when it has not been granted, it is together with a *dukkaṭa*. The construction is: for one who perceives [the other] as being subject to removal (*cāvana*), there is a *dukkaṭa* when others have spoken of the remaining offenses (*sesāpatti*) in his presence.
Even by merely causing the granting of the opportunity, there is only a *dukkaṭa*.
411. "With the intention of reviling" means with the intention of censuring. "Without having given an opportunity" means without having been granted leave;
this should be construed with the word "another. "By oneself" refers to the accuser; this should be construed with the phrase "without having personally granted an opportunity.
"Together with the *pācittiya*" means together with the *pācittiya* offense stated as "there is a *pācittiya* for insulting speech. "Of one who speaks" means of one who accuses.

Or for one who causes [another] to confess; here, the term “in the presence of” (*sammukhā*) is obtained by way of the opposite of the term “not in the presence of” (*asammukhā*) which will be mentioned later.
By the particle *ca*, there is a connection with the *dukkaṭa* offense in the alternative case of granting permission to act. 412.
Regarding the phrase “speaking not in the presence of,” the words “with the intention of reviling” (*akkosanādhippāyassa*) should be supplied and connected here.

“By one who has not granted the opportunity” means he does not comply. “By seven offenses” means by any one among the seven classes of offenses, namely: those classified as *pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*. By the word “likewise,” the term “not in his presence” is included.
“Formal act” (*kamma*) refers to the sevenfold formal act, beginning with the act of censure (*tajjanīya*).

413. Regarding the phrase "of one who is insane, etc.," the word "etc. includes what is stated [in the text]: "There is no offense for one who perceives as pure that which is pure; for one who perceives as impure that which is impure;
for one who is insane; for a first-offender. "Endowed with five factors" means:

(1) the fact that the one who accuses has attained the status of being "fully ordained"; (2) the perception of purity regarding that person; and (3) the specific *pārājika* offense with which one accuses him.

It is endowed with these five factors: being groundless by way of [false] vision and so forth, accusing someone in their presence with the intention of causing them to fall away, and that person’s understanding it at that very moment. 415.

The word "this" refers to the remainder, namely, the "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*); and by the term "training rule," it is precisely the offense (*āpatti*) that is to be established by that rule which is intended.
It is grasped (*gayhati*). "Arising from three" (*tisamuṭṭhāna*) means it arises from three conscious origins: from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from both body and speech and mind;

thus it is "arising from three. For this very reason, he says "with mind" (*sacitta*). It is "with mind" because it is accompanied by either of the two types of repulsive consciousness (*paṭighacitta*).
It is a painful feeling (*dukkhavedana*) by way of the feeling of mental displeasure (*domanassavedanā*) associated with that [consciousness].
Commentary on the Discussion of Faults (Duṭṭhadosakathāvaṇṇanā). 416.

Regarding the term *lesamattaṃ*: “It is called a ‘trace’ (*lesa*) because another basis is smeared (*lissati*), adhered to (*silissati*), or slightly attached (*īsakaṃ allīyati*) by way of mere conventional usage;
this is a designation for any one of the categories beginning with birth. This is shown among the etymological explanations given in the Aṭṭhakathā.
It is said that this refers merely to one of the ten stains (*lesa*) mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) by way of such passages as, “stain means the ten stains:
the stain of birth, the stain of name,” and so forth.
Among these, “birth” (*jāti*) refers to birth as a Khattiya, a Brāhmaṇa, and so on. “Name” (*nāma*) refers to the name [given] in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), such as “Chagalaka.”

There are two kinds of names: the name assigned by accusers, such as "Dabba the Mallian" or "the nun Mettiyā the Goat-Slayer," which is like a name established [by others], and one's own personal name, such as "Buddharakkhita. "Clan" (gotra) refers to clans such as Gotama or Moggallāna.
"Characteristic" (liṅga) refers to the diversity of physical shapes, such as tallness, and the diversity of complexions, such as blackness; this is the twofold characteristic.

"Offense-remnant" (*āpattileso*) refers to an offense such as a *pācittiya* that exists in a minor form or similar degree. "Bowl" (*patto*) refers to a bowl made of iron or other materials. "Robe" (*cīvaraṃ*) refers to one made of rags from a dust heap or similar materials.

"Preceptor" (*upajjhāyo*) refers to the preceptor of the one who is being reproved. "Teacher" (*ācariyo*) refers to the teacher of the one being reproved, such as the one who gave him the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
"Lodging" (*senāsanaṃ*) refers to the residence, palace, or similar dwelling place belonging to the very person being reproved.

"Chodesi" means: having seen a person of khattiya birth committing a *pārājika* offense, one accuses a person of khattiya birth who is an enemy, by way of such statements as, "A khattiya has been seen by me; you have fallen into a *pārājika* offense," and so forth.

A "grave offense" (*garukāpatti*) refers to a *saṅghādisesa*. If there is an intention to cause him to fall away—thinking, "Perhaps I might cause him to fall away from this holy life... [the offense is established].

Because it is stated, "he would cause [him] to fall away," it follows that if one accuses another with the underlying intention (adhippāya), "I shall cause this person to fall away from the Teaching," then— by way of contrast—
it is effectively stated that there is no other underlying intention. Thus, among the various types of intentions shown in the commentary on the preceding training rule (sikkhāpada)—
such as "the intention to cause falling away" and "the intention to revile"— it is only in the case of [the former] that there is an offense.
Having shown that the intention [to accuse] is a constituent part [of the offense], he rejects other intentions.
"Perceiving it thus" means perceiving that "this person has indeed committed a *pārājika* offense.
Because it is stated, "he accuses or causes to be accused," this term "perceiving it thus" should also be construed with "causes to be accused. Regarding the word "the rest" (*seso*) here:

Starting from the words “the *pārājika* offenses have been stated” and ending with “one’s own mind is a painful feeling,” this refers to all the determinations (vinicchaya) stated in the series of discourses that encompass the analysis of the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

From among those determinations, excluding that which is fixed to this specific rule—namely, the phrase “without ground” (*amūlakena*)—and also excluding the matter stated in this training rule as “there may be no offense (*anāpatti*) if [the monk] [accuses him] of a final offense (*antimavatthu*)... [etc.]”—all the remaining determinations are [intended here].
The meaning: it should be understood that "similar to the immediate" means it is identical to the training rule (sikkhāpada) stated immediately before.
This concludes the commentary on the second discussion of faults. 418.
"Of a united Saṅgha": "A united Saṅgha is one that shares the same communion and stands within the same boundary."
Because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it means "of the Saṅgha that has become one in mind and body.

The particle *ca* is for the purpose of completing the meter, or it has the sense of the particle *eva*; it should be understood as having the meaning of exclusion, i.e., "not of one who is not in harmony. "One should strive for the sake of schism" means:
thinking day and night, "How and when will these [monks] be divided?", and having sought a means, such as searching for partisans and so forth.
The meaning is "he should cause [schism]. For it is said in the Pāḷi: "He should strive for schism means: 'How might these [monks] become divided, separated, or split?
Thus he seeks out a faction and forms a group.
Regarding the "cause of schism," it is as stated in the passage beginning: "Here, Upāli, a monk proclaims what is non-Dhamma as 'Dhamma,' and he proclaims Dhamma as 'non-Dhamma. etc.
By way of this method, it states in the Khandhaka the cause for schism in the Saṅgha, known as the eighteen grounds for causing a schism.
For this very thing is stated in the word-commentary (padabhājana): “A legal issue conducive to schism refers to the eighteen grounds for causing a schism.
“Having taken up” means having grasped. “Should persist” means should not relinquish. Here, “elucidating” refers to one who is elucidating.
The meaning is "not relinquishing. As it is said: "He should remain" means "he should not relinquish.

419. "By the bhikkhus" means by the other bhikkhus who are modest and well-behaved, whether they are witnessing the efforts of that schismatic monk or, if he is far away, hearing of his conduct. For this has been stated: "By the bhikkhus..."
“By other monks. Those who see him or hear of it should say to him. To show the manner of speaking when they do so, he said:
“Venerable sir, do not strive for the schism of a united Saṅgha, nor stand up having taken up or maintained a legal issue conducive to schism; let the venerable one be at peace with the Saṅgha.”
Regarding the reading, “For a united Saṅgha, living in harmony, without dispute, and following a single recitation, dwells in comfort,” he stated “for the purpose of schism...
the cause of schism” in order to characterize it by way of including a portion [of that definition]. The construction is: “Thus it should be said. 420.
As for the phrase “vuccamāno hi,” here the word *hi* has the sense of the word *api*. Alternatively, the reading is *pī*, which means “by those modest bhikkhus.”
The meaning is that it has been stated three times separately according to the method beginning with “Venerable sir, do not. “He should relinquish, and not [otherwise]”:
even after having fallen into an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on account of not relinquishing that effort toward schism, he still does not give it up;
for this has been said: “If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Thus, one who does not relinquish it...

This is included by the following: having seized him by the hands and feet and brought him into the midst of the Saṅgha, even if he has been told three times in that same manner, if one does not release him, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For this was said by the Blessed One: "That bhikkhu, having been dragged into the midst of the Saṅgha, should be addressed:
'Venerable sir, do not... [etc. ...may you live in comfort. He should be addressed a second time. He should be addressed a third time."
[He] should be addressed: "If he relinquishes [the matter], that is good. If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
This wrong-doing in both cases will be stated generally as: "But for one who has spoken thus three times, even if he does not relinquish it.

Regarding the phrase "he should be formally admonished" (samanubhāsitabbo), the words "that monk" (so bhikkhu) should be supplied and connected here; "up to the third time" (yāvatatiyaṃ) is the ellipsis.
As it is said: “That bhikkhu is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhus up to three times.
Likewise, even when spoken to three times in the midst of the Saṅgha, if that bhikkhu who holds a stubborn position does not relinquish [his view], he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
the meaning is that he must be formally admonished by the Saṅgha after the formal procedure (kammavācā) has been recited three times. As it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
“‘He should be exhorted up to the third time’ means: he should be exhorted for as long as it takes until the third exhortation;

the formal act (kamma) should be performed with three formal proclamations (kammavācā). ‘That’ refers to the exertion toward schism and the taking up of a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) conducive to schism.
‘They transgress’ means even when the fourth proclamation of the formal act (*ñatticatutthā kammavācā*) is being uttered.”

"Transgressing": he incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense when, upon the third formal proclamation (*kammavācā*)—having reached the syllable "yya" in the phrase "he should speak"—he touches upon the grave matter.

421. The construction is as follows: for a monk who sees, hears, or knows another monk striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha and yet does not speak out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
422. Regarding how far away one must live to hear [the dispute] and then go and speak, he says "having gone," etc.; it is at a distance of exactly two-and-a-half *yojanas*.
"Half a yojana" means half a yojana or more than that. Regarding the sick person, "half a yojana" is prescribed; regarding others, it is said, "one may go even further than that.
For this very reason he says, "if one is able. "Tāvadeva" means at that very time;
the sense is "without delay."

423. "But when it has been stated three times" means: even for one who does not relinquish [the schism] after it has been stated three times—both individually and in the midst of the Saṅgha—by way of the formula beginning with "Venerable sir, do not," etc.; [this refers to] such acts as striving for that schism.
To show the offense incurred by one who, instead of going himself at the moment the schism is being carried out, sends a letter or a messenger, he says: "Or a messenger," and so forth.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “There is no release from the offense even for one who speaks by sending a messenger or a letter,” and so forth.

425. Regarding the syllable *yyakāra* in the phrase “when it is accomplished”: it refers to when the syllable *yyakāra* is uttered at the end of the third formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), [with the words] “He to whom it does not please, let him speak.
“They subside” means they are pacified; the sense is that they are completely settled. “The *dukkaṭas*, etc. refers to the offenses of wrong-doing and so forth.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the motion (*ñatti*), and two offenses of grave transgression (*thullaccaya*) for the two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*). As it is said:
"For one who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense, the offense of wrong-doing for the motion and the two offenses of grave transgression for the two formal proclamations are extinguished.
Therefore, even if [the offense] has been committed by not relinquishing [the matter] after it has been stated three times—both before the motion and outside the midst of the Saṅgha—the two...
It is understood that the *dukkaṭa* offenses are to be confessed.
Upon investigating whether the offenses committed by this formal act (*kammavācā*) are extinguished or not, it is determined:
"He who relinquishes [the offense] at the conclusion does not incur those offenses; therefore, they are extinguished as unincurred."

Having refuted the argument of the Elder Mahāsumma, "What is the purpose of the subsidence for those who have not committed [an offense]?", the position of the Elder Mahāpaduma—"those who have committed [an offense] are pacified [of it], just like offenses that are not common to both genders upon a change of gender"—is established. 426.
"But when the formal act has not been performed" means when the aforementioned act of admonition has not been carried out. "And even though they do not relinquish it" means...

This applies even to one who does not relinquish that effort toward causing a schism in the Saṅgha. By the phrase "with a *saṅghādisesa* offense," it is shown by way of contrast that, although the formal act has not yet been performed,
there is nevertheless an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the failure to desist when one has been told three times both in the midst of the Saṅgha and outside of it.

"Previously" (pubbe) means either before the motion (*ñatti*) has been made, or even when it is being stated three times in the midst of the Saṅgha. "At that very moment" (taṅkhaṇe) means at the moment of the motion;
it indicates the limit for this [offense] as being even after the motion has not yet been concluded, by saying "before the syllable *yya* has arrived.
Furthermore, it is declared in the first verse that there is no offense of *saṅghādisesa* for one who relinquishes [the course of action].
The latter half [of the rule] should be brought here and applied. At this point,
regarding the phrase "there is no offense for one who does not cause [the monk] to be admonished, for one who relinquishes [the view], for one who is insane, for one whose mind is deranged,

for one overcome by pain, or for a first-time offender," within the reading, concerning the items included under the term "for one who relinquishes" (*paṭinissajjantassa*), such as "by means of a motion" (*ñattito*) and so forth:
Having shown the analysis (*vinicchaya*), he said, "or even for one who relinquishes it," in order to conclude that matter.

The word *evaṃ* (thus) is obtained by implication as an indicator of the conclusion; the meaning is: "or for one who relinquishes it in the manner already stated, such as 'by means of a motion' (*ñatti*) and so forth.
*Taṃ* refers to the effort to cause a schism in the Saṅgha. *Asamanubhāsato vā* means "or for one who is not being formally admonished."
It should be understood that although it ought to have been said “asamanubhāsiyato,” it is stated as “asamanubhāsato” due to the elision of the suffix (*vikaraṇa-paccaya*).
As it says in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): “‘Asamanubhāsantassa’ means ‘of one who is being formally admonished (*asamanubhāsiyamānassa*)’.

Although the intended meaning is already established because the phrase “an offense of Saṅghādisesa has been declared” continues from the previous context, it is stated again as “anāpatti pakāsitā” (an offense has been declared) for the sake of clarity.

Does this not result in the fault of tautology (*punarutta*) in the phrasing? It does not result in such a fault, for the repetition of a phrase (*padāvutti*) is considered a form of literary ornament (*alaṃkāra*).
429. Regarding the origin of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), Devadatta, while requesting the five points for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, said:
"It would be well, Bhante, if the monks were to abstain from eating fish and meat for as long as life lasts; whoever eats fish and meat..."
When it was said, "If one were to eat it, a fault would touch him," Devadatta replied, "Enough, Devadatta! I have already authorized fish and meat that are pure in three respects:

not seen, not heard, and not suspected. Having thus authorized fish and meat, and having—without previously discussing the distinction between what is allowable and what is unallowable due to the lack of occasion—concluded the formal determination of the training rule, he now [addresses] the remainder of the bowl.

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “yañhi” has been commenced. Since the phrase “taṃ tassa” (that for him) will be stated later, the word “yaṃ” (which) should be construed both with the word “bhikkhuṃ” (the monk) and with the word “macchamaṃsaṃ” (fish and meat).
“Maccha” means aquatic creatures; “maṃsa” means the flesh of land-dwelling beings.
“Nibbematikoti” means one who is free from the doubt that has arisen as to whether [the food] was prepared specifically for him or whether it was prepared for the Saṅgha.
430. "Made specifically for" means made for the sake of either the Saṅgha or oneself. By the word "knowing," it is stated that there is no offense for one who eats without knowing [the source].
431. The construction is as follows: the meat of elephants, horses, bears, humans, snakes, dogs, leopards, lions, tigers, and hyenas is not allowable.

432. The state of being intentional (*sacittakatā*) is appropriate only in the case of an offense; however, here it refers to the meat itself caused by that [intention], using the term for the cause as a metaphorical designation for the result.

"Accompanied by consciousness" (sacittaka) is included [in the definition]. Here, "consciousness" (citta) refers to the mind that knows the fact that [the meat] was prepared specifically for oneself or for the Saṅgha.
"The rest" refers to unprepared (anuddissakata) and unfit (akappiya) meat. "Without consciousness" (acittaka) is exactly as described above. 433.
"Only after having asked" means, for the purpose of avoiding unfit meat, [asking] regarding the names among the ten types of meat and whether it was prepared specifically [for someone].

The meaning is: "only after having asked about the manner in which both [the meat and the water] were obtained for the sake of avoidance. Since there is no unallowable [nature] in fish found in water, the manner in which they were obtained must be known.
In the case of meat, if one recognizes it merely upon seeing it, thinking, "This is the meat of such-and-such," there is no fault even if one does not ask.
Regarding the givers, if there is an absence of meat [among them], there is no fault even if one does not ask about the manner in which it was obtained.

There is no fault. Or, when doubt has arisen—whether in one way or another—and one remains without accepting [the food], and upon being asked, "Why do you not accept it?", one explains the manner in which the doubt arose, saying, "We did not prepare this specifically for you or for other bhikkhus," and then says, "It was prepared with reference to us alone; it was prepared as a gift."

If they were to say, "This was prepared for the sake of guests," and so forth, describing the manner in which it was obtained by themselves, and further state, "It should be accepted without hesitation," then it is permissible to accept it;
all of this has been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The construction is:
"This is the proper conduct (*vatta*) for bhikkhus. Regarding "proper conduct" (*vattaṭṭhā*): it is that which was taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One out of great compassion.
Having purified the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, they are established in practice.

By the term “knowers of the Vinaya,” he excludes those who, not knowing the Vinaya, fulfill the duties solely by relying on oral instructions, for there might otherwise be a contradiction of the duties;
by the qualification “established in the duties,” he excludes even those who, though knowing the Vinaya, do not fulfill it. By both [terms], [he emphasizes] his own formulated judgment.
It illuminates the state of complete purity.

"This samanubhāsana" refers to the training rule (sikkhāpada) as previously stated. An offense that is to be settled by means of samanubhāsana is called a *samanubhāsanā* offense, by way of figurative usage (*kāraṇūpacāra*).
Otherwise, its status as having a single origin and so forth would not be logical. It has a single origin.

It is so called because it has a single origin consisting of body, speech, and mind. It is "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) because one has failed to desist from what ought to be done by the body, such as by means of hand gestures. It is "verbal action" (*vacīkamma*) because one has failed to desist from what ought to be done by speech.
It is "non-performance" (*akiriya*) because, according to the method already stated, it is the failure to exert effort to prevent the schism of the Saṅgha.
"Because it does not make itself known through either a bodily gesture or a verbal utterance, it is called 'non-action' (akiriya)," this is what is meant.
Commentary on the Discussion of Schism in the Saṅgha. 435.
"Something further must be said": regarding the monk who follows the schism in the Saṅgha, as mentioned in the phrase "one, two, or three."

"Having led those shameless monks who listen while passing by, both individually and into the midst of the Saṅgha, and having stated three times that following the schism of the Saṅgha is not to be done,
the formal act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma) must be performed against those who do not desist from it by means of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (ñatticatutthā kammavācā).
And this [is distinct] from the Saṅghādisesa offense incurred upon reaching the word "yya" during the third proclamation.

"Formerly committed *dukkaṭa* and *thullaccaya* offenses are pacified"—this was said with reference to this common legal determination (*sādhāraṇavinicchaya*) that it is also a mode of non-offense (*anāpattipakāra*).

However, there is indeed a distinction in the modes of expression; that should be stated concisely according to the *mātikā* and in detail according to the method presented in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). "Of this" refers to the second training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabhedasikkhāpada*).
It should be understood that by the phrase “origination... dead,” the common exposition has been extended [by analogy].
This concludes the commentary on the second discussion of schism in the Saṅgha (Dutiyasaṅghabhedakathāvaṇṇanā). 436.

Regarding the term “included in the enumeration” (*uddesapariyāpanne*), the word “training rule” (*sikkhāpade*) is to be supplied as the remainder; it refers to the detailed expositions of the Nidāna, Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, and Aniyata [sections].
The meaning is: "within the scope of the training rules included in the Pātimokkha characterized by the fivefold recitation.
By the phrase "training rules included in the recitation," he shows the scope of the statement, "he makes himself unaddressable.

Regarding the expression "a bhikkhu who is difficult to speak to," the word "who" (*yo*) is to be supplied. "Difficult to speak to" (*dubbacajātika*) means having a nature that is difficult to speak to; one who is impossible to address.

The meaning is as follows: according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), one who possesses nineteen qualities—beginning with *pāpicchatā* (evil desire), which serve as the causes for being difficult to admonish—and who, by failing to respectfully accept the instruction given to him, destroys it within himself, has the nature of being "difficult to admonish" (*dovacassa*). For this is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"He is of a difficult-to-admonish nature means he is difficult to admonish because of the factors that make one difficult to admonish."
“Endowed with these qualities, one is impatient and does not accept instruction.
To make oneself unaddressable means: “Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad;
nor will I say anything to you, venerable sirs, whether good or bad. Desist, venerable sirs, from addressing me!”
By the method already stated, "‘Do not speak to me,’ he makes himself one who is not to be spoken to.
Regarding the phrase "it may be grave," here the word "for him" (*tassa*) is obtained through the method of ellipsis (*ajjhāhāra-naya*). The construction there is as follows:
for that bhikkhu who, being of a bad-tempered nature, makes himself one who is not to be spoken to regarding a training rule included in the recitation, it may be grave for him.
What is meant? If a bhikkhu, even after having been told three times according to the method stated—by conscientious bhikkhus who see and hear his own difficult-to-correct nature, saying:
“Venerable sir, do not make yourself unadmonishable... [etc.
...by mutual restoration”—does not relinquish it even after having committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), that bhikkhu should be dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha.
Because it was stated, “he should be told,” even if he is led into the midst of the Saṅgha by taking him by the hand and dragging him there,
and even if he commits a *dukkaṭa* offense by speaking thus three times, if he still does not relinquish [his position], then for that person of a difficult-to-speak-to nature,

while the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) is being performed by means of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthā kammavācā*), at the third proclamation when the syllable *yya* is reached, as before...

By the same method as stated above, it is said that while the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) [arises] through the motion (*ñatti*), and the grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) through two proclamations (*kammavācā*), when these are being settled, there is a formal act of suspension (*saṅghādisesa*). 437.

Regarding the term "difficult to speak with" (*dubbaca*), the word "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*) is to be understood as the remainder; likewise, it is so in the commentary on the schism in the Sangha (*saṅghabheda*). Schism in the Sangha...
"One who praises the schism-maker" means one who speaks in praise of that schism-maker; what is that? It is the training rule (sikkhāpada).
And that must be understood as the very first training rule concerning the schism-maker, according to the method stated therein—this is the construction [of the sentence].
As it is said in the Commentary: "The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are exactly the same as those of the first schism-maker [offense]. "The entire exposition" (sabba-vinicchaya).
By this which has been shown here, namely the phrase "it may be grave," there is an extension (*atidiśati*)—

with the exception of the determination concerning the end of the *saṅghādisesa* offenses— to the types of non-offenses stated in the triad of verses beginning with "But when it is not done," and to the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth stated in the verse beginning with "This has a single origin."
Commentary on the Discourse on Abuse (Dubbaca-kathā-vaṇṇanā). 438.

The construction is as follows: that monk who is a corrupter of families, by bringing about a decision through favoritism (*chandagāmitā*) and other such means while formal acts (*kamma*) are being performed by the monks, incurs a grave offense;
he falls into a *saṅghādisesa* offense by transgressing that act of deciding through favoritism and the like.
Because of the statement, “A ‘corrupter of families’ corrupts families by means of flowers, or fruits, or powders, or clay, or tooth-sticks, or bamboo, or medical treatment,
or errands on foot,” [it is so called] because, when shameless monks—
relying on gains and winning over families endowed with faith through gifts of flowers and the like— fail to act accordingly, they corrupt the faith of those families.
A corrupter of families, O Bhikkhu.
When one sees or hears someone committing an act that corrupts a family because they lead them astray through favoritism and so forth, and speaks thus—"Venerable sir...
enough of staying here"—in order to release oneself from the dukkaṭa offense incurred by failing to speak out: [this is the case].

The meaning is that he joins the modest and gentle bhikkhus with the four ways of going astray, beginning with "going by way of favoritism" (*chandagāmin*), saying: "The bhikkhus who go by way of favoritism...
[etc. ...do not ordain certain people. Regarding the phrase "while the formal act (*kamma*) is being performed":
it refers to those who see the reviling and the censuring being directed at the bhikkhus who, according to the method already described, are reproaching themselves; and those who...
They hear [this], and when they say to him three times, "Venerable sir, do not speak thus; the monks do not act out of favoritism... [etc.

...do not stay here any longer," even though he has committed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for not desisting despite being told three times, they take him by the hand, drag him, and bring him into the midst of the Saṅgha;
then, having spoken to him again three times in the same manner, beginning with "Venerable sir, do not speak thus," etc.

This means that even for one who has committed a *dukkaṭa* offense and does not relinquish it, when the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) is being performed by means of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthā kammavācā*), [the following occurs].
Regarding "it would incur a grave offense": by the motion (*ñatti*), there is a *dukkaṭa*;

by the two subsequent proclamations, while the *thullaccaya* is being extinguished, at the conclusion of the third proclamation, upon the arrival of the syllable *yya*, he incurs a *saṅghādisesa*. This is what is meant.

439–40. To demonstrate the legal determination regarding the powders, leaves, and so forth that serve as the instruments for corrupting families—as described in the passage beginning with “He corrupts families with flowers”—the author says “powder,” and so on.
“Powder” (*cuṇṇa*) refers to the powder of *sirīsa* leaves and the like. “Leaves” (*paṇṇa*) refers to leaves such as betel leaves and palm leaves, whether they are chewed or not chewed.
“Fruit” (*phala*) refers to fruits such as the *tāla* and *panasa*. “Flower” (*puppha*) refers to flowers such as the *campaka*. “Bamboo” (*veḷu*) refers to a bamboo frame, a basket, and so forth.
"Bamboo. "Wood" refers to timber for a house and firewood. "Clay" refers to natural clay or clay of five colors.
"Powder" refers to that which belongs to oneself or has been taken on loan and so forth...

[omission] ...the connection is that for one who gives clay for the purpose of winning over a family, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) consisting in defiling the family. "By theft" means by robbery. "Of one giving"—this is a genitive case.

“Kātabbo” (should be done) is a word in the nominative case; depending on what is to be qualified, it should be construed with “dadanto” (giving), which is in the nominative case through a change of grammatical inflection. Here, “kātabbo” means “kāretabbo” (should be caused to be done).

By this [rule], one who gives to a family for the purpose of winning them over—whether it be powder or other items belonging to the Saṅgha, a group, or another individual—by means of theft, [is liable] by the value of the goods.
"Should cause [it] to be made" indicates this legal determination (*vinicchaya*). "Belonging to another Sangha" means belonging to the powder, etc., of another Sangha;
here, by the word "another," the inclusion of a group (*gaṇa*) or an individual (*puggala*) is intended.
"Or a valuable article belonging to the Sangha" means leaf-plates (*paṇṇa*), etc., which are equivalent in value to a valuable article belonging to the Sangha.

“Designated as a dwelling place” (*senāsananiyāmita*) means it has been so designated [by a rule] such as, “So many fruit trees and so forth are for the purpose of new construction at this dwelling place.
By the word “or” (*vā*) in the phrase “or by way of ownership,” the term “theft” (*theyya*) is excluded.
“Having carried away” (*haritvā vā*) means having carried it away by oneself; this connects with the phrase “giving flowers. This is the same.
The method applies to the subsequent cases as well. "Having had it brought" means having sent it into the hand of another. "Having summoned" means having called out;
"having had someone summon" is understood by way of implication (*upalakkhaṇato*). "Of one who has come" means either of one who has come by himself.
By the statement "for the purpose of supporting a family," it is indicated that "it is permissible when such an intention is absent. [Regarding] "the cetiya..."

"Even those performing worship, or those taking flowers while thinking 'we shall offer them,' give them here and there for the purpose of worshipping a cetiya encountered along the way; this too is not called a gift of flowers.
Thus, the entire exposition found in the Aṭṭhakathā is shown.
443. Having thus shown the general rule (*ussagga*), he says “or having brought,” etc., in order to show the exception (*apavāda*).

Because the word “or” (*vā*) to be construed with “having caused to be brought” has the sense of including what is unstated, it includes “or having summoned, or having caused to be summoned, or [having brought] those who have arrived.
By the particle “only” (*eva*) in the phrase “only for one who has arrived,” he excludes the giving and so forth after having brought [the food] oneself.
444. "And that" refers to that offering of flowers by one's mother, father, and others. "For the purpose of honoring the object" means for the purpose of worshipping the Triple Gem.
"But not otherwise" means it is not permissible to give in any other manner. To the question, "In what manner is it not permissible to give?
he says, "Siva and so forth," etc., meaning for the purpose of worshipping deities such as Mahesvara and others.

“For the purpose of adornment” means for the purpose of wearing as an ornament. By thus defining the types of things that must not be given, they say it is permissible to give [a child] to parents and others so that they might maintain their livelihood by selling it.

445. By the phrase “the decision regarding fruits, etc.…,” he shows that the decision previously stated—beginning with “having carried it away or having had it carried away”—is the same in all cases concerning fruits, leaves, and so forth.
“446. ‘At the time of distributing flowers and so forth’: at the time of distributing flowers, fruits, and the like.

‘By one authorized’ means by a monk authorized by the Saṅgha according to the method stated in the Khandhaka for the purpose of distributing flowers and so forth. ‘To him’ means to one who has come to the place of distribution.
‘By the other’ means by one who distributes flowers and so forth without the authorization of the Saṅgha. ‘It should be given after having informed’—all this [is required].”
Having informed the Saṅgha, it should be given. 447.
"Half a portion" means half of the share to be received by a single bhikkhu. By the phrase "little by little," even less than half is understood.
448. "Deprived of the means of subsistence" means one who lacks the fundamental requisites for maintaining life, such as rice and other provisions. "Even though possessing wealth and power" means...
And for a lord who has approached one’s presence—this is connected with the phrase, “one’s own fruit must be given.
In the *Khuddasikkhā* it is stated, “for those lacking provisions, one may give what belongs to oneself and others,” whereas here it is said, “one’s own fruit.
In that [former] context, the word “others” includes those who have placed their trust in one; however, here, having taken [the goods] by means of a trusted deposit...
Even when something is being given, it must be understood that the term "one's own" (*saka*) is used because it remains the property of the giver themselves. 449–50.
The construction is: "In whatever monastery the Saṅgha has established a boundary for fruit trees and made an agreement (*katikā*).
This means either having established a limit on the fruit by saying, "So much fruit must be given to guests," or [having done so] regarding so many trees.
"Having made a demarcation around the trees," means having established a boundary for the trees; "or by whatever manner the Saṅgha has made an agreement" is the meaning.

"Even for one who has come there" means even for one who has come to that Saṅgha monastery for the sake of fruit, where such an established agreement and rule exists. "According to the demarcation" means without exceeding the boundary set by the Saṅgha regarding the fruit-bearing trees. "Giving" means...
[This refers to] one who gives fruit that has been gathered and set aside, or fruit that has been caused to be gathered by those authorized to do so (kappiyakāraka).

Since there may be no one to gather the fruit and no one authorized to handle it, he says "or they should be shown" (*dassetabbāpi vā*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the proper procedure to be followed when those who have come for the sake of fruit find neither the gathered fruit nor an authorized person.

The word "having said" (*vatvā*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. By joining the particle *ca* with the particle *api*, the construction becomes "apicā" (or even). Having spoken thus, by the Saṅgha...
By the statement "the demarcated trees should be shown," the *Aṭṭhakathā* demonstrates through contrast that one should not say, "The fruits here are beautiful; take them from here.
(451) By the word "having dug," this also includes "having caused to be dug," because of what will be said later regarding the "kappiya-bhūmi" (consecrated ground).
In this context, "earth" is understood as "what is not allowable. For this very reason, it says, "by way of an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
By the term "flowering shrub" (*mālāgaccha*), both young flowering trees and thickets of *mallikā*, *sumana*, and other such plants are included.
As stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "For even young flowering trees and flowering shrubs are indeed called 'flowering shrubs' (*mālāvaccha*)."
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), one includes fruit-bearing trees, medicinal sap, and medicinal shrubs.
Because the term "ropāpane" (in causing to plant) will be mentioned later, the word "sayaṃ" (oneself) is construed with "ropane" (in planting).

Why is it not construed with "sayaṃ khaṇitvā" (having dug oneself)? Because there is no mention of "khaṇāpetvā" (having caused to dig), which will be mentioned later; for [the rule applies to] "yo... (who...).
Furthermore, because of the statement, "If a monk digs the earth or causes it to be dug, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," there must be an offense of expiation for causing it to be dug;
and since both digging and causing it to be dug must be understood by the word "having dug," [the interpretation of the term *kuladūsana* as referring only to one of these] is not tenable.
"In the defiling of families" means for the purpose of defiling families. Having dug unallowable earth...
The construction is as follows: after having had [the ground] dug, when one has personally planted flowering shrubs and the like, for that monk who has planted flowering shrubs and the like,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on account of defiling a family— on account of the defilement of the family— along with the Pācittiya offense caused by digging unallowable earth.
By the word “likewise” (*tathā*), the phrase “planting oneself” (*sayaṃ ropane*) includes all remaining modes except for that one.

The phrase “by an improper statement” (*akappiyena vākyena*) connects both with “having caused [the ground] to be dug up on unsuitable soil” (*akappiyapathaviṃ khaṇāpetvā*) and with “causing to be planted” (*ropāpane*).
This refers to making such improper speech as, “Dig this ground! Plant this tree! and so forth, regarding unsuitable soil.

The meaning is that for one who causes [the ground] to be dug and causes the planting of flower-garland trees and so forth, there is likewise an offense of expiation (pācittiya) and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Regarding the question of what occurs through the remaining methods of speech and application used by those desiring that purpose—namely, the two [offenses of] expiation and wrong-doing resulting from the digging and the planting—he says, "In all cases," and so forth.

In the phrase "in the defilement of a family" (*kuladūsane*), the locative case is used either in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*) or in the sense of the object (*visaya*). By means of what is improper...
Furthermore, by means of speech, having caused the earth to be dug, even if one causes [trees] to be planted with improper speech, there is likewise a *pācittiya* offense;

along with that, for a monk who corrupts families, a *dukkaṭa* is stated. In all these cases, as well as in all subsequent instances, the application is that for a monk who, desiring such things, engages in all kinds of worldly transactions for the purpose of corrupting families, a *dukkaṭa* is stated.
