453. Because there is no offense of *pācittiya* for digging a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area designated as fit for use) oneself, nor for having it dug by means of an improper expression (*akappiya-vohāra*), only a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated;
thus he said, "In both cases," and so forth. Here, the word "only" (*eva*) is to be supplied, which concludes the matter as previously stated.
Thus, according to the method already explained, even in the case of a *kappiya-bhūmi*, regarding the planting or causing to be planted of flowering shrubs and the like—
The construction is: "In two instances, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for a bhikkhu.
454. Regarding "a pācittiya together with a dukkaṭa": when one is commanded once, saying, "Dig a pit;
plant a tree," even if many pits are dug and many trees are planted, because the command was given as a single unit, there is a pācittiya together with a dukkaṭa.
This matter was stated with reference to an improper site (*akappiyabhūmi*).

As for the phrase “or simply an offense of wrong-doing” (*suddhaṃ vā dukkaṭaṃ*), this was stated with reference to the offense of wrong-doing that defiles a family, which must be incurred by one who, on an improper site, digs a pit using a term for what is proper, and by one who, on a proper site, digs a pit using a term for what is improper—both of whom have been given the single command: “Plant this tree.”

455. Regarding the phrase "by means of a permissible statement" (*kappiyena vākyena*): here, a "permissible statement" (*kappiyavākya*) refers to a statement such as, "Know there is a pit here; a pit is to be known here;
there must be a pit here," as well as statements such as, "Know this bush here; this bush is to be known here," and so forth.
By the word "only" (*eva*), both impermissible expressions (*akappiyavohāra*) and expressions that are a mixture of permissible and impermissible (*kappiyākappiyamissakavohāra*) are excluded.
He turns back. However, regarding the act of making a sign by speaking in a roundabout way (*pariyāyobhāsa*), it is permissible because of the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"The other three are allowable. And in both cases, "on the ground" refers to the two grounds: the allowable ground (*kappiya-bhūmi*) and the non-allowable ground (*akappiya-bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "in planting," here, by virtue of the connection and the context, the term "of flower-groves and so forth" is understood.
Because it is stated as “by means of speech” (*vākyena*), it should be said “causing to plant” (*ropāpane*);

if one asks, “For what purpose was ‘planting’ (*ropane*) mentioned?”—it was stated in that way for the sake of the metrical composition (*gāthābandha*), since the instigator (*payojaka*) must also be included by the description of the simple agent (*suddhakattu*).

By this, in the subsequent verse where it says “let him himself plant,” the word “himself” (*sayaṃ*) qualifies [the action] and thereby excludes the sense of “causing to plant. For the purpose of enjoyment...

"It should be understood that the commentary’s determination— that there is no offense when one causes [trees] to be planted using a permissible designation, whether on a permitted site or an impermissible site—
is summarized by this verse. 'No fault whatsoever' means that not even a single fault among those mentioned— namely, a *pācittiya* or a *dukkaṭa*— is found."
456–7. “Planted by oneself” (sayaṃ ropetuṃ) should be connected with the phrase “for the sake of monasteries and so forth” (ārāmādīnam atthāya).

By the word “and so forth” (ādi), forests and the like are included. Regarding the phrase “or of what is planted by oneself” (sayaṃ ropitassa vā), the word “or” (vā) includes the term “caused to be planted” (ropāpitassa);
for the purpose of qualifying this, the remainder of the text is “by means of allowable trade” (kappiyena vohārena). This, however—

The analysis (*vinicchaya*) should be understood according to the method found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "However, for the sake of a grove, a forest, or shade, it is not permitted to use even the mere expression of what is improper;

the rest is permitted. For the purpose of adorning the interior of a monastery or for the sake of shade outside [the monastery], as if for the sake of a forest, one may say with a pure mind using proper terminology (*kappiyavohāra*), such as "Know this," and so forth.

If one wishes to consume the fruit of trees planted by oneself in a plantation or on a prepared site— whether they were planted by oneself using improper terminology or caused to be planted by others—
or of trees planted by oneself in a non-prepared site— whether they were planted by oneself using proper terminology or caused to be planted by others—
it is permissible to consume them; this is the meaning.

The construction is as follows: it is permissible for monks to consume the fruit of a tree that was either planted by themselves on a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a site for allowable things) for the sake of a monastery (*ārāma*) or the like, or which was caused to be planted by others on a *kappiya-bhūmi* or even on a non-*kappiya-bhūmi* using allowable terminology.
In some manuscripts, at the place where this verse occurs, the reading "ārāmādīnamatthāyā" is written.
The verse beginning with “For the sake of supporting the family” is seen [in some texts]. Because it contradicts the sequence of the Canon (pāḷi), it is misplaced;
however, if spoken after the verse beginning with “Of flowers,” it is in its proper place.
458. “In all cases” means, as before, in regard to all [trees] planted by oneself or caused to be planted for the sake of a monastery and so forth.

Regarding "in garlands, groves, and so forth": "An offense of expiation (pācittiya) for using unallowable water" means that it is precisely an offense of expiation as stated in the rule, "Whosoever, a monk, knowingly sprinkles or causes to be sprinkled water containing living beings upon grass or clay, there is an offense of expiation," and not a minor offense (dukkaṭa);
such is the meaning.

459. Now he shows the scope of the *pācittiya* offense together with the *dukkaṭa*: “In a family... [etc. ... *dukkaṭa*. Regarding “sprinkling”: it refers to sprinkling with only suitable water (*kappiya-udaka*), as well as causing it to be sprinkled.

460. “But for the sake of those two” means for the sake of the two: defiling the family and using [the property]. Regarding “sprinkling and causing to be sprinkled,” the phrase “of flower-garlands and so forth” is understood from the context.

Regarding “*dukkaṭa*,” the word “only” (*kevala*) is to be supplied. 461. Regarding “causing to gather”: it refers to having others gather flowers. “And also in gathering oneself” means in gathering them by one’s own hand.

“With a pācittiya and a dukkaṭa”: because it is stated that “destroying vegetation is a pācittiya,” it is said that for the purpose of gathering flowers, there is both a pācittiya offense for the act of gathering and a dukkaṭa offense for corrupting families.
462. For one who causes flowers to be gathered or has them gathered for the sake of worship and so forth, or for the sake of supporting families...

In order to show the manner of committing the offense, he said, "of flowers. Because it is stated that "there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of flowers," the words "separately, one by one" are to be supplied after "picking flowers.

The meaning is that for one who picks each flower individually, there is an offense of expiation according to the count of the flowers. [This applies] to one who picks many flowers in a single effort.
However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "it occurs by way of counting the effort," which is understood here through the method of exclusion (*byatireka*).

By the term "one who plucks," both "one who causes to pluck" and "one who plucks himself" are shown, either because the specific [agent] is included within the general action, or as an illustrative mark (*upalakkhaṇa*).
And therein, regarding one who causes flowers to be plucked while specifying each flower individually, the offense occurs by way of the counting of the flowers; this alone is [the case].

One incurs [the offense]. It should be understood that the determination is such that when many flowers have been plucked on many occasions by means of a single command, the count is according to the number of commands.
To make it known that this applies to every variety within the method shown in the immediately preceding verse, he said:
"If it be for the sake of a *kulattha* (bean), there is a *dukkaṭa*. "*Kulatthan*" means for the purpose of gathering a family.
Because it is stated, “*sadukkaṭā*,” it is established that both the *pācittiya* and the *dukkaṭa* offenses occur according to the number of flowers.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “There are *dukkaṭas* and *pācittiyas* according to the number of flowers.

463. *Gantha* means tying; that which is produced by that is *ganthima*. This same method applies everywhere. He will explain the actual forms of *ganthima* and the others himself. *Saṅgahaṇaṃ* is *saṅgaho*; the analysis (*viggaha*) is “the gathering (*saṅgaho*) of flowers.”
464. To show these types of arrangements, such as the knotted (*ganthima*), etc., by way of their specific forms, he says:
“Therein, with stalk against stalk,” and so forth. Therein, “therein” refers to those six methods of gathering flowers.

“With stalk against stalk” is said with reference to flowers such as the *uppalā* (blue lotus) which possess stalks. “And stalk against stalk” is said with reference to red flowers and others that possess stalks. This is the method of arrangement.

“*Sabbam* (all)” means everything that has been made. Here, the classification of what is permissible (*kappiya*) everywhere will be explained in the verse beginning with “*sabbaṃ etaṃ*” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “having woven with thread, etc.,” the word “*vassika-puppha-ādīni* (jasmine flowers, etc. is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

A flower-work made by stringing jasmine and other flowers together with thread, or with plantain fibers (*kadalī-vāka*), and so forth, is called *gopphimaṃ*. That which has its stalks (*vaṇṭa*) joined together on one side is...

"Conflict" (*viggaha*). Regarding the term *ubhatovaṇṭikā*, the same principle applies here as well. The letter *ka* should be understood as having either the sense of "diminution" (*appattha*) or the sense of "self" (*sakattha*).
In the case of the feminine gender, the vowel *ā* preceding the letter *ka* undergoes substitution with the vowel *ī*.
A garland of flowers strung together by placing the stalks (*vaṇṭa*) of all the flowers in a single direction is called *ekatovaṇṭikā*; [as for] the stalks...
The meaning is that when a garland of flowers is made by tying it on both sides, it is called *ubhatovaṇṭikā*; thus, the *gopphima* is of these two kinds.

As stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: “Having doubled a reed, a creeper, or a rope, and having wound flowers thereon—excluding those with stalks such as the *nīpa* or *kadam̐ba*—the grasping [garland] is called *gopphima*.”

466. *Bundesu mūlesu*: By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "buds, etc.," flower clusters such as those of the *madhuka* tree that lack stalks, as well as flowers such as the *mallikā* that possess stalks, are included.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "needles, etc.," items such as palm-leaf needles (*tālahīrā*) are included.
"Flower-wreath fabrication" (*mālāvikati*) refers to the fabrication of flower garlands. [The text explains: by means of needles and so forth, buds and other flowers [are arranged] into clusters.
The construction is as follows: having pierced [the flowers], they are strung together;

this collection of garlands is called "veṭhima" (wound or wrapped). 467. Regarding the statement, “Veṭhima should be seen among flower-garlands and flower-bunches,” he shows the first of the types illustrated in the Commentary:
“or made by wrapping with garland-strings,” or [in the case of] a Dhamma-teaching or a statue.
Alternatively, those desiring to make an offering to a relic or a shrine place a cluster of garland strings upright upon the top;
then, for the purpose of showing the shape of a water-pot at the apex, they wrap them around many times.
Such making of a garland-braid is what is called "veṭhima" (the wrapped).
It shows another way: “or bound with fibers (vāka) and so forth. There is also the reading “having bound,” which connects with the word “made” (kata).

Some people, having made eight, nine, or ten long-stemmed flowers such as blue lotuses (*utpala*) into a cluster, place them at the tips of those very stems using fibers or whatever else is available, or separately.
Or, having tied them together, they make a lotus-hand gesture (*uppalahattha*) and so forth; this is what is meant by "a wreath" (*veṭhima*). Neither of these two is permitted.
It is not permitted for one to have flowers gathered and set aside by monastics (*kappiyakāraka*), place them in a cloth, tie them into a bundle, and then bind it.
Nor is it permitted [to do so] with a stalk that has not been cut from those very same flowers, or with a piece of bark (*vāka*) that has not been cut from that very same stalk.
It is permissible to tie it together by making a bundle or to carry it by placing it in a shoulder-bag. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“But it is permissible to tie those very [robes] with thread or with a cord, or to make a shoulder-bag.
And this phrase “with thread or with a cord” refers to tying them by encircling and binding [them].
"Speaking with intentional meaning," so it is said in the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada*.
It is permissible to insert lotus and other flowers into their respective leaves via the stalks, bring the stalks out, cover the flowers with the leaf, and tie them at the tip of the leaf.
However, it is stated in the very same commentary that "it is not permissible to tie them to the handle."
"Filled with flower garlands" (*pupphamālāhi pūraṇe*) means filled with rows of flowers. To the question "Where is this obtained?", he says "The Bodhi tree," and so forth.
What is called a "flower-cloth" (*pupphapaṭa*) is a cloth woven crosswise with rows of garlands, like those who weave cloth by spreading out rows of garlands like warp-threads.
This "flower-cloth" refers to the filling of the length [of the cloth] with rows of garlands.
What was taken previously refers to weaving horizontally; it should be understood that there is no tautology because what will be mentioned later also includes vertical weaving.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "cloth, etc.," the inclusion of shrines, relic caskets, railings, and so forth is intended.

It is said to "be applicable to enclosures" (*parikkhepesu*); this means it applies to the repeated encircling of the trunk of the Bodhi tree and other such objects. [The phrase] "the trunk of the Bodhi tree, etc."...
When the place called *purima*— which is reached by surrounding [the tree] with rows of flowers without overstepping the first row already established—
is attained, then, while another person holds it and brings it back while surrounding it,
one should again place the Bodhi trunk, the shrine (*cetiya*), or the relic casket (*dhātukaraṇḍaka*) in that spot by means of a floral mantle (*pupphakañcuka*).
"It is permissible to cover [the body]"—thus it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā. They say that even if only two monks stand on both sides and carry [the robe] in turn, it is indeed permissible.
This same legal decision applies to rows of flowers being spread out for the purpose of weaving a flower-cloth.
It is not permitted to insert a garland of long flowers (*dīghapuppha*) into the *nāgadanta* (peg-like supports) and then re-insert it later.

However, because it has been stated that “it is permissible to pass a flower-garland (*pupphavalaya*) through the *nāgadantas*,” it is permissible to insert a flower-garland—made from flowers given by others after they have fashioned them into a wreath—into the relic casket or the stupa-dome (*thūpikā*).
Furthermore, as for a flower-wreath (*pupphadāma*) made even with many strands of garlands...

Because it is stated, "Having obtained [the flowers], it is permissible to tie them to the tops of seats and so forth," it is permissible to tie flower garlands and flower strings to ropes, poles, and the like by means of the end of the string from which the flowers have been removed. 469.
Regarding "flower-figures": they make figures of elephants, horses, and so forth using *gopphima* flowers; these too [are made] in the weaving workshop.

Because it is stated [in the Vinaya] that "they stand," this refers to forms such as elephants and horses being fashioned by arranging rows of flowers after having assumed the respective shapes of those forms.
Furthermore, because it is stated in this reading of the Aṭṭhakathā that "those too stand in the place where they are woven," it is said:
"But when placing flowers within a boundary defined by others, it is permissible to make even the forms of elephants, horses, and so forth."
And because it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Regarding 'one who places flowers': this refers to one placing unstrung, natural flowers.
However, when placing a flower garland on the ground for the purpose of worship, whether touching it or not touching it, it is not permitted to place it by doubling it over.
Therefore, while filling out this form of an elephant and so forth...

It is understood that a method of worship exists wherein one joins a garland (*mālāvali*) with others already arranged in sections, places it upon stone altars, seats, couches, stools, elephant statues, and so forth, and offers it.
Regarding the "flower-cloth" (*pupphapaṭa*): by filling a flower-cloth of the type previously described, even a single row of flowers may be turned over.
It must not be left [unfastened]; while weaving, not even a single row of flowers should fall, even if it has been filled by others—this is the distinction regarding the "weaving-filler.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the "flower-net" (*pupphajāla*) is included; for one making that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of holes in the net.
Because it is stated, "The same rule applies to walls, parasols, Bodhi-tree pillars, and so forth," [the rule applies] to parasols and the like as well.
And a flower-net must not be given.
Because this training rule is common [to both], he said, "for monks and for nuns. Regarding the phrase "even for the Buddha," the particle *pi* here expresses inclusion;
it should be understood as "for the purpose of worship"; that is, even to make [an offering] for the purpose of worshipping the Buddha.
The meaning is that it is not permitted to have [it] made, either by oneself or by others. By way of illustration, the jewels of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also included.
The phrase "what need is there to say anything more regarding the rest? expresses a contrast. 471.
By the word "likewise" (tathā), [the text refers to] "whether by oneself or by others, for both monks and nuns, and even for the Buddha."
This refers back to what was stated in the preceding verse. *Kalambaka* means a hanging garland between two bows.
As it says in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "‘Kalambaka’ is said to be a hanging string of small bells (*ghaṭikādāma*) between half-moon-shaped pegs (*candanāgadanta*).
And here, ‘a hanging garland of small bells’ refers to a pair of hanging strings joined at their ends in the shape of small bells. *Kātuṃ* means...
The construction is: "It is not permitted to bind [it]. However, it is permitted to hang a single flower garland by binding it to the end of a thread that has been drawn out.
Even for one wishing to join two flower garlands together, it is permitted to join the ends of the threads only at the ends of the threads that have been drawn out.
"Or even in the shape of a half-moon" means "the encircling of the string of garlands in the form of a half-moon."
Or it is the form described in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

In this context, "encircling with a garland-string in the shape of a half-moon" means filling and encircling by repeatedly drawing out and bringing back the garland-string in the shape of a half-moon;
for that very reason, it is included in the previous [category]. Therefore...
It is said that filling even this half-moon shape by repeatedly taking up and putting down [the string] is not permitted;
however, it is permissible to take up the garland-string once in the form of a half-moon. The connection is: "it is not permitted to do so.
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Both of these are included within 'already filled'. "Filled by others" means by others.

"Having stretched it out long, a flower-cloth (pupphapaṭa) is filled. "To weave it as well"—this is connected with the phrase "it is not permitted," meaning that even to weave a single row of flowers crosswise is not allowed. 472.
"Made of rice-flour and clay" refers to a flower-garland made from rice flour and such, as well as from clay mixed with glass (kāca).
“Even those made of *bheṇḍu* flowers”: having fashioned them from *bheṇḍu* stalks to resemble jasmine, *sumana*, *campaka*, and so forth, and having made garlands from the perforated parts.
Some also write it as “made of *geṇḍu* flowers. “Made of coarse cloth (*kharapattamaya*)”:
here, they say that “coarse cloth” refers to a flower-cloth (*pupphapaṭa*) inlaid with copper filings. “To make”: to perform the acts of weaving, having woven, and so forth.

Because garlands made of *bheṇḍu* fruits or rough leaves have been prohibited, they say that even garlands made of cloth and such materials are not permitted, as they follow the same category of what is unallowable (*akappiya*).
473. "With thorns and so forth" means with the thorns of the palmyra palm, the coconut, and so on. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes grass needles and the like.
"For the purpose of a banner" means for the sake of worship in the form of a banner. By the phrase "of one piercing," both piercing with thorns and stringing with thorns and so forth are included.

In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated that one should fix a rope after directing one’s attention toward a *nāmacetiya* or a Bodhi tree for the purpose of inserting flowers;
therefore, it is understood that it is permissible to insert flowers between the *cetiya* and [the tree] using such a fixed rope.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it says: "A 'Dhamma-rope' is a rope that has been loosely coiled."
It is stated: "Having made a circle around the Bodhi tree or a cetiya, or having suspended [the garland] over the Dhamma-seat, one inserts flowers therein.
Therefore, it is understood that it is permissible to insert flowers even through the gaps in a loosely coiled rope;
having investigated this, the more appropriate view should be adopted. However, there is no contradiction between these two positions here—this is our own preference. Thus it was written.

476. By the word *pi* (also) in the phrase "even when extinguishing," the act of personally inserting thorns, pins, and so forth for the purpose of offering flowers on Dhamma seats, canopies, and the like, is included.

It is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: "The insertion of thorns, pins, and so forth onto canopies and such for the purpose of offering flowers is not permitted; this must be understood according to the authority of the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariya*)."
477. "Permissible speech" (*kappiyavacana*) refers to such permissible speech as found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), for example: "Know this; it would look beautiful if done in this way;
act in such a manner that these flowers are not scattered," and so forth. Regarding "worship of the object" (*vatthupūjana*), it means worship of the Triple Gem.
Among the "signs" (*nimitta*) and so on, "the sign" (*nimitta*) refers to those who know how to take flowers and weaving-cords and tie them into a garland.
"Placing nearby. Regarding "radiance": if one says, "Why do you not scatter the flowers you have worn?
and the other replies, "Because they are strung together," then there are such words as, "Is it not improper to string flowers intended for worship? Regarding "method":
there are such words as, "It is pleasing for the wise to worship by stringing the flowers in such a way that they do not scatter."
This is explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

Regarding the reading, “He defiles families by means of flowers,” etc., why was it stated—having set aside medical practice and the like from the category of “defiling families” as “by means of medicine or by errand-running on foot”—that “not only... [but] never”?
It was not stated that these should be done separately. However, the construction here should be understood as follows:

"Not only this aforementioned defiling of families through the giving of flowers and so forth must never be done, but furthermore, defiling of families through medical practice and the like must also never be done.

Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "medical practice and so forth," it includes the giving of protective charms (*paritta*), water, thread, and food-balls, as well as acting as a messenger or going on foot as a servant, which will be explained later.
479. Having prohibited [actions] in general by saying, "Never should one do [this]," he now demonstrates the method of exceptions by saying, "What should be done," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of the five fellow-practitioners" (*sahadhammika*): those for whom the Dhamma of the renunciant teaching is to be practiced together with these five—namely, monks, nuns, female trainees (*sikkhamānā*), male novices (*sāmaṇera*), and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*)—are called "fellow-practitioners."
"Of those who have reached [the limit]" (*saṅkhaṃ gatānaṃ*). "Even having made an unmade request" (*akataviññattiṃ katvāpīti*):

even after requesting medicine from an unrelated person who has not been invited, saying, "Venerable sir, please say what you need," such a request in a situation where it was not previously made is an "unmade request. "In one's own wealth" (*attano dhane*): within the sphere of what belongs to oneself. 480. "Likewise" (*tathā*):
this refers by extension to what was said regarding those of the same Dhamma (*sahadhammika*). "The beings who attend upon them" (*tadupaṭṭhākajantuno*): [refers to] those two.
"To one who performs services for one's mother and father"; "to a barber" means even to one staying in the householder’s dress who is seeking the going-forth.

"Also to one who performs services for oneself" means also to one’s own laborer. It is stated that medicine may be prepared for these people even without a formal request, just as it is for the five types of fellow-practitioners.
481. "Elder brother" (*jeṭṭhabhātā*) means a brother born before oneself. "Younger brother" (*kaniṭṭha*) means a brother born after.

Likewise, "two sisters" (*bhaginiyo dve*) refers to two sisters, the elder and the younger. "Younger mother" (*cūḷamātā*) means the mother’s younger sister. "Younger father" (*cūḷapitā*) means the father’s younger brother.
"Elder mother" (*mahāmātā*) means the mother’s elder sister. "Elder father" (*mahāpitā*) means the father’s elder brother.

482. "Paternal aunt" (pitucchā) means the elder or younger sister of one's father. "Maternal uncle" (mātula) means the brother of one's mother. Taking the two paternal aunts and the two maternal uncles together, they are stated as "ten. The connection [of the sentence] is: "it is permissible to prepare medicine [for them]. 484. The construction is:
"It should be given after making the mental resolve (ābhoga), 'These people will give to me. 485. Regarding these ten relatives:
how should the limit of the family (kula) be understood in the phrase "as far as the seventh generation"?
“With his children and wife, his brother’s family is one clan;
likewise, with his children or daughter, his [own] family is one clan”—in this manner, the circle of clans should be taken up as far as the seventh generation.
“With his children and sister-in-law, his family is one clan; likewise, with his children or daughter, his [own] family is one clan,” and so forth.
According to this method, [the lineage] should be traced back as far as the seventh generation of the family cycle.
They say that the ancestral succession of Cūḷamātā and others should also be understood by this same rule. Regarding the phrase "defilement of the family does not take root":

according to the method taught in such passages as "But a flower should be given to one's own kinsman who has arrived, rather than to another," the defilement of the family does not arise for one who conducts himself among these [relatives] in the manner prescribed.
"It grows," is what is meant. 486.
*Bhātujāyā* means the wife of one's own elder or younger brother. *Bhaginisāmiko* means the husband of one's own elder or younger sister.
487. *Bhātuno* refers to the elder or younger brother. *Anujā* means "born after," that is, a younger sister.

“*Anujā*” (younger sister) is a term used as an illustration; it includes the elder sister as well. The construction is: “If the wives of elder and younger brothers, and the husbands of elder and younger sisters, are unrelated (*aññātaka*).
Regarding the word “give,” the phrase “this medicine” is to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
488. “Of them too” refers to those brothers and sisters. By the word “sons,” daughters are also included. “Having done” means having said.
Regarding the phrase "Give it to your mother and father," here too, from the context of the matter, it is understood as "this medicine.
Because the term "mother and father" is an inclusive expression for both, it should be stated separately as appropriate: "to your mother" or "to your father.
In these cases, *tesaṃ* and *tumhākaṃ* are genitive (possessive) case endings, while *puttānaṃ* and *mātāpitūnaṃ* are dative (recipient) case endings.
489. Regarding those who are fit to receive medicine, the term "one who is not well" (*akallaka*) should be construed individually with each preceding word, such as "lord" (*issara*), and so forth.
"One who is not well" means one who is afflicted by illness. "Well" (*kalla*) is said to mean happiness;
that which possesses this is "well," and one who does not possess it is "not well. "Or rejected by kinsmen" means abandoned by one's circle of relatives.
490. *Etesaṃ sabbesaṃ* means "of all these people," namely those such as the lords and the afflicted.
Because of what will be said [later] regarding "by one who is good" (*sādhunā*), the word *sato* here means "by one who is mindful" (*apaccāsīsatā satā*).

This is a verb (*kiriyāpada*). The meaning is: by one who does not expect for their own benefit, thinking, "When this is done, they will give me such-and-such. By one who expects to be of service to the Saṅgha of monks.
It is appropriate to do so. "Hospitality" (*paṭisanthāra*) is twofold: hospitality with material things (*āmisa*) and hospitality with the Dhamma.
Here, hospitality with material things is intended. Since medicine is also a form of material thing, being included within it as a gift of the Dhamma is entirely appropriate.
"Paṭisanthāra" means the act of welcoming or providing for (*paṭisantharaṇa*). And regarding those who have received both material things and the Dhamma...
The meaning is: the spreading out evenly, in a fitting manner, within oneself.

Another method: *paṭisanthāra* is the smoothing over, closing up, and covering of the gaps, fissures, and breaches that may arise between oneself and another due to the non-attainment of material goods (*āmisa*) and the Dhamma. For this indeed—
The world’s dwelling is pierced by two gaps: by the lack of material goods and by the lack of the Dhamma.

Just as that gap is not visible when covered, so too the covering of that gap with material goods and the Dhamma—like a rug over a bench—is called "the welcome of material goods" (*āmisa-patisanthāra*) and "the welcome of the Dhamma" (*dhamma-patisanthāra*). "Well" (*sādhu*) refers to the noble qualities such as practicing with proper decorum (*sāmīcippaṭipannatā*).
The meaning is: "by a bhikkhunī who desires to be established through noble conduct.

The word "now" (*adhunā*) is said with the intention that this practice must be undertaken at all times, and especially during this degenerate age—the battle against the dark forces that produce evil—it must be practiced with particular heedfulness.

491–2. "By someone" (*kenaci*): because this is used as a characteristic term (*upalakkhaṇattā*), the meaning is "by a lay male devotee (*upāsaka*) or by a lay female devotee (*upāsikā*). "With the hand" (*hatthena*):

here, the fingers—the components of the hand—are meant, because a conventional expression that applies to a whole may also apply to its parts. "Having made" (*katvā*): here, the word "protection" (*parittaṃ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text;
since the verb *karoti* functions in the sense of action in general, the meaning is "having recited. And "belonging to those very [lay devotees]" (*tesameva ca santakaṃ*).
The thread and water belong to those who are having the *paritta* recited.

Because it has been stated thus, when someone says, "Bring your own thread and water, and for the sake of merit, move this with your hand or touch it while reciting the *paritta*," the thread and water must be prepared by that person.
When someone else says, "Give me the *paritta* water and threads," the monk [should provide them].

The construction is as follows: having stirred the water belonging to those very people with the hand, having kneaded the thread, and having performed a protective recitation (*paritta*), it should be given.

493. "Even if not touched" means even if not touched by the hand; it is said that it has been obtained from the hand of one who has not gone forth, and has not been grasped by oneself or by another monk.
494. "And of a bandit-robber" means of a thief who plunders villages.
495. *Paṇḍupalāsa* means: for Bhaṇḍuka, who was desirous of going forth, *paṇḍupalāsa* is a pale-colored leaf (*palāsa*).
He is like that, thus he is *paṇḍupalāsa*; this designation is applied to one who resembles it, as in such expressions as "this young man is a lion.
Just as a pale leaf stands on a tree facing its fall, its fall being certain, so too does he stand facing his departure from the marks of a householder.
One who is fixed upon entering the going-forth remains as such; thus he should be understood as being "like a withered leaf.
"Even in his own bowl" means even in the bowl used for his own consumption. This is merely an illustration; it should be understood that the alms-bowl is also included.
Regarding the word "setting aside," it should be connected with "alms-food" in the accusative case. "But that" refers to...

Almsfood given while being placed in one’s own eating bowl. Regarding the phrase “to mother and father,” since this is a statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the mention of “the father” here is illustrative;
thus the meaning is “to both mother and father. If a collective singular (*ekasesa*) is intended, the reading “to the parents also” (*pitūnampi*) would be appropriate.
496. “Running on foot” (*jaṅghapesaniya*): the work of carrying messages and errands for householders is called “running on foot. The word “also” (*api ca*) is a conjunction of what has been stated.

497. Having thus far shown the general rule (*sāmaññavidhi*), the words beginning with "bhaṇḍū" are now spoken in order to show the exceptional rule (*apavādavidhi*). "Sāsanaṃ" means a message. "Harituṃ" means to lead to the place mentioned. 498.
"Even by the eightfold [means]" refers to the eight types of actions, beginning with the offering of flowers and ending with the "service of the feet" (*jaṅghapesaniya*).

"By an act that defiles a family" means by an improper act that destroys the faith of families. Regarding the word "laddhaṃ," here the term "food" (*bhojanaṃ*) is understood from the sense of "to eat" (*bhuñjituṃ*).
Because it is stated [in the text] as "in the case of swallowing," and because it will be said later that "this same method applies to the remaining cases as well," [the rule] is obtained.
Since any requisite produced by even one of five fellow-monks through an act of defiling a family is not permitted for all of them,
the total prohibition is made with the words, "it is not permitted for the five fellow-monks."

499. *Sabbattha* (in all cases) is a qualification of the term *ajjhohāresu* (in swallowings); the meaning is "in all [swallowings]. This includes the reading found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: *ajjhohāre ajjhohāre*.
The phrase *ajjhohāresu* is said with reference to food that must be swallowed after being placed in the mouth.
Regarding the remaining conditions (*paccaya*), he says "in the rest" (*sesesu*) by way of consumption alone; that is, in the case of the remaining conditions which are not to be swallowed.
The meaning. What is meant? Regarding the requisite of robes, it is by counting each instance of use after having removed them from the body;
regarding the requisite of lodging, it is by counting each entry into the interior of a hut from the point where the water falls;

regarding lodgings such as beds and chairs, it is by counting each instance of use for sitting, lying down, and so forth; and regarding medicine to be prepared by way of anointing, smearing, and the like, without swallowing it.
"Having released from the body" means by way of counting the number of times; this is what is meant by "this method," which refers to the method stated as "the *dukkaṭa* offense is illustrated.

(500) "On account of conditions that have arisen" is said in reference to "by the reporting of what has not occurred. In reference to "having engaged in trade with money," the construction should be made as "on account of conditions produced.
The determination regarding trade with money is found in the section on *nissaggiya* offenses.
It will become manifest. The determination regarding the announcement of what has not occurred is stated in the fourth *pārājika*.
"Samānā" means "declared"; the meaning is that, according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*, they are similar by virtue of the requisites produced through the act of defiling families.
By this, he extends the application [of the rule], indicating that even in that case, the determination is exactly the same.

501. “Dwelling in saṃsāra is suffering”—having understood this, and having bound the mind to the attainment of Nibbāna, a clansman who has entered the Dispensation and desires to train, with reference to the practice leading to Nibbāna, must avoid from the very moment it is encountered any improper means employed for the sake of procuring unallowable requisites—such means being like foul urine mixed with poison, capable of taking one’s life at the very instant of contact.
All such varieties of improper methods [should be avoided] together.
To demonstrate this, he said, “viññatti,” and so forth. Therein, *viññatti* means requesting. *Anuppadāna* means giving alms-food in succession.
*Vejjakamma* (medical practice) is exactly as previously described. *Aneṣaṇā* means seeking the requisites by means of an effort that is inconsistent with fewness of desires.
*Pāribhaṭyatā* means [the behavior of] attendants who, having surrounded and served a lord, prattle whatever pleases their master’s mind.
The conduct of a monk who seeks gain toward those who provide the requisites should be understood as being like that of a servant.
One who "waits upon" (*paribhaṭati*) or "serves" (*sevati*) on all sides (*pari*) is a "servant" (*paribhaṭa*); a servant who moves about in the presence of masters is a *paribhaṭa*.
Like such a servant is the monk; the work of a servant is "servitude" (*pāribhaṭya*), and its state is [the quality of servitude].
*Pāribhaṭyatā*. Alternatively, one who "acts as a fosterer" (*paribhaṭati*)—that is, carries noble children upon his lap and so forth like a nurse—is a *paribhaṭa*.
The action of a *paribhaṭa* is *pāribhaṭyaṃ*; the state of that is *pāribhaṭyatā*.
This refers to the improper conduct of a monk toward noble children out of a desire for gain.
"Bean-soup-ness" means that, like cooked beans mixed with both ripe and unripe seeds, there is a mixture of truth and falsehood for the sake of pleasing the minds of donors through the hope of gain.
Just as when beans are being cooked, some do not cook while many do, even so, for one who speaks with donors, there is only a little truth and much that is untrue.
It exists; this is called "bean soup" because of its resemblance to bean soup. Its action is "bean soup-ness," and its state is "the condition of being bean soup.

What is called "site-science" (vatthuvijjaka) is the pointing out of sites for wells, houses, and so forth. That which is performed by those who practice site-science is "site-science" (vatthuvijjaka).
502. The "leg-scratcher" and the "messenger service" are exactly as previously described. "Corrupting a family" refers to what remains to be said.
"Speaking what is untrue" is also exactly as previously described. "Reprehended by the Buddhas" means that which has been censured and condemned by the Buddhas:

namely, the aforementioned wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*), as well as the unmentioned means of wrong livelihood consisting of the various branches of science such as *aṅgavijjā* (science of limbs), astrology (*nakkhattavijjā*), portents like falling meteors (*ukkāpāta*), conflagrations of the quarters (*disāḍāha*), earthquakes (*bhūmicāla*), and so forth.
"All. "One should avoid" means one should avoid from afar, as if it were poison or excrement and urine. By implication, the phrase "a clansman desiring training" is understood.

503. "Even from one who relinquishes" refers to the period prior to the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) or during the three proclamations (*kammavācā*) consisting of a motion followed by three announcements.
"Before the *antakammavācā* has reached the syllable *yya*" means: for one who is abandoning the act of corrupting a family.
"Equal to the first schism of the Saṅgha" means: equal to the first instance of causing a split in the Saṅgha.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of corrupting a family.
504. Regarding the word “knowing” (*jānan*), because it qualifies the term “by a bhikkhu,” it should be understood as “knowing [that he has committed an offense].
However, in the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada* written in the Pāli language, the meaning is stated as “having known: ‘I have fallen into such an offense.

The phrase “for however many days” (*yāvatīhaṃ*) refers to as many days as there are; it is connected with the word “concealed” (*chāditā*), and the accusative case is used here due to the absolute connection with the action of concealing.
*Chāditā* means concealed by the day on which one fails to inform one’s fellow celibates, thinking, “I have fallen into such-and-such an offense.
*Āpatti* refers to an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*). *Akāmā* means having fallen into a *saṅghādisesa* offense against one’s own will;

the intention is that for one who has not performed the atonement, it acts as an obstacle to heaven and liberation. *Parivatthabbaṃ* means that one must dwell having undertaken the probation (*parivāsa*).
Regarding the question "For how long a time?", he said, "for so many [days] here," meaning for that many days.
The meaning is: for as many days as one conceals the offense after having committed it, for exactly those many days [the concealment lasts].
As to the question "By how much is the offense concealed?", he said, "And the offense," and so forth. Therein, "and the offense" means:
"And a *saṅghādisesa* offense. And "not suspended" means one who has not himself been expelled by a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
And "capable" means one who is able to go in person to his fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*) and inform them.
And "free from obstacles" means one who is devoid of obstacles such as kings or thieves that would hinder his journey. "In these four" refers here to "among these."

"The remainder" means among these four; "perceiving it as such" means perceiving it as an offense, perceiving it as not having been suspended, perceiving it as frequent, and perceiving it as not being an obstacle—this is what is meant.

For one who perceives in this way, for that person who perceives those four things accordingly, there is the desire to conceal, which is the wish to hide [the offense] out of respect for teachers and others, or out of fear of censure and so forth, thinking, "I will not confess it."
“Concealing” (*chādana*) means hiding [the offense] after having thought thus: “I have fallen into such-and-such [an offense],” without saying so—thus, by these ten factors.
Because the word “by a bhikkhu” (*bhikkhunā*) is a designation of the agent, the meaning of “concealed” (*channā*) here is “hidden.

It shows the rule regarding time with the words “by the rising of the sun” (*aruṇuggamanena*); the meaning is that it becomes concealed together with the appearance of the dawn after the day on which the offense was incurred has passed.
The commentary on the two sections of the *Bhāṇavāra* is finished.

507. Thus, regarding the probation (*parivāsa*) prescribed for the purpose of performing the penance for a concealed *saṅghādisesa* offense—namely, that "one must undergo it even against one's will"—[the author] says "it is threefold," etc., to explain what its divisions are and what its procedure is. That probation is shown to be of three kinds.
The connection [of the verse] is as follows. To the question "By whom?", he says: "by one whose mind is free from the threefold conceit.

The meaning is: by the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose mind is free from the threefold conceit—that is, from the conceit designated by the term *vidhā* (conceit), which is said to be "the conceit 'I am better,' the conceit 'I am equal,' and the conceit 'I am inferior'"—as stated in the passage beginning with "three kinds of conceit."

"Concealed" (*paṭicchanna*) means that for this person there is a concealed offense. Because [the suffix] *-anta* occurs in words such as *ariyanta*, it should be understood as the addition of the suffix *-a* by including it therein. For this very reason, he will say: "It should be given for a concealed [offense]," and so forth.

Regarding "pure end" (*suddhanta*): because it is stated in the *Pāḷigaṇṭhipada* that "a probation to be given after both ends have been cleared is called 'pure end'," the "pure beginning" (*pubbanta*) refers to the time of ordination, and the "pure end" (*aparanta*) refers to the time of the confession [of the offense].

Furthermore, at the time of undertaking the probation (*parivāsa*) or during the period of probationing, having investigated and seen that both ends—the beginning and the end—are pure and counted as a time free from offenses, it is called "probation with a pure end" (*suddhanta-parivāsa*). Herein, he will explain the breach and so forth.
"Probation" (*parivāsa*) is where there is a "putting together" (*samodhāna*), which is the correct placing or insertion of the days and so on. Day by day...

The meaning is that, having gathered together all the offenses among those [offenses], or indeed all offenses belonging to various bases (*nānāvatthuka*), one should grant probation (*parivāsa*) after having concealed them.
Here too, he will explain the distinctions and so forth.

508. "Therein" means among those three types of probation. The word "who" (*yo*) is understood as the remainder. "Thus" (*iti*) should be understood in this sense. The construction is: "Who [has] the probation for what was concealed, this is proclaimed in such a manner."

509–10. To demonstrate the characteristic of effort (*padhāna-lakkhaṇa*) when the formal motion (*kammavācā*) is being recited at the time of granting the probationary period (*parivāsa*), he said: “By way of the offense (*vatthu*) and the clan (*gotta*),” and so forth.
In this context, “offense” (*vatthu*) refers to a transgression such as the emission of semen.

This very [transgression] is called a “clan” (*gotta*) because it protects and guards both the speech and the perception regarding the emission of semen and so forth; for it is so called by way of excluding those of a different nature while sharing a commonality with its own kind.
By not allowing [the organ] to go elsewhere, it guards the speech, the sound, and the perception directed toward those objects.

It is stated that this is done by means of these two statements: the specific terms denoting the two bases and lineages (*vatthu-gotta*), namely "emission of semen" (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) and "bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsagga*), as well as the general term "different bases" (*nānāvatthukā*).
For this is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Even by the expression 'emission of semen' and 'bodily contact,' etc."
“By the expression ‘having various bases’ (*nānāvatthukāya*), both the basis (*vatthu*) and the lineage (*gotta*) are included.

Regarding the phrase “by way of name and offense” (*nāmāpattivasena*): here, *saṅghādisesa* is a name common to its own class (*sajātisādhāraṇa-nāma*), while *āpatti* is a name common to all classes (*sabbasādhāraṇa-nāma*). Since that very thing must be incurred through the transgression of this or that [rule], it is called an “offense” (*āpatti*); thus, the meaning is “by way of both these names and the offense.”

Regarding the statement "the formal act (kammavācā) must be performed," the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even by way of the basis and the clan" includes the phrase "or by way of the name and the offense.
Here, "Saṅghādisesa" is a name shared by those of the same class, while "offense" (*āpatti*) is a name common to all;
thus, it collects these two names together. Therefore, the formal act must be performed by joining both together in one: "or by way of the name and the offense."

Regarding this, it is stated that by means of the particle *vā* in the sense of "option," and by means of the particle *matta* (mere) used in the commentary to exclude specific qualifications— such as the instruction that one should formulate [the confession] "Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses concealed for one day" merely by way of name—
one must indeed proceed by employing only the mere name and the mere offense, devoid of the details of the subject matter (*vatthu*) or the clan (*gotta*).

[The procedure] exists. However, the manner of performing the formal act (*kammavācā*) should be understood by applying the method found in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*, using the name of the person who has committed the offense and the expressions such as "concealed for one day" and so forth. The construction is: "it is to be given to him.
The term "probation" (*parivāsa*) is obtained from the context; the meaning is that probation is to be granted to the person who has concealed an offense.
"And by him" means: by the monk who has obtained the probation (parivāsa), sitting in the squatting posture (ukkuṭika) within the boundary (sīmā), with his hands joined in reverence (añjali).
"Having undertaken" (samādiyitvā): here too, the word "duty" (vatta) is understood by implication.
Because it will be stated later that "this same method applies even to the undertaking," one of these two—either "I undertake the duty" or "I undertake the probation"—[is to be recited].
Or having spoken either one or both [of the formulas] three times, it is said that he undertakes them for the purpose of fulfilling the duties prescribed in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.
The construction is: "At the outset, he should inform the Saṅgha. Having thus undertaken the duties while seated, he should first say to the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed one offense: intentional emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*)."

It was concealed for one day; I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for that one offense of intentional emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) which was concealed for one day.
The Saṅgha granted me a one-day probation for that one offense of intentional emission of semen which was concealed for one day.
I am currently undergoing that probation. I acknowledge it, venerable sirs; I acknowledge it.
“The Saṅgha should remember me”—thus it should be announced.

Furthermore, because of the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā that “it is permissible to announce this matter using any form of speech whatsoever,” it is permissible to announce it even in any language at all. Regarding the phrase “of those who have come again and again,” the word “monks” (*bhikkhūnam*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
[This refers to] those who have not yet reached the place where the announcement was previously made.
Also for visiting monks. "Announcing" means: if there is one monk, if he is senior, one should say "Venerable Sir," and speak according to the method previously stated;
if he is junior, one should say "Friend," and at the end say, "May the Venerable One remember me.
If there are two, one should say, "May the Venerable Ones remember me"; if there are three, one should say, "May the Venerable Ones remember me."

While announcing: "Without making a break during the night" means: either by living together (*sahavāsa*)—that is, by causing the dawn to rise while sharing a single dwelling place with a regular (*pakatatta*) monk, according to the method stated as "under one roof with a regular monk," and so forth;

or by being away from home (*vippavāsa*)—that is, by staying alone without other regular monks, according to what is stated as "staying alone without regular monks"; or [by staying] with visiting monks...
"By not failing to announce," means by not causing a break in the night that might occur through failing to announce as prescribed;
or, "without breaking the observances," means without omitting even a single one of the observances prescribed for one on probation in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.
"He should always dwell" means he should dwell for all the days designated for dwelling in probation until they are exhausted; this is the meaning.

512. "There, it is not possible to purify the probation" means that because the monastery is large, if one is unable to purify the probation without interrupting the nights—having sought out incoming bhikkhus who have arrived and informing them—one must set aside that duty;
that is, having set aside the duty undertaken in that manner according to the method to be explained below.
513. Regarding the question, "Where should it be deposited? he said, "Right there," and so forth.
"Right there in the midst of the Saṅgha" means in that very midst of the Saṅgha where one has undertaken one's duties.

"Or to an individual" means when the monks have risen and gone here and there, and while remaining within the boundary (sīmā), even if there is only a single monk left behind—or in the absence of such a person—when one who has gone outside the boundary remembers [the offense] at that moment.

When one is traveling together with [the preceptor], the formal observance (*vatta*) should be relinquished either in the presence of the persons belonging to that same retinue who are present at the granting of the probationary period (*parivāsa*), or by announcing it in the presence of an incoming bhikkhu.
As for how it is to be relinquished, he says: "I relinquish," and so forth. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he refers back to that very phrase, "I relinquish."
*Taṃ vattanti*: that practice (*vatta*) which one has undertaken for oneself.
514. *Ayaṃ nayo*: this method, namely the method just mentioned, beginning with "either by a single word or by two words.

515–20. *Pakatatto ti vuccatī*: he is called "one of natural integrity" (*pakatatto*). Because he stands firm in his own original nature (*pubbasarūpa*) due to the absence of any obstruction to heaven or liberation, he is thus described as "one of natural integrity. *Paccūsakālasmiṃ*: at the time of dawn, prior to sunrise.
Regarding the phrase "of an enclosed monastery": here, even a single lodging is called such because they dwell in it, considering it to be enclosed by walls and so forth.
The construction is: "having passed two clods' throws.
He shows the limit of those two clods' throws with the words "outside the enclosure" and "outside the place suitable for an enclosure from that which is unenclosed."
What is meant by "a place requiring a boundary"? In the *Visuddhimagga*, in the description of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), it is stated:
"In the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said that 'one should measure within the range of two stone-throws, having excluded the precincts of both the monastery and the village.
This is the measure here. Because this has been stated, for an unenclosed area, it is the first stone-throw; in a village...

If there is an enclosure around the lodging— such as a refectory, a sick ward, or other dwellings situated at the boundary of the monastery— then [the distance] is measured from that point; if there is no enclosure,
then it is measured from the place where water is poured out at the edge of the well, or from the spot where water used for washing dishes discarded by women falls,
or from the courtyard of the shrine (cetiyaṅgaṇa) or the courtyard of the Bodhi tree, provided one stands at a distance from the lodging such that a man of medium strength [could reach it].
The area within which a stone, thrown with one's own strength after extending the hand, falls is called the precinct of a monastery (*vihārūpacāra*);
that very same area is what is fit to be enclosed by walls and such.
Standing there, the distance at which a stone thrown in the same manner falls is one "throw of a clod" (*leḍḍupāta*); standing there again, the distance at which one thrown in the same manner...
"The place where a stone falls is one 'throw of a clod' (leḍḍupāta)"; thus, two throws of a clod should be understood.

"Having stepped off from the path" means having moved away from the path. "By a thicket" means by a dense growth of trees or a dense growth of creepers. "By a fence" means by a fence made of thorny branches and the like.
"Having undertaken the duties" means having formally undertaken the duties in the manner previously described. "Having announced" means having announced in the manner previously described.

"Having laid aside" means having laid aside the duties in the manner previously described. "A monk" refers to a monk who has come for the purpose of being within arm's reach of oneself. "Of anyone whatsoever"—here the word "in the presence of" is to be supplied. "Or having announced" means:
if he is junior to oneself, saying "Friend," and if he is senior, saying "Venerable Sir," and having announced it in the manner already stated.
"The rest" refers to the remaining analysis. "Of the Samuccaya" refers to the third Samuccayakkhandhaka found in the Cūḷavagga.
“And by the commentary” means also by the decision found in the commentary beginning with: “If some other bhikkhu [is there] for some business... “One should make it clear” means:
“If he sees a bhikkhu who has arrived there, or hears the voice of one speaking, he must inform him.
For one who does not do so, there is a breach of the night and a breach of the duty; he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”

If, having reached within twelve *ratana*s [of the monastery], he departs without that person knowing, there is a breach of the night-period (*ratticcheda*), but not a breach of the observance (*vattabhedo*).

If someone who came with him has gone away on some business, then having gone to the monastery, one should report it to the first person one sees and relinquish the observance (*vatta*). Thus, on the day thus determined...

If the period is full, for the purpose of dispelling remorse, and even if more than a day has passed, one who has fulfilled the duties but has not completed them at the very end is not eligible for *mānatta*.
Therefore, having approached the Saṅgha and undertaken the duties, he should request *mānatta* according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka.
For one who wishes to practice while not having laid aside the duties, the undertaking of the duties must be performed once again.
The distinction is merely this much: "it does not exist. This means that one should explain this determination as it appears in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the concealed probation (*paṭicchanna-parivāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "he does not know" (*na jānati*), the short vowel has been used here by way of metrical license (*chandavasena*). [He does not know] the delimitation of the offenses and the nights.

“Does not know” means that even after having committed many *saṅghādisesa* offenses, one does not know the limit of the *saṅghādisesa* offenses one has committed, thinking, “I have committed this many offenses”;
nor does one know the limit of the days, thinking, “The offense committed by me was concealed for so many days.
(522) Now, in order to show its classification, he says “This very same,” and so forth. “By those who are pure” means by the complete abandonment of all defilements (*saṃkilesa*).

By the former teachers beginning with the Elder Upāli, whose mental continuums were completely pure. "This very thing is the *suddhanta*" means that this probation (*parivāsa*) of the *suddhanta* type is of the nature already described.

And it is called by the name "Short *Suddhanta*" (*cūḷasuddhanta*) according to the method stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) beginning with, "He who, from the time of his full ordination (*upasampadā*), proceeds in direct order," and so forth; that is, proceeding in direct order starting from the ordination hall (*upasampadamāḷaka*).
Starting from the day it was announced, when the holders of the Vinaya ask, "How many days have passed since you were pure?
and one who has been reflecting in reverse order says, "I have been pure for this much time," then the *mahāsuddhanta* (great confession of purity) should be led through many days,
taking as its limit the days of purity stated by him, extending back as far as the day of his full ordination (*upasampadā*).
It is said that it is called the *cūḷasuddhanta* (minor purification) because it must be completed by including other days.
Since it has been stated, "For this probation known as the *suddhantaparivāsa* ascends upwards and descends downwards;
this is its characteristic," one should—after having undergone this probation—recollect, imagine, and apply the day following [the formal act], and so forth.
Whether one increases or decreases [the duration] from the day it was taken up— in both cases,
because of the statement, "There is no need to grant probation again," the probation previously granted remains the standard.
This is done erroneously by taking what was unconcealed as "concealed," or what was concealed for a short time as "concealed for a long time," or what was not numerous as "numerous."
The method found in the Aṭṭhakathā should be understood as follows: for one who performs a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) after having taken up [the offense], there is emergence from the offense;

however, this does not occur through the reversal of terms such as "unconcealed" for what was "concealed. Regarding the one named Mahāsuddhanta: "But he who, even when questioned according to the aforementioned method of direct and reverse order..."

The *Mahāsuddhanta* (Great Pure End) is defined in the commentary as follows: "If one does not know the limit of the night, nor remembers it, or is uncertain about it, the *suddhantaparivāsa* (pure-end probation) granted to him is called a *mahāsuddhanta*.
Because it is stated, "This [probation] does not ascend further, but descends downwards," this probation lasts back as far as the day of full ordination (*upasampadā*).

It must be filled up to that point; beyond that, it does not extend further. If one recalls by imagining one’s own state of purity during the intervening period, the count of days begins from that point, even though there is a lapse of days. 523.
“A certain bhikkhu had committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses; he [could not determine] the limit of the offenses...”

In the context of the narrative where it is said, “He does not know [the duration], he does not know the limit of the night,” because this *parivāsa* (probation) was permitted therein, that case was included by stating “and of the offenses. However, even after stating this, the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) refutes it by saying:
“But whether or not he knows the limit of the offenses—thinking ‘I have committed this many offenses’—is irrelevant.”

He said, "Even both kinds," etc., in order to show that the mere lack of full understanding regarding the duration of the night—specified as being up to the end of the night—is the sole criterion for [granting] the probation.

The construction is as follows: this *suddhantaparivāsa* (probation for one who has reached the end of purification) should be granted to one who does not know, or who is in doubt about, either a partial portion of the night's duration or the entire duration of the night.
Commentary on the Discussion of the *Suddhanta-parivāsa*.
524. The construction is: "That other [type] is also considered to be a *samodhāna-parivāsa* in three ways.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, "odhāna" refers to smearing. Thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "having shaken off, having smeared. "Samodhāna" means...
"Placement" (pakkhepa) is what is meant. As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "having combined" (samodahitvā).
"Odhāna" and "samodhāna" together form "odhānasamodhāna"; that wherein this probation occurs is to be understood as "odhānasamodhāna.

Because it is included within the group beginning with Ariṭṭha, the suffix -a should be seen here and in similar places above. And there is the smearing of the days already spent upon the root offense.
And the inclusion of intermediate offenses (antarāpatti) refers to that for which the probation (parivāsa) is stated. For this very reason, it will be said here:
"But when a day has been spent on probation, having shaken off [the offense], it is granted. As it is said in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
"Having shaken off—that is, rubbed away—the day-limit of the root offense on the day already spent on probation, one should merge the offense committed later with the earlier offense."
The construction is: "the probation based on value (aggha-pubbaka), the probation based on mixture (missaka-pubbaka), and the probation by combination (samodhāna-parivāsa).

What is meant is: "the probation by combination of value" (aggha-samodhāna-parivāsa) and "the probation by combination of mixture" (missaka-samodhāna-parivāsa). "Value and mixture" are *aggha-missakā*;

that which has these as its prior [components] is "that which has value and mixture as its prior" (*aggha-missaka-pubbaka*), namely the combination (*samodhāna*). A combination by way of value is "value-combination" (*aggha-samodhāna*); wherever that exists, it is "value-combination. Regarding the offenses committed...

The meaning is that for many offenses concealed for very long periods, there is a probation (*parivāsa*) joined by the inclusion of offenses committed subsequently, calculated by the value of the days [concealed]. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Value-combination (*agghasamodhāna*) means that among many offenses, whichever one, two, three, or several offenses were concealed for the longest period, having combined them according to their value..."
"Parivāsa is granted for the remaining offenses that are concealed for a lesser duration by way of delimiting those [offenses] according to their nights;
this is called 'aggregation by value' (*agghasamodhāna*). The aggregation of various offenses belonging to different bases is "mixed aggregation" (*missakasamodhāna*);
that is where such parivāsa is a mixed aggregation. [The offenses] of various bases belonging to different categories are combined together—
The meaning is that it is a probation (*parivāsa*) connected with the [remaining] portion. As it is said in the Commentary: "What is called 'the combination of mixed [offenses]'?
It is when various offenses belonging to different bases are combined and given [as a single probation].
(525–7) Thus, among these three kinds of probation by combination (*samodhānaparivāsa*), because they serve as the qualifications for the first probation, they are the constituent parts.
In order to establish the common form of both the words *odhāna* and *samodhāna* by restating their respective meanings, he says: “Having committed...
[etc. ...is explained. Therein, he states the restatement of the meaning and form of the first component, the word *odhāna*, as follows:
“Having committed... [etc. ...is given. Regarding the second component, the word *samodhāna*—
He states the restatement of the meaning and the form [of the rule] as: “For a previous offense... for a bhikkhu.

Precisely because both terms in the restatement of the two meanings—namely the two words “for a bhikkhu”—and both action-words—namely “is given” (*padīyate*) and “should be given” (*dātabbo*)—are taken separately, one should understand that there is no fault of tautology.

Thus, by way of restating the meaning of each component, he says, in order to show the aggregate of what is to be prescribed: “This is probation consisting of both the initial period and the concurrent period. (*Esodhānasamodhānaparivāso*)

"...is declared. Here, in the phrase "of one who conceals" (*chādentassa hi*), the particle *hi* indicates a reason. In the phrase "this is the probation for simultaneous restoration" (*esodhānasamodhāno*), the word "who" (*yo*) is understood through its connection with the pronoun "this" (*esa*).

The construction here is as follows: because one who, having committed [a new offense]... [etc. ...having shaken off [the previous concealment], is granted [probation]; and because it must be given for the prior offense... [etc. ..., therefore this probation for simultaneous restoration is declared.
In that context, "having committed an intermediate offense" refers to one who is either undergoing probation for a concealed offense or is deserving of the *mānatta* penance.
While practicing *mānatta* or being one deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*), he should at some time incur another *saṅghādisesa* offense.
"Concealing" means concealing for a period of time equal to or less than the time during which the first incurred offense was concealed.
"By means of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanā*)" means that all those days already spent in the *parivāsa* and all the days of the *mānatta* practice are to be discarded.
According to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), because the term "observed" (*parivutthe*) here is used as an illustration, it should be understood to include "and [those] practiced by conceited persons.
"Having shaken off" (*odhunitvā*) means having rubbed away by way of a formal sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanā*); the intention is that this was done on the previous day.
Since he from whom it is given is one who, having observed probation for sixty years, has become worthy of the trial period (*mānatta*) even while still subject to an intermediate offense...

The meaning is that if, after having committed [an offense], one conceals it for even a single day, all those days must be wiped out by means of a *mūlāyapaṭikassana* (sending back to the beginning), and those same sixty years must be given over again. As it is said in the Commentary:

"Even if one has completed sixty years of probation (*parivāsa*) and become worthy of the trial period (*mānatta*), if one conceals an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) for a single day, one must once again [serve] sixty years."
“He becomes one deserving of probation.
Regarding the “prior offense”: among the many offenses he has committed, it refers to the offense concealed prior to all the others. Regarding the “root day”:
the day of the initial transgression. Regarding “determined”: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a month...
"When the specific day has been determined as 'on such-and-such a day,' it should be given by placing [the days] together; this is the connection.
Regarding "to one who requests according to the procedure," it should be construed as "it should be given by the Saṅgha according to the procedure";

the meaning is that to one who requests according to the method stated in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*, it should be given by the Saṅgha according to the procedure stated in that very same place. The word-division is: "This is the *odhāna-samodhāna-parivāsa* (probation involving both piling up and combining)."
528–9. The connection is: "it is said thus. The particle *hi* in the phrase "by way of their value" (*tāsaṃ agghavasena hi*) indicates a reason.
Through its connection with the word *taṃ*, the word *so* implies *yo*. Here is the construction:

because a probation (*parivāsa*) must be granted to one who has combined [the concealment] of those numerous offenses... [pe] ...which are concealed for less than that duration by way of their value, therefore it is called "that."

Just as the *parivāsa* (probation) is called "the accumulation of the base" (*odhānasamodhāna*) by way of its constituent parts, so too it is called "the accumulation of the value" (*agghasamodhāna*).
In this context, "in many" (*sambahulāsu*) refers to those many offenses among which one desires to undergo probation; the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
"Either one," and so forth, is the description of that which is being selected. "Of those offenses" (*tāsaṃ āpattīnaṃ*). "By way of value" (*agghavasena*) means by way of number.
"By way of delimiting the night"—this is what is meant. As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "by way of delimiting those nights.
This connects with the word "to be given" (*padātabbo*). "From that" (*tato*) means from the offense concealed for a long time.

Regarding the phrase "of the offenses concealed for less than [that]," the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative; it means "having gathered together the offenses concealed for less [than that]."

530. Those for whom there are various bases, such as the emission of semen and so forth, are "those with various bases" (*nānāvatthukā*). Those offenses for which there are perceptions of various bases are "perceptions of various bases" (*nānāvatthukasaññāyo*).

Regarding the word "all" (*sabbā*), the word "which" (*yā*) is to be understood as the remainder; the meaning is: all thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses beginning with the emission of semen and ending with the corruption of families. In the phrase "all those," the particle "and" (*pi*) should be supplied.
Regarding the word "dātabbo" (should be given): here, the term "parivāso" (probation) must be supplied and connected. The construction is:
"Having combined all of those together, probation should be granted. The meaning is: "having combined even his thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses together.
[As in the example: "Venerable Sir, I have committed numerous *saṅghādisesa* offenses: one emission of semen... [and so on] ...one defiling of families."
“Venerable sirs, I, such-and-such a monk, request from the Saṅgha a simultaneous probation for those offenses.

Having made this request three times and having uttered his name during the formal motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamations (*kammavācā*) in accordance therewith, the probation to be granted is known as a “probation for mixed simultaneous offenses” (*missaka-samodhāna-parivāsa*).
This applies even to one who has committed two, three, four, or more offenses.
By means of this method, the subject matter should be grasped by distinguishing the names.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of simultaneous probation (*samodhānaparivāsa*). 531.
"Of one who has completed his probation" (*parivutthaparivāsassa*): this refers to one who has completed probation according to any one of the three types of probation.
"More than six nights" means more than six nights from the period of probation; "six days" is what is meant. The word "to practice" (*carituṃ*) is the ellipsis;
the accusative case is used because of the absolute connection with the action of practicing. The construction is: "The *mānatta* penance is to be given.
By implication, it is understood that "by the Saṅgha. Having applied the method stated in the *Samuccaya-khandhaka*, the six-night penance is also to be granted.
The meaning is that the procedure for honoring a bhikkhu must be given to the bhikkhu.

By the phrase “one who has completed the probation,” concealed *mānatta* is established; since there is no division therein, why is it said, “there are two according to whether they are concealed or unconcealed”?
This is because, without regard for the distinctions already established, [the rule applies] during the six-night *mānatta*.

This was stated in order to show the different types of objects currently available. For if that were the case, since the Pāḷi states, "Let him grant the *mānatta* for six days," when it is being combined [with the previous types], why was it not said to be "threefold" by including that as well?
Because that *mānatta* must also be granted only to one who has already completed the *parivāsa* for a concealed offense; thus, it is included by the very term "concealed *mānatta*."
Because it is included [within the others], it is not mentioned separately. For that very reason,

among the two types of *mānatta* to be shown apart from these two [other] fourfold *mānatta*, it should be understood that while the *pakkhamānatta* alone is shown by the verse beginning with "for one concealing" (*chādentiyā*),
the *samodhānamānatta* is not shown separately.
534–6. *Viniddiṭṭhappakāraṃ*: This refers to the manner demonstrated by the two verses previously cited, beginning with "Of an enclosed monastery" (*parikkhittavihārassa*).
Regarding the phrase "having undertaken that from them" (*ādiyitvāna taṃ tesaṃ*), the word "in their presence" (*santike*) is understood here because it will be mentioned later.
Having sat down in the *ukkhuṭika* (kneeling) posture before those four, having raised one's joined palms in reverence (*añjali*), and having formally undertaken that duty (*vatta*).

The meaning is as follows: “In their presence” also connects with the word “having announced. This refers to making the announcement—following the method found in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*—while sitting directly in front of them, saying:
“Venerable sir, I have committed one offense, intentional emission of semen,” and so forth.
By this, it is also understood that for others who are seen before dawn...
The announcement has been characterized.
One should deposit it in their presence; here, the phrase “when the dawn has risen” is to be supplied.
When the dawn has risen, having sat down in the presence of those bhikkhus in the manner already described, one says: “I deposit the *vatta*; [I undertake] the *mānatta*...”
Having said either one or both of these two phrases, “I relinquish the formal practice,” he should relinquish the *vatta*.
