537. Regarding the phrase “the interruption of the night, etc.,” here the word “etc. (*ādi*) includes the breaking of the formal practice (*vatta-bheda*). The construction is: “according to the commentary” (*aṭṭhakathā-vasena*) and “according to the canonical text” (*pāḷi-vasena*).
538. A group or assembly of twenty monks is a “group of twenty” (*vīsativagga*); that itself is the “one belonging to a group of twenty” (*vīsativaggika*). “They should rehabilitate” (*abbheyyuṃ*).
"Should reintegrate him" means she should make him one of those within [the community]. "By the rule" means by the procedure found in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*.

"One who has been brought within" means one who has been made part of the communal life; "one who is in his natural state" (*pakatatta*) means one who possesses his natural character, that is to say, one who is like someone who has not yet fallen into an offense.
539. The construction is: "of a bhikkhunī concealing an offense"; the word "having committed" (*āpajjitvā*) is understood, meaning having committed an offense.
"For a bhikkhunī who conceals her own offense"—this refers to a bhikkhunī who, by means of the ten factors previously shown in the method beginning with "an offense," is hiding her own offense.

Regarding the phrase "and not an offense," the word "her own" indicates that for one who conceals the offense of another, there is the offense of a pārājika termed "concealer of a fault. "For a bhikkhunī": [as before].
This indicates that for the monk, there is the state of having committed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
541. It is called *vinaya* because it leads to and abandons a contrary meaning; it is a *vinicchaya* (decision).

Because it abandons—by means of "abandoning through substitution of the opposite" (*tadaṅgavasena*)—the adversary known as delusion, which has as its object the specific distinctions of the decision regarding the meaning of the *Vinayapiṭaka*, it is designated as the "leading away" (*vinaya-naya*).
Therefore, it is "an illuminator of supreme intelligence" (*atibuddhidīpana*); it is called *atibuddhidīpana* because it illuminates the intellect to an extraordinary degree.
It specifically kindles the lamp of knowledge that determines the meaning of the Vinaya. Because it is endowed with various methods, it is "endowed with manifold methods" (*vividhanayayuta*).
Regarding the phrase "in the method of the Vinaya" (*vinayanaye*), it means in the bringing [of the teaching] into the mental continuum of others—that is to say, in the commentary on the Vinaya.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the Saṅghādisesa offenses in the *Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā*,
which is an elucidation of the essential meaning of the Vinaya.
Commentary on the Indeterminate Topics (Aniyata-kathāvaṇṇanā) 542–3.
Now, immediately following the discussion on the Saṅghādisesa rules, he says “through delighting in sitting in private,” etc., in order to show the discussion on the indeterminate topics.
Sitting in private is *raho-nisajjā*; the delight therein is *raho-nisajjassādo*; by that, [it is meant] “through delighting in sitting in private.”
The meaning is: by means of a defilement associated with the practice of sexual intercourse. For it is said in the Commentary:
“‘Delight in seclusion’ refers to a defilement associated with the practice of sexual intercourse. “Seclusion” (raho) means seclusion of the eye and seclusion of the ear.
“Seclusion of the eye” means that it is not possible [to maintain it] while the eye is being closed or the eyebrow is being raised.

Regarding the phrase "in order to see [something] when the head is being raised," the commentary states in its word-by-word explanation: "A 'secrecy' (raho) of the ear means that it is impossible to hear ordinary conversation.
Thus, it is the secrecy of the eye (*cakkhussa raho*) alone that is intended here. As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Although the text reads 'secrecy of the ear,' the delimitation should be understood as the secrecy of the eye alone."
Because of the seclusion of the eye, the term "concealed" (*paṭicchanna*) includes the term "unfit for action" (*alaṃkammaniya*) precisely because of that same state of being concealed.
By the inclusion of the word "sitting" (*nisajja*), the word "on a seat" (*āsane*) is also already included.

By the phrase "desiring to go into the presence of a woman," the phrase "together with a woman" is also already included. Thus, by the inclusion of words obtained through their inherent capacity (*sāmatthiya*).
"Whosoever, however, as a monk, should sit down alone with a woman in a secluded place, on a seat suitable for sexual intercourse"—
this is what is meant by "taking pleasure in sitting. Because of the seclusion from sight, even if it is a seat concealed by a wall or the like, and even if it is a human woman born on that very day,
he should be one who possesses the passion of delighting in sitting together with her on a seat suitable for the act of sexual intercourse.
The meaning. Herein, from where is it obtained that the phrase "of a woman" includes even a female born on that very day?
It is obtained from the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "A 'woman' (*mātugāma*) means a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, not a female animal;
[this applies] even to a girl born on that very day, let alone one who is older."
By the word “puts on,” this is indicated: “he fastens the waistband and robes himself in the outer robe.

The term “in all cases” includes both the aforementioned application and the preceding and succeeding applications. For that very reason, the distributive construction “in each and every application” is employed.
The connection is: “for him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for sitting down. [This applies] to both for the act of sitting down.
Since it will be stated [later] as "an offense of expiation" (pācittiya), this should be understood as referring to the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for sitting alone.
544. Regarding the phrase "for both while sitting": here, the word "once" (sakim) is to be supplied;
it means that by way of completing the act of sitting for both, whether before or after one another, or at the same moment, there is a single instance of sitting with either a woman or a monk.
This has been stated. For it is said in the Pāḷi: “When a woman is sitting, a bhikkhu sits down near her,” and so forth.
The construction is: “it becomes an offense of expiation (pācittiya). And it should be understood that there are offenses of expiation according to the number of applications (payoga);
that is, according to the number of applications of repeatedly sitting down near a woman, or a bhikkhu, or both, after each time they have risen.
The meaning is as follows: because it will later be stated, "even by three offenses," the mention of the *pācittiya* serves as an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) for the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*;

thus, what is meant is that [the offense occurs] when one of the three is present. Herein, the phrase "by counting the applications" (*payogagaṇanāya*) does not apply to a *pārājika*, because it is completed by a single application alone.
However, in the case of the *saṅghādisesa* involving bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*), [it applies] repeatedly from the body...
The *pācittiya* offense incurred through contact after having separated is obtained in the very same manner as previously described.
The construction is that when there are many women, there are many *pācittiya* offenses.
When many women are seated, by the mere act of sitting, through a single effort (*payoga*), there arise many *pācittiya* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses according to the number of those seated.
Regarding the phrase “and by counting the acts,” since this is also applicable here,
it follows that when those [women] rise up one after another and sit down again and again, and when he himself rises up one after another and sits down again and again,
the offenses incurred according to their count and according to the count of the acts are many. Here too, however, there is a *pārājika*.
It is not [a case of] *saṅghādisesa*; rather, a *pācittiya* offense is incurred.
545. Even one who is standing nearby, if blind, does not avoid the offense;
for although there is no "secrecy of the ear," because the primary factor—the "secrecy of the eye"—is present, it is stated: "within twelve cubits. By this...
The meaning is: "even though the presence of a woman is available. The construction is: "but even with a hundred women, he incurs no offense";
the intention is that this is because a conscious man is not present. Some write "pi itthīnampi satampi cā," but even there, this reading alone is superior.
Alternatively, the word *pi* should be understood in the sense of the word *tu*.
546. Regarding the word *nipajjitvā* (having lain down): here, the word *samīpe* (nearby) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Because the phrase *nipajjitvā* serves as a qualification for *niddāyanto pi* (even while sleeping), it excludes the possibility of one who is sleeping while sitting;
thus, it follows that even a sighted human male who sleeps while sitting nearby incurs no offense. By the qualification *kevalaṃ* (only/entirely), one who has fallen into a deep sleep is indicated.

The term "taken" (gahita) means that even one who sleeps with the "monkey-sleep"—a state occurring intermittently after having analyzed each offense as it arises, rather than remaining in that state—commits no offense;

this is the meaning obtained. When it should have been said "of a room with its door closed" (pihitadvāragabbhassa), it is stated as "of a room with its [door] closed" (pihitagabbhassa) by way of a compound in which the middle word is elided (majjhapadalopīsamāsa). By the word "at the door" (dvāre), that which constitutes a portion of the door is indicated.
It should be understood that this refers to the threshold or its vicinity by way of proximity (*upacāra*).

"If the womb [of the woman] is not closed off, there is no offense"—this is shown by way of contrast (*byatireka*). 547. In this *aniyata* training rule, although it does not appear in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*) in the Pāḷi, [it says]: "But whichever bhikkhu... with a woman...
“If one should sit down together with [a woman] in a secluded, concealed place on a seat, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Regarding this fourth training rule of the fifth section on the naked ascetics (acelaka-vagga), in the section on non-offenses, it is stated: “There is no offense if there is any other intelligent man as a companion;
if he stands and does not sit; if one is looking for an opportunity; if one sits while distracted by something else; or in the case of one who is insane or a first-time offender.”
In the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), he states the summary as “when there is no blind person,” and so forth. The phrase “in his presence” is understood from the context of the treatise.
Here, by the masculine designation, a male is understood; furthermore, that he “must be one who is not a fool” and “must be of human birth” is understood by this term “one who is wise” (*viññumhi*).
By the word “non-blind” (*anandha*), which expresses the opposite of the state of having entered into sleep like a blind person, [the meaning is conveyed].
“*Aniddāyante*” means “while they are awake”; the meaning is: while men who are conscious of what is pleasant and unpleasant are present within the range of sight.
This connects with the phrase “there is no fault on account of sitting down. In such a secluded seat, together with a woman—
The meaning is that there is no offense on account of sitting. The same phrase should also be applied to the word "of one who is standing.

Even when a discerning and capable male person is not present, and even if a woman is seated or lying down on a seat in private while he himself is standing, there is no offense on account of that because of the absence of sitting by him who is standing.
The meaning is as follows: there is no fault on account of sitting for one who perceives it as being with an arahant;
thus, even for one who sits with a woman in a secluded place, if he sits while devoid of the perception that it is "secluded," there is no offense on account of the sitting—this is the meaning.
The construction is: "there is no fault on account of sitting for one whose mind is distracted."

548. Having thus far shown the various modes of non-offense regarding the mere offense of a *pācittiya*, [the author] now says "there is no fault," etc., in order to show the modes of non-offense regarding the three offenses that constitute the grounds for the designation "undetermined" (*aniyata*) of this training rule. Regarding "even by the three offenses":
"When a monk admits to sitting [in private with a woman], he is to be dealt with according to one of three rules."

It is stated that this refers to all three types of offenses mentioned in the Canon— namely, "the first offense involving a pārājika, the saṅghādisesa offense of bodily contact, and the pācittiya offense"— as expressed in the passage beginning, "by a pārājika, or by a saṅghādisesa, or by a pācittiya.
This concludes the commentary on the first discussion of the undetermined (aniyata) rules.

549. Because it exceeds [the previous category] by way of being subject to discussion, and because its determination as the second *aniyata* (undetermined offense) is distinct from the determinations stated for the first *aniyata*, he says "not blind," etc., to show the specific distinction in its determination that was not mentioned there, while setting aside the determinations already stated.
Since the *saṅghādisesa* offense of "indecent speech" (*duṭṭhullavācā*) is also included here, he says "not deaf" in order to show what does not constitute an offense in that regard.
It was stated thus. The phrase "a man who is neither blind nor deaf" was said with reference to that [definition of a "man"].

With reference to that [definition of a] "woman," it should be understood as "neither blind nor deaf. The same applies to what follows. In order to show that he too must be within the range of hearing, it was stated: "standing within twelve cubits."
550. “A blind man and one who is not deaf commits no offense”—this was said with reference to the *saṅghādisesa* offense of bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*).
However, “Even one who is deaf but has sight commits no offense”—this was said with reference to the *saṅghādisesa* offense of indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*).
Thus, the intended meaning here should be understood in this way.

Since it is intended to state the second indeterminate case (*aniyata-kathā*) regarding the specific detail not mentioned in the first indeterminate case (*purima-aniyata-kathā*), this distinction must also be stated here. If it is asked, "What is this distinction that must be stated here?"—it is as follows:

whereas in that [first case] two factors of the seat were stated as "a concealed seat" and "not suitable for action," here [in the second case] it is said: "the seat is neither concealed nor unsuitable for action."
Having prohibited [the former], he stated this new addition: "It is indeed sufficient to address a woman with vulgar words.
In that context, "woman" includes even a girl born on that very day;

here, however, "woman" means a human female, not a *yakkhinī*, not a *petī*, and not one belonging to the animal realm—she must be intelligent and capable of discerning what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
"A woman who is wise and capable of discerning what is grave and what is not grave" is what is meant here.
In that context, three offenses were mentioned—*pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, or *pācittiya*; here, however, it says:
"If a monk admits to sitting [with her], he should be dealt with according to one of two rules: either a *saṅghādisesa* or a *pācittiya*."
...or" thus only two offenses are mentioned. Among the *saṅghādisesas*, in that context it is said:

"If she should say, 'I saw the venerable one sitting with a woman, engaging in physical contact,' and he admits it, he is to be dealt with according to the offense"—only the *saṅghādisesa* on physical contact was mentioned there; here, that too is mentioned: "If she..."

If one should say, “I have heard it from my noble sir that he was sitting and addressing a woman with indecent words,” and he admits it, he is to be dealt with according to the offense; thus the *saṅghādisesa* for indecent speech is stated.
This much is the distinction between the two *aniyata* rules.

Why is this not stated? It should be understood that this specific basis for full awakening (*sambodhavatthuvisesa*) was intended to be mentioned, but it was not stated because it is already included within the specific analysis found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). This [offense] has three origins (*tisamuṭṭhāna*);
that is to say, it has three origins by way of body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind.
By these two indeterminate training rules (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*) as well, the offenses and non-offenses prescribed within the other training rules have been shown;
no specific distinction regarding the offense itself has been stated. Therefore, what is the purpose of these words? It is said:

The Blessed One established the two indeterminate rules when a particular case arose, in order to set forth the defining characteristics for the adjudication of the Vinaya. How so? Even in the case of one whose word is trustworthy...
When being addressed by a female lay follower (*upāsikā*), one who confesses must be dealt with according to the offense, but not one who does not confess;

therefore, it should be understood that the defining characteristic of the legal decision has been established by these training rules (*sikkhāpada*) through the principle: "The procedure of acting upon what is confessed is the very factor [required] when one is charged with any offense whatsoever by anyone.
Now, why was the *aniyata* (undetermined) rule not stated for nuns?
It is not stated that this very characteristic follows everywhere.
This concludes the commentary on the second discussion on the indeterminate (aniyata).
Thus [ends] the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the discussion of the Indefinite Rules in the *Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā* is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of the Forfeiture Rules (*Nissaggiya-kathā-vaṇṇanā*).
551. Having thus shown the discussion on indeterminate matters, he now says "khoma," etc., in order to show the discussion on matters involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
"Khoma" refers to a robe of that name. "Khoma" is the name for a particular species of tree;
a robe made from its bark is called "khoma" by way of figurative usage based on its cause. "Kappāsa" refers to a robe made of cotton thread.
This too is called "cotton" in the manner already described. "Silk" (koseyya) refers to the cocoon of the silk-worm;
the thread produced from the cocoon is "silk. Here, however, the robe produced by that silk thread is what is called "silk.
"Hemp" (sāṇa) is a robe made by weaving hemp fibers; this should be understood in the same way as linen (khoma).
*Bhaṅga* refers to all types of linen thread (*khomasutta*) and so forth, or robes made by mixing some of these together.
This name is also derived from the manner of its manufacture. Some say: "Bhaṅga is a single species of plant;
a robe made by weaving it with threads of wool (*vāka*)"—in this view, it should be understood as being like linen (*khoma*). *Kambala* [refers to] human hair and animal fur, excluding [the former].
"It is said that a robe is one made by weaving with other fibers.
This was stated with reference to what is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)—"a robe is any one of the six kinds of robes"—and in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—"linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and jute.
"By way of genus" (*jātito*) is said because its divisions according to measurement and so forth will be explained later. "By way of genus" means...
"By way of the commonality of linen and so forth. For "commonality" (*sāmañña*) is called "kind" (*jāti*).

What is meant is that the commonality consisting in being made of linen thread—which encompasses all the constituent parts of cloth differentiated by length, shortness, thickness, fineness, blue, yellow, and so on—is what is called "kind.
The same applies to the others as well. 552. *Dukūla* is a robe made from the bark-fiber of a tree of that name. *Pattuṇṇa* is cloth produced in the country of Pattuṇṇa.
“*Pattuṇṇaṃ* is a specific kind of silk,” as stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*. *Cina* refers to cloth produced in the region of China.
*Somārapaṭṭaka* refers to cloth produced in the region of Somanera; some also write it as *somāracinapaṭaka*, which has the same meaning.
*Iddhija* refers to a robe produced through the merit-based supernatural power (*puññiddhi*) of those who have come forth as monks (*ehibhikkhus*). *Devadinna* means given by deities.
"Robe-cloth" (*cīvara*). For that [robe] is produced from the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*), similar to the cloth given by the celestial maiden Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha.
"Of that" means of the sixfold allowable robe-cloth. The meaning is that these six kinds of robe-cloth are stated to be appropriate according to their respective suitability.
For *dukūla* is suitable for *sāṇa* because it is made of flax; while *pattuṇṇa* and so forth are suitable for silk (*koseyya*).
Because they are made from threads produced by insects, even "supernatural" (*iddhija*) cloth is one of the same types as linen and so forth; thus it conforms to them.
"Gifted by the gods" (*devadinna*) cloth also conforms to those same types, such as linen and so forth, because it is a variety of them. As it is said:
"Linen is indeed [made] from *sāṇa* grass, while that which is supernatural and gifted by the gods..."
"But for those such as Khoma and so forth, it is suitable for silk.

(553) The term *ticīvara* is a collective designation for three robes; because it is the name specifically for a robe determined [as such] by its appropriate measure—namely the *saṅghāṭi* and the others—it refers only to that.
It should not be called "the triad of robes" merely by way of counting any three garments whatsoever. Even a single part of a collection [is so designated].
Just as it is said, "the ocean," so too, among the three robes that have been formally determined (adhiṭṭhita), any one of them is called "the triple robe" (ticīvara).
A "requisite cloth" (parikkhāracoḷa) is that which has not been determined by specific names such as the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) and so forth; it is the cloth permitted by the rule:
"Monks, I allow you a final robe eight finger-breadths in length by four finger-breadths in width, measured by the Sugata’s finger."
"Having made the western edge the limit" refers to the conventional designation for any robe, whether finished or unfinished.
"Face-wiping cloth" (*mukhapuñchana*) is the name for a specific type of robe permitted for the purpose of wiping saliva constantly flowing from the cheeks;
it is so called because one wipes the face with it. And "sitting mat" (*nisīdana*) is that upon which one sits.
This is the name of the robe that has been permitted for monks to spread out and sit upon.

"One should determine it" means one should determine it by taking its name according to the method to be explained hereafter, beginning with the words, "This is a kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi (an itch-covering cloth)," and so forth.
And "only a bedspread" refers to [a cloth] used upon a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha, for the purpose of being released from the offense incurred through physical contact with the body there.
And the robe for spreading out, which is permitted for the purpose of use as a bedspread.
554. *Ekāhaṃ* (for one day): this is the accusative case used to express continuous connection with the action of staying. *Ticīvaraṃ*: by means of the three robes. *Vippavaseyya*:

because it is stated [in the rule] as "with the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), or the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), or the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*"), it refers to being separated from even a single part [of them].

Because it is spoken of as a part by way of metaphorical designation for the whole, it is also said: "by any one of the three robes. By the word "tathā" (likewise), the word "vinā" (without) is referred back.

"Adhiṭṭhāti adhiṭṭhāya" means "having determined"; it should be understood that the phrase "after wise reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*) applies here, with the word "being used" (*vaḷañjiyamānaṃ*) as the ellipsis;
thus, it refers to the sitting mat being used after having been determined.
The construction is: "In that way, one should not live [there] for more than four months.

(555) *Kappiyaṃ* means the making allowable (*kappiyakāraṇa*), such as the application of colors like blue and so forth. And *kappiyaṃ* should be understood here by applying the name of the effect to the cause.
"Having applied a drop" means with the rust of iron and so forth mentioned as "blue, or mud-colored, or blackish-brown."
Having applied a drop [of dye] of any kind, even one the size of a bad back-wound or similar measure. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those things to be determined, such as the three robes;
the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "The three robes" (*ticīvara*) is that which is to be selected. "Appropriate" (*upapanna*) means suitable.

"By the measure" (*pamāṇena*) refers to the measure that will be explained immediately below. "It should be determined" (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) means by way of the formula: "I determine this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," and so forth.

Having stated the name according to the method that will be explained, it must be resolved (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). By the word "only" (*eva*), however, he shows that after stating the name, one must not assign it to another (*na vikappetabba*).
This same principle applies to the remaining robes as well. For this was said by the Blessed One: "I allow you, monks, to resolve upon the three robes, but not to assign them.
Therefore, by one who is resolving upon the three robes and so forth, [he should say]: "This outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)..."
One should perform the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by stating the name [of the robe] with the words, "I determine," and so forth.

However, one who performs the assignment (*vikappa*) should not state the specific name of that robe, such as "this outer robe" (*saṅghāṭi*), but should assign it by saying, "I assign this robe to you.
Whether it be the triple-robe (*ticīvara*) or something else, if one assigns it while grasping its specific name, it remains unassigned.
"It remains in the place of an extra robe" (atirekacīvaraṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati). "That robe" (taṃ cīvaraṃ) is the grammatical connection.
556–7. To show the measurement mentioned here in the phrase "produced according to measure" (upapannaṃ pamāṇena), he says "by the back seam" (pacchimantena) and so forth.
It is called a *saṅghāṭī* in the sense of being sewn together (*saṅghaṭita*). Because it is made by sewing together pieces of cloth, it is called a "saṅghāṭī."
"Cīvara" is the general name for robes. Here, however, by conventional usage, it refers specifically to a particular type of robe distinct from specific names such as "antaravāsaka" and so forth.

Regarding the term "five handfuls" (*muṭṭhipañcaka*): since words expressing numbers—ranging from one up to eighteen—function here to denote the objects being numbered, the word "five" refers specifically to the measure of the hand in *ratana*s (cubits) as established in the section on the measurement of robes.
Because it occurs [in that sense], the word *muṭṭhi-saddo* (the sound of a fist) also refers to a "fist-sized gem" (*muṭṭhi-ratana*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound.
One who completes five is the "fifth"; the fifth of a fist is a "fist-fifth" (*muṭṭhi-pañcamo*).

Since this [saṅghāṭī] has a measure of a "fist-fifth," although it should be called "*muṭṭhi-pañcamakā*," it is called "*muṭṭhi-pañcakā*" by the elision of the letter *m*. Thus the *saṅghāṭī* is described.

Regarding the term *muṭṭhittika*: according to the method explained here, the word *ti* (three), when occurring in a distributive sense (*saṅkhyeyya*), refers specifically to the number of cubits found in the section on the measurement of robes.
For that very reason, the word *muṭṭhi* (fist) also refers to a "fist-cubit" through the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).
Thus, *tatiya* means "the third," fulfilling the number three; *muṭṭhitatiya* means "the third of a fist"; [and] *muṭṭhittika*.
Because its measure is this, it is called “muṭṭhittikā”; although one should say “muṭṭhitatiyā,” by the elision of the suffix *tiya*, it refers specifically to the *saṅghāṭi*.
The same applies to what follows. “Tiriyan” means across. “By the upper limit” means by the maximum limit of measurement.
“Even the Teacher’s robe-measure” refers to: “In this regard, this is the measure of the Sugata’s Sugata-robe: [and so forth].
"Even less than a Sugata-cīvara of the dimensions stated as 'nine spans long by a Sugata-span and six spans wide.
The word *pi* (even) is used in the sense of inclusion; even that much is permissible according to the maximum limit, and anything less than that need not even be mentioned.
By indicating the two extremes, [it implies] whatever measure between the two is sufficient and acceptable."
This shows that it should be taken. 558.
The term *muṭṭhipañcaka* (five-fist) here refers to the long end (*dīghanta*) according to the method explained previously. The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"that which has five fists as its long end," or "in which the measure is five fists. What is meant is: "by a measure of five fists from the long end."
Some also write "muṭṭhipañcama" (fist-fifth). "Tiriyantato" means from its width. "Aḍḍhahattha" (half-hand) is [formed] by dropping the latter member of the compound;
it should be understood as that measurement which has two and a half as its third part; thus the meaning is that it is a measurement of two and a half ratanas.
"Dvihatthaṃ vā" (or two hands): the analysis is "that measurement which has two hands"; or it is a measurement of two ratanas.

The meaning is "it happens. And this is stated because it is found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Even two cubits across is permissible; for it is possible to cover the navel even with an upper robe (*pārupana*).
The phrase "in the remaining inner robes" is an indication of the robe measured according to the dimensions already mentioned.
Regarding the expression "of those that are unsoiled or made to appear unsoiled," the word "of cloths" (*vatthānam*) is to be supplied. "Of unsoiled cloths" means of new cloths.
"Unwashed" means slightly less than unwashed; that is to say, of those garments that have undergone the designation of being "new" and have been washed only a few times.
"Saṅghāṭī" refers to the robe named *saṅghāṭī*. "Double-layered" means having two thicknesses of cloth.
(560) "Seasonally removed" means those whose days [of use] have passed, having been set aside after being worn for a long time.
[The word] *hoti*. Alternatively, it should be understood as "of those robes taken out according to the season";
that is to say, of old robes remaining after one of the three seasons has passed. By the term "robes" (*cīvarānaṃ*), only those robes intended for use as robes are included.
"Fourfold" means having four layers. "The other two" refers to the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). "As is convenient" means...
According to one's preference. *Paṃsukūla* means a rag-robe consisting of pieces of cloth fallen in places such as cemeteries.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Even three," in the textual account where it is said, "When making the three robes, all [the material] cut [into strips] is not sufficient," there is the statement:
"I allow you, monks, two [robes] made of cut [strips] and one uncut. From this, the word "robe" (*cīvara*) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
"Should be cut" means that after cutting the cloth, it should be sewn and made [into a robe]. "If it suffices" means if, after cutting the cloth, it suffices for making a robe.
"In all" refers to the three types of robes. "If insufficient" means if they are insufficient by way of cutting and sewing the cloths.
"An extra piece" (anvādhika) refers to what is called an incoming patch, having removed any deficiency or excess from the cloth.
It is said that [the border] should be attached along the edge of the robe toward the wind, and in the middle, as appropriate, according to the measurements for long and short [strips].
562. "Or uncut" means uncut in the manner already described. "Not taken up" means a guest bowl that has not been formally accepted.
"The three robes" means one from each of the three robes. "By improper use" means by a faulty manner of using them.
Just as it is lost when used [inappropriately], so too by using it as an undergarment or the like without first washing or otherwise cleaning what has become soiled.
563–4. *Kusī* means a cloth of the same length and width as the robe, with a long strip of similar dimensions sewn along its length in the middle of the robe.
For this has been stated in the *Cīvarakkhandha-aṭṭhakathā*: "Regarding *kusī*, [it refers to] the length, the width, and the seam..."
This is a designation for those with long strips. *Aḍḍhakusī* means a robe that, like a winnowing fan, has short strips here and there in the middle.
This too has been said: “*Aḍḍhakusī* is the name for those with short strips interspersed.
*Maṇḍala* means a large circle in each individual section. This too has been said: “*Maṇḍala* [refers] to a robe consisting of five sections...”
"In each section there is a great mandala. An "inner mandala" (*addhamandala*) is a small mandala placed inside a [larger] mandala. This has also been stated:

"An 'inner mandala' is a small mandala. A "separated part" (*vivatta*) is a section sewn together in the middle by joining two [mandalas]—both a mandala and an inner mandala—into one. This has also been stated: "A separated part is a mandala and..."
The middle section is sewn together by joining two half-circles on one side.
The *anuvivaṭṭa* (outer edge) refers to the two sections of cloth, each consisting of two circles, sewn on both sides of that middle section. For it is said:
"The *anuvivaṭṭa* consists of two sections on both sides of it. The *bāhanta* (outer limit) refers to the outer side of those *anuvivaṭṭas*.
"Sewn" refers to two external patches. And this has been stated: "The 'outer edges' (bāhanta) are the individual patches on the outside of those [inner] curved seams.
A collection of five is a "pentad" (pañcaka); a robe sewn with the five types of patches already described is called a "pentad.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), robes sewn with seven patches and so forth are included. Therefore, it is said here: "It should be made..."
“...the three robes. Of a robe consisting of seven pieces, the single middle piece has the name *vivaṭṭa* (turning-back) alone;

on both its sides, there are two pieces each—those reckoned as the small turning-back (*cūḷānuvivaṭṭa*) and the large turning-back (*mahānuvivaṭṭa*)—which have the names *anuvivaṭṭa* (following-turning-back) alone.
And this is said in the Commentary: “Alternatively, they turn back following the *vivaṭṭa*, from one side of it, [namely] the two...”
"One side-seer" is the name for all four patches. "The two arms" refers to the two outer patches to be sewn at the two edges;

and because they are placed upon the top of the arm when the robe is folded together, they are called "arms" by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra), as in the expression "the beds are making a noise," where the term for the container is applied to the contents; furthermore, they are so called because they are constituent parts of the robe's edge.

It is also called "the edge" (*anta*). As it has been said: "When one puts on a robe measuring a *bāhanta*, having gathered it together, both edges placed over the upper arm remain facing outward; that is the name for them. This very seven-piece robe (*sattakhaṇḍacīvara*) was prescribed in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*;
therefore, even now, that alone is permitted. And this method has indeed been stated: [this very same principle...]
"...as stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Having shown the entire procedure—including [the rule] "by a bhikkhu... pe ... even while stretching out his arms"—the construction is as follows:
one must make the three robes (*ticīvara*) suitable for a recluse, which are divided into five types and so forth. 565–6.
Without violating the aforementioned procedure, having applied the "mark of fitness" (*kappabindu*) to the robe and having determined it by means of its name, such as "outer cloak" (*saṅghāṭi*), etc.
To explain how the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is broken for one who is consuming [the food], he says:

"By giving," and so forth. "By giving" means by giving it to another. "By taking it back by force" means by another person taking it away by force. "And by taking it on trust" means by another person taking it on the basis of confidence in oneself.
"By returning to the lower state" means by returning to the status of a householder without having formally renounced the training (*sikkhā*).
Just as in the case of giving to another, [the robe] is relinquished with a state of non-attachment toward the robe itself.
However, some— taking the phrase "returning to the lower state" to mean "a nun’s transition to the status of a householder"—
hold the view that even for a monk who has fallen away from the order, as long as he has not formally renounced the training, he remains defined as a "monk."
As for those who say, "She does not relinquish [the training]," that should not be accepted; because it was not stated with the qualification,

"by a bhikkhunī’s falling back to the lower state," and because in the case of a bhikkhunī’s return to the status of a householder, the relinquishment of the formal undertaking (adhiṭṭhāna) would have to be mentioned separately—
since she ceases to be a non-Samaṇa solely through her falling away from the order.
“By training” means by the training of a bhikkhu. “By abandoning” means by renouncing.

Here, the renunciation of training is mentioned for the purpose of showing that if one who remains in the marks of a bhikkhu renounces the training, he loses even his resolve regarding the robes clinging to his body.
Some write “by the abandoning of training,” which [is intended] to include “even by returning to the lower state.”

It is appropriate when the reading is "and by the abandoning of the training. However, the aforementioned reading, "and by the abandoning of the training, and also by returning to the lower state," is appropriate when that is the sequence of the text. Whichever way it may be, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
"By relinquishing" means by the relinquishing of the robe. "By death" is according to the commentary; [it also means] by destruction.
It is said that the very destruction of the life of the owner of the robe [constitutes the offense].
"The change of gender" means the change of the female gender of a bhikkhu, or the change of the male gender of a bhikkhunī; thus, by such a change of gender in either case.
All nine kinds of robes [are included]. Regarding "the determination": here the words "by these eight" are to be supplied. This meaning has already been stated.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says: "In that regard, by means of the first eight [rules], all robes lose their formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"Is broken" means it is relinquished. "The state of being torn" is *chiddabhāvo*; in that case, when there is a tear, it is said to be "born in a tear.
"The three robes" means any one among the three robes; it should be understood as "only the three robes."
And it is said: "But by way of having a hole, [it applies] only to the three robes.
(567) To the question, "In what measure of a hole does it arise?", he says: "Of the little finger," and so forth. By the phrase "the little finger... a span," he shows the lower limit.
(568) "Even a single thread" means even a single strand of yarn, whether long or across.
569. To show the procedure for a wearer of the three robes (*tecīvarika*) who applies a patch (*aggaḷa*) to a worn spot, he says "first," and so forth.
"First" means prior even to cutting the place where it was torn. "Having applied a patch" means having caused a piece of cloth to be attached.
Here, "formal determination" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is understood from the context, and "a monk who is a wearer of the three robes" is obtained; thus:
It is said that a monk who possesses only three robes (*tecīvarika*) maintains his formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) when he has a piece of cloth attached;
conversely, it follows that he breaks his determination. The construction is: "having first joined two edges.
When one cuts a determined robe in the middle because it is worn out in the middle, [the two edges] from before that point are already joined together as one.
"Having joined and sewn. "Afterwards" means after joining the two ends. "He cuts" means he cuts it in the middle to form both ends.
"He protects" refers to the manner already described. 570.
Regarding the question, "Where does the hole arise in the three robes that breaks the determination? he says, "Four finger-breadths," and so forth.

"Four and eight" (*cattāri ca aṭṭha ca*) means "four-and-eight" (*caturaṭṭha*); it should be understood as the combination of four and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), thus "four-and-eight-finger-breadth.
The construction is: "four finger-breadths" and "eight finger-breadths. "Inside" (*oraṃ*) means within. "One and two" (*ekañca dve ca*) means "one-and-two" (*ekadve*);
from the context, "of those one-and-twos," namely "of robes" (*cīvarānaṃ*), is understood; [this refers] to one robe.

The construction is "of two robes. According to the method of enumeration, the application is that for one robe it is less than four finger-breadths across, and for two robes it is less than eight finger-breadths across.
In both sentences, the phrase "it tears or breaks the hole" should be supplied.
"Of one robe" refers to the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*). "Across" means in width. "Less than four finger-breadths" means...
A hole [made] within four finger-breadths breaks the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). "Of two" refers to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*).
"Horizontally" means in width. "Below eight finger-breadths" means within eight finger-breadths.
The construction is as follows: for all three robes, a hole made below one span (*vidatthi*) in length certainly breaks the determination. Here, "span" (*vidatthi*) refers to the carpenter’s span.

It should be accepted. If a tear occurs within the limits thus described, because that robe has become an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), one must perform needlework and formally determine (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) it before ten days have elapsed.
However, for one who does not do so, it must be determined as a requisite cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*). 571.

Regarding the term "of the sitting mat" (*nisīdanassa*), it should be understood that this is stated with the elision of the latter member of the compound; that is, where "of the sitting-mat robe" (*nisīdanacīvarassa*) should have been said.

Regarding the term *diyaḍḍha*: here, the object to be qualified is the *vidatthi* (span). This is understood through the force of what has been stated, namely, “two spans” and “the span of the Sugata.

It is called *diyaḍḍhā* because it is half of a second; although it should be called *dutiyaḍḍhā*—meaning “that which has a second half”—it is expressed as *diyaḍḍhā* by means of the elision of the suffix *tiya*.
Thus, it is said to be “half of a second,” that is, one and a half. [The span] of the Sugata...
Because the measurement has been fixed by the rule "by a *vidatthi*," three carpenter’s *vidatthis* equal one *sugata-vidatthi*.
Thus, this sitting-cloth (*nisīdana*) is three hands long according to the carpenter’s hand, and two hands and six finger-breadths wide.
Since it is stated that "the border (*dasā*) is one *vidatthi*," it should be understood that there are ten [finger-breadths] in one and a half hands.

572. Here too, in the phrase "four cubits" (*catasso vidatthiyo*), the word "cubits" is understood by implication. The construction is: "for the purpose of covering itches" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādiya*) is joined with "length" (*dīghato*) through a change of grammatical case.
573. That which has two and a half as its third part is called "two-and-a-half" (*aḍḍhateyyā*); that is to say, "two and a third" (*aḍḍhatatiyā*). 574.
"Beyond that" (*taduttariṃ*) means exceeding each of those aforementioned measurements. "Excessive cutting" (*adhikacchedanaṃ*)...
"Excessive cutting" (*adhikacchedana*) refers to the confession of that *pācittiya* offense which consists in cutting away more than the prescribed measure;
having cut off a portion exceeding the stated measurement, the *pācittiya* must be confessed. "Uttered" (*udīrita*) means spoken in the *Pāḷi*.
(575) "By the Immeasurable One" (*appamāṇena*) means by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*), who is immeasurable by way of his qualities.
576. The connection is: “all is allowable. By the word “all,” it includes the blue and other colors mentioned in the commentary.

All bedspreads and robes, regardless of their size or distinctions, are allowable. 577. The phrase-break is: “one face-towel. Since another face-towel must be used while one is being washed until it is dry, he says:

“two are allowable in every way. 579. “Exceeding in measure and number” means exceeding both in measurement and in count. By the expression “exceeding in measure,” [the text refers to] the experts in the Vinaya (vinayadharas).
It shows the quality of being immeasurable; by the phrase "beyond counting," it indicates the state of transcending calculation.
Those who know what has been established (*pakataññū*)—that which was originally made and prescribed by the Buddha, the Blessed One—are the masters of the Vinaya (*vinayadharā*);

they are the "knowers of the established. [This lineage] has come down through a succession of great elder teachers, such as Upāli, Dāsaka, and others, who were adorned by a multitude of jewels of immeasurable qualities.
"Beyond the path of calculation" means they are holders of the Vinaya in numbers that exceed reckoning.

"Five hundred and eighty finger-breadths in length" means as long as a carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakiratanappamāṇa*). "Four finger-breadths in width" means as wide as a carpenter’s span (*vaḍḍhakividatthippamāṇa*).
"The last robe that reaches the allowance" is what is called the "last robe. "The last robe" refers to [robes such as] the water-strainer cloth (*parissāvanapaṭa*) and so forth.
The qualification refers to the measurement of the last robe; this is what is meant. 581.
A water-straining cloth (*parissāva-paṭa*) is a cloth for the purpose of straining water. A bowl-cloth (*patta-thavika*) is a sheath for a bowl.
A book-cloth (*potthaka-thavika*) is a sheath for a book. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), any cloth whatsoever, such as one of the final measurement and so forth, is included.
And he collects the staff and cloth. 582.
"To determine" means to determine it as a requisite cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*). "Set aside" means set aside without having determined it.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says, "There is no offense. "Absence of fault" (*dosatā*): fault itself is "fault-ness. [The phrase] "having released it from being one's own property..."
They say that, with reference to what was set aside, the *Mahāpaccarī* states there is no offense. One who sets it aside with the thought, "By means of this I will have medicine purchased;

I will give this to my mother," must perform the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). The intention is that once it has been released from the state of being one's own property by distinguishing it as "this is for the medicine" and "this is for the mother," there is no need for the formal act of determination. And on this point, there is [this verse]:
“Whatever cloth has been obtained by a bhikkhu, even if it was made for the sake of his mother or others, those who know the Vinaya say that it does not become an offense involving forfeiture.

(583) “In the four months of the rains” means during the four months of the rainy season. The accusative case is used here to express uninterrupted duration, meaning there is no interruption for four months through the act of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). A rain-cloth (*vassikasāṭikā*) is a garment to be worn during the four months of the rainy season.

584. It covers an itch, thus it is an "itch-covering cloth" (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*). This is a designation for the permitted robe intended for the purpose of covering the itch-disease of a monk who is afflicted by it.

And regarding this, there are [the following verses]: "In the commentary on the *Mātikā*, concerning that itch-covering cloth, it is not stated that there is a need to revoke its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) when the time limit has passed."
“Because it is stated specifically among the factors of relinquishment through resolution (*adhiṭṭhānapahānaṅga*), the wise should investigate whatever reason there may be in that regard.
(586) By the very words “this [is] not in his presence,” it is understood that “this” [is] in his presence. The construction is: “The discerning one should set it aside.”
587. *Adhiṭṭhitaṃ* means "formally resolved" (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
588. *Iti sabbamidaṃ*: thus, this refers to all the various regulations mentioned, such as the measurements of the three robes and so forth. *Tecīvarikabhikkhuno*:
for a monk who possesses the three robes by virtue of having formally resolved upon them—that is, for one who possesses the three robes according to the Vinaya. Of the three robes...

"Samāhāra" means the collection of the three robes; since it is the collection of the three triple-robes (*ticīvara*), although one should say "three-triple-robes" (*titticīvara*), by the method of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining the common form of one part), "triple-robes" (*ticīvara*) includes the nine robes.

One who is devoted to the triple-robes (*tecīvarika*) is called a "one whose triple-robes are his discipline" (*vinayatecīvarika*). This same rule applies to the triple-robes even for one who practices the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of the triple-robes; thus he too is included. In other [texts]...
Alternatively, among the six types of robes, only one accessory cloth (parikkhāracoḷa)—namely, the saffron-colored shoulder-cloth—is permitted.
"Having spoken thus" means having spoken according to the method beginning with, "I resolve upon this accessory cloth. That is the accessory cloth.
One who possesses such an accessory cloth, or one who is devoted to it, is called an "accessory-cloth wearer" (parikkhāracoḷika).

589. Having raised the inquiry, "Is it permissible or not permissible to determine the three robes as 'requisite-cloths' (parikkhāra-coḷa)?"—since the Commentary states that "it is permissible"—here the term "three robes" (ticīvara) refers specifically to the triad of robes themselves.

This is because of the statement, "Even a single robe may be determined for the sake of easy maintenance," which implies that the designation for the whole is applied to a single part by way of figurative usage (samudāyopacāra).
Even a single [robe] must indeed be formally assigned.

It is also permissible to make it a requisite-cloth (parikkhāra-coḷa). Thus, for one who lives outside the established boundary alone as a wearer of the three robes (tecīvarika), if at dawn he has not kept the three robes within the reach of his hand due to forgetfulness, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
It is stated that because suitable persons to perform the formal act of discipline (*vinayakamma*) are difficult to find, and for the sake of easy maintenance,
it is permissible— even if one has made a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding three robes by the name "the three robes" (*ticīvara*)— to relinquish them all or any one of the three,
and then determine them by the name "requisites-cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*).

Having thus rejected [that view], he said "And likewise in the case of the *udositaka* robe," etc., in order to show the opinion of the Elder Mahāpaduma, who stated: "If one were to determine the three robes as being for use as requisites-cloths, then the exemption in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada* would be rendered meaningless.
"And likewise" (*evaṃ ca*) means: having thus determined the three robes as requisites-cloths and wearing them...

If it is permissible: regarding the term *udosite* (in a covered place), the explanation for this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was stated in the immediately following second *kathina* training rule by way of the word-analysis (*padabhājana*), beginning with:
"There is a village belonging to a single family that is enclosed; having deposited the robe within the village, one must dwell within the village," and so forth.
And here [in this rule], it is stated by way of: "In places such as villages," and so on.
The method for wearing the three robes (ticīvara), which will be explained immediately following this rule, is "useless" (niratthaka);

the meaning is that it is purposeless because there is no offense for a monk who has formally determined (adhiṭṭhita) a robe as a requisite-cloth (parikkhāracola) by that name, even if he does not wear it as a set of three robes according to that procedure.
590. To avoid that [objection], he says “No,” and so forth. The construction is: “It is not without purpose. To show the reason, he says “Only for one who possesses the three robes,” and so forth.

For such a person possessing the three robes—who, having made a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) under the name of the “three robes” and not having relinquished it, and having established mindfulness, does not let go of the robe from his reach until dawn has risen—[there is no offense] in that training rule.
The meaning is: because the Blessed One has taught an exemption for one who has stored [robes].
Since an exemption is stated in the *Udositasikkhāpada* precisely for such a wearer of the three robes (*tecīvarika*), therefore: "all that" means all nine kinds of robes.
"Of the requisites-cloth" means: for one who wishes to use a robe after having determined it by the name "requisites-cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*).
It is permissible to perform the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati*).

Having thus established that the avoidance of keeping [extra robes] beyond the limit is not purposeless, he now addresses this further point: that it is indeed permissible to determine even the three robes by means of the name "requisite-cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*).
Regarding this additional meaning, there is an "additional statement" (*adhikavacana*)—consisting of the authorization of another action—which was authorized by the Greatly Compassionate One.
In order to show the state of being an indicative cause (*ñāpakahetu*), he said, “He resolves,” and so forth.

In this very training rule (*sikkhāpada*), within the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), in the passage: “There is no offense if one resolves or designates [the robe] within ten days,” since the state of non-offense is established by the word “resolves” alone, the permission for another action—namely, “designates”—is given as an alternative way, showing that there is no fault even in that manner.
The meaning is: "because the intention has been made known.
592. "Doing thus" means: having relinquished the formal determination by means of the name "three robes," one determines [the cloth] by means of the name "requisite-cloth.
Now, wishing to show an over-extension of the argument, the accuser states the following to reveal his underlying intention:
“Thus,” and so forth. Since there exist other types of things that must be performed apart from the fundamental resolve (*mūlādhiṭṭhāna*), the meaning of the question is:
why would there be no fault even for one who, having relinquished the three robes (*ticīvara*) and performed such acts as wiping the face, were to then make a formal resolve?
[The answer is: “No,” which serves to prevent an over-extension of the principle.
593. "By way of performing their respective functions" means by way of accomplishing the specific function of each, such as wiping the mouth and so forth.
The intention is that it is not appropriate to resolve upon such specific functions without referring to them by their respective names.

"Of what is not its function" means of that which is devoid of the function of wiping the mouth and so forth. "Of what is superfluous" refers to that which was set aside after the initial resolution [of the robe] had already been made.

"Because of having abandoned what is in excess. "Of this" means of the three robes (*ticīvara*). "But the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is appropriate" means that the formal determination by means of the name "requisite cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷa*), without exceeding ten days, is indeed appropriate. 594.
"The means for the opening of storage" is *nidhānamukha*; it refers to the formal determination by means of the names of the various robes, such as the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), and so forth.
The meaning is that whatever extra robe is kept as prescribed does not incur an offense; this is the method for its storage.
This is the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*). Regarding the *Mahāpaccarī*:

during the time of the danger posed by Brāhmaṇa Tissa, at the command of Sakka, Lord of the Devas, in order to lead the Saṅgha of monks to Jambudīpa, [the island] Mahāpaccarī was created by Visukamma.
Because it was written down after being recited, it is called by that name; in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, they also write, "in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other [commentaries].

(595) Regarding the question of what the prescribed measurement for the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is under the name of "requisites-cloth" (*parikkhāra-coḷa*), he says, "the robe" (*cīvara*), and so forth.
The word division is: "In the Nidāna, from its origin. In the Nidāna, regarding the phrase "the robe is complete," it says, "the triple-robe (*ticīvara*) is complete."
[This refers to] the matter reported by the monks to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, this extra robe exists; what should be done with it?
Regarding the phrase "from its arising": it means because the designation of requisites-cloth (*parikkhāra-coḷa*) has arisen [as a category], that is, because it was authorized.
"Now at that time, the monks' triple-robe (*ticīvara*) was complete, yet there was need for water-strainers (*parissāvana*) as well..."
[They reported this matter to the Blessed One: "Even with bags. The Blessed One said: "I allow you, monks, a requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷaka*).

Herein, according to the Pāḷi, it is established that for the sake of the comfort of being away from one's robes, it is permissible to rescind the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes by name and determine them instead by the name "requisites-cloth";
because they share the same means of establishment, even a single [robe] may be so determined.
It has already been stated that it is permissible to assign (vikappeti) a robe. For this very reason, the Commentary says:

"And this being so, for one who wishes to live apart from one of his three robes, the assignment of the three robes is rescinded, and an opportunity for assignment is granted for the sake of the ease of living apart."

596–8. Having thus far shown what constitutes a permissible robe (*kappiya-cīvara*) and what should be done with it, he now says, beginning with “*kusavākādī*,” in order to show what is an impermissible robe (*akappiya-cīvara*).
*Kusa* refers to *dabba* grass. *Vāka* refers to the bark of trees and the like. By the word “and the like” (*ādi*), a wooden board is included. The word *cīra* is a synonym for a robe (*cīvara*).
In this context, it refers specifically to a robe made by sewing together *kusa* grass and the other materials mentioned.
It is permissible. "A woolen cloth made of hair" refers to a woolen cloth woven from human hair. "A woolen cloth made of fur" refers to a woolen cloth woven from horse-tails or yak-tails.
"An owl-wing" refers to the wing-feather of an owl-bird; however, in this context, only a robe made by sewing those together should be understood as intended.
"A deerskin rug" refers to the hide of a black antelope. The phrase "for one who wears it, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya)" is to be connected with each [item] individually.
*Kadalidussa* refers to cloth made from plantain fibers (*kadalīvāka*). *Erakadussa* refers to cloth made from *eraka* grass.
*Akkadussa* refers to cloth made by taking either *akkadaṇḍa* stalks or their fibers. *Potthaka* refers to cloth made from coarse bark fibers (*makaci-vāka*).
*Tirīṭe* refers to the bark of a tree so named. *Veṭhana* refers to a head-wrap. *Kañcuka* refers to armor.

"Entirely blue" (*sabba-nīlaka*) means purely blue. This same method applies to "mañjeṭṭha" and the others. "Great red" (*mahānāma-ratta*) means red with the color of a thin lotus petal. "Great dye-red" (*mahā-raṅga-ratta*) means red with the color of a centipede. 599.

"With uncut fringes" (*acchinna-dasaka*) refers to that robe whose fringes (*dasā*) have not been cut. This same method applies to "long-fringed" (*dīgha-dasa*) as well. "Fruit-fringed" (*phala-dasa*) refers to that [robe] whose fringes are knotted like fruits.
"Flower-fringed" (*puppha-dasa*) refers to [fringes] where a rosette (*kaṇṇikā*) has been tied and opened out.
The meaning is: "for which [robe] the fringes have been made. "One whose robe has been stolen" means one whose robe has been plundered by thieves, leaving him naked.

"In this regard" refers to among materials such as *kusa* grass and so forth, and among all those that are entirely blue and so on. "Nothing whatsoever" means there is not even a single thing that is unallowable or unsuitable.
"By one who is naked, having obtained any of these unallowable robes, and having covered the private parts with it..."
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Later, when an allowable robe (*kappiya-cīvara*) has been obtained, one should accept that and relinquish this unallowable robe (*akappiya-cīvara*).

When robes of entirely blue color or other such colors are obtained, it is permissible to wear them after dyeing them with an allowable dye, or after destroying that color, or after attaching allowable cloth to both sides, or after covering them."
600. “Within ten days”: this should be connected with all the phrases beginning with “he determines.
“He relinquishes” means he gives it to another. Here, giving is twofold: giving in the presence [of the recipient] and giving in the absence [of the recipient].
Giving while seeing the recipient, saying, “I give this to you,” is called giving in the presence. In the absence, [saying], “This for so-and-so...”
"Give it," is a gift given in the absence [of the recipient]. Or, when it is said, "Take this," or "Take it for you," if one says, "I take it for myself," both the giving and the receiving are pure.
When the giver says, "Make this your own," "Let it be your own," or "It is yours," even if the recipient says, "It is mine..."
If one says, "I shall do so; let it be mine, let it be mine," both the giving and the receiving are impure.
However, when told, "Make it yours," if one replies, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I accept it," and then accepts it, the acceptance is pure.
When told, "Take this for yourself," if one says, "I will not take it," and [the donor] says again, "It is given..."

When [the first person] says, "I have [it]; take yours," and the other again refuses, that robe—because it does not belong to anyone—is not subject to forfeiture even if the ten-day limit is exceeded;
therefore, whichever of those two wishes may do so later, he should determine it for himself and use it.
All of this has been stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.

When one is in doubt regarding the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of a robe that has already been determined, one first makes manifest one's own doubt, thinking, "If it is not determined, then once this [act] is done, it becomes allowable (*kappiya*).
For one who then relinquishes it and performs the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*), no fault of false speech (*musāvāda-dosa*) arises.
As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "For there is no false speech for one who performs a disciplinary act after having made it known in this way."
"...occurs. "Some say that 'if one has taken a robe out of doubt in such a manner, it should be given back on the basis of trust,' but that is not good," it is stated right there.
"It perishes" means it is destroyed by thieves and so forth. "It is lost, it is burned, they seize it by force"—these [cases] as well...
Because they are modes of destruction, they are included by the very term “is destroyed.
In this context, “is lost” is said with reference to what has been seized by thieves and the like; “is destroyed” is said with reference to what has been gnawed by rats and so forth;
and “is burnt” is said with reference to what has been consumed by fire. “Is trusted” means that one who is seen, who is well-known, and who is addressed, continues to live.
"And when it has been taken, he is satisfied" means that it has been taken by another through confidence in himself, being endowed with the five factors.
"Explained" means as stated in the method beginning with: "There is no offense if one resolves [the robe] within ten days. 601.
As for this, the meaning is that it is called the *kathina-samuṭṭhāna* by name; that is, this is the *kathina-samuṭṭhāna*.

It originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind. It is "without consciousness" (*acitta*) because an offense occurs even when there is no conscious awareness of the designation (*paṇṇatti*), provided there is a mind that knows the state of having an extra robe.
It is "non-action" (*akiriya*) because it lacks formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and dedication (*vikappana*).
One who, while devoted to meditation or worshipping a shrine and so forth, causes the eleventh dawn to rise [with an extra robe], [commits this offense].
One commits [an offense] with a wholesome mind when one who is intent on quarreling and so forth, or one who knows the transgression, brings it about; one commits it with an unwholesome mind;

but one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), acting in that way through lack of mindfulness or not knowing the formal rule (paṇṇatti), commits it with an indeterminate (abyākata) mind—thus there are three types of consciousness.
For one who applies himself to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and so forth in the manner described, possessing a mind of joy (somanassa-citta):

There is pleasant feeling; for one possessing a mind of equanimity, there is neutral feeling; and for one whose mind is possessed of grief due to being intent on quarreling and the like, there is painful feeling—thus there are three feelings.
This same method should be applied to similar instances further on.
This concludes the commentary on the first discussion of the hard-to-understand points.

602. Regarding the phrase "in places such as villages, [groups of] three or five," this is stated in order to show the fault of being separated from one's robes after having deposited them there, and to indicate the locations where they might arise.

Thus, it is said that there are fifteen places for depositing robes, as enumerated in the Pāḷi by way of the following sequence: a village with a single precinct, and so forth—namely, a village settlement, a watchtower, a watch-station, a watch-tower, a palace, a hall, a mansion, a ship, a caravan, a field, a threshing floor, a monastery, a monastery-temple, the foot of a tree, and an open space.
It exists. Here, "village" (*gāma*) refers to a village consisting of a single hut and so forth.
"Dwelling" (*nivesana*) refers to a house such as one with four wings located outside the village. Therefore, it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada*:
"Those who explain the distinction between a village and a dwelling say: 'Furthermore, when many houses are established within a single boundary, they are called a dwelling.'"
Therefore, all this—such as dwellings and so forth—should be understood as "outside the village. And this was stated right there:

"If the dwelling and so forth are within the village, since they receive the same exemptions as those mentioned for the village itself, they should be understood as 'outside the interior of the village.'"
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the term *udosita* is defined by the description: "a hall for goods such as vehicles. The term *aṭṭa* is defined by the description:
"a specific type of dwelling with thick walls made of bricks, four or five stories high, built for the purpose of repelling rival kings and others.
The term *māḷa* is defined as: "a square palace comprised under a single roof-peak."
A multi-storied building (*māḷa*) is said to be comprised of a single story or four stories. A *pāsāda* is a long palace. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof.
A *nāvā* (boat) refers to a means of transport. A *sattha* (caravan) is a group of people, which is twofold according to whether it is a foot-caravan or a wagon-caravan;
each of these is further twofold according to whether they are settled or unsettled. Among those, regarding the settled [caravans]:
There is indeed even a boundary such as a fence and so forth.
"Field" refers to a field such as a barley field and so forth. "Granary" refers to a threshing floor. "Garden" (*ārāma*) means a flower garden and a fruit garden.
"Monastery" (*vihāra*) is said to refer to even a single lodging place. "A tree" (*rukkha*) is that which, at midday, [is surrounded] on all sides...
A tree covered by the extent of shade described as "the shadow extends" [is meant]. An open space (*ajjhokāsa*) is defined as within seven *abbhantara*s;
it is found in the Viñjā forest, in uninhabited wildernesses away from villages, on paths that fishermen do not travel, and on islands in the ocean.
A path that fishermen do not travel is one where, having gone out upon the surface of the water, they can return home again on the very same day.
A remote region of the ocean is called "distant" because it is impossible to reach.
This village and so forth is of two kinds: having a single boundary (*ekūpacāra*) and having various boundaries (*nānūpacāra*).

Among these, apart from an open space (*ajjhokāsa*), if a village and so forth belongs to a single family of owners—such as a particular king or other lords—whether they share a common purpose or have different purposes, it is "having a single boundary."
If it belongs to various families, it has multiple precincts. For this has been stated: “A village with a single precinct is one that belongs to a single family,” and so forth.
It is also said in the Commentary: “A village belonging to a single family is a village of a single king or a single chieftain”;
and “a village belonging to various families is a village of various kings or chieftains, such as Vesālī, Kusinārā, and the like.”
A monastery built by a single family has a single precinct; one built by various families has multiple precincts. As it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada*:

"The terminology of 'single family' and 'various families' regarding a monastery is stated according to the builders. However, in the case of an open space (*ajjhokāsa*), the division of precincts should be understood according to its interior.
And this has been stated in the Pāḷi: "An open space has a single precinct..."
"In a forest that is not near a village, an area extending seven *abbhantara*s all around constitutes a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*); beyond that, it is various precincts (*nānūpacāra*).
Here, one *abbhantara* is twenty-eight *ratana*s. As it is said in the Commentary: "One *abbhantara* is twenty-eight *hattha*s.
Thus, he spoke in order to show the fifteen locations, which have been described in brief according to their specific characteristics and divisions.
“In places such as villages, [in groups] of three or five”—this is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood from the commentary on the Pāḷi.
Regarding the phrase “one should be separated from the three robes”: it means by means of the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), or the inner robe (antaravāsaka).
Because of the statement, “having deposited the robe within the village,” in this context “the three robes” refers to any one of the three robes.
It should be stated thus: "for one night" (*ekarattaṃ*) is the accusative case used in connection with the action of being separated [from one's robes] to express duration.
By the word *api*, it is shown that this applies even for two nights and so forth.
"Except by the Saṅgha’s authorization" means that a sick monk who is unable to carry his three robes about may [remain apart from them] with the permission of the Saṅgha.
Having paid homage, sat down on his haunches, and extended his hands in reverential salutation, he said: "Venerable sir, I am ill; I am unable to depart taking my three robes with me.
Therefore, venerable sir, I request from the Saṅgha the authorization for non-separation from my three robes.

When he has thus requested it three times, the Saṅgha grants him the authorization for non-separation by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (ñattidutiyakamma). He understands this authorization for non-separation as having been granted.
This has been stated. Likewise, for a sick bhikkhu who has received such authorization, there is no fault— whether that illness remains unsubsided or has subsided—
nor when he returns to the place where his robe was deposited, provided that any other disease which has arisen remains unsubsided,
by virtue of that very authorization.
603. "Bhikkhunī" refers to a monk who has not received formal authorization. "With that robe-cloth" means it is not permissible to live apart from it;
that is, it is not allowed to dwell without it. What is meant? "There is a village belonging to a single family that is enclosed by a wall;
having deposited the robe-cloth inside the village, one must dwell inside the village. If it is unenclosed, [one must dwell] at whichever house the robe-cloth [is kept]."
"Where the robe has been deposited, one must stay in that house, or not depart from hand's reach.
If there is a village belonging to various families that is enclosed, one must stay in the house where the robe was deposited,
or in the assembly hall, or at the foot of the door, or not depart from hand's reach"— according to the meaning stated in the Canon by such methods as these.
It is meant that it is not permissible to cause dawn to rise outside [the boundary].
In this reading, the word "enclosed" (*parikkhitto*) is said with reference to what is enclosed by a wall, a fence, or a moat.
Regarding the phrase "within arm’s reach" (*hatthapāsā*), here "arm’s reach" (*hatthapāsa*) is two and a half *ratanas*. As it has been said:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "That house must not be left on all sides beyond the reach of one's hand;
it means that the area measuring two and a half ratanas above [the ground] must not be left.
To the question, "What is the fault for one who stays apart? he says: "There is... [up to] at the rising of the dawn. For [if one stays] outside the permitted place without the robe—
The meaning is that for one who causes [the robe] to be put on before dawn, that robe must be relinquished, and there is also an offense of expiation (pācittiya) caused by that.
For this very reason, he will say later: "Having relinquished... by a wise person. 604.
"Even while bathing" means even while bathing at a distance from the reach of the hand of the robe; the genitive case is used in a sense of disregard.

606. One whose robe has been snatched away or stolen is "one with a snatched-away robe" (*acchinnacīvara*); a *bhikkhu* who is such is "one in the state of having a snatched-away robe" (*acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāna*), and [the rule applies] in that case.

607. Regarding the word "having put on" (*nivāsetvā*), the remainder of the sense is "the inner robe" (*antaravāsaka*). Regarding the word "having taken" (*gahetvā*), the remainder is "the other ones.
This is an instruction for what should be done when there is no crowd of people on the path near the place to which one must go. In other cases, it is otherwise.
Having put on [the inner robe] and having wrapped the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) over one shoulder, one must go.

It is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that if no fellow monks are available in the monastery, one may even go to the seating hall (āsanasāla) and perform the formal act of the Vinaya in the presence of a fellow monk. By the word "having relinquished" (nissajjitvā), it is meant:
"Venerable sir, this robe of mine has been spent away from the community overnight, except by the consent of the monks."
"Having said, 'It is an offense entailing relinquishment; I relinquish this to the Saṅgha,' one relinquishes it to the Saṅgha;
or, having said before three [monks], 'Venerable sirs, this robe of mine... I relinquish it to you, venerable ones'; or before two;
or having said before one, 'Friend, this... I relinquish this to you, venerable one'—this is what is meant by 'having spoken and relinquished.'"
“By one who is wise” means by one possessing knowledge who understands the various types of procedures, such as the relinquishing of the article subject to forfeiture.
(608) That robe which is subject to forfeiture.
(609) By the statement, “And for one who does not accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the relinquished [article],” [it is meant that] by a learned and competent monk, the offense...

Because it is stated, "It should be accepted; the forfeited robe-cloth should be given," a competent person—one who knows this procedure and is capable of performing it according to the rules—should accept the offense in the manner prescribed in the Khandhaka.
Then, taking the forfeited robe-cloth in hand, having had [the offender] sit down, if there is a Saṅgha, he should say: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me."
“Venerable sirs, this robe-cloth, which was subject to forfeiture by the monk so-and-so, has been relinquished to the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe-cloth back to the monk so-and-so.
If there are three [members of the Saṅgha], [the motion is]: “Let the venerable ones listen to me; this robe-cloth, which was subject to forfeiture by the monk so-and-so...”
"Venerable sirs, this robe has been relinquished by you; if it is appropriate for you, venerable sirs, may you give this robe to the monk named so-and-so.
If he is alone, it should be given by saying, "I give this robe to the Venerable One.
