It is stated that if one takes the relinquished robe with the pure perception that "it was given to me alone" and does not give it away, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, for one who, knowing it is his property, robs him by means of a pretext, there are offenses of *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, and *pārājika* according to the value of the goods.
As it is said in the Commentary: “But for one who, knowing it is his property, seizes it by means of a pretext, he should be dealt with after having the goods valued.
Regarding the term *pariyāputa*: “Monks, a robe that has been relinquished must not be given back.”
The meaning is that it is stated in the Pāḷi: "Whoever does not give [the robe] incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the phrase "there, both while young," the construction is: "while both of these were going along the road. By the word "there," he indicates the state of being independent;
by the words "and while young," he indicates the state of being dependent. "Ohīne" means having retreated. If that elder...
He said “a teacher” with the intention that he might become the one who provides formal dependence (*nissaya*). Regarding that youth:

“The robe” refers to the robe held in his hand. “It does not subside” means that because he has not relinquished the burden and continues to have the effort to go, there is no cessation of the formal dependence;
this is the intended meaning. For that very reason, he said “for a moment,” and so forth.
614. The phrase “before dawn has risen” is connected with “having relinquished.

Having recognized the distance of the young bhikkhu and the time of sunrise, and having observed that the robe remains in his hand so as not to become subject to forfeiture (*anissaggiya*), one should relinquish it before dawn;
this is the meaning. “Gives away” means he gives it to another. “Is lost” means it is stolen by thieves and the like.
Commentary on the Second Discussion of the Kathina. 616.

Regarding "out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*): according to the statement, "Out-of-season robe-cloth means that which arises during the eleven months when the *kathina* has not been spread, or which arises during the seven months when the *kathina* has been spread, or that which is given specifically even during the [proper] season," it refers to a monastery where the *kathina* has not been spread.
“Robe-month” refers to the month beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of the former Kattika and ending with the full moon of the latter Kattika;

this is what is called the robe-month. Furthermore, it includes whatever [robe-material] arises during the eleven months following that in a monastery where the *kathina* has been spread, as well as whatever arises outside of those five months—namely, during the seven months consisting of the four winter months and the [following] three months.

The meaning of "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*) is as follows: it refers to that which is given to the Saṅgha during the five months when the *kathina* has been spread, within the period thus delimited, with the words, "I give this out-of-season robe";
and that which is given to an individual with the words, "I give this to you. The word "arisen" (*uppanna*) is to be supplied [to the end of the sentence]:
"it may arise from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from a relative, or from a friend, or from a rag-heap, or from oneself..."

The meaning is: "a robe arisen from what belongs to oneself" refers to that which has been given to the Saṅgha, or to a group (gaṇa) according to such methods as "we give this to the group of Suttantikas;

we give this to the group of Abhidhammikas," or that which arises from one's own *vassaga* (the end of the rains retreat), or from kinsmen and so forth, or from a cemetery and other places for discarded rags (*paṃsukūla*), or from cloth made of thread, cotton, and other allowable materials belonging to oneself.
"Storing for up to a month" (*māsaparamaṃ nikkhipati*): "A month is the maximum limit for this storing," thus it is *māsaparamaṃ*.
"Storing" (*nikkhipana*) should be understood as an adverbial modifier of the action; what is meant is: "One should perform the storing for up to a month.
"If a monk so desires, he may accept [the medicine]; having accepted it, he should have it prepared quickly. But if there is no completion [of the preparation]..."
Because of the statement, “That monk must store that robe for at most one month until the deficiency is fulfilled,” the meaning is this:
having accepted a robe that has arisen in such a manner, if he is able [to have it made], he should have it made within ten days;
if he is not able, he may keep it for at most one month for the purpose of fulfilling the deficiency.
When should it be laid aside? To this he said: "As long as there is hope.

This means: as long as there is hope from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from relatives, or from friends, or from rag-robes, or from one's own wealth—as stated in the passage beginning with "from the Saṅgha"—thinking, "I shall have what is deficient in this robe completed by that," so long as such hope exists, [the robe must not be laid aside].

The meaning is that it must be set aside. It is not permissible to keep it beyond that; the meaning is that it is not permissible to set it aside for a period exceeding one month, as this constitutes a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense.
If this is so, then [in the case where] "when the original robe has arisen on that very day, a robe expected in exchange arises... it should be made up within ten days... and so forth.
Why does it say, "When the original robe has arisen on the twentieth day, if a robe expected as a replacement arises, it must be made up within ten days"?
It is said thus because it is improper to keep a robe expected as a replacement beyond ten days, and because the original robe is subject to the same rule.
As it is said in the Commentary: "From the day the original robe arose until the twentieth day..."
“Until then, the expected robe-cloth (*paccāsācīvara*) that has arisen becomes one’s own property (*attano gatika*) as a basic robe-cloth (*mūlacīvara*).
This concludes the commentary on the third section concerning the Kathina. 618–9.
“The nun who causes [it] to be washed” is the connection. “A nun (*bhikkhunī*) is one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*) in both Saṅghas.”

By way of speech, one who has received full ordination through the formal act (*kammavācā*) consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) before the community of bhikkhunīs, and through the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations before the community of bhikkhus, is called a "bhikkhunī. Regarding "used": it refers to that which has been used, dyed, or accepted as permissible by a bhikkhu himself;
even if one merely places it on one's head with the thought, "I shall make use of it."
The meaning is: "even by merely sleeping in it, [the robe] has become old. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Even if, after dyeing and making it fit for use, it has been worn or put on even once—whether one has walked along a path carrying it on the shoulder or on the head, even as a mere token of use, or has lain down with it as a pillow—even this is indeed an 'old robe' (*purāṇacīvara*)."
"Robe" (*vattha*) refers specifically to the *cīvara*, by way of applying the name of the cause to the effect.

Regarding "one who is not a relative" (*aññātikā*): according to the statement, "One who is not a relative is one who is not connected through the mother’s or father’s line up to the seventh generation of ancestors," [it means] within the interval from one’s own self, or her mother’s or father’s lineage, up to the seventh generation. In this context:
"By anyone unrelated by blood" means she is not a relative (*aññātikā*). As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"The grandfather himself is the 'grandfather-generation. All ancestors beyond that are included by the term 'grandfather' alone.
Thus, she is one who is unrelated as far back as the seventh generation. "Has beaten" means has caused to strike.
"From that washing and so forth. "An offense entailing relinquishment" (*nissaggiyāpatti*) means an offense of relinquishment;
the meaning is that it is a *pācittiya* offense distinguished by the name of the robe that is to be relinquished.
This is the demonstration of the offense to be incurred at the conclusion of the three applications. For a nun who has her [robe] washed and so forth under such a mandate:
Therefore, it should be understood that for a monk, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the count of all prior efforts. As it is said in the Commentary:
"As long as she washes it and puts it aside, for every such effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk.
"By the first" means: of the three things he causes to be done, that which he causes to be done first; by that—this is the meaning. It is explained [in the context of] "an unrelated woman..."

It is taught by such passages as: "If one who perceives [the robe] as not belonging to a relative has an old robe washed, dyed, or beaten, there is an offense of *nissaggiya-pācittiya* and two offenses of *dukkaṭa*.
By this method, for one who causes two things to be done, the first results in an offense of *nissaggiya-pācittiya* and the second in an offense of *dukkaṭa*; this is the meaning summarized here.
620. By the phrase “gives for the purpose of washing,” it is understood from the context that this refers to “a garment already worn.
621. Regarding the description of a *sāmaṇera*: in that description as well—namely, the description [beginning with] “*sāmaṇerā*”—the construction is:
“he gives a garment he himself has worn for the purpose of washing”; that is, for the sake of washing a robe (*cīvara*) he himself has worn, he gives it to a *sāmaṇera*.

The meaning is "he gives. The word *pi* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The phrase "having attained" (*upasampajja*) is a prior action, while the subsequent action "washes" (*dhovati*) is understood through its functional capacity.

622. "And of young bhikkhus" means of those bhikkhus who are junior to oneself. "Entrusted" (*niyyādite*) means given. "This is the method" (*esa nayo*) refers to the principle that "there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for one [offense], and for the remaining two, or for one [of them], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in all applications."
623. *Cīvare* means in regard to a robe that has already been used. 624.
By the phrase “only for the purpose of washing,” he states that there is no offense because the other two [conditions] were not fulfilled due to the fact that the instruction had not been given.
626. Regarding the term *ñātikā*: here, as in the case of “*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*” and so forth, the letter *ya* is elided by virtue of the requirements of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
The meaning is "to a bhikkhunī who is a relative. The word-division is: "To one who is a relative, [thinking] she is not a relative.
"Bed-covering" (paccattharaṇa) refers to a robe used as a bed-covering that is to be spread upon a bed or chair.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the bhikkhunīs": if she has received full ordination within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as well, there is the possibility of an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
It has been stated. As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: "But for one who has received full ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the bhikkhus, it is according to the original basis [of her status].

If one first receives full ordination in the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs and subsequently receives full ordination in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, she is not said to have been "fully ordained solely in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Thus, those women were the first to go forth while the Blessed One was still living.
The five hundred Sākiyan women are so called. As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: “The five hundred Sākiyan women who received full ordination in the presence of the bhikkhus.
Since the change of gender for a bhikkhu is permitted as part of that very same act of ordination, he too must certainly be included.

628. "Washes without being told" means: if, upon seeing that a robe has become soiled, one takes the robe from where it was placed—even without being told, "Wash this robe"—and performs the washing of the robe and so forth either by taking it oneself or by requesting it through the method of asking, without having been instructed;
and "if it is not yet used" means: as explained in the manner stated below, if it is not yet used.
"Robe-cloth. "Another" means any requisite such as sandals, a needle-case, a bowl-bag, a cloth-bag, a bed, a chair, and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the account of washing old robes.
629. The construction is: "taking any robe-cloth whatsoever, starting from the last one that is subject to assignment. Here, [regarding] "a woman who is not a relative..."

Because it is obtained through the force of the statements that will be spoken— namely, "from the hand of a bhikkhunī," "if she perceives her as unrelated when she is actually related," and "he takes from the hand of one who is ordained on only one side"—
it follows, according to the method previously stated, that [the offense applies] to cloth measuring one vidatthi in width,
which has been formally assigned, taken from the hand of a bhikkhunī who is unrelated and fully ordained in both Saṅghas.

The meaning is: "for one who accepts any kind of robe-cloth starting from that [point]. Although it is stated generally as "an offense" (*āpatti*), it is understood—both from the context and because it will be stated later as "a forfeiture offense" (*nissaggiyāpatti*)—to mean specifically "a forfeiture offense. Regarding the phrase "except for an exchange":
this is based on the statement, "An exchange is when the small is for the large, or the large is for the small."
Because it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that “even with so little as a piece of harītakī,” one may receive even a piece of harītakī as the minimum;
thus, it is said that the triple robe (ticīvara) which is received by exchange is called *pārivattaka*. Having excluded that:
*parivattana* means exchange (*parivatta*); that which has this [exchange] is *pārivattaka*, meaning a robe to be received through buying and selling.

630. "In the effort for the purpose of taking" means in the effort of extending the hand and so forth in order to take. "Pariyāpūta" is taught [in the Vinaya] as: "For the effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) when one receives. 631.
"In the hand of one not fully ordained" includes all those other than monks and nuns; that is, everyone who is not fully ordained. As it says in the Commentary:
"But if it has been sent into the hand of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a novice monk (sāmaṇera), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), a male lay follower (upāsaka), or a female lay follower (upāsikā)..."

“If she accepts [it], there is no offense. (632) Regarding the phrase “from one”: here it should be understood as “from the community of nuns. On any other occasion, it is indeed a *pācittiya*. As stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “But for one who has received full ordination in the presence of monks, it is indeed a *pācittiya*.
(633) The construction is: “If she accepts [the robe] after forming the intention, ‘I will give it in exchange,’ no fault exists.”

634. Regarding "another requisite": one may take only a requisite that is either not subject to formal assignment (*avikappiya*) or not suitable for assignment (*avikappanupaga*), such as a bag, a waistband, and so forth.
However, that which is suitable for assignment is not permitted. As stated in the Commentary:
"Even a cloth water-strainer of the size of a later robe, if it is suitable for assignment, is not permitted. This concerns the receiving of robes.

"Action" (*kiriyā*) and "non-action" (*akiriyā*)—namely, the failure to give in exchange—is called "action-and-non-action" (*kriyākriya*) because it is to be incurred through both action and non-action.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the acceptance of robes. 635.
The word-division is: "to one who is unrelated and has not invited. The phrase "a householder or a housewife" is to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “A householder or a housewife who is not an acquaintance.
They are “not an acquaintance” because, according to the method previously stated, they lack the status of being a related kinsman up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
They are “uninvited” in the manner described by such phrases as, “I invite you to whatever is in my house. A “householder” (gahapati) is anyone who dwells in a household.
"Or a householder," as stated in the Pāḷi. "A housewife (gahapatānī) means any woman who dwells in a household," as stated in the Pāḷi; the meaning is "or a wife.
"There is an offense of expiation (nissaggiyāpatti)" means:
"If she requests [an item] except on an appropriate occasion, there is an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the undertaking; with the acquisition [of the item], it becomes an offense of expiation."
"In all the preliminary actions mentioned in the text, it is stated that there is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense together with a *dukkaṭa*.
‘Except at the right time’—regarding this, the summary states: ‘In this case, this is the right time:
the monk’s robe has been stolen or his robe has been lost. Here, ‘one whose robe is stolen’ means a monk whose robe has been taken away."
"It has been taken away by kings, or thieves, or rogues, or by anyone whatsoever.
"A monk whose robe is lost" means that his robe has been burnt by fire, or swept away by water, or gnawed by rats or termites;
the meaning is: other than the specific time explicitly indicated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).

636. It is said that there are three *pācittiya* offenses: “If one asks for a robe from one who is unrelated, perceiving them as unrelated, or being in doubt, or perceiving them as related—except at the proper time—it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*,” thus the Blessed One spoke these three *pācittiya* rules.

The phrase “in one who is related, perceiving them as unrelated” is the word-division (*padaccheda*). “In that [case]” means in that person who is related. “Of one who is in doubt” means [doubting whether they are] related...

"For one who is doubtful, thinking, 'Is this now a relative or not?'—there is likewise a double *dukkaṭa* offense. This is the construction. "Likewise" draws in the phrase "as stated," meaning that it was taught:
"If one asks for a robe from a relative perceiving them as a non-relative, or if one is doubtful, except on an appropriate occasion, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. This is the sense.

637–8. The construction is: “There is no offense for one who requests [it] at the proper time. Here, the phrase “a robe from one who is not a relative and has not invited [one to ask for it]” must be supplied and connected;

the meaning is that there is no offense for one who requests a robe from a non-relative who has not invited [one to ask] during either of the two specified times. In the phrase “or [from] a relative who has invited [one],” the word “one’s own” (*attano*) is also to be supplied.
It should be connected with the word “at the proper time. The meaning is that there is no offense for one who requests a robe even at an improper time when it has been invited by one's own relatives.
Regarding the phrase “for the sake of another,” the word “one’s own” is to be supplied as the remainder;

the construction is: there is no offense for one who requests [a robe] from one's own relatives or from those who have been invited on behalf of another. [This applies] depending upon another monk, [when requesting from] one's own relatives or those invited for another.

It is said that there is no offense for one who requests a robe [from those who have been invited]. He shows the other alternative with the words, "or from his relatives" (*tassa ñātake*) or "when they have been invited" (*pavārite*).
The word "his" (*tassa*) refers to the person previously mentioned as "another" (*aññassa*); it should be construed with the phrase "there is no offense for one who requests.
The word "or" (*vā*) refers back to the preceding alternative. Regarding the person with respect to whom one requests the robe, his relatives...
It is stated that there is no offense for one who asks for a robe specifically with reference to [a monk] who has already been invited or dismissed.
Regarding the phrase "or with his own wealth," which is mentioned as a factor for non-offense, the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the expression "insane, etc. includes those such as the insane and so forth.
This refers to the desire to receive [something] by means of an improper transaction after having given a permissible object—such as thread or cotton—that belongs to oneself.
The meaning is that there is no offense for one who asks.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding requesting from an unrelated person. 639.
Regarding the phrase "one who is not invited and is unrelated": here, the words "a householder or a housewife" are understood by implication.
“*Tatuttariṃ*”: from that which is beyond the limit of the inner and outer robes (*santaruttara-parama*), it should be understood as “beyond”;

because it is stated, “That bhikkhu may accept a robe beyond that limit of the inner and outer robes,” the meaning is that it is in excess of merely accepting the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) and upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) when one’s robes have been stolen.

Because of the expression “if he should accept beyond that,” the word “of one who accepts” (*sādiyantassa*) ought to be used; yet, although it ought to be stated thus, [the text says] “of one who requests” (*viññāpentassa*).
Why was it said? Because this training rule was laid down after the Buddha had rebuked the group-of-six monks,
saying, “How can you, foolish men, not knowing moderation, request so much robe-cloth?”—
in the case of monks whose robes had been stolen, regarding the matter of requesting robe-cloth from the group-of-six monks— and because of that, [the word] “should be accepted” is used here.
The meaning is "it must be requested"; for this very reason, it is stated in this word-commentary:

"If he should accept more than that" means "he requests more than that," and because of such statements as "if he requests a robe from one who is unknown to him, perceiving him as unknown, and it is more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). If this is so, [then] even in the training rule itself...

Regarding the phrases “it should be accepted” (*sāditabba*) and “he might accept” (*sādiyeyya*), why are they not stated as “it should be requested” (*viññāpetabba*) and “he might request” (*viññāpeyya*) in both cases?

It is because it was not stated that one must accept in this same way even when the robe has been lost, provided that one consents while the gift is being offered after it has been brought forward, even though no formal request was made.
Furthermore, this is said for the purpose of prohibiting an excessive request, even by one who speaks [on behalf of another].
“If a householder or housewife who is not related should invite him to accept many robes,

that bhikkhu may accept from them no more than an inner and an outer robe”— this was stated with the primary focus on the restriction regarding what may be accepted. Therefore, even for one whose robe has been stolen,
whether he himself requests it, or another requests it on his behalf, or even if no one requests it;
One should observe that the meaning intended in this training rule is stated with the understanding that even by one who consents when something is being given,
one must not exceed the limit of "an inner and an outer garment. To make this known,
it should be understood as the intention of the Teacher that, instead of saying "of one who consents," it is said "of one who requests."

640. Now, in order to show the restriction regarding both the act of making known and the act of consenting, he says "yassā" and so forth, to demonstrate the decision stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"If three have been lost, two may be consented to. If two have been lost, one may be consented to. If one has been lost, nothing may be consented to.
[Regarding the phrase: "For whom even all three have been lost, two..."

Having connected [the phrases] as "either all three are lost, or one is lost," the construction should be made accordingly: "By that person two robes may be accepted; by that person one robe may be accepted; by that person nothing at all may be accepted.
For one whose three robes are all lost and much is being given, only two robes may be accepted. If two robes are lost, one may be accepted.
The meaning is: if one [robe] is lost, it should not be accepted; what remains may be taken later when obtained through lawful and equitable means and by way of requisites.
As it says in the Commentary: “He will seek the remainder from a similar source.
However, for a bhikkhunī, if all five are lost, two may be accepted; if four are lost, one may be accepted; if three are lost...
"Nothing whatsoever should be accepted," so it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"It should be understood that there is no offense for one who brings back a remnant"—this is the construction [of the sentence]. The same should be applied to what follows as well.
For one who, having joined with a robe, takes back an extra cloth and goes away having taken much [of it], thinking, "I will give it [to you]";
The meaning is "there is no offense. There is also no offense for one who accepts what is given with the words, "Take even more yourself.
The construction is "not given because of [the robe] being lost"; the meaning is that there is no offense even when accepting many robes on the grounds of [the robe] not having been lost.
In the same way, this also demonstrates: "nor is it given because of [the robe] being destroyed. Regarding "when the robe has not been lost":
Because this training rule was formulated on the basis of the offense involving requesting more than that [allowance] of robe-cloth,
the phrase "for the sake of another" is not included in the section on non-offenses.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding "more than that."

643. “Because of the desire for what is beautiful”: the construction is that one would fall into the offense of *vikappana* (misappropriation) regarding a robe out of a longing for something beautiful and of great value. This refers to an additional specification beyond the standard allowance, as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
“Without having been previously invited [by the donor], [one asks]: ‘Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you need?
Is it long, or wide, or thick, or fine?’”—this constitutes a specific form of misappropriation.
The meaning is "he makes. Regarding the phrase "the acquisition of that becomes an offense involving relinquishment":

when one has not been invited [to choose], by means of the acquisition of a robe-cloth produced through an excessive arrangement made [by him], there are offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), relinquishment (nissaggiya), and expiation (pācittiya).

644. "He requests something of great value...": when a lay follower wishes to give a robe worth twenty [units of currency], he says, "Enough for me with this; give one worth ten or one of little value."
645. “Regarding ‘perceiving as non-relatives those who are relatives’—this is the word-division.
This concludes the commentary on the first introductory narrative. 646.
In the first training rule, harassment was received by one lay follower; here it is by two. This is the only difference.
"The remainder is exactly like the first training rule," he said, [concluding] "the second... explanation.
A training rule characterized by the word *upakkhaṭa* is "prepared" (*upakkhaṭa*). It is both "second" and "prepared," thus "the second-prepared" (*dutiyopakkhaṭa*); in that "second-prepared" one.
"Of it" (*assa*) means of the second-prepared one.
Commentary on the Second Discussion on What Is Set Aside (Dutiyopakkhaṭakathāvaṇṇanā). 647.

"From the king" (raññā vā) means from the monarch. One who has what is to be enjoyed (bhogga) from the king—that is, what is to be consumed—is called "one who enjoys the king's property" (rājabhogga).
The connection is that [the goods] are brought from anywhere by donors, being obtained as food and wages from the king. And not...
Regarding the phrase "it is allowable," one must supply here the words "because it would constitute an offense of expiation involving forfeiture" (*nissaggiyapācittiya*).
Here, what remains to be done will be explained by the verse beginning with "three times.
648. Whatever silver or other items have been acquired by means of cloth-money (*cīvaracetāpanna*) must not be accepted in any manner whatsoever.
To demonstrate this, he said, “silver, or,” and so forth. It is called *rajata* because it shines (*rājati*) due to its white nature; it is silver.
That which has arisen as form (*jātaṃ rūpaṃ*) and possesses the sense-sphere of color (*vaṇṇāyatana*) is *jātarūpa*, i.e., gold.
“Anything whatsoever” (*kiñci*) means even a small amount. The construction is: it is not permitted to accept anything being given, whether for one’s own sake or for the sake of another.

649. Since the offense for accepting [money] for oneself will be explained under the training rule regarding the acceptance of money (*rūpiya-gahaṇa-sikkhāpada*), he says "for the sake of another," etc., in order to show the offense incurred when accepting it for the sake of someone else.

Therein, "for the sake of another" means for the sake of another individual, a group, the Saṅgha, a shrine (*cetiya*), or for the purpose of new construction (*navakamma*). "Specified" (*niddiṭṭha*)...

The construction is as follows: it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that for a monk who accepts silver, gold, or anything else that is an object of forfeiture or an offense of wrong-doing (*nissaggiya-dukkata*), having been told by someone, "Take this," there is an offense of wrong-doing for him.
To clarify the meaning already stated in its own form, he says "having brought" (*netvā*), and so forth. "Having brought" (*netvā*) means having fetched. It is unallowable (*akappiya*).
They barter for "silver or gold," which refers precisely to the unallowable articles (akappiyabhaṇḍa) as previously described. "In this way" means by the manner that will be explained below.

Regarding the phrase "and it is not allowable," the word "and" (ca) here implies that it *is* allowable in certain cases, as permitted by the authorized tradition. As stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
"But if, when it has been refused with the words, 'This is not allowable for monks to accept,' [one says], 'It is for carpenters...'"

Or, having said, "It will be in the hands of the laborers; you need only know what has been well done or ill done," he gives it into their hands and departs—this is permissible. Or again, [if he says], "It will be in the hands of my men, or it will be in my own hands;
you need only send whoever is to be given whatever is to be given for that purpose"—[this is also permissible].
"He speaks; even this is permissible. 652.

Regarding the phrase "of the monastery": since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) as "of the new construction work" (*navakamma*), it was not mentioned here for the sake of the metrical composition of the verse. 654.
Regarding the phrase "silver or gold [given] to the Saṅgha": here it means "it was given with the instruction, 'Use these as the four requisites.'"
The rest is as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “But if someone brings even a great deal of gold and silver and says, ‘I give this to the Saṅgha;
please use it for the four requisites,’ and if the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the acceptance and in the use.
Thus, regarding what has been brought in that manner, if any bhikkhu in that Saṅgha [thinks], “This is not...”
If he rejects [the proposal], saying, "It is not allowable," then an offense occurs for the one who says, "This person is creating an obstacle to the Saṅgha’s gain.
As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "He who accuses him becomes the one who has committed an offense;

yet by that single individual, many have been rendered free from offense. Here, regarding the phrase "he himself becomes the one who has committed an offense," this refers to one who has committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"This is what is stated" is what is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. In this verse, some write "of the bhikkhu" (*bhikkhuno*) instead of writing "of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghassa*);
that is not correct. Since it is stated in the currently shown commentary text that "the Saṅgha accepts," the reading "of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghassa*) is the correct one.
"Of a *taḷāka*" means of a reservoir (*vāpī*). Because it is the source for the growth of crops, a *taḷāka* is a field;
therefore, the construction is that taking from it or using it is not permitted. In the phrase "and of a *taḷāka*," the word "and" (*ca*) includes arable land and building sites.
In the phrase "is not permitted," the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that it is also permitted [in certain cases].
656. To the question "What is that?", he says "four," and so forth. "All" means all [land], such as ponds, lotus-pools, fields, and so on. 658–9.

"In a portion not previously demarcated" means in a plot of land where the yield was not previously determined by saying, "Of the work done on this plot of land, such-and-such a portion is to be given.
"New crop" (navasassa) means that which has never been cultivated before. "Give such-and-such a portion" means...
“Give such a portion of a *kahāpaṇa*. “He causes to arise” means he produces. The construction is:
“having spoken an improper word, ‘Plow! Sow! Here, the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “and ‘Sow!
includes another improper utterance that is not explicitly mentioned here but is spoken at the time of the conjunction of those [actions]. And “that which has been produced”...
And here, the word *ca* (and) includes the *kahāpaṇa*. "All" means all [the coins] produced in that manner, as well as those produced by such improper speech;
thus, it refers to everything.
Without using such expressions as "plow" and so forth, one who [designates] the land, saying, "this much portion of this much land," [is at fault].

And he establishes [it]; this should be connected with what will be said later, namely, "for him alone this is improper. The word *ca* (and) refers to another person who will be mentioned later as "but whoever" (*yo pana*).
661–2. The construction is: "In order to know the measure of the ground by oneself, [he says] 'thus' (*tu*). "On such an extent of ground by us..."

When the farmers say, “The crop has been harvested; take such-and-such a portion,” the meaning is that, not believing their words, he himself desires to know the measure of the field. The word *tu* (but/however) highlights this very distinction. This should be connected with what will be said later:
“But for one who measures it, this is indeed unallowable. And [he may measure] with a rope or with a staff.
Regarding this, they say that it is not even permissible to measure with one’s foot. The same should be applied to the verbal forms such as “he guards” (*rakkhati*) and so forth.
“He guards while standing in the threshing floor” means that, while standing in the place where grain is processed, he protects it by not allowing others to take it.
How is it permissible to guard, and how is it not permissible to guard? As for that rice, [one should say]: “Do not take this much, or do not take that much.”
If he protects it by such means as saying, "This may not be taken," or "Take this away, make a heap here," and so forth, that is improper (*akappiya*).
If he protects it thinking, "While I am standing here, it is protected," or if, seeing them taking it, he says, "What are you doing?"—it is permissible.
This is the section on the training rule regarding the acceptance of money (*rūpiya-paṭiggahaṇa-sikkhāpada*).
It should be understood according to the method stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that "one must live having closed [the door] and guarding it," for it is so said.

Furthermore, it is stated in another *Gaṇṭhipada*: "When someone comes to take [something] away by force, they say: 'It is proper to ask back, "Sir, shall I report this matter to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?
Regarding the phrase "he causes to be brought out": here too, if by some means...

They say it is permissible; they say it is allowed. Regarding the statement, "This is not allowable for him alone," the two *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries state that because there is no other newly produced [grain] available—since it must be obtained from one who performs the measuring of the field and so forth—it is permissible for others.
663. The construction is: "If those to whom it was said, 'Bring this with so many grains of rice,' bring it... Herein, "This is not allowable for him alone" refers to the following.
This was stated because grain has already been discussed. As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “That [gift] is not allowable for him. Why?

Because grain has already been discussed. (664) “With gold” means with a *kahāpaṇa* coin. “That is not allowable” was stated because coins have already been discussed. As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “It is not allowable for anyone. Why? Because coins have already been discussed.”

665. *Pesakārakadāsaṃ* means either a slave known as a weaver (*pesakāra*)—a weaver being one who works with thread—or giving by means of the names of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), such as saying, "I give an attendant," or "I give a servant" (*veyyāvaccakara*), and so forth. 666.
Milk, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and fresh butter are the five products of the cow (*pañcagorasa*).
667. Regarding "among goats and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the buffalo is included.
"Even though forbidden" means even though it has been prohibited. "Having given the price" means having given the price for allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*).
However, chickens and the like should be released into the forest itself with the thought, "May they live happily. As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"It is permissible to release chickens and pigs into the forest with the thought, 'May they live happily. This also applies when pigs, peacocks, and so forth are obtained. Regarding them...
It should be bestowed only upon a suitable object. 671.

What is the connection with the verse beginning with “Three times”? By the method of inclusion set forth in the verse beginning with “By a king or by one belonging to the royal family,” [it refers to] a robe [obtained] from anyone among kings, royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and so forth, or by oneself, using cloth or the means for purchasing cloth.

Having had [the money] fetched and said, "Clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe," and having given that robe-fund—known as the robe-purchase money—the messenger sent by him approaches the monk and says, "Venerable sir, this robe-purchase money has been brought for the sake of the venerable one;
may the venerable one accept the robe-purchase money. If he should say this:

When the monk has said, "Friends, we do not accept cloth-money; however, we accept robe-cloth at the proper time and when it is allowable," if that person then asks, "But does the Venerable One have anyone to act as his agent?
the monk who needs robe-cloth should point out an attendant, saying, "Friends, this one is an agent for the monks. [He should point him out] to an attendant...
Or, if a lay follower has been pointed out [to him], and that person, having brought it himself, says:
"If this monk has need for a robe, purchase a robe with this and clothe him," and then approaches that monk and says:
"Venerable sir, the person whom the venerable one designated as a service-provider has been engaged by me; let the venerable one approach him at the proper time."
“If he should say, ‘I will clothe him with a robe,’ what should that monk who needs a robe do?”—this is what was said by the Blessed One, and this is the connection of this verse.
It is stated that the urging [of the donor] should be done three times: “Monks, a monk who needs a robe, having approached the attendant... [and so forth].
"He should be urged and reminded up to two or three times: 'Friend, I have need of a robe. Thus it is said that the urging should be performed three times.
"He stated the occasion for six times" means: "If, while being urged and reminded up to two or three times, he should produce that robe, that is good;
if he should not produce it, [he may go] four times, five times, or at most six times."

Since it is stated that "one should stand silently [waiting] for [the robe] to be designated," if after approaching three times and making the request, "Friend, I have need of a robe," the matter is not settled, he must go again;
however, without saying anything at all, he must observe the rule of "breaking the standing" (ṭhānabhañjanaka), according to the statement:
"He must not sit on a seat, he must not accept food, and he must not preach the Dhamma."
Without performing any such acts as sitting down and so forth, when asked, "For what reason have you come?", he said only this much: "Know it, friend.
This implies that standing for six times at most was taught by the Blessed One, the Supreme Wheel-Turner of the True Dhamma.

“If he merely urges” means: if he makes a mere urging without establishing a formal ground (*ṭhāna*), the construction is “he spoke six times. The term “urging” (*codanā*) is understood by implication; it is stated that after urging six times, one must not even stand [to speak further].

As for one who, without making six urgings, merely establishes a formal ground, [the question arises] how many grounds must be established by him? Thus he says: “The standing is characterized by the qualities beginning with urging”;
the word “must be established” (*kātabbā*) is the ellipsis to be supplied, and this should be construed with the word “spoke” (*abravī*). [He spoke] four times after having urged four times.
Because of the statement, "One should stand; having admonished five times, one should stand twice;

having admonished six times, one should not stand," and because it is established that standing for twelve times—being double the number of admonitions—is based on the rule that "it may be admonished up to six times," there is a case of twelve times for one who merely stands without performing any admonition at all.

The meaning is that one must indeed remain in the manner already described. By not showing what is to be done beyond that and indicating that one should desist with just this much, he shows that there is an offense according to the stated method:

"If, striving further than that, one brings about that robe, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort, and it is to be relinquished (nissaggiya) upon acquisition. Thus he demonstrates the nature of the offense.
672. “Obtained without having been asked for”: this is an indicative mark (*upalakkhaṇa*), since it is understood as including the phrase “obtained without having stayed [there].
End of the commentary on the King’s Training Rule (*rājasikkhāpada*).
The first chapter, the Chapter on Robes (*cīvaravagga*).
673. By the phrase “even by one,” it is implied: how much more so by two or many?

“Mixed” means mixed even with a single *kosiya* fiber brought by the wind. “Spread” (*santhatam*): according to the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), “spread” means that which has been made by spreading [fibers] and is not woven;
and [it refers to] having spread *kosiya* fibers one over another on a level patch of ground.

The meaning is that a *santhata* (rug or mat) should be made for the purpose of sitting, lying down, and so forth, by sprinkling it with sour gruel (*kañjika*) and other liquids as described in the commentary;
having sprinkled it with sour gruel and spread out silk threads (*kosiyaṃsu*), one should increase the thickness as desired.
Regarding "silk threads" (*kosiyaṃsunā*): it is called *kosiyaṃ* because it belongs to the silk-worm (*kosiyakimi*); it refers to the thread.

It is the fringe of that thread; thus, the meaning is "with a fringe of silk. Regarding the phrase "of one who has it made," because it is an indicative term (*upalakkhaṇa*), "of one who is making it" should also be understood.
For this has been stated: "‘Should have it made’ means he either makes it or has it made by mixing even a single fringe of silk with it.
Therefore he said: "Of one who is making it or having it made for the sake of another."

675. *Bhūmattharaṇaṃ* (ground-covering) is a rug that should be spread upon prepared ground for the purpose of protecting the skin. *Bhisi* refers to two types: the mattress for a bed (*mañcabhisi*) and the mattress for a bench (*pīṭhabhisi*). *Bibbohanaṃ* is a pillow. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning silk.
676. Regarding "black and white wool": "Black" refers to two kinds: black by birth (*jāti-kāḷaka*) or black by dyeing (*rajanakāḷaka*).
From the very words "or," this refers to black wool from sheep. "Pure" means unmixed with wool of other colors.
As it is said in the Commentary: "‘Pure black’ means pure blacks; the meaning is ‘blacks unmixed with others.
"Should make" means both for one who makes it himself and for one who causes it to be made. As it is said: "‘Should cause to be made’..."
"Does he do it himself or cause it to be done? Regarding "there is an offense," it is stated in the Pāḷi: "For the preliminary effort there is a *dukkaṭa*;
with the acquisition [of the object], it is a *nissaggiya*. This refers both to the *dukkaṭa* of the prior effort and to the *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of pure black [wool].
677. “Having taken all of it, whether white, or wool, or much”—this is the construction. “Or even brown”—here too it should be construed in exactly the same way.
Here, “all of it” refers to either the entire spread (*santhatassa*) that is to be taken, or all the hair.
Regarding the word “making” (*karontassa*), the term “spread” (*santhatam*) is understood by virtue of the governing context. This word “new” (*navam*) is connected with “making.”
It is obtained by means of the power of the words; the meaning is "for one making a new rug.
This is connected with the phrase "there is no offense. By the word "or," even in another manner, it includes the absence of offense for one who makes it.
For example: "When a monk is having a new rug made, two parts [of the wool] must be of pure black..."
The manner in which it was permitted according to the *mātikā* should be understood as follows: "Three parts of sheep’s wool are to be taken, white for the fourth, and [the remainder] of goat’s hair.

Here, by the qualification "much" applied to the phrase "white or even brown," it is indicated that not even a single fiber of black sheep’s wool may be included beyond the two aforementioned proportions; [this applies] to black wool alone.
Because it was already stated in the first training rule that wool from sheep is not to be accepted;
furthermore, by the phrase "or all of them," it is shown—just as in the preceding training rule—that these [materials], such as white and so forth, are not to be accepted in their entirety.
By the term "there is no offense," it is indicated through contrast (vyatireka) that an offense does occur for one who acts in a manner other than this.

For instance? This was indeed said by the Blessed One: "If a monk, without taking two parts of pure black wool, should have a new rug made with a third part of white wool and a fourth part of *gocariya* wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
To whatever extent of wool he intends to make a new rug, he should weigh those wools into four parts.

It is said that it is permissible to take two measures (*tula*) of black wool, or less; and having made one measure of white wool and one measure of either brown or black wool—whether by making both deficient or making both excessive—and excluding the black wool, it is permissible to make [the robe] or have it made by taking either one or both of those two.
Thus, by showing that there is no offense [in this case],...
It should be understood that the entire meaning of the training rules (sikkhāpada) is included.
By the phrase "in succession" (anukkamenā), it is indicated that one should not take only this [rule], but rather both the preceding training rules mentioned immediately before it.
The construction is: "even those obtained after having relinquished [the robe]. By the word "even" (api), [it refers to] "that which was made by another."
"Having obtained it, he uses it: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This refers to the *dukkaṭa* mentioned there;

and likewise, according to the method stated in the first *nissaggiya* training rule—"If he uses a robe that ought to be relinquished without having relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing"—here too, it is stated:
"If he uses a blanket (*santhata*) that ought to be relinquished without having relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
It should be understood that these two—the [offense of] *dukkaṭa* and that which was abbreviated by the compilers of the Dhamma by way of a formula (*peyyāla*)—are included here.
As for the third, however, the phrase "action-non-action" refers to this third training rule;

it is so called because it is committed by performing the act in an unauthorized manner, namely by taking more than the permitted amount of black wool, rather than following the method stated in the passage beginning with, "two portions of pure black wool."
“Kiriyākiriya” means: as it is said in the Commentary, “Because of performing [an action] both by taking up [the object] and not taking up [the object], it is called ‘kiriyākiriya’.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the two parts. 680.
“Within six years”: from the day previously spread out, counting upwards for six years.

"Within the rains" means during the rainy season. "There is an offense of expiation (nissaggiyāpatti)" means that within six years, the rug made is subject to forfeiture, and for the maker, there is an offense of confession (pācittiya); this is the meaning.
"Setting aside the consent of the monks" refers to a sick person who is unable to set out on a journey after taking up a rug, [thinking]: "Venerable sir, I..."
“I am ill and unable to depart taking my rug with me; therefore, venerable sirs, I request from the Saṅgha permission regarding the rug.

Having sat in the midst of the Saṅgha and extended his joined palms, when he has requested this three times, the meaning is that he understands the permission granted by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of one motion and a second announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*), which allows him to make a rug even within a distance of six *yojanas*.
682. Regarding the phrase "one who makes it for six years": here, the words "when they are complete" are to be supplied;
thus, the meaning is "one who makes the *santhata* (spread) when the six years have been completed. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"When the six years are completed, then he makes the *santhata*. "Even beyond that" means even after the six years. "In the canopy" (*vitāne*)...
"For one making a canopy" means for one making a covering resembling a wall. "And even when made after relinquishing" is to be construed as follows:
there is no offense even when, having given away an old rug to another, one makes a covered area within it for another rug during the six years.
This section on non-offenses is found neither in the Canon nor in the Commentaries.
It is seen; therefore, it is understood that this [tradition] has been handed down through a succession of teachers and was shown by a teacher.
However, regarding the common determination, he will say: "For this [case] as well, there is no distinction from the immediately preceding one.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the six years.

683. "Without taking" means that when a monk is making a new sitting mat (*nisīdana-santhata*), for the purpose of disfiguring it, he does not take from the edge of the old mat a *sugata-vidatthi*—which is prescribed in the text to be taken for the sake of disfigurement—by cutting it from the rounded end of the old mat. Thus it is.
How is it known that this has been stated? It is known from what will be said later: “By way of non-appropriation for that Sugata’s span.

Regarding the term *santhatam* (spread rug), the words “old” (*purāṇe*) are to be supplied here, and in the phrase “made to be used” (*kāretuṃ katañca*), the words “a new spread rug” (*navaṃ nisīdanaṃ santhataṃ*) are to be supplied.
When an old spread rug is not available, one should not, without taking up the Sugata-span from the vicinity, [use] a new one.
There is no offense for one who makes a new sitting mat (*nisīdana-santhata*). The construction is as follows:
there is no offense for having a new sitting mat made for the sake of another, nor for using a new sitting mat that has been obtained when it was made by someone else.
Regarding the phrase "to have it made for the sake of another," this should be understood here as showing that there is no offense [for the maker] precisely because of the *pācittiya* rule itself.

Therefore, because it is stated [in the Vinaya]: “If one makes it or causes it to be made for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” and because it is not seen in the Aṭṭhakathā or its commentaries, that [objection] should not be raised.
Alternatively, having referred to the immediately preceding training rule which states: “There is no offense if one makes it for six years...
or if one makes it or causes it to be made for the sake of another,” [the offense of] wrong-doing [is established].
And it is understood that this was written with reference to the state of non-offense [incurred] due to the pacittiya rule having been prescribed.

Regarding the phrase "and having used what has been made," the word "by another" (*aññena*) should be supplied; by this, the reading itself is shown: "Having obtained what has been made by another, he uses it;

there is no offense. 684. The construction is as follows: because of not taking up a span of the Sugata’s measure, and because of the making of this rug, the Teacher stated this training rule as both "to be done" (*kiriya*) and "not to be done" (*akiriya*).

685. But surely it was stated in the commentary on this training rule that "because of its being both an action and a non-action, its origins and so forth are similar to those of the two-part training rule";
why, then, are they said here to be "the same as those of the matchmaking rule"?
It is replied: in the two-part training rule, it was stated that "its origins and so forth are indeed the same as those of the silk-cotton rule."

It should be understood that these [points] were stated in the commentary because, in the case of the Kosiya training rule, the arising and other factors were said to be identical to those of the Sañcaritta [offense], and because the specific distinction known as "action" (kiriya) and "non-action" (akiriya) was shown separately after remembering the root itself;
thus, it was stated in this way with reference only to the remaining portion of the decision (*vinicchaya*). Apart from this specific distinction, regarding the remaining decision in both cases...
In order to show that there is no distinction in the common determination regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), he said, "of the one immediately following," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning sitting mats (*nisīdana-santhata*).
686–7. Regarding "while traveling": this refers to traveling beyond the distance of three *yojana*s. Regarding "vehicles": this refers to carts and the like.
"Wool" means sheep's wool. "Of the owner" refers to the owner of the vehicle and so forth. "Not knowing" is a term of address used in a sense of disregard.

Furthermore, when a monk traveling on a highway obtains sheep's wool, because it has been permitted that "it may be carried by one's own hand for a maximum distance of three *yojanas*," he may carry it by his own hand within the three *yojanas*;
however, upon exceeding three *yojanas*, [he must place it] in the vehicles and so forth belonging to others who are the owners.
The meaning is: if one should set it aside, thinking, "These [people] will take it," while they are unaware. Regarding the phrase "in them":

the construction is that when those vehicles and so forth—in which the wool was placed—have traveled more than three *yojanas*, even without the monk’s active involvement, an offense occurs for that monk once they have exceeded three *yojanas*.
For that monk, as soon as he causes the first foot to exceed the three *yojanas*...

There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If he steps beyond the second foot, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya); this being said, the meaning is that there are offenses of wrong-doing and confession.
"This is the method" means that where sheep’s wool has been placed, even without the monk's active involvement, an offense occurs when those vehicles or other conveyances travel beyond three yojanas;
this is how the matter is to be understood. 688. "While coming" means while situated within the three-yojana limit. "Having mounted" refers to the circumstances under which there is no offense.
To show one case, it was said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “For if one gives while standing on the ground, or calls out as one goes ahead, this is the same method.

Because of the statement in the section on non-offenses, “if he causes another to carry it,” [the author] said, “if she carries it, it is permissible,” in order to show that it is allowable when someone else carries it after being dispatched by oneself. For that very reason, he said: “But if he causes that other person to carry it...”
"...it contradicts the word. 690.
"In the ear-holes" means in the openings of one's own ears. 691.
In the section on non-offenses, because it is stated as "finished goods," therein even that which is merely tied with a thread [is included].

Regarding the phrase "having tied it with a string," he says this refers specifically to a bundle of goods. "Having made a braid" means having made a braid similar to one made of kudrūsa grass, sisu wood, or palāla straw.

The offense is clearly explained in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), which states: "If one carries it away after making a braid, this is called a 'storing-opening' (*nidhānamukha*); there is indeed an offense."
692. Regarding "a customs house" (*suṅkaghāta*): here, "that place" is the ellipsis; the construction is "if that place is a customs house. The meaning is:
if the location within a three-league radius were to be a customs-house site. "Having arrived" means having reached that place. The construction is:
"he goes either being harassed by thieves and the like, or he goes being occupied with something else. "An offense" (*āpatti*).
In this context, it is understood that "an offense falls upon him. Here, by the term "offense," he refers to the offense [incurred] through this training rule (sikkhāpada).
Because of this state of being unintentional, the offense occurs for both of them. However, the Pārājika offense of taking what is not given does not apply to them because it requires intentionality.
Therefore, it was said in the Commentary: "For whatever offense exists there, that is no offense here; whereas whatever [offense] exists here..."

“There is an offense; however, in that case, there is no offense. For one who carries away [an object] with the intention to steal, there is one among the offenses of *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, or *dukkaṭa*, depending on the value of the goods.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: “In the case of taking what is not given, however, there is an offense in the evasion of customs duties. 693.
Regarding the term “three *yojanas*,” this is the accusative case used to denote the direct connection (*accantasaṃyoga*) with the action of carrying. “Of one who carries... [is the construction].
The phrase "the body hairs" is obtained from the context as an illustration of this action.
The statement "no offense is declared" is to be connected with everything that will be said hereafter. The construction is: "for one who brings back those very same [hairs].
Regarding the term "three leagues," it is understood as "that very three leagues. Having gone three leagues oneself, and then taking those same hairs again—
"Of one who returns" means:
having gone for the purpose of residing, that is, having gone with the desire to dwell within three *yojanas* or within the boundary (*sīmā*) at a monastery;
"of one who carries it beyond that" means: not receiving a recitation (*uddesa*) and so forth at that monastery, one carries it beyond that to another [monastery].
The meaning is: "even when carrying it for three leagues out of a desire to dwell in a residence.

By this same method, it is also stated that there is no fault even for one who, with a pure mind, carries it from one place to another, and from that place to yet another, traveling in succession even for a hundred leagues; as it is said in the Commentary: "In this way..."
“There is no offense for one carrying [it] even a hundred yojanas. Regarding the phrase “or even having obtained what was stolen”:
this refers to one who obtains and carries away what has been carried off by thieves and then abandoned.

Here, in all instances within the section on non-offenses beginning with “having gone for the purpose of staying,” the meaning is understood to be that there is no offense for one carrying it even more than three yojanas, starting from the point where it was first obtained.
"Having received what has been forfeited" means having received what was given after it had been relinquished and the formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma) had been performed.

"By another" means by someone other than the one who took it away. "A manufactured article" refers to an article made from sheep’s wool—as stated in the Commentary—whether it be a blanket, a cloak, a rug, or anything else, even if it is merely bound together with thread; specifically, an article made from the wool of sheep.
"This is the origin" means this [offense] originates from sheep’s wool. Whether through ignorance of the rule (paṇṇatti) or even knowing it...
He says it is "unintentional" because this offense can occur even for an Arahant who travels beyond three *yojanas* with woolen cloth and other requisites,
even if he is unaware that the wool has become wet.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of wool.
697. The account regarding the washing of sheep’s wool is already explained.
[End of] the commentary on the account regarding the washing of sheep’s wool. 698.
Regarding the phrase “or should take,” the word “whoever” (*yo*) is to be supplied as the remainder. By the expression “should take or cause to be taken,” [the offense applies] therein to oneself...

Because it will be stated later as "for one's own benefit" (*panatthāya*) and because of the expression "having relinquished" (*nissajjitvā*), it is implied that one should either acquire [the object] for oneself or cause it to be acquired.
By the word "or" (*vā*), the phrase "or should consent to what is placed near" (*upanikkhittaṃ vā sādiyeyya*) is included;
the meaning is: if one consents to what has been placed near with the words, "Let this be for the noble one."
Elsewhere, "silver" (rajata) is said to mean lead; however, here it refers to coins used in commerce, such as the *kahāpaṇa* and so forth.
For this has been stated in the Pāḷi: "What is called 'silver' is the *kahāpaṇa*, the copper *māsaka*, the wooden *māsaka*, and the lac *māsaka*—those which enter into commerce.
Here, the specific nature of the *kahāpaṇa* and other such coins is explained in the Aṭṭhakathā:
“In this context, ‘kahāpaṇa’ refers to one made of gold, or one made of silver, or an ordinary [coin].
A ‘copper māsaka’ is a coin made from copper or similar metals. A ‘wooden māsaka’ is a coin made by carving out a shape from heartwood, or from a bamboo splinter, or even from a palm leaf.
A ‘gum māsaka’ is a coin made by forming a shape from lac or resin.”
But by this phrase, “those which come into common usage,” whatever comes into common usage in whichever country,
at whichever time— even including those made of bone, made of hide, made of tree-fruits or seeds,
whether they have a produced form or an unproduced form— all of them are included.
It should be understood according to the method already stated.
And here, "ordinary" refers to the current ordinary kahāpaṇa coin. "Made from the seeds of tree fruits" means made from the seeds of fruits of trees such as the *tintiṇika* and others.
"Jātarūpa" is gold; as it is said in the Pāḷi: "Jātarūpa is called that which has the color of a [burnished] sword. "Having relinquished" means...
Here, the word “by him” (tena) is understood; it connects with the word “by the bhikkhu” (bhikkhunā), meaning “by that bhikkhu who has accepted [it].

Having relinquished—meaning having accepted silver or gold, whether acquired by himself or caused to be acquired by another, or accepted by way of consenting to its being deposited—that bhikkhu, having approached the Saṅgha, [should] with one shoulder bared...

Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, having sat down on his haunches, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation—having thus approached into the midst of the Saṅgha, bowed at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, sat down on his haunches, and extended his hands in reverential salutation—he should say:
"Venerable sirs, I accepted silver; this is my article to be relinquished."
"I relinquish this," thus it is said after having relinquished.
"The offense is to be confessed" means that the *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense committed by oneself must be confessed right there in the midst of the Saṅgha while sitting in that very manner.
When the offense has been thus confessed, by one who is experienced, competent, and authorized by the consent of the Saṅgha...
It should be accepted by a bhikkhu. For this has been said: "An offense should be accepted by a competent and capable bhikkhu.
699. *Rajata* means silver. *Jātarūpa* means gold. By these two terms, everything—both wrought and unwrought—is included. Regarding "the coin of both":
it is meant that there is both a gold coin (*jātarūpa-māsaka*) and a silver coin (*rajata-māsaka*). Here...
Regarding the phrase "silver māsaka," the commentary on the words (*padabhājana*) takes the fivefold māsaka—such as the *kahāpaṇa* and so forth—as intended by the term "silver.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Every silver māsaka of the aforementioned types.
Since the "gold māsaka" is mentioned separately here, one must exclude the gold *kahāpaṇa* from the term *kahāpaṇa* and refer only to the other two [types].
“Bringing about forfeiture (*nissaggiyāvaha*)”: this is said with reference to one who performs the acts of acquiring, causing to acquire, or consenting to acquire for their own sake.
Furthermore, by the method that will be explained starting with the words “In that case,” it also brings about an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Although pearls and so forth are not mentioned in this analysis of the training rule (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*), they are [discussed] in the ninth chapter of the *Pācittiya-khaṇḍa*.

In the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) on the second Jewel Training Rule (*ratanasikkhāpada*), ten kinds of jewels are mentioned: "A jewel is pearl, gem, beryl, conch, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat's-eye.
In this training rule, having designated these ten jewels as objects subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiyavatthu*), [the text] excludes silver and gold and refers to the remaining ones.
In order to show that the status of these eight gems as objects of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭavatthu*) has been determined in this commentary, he says:
"pearls... pe ... musāragalva. Here, *veḷuriya* (cat's-eye) is not mentioned because of the requirements of the verse composition;

it is included by the very mention of the seven gems specified in the single compound. Pearls and the others are exactly as their forms have been shown. This is also [confirmed] by way of suttas such as the *Brahmajāla*.
“Unallowable” (*akappiya*) refers to the seven types of grain and so forth; he says “grains,” etc., to show the offense incurred in accepting them. 702.

Regarding the training rule on gems (*ratana-sikkhāpada*), he says “beans, peas, etc. to show that there is no offense for one who accepts allowable things (*kappiya-vatthu*) designated as gems. 703–4.
Thus, regarding the offense classifications that may arise from accepting an object established in these three ways, depending on the diversity of intention:
To demonstrate this, he said "In that regard" (*tattha*), and so forth. "In that regard" means among those three bases for forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and the rest. "Of the Saṅgha, etc.

means of the Saṅgha, the group (*gaṇa*), the individual (*puggala*), the shrine (*cetiyā*), and so on. "That" refers to the article subject to forfeiture. The analysis of the compound "sabbatthāya" is "for the sake of all" (*sabbesaṃ atthāya*).
Even for one who takes an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for their own sake or for the sake of the Saṅgha and others, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.

The meaning is "it happens. Here, by means of the particle *ca* used as a collective for what has not been explicitly stated, the inclusion of the specific determination mentioned in the Commentary—namely, that "if one accepts even all [of these] for the purpose of depositing them under the pretext of being a storekeeper, it is a *pācittiya* offense according to what is set forth in the subsequent Jewel Precept (*Ratana-sikkhāpada*)"—is made.
705. Regarding the phrase "kahāpaṇas, etc.," the word "etc. includes gold and so forth. The term "a thousand" is an illustrative example; thus, it is meant to include even a thousand.
706. Regarding the phrase “in bags, etc.,” the word “etc. includes vessels that are loosely filled.
By the qualifying term “loosely bound,” the commentary indicates through contrast that “if it is tightly bound, or if it is densely filled, there is only one offense. 707.
To show the act of consenting to what has been placed nearby, he says “this,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “even though desiring to take it,” [the thought] “let it be” is implied here.
The rest is as follows. "Only that which is to be prohibited" means that it must be rejected either by body or by speech, saying, "This is not allowable";
the meaning is that when this is so, there is indeed no offense. This very point has been stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"Even without rejecting it through body or speech, if one, being pure in mind, does not consent [to it], thinking, 'This is not allowable for us,' there is indeed no offense."
708. "That object" (*taṃ vatthuṃ*) refers to the object thus refused. "If he goes away after setting it aside" means:
if he goes away after having set it aside with the thought, "Whether you take it or not, it has already been given. The construction is: "It should be guarded in such a way that it does not perish.
[This is explained] by the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) beginning with, "Another person comes there and asks," and so forth.
In the manner described, when the Tathāgata asked the attendant, "What is this?", [the monk] revealed its nature and said, "I shall guard it, Bhante;

please show me a secure place. Without saying, "Take this and come," or "Go up to this seven-storied palace and put it here," [the Buddha] pointed out a well-guarded place, saying, "This is a secure place."
It means that after showing [the object] and placing a bolt there, it must be guarded.

709. To show the improper mode of speech that should not be used when a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable) goes away after taking charge of a protected place, he said: “‘Bring this, bring that,’ etc.
Here, the word “speech” (*vacana*) is understood following “what is unallowable” (*akappiya*). Thus is the unallowable speech.
If [the goods] have been brought and placed in a well-guarded location, what should be done? When tradeable requisites such as bowls and robes have been brought, one should say:
"We have need of this; it has such-and-such a price, but there is no one here to act as a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable).
When that person replies, "I am a kappiyakāraka; show it to me," if it is agreeable, one should open the door.

Without saying, "Take this," he should point out, "It was placed here," and accept it when the other person gives it after taking its value and measure. If the other person takes more than that, he should say, "We do not take your goods; you may go," and having turned it out and bolted the door, once a kappiyakāraka (an attendant for allowable goods) has been found, he should say, "We have need of such a thing as this. [He should then give it to him. If he takes more than that, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. If he does not give it to the kappiyakāraka, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. If he gives it to one who is not a kappiyakāraka, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. If he gives it to one who is a kappiyakāraka but who is not authorized, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. Having said, "There is a source," one should proceed according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: that when [the goods] have been purchased and given by him, they may be accepted.

710. "Except for one who takes gold" means, excluding a person who has received gold and other such precious metals (rūpiya), confessed their offense, and relinquished them—such a person being of the nature that will be explained in the immediately following training rule. "Exchanged after relinquishment" means...
Having relinquished it here and confessed the offense, one should— according to the method stated in the word-commentary beginning with “If a monastery attendant or a lay follower comes there”—
address the attendant who has arrived there as “Friend, know this,” and when that person asks,
“What should be brought by him? one should not say, “Bring this or that,” but rather the allowable item (kappiya) should be pointed out.

Because it is stated, "ghee, or oil, or honey, or molasses," the meaning is that when a suitable object has been indicated for the monks, whatever is brought back after exchanging it for the forfeited article is a "suitable commodity" (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*). 711.
"Even one's own share" means that when such a suitable commodity has been brought and is being distributed to the Saṅgha, [one's own portion].
"Even one's own allotted portion according to the rainy-season retreat. "A receiving bhikkhunī" is connected to the phrase:
"It is not permitted for a bhikkhu who has received gold or silver, incurred an offense, relinquished it, and confessed that offense.

"From another" means from someone other than oneself—from among any of the following: a human who has gone forth, a non-human, an animal, a female, or a male. "Obtained" means obtained by them or by oneself.
"Obtained from a portion received" means that the object was obtained by virtue of having been given from a portion [of property] already acquired.
"Any requisite whatsoever" refers to any one of the four requisites among those taken after exchanging that object;
it includes even water drawn by digging the earth, or fire kindled with wood, or [a lamp] with oil.

It should be understood that by this [phrase] alone, the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—namely, "even a burning lamp, or a tree, or a house, or natural shade, or a palm leaf, or anything else worthy of use and enjoyment"—is included. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Even if it has been taken away from there by monkeys and the like and placed in the forest, or [taken] from their hands..."
"Even if it has been discarded, it is not permissible even if it is rags (paṃsukūla) belonging to an animal," and so forth; and:
"Furthermore, in no way whatsoever is it permissible for one who accepts money to enjoy the requisites derived from that [money].
Here, "a bhikkhu" refers to a bhikkhu who accepts money.
713. "In a monastery" (*ajjhārāme*) means in a monastery delimited by the characteristics that will be explained below.

"That silver," with the words "having seen it fallen" as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Or in a dwelling" (*ajjhāvasathe*) means within the interior of a residence, according to the characteristics that will be explained.
"Of one who deposits" means when it is said, "He to whom it belongs shall take it," [the depositing occurs] at that place regarding that object, involving both counting and marking.
For one who places [it] down after having examined it.

714. It is stated that there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: "If one receives money while perceiving it as money, or while being doubtful, or while perceiving it as not money, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*," thus the Blessed One has declared a *pācittiya*. Regarding the term "offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*) here:
“Two *dukkaṭas*” is understood by implication. 715.
It is called “action-and-non-action” because it is an action due to being committed through the act of taking [money], and non-action because of the failure to perform the prohibition.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the acceptance of money.

"An object for a *nissaggiya* offense" (*nissaggiyassāpi vatthu*) means any one of the four objects, such as silver and so forth, specified in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*) as "the objects of a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*. "Or an object for a *dukkaṭa*" means any one of the *dukkaṭa* objects previously shown, such as pearls and so forth.
Here, in both cases, the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) expresses the relationship between cause and fruit.
"And a permissible object" (*kappiyassa ca vatthuṃ*): this refers to any one of the permissible objects such as mung beans, black gram, and so forth, as previously shown.

Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of a part-whole relationship. Although there is no actual difference between the part and the whole, it is expressed through a figurative distinction (*bhedūpacāra*), just as in the phrase "the body of the stone statue" (*silāputtakassa sarīraṃ*).
Thus, it is said "a permissible object," or "by means of a permissible object."

Because it will be explained [later]. Now, in this context, it should be understood that an offense occurs because an article subject to a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) or a suitable article has been exchanged for an article subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
The construction is: "For one who exchanges [something] with an article subject to forfeiture, there is an offense.
