If one exchanges an article subject to a *dukkaṭa* or a suitable article for an article subject to forfeiture, there is an offense.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: here, in both cases, because the object to be forfeited (*nissaggiya-vatthu*) has been exchanged, there is an offense (*āpatti*).
Thus, from the context, it is understood that in all three instances, by the general term "offense," specifically a forfeiture-requiring offense (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) is meant. 718.
Or, one exchanges the object of a wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the object of a wrong-doing; thus, it is a wrong-doing—this is the construction.
“*Vatthuṃ vā kappiyassā*” (or an article for something allowable) follows the same method already stated; that is to say, it refers to an allowable article (*kappiyavatthu*).
Since this allowable article has been exchanged for an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭavatthu*), it should be understood that an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) occurs. 719.

“*Vatthunā kappiyassā*” (by means of an article for something allowable) also follows the same method already stated. He says “*tathā*” (likewise) because when an exchange is made even by means of an allowable article, an offense of wrong-doing occurs on account of the article involving wrong-doing.
720. By the word “thus” (*tathā*), the term “of the object” (*vatthuno*) is drawn forward. By the word “of what is to be relinquished” (*nissaggiyassa*), he refers to the *pācittiya* offense.
“Formerly” means first; it is said to refer to the training rule concerning the acceptance of gold and silver (*rūpiya*) mentioned previously.
“By this” refers to the training rule concerning trade in gold and silver (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra*). The connection is: “the exchange was prohibited.”

721. Regarding "one who perceives it as silver" (*rūpiya-saññissa*): this refers to one who perceives as "silver" any of those things designated as "silver" mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), namely: "What is called silver? A coin the color of a teacher, a copper māsaka, a wooden māsaka, a lacquer māsaka—whatever enters into common trade.
Regarding "non-silver" (*arūpiye*): this refers to coarse leaves and so forth. By that non-silver. "For one who causes [it] to be bartered... (*cetāpentassa*).

The word-division is "arūpiyaṃ" (non-monetary). Because it is stated, "If one perceives what is non-monetary as monetary and causes it to be exchanged for money, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture," there is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the exchange of money, but rather the possibility of an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
therefore, money must not be accepted. This applies to one who perceives what is non-monetary as money, or to one who is in doubt, when causing that which is non-monetary to be exchanged.
The construction is: "thereby there are two *dukkaṭas*.
Regarding the phrase "one who perceives what is not *arūpiya* as *arūpiya*," the ellipsis here is "while exchanging what is not *arūpiya*.

In the expression "by five," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment; the ellipsis is "together with fellow-practitioners" (*sahadhammikehi*), meaning "together with five fellow-practitioners."
The meaning is: "of one who speaks" means of one who engages in worldly discourse; the meaning is, of one who performs buying and selling. The meaning is:
there is no offense for one who exchanges non-material things with the five fellow practitioners consisting of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, sāmaṇeras, sāmaṇerīs, and sikkhamānās.
(723) Because it arises through commercial transaction, it is an action-originated offense.
Commentary on the Discussion of Trading in Coin (Rūpiyasaṃvohārakathāvaṇṇanā). 724.
"Suitable" (kappiya) refers to the allowable articles mentioned in the word-commentary as: "robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
even down to a lump of face-powder, a tooth-stick, or a thread for a fringe."
As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: "It is manifold by way of allowable articles such as robes and so forth.
"By means of what is allowable" means by that very same allowable object. From the statement, "He would engage in buying and selling:
'Give this for that; bring this for that; exchange this for that; barter this for that,'" [it follows] "of one who exchanges."
The phrase "engaging in buying and selling" is a synonym for this.
In that context, "buying" (kaya) refers to receiving something from another's hand by exchanging it for a permissible article (kappiyavatthu);
"selling" (vikkaya) refers to giving something from one's own hand after exchanging it for a permissible article. As it is said in the Commentary: "Give this for that," and so forth.
"For by this method, one who takes another's allowable goods incurs buying, and one who gives what is allowable for oneself incurs selling.
Because it was stated, "excepting those of the same Dhamma," the phrase "exchanging" here implies "with others.
In this context, "others" refers to householders—both men and women—and renunciants outside the Dispensation. Therefore...
This buying and selling must not be done even with one's mother or father. As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"For this buying and selling is not permitted with anyone other than the five who share the same Dhamma, including all householders and renunciants, and even with one's mother or father."

725. Regarding the phrase "of an improper object": in this training rule, it refers to an object subject to forfeiture or an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) that is other than the permissible objects such as robes mentioned here. "By that very same" means by that very same improper object.

The words "and of a permissible [object]" are to be supplied; thus the construction is: "the exchange of a permissible object by means of that very same improper object. For it is in this way that the supplied words [are required].
The exchange of an allowable object for an unallowable object by means of an unallowable thing might be included under buying and selling;
however, that is not tenable, because such an act is already included specifically under the trading of money (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra*), and because here it is restricted to the definition:
"buying and selling is the exchange of an allowable object for an allowable object by means of an allowable thing. This is demonstrated [in the commentary], for "the exchange of unallowable goods..."
The meaning is that it is explained in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) thus: "It does not fall under the category of buying and selling.

726. Therefore, because buying and selling even of allowable goods is not permitted except with fellow-followers of the Dhamma (sahadhammika), and because the exchange of an unallowable thing for an allowable thing, as well as the exchange of an allowable thing for an unallowable thing, [are included] within the bartering of money (rūpiya-saṃvohāra);...
Because it is included [in the category of allowable things], it does not fall under the inclusion of buying and selling; therefore.
729. By the words "this or that," he refers specifically to allowable items such as cooked rice and so forth.
730–1. Having shown an illustration of the characteristics of the object by means of the verse beginning with "Having taken," [he explains] the classification of the offense.
To demonstrate this, he said, “Vighāsāda,” and so forth. *Challi* means the bark of a tree. *Valli* means a creeper. *Kaṭṭha* means firewood. *Dāru* means timber for building houses and the like.
It may also be stated by way of inversion: “Or else, a creeper or bark, or timber or even firewood.
*Vatthūnaṃ* refers to the materials such as bark and the rest that were caused to be brought after having been spoken of in that manner.
The construction is: "There are offenses for selling [the robe]" (kāyavikkaye āpattiyo honti); what is meant is that there are offenses of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiyapācittiya).
732. The word-division is "iti evā"; the meaning is: "in the manner stated," without applying the suffix denoting the prior time (pubbakāla) as in the case of the form "pivitvā" and so forth. 733.

Regarding the construction "in the smearing of the ground" (bhūmiyā limpane), this refers to the act of plastering the floor of the dwelling (senāsana) with decorative borders and the application of colors such as black and so on.
*Lepane*: in the washing of cloths, such as robes and other articles. *Ettha*: in those aforementioned instances.
Because the mention of these [specific cases] is illustrative (*upalakkhaṇa*), it includes other similar situations.
734. *Ayaṃ*: this refers to the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) incurred by means of cleaning the ground and so forth.
735. Regarding the phrase "except for the owner of the goods," here, by way of contrast (*byatirekavasena*), it is understood as "another person acting as a steward" (*kappiyakāra*).
736. The construction is: "there is no offense for one who speaks. The rest here is self-evident.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of buying and selling.

The second chapter, the Kosiya-vagga. 737. "Permissible bowls are made of clay or iron; there are two by way of birth"—this is the construction. "Sizes" refers to dimensions. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Three sizes of the bowl means three dimensions of the bowl. Therefore he says: "Large, medium, and small. 738.
"Of two *nāḷi*s of rice" means two *nāḷi*s of old *sāli* rice that has been well-husked and is free of broken grains.
It should be taken as described in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Of old, undamaged rice grains that have been well-husked and purified.

As for the *bhatta* (rice porridge), one must take only well-cooked rice that has had the water drained off, from which the broken grains have been removed, which is not soggy, not clumped together, very clear, resembling a heap of jasmine buds, and free of lumps.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Free of broken grains, not soggy, and not clumped together..."
“Extremely clear, like a cluster of kunda blossoms, and with the rice-water strained. “By the Magadhan *nāḷi*”: by the *nāḷi* used in the kingdom of Magadha;
that *nāḷi* holds eight *pasata*s of sesame seeds. Regarding this, the ancients said:
“Two hundred and fifty *khāris* make a *vāha*; a *khārī* is two and one-eighth *doṇa*s;”
“Two *nāḷis* make one *doṇa*; one *nāḷi* is eight *pasatas*.
One *pasata* of sesame seeds is a *lakkha* [in weight];

this is stated according to measure. Regarding this, it is said in the Andhaka-ṭīkā: “The Magadha *nāḷi* consists of twelve and a half *palas*. In its commentary (*vaṇṇanā*), it is stated: “Twelve and a half *palas* are to be taken by means of *māsas*. However, some have said:
Four *pasat*s make a *muṭṭhi*; four times that is a *pala*.
Four *kuḍuva*s make a *pasata*, and four *nāḷi*s likewise.
Four of those make a *pattha*, and four *pattha*s are called an *aḷhaka*.
"Four *aḷhakas* are proclaimed as one *doṇa*.
However, the teachers favor the former position, stating that "eight *pasatas* constitute a Māgadha *nāḷī*.
Furthermore, regarding the food, it is divided into four portions; when that meal is divided into four parts, one portion consists of a hand-held thick pea soup.

The meaning is as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "One should add bean soup made from all its constituent ingredients—neither too thick nor too thin, but such that it can be taken up by the hand—as a measure equal to one-fourth of that rice.
And the condiment (*byañjana*) is likewise proportionate to it; that is, the condiments such as fish, meat, and so forth, are in accordance with every mouthful (*ālopa*) until the very last morsel.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “One should add condiments such as fish and meat in an amount corresponding to each mouthful, up to the point that the last mouthful can be taken.

And here, regarding the phrase “corresponding to each mouthful,” since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Brahmāyu Sutta* that “the measure of a condiment is one-fourth part of a mouthful of rice,” [the meaning is] a quantity equal to one-fourth of a mouthful.
The sauce should be understood as being proportionate to the morsel of food.

Here, however, after showing the measure of the soup alone—being one-fourth the amount of the rice—and having thereby demonstrated its characteristic, the measure of the other [the sauce] is also already shown; thus, the measure of the sauce is not specified separately in that manner.
As for the ghee, oil, curd-serum, sour gruel, and so forth, which are to be added to the rice:

They do not constitute a formal group. 739. "All that" refers to the entirety of the aforementioned food and so forth without exception. "He takes" means he takes it in the three ways that will be explained.
"Of that" refers to the large bowl. "Half" refers to the amount of the material for the requisites taken within that bowl.
The bowl was called "half-full" because of its association with that [other bowl]. The same principle applies here in the phrase "half of that":
it should be understood as half of that medium-sized bowl. 740.
In these three types of bowls, all the food such as boiled rice and so forth, which has been stated for the large bowl, is placed in whichever bowl [is being used].
If the diamond being piled upon the rim of the mouth touches its lower part, it is called "superior-middle";
if more than the diamond remains, it is called "superior-inferior";
if it remains inside the bowl without reaching the lower edge of the rim, it is called "superior-superior. In this way, the middle and inferior types are each threefold.
He says “of the superior,” etc., to show that all nine bowls exist. “Of that very one” means of the superior one alone. “The inferior and the middling” refers to the inferior-middling.
Here, both the middling and the inferior are divisions of the superior alone; this same method applies to the other two pairs as well.
By the word “thus,” it is shown that just as there are “the superior-of-the-superior, the superior-inferior, and the superior-middling,” [so too for the others].
It should be applied; in this way, he shows the application according to the order for the medium and inferior types as well: "the medium-superior, the medium-medium, and the medium-inferior;
the inferior-superior, the inferior-medium, and the inferior-inferior. (741) "Among them" refers to the nine bowls.
"Therefore" means because they have not yet attained the state of a bowl. "They do not go" refers to both the superior-superior and [the other categories].
The plural form *omakomakañca* is used by referring to two things together. These are to be used by way of being a vessel (*bhājanasaṅkhepena*).
As it says in the Commentary: "Therefore, these are to be used by way of being a vessel.

(742) Regarding the phrase "joined with the characteristics of a bowl" (*pattalakkhaṇasaṃyuttaṃ*), here "characteristics of a bowl" means being endowed with the dimensions as previously stated; [it refers to] "an iron bowl..."
The perfection of firing is described as follows: a clay bowl fired with five firings, or one fired with two firings. If it is purchased, there are five qualities:
that the price paid is given without leaving any remainder, that it is free from holes, and that it is devoid of cracks or fissures.
And on this point, there is this [verse]:
“Proportionate size, excellence of color, having been given as the original basis, being without holes, and being unblemished—these are the five characteristics of a bowl.

Regarding the phrase “either by formal determination (adhiṭṭhāya) or by assignment (vikappetvā),” the word “or” (vā) should be construed [with both]. “By formal determination” means when it has first been used.
When there is another bowl, having relinquished the former, if that bowl to be determined is within arm’s reach,
one should either make a vocal utterance according to the method to be explained— saying, “I determine this bowl”— or, without making such a vocal utterance,

simply by thinking thus and taking hold of it with the hand, one determines it by means of the body through its movement; but if it is far away, beyond arm’s reach, [one determines it] by the place where it was set down.
Having observed it, one should break the silence by saying, "I resolve upon this bowl.

According to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā, this means that one may do so alone, or—should mindfulness fail—one may resolve it in the presence of another person capable of allaying anxiety by reminding one.
It is said: "In resolving it in the presence of another, there is this advantage:"
“If doubt arises in him as to whether or not he has determined [the bowl], the other will remind him and cut off the doubt”—this is the meaning stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
“One is not permitted to determine two bowls,” it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. Regarding the word “having determined”:
here, one must consider whether the bowl to be determined is one or many, and whether it is present or absent.

Having observed that one [bowl] is stored nearby, it is said that one should assign it according to the following method: "I assign this bowl to you," or "I assign this bowl to the monk Tissa," and so forth.
Since the word "should use" (*paribhuñjeyya*) is used here, [the meaning is]: "Use what belongs to me, or dispose of it as you see fit."

Or [you] may do so. Since it is improper to consume [the bowl] when it has not been relinquished by him, the specific term “having assigned it” (*vikappetvā*) must be understood as qualifying its relinquishment (*paccuddhaṭa*).

“Should keep it” (*dhāreyya*): it should be used without having formally resolved upon it (*anadhiṭṭhahitvā*) and without having assigned it (*avikappetvā*). The construction is: “he lets that time for the bowl pass.
By the word “offense involving forfeiture” (*nissaggiya*), this [term] “bowl” (*patta*) is also appropriately connected. The word “bowl” (*patta*)— [End of fragment]
It possesses two genders according to the Magadhī language; therefore, it is stated thus.

(744) Because [the bowl] is not included within what is determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) or what is assigned (*vikappita*), he said "whatever bowl" and so forth, in order to show its status as something additional (*atireka*).
(745) *Sammukhe* means a bowl situated within a space of two and a half cubits (*hattha*). *Dūrasmiṃ* means beyond two and a half ratanas.
Regarding the "other part" (*parabhāga*), it refers even to a distance such as that described in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as "inside a chamber, or on an upper story, or in a neighboring monastery.
At the time of making a formal assignment (*vikappana*), whether near or far, the distinctions between the terms for proximity and distance should be applied in exactly this way.
However, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that "many things may be assigned. This is the method: "this bowl..."
The method begins with “I relinquish,” and so forth.

Having shown the verbal determination (*vācādhiṭṭhāna*) among the two types of determination—verbal and physical—the text says “attention” (*ābhoga*), etc., in order to show the physical determination (*kāyādhiṭṭhāna*).
“Attention” means the mental attention [thinking], “I determine this bowl. By the word “mentally” (*manasā*), it is not...
It is said by way of speech (*vacasā*). A bodily movement itself is "bodily movement" (*kāyavikāraka*); the meaning is a physical action such as shaking with the hand.
By this very [term], it shows that a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) based on the body must not be made regarding something unreachable by the hand, such as a distant object.
747–8. The word-division is: “he abandons the resolution. “By giving” means by giving to another. “By causing division” means by causing a split.
"By death" means by the passing away of the owner of the bowl. "By renunciation" means by returning to the state of a householder without having formally renounced the training.

"By relinquishment" means by the act of giving it back. "By renunciation of the training" means by the formal abandonment of the precepts. "By transformation" means by the change of sexual characteristics.
"By taking on trust" means by receiving it through confidence, as well as by taking it after having seized it [by force].

"By the measure of a grain of *kaṅgu* rice" means by the measure of a grain of *kaṅgu*, which is the smallest among the seven types of grain. "By the mouth" means by the opening at the bottom of the rim of the bowl, which has the dimension of two finger-breadths.
"Or by a pin" means by a pin made of iron. 750–1. "A bowl made of gems" means one made of gems. "Arising from beryl" means made of emerald (*marakata*) gems.
"Arising from crystal" means made of crystal stone. "Made of glass" means made of glass-clay. "Made of bronze" means made of bronze metal. "Made of tin" means...
"Made of black metal" means made of iron. "Made of white metal" means made of silver; they also speak of it by way of a synonym (*vipallāsa*). "Made of brass" means made of silver. 752.
"Pot-sherd" means a fragment of a pot. "Lead-shard" means a skull from a corpse.
"Gourd" means a *alābu* (bottle-gourd). "Of this" refers to the eleven kinds of bowls. "Suitable" means suitable in the sense of not being forbidden. "Therein" means in those eleven kinds.
The construction is: "However, a bowl made of copper or iron is permitted. This means that while a plain leaf plate (*patta*) alone is not permitted, bowls made of copper or iron are permitted.
Regarding the phrase "trays and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes items such as *vaṭṭaka* bowls; a *vaṭṭaka* is shaped like a half-moon.
A specific vessel made of iron or other materials. "Of a person" means of a bhikkhu. "Householders and the Saṅgha" are *gihisaṅghā*;
that which belongs to them is *gihisaṅghika*. 754.
"Any bowl whatsoever" means any bowl among the seven types of bowls. "Having made it free of water" means having removed the water from it.
"Having done so. "Should restore" means: he should preserve it by way of depositing it in a place suitable for depositing, or by way of placing it in a bag and tying it up.
"To warm" means: to warm it in the sun or over a fire. "In that very heat" means: in that same [sun or fire]. "It must not be stored away" means: it must not be burned.
"Only the removal of the head is not permitted" means: it must not be stored away; this is understood through the exclusion of what is superfluous.
756. *Miḍḍhante*: at the end of the *miḍḍhi* (a circular grass mat). *Paribhaṇḍante*: at the front or at the edge of a large *miḍḍhi*. Some say:
“*Vitthiṇṇe* (in a wide space) means even in a space as small as two palms. The construction is: “it is permissible to place [the bowl]”;

the meaning is that it is permissible to place it even without a support such as a ring (*valaya*) and so forth. [The text continues: “At the front of the *miḍḍhi*, and on the rough ground of the *miḍḍhi*, etc.”
And they say, "It is permissible to place [the bowl] on top of a bowl-stand. 757. Regarding "a wooden support": it is a wooden support similar to a mortar.
"It is also permissible to place two bowls" means that by way of placing another bowl on top of the first bowl, it is permissible to place two bowls. By the word "also" (api),...

This shows that in one case there is simply nothing to be said. "This is the same method" means this method [applies] to the statement: "It is permissible to set down two bowls as well. Regarding "on a staff-base or a ground-base": here, a "staff-base" (*daṇḍādhāra*) is one made with many staffs.
A "ground-base" (*bhūmiādhāraka*) is a smooth base made on the ground in the shape of a circular basin or trench. Some say, "A ground-base is made of ivory, cane, creepers, and so forth."
758–9. *Taṭṭikāya*: on a mat made of palm leaves and so forth. *Potthake*: on a rug made of *makaci* fiber or tree bark. *Kaṭasārake*:
on a rug woven from palm leaves and so forth. *Paribhaṇḍakatāya*: on ground that has been smeared with cow dung.
By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that this applies even to ground that has been plastered with lime, polished with a stone, and made smooth.
He shows that [the ground] does not exist. "In sands" means in fine, subtle sands unmixed with clods, stones, gravel, potsherds, and so forth; thus it is said, "in such [sands]," and so on.

Even though dust may be present or absent, because it is stated separately that "[it] should not be placed on rough ground," the phrase "dusty" refers to soft ground covered with dust. "On rough ground" means on hard ground.

760. *Laggantuṃ* means to hang down. Placing [the bowl] by inserting it through the mouth of the bowl with either the tip of a staff or the tip of a peg is also called "hanging. *Chatthaṅkamañcapīṭhesū* means on a sunshade, in one's lap, and on a bed or chair. 761. *Aṭanīsū* means on the crossbars.
*Bandhitvā* means having tied it with a bag, a shoulder-strap, or whatever else is available. *Olambetumpi* means also to hang down. The word division is: “Ṭhapetuṃ upari. 762.
*Mañcapīṭhaṭṭake* means on the top of the crossbar of a bed or chair, so that the bowls placed there do not fall.
When a sturdy enclosure has been made, there are what are called "bed-and-chair stands"; the meaning is that it is permissible to place [the bowl] on such a bed-and-chair stand.
"Even when full of food" means even when full of cooked rice (*bhatta*). By the word "even" (*api*), the inclusion of [a bowl] filled with rice-gruel (*yāgu*) or oil is also intended.
The determination regarding an empty bowl is exactly as previously stated. *Pūraṇa* means "full"; the fullness of cooked rice is "bhattapūro."
The commentary on the section on the three recitations is finished.
763. *Kavāṭa* means the door-panel of a gate. For in such passages as, "In the lodging-place, the door-panel, the window-panel, and so forth," the panel of the door is indeed called a *kavāṭa*.
*Na paṇāmeyya* means he should not bend it, nor move it; and...
"Should cover" is the meaning. "Pattahattha" means one who has a bowl in his hand;

this is a *bahubbīhi* compound with a different case-ending (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*) for the external referent, as in the case of "Vajirapāṇi" (Thunderbolt-in-hand) and similar terms. The word division is "paṇāmeyya assā" (he should dismiss him).
"Na nīhareyya pattena calakāni" refers to things such as the seeds of madhuka fruit that have been discarded after drinking the juice.
One should not carry [anything] out with the bowl in order to discard it outside. "Bones" refers to bones such as those of jackfruit, coconut, or kola.
"Used water" refers to used water such as that from rinsing the mouth. The construction is "of one carrying it out with the bowl";
this means pouring it into the bowl in order to discard it outside. Otherwise, even the water used for washing the bowl would [be included].
It should not be taken out with that same bowl. 765.

"Accepts water for rinsing the mouth" means it is a receptacle; it is like a spittoon. "Removed from the mouth" refers to anything, such as a piece of meat or the like, that has been spat out from the mouth.
766. "Is lost" means it is lost either through renunciation of the monastic life, through formal relinquishment of the training, or through death.
Alternatively, *yo* is a word in the nominative singular; by transforming it into the genitive masculine as *yassa*, the construction is:
"For whichever bhikkhu the bowl is lost—whether by breaking, being cut off, or being stolen by thieves—for him there is no offense.
[767] *Paṭhamassa* means "of the first," because it is included at the beginning of the Bowl Chapter (*pattavagga*). *Pattassa* means "of the bowl" (i.e., of the training rule concerning the bowl).
"By the first" refers to the connection with "by the first *kathina*," because it is included as the first in the Chapter on Robes (*cīvaravagga*).
"Great Seer" (*mahesi*) means one who seeks or searches for the great qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).

All the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth of the first *patta* (bowl) are here [to be understood] as being similar to—meaning identical with—the first *kathina*, except for those points where a specific determination has not been stated.
The construction is: "thought by the Great Sage, approved, and permitted.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse regarding the first bowl. 768.
One whose [bowl] has five binding-rings less is "one with a bowl lacking five bindings"; regarding that [bowl], and also one without bindings...
The bowl with one, two, three, or four repairs is included under the category of "less than five repairs. As it is said in the Pāḷi:
"A bowl with less than five repairs means a bowl that has no repair, or one repair, or two repairs, or three repairs, or four repairs.

Even when a repair has not yet been made, if it possesses the lines with the characteristics to be described hereafter and is thus fit for repair, it is still considered "one with less than five repairs."
It should be accepted. Here, "without a binding" (*abandhana*) refers to that which has no binding at all. For this very reason, the Commentary says:
"Because even for a bowl without a binding, the five types of binding do not apply, owing to their absolute non-existence.
A space for a binding that is joined with a seam less than two finger-breadths in measure should also be understood as "without a binding. As it was said:
In the Pāḷi it says: “A bowl that is ‘without a binding-mark’ (abandhanokāsa) is one for which there is no line two fingerbreadths [in width].

769. Regarding the word “designated” (uddiṭṭha), it is stated in the word-commentary (padabhājana): “A bowl that is ‘with a binding-mark’ (bandhanokāsa) is one for which there is a line two fingerbreadths [in width].
The construction is: “a single binding [mark] with a line two fingerbreadths [in width]. “[Fallen] below the rim” means fallen from the edge of the mouth.
Based on the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated without doubt: "All rows [of stitches] must be understood as having fallen below, starting from the rim of the mouth.

Without the rim of the mouth, even if there are fewer than five stitches elsewhere, or if there is a space for fewer than five stitches, one cannot say that the bowl lacks five stitches; therefore, [the text specifies] "starting from the rim of the mouth..."
The statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* which establishes the rule as "starting from [this point]" should be examined. However, no such restriction is shown here;
therefore, this very analysis accords with and conforms to the Pāḷi text as stated in its general form.
Because the letter *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned, there are two bindings for each of the two finger-breadths.
And as for the phrase "and three bindings," this too has already been stated. As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"But for one who has two lines, or only one [line] four finger-breadths wide, two bindings should be applied.
For one who has three [lines], or only one [line] six finger-breadths wide, three bindings should be applied."
In order to show the classification of the last offense among those with fewer than five bonds, he says: “And the bonds,” and so forth.
This means that there are four bonds consisting of the four lines measuring eight finger-breadths on the rim of the bowl.
The word “and” (ca) serves to include what was stated previously. “Likewise for the eight-finger line” means from the rim of the bowl...

The meaning is: starting from the base, at intervals of two finger-breadths (aṭṭhaṅgula) along the length of the bowl, four bindings are made by that same method at places measuring two finger-breadths each, separated by a line (rājī). 770.
Having thus shown the bowl with fewer than five bindings, he now says [the following] to show the bowl with a full complement of five bindings:
“Or five,” and so forth. There are five lines that have descended from the edge of the mouth, each two finger-breadths in length.
By the word *vā* (or), the alternative of the five-fold binding is shown. “Or even one ten-finger-breadths long”: there may be a single line ten finger-breadths long from the edge of the mouth.
By the word *api* (even/also), the binding of that line according to the method of the five-fold binding is indicated. This...
“Five-fold binding” (*pañcabandhana*) refers to a bowl that has five lines or five bindings thereon;
or, if there are ten finger-breadths [in height] with one line or five bindings thereon, such a bowl is called “five-fold bound.
(771) Having thus shown the determination regarding earthenware bowls, he now says “an iron bowl,” etc., in order to show [the rules for] iron bowls.
Iron plates that must be fastened to cover the holes are called *lohamaṇḍalaka*; "bhaṇḍī" is also a synonym for them.
Even if a hole has been covered by fastening something that can be bound, if the food remains there because of its roughness, such a thing is not yet a bowl;
therefore he said, "it must be smooth. Or, [the bowl may be made] with iron filings.
Here too, it should be connected with the phrase, “it is allowable for him. 772.
The construction is as follows: “that bowl, which has been forfeited by him and relinquished to the Saṅgha, he does not take out of compassion for him”;
for, according to the statement, “it must be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha,” it is that bowl which has been relinquished by him in the midst of the Saṅgha.
[The offense applies] to one who, out of compassion, does not accept the bowl from that person to whom it was entrusted.

773. But when the bowl is being given away—in the case of a monk who has requested a new bowl with a bowl that has fewer than five mends—once he has relinquished that bowl in the midst of the Saṅgha and confessed his offense and is sitting there, there are four "non-goings," meaning he must not go [to those four places].
"Knowing what has been taken and what has not been taken" means that a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should first request the Saṅgha,

and after the Saṅgha has appointed a bowl-receiver by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*), he— being thus authorized— should take the relinquished bowl in his hand and,
approaching the members of that Saṅgha in order, beginning from the senior-most elder of the Saṅgha, [distribute it] as long as it is recognizable.
When [the bowl] has been offered after the virtues have been proclaimed: *yassa* (to whom) refers to whichever monk is seated in the midst of the Saṅgha;

it is the dative case used in connection with the sense of "for the purpose of pleasing. *So* (that) refers to the bowl being given. *Taṃ* (that) refers to the bowl being given. 774. *Dīpito* (declared): it is stated that "it should not be distributed to one who does not possess a bowl. *Tattha* (therein): in that assembly of monks.

Regarding the term *pattapariyanto*: here, because it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that "it is a bowl standing at the edge after being turned over in this manner," the meaning is that either the bowl brought by that turning over, or the very bowl brought because it was not taken by anyone else, is called the "edge.
*Tassa bhikkhuno* refers to that monk who has sat down after having relinquished his bowl.
775. That which was given to oneself is that bowl which has reached its limit [of use]. "In a small place" refers to a location such as a bed, a stool, or the like;
as it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: "in a place such as a bed, a stool, a canopy, or a peg. "He gives it away" means he gives it to another.
Without having it given by himself, he takes that bowl himself from another and, when another suitable bowl is being offered, [he accepts it].
"It is permissible to take it" is what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "He uses it without formal appropriation" means he uses it for purposes such as broth, fuel, and dyeing.
As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "‘Without formal appropriation’ means by way of broth, fuel, dyeing, cooking, and so forth.
Furthermore, "if an illness arises on the way and there is no other vessel, one may smear [a vessel] with clay and [use it for] broth..."
Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "it is permissible to cook [food] or to heat water," it is likewise permissible to consume [the food] in such a situation;
this is the distinction here. 776.
"Lost" (*naṭṭha*) means when one's own bowl, while being used by oneself, has been lost through theft or similar causes. "Broken" (*bhina*) means having reached a state of fracture.
“Non-offense” means there is no offense for one who asks for another bowl. “Expounded” means it has been taught in the Pāḷi according to such methods as:
“There is no offense for one whose bowl is lost, whose bowl is broken, for relatives, for those who have invited him, for the sake of another, or with his own wealth,” and so forth.
Here, because it is stated “for the sake of another,” even if one’s own bowl is still being used...
It is permissible to request an alms-bowl for the sake of another. Regarding the phrase "taking from relatives and so forth," the term "belonging to" (*santaka*) is understood here.
This is to be construed with "with one's own wealth. Here, "wealth" refers to allowable items such as thread, cloth, and so on.
In this context, the act of requesting is the action.
Commentary on the Second Discussion of the Bowl. 778.
Regarding the phrase "medicines such as ghee," etc., the text here enumerates them as follows: "That is to say: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses.
Then it defines ghee: "Ghee means cow-ghee, or goat-ghee, or buffalo-ghee; of these..."
Meat is permitted; ghee is specified as "the clarified butter of those [animals]"; fresh butter is specified as "the butter of those very same [animals]";
oil is specified as "sesame oil, mustard seed oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil";
honey is specified as "honey from bees"; and treacle is [specified as] "from sugarcane."
“Produced” is explained as molasses and so forth; the meaning is: whatever among this collection of five medicinal substances is a medicine.
“Before the meal” means prior to the meal. “Having received” means having accepted.
779. That medicine received before the meal. “For seven days”: here, [the verb] “is permitted” (*vaṭṭati*) is understood.
The accusative case is used for continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoge*). The word division is “*sattāhaṃ atikkamantassā*. Alternatively, the reading is “*sattāhātikkame tassā*.
*Sattāhātikkamo* means the passing of seven days; [it occurs] in that passing of seven days. *Tassa* refers to the monk who receives the medicine.
By the term “*nissaggiyan*,” the *pācittiya* offense itself is indicated. This is the subject matter of the forfeiture (*nissaggiyavatthu*).

One incurs an offense by counting according to the number of vessels. Even in a single vessel, one incurs an offense by counting individually the lumps of butter, lumps of sugar, granulated sugar, and layers of honey that have been placed therein.
780. "Having taken" means having received. "Sannidhi" means that which is stored; it refers to the stored object and its maker.

"Making a preparation" means setting it aside for the sake of another day; having done so, the meaning is that one has placed it down in such a way that what was received after the meal lasts until the following day.
"Enjoying it unworldly" means enjoying it without mixing it with worldly food.
781. *Uggahitaṃ* means taken with the hand without having it formally accepted (*appaṭiggahāpetvā*). *Sarīrabhogena* means by means of the external use of the body itself.
782. *Gahitaṃ* is what has been accepted (*paṭiggahitaṃ*).

*Tāpetvā* means having caused it to be melted. 783. The statement, “He melts it himself... [etc. ...he does not exist,” was said with reference to well-washed butter; it does not apply to that which is poorly washed.
However, when accompanied by curd balls and the like, it is indeed a *sāmaṃpāka* (cooked by oneself). The construction is: "The heating of butter by itself is not a *sāmaṃpāka*. 784.
"By anyone whatsoever" means by one who is ordained (*upasampanna*) or by one who is unordained (*anupasampanna*).
785. By the phrase "he cooks himself," the unordained person is excluded. However, that which was prepared by him on that very day before the meal [is permissible].
That which contains meat is also permissible. As it is said in the Commentary:
"Butter made from milk or curd received before midday, even if prepared by one who is not fully ordained, is permissible on that same day before midday.
(786) Regarding the term *savatthuka* ("with its basis"): here, "basis" (*vatthu*) refers to milk and curd.
787. *Assa* refers to ghee made from milk and curd that have been received. This is because it was stated, "having received those," in reference to this passage in the *mātikā*:
"Now, as for those medicines to be taken at the proper time for sick bhikkhus, namely:
ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—having received these... Here, the word "those" (*yāni*)...

It is implied that this refers specifically to the ghee and other substances already mentioned, because it was stated, "having received those"; the intention here is that milk and curd have not been mentioned. (788) Regarding "permissible ghee":

this refers to the ghee of animals whose meat is permissible. Regarding "impermissible ghee": this refers to the ghee of animals whose meat is impermissible; it is implied that [the offense occurs] when seven days have passed after receiving it.
Regarding the statement, "That ghee must be considered unallowable; how does this become an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)?", he says "all," and so forth.

Those for whom meat is unallowable are "those for whom meat is unallowable" (akappiyamaṃsā), namely humans and others. All of them and those for whom meat is unallowable are "all those for whom meat is unallowable" (sabbākappiyamaṃsā); [the term refers] to them.
790-1. If this is indeed the case, one might raise the objection: "Why is it stated in the Pāḷi that 'for those for whom meat is allowable, for them ghee is [also] allowable'?

Having raised this objection, he says "For those... and so forth, in order to resolve it. In this context, the question is being asked: what purpose does this statement—"for those for whom meat is allowable, for them ghee is [allowable]"—accomplish?
Now, [he explains] that which is termed the determination of the limit...
In order to show both that application (*payoga*) and its object (*visaya*), he said: “Of excellent food,” and so forth. The construction is: “The delimitation and restriction of excellent food.
This refers to the five kinds of medicine permitted for a seven-day period; the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

“Of the objects of what is to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*”) is the demonstration of that which is to be selected. Regarding the term “of what is to be relinquished,” it refers here to that which has that [relinquishment] as its cause.
The meaning is "of the *pācittiya* offense. Regarding "substances," only the two—ghee and fresh butter—are mentioned.

In the case of the *nissaggiya-pācittiya* concerning the seven-day period, the term "substance" refers to these very same ghees and fresh butters; it was stated in that way to show that "choice food" consists of those same milk, curd, ghee, and fresh butter.
It was not stated for the purpose of prohibiting ghee and so forth from unallowable meat-eating beings. This is the point.
In the Pāḷi, it is meant that the "meaning" (attha) is intended as the Tathāgata.

792. The construction is as follows: "In the case of what is taken up and what has been taken up, etc., and in the case of what is received and what has been received, etc., even regarding butter, the entire detailed exposition (vinicchaya) should be understood by the same method as stated for ghee.
By the word "etc. (ādi), [the inclusion is] of milk and curd received before the meal and after the meal.
Butter made from milk and curd that have been received is included as being exactly like that; likewise, unallowable meat-butter is also included.
"The entire determination" encompasses the whole system of determination beginning with offenses (*āpatti*), as it is said in the Commentary:
"the entire method regarding what is an offense and what is not an offense, and what may or may not be used."
793–4. Regarding the phrase "pouring for the bhikkhus," the word "into the bowl" is understood by implication. "Sun-cooked" means melted in the heat of the sun. "Mixed" means strained. 795–6.
Sesame oil, mustard seed oil, madhuka oil, and castor oil. "Taken" means received. The construction is:
"Before the meal, it may be tasted, whether with food or without food. "On account of those" refers to those [periods] exceeding seven days.
"By means of those oils"—this means by way of counting the oil vessels. 798.
"Of those three"—that is, of the three: castor-seed, madhuka, and mustard seed. 799.
An offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
800. Regarding the phrase "mustard seeds, etc.," here the word "etc. (ādi) refers, in reverse order, to the inclusion of *madhuka* and *eraṇḍaka* seeds.

"Having taken" means having accepted. The construction is as follows: for a monk who has kept mustard seeds and so forth for the purpose of oil, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) after seven days have passed.
801–2. *Nāḷikerañca karañjañca nāḷikerakarañjāni*; the connection is: "the oil of those [fruits], namely coconuts and *karañja* fruits, and of *nattamāla* stalks.
*Kuruvakassa* means of the *atasī* seed. *Nimbañca kosambakañca nimbakosambakāni*; the connection is:
"the oil of those [seeds], namely the *pucimanda* seed and the *phandana* seed. *Bhallātakassa* means...
“Of a tree seed of such-and-such a name. “With the passing of time” means after seven days have elapsed.

Regarding the phrase “and the classification of what is to be taken at the proper time” (*yāvakālika-bheda*): here, the analysis is “that which has ‘what is to be taken at the proper time’ as its specific classification.

This is the qualifier for that which is to be qualified as “this substance,” namely, that which is to be swallowed. “What is to be taken for life” (*yāvajīvika*) is also a qualifier of that very same thing.
This is the qualification. "The rest" refers to the entire category of specific types shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as:
"that which is cooked by oneself, that which has the same basis [of origin], that which is received before the meal, after the meal, or taken up, and the rules regarding the substance.

"In this case too" means even in this determination concerning oil (804). Of the clear ichneumon; of the fish born in water; of the boar, the pig; and of what is called the *susukā* (porpoise/dolphin).
Of the *makara*. Although the *makara* is already included by the term "fish," it is mentioned separately as a predatory fish;
this is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Of the donkey (*gadrabha*) and the ass (*khara*). The meaning is that, by way of these five creatures, there are five kinds of fat and five types of oil.
805. Regarding the phrase “of what is allowable and what is unallowable,” this means “of a being’s meat that is allowable or unallowable”;
it is connected with the statement that “all fat-oil is permitted. Here, in the text of the authorization which states, “I allow you, monks, medicinal fats:
bear-fat, fish-fat, porpoise-fat, pig-fat, and donkey-fat,” by the inclusion of bear-fat—

It should be understood that the inclusion of the term "unallowable" (*akappiya*) was made in order to encompass human fat, since the fat of all other unallowable meat-bearing creatures has been permitted by people.
As stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "By the expression 'bear-fat,' the fat of all unallowable meats—excluding human fat—is permitted.
Here, [the reference is] to the meats of unallowable meat-bearing creatures.

The state of being unallowable (*akappiya*) is to be understood from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) which states: "Regarding meats, the ten—human, elephant, horse, dog, snake, lion, tiger, leopard, bear, and hyena—are unallowable.
Regarding fats, only human fat is [unallowable]. Among milk and the rest, there is nothing called 'unallowable'. Since human fat is included by the term "unallowable," in that case...
He said "setting aside" (ṭhapetvā) in order to exclude [that which is not permissible]. 806. *Purebhattaṃ* means "before the meal. *Saṃsaṭṭhaṃ* means "mixed.
This term *purebhattaṃ* should be construed individually with each of these words: "having received," "cooked," and "mixed. As it is stated in the Pāḷi: "received at the proper time..."
"It should be used when it is cooked at the proper time and when it has been mixed with oil for consumption. 807.

"He gives it after having prepared it" means that he gives the oil after having taken it under the authority of one who has not formally received it (the non-ordained) and having cooked it. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"The cow's ghee and oil prepared by those who are not fully ordained, having been received before the meal..."
"Before the meal, even meat mixed with food is permitted. Beyond that, it should be understood as "not exceeding seven days.
As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Starting from after the meal, for seven days only meat-free [oil] is permitted.
Here, in both cases—whether at the proper time or at the improper time—the oil of permissible or impermissible meat and fat, when given, includes fine meat powder and so forth.
It is not subject to formal censure (*abbhohārika*). As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“But whatever there may be there that is like fine dust—whether flesh, sinew, bone, or blood—that is not subject to formal censure.
Regarding the words “to receive” (*paṭiggahetuṃ*) and “to make” (*kātuṃ*), the word “ghee” (*vasa*) is understood from the context in the former case, and the word “oil” (*tela*) in the latter.
"Kātuṃ" (to make) here means both "to cook" and "to strain"; this is the meaning.
"It is not allowable"—this is stated because there is a separate *dukkaṭa* offense for each of the three procedures beginning with receiving [the food]. As it is said in the Pāḷi:
"If, monks, it is received at an improper time, cooked at an improper time, and mixed at an improper time, and one should consume it, there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas*."

For these three *dukkaṭa* offenses arise from three modes of application. "The rest" refers to such specific details as the analysis concerning the objects consisting of what has been taken up and what has been received, the classification of offenses according to the counting of vessels, and so forth—all such particulars that ought to be stated. 809.

"Taken" means received. "Made by honey-bees" means made by the three types of honey-bees known as the honey-bee (*madhumakkhikā*), the small bee (*khuddakamakkhikā*), and the bumblebee (*bhamaramakkhikā*).
810. Regarding the "counting of the bases": if it remains as a honeycomb, it is by the count of the combs;
if it has been pressed and placed in a vessel, it is by the count of the vessels; if it is thick like glue, it is by way of the great masses or lumps of honey from large bees;
and if it has been separated into individual portions, it is by their count—this is the meaning.
811. Regarding the term *ghanāghana*: here, jaggery (*guḷa*) and various kinds of sugar that have been boiled down thickly are called *ghanapakka* (thick-boiled).
Thin boiled syrup is called *aghanapakka* (not-thick-boiled). The mere residue of sugarcane juice is called *apakkaghana* (unboiled-thick).

The juice extracted by pressing from the sugarcane stalks is called *apakkāghana* (unboiled-not-thick). This is because of the general scriptural statement: "Phāṇita is produced from sugarcane. Regarding "phāṇita":
And because of the commentarial statement, "namely, that which is derived from sugarcane juice," here the drinking of sugarcane juice is also included among the flavors and so forth.
Some describe sugarcane as being available during all four time periods; that should not be accepted as authoritative.
812. *Phāṇita* means one of the types of molasses mentioned above. *Gahitaṃ* means received.
“Unmixed” means not strained. “Phāṇita made by oneself” means phāṇita that one has made after straining [the juice].
“Taken before midday” means accepted before midday. Because it is said “made by oneself,” “made” here should be understood as sugarcane juice.
816. *Katvā* means having cooked and having made into molasses (*phāṇita*).
817. *Pacchābhattaṃ katañcāpi* means even molasses that has been prepared after the meal, either by oneself or by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
818. *Kataṃ …pe… sītavārinā*: honey-molasses (*madhuka-phāṇita*) is that which is made from the juice of *madhuka* flowers—having placed them in cold water, set aside, crushed, and strained.
819. *Assā* means of honey-syrup (*madhukaphāṇita*). *Dukkaṭaṃ* means an offense of wrong-doing according to the number of vessels used as its container.

Regarding the inquiry: "If honey-syrup made by adding milk is *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day), how can it become *sattāhakālika* (to be consumed for up to seven days) when made into sugar-candy or granulated sugar?"—in this consideration, it is permissible because the milk-scum is removed by washing it again and again.
They avoid [the fault]. As it is said in the Commentary: “But by repeatedly removing broken sugar and milk-sediment, they purify it;
therefore, it is permissible. Regarding the statement, “It is not permissible from the seed onwards,” the Commentary states that fermented liquor made from madhuka flowers is prohibited;
however, apart from that, both raw and ripe madhuka flowers are permissible before the meal.
820. "Of all fruits," however, refers to fruits such as plantains, jujubes, and so forth.

821. Because a general term can also apply to a specific instance, by the power of the statement "if there is a suitable condition after midday," one should understand that the three types of *kālīka* (time-limited) foods—excluding those that are *yāvakālika* (to be used until the end of the day)—are intended; this is indicated by the phrase "at will before midday."

All four [types of food] should be understood by their verbal definitions. With the exception of that which is for the time being (*yāvakālika*), the three types of "timely" (*kālika*) food may be consumed by a monk after the meal, at the wrong time (*vikāla*), provided there is a requisite cause such as thirst;

they may be used either entirely, individually, or mixed together. All four types of timely food may be consumed as one pleases before the meal, during the proper time, until midday, whether entirely or mixed together.
The construction is: "It is permissible for a bhikkhu to consume [it] even when there is no [other] requisite.
822. "Wounds and so forth" refers to ulcers and the like. By the phrase "it is not permissible to smear [it on]," external application is also prohibited.

823. In the section concerning non-offenses (*anāpatti*), within the context of "within seven days," [the text speaks of] "what has been relinquished, vomited, or released by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*)."

Because it is stated, "Having given without expectation, he receives and uses [it]," the phrase "having relinquished" (*cajitvā*) must be understood here as "within seven days for one who is not fully ordained.
Regarding the word "having received" (*labhitvā*), the sense that "even after the lapse of seven days" is obtained by implication.
Therefore, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "Indeed, there is no offense at all in using again what was given within the seven-day period."
"This was said in order to show that there is no offense in using [the oil] after seven days have passed.

"Having received" means having received what was given—whether respectfully or disrespectfully—by one who is not fully ordained, using the oil already taken. Regarding the word "to taste," the word "receives" (*labhati*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.

824. Regarding the phrase “there is no offense if he resolves (*adhiṭṭheti*”), the words “within seven days” are to be supplied between the two terms; it is also compatible with all the following terms.
“He resolves” means that within the interval of seven days, he resolves: “This ghee, oil, fat, or oil for the head, or an ointment;
honey as a salve for wounds; or molasses as incense for the house—these shall be used. He thus makes a formal resolution.
If that which was determined becomes mixed with that which was not determined, it must be determined once again.

"Gives away" means that within seven days he gives it to another person who has received full ordination. If it is given in such a manner, the Commentary states that there is no offense for either of them:
because it was not accepted by the other [recipient], and because it was accepted by the first [recipient] since it had already been given to him.
"It is destroyed" means that within seven days it is lost through some manner or other—such as by being stolen by thieves—in such a way that it becomes unusable.
As it is said in the Commentary: "It is destroyed means it becomes unusable.
"Another takes it after having snatched it away" means that another person seizes it by plundering it within those same seven days. "He takes it on trust" means in that very [interval]...
Within seven days, another takes up the *vissāsa* (trust/authorization).

825. The construction is as follows: by the Teacher, whose mind was not [bound by] the *kathina*, all matters such as the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth were explained as being identical to the first *kathina*. "By one whose mind was not [bound by] the *kathina*" means:
because it was saturated with the essence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), his mind was not harsh; that is, his mind delighted in non-violence (*avihiṃsā*).

It has been said: "By the Teacher" means by him who is the Teacher because he instructs the world together with its devas through matters pertaining to the present life, the future life, and so forth;
that is, by the Omniscient One, the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the medicinal training rule (*bhesajja-sikkhāpada*).

826. Regarding the word *gimhānaṃ* (of the hot season): here, by implication, the word *māsānaṃ* (of the months) is understood. The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). The meaning is "in the four months of the hot season.
It shows that which is to be selected with the words "one month remains" (*māso seso*); here, the phrase "at the time when it ought to be said" (*vattabbe kāle*) is to be supplied.
[This refers to] the three [periods] beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phagguna and ending with the full moon of the month of Jeṭṭha.

The meaning is: "when the months have elapsed. The "remaining month" refers to the period beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha and ending with the full moon of the month of Āsāḷha.
While it should be said that "a month of the hot season remains," the sense here is "in the time [of the remaining month].
In this last month of the hot season, if the rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) has not been obtained during the dark fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha...
The field for seeking, obtaining, and making [the robe] is not the field for the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the wearing (*nivāsana*).
The first half of the month of Āsāḷha is the field for seeking, making, and wearing, but not the field for determining.
From the first day of the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha up to the full moon of the last month of Kattika—this is the field for all four. This is the summary here.

“Should seek” means: without approaching those who previously gave a rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*)—in the manner described in the word-commentary beginning with “those people who previously gave a rainy-season robe”—and without requesting them by saying, “Give me a rainy-season robe-cloth,” etc., but rather [saying], “It is the time for a rainy-season robe;
it is the season for a rainy-season robe; other people as well give a rainy-season robe... [and so forth].
“Giving,” thus he should seek [the cloth] by merely arousing mindfulness.
“A rain-cloth” means a *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-season robe). “Half a month remains”—this connects specifically with the phrase “of the summer.
In that context, the words “at the time when it ought to be used” must be supplied; the meaning is: in the first fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha. Regarding the word “having made”: here—

“Obtained” means it is acquired by implication. It is said that it has been finished by means of the arising of mindfulness in the manner already described, or by means of the giving of small amounts of thread for sewing and dyeing from other families endowed with faith. “He wears” means he should put it on.
Regarding the phrase “at the time recognized as the back”: starting from the first day of the fortnight following the full moon of Kattika... [827-8]
Regarding the seven months indicated by the phrase, "From the full moon of Jeṭṭha to the full moon of Mūla, these seven months are called the 'back-season'":

the construction is "having aroused mindfulness toward relatives, non-relatives, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), both those who have invited [one to accept food] and those who have not are included.
As it is said in the Commentary: "from a place where one is not known or has not been invited."
“From those very same [persons]” means from those who are relatives or non-relatives, whether they have invited one or not.

By the word “likewise,” it is shown that “there is an offense entailing relinquishment. That offense occurs in the case of non-relatives who have not invited one, according to the training rule concerning requesting from non-relatives.
As it is said in the Commentary: “Having made a request in such a manner as ‘Give me a rainy-season robe,’ etc.”

"For one who causes it to be produced, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya) under the training rule concerning requests from those unrelated.

In the case of relatives or those who have invited him, there is no offense under that training rule; however, because the matter concerns the back [of the robe], an offense occurs under this [present] rule.

Furthermore, in the case of unrelated persons who have not invited him, it should be understood that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of the proper procedure, along with [the other offense].

829–30. The construction is: “having made [the food] from unknown persons, etc., there arises mindfulness. By the word “etc.,” those who have not been invited are included. Regarding the phrase “at the time known as ‘belly’”:
among the aforementioned periods of the back, the seventh month is mentioned, while the other five months are excluded.
As it is said in the Commentary: “But starting from the first day of the fortnight following the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla...”
“Up to the full moon of Kattika, these five months are called the ‘period of the womb’. *Vattha* means a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭika*).
Regarding the phrase *adinnapubbesu*: this states the reason for the breach of the rule (*vattabhedo*) with respect to those by whom a rain-cloak has not been given previously.

Here, "breach of the rule" refers to those people among whom it was previously said, “Those people who formerly gave the rain-cloak robe,” and so forth; [it applies] to those to whom it has been given before.
It is the performance, for the first time, of that which ought to be done by the arising of mindfulness. By contrast, it is shown that this does not exist in the case of things previously given.

"Therein" refers to the case of one who is unknown (*aññātaka*) and so forth. By the term "nissaggiya," he refers to the offense under the training rule concerning solicitation from one who is unknown (*aññātakaviññatti-sikkhāpada*).

As it was said in the fourfold summary on the stomach: "Even for one who, having made a request, brings [the gift] to completion, there is an offense under the training rule concerning solicitation from one who is unknown."
“...an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). This offense of confession (pācittiya) applies even to those who give a regular rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*);
this is understood from the statement in the Commentary: “But this [offense] indeed applies even to those who give a regular rainy-season robe. 831.
“He causes it to be rained upon” means he moistens the body with water fallen from the sky; by this, [it is implied that one should not] pour [water] from jars and so forth.
"It is allowable" is what is thus illustrated. "It is allowable to bathe with water that has been strained through a cloth" is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentaries).

"Even when a robe exists" means even when a *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloak) exists. By the phrase "an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the end," it indicates that this refers to the counting of drops.
"In an open space" means in a place not enclosed by trees or other such things.
832. "In the month" means in the last month of the summer season. 833.
Regarding the phrase "one whose robe has been stolen," it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that this refers specifically to the *vassikasāṭikā* (the rainy-season robe).
For one who is bathing while wearing the *vassikasāṭikā*, a danger from thieves constitutes what is called an "emergency. A "bathing enclosure" (*nhānakoṭṭhaka*)...

"A hut built for the purpose of bathing. By the word "pond" (*vāpī*), lotus ponds, natural lakes, and so forth are implied. "While bathing" means while bathing naked; this is understood from the context.
"By water falling from the sky alone" is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) itself. 834.

It is a "formal action" (*kiriya*) because it is an offense to be incurred through seeking [the water] at an improper time, making a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and wearing [clothing]. For one who performs the communication and so forth by both body and speech, there is bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Rainy-Season Robe (Vassikasāṭikakathāvaṇṇanā). 835.

Regarding the statement, “But whatever bhikkhu, having himself given a robe to a bhikkhu...,” the word “himself” (sāmaṃ) here implies “to a bhikkhu,” and the word “having given” (datvā) here implies “to a bhikkhu.
“Robe” (cīvaraṃ) refers to any one of the six types of robes.

The robe is the last of those that may be assigned. Regarding the phrase “of one who seizes,” because of the statement, “If, being angry and displeased, he should seize it,” the words “of one who is angry and displeased” are to be supplied;
the meaning is: of one who seizes or causes another to seize [the robe] while being angry and displeased.
“That” refers to the robe given by oneself. By the phrase “with the perception that it is his own,” [the offense of] pārājika is excluded.
It illuminates the state of being a basis. 836.
"Likewise" (tathā) illuminates that it is indeed a single offense. 837.
"Of cloths" (vatthānaṃ) means of robes. "His" (assa) means of the bhikkhu.
841. "Take the *saṅghāṭi*, take the *uttarāsaṅga*"—this is the construction.
842. Regarding the phrase "the last [robe] that is fit for assignment," the word "robe" (*cīvara*) is understood here.
A piece of cloth measuring one carpenter’s cubit in length and likewise one span (*vidatthi*) in width is, from its lower limit, "fit for assignment."

The construction is: "any other requisite whatsoever. This means that even if it is something as simple as a cloth, it is so stated. "Another person" refers to a different individual. Regarding the phrase "of one who causes to be cut":
this refers to one who causes [the cutting] to be done. Because the verb *kāreti* (causes to do) takes two objects, there is the grasping of two objects:
"another" and "requisite. "Another" is an adjective qualifying the requisite. There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each item and for each verbal expression.

844. Thus, just as there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when one perceives a person who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) as such, so too is there an offense of wrong-doing for one who is in doubt regarding a person who is not fully ordained;
this is the application of the rule. Regarding the phrase "of one who deprives":
here, the aforementioned term "one who is not fully ordained" should be transformed into the genitive case by changing its grammatical ending, and then joined with the supplied word "given."
“Robe” (*cīvara*) is understood from the context; it refers to one who takes back a robe given to a person not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
845. “Or he himself” means that very monk to whom the robe was given. The construction is: “whether pleased or displeased, he gives it. “Or simply out of confidence” means “taking it on trust.
846. “In this” means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Cutting Robe-cloth (Cīvaracchindanakathāvaṇṇanā).
847. “Having requested” means having asked for it, with reference to the weaving of cloth.
“Six kinds of thread” refers to the six types of thread mentioned in the word-commentary as: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and jute.

“Kambala” means woolen cloth made from sheep’s wool. The six types of cloth that are permissible should be understood according to what was stated previously in the *Cīvaravinicchaya* (The Determination of Robes).
Cloth intended for a robe is called “robe. “By weavers” means by spinners, both those who are allowable and those who are not.
In some manuscripts, the reading “it is not permitted to have it woven” is seen, followed by the word “if.”
Because this [reading] is inconsistent, it is not the correct reading. The reading “it is not permissible to have it woven” is consistent;
if one construes it as “if he has it woven,” the meaning is:

“if he should have it woven for his own sake. 848. Likewise, it is unallowable (*akappiya*). To the question “Of what kind? he says: “beginning with strangers” (*aññātakādika*). “Beginning with strangers” means that a stranger is the first among them.
"He is one who is unknown and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one who has not been invited is included. The meaning is:

when a weaver is unknown to a monk and has not been invited by him, that weaver—being requested by the monk—is "unallowable" (akappiya). 849. "By means of what is unallowable" means by means of what has been requested.

Regarding the phrase "for one who causes [it] to be woven," the remainder is: "for every act of effort there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); upon acquisition [there is an offense]. As it is said: "He causes it to be woven; for every act of effort there is an offense of wrong-doing. Upon acquisition, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya)."
850. To the question, "After how much has been woven does it become *nissaggiya*? he says, "When it is the measure of a span," and so forth. "The measure of a hand" means the measure of a *ratana*.
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it is stated that "it is *nissaggiya* by way of acquisition," whereas here it is said, "it is *nissaggiya* when woven.
Why was this said? Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. And why was it stated thus even there? Because immediately thereafter, it becomes one's own property.

The place for weaving has already been obtained; even in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it is stated that by this very intention of obtaining [the cloth], it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
Therefore, as long as the robe is being increased, so long do the offenses increase according to this measurement.
Regarding the phrase "and also on a board": here, a "board" (*phalaka*) refers to the place for spinning and weaving, where they keep [the materials] rolled up. On the board...
The construction is: "And it is stated that there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) even for a wooden board.

(851) "By that very person" means by the weaver who was specifically requested. "Suitable thread" means thread obtained without being requested. The construction is: "For one who has a weaver weave unsuitable thread using suitable [materials], there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
(852) The construction is: "Or, for weaving with threads that are alternately suitable and unsuitable, there is an offense of wrong-doing," meaning interspersed between them.
The meaning is that an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs through the spreading out of unallowable threads and through weaving them.

The construction is: "An offense of wrong-doing occurs when it is woven with both allowable and unallowable threads, whether lengthwise or crosswise. The meaning is: having spread out an allowable thread lengthwise, if it is woven crosswise with an unallowable thread, an offense of wrong-doing occurs. By the inclusion of the term "weaving," the opposite of what was stated [above] is also implied.
It should be joined. Having stretched out an unallowable thread lengthwise, one weaves across with an allowable thread;
this is the reversal here. Regarding "weaves," it should be repeated as "on each plank.
When planks have been woven by allowable and unallowable weavers, having mixed allowable and unallowable threads, [the rule applies].
The construction is: "It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for that bhikkhu on a wooden board. *Ve* is a mere particle; or alternatively, the meaning is:
"when that has been done, it is woven" (*vīte*). 854–5. Having shown the distinction between those weavers who are allowable and those who are unallowable, the construction is:
"if they weave an unallowable thread by means of restraint alone. It is woven by an unallowable weaver. It is stated as "woven" (*vīte*) for the purpose of protecting against [the arising of] desire.
"In the [proper] measure" means in that which does not exceed the maximum allowable measure. "Less than that" means less than that maximum allowable measure.

"By the other" means by one who weaves with permissible yarn. "In both cases" is to be construed as follows: in the case of the [proper] measure and in the case of being less than that, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 856.

If both a permissible and an impermissible weaver take hold of the loom at both ends and weave together in one place—this is the construction. Having inserted the thread crosswise, that loom by which they strike it to achieve density is so called.

857. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means: in all varieties of robes made by weavers using either allowable or unallowable thread and yarn—whether they are of the right measure, less than that, one interval [too large], long, or wide;

or in all variations of the types of cloth. "Distinction of offenses" (*āpattibheda*) means: if a robe is made with unallowable threads or with an unallowable weaver's weave, even if it is of the correct length and width and possesses the required intervals, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); in other cases, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is the distinction.
858. A weaver known as *kappiya* (a permissible person) may be either a relative, one who has invited [the monk], or one employed by means of a permissible fee.
859. "There is no offense in sewing a robe, or in [making] a waistband, a girdle, a shoulder-strap, a bag for the bowl, or a water-strainer;
[there is no offense] for relatives, for those who have invited [him], for the sake of another, or with one's own wealth"—such is the section on non-offenses.
To demonstrate this, he said, “There is no offense,” and so forth. Here, even that which is not explicitly defined by its characteristic should be understood as having been already indicated.
In this context, the construction is: “there is no offense for one who requests thread in order to sew a robe. “Wealth” (*dhana*) refers to allowable items such as rice and the like.

In the phrases “in a water-strainer” (*parissāvane*) and so on, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*); thus, it means thread intended for the purpose of making a water-strainer and the like.
It is stated that there is no offense for one who requests [cloth] from a weaver.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the request for thread. 860.

Regarding "from non-relatives who have not been invited": this refers to non-relatives who have not been invited [to choose], [as in the case of saying]: "Venerable sir, what kind of robe-cloth do you require?"
“What kind of robe-cloth shall I have woven for you?”—the meaning is “of unrelated persons who have not invited him,” according to the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
“Having approached” (*samecca*) means having gone near. “Specification” (*vikappa*) means a distinguished specification, an additional arrangement. “Enters upon” (*āpajjati*) means he performs it;
[as in the example: “Friend, this robe-cloth is being woven for me; make it long and wide.”

It is said that he makes an arrangement according to the method beginning with “Make it well-applied, well-stretched, well-woven, well-scraped, and well-shaved,” in order to make it longer and so forth than what was intended by the donors.
In this context, “long” (*āyata*) means extended; “broad” (*vitthata*) means wide; “well-applied” (*appita*) means thick; and “well-stretched” (*suvīta*) means well...
"Woven" means woven evenly in all places. "Well-woven" means well-woven, having been stretched out on the loom and made even in all places.
"Well-combed" means well-combed with a comb. "Well-carded" means well-carded with a carding brush; the meaning is "well-cleansed."
861. To show the manner of extending the thread, he said: "for the purpose of making it long, wide, or fitted.
And by that, in the word-commentary, only this triad—long, wide, and fitted—is stated: "By his word, one makes it long, or wide, or fitted;

there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of application, and upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya). Regarding the phrase "when [the robe] has been extended by the thread," immediately after this...
The construction should be made by supplying the phrase “there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort, [and] by acquisition,” along with the remainder of the text.

The meaning is that even if the entire effort made by him— including the lengthening of the thread beyond the amount given by the donors after they had weighed it— results in an offense of wrong-doing for the monk through that effort,
and an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya) by acquisition.
862. The construction is: "One should point out the non-offense for one who makes a formal determination regarding a robe among weavers belonging to relatives and so forth.
