Regarding the phrase "with one's own wealth," the word "employed" (*payojitesu*) is to be supplied as the remainder; this is an adjective qualifying "weavers. Thus, it means:
"One should point out the non-offense for one who makes a formal determination regarding a robe among weavers employed with one's own wealth."
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "for one who, having taken a permissible object belonging to oneself, undergoes alteration while having it woven"—this is the meaning.
Regarding "for one who undergoes alteration while having it woven for the sake of another," it should be understood that the construction includes the elided words (*pāṭhasesa*).
863. The construction is: "one desiring to have something expensive made, who has weavers weave something inexpensive—there is no offense; this is what is being pointed out."
Commentary on the Discussion of the Weaver: 864.
"Having designated the monks who have spent the rains" means having designated those monks who entered the rains during the earlier period (*purimikā*).

"Whatever robe-cloth is given even before the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*)" is the grammatical connection. This is what is meant: "Ten days before the full moon of Kattika, which marks the end of the three-month rains retreat."

In the Pāḷi it is stated that on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pubbakattika, prior even to the day of the Great Pavāraṇā Uposatha, whatever robe [is given] by sending a messenger—or by oneself—to any one among those mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) beginning with "one desiring to go to an army," namely:
a traveler, the sick, a pregnant woman, or one who has newly acquired faith; this is called an *accekacīvara*.
Having arrived and said, "I give the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe)," it is given. That is called an urgent robe (*accāyikacīvara*).
865. "Even before the invitation" means on any day from the fifth day onwards, prior to the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*).
Regarding the phrase "if it is taken after being distributed," the word "by whom" (*yena*) should not be used here, nor should the word "by that" (*tena*) be used here.
Regarding the phrase "and he makes [the interruption]," the expression "that interruption of the rains" is understood here by implication.
If, after the robe has been distributed, it is taken by someone, that person must not make an interruption of the rains. The construction is:

"If he does make an interruption of the rains, the robe taken after the distribution becomes the property of the Saṅgha. What is meant is that the robe must be given to the Saṅgha alone by one who has interrupted the rains.
866. “Right at the time” (antosamayameva): this should be construed individually with each of the phrases beginning with “he resolves” (adhiṭṭheti).

Within the very period of the time described in the word-commentary as “the robe-season is called the last month of the rainy season when the kaṭhina has not been spread, or the five months when the kaṭhina has been spread,” that urgent robe (accekacīvara) [must be used].
867. Regarding the phrase "but when the *kathina* has not been spread": this means that it is in whatever monastery the *kathina* has not been spread.

The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. "Parihāra" (the allowance) refers to the fact that here an urgent robe (*accekacīvara*) may be kept without having been formally resolved upon (*anadhiṭṭhāya*) or assigned to another (*avikappetvā*).
"Māsa" means a month; "ekamāsa" means that single month. [This period begins] from the first day of the month of Kattika.
The period from [the full moon of Kattika] until the full moon of the subsequent Kattika month is called the robe-season (*cīvarakālasamaya*).

"Ten days" (*dasāha*) is a compound of ten days; that which has this as its maximum or limit is "ten-day-maximum" (*dasāhaparama*), referring to the month. It means "having ten days more than the previously mentioned full moon of Kattika," as stated in the Pāḷi: "Ten days before the full moon of the Kattika three-month season."

The meaning is as follows: The construction is that when the *kathina* has not been spread, the privilege for that urgent robe-material is considered to last for ten days at most, or indeed for one month.
(868) "When the *kathina* has been spread" means in a monastery where the *kathina* has been spread; this is what is stated. The connection is with "for that urgent robe-material.

The connection is with "five months at most, [starting] from ten days. In a monastery where the *kathina* has not been spread, it is the month following the end of the rainy season, which is designated as the time for robes as previously described.

And from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika, which is reckoned as the day for the suspension of the *kathina*, until the full moon of the month of Phagguna—this constitutes the four months of winter; thus, there are five months. "Proclaimed" means it is explained that "when the *kathina* has not been spread, [the period is] the last month of the rainy season;
when the *kathina* has been spread, it is five months. "At most ten days" has the meaning already stated.
The construction is as follows: "When the Kathina has been spread, the period for the use of that urgent robe-material is five months at most, plus ten days; this was proclaimed by the Lord of Sages.
This limit of ten days mentioned in both contexts does not contradict the reading stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"When the Kathina has not been spread, it is one month plus eleven days; when the Kathina has been spread, it is five months plus eleven days."
It should be understood after such investigation. For if the text is read in this way, it does not contradict [the following]:
"Regarding that cloth for the rainy season residence, when the kaṭhina has not been spread, a delay of one month is permitted, but at most ten days."
“When the Kathina has been spread, five months are declared for it;
the privilege granted is for at most ten days.

(869) The construction is with the phrase “by the first Kathina. The word-division is “akriyam acittam. “Akriyam” means the non-performance of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and so forth within the prescribed period.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Early-Morning Robe (Accekacīvarakathāvaṇṇanā).
870–1. "A bhikkhu" refers to a bhikkhu dwelling in a forest lodging that is considered risky and dangerous.
As it is said: "Those forest lodgings which are considered risky and dangerous..."
“A bhikkhu dwelling in such lodgings... This is the connection: “having dwelt during the full moon of the former Kattika.
The full moon of the former Kattika is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Assayuja;

however, here, by way of association, the three preceding months of the rains-retreat characterized by that [full moon] are meant. Regarding the word “full moon,” it refers to the act of dwelling therein.

The accusative case is used for continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). The meaning is: having entered the rains retreat during the first period, having remained for the full duration of the rains, and having dwelt for three months.
As it is said in the Commentary: "But because one who, having entered the rains retreat, dwells until the full moon of the first *Kattika* month..."
“Robe” (cīvara) refers to any one of the three robes. “Having deposited in a village” is the connection;
here, the words “the full moon of Kattika” and “if he so desires” are to be supplied.
This means that a bhikkhu who wishes to put away his robe due to fear of robbers during the month of Kattika should deposit it in a village within the alms-round area adjacent to his forest dwelling.
The meaning is as follows: As it is said, “Now, having entered the rains retreat on the full moon of Kattika...
[omitted] ...desiring [to do so], he may deposit one of the three robes within the village.
Regarding the phrase “in the vicinity of the alms-village,” this means “he may deposit it within the village in the vicinity of the alms-village.”

It is stated because it was so stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). Furthermore, the phrase "in the month of Kattika" and "the full moon of Kattika" refers to the Kattika four-month festival (*cātumāsinī*), according to the word-commentary.

For here too, although "the full moon of Kattika" refers to the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the later Kattika, by way of association (*sahacariyanaya*), the fourth month associated with it is also mentioned.
In this context, for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has entered the earlier rains residence, performed the *pavāraṇā* at the Great *Pavāraṇā*,
and is dwelling in a forest lodging possessing the aforementioned characteristics, if there is a danger from forest thieves in the month of Kattika— the last month of the rains—

his separation from one of the three robes while he places it in the village where he seeks alms constitutes a breach of the robe [precept] as he fulfills the forest-dweller’s factor (*āraññaka-aṅga*).

The phrase "it does not exist in that month" indicates its permitted status. To clarify that very point, he will speak by way of demonstrating the method of its application: "In the month of Kattika itself... it is permissible.
Now, regarding this very month, if that bhikkhu goes elsewhere for some business while in the village—
By permitting the faultless nature of a monk who stays apart from the robe he has set aside, the Blessed One demonstrated the meaning stated in the passage:
“It may be that for that monk... he may stay apart from that robe. To show this, it was said: “When there is a requisite... [and] consent.
When such a requisite exists, it is because of the statement: “There may be a requisite; there may be business,” that [the rule applies] to such a case.
The meaning is: "when there is a necessity. "At most six nights" (*chārattaparamaṃ*): that dwelling-act for which six nights are the maximum is "at most six nights";
this is an adverbial modifier. The meaning is: "a dwelling-act at most six nights must be performed. "One may dwell apart from it":
one may dwell elsewhere than that residence apart from that robe which was left behind in the village. That alone is evident.
He will say: "For one living elsewhere, the maximum is six nights.
"From that" means from the six nights. "Living beyond" means living after the rising of the seventh dawn;
as it is said: "If he should live beyond that, there is an offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya) upon the rising of the dawn on the seventh day. "Fault" (dosa) means...
An offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). By the phrase "without the Saṅgha’s consent," what is meant?

After a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) was made regarding the *udosita* (loft) training rule, it was authorized at Kosambī that: "Monks, I allow you to grant to a sick monk the authorization not to be separated from his three robes (*ticīvara*).
Therefore, for a sick monk, by means of a formal motion and second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) of the Saṅgha...
This refers to the permission for non-separation (*avippavāsa-sammuti*) that was granted prior to the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).
The intended meaning is that for one who has received such permission, it is permissible to live even for a long time without that robe-cloth as long as the illness continues.
As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Except by the consent of the monks" refers to the Kosambaka consent regarding the *udositaka* training rule.
"It is permitted; apart from that formal authorization (sammuti), if it has been obtained, it is allowable to stay apart for more than six nights.
To demonstrate the laying aside of the robe, he said: "In the month of Kattika... it is explained.

"In the month of Kattika" means precisely in the last of the four months of the rainy season, namely the month of Kattika; this is one factor. "Having performed the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) on the first [day]"—
The second factor: here the construction is, "having entered the rains residence during the first *vassūpanāyikā*, he has performed the *pavāraṇā*";
that is to say, he has performed the *pavāraṇā* at the Great *Pavāraṇā*. As it is said in the Commentary:
"Having entered during the earlier period, he has performed the *pavāraṇā* at the Great *Pavāraṇā*. The third factor is: "he is endowed with the latter limit. Regarding the "lodging" (*senāsana*):

This is its qualification: here, the "western limit" of a forest dwelling refers to the vicinity of a house situated at the boundary of an enclosed village—whether surrounded by a wall, a fence, or a moat—at the gatehouse marked by the *indakhīla* (boundary pillar);
or, in the case of an unenclosed village, it refers to the vicinity of a house situated at the point where a surrounding wall would be required.
Starting from two throws of a clod by a man of medium strength standing at ease,
one should take as the limit either the entire enclosure of a walled monastery, or, in the case of an unenclosed monastery,
the boundary of the village in whichever direction it lies, or a shrine, or the Bodhi tree; and then, using the path leading to the monastery as the boundary...
In brief, it should be understood as a distance measured by five hundred bow-lengths using a teacher’s bow drawn along its natural path to a depth of one span.
The fourth factor is "reckoned as dangerous"; the remainder is "here in a place of peril. [The phrase] "reckoned as dangerous and perilous" [is used].
This is the Pāli. Both of these are qualifiers for the term “lodging” (*senāsana*).

In the case of a forest dwelling (*āraññaka*) that is dangerous (*sappaṭibhaya*)—due to the visibility of places where thieves have sat, lain down, stood, eaten, or drunk within the monastery grounds (*ārāma*) or its vicinity (*ārāmūpacāra*), and due to the specific presence of fear caused by the visibility of people who have been struck, killed, or plundered right there in those monasteries and so forth—it is [dangerous].
The meaning is "in a dwelling" (*senāsane*). Regarding the phrase "a monk who is staying": here, the particle *eva* is used in the sense of "not in that place.
Therefore, having brought it from there, it should be construed with "only when there is the combination of the four factors" (*caturaṅgasamāyoge eva*).

"Only when there is the combination of the four factors" means precisely when there is the combination—that is, the coming together—of the four factors as previously described. Here, by the particle *eva*, [it is indicated] that in the absence of that factor...
It indicates the state of being unobtainable. "Explained" means it was stated in the commentary beginning with, "In this regard, this is the perfection of the requisites.
874. That robe-cloth. "For one month" means for one month consisting of the final month of the rainy season.
If a village falls within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) established by the previous binding, one may keep [the robe] there even beyond one month.
"It is permissible" is what the Elder Vajirabuddhi stated. 875.
"In another sense alone" means: outside of that forest dwelling (*āraññaka-senāsana*) in which the robe was deposited within the alms-village (*gocara-gāma*).
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) of the two meanings set forth by the one-and-a-half stanzas beginning with "Whatever village... and so forth.
The intention [is as follows]. "Assā" means of the training rule concerning danger.

Thus, because it is permitted by this training rule that "one may dwell in the forest during the month of Kattika without a robe," [the text says] "that bhikkhu may be separated from that robe for a maximum of six days.
Having left that [robe] in the alms-resort village and having dwelt in that forest dwelling, if for some reason he [leaves] from there...
Because the delimitation of the day is understood even for one who has gone outside the residence and is staying there, he says, "whether concealed or exposed.

To show the legal determination according to the method explained in the Aṭṭhakathā— namely, "If the lodging is in the eastern direction from the village where one goes for alms, and this person has gone to the western direction," and so forth— he says, "But having not returned to the lodging," and so on.
“Dwelling” (*senāsana*) refers to a forest dwelling where one has resided oneself. “Having come back” means having returned from the place where one had gone out.

Having deposited one’s robe in the alms-village and then departing from that monastery while staying in a forest dwelling in the eastern direction, one goes to a distant place in the western direction from that alms-village;
[the phrase refers to] from the place where one has thus arrived.
The application here is this: for a monk who has come to that lodging and is unable to raise the seventh dawn because of the great distance, what is prescribed?
"Or having gone even to the village boundary" means that he must go to the village boundary where the robe was deposited before the dawn breaks. 877. Or having gone even to the village boundary.
"Having come. "Anywhere whatsoever" means in any suitable place, such as an assembly hall, a temple, a gatehouse, or a wall enclosure.

Because it is stated in general terms as "anywhere whatsoever," if a distant spot within the village boundary is found that is fit to serve as a forest-dweller’s fire-keeping site, one should cause the dawn to rise there without violating the constituent factor [of the practice], even though the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) itself may not be present there.

Even if one has entered the village boundary and the dawn has risen, it should be understood that the formal procedure for the robe (*cīvarapavatti*) itself must take place in order to avoid an offense.

As it is said in the Commentary: "Having entered even the village boundary and stayed in an assembly hall or anywhere else, once the formal procedure for the robe has been performed, it is permissible to depart."

878. "And even if unable" means being unable to go and cause the dawn to rise either without breaking the [robe] parts or having broken them within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*). "Knowing" means having observed the place where one's own robe was placed.
"Right there" implies that the word "standing" is understood here. "Quickly" means speedily; it is said, "before the dawn. "In a place beyond" means...
The construction is as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Thinking, ‘It will remain in the status of an extra robe,’ or ‘It remains in the status of an extra robe’—this is the meaning.
(879) “He gives it away” means he gives it to another before the rising of the seventh dawn. The same should be said for the subsequent cases as well.

880. Regarding the training rule (sikkhāpada) known by such a name as "Sāsaṅka" (the one involving suspicion), the Muninda [the Buddha] considered all factors—beginning with its origin (samuṭṭhāna)—to be the same as that second Kathina; thus they are "thought" (mata), "approved" (anumata), and "permitted" (anuññāta).
This is the explanation of the discussion on "Sāsaṅka. 881.
"They know" means knowing in whatever manner the fact that it has been dedicated by the statement, "We give this to the Saṅgha."
As it says in the *Padabhājana*: “He knows for himself,” and so forth. Regarding the term *pariṇataṃ* (dedicated):

here, according to the rule stated in the *Padabhājana*, “*Pariṇataṃ* means that the speech [of dedication] has been uttered, ‘We shall give; we shall do,’” the meaning is that it has been dedicated to the Saṅgha.
*Lābhaṃ* (gain) refers to anything that is to be obtained, such as robes and so forth. As it says: “*Lābhaṃ* means robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“Even if it be as little as a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, or even a thread from a cobweb. To divert for oneself means:
“Friends, there are many donors to the Saṅgha, many supporters of the Saṅgha;
it is because of you and out of regard for you that we dwell here. If you do not give to us, who indeed will give to us? Give, friends!”
The meaning is that one should dedicate [the robes] to oneself according to the method found in the text: "These robes are ours.

Regarding the phrase "it is to be relinquished" (*nissaggiya*), the remainder of the rule is: "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the attempt, and [an offense of expiation] upon acquisition.

This term "to be relinquished" is stated with reference to one who perceives as dedicated that which has been dedicated. However, for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing. As it is said: "When dedicated..."
“If one who is doubtful dedicates it to oneself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense for one who perceives it as not dedicated. As it is said:
‘If one who perceives it as not dedicated when it has been dedicated dedicates it to oneself, there is no offense. 882.
‘If one dedicates it [thinking], “Give this to another,” while knowing that it has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, [then] to another...”
"If he dedicates it [thinking], 'May it be for the sake of a body,' it is a *pācittiya* offense.

"A pure *pācittiya*" means a mere *pācittiya* devoid of any object that must be relinquished (*nissaggiya*). "With a pure mind" refers to the Blessed One, whose mind was purified by the abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanānavasesakilesappahāna*).
"The *pācittiya* was proclaimed" [occurs] at the conclusion of the eighth chapter, the Sahadhammika-vagga, among the *pācittiya* rules.

“Whatever monk, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been assigned to an individual, should assign it to that individual, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Thus it was taught. 883.
“One robe” means one robe from among the robes assigned to the Saṅgha. In the phrase “or a robe,” the word *vā* (or) has the sense of an alternative regarding the condition.
In the phrase “or again,” the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative regarding the meaning. One robe.
The construction is: "or he should divert another requisite belonging to another, but [he] himself [should divert] one.
*Saddhim* means "together," which is to say "at the same moment. The construction is: "there may be two *pācittiyas* together.

The meaning is that by the act of diverting it for another, there is a simple *pācittiya*, and by the act of diverting it for oneself, there is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*; thus, two *pācittiyas* occur at one and the same moment.

884. Having set aside [the case] after it has been brought forward, and having shown the decision and relinquished it, he says "Of the Saṅgha," etc., in order to show the decision regarding what was given.

"Defeat" (parājaya) is said with reference to a matter sufficient for a formal charge; however, depending on the specific matter, offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) or grave offenses (thullaccaya) may also be mentioned.
885. The construction is: "If one should divert what was intended for another shrine (*cetiyassa*) to another shrine, or to the Saṅgha, or even to an individual (*puggalassa*).
In both phrases, "to the Saṅgha" and "to an individual," it should be construed in exactly the same way.
As it has been said: "If one diverts what was intended for the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a shrine, or to an individual..."
“There is an offense of wrong-doing,” and so forth. “If one should divert [the gift] intended for one person to another person.
(886) He said, “Whosoever,” and so forth, in order to show that this applies to the domain of all sentient beings.

(887) This is the training rule concerning what has been diverted (*pariṇata-sikkhāpada*). It has three origins (*tisamutthāna*), namely: body, mind, and speech; mind, body, and speech; and mind, body, and speech.
It is "threefold in origin" because it originates from the three types of origins involving consciousness. It is "action" because it must be committed through the condition of dedication.
It is "liberation by perception" because it is released through the absence of the perception that the Sangha or others have received the dedication.
It is "bodily action" and "verbal action" because it is to be dedicated by means of bodily intimation and verbal intimation.
Commentary on the Story of Pariṇata.
The Third Chapter, the Section on the Bowl (Pattavagga).
888. The construction is: "Those who cross this determination cross the great ocean of conceptual designation. That which is designated as...
The Vinaya Piṭaka itself is like the great ocean; this refers to the "great ocean" as it is designated. Having thus shown the whole, he says "nekā" and so forth in order to show its parts.

The analysis (*viggha*) is: that which has many various observances (*vatta*), such as the observances regarding lodgings (*senāsana-vatta*) found in the Khandhaka, as its high, lofty, and surging garlands of waves and succession of great whirlpools.
[It is so called] because of the succession of great waves consisting of the various kinds of observances mentioned in the Khandhaka.
The meaning is "equipped. *Sīlanta*: that which has the boundary of the ocean (*velāvalaya*) as its limit (*anta*)—namely, virtue (*sīla*) such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha—is called *sīlanta*.
The meaning is that the fourfold purity of virtue, beginning with the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, constitutes the boundary and the oceanic rim because it is that which must be practiced.
The offenses (*āpatti*) are the seven classes of offenses; and the transgressions of virtue, conduct, view, and livelihood are the seizing creatures, such as crocodiles and the like.

The analysis of the compound is *yassa* (of whom). The meaning is: "one who possesses the 'gentle beings' consisting of the perfection of virtue, conduct, livelihood, and view, and who possesses the 'fierce beings' such as crocodiles and monsters consisting of the failure of those [same] factors.
Thus, it should be understood that this verse is composed using the figure of speech (*rūpakālaṅkāra*) for both the whole and all its parts.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the Nissaggiya offenses in the *Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā*,
which is an elucidation of the essential meaning of the Vinaya.
Commentary on the Pācittiya Rules:

889. Having thus shown the determination of the Nissaggiya rules by way of neither excessive detail nor brevity, [the author] now begins the section beginning with "in intentional lying" (*sampajānamusāvāde*) in order to show the determination of the Pācittiya section (*kaṇḍa*) which was indicated immediately following that.

Regarding "knowingly speaking falsehood" (*sampajānamusāvāda*): the meaning should also be understood as the act of speaking falsely by one who knows the falsity of their own words, knowing through such modes as "what was not seen was seen," and so forth. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"In the case of speaking falsely by one who knows, having known. For in the phrase "in speaking falsehood" (*musāvāde*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; thus, the meaning is "on account of speaking falsehood."

The construction is: "of one who speaks falsely" (*davā bhaṇantassa*). The meaning is: of one who, without investigating, says out of impetuosity regarding even what has been seen, "It was not seen by me.
As it is said in the *Padabhājanīya-aṭṭhakathā*: "To speak falsely means to speak impulsively"; and in the commentary on that phrase:
"To speak impulsively means to speak without examining or reflecting, saying out of haste, 'It was not seen by me,' even though it was seen."

"Speaking distractedly" means speaking something else because of dullness or delusion, intending to say one thing but saying another—just as one who wishes to say "robe" (cīvara) might say "tattered cloth" (cīra).
As it is said: "One speaks distractedly when, intending to say one thing, one says another. 890. "In another matter" refers to the fourth *pārājika* offense and so forth.
[Claiming] a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) not attained by oneself as "attained"—
If one speaks falsely, saying "I have [done this]" to someone who hears it at that very moment and understands its meaning, there is a *pārājika* offense;

if the meaning is not understood at that time but is understood later, or if it is understood through indirect speech (*pariyāyavacana*), there is a *thullaccaya* offense; if it is understood through indirect speech but not directly, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense;

and for one who has not committed a *pārājika* under the rule concerning corrupting faults (*duṭṭhadosasikkhāpada*) but speaks falsely, saying "I have committed it," there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.

Since both the offense of intentional lying and the offense of frivolous speech are mentioned in the training rule on malicious speech (*omasavāda-sikkhāpada*), it is said: "There are five offenses as causes for lying.
Together with this *pācittiya*, there are six classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of intentional lying.

891-3. The construction is: "among the ten bases of abuse stated [in the Sutta] beginning with birth. The meaning is: among the ten bases of abuse stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) by way of abuse concerning birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, illness, gender, defilement, and offenses.

Among these, excluding defilement, all of them are of two kinds according to whether they are inferior or superior. As it is said in the word-commentary: "Birth means two types of birth: inferior birth and superior birth," and so forth.
In this context, the castes of the *caṇḍāla* and so forth are low, while the castes of the *khattiya* and *brāhmaṇa* are high.

Among names, names such as *Avakaṇṇaka* and *Javakaṇṇaka*, which are merely slave-names, are low; names such as *Buddharakkhita* and so forth are high. The lineage of *Kosiya* and so forth is low, while the lineage of *Gotama* and so forth is high.
Among occupations, the work of carpenters, jewelers, and so forth is low, while the work of agriculture, trade, and cattle-herding is high.
Regarding crafts: the crafts of reed-workers, potters, and so forth are inferior; the crafts of arithmetic, calculation, and so forth are superior. Regarding diseases: all diseases are inferior;
however, diabetes (madhumeha) is superior because it does not produce [intense] affliction. Regarding physical characteristics: being excessively tall and so forth are inferior;

not being excessively tall and so forth are superior. All defilements (*kilesa*) are inferior. All offenses (*āpatti*) are also inferior; however, the attainment of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-samāpatti*)—[is superior].
*Ukkaṭṭhā* (superior). Regarding insults: "You are a camel, you are a ram, you are an ox," and so forth, is inferior; "You are wise, you are competent," and so forth, is superior.
*Aññatraññāpadesena* means without figurative speech. *Omasantassa* means of one who pierces with the goad of words.
*Sambuddhena pakāsitā* refers to [the Buddha] saying, "You are a caṇḍāla, you are a weaver, you are a hunter, you are a cartwright, you are a scavenger."

"An offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every single word spoken. This was taught by the Blessed One, who is designated as "the Fully Enlightened One" (Sambuddha) because of his personal realization of all phenomena.

894. "By those very same [grounds]" means by those very grounds of abuse such as birth and so forth. The connection is that for one who abuses an unordained person using other designations—whether true...
pe ...or even if it is an offense already incurred—the offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) has been proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One. Here, the terms refer to both what is true and what is untrue.
The words beginning with *tehi* should be construed as plural forms, referring back [to those previously mentioned].

By this, it should be understood that while the second section beginning with “There are some here” (*santi idhekacce*) demonstrates the establishment of the *dukkaṭa* offense, the third section—which shares the same function—and the fourth section beginning with “They do not think so” (*na maññanti*), which constitutes the deficiency-section, are also included. As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): “There are some here...”

But in the section [beginning with] "having avoided," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because of the fact that it has already been stated. This same method applies to the sections beginning with "Is it not that... and "...we do not.
Regarding the phrase "even by means of words outside the Canon" (*pāḷimuttapadehi*): here too, the phrases "whether by truth" (*bhūtena vā*) and so forth should be connected in the same way.
An example of a phrase outside the Canon is: "You are a thief! You are a cutpurse! "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in all four sections.

And regarding passages outside the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*), it is indeed stated: “In the case of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in all four instances.
However, by means of such words as ‘You are a thief! or ‘You are a cutpurse!’, there is only an offense of wrong-doing in every instance, whether the person is fully ordained or not.
By the term “one who is not fully ordained,” [it is meant] that in this training rule, setting aside the *bhikkhu*, all others—*bhikkhunīs* and so forth—are included.
“Beings standing in a place where they have not received full ordination”—thus those who have not received full ordination are included as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For this very reason, it will be said here as well: “Having entered a place where they have not received full ordination, and here [in this case] a bhikkhunī.
895. Regarding the term *davakamyatā*: here, as in the expressions “reflecting thoroughly” (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*) and so forth, there is an elision of the letter *ya*. “In all cases” (*sabbattha*).

"In all cases" means in all instances, both among the stated bases for *pācittiya* offenses and among the bases for *dukkaṭa* offenses. "An ill-spoken word is uttered" means that when one says, "You are a Caṇḍāla...
[and so on] ...you are a Pukkusa," it is stated: "For every single utterance, there is an offense of *dubbhāsita*.
However, when one reviles someone in their absence by means of the bases for *pācittiya* or *dukkaṭa* offenses, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Likewise, the teachers say that even for one who speaks behind another’s back out of a desire for sport, it is indeed a *dubbhāsita* (ill-spoken word).

896–7. The construction is: “There is no offense for a bhikkhu who speaks with the meaning (*attha*) in mind. “Dhamma” refers specifically to the canonical text (*pāḷi*), such as “You are a caṇḍāla,” and so forth.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “One who recites the *pāḷi* has the Dhamma in mind. “Instruction” (*anusāsanī*) means “even now... [and so on].
For one who speaks with the primary intention of instruction—using the very same form of words as those stated in the Commentary, such as “You are a caṇḍāla;
do not commit an evil deed; do not go from darkness to darkness”—there is no offense even if anger should arise in the interim, because of the mind’s state of rapid transformation.
"Herein" means in this training rule concerning slanderous speech (*omasavāda*). Because it must be committed with a mind associated with aversion (*paṭigha*), there is only mental painful feeling.

This concludes the commentary on the discussion of slanderous speech. 898. The construction is: "In two ways, there may be an offense in the case of a monk’s malicious tale-bearing (*pesuñña*). It is called *pisuṇā* because it "grinds" (*pisati*) [the harmony]; it is speech [that grinds] those who are in concord.
The meaning is that he causes a division among beings who constitute a single group. *Pisuṇā* (slanderous) is itself *pesuñña* (slander);
a person endowed with such speech is "slanderous" (*pisuṇo*) by way of association, and his action is *pesuñña*. "Slander of monks" (*bhikkhupesunña*) means the slander of monks;
[it refers to] in that slander of monks. In the word-commentary: "One who is fully ordained, having heard from one who is fully ordained..."
Because it is stated: “If one, being fully ordained oneself, brings about slander against another who is fully ordained, saying, ‘So-and-so calls you an outcaste...

[and so on] ...a Pukkusa,’ there is an offense... [and so on] ...of *pācittiya*,” then having heard another who is fully ordained insulting someone else—being fully ordained oneself—behind that person's back by means of any one of the ten grounds for abuse such as birth and so forth, [one incurs an offense].
Having gone into his presence, based on either of the two reasons— namely, one's own desire for affection or the intention to cause division—
as will be described in form, one brings slander by saying, "So-and-so says this to you.
The meaning is that for the purpose of speaking such slander, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Regarding the phrase "in two ways" (*duvidhākāro*): here, the word *ākāra* is a synonym for "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

As it says in the Commentary: "In two ways means by two causes. Here, "cause" refers to a specific intention. To show that cause by way of its intention, he said "of one who desires his own [favor]," and so forth.
"Of one who desires his own favor" means of one who desires to be dear to himself; [it is] slander (*pesuñña*).
"Of one who speaks" means of one who desires his own dearness; that is to say, with such an intention.
As it is said in the Commentary: "Of one who aspires to his own dearness, thinking, 'In this way I shall become dear to him.
"And also of one who desires the division of others" refers to both the slanderer and the one who hears his own slanderous words.
The meaning is: "of one who desires the schism of both," which is to say, "with the intention of causing a schism. As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"Of one who desires the schism of another by means of another. 899. The construction is:
for one who insults by way of figurative expression (*pariyāya*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [this refers to] speech that is insulting by way of figurative expression.
The meaning is that for a monk who, having heard [the report], goes into the presence of another and speaks [thus], there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. As it was said:
“‘A certain person here says that some outcasts... he does not say anything else;
he says that very thing’—for every word, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*,” and so forth. This refers to the speech of one who reviles according to the method set forth in the *Pāḷimutta*.
The construction is: "it is an *dukkaṭa* offense. Here, the method called "the way apart from the Canon" (*pāḷimuttanaya*) is shown by such statements as, "You are a thief!
You are a cutpurse! [Rule 900]. The construction is that it is likewise an *dukkaṭa* offense for one who conveys a verbal abuse directed at a person not fully ordained to a person fully ordained;

and by the word "and" (*ca*), it includes the case where one conveys a verbal abuse directed at a person fully ordained to a person not fully ordained, and where one conveys a verbal abuse directed at a person not fully ordained to a person not fully ordained.

The phrase "even for one who takes [it] away" likewise combines two alternatives, namely *dukkaṭa*. From the commentarial statement, "In this case as well, starting with the nun, all those who are not fully ordained are called 'anupasampannā'," the term "nun" (*bhikkhunī*) is used as an illustrative example (*upalakkhaṇa*). 901.
"And not for one desiring affection" means for one not desiring a state of affection. "Nor even for one seeking a schism" means for one seeking a division.

"And for one who does not wish [to speak]. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of censuring the wicked," the word "merely" (*kevalam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. As it is said in the Commentary:
"Having seen one person reviling and another being patient, if one speaks merely for the sake of censuring the evil—thinking, 'Oh, how shameless!
He thinks he can even speak again to such a venerable one'—there is no offense."
Commentary on the Discussion of Slanderous Speech (Pesuñña-kathā-vaṇṇanā).

903. “By another” means by a novice (sāmaṇera) or others. Because it is stated in the Word-Commentary (*padabhājana*) that “whatever word, whatever following word, whatever syllable, and whatever following phoneme—all this is called ‘by words’ (*padaso*)”—the term “the Three Piṭakas” (*piṭakattaya*) is used here by way of applying the name of the whole to its parts (*avayave samudāyopacāra*).

It should be understood that only a portion of such [a verse], beginning with a word (*pada*), is what is spoken of here. In this regard, the specific form of the words and so forth should be understood from the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For it is said there: "A 'word' (*pada*) is intended as one quarter-verse (*gāthāpāda*). A 'subsequent word' (*anupada*) is the second quarter-verse.
'Letter by letter' (*anvakkhara*) means each individual syllable (*akkhara*). 'Syllable by syllable' (*anubyañjana*) means a subsequent syllable that resembles the preceding syllable. This is...

This was said with reference to teaching consisting of verses (*gāthāmayadesanā*). It is also stated: "Whatever there may be, even a single syllable (*akkhara*) or each successive syllable; a collection of syllables is a phoneme (*anubyañjana*);

a collection of syllables and phonemes is a phrase (*pada*); the first phrase is simply a 'phrase' (*padam eva*), while the second is a 'subsequent phrase' (*anupada*)—in this way, the distinction here should be understood.
This, however, was said with reference to teaching in prose fragments (*cuṇṇiyadesanā*).

"Dhamma" refers to the canonical Dhamma spoken by the Buddha and so forth. For in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, within the "Fivefold Dhamma," even the canon itself is called "Dhamma. The "Fivefold Dhamma" is defined as follows:
the cause that produces the fruit, the Noble Path, what has been spoken, and the wholesome and unwholesome;
these are designated as "Dhamma. Here, "what has been spoken" refers to the canon (*pāḷi*). It also includes that which is based on the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
This is included right here. And that [text] should be understood as having been established previously in the Magadha language and recorded in the three councils.

Regarding the statement, "If one recites together, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," this refers to the manner found in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) such as, "Having begun together, they conclude together," which concerns the recitation of a word together with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Whether he speaks word by word, letter by letter, or syllable by syllable, it is stated that there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the counting of the words and so forth.

904. The construction is as follows: among those teachings not included in the *Saṅgīti*, the *Rājovāda* and other such discourses (*suttanta*) indeed give rise to an offense, as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries. The *Rājovāda* is one specific discourse; by the word "and others" (*ādi*), discourses such as the *Tikkhindriya* are included. 905.

For a monk who perceives another monk or a nun as not ordained, or for a monk who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) regarding the recitation of the words in that manner. This is the construction.

"906–7. *Ekato uddisāpetī* (causes to recite together): he causes [the student] to recite together with those who have not yet received full ordination (*anupasampanna*) by way of simultaneous vocalization. *Sajjhāyaṃ vā karoti* (or practices recitation): likewise, he practices recitation together. Regarding the phrase *paguṇagandhaṃ* (a text mastered by heart), according to the statement in the Commentary:
"If even one quarter of a single verse does not come [to mind], while the rest comes, this is called 'a text mastered by heart for the most part' (*yebhuyyena paguṇagandho*);
this same method is to be understood regarding the Suttas as well,'" it follows that here the word *yebhuyyena* (for the most part) refers to the mastery of the text.
The rest is clear. *Opāpeti* means he speaks from one side, saying, "Speak thus. *Uddesaṃ* means that which is to be recited. *Tenā* means by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). 908.

Since this training rule on the memorization of words (*padasodhamma*) arises from speech, and arises from both speech and mind, therefore the construction is: "This origin is called by the designation ‘memorization of words’.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the memorization of words.
909–10. Regarding a lodging that is entirely roofed and entirely enclosed:
the construction of the rule is as follows—"If a monk, having set aside another monk, should lie down at night for three nights, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him.
According to the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), "whatever is capable of providing concealment should here be understood as both 'roofed' (chadana) and 'enclosed' (paricchanna)."

Because it is stated [in the commentary] that a lodging is "completely covered" (*sabbacchanna*) when it is entirely roofed over with any material whatsoever— such as bricks, stone, plaster, grass, or leaves— it is "completely covered" by whatever means. Furthermore,
because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that it is "enclosed" (*parikkhitto*) from the ground up to the roof by a wall,
or by anything else, including even a cloth, it is [defined] by whatever means.
"Having surrounded it, a dwelling that is concealed is 'completely enclosed' (sabbaparicchanna).

Even if it is surrounded by a wall or the like reaching one and a half cubits in height at its lowest point, without touching the roof-covering, it is still 'completely enclosed'—so it is stated in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā;
this will be explained later with the words 'one and a half [cubits]' and so forth."
Thus, in a single dwelling that is entirely covered and entirely enclosed, whatever monk— having shared a sleeping place for three nights with another person,
whether one or many, subsequent to his full ordination— spends the fourth night and onwards, throughout all nights,
from the time of sunrise until the end of the entire night, either at the beginning, at the end, or continuously without interruption;

Regarding the rule that "if, after stretching out one's back, one makes one's bed on a single seat, there is a daily *pācittiya* offense for him," this regulation was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) as:
"Furthermore, in this case, even the fourfold set beginning with 'one dwelling' (*ekāvāsādi*) should be understood.
The meaning should also be understood by applying it in exactly the same way to the phrase "mostly covered and sheltered" (*yebhuyyena paricchanne channe*). [The text continues: "Of whom..."

However, when the upper part is mostly covered and only a little is uncovered, and it is mostly enclosed on all sides and only a little is unenclosed, this should be understood as "mostly covered and mostly enclosed" (*yebhuyyena-channaparicchanna*) according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The meaning is exactly as described. "Mostly... [The rest follows].
In the commentary on the phrase "paṃsukā," "the majority" refers to two out of three; however, here,
regarding the phrase "a text that is mostly mastered" in the commentary on the *padasodhamma*, it should be understood that "the majority" means three out of four,
as in the explanation beginning with "of even a single verse."

911. Regarding the phrase "having lain down with a person": the basis for sexual intercourse that was specified in the first *pārājika*—even if it be as small as an animal—is the same basis as that first *pārājika*.
The construction is: having lain down together with such a person, there is an offense of lying down together (*sahaseyyāpatti*).
912–3. As for the alternative "or both lie down," since its meaning has already been shown by the first two verses, [it is not repeated here].

In order to show that [the offense] may also occur by way of sequence (pubbāpariya), he says "when they have lain down," etc., to illustrate the two sides shown by the method beginning with "one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*).
"Having risen" (*uṭṭhahitvā*) is to be understood here as an iterative expression (*vicchā*).

"Even by the counting of those not fully ordained" (*anupasampannagaṇanāyapi vā*) means either by the counting of many non-ordained persons or by the counting of those [non-ordained persons] when there are many non-ordained persons.
By the statement, "A single bhikkhu has many offenses," it is also shown that when there are many who are ordained and one who is unordained,
there are many offenses to be incurred by them according to the count of their respective applications; and likewise,
when both groups are numerous, there are many offenses for each individual who is ordained according to the count of the unordained.
914. Because it must be used through a single door, even in a dwelling with one hundred rooms that has a single common area,
if one who is fully ordained stays in one room and sleeps on the fourth night in his own bed-chamber— whether he has closed the door or not—
the rule regarding the offense previously stated applies equally to those who are not fully ordained sleeping on the upper floor or in the remaining rooms.
He said, "If she covers herself," and so forth, for the purpose of clarification. By eliding the latter member of the compound, "womb-door" (gabbhadvāra) is expressed simply as "womb" (gabbha).

The construction is: "On the fourth day, when the sun has set, if she lies down, there may be an offense. The phrase "together with one who is not fully ordained" is understood from the context of the section. The offense is a *pācittiya*.
915. "By one and a half cubits high" means by one and a half *ratanas* (cubits) according to the measurement of a carpenter.
Thus, what is called a "wall" (*pākāra*) is finished. They also say that what is called a "mound" (*caya*) refers to a wall that is unfinished.

Furthermore, since the porch (*āḷinda*) is not included here, the *Aṭṭhakathā* is the authoritative standard [for this rule], stating: "Even a terrace (*jagati*) one cubit high does not count as part of the enclosure."
They say: "Jagatī" means a veranda (*āḷinda*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of walls, curtains, screens, and so forth is intended.
916. "Dussakuṭi" means a cloth-hut (*vatthakuṭi*). 917.
In the phrase "from the distinctions of 'completely covered,' 'partially covered,' etc., and from the distinctions of 'mostly,' etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) applies to each [term] individually.

It should be applied. By the first word "all" (*sabba*), four types of lodgings are included: those that are entirely covered, mostly covered, half-covered, and entirely enclosed; as well as those that are mostly covered, entirely enclosed, and half-covered.
Together with the "entirely covered" and "entirely enclosed" types explicitly mentioned by their own names in the verse, five types of lodgings are thus shown. By the second...

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), three types of lodgings are included: those mostly covered and mostly uncovered, those mostly covered and half-covered, and those mostly uncovered and half-covered. These eight permutations are possible.
Why, then, is it said that there are "seven *pācittiya* offenses"? Because it is stated so in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. As it says:
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "If it is entirely enclosed and mostly covered, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
if it is entirely enclosed and half-covered, there is an offense of expiation; if it is mostly enclosed and half-covered, there is an offense of expiation;

if it is entirely covered and mostly enclosed, there is an offense of expiation; if it is entirely covered and half-enclosed, there is an offense of expiation; if it is mostly covered and half-enclosed..."
“[In the case] of one half-covered, there is a *pācittiya*; together with the *pācittiya* stated in the *Pāḷi*, there are seven *pācittiya*s,” so it is said.
But why, after stating “eight *pācittiya*s” in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, was the numerical limit set at “seven”?
Without doubt, [the *Aṭṭhakathā* states]: “A ‘bed’ (*seyyā*) is one entirely covered and entirely enclosed, or mostly covered and mostly enclosed.”

Regarding the two alternative interpretations found in the Pāli, the resolution is shown by taking one of the stated *pācittiya* offenses and explaining that the term "seven" refers to the *pācittiya* mentioned in the Pāli itself.
Furthermore, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is stated: "The 'seven *pācittiyas*' are spoken of by taking the two *pācittiya* offenses mentioned in the Pāli as a single unit in a general sense;
however, if they were taken separately, [the number would differ] in the case of a completely enclosed [space]."

"The resolution stated is: 'If it is entirely covered, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); if it is mostly covered and mostly enclosed, there is an offense of expiation'—thus there are exactly eight offenses of expiation.
When the terms *sabba* (all), *yebhuyya* (most), and *upaḍḍha* (half) are joined with the terms *channa* (covered) and *paricchanna* (enclosed), nine permutations are possible.

Among those, since an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is shown in the ninth option—where the roof is half-covered and half-uncovered—by process of elimination (*pārisesato*), only the eight *pācittiya* offenses are possible in the remaining eight cases.

However, it should be understood that in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated as "seven" because a small amount that is either deficient or excessive does not count toward the required number. "In this" refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
918. The construction is: “half-covered, half-enclosed. The construction is respectively: “completely enclosed, slightly covered.
By this, having shown the third of the five alternatives found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) includes the remaining alternatives, such as “completely covered,” and so forth.
As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “completely covered, slightly enclosed.”

“There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); when it is mostly covered and slightly uncovered, there is an offense of wrong-doing; when it is entirely covered and slightly uncovered, there is an offense of wrong-doing;

when it is mostly covered and slightly uncovered, there is an offense of wrong-doing—it is said that there are five offenses of wrong-doing, including the offense of wrong-doing mentioned in the *Pāḷi*. As for the offense of wrong-doing mentioned in the *Pāḷi*, it is right at the beginning of this very verse.”
This is the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). As it has been said: "If it is half-covered and half-enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Furthermore, the minor coverings (*cūḷacchanna*) and so forth should be understood here as follows: that which is covered in one of its four parts while the remaining parts are uncovered is a "minor covering" (*cūḷakacchanna*).
That which is covered in two of its three parts while one part is uncovered is "mostly covered" (*yebhuyyenacchanna*).
When one of two parts [of a dwelling] is covered and the other is uncovered, this is called a "half-covered" lodging (*senāsana*).

The "small-covered" (*cūḷaparicchanna*) and other types should be understood according to this same method. In the phrase "by means of the covered, etc.," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment.
The particle *pi* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). [The term refers to] together with all four: the small-covered, the covered, and so forth, including the half-covered and half-enclosed.
The construction is: "the fivefold *dukkaṭa* is elucidated.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of one completely covered, etc.," here the word "etc.

includes the remaining cases of non-offense mentioned in the Canon as "completely covered, completely uncovered, mostly uncovered, mostly not covered," as well as those mentioned in the Commentary as "half-covered" (*upaḍḍhacchanne*).
By the phrase "covered with a canopy," "half-covered," "covered at the top," and "covered at the top and half-covered," three sections on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*) are included.

Regarding the phrase "even when he is lying down": here, the word "even" (*pi*) includes other modes mentioned in the Canon, such as "the monk is lying down while one not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) sits," or "both sit."
Commentary on the Discourse on Sleeping Together. 922.
By the word "even" (*api*), he shows that it is all the more so for one who is of greater seniority. "One should arrange sleeping together" means:
having entered a dwelling—such as one entirely covered or entirely enclosed—that possesses the characteristics already mentioned, from the time the sun sets onwards, [one should do so] before...
In the manner already described, one should prepare a bed characterized by having the back turned away [from another].
923–4. *Devī* means a female deity; *tiracchānagatitthī* means a female animal such as a monitor lizard (*godhā*).

By the phrase "one who has become the basis for sexual intercourse," he shows that there is no fault in sharing a bed with one who has not become the basis for the act of sexual intercourse. *Vatthūnaṃ gaṇanāyā* means...
"By the counting of women" means by the counting of those [women] and by the counting of one's own acts. "Assa" means of the bhikkhu.

Having committed an offense under this training rule by sharing a sleeping place with a woman for three days, on the fourth day, by sharing a sleeping place, he commits an offense under both training rules. Here, regarding the woman who constitutes the basis for the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) offense, right there...
It should be understood that by sharing a sleeping place on this training rule, having committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), on the fourth day at night, while sharing a sleeping place,
one commits a formal confession offense (pācittiya) together with the previous training rule, along with the offense of wrong-doing incurred under this training rule.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the second rule concerning sharing a sleeping place.
926. The connection is: "for one who speaks the Dhamma to a woman beyond five or six words. Regarding "to a woman":

"A woman" refers to a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, and not a female animal; she must be a human woman who is wise and capable of discerning what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, and what is grave and trivial—thus it is said in the Pāḷi. "Speaking" has the characteristic that will be explained below.
"Of one who speaks further on the Dhamma by way of six points": excluding a "wise person" (viññu) who is a human being—
meaning a male human being who has come within earshot as stated in the Pāḷi, "a wise person is capable of discerning what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, and what is grave and not grave"—
[and] "Dhamma" refers to the teaching-Dhamma whose specific nature will be explained below.

927. There are two kinds of teaching: that consisting of verses (*gāthāmaya*) and that consisting of prose (*cuṇṇiyaganthamaya*). Regarding these, in order to show that in the case of the teaching consisting of verses, "speech" (*vācā*) refers to the characteristics of the lines of a verse, he says, "a line of a verse" (*gāthāpādo*), and so forth. However, in the case of the prose teaching, the delimitation of speech should be understood by way of the case endings.
Therefore, it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "A single line of a verse" refers exclusively to the construction of a verse.
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*); however, in other instances, only the word ending in the case-suffix should be taken.

By the term "the Dhamma," which is explained as "the recitation of words" (*padasodhamma*), the Three Piṭakas are meant. By the term "the Commentary" (*aṭṭhakathā*), the ancient commentaries recorded in the three councils (*saṅgīti*) should be understood.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "The Commentary, as well as the stories (*vatthu*) of the *Dhammapada*, the *Jātaka*, and so forth."
They say that by this [statement] as well, it is indicated that the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) has been spoken exactly as it was entered into the ancient recitation (*saṅgīti*).
Apart from the reading of the commentaries and so forth, it is permissible to speak in other languages such as Tamil according to one's preference.
928. The construction is: "of one teaching the Dhamma over the six languages by means of the words (*pada*) and so forth. Regarding "desentassa": [it refers to the one who is teaching].
[The offense applies] to one who teaches the Dhamma beyond six sentences that are similar in form to the words and so forth characterized as being "spoken" (vutta-lakkhaṇa).
"By counting the words and so forth" means by counting the words, phrases, syllables, and phonemes as they have been described. 929.

"A human form" means the appearance of a human male. Here, "animals" refers to those possessing psychic power (*iddhimanta*), such as *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas*, who are capable of assuming various appearances.
931. *Vadatoti*: speaking further, that is, while he is discoursing on the Dhamma.
932. *Itthirūpan*ti: the appearance of a human woman. *Tiracchānagatitthiyā*ti: of a female animal of the specific kind already mentioned. 933. The connection is as follows:
there is no offense declared for one who, having himself stood up and sat down again, continues to teach the Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase "or likewise for a woman": here, by the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the specific manner already described is included;
thus, it is stated that there is no offense for one who, having risen, teaches the Dhamma again to a woman who is seated.
By the expression "having risen" and so forth, which demonstrates a change in posture, he indicates that there is no offense even when different postures are involved.

934. Regarding the phrase *aññissā puna aññissā* (“to another, and again to another”), the words *“āgatāgatāya”* (to each one as they arrive) are to be understood as the remainder. As it says in the Commentary:
“‘To another woman’ means that having taught to one, he then teaches to another who has arrived; thus, sitting on a single seat, he teaches even to a hundred thousand women.
And by the particle *ca*, which has the sense of including what was not explicitly stated, [it implies] “the question...”

This [phrase] "when asked, he speaks" summarizes the following: for one who asks the question, "Venerable sir, what is the purpose of the Dīgha Nikāya?", there is no offense even if she explains the entire Dīgha Nikāya to that woman. As it is said in the Commentary:
"He asks a question; when asked a question, he speaks"—referring to a woman who asks, "Venerable sir, what does that which is called the Dīgha Nikāya illustrate?"
“If he asks, and when thus questioned the bhikkhu recites even the entire Dīghanikāya, there is no offense.
And here, “if he recites even the entire Dīghanikāya” means that he continues to recite even on the following day until it is finished.
This is a *kriyākriya* (offense through action and non-action) because it is an offense incurred both by teaching the Dhamma and by not remaining present for a person who understands.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching of the Dhamma. 936.
"Exalted" refers to the fine-material and immaterial jhānas. "Sublime" refers to the supramundane Dhamma. It is called "sublime" because it has been brought to a state of excellence.
"Of one proclaiming" means [proclaiming] in the manner of the fourth Pārājika: "I enter the first jhāna," and so forth.

For one who speaks in the manner already described. And because it must be announced to monks and nuns at the time of their own parinibbāna and when they are questioned regarding the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) attained by themselves, it is said: "Except for a nun, [it may be told] to a monk.
The word "to another" (aññassa) is the remainder [of the phrase]. As it is said in the Commentary: "One announces what is true to one who is fully ordained; that is, only the superhuman state."

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For at the time of his final *parinibbāna*, it was permitted for one who had been ordained—even if being dragged along—to report what had actually occurred.
Regarding the word "actually" (*bhūte*), it should be understood as "when superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) have been reported";

here the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). The meaning is: "on account of the reporting of superhuman states accomplished within one's own continuum in this present existence."

937. "If he does not know what was said" means that the person to whom one reports it does not know, at the very moment of hearing, what was said according to the method described, such as "this person is an attainer of the first jhāna," and so forth.
"In figurative speech" refers to figurative expressions such as "he who dwells in this monastery is an attainer of the first jhāna. Regarding "whomsoever's superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)..."

The connection is as follows: if, immediately after hearing it, the monk does not know that "this person spoke thus," then for the monk who reports it to such a person, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The construction is: "And when reporting a true matter by means of a figurative expression, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk."

938. "When such a cause exists" means when there exists a cause characterized by the recognition of another's causal status, as well as by the functions of demonstrating the fruitfulness of practice, providing encouragement, and offering praise.
"Of everyone" refers to everyone, whether ordained or unordained. "Virtue and so forth" refers to the qualities of virtue, learning, and mastery of the scriptures.
Regarding the word "speaking," the term "monk" is understood here from the context of the treatise.
939. "Because of the impossibility of that": because madness and so forth are impossible for one endowed with right view (*diṭṭhisampanna*). As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"For those endowed with right view, there is an absence of madness or mental derangement. This has also been examined in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
By stating the reason for not including the term "insane" (*ummattaka*), the reason for not including the terms "mentally deranged" (*khittacitta*) and so forth is also stated.

It should be understood that this has been shown by way of illustration. Furthermore, it must be seen that only for Noble Ones (ariya) who possess the vision of the Path and its Fruit is there no state of madness or similar conditions.
However, for those who have attained meditative absorption (jhāna), if such a state occurs, they fall away from that absorption;
therefore, in their case, it should be said that there is no offense on account of reporting what is untrue, but not on account of reporting what is true.

940. Since this offense is impossible for anyone other than those who have attained the jhānas, paths, and so forth, it is stated that "there are two types of consciousness: wholesome and indeterminate.
Furthermore, this is said with reference specifically to noble persons (ariyapuggala) by way of the highest possible limit.

However, worldlings (puthujjana) who have attained jhāna but do not know the formal designation (paṇṇatti) may, through greed, [commit an offense] even with an unwholesome mind regarding various objects.
It is not that they do not declare [the three types of consciousness]; therefore, it might be said that there are "three consciousnesses.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated because, for the most part, only wholesome and indeterminate [consciousness] are possible [in this context]. The two feelings are by way of pleasure and equanimity.

Furthermore, this training rule (sikkhāpada) arises without consciousness (acittaka-samudhāna) due to ignorance of the formal rule (paṇṇatti). And herein, the Noble Ones (ariya), knowing the formal rule, [do not commit] a transgression.
Ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), however, even though they know the formal designation (*paṇṇatti*), commit transgressions.
It should be understood that because of the powerful unwholesome state of the volition (*cetanā*) that transgresses the Teacher’s injunction, they fall away from the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
This concludes the commentary on the account of the announcement of what has occurred.

941. The construction is as follows: for a monk who reveals a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*) to one who is not fully ordained, setting aside the authorization of the Saṅgha, there is an offense for that monk. "A grave offense" refers to a *saṅghādisesa*.

But is it not the case that, according to the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), "grave offenses are the four *pārājikas* and the thirteen *saṅghādisesas*," thus including both *pārājikas* and *saṅghādisesas*?
It has been shown [that both offenses are included], so why is only the *saṅghādisesa* taken here? It is said:

the *pārājika* was mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the term *duṭṭhulla* (grave offense), but it has been discussed in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that here the Blessed One intended only the *saṅghādisesa*.
For it is stated there: "The *pārājikas* were mentioned for the purpose of showing the meaning of the term *duṭṭhulla*; the *saṅghādisesa*..."
"But here, that which is intended [is different]. And he will say: "In this context, only the *saṅghādisesa* offenses are considered grave offenses (*duṭṭhulla-apatti*).

Regarding the term "one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*), it means "informing one who is designated as 'not fully ordained' in the word-commentary as 'anyone remaining after excluding both a bhikkhu and a bhikkhunī. This is what is meant.

“Except for the authorization of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus” means: as shown in the word-commentary with the passage, “There is an authorization of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus that has a limit regarding offenses but no limit regarding families,” it refers to the offenses of a bhikkhu who commits them frequently—
whether those offenses, the lay families, or both are delimited or undelimited— for the sake of future restraint and for the sake of generating shame and moral dread.
It means that after the Saṅgha has made the formal authorization (sammuti) by announcing it three times in the midst of the Saṅgha, [the procedure] is established.

As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Upon seeing a monk who repeatedly commits offenses, thinking, 'In this way he will attain restraint for the future through shame and fear of wrongdoing toward others,' the Saṅgha should perform [this act] after seeking permission three times out of a desire for that monk's welfare."
942. Regarding the phrase *ghaṭetvā vadantasseva* (“speaking while having joined [the parts]”), the particle *eva* should be applied to its proper place.
He will explain the meaning excluded by that *eva*-particle with the words beginning with “the basis” (*vatthu*). By the phrase “having emitted semen,” he states the basis;

by the phrase “an offense entailing suspension” (*saṅghādisesa*), he states the offense. “Fault” (*vajja*) is simply the state of being faulty. “An offense of expiation” (*pācittiya-āpatti*) is another synonym for this. “This [is] semen...”

The construction is as follows: for one who speaks of an offense by connecting it with the basis [of the case], saying, “Having confessed [the previous offense], he has fallen into a *saṅghādisesa*,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (*vajjā*) which is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). 943.

“Of one who is pure” means of one who has not fallen into a *pārājika*. “They speak” means on account of speaking; the meaning is: because of stating a *saṅghādisesa* together with the basis [of the case].

944. *Aduṭṭhullāya* means: other than an offense involving a *saṅghādisesa*. *Duṭṭhullasaññino* means: those who perceive it as a *saṅghādisesa*. *Sesā āpattiyo pi vā* means: the remaining six classes of offenses, excluding the *saṅghādisesa*. 945.

*Tathā* extends the application to the *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). The construction is: for one who reports a grave transgression (*duṭṭhulla ajjhācāra*) that is considered fivefold for one not fully ordained, there is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. "A grave transgression considered fivefold for one not fully ordained" means: [the five types of grave transgressions].
And the transgressions of the five training rules, beginning with the destruction of life, are included. Some, however, say that "the five beginning with the emission of semen" are meant;
that should not be accepted. For only ten training rules, beginning with the destruction of life, have been prescribed for novices.

And the consideration of what constitutes a grave or non-grave offense must be made only regarding those training rules that have been prescribed, and not regarding the emission of semen and so forth.
"They have separate designations for each.

Now, what indeed are the offenses such as the emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) and so forth—reckoned as grave matters (*duṭṭhulla*) for a monk—when committed against one who is not fully ordained?
They are called "transgressions" (*ajjhācāra*). As it is said in the Commentary: "The emission of semen... [and so on] ...is a transgression."
...is what is meant by ‘named. By this also it is established that for one who is not fully ordained, the emission of semen and so forth is not called ‘grave’ (*duṭṭhulla*).

For when he says, “It is called ‘transgression’ (*ajjhācāra*),” he indicates that while for one who is not fully ordained the emission of semen and so forth is merely a transgression, it is not a grave transgression. “Transgression...”

Because it is stated as "names" in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), and because they are not of a nature to be performed [by one who is ordained], the emission of semen and so forth by one who is unordained fall under the category of matters for disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*).

And they say that a monk who reports these to another unordained person out of a desire to disparage him incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, here, by the mention of "unordained," one should understand the inclusion of male novices (*sāmaṇera*), female novices (*sāmaṇerī*), and trainees (*sikkhamānā*).
The construction is: "a non-gross offense of transgression. And the words "of one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampannassa*) are to be supplied [from the preceding context].

This refers to either a non-gross offense of transgression, such as eating at the wrong time (*vikālabhojana*), or any other [offense] besides the five training rules already mentioned for one who is not fully ordained.
As it is said: "A gross or non-gross offense of transgression for one who is not fully ordained," and so forth.
"Of one who reports only the basis" means: of one who reports merely the basis in such a manner as, "This person has committed an emission of semen," and so forth.

"Or of one who reports only the offense" means: of one who reports merely the offense in such a manner as, "This person has committed a *pārājika*, this person has committed a *saṅghādisesa*, and so forth. "By the authorization of the bhikkhus" means:

In this context, it should be understood as "one who confesses an offense by connecting it with the basis. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the phrase "there is no offense" (*anāpatti*) is referred to.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the confession of grave matters. 948.

Regarding the phrase "improper earth," the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) first enumerates: "There are two kinds of earth: earth that has been formed (*jātā*) and earth that has not yet been formed (*ajātā*). Then—

“‘Born earth’ means earth that is pure soil, pure clay, with little stone, little gravel, little pebbles, little sand, and little grit; it is mostly soil and mostly clay. Even earth that has not yet been burnt is called ‘born earth.
And even a heap of soil or a heap of clay that has lain for more than four months is also called ‘born earth. Thus it was said.
“Unborn earth” means earth that consists of pure rock, pure gravel, pure pebbles, pure sand, and pure grit;
it has little soil and very little dust, being for the most part rock, for the most part gravel, for the most part pebbles, for the most part sand, and for the most part grit.
Even when burnt, it is called unborn earth. Also, a heap of dust or a heap of clay...
Or, if it has been covered for less than four months—this too is called "earth that has not yet arisen.
Thus, among the two types of earth specified, this refers to the unallowable earth known as "arisen earth.
Regarding the characteristics of stones and so forth here, the Commentary states: "Stones should be understood as those exceeding the size of a fist."
"Gravel the size of a fist," "potsherds" means fragments of broken vessels, "marumba" means coarse gravel, and "sand" means sand itself;
this should be understood according to the method already stated. Regarding the characteristics of soil and so forth that are "mostly soil":
"mostly soil" means that out of three portions, two portions are soil and one portion is any one of the categories such as stones; and "even if not burnt... [and so on].

It should be understood from the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) as follows: "It was not burnt in such and such ways by means of [being used for] a hearth, a cooking pan, a potter’s kiln, a sowing pit, and so forth.

Regarding the two phrases "little dust" (*appapaṃsu*) and "little soil" (*appamattikā*), the pentad of terms beginning with "mostly stone" (*yebhuyyena pāsāṇādi*) is stated in the form of a *niddesa* (exegesis).
Even there, the meaning should be understood according to the inversion of the order found mostly in the terms beginning with "dust" (*paṃsu*). As it has been said:
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it says: "This is merely a demonstration of the subdivisions of those same two [types of earth].
"Or he should dig" means that he himself digs such an improper area of ground, even if only with his big toe or a broom-stick.
"Or he should have it dug" means that he causes another to dig by means of improper speech, such as saying, "Dig this," and so forth.
"Should have it dug up. "Should have it broken up" means he should have it broken up in that same manner. Or "he should break it up" means he might also break it up with urine, water, and so forth.
