Alternatively, since the word *vā* (or) can be connected with all the verbs by virtue of its governing function (*adhikāra*), the word *ca* (and) in the phrase "should have it broken up" (*bhedāpeyya ca*) serves as a conjunction for the two phrases not explicitly mentioned here: "he burns it" (*dahati*) and "he has it burned" (*dahāpeti*).

It should be understood. Even regarding the cooking of a mere alms-bowl, whether one burns it oneself or causes another to burn it—this and so forth should be understood by means of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on these words.
"There may be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)" means that for one who digs or breaks [the earth], there is an offense of expiation for every blow.

949. Regarding the statement, "For one who causes [it] to be dug, it is according to the number of commands; for one who burns [it], it is according to the number of times the fire touches," this should be understood by way of the commentary’s (Aṭṭhakathā) words, "For every blow, there is a *pācittiya* offense," and so forth.
To demonstrate this very point, he said, "If he himself," and so on.

950. "Causing to be dug" means causing it to be dug once. 951. He stated, "One should have it dug; dig a lotus pond," and so forth, in order to show an exception (*apavāda*) to the general statement (*sāmaññavacana*).

Regarding the statement, "No fault is found," the intention is that there is no offense because words such as *pokkharaṇī* (lotus pond) and *āvāṭa* (pit) do not function as synonyms for "earth" (*pathavī*). 952.

Because the phrases beginning with "this here" denote the intended ground as something directly perceived, he says "this" and so forth to show that the very same application, when joined with those [words], constitutes an offense.
953. *Kandanti* refers to the bulbous root of the *tāla* palm and other such plants. *Kurundanti* refers to the *kulacoca* tree. *Thūṇanti* refers to a pillar or post.
*Khāṇukanti* refers to a portion of a tree devoid of branches and foliage. *Mūlanti* refers to that part of the tree which causes it to be firmly established in the earth.
*Vaṭṭatīti* means "it is permissible"; because there is no offense due to the statement being made without specifying [the particular type], it is permissible.

954. Having established this by means of the phrase "misapprehension through direct perception," he says, "It is an offense because it is spoken [as such]," adding, "But it is not permissible to speak after having made a restriction.

955. "To pour out with jars" means to take up water with jars and pour it out. "Thin mud" refers to *jambāla* (mud). It should be construed as: "It is not permissible for a bhikkhu to remove thick mud. 956. Regarding the phrase "of rivers, etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) includes the Gaṅgā, mountain caves, and so forth. This is to be connected with the word "bank" (*taṭa*).
"Vaṭṭhati" means it is permissible even if it has been submerged by rains. "Cātumāsaṃ" is the accusative case used in connection with the action of breaking [the boundary] to express duration;
the meaning is that it is permissible to break it within the four-month period. 957.
The construction is: "If it falls into the water, it is permissible," meaning if the bank breaks and falls into the interior of the water.
“Even when it has rained” means even when the rain-god Pajjunna has rained. The word *vuṭṭha* functions as a term for the agent. The construction is: “even when four months have elapsed.
In that regard, he says, “For the god rains upon the water,” in order to show the reason.
958. “A *soṇḍī*” is a stone lotus-pool. “Therein” means in that dry pit of the *soṇḍī*.
959. The construction is: "to clear and to break" (*sodhetuṃ bhindituṃ*).
By bringing the object-phrase "dust" (*rajaṃ*) and connecting it with the action-phrases "to clear," "to break," and "to disturb," the meaning should be understood.

When the rain falls upon that mass of dust, because the water has subsequently ceased, even though the ground has become thick and dry, within the four-month period starting from the day the rain fell—
The meaning is that it is proper to disturb or break [the rain-cloud].
960. The construction is: "When the *soṇḍi* (water-channel) is full, it is proper to disturb that dust after four months have passed.
961. By means of the word "phusāyante," one should transform the word "devo" (god/rain) according to its locative sense as "deve phusāyante" (while the god rains).
It should be joined [to the previous context]; the meaning is: "when the rain-god Pajjunna causes a downpour. *Piṭṭhipāsāṇake* means on the surface of a rock.
*Tampi* refers to that dust which has likewise adhered to the surface of the rock. 962.

*Akatapabbhāro* is a portion of a mountain situated so that its lower part is not moistened by rain-drops; it stands tilted in such a way. This is an illustration of anthills that have arisen in a place sheltered from the rain (*anovassaka*).
963. The connection is as follows: if an anthill that has arisen in the open air is covered over, for how many months is it permissible to disturb it?

"For four months" (*cātumāsam*) is used in the accusative case to express the duration of the action of disturbing. The word "tree" (*rukkhe*) is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) for pillars, stones, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "ants and so forth," black ants, termites, and others are included. That method [is as follows]: from the day it was covered...
The method as stated is that it is permissible to repair [a dwelling] within the subsequent four-month period.
964. "Mūsikukkira" means dust dug up by mice; the analysis of the compound is: the scattering (*ukkira*) of mice is "mūsikukkira.
"Gokaṇṭaka" means the clay raised up by the hooves of cattle. "Gaṇḍuppādamala" means the clay from the surface of the ground.
However, it is permissible to take [the soil] from the top without disturbing the natural ground. 965.
*Kasī* means a ploughed area; the clay dug up there by the plough is *kasinaṅgalamattikā*.

By the word "uncut" (*acchinnā*), he speaks in order to dispel the suspicion that even a layer of clay remaining as a long strip, having been broken into pieces, might still be considered "unborn earth."
“Connected with the ground”: this refers to the clay from the site of the meditation object (kasiṇa). 966.

Regarding “lodging,” the word “old” (*purāṇa*) should be understood as a textual supplement here. The construction is: “One should not disturb what has been plastered after four months have passed. 967.
“From there” means starting from the day it was plastered, [referring to] a house that has exceeded the four-month period. By the word “rafter” (*gopānasi*),...
This indicates that there is no offense even when the dust of an ant-hill situated at the top of a rafter collapses.

By the term "wall," it refers to the wooden parts such as the wall-footings which constitute a portion of that wall. This too is stated with reference to the clay of the wall and the clay of the ant-hill.
By the term "pillar," this likewise refers to the dust of the clay from the surrounding enclosure, the ground, the ant-hills, and so forth, associated with it.
It has been said. "A floor-covering" (*padarattha*) means a floor that has already been laid. This too is said with reference to the layer of clay, plaster, or dust upon the floor-boards.
The words beginning with "rafters" (*gopānasi*) should each be construed individually with the phrase "I shall take.
By the phrase "I shall take," he indicates the absence of any intention to disturb [the structure].

968. Regarding the phrase "of one who takes": here the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). The words "with a pure mind" (*suddhacittena*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the reading.
"Bricks" (*iṭṭhakā*) refers to roofing bricks. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), stones, sea-foam, and so forth are included. "Falls":
the meaning is that if, while one is taking it with a pure mind, the clay breaks off and falls, there is no offense. "Clay" refers to [clay used for] a wall or a roof.
And regarding the clay for the floor that has been soaked for more than four months: if it has not been soaked, it is permissible to take it. As it is said in the Commentary:
"If one takes whatever [clay] has not been soaked, there is no offense. The construction is: "If one takes it, there may be an offense.
(969) "Not soaked" means not soaked by rainwater; by this, he shows the object to be determined. Within his own house...
And in order to show the determination for one standing within the house as opposed to outside, he said, "If it should be within the house.
To first show that which is not soaked among two mounds of clay, both of which have been moistened by rainwater, he said, "and unsoaked. 970.
To show the determination regarding that which has been soaked by rainwater, he said, "But when it has rained," and so forth. "When it has rained" means...
By changing the word “mattikāpuñjo” (a heap of clay) here to the locative case, it should be connected with “vuṭṭhe mattikāpuñje” (when the heap of clay has rained upon).
The phrase “even for a single day” is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase “gehasmiṃ” (in a house), the word “ṭhite” (standing) should be supplied;
thus, it means that when the heap of clay is standing in the house, it becomes soaked by rainwater even for a single day. According to the method to be explained later, having struck it elsewhere...
Having risen, one should understand that [the robe] is "wet" by the raindrops that have fallen straight down after soaking it.
The construction is: "If it is entirely wet. This connects with the phrase "a heap of clay.
To show the determination regarding a case where only a portion is wet—which is excluded by the qualifier "entirely"—he says: 971. [The following].
“*Yattaka*,” etc. The word *tu* (but/however) highlights this very distinction. *Yattaka* means as much as the measure [of the clay] from the top down, not going further down, and from the boundary.
*Tattha* means in the heap of clay. To the term “*akappiya*” (unallowable), the phrase “after the lapse of four months” is supplied by way of ellipsis.
By the phrase “*atintaṃ…pe… kappiyaṃ*,” one avoids the unallowable state, or [one acts] through those who make it allowable (*kappiyakāraka*).
The meaning shown here is that, having had [the food] brought by means of a permissible statement (*kappiya-vacana*), one may use it as desired in a place where it has not been cooked.
As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "By the preparers of what is permissible" (*kappiyakārakehi*), and so forth.
972. *Vārinā* means by rainwater falling directly from the sky; it does not refer to water that has fallen there after being splashed elsewhere.
It is permissible to moisten it. That refers to the mound of clay. "Beyond that" means:

if, after the time when it has become a single solid mass, that mound of clay is moistened with water and becomes one with the ground, then beyond that point it is simply earth that has been produced;
it is not permissible to disturb it—this is the construction of the sentence.

By the word “enclosed” (*ovaṭṭha*), he shows by way of contrast that what is not enclosed is permissible (*kappiya*). By the qualifying term “made of clay” (*mattikāmaya*), he excludes walls made of bricks and the like;
his statement of its permissibility will follow with the words “if it is a wall of bricks,” etc.
By the phrase “at the end of four months,” he shows that within that period it may be disturbed.
974. *Tattha* means in the enclosed clay wall. *Aghaṃsanto vā* means without disturbing the clay of the wall.
*Mattaso chupitvā* means having touched it slightly, that is, having placed the palm of the hand there after making it soft according to measure.
*Allahatthena* means with the palm of the hand moistened with water; "hand" refers to one part of the hand.

975. “On a site mostly consisting of gravel” means, according to the method previously stated, on a suitable plot of earth where two out of three parts consist of gravel. 976. Regarding “in the open air”:
because this is an indicative term (*upalakkhaṇa*), it should be understood that even within a house, it is not permissible to disturb the earth by moving a pillar.
In both these places, one must remain free from fault through a pure mind, as has been described.
He spoke according to this method: "With the perception, 'I shall take a pillar or a stone slab,' it is permissible to take them.
"Earth" refers to unallowable earth. 977.
The construction is: "There is no fault for one who pulls it up straight."
"Having lifted up" means having raised, moved, and turned over. "It rolls" means that having rolled it here and there, one carries it away;
this is the meaning. "Of one with a pure mind" refers to one who, without observing that "the ground is breaking," possesses a pure mind thinking, "I will carry it away by rolling it over and over."
979. The construction is: “even for one splitting wood on the ground, or dragging branches and such like on the ground.
980. *Kaṇṭaka* means either a tree-thorn or a fish-bone. A *sūci* (needle) is any one among needles made of iron, ivory, copper, wood, and so forth.
*Aṭṭhiṃ vā* means a bone of cows, buffaloes, and the like. *Hīraṃ vā* means a coconut-shell or similar shell. *Ākoṭetuṃ* means to strike.
"Just as one enters the earth at a single point, so too [should one] strike it. "To cause to enter" means to cause to go into the earth. 981. "Urine" (*passāva*) means what is voided.
"Mud" (*medani*)—here this refers to improper earth (*akappiyapathavi*). Regarding "I shall break it," the words "having thought thus" are to be supplied. 982.
Regarding "of one who is doing it," it should be construed as "of one who is voiding urine with a pure mind. "While sweeping"—this...

“By one sweeping” (*sammajjantena*) is what should be taken; “with a broom” (*sammajjaniyā*) is the remainder. Immediately following, the word *medanī* should be taken in the objective case as “the ground” (*medani*);
“uneven” (*visamaṃ*) is the remainder, and this should be construed with “to make level” (*samaṃ kātuṃ*).
By one sweeping, having pressed down the high places and filled in the hollow places, one should sweep so as to make it level; [one] should not rub it with a broom.
The meaning is "it is allowable. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Even to rub [the ground] with a broom with the thought, 'I will make the uneven ground level,' is not allowable.

Regarding the phrase "or with the big toe," the word "or" (*vā*) here has a conjunctive sense; thus, what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* regarding "with a walking-stick" (*kattarayaṭṭhiyā*)— [...is also included.]
This includes the phrase "digging the ground. "Even to scratch" means even to make a line by breaking the ground;
this is how the construction should be understood. "With feet" means with the soles of the feet.

"Ground" refers to improper ground (*akappiya-bhūmi*). Regarding the phrases "he burns" and "he causes to burn," here the connection is established through the relationship between "whoever" (*yo*) and "of that" (*tassā*).
It is obtained. "One who burns a bowl" means one who takes up a bowl with grass torches or the like after having it smoked for the purpose of hardening its surface.
986. "Just as many" means exactly the measure of the spot. Here too, the words "whoever" (*yo*) and "of that" (*tassā*) are understood by implication.
987. "On the ground" means on improper ground. "Bowl-cooking" (*pattapacana*) is so called because the bowl is cooked there; it refers to a potsherd, and [the offense occurs] in that potsherd.
988. Thus, the construction is as follows: if that fire, while burning those logs, should go on to burn the ground exclusively, therefore it is not permissible to place the fire upon the logs.

989. A "brick-pit" (*iṭṭhakāvāpa*) is so called because bricks are scattered (*āvapīyanti*) and baked (*paccanti*) therein; it is precisely this brick-pit, meaning a place for baking bricks. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes the potter's kiln and similar sites.
990. That which is taken up (*upādīyati*) is "clinging" (*upādāna*); fuel is clinging. That which is not clinging is "non-clinging" (*anupādāna*), meaning something other than fuel. From that...

The meaning is "without taking up [fuel]. Regarding a "stump": it is permissible to give fire to a dead stump or a dry tree with the intention, "I shall extinguish it," provided that one does not give the fire to what has already entered the ground.
Even if effort is made later, if it does not go out, there is no fault. As it is said in the Commentary:
"But if, however, [the fire] has not yet reached the ground," and so forth.
991. "Tiṇukka" means a fire made by binding together grass. "Tiṇukka" is a term used as a characteristic; fires bound with coconut leaves and so forth are also included. 992. The construction is:
"In the Mahāpaccarī, it is stated that it is permissible to place fuel in the spot where that fire has fallen and then rekindle that fire. 993. The word division is "tassa apathaviyaṃ.

"Vimatissubhayatthāpi" means for one who is in doubt regarding both states—that is, regarding both earth and non-earth. Therein, that which is born from the earth is "pathavī," while the other is "apathavī."
994. These [refer to] a pit, clay, or soil.
Explanation of the Discussion on Digging the Earth.
The First Chapter: On False Speech.
995. *Bhavantassa* means of one who is being born and of one who is growing. *Bhūtassa* means of one who has been born and of one who has grown;

such is the meaning. As it is said in the Commentary: "They become (*bhavanti*) and they have been (*ahuvuṃ*), thus they are 'beings' (*bhūtā*); they are born and they grow, and having been born and having grown.
And here, by the word "becoming" (*bhavanti*), [it refers to] having attained the state of greenness when the roots have already sprouted.
It shows a young grove that is still growing. By the word "ahuvuṃ" (they were), it shows large trees, groves, and so forth, that have grown and remain established.
"Bhavanti" (they are) is explained as "they conquer" or "they grow," while for "ahuvuṃ" it is "born" or "grown.
Thus, he shows that the word *bhūta* has both the present and the past as its objects. [Regarding] "of one who is becoming..."

By these two phrases, "of what has come to be" (*bhūtassa*), through the demonstration of their having a common substratum with the phrase "of the community of beings" (*bhūtagāmassa*), [the author] states the position that the word *gāma* (community) occurs in the sense of the word *bhūta* (being), just as the words *diṭṭhigata*, *vana*, *anta*, and so on, occur in the sense of the words *diṭṭhi*, *vana*, etc.
As it is said in the Commentary: "Or else, the community itself is the 'community of beings' (*bhūtagāma*); this is a term for established green grass, trees, and so forth."
“Designation”: Or, it is a “community of spirits” (*bhūtagāma*) because it is the village—the dwelling place—of elemental spirits.
For grasses, trees, shrubs, and so forth, having become established upon the earth and attained the state of being green, are possessed by spirits.
The meaning is: of trees and so on that are being born, growing, or have reached the limit of their full development.
Regarding the phrase "the cause of being drinkable" (*pātabyatā-nimitta*): here, *pātabyatā* means the state of being drinkable;

based on the commentarial statement, "it means that it may be consumed as one pleases through cutting, splitting, and so forth," the meaning of the word *pātabyatā* should be understood as "that which is to be consumed.

That for which this offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is the cause or reason is "the cause of being drinkable. [This refers to] by way of cutting, splitting, and so forth, trees and other such things.

The meaning is that an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*) is proclaimed and stated as the cause for consuming [food] that has the characteristic of being subject to destruction, which is defined as being liable to be disturbed.
996–7. *So* refers to the "community of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*). "Beginning with sesame seeds" means that here, the sesame seed includes fine leaves, moss, and so forth;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other similar types of moss are included. "Above, there are minor and very minor leaf-sprouts; below, there are minor and very minor root-sprouts."
"Sevāla is called *tilabīja*," so it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. "For one who destroys all of that" means:

for one who destroys all that *sevāla*—namely, the *sevāla* and so forth growing in water that has taken root in the earth by way of uprooting and cutting from the ground, and the fine green moss and such that have established themselves in the water itself by way of lifting out and cutting from the water.

998. *Hatthena viyūhitvā* means having removed it from afar with the hand, without having released it from the water. The phrase beginning with *“hoti”* is for the purpose of showing the reason for that. The meaning is: because the entire, complete, and whole body of water is its [the moss’s] place;
therefore, [it is not allowed]. 999. *Cecca* means knowing. The construction is: it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to extract that mossy growth from the water without the water.
For the phrase *“ṭhānasaṅkamanan”* is the statement of the reason (*hetu*). Because performing it in that manner constitutes a change of location (*ṭhānasaṅkamana*).
“Dislodging from its place”; therefore, the construction is: “that is not permissible.

(1000) To show the contrast with what was stated above, he said: “By water,” and so forth. Therein, “by water” is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*). That [water] is of the nature of algae. “In waters” (*vārisu*): here, they are called *vārī* because they ward off (*vārayanti*) dwelling;

in those [waters]. (1001) “Climbing plants, grasses, etc., in the water”: climbing plants growing on the surface of the water, as well as *karavalli* grasses and so forth. “Of one who is pulling up”: [refers to the person].
For one who lifts [something] from the ground that is established on the ground, or from water that is established in water.
Therein, in order to show the side of the end, he said "from the water" (*toyato*). "Of one who disturbs" means of one who disturbs by means of breaking it into pieces and so forth.
"Therein" means in that water; the particle *eva* is indicated as elided, according to the commentary’s statement: "right there" (*tattheva*).
"1002. *Ettha* means in water itself. *Vikopentassa* means one who performs acts such as cutting without having it made allowable (*kappiya*).

*Tāni* refers to creepers, grasses, and so forth, which have been freed from the status of being a "habitat of beings" (*bhūtagāma*) because they were uprooted by others in that manner. *Bījagāmena* means by way of the habitat of root-seeds and so forth."
1003. Having thus shown the decision regarding that which is situated in water in brief, he now says "on land" (*thalaṭṭhe*) and so forth, in order to show the decision regarding the other as well.
Regarding the term *haritakhāṇuko*, the word "which" (*yo*) is to be supplied;

it is connected with the word "of that" (*tassā*). What is meant is: "a stump remaining after being cut from the *kakudha*, *karañja*, or other such trees. Regarding "by a community of beings" (*bhūtagāmena*):
By the phrase "it is a gathering," he indicates that destroying it constitutes an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). The same applies to what follows.

Regarding the phrase "the stump of coconuts and so forth," here too the term "green above" is understood by implication. By the phrase "it is a gathering of seed-plots," he states that this is a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The same applies to what follows. For although the stumps of palm trees, coconuts, and so forth—

Although that which does not grow upward is not a cause for the class of beings (*bhūtagāma*), it is nevertheless included within the category of the "seed-group" (*bījagāma*) because it arises from leaves, roots, or seeds produced within what is reckoned as the class of beings. Thus it is designated as the "seed-group.
1005. It is described in that manner as being called the "seed-group."

1006. The construction is as follows: "As long as the plantain tree has not yet produced fruit and its leaves are still green, so long is it declared to be included within the 'community of beings' (bhūtagāma).
As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: "But the plantain tree, as long as it has not produced fruit and its leaves are still green, is included within the community of beings itself.
*Naḷa* means small bamboo; *veḷu* means large bamboo. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "grass and so forth," crops and the like are included.
1007. Furthermore, the construction is as follows: when this bamboo dries from the top downwards, it is then said to be included within the category of seed-plants (*bījagāma*).

By "seed-plant" is meant a plant propagated by means of joints or slips (*phaḷubījagāma*). As it is said in the Commentary: "By which category of seed-plant? By the category of seed-plant consisting of joints and slips. 1008. *Indasāla* is the *sallakī*.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *sobhañjana* and other such plants is intended. By the particle "tu," [the reference is] to the Commentary.
This clarifies the specific detail stated [in the Vinaya]: "Even though branches as large as a *ratana* in length protrude from the stakes driven into the ground.

This is the determination known by those learned in the Vinaya for the benefit of the conscientious: that when branches even the size of a *ratana* have grown on the stakes that were cut and set up, it constitutes a "seed-planting" (*bījagāma*) rather than a "living-thing" (*bhūtagāma*), because the roots have not yet taken hold.
He said, "It is to be understood by one who knows the Vinaya. He will explain this same point with the words, "Or even at the root," and so forth.
"For the sake of pavilions, etc. means for the sake of pavilions, huts, walls, and so on.

"If they bury them" means if they bury those poles of the Indasāla and other such structures in the ground. "When the leaf at the root has fallen away" refers to [the pole] having been buried in that manner from its base.
“When the roots and leaves have grown”: here, by implication, the word “of them” (*tesam*) is understood, and “to be known” (*viññeyyo*) is the governing term (*adhikāra*).
Regarding the phrase “even when they have gone out,” the third particle *pi* indicates extreme smallness.

1011. *Sakandā tālaṭṭhī* means the seed of the *sakanda-tāla*. *Pattavaṭṭī* refers to a sprout-leaf tube shaped like a needle. The construction is: "and it is not called a 'seed-group' (*bījagāma*). The term "*bhūtagāmo*" (a group of beings) is shown here by way of contrast with what was previously stated.
1012. *Nāḷikeratacaṃ* means the rind of a coconut fruit. *Dantasūcīvā* means like a needle made of ivory. *Sopī* means even that coconut.
Even when the words *rukkha* (tree) and *taca* (rind) refer to fruits, their grammatical gender is not contradicted.
“He says ‘so’” is understood as [the response]. 1013.
“Resembling a deer’s horn” means like a green antelope horn. “A ring of leaves” means a ring of sprout-leaves.
“While mindfulness is present” means while it exists. “It is called a ‘group of living beings’” means it is called a “rootless group of living beings. This refers to the coconut.
This was stated by way of an exclusive (āveṇika) application.
The commentary on the four sections (catubhāṇavāra) is concluded. 1015–6.

*Ambaṭṭhī* means the seed of the mango (*amba*). *Jambuṭṭhī* means the seed of the rose-apple (*jambu*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the seeds of the *madhuka*, the breadfruit tree (*panasa*), and so forth are included.
*Gahaṇaṃ* means a thicket. *Vandākā* refers to the *rukkhādanī* (tree-eater) plant. *Aññaṃ vā* means either the *bhaṇḍakadali* or the *manoraha* plant. *Assa* refers to the *vandākā* and so forth.
*Amūlavallī* is a creeper of that name.
The construction is: "That is the *sevāla* (moss)."
1018. *Ghaṃsitvā* means having struck it with anything whatsoever. *Taṃ sevālaṃ* refers to that moss. *Tasmā* means from that wall. 1019. *Sevāle apanīte*: when the moss has been removed.
*Anto* means inside the interior cavity of water-jars and the like. The construction is: "the *kaṇṇaka* [moss] is not to be discarded.
Because the moss on the outside of water-jars and the like does not remain fixed in the water, and because it conforms to the category of seeds (*bījagāma*), it is a basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense.
They say this. Even blue-colored *kaṇṇaka* is indeed not subject to the designation [of "flower"].

1020. *Pāsāṇadaddu*: this is a designation for that which grows on stone in the form of a disease upon the human body. *Sevāla* means stone-moss. *Selyyaka* is a certain fragrant species produced from stone.
*Apattāni* means leafless. 1021. *Pupphita* means blossomed; that is the *ahicchatta*. *Makula* means unblossomed.

1022. The construction is as follows: just as it is not permissible to take [bark] after damaging the bark of a living tree, so too it is not permissible to take either *pappaṭika* (resin) or sap after damaging [the tree]; the intention is that this constitutes a *pācittiya* offense.
"*Pappaṭikam-pī*" refers even to a layer of dried bark on top of fresh bark. By the contrast with the word "fresh" (*alla*), the absence of fault regarding a dead tree is indicated.

It illuminates [the meaning]. Because of the statement, "having peeled off the bark," it is permissible to take even the tree itself, the shoots, or the sap of *sālakapittha* and other such trees, provided one cuts them from the top without damaging the fresh bark. 1023.
Regarding trees such as the *nuhika* and *kadali*, which are suitable for being split into syllables (*akkharacchindana*), and the palm leaves and so forth produced thereon—

The construction is: “for one who writes a syllable, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). By the phrase “growing on that [tree]” (*tatthajātesu*), it is indicated by way of contrast that it is permissible to write on leaves removed from the tree.
Because of the separate mention of “or even ripe,” the term “fruit” (*phalaṃ*) here includes unripe fruit as well.
1025. "A branch bearing fruit" (*phalinisākha*) means a branch such as that of the rose-apple tree (*jambu*) which possesses fruit fit for eating.

"For one who is not fully ordained taking [it]" means it is to be taken. "And desiring to eat it himself" means that if, having bent down in that manner and plucked it from the branch, he desires to eat the fruit given to him himself.
"To give in this way" means to bend [the branch] in the aforementioned manner and give it.
"Having lifted up someone else" means having lifted up another person who has not received full ordination (*anupasampanna*). "While plucking flowers" means while cutting blossoms.

"This is the very decision" refers even to the general description here: having bent down one's own [branch] and given it, flowers from a branch thus offered must not be taken for the purpose of drinking water or bathing.
Having had an unordained person lift [the branch] and pluck the flowers...
The distinction here is that flowers already gathered may be taken. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"One should not infuse drinking water with those flowers. One who wishes to infuse drinking water should have a novice monk pluck them by lifting him up.
(1027) "Branches" (*sākhā*) refers to what has been loosened by breaking or cutting. "Of branches" (*sākhīnaṃ*) means of trees. "That" (*taṃ*)...
As for the phrase "from a tree as previously described" (*yathāvuttarukkhato*), the construction is as follows:
it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who, without having had the branch of those trees from which branches grow made *kappiya* (rendered allowable), damages that branch.
Because it is stated, "of those trees whose branches grow," they say that for those [trees] from which branches do not grow, there is no necessity to perform the act of making them *kappiya*.
1028. Regarding the phrase "allasiṅgiverādikesupi," the word *ādi* (etcetera) includes *vacā*, *lasuṇa*, and so forth.

1029. The construction is: "it is permissible even without a specific restriction. To show the nature of a specific restriction (*niyāma*), since the words "this tree" and so forth will be stated later, it should be understood that in the general designation "without restriction" (*aniyāmato*), there is an absence of a restrictive term such as "this.

1032. In the expression *ucchukhaṇḍānaṃ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of a complement (*pūraṇayoga*); thus, it means "by means of pieces of sugarcane" (*ucchukhaṇḍehi*). The phrase *sabbameva* (all indeed... [is used].
"Everything remaining in the basket has been made allowable (*kappiya*). "Made" means it has become allowable.
"When one allowable portion has been made" means when, among all the pieces remaining in the basket, one allowable piece has been prepared by touching it. [The Buddha said:
"Monks, I allow you to consume fruit that has been rendered allowable by the five ascetic methods: that which is cleared by fire, that which is cleared by a knife..."

Regarding the statement, "The fifth is the 'nail-destroyed' [seed], which is seedless, having its seed extracted," one [commits an offense] by piercing with any one of these: fire, a knife, or a nail;
or with a red-hot iron bar, or a blazing fire, or a needle-point, or a nail-cutter, or the edge of a blade;
or with the claw of a human, a lion, or other such creatures, whether it has been plucked out, not plucked out, or is not putrid.

Or, having cut it, it should be made allowable (*kappiya*). And when a non-ordained monk says, "Make it allowable," the one making it must first say, "It is allowable," and only afterwards take hold of the fire-purified portion and so forth as the crow's share.
For it will be said: "'It is allowable'... ...is permissible. As for the word "allowable," by which—
They say it is permissible to speak of it with body or speech. Having first set aside the fire, one should make it "allowable" (kappiya) by piercing or cutting it with the nails or other means.
They say that when making it allowable, it is permissible to do so without removing it, provided one says "allowable" and removes it afterwards;
some say that if one wishes to say "allowable" but says "kappa" instead, it is also permissible.

1033. "A log together with sugarcane" (*dārunti ucchūhi saddhiṃ*) means a log tied to one end [of a string] with sugarcane. Regarding the phrase "pierces the log" (*dāruṃ vijjhati*), whether one pierces it oneself or causes another to pierce it, even if one knows [the rule], it is permissible. The same principle applies here as well in the phrase "even a single grain" (*ekasitthepi*).
1034. "Those sugarcane logs" refers to those pieces of sugarcane. "That" refers to the creeper or the rope. 1035.
"By means of pepper preparations" (*maricapakkehi*) means by means of matured pepper preparations. However, for immature ones, because they lack seeds, they are allowable (*kappiya*).
It is also permissible when it has not been prepared. This is an illustration for rice mixed with white garlic, red garlic, and so forth.

In this context, the state of being "connected as one" (*ekābaddhatā*) should be understood by way of the connection between the rice and the grain, and not merely by way of the mutual connection between the fruits and so on themselves. 1036. Regarding the phrase "in the case of sesame, rice, and so forth":
this refers to rice and other grains that have been mixed with sesame seeds that have been made allowable (*kappiya*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other items] are included.

Other instances are included as being mixed with those things that ought to be done. "Even in a single connected wood-apple" means even in a ripe wood-apple fruit whose seed is bound within its rind (*kaṭāha*).
"In the rind" means in the shell where the pulp (*miñja*) is bound. 1037.
"Having released the rind" means having released the rind on all sides because it has dried. "Pulp" means the pulp of a ripe wood-apple fruit.
"Having had that wood-apple split open" means having had the shell of the wood-apple split open; this is stated because the shell, being freed from the seed, functions as a vessel. 1038.
The word division is "abhūtagāma-abījesu," meaning "in non-living things and in seeds. But is it not the case that [the rule] says "in non-seeds"?
If one perceives it as seed while being in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Since the reading "perceiving what is not a vegetable-growth as a vegetable-growth" does not exist apart from that text, why was the inclusion of the term "not a vegetable-growth" made? It is said:

in that text, both seed and vegetable-growth—though they should have been called "seed-vegetable-growth" and "seed-and-seed"—were designated by the term "seed" according to the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*), and thus analyzed.
This was stated for the purpose of showing both categories after having distinguished them.

Therein, regarding that pair consisting of the non-seed-group (*abhūtagāma*) and the seed-group (*bījagāma*), four instances of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) are shown by this verse: "For one who perceives a non-seed-group as a seed-group, there is wrong-doing; for one who is in doubt, there is wrong-doing.
For one who perceives a seed-group as a seed-group, there is wrong-doing; for one who is in doubt, there is wrong-doing. Therein, "non-seed-group" means...
Seed-crops should be taken. "Non-seed-crop" means that which is not seed.
1039. Regarding the phrase "in those two [cases], the seed-crop and the living-plant," in expressions such as "those who perceive otherwise," the remainder is "of one who destroys a living-plant";
the connection is that "no offense is declared. This refers to one who perceives what is not a living-plant, or what is not seed, as being a living-plant.
The meaning to be understood is that no offense is declared even for one who damages a seed. As it is said in the Pāḷi: "If one cuts [a plant] perceiving what is a seed as not a seed...
[etc. ...there is no offense. The construction is:
"There is no offense for one who unintentionally damages a living organism (bhūtagāma). This should be applied in the same way to the subsequent cases as well. For one who is walking...

The meaning is that there is no offense because one has not directed the mind [to the act], even if the grass or other materials are cut while being held by the feet or struck against a support or a walking stick with the thought, "I will cut this.
"Of one who is absent-minded" means of one whose mindfulness is distracted elsewhere, or of one speaking with another, or of one cutting grass and so forth with the big toes and such.
By the word "and" (ca), the phrase "of one who does not know" is included here, though it was not explicitly stated.

This is a summary. The meaning is that there is no offense for one who does not know: "this is a collection of living beings," or "when this fire falls upon it, this is being burned," or "by this, this is broken or cut," and so forth.
1040. "And this" refers to this training rule on plants (*bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*). It has three origins: by way of body, mind, and speech; and by way of body-mind, speech-mind, and body-speech-mind.
It has three origins (*tisamuṭṭhāna*). It is *kiriya* (functional) because it is committed through acts such as cutting. Regarding "three types of consciousness" (*ticitta*):

for one who, unaware of the designation (*paṇṇatti*), clears away grass thickets and the like at shrines and so forth, it is wholesome (*kusala*) if they are one whose taints are not yet exhausted (*akhīṇāsava*), and functional (*kiriya*) if they are one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

For trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) who destroy [the vegetation] out of greed for fruits, flowers, and the like, it is unwholesome (*akusala*). Thus, there are three types of consciousness.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Grove of Spirits (Bhūtagāmakathāvaṇṇanā). 1041. The construction is: "the act performed by the Saṅgha regarding those who speak otherwise and those who cause harassment.

The meaning is: "each [act] was performed individually by the Saṅgha through a formal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*) regarding the charge of being one who speaks otherwise and one who causes harassment. 'He speaks otherwise' means he is a speaker otherwise (*aññavādaka*)."
“Evasive speech” (aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇa) is its name. From the statement, “One who harasses is a harasser (vihesakā);

this is the name for one who remains silent,” it means that when a charge regarding a matter or an offense has been made in the midst of the Saṅgha, one who does not wish to speak about it—having set aside what was asked according to the sequence of the word-analysis, such as “Who has committed [the offense]? What has he committed? In what has he committed?”—[is called a harasser].

Not speaking of one thing but evading with another is "evasive speech" (*aññavādaka*); one who does this is an evasive speaker. Here, however, the action is understood in the sense of its underlying state (*bhāvappadhāna*).
Likewise, being thus accused and wishing not to answer what was asked, yet not evading with another thing out of fear of an offense, one remains silent in order to harass the Saṅgha;
such a person is called a "harasser" (*vihesaka*). In this case as well, it is understood in the sense of its underlying state.
Only the action itself should be grasped. Here, however, it is stated in brief that the act of attributing that state [of falsehood] is what is meant.
"Again, for one acting in that way" means again acting in that same manner by making separate instances of speaking otherwise and causing vexation.

"There are two *pācittiya* offenses" refers to the method in the word-commentary beginning with "when the speaking otherwise has been attributed" and likewise beginning with "when the vexation has been attributed."

And because it is stated separately for each case according to the method [of the rule], one should understand that there are two *pācittiya* offenses, since a single offense arises for each individual instance.
1042. Regarding the term "dhamma" (righteous), the word "kamma" (formal act) is to be understood as the remainder.
Thus: one who perceives a righteous formal act as such, one who is in doubt, and one who perceives an unrighteous formal act as such.

Regarding the three alternatives: the same principle applies here as well for the phrase "in what is not Dhamma. Regarding "when the legal action has been brought forward": this refers to when the bringing forward of the legal action against one who speaks otherwise has not yet been performed.
Regarding "of one who speaks thus": this refers to one who speaks such things as, "Who has committed an offense? and so forth. And regarding the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "vadantassa ca":

by means of this *ca*, it includes the fact that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who thus harasses [the accused] even when the legal action has already been brought forward. In this interpretation, the phrase "when the legal action has been brought forward" indicates the time of the harassment.
1043. "One who has fallen" means one who has himself fallen [into an offense]. "With the perception that there will be a quarrel" means:
when I have said this, he remains silent with the perception that there will be quarrels, strife, and so forth for the Saṅgha. "Of one who is ill" means:
of one who is unable to speak due to being afflicted by mouth-disease or other such ailments.
1044. Action (*kriyā*) is the performance of various services for one another. Silence is non-action (*akriyā*). [This concludes] the commentary on the talk of those who speak otherwise.
1045–6. "Of one authorized" (*sammatassa*):
this refers to the thirteen types of authorization (*sammuti*) found in the *Khandhaka*, such as the authorization to assign lodgings and so forth.

To one who has been granted permission by the Saṅgha after the motion (*ñatti*) has been established and the formal act (*kammavācā*) has been recited—whether for one, several, or all [of the duties]—the term "bhikkhu" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), based on the statement: "He has been ordained by the Saṅgha and is authorized.
The connection is: "desiring to perform this task. As for the word "speaking": "By his consent, so-and-so prepares the lodgings; by his consent, the meals..."

While reciting the passage beginning with “he points out,” the term “to one who is ordained” (*upasampanne*) is the accusative plural used as the object in relation to the action “he censures” (*ujjhāpeti*).
This is the meaning here: he censures means he causes [the person] to be looked upon with contempt, or he causes them to be thought of as inferior;
he reviles means he proclaims by saying such things as, “By his own will, so-and-so assigns lodgings.”

In this context, where one should have said "of those who are ordained" (*upasampannānaṃ*), it is stated as "to those who are ordained" (*upasampanne*) by means of the accusative case in the sense of the genitive; the meaning is that one makes a disclosure in the presence of those who are ordained.
Regarding the phrase "there are two *pācittiya* offenses," this refers to the two bases [of offense]: "a *pācittiya* for reviling and a *pācittiya* for disparaging."
Because it was stated [in the previous section] as a single unit, it is also stated here as a single unit; however, they should be understood separately.

Regarding the term *dhamma* (righteous), the word *kamma* (formal act) is to be supplied as the remainder; thus, the meaning is: "if the formal act of granting consent by the Saṅgha to one who has been ordained is a *dhammakamma*.
Regarding the term *adhamma* (unrighteous), the same principle applies here as well.
1047–8. "Bhikkhunā" means by a bhikkhu who has been authorized (*sammatassa*). The construction is: "he speaks dispraise of a bhikkhu who has not been authorized.
Regarding the phrase "of anyone whatsoever" (*yassa kassaci*), the word "in the presence of" (*santike*) is to be supplied;
the meaning is "in the presence of anyone whatsoever, whether ordained (*upasampanna*) or unordained. One who was authorized at the time of ordination but later [became] a novice...
With reference to one who has approached [the Saṅgha], it is said, "of a novice monk who has been formally authorized" (*sammatassa sāmaṇerassa*). The construction is: "speaking dispraise.
(1049) "One who acts" refers to one who has been authorized. "Speaking" means complaining or disparaging. The meaning, however, is exactly as previously stated.

It is an *action* (*kriya*) because it is committed through the acts of complaining and disparaging. Since both complaining and disparaging occur only by way of false speech (*musāvāda*), [it is classified as such].

Because it has occurred [previously], it should be understood that the statement “there is no offense for the first offender” is spoken for the purpose of showing there is no offense both in the case of a *pācittiya* and in the case of a *dukkaṭa*. And this being so,
it follows that for one who reviles and for one who finds fault, there are two offenses each at a single moment.
Commentary on the Discourse on Causing Resentment. 1050.
The connection is with the phrase "a bed or chair of the Saṅgha. This refers to beds and so forth belonging to the Saṅgha, as shown in the Canon by the words:
"A bed or chair or cushion or mat of the Saṅgha. And here, "bed" (mañca) is defined in the Canon as follows: "Four..."
The fourfold bed is shown as: "a bedstead, one with removable legs, one with removable cross-bars, one with curved legs, and one with detachable legs.
Among these, a *masāraka* is a bed made by boring holes in the bed-legs and weaving them together with strips of bamboo;

what is currently in use today is called a rattan bed (*vettamañca*). A *bundikābaddha* is [a bed] where the bed-legs are inserted from within the spaces between the bamboo strips at the ends of the cross-bars.
One should observe that a cane bed or a wooden plank bed is made by having [the frame] bitten [into shape].
A "crab-legged" bed (*kuḷīrapādaka*) is a bed joined with curved legs resembling the legs of a crab, having displayed the shape of a horse's hoof or similar form at the base of the legs.

A "striking-legged" bed (*āhaccapādaka*) is one where, after boring holes in the crossbars (*aṭani*), a crest is formed at the head of the leg and inserted into the hole in the crossbar; when it emerges above the crossbar, the crest-tip is positioned upon it.
A bed (*mañca*) is made by boring through [the legs] horizontally and inserting a pin.
A chair (*pīṭha*) is likewise made; it is of four kinds, each bearing its own name.
As for a mattress (*bhisi*), according to its constituent materials, there are five types: woolen mattresses, cotton mattresses, bark-fiber mattresses, grass mattresses, and leaf mattresses.
Five kinds of bedding were shown. Therein, "wool" (*uṇṇā*) refers to all body hairs except human hair.
"Cotton cloth" (*coḷa*) refers to rags. "Bark-fiber" (*vāka*) refers to *makaci*-bark and the like. "Grass" (*tiṇa*) refers to *dabba* grass and the like.
"Leaf" (*paṇṇa*) refers to all leaves except for the *tamāla* leaf.
In the Pāḷi it is shown: “A *koccha* is that which is made of *vāka* grass, or *usīra* root, or *muñja* grass, or *pabbaja* grass, and is bound after being wrapped around the inside.
Thus, having taken *vāka* grass, or *usīra*, or *muñja* grass, or sheep’s wool, or *pabbaja* grass, one spreads them out at both ends, presses them together in the middle, and contracts them.
Having bound it and covered it with the wrapping bindings of lion skins and so forth, they say it was made as a seat for sitting, like a foot-wiping cloth.

As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "It was bound having been made wide at the bottom and top, narrow in the middle, and in the shape of a drum (paṇava); it is said that even though its middle was encircled by lion and tiger skins..."

“They do so; for there is no such thing as an improper skin here,” and so forth. “Having had it spread out” means having had it spread out by either one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or one who is not fully ordained.
The detailed explanation (*vinicchaya*) regarding this will be stated later. “Having spread it out” means having spread it out oneself.
“One should neither remove it” means that after removing it from the place where it was laid out, one should not put it away. “Nor should one have it removed.”
One should not have it carried by another in such a manner. "That" refers to the bed and so forth. Regarding "departing": here, the phrase "whatever monk" is understood;

the meaning is that he goes beyond the point where a stone, when thrown with an outstretched hand from the place where the bed and so forth are spread, would fall for a man of medium strength. As it is said in the Pāḷi:
“Of a man of medium build throwing a clod.
(1052) “During the four months of the rains” means within the four-month rainy season. Regarding the phrase “if it does not rain,” the words “in some region” are to be supplied.
For this very reason, he says “if,” indicating uncertainty. [This refers to] those regions where it does not rain during the rainy season.
"Even in those [other regions], it is likewise not permitted to store [the robes] for four months," so it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.

"And likewise even there" means even in those other places where, during the winter, it does not rain for four months. 1053. "Where" means in a region such as the island of Laṅkā, where even in other winters it does not rain for four months.
The construction is as follows: "When it rains, for eight months it is not permitted to place beds and such things in the open air.
By contrast, it shows that "during the four months of summer, however, it is permitted to place them outside.

1054. "In a dwelling" (*nivāsasmin*) means when there is continuous residence after having built a nest in a tree; as it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "But in whatever [tree] they dwell, having made a nest through constant residence. "Even at any time" (*kadācipi*) means even during the dry season when it does not rain.
1055–6. “Whatever belongs to the Saṅgha,” such as beds and so forth—this is the construction. “If it is spread” means if it has been laid out without formal authorization;
what is meant is that it has been prepared. “In any place whatsoever” means in any location, such as at the foot of a tree, in a pavilion, or in the open air.
“By anyone whatsoever” means by a co-resident, or by a pupil, or by another.
“By a bhikkhunī” means by one who is fully ordained (upasampanna). “He” refers to that bhikkhu for whose sake [the rule] was prescribed. 1057.

“That” refers to that bedstead made of cane belonging to the Saṅgha and so forth. The word *santharāpita* is formed with the agentive suffix; thus, the meaning is: “by a bhikkhunī who has instigated [another] to spread it. 1058.
Regarding the term “by a bhikkhunī,” since the word “one who commands” (*āṇāpaka*) will be mentioned later, it means “by a fully ordained bhikkhunī who has been commanded.”
It is obtained. "Of that very person" means of that very monk who was instructed to prepare the seat.

Because the word "sits down" is illustrative (upalakkhaṇa), it should be understood that if [the monk] comes and places either a bag or a robe—or anything at all—there, or says, "This burden is mine alone," the preparer is released from responsibility.

1059–60. Regarding the term *anāpuccha* (“without having asked for permission”), the meaning is: “anyone whatsoever without asking,” according to the specific form stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as: “Whatever monk, novice, or monastery attendant is conscientious and regards [the person] as his own impediment.
Because it is stated that “a monk, novice, or monastery attendant must be conscientious,” one may go after asking someone who lacks such conscientiousness.
They say it is not permissible. If one asks: "Having said, 'We shall go,' the obtaining of consent is called *āpucchanā* (asking for leave);
how can that be a factor in the absence of an offense? It is because permission for the journey has been obtained.

Since there is the statement, "One should go after having obtained the *kappa* (formal authorization)," it is as if the one granting the consent has accepted both the regular and the irregular duties; thus, the *kappa* is considered obtained.

If he goes in this manner, it is permissible. "Without having handed over" means without having performed the act of handing over—that is, without having arranged for the regular and occasional duties, or without having caused them to be accepted;
this is what is meant. "He stops" means at every step. 1062.
"Therefore, from the place" means from the dining hall where he himself stood while giving orders. As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Having departed from the dining hall, he goes elsewhere."
1063. Regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses based on the perceptions of "belonging to the Saṅgha," "doubtful," and "belonging to an individual.

"By means of a triad that has passed beyond" means by means of having transcended—through the abandonment of uprooting along with the latent tendencies—the triad of unwholesome roots and so forth. "A triad of *dukkaṭa*" refers to:

"If one perceives what belongs to an individual as belonging to the Saṅgha, or is doubtful, or perceives it as belonging to an individual; or if one [takes] another’s property belonging to an individual, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*."
Regarding the words [of the rule], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each of the three cases.
1064–5. "Cimilika" means a piece of cloth to be spread over ground that has been prepared as a work-surface, for the purpose of protecting the skin.
"Taṭṭikā" means a mat made from palm leaves and so forth. "Leather" refers to lion-leather and the like; among the requisites for lodgings, it is unallowable leather.
There is no such thing [as a prohibition against using skins]. As it is said: "For in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), no skin is seen to be prohibited for the use of lodgings;
therefore, the prohibition should be understood as applying only to the carrying about of lion skins and the like.
And the meaning of this commentary passage is explained in the *Sāratthadīpanī* as follows:
By the statement, “The prohibition should be understood as applying specifically to the wearing of lion skins and so forth,” he clarifies the intended meaning of the Khandhaka passage which says:
“Monks, great skins are not to be worn—namely, a lion skin, a tiger skin, or a leopard skin;
whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This means that even within a bed...

In this case, because the training rule was laid down on account of the fact that [bedding] had been prepared inside and also prepared on the bed outside, it was precisely the use [of bedding] after spreading it upon beds and chairs that was prohibited;
however, use by way of spreading it upon the floor was not prohibited. If this is so, why is it said that "the prohibition concerns only the carrying [of the bedding]?"

Is it so stated? Just as from the statement, “I allow you, monks, the use of all palatial dwellings,” it follows that although items such as golden water-pots—which are determined for use as furniture even in a private dwelling—are permitted for use, they are not allowed to be used by making them one's own private property; so too is this [the case] with regard to floor-coverings.

It is stated that "the prohibition should be understood as applying specifically to the carrying away" in order to show that it is not permissible to take various items belonging to one monastery to another monastery to use them there, even while they are being used.
By the word "board" (*phalaka*), only the board-stool (*phalakapīṭha*) found in the textual tradition is indicated; as it says in the Commentary: "The board-stool..."
"A bench made of wood. A "foot-wiping cloth" (*pādapuñchanī*) is a foot-wiper made from plantain leaves, *vāka* grass, or similar materials.
A "floor-covering" (*bhūmattharaṇa*) is a matting or similar item that should be spread upon a floor-cloth if one exists, or upon the bare ground if none exists.
An "upper covering" (*uttarattharaṇa*) is a bedspread that should be spread over communal beds, benches, and so forth.
“Alms-bowl support” means a bowl-stand. That refers to the aforementioned requisites. “Going” means going beyond the distance of a stone’s throw.

However, if at the very time of giving, donors give even a woolen blanket worth a thousand coins, saying, “Use this as a foot-wiper,” it is permissible to use it exactly as given. Therefore, this bedding such as beds and chairs— [End of excerpt]
"If it has been given by donors with the instruction, 'Enjoy it at your pleasure even in the open air,' they say it is permissible to leave it in the open air at all times.

(1066) "If one who dwells in the forest must go away, he may go as he pleases after hanging his bed, chair, and so forth on a tree in a place sheltered from the rain; such is the application of the rule."
1067. Regarding the phrase "by upacikās, etc.," the word "etc. includes mice. "Is not destroyed" means it does not perish. "All of that" refers to the entire set of items such as beds and so forth.
1068. "In what belongs to oneself" means in the case of one's own personal belongings, such as beds and the like.

"Obstructed" means when the bed and other items are obstructed—meaning occupied or seized by a senior bhikkhu, or by lords and the like, or by yakkhas, lions, and so forth—having been overcome and taken possession of.

The meaning is as follows: "Even in times of distress" means even when obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) and so forth exist. The construction is: "There is no offense for the monk who goes. (1069) Regarding origination:
it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; thus it is called the *kathina* origination.

For one who does not know the rule (*paññatti*) and does not himself remove [the robe], there is an offense by way of the body; for one who does not ask permission, there is an offense by way of speech; [and regarding] the rule...
It should be understood that for one who acts thus intentionally after having known [the rule], it originates from those same two factors.
Exceeding the range of a clod’s throw is an action; not removing beds and so forth is a non-action.
This concludes the commentary on the first section concerning lodgings.

1070–3. "Bhisī" refers both to the five kinds mentioned in the first training rule and to the kind of mattress shown in this commentary as "a mattress for a bed (mañcakabhisī) or a mattress for a bench (pīṭhakabhisī).
"Bed-covering (paccattharaṇa)" means a woolen rug (pāvāra) or a blanket (kojava).
"Only this much was stated" is what is recorded in the commentaries. [This is] for the purpose of showing that it was stated in such a manner in the commentaries.
"It has been stated [in the Vinaya], and other such items as well, which are to be spread upon beds and chairs, are indeed 'spreading-cloths' (paccattharaṇa)";
this is written in the *Sāratthadīpanī* according to what is stated in the three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. "Sitting-cloth" (nisīdana) refers to the sitting-cloth (nisīdanacīvara).
"Grass-spreading" (tiṇasanthāra) is a spreading made by arranging grasses such as *eraka* in two or three places. "Leaf-spreading" (paṇṇasanthāra) [is likewise].
A *nāma* is a bed made by covering [the ground] in the same way with leaves such as those of the coconut palm. A *seyyā* is that upon which one lies.

The phrase "whether completely covered or partially covered" has the same meaning as what was stated in the discussion on sleeping together (*sahaseyya*). "One of the ten kinds of beds" means one among the ten types of beds. Or, "even after having spread it."
Here, the word *pi* has the sense of inclusion; it includes the phrase "even after having had [the bedding] spread.

By connecting the word *vā* with "without having removed it himself" (*sayaṃ anuddharitvā*) as "or without having removed it" (*anuddharitvā vā*), this alternative (*vikappa*)—namely, "or without having had it removed" (*anuddharāpetvā vā*)—is comprised.
That is the bed (*seyya*).

“Within the vicinity of the monastery” (*ārāmasūpacāraṃ*) refers to the vicinity as described in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “The vicinity of an unenclosed [monastery] is two *leḍḍupāta*s from the dwelling. “*Assa*” means of the enclosed monastery. “1074.
Of both” refers to the dwellings and the beds. The connection is: “having spread [it] inside the inner chamber, he goes. 1075. Regarding “in the vicinity of the monastery”:
here, “monastery” (*vihāra*) refers to any protected dwelling that is completely enclosed, such as an inner chamber and so forth.
As it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “‘Vihāra’ should be understood as either an inner chamber or any other well-enclosed, protected dwelling.
In that context, “vicinity” (*upacāra*) refers to the area near it. As it is said: “‘Vicinity’ means the space close to its exterior.
A “pavilion” (*maṇḍapa*) is a pavilion for assemblies, whether enclosed or unenclosed. As it is said: “In a pavilion...”

“He walks in an unenclosed place, or even in an enclosed one, or in a pavilion where many have gathered. By the word “etcetera,” the assembly hall (*upaṭṭhānasālā*) and the foot of a tree are included.
An “assembly hall” is an unprotected dining hall. As it is said: “In an assembly hall or in a dining hall.
And its state of being unprotected is to be understood from the commentary’s statement: “due to the unprotected nature of the place.”

1076. It is said that "the threefold offense of expiation (pācittiya) has been stated" because the three offenses of expiation have been stated in the three cases: "perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha when it belongs to the Saṅgha," "being in doubt," and "perceiving it as belonging to an individual.
It is called "ten-based" (dasavatthuka) because it exists within those ten items;
or, the basis for the ten is the "ten-basis" (dasavatthu), and that very thing is the "ten-based. This refers to any one of the bedding articles, such as a mattress (bhisi) and so forth.

“Of that” means of the mat. The threefold triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses is illustrated by the following: [if one uses] what belongs to an individual with the perception that it belongs to the Saṅgha; if one is doubtful; or if one uses what belongs to another individual with the perception that it belongs to an individual—there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
1077. “Having removed” means having put away the bedding so that it is not eaten by termites.
The word "gacchato" (of one going) is connected with this. "By another" means by an elder monk, a superior, or the like. "Palibuddheti" means when the lodging has been obstructed or prevented.
"And having gone while still having concern" means having gone with the thought, "I shall go back today and put this away," thus accompanied by concern.

"Having gone to another village, etc."—as it is said: "Thinking, 'I will return this very day and look after [them],' one who is thus full of concern goes to the other side of a river or to another village.
Regarding that, "having stood there" means having stood at the place already reached;
it is meant that the thought has arisen, "I am going beyond from here. As it is said: "He stands right where the intention to go has arisen."
"He asks him" is the connection. It is said that he asks by sending someone to that bed; as it was stated: "having sent someone, he asks.

And here, whereas in the previous training rule the offense of *pācittiya* occurred by exceeding the range of a clod's throw—whether inside or outside the monastery—from the place where the beds and so forth were arranged, here it occurs by exceeding the precincts (*upacāra*).
This distinction should be understood:
there is no fault for one who departs after abandoning beds and such in an open space, or merely his bedding in a monastery,
provided he remains within the range of a stone’s throw.
Commentary on the Second Discussion of Lodgings (Dutiyasenāsanakathāvaṇṇanā). 1079.

The construction is as follows: if a monk, knowing that another monk has already arrived at a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, should occupy a bed by encroaching upon him, there would be a *pācittiya* offense for that monk.
"One who has arrived first" means one who has attained [priority] by means of the *vassa* (rainy-season retreat).
Having taken a lodging that has been assigned, he dwells there. "He knows" means he knows: "This person is not to be moved.
Those who are "not to be moved" are the elders and so forth. As it is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana): "He knows means he knows:
'He is an elder,' or 'He is ill,' or 'He has been assigned by the Saṅgha. "Having intruded" means having entered; [he sits] closer than the bed or other furniture already arranged for him.

The meaning is: having entered the access concentration (*upacāra*) characterized as will be explained [later]. "He might lie down" means that having spread out one of the ten kinds of bedding, he would make his bed;
it is said, "he would recline. And he will say: "one of the ten kinds of bedding," and so forth. The words "or sitting" are to be supplied.
As it says in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "he sits down or he lies down."
1080-2. Desiring to explain the meaning that has been stated, [the author] first says, "He should not occupy a bed in an intrusive manner," in order to show the determination regarding this point:
"The stone for washing feet... [down to] an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For a monk entering a dwelling, [this refers to] the stones for washing feet up until he leaves that bed or bench; however, for one leaving from the bed or bench—
The construction is as follows: "Whatever place lies between [the dwelling] and the place for urination—this alone is called the precinct (upacāra).
In this context, the word "precinct" (upacāra) is used in the sense of "surrounding area. "Desiring to trouble" means one whose mind has arisen with the thought:
"He who has a pressing need will depart. The analysis of the compound is: "They lie here" (sayanti ettha).
1983. Regarding the phrase "of an offense entailing expiation" (*pācittiyassa*), he says "of one sitting down," etc., in order to demonstrate what was stated in the summary.
"Therein" means: in that bed which has been occupied by intruding in such a manner.

The expression "two offenses entailing expiation" is stated with reference to this latter alternative, namely, "of one doing both. However, regarding the two preceding alternatives, [it is said]: "for one sitting down, there is an offense entailing expiation;..."

It should be stated: "or for one who lies down, there is a *pācittiya*. Regarding these three modes of classification (*vikappa*), it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that for each one, both "three *pācittiyas*" and "three *dukkaṭas*" should be stated. How so?

If one uses a seat belonging to the Saṅgha while perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha, being doubtful, or perceiving it as belonging to an individual, and sits down, there is a *pācittiya*. Thus, regarding sitting, there are three *pācittiyas*.
Thus, regarding a bed, there are three *pācittiyas*; regarding both [bed and seat], there are two sets of three *pācittiyas*. Thus, in these two alternatives, there are twelve *pācittiyas*.

Regarding what belongs to an individual, if one perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, or is in doubt, or perceives it as belonging to another individual, and one uses it for sitting, there is an *dukkaṭa*.
Thus, for sitting, there are three *dukkaṭas*; likewise, for a bed, there are three *dukkaṭas*. In both cases...
"Two sets of three *dukkaṭas*" means that twelve *dukkaṭas* are to be understood. Regarding "one who is doing":
here, "the sitting mat, etc. is obtained from the context. It is stated as "threefold *pācittiya*":
in the three alternatives—[thinking it belongs to the Saṅgha] when it belongs to the Saṅgha, being in doubt, or thinking it belongs to an individual—one incurs a threefold *pācittiya*.
This is stated in the Pāḷi. Thus, regarding the individual (puggalika), a triad of dukkaṭas is also stated. Therefore, he said: "For an individual, there is a triad of dukkaṭas.
By this, it should be understood that the aforementioned pācittiya and dukkaṭa offenses are stated by including them generally within the triad.
1085–6. Regarding the pair of verses beginning with “Vuttūpacāraṃ,” one should exclude the precincts already mentioned for the monastery, or [refer to] the precincts [in general].
It is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who spreads [a rug] in the open air, or causes it to be spread, or sits down there.
The construction is: "In all those cases, his dwelling is prohibited. Therein, "of the monastery" refers to the aforementioned lodging.
"In the vicinity" means not far away. "In the open air" means in the courtyard area immediately adjacent to that lodging.
The phrase "whether sitting down" includes, by the inclusion of the word "or," both lying down and doing both together. As it is said in the Pāḷi:
"Whether he sits down or lies down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"Therein" means in that dwelling place (senāsana) which was already occupied. "In all cases" means both inside and outside of the aforementioned precincts, even including...
“Even in the open air” means in all places whatsoever. “Of him” refers to that person of discordant character who, being displeased, lies down intruding upon another.
The meaning is that his dwelling is forbidden because living together with one who harasses others causes great harm.
As it is said in the Commentary: “For with such a person of discordant character, in the same monastery or on the same courtyard...”
"Or there is no need for the spring; therefore, his dwelling is prohibited in every respect.
(1087) "Of one afflicted by cold and so forth"—this is the word-division (*padaccheda*). The meaning is: of one who is afflicted or oppressed by cold and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the text] includes "or by heat," and so on. As it has been said: "Afflicted by cold or by heat, he enters [the dwelling]."
In this context, "emergency" (*āpadā*) refers to the occurrence of an obstacle to life or to the holy life for one who sleeps outside [the monastery]. 1088.
The construction is: "This training rule results in painful feeling.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of "intruding" (*anupakhajja*).
1089. *Nikkaḍḍheyya* means he would drive out. *Nikkaḍḍhāpeyya vā* means he would cause [someone] to drive out. 1990. *Bahubhūmo*:
that which has many floors (*bhūmi*) counted as levels of sand is a "many-storied" (*bahubhūmo*) palace. It is called "many-storied" by virtue of the rules governing compound endings.
1091. *Ṭhapetvā ṭhapetvā* means having repeatedly halted his movement at this or that spot.

1092. This is the method: regarding the command "Go out!", even if many people go while it is given as a singular command, there is only one offense for the commander once they have passed through the gatehouse;
however, for one who stands at the spot where he gave the order and repeatedly sends them out, the number of offenses corresponds to the number of gatehouses.
Regarding "at the very moment of the command," this means at the very instant of the command, such as "Drive this person out!"
1093. In this context, it should be stated: “There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one [person]. And in the phrase “many,” it should be stated: “gateways”;
the connection is with the word “passes through. [Examples include: “Having made him pass through so many gateway-towers, drive him out!
and “Drive him out as far as the gateway-tower at the boundary! and “Having made him pass through many gateway-towers, drive him out!”
And because of being commanded, if he drives [them] out after passing through many door-chambers—that is the meaning. As it is said in the Commentary:

“But if he is commanded with such a restriction as ‘drive them out through so many doors,’ or ‘drive them out as far as the main gate,’ there are offenses of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of doors. The construction is: “there are many offenses of expiation.”

1094. Regarding the phrase "from the assembly hall, etc.": here, because it is in the ablative case used in the sense of departure (*nissakka*), the meaning to be understood is "from the assembly hall, etc.
Because it stands in grammatical apposition with the word "vicinity" (*upacārato*), what is meant is that it is from the vicinity of the monastery, starting from the assembly hall, etc.
As stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "Vicinity (*upacāra*) means merely the area consisting of the assembly hall, etc. Also by way of the body...

The phrase "even by speech" and "in the case of ejecting" are to be construed with what will be stated later regarding the *dukkaṭa* offense. "Of him" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
By the word "etcetera," pavilions and so forth are included. As it has been said:

"If one ejects, or causes another to eject, [a person] from the vicinity of a monastery, or from a hall for attendance, or from a pavilion, or from the foot of a tree, or from an open space, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*."
By the word “vācāya” (by speech), both the command “go out” and the command “expel this person” are included.

By the word “tathā” (likewise), he restates the manner already explained: that there is a single offense through a single effort, whereas in the case of multiple efforts, there is an offense according to the number of efforts or the number of doors.
"1095. ‘Likewise’—this should also be connected with the statement: ‘For one who ejects another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Just as there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who ejects, or causes another to eject, a fully ordained person (upasampanna) from the vicinity of a monastery (vihāra), such as from the assembly hall (upaṭṭhānasālā) and so forth, likewise [there is an offense] for the ejection and so forth of one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) from a monastery or from the vicinity of a monastery."

The meaning is that for a bhikkhu who does so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Likewise, the construction is: for one who drags out the requisites of all [monks], whether from the vicinity of a monastery or from the monastery itself, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

"Of all" refers to both those who are fully ordained and those who are not. "Requisites" includes even the bark used for dyeing, as it is said in the Commentary: "even down to the bark used for dyeing."
1096. By the phrase “asambaddhesu” (in those not bound), he shows, by way of contrast, that a single offense arises only in the case of requisites that are not loosely bound.
As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: “But when they are placed after being bound tightly, there is only one offense,” which is stated in the Mahāpaccarī. However, a loose binding is not a proper binding.
"It happens" should be understood as being included by way of irrelevant speech.

The construction is: "He indicates the *dukkaṭa* offense by counting the items of that bhikkhu"; what is meant is: "of that bhikkhu who is having requisites removed, or who is causing them to be removed. 1097–8.
Regarding the terms "pupil" (*antevāsin*) and "co-resident" (*saddhivihārika*), the word "one who does not behave properly" (*asammāvattanta*) is to be supplied here. As it has been said:
In the section on non-offenses, it says: “He ejects a pupil (*antevāsika*) or a co-resident student (*saddhivihārika*) who is not conducting himself properly,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “of one who ejects,” the word “or of one who causes [another] to eject” (*nikkaḍḍhāpentassa*) is to be understood as the remainder.

This refers to a pupil who is not conducting himself properly, or one who is shameless; or likewise, a co-resident student who is not conducting himself properly, or one who is insane—[regarding these] pupils and the rest.

The construction is as follows: there is no offense declared for one who himself drives out personal requisites from his own residence or from the residence of a person who trusts him, or causes them to be driven out;
nor for one who drives out, or causes to be driven out, either one who is fully ordained or one who is not fully ordained from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, provided he himself is insane.
