In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "But those who are shameless and so forth should be expelled from their very own dwelling place";
and in the *Pāḷi*, it is stated: "There is no offense regarding one's own personal [dwelling].
If one asks, "Why was this [phrase] 'from the dwelling place of one’s own trusted person' stated?"—it was stated as a corollary to that very reading. First, among the terms such as *antevāsika*...
If one thinks, “I will expel him,” because of his improper conduct and so forth, there is no offense even if anger arises due to the rapid shifting of the mind while actually expelling him.
By the word “likewise” (tathā), the remainder of the phrase “while expelling” is understood to mean “while causing [another] to expel. 1099.
And he provides him with "his requisites" as previously stated. The phrase "even from the entire Saṅghārāma" should be connected specifically with the one who creates quarrels.
As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: "He is permitted to expel only the one who causes strife and the one who creates quarrels from the entire Saṅghārāma;
for such a person, having gained a faction, might even cause a schism in the Saṅgha."

The word *tu* here, which indicates a specific distinction, points out that apart from the particular qualification stated [by it], the remaining analysis is exactly the same as in the immediately preceding case.
It is "arising from three origins" because it originates from body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of expulsion.
"1100-1. *Majjhimāsīsaghaṭṭāya*: that which does not touch the head is *asīsaghaṭṭā*; that which is of medium height and does not touch the head is *majjhimāsīsaghaṭṭā*.
By this [term], the meaning is: 'having a floor level with the bottom of the head of a man of medium stature.
*Vehāsakuṭiyā*: in a hut whose upper surface is not covered by tiles or the like, consisting of two stories or more."
“Upari” means on top; it refers to the upper floor of a dwelling that has not been spread with carpets or similar coverings, but is merely fitted with a frame.
As stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: “Any two-storied or three-storied hut whose floors are not covered above is called a ‘vihāsa-kuṭī’ (lofty hut);
however, in this context, those where the head does not strike [the ceiling] are intended. Regarding a bed with removable legs: [text continues].
Regarding the phrase “a bed with fixed legs (*āhaccapādako mañco*) is one that stands by piercing through the frame,” as shown in the Canon, the meaning is:
a bed that stands with its upper crossbar not struck against the lower crossbar, having the corner-posts pierced and the leg-ends fastened to them.
This is to be connected with the phrase “a stool with fixed legs (*āhaccapādakaṃ pīṭhan*”). As it says in the Canon: “A stool with fixed legs is one that stands by piercing through the frame.”
“...occurs. This is the meaning.
The construction is as follows: for that bhikkhu who sits or lies down on a bed or chair with detachable legs, there may be *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of his actions (*payoga*).

1102–3. Regarding the threefold *pācittiya* based on the categories of "belonging to the Saṅgha," "perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha," "being doubtful," and "perceiving it as belonging to an individual" (*puggalika*): [the term] "individual" refers to...
In a dwelling belonging to an individual (*puggalika-vihāre*). In a gabled upper room (*vehāsakuṭiyā*)... [and so on]...

the construction of the phrase is that for him there is a triple offense of wrong-doing (*tikadukkaṭa*) by way of counting. There is a triple offense of wrong-doing by way of [the cases of] perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha when it belongs to an individual, being in doubt, or perceiving it as belonging to another individual.
"Below, where there is no use" means on the lower floor or in a place without a drip-ledge, by way of timber materials and so forth. "Where the head strikes" (*sīsaghaṭṭāya*).
Or in a hut whose floor is level with the striking of a hammer-head. "In a dwelling free from fear" means in a leaf-hut or similar structure built on the ground within a dwelling free from fear.
Here too, the phrase "in a dwelling of trust" is stated as a corollary to the rule "there is no offense regarding one's own personal property."

1104. Regarding the phrase "where a pin has been inserted": the construction is that there is no fault for one who sits down or lies down on a bed where a pin has been driven horizontally from the top of the headboard across to the footboard.
"There" (tattha) refers to a bed or a bench where a pin was previously mentioned as not having been inserted. By the word "standing," lying down is excluded.

"Lageti" means he attaches any kind of equipment, such as a hook or a training device, to the upper part [of the body]. This training rule (sikkhāpada) is considered equal to the training rule concerning sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada) from the perspective of its origin (samuṭṭhāna);
this is the construction [of the sentence]. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the "Air-House" (vehāsakuṭika).
Regarding the phrase "as far as the space of the door," the remainder of the sentence is "of a large vihāra.
Since it is stated in the Pāḷi that "a 'large' vihāra is said to be one that has an owner," and because such a vihāra would likely have been built by donors,
it refers to a "vihāra"— the distinctions of which are shown to be "either plastered inside, or plastered outside, or plastered both inside and outside."

The meaning is: taking as the limit the vicinity of the door-posts, which is the width of the door-panels as stated in the text for a "door-chamber" (*dvārakosa*)—that is, a "plank-jointed wall" (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*)—"within a hand’s reach on all sides. As it says in the commentary:
"A 'door-chamber' is the space surrounding a plank-jointed wall, measuring the width of the door-panels."

Regarding "for the fixing of the bolt" (*aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya*): here, because the term is used in association with the bolt, it refers specifically to the door-posts that are joined with the door-leaf along with that bolt;
thus, the meaning is "for the sake of making the door-posts immovable. As stated in the Commentary: "The meaning is 'for the sake of the immovability of the door-fastening together with its leaf.
Regarding "should be smeared" (*limpitabbaṃ*): here, the word "again and again" (*puna-punaṃ*) is to be supplied. As stated in the Commentary:
“‘It should be smeared again and again, or one should have it smeared’ means that a coating of clay should be applied repeatedly over the grass and clay.

(1106–7) “That which is to be known is this method (*naya*)” is the connection; the meaning is that whatever was stated as “it should be smeared again and again, or one should have it smeared,” this is to be understood as the method. It is called an *ālokasandhi* because it directs or covers the light.
This is a designation for the openings of the windows. As it is said: "The term 'light-entrances' refers to the window-openings.
Here, the plastered area surrounding the opening is equal in extent to the width of the door-panel of the window. As it is said:
"In all directions, the space is equal in extent to the width of the door-panel."

The intended meaning here is as follows: in the space around the window-frames, equal in width to the door-panels, and extending upwards as thickly as desired with the three types of clay, the light-opening should be plastered or caused to be plastered for the purpose of finishing.
Regarding the phrase, "He had it roofed again and again; he had it plastered again and again": [this refers to that].
Because the training rule was established due to the fault arising regarding the matter,
and because plastering was permitted only within a space measuring two and a half cubits around the door-frame,
for one who repeatedly applies plaster or causes it to be applied elsewhere than that, or who finishes the work to be done with clay on the wall—
They say that when a fourth application is given, it must be an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, in the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries,
since no offense of expiation is mentioned for the repeated application of plaster other than what has been specified as prohibited,
it is stated that an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is the appropriate consequence.
"Of a roof" (*chadanassa*) means of any one among those mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): roofs of brick, stone, plaster, grass, or leaves.
Regarding "two or three layers" (*dvattipariyāyaṃ*), since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "By 'layer' (*pariyāya*) is meant by way of encircling;
thus, a roof is obtained by means of grass or leaves," "layer" here refers specifically to the roofing itself after having been encircled with either grass or leaves.
It should be understood as follows: when a roof-covering made of bricks, stone, or plaster is available, the term "roof-covering" is used here by way of illustration.

Furthermore, regarding the two or three layers of roofing, it should be understood as referring to successive layers of roofing, based on the commentary’s statement: "And all this roofing should be understood as being above the roofing."
“Harita” (green) refers to paddy and other such crops. As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā:

“In this context, ‘green’ intends both the seven varieties of paddy (pubbaṇṇa) and the other types of grain (aparaṇṇa), such as the varieties of beans, peas, sesame, horse-gram, bottle-gourd, and pumpkin.
That which lacks any one of these is called “aharita” (not green).
"Adhiṭṭheyya" means it should be determined. "Beyond that" means above [the three] either by way of the three methods (*pariyāya*) or the three paths (*magga*).

As it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Above the three paths or the three methods. "It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)" refers to when one stands in a place not yet cultivated, makes an agreement, and has it covered three times, according to the distance to be described hereafter.
On the third occasion, having commanded, "Do it thus," one should depart. One who does not depart must remain silent;

beyond that, on the fourth occasion, for one who prepares [the site] for the purpose of roofing, it is stated that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the counting of bricks and so forth, according to the counting of grasses among the grasses, and according to the counting of leaves among the leaves.
As it is said in the Pāḷi: "For one who roofs with a path..."
“Having resolved upon two paths and having directed [the intention] toward the third path, one should depart,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “toward the third path” (*tatiyāya maggaṃ*):

here, *tatiyāya* is a dative-accusative form used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is “the third path. As for the word “therein” (*tattha*), it refers to green grass. This is because of the statement:
“If one resolves while standing on green grass, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); therefore, one stands for the purpose of resolving.
It is so called. From the time of sowing the seed until the crop stands, it is called "green.
As it is said in the Commentary: "In whatever field the seed has been sown, though it has not yet come to fruition, once the rain has fallen, it will come to fruition," and so forth.
1108–9. To show the boundary for one who stands even in a place other than the sitting area, he says “on the back beam,” and so forth.
“On the back beam” is stated by way of a lodging connected with a beam; it is also an illustration for a lodging made by taking hold of a pillar.

And in the phrase “on the back beam,” the locative case is used in the sense of a location by proximity (sāmīpikādhāra), as in expressions such as “the sound on the Ganges. From where does this [arise]?

Is a distinction obtained? It is obtained from the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "He is seated either above the ridge-pole of the back-rafters, or above the pinnacle of the gable-roof, or at the side of the spire.

From the *Aṭṭhakathā* statement "seated," it should be understood that the word "standing" is also included here by virtue of the commonality of the cessation of movement. Regarding the phrase "in whatever place": [the rest follows].

“*Aharite*” (in what is not cultivated) is understood from the context. Regarding the word “*ṭhātuṃ*,” it is stated that one has taken up a standing position for the purpose of making a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*);
this is understood from the commentary’s statement: “It is not permitted to make a resolve even while standing within that [area] which is not cultivated.
In the phrase “*patanokāsato*,” the suffix *-to* is used in the sense of the first case (nominative). For that place is the falling-place of the monastery.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: The word *hi* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetuatthe*). Therefore, since this spot is the place where one falling from a non-green area would land upon the monastery, it must be understood that it is not permissible to stand there. 1111.
In this training rule, first of all, regarding the term *vihāra* in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it says: "A *vihāra* is called... [and so on].
Because it is stated [in the text] as “or,” and so forth, by way of its opposite, a hut whose roof and walls are made with grass alone is understood to be a “grass-hut”;
thus, a hut with a grass roof is a “grass-hut.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the two or three alternatives.

1112. "Knowing" means knowing that the water contains living beings. Regarding the words "he should sprinkle or cause it to be sprinkled," the phrase "with that water" should be supplied here. As it says in the Aṭṭhakathā: "He himself should sprinkle with that water," and so forth. 1113.
However, if one should sprinkle clay without breaking the stream, the construction is: "of him who is sprinkling in this manner. 1114–15.
"A flowing stream" (sandamānaka) means a channel carrying water. "A trench" (mātikā) means a bank or embankment. "Making it face him" means [making] the water intended for bathing.

If [the water] turns toward him as he himself directs it—this is the construction for the phrase "there might be an offense for that bhikkhu according to the count of his efforts" when binding it here and there.
"Count of efforts" means by the count of efforts; the meaning is: by the count of the efforts made to turn the water toward whichever direction is desired after having bound it again and again.
1116–7. Regarding the water which, when grass or the like is thrown into it, undergoes either depletion or turbidity—in such a case...
If one were to throw clay, or even grass, into water—even if it were as much as a full cartload—all at once, there would be one *pācittiya* offense for each such act of throwing.
The word "or" (*vā*) implies that for one who throws clay, grass, or even wood, cow dung, and so forth, the *pācittiya* applies according to the number of individual acts.
"Turbidity" (*āvilatta*) refers to the state of being stirred up in such a way that living beings perish.
This demonstrates that there is no offense for one who throws grass and such into great water where living beings do not perish.
As it is said in the Commentary: "But this was said with reference to great water... (1118).
"There is an offense of wrong-doing" means that an offense of wrong-doing arises by reason of the command. There is one *pācittiya* [offense].
1119. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means both where there are living beings and where there are no living beings.

"With doubt" (*vimatissa*) refers to one accompanied by doubt due to association [with others]. 1120. In the phrases beginning with "In all cases perceiving it as containing living beings," that which is obtained through the context—namely, "doing anything such as pouring water and so forth"—should be connected to each [term] individually.
"In all cases" means both where there are living beings and where there are no living beings. "Perceiving it as containing no living beings" (*apāṇasaññissa*)...
Thus, for one who perceives that there are no living beings because they have perished through such an application of effort:

"Unintentionally" (*asañcicca*) means, for example, when water containing living beings has been taken in jars or other vessels, and while pouring it out or having it poured out so that the living beings do not perish, grass or other debris falls into that water; this is called "done unintentionally. "Unmindful" (*asatiyā*) means by way of lack of mindfulness.
"Of one who does": of one who does so without knowing that there are living beings present.

(1121–2) Since the seventh section on "With Living Beings" concerns the scope of the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*) when a murderous intent is present, he says "without a murderous intent" in order to distinguish it from that.
In the Pāḷi of this training rule, [it says] "with living beings..."
By the word "water," the first factor as found in the commentary is stated; by the word "knowing," the second factor is stated;
and by the phrase "should sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled," the fourth factor is stated. The third factor is not explicitly stated here;

however, its absence is indicated because that [factor] is defined by the mention of a *pācittiya* offense in the first training rule of the seventh chapter on the mind of a murderer (*vadhakacitta*).
With the intention that the third factor has already been explained, he said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, “without the intent to kill. For this very reason, he said:
“The four factors of this [offense] have been pointed out by the Great Sage. “Of this” means of this training rule (sikkhāpada).
1123. Regarding one who perceives water as containing living beings—even if they previously knew, “By using this, living beings will die”—
Sprinkling and causing to sprinkle—just as lighting a lamp while knowing that insects such as moths will fall into it and die occurs even without the intention to kill, so too [this action] occurs;
thus it is said: "A formal offense (paṇṇattivajja) involving three types of consciousness.

In this regard, for one who sprinkles out of anger or while preoccupied with play, there is unwholesome consciousness; for one who sprinkles a flower-grove and the like, there is wholesome consciousness.
The "threefold mind" should be understood as the indeterminate mind of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and who is unaware of the designation (paṇṇatti).
"Of that" refers to the first training rule in the seventh chapter. "And of this" refers to this training rule concerning pouring.
"This distinction" means this difference; the meaning is that it is explained or made manifest here in this treatise. That is a worldly offense (lokavajja).

This is an offense by way of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*). That is an unwholesome mind; this refers to the three types of consciousness. That is painful feeling; this refers to the three types of feeling—this is what is meant.

If it is asked, "What is the distinction between this [offense] and the second one in the seventh chapter?"—it is because this training rule was first formulated with reference to external use, stating, "If one should sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled," whereas [the other] states, "If one should use water containing living beings."
It should be understood that this training rule was formulated with reference to one's own use of bathing, drinking, and so forth. Alternatively,

even though it was formulated first in that context, since it was formulated specifically for one's own use, it should be understood that this present training rule was formulated with reference to external use.
Commentary on the Discourse on Water with Living Beings.
The second chapter, the Section on Lodgings.
1124–6. Regarding the phrase "endowed with eight factors": here, "virtuous" and so forth constitutes one factor; "learned" and so forth constitutes the second.
“Moreover, both of these [qualities] in her” and so forth is the third; “she is one of beautiful speech” and so forth is the fourth;
“she is for the most part dear and pleasing to the bhikkhunīs” is the fifth; “she is capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs” is the sixth;
“but this was not undertaken specifically for the Blessed One” and so forth is the seventh; “or she has twenty years of seniority.”
"Or more than twenty years"—these are the eight factors mentioned in the text. The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs" and "the formal authorization for that purpose.
"Herein" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The analysis is: "of which formal act the motion is the fourth.
The word "by the formal act" (*kammena*) is the remainder [to complete the sentence].

The construction is as follows: "that monk who is not authorized by that authorization as a teacher of bhikkhunīs which was permitted here by the Great Seer through a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation for a bhikkhu endowed with the eight factors.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the eight *garudhammas*," these refer to those rules found in the Canon beginning with: "A bhikkhunī ordained for a hundred years must perform salutation, rising from her seat, joining of palms, and respectful service toward a bhikkhu ordained on that very day."
"By means of the eight *garudhammas*. "A single bhikkhunī, or several bhikkhunīs"—this is obtained from the context.
"While reciting" (*osārento*) means while vocalizing the text (*pāḷi*). As it says in the Commentary: "It should be recited means the text should be spoken.

"Those rules" refers to those eight *garudhammas* mentioned previously. "He should exhort" (*ovadeyya*) means he should perform the exhortation consisting of the recitation of the text of the eight *garudhammas*.

What is meant? On the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), the bhikkhunīs, having come for the purpose of receiving exhortation, having paid homage, and sat down to one side, [the bhikkhu] asks them according to the method set forth in the text beginning with "by that bhikkhu": "Are you, sisters, living in concord?

If they should say, "We are living in concord, venerable sir," he should ask again: "Are the eight weighty rules (garudhamma) being observed by you, sisters? If they should say, "They are being observed, venerable sir,"...
If they should say, “Sisters, this is the exhortation,” he should hand it over.

If they should say, “It is not proper for you [to do so],” he should provide the exhortation by reciting the text of the Eight Garudhammas, beginning with, “[Even] one ordained for a hundred years...,” as it is said: “He should exhort them while reciting those very rules.”
1127. “By another teaching” means by either the Sutta-piṭaka or the Abhidhamma-piṭaka. “Ordained on one side” means ordained within the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs alone.
As it says in the Commentary: “of one who has been ordained on one side in the presence of the bhikkhunīs.
“In that manner” indicates that for one who exhorts [the bhikkhunīs] in such a way, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
1128. “In the very presence of the bhikkhus” includes the five hundred Sakyan women who went forth together with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
Regarding the change of gender: the meaning is that when a bhikkhu undergoes a transformation of gender, it is declared that there is likewise a *pācittiya* offense.

1129. "Without having handed over the exhortation" means that even when [the nuns] have been asked, "Sisters, do the eight *garudhammas* prevail? and they reply, "They do prevail, Venerable Sir," the same meaning applies here as well. 1130. The construction is:
"There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who exhorts [them] by means of the *garudhammas*.
1131. Regarding "for one who does not accept the exhortation": here, the request or message for the purpose of the exhortation is understood as "exhortation" because it has that purpose.

"Not accepting the instruction" means not receiving the exhortation. "Nor bringing it back" means even for one who, having announced that exhortation received by herself at the Uposatha hall, does not speak after delivering to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha the reply given by the reciter of the Pātimokkha.
"Foolish" refers to both the failure to accept the instruction and the failure to announce it after going to the Uposatha hall.

One is "foolish" due to ignorance regarding how to carry back the response and how to announce it accordingly to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, a group, or an individual on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada).
"The sick" refers to one who, even after going to the Uposatha hall, is afflicted with an illness that prevents them from making the announcement.
"One who is traveling" refers to one who must depart on urgent business without remaining for the first day of the fortnight.
The connection is: "except for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), it may be so.

Regarding the phrase "in the formal act" (kammasmiṃ): it is stated in the Commentary that here, by the word *kamma*, what is intended is the formal act of authorization (*sammutikamma*) granted to the instructor of bhikkhunīs by means of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*). Having omitted both the motion and the formal statement (*kammavācā*), [the offense occurs].
If it is done after having been reversed, it is called an illegal act (*adhammakamma*).

It is "in a faction" (*vagge*) when there is a division due to the failure to bring the consent of those entitled to give consent, or by the reopening of a matter already settled among those assembled. "There may be three offenses of expiation" (*tikapācittiyaṃ siyā*) means:

if one instructs a factional community of nuns while perceiving the illegal act as illegal and perceiving the community as factional; or if one instructs them while being doubtful; or if one instructs them while perceiving the community as united.
“There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)” refers to the triad of offenses of expiation mentioned in the case of one who perceives an illegitimate legal act (adhamma-kamma) as such.
1133. The construction is: “but also for one who is doubtful regarding an illegitimate legal act. By the word “likewise” (tathā), this includes the statement:
“In a quorum [of monks], in the community of nuns, there may be a triple offense of expiation. What is meant? In the case of an illegitimate legal act, in the category of those who are doubtful...

“If one exhorts a factional Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs while perceiving it as factional, or being in doubt, or perceiving it as unanimous, there is an offense of pācittiya”—this means that in the section on uncertainty, the pācittiya consisting of three cases applies precisely to an illegitimate legal act (*adhammika-kamma*).

By the phrase “perceiving it as a legitimate legal act,” this should also be connected with the statement “but in the case of an illegitimate legal act”; thus, the connection is made by the word “likewise.”

By this, he includes the passage beginning with “in a faction” (*vagge*). It is stated: “If one instructs a factional community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*) while perceiving it as a legal act (*dhammakamma*) when it is an illegal act (*adhammakamma*), or while being uncertain of its factionality, or while perceiving it as a united assembly (*samagga*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
thus, there is a triad of expiations. It is with reference to these expiations that he says, “nine expiations are stated.”
In this section on illegal formal acts (*adhammakamma*), just as in the alternative case of "in a united community of bhikkhunīs," nine *pācittiya* offenses likewise occur;
thus, pointing this out by extension, he said, "And even in a united [community], there are that many. As it is said:
"If one perceives an illegal act as an illegal act, and addresses a united community of bhikkhunīs while perceiving it as divided, or being doubtful, or perceiving it as united..."

There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If it is an illegitimate legal procedure (adhamma-kamma), and one is in doubt, yet instructs a united community of nuns while perceiving it as a divided one, or being in doubt, perceives it as a united one—there is an offense of expiation. If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure (dhamma-kamma), and one instructs a united community of nuns while perceiving it as a divided one, or being in doubt, perceives it as a united one—there is an offense of expiation.”

1134. "Of two groups of nine" refers to the group-of-nine in discord and the group-of-nine in concord, according to what has been shown, by way of these two groups of nine. "These" refers to the *pācittiya* offenses.

"If one perceives a legal act as an illegal act, and instructs a group-of-nine Bhikkhunī Saṅgha while perceiving it as a group in discord, or being doubtful, or perceiving it as a group in concord, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If one is doubtful regarding a legal act, and instructs a group-of-nine Bhikkhunī Saṅgha while perceiving it as a group in discord..."

If one who is doubtful, perceiving the Saṅgha to be united, instructs [the nuns], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If, in a legitimate legal procedure (dhammakamma), one who perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, perceiving the nun-saṅgha to be incomplete or being doubtful about its incompleteness, yet instructs them while perceiving it to be complete, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Thus, there are nine offenses of wrong-doing on the side of the incomplete assembly. “If, in a legitimate legal procedure, one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure [instructs] a complete nun-saṅgha...”

If one who perceives a schismatic assembly, or is in doubt, or perceives it as a united assembly, exhorts [the nuns], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If, regarding a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma), one who is in doubt, perceiving a united Bhikkhunī-saṅgha as schismatic, or being in doubt, or perceiving it as united, exhorts [them], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, regarding a legitimate legal act, one who perceives it as a legitimate legal act, perceiving a united Bhikkhunī-saṅgha as schismatic, or being in doubt, exhorts [them]...

There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In the case where one perceives a legitimate legal act as legitimate, and perceives the united Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs as united, and exhorts them, there is no offense—this refers to the section on non-offenses mentioned at the end. Excluding that, in the remaining eight sections, there are eight offenses of wrong-doing for the side of unity.
Thus, there are nine [offenses] in the preceding cases and these eight in the side of the legitimate legal act.
"There are seventeen *dukkaṭas*," he said, [expressing this by]: "There may be a *dukkaṭa* even in a formal act (*dhammakamma*), and it may be of seventeen kinds.
1135. The construction is: "When told, 'Recite [the Pātimokkha],' he recites it"; or when told, "Recite the eight *garudhammas*," he recites them;
or when asked a question, he answers—namely, when asked a question concerning the eight *garudhammas*, he answers that very thing.
"He speaks" or "he tells the training rules to a *sikkhamānā*": this is the connection. The meaning is that there is no fault if he explains the eight *garudhammas* to a *sikkhamānā*.
The construction is that for one who speaks while insane and so forth, there is likewise no fault. 1136.
Now, when the characteristics of all three types of learned ones (*bahussuta*) have been shown in one place, the distinction of the instructor of nuns (*bhikkhunovādaka*) [is as follows]:

To show that it is easy to understand, he said: "It should be made familiar by being recited from memory," and so forth. The construction is: "The two matrices (mātikā) should be made proficient and recited from memory.
The construction is: "In the Vibhaṅgas of the Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs, the matrices should be made proficient and recited from memory";
that is, having mastered the matrices of the Bhikkhu- and Bhikkhunī-Vibhaṅgas and having learned their commentary (aṭṭhakathā) both according to the text and according to the meaning.
The meaning is that they must be made such that they have ascended the path of speech and are fit for conventional usage.

The construction is as follows: it is declared that the four recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) must be made both proficient and committed to memory. By the word "proficient" (paguṇā), he shows that one should master the text, retain it, and then inquire about it.
By the phrase "must be made committed to memory," he indicates that after hearing and retaining its meaning, [one should practice recitation].
This shows that it must indeed be questioned.

"For the sake of a preliminary discourse" means for the purpose of giving a Dhamma talk to those who have assembled. "The path of discourse" refers to the path of discourse concerning the Mahāsudassana. "Auspicious...
[omission] ...thanksgiving" refers to the discourse on giving, which consists of the thanksgiving for the meal among the auspicious events such as the first gift and so forth.
And there is the rejoicing in blessings such as the *Mahāmaṅgala Sutta* during the *kumāramaṅgala* ceremonies and so forth;

and what is called "inauspicious" is the passing away [of a person], wherein there is talk such as that from beyond the wall regarding funeral meals and the like—thus, there are exactly three kinds of rejoicing. 1138.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the Uposatha and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *pavāraṇā* ceremony and others. "The determination of what is a formal act and what is not" (*kammākammavinicchaya*).
The analysis stated in the *Kammavagga* refers to the analysis of minor and very minor formal acts (*kamma*) found in the *Parivāra*, Kammavagga.
By the term "meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he refers to the meditation subject for insight (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*), because of what will be said later: "the ruin of the highest goal.
And it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*s that one who learns by way of insight should learn it by means of the determination of the elements (*dhātu-vavatthāna*).
It has been said. "Of the supreme goal" means of arahantship. 1139.
"Having mastered this much, he is one of great learning": because he has mastered the teachings as they have been described, he is one of great learning (*bahussuta*).
"Five years old": having completed five full years since his full ordination (*upasampadā*). Regarding the phrase "ten years old," it is the same here as well.
The same method applies here. According to the reckoning of years, when five years are complete, it is "five years" even if the rains-residence (vassa) has not been completed;
otherwise, it should be understood as "less than five years.

Just as in the case of full ordination (*upasampadā*) for those who have completed twenty years, some do not consider the calculation of the solar year (*saṃvacchara*), but rather take the mere common term "five years" to mean the counting of completed rains-residences.
To grasp [them] in that way is improper; or rather, the propriety regarding such graspings must be sought. "Having released them" means having abandoned the life of dependence (*nissayavāsa*).
"Independent" (*issara*) means being independent due to the absence of a formal preceptor for dependence; by this, the characteristic of being free from dependence is shown.

(1140) "The two Vibhaṅgas" refers to the pair of the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga. Here, the term "committed to speech" (*vācuggata*) also includes the *paripucchā* (the detailed interrogation).
It is also said with this underlying intention (*sandhāya*). Therefore, it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*: “The two Vibhaṅgas should be made familiar and mastered by recitation”;
they say this was also spoken with reference to learning by means of questioning. Regarding the phrase “beginning with the phrasing (*byañjana*)”:

here, “phrasing” (*byañjana*) refers to a word (*pada*), while by the word “beginning” (*ādi*), that which is included as “sub-phrasing” (*anubyañjana*) refers to a syllable (*akkhara*); thus, [it refers to] the words and syllables.
"Without omitting" is what is meant. "In all four Nikāyas" refers to the Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, and Aṅguttara Nikāyas;
the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). The construction is: "either one Nikāya, or even a single book.

By the word *api* ("even/also"), the inclusion of the Khuddaka Nikāya is to be understood. By the phrase "or even," it is indicated that [the reciter] should recite the Jātaka together with its commentary from the Khuddaka Nikāya.

Having mastered the *Dhammapada* together with its narrative contexts (*vatthu*), one should indeed master it further; thus it is shown that one compiles two manuscripts, or the four sections of the *Khandhaka-vatta*. 1142.
"A leader of the quarters" means wherever he dwells, he is the leader, the foremost, of that respective quarter. "One who goes wherever he wishes."
The meaning is that he has his livelihood wherever he may be, according to his wish. The construction is: "He obtains the mastery to cause a retinue to attend upon him.
The meaning is that, being master, he is able to have himself attended upon by a retinue of monks according to his own preference.
Up to this point, the characteristic of one who causes a retinue to attend upon him has been stated.

1143. *Vācugga* means that which has reached the mouth. And here, it is stated without doubt: "Now, since this procedure for reciting the text (*bhaṇḍapāṭhāvidhi*) does not exist, it should be understood that the formal decision (*atthakaraṇa*) made according to the sequence of the inquiry and discussion is not what is called 'bringing [the matter] to the mouth' (*vācuggatakaraṇa*).
By this, only the second factor as previously described is included.

1144. *Assā* refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "The three factors beginning with being unappointed" means these three factors: one's own lack of appointment, the fact that the nun is fully ordained (*paripuṇṇūpasampannā*), and the speaking of the eight weighty rules (*aṭṭhagarudhamma*) by way of exhortation.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse regarding exhortation.
1146. Regarding the "threefold offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*): "When the sun has set, perceiving it as having set; being in doubt; perceiving it as not having set."

Regarding the three types of formal determination (*vikappa*): "one ordained in one [community]" refers to one ordained in the community of nuns (*bhikkhunī-saṅgha*). However, the Commentary states: "But for one who exhorts [nuns] who have been ordained in the community of monks (*bhikkhu-saṅgha*), it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone.

(1148) "By way of recitation and so forth" means by way of the section on non-offenses, such as: "There is no offense when giving a recitation (*uddesa*), when giving an interrogation (*paripucchā*), and so forth. "His" refers to the monk (*bhikkhu*).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Setting Sun (Atthaṅgatasūriyakathāvaṇṇanā).
1149. Because it will be stated later, “If he is not authorized,” the word “authorized” (*sammatassa*) is understood here in the phrase “while exhorting.
“The nunnery” (*bhikkhunupassaya*) means the dwelling place of the bhikkhunīs. “Except at the proper time”: “In this case, the proper time is when she is ill...”

"Except at the time when it is said, 'a bhikkhunī,'" this means that there is no offense during the period of illness as indicated by the statement: "A sick bhikkhunī is one who is unable to go for the exhortation or to join the communal residence.
"There are two *pācittiya* offenses" means that there are two *pācittiya* offenses: one under the first training rule and one under this training rule.

"They are" means that "three *pācittiya*s" should be connected [to the rule]; the meaning is that three *pācittiya* offenses arise by virtue of the first, second, and third training rules (*sikkhāpada*). 1151.

"By another teaching" means by another word of the Buddha other than a heavy offense (*garudhamma*). "Two *dukkaṭa*s" refers to those rooted in going to a nun's residence that has not been formally authorized.
Two *dukkaṭa* offenses. Regarding the term "nun" (*bhikkhunī*), it is because [the text] will later state, "even for one who is authorized.

It is said to be "caused by night" because it is stated in the rule concerning the eight *garudhammas* that "if she exhorts her with the eight *garudhammas* or with any other teaching, there is an offense of *pācittiya*"; thus, the meaning is that it is rooted in exhortation during the night.

"1152. 'The two Pācittiyas' refers to those rooted in the second and third [Garudhammas]. The analysis is: 'An instruction by means of a Garudhamma is a Garudhamma'; that which has such a Garudhamma as its source (nidāna) is the Pācittiya.
The connection is: 'Because there is an absence of a Pācittiya offense whose source is a Garudhamma, due to the fact of being formally authorized.
By this first training rule, he demonstrates the state of non-offense."

1153. *Tasseva* means of one who has been authorized. There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) under this third training rule. There is no offense under the first training rule; therefore he said, "because of being authorized. There is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) under the second training rule; therefore he said, "during the night. 1154. It is stated that there is a triad of offenses of expiation:

"If, regarding one who is fully ordained, he perceives her as such, or is doubtful, or perceives her as not fully ordained, and having approached the nuns' quarters, he exhorts her except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation"—this is the triad of offenses of expiation.

It has been stated. Regarding "the other two": this refers to the other two cases shown [in the text] as: "If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if one is uncertain regarding a person who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Regarding "one who exhorts": this refers to anyone who exhorts.

(1155) To show that there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses and that in the place of *dukkaṭa* there is only *dukkaṭa*, he said "likewise" (*tathā*). The construction is: "Likewise" applies to one who, having gone to the nuns' quarters, exhorts them by means of some other teaching.
Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Nuns’ Quarters (Bhikkhunupassayakathāvaṇṇanā).

1156. Regarding the phrase "robes and so forth" (cīvarādīnaṃ): by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the other three requisites beginning with almsfood (piṇḍapāta) are included, as well as honor, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship. "Appointed" (sammateti) means appointed by the formal authorization (sammuti) as a teacher of the nuns (bhikkhunovādaka). 1157. It is stated that there are three types of offenses of expiation (pācittiya):
"perceiving a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma) as legitimate," "being in doubt," and "perceiving it as an illegitimate legal act (adhammakamma)."

"If she speaks thus, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. Thus, the triad of *pācittiya* offenses is already shown in the Canon (*pāḷi*). Here, "formal act" (*kamma*) refers to the aforementioned formal act by convention (*sammutikamma*).

Regarding an illegitimate formal act (*adhammakamma*), there is a triad of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) based on one who perceives it as legitimate, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as illegitimate.
"Twenty years old or more than twenty years old" are the constituent factors for the convention.

1158. If it is asked, "To whom does the phrase 'one who is ordained but not fully admitted' refer? It is said with reference to one who, having been ordained, has renounced the training and returned to the state of a novice (sāmaṇera). "For the sake of material things" means for the sake of robes and so forth. This concludes the commentary on the talk concerning material things. 1162.

Regarding the phrase "given by a bhikkhunī," the word "by a bhikkhu" should be supplied. The construction is: "given by a bhikkhu. The word "by a bhikkhunī" is the remainder [of the sentence]. "Therein" refers to the training rule (sikkhāpada) concerning the acceptance of robes. "Indicated" means made manifest.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Giving of Robes. 1163.
The construction is: "a robe from a nun who is not a relative.
1164. "In this" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
1165. “Having inserted the needle into the robe” is the connection [of the sentence]. “In the drawing out of the needle” means from the robe. 1166.

“By way of the effort” means by the counting of the efforts of drawing out the needle after having sewn many [stitches] in a single moment. “Many *pācittiya* offenses” is the construction; the meaning is that there are as many offenses as there are instances of effort.

1169. “There are many *pācittiya* offenses” is the construction. “In the path of the needle” means in the track of the needle. In the second line, it should be understood that the word *āra-* has been elided for the sake of the meter’s ease.
1170. What indeed is the meaning of the phrase “there are many offenses”? Here, the sense is: what is there to be said? Regarding the *triplet of pācittiyas*:

it is the triplet of pācittiyas stated thus: “If one sews or causes to be sewn a robe for a woman who is not related, perceiving her as not related, or being in doubt, or perceiving her as related, there is an offense of pācittiya.”

1172. "Another requisite" refers to items such as sandals and bags. Regarding the term "sewing," the sense of "having [someone] sew" is understood here by virtue of the governing context. "Those undergoing training" refers to probationers (*sikkhamānā*) and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*).
1173. It is called an "action" (*kriya*) because it is an offense incurred through the act of sewing.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of sewing robes.
1174–5. *Saṃvidhāya*: having made an appointment in the manner of saying, "Let us go today," or "Let us go tomorrow," and so forth.

As it is said: "He makes an appointment, thinking, 'We shall go either today, or yesterday, or the day after. *Maggaṃ*: a single road for traveling, even if it is merely the distance between two villages.
*Aññatra samayā*: except at the proper time. Regarding this, the proper time is as follows: "The road is one that must be traveled by a caravan and is considered dangerous."
"Except at the specific times mentioned as 'frightening'—this is what is meant by 'except. A road that cannot be traveled without caravan leaders is called 'a road for caravans.
A road where the places where thieves lie down, sit, stand, eat, or drink are visible is called 'dangerous. Where people have been struck down, killed, slain, plundered, or robbed by thieves..."

That which is perceived as such is called "frightening. "Here" means at this time when, having made an appointment with a bhikkhunī and not breaking it, one sets out on a journey along the same road with her.
"Another village" is *gāmantara*; "entering" (*okkamana*) or approaching that is "entering another village" (*gāmantarokkama*); the meaning is: "when [that] has been done."
"In a forest devoid of a village, beyond half a *yojana*"—this is the construction; the meaning is: "even on a forest path free from a village, when one has gone beyond two *gāvutas*.
Regarding the phrase "there is an offense," he says "herein," etc., in order to show the classification and non-classification of the offenses shown in general terms.
"In this" means in this exposition of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), or in this treatise (*pakaraṇa*). The connection is: "an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is explained.
Regarding the phrase "standing on improper ground": here, "improper ground" refers to such places as the gatehouse at the entrance to a nunnery within a village.
As it says in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "But if [he stands] at the gate of a nunnery within a village, on a carriage road..."

“Or if they make arrangements in other places such as at crossroads (*catukka*), intersections (*siṅghāṭaka*), elephant stables, and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the monk.
In this context, a *catukka* is a place where four roads meet; a *siṅghāṭaka* is a place where three roads meet.
A “proper ground” (*kappiyabhūmi*) refers to a dwelling for bhikkhunīs and the like, as it is said: “If both [the food and the storage] are in a dwelling for bhikkhunīs...”
If they make an appointment while standing in a monastery grove, in a sitting hall, or in a lodging for non-Buddhist ascetics, there is no offense.
For this is indeed a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area where things are permissible). Therefore, they do not say that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) here on account of making an appointment.
Thus he said: "There is no wrong-doing for one who does not speak. The analysis of the phrase is: "They do not speak [to him]."

1178. "In both cases" (*ubhayattha*) refers to the two alternatives: departing after making an appointment while standing on unallowable ground, and departing after making an appointment while standing on allowable ground.
"Only for one who is going" (*gacchantasseva*)—the word "only" (*eva*) indicates that there is no offense for one who has already departed.
As it is said: "There is no offense at the moment of departure. By the phrase "for a bhikkhu," he indicates that there is no offense for a bhikkhunī.
He said, “of the one immediately following,” and so forth, for the purpose of defining the field of offenses. 1179.
“There too” means even when stepping outside the precinct of a formal enclosure (kappiyabhūmi). It was stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*; as it says, “it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. 1180.
“Between” means in the middle between the village from which one has departed and the next village. As it says, “from the village...”

"But having gone out, as long as one has not yet entered the precincts of the next village, even if an appointment has been made within this interval, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the bhikkhu.
Regarding this training rule, there are three types of appointments and non-appointments based on time, doors, and paths.
Among these, he said "door... is called" in order to show that an offense indeed occurs even in the case of non-appointment regarding the path and the door. Regarding non-appointment regarding time:
However, he will state the non-offense. The offense is a *pācittiya*. 1181.
Regarding "at an unappointed time": this refers to a time not previously appointed, such as after the meal, for those who have made an appointment saying, "We shall go before the meal," and so forth;
it is in that [time]. "In the case of an appointment by a monk" means an appointment by a nun.
If there is no arrangement made by the monks themselves, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 1182.

The construction is as follows: there is no offense for one who goes after having made an arrangement at the proper time, or for one who goes after having made an arrangement at an improper time but without breaking the agreement, or for one who goes after having made an arrangement in the event of an emergency.
The word "likewise" (tathā) refers back to this: "there is no offense for one who goes after having made an arrangement."
In this context, "agreement" (*samaya*) refers to a specific time as previously described. "Misunderstanding" (*visaṅketa*) refers to a misunderstanding regarding the time;

that is to say, having made an appointment, thinking, "We shall go on such-and-such a day at such-and-such a time," there is a failure to appear at that appointed time when it is actually the time to go.

As it is said: "There is no offense only in the case of a misunderstanding regarding the time. "Calamity" (*āpadā*) refers to [disturbances] such as the division of kingdoms or [the upheaval of] provinces.
It is time to flee. As it is said: "When there is a division of the kingdom, the people mounted on their vehicles wander about;

such is the case in times of calamity. Here, "division of the kingdom" means the destruction of the kingdom. "Mounted on their vehicles" means mounted on a vehicle consisting of postures (*iriyāpatha*) or a cart-wheel (*sakaṭacakra*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those with deranged minds and others are included.

1183. Regarding the phrase "the triad beginning with body and speech" (*kāyavācādikattaya*): here, by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), "mind" (*citta*) is included; thus, it means "body, speech, and mind. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of arrangements.
1184. It moves upward, thus it is "upward-moving" (*ujjavanī*); it refers to a boat going against the current. It moves downward, thus it is "downward-moving" (*ojavanī*).
"A boat going with the current"—this refers to that. "He should board" (*abhiruheyya*): here, the word "having made an appointment" (*saṃvidhāya*) is to be supplied. As it is said:
"Whatever monk, having made an appointment with a nun, should board a single boat.

The meaning is: having boarded that boat due to friendship characterized by worldly pleasure, and making the intention to play the precursor, they have made an appointment with one another. As it is said:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says: "Having made an appointment with the intention of sporting, by way of worldly pleasure and intimacy with friends.

(1185) When traveling along the side of a village boundary, it is a *pācittiya* offense by way of crossing into another village; when traveling along the side of a non-village boundary, it is a *pācittiya* at half a *yojana*, and for a distance exceeding half a *yojana*, whether a village exists [within that range] or not.
(1186) He speaks thus in order to show that for one traveling through the middle of a river one *yojana* in width, the offense occurs by way of half a *yojana*.
“‘Tathā’ and so forth. ‘It divides both sides of the middle of a river that is less than a *yojana* in width;
thus, for one traveling through the middle of such a river, there is an offense according to the calculation of crossing between villages and the calculation of half a *yojana*,’ so they say.
Regarding “as one pleases in the ocean,” the word “should go” (*gantabba*) is to be supplied as the remainder. By the phrase “in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)” and so forth...
He shows the reason for permitting travel according to one’s convenience. By this very [statement], it is understood that there is no offense regarding ponds and the like where water does not flow.
1188. "For the purpose of reaching the opposite bank" means to cause her to reach the other shore. "That boat. "Those who have harnessed [it]" refers to the boatmen. 1189.
By the word "likewise," he includes the phrase "no offense has been declared" in relation to [the case of] a nun who has not made an appointment.

The construction is as follows: "whether he should board a single boat together [with her]; or, having made an appointment with a bhikkhunī, he should board a single boat for the purpose of crossing over;
or, in cases of emergency, he should board a single boat together with a bhikkhunī—even having made an appointment—there is no offense; thus it is declared."
By the phrase “equal to what follows immediately,” he includes the determination stated by the passage beginning with “at a time not previously arranged.

Here too, there is no offense when there is a discrepancy regarding the time; however, there is indeed an offense when there is a discrepancy regarding the landing place or the boat. As it is said: “Here too, there is no offense precisely because of a discrepancy regarding the time,” and so forth.
This is because of the statement: “having made an arrangement out of a desire for sport, due to worldly pleasure and intimacy with friends.”
Some say that this training rule is an unwholesome state of mind and is "worldly-offense" (*lokavajja*); that should not be accepted.

For if one mounts [a vehicle] with the intention of sport and enters another village, or travels beyond half a *yojana*, one incurs an offense even while possessing a wholesome or indeterminate state of mind.
Indeed, if such a person were to attain a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and realize *arahantship*, [the offense would be nullified].

Whether one falls asleep or goes about attending to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), how could there be for such a person possession of an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta-samaṅgitā*)—on account of which this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) would be called "unwholesome mind, a worldly offense" (*lokavajja*)?
Therefore, it is established that this is an offense by formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*) and involves three types of consciousness (*ticitta*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding boarding a boat.

1190. The construction is as follows: for a bhikkhu who, having abandoned the undertaking of householders, knows that the meal has been prepared by a bhikkhunī and then eats it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Prepared" (paripācita) means produced by speaking to families of the bhikkhu’s virtues, such as his moral discipline (sīla), learning (suta), and so forth.
As it is said: "Prepared by a bhikkhunī" means obtained and made ready through the manifestation of one's virtues.
"Meaning": "Prepared by householders" means that which was already prepared by householders prior to the nun's ripening [of the meal]. As it is said:
"The meal that was first prepared by householders for the ripening of the nun. For he will say later:
"Or even without what is prepared by householders."

1191. Since the word “tassā” (of her) will be explained later, it should be construed with “yaṃ bhojanaṃ” (whatever food). “Tassā” refers to the food mentioned in its fivefold form. “In all instances of swallowing” means in all applications of the act of passing [food] down the throat of another.
1192. The construction is: there is an offense for a bhikkhunī who eats food prepared [for her].

1193. “In both cases” means whether it was prepared or not prepared. “In all instances” means that for one who consumes these two [kinds of food], there is a dukkaṭa offense by way of the act of swallowing; this is the construction.
1195. The construction is as follows: "There is no offense for one who eats anything other than the five kinds of cooked food, such as rice-gruel, solid food, fruit, and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding what has been prepared. 1197.
All of this tenth training rule is identical to the second indeterminate rule (*aniyata*) in terms of its origin, method of transgression, and so forth.

The word *matanti* means "they consider. "This training rule" refers to the training rule concerning sitting in private, which was stated as: "Whatever bhikkhu should sit down alone with a bhikkhunī in a secluded place, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of sitting in private.
The Third Chapter on Bhikkhunīs.

1198. *Eko* means lasting for one day. *Āvasathapiṇḍo* (alms-food at a rest-house) refers to any one of the five kinds of cooked food prepared in halls and such places by those seeking merit to give as much as desired to a single religious sect. As it is said: "Alms-food at a rest-house..."
“...one of the five kinds of cooked food has been prepared there to one’s satisfaction, either in a hall, or in a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree, or in the open air.
Regarding the term “not being ill,” the commentary on the word-analysis (*padabhājaniya-aṭṭhakathā*) states:
“One who is not ill is one who is able to depart from that lodging,” and [it continues]: “half a *yojana* or a *yojana*...”
Because it is said, "or he is able to go," the meaning is: by one who is not ill and capable of going from that lodging either half a *yojana* or a full *yojana*.
"Beyond that" means further than the second day. 1199.
The construction is: "he collects alms-food even where it is not specifically designated," or "from among these very ones," referring to a particular sect (*pāsaṇḍa*).
The phrase “or for just so many” means that, without making a specific limit on the number of persons there, it is established as a common provision for all;
thus, the meaning is “in the alms-food provided for the guest-house. The construction is: “it is established for alms-food sufficient for one’s needs. The analysis (*vigga-ha*) is:

“alms-food” (*piṇḍa*) is so called because its purpose (*attha*)—namely, filling the belly and so forth—is measured by the amount required; it is not limited by saying “only this much should be given,” but rather [it is for those] who are eating.
The meaning is: "only when the alms-food has been prepared [with the thought] 'it should be given as much as required'.

"It should be eaten" (*bhuñjitabba*) is either a karmasādhana (denoting the object) or a bhāvasādhana (denoting the action). "Food" (*bhojana*) is that which is to be swallowed. "Once" (*sakim*) means a single time. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the lodging. 1200. "Of that alms-food" (*tassa piṇḍassa*).

"In all swallowings" (*ajjhohāresu sabbesu*) means when all the acts of swallowing have been performed. "For that swallower" (*tassa ajjhohārakassa*). It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the number of applications.
1201. The construction is as follows: “Is it prescribed by one family in various distinct locations? or “Is it prescribed by various families in various distinct locations?
The governing term is “in a group” (*piṇḍe*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is: *nānā* (various) and *eko* (one) are *nānekā*; *ṭhānānaṃ bhedā* are *ṭhānabhedā* (distinctions of locations);

and *nānekā* and those *ṭhānabhedā* together form the compound. [The phrase refers to] among those. “Sharing in one” (*ekabhogī*) means sharing in the consumption of a single group meal (*ekapiṇḍaparibhogo*).
By the word "only" (eva), the consumption [of food] on the second day and subsequent days is excluded.

1204. Regarding "for one who is ill": the construction is that there is no offense for one who, having become ill according to the stated characteristics, eats again and again while going or coming—even if going as far as half a *yojana*, or having gone and then returning.
It is said that there is no offense for one who eats on a single day while traveling on the road and at the place where he has arrived.
As it was said: "If one who is going eats for one day on the road and for one day at the place where he has arrived, for him too there is no offense.
This same principle applies to one who is returning. Regarding the phrase "prescribed specifically," here [the term] "monks" refers to...
The rest is as it has been said: "It is prepared specifically for the sake of the bhikkhus. Regarding *paritta* (meager):

this refers to a small amount of food that is insufficient to fill the stomach. As it has been said: "If it is not prepared for as much as one needs, but is obtained little by little, it is permissible to consume such a thing even regularly.
*Sakim* means that which is prepared for as much as one needs, according to the method already stated.
There is no offense for one who eats only once. 1205.
Regarding the phrase "rice-gruel and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes other edible items apart from the five kinds of solid food.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning public rest-houses.
The construction is: "except for the stated occasions. This refers to the seven types of times mentioned [in the Vinaya]: "In this regard, these are the occasions:

the occasion of illness, the occasion of giving robes, the occasion of making robes, the occasion of traveling on a journey, the occasion of boarding a boat, the occasion of a great assembly, and the occasion of a meal for recluses"—it is except for these stated times.
In this context, when one is unable to go for alms because one’s feet have become cracked, this is the time of illness.
When the *kaṭhina* has been spread, there is a period of five months; for others, it is the month of Kattika—this is the time for the distribution of robes.
When, while a robe is being made, one performs even a small amount of work on the robe, this is the time for making robes. When one desires to travel even half a *yojana*...
Whether one is about to set out, is setting out, or has already set out—this is the occasion for traveling on a journey. The same principle applies to the occasion of boarding a boat.
When four monks, having wandered for alms in the village where they seek food, do not find enough to sustain themselves, this is the "great occasion" (*mahāsamaya*).
When anyone who has gone forth invites [monks] to a meal, this is the "occasion of a meal for recluses" (*samaṇabhattasamaya*). To the question "What is a group? he said: "A group," and so forth.
1207. Regarding "group-meal" (*gaṇabhojana*), what is it? It says "that which," and so forth. The construction is as follows:
that which is obtained either through an invitation (*nimantana*) or through a request (*viññatti*) from among the five [kinds of food] is intended here by the term "meal.
By "invitation," he refers to an improper invitation made in the manner that will be explained later with the words "of meals," and so on. Also, by "request"...
By the method that will be explained with the words "Even if... and so forth, he indicates a request for what is unallowable (*akappiya-viññatti*).
Regarding the phrase "of foods" (*bhojanānaṃ*), this is a genitive used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*);
the word "of one or another" (*aññatarassa*) is to be supplied. It refers to one of the five types of food included in the summary: "Boiled rice, flour, gruel, fish, and meat are the foods."

“Names” refers to the names of rice and so forth that will be mentioned. Regarding the phrase “he invites the bhikkhus,” the words “either together or separately” are to be understood as the ellipsis.

As it has been said: “Invited together; invited separately. An invitation together means inviting all the bhikkhus while they are standing together. An invitation separately means inviting the bhikkhus one by one.
An invitation from various sources occurs when one goes to the place where they live or to the place where they are standing together. As it is said:
"Having gone to four different cells or to the monastery, they are invited from various places;
or even when they are standing in one place, one is invited by his son and another by his father—this too is being invited from various sources."
"Synonym" (vevacana) refers to alternative expressions for all terms such as "rice," as well as for verbal phrases such as "accept.

"Other language" (bhāsantara) refers to linguistic systems other than the Māgadha language, such as the Sinhala, Tamil, and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is: "He invites either by means of synonyms or by means of another language."

“Then, immediately after the invitation”: *nimantana* refers to the aforementioned improper invitation (*akappiya-nimantana*). “Taking together”: standing or sitting while not releasing each other’s distance of twelve finger-breadths, they take [the food] together.
Regarding the phrase “the reason for eating in a group,” this offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) due to the condition of eating does not occur without such taking together; thus it is said.

1212. The construction is as follows: "Whether it be going together or separately, or even eating [together], the wise say that this is not a cause for *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group). Regarding "whether together or separately," the words "standing or sitting" are to be understood as the ellipsis. 1213–14.
"Having requested" means having requested either collectively, saying, "Give food to all four of us," or individually, saying, "Give to me, give to me.
"Even in this way" means even by means of such a request. 1215. "Of the two kinds" refers to the one who invites and the one who requests.
1216. The construction is: "There is no offense for those eating during even the seven occasions. From the context, this refers to "eating in a group" (*gaṇabhojana*). The meaning is:
for those eating without any pretext during the seven times previously mentioned, such as when one is ill, and so forth.

This word "together" (*ekato*) should be construed with the word "having taken" (*gahetvā*). "Eating" (*bhuñjantaṃ*) means "of those who are eating. The word "thus" (*tathā*) refers back to the phrase "there is no offense" (*anāpatti*).
1217. "Anupasampanna," "cārī," "patto," and "animantito" [refer to] one who is not ordained... [and so on] ... "nimantitā";

the meaning is that these four are made the fourth. The Sage has declared the breaking of the group for those who eat together after making an unordained person, or an alms-collector, or a bowl, or one who was not invited the fourth, and taking them all together.
It is meant that the incompleteness of the *gaṇa* (the group) is being illustrated. One who wanders for alms by way of his habit is a *piṇḍacārī*;

here, he is called simply "wanderer" (*cārī*) through the elision of the first member of the compound, meaning a *piṇḍapātika*. For he, not accepting invitations, does not become one who eats in a group or one who consumes from a group—this is the intended meaning.
A bowl (*patto*) is [that which is used] after sitting down in a monastery for the purpose of obtaining food for oneself as the fourth [member of the group].
"Sent" means brought. "Invited" refers to one who has been invited by an improper invitation, yet is not included within the limits [of that invitation], and is fully ordained.
"In this" refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The word "also" (*api*) refers back to the determination stated above regarding the cases of two or three [people].
1218. *Samayaladdhānaṃ*: those by whom the seven occasions—such as being ill and so forth—have been obtained are "those who have obtained an occasion" (*samayaladdha*);
for them, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). The word "of a certain one" (*aññatarassa*) is to be supplied, which connects with the word "by means of" (*vasena*).

The construction is: "there is no breach of the group. Taking that [person] who has obtained an occasion—who is himself free from offense—as the fourth member, there is a "group meal" (*gaṇabhojana*).
However, because an offense may arise for those who accept [the invitation], it is said: "The offense must be understood. As stated in the Mahāpaccarī:
"One who has obtained [an invitation] at the proper time is released by himself; as for the others, because they act as the completer of the group, they become liable to an offense. 1219.
Having invited someone by mentioning one of the five kinds of food, if another [of those same five] is given to them...
In order to show the absence of a breach of convention for one who accepts [the food], he said, "And of the foods," and so forth.
"Of the foods" is a genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*); what is meant is "by way of one or another.
This means that for one who accepts rice gruel and so forth after being invited by the specific names of rice and other such items, it does not constitute a "group meal" (*gaṇabhojana*).

1221. “Constant meal” (*niccabhatta*) refers to a fixed meal. When they say, “Take a constant meal,” it is permissible for many people to take it together. This same principle applies to tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*) and so forth.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding group meals (*gaṇabhojana*). 1223–4.
“By many people” means by numerous individuals who have been invited separately. Of the five [offenses], for whom...

Regarding the word *kassa*: here, the phrase “among fellow practitioners” (*sahadhammikesu*) is to be supplied; it is used in the locative case for the purpose of specification, meaning “whichever among the five fellow practitioners.

What does he say by the words “having abandoned,” etc.? [He says: either by way of a formal assignment (*vikappana*) in the presence of the person to whom he assigns it, saying, “I give my expectation of food to you,” when that person is present; or, when that person is absent...
Having mentioned his name, one says, "I give my share of food to [so-and-so]";

this refers to the act of assigning by way of indirect designation (*vikappanā*) when not in his presence, or having set aside the assignment made at the first invitation—it is said, "without assigning that.
Regarding the word "food" (*bhatta*), the ellipsis is "he who eats it. He who, having been invited, subsequently eats the food for which he was invited later.

"For him, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)"—this is the construction. "For one who eats even a single grain out of order, for him there may be an offense of expiation"—this is the construction.

What is meant? For one who first eats the food of those invited later, and afterwards eats the food of those invited first; and for one who, in the very same bowl, first [places] the food of those invited first underneath...
This means that after putting the food in and placing the other [food] on top, one lowers the hand;
it refers to one who, without first eating even a single grain of the food situated below, eats first that which is situated above.
For this very reason, there is no fault for one who eats the mixed food in such a way that no reverse order occurs.

In the *Mahāpaccarī*, the analysis is shown by way of contrast. As it says: “Having invited two or three families and having had them sit down in one place, they bring food from here and there and pour it out; they pour out curry and condiments;
it becomes a single mixture. In this case, there is no offense—so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.”
1225–6. To show the specific nature of *paramparabhojana* (successive eating) according to the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), he says:
“‘Of foods also,’ and so forth. The construction is: “he partakes of one or another of those same five kinds of food.
That which was elucidated by the Great Sage is stated in the word-commentary by way of the method beginning: “*Paramparabhojana* is [the eating] of the five kinds of food,” and so on.

1227. *Yattha* means "in which," referring to the food into which many [items] have been placed in a single vessel; because there is no discernment when it is given by one person alone, it is said: "All may become of one taste. This means that, instead of having tastes perceived individually, it becomes of one and the same taste. 1230. By the word *gāmena*, only the village (*gāma*) itself is expressed.
The phrase "there is no fault for one who is invited" should be applied separately to each of the village, the group (*pūga*), and the town (*nigama*).
Just as in the expression "from the village or from the forest," the word *gāma* is used here [to represent the entire category].
The city is also included. A *pūga* refers to righteous people who perform meritorious deeds, having formed various separate groups.
A *nigama* refers to a large village with shops. The meaning is that there is no offense for one who, having been invited by an entire village, eats in whichever house he arrives at.
This same principle applies to *pūgas* and the others as well. As it is said: "By the entire village..."
"There is no offense for one who, having been invited as a single person, eats anywhere at all. The same principle applies to a group.
Regarding the statement "there is no fault in a regular meal," it means there is no fault for one who eats out of order even when receiving a regular meal being given from many different places.
1231. That which is committed through body, speech, or both body and speech and mind is called an offense originating from the *kaṭhina*.
Here, "action" refers to eating, while "non-action" refers to not designating the first invitation; these two alone are referred to as "eating and non-designation.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding successive eating.
1232–3. *Pūva* refers to flavors such as those that are exceedingly sweet. *Paheṇakatthāya* means for the purpose of a gift or present. *Paṭiyattā* means prepared or accomplished.
*Pātheyyatthāya* means for the purpose of provisions for one who is traveling. This is connected with the phrase "or gruels (*mantha*) have been prepared.
*Mantha* refers to bound grain, unbound grain, sesame, rice, and so forth. As it has been said: "Bound grain, unbound grain, sesame, rice, and so forth..."
“All this here is reckoned as *mantha*. The construction is: “those cakes (*pūva*) or *mantha*s.
The particle *hi* is merely an expletive. Therein, regarding those prepared cakes or *mantha*s: “by a bhikkhunī”—here the words “desiring [to receive them]” are to be supplied.
The analysis of “two or three bowls” (*dvattipatta*) is: “two or three bowls. “Full” means up to the level of the lower rim of the mouth.
“Full. As it is said: “having taken a bowl filled level with the lower line of the rim. And here, by the phrase “two or three bowls full,” the measure is shown;

because of the metaphorical treatment of the measure and the measured as non-different, the cakes and gruel are to be understood [by the term “full”], just as in the expression “two or three measures of rice. Or the construction is: “with cakes or with gruel. Regarding “gruel” (sattu):
The inclusion of both "bound" and "unbound" cakes is by this very [rule]; likewise, sesame seeds and so forth are indicated by this.
Furthermore, that which is placed above the lower line on the rim of the third bowl is included by the phrase "beyond that.
As it has been said: "If one takes a third bowl full of cakes, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the number of cakes."
1237. In this context, the construction is: "If two bowlfuls are obtained from those cakes or dough-balls.
The construction is: "One bowlful is to be given away. The construction is: "From one [bowlful], nothing is to be given away"—that is, even a little must not be given against one's will.
As it is said: "By whom one [bowlful] has been taken, by him nothing must be given against his will; [it may be given] according to one's pleasure."

"Thus it should be done. When giving in this manner, one should give by way of a gift shared with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus seen in the assembly hall or at one's own fixed place of residence; one should not give exclusively to friends. As it is said:
"But it is not permitted to give according to friendship."
1238–9. The connection is with the phrase "giving those who provide provisions for a journey (*apaheṇaka*) or travel rations (*apātheyya*).

As it is said: "They give what has been prepared neither for the sake of provisions for a journey nor for the sake of travel rations. The word "from" (*tato*) means from those provisions for a journey and travel rations.
