By the particle *vā*, the text includes what is not explicitly stated here but is mentioned in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*), namely: "giving when the journey has been abandoned. "Less than that" (*tadūnakaṃ*) means less than that.
Less than two or three bowlfuls. As it is said: “He receives less than two or three bowlfuls.

Even for one who takes provisions and so forth with the perception that they have been prepared for the purpose of travel and the like, there is indeed an offense, because the training rule is unintentional (*acittaka*).
It is a verbal action (*vacīkamma*) because an offense is incurred even by saying, “Give this into his hand,” for the purpose of taking it oneself.
Commentary on the Story of Kāṇamātā. 1240.
*Aññena* (by another) is an expression formed by the elision of a *taddhita* suffix; the meaning is *aññatarena* (by one or another). It is to be connected with *pavārito* (invited).
*Bhojanānaṃ* (of foods) is used in the locative case for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇe*). *Pavārito* means: "Venerable sir, please take as much as you wish"—thus [he was invited].

The meaning is that he has been invited according to the two modes described in the Commentary: first, by an invitation for as much as needed (*yāvad-attha-pavāraṇā*), and second, by an invitation involving a refusal such as, "Enough, friend, give only a little.

In these two modes, within the two types [of invitations], the meaning of the word *pavārita* (invited) should be understood through the sense of "preventing" (*vāraṇa*) a request (*patthanā*) from the verbal root *var*, as in the rule:
"It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) if it is not left over (*anatiritta*)."

The word-analysis (*padaccheda*): Having regard for the qualification "food that is not left over" (*anatirittaṃ bhojanaṃ*), one should change the case-ending of "by another" (*aññena*) and construe it as "one of the five kinds of food.
The meaning is: one of the five kinds of food mentioned in the definition of food that is not made left over (*anatirittakatabhojana-niddesa*) which will be explained later.

Regarding the phrase “either solid food (khādanīya) or soft food (bhojanīya),” because they were taught together, it should be understood according to the principle of a single compound as “solid food.
With the exception of the five kinds of soft food and the three [types of] time-bound [medicines], everything that is time-appropriate (yāvakālika) is called solid food.
1241. Here, “eating” (asana) refers to food that has not yet been finished; if the person is still eating, the act of eating has not ceased.
The meaning is "it proceeds. "Food" refers to rice and other items sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*), which are seen in the hands and so forth.
"Within arm's reach" (*hatthapāsa*) means that the space where one stands after bringing forward food sufficient for an invitation is measured at two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyyahattha*);
this is what is stated. "Bringing forward" (*abhiharaṇa*) is "bringing" (*abhihāra*); that itself is "the state of bringing" (*abhihāratā*). By the body of one standing thus to give [food],...

"What is seen as an act of offering?"—this is what is meant. "A physical or verbal refusal" means that when food has been brought in that manner, a physical refusal, such as a movement of the hand by the recipient, or a verbal refusal, such as saying "Enough," becomes manifest.

(1242) "By the one free from proliferation" means by the Tathāgata who is devoid of the threefold proliferation of craving and so forth, together with their underlying tendencies, having abandoned them.
1243. *Tattha* means "among those," namely among the boiled rice and so forth. *Sattannaṃ* refers to the seven kinds corresponding to what will be stated beginning with "rice" (*sālī*).

1244. *Oda-ka* means "that which exists in water. *Ettha* refers to the fivefold invitation (*pañcaṅga-pavāraṇā*). *Ayaṃ nicchayo* indicates the detailed exposition of the method that is about to be stated.

1245. *Sālī* refers to all varieties of rice. *Vīhī* refers to all varieties of paddy. *Kaṅgū* refers to all varieties of millet, distinguished as white, red, and black. *Varaka* is the white *varaka*. By the Blessed One, who has accumulated a store of merit through his grain.
1246. *Tiṇa* means precisely grass-seed; it is explained and included [in this sense]. *Varakacoraka* means fine *varaka*.
1248. To demonstrate the perfection of the limbs, he said, “with the hand,” and so forth.
1249. *Tanū* means slender.
1250. It does not preserve the invitation (pavāraṇā).
1251–2. Regarding "grains, juices, and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), curd and other such items are included. "Having placed upon" means having placed upon the hearth.
"Fruits" refers to fruits such as cardamom and garlic. "Leaves" refers to soup-vegetables. "Shoots" refers to the shoots of bamboo and the like. "Many" refers to...

This is a further qualification of those very same [terms]. In that context, “in that” (*tattha ca*) refers to the buttermilk and so forth into which leaves and other ingredients have been added. “He shows the limit” (*odhiṃ dasseti*): here, the word “at the time of consumption” (*paribhogakāle*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

“He produces” (*sañjaneti*): here, the phrase “rice-gruel with fruit and so forth” (*phalādiyāgu*) is obtained. 1253–4. Regarding “in the flavor” (*rase*): it refers to the flavor of meat and so forth.

It should be construed as either saying “take the rice-gruel” (*yāguṃ gaṇhatha*) or simply “rice-gruel” (*yāgu*). Regarding the statement “the rice-gruel is included” (*yāgu saṅgahitā*): the intention is that within the two alternatives—the manifestation and non-manifestation of the limit (*odhi*)—there is an identical determination concerning the rice-gruel.
1255. *Chupanti* means they touch. The verbal root *chupa* signifies touching; it is synonymous with "placing. As it is said:
"where they place fish or meat. The construction is: "if even a portion the size of a mustard seed of fish or meat is discernible.
Regarding the word *pavāraṇa*, the word "produces" (*janeti*) is to be supplied here. The word *yāguya* is used in the nominative case.
It should be construed as: "having transformed it, it produces gruel. 1256.
"Mixed" (saṃsaṭṭha) should be construed as: "it does not produce [fermentation] when strained.
1257. "Having set aside entirely" is the connection. It is a limb [of the offense] due to the remainder of the preparation, such as rice into which meat and so forth have been put.
To show this, he said "in every way" (*sabbaso*). The construction is: "he does not invite [to eat] in every way.
"Bamboo-rice" (*veḷutaṇḍula*) means the grain of bamboo-ripened rice (*veḷuvīhī*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), bulbs and roots are included. As it was said:
"food prepared with bamboo-rice and so forth, or with any kind of bulb, root, or fruit."

1258. "From that" means from rice and so forth, and from bamboo and so forth; the meaning is that the parched grains produced therefrom are blown away. "By those" means by the parched grains. "Pure" is connected with "they do not offer," meaning unmixed with parched grains and the like.
1259. "Of the roasted" means of those that have been fried. "Combined with flour" (*sattusaṅgahita*) means that which is gathered together with flour.
1261. "A sweetmeat of flours" means bound with flour; the meaning is "flour-bound."
1263. *Teheva* means by the kings themselves. *Suddhaṃ khajjakaṃ vā* means solid food unmixed with fish and so forth, according to the method that will be explained later.
1264. By the words “*pūritaṃ*” and so on, he shows the opposite of that. *Taṃ* refers to the *kuṇḍaka* (rice-scum) and other such items.
1266. *Akappiyaṃ maṃsaṃ* means unallowable meat. *Avatthuttā* means because of the absence of a fixed occasion for the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), since unallowable meats must be prohibited.
1267. *Vatthukattā* means because it serves as the basis for the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) regarding allowable meat (*kappiyamaṃsa*).
Regarding the phrase *pavāreti*, the remainder of the sentence should be understood as: "and because it is meat while being eaten. As it has been said:
"But that which one eats, although it stands in a place where it ought to be rejected, does not lose its nature as meat while it is being eaten."
1268. "Any kind of allowable food" means any of the five kinds of edible food that is allowable. 1269.
"Other unallowable meat" refers to food obtained by means such as corrupting families and so forth, which remains after the unallowable meat has been excluded.
As it is said: "That which is produced by corrupting families, by medical practice, by claiming superhuman states, or by [accepting] money and so forth..."
“He rejects unallowable food that has arisen through improper search, which is censured by the Buddha, and he does not partake of it.
To show the determination regarding the two factors—“seat” and “food”—he said, “If it has been swallowed,” and so forth.
“Swallowed” means it has entered the throat of another. By the word “in the bowl,” vessels such as platters and the like are also included. In some places...
The construction is: "there is no food. This means that in the bowl, the hand, the mouth, or wherever else, not even a trace of any of the five kinds of solid food is found;

only its scent is perceived. Regarding the word *ādāya* (having taken), the phrase *aññatra bhuñjituṃ* (to eat elsewhere) is to be supplied as the remainder. [This applies to] one who, desiring to go elsewhere to eat, [takes it along].

Because the statement in the *Mahāpaccarī-aṭṭhakathā*, "Having swallowed the food in the mouth, taking the remainder," and so forth, is authoritative, he said, "He does not invite [others to eat]. 1273.
"Food has been swallowed in the mouth; one desires to give food from the hand to a scavenger; food in the bowl..."
In order to include the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, which has come down as stating, "If one wishes to give to a bhikkhu and he refuses at that moment,

he does not invite [him to eat]," and because the phrase "food in the mouth" (*mukhe ca bhattaṃ*) and so forth is consistent with the reasoning to be explained later in the passage beginning with "the interruption of the meal" (*asanassa upacchedā*),
the reading "desiring to eat" (*bhottukāmo*) was not adopted for this verse.
The reading “dātukāmo” (desirous of giving) should be accepted.

Regarding the phrase “asana-ssupacchedā” (the cutting off of expectation regarding the seat), this indicates the cutting off of expectation while still on that very seat, remaining seated exactly as one was;
as it is said in the Commentary: “But if he does not wish to eat on that seat, [he should go] to the monastery...”
"Having entered, he wishes to eat, or he wishes to give to another.
Because this analysis was presented in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, the term "of great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*) refers to the teacher of the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*.

"Knowing what is a valid reason and what is not" means knowing that "this is a valid reason for an invitation (*pavāraṇā*), and this is not a valid reason. In some places, it is read as "by one who knows what is a valid reason and what is not."
They write it in the book. Therein, the teachers of great wisdom, who know what is the cause and what is not the cause, state:
"‘It is’ is the cause"—this is how the construction should be understood.
(1275) To show the determination regarding the range of the hand, he says: "Of one who takes... [up to] ‘stretched out’. Of one who takes:
When one receives [an object] while endowed with a certain posture (*iriyāpatha*), it refers to receiving in such a manner.

"The posterior limb" (*pacchimaṃ aṅgaṃ*) refers to that part of the recipient which is situated behind the part given by the donor; for a recipient endowed with a posture such as standing, it is the heel and so forth—the posterior limb.
Without the hand extended by the giver, there is no "prior limb" (*purimaṃ aṅgaṃ*).
The construction [of the compound] is as follows: in the phrase "stretched-out hand" (*pasārita-hattha*), the word "to give" (*dātuṃ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

In the phrase "of both," the word "between" (*antare*) is to be supplied as the remainder; that is, in the space or interval between the two parts—the latter and the former—of the recipient and the giver respectively.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a hand measuring half, or a third (*teyya*). The meaning is: a measure of more than one *vidatthi* or two *ratana*s.
1276. To demonstrate the legal decision regarding the act of bringing [food], he said "In that," and so forth.
The construction is: "having stood in that place measuring two and a half [ratanas]. The meaning is: having stood in that place measured by two *ratana*s and one *vidatthi*.

"Bringing" (*abhihaṭa*) means brought near or presented. "Such as that" (*tādisa*) means similar to what was brought; the meaning is: any one of the five kinds of food sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*).
1277–8. *Ādhārake vāpīti*: even on a support such as a ring or a leaf-stand. *Ūrusūti*: between the two thighs; the meaning is "in the lap" (*aṅke*).
*Āharitvāti*: having brought forward. Regarding "he takes the food," the word "from here" (*ito*) is to be supplied as the remainder;
the construction is: "He speaks while sitting nearby, saying, 'Take food from here. The term "food" (*bhattaṃ*) is illustrative; it refers to any of the five kinds of edible food.
"Whatever" is the meaning. "That" refers to the food, such as the meal already mentioned, which was taken in that manner.

Regarding the phrase "and of an offering," here the word *ca* (and) serves either to complete the metrical line or has the sense of the particle *eva* (only); thus it should be construed as "only because of its absence.
The term "rice-tray" (*bhattapacchī*) is an illustrative designation (*upalakkhaṇa*).
1280. Regarding the phrase "When being given," the word "food" (*bhojana*) is to be understood as the ellipsis here. "The other" refers to one sitting within arm's reach.

Because the factor of "bringing forth" (*abhihāra*) is absent, he has not been invited to stop further giving (*pavārita*). 1281. To show the analysis regarding the factor of "refusal" (*paṭikkhepa*), he says "By body," and so forth. Since verbal bringing forth is not a constituent factor [of the offense], he says "brought by body.
As it has been said: "For one who refuses what is brought by speech, there is no invitation to stop further giving."
To refuse food that has been brought to one, by making any bodily gesture such as moving the fingers, the hand, or anything else belonging to the hand;
or by raising the eyebrows; or by looking on with anger—one is said to refuse it by means of the body.
Or [one refuses it] by saying: "Enough," or "I will not take it," or "Wait," or "Be patient," or "Do not scatter it."
Or, by saying such things as "Go away," one is said to reject [the invitation] by speech. 1282–3.
Regarding the word *ākirāti*, here too it should be construed with "and thus" (*iti ca*).

Although there is a desire to prevent [the invitation] in the mind of one who speaks in this way, because it occurs through words of prohibition, the invitation does not take place; therefore he says: "No."
"But *pana* means ‘invitation’ (*pavāraṇā*); however, the construction is ‘but there is no invitation.
(1284) The connection is that he says, “Take the flavor. “Having heard that” means having heard those words.
(1285) “The essence” (*sāra*) is merely a way of praising it. “This” refers generally to fish and meat.

It is a constituent of the invitation (*pavāraṇaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "fish broth, meat broth," since a *dvanda* compound is also possible here, it is stated as "take fish and meat," and that too is a constituent.

However, when it is said "take broth" (*rasaṃ gaṇhā*), because there is no option for this particular alternative, it is not a constituent of the invitation. For this very reason, he said: "There is [broth] and there is meat."
1287. "Wait a moment" means look for a short time. 1288.
"With jackfruit and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of *vettaṅga* and other such items is intended. 1290.
Regarding "fish soup" (*macchasūpa*) and "meat soup" (*maṃsasūpa*), the alternative compound forms here should be understood as being like "fish juice" (*maccharasa*) and "meat juice" (*maṃsarasa*).
1291. *Karambaka* is the name for a particular kind of curry mixed with minced meat, fish, or other ingredients.
For this very reason, when it is said, "Take the meat *karambaka*, take the fish *karambaka*," there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) by way of restriction;

however, when it is simply said, "Take the *karambaka*," because the expression is indefinite, there is no such invitation. This is the same as the determination [of the rules] regarding bamboo-shoot curry (*kaḷīrasūpa*) and so forth.
To demonstrate this, he said: "This same method has been stated.
(1292) When it is said, "when it has been stated.

(1293) "By which" means by the meal. "Having been asked" means having been told, "Take [some]. "Of that meal": because of its existence, that is, because the rice-gruel (*yāgu*) was present. "Thus, the reason": this is the reason for the invitation (*pavāraṇa*).
1294. When it is said, "Take the rice-gruel mixed with [the food]," if that gruel is equal to or greater than the food placed there in the vessel brought to him, the construction is as follows:
"It is said (kira) that the monk does not refuse the offering brought to him after having spoken thus.
The word *kira* indicates a lack of approval. For this very reason, he will say later: "But the reason is difficult to see."
1295. *Sabbattha* means in all the Aṭṭhakathās. 1296.
*Visuṃ katvā* means having separated the flavor or the milk from the rice in such a way that not even a single grain remains [mixed].
1297. *Gacchanteneva* means by one who continues walking until the meal is finished. As it is said: "By one who is walking..."
"Even when one has not stood on the bank of a river that is overflowing, but is wandering after surrounding a grove;
or when one has not boarded a boat or a bridge, but is wandering after having encircled [the area].
Here, "he" refers to one who is walking. "From there" means from that place; the intention is that the posture of walking has been disturbed.

1299. *Āsanaṃ avicāletvā* means not moving the place touched by the act of sitting; that is to say, not rising from it. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "In the case of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), the shifting of one's position (*ṭhānācāvana*) must be understood [as a factor].
1300. *Tato* means after the time of having been invited to leave, or from that seated place. *Ito vā etto vā* means to move even slightly from the seated place here or there;
the meaning is to shift or depart. 1301. *Sabbattha* means on every seat that can be moved, such as a bench and so forth. By the phrase "by one who knows the Vinaya," if...
"But if they lift him up together with the bed and carry him elsewhere, it is permissible"—this is what is meant by [the author] stating that he knew the fact expressed in the Commentary:
"This same decision applies to benches and so forth as well.
Regarding the phrase "having lain down": here it is said, "While turning over, one must not pass beyond the position of whichever side one was lying on."
The meaning is: having lain down without leaving the place where one was previously lying. "In the same way" means: having remained in a squatting position;
this is what is intended. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "However, beneath him a straw mat or some other seat should be provided."
1303. The construction is as follows: when a monk makes food "leftover" (*atiritta*), he should incline the vessel and, once the food has been presented, say, "This is enough for all.
In this context, "making it leftover" means: it is made permissible (*kappiyakata*); it is made accepted (*paṭiggahitakata*);
it is made by verbal declaration (*uccāritakata*); it is made within arm's reach (*hatthapāse kata*); and it is done by one who has already finished eating (*bhuttāvinā*).
It is said: "It has been made [ready]"; it has been made by one who has finished eating, refused further food, and not yet risen from his seat;

it has been declared, "This is enough for all"; and it is the remainder of one who is ill—among these eight modes mentioned, it means making it "leftover" (atiritta) by means of the first seven modes of formal monastic procedure (vinayakamma), excluding the last one. As it is said: "By these seven modes of formal monastic procedure..."
"Whatever is left over," and so forth.

Here, food brought for the purpose of making it "left over" (atiritta) is indeed permissible (*kappiya*). It is called "prepared" (*kata*) because it is associated with permissible items such as ginger, turmeric, garlic, and the like;
because it is devoid of impermissible meat; and because it has not been produced through acts such as defiling a family.

"It is sufficient for all this" means that because it has been made into leftovers (*atirittaka*), it is both permissible (*kappiya*) and prepared (*kata*); thus it is called "permissible-prepared" (*kappiyakata*).
In the same way, the meaning and the analysis of the compound for the word *kata* should be understood in the subsequent instances as well.
In the remaining passages, what has been received by a monk is called "received. Having had that prepared, when a monk returns, [he may take] a small amount...
That which is shown after having been uttered or poured down is called "made by utterance" (*uccāritakata*).

For one who has come to have something made allowable (*kappiya*), that which is within arm's reach—within a distance of two and a half cubits—is called "done within arm's reach" (*hatthapāse kata*) even if it is not leftover (*atiritta*).

One is considered "one who has eaten" (*bhuttāvī*) because of having eaten even as much as a blade of grass from any food whatsoever, including that which generates the invitation (*pavāraṇa*). As it is said: "Of the five kinds of soft foods, any one..."

“Even a morsel as small as the tip of a blade of kusa grass has been eaten. One who, while eating, having been invited, does not leave his seat, is called “one who has finished eating, having been invited, and has not risen from his seat. Therefore, it is said: “done by one who has finished eating... and has not risen.
Having made the verbal utterance, “This is enough for all,” it is said: “This is enough.”
"‘All’ is what has been stated," thus it is shown. This is called the sevenfold manner of formal acts (vinayakamma).

Furthermore, although "the remainder of one who is ill" (gilānātirittaka) is not mentioned in this verse, it should be understood as the opposite of the phrase "nor the remainder of one who is ill" found in the verse beginning with "done" which is to be recited later, for the purpose of indicating what is not a remainder. From the state of being ill...
“Leftover” (atiritta) refers to that which has been set aside for the purpose of eating on another day; this is what is called “leftover from one who is ill.

By the phrase “by that bhikkhu,” he refers to a bhikkhu who is distinguished by the specific characteristics already mentioned—namely, “one who has eaten,” and “one who has eaten and refused further food and risen from his seat”—and thus makes him clearly identifiable. [This applies] to those who cause the invitation (pavāraṇā).
"By one who has eaten even a small amount of any of the five kinds of food"—this refers to a bhikkhu who, having finished eating and being invited to stop, has not yet risen from his seat.
Regarding the phrase "having bent down over the vessel," the words "when the food has been shown" are to be supplied as the remainder;
this connects with the word "then. "Things worthy of being made allowable" refers to ginger and so forth, which are *kappiya* (allowable).
Having had [the food] prepared and received, and having returned until he is within arm’s reach, the monk who is making it *atiritta* (leftover) must slightly incline the vessel and hold it up;
this refers to the moment immediately after it has been shown. To demonstrate what must be done beyond that, he says "Enough," and so forth.
To this extent, by the phrase "by that bhikkhu," two factors are included: "done after having eaten" and "done after having been invited to stop eating and not having risen from the seat.
By the phrase "having lifted up the bowl," this is included: "it must be done after [the food] has been announced. "Made allowable," "made accepted," and "made within hand's reach"—this...
This is included by the word *atha* used in the sense of "immediately following.
However, it should be understood that the phrase "all this is sufficient" is shown here in its own specific form.
There is no requirement that only food placed in a bowl may be made *atiritta* (leftover); rather, it may be done in any vessel whatsoever, such as a basket or the like.
To show that it should be done even when [the food] is placed in a vessel, he said, “But what is allowable (kappiyaṃ).
“In a bowl” (kuṇḍe) means in a small wooden bowl. “In a vessel” (bhājane) refers to any kind of vessel taken.
1305. “This” refers to this food that has been made leftover. The construction is: “having set aside only that. “It is indeed permissible” (vaṭṭatevā).

Even though it was said [that one may take it] for the purpose of anointing and so forth, he said "it should be eaten" to address the possibility that others might take it; the meaning is that it should be consumed by others alone, without that one person. 1306–7.

"Having made it allowable" means having made it leftover (atiritta). "And they pour it in" means if they place it inside. The construction is: "Once again, having made it leftover in that same way, it should be eaten."
To the question, "By whom should that be made *atiritta* (leftover)? he says, "by whom," and so forth. "That" refers to the food that has been made *atiritta*. The connection is:
"by whom it was not made"—that is, by whichever monk it was not first made *atiritta*, by him it must be made.
As it is said: "By whom it was not made means: by another monk by whom it was not first made; by him it must be made. Or rather:
The construction is: "that which was not made [into leftover] must be made [so] separately by him. Or, regarding "that which was not made":
it refers to that food which was placed into that meal already made into leftovers, but which itself had not been made into leftovers.
"It must be made separately by him" means that the food subsequently added must be placed in another vessel so that it remains unmixed with what has already been made into leftovers.
Having set it aside as a separate portion by way of taking it up, one should make it *atiritta* (leftover) even with that which was first made *kappiya*. As it is said:
"And as for that which is not yet made [kappiya]: even by him who first made the *kappiya*, that which remains unmade must be made [kappiya].
However, it is not permitted to do so in the first vessel; for if it were done there, it would be together with what was first made."
“It has been made [into a meal]”; therefore, the intention is that it is permissible to make it in another vessel.

(1308) Regarding the seven [factors] beginning with the unallowable: “What is called ‘not left over’ is that which has been made unallowable, made without having been formally accepted, made without words being uttered, made outside the reach of hand, made by one who has not yet eaten, and made by one who has already eaten.”

And it is considered "made" (prepared) when one has finished eating, risen from the seat, and it has been stated by those [who have finished] using the seven formal modes of the Vinaya that "this is enough for all.
The construction is: "it is made into a leftover (*atiritta*). The word division is: "it is not a non-leftover (*anatirittaka*). 1309.
Even when the time is near [the end of the meal], one who makes it a leftover should say, "I have already eaten this morning," or "I have eaten only a little."
In order to show that it should be done without reflecting, he says "whosoever," and so forth. "Even when brought at the approaching time" means even food brought at the time when [the meal] is near.

"Of the watch-period and so forth" means belonging to the periods of a watch (*yāma*), seven days, or as long as life. "Unmixed" means unmixed with worldly gain (*āmiṣa*). The connection is: "he partakes of that which belongs to the watch-period and so forth."

1312. It is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that even food set aside with the intention, "He will eat it at some time," like the leftovers of one who is ill, is called "leftover from one who is ill" (*gilānātiritta*).
They say, "Even a portion of food intended for a sick person in a monastery or similar place is called 'leftover from one who is ill'.
1313. "By the *kathina*" means by the first *kathina*.
Commentary on the First Discussion of Invitation (Pavāraṇā). 1314.
Regarding the phrase "not with what is not left over," the words "either as fresh food or as soft food" are to be supplied here.

Here it is stated: "Fresh food (khādanīya) means everything remaining after setting aside the five kinds of soft foods, the food for the watch of the night, the food for seven days, and the food for life."
Everything other than the five kinds of food is called "hard food" (khādanīya) that may be consumed at the proper time. It is said: "Food (bhojanīya) means the five kinds of food:
boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat. The detailed explanation here is stated in the immediately preceding training rule (sikkhāpada).
Regarding the term *pavāreyya*, the word *abhihaṭṭhuṃ* is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, *abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya* means "having brought [food], one should invite [the other monk]."
“Come, monk, take as much as you wish and eat or consume”—thus one should invite.
The word “invited” (*pavārita*) has the meaning already stated. “Knowing” means knowing his state of being invited, either by hearing or by seeing.
“Aiming at reproach” (*āsādanāpekkho*) means looking toward reproach, censure, or the state of being made to feel shame. “Having eaten” (*bhutto*)...

By means of his action, when the other has finished eating and the meal is concluded. "Of him" means: of the one who, having learned of his state of being invited (*pavārita*), directed him, saying, "Eat.
[Regarding the rule: "How is it that by one person's eating there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for another?"—it was stated thus because of such a doubt.

To avoid [this], he says: “An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)... it has been shown. Regarding “the taking by the other”: this refers to the acceptance for the purpose of eating by the monk who has already finished his meal (*pavārita*).
And regarding “in the acts of swallowing”: here too, the connection is with “by the other.

All of this constitutes an offense of wrong-doing and an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*). It has been shown: “If he brings it forward, there is an offense of wrong-doing. By his word: ‘I shall eat’...”

The meaning is that this was taught by the Blessed One: "If one accepts [food] thinking, 'I will eat,' there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

At the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). 1317. "In both cases, for one who is doubtful" means: for one who is doubtful whether he has been invited to stop eating or not invited to stop eating. "An offense of wrong-doing is illustrated" means it was taught: "If one is doubtful when invited to stop eating; if one is doubtful when not invited to stop eating, there is an offense of wrong-doing."

1318. Regarding the phrase "having caused [it] to be made": here, the words "Eat! are to be understood as the remainder. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of another": here, the words "go while offering it" are to be understood as the remainder.
1319. Regarding the phrase "equal to verbal abuse": this was said with reference to the origin (samuṭṭhāna) of taking what is not given.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the second invitation (pavāraṇa).
"Khādanīyaṃ" (hard food) means any of the five types of solid foods, excluding those belonging to the three times; or, among the remaining [foods], anything whatsoever.
"Bhojanīyaṃ" (soft food) means any one of the five types of soft foods. "Vikāle" means when the time has passed.
"Kāla" (the proper time) refers to the period from sunrise until midday; any other time than that is "vikāla" (the improper time). As it is said: "Vikāla is [the time] after midday..."
“Until the rising of the dawn. This includes even the time when midday has passed. As it is said: “The time when midday has passed is also included within the [permissible] time.
However, from that point on, one is not permitted to chew or eat;
yet it may be possible to drink [liquids] suddenly. Nevertheless, one must not do so out of scruple. And this is for the purpose of knowing the limits of the time.”
“The time-marker must be joined; the meal-duty must be performed within that very time limit. Regarding the offense: it is a *pācittiya*.

In the phrase “hard food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*),” since the nature of soft food has already been shown in the training rule concerning the invitation (*pavāraṇa-sikkhāpada*), he says “that which pertains to meat,” etc., in order to show the nature of hard food first. “In these” means among these [categories of] hard and soft foods.

As for that which consists of forest roots, fruits, and so forth—belonging to the category of material food (*āmisa*), included within the category of food for the time being (*yāvakālika*)—that is to be construed as "edible food" (*khādanīya*).
In the phrase "for the sake of non-delusion regarding things pertaining to the time," the letter *m* is elided due to the requirements of metrical composition;
thus, it is said to be "for the sake of non-confusion. He says "this" with reference to what is about to be explained.

1322. “Root” (*mūla*) refers to whatever root belongs to trees or creepers. “Bulb” (*kanda*) refers to the bulb of those very same trees or creepers. “Rhizome” (*muḷāla*) refers to the root-bulb of the lotus plant.
“Top” (*matthaka*) refers to the crown of palm trees, coconut trees, and so forth; the sprouts of bamboo, *kaḷīra* reeds, and young shoots are also included herein.
“Stem” (*khandhaka*) refers to the stem of sugarcane and similar plants. “Bark” (*taca*) refers to the outer skin. “Leaf” (*patta*) refers to foliage.
“Blossom” means flowers. “Fruit” means the fruit of trees, creepers, and so forth. “Seeds” means the seeds of trees, creepers, and so forth.
“Flour” means the flour of grain and so forth. “Resin” means gum. The term “hard food” (*khādanīya*) is applicable everywhere according to the context.
Having thus set out the matrix (*mātikā*) for hard foods, he says “of hard foods such as roots,” etc., in order to show them in their specific forms.
In this context, the analysis of the compound is: "that which has the root of a tree as its primary edible.
Regarding the phrase "understand it as a mere indication of the entrance," the word "by me being composed" is to be supplied. "Mere entrance" means the mere door of entry;
it is said that the edibles will be shown in brief because fear arises in those who dread prolixity when there is a desire for a complete exposition.
He states the purpose for this exposition as: "for the sake of proficiency among monks regarding names and their meanings.
The meaning is: for the purpose of producing proficiency among monks concerning the names of roots, edible plants, and so forth, as well as their respective meanings.
The specific details of the roots, sub-roots, and so on, should be understood from the instruction itself; for even if they were stated by means of synonyms, they would not be clear.
It is possible to understand [this]. For even when it is stated by another method of expression, there would only be confusion for those who do not know each of those names;
therefore, we shall say nothing further on that point. *Sākānam* means of leaf-vegetables used as curry. *Idha* means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
*Āhārattham* means the purpose to be accomplished by food; what is meant is the function of food. It is also called *āmisa-atthaṃ*.
They write. "Spreading" means extending. "Jaraṭṭha" means an old bulb.
The connection is with that which is "jaraṭṭha. The construction for the others is: "The *jaraṭṭha* of the remaining [roots] is *yāvakālika* (to be used within the same day).
By "the remaining," radishes and so forth are meant. As it is said: "Of radishes, *khāraka*, *jajjharī*, and roots..."
"However, even those that have become withered are still subject to the same destination as [other] food.
1331. "Washed" means having its back surface produced.

1332. The construction is: "the root of the milk-creeper is unwashed. "Beyond the path of speech" means they are beyond the reach of verbal expression because it is impossible to bring them to a conclusion by saying, "It is this one or that one."
1333. The *puṇḍarīka* is white; the *paduma* is red. 1334.
*Sambhava* means born.
1338. *Jaraṭṭhabunda* refers to the part of the bulb that has become extremely decayed at its base.
1339. "Gone into the earth" means gone into the interior of the earth; it is said that he has gone having submerged into the earth like a young stalk.

1340. Thus he has gone into the interior of the ground. The phrase-break is: "The leaf-stalks of the *utpala* and so forth. "All" means both the young and the mature. The construction is: "All the leaf-stalks of the *utpala* and so forth, as well as those of the *paduma* species, are 'to be used for the time being' (*yāvakālika*).
1345. "What is called 'leaf-eatables'? means what is called edible food consisting of leaves.
1348. "Of radishes, etc. refers to the radishes and so forth mentioned in the verse beginning with: "Radishes and also salt... 1349.
"The pericarp" means the pericarp of a lotus. 1360.
"Of ketakas, etc."—here, by the word "etc.," the *timbarusaka* is included. "The kernel of a palm fruit" means the seed of young fruits.

1361. Regarding the phrases “*puṇṇāga-madhuka-ṭṭhīni*” and “*puṇṇāga-madhuka-ṭṭhicā*,” both readings are found in the manuscripts; however, the meaning is the same. The word division is “*selu-aṭṭhī*. *Anāmise* means for as long as life lasts. 1363. “Washed palm-powder” (*dhotaṃ tālapiṭṭhaṃ*) means:

having pounded the inner bark of the palm tree, kneaded it in water, strained it, and when the thick paste has settled on the surface of the vessel, the clear water is removed and the palm-powder that remains is taken—this is what is meant. Likewise...
The construction is "the flour of milk-creeper. The meaning is: having likewise pounded and strained it, [one uses] the flour of the milk-creeper that has been taken.
1364. "Unwashed" should be understood as the opposite of what was stated.

According to the statement, "All that which does not serve as food [is] for life-long use," roots and so forth that do not perform the function of food for people in various regions are for life-long use.
"In that case, another [type of food] is 'to be taken at the proper time' (yāvakālika)"—this is how the concise definition should be understood.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of eating at improper times. 1369.

Regarding the phrase "eating food after it has been stored," here "food" (bhojana) and "hard food" (khādanīya) refer specifically to those things categorized according to the distinctions already mentioned.
"Having stored up" (*sannidhiṃ katvā*) means having accepted [the food] and allowed even a single night to pass; thus it is said "having stored. As it has been stated:
"This is a designation for that which has been passed over for even one night after being accepted. He will explain this very point with the words beginning "by oneself," etc.
"Chewing" (*khādana*) is a term formed by the *kamma-sādhana* (instrumental) case; it has the same meaning as "that which is chewed" (*khajja*).
1371. Regarding the phrase "having stored up" (*sannidhiṃ katvā*), he says "by himself," etc., in order to show the explanation (*niddesa*).

1372. Regarding the phrase "that is not permitted," he says "from that," etc., in order to show the meaning. "From that" means from food stored up. "With a pure mind" means with a stainless mind due to the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).
"As one who is such" (*tādī*) refers to one who is unaffected by the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).

By being "such-like" (tādin) through the state of being free from agitation (*nibbikāra*). Alternatively, it means by the Blessed One who was "such-like" as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were in terms of their qualities of form and formlessness.

Regarding the five kinds of food, such as boiled rice and so forth, [the text] says "in the case of what is unallowable" (*akappiyesu*) and so on, in order to show the specific offense of a *pācittiya* and other offenses arising from the storage of unallowable meat. "Pācittī" refers to the *pācittiya* offense of storage. "The others" refers to...
Regarding "in the meat of lions and so forth": the construction is that there is a *pācittiya* together with a *dukkaṭa*.
In the phrase "consuming what is designated as for the duration of a watch," the term "having stored it" (*sannidhiṃ katvā*) is understood by virtue of the governing context.
Since it is stated as "*pācittiya*" rather than "together with a *dukkaṭa*," it should be understood that one consumes it when there is a valid reason (*paccaya*).
As it is said: "If one consumes [food] that is not within the proper time, even when there is a valid reason, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one consumes it for the purpose of food, it is an offense of expiation together with an act of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding the word "food" (anna) here as well, the term "stored" (sannidhikata) is to be understood as before; the term "natural" (pakati), however, is...
"Food" (*anna*) is a qualification of this [term]; the meaning is "merely food that is unmixed with human flesh and the like, and not made into leftovers" (*anatiritta*).

"The two offenses of expiation" (*pācittiyadvaya*) refers to the two *pācittiya* offenses arising from the condition of [eating] what is not leftover and the condition of [eating] what has been stored.
In both instances of "two" (*dve*) and "pair" (*dvaya*), the meaning is exactly this.

Regarding the phrase "two [offenses] by means of food with flavor": since it is stated here that "the five kinds of cooked food, excluding the 'time-for-a-watch' (yāmakālika), the 'seven-day-time' (sattāhakālika), and the 'life-long' (yāvajīvika), are called 'chewable food' (khādanīya)," there are two offenses of expiation for storing (sannidhi-pācittiya):

one because it is mixed with that time-for-a-watch food which is not included under chewable food, and the other because it is based on the flavor that has entered the mouth through the act of storing.

The meaning is "there are. Regarding the phrase "by means of a mouth mixed with worldly things" (*sāmisena mukhena*), because it is used as a defining characteristic, it should be understood that however much [food] has become mixed with worldly things (*āmisa*), there are this many offenses.
The construction is: "for one who eats non-worldly (*nirāmisa*) post-midnight food (*yāmakālika*), there is exactly one *pācittiya* offense";
the meaning is that for one who consumes post-midnight food in any manner whatsoever when it is unmixed [with worldly things], there is exactly one *pācittiya* offense.

1378. "That very same" refers to that which is proximate, namely the *kālika* (time-bound) [gift]. Regarding those two alternatives: this means within the two alternatives of "with worldly gain" (*sāmisa*) and "without worldly gain" (*nirāmisa*).

"Only a *dukkaṭa* offense increases" means that in the first alternative, there is a *dukkaṭa* together with two *pācittiya* offenses, while in the second alternative, there is a *dukkaṭa* together with one *pācittiya* offense; thus it is stated.
1379. Regarding the word *suddhaṃ* (pure/clean) here, the phrase “stored food” (*sannidhikataṃ bhojanaṃ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound].

This is understood from the fact that in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is called “normal food” (*pakatibhojanaṃ*), and here it is stated that “there is no fault regarding what is for the watch of the night” (*na doso yāmakālike*), since what is for the watch of the night will be explained separately;
thus, it means food unmixed with unallowable meat or what is for the watch of the night.
1380. Regarding the word *maṃsaṃ* (flesh) here, the phrase "in what is not allowable" (*akappiye*) is understood through the mention of the grave offense (*thullaccaya*) and so forth.

It "increases" means that, together with the two previous *pācittiya* offenses mentioned, there is an increase of a grave offense for human flesh and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the flesh of lions and other such animals.
And for human flesh and the remaining unallowable flesh such as lion-flesh and so on, there is a grave offense respectively.
The construction is: "the two—[namely] *dukkaṭa* and [the other]—increase. 1381. The construction is:
for a monk who consumes even non-leftover food at an improper time (*vikāla*), there is no fault on account of that in any of the aforementioned alternatives.
This is because, in the phrase "at an improper time... [and] what is for the day," that which is for the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*) will be explained separately.

Since both the act of making [food] leftover and the act of eating occur only in relation to food, the phrase "not leftover" (*anatiritta*) here has "food that has been set aside" (*nihitabhojana*) as its implied referent.

Because of the commentary’s statement, "But on account of it not being leftover, there is no offense in all cases of eating at the wrong time," the term "on account of it not being leftover" refers to the *pācittiya* offense.
For this very reason, he will later say "having that as its cause," meaning having the state of not being leftover as its cause.

The meaning is as follows. "In all alternative cases" means in all alternatives such as: "whether it is pure, or mixed with human flesh, or mixed with the flesh of lions and so forth, or mixed with food that is to be taken during the watch of the night.
By the very expression "having that as its cause," he shows the possibility of the fault arising from causes such as taking food at the wrong time (*vikāla*), which has already been prohibited.

Regarding the phrase "or because of the condition of the wrong time" (*vikālapaccayā vā*): here, by the word "or" (*vā*), the phrase "because of the condition of not being left-over" (*anatirittapaccayā*) is included as a conjunction.
The word *api* (even/also) should be construed with the phrase "even in the case of what is for a watch of the night" (*yāmakālikepi*).

The construction is as follows: for one who accepts [medicines] for the purpose of food—whether it be that which is for seven days (*sattāhakālika*) or that which is for life (*yāvajīvika*)—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of accepting; however, in the case of the aforementioned two-fold division of what is for seven days and what is for life, there is an offense of wrong-doing during the acts of consuming or when it is not mixed with non-food (*nirāmise*). The particle *tu* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

1384. *Atha* is a particle used to introduce a statement. The construction is: "mixed with food, [whether] for seven days or for as long as life. *Gahetvā* means having formally accepted (*paṭiggahetvā*). *Ṭhapitaṃ* means set aside after the dawn has passed.

*Pācittī* refers to the offense of expiation (*sannidhipācittiya*). 1385. *Kāla* (time) refers to the period beginning from sunrise until the end of midday. *Yāma* (watch) refers to the period beginning from midday until the end of the second sunrise.

The construction is: "there is an offense for one who lets pass that respective time-period. The word *tu* has the sense of emphasis (*evakāra*). Or, *taṃ*... [etc. (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on the Vinaya rules regarding the storage and consumption of medicinal substances.)
"Kālika" means, respectively, "yāvakālika," "yāmakālika," and "sattāhakālika"—this is what is meant. 1386. The construction is:
"The *yāvakālika* brings the other three types of *kālika* that are mixed with it into its own nature. Its own state is its "nature" (*sabhāva*); that [it brings them to]. 1387–88.

"In the same way, one should demonstrate" means one should explain: "Each preceding *kālika*, when mixed with itself, causes each succeeding one to take on its own nature alone. This is what is stated.

In the phrases beginning with *imesu*, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "It becomes stored within" means that by placing it inside an improper hut and causing the dawn to rise [while it remains there], it is said to have become "stored within.
"And it becomes kept in reserve" means that by receiving it and not relinquishing the act of reception, and then causing the dawn to rise, it is said to have become "kept in reserve.
In the manuscripts, the reading *sannidhiṃ* with a nasalized vowel is seen; however, [the word] "becomes" (*hoti*)...
Because it is connected with the sense of "action" (*kiriyā*), the word *sannidhi* is in the nominative singular;

thus, it should be understood that the nasal [consonant] is an augment (*āgama*) resulting from euphonic combination (*sandhi*). "Both as well" means both that which was previously mentioned as being stored inside, and the "accumulation" (*sannidhi*).
"It certainly does not exist" means it certainly does not exist unmixed with the two preceding time-periods.
1389. Briefly, it should be understood that a lodging which is not made into a *kappiyakuṭi*, not formally authorized, and not enclosed by a wall or similar structure is called an *akappiyakuṭi*.
"By the two ends" means by the seven-day [allowance] and the lifetime [allowance];
the word "by" (*saha*) expresses the sense of agency. "Mixed" is the remainder [of the sentence]. "Taken" means received. That [refers to] the former two.
This refers to the two periods: the "until-mealtime" (yāvakālika) and the "for-a-watch" (yāmaka).

It is stated that whatever has been received on the same day during the first two periods, even if it was kept in an improper storehouse, becomes what is called "stored overnight" (antovuttha) when mixed with anything at all during the latter two periods by one who has allowed the dawn to rise.
1390. The *Aṭṭhakathā* states that when the two earlier periods are combined with the two later periods stored within, this is called "storing in the mouth" (*mukhasannidhi*).
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated emphatically that what has been stored within is not permissible; such is the construction of the meaning.
In this context, the difference between the names “stored in the mouth” (*mukhasannidhi*) and “grown inside” (*antovuttha*) is merely nominal;
it should be understood that there is no difference in meaning between these two commentarial statements, as they refer to the very same thing.

For the word *mukha* (mouth) is a synonym for *anta* (inside), and the word *sannidhi* (storage) is a synonym for *parivuttha* (grown). Thus, “storage in the mouth” (*mukhasannidhi*) is an analysis based on the object (*kamma-sādhana*).
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the mention of "mouth" (*mukha*) and the inclusion of "inside" (*anta*) are made for the purpose of excluding external storage (*bahi sannidhi*).
Furthermore, "outside" (*bahi*) refers to whatever has been stored anywhere outside an improper storehouse (*akappiyakuṭi*) after being received;

it is intended as the latter pair of meal-times mixed with the former pair of meal-times. There is no difference in meaning between the terms "mouth-storage" (*mukhasannidhi*) and "inside-stored" (*antovuttha*).
This is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. As it says:

"If a novice brings food such as rice to a monk, places it in a *kappiya-kuṭi* (a place where things are made allowable), and then cooks and gives it to him on the following day, it is not considered 'stored overnight' (*antovuttha*).
In that regard, [the same applies] to ghee and other items placed in an *akappiya-kuṭi* (an unallowable place)..."
Whatever one gives after having put something [else] inside is called "stored in the mouth" (*mukhasannidhi*).

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* it is stated: "It is what has been kept overnight"; in that case, the only difference is merely the terminology. But there is no doubt that it is understood as if stated otherwise;
even there, this same principle should be understood to apply.

1391. "There is no fault" means there is no fault of storage (*sannidhi-dosa*). "Having stored away" means having received [the food] and not relinquishing that receipt, having stored it away within the respective time limits for each [type of food]. And here, in order to show the minimum limit for storage, it is said:
"After washing the bowl, one should know whether it has lost its moisture by pouring clear water back into it again or by rubbing it with a finger."

It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "By this [statement], it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that when one has accepted [an alms-bowl] with indifference, and without relinquishing it, one makes it empty—either by oneself or by another—and after washing it properly, when it is finished, even what was stuck [to it] remains as something accepted without being abandoned;
therefore, an offense is stated in that case. Regarding acceptance with such indifference...
It is established that there is no fault even in such a discarded bowl.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of storage (*sannidhi*). 1393.
Regarding "exquisite foods," the Pāli text enumerates them as follows: "That is to say: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, and curd."
“Ghee (sappi) means cow’s ghee, or goat’s ghee, or buffalo’s ghee—the ghee of those whose meat is permitted.
Butter (navanīta) means the butter of those same animals. Oil (tela) means sesame oil, mustard seed oil, madhuka oil, castor oil, or fat oil.
Honey (madhu) means honey from bees. Molasses (phāṇita) means that which is produced from sugarcane.”
“Fish” refers to aquatic creatures. “Meat” refers to the meat of those animals whose flesh is permitted.
“Milk” refers to the milk of cows, or the milk of goats, or the milk of buffaloes—the milk of those animals whose meat is permitted.
“Curd” refers to the curd of those same animals.”

The meaning is that nine kinds of choice food have been specified. "One who is not ill" refers to one for whom there is comfort even without choice foods; this is what is meant by "one who is not ill. In this context, the word "having been" (*hutvā*) is to be supplied after "one who is not ill.
Regarding "give with ghee," etc., these are the modes of requesting. As for "ghee-rice" (*sappibhatta*):

although it could be understood as rice mixed with ghee, or ghee and rice taken together as "ghee-rice," in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is explained as "rice [prepared] with *sāli* grains."
Having stated the reason, "There is nothing like ghee with rice," and having made the *dukkaṭa* offense even more stringent because it was so stated, it is not possible to say anything else.
For the masters of the *Aṭṭhakathā* are indeed the authority in such instances.
1395. Regarding the *pācittiya* for "swallowing": it is called a *pācittiya* according to the count of swallowings, as it is said, "For every swallowing, there is an offense of *pācittiya*."
1396. "Pure" means unmixed with cooked food (*anna*). "In the training rules" (*sekhiyesu*) means it is stated among those things that ought to be practiced; this is the meaning. 1397.

Since requesting and consuming pure, choice foods constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), therefore [the text specifies]: "Consisting of the seven grains" means being a derivative product of any one of the seven grains, such as rice and so forth.
1398. The construction is: "If he gives. It is stated that there is no offense (*anāpatti*) when there is a misunderstanding (*visaṅketa*).

1399. The connection is with *deti* (gives) and *ceti* (takes). In the phrase *aññatarena*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*). The word "food" (*bhatta*) is understood from the context.

"Of this bhikkhu" refers to the recipient. "A breach of agreement" means that because something different from what was requested was given, there is no offense due to the failure of the agreement; this is what is meant.
In the phrase "by whatever," here too the word is used in the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) as before.
"Viññattaṃ" (solicited) is a qualifier for the additional term "bhattaṃ" (food). "By whatever" refers to any kind of refined food without restriction.

By this, ghee and so forth are already included individually; furthermore, the various types of ghee, such as cow-ghee and the like, are also encompassed. "Even when that has been obtained" means precisely when it has been requested.
"When it has been obtained. The construction is to be understood distributively as "obtained at the root of each respective [item].

What is meant? If one who makes a general request, saying, "Give me food with ghee," is given that very thing, or if one gives another item such as fresh butter (*navanīta*)—saying, "Take this and make ghee from it"—or if one gives a cow or the raw material for ghee, then [it is considered] "ghee from a cow" (*gosappi*).
If one makes a request specifying [the food] by saying, "Give me alms-food," or if the person gives that very same thing, or butter from a cow and so forth,
or a cow itself, saying, "Having given this, take ghee," or if they give the price, there is no deception;
it is said that one incurs an offense exactly according to the original category of the object.

"Na aññathā" (not otherwise) means: when someone has requested ghee, instead of saying, "Take this and make ghee with it," one says, "There is no ghee, take this," or remains silent, and then gives any of the other items such as fresh butter;
even though something else was given, there is still a lack of coordination (*visaṅketa*) because there was no specific indication of that particular item.
Even if [the item] was given without being mentioned in the formal text (*pāḷi*), there is still a lack of coordination.
"But if one gives something else, whether it has come down in the Canon (pāḷi) or not, it is a violation," so it is said in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

1401. "In the Canon" refers to the explanatory text (niddesa-pāḷi) previously shown, beginning with "Ghee (sappi) means cow's ghee," and so on. As it says: "Setting aside the fresh butter and other items that have come down in the Canon," and so forth. [The phrase] "by others" refers to fresh butter and the like; the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (sahatthe). 1402.

The word "having requested" (*viññāpetvā*) has "alms-food" (*bhatta*), which serves as its object, as the subject under discussion. This is due to the requirements of the metrical composition (gāthā-bandha).
The short vowel of the word *vā* has been applied. The construction is "or from one [place]" (*ekato vā*);
"from different [places]" (*nānato*) is also implicitly included, meaning "either from one place or from different places. As it was said:

"But if, having requested [permission] with all [the substances] such as ghee, etc., either in one place or in different places," and so forth. For that very reason, in the phrase "he eats" (*bhuñjati*), the word "if" (*ce*) indicates a hypothetical supposition.
And this phrase "even a single drop on the tip of a blade of kusa grass" is to be supplied here for the purpose of illustrating the dipping-spoon (avakaṃsa).
The statement "it is considered [an offense]" (*matā*) is said with reference to what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

The construction is as follows: if, having requested food from one or several places, one makes it of a single flavor and eats even as much as a single drop on the tip of a blade of kusa grass, nine *pācittiyas* are considered [to have occurred].
1403. The construction is: "even when told, 'Give [me] ghee that is not allowable' (*akappiya*). The instrumental case is used in the sense of the direct object.
"Food" (*bhatta*) is the subject under discussion. "Unallowable" (*akappiya*) should be understood as the opposite of the type described in the statement, "The ghee of those whose meat is allowable.
"If he gives with that" means if, together with that very unallowable item requested, he gives rice.
1404. *Tathāsaññissa* means "of one who perceives it thus"; the meaning is "one who perceives himself as being ill. As it is said:

"If one is ill and perceives oneself as ill, there is no offense. 1405. The construction is: "No offense is declared for one who, having requested [food] at a time when he was ill, eats it while not ill.
The same should be applied to the other two phrases as well. As it is said: "There is no offense if, having made a request while being ill, one eats it after having become non-ill," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of relatives and so forth," the word "dependent" (*āyatta*) is to be understood as the remainder. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), this includes: "when invited [to eat], for the sake of another;
by means of one's own wealth; of one who is insane; and of a first-offender.
(1406) To show the four origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), he says "from the body," and so on.
Commentary on the Discussion of Exquisite Food (Paṇītabhojanakathāvaṇṇanā).

1407. Regarding the term "not given" (*adinnan*): unlike in the training rule on taking what is not given (*adinnādāna-sikkhāpada*), one should not say "appropriated by another," but rather simply "not received.
As it is said: "What is called 'not given' is said to be that which has not been formally received (*appaṭiggahitaka*). "The mouth-door" (*mukhadvāra*) means in the mouth.

“Door” means the mouth-door or the throat-pipe. By this statement, it is indicated that whatever is to be swallowed—whether it enters by the mouth or by the nose—once it has entered the cavity of the throat, it constitutes an offense.
“Food” refers to anything other than water and tooth-sticks that is to be swallowed, such as the *yāvakālika* (food for the appropriate time) and so forth. As it is said: “What is called food...”
"Having set aside water and tooth-cleansing wood, anything that is to be swallowed.
"One might swallow" means one might introduce it into the mouth; by this, it is indicated that there is no fault even when receiving with the mouth without [the food] passing down the throat.
For this very reason he said, "except for water and tooth-cleansing wood. For this same reason it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*:

“By the very statement that there is no offense in placing a tooth-stick in the mouth of the Blessed One, it is stated that there is no offense in placing anything whatsoever in the mouth without making it go down the throat.
For it is permissible to drink water as one likes and to use a tooth-stick for the purpose of cleansing the teeth; however, one must not swallow its taste.
It is not permissible. Even if the taste of a tooth-stick enters the mouth of one who is unaware, it is still an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
It is called *dantapoṇa* because by means of it, the teeth are cleansed and made free from impurities. 1408–9.

Showing first the characteristic of what has been given according to the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), he says “within arm’s reach,” etc., by way of contrast to the characteristic of what has not been given. Regarding “within arm’s reach,” this is as stated in the *Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*:
"The last factor for the one taking, but the first for the one giving;
if it is two and a half [fathoms] for both, excluding the extended hand"—this is the characteristic of the "hand's reach" (*hatthapāsa*) as stated.
"Directing toward" (*abhinīhāra*) means carrying [the object] forward by facing it, according to the method stated right there.
“Capable of being lifted by a person of medium strength” means that it is fit to be lifted by a man of medium physical power, according to the highest limit of what can be received.
This description emphasizes the state of the object (*bhāvappadhāna*). However, the minimum limit should be understood from the commentarial statement:
“at least as much as the dust raised by a chariot wheel. *Uccāraṇa* means lifting. By the term “non-human being,” [the text] refers to its commonality with other beings.
It should also be understood as applying to animals (*tiracchānagata*). Alternatively, it should be understood by what will be said later, beginning with “or a bird.
“By means of the body, etc. refers to any one of the offenses involving the body, the body’s attachments, or what is to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*).

For this very reason, he says “in three ways. “In two ways” means either by the body or by what is attached to the body. Regarding “the conjunction of five factors,” here the first factor is “the range of the hand” (*hatthapāsa*).
“Abhinīhāro” is the second; “majjhimuccāraṇakkhamo” is the third; “manusso…pe… tidhā” is the fourth;
“paṭiggaṇhāti…pe… dvidhā” is the fifth—these are the five factors.
The conjunction, meeting, and assembly of these five factors is the "fivefold conjunction" (pañcaṅgasaṃyogo); [it occurs] therein. “Gahaṇaṃ” means receiving. Of that...
For a bhikkhu. It grows; it succeeds. 1410–12.
"The other" refers to the recipient. Of that limb. "Naga" means that which does not move; by "naga," both a tree and a mountain are called. "In such a place" means in such high or low locations.
1413. "With the trunk" means with the hand.
1415–6. Having bent slightly and lowered it a little, that bhikkhu should cover that lower vessel even with a single part;
this is the construction of the sentence. 1417. “Having opened” means having lifted up; it is said, “having set the vessels down separately.

1418. “A basket of food” means a basket of cooked rice; it is said, “a basket filled with rice. “Giving while bending” means she herself, having bent down, gives the *byābhaṅgi* (a type of ladle or serving spoon).
1419. Regarding the phrase “thirty cubits”: this was said for the purpose of showing that if it is merely thirty *ratana*s in measure, one should not suspect it of being "far away.

In the case of "when it has been taken," when a donor standing within arm's reach offers a bamboo pole thirty cubits long to be accepted—while two jars have been placed at both ends—one who accepts it must do so with some part of the body.
Or, having made the mental application (*ābhoga*) "I take this" with something connected to the body, it is said that it is "received" once it has been touched anywhere on a bed or similar object.
"All of that" means everything placed in those two jars.
"It is indeed taken" means it is indeed received, because it has come within the reach of the donor's hand; this belongs to him.
By the word "only" (*eva*), it is indicated that no suspicion should be raised regarding anything "connected to the body.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "Even when two jars are placed on the ground, by the mere act of receiving [the food] upon the bamboo pole binding them, it is considered received.

(1420–24) By the term "on a straw mat" (*kaṭasārake*), items such as wooden platters and the like are implied. The phrase "he sits down" (*nisīdati*) serves as a representative for "he stands," and so forth.
This is an illustration. Regarding the phrase "having touched the beds and so forth," the word "even with a finger" (*aṅguli-yāpi*) is to be supplied here. As it is said:
"By one who stands, sits, or lies down, having touched the beds and so forth even with a finger, while perceiving them as a receiving bowl" (*paṭiggahaṇasaññāya*), and so on.

Regarding the phrase "in the bowls," this refers specifically to all the bowls placed in that manner. Regarding the phrase "and what is given," the expression "by one standing in that manner" is understood by implication (*sāmatthiyā*).

Having shown that even when [food] is merely touched by a finger or any other part on a bed or similar object, it constitutes acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*), he now says “I shall accept,” etc., to show that it is also accomplished by climbing onto such objects. The construction is as follows:
if one climbs onto beds and so forth with the very thought “I shall accept” and sits down, and if the donor also stands within arm’s reach while giving, all of that is considered accepted.

The construction is as follows: regarding those alms-bowls that have come from one bowl to another and are now resting on the ground, if he sits and touches whichever bowl with his finger or even with a needle, he may accept what is given right there; it is permissible.

(1425) If the *kaṭasāra* (wicker stool) and such items were large, there might be the thought that they would not constitute a "receptacle" (*paṭiggahaṇa*); therefore, to preclude that, he says "on a wicker stool," and so forth.
By the word "large," he provides the reason for mentioning the wicker stool again. [He then mentions] the elephant rug.
"Name" refers to a rug that should be spread upon the back of an elephant. By the word "etcetera," one includes horse-blankets, chariot-covers, and so forth.
The phrase "while within arm's reach" indicates the reason for the offense of receiving or mounting [the gift] when it is being given while standing;
the particle *tu* (but/then) merely clarifies the specific qualification already stated.

1426. *Tatthajātakapaṇṇesu* means on leaves that have grown right there on the tree itself. *Gahetuṃ* means to receive. The passage beginning with *“Na panetāni”* is a demonstration of the reason why it is not permissible.

The word *hi* indicates what is well-known. 1427. *Asaṃhāriyaṃ* means that which cannot be lifted up by a man of medium strength; it is unportable. *Tādiseti* means in such a manner; it is said to be unportable. *Khāṇubaddheti* means tied to a stump driven into the ground.
1428. *Tintiṇika* means *ciñcā* (tamarind). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of small [leaves] such as those of the *kadamba* flower and so forth.
From the statement "on leaves of the *tintiṇika* and others," it should be understood that receiving [alms] on branches is permissible.
It should be connected with the phrase "spread upon the ground. As it has been said: "Even on very fine leaves of the *tintiṇika* and others spread upon the ground..."
"Receiving [the food] is not permissible. 1429.
"The distributor" means the donor. 1430.
"Having wiped it off without remainder" is the construction.
1431. *Paṭiggahetvāva*: having received [the bowl] indeed. It is to be connected with "alms are to be taken. 1432. *Apaṭiggahite*:
here the word "in the bowl" (*patte*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The construction is: there is no offense for one who uses it after receiving it later.
1433. *Anādiyitvā*: not taking; what is meant is that he did not pay heed to that instruction.
1435. To another person who has not received full ordination.
1436. Regarding the previous intention, it was stated according to its specific nature: “Having given that to a novice... [etc. ...it is permissible.
However, since that [object] does not become the property of another merely by the arising of the thought, “I will give this to another,” therefore—
Even if it has not been given [to him], it is permissible for him to accept and consume it.
1437–9. "A bhikkhunī" refers to another bhikkhu. "Of food" refers to food mixed with liquid such as sour gruel (*kañjika*).

"It floats" means it floats on top. "Sour gruel" (*kañjika*) means fermented rice water (*āranāla*); since this is an illustrative term (*upalakkhaṇa*), it includes liquids such as milk, buttermilk, and so forth.
"Collected. "Having swept away" means having blown it off from the top. "If it has entered inside":

if that dust has entered into the food, it should be accepted; that is, if there is no one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) present, one should accept it without releasing it from the hand, having led it to a place where someone who is not fully ordained is present.
1440. Regarding the phrase *apanīyāvāti*: here, the term “coarse” (*thūla*) is understood by way of contrast with what will be stated later as “if it is fine” (*sukhumaṃ ce*).
The connection is “having removed [the food] together with the rice. As it has been said: “It should be removed along with the rice on top, or, having received it, it may be eaten.

1441. *Thevo* means a drop (*bindu*). Regarding the statement “a drop... is permissible”: just as there is no fault when a drop falls first, likewise, for those who remove [food] after having scattered it, there is no fault even if a drop falls later, because it was brought [into the bowl] [along with the rest].

“*Carukenā*” means by means of a small ladle (*khuddakaukkhalī*). “*Tato carukato*” means from that ladle. “*Masī*” refers to soot, ash, and the like. “*Bhājane*” means in a vessel such as a bowl or other container. “*Tassa cā*” means of that [soot] and so forth. The construction is as follows:
if, while being given to the immediately following monk, something falls from the bowl into the bowl of the other monk, it is considered already accepted;
therefore, it is indeed permissible. Regarding the word “*dīyamānan*,” it refers here to food and so forth.

The phrase "whatever" is obtained from the context of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*). Regarding the expression "it is indeed allowable," one should not make the word-division "this is indeed allowable" (*vaṭṭateva ayaṃ*), because there is nothing with which the word "this" (*ayaṃ*) could be connected.
Therefore, it should be understood that the letter *va* has been pronounced long for the sake of the meter of the verse.
1445–6. Regarding "of porridge" (*pāyāsassa*): here, the genitive case is used in the sense of a container; thus, it means "by means of porridge. "Because of heat" (*uṇhato*) means "due to being hot.

"He is not able" (*na sakkati*) means "he is unable. "It is allowable to [take it] at the rim of the mouth" (*mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ vaṭṭati*) means that it is allowable to take it after lifting the rim of the mouth so that it touches the hand.
Likewise, the construction is: if it is impossible to take it by the rim of the mouth, it may also be taken with a support (a spoon).
1447–8. The construction is: "He does not know it being brought, nor does he know it being given.

In accordance with the requirements of the verse meter (*gāthābandha*), the form *jānatī* has been shortened to *jānati*. "Intention" (*ābhoga*) means the intention [thinking], "I am taking. As stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "In this case, the mere presence of intention is the criterion.

Because it is said, "He receives either with the body or with what is connected to the body," the bowl— [...is implied as the instrument... (Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence regarding the bowl; the translation reflects the available text.)
Because he sat down after having taken [the bowl], it is also appropriate to say that he formed the intention, "I shall take it with what is connected to my body.
Regarding the phrase "having released it from the hand," this should also be construed with the words "or even the stand.
However, the phrase "having nudged it with the foot" should be construed only with the word "stand," as it is said: "having released the stand from the hand..."
“Having kicked with his foot, he sleeps. *Pelletvā* means having pressed down; it is said to mean “having stepped upon.
In the root *kami*, the division of the word as *akka* in the middle is a fault of deficient rhythm (*yati*).
“The wise know that the division of words and the rhythm are fixed places within a verse (*siloka*).”
"That which is devoid of that [consonant], having lost its status as a *yati*-pause, is like a hair-raising [shudder]"—
having thus analyzed it so that no fault arises from the definition stated by Daṇḍin, it should be accepted. However,
some here maintain that because the augment *i* functions as a grammatical condition (*paccaya*), the letter *m* accompanied by it is included within the mention of that [augment].
They resolve the objection by stating that there is no fault because, among the *dhātu* and *paccaya* suffixes, a *yati* (caesura) is desired between the two parts.
"Even for one who is awake" (*jāgarassāpi*) means even for one who is not sleeping. "Disregard" (*anādaro*) is the state of disregard. 1451.
"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of the state of disregard for such a grasping. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to that supporting surface, having stepped upon it with the foot.
And [the phrase] "receiving. "Being given" means being offered by the donor while being received.
"Falls" means that without touching the hand of the recipient, it falls upon clean ground free of dust, or upon lotus leaves and the like. As it has been said:
"That which, while being given, slips from the hand of the donor and falls upon clean ground, or upon lotus leaves, cloth, baskets, and so forth..."
"Or if it falls [on the ground], it is permissible to take that [food] and consume it oneself.

Regarding the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "If it falls on dusty ground, after wiping away the dust, or washing it, or having it formally accepted (*paṭiggahāpetvā*), it may be consumed"—here, the word "take" (*gahetuṃ*) implies "to consume" (*bhuñjituṃ*).
Regarding the phrase "it is allowable," the words "given away by the donors" are to be understood as the ellipsis. As it was said:
"I allow you, monks, to take for yourselves what falls while being given and to consume it; that, monks, has been relinquished by the donors.
Since this was stated without distinction as "what falls while being given," this principle should be understood to apply to all four types of requisites (kālika).
1452. To demonstrate the method of *abbhohārika* (the way of inclusion), he said:

“of those eating. 1453–4. That is the impurity. “In them” means in the substances such as sugarcane and so forth. “That” refers to the substance such as sugarcane mixed with impurity. “Is not discerned” means that it is indeed not discerned. “In that” means in the substance such as sugarcane and so forth. 1455.
Regarding the phrase “seats, mortars, and so forth,” by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), items such as grinding-stones, cloth-bags, pestles, and the like are included.
