1456. Because the razor is used as an illustration, any kind of blade of that same nature should be understood to be included. "Milk" refers to milk heated by one who is not fully ordained;
this is understood from the separate mention of "raw" [milk] below. "Blue" means blue-colored. "As with a blade" implies a definitive determination;
thus, having received it like a piece of sugarcane from which the impurities have been removed by a blade, it may be consumed.
The detailed analysis (vinicchaya) should be understood.
1457. "That" refers to that axe heated by fire and so forth; the axe is to be taken from the object of heating.
1459. "That" refers to that limb of the body such as the hand, or the robe, after washing it, [or] rice mixed with the dirty water that has fallen [from it].
To show that the same decision applies even when one eats while sitting at the foot of a tree or elsewhere, having washed leaves and such from a bowl in fallen, dirty water, he said:
“This very [same]...,” etc. 1460. The construction is:
“If pure water falls, it is permissible. The word “from a tree” is understood. This refers to the open air.
And if pure water falls, it is permissible; here, the word "from the sky" is understood.
In both cases—on the leaves of trees and in the air—it is called "pure" because the dust was washed away by the rainwater at the very outset. 1461.
"Without touching" means without making contact. "Of him" refers to that novice.
1462. They take the bowl of one who is not fully ordained. "Having touched" means having touched the boiled rice contained in the bowl of one who is not fully ordained.

That [rice] is the food in one's own bowl. As it is said: "If, after touching the boiled rice while it has not yet been formally received, one takes more boiled rice into one's own bowl, it constitutes an offense of taking what is not given."
1464. *Pacchā* means after, whether that [food] has been accepted or not accepted. *Taṃ* refers to that food which has been accepted. 1467.
*Tassa* refers to that alms-food contained in one's own bowl.
1468. *Parena* means by one whose bowl has not been accepted.
1469–70. The connection is: “In the vessel of the monks for the cooking of rice-gruel and so forth. It is a *pacana* because they cook therein;
it is a vessel (*bhājana*). “In the hands of the novice above the vessel” means in the hands of the novice which have been placed above the vessel.
“Fallen from the hand into that” means having slipped from the hand of that novice, it fell into that vessel.
1471. Regarding the statement, “He does not make it unallowable,” the reason is given here: “For that has been relinquished.
Since it has indeed been relinquished, therefore he does not make it unallowable; this is what is meant. “Having not done so” means having not done it in the manner just described.
“And he pours [it] in” means if he pours it into the vessel. That food-vessel is thus filled.
"Having made it free from food" (*nirāmisaṃ katvā*) means that one should wash [the bowl] so that the food fallen therein does not remain, and then eat; this is the connection.
1472–3. "A *kuṭa*" is a jar. "He pours" means he inclines the jar and pours the rice-gruel (*yāgu*).
1474. "In the hands" refers to the two hands. "Therein" means upon the two palms placed there on the ground.

1475–6. *Ekassa gahaṇūpagaṃ ce bhāran*ti: if there should be a load that is capable of being carried by one person, meaning a load that can be lifted by a single man of medium strength. By the word “tathā,” he refers back to this phrase: “a load capable of being carried by one.
1477. *Laggentīti*: they hang down. *Tatthāti*: in that bed or chair. *Vaṭṭatevāti*: it indicates that it is not something already grasped (or held).
1478. *Sammujjantoti*: sweeping. *Ghaṭṭetīti*: he touches [the bed] with the broom unintentionally.
1479. "Having known that" means having known the state of it being accepted. The intention is that it is permissible to set it aside, as it does not constitute an "accepted" (uggahitaka) item.

1480. "That" refers to what was taken with the perception that it had been accepted; that is "not accepted. Otherwise, it should not be done: the meaning is that it is not permissible to cover what is uncovered, nor to uncover what is covered.
1481. "And if he places it outside": if he places it outside the place where it was previously placed. "By that" means by having placed it outside.

"By that monk with hands released": by him whose hands have been released from [the bowl]. "That": that which was placed outside and thus released from the hand. "Having known": having known its state of not having been formally accepted (*appaṭiggahita*).
Having known it to be thus, it was placed there. 1482–3. "If a *kaṇṇikā* arises":
if a *kaṇṇikā* (a small growth or blister) is produced. "In the case of ginger, etc.": here, by the word "etc.," [other items are included].

The mention of *pipphalī* and so forth refers to [the group of] roots, such as the five roots (*pañcamūla*). "Root" (*mūla*) refers to the root [of the five roots, etc.]. "Worm-powder" (*ghuṇacuṇṇa*) means powder produced by worm-creatures (*ghuṇapāṇaka*).

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the action "arises" (*uṭṭheti*) is referred back. "Because it originates from that" (*taṃsamuṭṭhānato*) means because it has arisen from the oil and other substances already received.
"That very same thing is called [it]" (*taññeva pavuccati*) means that very first-received oil and so forth is what is being spoken of.
Therefore he said: “There is no receiving... [etc. ...it does not exist.

(1484–5) “Any person whatsoever” means any being at all, such as a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*), a traveler, and so forth. “A palm-clump” means the fruit of the *tāla* tree, specifically the nut. “Another person standing on the ground” means any other person—whether a woman or a man—standing upon the earth.
“Having cut” means having performed the act of cutting. “A fence” means a thick enclosure sufficient to reach arm’s length. As it has been said:
“While within arm’s reach”: this means without touching the handle; that is to say, for as far as the momentum of the movement subsides, or without striking the handle of the fan.
If one strikes it and then stands still while walking, it is not permitted.
As stated in the commentary: “But we [say] that from the place where it was struck, it is as if it fell of its own accord...”
"We think it will happen. When he does not stop there but continues on, it is appropriate [to consider it] like goods that have been turned over by a customs officer and fallen outside. 1487–8.
Regarding "rampart," since "or a fence" is mentioned here in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, this should be understood as being included by way of context.
Regarding the phrase “not broad,” he says “inside... if it fits” in order to show the intended measurement.
By the words “having gone up a hundred cubits,” he makes known that the donor, through the desire to give, has lifted it into the air and released it.
“Attained” means reached by hand. “Taking” means taking with the perception that it is being received.
1489. “A novice” (sāmaṇera) is an indicative term; thus, householders are also included. “Right there” means right at the trunks [of the trees]. “The novice was sitting. 1491–2.
“A fruit-bearing branch” means a branch possessing fruit. “In order to eat”—this should be connected with the phrase “when the thought arose.
The construction is: “If he eats the fruit, it is permissible to eat it in this way. [This refers to] flies.
"For the purpose of warding off" means for the purpose of keeping away flies.

1493. If a fruit-bearing branch is taken for the purpose of shade and for warding off flies, and it has been made allowable (*kappiya*) and accepted for the purpose of comfortable enjoyment, then when there is a desire to eat, it is permissible even if it is not accepted again.
In order to show this, he said, “But having had it made allowable,” and so forth (1494–5).

Since it will be stated later, “Having had that accepted by him,” it should be understood that the word “having taken” here refers to taking [the food] without first having it formally accepted. Regarding the phrase “that was accepted,” the words “if [it was] already” are to be supplied as the remainder (1496–9).
The connection is with “the rice for a bhikkhu’s provisions. “He” refers to the novice. “By the others” means by the rice belonging to himself which has been taken by the bhikkhu.
“Regarding ‘in two bowls’: this is an illustration; the same principle applies even to many.

It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that it is permissible to give even to many by means of giving to others after having given to monks what one has received oneself, and taking from them what they have received to give to oneself.
To demonstrate this very point, he said: “‘Give the rice-gruel to me, friend,’ [saying] to a monk,” and so forth. “‘Friend, give your rice-gruel to me.’”
Thus, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Even if the elders have requested [the food] in turn, it is permissible for them to drink [the gruel], as everything has been consumed by the novices alone.
Regarding the phrase "because it was drunk by the novice," the word "of the gruel" (yāguyā) is understood from the context.
1500. *Imassa* means "of this rice-carrying traveler. By the phrase "not a distinction," he indicates that it should not be stated separately.
1501. *Assa visesassa* means "of this distinction"—the remainder of the sense being "of the state of being stated separately" regarding the aforementioned specific determination (*vinicchaya*).
*Tassa* refers to the bhikkhu who was a novice (*sāmaṇera*) carrying rice. *Sālayabhāvaṃ* [means] "the state of attachment" toward the rice grains taken by himself.
When things have been completely exhausted, the state of attachment (*sālayabhāva*) is the thought: "This will also serve us.
Regarding a branch being taken for the sake of its shade and so forth, if there is a desire to eat its fruit, one can indeed form an attachment (*ālaya*) thinking, "It is fit to be eaten";
thus this too is understood as no different [from the previous case]. However, it is appropriate to say that he spoke in order to show the distinction that is possible therein.
"Cannot move it constantly" means that after moving it, one cannot remove the pebbles. "Celaka" refers to a junior novice (cūḷasāmaṇera). The construction is:
"At the time when it is cooked, having opened [the vessel], the state of being cooked is to be known. The word *pi* has the sense of the word *pana*.

"Having removed" means having removed from the hearth. This is because the measure [of what may be accepted] applies only to that which has already been received for the purpose of washing the previous rice.
He said: "It is not for the purpose of receiving [food] afterwards.
*Assa* means "of food. (1505) Because the verb *kāreti* takes two objects, he said: "the hearth and the clean vessel"; that is to say, it is stated as "on the hearth.

(1506) *Koci* refers to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). "By that bhikkhu" means by the bhikkhu who, having placed [the food] on the hearth and the clean vessel, lit the fire. And this is an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), because it should not be done by anyone else either.

1507. *Pacchā* means after the throwing in of rice. *Taṃ yāguṃ* refers to that gruel. *Sace pacati* means he cooks while applying fire. *Na muccati sāmapākā* means that by drinking that gruel, one is not released from the *dukkaṭa* offense of cooking for oneself.

1508. The construction is as follows: if one shakes even slightly any fruit grown on a creeper there, together with the creeper itself, then whatever fruit is obtained from that is not permitted for that very bhikkhu;
for one who consumes it, there is the *dukkaṭa* offense of improper conduct (*durupaciṇṇa*).
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāyo*). By the word "of that very" (*tasseva*), the particle *eva* indicates that it is permissible for others as well.
1509. *Parāmaṭṭhuṃ* means to touch. *Apassayituṃ* means to lean against, or to provide support. By the word "it is said" (*kirā*), he indicates that this is merely stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
1510–1. *Tattha* means in that oil. *Hatthena saṇḍāsaggahaṇaṃ amuñcantena*: with the hand not releasing the grip on the tongs. *Taṃ telaṃ*: that oil.
“Loṇakiccaṃ” means the task that must be performed with salt in a place where there is no salt.

He said “reckoned as ‘for-life’ (yāvajīvika),” and so forth, to show that sea water is not subject to storage (asannidhi), just like [medicines] that are mixed with what is stored and what is for the remainder of the day.
“Kālavinimmuttaṃ” means free from time-restriction (akālika); the meaning is that it is not included among the four types of medicines restricted by time.
1517. "Like snow" means like pearls from frozen water; "like gravel" means like pebbles.

"Even though thick" refers to water that is so thick it does not appear as mud-colored in the place where it is poured, whether in the mouth or elsewhere; such water may be drunk even if it has not been formally received.
However, if the color of mud is discernible, it is not permitted. As it was said: "But if, in the mouth and in the hand..."
"It clings; it is not permitted; having accepted it, it may be consumed.
(1518) "In a ploughed place" means in a place where wood has been cleared. It is not permitted [to take] what has not been formally accepted. This applies everywhere.
(1519) A "sobbha" is a reservoir of water difficult to plunge into. Some say it is a "pit" (*āvāṭa*). A "kakudha" is a *ajjuna* tree.
1520. *Pānīyassa ghaṭo* means a water-jar; *taṃ pānīyaghaṭaṃ* refers to that water-jar. 1521.

Flowers for the purpose of scenting are *vāsapupphāni*. *Tattha* means in that water-jar. *Kamallikāsu* means among the thorny jasmine (*kaṇṭakamallikā*) as well as with flowers such as the *pāṭali* and others. *Dinnāsu* means when they have been placed into the water.
1522. *Visati* means it enters into the throat. For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary: "That which was set down without being formally received..."

It is stated that [food] "should be accepted. If it is argued that this commentarial statement contradicts the canonical text (pāḷi) which says, "except for water and tooth-wood," it does not contradict it.
For that [text] was spoken specifically with reference to the function of the teeth, whereas this was spoken with reference to the flavor.
For that very reason, immediately following that, it says: "Even if the flavor has entered the mouth of one who is unaware, there is still an offense. For it is unintentional..."

"This is the training rule" is what was stated. The fact that this training rule is "without intention" (acittaka) is understood from the Pāḷi text beginning with "perceiving as received what is not received," because an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated even for one who perceives it as allowable (kappiya).

Furthermore, since clear water may be consumed even without being formally received, it is similar to a tooth-stick; thus, it is understood that those items taught in a single grammatical connection (ekayoga) function together.
One should consider water and tooth-cleansing wood to be equal in their faults.
(1523) Because liquid urine, water, snot, and so forth, as well as liquid milk, blood, and so forth, are manifestations of the water element (*āpodhātu*),
and because solid earwax and the like are manifestations of the earth element (*pathavidhātu*), the phrase "among the beings residing in the body" refers here to milk and the rest.

The word “*kiṃ*” (what) should also be construed with the phrase “this is not allowable. Regarding the expression “of meat that is allowable or unallowable,” the term “of beings” is understood here by implication (*sāmatthiyā*).
Regarding the word “salt,” the phrase “all this as well” is understood here by virtue of the context (*adhikārato*).
1525. *Ettha* means: among these aforementioned things, such as ear-wax and so forth. 1528.
*Cattāri vikaṭānīti*: the four "loathsome things" (*vikaṭa*) are said to be excrement, clay, urine, and ashes;
these four are called "loathsome things" because they are repulsive, having been rendered foul like the poison of a snake.

“*Nadāyakaṃ*”: a place where there is no giver (*dāyaka*) is *nadāyaka*; [it refers] to that [place]. Because it is stated that “*na*, *a*, *no*, *mā*, and *alaṃ* express negation,” there is a compound with the word *na*, which expresses negation.
This has no difference in meaning from the term “*adāyake*” (in the absence of a giver). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“One who is ill-behaved and incompetent is called ‘unvirtuous’ (*asanta*). This is what is known as *kālodissa*.

1529. *Pathavin* means improper ground. *Tarunti* means [they cross] over a tree that is still moist. By this, he shows what must be done by oneself for the sake of *vikaṭa* (raw food) when one has been bitten by a snake and there is no one to perform the ritual purification (*kappiyakāraka*).
1530. *Acchedagāhato* means from taking [something] after plundering it. The word *“tassā”* connects with all the causal phrases.
*“Tassā”* means of that which has not been formally accepted (*appaṭiggahita*). The construction is: “and by giving to another who is without monks (*abhikkhuka*)”; thus, *“abhikkhukassa”* [is used].
However, this indicates that when [food] is given to one who has been fully ordained (*upasampanna*) by means of a qualification, the act of receiving does not cease.
"All" refers to everything mentioned above, such as the various modes of taking with the body and so forth. "In this way" means according to this method.
1531. "Ill-performed" (*durupaciṇṇa*) means poorly performed or improperly handled; it refers to food, alms-bowls, and so forth, which have not been formally received.
The meaning is: by touching with the hand for the sake of play, and by grasping a fruit-bearing branch or creeper grown there and shaking it.
"In the case of what has been taken up" means: in the receiving of any object that was taken while knowing its state of not having been formally received (*appaṭiggahita*).
"And when it has entered within" means: when dawn has arisen after it has been placed inside an improper hut (*akappiya-kuṭi*).
"And by oneself cooked" means cooked by oneself anywhere at all. "Cooked inside [an improper hut]" means cooked inside an improper hut (*akappiyakuṭī*).
The connection is that "an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is specified.
1532–3. "Regarding what has been accepted, one who perceives it as accepted"—this is the connection. "Tooth-cleanser" (*dantapona*) means a tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*).
“Of the bhikkhunīs” means of both the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī; “of the bhikkhunīs” is a singular collective form (*ekadesasarūpeka-sesa*).

Regarding this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the explanation (*vinicchaya*) for the nine classes of bhikkhunīs—beginning with the junior, the middle-ranking, and the senior—should be understood without distinction.
Therefore, for that reason, this entire explanation has been stated by me in its entirety and without abbreviation. This is the construction of the sentence.
Since it is possible to state the full meaning merely by way of a summary of the meaning— as is done in the *Kusalattika* and other such works— he said "in its entirety" (*sakalo*),
and then said "not in brief" (*asamāsato*) to show that the discussion has been set forth in detail.
This concludes the commentary on the *Dantapona-kathā*.
The fourth chapter on Food is concluded.

1535. Regarding the phrase "of those such as the naked ascetics" (*acelakādi*), it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that "a naked ascetic (*acelaka*) is anyone who has entered the state of a wanderer (*paribbājaka*) and is naked.
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on that, it is said: "One who has entered the state of a wanderer means one who has entered the life of renunciation (*pabbajjā*). Therefore...
In this context, one who has indeed entered the ascetic wandering life is called an *acelaka*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), two items found in the matrix (*mātikā*)—"of a male wanderer (*paribbājaka*) or a female wanderer (*paribbājikā*)"—are included. Regarding these two, a "wanderer" is defined as:

"anyone who has entered the state of a wanderer, with the exception of a monk (*bhikkhu*) and a novice (*sāmaṇera*). [The same applies to] a "nun" (*bhikkhunī*) and a "probationary nun" (*sikkhamānā*).
"Any woman who has entered the state of a wanderer (paribbājikā), with the exception of a female novice (sāmaṇerī),"—this is how those called "wanderers" (paribbājikā) should be understood.
However, in this context, only those [wanderers] who are disguised (channā) should be taken. Regarding the phrase "of one giving," the word "of a monk" (bhikkhussa) is obtained from the context;
here, the words "by means of the body, etc. (kāyādinā) are to be supplied. As it is said: "He should give" means by means of the body or by means of what is connected to the body.
“Or he gives with something that has been relinquished.

1536. Regarding “threefold offenses of expiation” (*pācittiya*): there is a triad of expiations consisting of [the cases where one] perceives a non-Buddhist as a non-Buddhist, is doubtful, or perceives someone who is not a non-Buddhist as a non-Buddhist.
1537. The construction is: for a monk who perceives one who is not a non-Buddhist as a non-Buddhist, or who is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
1538–9. *Tesaṃ* refers to the heretics (*titthiyānaṃ*). *Bahilepanaṃ* means giving anything to be smeared upon the exterior of the body. The construction is as follows:
there is no offense for one who, having placed his own food, bowl, or other such items near those heretics—close to them—says, "Take the food.
The phrase *samuṭṭhānaṃ eḷakūpamaṃ* is to be analyzed as a compound word.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakakathāvaṇṇanā). 1540–2.
“A bhikkhu, having caused some kind of material gift to be given to another bhikkhu, or not having caused it to be given”—this is the construction. What is meant?
It is according to the method stated in the training rule: “Come, friend, let us enter a village or town for alms.”

Having spoken thus, whether he causes some kind of material gift—such as hard food (*khādanīya*) and so forth—to be given to that monk with whom he has entered the village for alms, or whether he does not cause it to be given;
the construction is: "he dismisses that monk by saying, 'Go! What is meant? Thus, whichever monk...
Having entered the village with him, he says to him, “Go, friend; neither conversation nor sitting together with you is comfortable for me;
conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me,” and on that account, he urges him to go for the purpose of engaging in improper conduct such as speaking with those women.
“On that account” (*tappaccayā*) refers to “the mere urging” (*uyyojanamattasmiṃ*).

This is the qualification. Regarding the phrase "and by the first," the word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of a locative (*aṭṭhāna*) and should be construed with "even in the mere act of inciting" (*uyyojanamattasmiñca*).
"Of him" (*tassa*) refers to the one who incites.

"Of it" (*assa*) refers to the one who is incited; this is a genitive case used to express a relationship between parts (*avayavasambandhe*). [This occurs] when one has transgressed the vicinity, according to the definition that will be stated later.

The meaning is: "having passed beyond the range of sight or the range of hearing"; the locative case is used here to characterize a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇe*). Again, "of that" refers to the precinct (*upacāra*).
The limit of the precinct (*upacāra-sīmā*) is defined as extending twelve *ratana*s, or whatever is included within that, such as the enclosure wall and so forth.
To show this according to its specific form, he says: "In the case of seeing," and so on. In the open air (*ajjhokāse*), regarding the precinct of twelve [ratana*s] in the case of seeing...
The construction is: "twelve cubits are taught as the measure. And regarding the hearing area (*savana*), in the open air (*ajjhokāsa*), the construction is:

"twelve cubits are taught as the measure for the vicinity of the hearing area in the open air"; the meaning is that it is stated that the boundary of the vicinity of the hearing area is precisely twelve cubits in measure.
"And not otherwise" means that in the other case, which is not the open air, the measure of the vicinity is likewise twelve cubits.
Nor has it been taught [that these are boundaries]; rather, what is meant is that walls and so forth—which create an obstruction—are not taught as the measure for the vicinity (*upacāra*).

And this has been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "But if there are walls, doors, enclosures, and so forth in between, the very fact of being separated by them constitutes the transgression of the vicinity of sight;
the offense should be understood according to that. Here, in the two types of vicinity...

Even though they are equal [in status], it is understood that this is stated with reference to the non-occurrence of an *āsava* (outflow) when one has been dismissed and has reached the limit [of the offense].

"Threefold *pācittiya*" means: regarding one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), for one who perceives them as such, one who is doubtful, or one who perceives them as not fully ordained, there is a threefold *pācittiya*.

"The others" refers to those who are not fully ordained. "Threefold *dukkaṭa*" refers to [the offense] for one who perceives a person who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, or is doubtful, or perceives them as not fully ordained.
Accordingly, there is a triple offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). “The others” refers undoubtedly to novices (*sāmaṇera*) alone; this has been written down.

The fact that this very same meaning was also stated by Vajirabuddhi is demonstrated. If that demonstration is said with reference to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), as intended here among the five types of co-religionists, it is appropriate.
Otherwise, [it would contradict] the general term “one who is not fully ordained” used in the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Since it has been specified [in the rule], it is our view that there should be no offense for one who incites even a householder who is not fully ordained;

this is because [the rule] refers to "both," meaning both those who are fully ordained and those who are not. However, to avoid any doubt, it is written as "monks and novices. Regarding the phrase "imposing the message of *kali*":
here, *kali* means anger; its "message" (*sāsana*) is its command, thus "the message of *kali*" (*kalisāsana*), and the act of imposing that is "imposing the message of *kali*."
The propagation [of the teaching] is the planting of the message of the Kali age. Regarding that, by way of anger, one displays fault in standing, sitting, and so forth, saying:
"Look, sirs, at this man's standing, sitting, looking forward, and looking around!
He stands like a stump, he sits like a dog, and he looks here and there like a monkey. Thus, thinking, "Perhaps he will be provoked by this too..."
"Should depart" means the speaking of unpleasant words.
"By one who sends [someone] on account of a task" means by one who dispatches a monastery guard or others for tasks such as bringing food;

because this is an illustrative example (*upalakkhaṇa*), it includes the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) such as: "There is no offense if one sends [them away], thinking, 'We two shall not live together.'"
All modes [of speech] should be understood. This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning dismissal (uyyojanakathā). 1546.

Regarding the term "in a small place" (khuddake), the words "in a bedchamber" (sayanighare) are to be supplied as the remainder, based on the subsequent phrase: "for him who is in a non-bedchamber, perceiving it as a bedchamber."
It is obtained because it will be explained [later]. The same principle applies here to the term “large. The meaning is:
in such a small bed-chamber whose middle is two-and-a-half cubits in measure from the back wall. “The backbone” (piṭṭhivaṃsa) refers to the center of the house fixed by the backbone.
Therefore, the Commentary says: “By the phrase ‘having passed beyond the backbone,’ the passing beyond the middle is indicated.”
"...shows. Regarding "with food" (*sabhojana*): *sabhojanaṃ* means together with food; [it refers] to that which is "with food. Alternatively, "with food" (*sabhojana*) means with wealth (*sabhoga*).
For a man who is obsessed by lust, a woman is his wealth, and for a woman, a man is her wealth; thus, it is said to be accompanied by men and women who are impassioned by sexual desire.
As it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "A family 'with food' (*sabhojana*)..."
"She is a woman and he is a man; both the woman and the man have not departed [from the household], and both are not free from lust.
By this, the state of being ignited at that very moment by the fire of sensual passion for sexual intercourse is illustrated. "In the family" means in the house.
"Within arm's reach" refers to a space measuring two and a half ratanas. "And of the door-panels" refers to the closing of the door.
*Ca*. "Of a bed" (*sayanassa*): it is called a "bed" (*sayana*) because they lie upon it; of that [bed].
One who sits in a place near [a bed] in a family that provides food should be connected with this word "of him" (*tassa*). The meaning is: one who sits in a place in the vicinity of a bed.
"In a large one" (*mahallake*): in a bedchamber larger than the dimensions previously mentioned. "And such a bedchamber [is found] in great four-winged halls (*mahācatusālā*) and so forth."
“...occurs,” so it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
1548. *Sayanī* means “one who has a bed”; the analysis (*viggaha*) is: “he is a bed-user (*sayanī*) and that is a house. *Tattha* means “in the bed-house. 1549–50.
*Dutiye sati* means “when there is a second person, a monk. As it is said in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*): “a monk is the second [companion].”
“...occurs. Regarding “among those free from lust”: this refers to those whose obsessions with lust have been abandoned. “A place with the characteristics already described”:

this refers to a location in a small or large dwelling that possesses the characteristics already mentioned. “For one sitting without overstepping”: for one who sits without having transgressed [the limits].
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning eating together.
1552. "Tesam" refers to the two indeterminate training rules (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*). "Esam" refers to these two training rules concerning secret concealment and sitting in private;

the construction is that this very distinction—namely, the distinction characterized by their mode of origin (*samuṭṭhāna*)—is illustrated as being the same as the immediately preceding training rule.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of secret concealment and sitting in private.

1553–6. *Vutto* means invited. *Santaṃ bhikkhunī* means a bhikkhunī standing within twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*) in the vicinity of the place where the thought arose, "I shall visit a family. As it is said:
"From the point where the intention to visit families arose while standing, [counting] from there—whether to the side or in front..."
“Or one sees [him], or it is possible to inform him by means of ordinary speech; this is what is called ‘one who is present.
In this context, that which can be heard by someone standing within twelve cubits is called “ordinary speech.
“Without having asked permission” means [not saying] such things as, “I am going to the house of so-and-so,” or, “I ask for permission to go on a journey.”
"Without having asked for permission by word. "Should enter upon wandering" means: it is said that she would go about.

"Except at the proper time" refers to the two kinds of proper times mentioned according to the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) in the training precept: "In this regard, this is the proper time: the time for giving robes and the time for making robes"—at any time other than these.
In order to show the classification of offenses, he said, “excepting,” and so forth. By the phrase “when midday has not passed,” both before the meal and after the meal are included.
Here, “before the meal” and “after the meal” mean whether that meal for which one was invited has been eaten or not yet eaten.
As it is said: “Before the meal means [the time] when one has not yet eaten that for which one was invited.”

"One who has not eaten. Regarding "after the meal," it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "By whomsoever one was invited, even if that person has eaten as little as a blade of *kusa* grass.

"The house of another" means the house of someone other than the one who invited him. The connection is: "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) upon stepping onto the precincts of the house. The meaning is:
"there is an offense of wrong-doing upon stepping onto the precincts of the house to which he himself has gone. The connection is with the phrase "with the first foot."

“Gharummāre” (at the threshold of another’s house) means at the threshold of another’s dwelling. The phrase “and another too” is stated with reference to the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) committed within the vicinity of a house (gharūpacāra).
Together with the word “samatikkame” (upon crossing over), the term “gharummāre” should be construed by changing its case-ending to “gharummārassa.
1557. “In the place where he stands” means within twelve cubits of that spot where he was standing when the intention to go arose.
This should be understood according to the rule already stated. "Having looked" means having looked at both sides and having looked directly ahead;
this is what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Whatever he sees either on the side or directly in front.
(1558) "At a distance" refers specifically to a distance of twelve *hattha*s. The construction is: "There is no need for a report after searching here and there."
1559. "There is no fault" means there is no offense (*anāpatti*). Regarding "at the proper time," the phrase "without having asked permission" is to be understood as the remainder here.

And in this case, as well as in the subsequent instance, the phrase "there is no fault" applies respectively to each. "A bhikkhunī who is present" is the connection [of the sentence]. "By way of another's house" means by another person's house;
here, the phrase "and by way of the vicinity of the house" is to be understood as the remainder. Regarding "going to the monastery," it is implied that this is done "by that path."
Regarding the two phrases “by that path” and “of one going,” the word *tathā* (in that manner) applies to both “to the lodging of the sectarians” and “to the lodging of the nuns.
The meaning is: there is no offense for one who goes to a monastery of sectarians or to the lodging of nuns by way of that house or the vicinity of that house which is the path to be traveled.

The construction is: "He goes by way of an emergency" (*āpadāya gacchati*). An "emergency" (*āpadā*) refers to obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) or to one's livelihood. "Or to a dining hall" (*āsanasālaṃ vā*):

this means either a dining hall (*bhojanasālā*), like those in the island of Sri Lanka where seats are prepared by donors for the monks to eat; or it refers to a hall where seats (*āsana*) are provided.
Although one should have said "to an emergency-dining-hall" (*āpadā-āsanasālam*), the letter *ya* has been elided for the sake of metrical composition in the verse.
"Bhattiya’s house" refers either to a house where one is invited to eat or to the houses of those who provide tickets for meals.

Entering is the action (*kriyā*); not asking permission is the non-action (*akriyā*). Because it originates from a state that is both with and without intention (*acittaka*), it is described as "without intention.

It is stated to be "associated with three types of consciousness" with reference to the fact that it must be committed by one possessing any one of the wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate types of consciousness.
Commentary on the Discussion of Conduct (Cārittakathāvaṇṇanā). 1562.
Explaining the word “all,” he shows the three types of invitation (*pavāraṇā*): the four-month invitation, the repeated invitation, and the constant invitation.
And herein, [it is said]: “The four-month requisites-invitation may be accepted; the illness-requisites-invitation may be accepted.”
This is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). Furthermore, there is the invitation for medicine for exactly four months. Therefore, it was said in the *Aṭṭhuppatti*:
“In that case, Mahānāma, invite the Saṅgha again for another four months with medicine.
What is called the perpetual invitation (*niccapavāraṇā*) is the invitation for medicine for as long as one lives. And this too was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Aṭṭhuppatti*.
“Therefore, Mahānāma, invite the Saṅgha for medicinal requisites for as long as you live.
All these invitations are fourfold, according to whether they are limited by the medicine, limited by the night, limited by both, or unlimited. As it is said:
“Limited by medicine means that the medicines have been specified: ‘I invite [the Saṅgha] with this much medicine.’”
"Having a limit of nights" means that the nights have been delimited, [thinking]: "I shall perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) within these many nights.
"Having a limit of medicine and a limit of nights" means that both the medicines have been delimited and the nights have been delimited, [thinking]:
"I shall perform the invitation ceremony with these many medicines within these many nights. "Neither having a limit of medicine nor having a limit of nights" [means...].

“Medicines are unowned and the nights are unowned. When it was said, “It may be accepted,” he spoke the words beginning with “I shall request” in order to show the manner of acceptance. The construction is: “Even medicine, when there is a requisite for me, I shall request”;
this connects with the phrase “it may be accepted. That very point [is explained] by way of contrast:
To show this, he said, "It should not be refused. To show the reason for refusing, he said, "And 'I am now afflicted by disease.
That invitation (pavāraṇā) is threefold. 1564.

Regarding what was stated as the triad of offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya): "If it exceeds that [limit], perceiving it as exceeding that, being in doubt, or perceiving it as not exceeding that..."
“[If] one requests medicine, there is an offense of *pācittiya*”—thus is stated the triad of *pācittiya* offenses.
Here, the phrase "more than that" (*tatuttari*) means: more than or exceeding those medicines with which one has been invited [to partake], and those nights during which one has been invited.
As it is said: "At the limit of the medicines, those medicines with which one has been invited..."
The construction is as follows: "If, setting aside other medicines, he requests them, there is an offense of *pācittiya*";
and "If, setting aside those nights which constitute the limit of the night during which he has been invited, he requests them on other nights, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
In this regard, it is stated that for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
1565. "Beyond four months" means more than that; "not beyond that" (*natatuttari*) means there is no further [period] beyond that.
"One who perceives it as not beyond that" (*natatuttarisaññī*) means one who possesses the perception that it is not beyond that. The construction is: "for such a monk, there is no offense.
The phrase "there is no offense for one who asks for those medicines with which he was invited" should be connected with the remainder of the text. As it has been said:
“There is no offense if one asks for those very medicines with which one has been invited. Or rather, this should be construed together with the remainder:
“There is no offense for one who, having described exactly what [was offered], asks for more, whether it be by means of certain medicines, or on certain nights, or something else besides that.
Regarding the phrase “having described exactly what [was offered], asking for more”:
In this context, having spoken truthfully according to the statement:

"Having informed you, 'We have been invited by you with these medicines, and we have need of this and that medicine,' one makes a request; or, having informed you, 'On those nights that we were invited by you, those nights have passed, and we have need of medicine,' one makes a request."
The meaning is: "for one who requests more.
1566. The construction is: "there is no offense for a monk who requests on behalf of another monk.
Regarding the phrase "there is no offense for one requesting for relatives," the meaning here is: "there is no offense for one requesting what belongs to relatives."
The construction is: "There is no offense for one who requests [it] using his own wealth. Here, "wealth" refers to allowable items such as rice and so forth.

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the phrase "requesting" is referred back. Since the qualification "of those who are insane, etc. is required, the plural form "requesting" (*viññāpentānaṃ*) must be employed. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of medicine.
1568. "Uyyutta" means one who has made preparations for battle; that is, one who has gone out from a village, or one who is stationed at a certain place.
As it is said: "An army is called 'mobilized' when, having gone out from a village, it is either stationed or on the march.
"Except for a requisite" means setting aside such a requisite as that.

1569. Regarding the phrase "within the vicinity of sight" (*dassanassupacārasmiṃ*): here, the "vicinity of sight" (*dassanūpacāra*) refers to that place where, from which position one stands, the army is visible.
As it is said: "Wherever one stands and sees [it], there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
"Looking while having left the vicinity" means not looking while standing in the aforementioned place that constitutes the vicinity of sight.
It is said that by means of such reasons as "it is easy," one leaves that place and looks elsewhere.

Just as it is impossible to look at a low-lying place—even if it is concealed by something and thus invisible, or even if it has been entered and is known—so too should this analysis be understood. As it was said: "Or [an object] obstructed by something, or low-lying..."
“Or having entered, he is not seen,” and so forth. “By way of application” means by way of counting the applications for the aforementioned seeing.
1570. Now, in order to show the characteristics of a fourfold army, he said: “The riders, however, are four,” and so forth.
“Riders” (ārohā) here should be understood as elephant-riders. “Tappādarakkhakā” is a compound analyzed as *tassa pādarakkhakā* (his foot-protectors). “Two by two.”

"Protecting each foot by twos. The analysis (*viggaha*) of *dvādasaposā* is "one who has twelve men. A single elephant is said to be "yoked with twelve men. 1571. "Rider": here, it refers to a horse-rider. "Three men":
the analysis is "one who has three men. "Horse" (*hayo*) means a steed. "A single charioteer" (*eko sārathī*) means one who drives the chariot.
"A single warrior" (*yodho eko*) is the word-division. "Guarding the linchpin" (*āṇirakkhā*) refers to [the guards] of the two wheels of the chariot.
To prevent the axle from slipping, two pins driven into both ends [of the axle] serve as protectors.
1572. *Catuposā*: the analysis of the compound is "one who has four attendants. *Catusaccavibhāvinā*: by the Blessed One, the teacher of the Four Noble Truths.
*Padahatthā*: those with weapons in hand. It is so called because by means of it one proceeds, goes, or strikes others.
*Pada* (foot) and *āvudha* (weapon)—those whose hands have feet and weapons as their [components] are called *padahatthā*;

this is a bahubbīhi compound with different grammatical bases (*bhinna-adhikaraṇa*) for the external referents, just like the term "Vajirapāṇī" (the wielder of the thunderbolt). The word *pattipadā* is synonymous; it is a designation for an army of men.
1573. *Caturaṅgasamāyuttā*: the analysis is "joined with four limbs or components."
1574. *Hatthiādīsu* means: in the four components (*aṅga*) known as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, which possess the characteristics already described;
the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). *Ekekam* means each individual component.
Among these, taking at least one elephant mounted by a man, and likewise one horse, and one foot-soldier carrying a hand, he says "each one" for the purpose of showing them individually.
"...as they go. As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "At the very least, even a single elephant mounted by a single man," and so forth.
"Even when not mobilized" means when they have gone out for reasons other than war.
As it says: "Those who are 'mobilized' [are those] when the king goes to a park or to a river; thus he is mobilized."
1575. Here, the word "army" (*sena*) is understood from the context of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*). Regarding "in times of distress" (*āpadāsu*):

when there is an obstacle to life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), there is no offense for one who goes with the thought, "Having gone there, I shall be released. The construction is as follows: when such conditions exist—such as visiting the sick or other conditions conducive to going—there is no offense.
Commentary on the Discussion of Military Expeditions (Uyyuttakathāvaṇṇanā). 1576–7.

Because it has been authorized that "if there should arise for that bhikkhu some occasion for going to the army, he may stay with the army for two or three nights," [the rule applies] when [the army] has set out for the sake of battle due to some business.
Having stayed with the army in succession for two or three nights, he says “on the fourth,” etc., to show the offense incurred by a monk staying on the fourth night.
In the section on non-offenses, because it was stated that “one who is ill stays,” he says “one who is not ill.
Regarding the word “with the army” (*senāya*), here the army is defined either by the area capable of being enclosed or by the limits of its movement.
It should be delimited; the meaning is: "within such a delimited army.

Regarding the three *pācittiya* offenses: "If one stays in an army for more than three nights, perceiving it as more, or being in doubt, or perceiving it as less, there is an offense of *pācittiya*"—thus the triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of staying in an army.
1580. *Uyyodhikaṃ* is a place for battle. As it is said in the Commentary:
“Because they fight here, rising up again and again, it is called *uyyodhikaṃ*; this is a designation for a place of conflict.
*Balaggaṃ* is the place for counting the army according to the method found in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*), such as “there are so many elephants,” and so forth. As it is said: “Of the army...”
“Balagga” means they know the highest point (*agga*) therein; the meaning is “the place for counting forces. Regarding “arraying the army” (*senābyūha*):
it is the location for the deployment of troops as stated in the word-commentary—“let there be elephants here, horses there, chariots there, and infantry there”—this is called “arraying the army.
As it is said: “The arraying of the army is ‘senābyūha’; this is a designation for the stationing of troops.”

1581. *Purima* refers to the immediately preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The construction is: “The elephant consists of twelve men”—this is the elephant that was mentioned. *Tenā* means by that elephant acting as the cause. 1582.
By the word *sesesu* (“in the remaining [units]”), the cavalry units, chariot units, and infantry units are included.

Regarding the infantry unit (*pattānīka*), it is defined without distinction among the military divisions (*senanga*) in the explanatory list: “Four men with hands raised are a foot soldier; four such foot soldiers constitute the rear infantry unit.”
Thus it was said. "Of these" refers to those [monks] who are engaged in such activities as military exercises.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of military exercises.
The fifth chapter, the Section on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-vagga), is finished.
1583. Regarding the phrase "with flour and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) here includes cakes and the like. As it is said:
"Liquor (surā) means flour-liquor, cake-liquor, rice-liquor, that into which grain has been put, or that which is prepared from various ingredients.

And herein, flour-liquor is that made by putting flour into a vessel, adding the appropriate water, and then fermenting it. Likewise for cake-liquor and rice-liquor, having put the cake or the rice into a vessel...

That which is made by adding water produced from that [grain], kneading it, and fermenting it is called "cake-liquor" (*pūvasurā*) or "rice-liquor" (*odanasurā*). Furthermore, the term "*kiṇṇa*" refers to the seeds of that liquor;
those made by adding what are also called "fermented seed-grains" (*surāmodaka*) are called "those into which seeds have been added" (*kiṇṇapakkhittā*).
That which is mixed with various ingredients such as *harītaki*, *sāsa*, and so forth, is called "combined with ingredients" (*sambhārasaṃyuttā*).
Regarding the phrase "with flowers, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes fruits and so forth. As it is said:
"Liquors (*meraya*) are flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, honey-liquor, molasses-liquor, and those compounded with various ingredients.

Among these, "flower-liquor" refers to the juice of *madhuka* flowers and the like, as well as the juice of palm and coconut flowers, which has been aged for a long time. "Fruit-liquor," however, consists of grapes, jackfruit, and other such fruits.
Having crushed [the fruits], it is made from their juice. That which is called *madhvāsava* is made from the natural juice of *muddika* (grape) fruits;

they say it can also be made with honey-bee honey. *Ucchurasa* is molasses-liquor (*guḷāsava*). *Āsava* is liquor (*meraya*) produced by the juice of various ingredients such as *harītaka*, *āmalaka*, *kaṭuka*, and *bhaṇḍa*, which has been fermented for a long time and mixed with those ingredients. This is how the construction of the sentence should be understood.
“Starting from the seed” means starting from the time the ingredients have been prepared and placed in the vat;

for palm and coconut [liquors], it means starting precisely from the time the fresh juice has dripped from the flower. Regarding the phrase “for one drinking,” the words “with the tip of a blade of kusa grass” are also to be understood as an ellipsis here.
“Both of them” refers to both *sura* and *meraya*. Furthermore, starting from the seed with the tip of a blade of kusa grass...
It should be construed as: "Even for a monk who is drinking, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
To show the abundance of offenses due to the abundance of applications (payoga), he said: "In each and every application. This should also be construed as:
"For a monk who drinks by repeatedly pausing, there is an offense of expiation in each and every application. As it was said: "Having paused..."
“For one who drinks after having interrupted [the flow], there are offenses according to the number of applications.

This explains, by contrast, that even for one drinking a great deal with a single application, there is only one offense. As it says: “But for one who drinks a great deal with a single application, there is one offense.

1585. Regarding what was stated as the threefold *pācittiya*: “If one drinks alcohol perceiving it as alcohol, if one drinks alcohol while in doubt, or if one drinks alcohol perceiving it as non-alcohol, there is an offense of *pācittiya*”; thus the threefold *pācittiya* was stated.

1586. Because it is stated, “There is no offense if it is not liquor, yet has the color of liquor, the smell of liquor, and the taste of liquor, and one drinks it,” he said, “not liquor, yet having the color of liquor,” and so forth.
*Ariṭṭha* is a specific kind of fermented liquor (*āsava*) made from the juice of the *āmalaka* fruit and other ingredients.
Regarding *loṇasovīraka*, it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): [text follows]
“Having added the decoctions of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *vibhītaka*; all kinds of grain; all kinds of vegetables;
rice from even the seven types of grain; all fruits such as plantains; all types of shoots such as those of *vetta*, *ketaka*, date palms, and *kaḷīra*;
pieces of fish and meat; and many medicinal substances such as honey, molasses, rock salt, sea salt, *tikaṭuka*, and so forth—”
Having smeared the opening of a jar, they leave it for one, two, or three years; when it has fully matured, it becomes the color of rose-apple juice.

For those suffering from wind-disorders, skin diseases, leucoderma, hemorrhoids, and the like, as well as for those who have eaten oily food, there is no superior drink or medicine for digesting a meal like this. Moreover, this may be taken by monks even after the meal.

"It is permissible for those who are ill [to use it] in its natural state; however, for those who are not ill, it is permissible by way of consuming it as a drink when mixed with water."—Thus the specific medicinal quality is explained.
"Sutta" (brew) refers to a particular fermented liquor (*āsava*) prepared from various medicinal ingredients that is devoid of intoxicating strength (*majja*).
"For the purpose of making it take on a fragrance" means for the purpose of making it acquire a sweet scent. "Slightly" [refers to] the color, aroma, and taste of intoxicants.
"It is 'insignificant' (appamattaka) insofar as it does not appear [as such]. As it was said: 'There is no offense as long as the liquor has not yet been poured out.
But when the liquor has been poured out—wherever the color, smell, and taste of the liquor are perceived—in that case there is indeed an offense.
Regarding the phrase 'in the cooking of rice-gruel, etc. (sūpādīnaṃ),' the word 'etc. includes the cooking of meat and so forth. As it was said:"
“In a meat broth, in a fish broth, in an oil broth. (1588) The connection is:
“lack of awareness regarding the substance is ‘without intention. As it is said: “And here, the state of being without intention is to be understood as the lack of awareness regarding the substance.
And what is called “lack of awareness regarding the substance” is the state of not knowing that it is “liquor. “This” refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

By the word "ca" (and), he includes other training rules such as those concerning the village festival on the mountain-top (*giraggasamajja*). "By unwholesome [mind] alone" means by an unwholesome consciousness alone.

"From drinking" means from that which is to be drunk. "World-reprehensible" (*lokavajjaka*) means that which is to be avoided (*vajjetabba*) by the world of the virtuous; it is "world-reprehensible" because it is reprehensible to the world.

Now, in this case, since there is a state of mindlessness due to the lack of knowledge regarding the object, would that lack of knowledge regarding the object not also apply to one who possesses a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness?
Since it is possible [for intoxicants to be drunk unintentionally], why is it said that "it is unwholesome alone that constitutes a worldly offense by drinking"? It is replied:

because for one who drinks with the perception that it is not liquor, or even for one who drinks with the perception that it is liquor, the liquor serves as a condition for the arising of defilements according to the nature of the object;
just as liquor, even when drunk by one who does not know it is being drunk, is a condition only for unwholesome states and not for wholesome ones, so too [is this case].

It is said, "It is a world-transgression by drinking only through unwholesome [intention]," because even at the time of swallowing, it serves as a condition for unwholesomeness alone according to the nature of the object.
This is just as in the *Niḷinijātaka*, where a boy, with the perception that it was medicine, inserted his organ into a woman's path on the road;
or as when one has the perception, "This is a woman," or "I am engaging in sexual intercourse in her path."
Even in the absence of the arising of sensual lust, there was a loss of qualities such as virtue due to the restriction of the object;

it should be understood in this way here as well. However, some, thinking that the phrase "by taking life with an unwholesome mind" refers specifically to the intentional aspect of this training rule—otherwise there would be an over-extension even to cases like killing—and thus [asserting] many reasons and restrictions, [argue as follows].
They showed [this]. However, because in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, and others,
it is stated as "unwholesome consciousness" (*akusalacitta*) rather than "threefold consciousness" (*ticitta*),

and because it would be inappropriate to demonstrate a characteristic of an alternative position while demonstrating the general characteristic of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), one must follow the literal sense of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
And since no contradiction arises regarding the grasping of the meaning, this refers exclusively to the position that [the person] possesses consciousness;

thus, it cannot be said here that there is a "worldly offense" (lokavajjā) for the state of unwholesome consciousness. As for what was stated: "For a bhikkhu who drinks liquor, whether he knows the substance or not, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). But for a sāmaṇera, there is a breach of virtue only if he drinks knowing [it is liquor], not if he drinks unknowingly."

In that regard, the reason must be sought. Since the formulation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is the exclusive domain of the Buddhas, that reason need not be sought; one should simply act in accordance with what has been prescribed.
Furthermore, this training rule pertains to unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*) and, by way of pleasant and neutral feelings (*sukha-upekkhā-vedanā*), involves two types of feeling.
However, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that "it involves three types of feeling" (*tivedana*).

The reading is seen in the *Khuddakapāṭha-vaṇṇanā*, the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, and other works, where it is stated that "it has two feelings by way of pleasant and neutral feeling" and "it has two roots by way of greed and delusion"; therefore, that [reading] should be understood as a "reading of negligence.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of drinking fermented liquor.
1589. "By any limb whatsoever" means by any part of the body, such as a finger and so forth.
"With the intention of laughing" (*hasādhippāyino*): the analysis of the compound is "the intention for laughter is *hasādhippāyo*; he who possesses that is [so called].

By this, the absence of offense for one devoid of the intention to play is indicated through contrast. And it will be said: "There is no offense for one who does not have the intention of laughing. "Of one touching" means of one who is in the act of touching.
1590. "In all cases" means among all those who are ordained and those who are not ordained. "In the method beginning with 'connected to the body'" refers to the method shown by such passages as:
"If one touches what is connected to the body with the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
It is said that three offenses of wrong-doing are stated with respect to one who perceives a non-ordained person as ordained, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives them as non-ordained.

“Likewise, in the case of one who is not fully ordained, a triad of dukkaṭas is indicated. Here, by the phrase “likewise,” it is indicated that a triad of pācittiyas has been stated with respect to one who is fully ordained when one perceives them as such, when one is doubtful, and when one perceives them as not fully ordained.
The construction is: just as a triad of pācittiyas is indicated in the case of one who is fully ordained, so too a triad of dukkaṭas is indicated in the case of one who is not fully ordained.
1591. Herein... "a nun": here, it should be understood that even a monk, when standing in the position of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) relative to a nun, is included.

1592. "Touches with a motive of laughter": this refers to one who touches another with a limb of the body, such as a foot, for purposes such as salutation, and so forth, without a motive of laughter. "When there is a purpose": when there is a purpose such as massaging the back, and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the poking with a finger.
1593. Regarding the word *jaleti* (in water): here, the phrase “above the ankles” (*uparigopphake*) is to be supplied as the remainder, as it is said:
“in water above the ankles. Regarding the phrase “immersion and so forth” (*nimujjanādīnaṃ*): here, by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), emerging and swimming are included, as it is said:

“with the intention of playing, one immerses oneself, or emerges, or swims in water above the ankles. By the word “only” (*kevalaṃ*), it is indicated that there is no offense for one who enters [the water] for the purpose of bathing and such duties.

1594. "In water reaching above the ankles" means in water at the height of the upper part of the ankles. "He might even submerge" means he might enter into the water and sink; "or he might cross" means he might swim across. 1595–6. The construction is:
for one who, having submerged himself right within the water, moves about by means of the application of his hands and feet, it is declared to be a *pācittiya*.

1597. To include all the limbs of the body, such as the hands and so forth, he uses the indefinite repetition "by whichever [limb]. The construction is: for a monk crossing the water, by whichever limb the crossing takes place.

1598. "From a tree or from a well" means: regarding the threefold *pācittiya*, it is a threefold *pācittiya* by way of one who perceives [the water] as having the nature of play (*hasadhamma*) when it does have that nature, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as not having the nature of play.
The reading "threefold *dukkaṭa*" is seen; after stating, "If one perceives water that does not have the nature of play as having the nature of play, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*;
if one is doubtful regarding water that does not have the nature of play, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*," it says, "In water..."
In the third alternative, the text states, "If it is not a non-Dhamma and he perceives it as not a non-Dhamma, there is no offense";
thus, that reading is a careless error, and the reading "two dukkaṭas" alone should be accepted. 1599.
The connection is "even while hauling a boat onto the bank. "Hauling" means causing it to ascend the bank. The word "playing" should also be construed with this term "driving."
1600. *Kathalāya* means in a small potsherd. Regarding "water," the word "contained in a vessel" (*bhājanagataṃ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase].
For it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "or water contained in a vessel. 1601. *Kañcikaṃ vā* means or grain-juice.

The word *api* includes those items mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), namely: "or milk, or buttermilk, or dye, or urine. *Cikkhallaṃ vāpi* means or mud-water. Here, by the indicator of the distinction...

By the word "api" (also), one should understand the specific legal determination found in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Furthermore, setting aside the aforementioned acts such as emerging from the water while standing above the ankles,
if one plays by throwing water— even if one has entered the water in some other manner,
or even if one has not entered it at all— whether standing anywhere or taking up even a single drop, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who plays."
He collects [the items]. Having scattered them, they scatter them. 1602. The construction is:
"There is no offense for one who, when there is a task to be done, plunges into the water and performs such acts as submerging. A "task" refers to bathing and so forth. 1603.

"Of the immediately preceding" means of the training rule concerning the poking with a finger. "Distinction" (visesa) means the state of being distinct; the meaning is that there is no distinction whatsoever.
Commentary on the Discourse on Envy (Hasadhammakathāvaṇṇanā). 1604–5.

The construction is as follows: "If a bhikkhu, when being addressed by another bhikkhu regarding what has been prescribed, does not show respect because he is unwilling to act upon those words, then for that lack of respect, one should pronounce the *pācittiya* offense. By this statement, [the meaning is established].
An offense of expiation (pācittiya) rooted in disrespect toward persons has been stated. As it is said: “Disrespect means two kinds of disrespect:

disrespect toward persons and disrespect toward the Dhamma. Regarding “disrespect toward persons”: when one who is fully ordained is being addressed by someone established [in the discipline], thinking, “This person is suspended, or reviled, or censured;
his word shall not be heeded,” [one acts accordingly].
"He commits an act of disrespect; there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

Furthermore, if a monk—who does not wish to train in the Dhamma itself—does not show respect when being addressed by another monk regarding what has been prescribed, then for that act of disrespect, one should pronounce an offense of expiation against him.
The *yojanā* (explanation): By this, the *pācittiya* offense rooted in disrespect for the Dhamma is stated. As it is said: "Disrespect for the Dhamma means:
when one who is fully ordained is being spoken to regarding what has been prescribed, [if] he would lose, destroy, or cause the disappearance of that discourse;
desiring not to attend to it, he acts with disrespect—there is an offense of *pācittiya*. In the word *anādariye*, the locative case is used in the sense of a causal sign (*nimitta*).

1606. It is said that there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: "If one treats [a person] with disrespect when they are fully ordained (*upasampanna*), perceiving them as fully ordained, being in doubt, or perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

Thus the triad of *pācittiya* is stated. "By one who has transcended the triad" means by one who has transcended the three worldly states. Regarding the triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses for treating those not fully ordained with disrespect:
[this applies to] one who perceives a person not fully ordained as fully ordained, one who is in doubt, and one who perceives them as not fully ordained.
According to this, there is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the Sutta and the Abhidhamma" (*sutteneva abhidhammena*), the particle *eva* (only/just) should be construed with the word "*dukkaṭaṃ*".

By the two terms "Sutta" and "Abhidhamma," through the metaphorical application of identity (*abhedopacāra*), the Dhamma of the formal teachings (*pariyattidhamma*) contained within the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas is expressed.
"By what is not laid down" (apaññattena) means by that which is other than the Vinaya known as "laid down" (paññatta).

This term "by what is not laid down" is a qualification of the two terms "by the Sutta" and "by the Abhidhamma. For a monk who shows disrespect toward what has been spoken by another monk, or toward the Dhamma, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) alone.
For a novice (sāmaṇera), there is an offense by both—whether it be what is laid down or what is not laid down.

The construction is as follows: for a bhikkhu who shows disrespect toward that which has been spoken, whether toward that novice (sāmaṇera) or toward the Dhamma—whether it has been formally prescribed or not—there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
1608. “Fault” (dosa) refers to some fault consisting of either an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) or an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
1609. *Ettha* means "in this" [context] of the teachers' manual (*ācariyuggaha*). The construction is: "The teachers' manual is to be censured;

it should not be accepted at all. Regarding the phrase "the teachers' manual is to be censured": here, because sugarcane juice is for seven days, its dregs are for life, and the stalk of sugarcane is merely the combination of these two, therefore it is permissible to eat the sugarcane stalk at an improper time, as is the case with sugar and myrobalan fruits.
"Thus it should be known"—this and similar statements constitute the venerable teaching of the teachers (ācariyavāda) recently formulated. But which one should be accepted?
Only the acceptance of the teachers that has come down through the lineage (paveṇi) should be accepted.

However, in the *Kurundi*, it is said: "In the case of a world-transgression (lokavajja), the acceptance of the teachers is not permitted; but in the case of a formal transgression (paṇṇattivajja), it is permitted."
It has been stated. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is said: “For those who have mastered the Suttas and what is in conformity with the Suttas, the learning of their teachers alone is authoritative;
the discourse of those who do not know is not authoritative. It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “All that accords with what has come down through the tradition (*paveṇī*) reaches agreement.
In this regard, regarding the offenses of worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), the learning of a teacher is not permitted within the training rules on worldly transgressions.

The teacher’s opinion regarding a point of offense (āpattiṭṭhāna) should not be accepted; the intention is that for one who says, "This is our teacher’s tradition," having transgressed what is forbidden by the world, such a tradition is not permissible.
The *Aṭṭhakathā* is called "in conformity with the Suttas" (*suttānuloma*).

Because it accords with the convergence [of the teachings] as they have come down through the lineage (*paveṇi*), it is said: "Only that which has come down through the lineage as the teacher’s tradition should be accepted."
When this was said, the intention is that it is included within the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā-vāda itself.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding disrespect. 1610–1.
Regarding the rule: "Whatever monk should frighten another monk, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," because of this word in the *mātikā*, [the act is] for the purpose of producing fear.
Here, the words “of a bhikkhu” are to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. For this very reason, he will later say: “but for the other bhikkhu. “Forms, etc.
means forms, sounds, odors, and so forth. “Presents” means establishes; that is to say, he shows it.
“Terrifying talk” refers to talk concerning robbers, wildernesses, and the like. As it is said: “He describes a wilderness of robbers, or a wilderness of wild beasts, or a wilderness of demons.”
Regarding the phrase "near another": here, by the method already stated, "another" should be understood as one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
"Having seen" means having seen that form or other object presented [to him]. "Or having heard" means having heard that terrifying account.
Whether the person for whose sake it was presented sees the danger or not, let him fear or not; as for the other...
Of the monk who attends to him. "At that moment" means at the moment he has been attended to. 1612. Regarding the threefold *pācittiya*:

it is stated, "If one frightens one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), perceiving them as fully ordained, being in doubt, or perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of *pācittiya*";
thus the threefold *pācittiya* is stated. Regarding the threefold *dukkaṭa*: [it applies] when [the person] is not fully ordained.

There is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses based on the cases of one who perceives [the person] as fully ordained (*upasampanna*), one who is doubtful, and one who perceives [the person] as not fully ordained.

In the section on *dukkaṭa* beginning with “desiring to frighten one who is not fully ordained,” since the mention of “one who is not fully ordained” includes householders as well, he says, “a novice or a householder.
The construction is: for one who likewise frightens a novice... or a monk, a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses is stated.
Commentary on the Story of the Terrifying One (Bhiṃsāpanakathāvaṇṇanā). 1614. "Joti" means fire. "Desirous of warming oneself" means desirous of making warm.
Regarding the occasion when it was said, "At that time, monks were apprehensive even regarding lamps, torches, and steam-baths," [the Buddha said]: "I allow you, monks..."

Because it is stated, "to kindle or cause to be kindled a fire by means of such-and-such conditions," here the phrase "such-and-such conditions" should be understood as including the lighting of a lamp,
the work of cooking in a vessel or bathing the body, and the maintenance of a sauna. And in this context,
"even in the case of a lamp" means making it serve as a light for the tasks of cooking in a vessel, bathing, and so forth.
1615. *Sayaṃsamādahantassa*: "of one kindling by oneself," that is, of one maintaining [the fire] personally.
1616. *Jālāpentassa* ... *dukkaṭaṃ*: this refers to the *dukkaṭa* offense to be incurred through an order.

Regarding the offense to be incurred when [the fire] has been ignited by an order, it is because the following [verse] continues: "But for the act of igniting, the offense is declared to be a *pācittiya*."
It is not stated separately that [the offense] is established.
1617. "Of one who is ill" refers to the one described as "ill" in the sense that he finds no comfort without fire.
"Of one throwing up an unextinguished ember" refers to an ember that has fallen from being held and is not yet extinguished, [thrown] near a fire.
"Of one who is warming [it]," meaning "of one who is placing it in its proper position.
1618–9. "An extinguished firebrand" means a firebrand whose flames have been quenched. "An offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the basis [of the object]" is what is stated.
The construction is: "There is no offense for one warming [it] that has been prepared by another. "Warming" means heating. "Embers" means...
"A charcoal without a flame. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the lighting of a lamp, etc.," it includes what is mentioned in the passage: "in a fire-pit or a sauna, by such a requisite.
And here, "by such a requisite" means by any other such requisite besides a lamp and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the kindling of a fire.

1620–1. He teaches that it is in the Middle Country of Jambudīpa, where the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍala) is located—within that central region measuring nine hundred yojanas in circumference—that this training rule (sikkhāpada) is restricted by being designated as specific to that very place.
For this reason, he will later say in the section on non-offenses: "or even in a border region. *Cuṇṇa* refers to things such as *sirīsa* powder.
*Cuṇṇaṃ*: "Of one who prepares" means of one who makes ready.

1622–3. The word-division is: *māse ūnasaññino*. The construction is: for one who perceives [the time] as less than a month, or for one who is in doubt regarding more than half a month, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The construction is: there is no offense for one bathing when more than half a month has passed. Regarding the [permitted] occasions (*samaya*):
Regarding the phrase "there is no offense for one bathing," the meaning is that when any one of the six occasions specified—
“the time of heat,” “the time of feverish distress,” “the time of illness,” “the time of work,” “the time of traveling on a journey,” or “the time of wind and rain”— is present,
there is no offense even for one who bathes in less than a month, provided they have established mindfulness.
In this context, the month of Jeṭṭha and the first fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha—these one and a half months are called the "hot season.

As it is said: "The hot season is defined as the remaining one and a half months of the summer. The first month of the rains is called the "feverish season. As it is said: "The feverish season is defined as the first month of the rains. "Of whom..."
When it is said, “Without bathing, we are not at ease,” this is called the occasion of illness (*gilānasamaya*).
When it is said, “At the very least, even the surrounding courtyard has been swept,” this is called the occasion of work (*kammasamaya*).

When it is said, “One may bathe thinking, ‘I will go half a *yojana*’,” this is called the occasion of traveling on a journey (*addhānagamanasamaya*). When monks are covered by a dusty wind, or two or three...
When it is said, "or drops of water have fallen upon the body," this refers to the occasion of wind and rain.

The construction is: "Even for one going to the other side of a river, there is no offense for bathing for less than half a month. Regarding the phrase "having scattered sand," this means having scattered sand in a dry riverbed. Even for one bathing for less than half a month in places where embankments have been constructed, [there is no offense].
"An offense does not occur" means: by the word "likewise," this refers back to the statement, "there is no offense for one who is bathing.
1624. Or, "even in border regions" refers to those outside the aforementioned Middle Country, namely in the frontier provinces and in small islands.
"Of all" refers to both those who have received the training rules and those who have not.
"For all bhikkhus. "In emergencies" means in emergencies such as being pursued by bees and so forth. As it is said:
"For one who is being pursued by bees and the like, it is permissible to submerge oneself in water. That which originates from both body and mind is called "originating from wool.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of bathing.

1625–7. From the canonical statement, “‘New’ (nava) is said to mean ‘not yet made allowable’ (akatakappa),” and from the commentary’s statement, “the meaning is ‘a new robe that has been obtained,’” the word “robe” (cīvara) is to be understood here as having “new” (nava) as its remainder. The connection is as follows:
if a monk uses a new robe without having had the allowable mark (kappabindu) applied to it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for him so using it. “Covered” (channaṃ).
The genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used for selection (*niddhāraṇa*) from among the *khoma* and other [fabrics]. One of the nine new robes is that which is to be selected.
"In any place whatsoever" means in any of the robe’s corners—whether in four, three, two, or even one corner—according to the statement in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
