"Kaṃsanīla" means the blue of a tanner. "Tanner-blue" refers to natural blue. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"Tanners make leather black by throwing the three fruits (*tiphala*) and iron dross into water;
that is 'tanner-blue'. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it is stated: "Iron rust and copper rust—this is called 'kaṃsanīla'."
“By green leaves” means by green leafy material, as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Whatever is green in color and consists of leaves.
“By anything black” means by any black-colored substance whatsoever, such as charcoal, soot, and so forth.
Because it is said, “Mud is called that which is mixed with water,” the term “mud” includes dry mud and the like that is carried along by water.
The construction is according to the respective order: “the size of the back of a *maṅgula* [crab], the size of the eye of a peacock.
(1628) The construction is “shaped like a *pāḷi* and shaped like a *kaṇṇika*”;

the meaning is that it is fashioned in the form of a string of pearls (*pāḷi*) and fashioned in the form of a *kaṇṇika*. Regarding the word “in some places,” the remainder is “in the aforementioned location.”
Because it is stated, “either at four corners or at three,” he said “or more than one. “A circle” (*vaṭṭa*) is indeed a circular shape (*vaṭṭaka*);

by this, he shows that no other modification is permitted. As it has been said: “Except for a single circular dot, the boundary-mark (*kappa*) must not be made with any other modification whatsoever.”

1629. “*Anāpatti pakāsitā*” (no offense is declared) refers to the third alternative, “*ādinne ādinnasaññino*” (perceiving it as taken when it has been taken), which is conjoined here by the word *ca* (“and”) in the phrase “*vimatissacā*. As it is said: “*Ādinne ādinnasaññī, anāpattī*” (if one perceives it as taken when it has been taken, there is no offense). 1630.

This should also be construed with the phrases beginning with “*kappe naṭṭhepi vā*” (or even when the [boundary] marker is lost). By the word *pi* (“also”), this phrase “*kappakatokāse jiṇṇe*” (when the marked-off place has become worn out) is included.
As it is said: “*kappakatokāso jiṇṇo hotī*” (the marked-off place has become worn out). Therefore, the term *kappakatenā* is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*).

This is a statement regarding the instrument (the means). Regarding the phrase "in those that are sewn together," the words "not made allowable" (*akappakate*) are to be understood as the remainder. As it has been said: "That which is not made allowable becomes sewn together with that which is made allowable.

Making [the robe] into an undergarment or an upper garment is the action (*kriya*); the non-taking of the formal mark of allowance (*kappabindu*) is the non-action (*akriya*). This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning the making of the discolored color (*dubbaṇṇakaraṇa*).

1631–4. Because it is stated, “What is called ‘assignment’ (vikappanā) consists of two kinds of assignment: assignment in the presence (sammukhā-vikappanā) and assignment in the absence (parammukhā-vikappanā),” he says, “There are two kinds of assignment,” and so forth.
“Iti” is used as an indicator; its meaning is “thus. To the question, “How does assignment in the presence come about?
he says, “In the presence... [etc. ...one should point out. Regarding the word “of one,” the word “of one who is competent” (byattassa) is to be supplied as the remainder. Here, “competent” means—
One who knows the procedure for designating, assigning, and relinquishing [robes].
Regarding "according to the connection of the words," this means not overstepping what is stated in the Commentary:
"‘This robe,’ or ‘these robes,’ or ‘that robe,’ or ‘those robes’"—[this refers to] following the sequence of the grammatical connection of the words.
This is the meaning. He shows a partial similarity [to the previous rule] by saying, "this robe.
By the phrase "because it has not been relinquished," he shows the reason for the statement "it is not allowable.
"The property" and so forth refers to the manner of relinquishment. "Act according to your requirements" means: do as you please.
1636. To show another instance of assigning [a gift] in the presence [of the recipient], he said: “Another is stated in the presence,” and so forth. The construction is:

“having taken the name of anyone whatsoever who is pleasing to oneself. Regarding the term *sahadhammīnaṃ*, the word “of the five” (*pañcannaṃ*) is to be supplied as the remainder; it is a genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
1639. The word *evaṃ* refers to what is about to be stated. The particle *api*, however, has the sense of the word *saha*.

1640. Regarding the phrase *mitto ti daḷhamitto*: because of the statement, “He should be asked, ‘Who is your friend or acquaintance?’”, this is an indicative mark (*upalakkhaṇa*). The construction is: “Furthermore, that monk also should be asked. 1641–2.

The reading beginning with *idaṃ* (this) and so forth should be connected with the remaining text from the Aṭṭhakathā: “‘I give it to the bhikkhu Tissa’... or ‘I give it to the novice nun Tissā. 1643. In the word *dvīsu* (in two), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
Here, the term *vikappanāsu* (in the cases of assignment) is understood from the context.

1644–5. Herein, however, in this teaching, if a monk should use that robe without the trust—that is, without the state of confidence—of the monk with whom the legal act (*vinayakamma*) was performed by the owner of the robe, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for that monk;
such is the construction. The term "legal act" (*vinayakamma*) is used for the purpose of preserving the consent [of the Sangha].

The addition of the prefix *anu-* should be understood; the meaning is "a formal act of the Vinaya. The construction is: for one who either determines (*adhiṭṭhahantassa*) or relinquishes (*vissajjantassa*) that robe, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

1646. Regarding "in the case of garments that have been relinquished": this refers to garments that have been formally given up (*paccuddhaṭavatthesu*). "One who perceives them as not relinquished" means one who has the perception that they have not been relinquished (*apaccuddhaṭasaññino*).

*Therein*: regarding items that have not been formally relinquished (*apaccuddhaṭavatthesu*). *Of one who is in doubt*: of one who has fallen into uncertainty, thinking, "Have these been relinquished by me, or have they not been relinquished?
*Of one with the perception of relinquishment*: of one who perceives, "This has been relinquished. *By way of trust*:
either from the person to whom one assigned the robe, even though it has not been relinquished by him, or from the trust of one who uses it; as it is said: "Or of him..."
“...he uses it while placing his trust [in others].
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the *vikappana* (assignment). 1648–9.
Regarding the statement, “A bowl (*patta*) means two kinds of bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl,” this is said because allowable bowls (*kappiya-patta*) are defined by their material.
He said: “A bowl that is subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*). “Such” means subject to formal determination. A needle-case is one that either has a needle or does not have a needle.
A waist-band is a strip of cloth or a pig-girth. A sitting mat is said to be one with a border.
With the accusative endings in “the bowl,” etc., the phrase “having removed [it] and storing it” should be construed with each [item] individually.

“Of one who is putting away” (*nidhentassa*) is a qualification for this term “of one who expects laughter” (*hasāpekkhassa*). As it is said: “‘Even one expecting laughter’ means one whose intention is for sport.
By the word “merely” (*kevalaṃ*), he indicates the absence of any other intention—such as the intention to put it back in place—for that which has been wrongly set down.
And he will say: “There is no offense for that which was wrongly set down, provided one puts it back in place.”

"By him too" means by the one who has been commanded. "Of him" refers to the commander. "A triad of dukkaṭa offenses is stated" means that a triad of dukkaṭa offenses is stated with respect to one who perceives as ordained, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives as not ordained when [the person addressed] is actually unordained.
And by this, it follows that there is a triad of pācittiya offenses regarding what belongs to one who is ordained; thus, this too is already stated.
1651. "Other" refers to requisites such as alms-bowls, bags for robes, and so forth, which are not mentioned in the canonical text (pāḷi).
1652. "In all" means in all requisites, both those mentioned in the canonical text and those not mentioned.
1653. "Having given a discourse on the Dhamma" means: "It is not fitting for one who calls himself a recluse to possess unrestrained requisites."
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma according to the method found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "With requisites not deposited" means with requisites that have not been returned.
The construction is: "If he deposits them, there is likewise no offense. "One who does not intend to harm" means one devoid of the intention to cause injury.

"One who is not playing" means one devoid of the intention to play, merely depositing [the items] under the pretext of formal conduct (*vattasīsa*) with the thought, "I will give them back after having returned them."

1654. Because offenses originating from taking what is not given (adinnādāna-samuṭṭhānāpatti) are also "with consciousness" (sacittaka) by way of being unwholesome (akusala) and so forth, it says: "This is with consciousness only through the unwholesome.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion on the Misplacement of Robes (cīvara-apanidhāna-kathā).
The sixth chapter, the Section on Drinking Liquor (surāpāna-vagga), is finished.

1655. By the phrase "an animal" (*tiracchānagataṃ pāṇaṃ*), he indicates the "living being" intended in this training rule: "Whatever monk should intentionally deprive a living being of life, it is an offense entailing expiation" (*pācittiya*).
He says "whether large or small" because there is no difference in the nature of the offense. As it has been said: "And in this training rule, only an animal is meant by the term 'living being'."
It should be understood that for one who kills, whether the victim is small or large, there is no difference in the nature of the offense;
however, in the case of a large being, because the effort is greater, the unwholesome karma is greater. The word-division is: *mārentassa assa*.
By the phrase "or for one killing even a small [being]," the commentary [refers to] "even while cleaning a bed or a chair..."
If one perceives it as a living being even when it is a seed with a rotten core, and removes it by breaking it out of cruelty, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Therefore, the determination stated—"in such cases, one should establish compassion and perform the proper conduct with diligence"—is also included here.

Regarding "in both cases": this refers to both when it is a living being and when it is not a living being. Furthermore, the remaining determination in this matter should be understood according to the method already explained in the section on the human form.
Commentary on the Discussion of Intentional Killing (Sañcicca-pāṇa-kathā-vaṇṇanā).
1658. *Sappāṇakan* means "containing living beings" (*saha pāṇakehi*). Here, those that die through being consumed are intended by the term "living beings. *Assa* refers to the bhikkhu. 1659.

By the word "without interruption" (*avicchijja*), it is indicated that there is a difference in the application [of the act] precisely because of the interruption. In the phrase "even a bowl-full," the particle *pi* is used in the sense of exclusion (*byatireke*).
The connection is: "For him, a *pācittiya* offense is explained. "By such [a thing]" means by that which contains living beings (*sappāṇaka*).
"Having stirred" means having caused it to whirl around. Regarding the word "gruel" (*yāgu*), the term "hot" (*uṇha*) is understood here by implication.

And this is an illustration for any hot substance whatsoever that one might not extinguish with water containing living beings for the purpose of killing those beings. That [substance] which contains living beings—
“Water. Regarding the phrase “even when bathing,” the word “even” (*pi*) here includes, according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“Even for one who, having entered a water-pool or a lotus pond, stirs up a wave for the purpose of exiting;
or by those cleaning a pool or a lotus pond, the water taken from it must be poured back into the very same water. In its vicinity...”
"If there is no water, one should pour eight or ten pots of *kappiya*-water onto a spot prepared for water in its shape, and then pour [the water] there.
One must not pour water onto a hot stone thinking, 'It will roll off and fall into the water.
However, it is permissible to pour [water] after extinguishing the heat of the stone with *kappiya*-water."
It summarizes the *Vuttavinicchaya*.
1662. Regarding "in both cases": this means in both instances—namely, whether there are living beings (*sappāṇaka*) or no living beings (*appāṇaka*). 1664–6.
To show the reason for its being connected with living beings, he says "falling," and so forth. "Of moths, etc. refers to grasshoppers and the like.

In the phrase *ñatvā* (“having known”), the particle *pi* is indicated as being elided; this is also the case in the following instances. In the phrase *padīpujjalanaṃ* (“the lighting of a lamp”), the word *viya* (“like”) is to be understood as the remainder.

*Ettha* means “in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*)”. *Sappāṇabhāvatā* is the state of containing living beings; that [state]. *Bhuñjato* means “because it is to be eaten”. The construction is as follows:

even though one knows the falling of moths and so forth, just as there is the lighting of a lamp with a pure mind, even though one knows the presence of living beings, because it is to be eaten with the perception that it is water, the nature of an offense against the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*) is to be understood here.
This being the case, one might ask: "What is the distinction between both the training rule on pouring water and the training rule on water containing living beings?

To this he says, "In the case of pouring," and so forth. The connection is as follows: "Pouring" refers to the training rule on pouring; it was spoken regarding pouring and prescribed for the domain of pouring.

However, this training rule on water containing living beings was spoken regarding consumption and prescribed for the domain of swallowing. This alone is the distinction between that [rule] and this one.
Commentary on the Discussion on Water with Living Beings (Sappāṇakakathāvaṇṇanā).
1667. “In accordance with the Dhamma” (yathādhammaṃ) means by that very Dhamma which has been taught for the settling of whichever legal issue (adhikaraṇa).
By the term “legal issue arising from business” (kiccādhikaraṇa), the other types of legal issues are implied. As it is said: “The legal issue... [and so forth].

"Namely, the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*): the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

The four acts of the Saṅgha, beginning with the act of obtaining permission (*apalokanakamma*), are called "business of the Saṅgha. That very same [business] is a "legal issue" because it must be settled and must be resolved by means of the methods of settling disputes;
thus, it is the "legal issue of business" (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, "to be brought out again" (*punar nīhātabba*) means it must be removed again; that is, it must be resolved.

This is the meaning. By this, it should be understood that the twelve "reopenings" (*ukkoṭa*) shown in the Pāḷi, beginning with "the action was not performed," are characterized. "Of one who reopens" means:

having gone to the presence of each respective monk and saying such things as "the action was not performed," one who agitates [the Saṅgha] and does not allow [the decision] to stand by its established state. And here, regarding "to stand":
"Not giving" is stated for the purpose of showing the manner of its occurrence. However, whatever legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) has been settled according to the Dhamma, that is indeed properly settled.
1668. The construction is as follows: "When a monk says, 'This action was not done; it is a wrongly done action; the action must be done again,' he is not permitted to overturn that action."

1669. *Vippakata* means commenced but not finished. *Taṃ* refers to one who protests against it. *Saññāpetvā* means having made known the blameless nature of the action performed. *Na pan’ aññathā* means without having made it known in that way. 1670.

*Adhamme pana kammasmiṃ* means regarding an action as it appears in the text [of the Vinaya]. *Ubhayatthāpi* means in both cases: whether it is a legal action (*dhammakamma*) or an illegal action (*adhammakamma*). 1671.
Regarding the phrase *na ca kammārahassa vā*, the word *ca* here should be construed with the words “and by an incomplete assembly” (*vaggena ca*). The word *ca* has the sense of the word *vā*.

It should be seen thus: the construction is that there is no fault in reopening [a legal act] for one who knows, "It was performed contrary to the Dhamma, or by an incomplete assembly, or on one who does not deserve it.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of reopening. 1673.
Because of the statement: "A grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*) consists of the four *pārājika* offenses and the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses."

Because the *pārājika* offenses are also grave (*duṭṭhulla*), yet because a *pārājika* is not intended here, the term "grave" is qualified by the word "offense entailing suspension" (*saṅghādisesa*) in order to show precisely what is intended here.
As it has been said: "In this context, the four *pārājikas* are shown by way of enumeration, but the offense of *saṅghādisesa* is what is intended. "Having known" means either by himself...

"Or having learned from another. "For one who conceals it, the offense is a *pariyāpatti*": for one who conceals it, thinking, "Having learned this, they will accuse me, they will press me for an answer;
I will not tell," the offense of concealment (*pariyāpatti*) is prescribed for him.
"Having laid down the burden": having made a resolve, thinking, "I will not tell another. "Of him": [refers to the one who concealed it].
*Duṭṭhullassa*: the analysis (*vigga-ho*) is "that confession whose cause or reason is concealment. *Paṭicchādanahetukaṃ* is an adjective qualifying the act of confessing;
what is meant is that one makes the confession after saying, "So-and-so has committed such-and-such a *saṅghādisesa* offense;
do not tell anyone else. *Iti* is used in the sense of indicating what has been stated; *hi* is used in the sense of the particle *eva* (emphatic).
The meaning is: "He speaks in this very way.
The construction is: as long as the limit is not broken, even if there are a hundred or a thousand monks, they all incur that same offense.
(1676) "By the root" means by the person who has incurred a *saṅghādisesa* offense. "Of the second who has been informed" is a grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

The construction is as follows: when a third person, having heard from a second bhikkhu who was told by the first (the *mūla*) "Do not inform anyone else that you have fallen into an offense," turns back and informs that very second bhikkhu, it is said that the limit (*koṭi*) of the informing has been reached.
"Limit" (*koṭi*) refers to the conclusion of the act of informing.

1677. Regarding the phrase "and [if one] perceives it as grave when it is grave," the word "announcing" (*ārocento*) is understood here from the context of the section. However, regarding the other two cases—namely, being doubtful about what is grave and perceiving it as not grave—there are two [cases].
1678. "Not grave" refers to the five kinds of light offenses. "In all instances" means in all the various permutations. The triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses is specified by way of:
(1) perceiving what is not grave as grave; (2) being doubtful about what is not grave; and (3) perceiving what is not grave as not grave. Thus, there is a threefold *dukkaṭa*.
The meaning is that it is shown in the Pāli text. "In all cases" means in all [instances].

"In the sections concerning those not fully ordained" means in the three alternatives regarding those not fully ordained. "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that there is a triad of offenses of wrong-doing based on the cases of one who perceives a person as fully ordained when they are not, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives them as not fully ordained. 1679–80.
"If he does not report it," by means of all the phrases beginning with "there will be a schism in the Saṅgha," etc.
"There is no fault"—this should be applied to each case individually. If one does not report because one does not see [the offense] as it is, there is no fault.
If one does not report because one thinks, "He is harsh," there is no fault.
It is called "non-action" (akiriya) because it is an offense incurred by failing to report it to another. Regarding that which has been permitted as "it must be reported":
Since non-disclosure does not occur without disrespect, it is called "painful feeling.
In this context, while the Commentary on the Mātikā states, "they are exactly like samanubhāsana," here it says, "they are equal to dhuranikkhepa";
one should understand that in both cases the only difference is the name, as the origin (samuṭṭhāna) is the same.
Commentary on the Discussion of Improper Speech.
1682. Regarding the phrase "one under twenty years of age," the word "knowing" is to be supplied; thus, the meaning is "knowing [him] to be under twenty years of age.
"One under twenty years of age" means one who has not completed twenty full years from the moment of conception. "Who" refers to whichever bhikkhu.

"Having become a preceptor. "Should do" means "should cause to be done. "Ordains" (upasampajjati) refers to ordination (upasampadā); that [is what is meant]. The construction is as follows: for a monk who knowingly ordains a person less than twenty years of age, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for that monk who thus ordains him.
Regarding the others: "For the group and for the teacher, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
This refers to the inclusion of those cases shown in the Pāḷi.
1683. Whether a monk knows or does not know that a person is under twenty years of age, if he has been ordained, he remains unordained;
once he has reached the full twenty years of age, he must be ordained again.
The construction is: "He must indeed be ordained.

(1684) Having reached ten years [of seniority], being one who has completed ten years, if there is some fault in ordaining others while having a preceptor who is merely a monk in name, that is absolutely not the case; it does not exist—this is the construction.
(1685) "That monk" refers to a preceptor who, having been ordained at less than twenty years of age, has now completed ten years [of seniority].
Having performed the offering, he ordains that one who claims to be a monk. "If the group is complete" means: in the Middle Country, a group of ten;
in border regions, a group of five—if such a group is not deficient. "They" refers to those who have been ordained. "Well-ordained" means properly ordained. 1686–7.
A monk who, having acted as preceptor, thinks, "I shall ordain a person less than twenty years of age," [is at fault].
If he seeks out a group, a teacher, or even a bowl, or if he appoints a hall and binds a fixed boundary, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him in all such undertakings.
Likewise, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the motion (ñatti); likewise, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the two proclamations (kammavācā)—this is the application [of the rule].
1688–9. "Twenty and those years" means twenty years; one who has fewer than twenty years is "one under twenty years."
“Perceiving less than twenty years” (*ūnavīsativassasaññī*) means: the perception that one is less than twenty years old is “perception of being less than twenty years old” (*ūnavīsativassasaññā*).

Since he possesses this, it should be called “one who perceives [himself as] less than twenty years old”; however, by applying the rule of elision (*nipātanalakkhaṇa*), the word *vassa* is dropped, and thus it is stated as “one who perceives [himself as] less than twenty” (*ūnavīsatisaññī*). For such a person who perceives [himself as] less than twenty—[the phrase] “one whose twenty years are complete” (*paripuṇṇavīsativasso*) should be stated as follows:
he who has twenty full years is “one with twenty full years. (In the case of the compound *paripuṇṇavīsativasso*, the word *vassa* is likewise elided.)
By means of the grammatical rule for elision (*nipātana-lakkhaṇa*), the word "twenty years" (*vīsati-vassa*) is dropped, and thus a person is called "full" (*paripuṇṇo*).
In that "full one," the meaning is: in a person who has completed twenty years. "In both cases" refers to both types of persons: those under twenty years and those full twenty years.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning those under twenty years of age.

1691. "Together with a caravan of thieves" means together with a multitude of people designated as a "caravan," in the form described in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) beginning with: "A caravan of thieves is one consisting of robbers who have either committed their deeds or not committed their deeds," and so forth.
The instrumental case is used here due to its connection with the particle *saha* (together). "Knowing" means knowing that it is a "caravan of thieves. "Having made an agreement" means...

“Let us go, friend; let us go, venerable sir; let us go, friend; today, or yesterday, or tomorrow, or the day after—we shall go,” this is the meaning of “having made an appointment” according to the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).

“A road” means a single-way path; here, the phrase “even as far as another village” is to be understood as the remainder, as it is said: “One might set out on a single-way path even as far as another village.”

“It may be a *pācittiya*” means: it would be a *pācittiya* offense of the kind described as, “In a village, for every interval between villages, there is an offense of *pācittiya*; in a forest outside a village, for every half-yojana, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
“Not recited” means not stated here [in this context].
1693–4. *Maggāṭavīvisaṅkete*: in a false indication of a road, and in a false indication of a forest. *Yathāvatthukameva*:
it is indeed a *pācittiya* according to the specific basis [of the offense]. *Tesu*: among those caravan-leaders. *Asaṃvidahantesu*: not making arrangements. *Sayaṃ vidahatopica*:
and for one who makes arrangements himself. *Ubhayattha*: in both cases—that is, whether it is a caravan of thieves or a caravan that is not thieves.
1695. Regarding the phrase "perceiving it as a non-road": here, the word "in both cases" (*ubhayattha*) should be understood as carrying over.
"Kāliko" means that which belongs to the time; thus, there is no offense in the case of a sign (*visaṅketa*) or in a sign connected with that time.
By this specific qualification "belonging to the time," it is indicated that even in a sign such as a road or a forest, there is indeed an offense.
1696. The construction is as follows: this training rule is said to originate from a caravan of thieves by way of arising from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the caravan of thieves. 1697.
"The seventh" refers to that which was recited [in the Pātimokkha] beginning with: "Whatever bhikkhu, having made an appointment with a woman... and so forth.
The seventh training rule. "In consultation with a bhikkhunī" means by the training rule concerning consultation with a bhikkhunī.
"By way of origin and so forth" means by way of the analysis beginning with the origin. "Equal" means similar. "Even a little" means even a small amount.
Explanation of the Discussion on Consultation.
1698. The construction is: "These five things have been declared to be obstructors.
Here, this term *antarāyakara* (obstructor) has the same meaning as the term *antarāyika* (obstructive) found in the Pāli Canon.

Therefore, these five obstructive things are: the obstructive factor of karma, the obstructive factor of defilements, the obstructive factor of kamma-result, the obstructive factor of slander, and the obstructive factor of transgression of the Teacher's command.
It means "proclaimed by the Blessed One.
In this context, it is called an *antarāya* because it comes (*eti*) into the midst or interior (*antara*) of a being’s mental continuum (*santāna*) by way of obstructing various forms of success;
it refers to misfortune pertaining to the present life and so forth. In the sense of not being able to transcend that obstacle, one is "engaged in" (*niyuttā*) that *antarāya*. *Antarāyaṃ*...
Or, they are "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) because they are either worthy of [receiving] fruit [that hinders progress] or have the nature of creating an obstacle.
Only the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariyakamma*) are obstructive to [the attainment of] karma; likewise is the act of violating a nun.
However, that [act] creates an obstacle only to liberation (*mokkha*), not to heaven (*sagga*). And this is stated because it lacks the characteristic of sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*). For indeed—

A bhikkhunī possesses the quality of being protected by the Dhamma; this is said with reference to an ordinary bhikkhunī. However, for a noble one (ariyā), what occurs leads only to rebirth in the states of woe.
In this regard, the young man Nanda serves as an illustration. Alternatively, there is no obstruction to heaven for both [the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī] due to their having the same aspiration;
however, there is an obstruction to liberation because it defiles the practice undertaken for the sake of liberation.
They say that once these have been overcome, it is impossible to prevent them from becoming obstacles to rebirth in the heavenly realms (*sagga*) during the course of existence.

Wrong views—namely, the view of no-cause (*ahetuka-diṭṭhi*), the view of non-action (*akiriya-diṭṭhi*), and the view of nihilism (*natthika-diṭṭhi*)—when they have reached a state of certainty, are called "defilements that are obstacles.
The states of consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-citta*) for those who are eunuchs, animals, or hermaphrodites [are also such].

"Obstructive to fruition" (*vipākantarāyika*) means this. Here, the mention of eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and so forth is merely an illustration, because all rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) that is without root-cause (*ahetuka*) possesses the quality of being obstructive to fruition.

"Slandering the Noble Ones" (*ariyūpavāda*) is called "obstructive to reproach" (*upavādantarāyika*). However, these [acts] remain such only as long as the Noble One has not been asked for forgiveness;
not beyond that. The seven classes of offenses committed intentionally are "obstructive to the transgression of the command" (*āṇāvītikkamantarāyika*).
...by name. Even they [are obstructive] only as long as one claims the status of a monk, or does not emerge from the offense, or does not confess it—not beyond that.
"These are obstacles; as they are, so am I."
“He who says, ‘I understand the Dhamma taught by the Sage’”—thus should the second verse be recited.
Since it was not stated thus, the connection with the first verse of the verses beginning with “three times” would not be possible. Therefore, it is understood that this verse has been omitted here.

The connection is as follows: if a bhikkhu should say, "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Sage in such a way that these five things proclaimed by the Blessed One as 'obstructive' (antarāyika) are not, in fact, obstructive," then that bhikkhu is to be addressed three times.
To the question of by whom and how he is to be addressed, he says: "Those who see... and so forth. [He is to be addressed] by those who see him speaking in such a manner.
They see a bhikkhu, or they hear from others that "such-and-such a venerable one speaks thus.
The construction is: that bhikkhu is to be addressed three times, [saying], "Venerable sir, do not speak thus. 1701. Regarding "if he does not speak":
this refers to one who, having seen or heard [the matter], does not speak according to the manner described above. It is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

The offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) has been understood. That is the attainment [of the offense]. "Of one who does not relinquish" means: even when the monks have spoken thus, for one who does not relinquish it. In this way, he extends the application to the offense of wrong-doing. 1702. "At the formal proclamation" (*kammavācā*) means:
at the third formal proclamation. "At the conclusion" (*osāne*) means: at the end; the intention is that the offense is incurred at the syllable *yy*.

The triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated thus: “If one does not relinquish [the action] while it is a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), perceiving it as a legitimate legal act, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

If one does not relinquish it while it is a legitimate legal act, being in doubt about it, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. If one does not relinquish it while it is a legitimate legal act, perceiving it as an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*), there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Thus the triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated. For an illegitimate legal act, there is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses.

"Stated" means that regarding an illegal act (*adhammakamma*), three types of offenses are stated for one who perceives it as a legal act (*dhammakammasaññī*), one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as an illegal act. 1703. The word-division is:

"There is no offense (*anāpatti*) for one to whom the act has not been performed. An "act" (*kamma*) here refers to the act of formal admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*). As it is said: "There is no offense for one who does not admonish.
This concludes the commentary on the account of Ariṭṭha.
1704. *Ñatvā* means having known—either by oneself, from another, or from that person—the state of not having been reinstated (*anosārita*).

*Akatānudhammena*: one for whom the *anudhamma* (the rule) consisting of reinstatement has not been performed is *akatānudhamma*; this is used in the instrumental case because it is joined with the word *saha* (with/by). *Tathāvādikabhikkhunā*:
by a monk who speaks thus, saying, "I understand the Dhamma as taught by the Blessed One," and so forth.
“By a bhikkhu. This is in grammatical apposition with the term “one who has not acted in accordance with the Dhamma.

“Should live together” means he should perform sangha business such as the Uposatha ceremony and so forth. “And should eat together” means he should engage in either the enjoyment of material goods or the enjoyment of the Dhamma.
“Or lie down together” means he should lie down under one roof, even if in separate quarters.
1705. Now, in order to show the determination of the field for the aforementioned pācittiya, he said: “The formal act such as the uposatha,” and so forth.
By the word “such as” (ādi), the invitation (pavāraṇā) is included, as it is said: “either the uposatha or the invitation.

“Together with that” means together with the one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka). “At the conclusion of the formal act” is an indication of the field of offense by way of communal association (saṃvāsa).
1706. For one who takes much food, such as that which may be kept for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*), by a single act (*payoga*), there is one *pācittiya*.
Likewise, for one who gives much food by a single act, there is also one *pācittiya*. The application is that for many acts, there are many *pācittiyas*.
And by this mention of the enjoyment of material goods (*āmisa-sambhoga*), he implies by association the enjoyment of the Dhamma (*dhamma-sambhoga*), which bears an equal fruit.

It should be understood. In that regard, however, for one who is being recited from or causing to be recited from [the text] starting with the words (*pada*), the offense should be understood according to the method stated in the *Padasodhamma*.

1707. "The other" means one who is of regular standing (*pakatatta*). "The other" means one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*). "The third" means one of regular standing. "Both of them" means both the one of regular standing and the one who has been suspended.
The phrase "they lie down together in one place" is to be supplied as the remainder. In these three instances, the term "offense of expiation" (*pācitti*) is obtained by the context of the section.

1708. One should apply the method of supplying missing words (*ajjhāhāra-yojanā*) as follows: "There may be offenses by way of the acts of lying down for one who, having risen again and again, lies down.

To the question, "Where does the determination (*vinicchaya*) of the offense stated in the passage beginning 'When [a monk] has lain down with one who has been suspended' (*ukkhittake nipannasmiṃ*) occur?", he says:

"The determination is in cases of different precincts (*nānūpacāra*) and in cases of being covered by the same roof (*ekacchanna*). Regarding the term "in cases of different precincts" (*nānūpacāresu*), the particle *pi* (and) is used here.
And here, "and they come" (*ayanti*) should be connected with the word "determination" (*vinicchayo*). That which has a single precinct is "single-precinct" (*ekūpacāra*);

that which has various precincts is "various-precinct" (*nānūpacāra*). "Single-precinct" and "various-precinct" form the compound *ekanānūpacārāni* by means of the *ekadesasarūpekasesa* (the elision of all but one of identical parts).

Among those [places], "covered together" is *ekacchannāni*. While it would have been more formally correct to say *teṣu ekacchannesu*, the form *ekacchannesu* is used either through the elision of a phoneme (*vaṇṇalopa*) or through a transposition of words (*vacanavipallāsa*).

Or it is stated as “under one roof. The meaning is that this determination regarding the offense as previously described should be understood to apply even to dwellings that have a single common precinct (*nānūpacāra*), provided they are under one roof.
1709. “In both cases” means in both instances, whether [the monk] has been suspended or not suspended. 1710. The word-division is:
“*saññissa osārito* (‘if he is reinstated while being conscious [of the offense]’) and so forth.”
Commentary on the Discussion of Suspension (Ukkhittakathāvaṇṇanā). 1712.

Likewise, "one who has been expelled" means: "From this day forward, friend novice, you are no longer to be designated as 'the Blessed One is your teacher,' nor are you to receive from the bhikkhus the two or three nights' stay that other novices receive with the bhikkhus."
“Even that common lodging you do not have; go away, perish!”—it was expelled according to this manner of speaking.

From the statement, “O novice, you have been expelled thus,” the term “novice” (*samaṇuddesa*) is understood as the remainder. “Knowing” means knowing, in the manner already stated, that “this one has been expelled.
“Should entice” means: “or should entice him [by offering] his bowl, or his robe, or the formal instruction (*uddesa*), or the detailed questioning (*paripucchā*).”
One should include [this] according to the method found in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "or I will give.

"By him" means by that one who has been expelled. "Or should cause to wait upon" means that, while consenting to the powders, clay, and so forth being given by him, one should cause oneself to be waited upon by him.
This term "by him" (*tena*), used in the sense of the instrumental case, should also be construed with "should associate" (*sambhuñjeyya*) and the following terms. "Or" (*vā*).
Here, it is short by way of the metrical composition of the verses. Sharing enjoyments and sharing a bed are exactly as described in the immediately preceding training rule (sikkhāpada).
Therefore, the delimitation of the offense here should be understood according to the method stated therein.
To show the three ways of losing [the status] mentioned in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) by way of an enumeration of meanings, he said: “By living together... pe...”.
“Three. Regarding that, he says “herein,” etc., to clarify which of the three is intended. The construction is: “expulsion by means of penal action (*daṇḍakamma*) is what is intended here.
Their classification is as follows: “In that context, expulsion due to non-acknowledgment of an offense and so forth is called *saṃvāsanāsanā* (expulsion from communal living).
‘The violator is to be expelled; expel the nun Mettiyā’—this is called *liṅganāsanā* (expulsion of the gender-mark). ‘From this day forward... [and so on].
"Friends, that bhikkhu should not even refer to the Blessed One as his Teacher"— this is what is called "the suspension by means of a formal act of censure" (*daṇḍakamma-nāsanā*),
as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the phrase "spoken in reference to the formal admonition," because it was spoken therein, he said, "considered equal to [the case of] Ariṭṭha."
Commentary on the Story of the Thorns.
The Seventh Chapter: The Section on Living Beings.
1716–7. Whatever monk, while transgressing a training rule, is seen or heard by others regarding that transgression...

When being addressed by those monks according to the training rule, saying, "Friend, do not do this; this is not allowable for a monk," and being addressed according to the method stated in that training rule, [he thinks]:

"Regarding this training rule, as long as I do not ask another who is competent, learned, experienced, and a master of the Vinaya—about whom you would speak regarding the meaning of this training rule—"

The construction with the underlying intention (*sādhippāyayojanā*) is as follows: if one says, "I will not train [in this] until then," for one who speaks thus, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Regarding the rule concerning those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*): the Teacher has explained three sets of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) based on the cases of perceiving someone who is not fully ordained as being so, being doubtful, or perceiving them as not being fully ordained.
By this same principle, [the offenses for] perceiving someone who is fully ordained as being so, being doubtful, or perceiving them as not being fully ordained [are also explained].
By way of one who has been ordained, the threefold offense of expiation (pācittiya) is illustrated. To show the manner of advising by means of what has not been laid down, he said:
"This is not for effacement. Regarding both those who are ordained and those who are not ordained:
for a monk who says "not yet" and so forth when being told by one who has not [yet] laid it down, "This is not for effacement," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The construction is: "it occurs. The word-division is: “There is no fault for those who are insane, etc.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
1720. From the recitation of the training rule beginning with: “Whichever bhikkhu, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, should speak thus... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "recite them": here, the remainder is "by means of the minor and lesser training rules. With the exception of the *pārājika* offenses, the rest are designated as "minor and lesser" (*khuddānukhuddaka*) one by one.
Here, the word *kiṃ* functions as a negation; it means "what is the use of these?"—that is, there is no purpose for them.
In the expression "by these" (*ete hi*), the term is used in the sense of proximity (*samīpatthe*), and by virtue of its general grammatical form, it is a synonym for "by these" (*imehi*).
“Why, then, these?”—this phrase shows the reason for the prohibition in the recitation of the training rules (sikkhāpada) by stating, “because they are the source of remorse and so forth.

Here, by the word “and so forth” (ādi), vexation (vihesā) and scruples (vilekhā) are included. In this context, “remorse” (kukkucca) means the state of being anxious, thinking, “Is it allowable, or is it not allowable?
“Vexation” (vihesā) means regret (vippaṭisāra). “Scruples” (vilekhā) refers to what is termed doubt (vicikicchā).
“Mental remorse” (*manovilekhatā*) means mental distress (*manovilekhā*). By all these terms, the manner of disparaging the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is shown.

The word “iti” should be supplied and connected [to the phrase] “thus, in the disparagement of the training rules. In the term “vivaṇṇane,” the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).

The construction is as follows: “In the disparagement of the training rules—due to the causes such as anxiety (*kukkucca*) and so forth—is there an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for these minor and lesser training rules that have been recited?”
1721. It is said that there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: "If one disparages the Vinaya regarding one who is ordained, perceiving them as ordained, it is an offense of *pācittiya*.

If one is doubtful regarding one who is ordained... [and so on] ...if one perceives them as unordained... [and so on] ...it is an offense of *pācittiya*. Thus, three *pācittiya* offenses have been stated.
However, if one disparages that same Vinaya in the presence of one who is unordained, the application is that there is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses.
“Of both” means of those who are fully ordained (*upasampanna*) and of those who are not fully ordained; the word “in the presence of” (*santike*) is understood to follow.

“Censuring other teachings” (*aññadhammavivaṇṇanā*) refers to the disparagement of the Suttas and the Abhidhamma as distinct from the Vinaya. To show the scope of what constitutes no offense (*anāpatti*), he says:
“For one not wishing to disparage,” and so forth. There is no offense for one who speaks thus: “Come now, master the Suttanta first; you shall master the Vinaya later.”
The exposition. "Similar" means exactly similar.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of "scratching.
Regarding the discussion of "deluding" (mohanaka) first: [1725]
“The monk who, every half-month,
when the Pātimokkha is being recited in its entirety, [remains] ignorant— ”
"She asks by means of her own [ignorance]"—this must be the first verse.
For if this were so, it is understood that the verse beginning with "By ignorance" would have a complete connection.

Or, in the phrase "by ignorance," the word "because of having committed [an offense]" (*āpannattā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "Release from offense" (*āpattimokkho*) means release from an offense. By ignorance...

The construction is: "Because it has been committed, there is no release from the offense. To the question "What should be done?", he says: "He should be made to act," and so forth. The connection is:
"The monk should be made to act in accordance with how the Dhamma stands. The word *dhamma* here refers to the Pāḷi;
the meaning is that he should be made to act exactly as stated in the Pāḷi. If the offense is one that requires confession (*desanā*), he should be made to confess it.
If it is an offense leading to rehabilitation, it is said that he must be rehabilitated. As it is said: "He should be dealt with according to the Dhamma.
Because he has fallen into that offense through ignorance, there is no release from it. However, the bhikkhu should be dealt with in accordance with how the Dhamma and the Vinaya stand:
if he has fallen into an offense leading to confession, he should be made to confess it; if he has fallen into one leading to rehabilitation...
The meaning is that he should be reinstated. 1726.

"Uttarin" means beyond the performance according to the Dhamma. "By the second [motion]" means by the motion-and-second-vote (ñattidutiyakamma) alone. "Having censured" means having reproached him with such words as, "Friend, it is a loss for you.
1727. "When the offense has been thus brought forward" means when, after the performance according to the Dhamma, that person has been dealt with in the manner previously described.

Having censured him with a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma), when such delusion has been imposed upon him, the construction is: "If he deludes [him] again. The construction is:
"In that person who causes delusion, a *pācittiya* is stated. 1728. The triad of *dukkaṭas* is illustrated as follows:
"If one deludes [another] while perceiving a non-dhamma act as a dhamma act; if one is in doubt; if one perceives it as a non-dhamma act..."
“...if she causes confusion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); thus the triad of *dukkaṭas* is shown.

From the reverse of this, the triad of *pācittiyas* is to be understood. As it is said: “If it is a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*) and she perceives it as such, yet she causes confusion; or if she is in doubt;

or if it is an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*) and she perceives it as such, she commits an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Here, “legal act” refers to the act of imposing confusion. As it is said:
“In ‘a legal act concerning the Dhamma’ (dhammakamma) and so forth, what is intended is an act that imposes delusion. 1729–30.
Regarding the passage beginning with “And not for one who wishes to delude,” this should be construed individually with the phrase “there is no offense.
The word division is “vitthārena asutassa. Here, the term “Pātimokkha” should be understood as referring to the formal act (kamma).

The construction is: "and for one who has heard it less than two or three times in detail. By the word "thus" (*tathā*), one refers back to the phrase: "it should be understood as 'there is no offense'.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse that causes confusion.
1731–2. "Angry" means provoked. "Gives a blow" means [gives it] with the body, or with something connected to the body, or with something released from the hand.

Or, at the very least, one gives a blow even with a lotus leaf. As it is said: “‘Should give a blow’ means one gives a blow with the body, or with something attached to the body, or with something released, or at the very least even with a lotus leaf. Here, the words “of another monk” are to be supplied as the remainder.
By looking back at that [phrase], the word “whoever” (yo) is obtained.

In order to show the determination as it appears in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), he said, “by one desiring to strike,” and so forth; by this it is meant that if [one] strikes with the intention of causing death, it is a *pārājika* offense.

(1733) “Thus, when this has been done, he shines in the midst of the Saṅgha”—regarding this, “desiring disfigurement” means one who has regard for disfigurement; and if such a person cuts off the ear or the nose of the monk who is the object of that regard, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense—this is the construction.
(1734) In the term “anupasampanne,” the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive. By the words “of a woman,” and so forth, [the rule applies] as appropriate.
It should be applied as: "to an unordained woman and an unordained man.
Regarding the phrase "even to an animal," the word "at least" (*antamaso*) is to be supplied here, as it is said:
"at least even to an animal. 1735. The analysis of the phrase is: "if she strikes, and [he strikes] the woman. "With a mind full of passion" means with the lust for physical contact.

"With a lustful mind": this is shown by such rules as, "Whatever bhikkhu, with a mind that has descended [into passion] and is perverted, should engage in physical contact with a woman," and so forth. "With the intention of release" means:
aspiring for one's own release from that [contact]. "No fault is found" means: there is no fault, not even a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) or similar offense.
1737–9. The construction is: "Having seen on the road even a thief or an enemy who is coming with the intent to harm.
Having seen them, he states how one should act: "O lay follower, do not come here," and so forth;

by forbidding his approach, it is meant that he should remain right there. Regarding the word *āyantaṃ* (coming): when this is said, it refers to one who is approaching while disregarding [the warning]. As it has been said:
“Coming without having accepted the instruction.
This is the same method: even when told, “Do not come,” there is no offense for one who comes, even if they have been struck or have died; this is the method. 1740.
The triad of *pācittiya* offenses has been stated: [namely,] “perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained,” “being in doubt,” and “perceiving one who is not fully ordained.”

"Striking [another] constitutes an offense of expiation (pācittiya)"—thus the triad of *pācittiyas* is stated. Regarding "the rest": this refers to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). The triad of *dukkaṭas* is stated as follows:

"If one strikes one who is not fully ordained while perceiving them as fully ordained, or while being in doubt, or while perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)"—thus the triad of *dukkaṭas* is stated.
Because it is not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*), he says: "arising from body and mind."
Since pleasure and equanimity can also arise in the body and mind, he says "painful feeling" (*dukkhavedanā*) in order to distinguish it from those.

This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the blow. 1741. "Body" (*kāya*) refers to a portion of the body, such as a limb like the hand. "Or" (*vā*) is used for the purpose of combining a second meaning. "Attached to the body" (*kāyabaddha*).
“Connected with the body” refers to any one of the items suitable or unsuitable for use as a weapon, such as a knife, a staff, or a sword.

“If he should utter it” means if, having displayed the manner of striking, he should lift it up; this [phrase] is to be construed individually with each of these terms: “the body or what is connected with the body. “Of that” refers to the body and so forth that has been uttered. “On account of the lifting” means on account of the cause of raising it up.
"By one not wishing to strike back" means by one who does not desire to return a blow. "Because it has been given" means because the blow has been delivered.
Because there was no desire to strike back, there is no *pācittiya* offense under the previous training rule;

and because the effort was made with the intention of vomiting [the food] rather than remaining at the mere act of vomiting, there is no *pācittiya* offense under this rule either, due to the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
Because the application (payoga) is impure, there must not be a lack of offense; therefore, a *dukkaṭa* is stated.
1743. If by that blow any limb, such as the hand or other parts of the body, of the bhikkhu is broken, the connection is that it is a *dukkaṭa* for the one who struck the blow. 1744.
The remaining analysis—beginning with "one whose intention is liberation"—is the analysis not stated here, [to be understood] by way of its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
The construction is: "It should be understood by one learned in the Vinaya according to the method stated immediately preceding.
They say: "Even if one emits [semen] out of anger while desiring to frighten away animals and the like after seeing them defecating and so forth, it is still with the intention of emission.
This concludes the commentary on the Discussion of the Hand-Clap.
1745. *Amūlakena* means "without a root," that is, devoid of a root such as what was seen and so forth;

here, the word "monk" (*bhikkhu*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. *Saṅghādisesena* means by any one of the thirteen [offenses]. *Tassa* refers to the accusing or inciting evil monk. The construction is:
"If, at that moment, the accused monk knows, 'This person is accusing me,' it would be a *pācittiya* offense. By this [it is implied] "if thus..."
"It is established that if one does not know, or knows only after a long time, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

(1746) "Therein" means regarding one who is fully ordained (upasampanna). "Three offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya)" refers to: "If one accuses one who is fully ordained, perceiving them as fully ordained, with a groundless charge of an offense involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), it is an offense entailing expiation. If one is in doubt... [and so on]... if one perceives them as not fully ordained..."
“If one accuses [another] of a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. This is the triad of *pācittiya* offenses.

Regarding “the accuser of failure in view or failure in conduct incurs an offense of *dukkaṭa*”: the meaning is that for one who accuses another of a groundless failure in view or failure in conduct, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
“In the rest” means: in the case of those not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). “The triad of *dukkaṭa*” refers to [accusations against] those not fully ordained.
The meaning is that there are three *dukkaṭa* offenses based on one who perceives [the person] as ordained, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives [the person] as unordained.

1747. The word-division is: “There is no offense for one who perceives it thus. “One who perceives it thus” means one who perceives it as having a basis (*samūlaka*). This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the lack of a basis (*amūlaka*).
1748–9. *Sañcicca* means knowing full well that he is twenty years of age or older. Regarding the term *bhikkhu*, the word *aññassa* (of another) is to be supplied as the remainder.
In the phrase *ūnavīsativasso tvaṃ maññe*, the particle *maññe* expresses a hypothetical sense;

by this particle signifying a supposition, it demonstrates that there is no offense of lying, just as in expressions such as "I suppose the water is burning. This is due to his benevolence (*hitesitā*).
In the absence of such things as giving instruction or other similar requisites or causes,
if a bhikkhu should intentionally cause remorse in another bhikkhu by saying, "I think you are under twenty years of age," and so forth—
this is the construction: for that bhikkhu who thus causes remorse, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every single word.

1750. It is said that there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: “If one intentionally causes remorse in one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), perceiving them as fully ordained, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. If one is in doubt... [and so on] ...if one intentionally causes remorse in one who is not fully ordained, perceiving them as fully ordained, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Thus the triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated. “And in the rest” means in the case of those who are not fully ordained. This is the triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses.
There is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses based on the cases of one who perceives another as ordained when they are not, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives them as not ordained.
"Fault" (*vajja*) is simply the state of being faulty (*vajjatā*). 1751. The connection is: "one speaks out of a desire for their welfare.

Regarding the phrase "do not do so," the word "act" (*karohi*) is understood; thus, the meaning is "do not act in this way again. "I think you were sitting with a woman; I think you ate at an improper time."
The construction is as follows: "There is no offense for one who speaks out of a desire for benefit, saying, 'Do not do this again.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of intentional speech (sañciccakathā).

1753. "Quarrel" (bhaṇḍana) means a dispute. The analysis of the compound *jātabhaṇḍanānaṃ* is: those in whom a quarrel has arisen (*bhaṇḍanaṃ jātaṃ yesaṃ*). Thus, the meaning is "of those among whom a quarrel has arisen."

The word "speech" (*vacana*) is understood as the remainder [of the compound]. The construction is: "should stand eavesdropping in order to hear. For it is called *upassuti* because one hears (*suyyati*) by approaching (*upecca*) there;
that is, a place. The meaning is: "in that place which, having approached, one is able to hear the sound of those speaking.
Now, if a monk should stand eavesdropping in order to hear the speech of monks who have fallen into a quarrel, [he commits an offense].
"For him there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya)"—this is the construction. 1754. "For one going with the desire to provoke"—this is the construction. 1755.
"To hear" means to hear the words of those who have fallen into quarreling as they walk behind. "Of one lagging behind" means...
The construction is as follows: for one who falls behind after having abandoned their natural pace, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense for the monk walking in front.
"Or [for one] going hurriedly" means even for one who goes quickly from behind in order to hear the words of those walking in front who have become quarrelsome.
"This very same determination" means that at every step, this indeed is the determination.

1756. “One’s own standing place” is the connection [of the phrase]. “Even by clearing the throat” means even by making the sound of clearing the throat. Here, the construction is: “having said ‘I am’ here, it should be made known. 1757.

A triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated with reference to one who is ordained (*upasampanna*), whether perceiving them as ordained, being doubtful, or perceiving them as unordained (*anupasampanna*).

“In the remaining cases” refers to those who are unordained. A triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses is stated with reference to one who is unordained, whether perceiving them as ordained, being doubtful, or perceiving them as unordained.
1758. "I shall abstain" means I will refrain from the wrong grasp that has been taken up by me. 1759.
Regarding the origin: it originates from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
It may be an action in the sense of going with the desire to hear [the secret], or it may be a non-action in the sense of remaining where one stands while others are conversing.
By way of causing [another] to know; therefore he said, "This is an act and a non-act. It is bodily action because it is accomplished through going.
It is vocal action because it is accomplished through silence. "With hatred" means blameworthy; what is meant is "unwholesome mind.
Explanation of the Discussion on Eavesdropping.
1760. "Of those that are lawful" (*dhammikānaṃ*) means of those performed according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.

"Of legal acts" (*kammānaṃ*) refers to these four types of legal acts: an act consisting of a motion (*apalokanakamma*), an act consisting of a single motion (*ñattikamma*), an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and an act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*). "Is dissatisfied" (*khīyati*) means he expresses his lack of approval. 1761.
"In both cases" (*ubhayattha*) means in regard to what is not-Dhamma (*adhamme*) and what is Dhamma (*dhamme*).
1762. Regarding the term *adhammena*: here, the word *kammena* (by means of an action) is to be understood as the remainder; thus, the meaning is "by an action contrary to the Dhamma.
The word *kammamhi*, having changed its case-ending, should be construed as *kammena*. Regarding *vaggena*:

this is because it is contrary to the characteristic of concord (*sāmaggī*) as defined by the statement, "consent has been brought from those entitled to give consent, and those present do not protest."

"In a non-unanimous [assembly]," here the word "by the Saṅgha" is to be supplied as the remainder. The phrase is to be divided as "tathā akammārahassa" (likewise for one who does not deserve a formal act).

[The meaning is: "These are performing a formal act by means of an illegal act," and "These are performing a formal act by a non-unanimous Saṅgha," and "These are performing a formal act by a factional Saṅgha through an illegal act," and likewise, "These are performing a formal act upon one who does not deserve a formal act."
The construction is as follows: having understood that [the offense] is being committed, there is no offense declared for one who censures it.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the obstruction of formal acts (*kamma*). 1764–5.
The construction is: "The matter reported until it has not yet been adjudicated," [referring to] "by the accuser and the accused..."
Since it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: “The person’s own account has been told, and an investigator has been appointed;
even by this much, the matter itself has been reported,” the meaning is that the matter is considered “reported” until it has been formally decided.

The construction is as follows: “As long as the motion (ñatti) has not been put, or the formal act (kammavācā) has not reached its conclusion, in this case... there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
1766. “If one has not given consent and [the person] has left the reach of his hand, it shall be a *pācittiya* for him”—this is the construction.
1767–9. “Even in a non-Dhamma legal act (*adhammakamma*), if one perceives it as a Dhamma legal act (*dhammakamma*), it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)”—this is the construction.

The case where one perceives a Dhamma legal act as a non-Dhamma legal act and there is no offense is not mentioned here; however, because it is mentioned in the *Pāḷi*, it should also be applied here.
The construction is as follows: there is no fault for one who goes while perceiving that "there will be disputes and so forth in the Saṅgha";
nor for one who is ill; nor for one who goes on account of a task for the sick; nor for one who does not wish to interrupt the formal act (kamma);
nor for one who goes because oppressed by the need to void urine and so forth; nor even for one who goes with the thought, "I shall return. There is no offense in such cases.
In this context, fault itself is "faultiness," which is an offense; lack of fault is "non-faultiness," which is not an offense.

Because it is committed by departing after having left the reach of hand-contact and by not giving one's consent, it is classified as both an act and a non-act (*kriyākriya*). This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding departing without having given one's consent.
"With a complete Saṅgha" means together with a Saṅgha that is of common affiliation and stands within the same boundary.
For it is said: "A 'complete' Saṅgha is one that is of common affiliation and stands within the same boundary.
"Robe" (*cīvara*) refers to that which is subject to formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*). As it is said: "'Robe' means any one of the six kinds of robes that is subject to formal assignment."
"Last. "Of one who is authorized" means of any one among those who have received authorization as a distributor of lodgings and so forth.
"He disparages" means he speaks dispraise in such a manner as, "She gives to whoever is her friend," and so on.

Regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), a triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated based on the cases of one who perceives it as a legitimate legal act, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*).

1772–4. The construction is as follows: even for one not authorized by the Saṅgha, if the Saṅgha—being complete and unanimous—gives him a robe or some other requisite in that same manner, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the phrase "to one who is not ordained" (*anupasampanne*): it is used in the sense of the dative case. The construction is that for a robe or any other requisite given in that same manner by a complete and unanimous Saṅgha to one who is not ordained, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense in every instance.
"Of the ground," meaning "of one who is not fully ordained.

The construction is: there is no offense for one who acts according to their own disposition by way of desire and so forth, and for one who is exhausted. These are the methods and the sequence of the determination.
This is the commentary on the discussion of weakness.

1775. The connection is with the phrase “this is the twelfth”; the meaning is: “This is the twelfth training rule (sikkhāpada), namely: ‘If a bhikkhu, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been dedicated, should dedicate it to an individual, he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).

This occurs in the section on the thirty [offenses] within the section on offenses entailing relinquishment (nissaggiyakaṇḍa). Regarding the word “by the last,” the term “by the training rule” is understood here from the context. The word “and” (ca) [is used].

The meaning of the word *eva* (only). The construction is as follows: “Whatever monk, knowing that a gain belonging to the Saṅgha has been dedicated, should dedicate it to himself, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*)”—by this very last training rule (*sikkhāpada*), everything that is to be said is identical in every respect.
Regarding the phrase “this alone is the distinction”: here, the distinction itself is the state of being a distinction; the meaning is “this alone is the distinction.”
1776. *Tattha* means in that training rule at the conclusion of the section on forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). *Attano pariṇāmanā* means for the sake of one's own dedication.
This is the commentary on the discussion of dedication. The eighth chapter, the Section on Fellow-Practitioners (*sahadhammika-vagga*), is finished.

1777–8. Should any bhikkhu, having entered unannounced and without the king’s or queen’s knowledge, cross the threshold or the doorpost of the royal bedchamber while the king has not yet departed and the queen has not yet departed— if he crosses it,
for that bhikkhu there shall be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on the first footstep, and on the second footstep...
The construction is: "it may be an offense of expiation" (*pācittiyaṃ siyā*). 1779.
*Paṭisaṃvidite* means when one has announced one's own arrival. *Nevapaṭisaṃviditasaññī* means one who perceives it as not having been announced.
*Tattha* means in that case of having announced one's arrival. *Vematikassa* means of one who is in doubt: "Has it been announced, or has it not been announced?"
"Is it not so?"—this refers to one who has fallen into doubt.
The construction is as follows: there is no fault for one entering even without having informed a khattiya, or even without having informed one who has been consecrated by the khattiya-consecration;
the meaning is that there is no offense for one entering even when such persons have not been informed.
The construction is as follows: there is no fault whether one enters when both the queen and the lady have gone out from their bedchamber, or even if one enters when only one of the two has gone out.
Regarding the term "by means of the *kathina*," the remainder—"equal in terms of origin and so forth"—is to be supplied;
this training rule is equal to the *kathina* training rule by way of its origin and other such factors.

This has been stated. Entering a bedchamber is an act (*kriya*); not experiencing it is a non-act (*akriya*). This concludes the commentary on the talk concerning the inner apartments. 1782. The construction is as follows:
for one who acquires silver or gold for their own sake, or causes it to be acquired, there is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiyāpatti*).

1783. The construction is as follows: for one who causes [gold or silver] to be acquired for the sake of a *gaṇa*, an individual, or a *saṅgha*, or for the sake of new construction (*navakamma*) on a *cetiya*, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both the one who causes it to be acquired and the one who acquires it. The specific nature of gold and silver should be understood in the same manner as stated under the rules concerning forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

1784. Jewels such as pearls and so forth are of the same specific nature as those already mentioned. Regarding the phrase "for the *saṅgha* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *gaṇa*, the individual, and the *cetiya*. 1785–6.
Whatever belongs to a householder—whether it be a permissible object (*kappiyavatthu*) or even an impermissible object (*akappiyavatthu*)—[is subject to the rule].

The construction is as follows: whether it be an earring worn on the mother’s ear or even a palm leaf, for one who puts it away under the pretext of being a storekeeper, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
"It must not be stored" means it must not be put away.
1788. Since this is indeed called an impediment (*palibodha*), the construction is: "therefore it is permissible to set it aside. 1789.
Regarding the phrase "in a permitted place" (*anuññāte ṭhāne*), the word "fallen" (*patita*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

Here, a "permitted place" refers to either within a monastery (*ajjhārāma*) or within a dwelling (*ajjhāvasatha*). As it has been said: "I allow you, monks, [to take] a jewel or what is considered a jewel within a monastery..."
Or, having taken it up or having had it taken up in a monastery enclosure (*ajjhāvasatha*), one may deposit it [with the thought]:
"Whoever it belongs to, he shall take it away. And herein, "monastery enclosure" (*ajjhārāma*) means: within the boundary of that which is enclosed;

for that which is not enclosed, it is within two *leḍḍupāta* (the distance of a stone's throw). "Monastery dwelling" (*ajjhāvasatha*) means: within the boundary of that which is enclosed; for that which is not enclosed...
“Within the distance of a mace’s throw. The term “having taken up” is illustrative; it is also said to mean “having caused to be taken up.

However, in a permitted place—such as the aforementioned locations within the monastery precincts (*ajjhārāma*) and so forth—for one who takes and deposits either a jewel, or what is considered a jewel, or an object for human use and enjoyment, or a bed-furniture item, [the rule regarding] what is considered a jewel [applies].
The construction is as follows: there is no offense for one who receives it on trust, or for one who receives it only for a limited time, or in both cases for those who are insane and so forth.

Regarding "of the same origin as the act of matchmaking" (*sañcaritta-samodaka*): here it should be stated that "this training rule [arises] by way of its origin and so forth"; the meaning is that this training rule is of the same class as the act of matchmaking in terms of its origin and other such factors.
End of the commentary on the Discourse on Jewels (*Ratanakathā-vaṇṇanā*).
1792. *Pureti* means in the first part [of the day]. 1793–4.

*Santanti* refers to the specific form stated in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) concerning conduct. *Anāpucchāti* means without having asked for permission, saying: “I ask for permission to enter the village at an improper time.
*Paccayaṃ vināti* means without such an urgent necessity (*accāyikaṃ karaṇīyaṃ*). *Parikkhepokkameti*...
[It refers to] entering within the enclosure. The same method applies here for "stepping out of the precinct" (*upacāra*) as well.
1795. *Atha* (then) marks the commencement of another statement.
1796. *Tato aññaṃ* (other than that): having first requested permission to enter a village at an improper time, [one may then do so] from the village already entered.
“To another village. Again, the word “from there” (*tato*) refers to the second village. In some manuscripts, the reading “the duty of asking permission” (*āpucchane kiccaṃ*) is seen;
however, the reading “the duty of asking permission” (*āpucchanakiccaṃ*) is more appropriate. He says “or even in a hundred villages” to show the extent as desired.
1797. “Having calmed” (*passambhetvāna*) means having dispelled. The construction is: “and they enter another village along the way.”

1798–9. Having performed his meal duties either in a family home or elsewhere in a dining hall, the construction of the sentence is: "if that bhikkhu should wish to go for alms of ghee or alms of oil.

"Sees" means [sees] someone in his own vicinity who is fit to hear ordinary speech; by this very fact, it is shown through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*) that one who has moved a certain distance away is called "not present.
"Not present" (*asanta*) means either non-existent or [situated] beyond the aforementioned measure.
Or when [the person] has gone far away. Regarding the phrase "it does not exist," the word "having reflected" is to be supplied as the remainder.
1802. *Anokkamitvā* means without having approached. *Maggehi* means by the paths that ought to be traveled. 1803. *Tikapācittiya*:

A triple offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is stated with reference to one who perceives it as the wrong time when it is the wrong time, one who is doubtful about it, and one who perceives it as the right time.
1804. “Or in an urgent matter” means: when there is an urgent matter that must not be delayed, such as seeking medicine for those bitten by snakes and so forth, for one who goes [on account of it].

1805. “Within the monastery” means a Saṅgha monastery within the village. “The dwelling of the bhikkhunīs” means a bhikkhunī vihāra. “The dwelling of the sectarians” means a sectarian monastery. 1806–7.

Regarding going within the monastery and so forth, there is no offense not only for one who goes without having asked permission, but also for one who goes without having fastened the waistband or without having put on the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).

"In times of distress as well" means that even when a lion or a tiger approaches, or a cloud rises, or some other calamity arises—when such distress occurs, there is no offense for one going from outside the village into the village; this is the meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding entering a village at an improper time.
1808. "A needle-case made of bone, ivory, or horn"—this is the construction. "Bone" refers to any kind of bone. "Ivory" refers to elephant tusks. "Horn" refers to any kind of horn.
1809. *Lābheti* means "in obtaining. *Bhedanakaṃ*: "breaking" itself is *bhedanakaṃ*; that which has this [breaking] is *bhedanakaṃ*.
Because it must be confessed after first having broken [the rule], that *pācittiya* offense has this "breaking" as its characteristic; thus it is *bhedanaka-pācittiya*.
The suffix *-a* is used here in the sense of "having the nature of" (*assatthiatthe*).
1810-1. “There is no offense regarding a fire-drill” (*anāpatti araṇike*)—this is the word-division. “Araṇika” means a fire-drill and its lower block.
