“Vidha” means a fastener for a waistband. “Añjanikā” means a tube for ointment. “Dakapuñchanī” means a cloth for wiping water from the limbs of one who has bathed.
“Vāsijaṭa” means a handle for a chisel.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Needle Case (Sūcigharakathāvaṇṇanā).
1812–3. The nature of the bed and chair has already been stated in the fourth training rule of the second chapter on living beings (Bhūtagāmavagga).

Because it is stated that "the legs are eight finger-breadths [in length] by the Sugata’s finger-measure," the word "by the leg" is to be supplied here after the phrase "measuring eight finger-breadths."
"Below the lowest crossbar" (*heṭṭhimāṭanī*) means the lower surface of the crossbar. "The lowest of the crossbars" (*heṭṭhimāṭanī*) refers to the bottom part of the crossbar;
the meaning is that it is "except for the lower crossbar. It is "with the cutting" (*sacchedā*) because it occurs together with the cutting of the bed-legs prior to the teaching.
"That is the measure. "Of one who exceeds" (*atikkāmayato*) means of one who causes [the length] to exceed; the letter *y* is elided due to the requirements of the verse composition (*gāthābandha*).
1815. "For one making it with a measure" means for one who joins and makes it with a foot-measure of one *vaḍḍhakiratan* below the handle (*aṭani*).
By this very [phrase], the expression "for one making it deficient" is implied. "Of that" refers to that which lacks a measure.
"Having cut off" means having cut off the portion exceeding one *vaḍḍhakiratan* from below the handle.
1816. Regarding the phrase "having dug down to its measure": here, by implication, the word "exceeding" (*adhika*) is understood;
thus it means having dug a place exceeding the measure, that is, having caused it to enter into the ground.
"Or having placed it on the surface" means having set it upon the ground with its base upwards, or upon wooden blocks. "Or having built a platform and using it" means having lifted it up.
There is no offense for one who places [the bedding] upon a frame of cotton, secures it with a binding, and uses it.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning couches.
1817. "Cotton is stuffed therein" means *tūlonaddha*; that is, having inserted cotton, it is covered on top with a cloth (*cimilikā*).

“Cotton (*tūla*)” means that after inserting any one of the three types of cotton mentioned—namely, tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or *poṭaki*-cotton—and sewing it over with a piece of cloth, it is made;

this is what is meant. *Poṭaki*-cotton refers to the cotton of any kind of grass species, such as *eraka* grass and so forth. *Uddālanaka* is simply "tearing apart" (*uddālana*); because it possesses that quality, it is called *uddālanaka*.
It is exactly as previously stated. "Anīti" means one by whom calamity (*īti*) and affliction (*upaddava*) have been transcended; thus, [he is] the Blessed One, the Anīti.
1818. *Āyoge*: on a carrying-yoke. *Bandhane*: on a waist-band. *Aṃsabaddhake*: on a shoulder-strap. *Bibbohane*: on a pillow. *Thavikā*: a bowl-bag.
In the phrase "thavikādi," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes items such as needle-cases (*sipāṭika*).
The summary: The construction is that there is no offense for a monk when cotton-filled items such as bags (*thavikā*) and the like have been used.

1819. Regarding the phrase "made by another," the context provides that this refers to "a bed or a chair. "Having torn out" means having ripped away the cloth and removed the cotton. "Guidelines" refers to the origins and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of cotton-filled items.
1820. "Sitting mat" means a sitting-cloth (*nisīdana-cīvara*). "In respect of measure" refers to the measure stated as: "In this regard, this is the measure:
two spans long according to the Sugata-span, one and a half spans wide, and a border of one span. The construction is:
"If there is an application [of making it] exceeding the measure, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for that."
1821. "Sacchedan" means that the *pācittiya* offense is declared to involve the act of cutting down to the proper measure, along with the subsequent remedy for the excess portion;

this is the meaning. "Tassa" refers to the sitting mat (*nisīdana*). The construction is: "having cut it in two places, three fringes (*dasā*) should be made. 1822. "Tadūnakan" means less than that measure.

Regarding the phrase "for one making a canopy, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes rugs, floor-coverings, walls, pillows, and bolsters. "The same method as for a go-between" has already been explained.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Sitting Mat (Nisīdana).
1823. "When there is disease" means when there is a disease such as itch, boils, or abscesses. As it was said:
"I allow you, monks, for one who has an affliction such as itch, boils, an abscess, or severe scabies, a covering for the itch. Herein, "itch" (kaṇḍū) refers to...

*Kacchu* (itch) refers to small, red-tipped pustules. *Piḷakā* (boils) refers to small pustules with red tips. *Assāva* (discharge) refers to the trickling of impurities by way of fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, anal fistula, diabetes, and so forth.
*Thullakacchū vā ābādho* (or the disease of severe itch) is said to be a disease of large pustules.
*Pamāṇato* (by measure) means according to the measure stated thus: "In this regard, the measure is four Sugata-spans in length and two spans in width."
Commentary on the Discussion of the Rain-Cloak (Kaṇḍupaṭicchādikā). 1825.
"Only by the proper measure" means by the measure stated as follows: "In this regard, the measure is six spans long according to the Sugata-span, and two and a half spans wide.
Regarding "exceeding the measure," it refers to exceeding the aforementioned measure of the rain-cloak.

In the phrase "atikkamane," this locative case (*bhummavibhatti*) has the sense of a cause or condition (*nimittattha*). "Tassa bhikkhuno" means "of that monk. "Nayo" refers to the method of legal determination (*vinicchayanaya*), beginning with the *pācittiya* offense for cutting [the robe]. This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭika*). 1826. The construction is as follows:

"If a monk should have a robe made equal in measurement to the robe of the Sugata, there would be an *dukkaṭa* offense for that monk in the making of that robe. The analysis (*viggaha*) of the compound is: "that whose measurement (*pamāṇa*) is equal (*tulya*)."

1827. There is no acquisition [of robes] other than through making them oneself or having them made; here, "acquisition" is understood as the obtaining of the robe in its proper form at the conclusion of the tailoring work.
1828. "Of that" refers to that Sugata-cīvara which was mentioned in the phrase "with the robe of the Sugata.
By way of length, it is specified as nine spans (*vidatthi*) of the Sugata’s span; by way of width, it is six spans.
The construction is: "It was spoken in the training rule itself.
This concludes the commentary on the Story of Nanda.
The Ninth Chapter, the Rājavagga.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the *pācittiya* offenses in the *Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā*, which is an elucidation of the essence of the meaning of the Vinaya.
The first part is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Vinaya Piṭaka,
the Vinayavinicchaya-Ṭīkā (Second Part).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Pāṭidesanīya Offenses (1830–1).

Having thus shown the ninety-two *pācittiya* offenses by a method that is neither too concise nor too prolix, he said, “Whoever, within a house,” etc., in order to show the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses which were indicated immediately thereafter. Therein, “within a house” (*antaraghara*) means:
He explains what constitutes "within a house": as it is said, "Within a house means a carriage road, a military array, a crossroads, or a dwelling.

Now, if a monk should with his own hand receive from the hand of an unrelated nun who has entered within a house any kind of solid food or soft food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for that monk at the moment of receiving it.
The construction is: "If one swallows food, it may be an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
From this point onward, four verses have been written in the manuscripts out of sequence; their correct order is as follows:
the third is "In this case, within a house," the fourth is "Therefore, for a bhikkhunī," and the fifth is "On streets and so forth."
“Or even on a chariot-road”: this is the genitive case. Furthermore, this sequence should be understood according to the order of the commentary on the *mātikā*.
Following this sequence, there is the explanation of their meaning—1832–3.

Having shown the general determination found in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*) by means of the preceding two stanzas, [the author] now [presents] that which is found in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
In order to show a distinction, he said, “In this,” and so forth. Therein, “in this” means in this first *pāṭidesanīya* training rule.
“Of her” refers to the unrelated nun. “From the statement” means from the words “having entered among the houses. The word “for” (*hi*) indicates a reason.
Since it is described in the Commentary that the standing place of the bhikkhu is not the measure [of distance], therefore...

The construction is as follows: if one who stands in the street or elsewhere should receive [food] from the hand of a nun standing in a monastery or similar place while she is giving it, there is no fault for that monk receiving it in this manner.
Since the acceptance is the root of the consumption, there is no fault. By the word "receiving," it is also indicated that there is no offense of *pāṭidesanīya* regarding the consumption.

1834. If a nun, standing on a carriage road or similar place, gives food, and a monk, standing within the monastery grounds, receives it, there is an offense for him—this is the construction [of the sentence].
Due to the requirements of the metrical verse, the word *bhikkhunī* is shortened to *bhikkhuni*, and *bhojanaṃ* to *bhojana*.

The term "offense" (*āpatti*) is stated with reference to the offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and an offense requiring confession (*pāṭidesanīya*) regarding both the receiving and the consuming [of the food].
1835. If a bhikkhunī, standing on a carriage road (*rathikā*) or elsewhere, gives food, that [act] occurs even on a carriage road...
such is the application of this method (*naya*). Therein, "carriage road" (*rathikā*) means a street. "Byūha" refers to a street where people go back and forth without it being partitioned off.
"Sandhi" means a house junction. "Siṅghāṭaka" is a place where roads meet, whether four-cornered or three-cornered.
“This method” refers to the method stated in the immediately preceding verse beginning with “an offense. 1837.

This *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is spoken with reference to that which has not had its flavor mixed with food (*āmisa*). The construction is as follows: when [food] such as that allowable for the watch of the night has its flavor mixed with food and becomes of a single flavor, there may be an offense of *pāṭidesanīya* upon receiving it and consuming it.
1838. “From the hand of one fully ordained on only one side” means from the hand of one who has received full ordination in the presence of nuns. As it has been said:

“‘To one who has received full ordination from one side’ means: to one who has received full ordination in the presence of the bhikkhunīs. But for one who has received full ordination in the presence of the bhikkhus, it is exactly as in the original case. 1839.
The construction is: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who perceives a non-relative as a relative, and likewise for one who is in doubt.

1840. The construction is as follows: there is no offense for a monk who accepts [food] from one who causes it to be given by a woman unrelated to him, whether she places it on the ground to give it, or stands within the monastery grounds (*antarārāma*) and so forth to give it.

Regarding the phrase "within the monastery grounds and so forth" (*antarārāmādīsu*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the nuns' quarters, the dwellings of heterodox ascetics (*titthiya*), the refectory (*paṭikkamana*), and others. The "refectory" (*paṭikkamana*) is the dining hall.
1841. The construction is: "having brought it out from the village, he gives it. 1842.
Regarding the word *hatthato*, the word "taking" (*gahaṇe*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "Likewise" means there is no offense. This training rule is considered equal to that on wool;
such is the construction. The commentary on the first *pāṭidesanīya* [offense].
1843–4. *Avutte*: not having been told, according to the method that will be explained. This is to be connected with the phrase "even by a single bhikkhu. *Apasakkā*: go away.

It should be understood that by the word *iti*, which expresses the sense of "beginning," the remainder of the sentence—namely, "Go away for now, sister, as long as the bhikkhus are eating"—is included.
By this, the manner of dismissal is demonstrated. [The phrase] "even by a single bhikkhu" [is used].
By this, the minimum [requirement] is shown. The maximum, however, should be understood from the text as well: “That nun is to be censured by those bhikkhus.
Although the term “material gift” (*āmisa*) is a general expression, it refers specifically to any one of the five kinds of cooked food;
as it is said: “by any one of the five kinds of cooked food. The terms “one who has enjoyed” (*bhoga*) and “one ordained on one side” (*ekatoupasampannā*) have meanings already explained.
1845. “In that same way” means there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). “Therein” means in the case of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampannā*). 1846.

Even if food has been given for oneself, there is no offense under this training rule (*sikkhāpada*); however, because an offense may arise under the previous training rule, it is stated, “she does not give.
As it was said: “She causes her own meal to be given; ‘she does not give’—here [the meaning is]...”
"Even if one gives their own food, there is no offense by this training rule, but there is an offense by the previous training rule.
Thus, "tathā" means there is no offense. To show that there is no offense under both training rules as well, he said, "if one causes it to be given. As it is said:
"One gives food to others, but does not cause it to be given"—here, however, even if one were to cause it to be given, by this training rule...
“There would be an offense; however, for the one giving, there is no offense by this [act], nor by the previous one.

1847. If a bhikkhunī causes that which has not been given to be given, or causes it to be given where it was not previously given, and she causes it to be given equally to all—both friends and enemies—even in that case there is no offense. 1848.
If a female trainee (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerikā), while urging [others] by saying, “Give soup here, give rice here,” [indicates] the distribution...

There is no offense for one who does not dissuade her while she stands there making [the request]. There is no offense for one who does not dissuade a nun who is soliciting for the five kinds of food specifically, and not for anything else.
The construction is that there is also no offense for one who does not dissuade her when she is insane, and so forth.

1849. Regarding the "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*): the word "of this" (*imassā*) is to be supplied as the remainder here. Food is the action (*kiriya*); the failure to prevent the one who is soliciting is the non-action (*akiriya*). Thus, this is a case of both action and non-action (*kriyākriya*).
Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya: 1850–1.
Regarding "one recognized as a trainee" (*sekkhasammata*): "A family recognized as a trainee (*sekkhasammataṃ nāma kulaṃ*) is a family that increases in faith but decreases in wealth;
for such a family, the recognition as a trainee has been granted by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyena kammena*)."
This family is called "one recognized as being for those in training" (sekkhasammata). Therefore he said, "in a family that has received such recognition.

The analysis of the compound is: "that by which recognition has been obtained. He said, "even before entering the vicinity of the house," because even one who has been invited becomes as if uninvited once he has entered the vicinity of the house.
As it is said: "One who is 'uninvited' is one who has not been invited for either today or for tomorrow, [once he has entered] the vicinity of the house..."
"He invites [the monk] as he is entering; this is what is meant by 'not invited.
Since it is stated, "One who is not ill is one who is able to go for alms," one who is capable of going for alms is called "not ill.
"Having taken" means having received with his own hand. This is connected with the word "food" (*āmisa*). As it is said: "Edible food..."
“Or having received with one’s own hand either solid food or soft food. Regarding the word “receiving,” the phrase “for the purpose of nutriment” is to be understood as the ellipsis here.
1853. “Therein” means in a family regarded as belonging to those beyond training (*asekha*). “In that very way it is explained” means that an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is explained. 1854.
Regarding the phrase “or for one who has been invited,” the word “or” (*vā*) here includes the remainder of the case of one who has been invited. As it was said: “For one who has been invited...”
“Or he eats the leftovers of one who is ill. The construction is: “Alms for others are given there.
“There” means in that family regarded as *sekkha*.

“In any place whatsoever” means in any place such as the dining hall (*āsanasālā*) and so forth. “Or in the case of a regular meal (*niccabhatta*) and so forth”—here, by the word “and so forth,” meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*), fortnightly meals (*pakkhika*), Uposatha-day meals (*uposathika*), and meals on the first day of the lunar half-month (*pāṭipadika*) are included.

1856. Regarding the word *dvāre* (at the door), the word *ṭhapetvā* (having set aside) is to be supplied. Regarding the word *sampatte* (when he has arrived), the word *pacchā* (afterwards) is to be supplied. As it is said:
"Even if, when a monk has not yet arrived, they first take [the food] out, set it at the door, and afterwards give it to the one who has arrived, it is permissible.

1857. To show the determination (*vinicchaya*) as found in the *Mahāpaccarī*, he says "a monk," and so forth. Regarding the phrase *samuṭṭhāneḷakūpamaṃ*, the meaning is that, in terms of its origin (*samuṭṭhāna*), it is similar to the training rule concerning wool (*eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*).
Commentary on the Third Pāṭidesanīya: 1858–9.

Because of the statement, "Of the five, that which is acknowledged is what is called 'unacknowledged,'" and because it will be stated here as well that "it is requested by one who is in accordance with the Dhamma," the term *agahaṭṭha* (not a householder) includes wandering ascetics (*paribbājaka*).
He said, “By a woman or by a man,” in order to show the same method expressed through different terminology.
Because of the statement, “Those forest lodgings,” he refers to a monastery as a “forest monastery. The construction is:
“If it has been announced in this way, it is ‘authorized’ (paṭisaṃvidita),” as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). “Authorized” means previously informed.

1860. Afterward, whether it be that very thing as it was announced, or having made its retinue [the object], or even bringing many other things—this too is called "experienced" (*paṭisaṃvidita*); such is the construction. 1861.

Regarding the phrase "having made it known by means of the rice-gruel," here the expression "setting that aside" is obtained by implication (*sāmatthiyā*). This too is stated in the *Kurundi* commentary that "making it known" is permissible; such is the construction. 1862. *Panā* has the sense of the word *api* (also/even).
"Other families as well"—such is the construction. Here, "a certain family named so-and-so is experienced" [is the meaning].
The remainder of the commentary states: "Having heard that [the donor] goes after having prepared and taken hard foods and so forth.
*Tenā* means "by that which has been experienced. The construction is:

"And all of that is permissible. 1863. Thus, regarding "that which was not announced," it refers to what was first [mentioned] by way of the method beginning with "having entered the monastery or its precincts," and so forth.
"Unannounced" (*anivedita*): this word "thus" (*evaṃ*) should also be connected with the phrase "whatever has been brought to the monastery.
"Thus" means in the manner described by the passage beginning, "having made it an attendant [to the meal]. "That is called 'unannounced'" (*taṃ asaṃviditaṃ nāmā*):

this should also be connected with the phrase "announced according to the Dhamma" (*sahadhammikañāpita*). As it is said: "Of the five [types], that which is announced—this is what is called 'unannounced' [in the context of the other four]."

And in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: “Regarding the phrase ‘informed among five,’ even if one has sent something to any of the five fellow practitioners and informed them, saying, ‘We shall bring hard food or soft food,’ the meaning is that it is as if no information had been given at all.
(1864) In the expression “having caused [it] to be made,” the word “informed” (*paṭisaṃvidita*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

1865. The construction is: "Or, having gone, it should be taken by the bhikkhu on the way. "Without doing so" means without performing the procedure stated [in the rule] beginning with "having sent [a messenger] outside the monastery. Regarding the term *upacārato*, the suffix *-to* should be understood here in the sense of the locative case (*bhumm-atthe*). 1868.

The connection of the words beginning with "if informed" (*paṭisaṃvidite*) is with the phrase "there is no offense" (*anāpattē*). Regarding the word "if informed," the remainder of the phrase is "of one who is ill" (*gilānassa*).
There is no offense if informed; there is also no offense for one who is ill, even if not informed.
The connection is: "there is no offense for one who eats the remainder of what has been formally assigned, or the remainder of what belongs to a sick person.
As it is said in the section on non-offenses: "He eats the remainder of what has been formally assigned, or of what belongs to a sick person. The construction is:
"There is no offense for one who, having received [food] outside the monastery, eats it only inside. Regarding the phrase "or having taken," the word *vā* (or) here...
The phrase “of her,” and so forth, should also be applied [to the preceding rules].

1869. Regarding the phrase “therein”: it means in that forest monastery (*āraññakārāma*). The construction is: “There is no offense for one who eats,” with the remainder being: “provided they have been made allowable by another and given.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* (offense requiring confession).
Thus ends the commentary on the Discussion of the Pāṭidesanīya rules in the Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā, which is an elucidation of the essence of the meaning of the Vinaya.
Now begins the commentary on the Discussion of the Sekhiya rules.

1870. Having thus shown the determination (*vinicchaya*) of the offenses entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*), he said, beginning with “Whoever, out of disrespect...,” in order to show the determination of the training rules (*sekhiya*) that were recited immediately thereafter.
“Whoever” refers to one who is senior, junior, or of middle standing.

Here, “disrespect” means intentionally committing an offense and being lacking in effort when taking up the robes for wearing, such as the lower robe (*nivāsana*), and so forth. Even behind [the person].
In the phrase *vāti*, the word *vā* includes the expression “or even one who sees. In the phrase *tassa ca*, the word *ca* is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for what is about to be stated.

(1871) It is not only for one who wears [the robe] in the manner already described that this applies; it also applies when [the robe] has the shape of an elephant’s trunk and so forth as found in the Khandhaka.
It is said that for one wearing [it] improperly, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); thus he says, "like an elephant’s trunk," and so forth.
The wearing of the robe like an elephant’s trunk and so on will be explained later in the *Khuḍḍaka-vatthu-kkhandhaka*. "Circularly" means having made it circular all around.
"Should be worn" means it should be put on; the sense is that it should be used as a lower garment (*nivāsana*).
1872. Regarding the phrase "below the kneecap," the words "starting from the head of the shin bone" are to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Measuring eight finger-breadths" means it should be about eight finger-breadths according to the carpenter's finger, say the teachers.
However, for one who has a thin shank or large calf muscles, one may lower it even more than eight finger-breadths below the kneecap in order to provide a proper fit when putting on the lower robe.
To include the commentary [on this], he said: "Less than that is not permitted.
(1873) The construction is: "There is no offense for one who, unintentionally, wears the lower robe unevenly.
The same applies to what follows. "Unintentionally" means: not intentionally thinking, "I will wear it unevenly," but rather thinking, "I will wear it evenly."
There is no offense for one who, having become dispassionate, wears it unevenly. "Even if unaware" means there is no offense for one who wears it in that manner while distracted by something else.
"Not knowing" means there is no offense for one who simply does not know how to wear it evenly.
Furthermore, the procedure for wearing the lower robe must be learned. Even one who has learned the procedure, if [he thinks], "It is pulled up," or "It is pulled down,"...
Or if he does not know, there is likewise no offense for him. "For one who is ill" means:
for one who has a wound on the calf or the foot, there is no offense for him while putting it up or taking it down to dress it.
And here, "foot" is intended to mean the vicinity of the foot. "In cases of emergency" means: when wild beasts or thieves are pursuing him; in such emergencies, there is no offense.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Circular Manner (Parimaṇḍalaka). 1874.

“Having made both corners even” means that when the upper robe is worn over one shoulder, having made the two corners—which would otherwise hang down at the back and the front of the abdomen—level like the two humps on the back of an elephant. “Having made it circular” means...
This is for the sake of that very same purpose. *Sādaraṃ* is a neuter noun used adverbially. Alternatively, the construction is: "it should be worn with respect";

the meaning is that the act of wearing it should be performed with respect. "For one who does not do so" means for one who fails to wear it in this manner, despite having generated respect for the duty of wearing it.
(1875) "The training is to be observed: 'I shall put on the lower robe evenly all around,' or 'I shall put on the upper robe evenly all around.'"
Because it was stated without specifying whether it refers to "the training should be observed" or "within a house," he says, "stated without distinction.
Since these two training rules were stated without distinction, the construction is: therefore, whether in a house or in a monastery, the robes must be worn evenly all around (*parimaṇḍala*).
"In a house" means within a house (*antaraghare*). "Or in a monastery" is said with reference to times such as when attending upon the Buddha. *Parimaṇḍala*.
"Should be made" means it should be worn wrapped perfectly circularly; this is the meaning. This is the second [section]. 1876.
"Having made both corners equal" is the connection. "And having covered the neck with the windward side" is the construction.
1877. "Without having done so" means without having performed the procedure as previously described. "Even both shoulder-tops" refers to both the tops of the shoulders.
"And the chest" refers to the heart. "Having uncovered" means without concealing it. "According to desire" means in accordance with one's wish.

Regarding the word "going," the phrase "within an inhabited area" (*antaraghare*) is to be supplied here. An "inhabited area" may be either in a village or in a monastery; [the rule applies] after having cooked and eaten there.
The dwelling place of householders.
Third.
1878–9. By the phrase “from the wrist,” it should also be connected with “below. Regarding the term “vāsūpagassa,” here [the word] “kāyaṃ”...
The remainder of the phrase is “sitting after having uncovered [the bowl]. “One who has gone for the night’s stay” (vāsūpaga) means one who has approached for the purpose of staying overnight;
by this it is indicated that one approaching a house for the sake of a night’s stay must do so well-covered.
By this very point, it is also stated that there is no fault in departing as one pleases from one who has approached the presence of someone who has gone for the night’s stay.
Therefore, it is said in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "It is permissible to go as one pleases to the presence of one who has entered upon residence for even a single day;
what need is there to mention the case of monks who have resolved to stay for four or five days?
This is the fourth [section].
1880. *Suvinītena*: by being well-disciplined through not playing with the hands and feet.

This is the fifth [clause]. 1881. In accordance with the requirements of verse composition (*gāthābandha*), the word "satīmatā" has been lengthened. *Avikārena*: without agitation, that is, without being distracted by various sights.
“Yugamattaṃ” means that which has a yoke as its measure or extent; a chariot-yoke is four cubits in measure, and such is the area [referred to].
“Pekkhinā” means by one who is looking. The word-division is: “bhikkhunā okkhittacakkhunā. Even though it is stated thus:
“standing anywhere at all within an inhabited area, even in a single spot,” this is the construction. Although it has been said in this way...

When such an obstacle exists, it is permitted even for one who is walking to look [back]. However, regarding the phrase "standing in one place," it is stated here that even one who is walking is indeed permitted to look for the absence of danger.
This is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries as: "Likewise, in the village, there is honor.
The word *pi* has the sense of the word *pana*; thus, it is meant to say: "but it is permissible to look."
1883. "Looking here and there": this refers to one who, out of disrespect, looks toward various directions, toward a palace, a gabled chamber, or a street.

This is the seventh [offense]. 1884. "Or from one side" means from one shoulder-joint. "Or from both sides" means from both shoulder-joints. "Inside from the threshold post" means inside from the threshold post of the village gate; it is said to be "inside the house."
The ninth [section].
1885. "Even while sitting in that manner" means even while sitting inside the gateway pillar (*indakhīla*).
The construction is: "When taking out the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), one should give the water-pot without having thrown the robe over it. Furthermore, "water-pot" is used merely as an illustration.
The same method applies to the cases beginning with *dhammakaraṇa*.
This is the tenth [chapter]. The first section.

1886. The construction is: "It is not permitted both to go and to sit. The word *ca* (and) is a conjunction of actions (*kiriyāsamuccaya*). "In a matter that is laughable" means in a cause that produces laughter. "A mere smile" means a gentle smile. [These refer to] the first and second [offenses].
1887. "With little noise": "To what extent is one 'with little noise'? In a house twelve cubits square, the senior of the Saṅgha at the beginning..."

When they are seated in this manner—with the second elder in the middle and the third elder at the end—if the senior of the Saṅgha consults with the second elder, the second elder hears both the sound and discerns the meaning;
however, the third elder hears only the sound and does not discern the meaning. To this extent, it is "with little noise," as described by the term *appasadda*.
But if the third elder explains it thus: "There is what is called a loud noise," this is the third [explanation].

(1888) "Making the body shake" means shaking the body again and again. The same method applies to what follows as well. Because the hand has already been defined by its characteristics, "the arms" should be understood as the portion from the wrist up to the shoulder-joints.
1889. *Ujuṃ paggahetvā* means having placed [the body] straight. *Āsitabbaṃ* means it should be sat upon. The word division is: *“samena iriyāpathena tu.”* 1890.

This is an instrumental case used in the sense of a state of being (*itthambhūte*). Since walking is impossible in the training rules connected with walking, he said, *“connected with sitting.”* These are the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth [rules].
The Second Chapter.
1891. "Having placed a hand on the hip" means having bent the hand from the armpit joint toward one or both sides of the waist and placing the hand there.
As it is said: "One who has placed a hand on the hip is one who has made a 'hand-on-hip' gesture."

The construction is: "or walking on tiptoe. "On tiptoe" (ukkuṭikā) refers to walking while lifting the heels and touching the ground with the tips of the feet, or lifting the tips of the feet and touching the ground with the heels.
"With a cloth wrapped around [the body]" means with a cloth bound around the waist.
The construction is: for one sitting inside a house in such a manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
1893. "And in the second" refers to the training rule: "I shall not sit with hands on hips in inhabited areas.

"And in the fourth" refers to the training rule: "I shall not sit with head covered in inhabited areas. "In the sixth" refers to the training rules beginning with: "I shall not sit with legs crossed in inhabited areas," and so forth.
Thus, these twenty-six [rules] are appropriate and suitable for the conduct of a recluse.
The training rules have been proclaimed:
the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth.
(1894) A wise bhikkhu, being diligent, endowed with mindfulness, and perceiving the bowl as full, [should eat] almsfood with equal curry.
"It should be taken" is the construction. Thus, by this verse, the triad of training rules is summarized.
"Carefully" means having established mindfulness. "Endowed with mindfulness" is a synonym for "carefully," for it is said in the Commentary:

"having established mindfulness. "Bowl-perception" (*pattasaññā*) is the perception regarding the bowl; one who possesses that is "one endowed with bowl-perception" (*pattasaññī*), meaning one who acts according to the specific rule and not otherwise.
The meaning is: "one whose perception is fixed solely upon one's own vessel. 1895.
*Bhattacatubbhāgo* means a portion equal to one-fourth of a meal. For one who takes more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
1896. Although it should have been stated as *rasarase*, it is expressed as *raserase* due to the requirements of the verse composition (*gāthābandha*). Having set aside two soups...
The remaining items—such as sour gruel (*oloṇī*), vegetable soups, meat soups, and meat juices—are to be understood as "flavors" (*rasa-rasa*).
Regarding this, some say: "Sour gruel (*oloṇī*) is cow’s milk product that has turned sour. Others say: "It is a particular kind of sauce (*byañjana-vikati*). Still others say:
"It is any pure liquid flavor such as rice-water (*kañjika*) or buttermilk (*takkā*). By the inclusion of the term "vegetable soups," any sauce prepared with edible vegetables is meant.
[The phrase] "meat broth, etc."—by the word "etc.," it should be understood that all remaining varieties of condiments are included.

Regarding "of relatives, etc.," the words "taking what belongs to them" (*santakaṃ gaṇhantassa*) are to be supplied. Regarding "for another purpose," the words "taking what has been prepared" (*kataṃ gaṇhantassa*) are to be supplied.
Regarding "with wealth," the words "his own," "bought," and "taking" (*gaṇhantassa*) are to be supplied. [This applies to] relatives, etc.

The meaning is that there is no offense for one who takes what belongs to another, for one who takes what was made for another purpose, or for one who takes what has been purchased with his own wealth.
[This concludes] the seventh, eighth, and ninth [cases]. 1897.
The construction is: a bowl that has reached the limit of its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) must be taken only when it is filled to the extent of the inner rim of its mouth.
1898. Having shown the scope of what is not an offense (*anāpatti*), he says "therein" (*tattha*) and so forth to show the scope of what is an offense (*āpatti*).
"Therein" means in the bowl that has been determined. Regarding the phrase "having made it into a heap" (*thūpīkataṃ katvā*), the word "being given" (*diyyamānaṃ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

The connection is: for one who accepts [the alms] being given after they have been made into a heap in such a way that it exceeds the aforementioned limit of writing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). By this...

It should be understood that both the subsequent receiving of alms-food after it has been heaped up in a bowl that was not previously determined [as a vessel], and the subsequent receiving of food after it has been heaped up in a bowl already received first, are prohibited. (1899) The construction is:

"Only the three types of timely food (kālaka), when heaped up, are permitted. Regarding the word "the rest": this refers to a bowl that was not previously determined. The construction is: "All four kinds of timely food, when heaped up, are permitted."
Regarding the word *peseti* (sends): here, the word "monks" (*bhikkhū*) is to be understood as the remainder. The construction is: "if a monk sends [something] to monks.

By the expression "of the monks," used to show the intention of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "it is permissible to send it to a monastery," it is indicated that there is no offense for those monks who receive what has been sent by a monk himself, provided they do not abandon the status of being recipients.
Otherwise, it would be understood that only this much should be said: "It is permissible to fill [it].
(1901) "Being inserted" means being inserted into the middle after having been raised above the rim of the opening.
"Fruit, etc."—by the word "etc.," rice and so forth are also included. "It descends downward" means it moves because there is space available on all sides.
It falls below the level of the mouth-opening. (1902) Regarding the phrase "of cardamom, etc.," the word "etc.
includes betel nuts and so forth. "Having placed" means having set it down upon the food. "A wreath" (*vaṭaṃsaka*) means a non-wreath (*avaṭaṃsaka*).

(1903) In the expression "of cake" (*pūvassa*), the genitive case is used to indicate a relationship of modification; thus, it is meant as "a cake-wreath. Because the cake is a "timely" (*yāvakālika*) substance, he says: "This may be made into a heap."
1904. Because the various types of food require separate containers, he said, "It is allowable.

1905. "Of him" means of the bhikkhu. "But all that" refers to everything that was stated as "it is not allowable because it has been heaped up"; all that [is meant]. "Well received" means that if it was received without violating the rules, it is properly received.
The tenth [section].

The Third Chapter. 1906. The word-division is “upari odhin” (above the limit). “Upari” means above the meal. “Odhin” means a boundary or limit. “Paṭipāṭiyā” means in successive order, starting from the edge of one’s own direction. 1907.
Regarding “aññesaṃ” (to others), the word “dento” (giving) is to be understood as the remainder. When giving one’s own food to others, [one should give] into another’s bowl...
The construction is as follows: if, while scattering [the food], one scatters it here and there even without following the proper sequence, there is no fault.
Likewise, if while scattering the *uttaribhaṅga*, one scatters it here and there, there is no fault. Furthermore, one who takes it for the purpose of eating should also be addressed in this regard.
*Uttaribhaṅga* means a condiment (*vyañjana*).
The third [offense].
1908. The construction is: “There is an offense for one who consumes [food] after pressing down the top.

According to the commentary’s statement, “‘Made into a mound’ means from the top, from the middle,” here the word *matthaka* refers to the top of the meal. “Having pressed down” means having pressed the food down with the hand.

1909. “Even when what remains is small” means even when the remainder is little. “Having gathered together” means having collected what was situated in its respective place. The construction is: “there is no offense for one who eats after having mashed it all into one. This is the fifth [offense]. 1910.
“Because of a desire for more” means because of a wish to take again. “Soup” means soup made of mung beans and so forth. “Condiment” means a further curry (*uttaribhaṅga*).

The sixth [offense]. 1911. Regarding "by means of a request": this refers to a request for soup or boiled rice. The phrase "from relatives, or from those who have invited him, or for the sake of another, or with his own wealth" is additional to the cases where there is no offense.
Even being ill, if one, with a sense of reproach, [takes] the bowl of others...

"An offense occurs for one who looks [at another's meal]"—thus he said: "Even if ill, one is not exempt from censure. In the phrase *ujjhāne*, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). "I will give":
having looked at this person's meal, thinking, "I will give what is missing there," or "I will have it given.
*Ujjhāna* is the state of mind that censures after having looked down upon [another]. *Ujjhānasaññā* is the perception regarding such censure; one who possesses that is so described.
The construction is: "It should be understood that there is no offense for one who does not perceive [the act] as a formal dispute.
This concludes the seventh and eighth [rules].
(1913) By the phrase "by their medium measure," it should be understood that the prohibition against small [measures] is established by way of what is inappropriate.
Regarding the phrase “not too large,” since what is excessively large is specifically prohibited, no offense is seen in the case of something small. *Kabaḷo* means a mouthful.
In the phrase “and in all cases of chewable food such as roots, etc.,” the construction is to be applied as follows: *phalāphale* refers to both small and large fruits. Ninth.
1915. There is nothing further to be said regarding the tenth [chapter].
The tenth.
The fourth section.
1916. Regarding the phrase “anāhaṭe,” its meaning is “not having reached the mouth-door. As it has been said:

“‘Anāhaṭe’ means ‘not brought in,’ the sense being ‘not having been delivered to the mouth-door. When only the words “of one opening the mouth-door” are stated, because the word “mouth-door” is a relative term, there arises an expectation for the question “whose?”;
thus, by means of the first person singular form “I shall open the mouth-door,” [the agent is specified].
It should be understood that he mentions himself in order to clarify this very meaning. The word *ca* has the sense of the particle *eva*;
it should be construed with *appatte va*, meaning "even when not yet arrived.
First.
1917. Regarding the phrase "the whole hand" (*sakalaṃ hatthaṃ*): here, the word "hand" (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to the fingers, which are parts thereof.

This is because, just as in expressions such as "a hand-seal" (*hatthamuddā*), a conventional term that applies to a whole may also apply to its individual parts; therefore, it is not permissible to put even a single finger into the mouth.
1918. "Of him" (*assa*) means of the bhikkhu. "Speaking" (*byāharantassa*) means while talking.
The second and third [cases] are the same.
1920. *Piṇḍukkhepakaṃ* means having repeatedly tossed up morsels of food.
Here too, there is no offense regarding cakes and fruits. *Kabaḷacchedakampi vā* means having cut the mouthfuls. Here, together with cakes and fruits...
There is no offense even regarding the subsequent portion of the meal. Regarding the phrase "having made a lump": here, there is no offense for merely taking a morsel of fruit.
[This concludes] the fourth, fifth, and sixth [rules].
1921–2. Regarding the phrase "having shaken the hand": this is to be connected with the statement "he eats his meal having shaken his hand."
"Scattering rice" means scattering grains of rice again and again. "Or protruding the tongue" means protruding the tongue again and again.
"Making the sound 'capu capū'" means making such a sound as "capu capū.
The seventh [training rule] is the precept: "Not shaking the hand. The eighth is the precept: "Not scattering rice."
"Throwing out the refuse" means the removal of rubbish.
The seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth [rules].
The fifth chapter.
1923. The construction is: one must not eat while making such a sound as “suru surū. Or, “licking with the hand” means licking the hand repeatedly.
1924. The construction is: it is permissible to eat even molasses or thick gruel by taking it with the fingers and inserting the fingers into the mouth.
1925. Even a single finger must not lick the bowl. Not even a single lip must be licked with the tongue.

The application [of the rules]: One must not lick the outer lip with the tongue. Whatever food, such as a grain of rice, may stick to the lip, it is permissible to take it up with both the lips themselves and place it inside the mouth.
[This concludes] the first, second, third, and fourth [rules].
1926–8. And it should not be taken; the construction is: "it is rejected because of its repulsiveness.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because," for which reason he will later say "therefore" (*tasmā*).
"A water vessel" (*pānīyathālaka*) is merely an illustration, since conch shells and other such items are likewise not to be taken. "Or a cup" (*sarāvaṃ vā*) means a shallow bowl (*taṭṭaka*).
"With a hand free from food" means with a portion of the hand that is devoid of food. As it is said:

"If, however, one part of the hand is not smeared with food, it is permissible to take [the bowl] with that portion. But there is no offense for one who takes [the bowl] with a hand smeared with food while thinking, "I shall wash it," or "I shall have it washed.
This is the fifth [offense].

1929. "Having removed" means: having removed the grains of rice from the bowl-washing water that contains them, there is no offense for one who discards that bowl-washing water outside the house, within the inhabited area (*antaraghara*). "Having broken up" means:

having crushed the grains of rice in the bowl-washing water that contains them, having mixed them with water and rendered them as mere water, [there is no offense] for one who [discards] that water outside the house.

There is no offense for one who discards [the water] within a house. Regarding "having taken": there is no offense for one who, having taken bowl-washing water containing rice grains, discards it into a receptacle.

The construction of the sentence should be understood as: "There is no offense for one who, having carried bowl-washing water containing rice grains outside the house, discards it within a house. In this context, "receptacle" (paṭiggaha) means:
Spittle, wrestling matches, and so forth; specifically, the vessel used for washing hands after eating. This is the sixth [category]. 1930.
"Any kind of umbrella" means: "An umbrella" refers to three types of umbrellas: the white umbrella, the palm-leaf umbrella, and...
Among the three types of umbrellas mentioned—“the leaf umbrella,” “the one bound with rings,” and “the one bound with strips”—it is any one of these.
Here, the “white umbrella” refers to a pale white umbrella covered with cloth. The “palm-leaf umbrella” refers to an umbrella made of *vilīva* leaves.
The “leaf umbrella” is made from any kind of leaves, such as palm leaves and so forth. Regarding the phrases “bound with rings” and “bound with strips”:
This, however, is stated for the purpose of showing the framework of all three types of umbrellas;
for they are indeed both circularly bound and bound by spokes. By the phrase "whatever [there may be]," which expresses an exhaustive inclusion, the *Aṭṭhakathā* states:
"Even that single-leaf umbrella made with a handle grown from right there is also indeed an umbrella."
He takes a particular kind of umbrella. Regarding the word "with the hand," the phrase "without letting go" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Regarding the phrase "with a part of the body," the word "having taken" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The particle *vā* has the sense of the particle *api*. The meaning is: even when holding it with a part of the body such as the shoulder, provided that one does not let go of it with the hand.
However, if someone else holds his umbrella for him, or he is standing on an umbrella-stand, or he is standing at the side, then as soon as the umbrella has left his hand,
he is no longer considered "one with an umbrella in hand" (chattapāṇi), and it is permissible to teach him the Dhamma. This is because of the statement,
"Not to one who has an umbrella in hand and is not ill," and because it will be stated here later that "in all cases, [it is not permissible] for one who is not ill."
And here the phrase “one who is not ill” is applicable. Furthermore, the analysis of the Dhamma (dhammapariccheda) here should be understood according to the method stated for the *padasodhamma*.
The same applies to what follows. This is the seventh [section].
1931. Regarding the phrase *daṇḍapāṇimhi*: here, the analysis (*viggaha*) is "one who has a staff in his hand.

To the question of what the measure of the staff is, he says, "measuring four cubits," and so forth. "From the middle-length hand" means from the hand of a person of medium stature, which is called a "carpenter’s cubit" (*vaḍḍhakihattha*).
The eighth [section].
1932. Regarding the term *satthapāṇissa*: here too, the analysis (*viggaha*) follows the same method as previously stated.

Excluding all varieties of bows and arrows that will be mentioned later, the remainder—such as swords and so forth—is called a weapon (*sattha*). Even one who stands having girded himself with a sword...

He said "one with a weapon in hand" (*satthapāṇī*) and so forth in order to dispel the suspicion that [the term] might mean "one with a sword in hand. The word division is "na hoti asiṃ" (it is not a sword). This is the ninth [section]. 1933–5.
[It refers to] a bow together with an arrow, or a plain bow, or a plain arrow, or a bow-staff equipped with a string.

The construction is as follows: even for one who stands, sits, or lies down while holding either a bow or a staff, if someone teaches him the true Dhamma characterized by the "step-by-step" (padasodhamma) method as described, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, if his bow is slung over his shoulder and he has not yet taken it up, it is permissible for that duration.
It occurs together with strife; thus, it is "with strife. Tenth.
The sixth chapter.

1936. Regarding "one who has put on sandals" (*pādukāruḷhaka*): one who has ascended onto sandals is "sandals-ascended" (*pādukāruḷha*); he himself is "the sandals-ascended one" (*pādukāruḷhaka*), [meaning] of him.
To explain how he has ascended, it says "having stepped upon," and so forth.

"Standing having stepped upon" means standing after having merely stepped upon the sandal itself, without inserting a space between the fingers and the handle of the parasol. "Or having fastened them" means standing after having fastened them.
Both of these are explanatory phrases for the term “of one who has put on sandals. As it is said:

“The Dhamma should not be taught to one who has put on sandals and is not ill. Whoever, out of disrespect, teaches the Dhamma to one who is not ill—whether that person has stepped into them, is wearing them, or has taken them off—commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
"Even for one who has sandals on" means even for one who has stepped onto or put on sandals in such a manner as walking upon them, and so forth; as it is said:

"whether stepping on them or having put them on. "In all cases" refers to all training rules (sikkhāpada), such as those concerning one with a sunshade in hand, and so forth. "For one who is not ill" means...
"This is to be connected" is the remainder [of the sentence]. The construction is: "If one teaches the Dhamma to someone who has gone by vehicle and is not ill, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
In that context, "having gone by vehicle" means: if two people are traveling together holding hands; or if they are being carried on a pole after being placed upon a mat;
or if they are in an unsuitable vehicle such as a cart (*vayha*) and so forth; or even if the vehicle is stationary, having been unhitched, for the distance of a wheel's breadth.
He is sitting; he is reckoned as one who has gone by vehicle.
Or, even when lying down—whether on a straw mat or on the bare ground—even for one who is not ill: this is the construction. As it is said:
“For one who has gone to bed means: even for one lying on a straw mat or on the natural ground. On a high seat...
The construction is as follows: it is not permissible for one sitting on a high seat, or standing, to teach while another is lying down.

By the word "standing," the phrase "sitting" is also included. Furthermore, when teaching one who has gone to a bed, it is permissible for the teacher—whether on the same level, or even on a higher level—to be likewise lying down; such is the construction.
1941. By the phrase “and likewise,” the word “is permissible” (*vaṭṭati*) is included.
[This concludes] the second, third, and fourth [sections].
1942. Although one should say “pallatthikāya nisinnassa” (of one sitting in the pallatthikā posture), the letter *y* has been elided for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse.

“Of one sitting in a cross-legged posture”: this is said; the meaning is: of one sitting in any kind of cross-legged posture, whether it be the *āyoga*-posture, the hand-posture, the cloth-posture, or any other such posture. “Of one with the head wrapped”:
of one whose head is wrapped—either with a cloth-wrapping or with a *moli* (turban) and so forth—in such a way that the hairline is not visible.

1943. If one teaches after having had the hair at the edge of the head uncovered, it is permissible—this is the construction. By the phrase “this alone is the determination,” the category of non-offense (anāpatti) is also stated, namely: “if one teaches after having had the head uncovered, it is permissible.
[This concludes] the fifth, sixth, and seventh [rules]. 1944–5. Regarding the eighth: “of one sitting on a seat” means even if one is sitting after having spread out a cloth or even blades of grass.
Regarding this, in the ninth [chapter], it is stated: “‘On a high seat’ means that it is not permissible to teach one who is seated even on a slightly elevated spot of ground”;
and in the tenth, setting aside the specific determination that will be explained starting with “Even if...”, because there is no further distinction to be stated, he says:

“In the eighth, or even in the ninth, in the tenth there is nothing at all. Here, the word “to be stated” (*vattabba*) is understood as the remainder. This concludes the section on the attendance upon elders (*therupaṭṭhāna*).
The construction of the sentence is: "If the elder, having approached, asks a question while the youth is standing and he himself is seated on a seat.
To show the method by which it should be explained, he said: "But when there is another person nearby, it should be explained by one who understands.

Here, the word "standing" (*ṭhitassa*) is understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. In the absence of anyone else present near him, it is permissible to speak even after resolving upon a recitation (*sajjhāya*).
The eighth, ninth, and tenth [rules].
The seventh chapter. 1946.
Regarding the phrase "in front of one who is walking," the remainder is "by one walking behind. By one walking behind...
The construction is: "One should not speak a question to one who is walking ahead. If the one walking ahead asks a question, he says "of the one behind," etc., to indicate what should be done. 1947.
While walking behind, one should recite the Dhamma already mastered together with the one walking ahead.
"It is appropriate" is the construction. "It is appropriate to speak of holding the yoke for those walking together" is the construction.
"Holding the yoke" means mutually; for the word *yugaggāha* is a synonym for the word *aññamañña* (mutually).
First.
1948. It is permissible to teach the Dhamma to one who is walking along the track of each wheel of a cart on a cart-track, provided they are walking at the same pace as the track of each wheel.
It is also permissible to teach the Dhamma to one who is walking off the track, provided they are walking at the same pace as the off-track path—this is the application of the phrase *ajjhāhāra*.
"Off the track" (*uppathena*) means by a non-path. Thus, regarding the sphere where there is no offense:
It should be understood that by way of the opposite of what has been shown, the scope of the offense is already indicated.
Second. 1949.
Regarding the third [offense], there is nothing further to be said: "I shall not, while standing and not being ill, void excrement or urine."
The analysis of this is stated on the grounds that it is easily understood according to the literal meaning.
If, while going to a concealed place, excrement or urine is discharged suddenly, it is called "done unintentionally," and there is no offense.
This is the distinction to be observed here. Although nasal mucus is included within the category of saliva, among the thirty-two bodily constituents—
Since a single category was shown separately, he said "the fourfold beginning with excrement," including even that which is not mentioned among the training rules (sikkhāpada).
1950. Here, in order to show what is meant by "greenery" (harita), he said "of a living tree," and so forth.
The word "tree" is an illustration (upalakkhaṇa), because living grasses, creepers, and the like are also included within "greenery. By the very statement "it goes while being seen,"...
"It is not green when it has gone out of sight" is understood through contrast (*byatirekato*). "Or a branch touching the ground, even if visible, passes by;
all that is indeed green"—this is the construction (*yojanā*).

1951. "Feces come out suddenly"—this is the connection. "Of this monk" refers to the bhikkhu. "Feces" (*vacca*) is an indicative term (*upalakkhaṇa*), since urine and so forth are also shown [to be included]. "It is allowable" (*vaṭṭati*); here the remainder is "because he is standing in a place for the sick."

1952. “In a heap of straw” (*palālaṇḍupake*) means even in a bundle of straw. Here, the phrase “by one who cannot find green grass” is to be supplied as the remainder. “On anything whatsoever” (*kismiñci*) means on any [dry] grass or the like. The construction is: “He covers that excrement afterwards with green grass;

it is permissible. 1953. “Goes” (*eti*) means enters. “In this” (*ettha*) refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The word division is “and by spittle alone” (*kheḷena eva cā*). These are the third and fourth [sections].

1954. Regarding the phrase "in the waters of Vaccakuṭi, the ocean, and so forth": here, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), all water that is unfit for use is included. For this very reason, he states the reason as "because they are unfit for use.

1955. Regarding the phrase "in a water-hole": here, the word "when it has arisen" (jāte) is to be supplied. "Non-water" (ajala) refers to a place that is not water. "In water" (jala) refers to water fit for use. Here too, if water flows over from dry land, there is no offense. This is the fifth [offense].
The Eighth Chapter. 1956–7. To demonstrate the miscellaneous determinations (*pakiṇṇaka-vinicchaya*), he says: "Origination and so forth," etc.

"Are to be known" means they are to be understood by the method that will be explained. "In this" refers to these rules of training (*sekhiya*). The analysis is: "those for whom laughing loudly and so forth are primary"; this is a term used to indicate their specific qualities.
This is a *bāhirattha-samāsa* (compound with external referent); the meaning is that these are four training rules connected with loud laughter and low voices.
"The ground, a low seat, standing, behind, and a by-path" constitute *chamā-nīcāsana-ṭhāna-pacchā-uppathā*;
since those sounds are present in these training rules, they are the training rules connected with them, namely: *chamā... pe ... uppathavā*.
The meaning is: "the five training rules (sikkhāpada) beginning with the one on touching (chamā).

Here, by the word *ṭhāna*, because it is simply a form of the verbal root *ṭhā*, the word *ṭhita* occurring in the training rule is understood. Where "in ten" (*dasasu*) should have been said, it is stated as "ten" (*dasā*) either through the elision of a vowel (*vaṇṇalopa*) or by a transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*).
Regarding the formal origination (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors in the admonition (*samanubhāsana*), [one should know] the formal originations and so forth among these ten training rules.
The construction is: "they are said to be equal.
What is meant? It is meant that these ten training rules (sikkhāpada) originate from formal admonition;

each one here is an action (kiriya), is exempt from [the need for] perception (saññāvimokkha), involves consciousness (sacittaka), is a worldly offense (lokavajja), is bodily action (kāyakamma), is vocal action (vacīkamma), is an unwholesome state of mind (akusalacitta), and is painful feeling (dukkhavedanā).
“*Chatta*,” etc., are the characteristic terms for the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). The construction is as follows:
these eleven training rules are indeed equal—that is, identical—in terms of their origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth, as well as in the teaching of the Dhamma.

This is what is meant: these eleven training rules originate from the teaching of the Dhamma; they are actions that do not entail transgression (*kiriya-akiriya*); and they are released through mere perception (*saññā-vimokkha*).
[These are] states accompanied by consciousness, offenses blameworthy according to the world, verbal actions, unwholesome states of mind, and painful feelings.
"A request for rice and curry" refers to the training rule on requesting indicated by the words "rice and curry. Because there are many training rules on requesting, this one alone is specified.
It is considered equal to the "caravan of thieves" training rule in terms of its origin and other characteristics.
"They consider it the same" means the sense [is identical]. This is what is stated:

the training rule regarding the solicitation of soup and rice is originated by theft, is an action, is liberated by awareness, involves a conscious mind, is a worldly offense, is bodily action, is verbal action, is unwholesome consciousness, and is painful feeling.
(1960) "The remaining fifty-three" refers to the remaining fifty-three training rules. "But they are the same as the first" means...
The meaning is that they are identical in terms of their origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth with the first *pārājika*; it is said that they have an origin similar to the first *pārājika*.

The word-division is: “There is no offense in cases of distress (*āpadāsu*). “Distress” refers to dangers such as attacks by thieves for those who are walking about having dressed and covered themselves properly.
By the word “also” (*api*), crossing a river and so forth are included. Regarding “in all the *sekhiyas*”:
This was stated by way of the majority.

As for the section on non-offenses beginning with, “I shall not look at the bowl of others with a critical mind,” it was not mentioned in the Pāḷi because it is impossible for such a case to occur within this [category]. Nevertheless, the offenses for that [section] should be understood as being exactly according to their respective bases (vatthu).
Thus ends [the portion from] the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.

This is the second [offense]. 2104. If she herself seizes it, having exchanged the robe with another nun, and afterwards...
"If you take your robe, give me mine"—if one seizes [the robe] oneself in this manner, the phrase "with the perception that it is one's own" (*sakasaññāya*) is to be supplied here.
Because it was taken with the perception that it is one's own, a *pācittiya* offense and a *dukkaṭa* offense are stated;
otherwise, one is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
2105. *Itaresu* (in the others) includes both the absence of binding and the multiplicity of commands. Therefore he said: "It may be according to the basis and the application. 2106.

With reference to the phrase "threefold pācittiya," it should be connected with the word "declared" (*uddiṭṭhā*). The meaning is that a threefold pācittiya is stated by way of these three cases: [the nun] perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained, being in doubt, or perceiving one who is not fully ordained as such. In another...
“He exchanges” means [exchanging] one requisite for another requisite among those who are ordained and those who are not ordained. “For the other” means for one who is not ordained.

Regarding the “triple offense of wrong-doing” (tikadukkaṭa): it is taught as a triple offense of wrong-doing by way of the cases where one perceives a person who is not ordained as being ordained, where one is doubtful, and where one perceives them as not ordained.

2107. The construction is as follows: there is no offense for one who receives what is being given by her, or what is being given by another nun—whether that other nun be ill-disposed or well-disposed—or for one who receives it out of trust in her.
“It is considered to have three origins” means exactly what has already been stated.
The third [case].
2108. But whichever nun, when addressed with the words, "What is your discomfort, noble lady?

What should be brought for you?", requests something else, and having rejected what was brought, desires to take both that and the other, if she then requests the other, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the request;

if she obtains it, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). This is the construction according to the underlying intention. An offense of wrong-doing for the requesting is "offense-of-wrong-doing-for-requesting" (*viññattidukkaṭa*).

2109–11. It is said that there is a triad of *pācittiyas*: “If one asks for one thing while perceiving it as another, or while being in doubt, or while perceiving it as not another, and then receives what was asked for, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.

Thus the triad of *pācittiyas* is stated. Regarding “not another,” there is a dyad of *dukkaṭas*: by way of perceiving what is not another as another, and by way of being in doubt. This is according to the passage beginning, “Perceiving what is not another as another,” and so forth.
The scope of non-offense has been shown. The phrase “regarding what is not another, with the perception that it is not another” is to be analyzed as follows:

there is no offense for one who makes herself understood regarding what is not another, with the perception that it is not another. There is no offense for one who makes herself understood [only] when that which was first requested is not being provided, or who makes herself understood regarding that very same thing.
There is also no offense for one who, while there is another purpose, makes herself understood regarding something else along with that [other purpose]. This is what was said.

There is [no offense]: if ghee was first requested, and because the physician stated that "raw meat must be cooked," there is a need for oil, and she then requests another thing saying, "I also have need of oil.
It should be understood that there is no offense even for one who requests something else after pointing out a benefit. This is what is meant.
"If ghee has been brought for one kahāpaṇa, twice as much oil can be obtained for this same price;
and since this purpose can also be accomplished with oil, therefore bring oil"—having thus shown the advantage, he makes the request.
This is the fourth [case].

2112–3. *Pubbaṃ aññaṃ cetāpetvā* (having exchanged something else for what was previously [given]) is the construction; the meaning is: having caused another thing to be traded for one's own allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*) by saying, "Bring such-and-such.
In the word *evaṃ*, the word *vutte* (when it has been said) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Grain produced by means of wealth—here, oil and the like are intended by the term "grain" (*dhañña*) because they are accomplished through one's own wealth, not rice and so forth.
When this has been said, the construction is as follows: with the thought, "He will bring another grain and give it to me," one might later cause another to be bartered for;

or, when told, "I have no need of this, bring something else," with the thought, "Having given this, he will bring and give another," one might later cause another to be exchanged, thinking, "This does not please me, bring something else. This is the meaning.
"By means of causing to be purchased" means by way of the act of purchasing on behalf of one who has been commanded. "From the original source" means from the one who gave the command.
The construction is: whether it has been brought by that person or by another, upon the acquisition of it, there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya).
2114. "The rest" refers to the specific details of the classification beginning with the three offenses of wrongdoing (pācittiya).
The fifth [offense].
2115–6. "Given for another purpose" means given by lay followers (*upāsaka*) for the sake of something else, with the instruction: "Having taken this, divide it and consume it.
This is connected with the phrase "with requisites belonging to the Saṅgha. Regarding "requisites":

"By means of an allowable article. "Belonging to the Saṅgha" means that which has been relinquished to the Saṅgha. "Here" means in this Dispensation. "Of her" refers to the one by whom it was caused to be bartered.
"It may be subject to relinquishment": here it should be stated that what is obtained after having been relinquished must be returned to the giver.
As it is said: "Having obtained what was relinquished, it must be returned to the giver. This [is explained] below.
The meaning and intention are exactly as stated. Regarding the phrase "in this [case]": it refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Because it is stated, "If one perceives something not intended for another purpose as being intended for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); if one is in doubt regarding something not intended for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing," he said, "In the case of what is specified as 'not intended for another purpose,' two *dukkaṭas* are indicated.
By this, it is already implied that "in the case of what is intended for another purpose, there is a threefold offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)."

“For one who exchanges [something] for something else when it is intended for something else, or when she is in doubt, or when she has the perception that it is not intended for something else—[if she] causes another to exchange [it], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Thus it is said. 2117.
“The remainder”: having exchanged for something else what was given for a specific purpose and brought it back, [if she uses] the surplus value for another purpose...
It should be construed as: "there is no offense for one who brings it.
"Having asked the owner" means having asked the owner thus: "This was given by you for the sake of robes; we already have robes, but we have need of oil and such things.
"That" refers to that which was used for exchange. "In times of distress" refers to a calamity necessitating that the bhikkhunīs leave the monastery.
As it is said: "In times of distress" means that when such calamities arise, the bhikkhunīs abandon the monastery and depart;
in such emergencies, it is permissible to have whatever is needed procured. 2118. Regarding "woven from what was personally requested" (*saṃyācitaka*):
this is stated because, without the word *vināti* (weaves), this term alone is distinct [from the others].

The sixth and seventh [sections]. 2119. To show the additional statement, he said: "By means of what is common to the multitude, by what is borrowed, and by what is requested. *Padatādhikā* means that the word itself is the state of being a word (*padatā*). *Mahājanikena* means by what has been relinquished to a group. *Saññācikenā* means by what one has personally requested. 2120.

*Anantarasamā matā* means that here, the term "by what belongs to an individual" (*puggalikena*) is understood together with the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), etc., even without the explicit mention of that word.

The meaning is that all the legal decisions (*vinicchaya*) are considered similar to the immediately preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*). For the training rule states: “Whichever nun, however, with a requisite intended for another purpose and designated for another, [uses it] as personal property (*puggalika*)... Here, “personal property” means what has been relinquished to a single nun.
They write “kiñcipi” (even a little), but the reading “kocipi” (even some) is better, because it shares the same grammatical core (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) with the word “viseso” (distinction).
The eighth, ninth, and tenth [rules].
The First Chapter.
2121–2. Four *kaṃsas* combined, or the collection of four *kaṃsas*, is a "four-*kaṃsa*" (*catukkaṃsa*); from a four-*kaṃsa*...
"Exceeding by more than four kaṃsas" means a cloak worth more than four kaṃsas;
it is stated as "exceeding by more than four kaṃsas" by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*). As for the measure of a *kaṃsa* here, he himself will state:
"Four kahāpaṇas, indeed, are called a *kaṃsa*. Therefore, the meaning is: worth more than sixteen kahāpaṇas. "A heavy cloak" (*garupāvuraṇaṃ*)...
A cloak to be worn during the cold season. "Should cause to be given" means should request it. The Four Truths taken together, or the collection of the four truths, is the "Four Truths" (catusacca);
one who has the nature of proclaiming that is a "Proclaimer of the Four Truths" (catusaccappakāsī).
By him—by the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), the expounder of the Four Noble Truths. In the application [of the phrase], such as "Give!"—thus.
In the act of making known. "Acquisition" means obtaining.
A group of four is a "tetrad"; a tetrad of kahaṇapas is a "kahaṇapa-tetrad.

And here, the kahaṇapa should be understood as that which is current in currency at the particular time and in the particular place. These aforementioned offenses, ending with those involving forfeiture (nissaggiya).

Regarding the phrase "and in the possession of relatives," since this will be explained as a sphere where there is no offense, it should be understood that this applies to a place where an invitation has been made in the following manner—

not by making a permanent invitation (niccapavāraṇā) such as, "Whenever you have need of anything, then please speak for it," but rather, having gained confidence in someone's virtue at that time, saying, "Please speak for whatever you have need of.
It is to be seen as occurring in such a situation where an invitation has been thus granted.

Because it is stated: “If [the value] is less than four kārṣāpaṇas and one perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If [the value] is less than four kārṣāpaṇas and one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing,” he said: “But when [the value] is less than four kārṣāpaṇas, two dukkaṭas are prescribed.

By this, [it is shown that] if one causes [an item] to be bartered for when it is more than four kārṣāpaṇas—whether perceiving it as more, being doubtful, or perceiving it as less—it is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
The phrase "an offense entailing expiation" (pācittiya) thus indicates both the triad of expiations.
"Heavy" refers to a heavy cloak. "Or less than that" means less than four kamsas.

Regarding the phrase "and for relatives," the word "and" (ca) here includes those who have invited [the monk to accept food). As it is said in the section on non-offenses: "for relatives, for those who have invited."
And here, it should be stated as “even more than fourfold,” because by the phrase “or less than that,” a deficiency of fourfold is expressed.
By the phrase “or even a small amount,” it should be understood that something of greater value than even fourfold is also expressed.
The eleventh [section].

2126–7. Regarding the statement, “When a bhikkhunī has light clothing made, it should be made at a maximum value of two and a half kaṃsas,” the words “by the bhikkhunī having [it] made” are to be supplied after “light clothing,” and the words “should be made” are to be supplied after “worth two and a half kaṃsas.
“Light clothing” refers to a cloak for use during the hot season. It is that which fills three [kaṃsas].
"Three and a half" means "three plus a half," hence *aḍḍhateyya*. That which is a *kaṃsa* weighing three and a half [units] is called a *aḍḍhateyyakaṃsa*;
that which is worth such a [weight] is *aḍḍhateyyakaṃsagghana*, meaning it is worth ten *kahāpaṇas*. "From that" means from that which is worth a *aḍḍhateyyakaṃsa*.
Furthermore, the cloak (*pāvuraṇa*) that is worth a *aḍḍhateyyakaṃsa* is a light cloak (*lahupāvuraṇa*). From that [cloak] worth a *aḍḍhateyyakaṃsa*.

Regarding "from a light cloak": *uttariṃ* means "in excess. The construction is as follows: "If a nun causes a cloak worth two and a half *kaṃsa*-coins to be purchased, upon the acquisition of that cloak, an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) is stated for that nun.
To support the statement "the remainder is equal to the preceding," he said, "there is no distinction whatsoever. *Visesatā* is simply the state of being a distinction (*viseso*).
The Twelfth. 2128.

Now, in order to show the reason why some of the thirty-two *nissaggiya* offenses mentioned in the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* are not mentioned by himself, and to show that those mentioned together with those not mentioned are included [in the category of common offenses], he says: "They are common," and so forth. For...
