The construction is as follows: since there are eighteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) common to both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs— namely, those other than the ones mentioned here— and twelve training rules of the same form as those mentioned here,
there are exactly thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* training rules in total for bhikkhunīs.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discussion of the Nissaggiya Offenses within the Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā,
which is an Elucidation of the Essence of the Meaning of the Vinaya.
Now begins the commentary on the Discussion of the Pācittiya Offenses.
2129–30. Having thus shown the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* rules, he now says “garlic,” etc., in order to show the pure *pācittiya* rules.
Regarding the word “garlic” (*lasuṇaṃ*), the particle *iti* here is indicated as being elided.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that “garlic” refers to a bundle; garlic is defined as a bundle consisting of four or five cloves and so forth, but not less than that.

Therefore he said, "not having even one, two, or three seeds. He stated the distinction [of this garlic] from that which grows in a cultivated field and from that which originates on the island of Sīhaḷa by saying, "only raw Māgadha.
"Māgadha" means grown in Magadha; it connects with the word "sown. As it has been said:
"Only the garlic grown in the kingdom of Magadha is intended here by the term 'garlic' (lasuṇa). Thinking, "I will eat that,"...
The connection is with the word "takes. To show that the aforementioned *pācittiya* offense occurs by way of swallowing, he said:
"One should indicate the *pācittiya* precisely by way of swallowing.

He will state this very point in the passage beginning with "two or three," and so forth. "Together" means at once. "Having chewed" means having crushed it with the teeth without having first introduced it into the cavity of the throat. "Swallows" means one makes it go down into the gullet.

2132. *Tattha* means in that *bhaṇḍikala-suṇa*. By the phrase “by the counting of the kernels (*miñjānaṃ gaṇanāyā”*), it is shown that the counting refers specifically to the number of instances of swallowing. As it has been said: “But for one who eats each kernel after breaking it open, there are offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the count of the instances.
2133. The construction is: “...is permissible by its very nature (*sabhāvato vaṭṭanteva*). 2135.
In order to show the distinctions among the aforementioned onions (*palaṇḍuka*) and so forth, he says: “One kernel,” and so on. Here, regarding the kernels...
The diversity has been shown by way of [their] function alone. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is also by way of color.
As it says: "The *palaṇḍuka* is pale in color; the *bhañjanaka* is red in color; the *haritaka* is green-leaf-colored. 2136.
The word division is "sāḷave uttaribhaṅgake. This is because of the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "In cases such as *badara-sāḷava* and so forth."
In this context, the word *badara* is the remainder [of the compound]. A *badarasāḷava* is a type of food preparation made by drying and pulverizing jujube fruits (*badaraphala*).
Regarding the phrase "for one who is insane, etc.," the word "etc. includes a beginner. As it is said: "For one who is insane, for a beginner.
The first [section].
2137. *Sambādheti* means in a concealed place. To show its classification, he says: “or even in making urine on the pubic hair. 2138. The connection is:
“for her, there is likewise a *pācittiya* offense. By the phrase “not by counting the hairs,” this very point—that it is “by counting the acts” (*payoga*)—is supported.
2139. *Ābādheti* refers to diseases such as itching and the like. As it is said: “‘On account of an affliction’ means on account of afflictions such as itching, scabies, and so forth.”
"Considered equal to the preparation for the path" means it is considered and known to be similar to the training rule concerning traveling together with a nun after having made such an arrangement.
This is the second [offense]. 2140. Even by the mere filament of a red lotus or a white lotus, [one should not touch] the urinary organ with lustful desire.
The construction is as follows: "In striking the palm [of the hand], even the giving of a blow with the urinary organ is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even with the filament" (*kesarena pi*), it is indicated that there is no need to mention [striking] with large lotus leaves. As it has been said:
"At the very least, 'even with a lotus leaf'—here, the leaf is indeed large; yet for one who gives a blow even with the filament, there is an offense."
2141. “Therein” means on that surface of the urinary organ. This is the third [offense]. 2142.
But whichever bhikkhunī, overcome by sensual lust, oppressed by sensual lust, [inserts her finger] into her own female organ...
The construction is: "If she inserts even a lotus petal, it is not permitted; it is a *pācittiya* offense. By the word "even" (*pi*), the *Aṭṭhakathā* is alluded to:
"But for one who inserts even a mere filament, there is indeed an offense. [Sutta 2143–4:
If this is so, why was it stated that "in the case of a dildo (*jatumaṭṭhaka*), it is a *pācittiya*"? To this he says: "This... [is] the dildo."
This account of the "lump of resin" (*jatumaṭṭhaka*) was spoken by way of the actual event:
"Then that bhikkhunī, having taken the lump of resin and forgetting to wash it, threw it aside to one side.
When the bhikkhunīs saw it surrounded by flies, they said, 'Whose work is this? She replied, 'This is my work. Those bhikkhunīs..."
The modest nuns were indignant, critical, and complained, saying, “How can a bhikkhunī take up a waxed dildo?
This was stated specifically in reference to the case that has come down to us; the intention is that no other type of dildo could possibly exist apart from that one.
A "waxed dildo" (jatumaṭṭhaka) is a smooth rod made of wax.

Regarding the word *daṇḍa* (staff), the phrase “anything whatsoever” (*yaṃ kiñci*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the definition]. As it is said: “Even so little as a lotus leaf, she inserts into the urinary tract.
And this [measure] is still too much; for one who inserts even a mere filament, there is indeed an offense.
*Eḷāluka* refers to the fruit of the *kakkāri* plant. *Tasmiṃ* means in her own urinary tract.
2145. *Ābādhapaccayā* means by way of the condition of a wound or the like arising in the region of the urinary organ; that is, by way of the condition of applying ointment to the site of a wound.
This is the fourth [condition]. 2146. *Aggapabbadvayādhikaṃ* means exceeding even by the measure of a hair-tip the two top joints. As it is said: "At the very least..."
“If she exceeds [the limit] by even as much as the tip of a hair, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
Regarding “performing water-purification”: this refers to performing a washing in the place of the urinary organ. As it is said: “Water-purification is called the washing of the urinary organ.
By the word “three,” he indicates that there is no fault in washing after inserting two joints of a single finger.

"Longitudinally" means along the length of the finger. The construction is: "If she inserts three joints into the urinary organ and takes up water for purification, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). 2148.
If one inserts [the finger] in width by joining three or four fingers together, it constitutes an offense even if only a single joint has entered.
Regarding the phrase "not exceeding two finger-joints," it is said "even a single joint" because it refers to exceeding the fixed measure.
The construction is as follows: for whatever nun who inserts even a single joint of four or three fingers in width [into the vagina], there shall be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

2149. *Iti* means "thus. *Sabbappakārena* means by every manner, such as the entry into the deep and so forth. *Abhibyattataraṃ katvā* means having made it more clearly manifest. *Ayam attho* refers to this meaning stated [in the rule] beginning with "three [finger-joints] on one finger," and so forth.
2150. The construction is: "there is no fault in [measuring] two finger-joints.

However, even when there is the acceptance of contact, provided it is for the purpose of cleansing with water, there is no offense within the aforementioned limit. *Adhikaṃ pi* means even more than two finger-joints. [This applies to] cleansing with water.
The construction is: "There is no fault for her who performs [the act]" (2151).
Likewise, the construction is: "It is declared that there is no offense for those who perform purification with water, such as women who are insane, etc.
This is the fifth.
"But for a bhikkhu who is eating" means for a bhikkhu who is eating any one of the five kinds of cooked food.
As it is said: "For one who is eating means for one who is eating any one of the five kinds of cooked food.
"Or a drink, or a fan" refers to the drink and the fan that will be mentioned later. "Should stand near" means within arm's reach.
From the statement "he stands," it should be understood that here the prefix *upa-* denotes proximity, defined as being within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*).

2153. The construction is: "any [object] such as a corner of a robe-cloth (*vatthakoṇa*) or the like is called a 'fan' (*bījanī*). By this, the meaning is: anything of the nature of a corner of a robe-cloth taken up with the resolve, "I shall perform the function of fanning," is called a "fan.
2154. "Then that bhikkhunī, while that bhikkhu was eating, [served him] with drinking water and a fan..."
Having approached and addressed her, that bhikkhu then rebuked the bhikkhunī, saying: “Sister, do not do such a thing;
this is not allowable. [She replied: “Previously you were doing such and such to me, but now you cannot endure even this much!
Having struck the water-bowl against her head, she dealt a blow with a fan. In this regard—
When the matter had been reported by the monks, [the Buddha] said, "How indeed, monks, could a bhikkhunī give a blow to a bhikkhu?

and so forth; then, because it was stated, "Whichever bhikkhunī should stand near a bhikkhu while he is eating, whether with drinking water or a fan, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," [the author] says this in order to dispel the suspicion that [this rule] might instead be a cause for the offense of giving a blow.
“The offense due to the condition of standing within arm’s reach is explained here. And here, “having struck” means having caused to fall.
“Here” refers to this training rule. Having taken what was stated in the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka—“Monks, a blow must not be given by a bhikkhunī to a bhikkhu.
Whoever should give one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)”—he said, “it was spoken regarding the condition of a blow.”
"In the Khandhaka, the *dukkaṭa* [offense] is separate"—by this, the reason for what was stated is shown. 2155.
Regarding "having left the reach of the hand" (*hatthapāsaṃ jahitvā*): here, in the phrase "for one eating food" (*bhojanaṃ bhuñjato*), it should be said "having left the reach of the hand";

and in the phrase "eating a hard food" (*khādanaṃ khādato*), it should be said "within the reach of the hand" (*hatthapāse*). For one who stands near while another is eating food having left the reach of the hand...
The construction is as follows: there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for one who stands within arm’s reach of someone who is eating or chewing.
2156. "Gives" means she gives water or curry and so forth, saying, "Drink this; eat with this. She gives a palm-leaf fan, saying, "Fan yourselves with this while you eat.
"Causes to be given" means she causes both to be given by another. This is the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The construction is: "They consider it equal to wool from a sheep's fleece by way of its origin.
This is the sixth [case].
2157. "Having requested" means either having requested oneself, or having had another request it on one's behalf. "Either having requested or having had it requested."
This is indeed a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Raw grain" (*āmaka-dhañña*) refers to the seven kinds of grain, such as *sāli* rice, that are uncooked and unhusked.
As it is said: "Raw grain means *sāli*, *vīhi*, barley, wheat, *kaṅgu*, *varaka*, and *kudrūsaka*.
"Having pounded" means having pounded with pestles. The construction is: "if he consumes [it]."
“‘He receives it [thinking], "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)'—this is called an offense of wrong-doing in the preliminary action (payoga-dukkata).

Therefore, the offense of wrong-doing does not occur only at the moment of receiving. By saying this, he states the classification found in the Aṭṭhakathā, beginning with "But not only in the case of grains," etc.
The word *pana* has the sense of the particle *api*; thus, the meaning is "even in the case of drying. "For the purpose of roasting" means...
Here, the phrase “on the day of the storm” is to be understood as the ellipsis. “In the preparation of the pans and the preparation of the hearth” should be construed with each [term] individually.
“In the preparation of the pestle” means in the making of the ladle. Therein, the construction is: “in the throwing of grain into the pan.
Although one should have said “rubbing and pounding,” the letter *na* has been elided for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse, hence it is stated as “rubbing-pounding” (*ghaṭṭakoṭṭane*).
2161-3. Because the word *pamāṇa* (measure) possesses fixed gender and number, it is said: "The measure of the intimation is the food itself.
Fixed gender and number means having a restricted gender and singular or plural number. Thus, here the word *pamāṇa* is used in the fixed neuter gender and the fixed singular number.
Herein, in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), these two—namely, the food itself and the intimation—are [the factors].

The construction is as follows: since it is indeed the measure (*pamāṇa*), therefore, whether she herself has it cooked, or causes others such as her husband to cook it, or having had it cooked by another, she herself cooks it, whichever nun consumes it, for each act of consumption she incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
This is the application of the rule.
In order to show the determination as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*, he said: "Having asked his mother," and so forth.
Here, the word *vā* (or) is used for the purpose of indicating an alternative; the word *pi* (also/even) is used in the sense of inclusion.

Whoever, having asked his mother, or his father, or another relative, or having been invited [to accept], asks for raw grain, or causes it to be prepared by another, and then consumes it—[that is the offense].
The construction is: "for her, it is a *pācittiya*.

2164. The construction is: for one who consumes what was obtained without a formal request—either having roasted it herself, or having had another do so, or having had someone else prepare it—it is a *dukkaṭa*.
2165. However, for one who swallows what was obtained through a formal request made by another—whether she had it prepared by that person or prepared it herself—[it is a *pācittiya*].
The construction is: "In that case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This is stated by adopting the method found in the *Mahāpaccarī*.

However, since it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that "there is a dukkaṭa for one who eats what has been requested by another," it should be understood that a dukkaṭa is indeed prescribed even for one who, having obtained raw grain through a request from another, causes it to be prepared by her or prepares it herself and then consumes it.

“2166–7. For the purpose of fomentation and so forth”: for the purpose of treating those afflicted by wind-diseases (*vāta-roga*) and the like with fomentation and other such remedies. Here, the phrase “even in a place where one is not related or has not been invited” is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule].

This same principle applies to monks as well. The construction should be understood as follows: “Excepting the seven types of grain, there is no offense even for requesting other things in a place where one is related or has been invited.

“For the purpose of requesting other things” means for the purpose of requesting things other than the grains already mentioned, such as mung beans, black gram, bottle gourds, pumpkin gourds, and so forth.

Because it has been stated that the seven types of grain, beginning with rice, constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and because they are not to be touched, he said "even from relatives" and so forth to show that they are in no way whatsoever permitted.
2168. "Obtained" means being currently received. "In regard to new construction works" means for the purpose of new construction; the locative case is used here in the sense of a cause or occasion.
Here, the word "to accept" is to be supplied. However, that which is obtained without prior solicitation may be accepted for the purpose of new construction works.
"It is permissible," so it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
Seventh. 2169.
"Refuse" means rubbish. "Or scraps" refers to fish bones, meat bones, bone fragments, mouth-wash water, and so forth that have been left over.
"Whatever. Regarding "should discard": here, the word "himself" (*sayam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis, because it will later be stated that "he should have others discard it.
"Across the wall" (*tirokuṭṭaṃ*): this means on the other side of the wall; the meaning is "on the far side of the wall.
Alternatively, since it will later be stated that "this same principle applies to a rampart," "wall" (*kuṭṭa*) should be taken here as referring to a partition wall.
2171. Here, the word “offense” (*āpatti*) is the remainder [of the sentence]. It is connected with the word “of that” (*tassā*). 2172.

Regarding the phrase “in discarding,” the particle *pi* is indicated as being elided. The construction is: “Even in the discarding of a tooth-stick, it is shown that for a bhikkhunī there is a *pācittiya* offense.
2173–4. “In all cases” means in all the aforementioned alternatives. To show the scope of non-offenses (*anāpatti*), he said:

“Even when discarding,” and so forth. The construction is as follows: there is no offense even for one who discards [the object] without looking at a place where it is not used (*avalañja*), or even for one who discards it after looking at a place where it is used (*valañja*).
Discarding is an action (*kriyā*); not looking is a non-action (*akriyā*). This is the eighth [offense].

2175–6. Furthermore, if a bhikkhunī herself discards, or causes others to discard, those four things— namely, food scraps, excrement, sweepings, and urine— in a field, in a coconut grove or similar garden, or anywhere else where cultivated greenery grows,
the determination of the offense for that bhikkhunī is according to the method already stated beginning with the words "each one," and so forth.
The construction is: "in the manner already described.

2177–8. Furthermore, if a nun sits down in a green field and eats, or likewise, while eating sugarcane and such things in that green field, or if she walks away while eating, or if she leaves behind leftover water or scraps of food, etc., [she incurs an offense].
The construction is: "If she discards it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). "Calaka" means that which causes vomiting.
2179. The construction is: "In such a green place, even for one who discards a coconut—though its top has been cut off—after drinking its water, there may be an offense.
2180. "Of all" refers to both monks and nuns.

2181. Even if a field has been cleared, if people guard it for the purpose of sowing again, then for that nun who voids excrement or urine in that very field, the offense is a *pācittiya* exactly as it was in the original case;
this is the construction of the meaning. By the phrase “for her, as in the original case,” it is already stated that for a monk there is a *dukkaṭa*.
2182. "In a field abandoned by people" means in a field from which the crops have been harvested by humans.
As it is said: "When humans have harvested the crop and departed, it is called an 'abandoned field';

there, it is permissible. Thus, even in a field where no work has been done, it is permissible to do so after asking the owner's permission. As it is said: "Having asked the owner, he abandons [the field]. Here, the field-keepers...
And the guardians of parks and so forth are indeed the owners themselves.

Regarding a field or park belonging to the Saṅgha, if there is no agreement that "rubbish must not be discarded there," it is permissible for a monk to discard it because it is included within the property of the Saṅgha;

however, it is not [permissible] for nuns. For them, however, it is not permissible according to the method stated for the community of monks, nor is it [permissible] for that monk [if it belongs to the nuns].
Even though this is so, it should be performed in accordance with what is appropriate. "All" refers to the fourfold [offenses] beginning with excrement.
Ninth. 2183.
Herein, "dancing" means any kind of dancing whatsoever; "singing" means any kind of singing whatsoever; "instrumental music" means...
Because of the expression “whatever instrumental music,” the word “whatever” (yaṃ kiñci) is understood as the remainder [of the phrase].
The construction is: “Whatever nun should go for the purpose of seeing whatever dance, whatever song, or whatever instrumental music.
In that context, “whatever dance” means whether it be dancers such as actors and the like, or drunkards, or even down to peacocks, monkeys, and so forth.

All of this is indeed dancing. Whatever is called "singing"—whether it be the singing of actors and the like, or the well-performed singing associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem at the time of the Noble Ones' parinibbāna, or the chanting of Dhamma by unrestrained bhikkhus—all of this is indeed singing.
Whatever is called "instrumental music"—whether it be played on instruments such as drums and the like—[all of this is instrumental music].
Whether it be the sounding of a small drum or even the sounding of a belly-drum, all of this is indeed instrumental music (*vādita*).

Although one should have said "for the purpose of seeing and hearing," it is stated as "for the purpose of seeing" by way of the grammatical rule of *virūpekasesa* (retaining only one member of a heterogeneous group). Alternatively, it is stated as "for the purpose of seeing" because the five types of consciousness have the intrinsic nature of perceiving their respective objects.

2184. To show that there is a *pācittiya* offense together with the *dukkaṭa* of prior preparation, he said, “for the purpose of seeing dancing,” and so forth. Regarding the word “of singing,” the phrase “of instrumental music” is understood here by the context.
2185. “By a single act of preparation” means by a single act of looking in one direction. For this very reason, he will say later: “…in another case also… they may be.
Regarding the word “sees,” the word “dancing” is the ellipsis. The word “their” refers to those whose dancing one sees. By the particle “pi” (also), “instrumental music” is also included.
He summarizes: as it is said, “If one hears their singing and instrumental music [together], there is only one *pācittiya* offense.
(2186) “From another” means in another direction or location.
(2187) To clarify the point that “there may be separate *pācittiya* offenses,” he says: “In this case, the count of offenses is according to the count of the applications (*payoga*).”

“Could it be so?”—here, “in this” means in this place where various directions meet. To show the determination (vinicchaya) as found in the commentaries regarding the viewing and hearing of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, he said:

“‘To dance,’ etc. The word division is *nacca iti*; there is also a reading *naccāhi*. “Attendance” (*upaṭṭhāna*) refers to the honoring with the sound of drums. “To accept” means to consent by saying “Very well. Because this is stated as an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), the same principle applies to dancing and singing as well.

2189–90. *Sabbattha* means in all cases, such as dancing and so forth. *Upaṭṭhānaṃ karoma* means “we shall perform an offering for your shrine with dancing and so forth. *Upaṭṭhānaṃ pasatthaṃ* means that the performance of an offering is indeed excellent.
The construction is: “or stands right there in the monastery and sees or hears [it]”; here, the remainder of the phrase is “or within the monastery,” and so on.
“If one stands in the monastery, or within the monastery, or outside the monastery, and sees or hears dancing and so forth, there is no offense.”

This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Although the word "standing" (*ṭhatvā*) is used, it applies to all postures (*iriyāpatha*). The phrase "standing in the monastery" (*ārāme ṭhatvā*) indicates that it is not only while standing, but also while walking and so forth—that is, it applies to all postures.
However, the expression "standing in the monastery" is stated for the purpose of showing that one must be within the boundaries of the monastery;
otherwise, one would not obtain [the benefit] even when sitting, according to the *Gaṇṭhipada* and other commentaries.
Thus it was said. The same principle applies to monks as well.
2191. The construction is: "she who, having come to her own place of standing, sees or hears [the act] being performed.

Regarding "place of standing," here, by the common usage of the term for a place where one has stopped, lying down and sitting are also included. For such causes exist when she goes and sees [the act].
The construction is "or [there is] a cause. A "cause" refers to such reasons as *salākā-bhatta* (tickets for meals) and so forth. As it is said:

"If there is something to be done—whether for the sake of *salākā-bhatta* and the like, or for some other business—one goes; having gone, if one sees or hears [the performance] at that place, there is no offense. 2192.
"While walking along a road, she sees a dance performed on the opposite path"—even for one seeing in this manner, it is likewise [an offense].
“Non-offense” (*anāpatti*) refers to the application of the phrase “having inserted [the words]. “On the path” (*paṭipathe*) means facing the way of travel.

“In cases of distress” (*āpadāsu pi*) means that if, being afflicted by such a calamity, she enters a place of assembly, there is no offense for her if she sees or hears [the talk] after having entered in this manner.
This training rule (2193) is considered equal to the training rule on wool (*eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*) from the perspective of its origin; it is understood as being “the same.”
The Tenth.
The First Chapter on Garlic. 2194–5.
Herein, in this teaching, whichever nun [should enter] in the darkness of night, where there is no lamp, together with a man...
The construction is as follows: "If she stands alone together [with a man], for her a *pācittiya* has been declared.

"In the darkness of night" means during the night; for the term *rattandhakāra* (darkness of night) is a synonym for *ratti* (night). As it says in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "In the darkness of night means when the sun has set.
"Without a lamp" means not illuminated by even one of these: a torch, the moon, the sun, or fire; by this, the nocturnal domain is defined.
This is shown. By the word "stands still" (*santiṭṭhati*), it should be understood that the triad of postures consisting of walking, sitting, and lying down is also implied.
For it was said by Vajirabuddhi: "In the phrase 'she should stand still,' the fourfold posture is included by way of the mention of standing;
therefore, even for one who is performing walking meditation and so forth together with a man, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)."
"...is found. "Together with a man" means: to stand together or to converse with a wise human male.
The construction is as follows: for one who, by way of secrecy or intimacy, comes within arm's reach of a man and converses with him, a *pācittiya* offense is stated.
2196–7. But whichever nun stands together [with a man] after having left the reach of a human male's hand...
The construction is as follows: "Whether she stands or converses within arm’s reach of a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or an animal, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is declared for her.
By the inclusion of the term "one who understands," it is indicated that there is no exemption from the offense for a man who does not understand.
2198. *Aññavihitāya*: thinking of something other than the secret enjoyment [of sexual intercourse]. As it is said: "Having become intent on something other than the secret enjoyment.
With the fourth and sixth modes of origination (*samuṭṭhāna*), it originates from the category of theft (*theyyasattha*).
It constitutes an action by way of standing together and conversing. It is called *saññāvimokkhaka* because liberation from it occurs through perception (*saññā*).
First. 2199.
"In a concealed place" means in a place concealed by anything whatsoever, such as a wall and so forth. This is the statement.
Second.

In the third [case], having excluded the word “in the open air,” and in the fourth, having excluded the words “on a carriage road, in a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads,” he says with reference to the remainder: “There is nothing whatsoever new. Here, the word “should be stated” is to be supplied.
And here, “carriage road” means a street; “cul-de-sac” means a street that has not been pierced through; “crossroads” means a place where four roads meet.
"Whether triangular or quadrangular" means at a place where roads meet;
this refers to the third and fourth [offenses]. 2201–2.
"Whichever nun, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, [speaks] to the owners..."

"Should she depart without having asked for permission, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). According to this statement, if a nun, having visited families before the meal and sat on a seat within the covered area, passes beyond the sheltered place without asking the owners for permission;
or if, having sat in the open air, she passes beyond the precinct (upacāra), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her at the first step.
The construction is: "In the second phrase, 'there is an offense of expiation' (*pācittiya*) is supplied.

By the word "on a seat" (*āsane*), what is intended is a seat suitable for sitting after folding the legs in the cross-legged posture (*pallaṅka*). As it is said: "A 'seat' is called the space for the cross-legged posture.
"A place sheltered from rain" means within the threshold. He says "even the precinct" (*upacāraṃ pi*) in order to show the field of offense even in the open air.
"Or if," [it is said]. "Vicinity" (*upacāra*) refers to an area measuring twelve *hattha*s in extent. As it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "The vicinity is twelve *hattha*s. "Likewise" (*tathā*):
by this word, one refers back to the phrase "a *dukkaṭa* offense has been proclaimed. The construction is as follows:

for one who departs when [the robe] has been folded, while perceiving it as not folded, or while being in doubt about it having been folded, there is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. And here, the term "by a bhikkhunī" [is used].

Because it shares the same meaning as *sambandhinī* (a female relative), it should be understood that although one ought to say "of her who is doubting" (*vicikicchantiyā*), it is stated as "of him who is doubting" (*vicikicchato*) by way of a change in gender.

"Of one who is ill" means: she who, due to such an illness, is unable to obtain permission. "In cases of distress" means: there is no offense for one who departs without obtaining permission when such a misfortune has arisen, such as a fire breaking out in the house or the presence of thieves.
The fifth [offense].
2205–6. The phrase “of one who is walking or going” is stated for the purpose of showing that the offense concludes with sitting or lying down.
However, it is a *pācittiya* offense if, after a meal, one sits or lies down here without having asked permission from the owners, saying, “Let us sit or lie down here.”

It should be understood that this is a condition for one who is sitting or lying down. The construction is as follows: for one who, after a meal, sits on a seat and departs without having asked permission from the owner, there is one *pācittiya* offense. This same method applies to the cases of "having lain down," and so forth.
However, just as there is no offense in that case when the seat cannot be moved away, so too here there is no offense when the seat has been permanently assigned.
The sixth. 2207.
"Arising from three origins" means because it arises from the three origins associated with one's own mind.
The eighth.

2208. However, whichever nun should curse either herself or another with curses involving hell or the holy life (*brahmacariya*), for every such word there shall be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
this is the construction [of the rule]. In that context, "should curse" means she should make an oath, such as: "May I be reborn in hell;
may I be reborn in Avīci," or regarding herself, "May [she] be reborn in hell; may [she] be reborn in Avīci."

It is said that one might either curse another, saying, "May [this] arise," or "May I become a householder, may I wear white garments," or one might curse oneself, saying, "May I become a householder, may I wear white garments," or one might curse another.

(2210) "He reviles either himself or another" is the connection. "An offense of expiation for three cases" refers to the cases of perceiving one who is fully ordained as such, being in doubt about it, or perceiving one who is not fully ordained as such.

"Of one who is not fully ordained" means of one who has not received full ordination (*anupasampannā*). If one reviles her while perceiving her as fully ordained, being in doubt, or perceiving her as not fully ordained, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
thus there is a "triple wrong-doing. 2211. The construction is:
"There is no offense for those speaking while placing the instruction in the meaning and the Dhamma foremost. As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
“With the welfare as her primary concern” means while she is delivering a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). “With the Dhamma as her primary concern” means while she is reciting the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
“With the instruction as her primary concern” means: “Even now you are like this; it would be well if you desisted.
If you do not desist, certainly by performing such deeds again, you will arise in hell, or you will arise in the animal realm.”
“There is no offense for one who speaks while standing in such instruction.

This is the ninth [case]. 2212. “Having struck”: having struck with a weapon or the like. Regarding the phrase “or having struck,” the word “or” (*vā*) here indicates the repetition (*āmeḍita*) expressed in the Pāḷi as “having struck, having struck” (*vadhitvā vadhitvā*).

"2213. *Ettha* means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). That which originates from body, speech, and mind, and that which originates from the laying down of the burden—this is also the name for that which originates from formal admonition.
Tenth. The second chapter, the Chapter on Darkness."
2214. But whichever nun, being naked, unclothed, and uncovered, bathes, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every act involved.

At the conclusion, at the end of that bathing, that nun incurs and falls into an offense of expiation (pācittiya), which is called "the fault spoken by the Victor," prescribed for nuns by the Victor, the Blessed One;
such is the construction of the meaning. [End of] Bhikkhunī [Pātimokkha].
In this context, the vowel has been shortened for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse.

2215. "Those whose robes have been snatched away" means those whose *udakasāṭika* robes have been snatched away. "Those whose robes have been lost" means those whose *udakasāṭika* robes have been lost by thieves and the like.
"Or in times of distress" refers to such times of distress as when one thinks, "Seeing that this is of great value, even thieves might carry it off," and thus [one remains] naked.
There is no fault for one who is bathing.
First [case].
Regarding the second: it refers to the training rule beginning with, "But for a bhikkhunī who is having a bathing cloth made... and so forth. (2216) Second.
The second [offense].
2217–8. "A poorly sewn robe" means a robe that has been sewn without care.
"Having unsewn" means having oneself made the sewing undone for the purpose of sewing it again; "having had it unsewn" is the remainder [of the phrase]. As it is said:
“Having sewn it oneself or having had it sewn by another. “Without obstacle” means free from any of the ten obstacles.
That robe which has been sewn or caused to be sewn—where it should have been said “without obstacle after that,” the short vowel is used for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse.
“One should not sew” —here too, “nor should one cause it to be sewn” is the understood remainder. As it is said: “Neither should one sew...”
"One should not make an effort for the purpose of having [the robe] sewn.

Regarding the phrase "four or five days": here, although a higher number is included within a lower number—as in the cases of "more than six or five words" or "more than two or three nights"—both terms are used by way of worldly convention and for the sake of euphony in speech.
It should be seen. *Dhure* means in the effort of sewing. *Nikkhittamatte* means as soon as it has been set down. 2219.

"The triad of *pācittiya*s is stated" means that the triad of *pācittiya*s is stated in three cases: when one perceives a person who is fully ordained as being fully ordained, when one is in doubt, and when one perceives them as not fully ordained.
*Sesāya* means to one who is not fully ordained. *Tikadukkaṭaṃ* means a triad of *dukkaṭa*s for each of the three cases.

2220. "Of both" means of those who are fully ordained and those who are not. "In another" means other than the robe. "Or even when there is an obstacle" means when any one of the ten obstacles—such as kings, thieves, and so forth—is present.

2221. "'Abandoning the burden'—this is considered the origin": this was stated by taking exactly what is called "originating from abandoning the burden" (*dhuranikkhepa-samuṭṭhāna*) in the Commentary;
among the thirteen types of origins, it is designated as "originating from abandoning the burden."
There is no such thing as a separate heading for the origin (samuṭṭhāna-sīsa). In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated as "originating from formal admonition" (*samanubhāsana-samuṭṭhāna*);

this is already included within the headings of origins themselves. Therefore, this term "originating from the laying down of the burden" (*dhuranikkhepa-samuṭṭhāna*) should be understood as merely a synonym for "originating from formal admonition."
The third [section]. 2222. *Pañca ahāni* means five days; *pañcāhaṃ* means for five days; *pañcāhikaṃ* means that which lasts for five days.

Regarding the word “*atikkameyya*” (should exceed), because the verb takes two objects, the accusative case is used for both “*pañcāhikaṃ*” and “*saṅghāṭicāraṃ*” in the sense of the direct object (*upayoga*). In the sense of being sewn together (*saṅghaṭita*), [it refers to the robe].
“Saṅghāṭi” is a designation for the five robes that are about to be mentioned. “Saṅghāṭicāra” means the movement of the saṅghāṭis;
the meaning is that they are exchanged either by way of use or by way of being brought out.
“If he should exceed the five-day limit for the movement of the saṅghāṭis” means that on the fifth day, he neither wears nor puts on nor brings out the five robes.

Because of the statement, "If she lets the fifth day pass, there is an offense of *pācittiya*," it is said, "if she should let [the time] pass," etc., in order to show that for one who lets [the time] pass without doing anything at all within the five days, there is a *pācittiya* offense for each garment (*cīvara*). 2223.

"The three robes" refers to the set of three robes consisting of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*). "A belt" (*saṃkacci*)... [text continues]
And the robe known as the *thanaveṭhana*. The *dakasāṭī* is the water-bathing robe to be worn during the hot season.
Thus, these are five. "Five indeed" means they are called the five robes.

2224–5. Regarding the three *pācittiya*s: there are three *pācittiya*s based on the three alternatives of perception—perceiving [the period] as having exceeded five days, being doubtful, or perceiving it as not having exceeded five days. For those who perceive it as having exceeded five days when it has not, or who are doubtful, there are two *dukkaṭa*s.
“On the fifth day,” and so forth, is the demonstration of the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*). “Wears” means either puts on as an undergarment or wraps around as an upper robe.
Regarding “dries [it]”: here the word “or” (*vā*) is indicated by elision; the meaning is “or dries it.
“Even in cases of distress” means that there is no offense in such a calamity when a costly robe cannot be used due to fear of thieves and the like.
The Fourth.
2226. The construction is as follows: if one takes a robe belonging to another that is to be transferred and uses it without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her;
[this refers to] any one of the five types of robes belonging to another fully ordained nun (upasampannā).
The meaning is: having taken it without first returning it, it must be given back to her; for whichever nun uses it without having returned it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

"Cīvara that is to be transferred" (*saṅkamanīya*) and "cīvara to be transferred" (*saṅkametabba*) are synonymous terms. As it is said: "Cīvara that is to be transferred means cīvara that must be transferred;
the meaning is that cīvara belonging to another which was taken without asking permission must be returned again."
2227. It is said that there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: “If she, perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained... [and so on]... being in doubt... [and so on]...

perceiving one who is not fully ordained as such, wears a robe that should be transferred, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. Thus, the triad of *pācittiya* offenses is stated in the Canon. “The rest” means: for one who is not fully ordained. “A triad of *dukkaṭa*” offenses is also to be understood according to the same method just described. “In cases of emergency” means: if it is uncovered...
Or thieves carry off what has not been worn; such are the kinds of misfortunes. 2228.

The application is that these origins are equal to those of the *kathina* robe. Taking it up and using it constitute an action (*kriyā*). Not asking for permission constitutes a non-action (*akriyā*).
This is the fifth [case].
2229. "A robe that ought to be obtained" means a robe that has reached the stage of being formally assigned (vikappanupaga).
"She prevents it" means she exerts herself to create an obstacle so that those who wish to give do not give.
"She indicates a *pācittiya* offense" means that if they do not give because of her words, one should declare a *pācittiya* offense for the nun; this is the meaning.
2230. Here, because it is stated first as “of the Saṅgha,” two or three groups must be understood [as included].
Regarding “gain”: the word “if he prevents” (*nivārite*) is to be supplied here. The construction is: if he prevents another requisite, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
“Another” means other than a robe that has reached the stage of formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*). “Requisite” means any one of them, such as a bowl-stand and so forth, or ghee, oil, and so forth.
“Having pointed out the advantage” means: he asks, “How much do you wish to give as the price?
When they say, “This much,” he says, “Wait for now; the raw material is expensive at present, but after a few days, when cotton has arrived, it will be of equal value.
Having thus pointed out the advantage, there is no fault—that is, there is no offense. This is the meaning.
The sixth. 2232–3.

When a lawful distribution and apportioning of robes is being carried out by a complete Saṅgha that has assembled together, whichever bhikkhunī should prohibit or obstruct it—for her, thus prohibiting it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

The construction is: "it happens. The construction is: "the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is illustrated by the perception of what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma. Regarding the phrase "or when both are in doubt," it means "when there is doubt regarding both.
The word *su-* is elided due to the requirements of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*). The construction is:

"the offense of wrong-doing is illustrated for one who prevents [the distribution] while being in doubt concerning whether the distribution of robes is in accordance with the Dhamma or not in accordance with the Dhamma. As it is said: "being in doubt regarding what is in accordance with the Dhamma..."
If she prevents it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If she prevents it while being doubtful whether it is contrary to the Dhamma, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Having pointed out the advantage: having shown the advantage by saying, “One robe is not enough for one person; wait a moment, it will appear in just a few days, and then we shall share it.”
The seventh. 2235–6.

Whatever robe there may be—whether suitable for an inner garment, or suitable for an upper garment, or marked with the allowable spots—if one gives it to any other householder whatsoever, excluding the five who share the same Dhamma and even one's own mother and father, [it is an offense].
The construction is as follows: "If she should give [it] to a wanderer (paribbājaka), for her too there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

And here, in the phrase "parents" (pitaro), although one should say "mother and father" (mātāpitaro), it should be understood as a designation based on the grammatical principle of *virūpekasesa* (retaining only one of two dissimilar members). 2237.
Herein, regarding this training rule (sikkhāpada), the construction is: "Those offenses of expiation, moreover, are to be counted according to the number of robes."

2238. "Tāvakālika" means that the time for it has been accepted for such a short duration; thus, it is a "temporary robe. Regarding the phrase "of another": because the previous term "another's" was distant [in its application], he says again "of others," which carries the same meaning. This is the eighth [offense]. 2239.
But whichever nun, having made a verbal distinction by saying, "If we are able, we will give [it] or we will make [it]," [and then fails to do so]... [the rule continues].

The construction is as follows: if, having set aside the distribution of a robe due to a weak expectation of receiving one—where it is said, "it happens"—one should let the time for the robe pass, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) on account of that fault. Regarding "the time for the robe," the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states:
"The robe-season is called the last month of the rainy season when the Kathina has not been spread; it is five months when the Kathina has been spread."
The time for robe-making has been stated. "Should she let it pass" means she would let pass the rule as stated: "If the kaṭhina has not been spread, the last day of the rainy season;
if the kaṭhina has been spread, the day of the kaṭhina-removal. Regarding the phrase "if the robe is very fragile":
because of the statement, "If there is a perception that a robe is fragile when it is actually fragile, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," [it refers to] one that is very fragile.

In the phrase *cetasā*, the word *su-* is used here for metrical completion (*padapūraṇe*). *Ubhosu* means both when they are weak and when they are not weak. *Kaṅkhitāya vā* means either when one is doubting or when one is perplexed.
2241. *Ānisaṃsaṃ nidassetvā* means having pointed out the benefit as follows: "Even though they say, 'Venerable lady, we are not able,' now cotton will come to them;
a faithful and confident man will come, and he will certainly give it."
Having shown the benefit according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Ninth. 2242.

Regarding the "legitimate suspension of the *kathina*": this refers to the suspension of the *kathina* as it is stated: "The legitimate suspension of the *kathina* is when the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, being complete, having assembled, suspends it."

2243. *Yassa* means "of which kaṭhina. The benefit rooted in the spreading (*atthāramūlaka*) is the benefit consisting in the cloth for robes arising in that monastery, which was authorized [by the Buddha] with the words: "Whatever robe-material arises there shall belong to them.
The benefit rooted in the suspension (*uddhāramūlaka*) is the benefit consisting in the cloth for robes given by lay followers who are having an interim suspension performed.
“Even with equal benefits” means that even an *ubbhāra* (lifting/setting aside) is one where the benefits are equal by virtue of the benefit of spreading [the cloth].
“For the purpose of protecting faith” is to be construed as: it should be given for the sake of guarding one’s serene confidence (*pasāda*).
“Having pointed out the benefit” means having shown a benefit such as: “The community of bhikkhunīs has worn-out robes; there is a great gain rooted in the benefit of the *kathina*.”
2246. Furthermore, the remaining portion of the analysis, together with its origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth, is considered entirely identical in every respect to the seventh training rule;
it is understood as "similar. The construction is: there is not even the slightest thing therein that is new or different from the method already stated.
The Tenth.
The Third Chapter on Nakedness.
2247. “Whichever bhikkhunīs should lie down on the same bed, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)”—thus was the training rule (sikkhāpada) laid down.
To show the legal determination (*vinicchaya*), he said: “By one,” and so forth. “By one” means by one nun. “The other” refers to another who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
“Should lie down”—here the words “on the same bed” are to be supplied as the remainder. “Two” means two nuns. 2248–9.

“And by one,” and so forth, is the exposition of the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*). “Both sitting together equally” is the construction. “By the *eḷaka* rule” means by the training rule concerning sheep’s wool (*eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*).

Regarding the phrase *pāvārakaṭasārādi*, this is the singular locative case. Because it stands in grammatical apposition with the word *saṃhārimesu* (in those things gathered together), which is plural, one should understand that the singular designation here is used by way of a shift in number (*vacanavipallāsa*). And the *pāvāra*...
The analysis of the compound is: "that of which the mat (kaṭa) is the primary substance (sāra). This is a locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

"A single one" (*ekakaṃ*) indicates that which is to be selected. "Only one" is what is meant by "a single one. The meaning is: "one among those things that can be rolled up, such as a woolen rug (*pāvāra*) and so forth.

They say, "A 'woolen rug' refers to a *kojava* and similar items. "Mat" (*kaṭa*) means simply a mat. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), everything suitable for lying upon after being spread out is included.
“By that very [blanket]” means by that which has been spread out. The construction is: “If, having put it on, two lie down together, there may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for them.

And here, since the functions of spreading and covering are assigned to one [blanket] alone, it is understood that the spreading is done with one end and the covering with the other end. As it is said: “Of those that are portable...”
"This is a designation for those who lie down after spreading one end of a woolen rug (*pāvāra*), a mat (*attharaṇa*), a grass mat (*kaṭasāraka*), or the like, and covering themselves with the other.

The connection is that when two bhikkhunīs lie down on a single rug or a single cover, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both of them. Thus, "two offenses of wrong-doing" have been stated:
"When they are on different rugs and covers, yet perceive them as being on a single rug and cover... and so forth.
"Being in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Thus, two *dukkaṭa* offenses have been stated.
2252. "Having demonstrated the determination": the meaning is that if one lies down after placing a yellow robe, a walking stick, or even a waistband in between, there is no offense.
The rest concerns the method of origin and so forth. By the word "and so forth," [it refers to] this very [category].
By the first training rule in the section. "Tulya" means equal or similar.
Second. 2253.
Of another bhikkhunī. "Aphāsukāraṇā" means for the purpose of causing discomfort. "Anāpucchā" means without having asked permission.
The construction is as follows: if one should perform such acts as walking back and forth (*caṅkama*) in front of her, for one doing so there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Regarding the phrase "walking back and forth, etc.," the word "etc. includes those acts mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), namely: "standing, sitting, lying down, reciting, causing to recite, or performing private study."
"By counting the turnings" means by counting the turns made when one walking on a path reaches both ends of that path and turns back.
"Only by the application" means only by the counting of the applications; it is said to mean only by the counting of the changes in posture.
"Faults" refers to the offenses of *pācittiya*.
2255. Regarding the phrase "the counting of words" (*padānaṃ gaṇanāvasā*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) here is indicated as being elided. As it is said: "by the counting of words, etc. (*padādigaṇanāyā*).

"A threefold offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is stated" means that a triad of offenses of expiation is stated by way of the three alternatives: perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained, being in doubt, and perceiving one who is not fully ordained [as fully ordained]. "To the rest" means to one who is not fully ordained.

2256. “And not for one who desires discomfort”: the construction is that there is no offense for one who, having asked permission, performs walking meditation (*caṅkama*) and so forth in front of that nun.

2257. “Doing and not doing”: performing walking meditation and so forth is “doing” (*kiriya*). Not performing [the act of] asking permission is “not doing” (*akiriya*). “Evil-mindedness” is an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*). This is the third [section].
2258–9. *Anantarāyā*: a nun who is free from any of the ten obstacles that will be mentioned, such as the obstacle of a king (*rājantarāya*), etc.
*Dukkhitā*: one who is ill. As it is said: "One who is 'afflicted' (*dukkhitā*) is called one who is ill.
*Sahajīviniṃ*: a co-resident (*saddhivihārinī*). As it is said: "A 'co-resident' (*sahajīvini*) is called a co-resident nun. *Vā aññāya nupaṭṭhāpeyya*: or she should have another nurse her.
One should not cause another bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), or a female householder to provide attendance.
Nor should one attend oneself; that is, one should not personally provide attendance. "As soon as the burden is laid down" means:
as soon as one has relinquished the effort and resolve regarding the burden, thinking, "I will no longer attend, nor will I make an effort to have [another] attend."
“Of her” means of the preceptoress (*upajjhāyā*).

“Or of a female pupil (*antevāsini*)” refers to any one among the four types of female pupils—distinguished by way of going forth, full ordination, the Dhamma, or dependence. “The other” refers to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampannā*).
“If she is ill” means if she herself is ill. The phrase “if, having sought [another], they do not find one” is the word-division; it refers to another attendant (*upaṭṭhāyikā*).
The meaning is: "not finding [them] despite having searched. The word-division is: *āpadāsu ummattikādīnaṃ*.

Due to the requirements of the metrical structure of the verse (*gāthābandha*), the elision of a vowel (*vaṇṇalopa*) should also be understood. *Āpadāsu* means when such a calamity (*upaddava*) occurs.
*Dhuranikkhepodayaṃ* means the arising of the relinquishing of responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa-samuṭṭhāna*). Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated below.
The fourth [section].

2261–2. Because one's own property (*puggalika*) is not restricted by way of being dependent on oneself (*attāyatta*) or dependent on another (*parāyatta*), it is specified by the term "one’s own" (*saka*).

"One’s own property" (*sakaṃ puggalikaṃ*) means one's own personal property. Regarding the word "having given" (*datvā*), the word "to a nun" (*bhikkhuniyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "One’s own woven cloth" (*sakavāṭaṃ*).
"Equipped with a revolving door and a door-panel. *Upassaya* means a dwelling or house. Regarding the phrase "at the doors, etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) here includes the inner chambers and the main halls; this locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
"Even many" indicates that which is to be selected: either many doors, or many inner chambers, or many main halls. "Her" refers to that nun to whom the dwelling was given.
"Of one who ejects" means of one who causes [the person] to pass beyond [the boundary]. "Of her" means of her who ejects. 2263.
"In this case" refers to the act of ejecting. "The same method" refers to the method shown by the statement, "the offense is according to the number of applications.
Here, "application" (payoga) means the act of commanding; by this it is shown that even if [the person] passes beyond many doors through a single command, there is only one offense.
This summarizes the analysis found in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), beginning with the words "it happens," and so forth.

To show one specific point among those analyses, he says: "There are only this many doors," and so on. "Offenses by way of door-count" (*dvāragaṇanāpattiyo*) refers to offenses according to the enumeration of the doors.

Regarding the phrase "from a place without a door": the construction is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is being expelled from a residence (*upassaya*) that lacks a door-bar. As for the remaining [cases]...

"Regarding one who is not fully ordained": "The triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses" means that there is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses based on perceiving her as fully ordained when she is not, being in doubt, and perceiving her as not fully ordained. "Of both" refers to those who are fully ordained and those who are not.

"In regard to requisites" refers to requisites such as the bowl, robes, and so forth. "In all instances" means in all applications; it is said: "both when they are being driven out and when they are being caused to be driven out."

2266. Here, the construction is as follows: together with the determination of the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth for this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the remaining body of determinations (*vinicchaya-jāta*) is to be understood in its entirety and in all its aspects as being considered "similar" (*sadisa*) to the training rule concerning the expulsion from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.
The fifth [section].

2267. Regarding the sixth: this refers to what is to be stated here in this Vinaya adjudication concerning the sixth training rule (sikkhāpada) indicated in the matrix (mātikā), beginning with: "Whatever bhikkhunī should live in association with a householder or a householder’s son," and so forth.
It should be explained. "By the training rule of Ariṭṭha" means by the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha. "The analysis" refers to the origin and so forth. This is the sixth [section]. 2268.

Regarding the phrase "in what is considered dangerous," the word "where there is peril" (*sappaṭibhaye*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Both of these have already been explained in meaning below.
"Within the kingdom" means within the kingdom of the one whose realm she dwells in. The construction is as follows:
"For a nun who wanders on tour without a caravan through a region considered dangerous and fearful within the kingdom, there may be an offense.

(2269) "For her wandering in this manner, the sequence for the *pācittiya* offense—the method for the establishment of the *pācittiya* offense—should be known and understood by a monk skilled in the Vinaya regarding entry into another village within a village-enclosure, and regarding the half-yojana in the forest where there is no village. This is the construction.

2270. "There is no offense for one traveling with a caravan" is the construction. "There is no offense for one traveling in a secure place, or for one traveling in times of distress" is the construction.
The seventh [section].
2271. Regarding the eighth or ninth [sections], namely the eighth training rule beginning with "But whatever nun [travels] across a foreign kingdom," etc.:
And also in the ninth training rule stated thus: “Whatever bhikkhunī should go on a walking tour during the rains, it is an offense entailing expiation.
There is nothing obscure; everything is indeed clear. Therefore, the intention is that I shall not investigate this here.
[These are] the eighth and ninth.

2272. Regarding the training rule stated thus: “Whatever bhikkhunī, having completed the rains residence, should not set out on a journey—even if it be only five or six *yojanas*—it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*),” he says “it is an offense of expiation,” etc., in order to show the analysis of that rule.

The construction is as follows: when she has relinquished her responsibility by thinking, “I will not go; I will not set out,” it is an offense of expiation. “In that way” means: it is an offense of expiation.
2273. After having completed the rains residence and performed the *pavāraṇā*, it is permissible to travel even as far as five *yojanas*.
To show that the word "even" (*api*) here has the sense of inclusion, he says "in six," and so forth.
Here, in this section concerning non-offenses, what could possibly be said regarding the six *yojanas*? The meaning is that there is nothing at all to be said. Having performed the *pavāraṇā*...
It is pointed out that for one traveling six *yojanas*, the state of being without offense (*anāpatti*) is established even without being explicitly stated.
2274. Three *yojanas*. "By that very [path]" means by the same route by which she went. "By another path" means by a way other than the path already traveled. 2275.
"When ten kinds of obstacles exist" means when any one of the obstacles to be mentioned hereafter exists. For her...
The construction is: "there is no offense. "In calamities" (*āpadāsu*) means in calamities characterized by being obstructed by someone due to reasons such as danger and so forth.
"For one who is ill" (*gilānāya*) means for herself when she is ill. There is no offense if she departs because a second nun is not available, or if she departs [due to other causes].
2276. The analysis of the compound is: "kings and thieves and non-human beings and fire and water and beasts of prey and reptiles."
“Manussa” (human being): here, due to the requirements of metrical composition, there is an elision of the first member of the compound, as in expressions such as “gourd-sinking” (*lābu-sīdanti*).
“Jīvitabrahmacariya” is a collective dvanda compound meaning “life and the holy life”; [the phrase refers to] “of that life and holy life.
“Antarāyikā” means “obstacles” (*antarāyā* itself). There is no offense for one who departs because of any one of these ten. As it has been said:

“Regarding ‘obstacle’: there are ten kinds of obstacles. For one who has set out thinking, ‘I shall go to another place,’ it is proper to turn back if a river is in flood, or if there are thieves on the road, or if a storm arises.
[The commentary states: Departure is non-action. It is called “painful feeling” because it is incurred through disrespect.
The tenth.
The fourth chapter, *Tuvaṭṭa-vagga*.
2278–80. “*Rājāgāra*” means the king’s pleasure-house. “*Cittāgāra*” means a picture gallery for recreation. “*Ārāma*” means...
A pleasure grove (*kīḷana-upavana*). A pleasure park (*kīḷa-uyyāna*) is a park made for the purpose of recreation. Regarding "a pleasure pond" (*kīḷā-vāpi*):
although a lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*) is mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), that is stated as a representative example of all water reservoirs constructed for recreation;
thus he says "a pleasure pond," meaning a pond made for the purpose of recreation. "In various ways" (*nānākāraṃ*): this [is explained] by the aforementioned terms.
Each [offense] should be applied individually. The term "those" (*tāni*) is used in the sense of including all of them collectively.

The construction is as follows: for those bhikkhunīs who go to see various types of royal palaces, picture galleries, parks, pleasure groves, or pleasure ponds, the Sage has prescribed a *dukkaṭa* offense at every step for all of them, whether they go to see them one by one or together.

The construction is as follows: "In all five cases—the five [offenses] such as the royal palace and so forth—it is explained that there is only one *pācittiya* offense. The construction is: "If, having gone to each respective direction, they see [the object], there would be separate offenses according to the number of applications (*payoga*).

Having demonstrated the abundance of offenses through the abundance of journeys, he says, "There may also be an abundance of *pācittis* due to the abundance of applications," in order to demonstrate the abundance of offenses even by means of what is termed the abundance of applications consisting in the turning back of the neck. "In all instances" means...
"Wherever an offense of expiation (pācittiya) has been stated for a bhikkhunī, [the same applies] everywhere.
2282. "The remainder is also non-offense" (avasesopi anāpatti): this is the word-division. Non-offense and the method of discourse regarding it constitute "non-offense-discourse-method";
the analysis of these is the "analysis of the non-offense-discourse-method," beginning with the statement: "There is no offense if she sees while standing in a monastery," and so forth.
The meaning is: the determination regarding non-offenses as found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and the determination for the remainder.

By the phrase "standing in the monastery," this section on non-offenses is shown: that there is no offense for one who sees royal palaces and such things while standing within the monastery grounds (*ajjhārāma*).
By this very [statement], it is implied that one may go here and there within the monastery to see royal palaces and so forth, just as one might go to see dancing and other performances.
"Obtains" is also established. By the word "etcetera," the following exemptions from offense (*anāpattivāra*) are included:
"If she goes on the road for the sake of alms-food and so forth, and sees them, there is no offense. Having gone to the presence of a king on some business, she sees them, there is no offense.
Being harassed by someone, she enters [the house] and sees them, there is no offense. [The same applies to] watching dancing... and so forth.
This is similar to the training rule on watching dancing, etc., in its analysis beginning with the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*). First. 2283. *Mānātītā*:

that which has passed beyond or gone away from the measure (*māna*) is "exceeding the measure" (*mānātītā*); it refers to a high-backed chair (*āsandi*). *Vāḷūpeto*: that which is possessed of wild animals is "furnished with wild animals" (*vāḷūpeto*); it refers to a divan (*pallaṅka*).

Regarding that: because of the statement, “An *āsandī* is said to be one exceeding the [prescribed] measure,” an *āsandī* is a specific type of bed or stool with legs higher than a carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakihattha*) from the bottom frame;
it is square in shape, and its being square is permitted even if it exceeds the measure.
Because of the statement, “A *pallaṅka* is made of exotic animal skins,” such a thing—even if it conforms to the measure—is likewise [prohibited].
It is not permitted. "Brought-in furs" (*āharimavāla*) refers to fur objects that, having been brought, are to be placed in a suitable location;

what is meant is that [the bed] is furnished with such brought-in fur objects. For those bhikkhunīs who use, sit upon, or lie down upon a high couch (*āsandi*) or a luxurious divan (*pallaṅka*) equipped with such furs, the Teacher has declared an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
2284. For those [offenses], the counting of the *pācittiya* rules occurs by way of the multiplicity of applications for both sitting and lying down;
thus, this enumeration has been demonstrated. The construction is as follows: "In this way, this enumeration was spoken by the Blessed One through his absolute mastery and infinite retinue.
And here, *iccevaṃ* is a collection of particles; the word *iti* indicates a reference, and the word *evaṃ* [indicates]...
This is how it should be understood. 2285.

"Having cut off the feet of the chair" means having cut them by removing a portion exceeding the proper measurement of the chair's feet. "The claw-ornaments on the feet of the couch are 'couch-claws'; having removed those, [if one uses it], there is no offense"—this means there is no offense for those who use it.
The second [section].
2286–7. *Channaṃ* means “of the various cloths” such as linen (*khoma*) and so forth; this is a genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
*Aññataraṃ suttaṃ* indicates that which is to be selected. *Hatthā* means “with the hand”; here it is an ablative used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*).
*Añcitaṃ* means drawn out by the extension of the hand. *Tasmiṃ* refers to that portion of the thread being drawn out. *Takkamhi* means in the spinning needle.
*Veṭhitā* means wrapped around.
*Sabbapubbapayogesū ti suttakantanato* means in all previous operations prior to the spinning of the thread; that is, in all operations beginning with the picking of the cotton.
*Hatthavāratoti* means by the count of hand-turns. As it is said: "Beginning with the picking of the cotton, in all previous operations..."
"By counting hand-waves, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
2288. "Spun thread" refers to thread such as that for tassels which has already been spun once. "Spinning again" means spinning it again after joining end to end.
This is the third [case].

2289. The construction is as follows: for a woman performing domestic service for householders, starting from the threshing of rice, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all prior preparatory acts.
2290. Regarding drinks such as rice-gruel that are to be prepared, one should indicate the offense of expiation (pācittiya) by counting the vessels that serve as their containers;

regarding solid foods such as snacks, one should indicate the offense of expiation by counting the individual items—this is the construction. In the phrase "regarding rice-gruel and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) [includes other similar items].

This is the inclusion of cooked rice, soup, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the case of snacks and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes fish, meat, and other supplementary foods (uttaribhaṅga).

2291. Even if one's mother and father should arrive, it is permissible to cook anything at all provided that one first has them perform some task—such as making a fan or sweeping with a broom—and then places them in the position of a service-provider (veyyāvaccakara). This is the legal decision (vinicchaya) found in the Aṭṭhakathā.
He said "If," and so forth, in order to show this. Here, the words "if one's mother and father come" are to be supplied as the remainder.
The construction is: it is not permissible to perform any action whatsoever without first having one's own mother and father—who have arrived in such a manner—perform some action [on their behalf].
The word *api* (even/also) expresses a high degree of probability; by it, he indicates that there is no talk of anyone else at all.
2292–3. The construction is: “There is no offense for one who performs service at the time of the Sangha’s drinking of rice-gruel.
The same principle applies to the phrases “at the Sangha’s meal,” and so forth. The connection is with “or for one who performs service for oneself. As it is said:
“At the drinking of rice-gruel” means, when rice-gruel or a meal for the Sangha is being prepared by people for the sake of the Sangha, [the nun acts] by way of being an assistant to them.
There is no offense for something [prepared] by one who is cooking. It is permissible to act as an assistant in the worship of a cetiya and to offer perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
This is the fourth [case]. 2294. “But whichever bhikkhunī, when addressed thus: ‘Come, noble lady, settle this legal issue,’ says: ‘Very well’...”
Having promised, if she subsequently, being without obstacle, neither settles the matter nor makes an effort to settle it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
thus he spoke "an offense of expiation upon abandoning the burden," etc., in order to show the analysis of this training rule.
"Abandoning the burden" means: [thinking] "I will not settle this now, or I will not have others settle it"—thus, the abandoning of the responsibility.
The construction is: "In the relinquishing of the effort, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The construction is:
"Just as a five-day exemption is obtained in the case of sewing a robe, here, however, not even a one-day exemption is obtained.

2295. "The rest" refers to the various points of legal decision such as: "If they decide after having laid down the burden, they decide only after having incurred an offense," and so forth. The construction is: "In that regard, it should be understood according to the same method stated for the sewing of a robe."
The fifth [offense]. 2296–7.

Whatever nun, except for householders or fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, should with her own body give to other male or female wanderers any kind of edible food—whether solid or soft—to be swallowed, other than water for cleaning the teeth; [this is an offense.]

The construction is: "If she gives [it] by means of her own body, or by something connected to her body, or by something that must be relinquished, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
2298–9. Here, in this training rule, the construction is: "The Sage has stated that [using] tooth-sticks or water constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Furthermore, as for the nun who does not give it herself by means of her body or other such means, but causes another to give it—having not given it herself by means of her body or other such means...

The construction is as follows: even for one who gives after having placed it on the ground, or for one who gives an external ointment, there is no fault and there is no offense for that person, as well as for one who is insane.
This is the sixth [case].
2300–1. *Āvasathacīvara* (lodging robe) means a robe given [with the instruction], “Let the nuns who are menstruating use it.

If a nun, having washed that robe designated as an *āvasathacīvara* on the fourth day, should use it herself without giving it—even for a single moment—to one who is menstruating or to a novice nun, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) is stated for her.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "There may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the triad" means that there is an offense of expiation as stated in the rule: "If she uses [the robe] while it has not been relinquished, perceiving it as not having been relinquished... or being in doubt... or perceiving it as having been relinquished, there is an offense of expiation. 2302–3.
Regarding that robe, whether by the perception that it has not been relinquished or by being in doubt when it has been relinquished, for that bhikkhunī...
The construction is: "two *dukkaṭas* are stated. There is no offense for one who uses [the robe] even without giving it away, provided there are no other women in their fertile period (*utu*).
"Again, in turn" (*puna pariyaye*) means there is no offense for one who uses it at the proper time during another turn of the fertile period.

"And there is no offense for those whose robes have been stolen, etc."—this is the construction. In the word "turn" (*pariyaye*), the short vowel is used for metrical reasons (*gāthābandha*). Regarding "those whose robes have been stolen, etc."...
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of lost robes and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even in times of distress":

even if one has carefully hidden a costly robe after removing it from one's body, thieves may still carry it off; in such times of distress, there is no offense for one who uses [the robe]. This is the construction.
The seventh [section].

2304. “A monastery with a door” (*sakavāṭakaṃ vihāraṃ*) means a monastery secured by a door-panel; what is meant is a well-guarded dwelling provided with a door-panel. “Without giving for the sake of protection” means without having asked permission in this way:

“Please keep watch over this. 2305–6. He said, beginning with “From her own village,” etc., in order to clarify what was stated as: “There is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for her when she sets out on a journey.
“From her own village” means from the village where she herself resides. “Likewise for the other” refers to that which is not enclosed.
The enclosure and the precinct of the monastery. In the triad of phrases beginning with "in that," the accusative case is to be understood as having the sense of the locative.
For a walled monastery, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when one has crossed the enclosure by means of the first phrase;
likewise, for the other, the unwalled monastery, there is an offense of wrong-doing when one has crossed its precinct by means of the second phrase. By the second phrase...
The construction is: "It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) when one has merely transgressed the boundary or the precinct. (2307) Regarding "in a dwelling without a door-bolt":

this illustrates that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does not relinquish [the bedding] in such a monastery that lacks a door-bolt. Regarding "not obtaining a caretaker": here the word "having sought" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Caretaker" means a person who looks after the monastery. (2308) "In cases of emergency":
this refers to emergencies such as when the kingdom is in turmoil and they depart, leaving the residence behind. "If she is ill": this means if she is unable to make vocal utterance.
The eighth. 2309–10.
