*Hatthī* (elephant), *asso* (horse), and *ratho* (chariot) constitute *hatthi-assa-ratha*; those for which these are the beginning are *hatthi-assa-rathādayo* (elephants, horses, chariots, etc.).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the two terms *dhanu* (bow) and *tharu* (spear) are included. *Saṃyuttaṃ* means [connected] with the aforementioned words such as elephants, horses, and so forth.
“Combined” means a compound formed by [the rule] “elephant-training is *hatthisippa*,” and so forth;
it refers to whatever craft has been mentioned in such passages as “elephant-craft, horse-craft, chariot-craft, archery-craft, and swordsmanship-craft.
By the metaphorical identification of the expression with its referent (*vācya-vācaka-abheda-upacāra*), the treatise that illuminates elephant-training and the other crafts is called “craft.”
It should be understood as "spoken thus. For that very reason, he will say: "By way of the words and so forth.

"Any [craft] that harms others" means any craft such as the various types of *āthabbaṇa* spells—including those for causing obstruction, paralyzing, subjugating, or withering—as well as those for poisoning and the like; this is the meaning.
And here, a "stake-mantra" (*khilamantra*) is a mantra for killing that involves consecrating a stake made of heartwood and driving it into the earth.

A "subjugation mantra" (*vasīkaraṇamantra*) is a mantra that brings another under one's own control. A "withering mantra" (*sosāpanamantra*) is a mantra that causes the body of another to become parched through the depletion of the bodily constituents such as the fluids.
By the word "etcetera," there is an inclusion of mantras for driving away and so forth.
"Sowing dissension" means causing friends to fall into mutual enmity. Here, in this teaching, the construction is as follows:

if any bhikkhunī should master or study anything—such as [the training rules on] elephants, etc.—in the presence of anyone whatsoever by way of the words and so forth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
"In writing" means in the craft of calligraphy. "And for the purpose of memorizing" means in the science of memorization;
by practicing according to the method described therein, one can retain even many texts. "For protection" means for the sake of protecting oneself or others.
"And in all protective charms" means in all protective charms such as those against *yakkhas*, thieves, wild beasts, and so forth.
The ninth. 2312.
Regarding the tenth: when it is proclaimed, "Whichever nun should teach worldly lore, there is an offense of expiation," this refers to the tenth training rule. This is the tenth training rule.
The tenth.
The fifth chapter on the Hall of Paintings (Cittāgāravagga). 2313.

"An arama with monks" refers to that area where monks reside, even if only at the foot of a tree. "Knowing" means knowing that it is "with monks. "Any [person]" means any monk, novice, or monastery attendant. 2314–5.
Because of the statement, "An 'arama with monks' is one where monks reside, even if only at the foot of a tree," he says:
“‘If, at the very least’ and so forth. However, if a nun, without having asked permission, crosses the enclosure—at the very least even that of the root of a tree—the formulation is as follows:

for her first step, there is a *dukkaṭa*; even if that monastery is not enclosed, when she steps across its precinct, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the nun; when the second step has been crossed, it shall be a *pācittiya*.”

2316. "In a monastery without monks, perceiving it as one with monks"—the meaning is: for one who has given rise to doubt through uncertainty regarding both types of monasteries, those with monks and those without monks; for her, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—this is the construction. 2317.
"For the nun who walks looking back over her shoulder, no offense is declared for her"—this is the construction. It is the same for what follows.
She goes thinking, "I am going into the presence of those nuns where they have assembled. As it is said:
“It is permissible to go thinking, ‘I shall go into the presence of those nuns where they have entered first to perform recitation or pay homage at the cetiya and so forth. 2318.
By the very words “without having asked a monk present,” it follows that one may go to a monastery devoid of monks without asking anyone at all.
"It is explained that there is no offense for one who enters. This also applies to one who goes by way of a path that runs through the middle of the monastery.
Regarding 'in cases of distress': she is afflicted by some kind of misfortune; for one who enters in such cases of distress, there is no offense. First [case concluded]."
2320. "Should revile" means: he should revile him either in his presence or in his absence by means of one or another of the ten grounds for reviling.
"Or should insult" means: he should instill fear in him. "A triad of *pācittiya* offenses" refers to: "If [the person] is ordained, and he perceives him as ordained... or is in doubt...
or perceives him as unordained, and he reviles or insults him, there is an offense of *pācittiya*."
A triad of *pācittiya* offenses has been stated. Regarding the word "the rest": it refers to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

The construction is that for her there is a triad of *dukkaṭa* offenses. 2321. As for what should be said regarding the phrases beginning with "having placed in front," that is exactly according to the method already stated in the training rule concerning "should curse.
Second.
2322–3. *Saṅghanti bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ*: "He reviles" means he reviles according to the method already stated: "These women are fools; these women are incompetent;
they do not know the legal act (*kamma*), nor the defect in a legal act, nor the failure of a legal act, nor the success of a legal act.
In the phrase "to the other one" (*itarāya*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative. [This refers to] either a single bhikkhunī or several bhikkhunīs.
The construction is as follows: "For her who reviles another, whether one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or likewise one who is not fully ordained, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared.
This is the third [offense].

2324–6. Both the invitation (*nimantana*) and the formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*) are included in the training rule regarding eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada*), as well as in the training rule regarding the formal invitation (*pavāraṇa-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding those [prohibitions] with the characteristics already stated: if a bhikkhunī, whether she has been invited by both [methods] or has been offered the *pavāraṇā*,
should accept any kind of edible food (*āmisa*) for the purpose of consumption— excluding the morning meal (*purebhatta*), rice-gruel (*yāgu*),
and the three [types of food] permitted at the appropriate time (*kālika*)— there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in that acceptance.
The construction is: "It may be that, by way of swallowing [food], an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is indicated here in this training rule.

And here, "one who has been invited" (*nimantitā*) refers to one who has been invited with any one of the five kinds of cooked food, according to the definition stated in the training rule regarding eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*).
Furthermore, "having been served" (*pavārita*) means: "food is perceived, a meal is perceived, within arm's reach..."
It should be understood that these are the characteristics stated in the *Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*: "When standing, one brings [the food]; thus the refusal is made known. 2327.
"And there are only three [types of] timely [food]" means that the three types beginning with "for a watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*) are indeed timely.
2328–29. Having shown the common offense for two people who have been invited and then refused further offerings, he speaks in order to show the non-offense:

“Invited,” and so forth. Herein, the meaning is: if a bhikkhunī who has been invited but not formally offered [food] drinks rice-gruel in this Dispensation, it is permissible; there is no offense. “Of the host” means of that very person by whom she was invited, the owner of the invitation.
“Other food” means food other than that from which she was invited. The construction is: if she eats that, it is likewise permissible.

“Only three are for the time of Kālika” means that the three beginning with *yāmakālika* (lasting until the watch of the night) are indeed *kālika*. “When there is a requisite condition” means when there is a condition such as thirst.
2330. The construction is: “The origin of this training rule is equal to [the offense of] traveling.
To show the status of being an action (*kiriyā*) or a non-action (*akiriyā*) depending on whether one has been invited or not invited, he said “being invited,” and so forth.
However, if one who has been invited eats without asking the host, this training rule (sikkhāpada) becomes "action-and-non-action" (kriyākiriya) by virtue of that act.
Herein, eating is action; not asking the host is non-action.
The phrase beginning with “having had something made allowable” (kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā) was said specifically with reference to one who has already been invited. If she should consume it, for her—
And the construction is: "It may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) by way of action. "May be" (siyā) means necessarily.

The meaning is that for one who consumes [the food]—whether having had it made allowable according to the method stated in the Pavāraṇā training rule or not having had it made allowable—an offense necessarily arises by that very act of consumption through this training rule.
The Fourth.

2332. Regarding this training rule, “Whatever bhikkhunī should be stingy with respect to families, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),” he says “of bhikkhunīs,” etc., in order to show the detailed exposition (vinicchaya).
For one who speaks dispraise of bhikkhunīs in the presence of a family, there is an offense of expiation.

The connection is as follows: "in the presence of a family" means there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who speaks dispraise of the bhikkhunīs, saying, "The bhikkhunīs are immoral and of evil character. Or, "or dispraise of the family":

there is an offense of expiation for one who, in the presence of the bhikkhunīs, speaks dispraise or faults of that family, saying, "That family is faithless and lacks confidence. This is the connection.
2333. To speak of a fault when there is no fault means: for one who, being without envy, speaks of a fault or danger that actually exists regarding either a family or the bhikkhunīs.

This is the fifth [offense]. 2334–5. "One who gives exhortation" means: one who gives exhortation by means of the eight *garudhammas*. "To one who has entered the rains residence" means: to one who is observing the rains residence.
2336. "Bhikkhus" refers to those bhikkhus who give exhortation. This is the sixth [section]. 2338.
That bhikkhunī who has completed the rains residence, having stayed for either the first or the second three-month period, immediately thereafter—
The construction is as follows: he renounces his responsibility by saying, "I will not perform the *pavāraṇā*," before both Saṅghas—that is, both the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

This is the seventh [case]. 2341. "For the sake of the exhortation and so forth" means for the sake of hearing the eight weighty rules (*garudhamma*) and so on. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inquiry regarding the *uposatha* and the *pavāraṇā* are included.
2342. By not going for the sake of exhortation and so forth, there is non-performance. "Bodily" means bodily action. This is the eighth [offense]. 2343.
"Every half-month, two things must be expected from the Saṅgha of monks by a bhikkhunī: the inquiry regarding the Uposatha and..."

Regarding the training rule: "There is an offense of expiation for one who transgresses the approach for instruction," he said "I will not ask" and so forth in order to show the analysis (vinicchaya) of this rule. This has a self-evident meaning.
The ninth [section].
2346–7. *Pasākha* means the region below the navel and above the kneecaps.
For it is called *pasākha* because both thighs have branched out from it like the branches of a tree;
[the word refers] to that *pasākha*. *Sañjāta* means arisen. *Gaṇḍa* means any kind of boil. *Rudhita* means any kind of wound.
“Or to the Saṅgha” means to the community of bhikkhunīs. “Or to a group” means several bhikkhunīs.
Regarding the word “with one,” the word “by a man” is to be supplied; this is an instrumental case used in the sense of accompaniment. As it is said: “one [woman] with one man.
And by “man,” only a human male is to be understood.

By the word *iti*, used here in the sense of "beginning with," the triad of commands—"anoint, bind, release"—is included, because it encompasses the other three training rules (*sikkhāpada*) found in the text: "or have [her] anointed, or have [her] bound, or have [her] released.
For this very reason, he will later say: "There are six offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and six of expiation (*pācittiya*)."
However, if a nun, without having informed the Saṅgha or a group,

instructs a single man while she is alone with him regarding a boil, a wound, or an abscess occurring in the groin— commanding him to "cut it," "split it," "wash it," "anoint it," "bind it," or "loosen it"—
there are six *dukkaṭas* for her. The application is that when the six acts, such as cutting and so forth, have been performed, there are six *pācittiyas* for her.
"2348–9. *Ettha* means in a boil or a wound. The construction is: "If she should command thus: 'Do everything that is to be done,' [then there is an offense].
The construction is: "By that single act of commanding, there may be twelve offenses—namely, six *dukkaṭas* and six *pācittiyas*."
"Having asked permission" means having asked permission from either the Saṅgha or a group. "A companion" means a female companion. The construction is: "or even taking a wise person as a companion.
This is the tenth [offense]. The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga), is concluded.
2353. Although it should have been stated as *gaṇapariyesanādismiṃ*, the elision of the nasal (*niggahita*) is for the purpose of preserving the meter.

*Gabbhiniṃ* means one who has conceived; the meaning is one who has entered a being into her womb. *Vuṭṭhāpentiyā* means by one who is conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*). *Kammavācāhi* means by two formal acts (*kammavācā*). 2354–5.
*Kammavācāya osāne* means at the conclusion of the third formal act; the meaning is when the syllable *yya* has been reached.

"Perceiving her as pregnant when she is not pregnant" means perceiving one who is not pregnant as being pregnant. "When doubt has arisen regarding both" means when uncertainty has arisen concerning both;
the meaning is: when there is hesitation regarding whether she is pregnant or not. Here, the word *su-* is elided for the sake of the metrical composition of the verse. Thus, the construction is:
"For the preceptor who ordains [her] in such a manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). [This applies to] the teacher (*ācariyā*).
“Of her” (*tassā*) refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāyā*) who ordains a pregnant woman, and to the teacher (*ācariyā*) who causes her to hear the formal act (*kammavācā*).
“Of the group” (*gaṇassa*) refers to another group of nuns other than the preceptor and the teacher. The construction is: “In that way, the *dukkaṭa* offense is explained. 2356. The word-break is:
“In the two cases, with the perception of ‘not pregnant’” (*dvīsu agabbhinisaññāya*). “In the two” (*dvīsu*) means: in the case of one who is pregnant and in the case of one who is not pregnant.
First. 2357.

Regarding the second: “Whichever nun should ordain a woman who is nursing [an infant], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This is the training rule. In this training rule, the distinction is that one called “nursing” is either the mother or the nurse.
Second.
2358. But whichever nun should ordain a *sikkhamānā* who has not trained for two years in the six rules, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
such is the construction [of the rule]. In this context, "two years" means two full years by way of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
"In the six rules" refers to the six beginning with abstaining from taking life and ending with abstaining from eating at the improper time.

Regarding "in the dharmas": "one who has not trained in the training" refers either to one who has not undertaken the precepts according to the method beginning with, "I undertake the restraint from taking life for two years without transgression," or even if they have so undertaken them, one whose training has become corrupted.
Or, it refers to a *sikkhamānā* because she trains in those six dharmas, or because she honors those dharmas which are termed "training."
"Thus named" refers to one who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*). "Should ordain" means she should grant full ordination.

"There may be an offense" means that, according to the method explained in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*), at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), there may be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); the meaning is that it becomes an offense of expiation. 2359.
"If it is a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*) and she perceives it as a legitimate legal act, and she ordains [her], there is an offense of expiation. If it is a legitimate legal act..."

If she ordains one who is doubtful, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). If, regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), she perceives it as an illegitimate legal act and ordains her, there is an offense of expiation.
Thus, regarding a legitimate legal act, the Teacher has stated three cases of expiation.

“If, regarding an illegitimate legal act, she perceives it as a legitimate legal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If, regarding an illegitimate legal act, she is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Regarding an illegitimate legal act...”

“If one restores [a person] while perceiving the formal act as illegitimate, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Thus, regarding an illegitimate formal act, the Teacher has illustrated three sets of wrong-doings.
2360. “Unbroken” means not having made it broken.

2361. If one who desires full ordination (upasampadā) has been a wanderer (pabbajitā) for sixty years, these six training rules (sikkhā) must be given to her so that they are not transgressed for two years; the construction is: "Without giving these, one should not cause [her] to act, nor should one cause her to be ordained.

This is the third [section]. 2362. Regarding the fourth, there is nothing further to be said; because of the specific distinction that will be explained, there is nothing else to be said, and thus it follows the same method as previously stated.
The intention [of the text] is as follows. By the words “here” (*idha*) and so forth, it shows the specific qualification found in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The construction is: “In this case, for the nun who is ordaining that *sikkhamānā* who has been approved by the Saṅgha, there is no offense (*anāpatti*) in this training rule.
[And: “For a *sikkhamānā* who has trained in the six rules for two years, by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha... [2363]

Regarding the formal act (*kammavācā*) consisting of one motion and two proclamations (*ñattidutiyā*) prior to full ordination (*upasampadā*), the permission for recovery (*vuṭṭhānasammuti*) must be granted;
if that permission for recovery has not been granted first, it must indeed be granted there, even in that ordination hall (*upasampadamāḷaka*). 2364.
"And the third" refers to the third training rule (*sikkhāpada*); "and the fourth" refers to this fourth training rule.
"By the first, it should be known as equal" means it should be understood as being identical to the first training rule in its determination, such as its origin and so forth.
However, the fourth training rule is "action/non-action" (kriyākriya) by way of giving the full admission (*vuṭṭhāpana*) without having obtained formal authorization (*sammuti*).
This is the fourth.

"2365. *Gihigataṃ* means one who has gone over to another man; the meaning is that she has reached union with a man. *Paripuṇṇā dvādasavassā* [means] "full twelve years," by the elision of the latter member of the compound.
The construction is: "even though there is no fault. *Vuṭṭhāpentiyā* means by her who, having become a preceptor (*upajjhāyā*), confers full admission (*upasampadā*).
2366. It is said: "the rest. [This means] completely, in every way."
The fifth [section].
2368. Regarding the phrase "a co-resident who is suffering," the word "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*) is to be understood as the remainder.
The eighth [training rule] is that which was stated in the Tuvaṭṭaka-vagga as being connected with these two words, "a co-resident who is suffering."
The object of knowledge is equal; there is no distinction because there is no difference—this is the construction. "The eighth" refers to the training rule stated thus:
"Whatever nun, having given the full admission to a co-resident, neither herself instructs nor causes her to be instructed for two years, commits a *pācittiya* offense.
In this context, "co-resident" means a student (*saddhivihārinī*). "Neither herself instructs" means she does not herself instruct her through recitation and so forth.
"Should not cause to assist" means: she should not cause another to assist her by saying, "Noble lady, give this woman the recitations and so forth.
It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) as soon as the duty is abandoned.
The eighth [offense].
2369. Whatever nun does not attend upon the preceptor who has ordained her for two years, for her there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
this is the construction of the phrase "explained by way of enumeration. "One who ordains" means one who has ordained;
"one who attends" means one who causes [the pupil] to train well; "one who has ordained and is an attendant" is *vuṭṭhāpitapavattinī*, which is a designation for the preceptor (*upajjhāyā*).
“Toward that preceptor. “One should not follow after him” means one should attend to him with various necessary services, such as with powder, clay, tooth-sticks, or water for rinsing the mouth.

If she lays down her burden by saying, “I will not follow for two years,” then the construction is that at the mere moment the burden is laid down, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.

2371. However, regarding the nun who does not follow her preceptor when he is foolish or shameless: the construction is that there is no offense for her if she does not follow him due to illness, or due to emergencies, or if she is insane.
2372. It is said that "it occurs through non-attendance," thus [the text] says, "the non-performance has been stated.
The ninth [section].

2373–5. Whatever bhikkhunī, having had a co-resident or a student (saddhivihārinī) ordained and having taken her along, should not go even as far as five or six yojanas, nor should she command another, saying, "Go, noble lady, taking this one," nor should she direct anyone else;
if, at the very moment the responsibility is cast off, she thinks, "I will not go now," [she commits an offense].

The construction is as follows: "If, having abandoned her resolve, she takes another [person] and does not direct her to go, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The construction is as follows:
"There is no fault if there is an obstacle, or if she cannot find a companion, or in cases of emergency, or if she is ill, or if she is insane.
This is the tenth [offense].
The seventh chapter: On Pregnant Women.

2376. “By the three rules concerning those who have gone to a house” means by the fifth, sixth, and seventh training rules associated with the word “gone to a house” in the immediately preceding chapter on pregnant women.
“Are similar” means that here the mention of “twenty years” and the mention of “a maiden” correspond to those [in the previous chapter].
Excluding the expressions *dvādasavassa* (twelve years) and *gihigata* (married), the remaining determinations (*vinicchaya*) are exactly similar according to their respective order.
Regarding the term *mahūpapadā*: those *sikkhamānā* (probationary nuns) for whom there is a prefix (*upapada*) of "great" (*mahā*) are called *mahūpapadā*.
Since a prefix is appropriately applied only to words and not to meanings, the word *yāsaṃ* (of whom) is used as a separate term to include the words *sikkhamānā* and so forth.
However, because the non-differentiation of the referents of the terms is intended here, it should be understood that those who have taken up the training of a *sikkhamānā* are included;
thus, the term "great *sikkhamānās*" (*mahāsikkhamānā*) is used. Regarding the word "from the beginning" (*āditoti*), the word "stated" (*vuttā*) is to be supplied as the remainder;
this refers to the two *sikkhamānās* mentioned in the first and third training rules of the three sections concerning women who are pregnant.

The meaning is as follows: Since a distinction has been stated on the basis of years—namely, that for one who has gone to the household life it is "full twelve years," and for one who is still a maiden it is "full twenty years"—the author says, "She who has reached twenty years should be understood by the discerning," in order to show that the distinction between those two and the *mahāsikkhamānā* is likewise based solely on the number of years;
the meaning is that she who has exceeded twenty years is called a *mahāsikkhamānā*.

2378. Those two types of *mahāsikkhamānā*s—whether they be married women or not yet married to men—must be addressed as "sikkhamānā" during the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*) for the granting of consent (*sammuti*) and so forth;

this is the construction [of the meaning]. Herein, "consent" (*sammuti*) refers to both the consent for the training (*sikkhā-sammuti*) and the consent for the higher ordination (*vuṭṭhāna-sammuti*), which must be performed by a formal procedure consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyā kammavācā*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) is included.

2379. Having shown what should be recited in the motion (*ñatti*) and the formal act (*kammavācā*) regarding the granting of consent (*sammuti*) and so forth for these two types of women, he now says "not those," etc., to show what should not be recited.

Since neither of these two types of *mahāsikkhamānā*—whether called "virgins" (*kumāribhūtā*) or likewise "married women" (*gihigatā*)—should be mentioned by name in the formal act, therefore it is not permissible to speak in that manner.
The construction (*yojanā*). By the phrase "it should not be said," it is indicated that if the formal act (*kammavācā*) were recited in such a manner, that act would be invalid.

Here, however, since the word *pana* has the sense of "because" (*yasmā*), the construction is shown according to that meaning. 2380. "Consent" (*sammuti*) means consent for a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*).
Regarding the phrase "for one who is ten years [old]," the words "who has gone to a householder" (*gihigatāya*) are to be supplied as the remainder. As it has been said:

—“When she has reached ten years of age while living as a householder, the formal permission for training (*sikkhāsammuti*) should be granted, and when she has reached twelve years of age, the full ordination (*upasampadā*) should be performed.
Regarding the others as well: having granted the permission for training at eleven years of age, it should be performed at thirteen;
having granted the permission for training at twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, or eighteen years of age, [the ordination] should be performed at twenty years of age.
"It should be done" refers likewise to the remaining *sikkhamānās* who have reached the age of eighteen. "This method" means:
"She should be ordained in the second year following the year in which the formal authorization (*sammuti*) was granted. For this very reason it is said:
"Having granted [the authorization] at the age of eleven, it should be performed at the age of thirteen," and so forth.

2381. The construction is as follows: it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that it is permissible to refer to her either as a "virgin" (*kumāribhūtā*) or as one who has "gone to a householder" (*gihigatā*).
2382. However, a female novice (*sāmaṇerī*) who is twenty years of age and is called a "virgin" must be addressed as such during the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*);
otherwise, she should not be addressed as one who has "gone to a householder" (*gihigatā*) or as one who has "gone to another man" (*purisantaragatā*).
The construction is: "or they should not be so called. As it is said: "But a maiden who has gone forth as a householder (gihigatā) should not be called 'one who has gone forth as a householder';
she should be called simply 'a maiden' (kumāribhūtā). "But these three," however, refers to those spoken of as both a *mahāsikkhamānā* and a *gihigatā*, as well as a *kumāribhūtā*.
By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that it is permissible to refer to the two—the *gihigatā* and the *kumāribūtā*—by their respective individual names as well.
He illuminates [the point]. Someone might think that it is not permissible because it is not mentioned in the Pāḷi as “for a *sikkhamānā* who has become a maiden”;
therefore he says, “there is no doubt. He says, “because of the granting of the authorization for training,” in order to show the reason why it ought to be stated in that way.
[This concludes] the first, second, and third [sections].
2384–5. But whichever nun, being less than twelve years [of standing] and thus not having completed the twelve years required for full ordination (*upasampadā*),
acts as her own preceptor (*upajjhāyā*) and formally ordains another trainee (*sikkhamānā*),

then immediately following the offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) incurred during the search for a group and so forth, up to the conclusion of the second proclamation, as previously described, [there follows the offense of the formal act].
The construction is as follows: when the third proclamation has been completed and the motion has reached its conclusion, that *pācittiya* offense is thereby revealed.
This is the fourth [case].
2386. Regarding the fifth: "Whichever nun, though being twelve years of age and complete, should give the full admission (*vuṭṭhāpeyya*) without having been authorized by the Saṅgha..."

In the training rule (sikkhāpada), it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). It has three origins (samuṭṭhāna): by way of body and mind, by way of speech and mind, and by way of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding "action and non-action" (kriyākriya): ordination (vuṭṭhāpana) is action; the failure to obtain the formal authorization of the Saṅgha is non-action.
This is the fifth [category].
“By the Saṅgha” means by the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*). “Having investigated” means having investigated her state of shamelessness and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “Enough for you now,” the words “those ladies” (*te ayye*) are to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the word “restrained” (*vāritā*), the words “having assented, saying ‘Very well’” (*sādhūti paṭissuṇitvā*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
Thus, having been restrained with the words, “Enough for you now, lady, with this full ordination,” and having assented, saying “Very well,” [the following occurs] here, in this context.

The construction is as follows: if, after the *pavāraṇā*, one criticizes [the Sangha], proclaiming dispraise by saying, "Surely I alone am foolish," "Surely I alone am shameless," and so forth, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) due to the fault [of such criticism].
Regarding the phrase "one who acts out of malice toward the consent, etc.":

here the word "by nature" (*pakatiyā*) is to be supplied. The construction is: if one criticizes [the Sangha] when she is acting to prevent them from naturally following wrong paths due to malice toward the consent, etc., there is no fault.
The sixth [offense].

2389–90. Regarding "when the robe has been obtained": after a female trainee (*sikkhamānā*) has said, "If you, Noble Lady, will give me a robe, I shall ordain you," and it has been requested, [the offense occurs] when that robe has been obtained. "Afterwards" means after the obtaining of the robe.

"Without obstacles" (*asante antarāyike*) means when none of the ten obstacles are present. "I will not ordain you" (*vuṭṭhāpessāmi nāhan-ti*) means "I shall not cause you to arise [in the higher training]";
the construction is that there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for such a relinquishing of one's duty. 2391.
"This" (*idan-ti*) refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). It is non-action by virtue of not ordaining.
The seventh. 2392.

The eighth is the training rule beginning: "Whatever bhikkhunī should say to a *sikkhamānā*: 'If you, noble lady, will follow me for two years, then I will give you the full admission (*vuṭṭhāpessāmi*),' and so forth. The ninth is: "Whatever bhikkhunī..."

Regarding the training rule stated as: "If one should ordain a female trainee (sikkhamānā) who associates with men, associates with youths, is fierce, or dwells in grief, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya)":
the phrase "there is nothing to be said" is stated because the legal determination (vinicchaya) is easily understood without needing a specific distinction in the meaning of the words.
For that very reason, he says: "This is indeed clear."
The meaning of the words should be understood as follows: "Associated with men" means associated with a man who has reached full twenty years of age through improper bodily or verbal actions.
"Associated with boys" means similarly associated with a boy under twenty years of age.
"Fierce" means prone to anger. "A dwelling place for grief" refers to [a situation where] men come after having made an appointment.

"Those who enter into sorrow are 'dwellers in sorrow' (sokāvāsā); that is, the dwelling in sorrow. Alternatively, just as the owners of a house [enter] the house, these women, not obtaining the company of men, are entered by sorrow;
thus, because they are entered by it, that [sorrow] becomes their dwelling—hence "dwellers in sorrow.
For this very reason, its word-commentary explains it in two ways: "Dwellers in sorrow means they produce suffering for others and they are entered by sorrow."

The meaning has been stated. Regarding the term *pācittiya*: for one who ordains such a person, at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*) according to the method already described, there is a *pācittiya* offense for the preceptor (*upajjhāyā*). 2393.

The phrase "there is no [offense] for one who does not know" is the break in the text; the meaning is: for one who does not know that the female trainee (*sikkhamānā*) is associated with men and so forth.
The eighth and ninth [rules]. 2394.

The construction is as follows: for a nun who ordains (*vuṭṭhāpeti*) a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) who has not been permitted by her mother or father—whether she be the biological mother or father, or the husband or the husband who has taken her in—and who is not permitted for the sake of full ordination (*upasampadā*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
2395. "By a nun" means that it should not be asked twice; it should be asked only once.
This has been stated. As it was said: "The nuns must request permission twice—at the time of going forth and at the time of full ordination;
however, for the monks, it is permissible even if they have requested only once.
(2396–7) *Atthitaṃ* means existence (*atthibhāva*). It originates from four [factors], or its origins are four.
It has four origins. To the question, "By which four does it originate? he says: "From speech... and also from body, speech, and so forth.

How does it originate from the four, such as speech? For instance, when those sitting within a broken boundary for some business such as a *abbhāna-kamma* (act of rehabilitation) say, "Call the *sikkhamānā*;
we shall ordain her right here," and they thus perform the ordination—thus [it originates].
It originates from speech. Having said, "I will confer the full ordination starting from the monastery," it originates from body and speech for one who goes to a broken boundary (khaṇḍasīma).
For one who, having understood the rule in both instances, commits a transgression, it originates from speech, mind, and body-speech-mind.
Conferring the ordination is an action; not asking permission is a non-action.
The Tenth. 2398.

Herein, the construction is as follows: if a nun, by means of the giving of consent by one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*), should ordain a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for her.
In that context, "by means of the giving of consent by one who is on probation" refers to the fourfold [consent].
There are five kinds of postponement: postponement by the assembly, postponement by night, postponement by consent, and postponement by intention.

Among these, "postponement by the assembly" means that when the monks have gathered for some business, then either a rain cloud arises, a signal is given, or people arrive overwhelming them; [the monks]...
Thinking, “This is not the proper time; let us go elsewhere,” they rise without having relinquished their consent (*chanda*). This is called “the assembly being dispersed.
Even though the assembly has been dispersed, because consent has not been relinquished, it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*).
Again, monks, having gathered at night thinking, “We shall perform the Uposatha and other rites,” [wait] until all have assembled.
They request one [monk], saying, "Let us hear the Dhamma," and while he is still delivering the Dhamma talk, the dawn breaks.
If they were sitting down thinking, "We will perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day," it is permissible for them to perform it on the fifteenth.
If they were sitting down to perform the Uposatha on the fifteenth, they must not perform the Uposatha on the first day of the month, which is not an Uposatha day.
It is permissible. However, it is also permissible to perform other business of the Saṅgha. This, then, is what is called "postponement for a night.

Furthermore, suppose monks have sat down thinking, "We shall perform some business of the Saṅgha, such as a formal act of rehabilitation (abbhāna)," and there a monk who is an astrologer says, "Today the constellation is inauspicious; do not perform this business."

Having relinquished their consent at his word, they remained sitting right there; then another person came and, having said, "The purpose has passed the fool who was waiting for the auspicious moment," he added, "What is the use of the auspicious moment?
Do [what needs to be done]! This is both the relinquishing of consent and the relinquishing of intention.

In this case of one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*), it is not permissible to perform a formal act (*kamma*) without again bringing forward their consent and purity of conduct (*chandapārisuddhi*).
It is with reference to this that it was said: "by the giving of consent by one who is on probation.

"There may be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)" means that for her who performs the formal act of restoration in the manner described, there may be an offense of expiation at the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).

2399. The construction is as follows: there is no offense for one who ordains [a woman] while the assembly has not yet departed—that is, without having dismissed them or without their having risen—while the assembly remains seated as it was. The word *vā* (or) has the sense of *eva* (only/just). This is the eleventh [offense]. 2400. Regarding the twelfth:

in the training rule, “Whichever bhikkhunī, however, should ordain [a woman] every year, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Regarding the thirteenth: in the training rule, “Whichever bhikkhunī, however, should ordain two [women] in one year, there is an offense of expiation.”
The twelfth and thirteenth [rules].
The eighth chapter: The Chapter on the Maidenhood. 2401.
"Not ill" means free from a disease that must be alleviated by means of an umbrella or sandals. As it is said: "One who is not ill is one for whom..."
“It is comfortable without the sunshade and sandals. “Sunshade and sandals” (*chattupāhana*) refers to the sunshade and the sandals. Herein, the sunshade has the characteristics already described;
the sandals will have their characteristics explained later. “She should carry” means she should carry both together.
For he will state that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who carries them separately.
2402. *Divasanti* takes the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) because it denotes continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). The construction is: "if he carries [it]. 2403.
Regarding the phrase "mud and so forth" (*kaddamādīni*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here includes "vast quantities of sand" (*mahāvālukā*) and other such things.
2404. The connection is: "if he goes. Having seen [the ground], he goes toward a place that is lower, suitable for attaching the umbrella, and so on.
"Having seen a tree, etc."—by the word "etc.," groves and so forth are included. "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that for the mere wearing of sandals, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

2405. "Having removed" means having removed them from the head. "Having taken off" means having taken them off from the feet. "There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)" means that it becomes an offense of expiation once again. 2406.
"Only by the counting of the acts" means by the counting of each act of wearing the umbrella and sandals after having repeatedly removed them together.

The "triple *pācittiya*" is stated as follows: "If one who is not ill perceives herself as not ill, or is in doubt, or perceives herself as ill, and she uses a sunshade and sandals, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

Thus the triple *pācittiya* is stated. The connection is that the "double *dukkaṭa*" is likewise stated thus: "If one who is ill perceives herself as not ill, or if one who is ill is in doubt, and she uses a sunshade and sandals, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. Thus it is stated.

2407. Wherever monks or nuns reside—whether in that monastery (ārāma) itself, in its vicinity (upacāra), or in the vicinity of an unenclosed monastery. "In times of distress" means in times of distress such as civil war and the like.
First [section]. 2408. Regarding the term "nun": here the phrase "who is not ill" is understood as a supplement; it refers to one who is not ill and is capable of traveling on foot.
The meaning is "a bhikkhunī. As it is said: "One who is not ill is one who is able to go on foot. A "vehicle" means a chariot and so forth;
its specific nature has already been explained below. 2409.

"In cases of distress" refers to such distresses as civil war and the like. In the training rule concerning the umbrella and sandals, no offense was stated for being within an *ārāma* or in the vicinity of an *ārāma*; since that is not stated here, it should be understood that there is an offense everywhere.
The second [section]. 2410. “Whatever is for the waist” is a synonym for “waist-band” (*saṅghāṇi*). As it is said: “What is called a ‘waist-band’ is anything that goes around the waist.
A “waist-band” refers to an ornament worn on the waist, such as a girdle (*mekhalā*) and so forth. “For the waist” means that which reaches the region of the waist.
2412. *Kaṭisuttaṃ* means a cord or string worn as an ornament around the waist.

2413. Here, in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the mind is unwholesome; furthermore, this training rule is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*). Thus, these two factors constitute the distinction and difference between this [rule] and the preceding training rules.
The third [section].
2414. The construction is as follows: if she wears anything among head-ornaments and the like, there would be offenses according to the number of those items.
"Head-reaching" (*sīsūpaga*) means that which reaches the head; the meaning is that it is fit to be worn on the head.

By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), neck-ornaments and so forth are included. As it has been said: "Female ornament (*itthālaṅkāra*) is that which reaches the head, that which reaches the neck, that which reaches the hands..."
"Reaching the feet, reaching the waist"—this is the construction.
And it is not a fault [to say this]. When it should have been said, "It is explained as 'they resemble' (*sadisaṃ*)," the word *iti* is indicated as being elided.
This is the fourth [section].
"By whatever scent" means by any kind of fragrant paste, such as sandalwood, tagara, and so forth. "With color or without color":
that which exists together with color is "with color" (*savaṇṇaka*), such as turmeric paste;

that for which no distinct visible color is perceived due to the application of an ointment is "without color" (*avaṇṇaka*), such as mustard-seed paste; "with color or without color" refers to both the colored and the colorless types.

The construction is as follows: for one who bathes after having rubbed [her body] with both scented and unscented [powders], at the conclusion of the bath, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is declared.
2417. "In every application" means in every prior application. "On account of illness" means on account of diseases such as ringworm, skin eruptions, and so forth.
2418. "The sixth" refers to the training rule: "Whichever bhikkhunī should bathe with scented oil-cakes, there is an offense of expiation."

The fifth and sixth [rules]. 2419. However, the construction is as follows: "If a nun should have another nun rubbed or massaged, that nun incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). 2420. Herein, regarding this rubbing and massaging:

if she rubs her without releasing her hand, there may be a single offense; if she rubs her by repeatedly releasing her hand, there may be offenses according to the number of applications (*payoga*). This is the construction.

"2421. In times of distress (*āpadā*) means during bodily tremors caused by fear of thieves and the like. 'To one who is ill' (*gilānāya*) means to one who is afflicted with disease, even if it is merely from the fatigue of traveling on a road.

2422. In order to show that, excluding the specific distinctions of 'a trainee nun' (*sikkhamānā*) in the eighth training rule, 'a novice nun' (*sāmaṇerī*) in the ninth training rule, and 'a female householder' (*gihinī*) in the tenth training rule, the remaining analysis is identical to that of the seventh [training rule], he said:"
“‘The three beginning with the eighth’:
[this refers to] the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth.
‘Within the precincts’ means within twelve *ratana*s. ‘In front of a bhikkhu’ is an illustrative expression (upalakkhaṇaṃ).”
Therefore, whether it be in front, behind, or within sight—this is an illustrative phrase meaning "within twelve ratanas all around.
"Even on the ground" means even on ground that is not covered by grass; this is to be connected with the word "should sit. It is not permitted; the meaning is that there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
2424. The threefold *pācittiya* has been stated: [the cases of] perceiving as unpermitted when it is unpermitted, being doubtful, and perceiving as permitted.
In the three alternatives, the three *pācittiya* offenses have been stated.

In the two alternatives—where one sits down in front of a monk while having requested permission but perceiving that it was not requested, or being in doubt—a pair of *dukkaṭa* offenses occurs. "In cases of emergency" refers to emergencies such as civil unrest in the kingdom and so forth;
[it applies] to a sick nun who is unable both to request permission and to remain standing.
2425. Lying down is an action; not asking permission is a non-action. This is the eleventh [offense]. 2426.

One by whom leave has been given is "one for whom leave is granted" (*okāsakata*); one who is not one for whom leave is granted is "one for whom leave is not granted" (*anokāsakata*), meaning one who has not had leave granted.
“‘In such-and-such a place I shall ask’—this refers to the time when one requests permission by mentioning the name of the Vinaya or other subjects one intends to inquire about;
it is said that ‘no permission has been granted’ because of the refusal [of the request]. Regarding ‘fault’: it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Even for one who has requested permission regarding one Piṭaka but asks a question concerning another Piṭaka, there is an offense of expiation.”
To show this, he said, “In the Vinaya,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “even for one who asks,” the word *pi* (also/even) here implies “even for one who asks about the Abhidhamma. Furthermore, by the particle *ca* (and) used in the sense of an inclusive conjunction, it means:
“Having requested permission regarding the Sutta, she asks about either the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma; there is an offense.”
This is also included [in the rule]: "If, having requested an opportunity for the Abhidhamma, one asks about the Suttanta or the Vinaya, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
(2427) "Without specifying" means not determining it thus, "I am asking about such-and-such," but simply saying, "There is something to be asked; I ask you, Venerable Sir."
The Twelfth. 2428–9.
*Saṃkaccika* means a robe for wrapping around the breasts; it must be worn by one who covers the area below the collarbone and above the navel while putting it on.
Therefore, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "Not wearing a *saṃkaccika* means [not covering] that which is defined as the area below the collarbone and above the navel..."
"She is one who lacks the *saṃkaccika* robe permitted for the purpose of covering the body. Regarding the measurement of the *saṃkaccika*, the Elder Vajirabuddhi states in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*:
"Its measurement across is one and a half cubits. "In entering the enclosure" means in entering within the boundary of the enclosure.
"Also in entering the vicinity" means even in entering within the range of a second stone's throw from an unenclosed village.

“In this” means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). “The same method” means that the method already stated—namely, “there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the first step, and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the second”—is considered and understood; such is the meaning.
“Even in cases of distress” means: if the bodice (*saṃkaccika*) is of great value, and a danger arises for one who is going after having put it on, there is no offense in such cases of distress.

2431. They understand it here both from its own form and as that which is not explicitly shown. "By the very method already stated" means by the very method stated in the summary headings (*mātikā*), the word-commentaries (*padabhājana*), and so forth.

One who "makes manifest" (*vibhāvī*)—that is, one who clarifies and reveals in various ways the nature of the phenomena (*dhammajāta*) and the nature of the meanings (*atthajāta*) in a most skillful manner—is a "maker-manifest" (*vibhāvī*); [the term refers] to such a maker-manifest. This is the thirteenth [chapter].
The ninth chapter: On Sandals.

Having thus shown the ninety-six training rules for bhikkhunīs that are not shared with bhikkhus through nine chapters, in the seven subsequent chapters beginning with the Chapter on False Speech, the training rules shared with bhikkhus [are explained] according to the exposition of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha.
They are to be understood in the manner already stated, and thus they are not shown here.
All together, there are one hundred and eighty-eight training rules (sikkhāpada): ninety-six for nuns in the Minor Rules (Khuddaka-vagga) and ninety-two for monks.
Beyond that, there is the entire Bhikkhunī-vagga, as well as eating in succession (parampara-bhojana) and eating what is not left over (anatiritta-bhojana).
These are: inviting [a meal] with food that is not left over; requesting exquisite food; the training rule concerning the naked ascetic;
concealing a grave offense; ordaining one who is less than twenty years of age; traveling by appointment with a woman; entering a royal palace;
entering a village at an improper time without asking a monk who is present; using a sitting mat; and the rainy-season robe—these are they.
It should be understood that, excluding the twenty-two training rules (*sikkhāpada*), the remaining one hundred and sixty-six training rules are recited by way of the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.
Herein, this is the summary of the determination of the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) regarding the non-common training rules: the Giraggasamajja [incident].

The ten training rules (sikkhāpada) concerning the following—namely, the rule on the house of women (cittāgāra), the hip-string (saṅghāṇi), female ornaments, scents and cosmetics, scented sesame oil, and being massaged or rubbed by bhikkhunīs and so forth—are without intention (acittaka), offenses against worldly standards (lokavajja), and associated with unwholesome states of mind (akusalacitta). This is the intended meaning here:
they are "without intention" because they must be committed even without a [specific] intention; however, when there is a mind...

Because they must be committed by an unwholesome mind alone, these are both world-transgression offenses (*lokavajja*) and unwholesome states of consciousness. The remainder, being without a [specific] mental state, are only formal-rule transgressions (*paṇṇattivajja*).

These include: the instigation of thieves, the offense regarding traveling between villages, the training rule on entering a monastery, the seven rules beginning from the first in the section on pregnant women, the five rules beginning from the first in the section on unmarried girls, the rule on associating with men, and the giving of consent while under probation.

The annual ordination (*anuvassavuṭṭhāpana*) and the intermittent ordination (*ekantarikavuṭṭhāpana*): these nineteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) involve intentional action (*sacittaka*) and are offenses by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
All the remaining ones involve intentional action and are offenses against the world (*lokavajja*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya*, titled the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the discussion of the *pācittiya* rules is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the *pāṭidesanīya* rules: 2432.
Having thus shown the determination of the *pācittiya* rules, he now says “one who is not ill,” etc., in order to show the *pāṭidesanīya* rules.

The construction is as follows: "But whichever nun, not being ill, takes ghee that she herself has requested, thinking 'I shall eat it,' for her taking it in this manner, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared.
In this context, one who finds comfort without ghee is called "not ill. "Ghee" refers specifically to cow-ghee and so forth, as previously defined and included in the Canon.
2433. Regarding "three *pāṭidesanīyas*": for one who is not ill, perceiving oneself as not ill, or being in doubt—among these three alternatives, there are three *pāṭidesanīyas*.

"For one who is ill, there are two *dukkaṭas*": for one who is ill, there are two *dukkaṭas*. For one who is ill, perceiving oneself as not ill, or being in doubt—among these two alternatives, there are two *dukkaṭas*.
2434–5. Having been ill and having requested ghee, if she later uses it after her illness has subsided;
or if she uses what remains when she is no longer ill; or if she uses what was requested from a relative or from a place where relatives have invited her;
or if she uses what was requested for the sake of another; or if she uses what was obtained with her own wealth.
The construction is: "There is no offense for one who is eating or for one who is insane.
First [offense]. 2436.
Regarding the second and subsequent rules among the remaining ones: "Whichever nun, however, not being ill, [uses] oil... pe... honey... pe... molasses... pe..."
If she should request and eat fish... [etc. ...meat... [etc. ...milk... [etc. ...or curd, that bhikkhunī must confess:
"Venerable ladies, I have committed an offense that is blameworthy, unbecoming, and one requiring confession;
I confess it. Thus it is for the second through the seventh *pāṭidesanīya* rules. There is no difference [in the procedure]; it is the same except for the words beginning with "oil" and so forth.
The meaning is that there is no other distinction whatsoever.
2437. The construction is as follows: even for one who, having requested any one of the eight substances beginning with ghee—which are not mentioned in the Pāḷi—eats them, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya* in the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the discussion of the *pāṭidesanīya* rules is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the training rules (*sikkhākaraṇīya*):
2438. Following the *pāṭidesanīya* rules, the seventy-five *sekhiya* rules that were recited have their detailed analysis already stated in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*.
Extending that same [principle] by way of analogy, he says: “But as for those rules of training (sekhiya-dhamma),” and so forth. The construction is as follows:

since the analytical exposition of the meaning of those seventy-five rules of training which were recited immediately after the rules on offenses entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) has already been stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga, they should be taken from there by those who desire them;
my intention is that I shall not present them again here.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discussion of Training and What is to be Done, within the *Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā*,
which is an elucidation of the essence of the meaning of the Vinaya. [2439–40] Of the two Pātimokkhas together with their respective Vibhaṅgas, for both monks and nuns...
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Having taken up all that essential meaning— which is the core of the commentaries on the Pātimokkhas,

which constitutes the essence of all commentaries, and which has been stated specifically in the *Samantapāsādikā*— this exposition of the Vinaya has been composed and arranged by me for the benefit of both monks and nuns."
2441. This Vinaya-vinicchaya, which has arisen from our own inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāṇa*), is beneficial for those beings who hear it;
it is beneficial for the world of beings because it elucidates the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
It is "well-thought" (*sumata*)—that is, thought by the Buddha and others—or it is "thought by the well-thought [ones]," namely, the Buddha and others. It is thus helpful to the people of the world.
For those who know the Vinaya— the Vinaya Piṭaka— which is the path and the straight way for reaching the great Nibbāna of the Deathless that has been penetrated,
and which serves as a refuge by warding off the fear of the states of woe because it is the antidote to transgressions of body and speech:

the meaning is that they become "knowers of that," knowing things according to their true nature, and thus they become those who know each respective thing as allowable or unallowable, and as fit to be practiced or not to be practiced.
2442. Because many essential principles (*sāra*) are found herein, it is called the *Bahusāranaya*;

in that *Bahusāranaya*. A wise ascetic, possessing the power of knowledge, who especially desires—by earnestly seeking—the state of fearlessness (*vesārajja*), which is unshakable knowledge, within the supreme and highest discipline (*vinaya*), namely the Vinaya Piṭaka, [should strive] at all times for the fulfillment of the threefold training.

The meaning is this: a monk who practices right effort with unwavering persistence must especially exercise the highest, most supreme, great, and most essential degree of reverence toward this exposition of the Vinaya; indeed, it is precisely this that must be done. 2443.
Thus, because it is the cause for confidence (*vesārajjahetutāya*), this exposition of the Vinaya [is included] within the Vinaya Piṭaka, which accomplishes purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).
In order to show that [the study of grammar] is the very root for attaining the deathless Great Nibbāna—
which must be realized through the succession of the seven purifications beginning with purification of virtue—
he said, "He understands," and so forth. Furthermore, that bhikkhu who possesses what is meaningful— that is, endowed with great purpose and with a subject matter— is...
One who understands this exposition of the Vinaya and knows it as it truly is through direct penetration attains the state of peace— the deathless because there is no further succession of death,

the ageless because there is no aging, the stainless because it is the antidote to the dust of defilements such as lust, the painless because it is the cause for the non-occurrence of manifold diseases,
and the state of peace because it is the cause for the subsiding of all the distress and fever of the defilements.

The construction is as follows: one attains the state of Nibbāna, which is designated as "peace," by penetrating it after proceeding through the succession of the seven purifications beginning with purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya* within the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the analysis of the Bhikkhunī rules is finished.
The Khandhaka Analysis:
The Mahāvagga.

Thus, in this manner, [the account] has been presented in the two Vibhaṅgas and their respective commentaries by a method that is neither too concise nor too prolix. 2444. [End of] the Explanation of the Discourse on Going-forth in the Mahākhandhaka.
Having shown the exposition [of the Sutta], he now began to show the exposition found in the Khandhakas, saying:

"Endowed with the aggregate of virtue, etc. Therein, "endowed with the aggregate of virtue, etc. means endowed with—possessed of—the five aggregates which are heaps of qualities, namely: virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. "With a beautiful trunk" means because of having a rounded trunk resembling a golden pillar.
The Blessed One is called *Subhakkhandho* because he has a beautiful (*subha*) and handsome (*sundara*) shoulder (*khandha*).
By this statement, which illustrates the characteristic of having well-rounded shoulders— a single part of the thirty-two marks— by way of the "supplying of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇāhāranaya*),
it should be understood that the entire splendor of the physical body, beginning with the thirty-two marks, is thereby demonstrated.
*Khandhaka*: A *khandhaka* is a collection (*samūha*) of sections (*khandha*); or, it is called a *khandhaka* because it illuminates (*dīpana*) the body (*kāya*) of the sections.

Here, by "sections" (*khandhā*), what is intended are the formal acts of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) such as going forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*), as well as the rules of training (*sikkhāpada*) consisting of proper conduct (*cāritta*) and prohibited conduct (*vāritta*).
For these, such as going forth and so on, are called "rules" (*paññatti*) because they were laid down (*paññatta*) by the Blessed One.
Furthermore, the word *khandha* is seen in the sense of a designation (*paññatti*), as in such examples as "a log of wood," "a mass of fire," and "a body of water.
Moreover, the meaning of "a portion and a heap" is indeed appropriate here, because those designations are analyzed both by way of their parts and by way of their collection.
In that section on the aggregates (*khandhaka*), the word "also" (*pi*) refers back to the previously mentioned sections on the five hundred and seven hundred aggregates.

Having excluded two [sections], because the twentyfold determination (vinicchaya) stated in the sections beginning with the Pabbajjā-khandhaka and ending with the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka will be explained here,
he said with reference to that very point: "I shall also explain the determination in the Khandhakas in brief."
Regarding the phrase “by mother and father,” it is the biological parents who are intended.

“Shaving (bhaṇḍukamma), making a novice (samaṇakaraṇa), and ordination (pabbājanā) are synonymous terms”—this is stated in the commentary on this passage: “I allow you, monks, to seek permission from the Saṅgha for the purpose of shaving.
In the expression “having asked permission,” the word “Saṅgha” is to be supplied as the object.
“Vāvaṭo” means diligent; the sense is “one who is engaged and applied. The phrase “having ordained, bring him back” (*pabbājetvā ānaya iti*) is the word-division.
Here, ordination (*pabbājana*) should be understood as threefold: the cutting of hair, the donning of the saffron robes, and the granting of the refuges.
One who performs these three is said to “ordain. Even one who performs only one or two of them is designated by that same term.
Therefore, it should be understood that by the phrase "having caused him to go forth," the meaning is: "having shaved his hair and clothed him in the saffron robes, bring him here.

2447. "Uninstructed" means not commissioned by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). The construction is: if that youth himself performs the shaving of the hair and the donning of the saffron robes when he causes him to go forth, it is permissible.
2448. "Therein" means in one's own presence. "Having led him to a partial boundary" (*khaṇḍasīma*) is for the purpose of avoiding the announcement of the formal act (*bhaṇḍukamma*).
It has been stated. Therefore, it is not permissible to say to another monk in a monastery where monks are present, "Shave this man's hair.
By the phrase "having ordained," he is speaking with reference to the shaving of the hair.
(2450) The statement, "It is not permissible for one other than a monk to ordain a man," is said with reference to the granting of the refuges; for that very reason, he says "a novice" and so forth.

2451. The construction is as follows: by the command of both the elder monk and the elder nun, "Clothe him with these robes," whether it be a novice (*sāmaṇera*) or likewise a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), both the novice and the novice nun are permitted to give the saffron-colored robes (*kāsāyāni*).
2452–4. Regarding the phrase "by the monk who ordains": here it should be stated, "having given the meditation subject of the 'five-fold skin' (*tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).
For it is by doing so that the removal of hair is mentioned in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Indeed, it is said there: "Friend, well..."
Having said, "Consider this; establish mindfulness," the meditation subject of the "Fivefold Skin" (tacapañcaka) should be explained.

And while explaining it, one should explain it by making evident its impurity, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness according to its color, shape, smell, location, and source—or its lack of life and lack of a sentient being—and so forth.
If one asks, "For what purpose is this done?"—it is for one who is endowed with a sufficient basis (upanissaya).
...it exists for the sake of his attaining Arahantship right at the tip of the razor. And this has been said in the Commentary:

"Whosoever have attained Arahantship at the tip of a razor, they all did so after obtaining such a hearing and relying on the method given by a teacher who was a good friend, not without such reliance; therefore, from the very beginning, such a discourse should be delivered to him.
By this very statement, it is shown by way of contrast that other discourses which do not lead to liberation should not be delivered. "With cow dung, etc. means...
"By means of cow-dung powder, etc."—by the word "etc.," clay and so forth are included. "A boil" means a large boil; "scabies" means fine scabies.
"One's own son" means one's own child. Because of the distance between the words, he said "by the ascetic" (*yatinā*) instead of "by the bhikkhu" (*bhikkhunā*).
2455–6. But why should he be bathed in this manner? To answer this, he says: "Even by this much," and so forth. "He" refers to the one seeking admission to the going-forth (pabbajjā).
Regarding the phrase "among the preceptor and others": here, the word "others" (ādi) includes the teacher, co-students, and so on.

In the expression "for they reach [him]," the particle *hi* functions in the sense of a causal conjunction (*yasmā*). This is because even by this much, he is respectful toward the preceptor and the rest.

And because, having received such assistance, sons of good family will dispel arisen discontent, fulfill the trainings, and reach Nibbāna, therefore such assistance should be rendered; this is the meaning. 2458.
"Together" means having gathered all the robes into one place.

2459. Now, *atha* is a particle used at the beginning of a new section. The construction is as follows: even without giving it into his hand, it is permissible for either the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or the teacher (*ācariya*) to clothe that person seeking admission to the order himself.

2460. Because one must not accept a robe that has not been given, he says: "Having removed all of that from him, it must be given back again. "From him" means from his body; "that" refers to the robe. 2461–2.

He states this very point with the words beginning "by a monk" (*bhikkhunā*). Regarding the phrase "what is not given is not permissible," here it means that the going forth (*pabbajjā*) does not take root.

They say: even a robe belonging to that very person, if not given, is not permitted; what need is there to mention robes belonging to oneself, or those belonging to one’s own teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya)?
The meaning is that there is simply nothing to be said [in favor of taking them]. "Bhikkhus" refers to those who have assembled there.
Regarding the phrase "having made [them] squat," the verb *karoti* here is understood as encompassing the meanings of all verbal roots (*dhātu*); thus, it means "having made [them] squat."

The meaning to be understood is "having caused [them] to sit. Regarding the term "ukkuṭika," the reading in the Aṭṭhakathā is indicated here with the elision of the letter *k* for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.

"Or even a single word" means even a single word such as "Buddha" and so forth. "Or even a single syllable" means even a single syllable among the phonemes beginning with the letter *b*. "In succession" means the sequence of words beginning with "Buddha" and so forth.
2465. To show another type of improper procedure, he said, “If three times,” and so forth.
“Likewise for the others” means that if one gives the refuge in the Dhamma three times, or if one gives the refuge in the Saṅgha three times—even in this way, the three refuges remain unbestowed.

The connection is: "having made them end in a nasal, they are to be given. To show that they are to be given at the time of recitation having been made to end in a nasal, without making an interruption in the middle, it is said: "or else, as a single continuous whole. This means:

having separated them according to the sequence of words, and having made them end in the letter *m*, one makes an interruption at the time of giving [the recitation]. Regarding the word "mantrāni" (mantras), it refers to [the formula] beginning with "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī" and so forth.

[The words] ending in the letter *m*—such as "I go for refuge to the Buddha" (*buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi*) and so forth—should not be given [as they stand], because the final nasal stop (*niggahita*) must be changed;
thus he said, "then. 2467.
"Purity" (*suddhi*) refers to the teacher’s purity in the pronunciation of the motion (*ñatti*) and the formal act (*kammavācā*). "Going forth" (*pabbajjā*)...

The going forth for novices and the state of being a novice. "Without the purity of both sides" means that without the purity of recitation by both the teacher and the pupil—regarding the threefold giving and receiving of the refuges—even if there is the presence of a single faulty syllable, it does not [constitute the going forth]; such is the meaning.

2468–9. The phrase “desiring the virtues of the going-forth” (pabbajjāguṇamicchatā) should be understood as a qualification of the two terms “by the teacher” (ācariyena) and “by the pupil” (antevāsikena).
That is to say, by the teacher who desires the virtues of the pupil’s going-forth, and by the pupil who desires the virtues of his own going-forth;
[the term] “syllables” (akkharā) refers to the phonemes beginning with the letter *bu* and the letter *dha*, such as the syllable *bu* and the syllable *dha*.

The construction is as follows: it should be spoken by one who does not lose or neglect the perfection of place (*ṭhāna*)—which consists of the divisions of throat, palate, lips, teeth, and nose—and the perfection of instrument (*karaṇa*)—which consists of the tongue-tip and so forth that are most effective in producing the phonemes. Why is this stated with such emphasis?

He says: "By the destruction of even a single phoneme," and so forth. The word *hi* (for) has the sense of the causal particle *yasmā* (since), because [even] by the destruction of a single phoneme...
The intention is that the going forth does not take root through either mispronunciation or failure to pronounce at all; therefore, it is said thus.

By the phrase "if [the words] are mastered," which implies a state of apprehension, the difficulty of achieving purity in the pronunciation of both [teacher and pupil] is illustrated, and thus the instruction is given to both the teacher and the pupil: "One must be heedful. "From the moment of going for refuge..."

By this restriction, it is shown that the going forth as a novice (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) does not occur through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma), as is the case with full ordination (upasampadā);
rather, even now, it is accomplished by the mere going for refuge alone. The word "hi" (for) expresses a well-known fact. As it has been said:
"Since full ordination by means of going for refuge was rejected later on, therefore it is [now] accomplished by the mere going for refuge."

It does not take root. However, as for the going forth of a novice (sāmaṇera), since it was already authorized by the Blessed One even at another time—by the words, “Monks, I allow this going forth of a novice by means of these three goings for refuge”—therefore, even now, it takes root by the mere act of going for refuge alone.
Although the going forth is thus established and accomplished through the goings for refuge alone, nevertheless, for this novice...
The construction is as follows: having understood, "This and that virtue must be fulfilled by me," the ten precepts should be given by a monk for the purpose of their fulfillment.
As it was said: "I allow, monks, ten training rules for novices, and they should train in them.
[They are: abstention from taking life," and so forth.

Commentary on the Discourse on Going Forth (Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā). 2471. Regarding the term *upajjhāya*: one is called an *upajjhāya* because he reflects (*upanijjhāyati*) upon what is blameworthy and what is blameless. This refers to a person endowed with the qualities mentioned by the Blessed One and possessing ten years of seniority.
Having dressed [the candidate] and having clothed [him], [he should place] his hands in *añjali* at the head...
Having taken hold [of him], he should sit down squatting facing him and say three times, "Venerable sir, be my preceptor. When this request has been made,

[the preceptor] should communicate by means of body, speech, or both, one of these five points— namely, "Good," "Quickly," "Appropriate," "Suitable," or "Accomplish it with a pleasing demeanor"— and then, toward that [candidate]...
One who, having accepted [the candidate] and taken his place in the father’s role, takes him as if he were his own son,
examines what is blameworthy and what is blameless, restrains him with fault-finding, and trains his co-residents, is called an *upajjhāya*.
One who should be respectfully served and attended upon by those desiring to learn knowledge, craft, or proper conduct is called an *ācariya*.
The person who possesses exactly the characteristics described for an *upajjhāya* should sit down in the same manner as previously stated and say three times:
"Venerable sir, be my teacher; I shall live in dependence upon the Venerable One.

When this request has been made, and after [the other] has said one of the five responses beginning with "Very well," and having accepted, he should stand in the position of a father toward the one standing in the position of a son.
One who trains a resident pupil is called an *ācariya* (teacher).
In this context, *sāhu* means "well" (*sādhu*). *Lahu* means "not heavy" (*agaru*); the meaning is: "In my being your preceptor (*upajjhāya*), there is no burden for you.
*Opāyika* means connected with a means (*upāya*); that is, "by this means, you [should accept] the taking of me as your preceptor."
The meaning is: "From this point on, you have become a burden. "Suitable" means that taking [this person] as your preceptor is appropriate for you.
"With pleasing" means with a physical and verbal application that inspires confidence. "Accomplish" means bring to completion the threefold training.
"Or by body" means by showing hand gestures and so forth with the body. Regarding the duties to be fulfilled without specifying particular names:
Because of their equality, both are stated together.
These duties must be performed by the *saddhivihārika* toward the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), and likewise by the *antevāsika* toward the teacher (*ācariya*).

"While dwelling" means while living there. "By one of lovely virtue" (*piyasīlena*): he whose virtue (*sīla*) is dear is "one of lovely virtue"; by him; that is to say, by one who desires to fulfill virtue.

2472–3. Regarding the instruction, "The seat should be prepared," the preliminary duties mentioned here—namely, "having risen early, having removed one's sandals, and having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder"—should be stated.

As for the phrase "the seat should be prepared," after sweeping the place where the tooth-stick is chewed, a seat should be prepared for sitting. By this [same principle], seats should also be prepared for the place where rice-gruel is drunk, and so forth.
It is shown that [the tooth-stick] must indeed be provided.

Regarding the instruction "a tooth-stick should be given": having brought three types of tooth-sticks—large, medium, and small—one should give the same kind as the one taken on the third day, starting from the fourth day onwards. If...
If one makes no specific restriction and takes whatever is available, then whatever kind is obtained should be given.
Regarding "water for the mouth" (*mukhodaka*): it is water for rinsing the mouth; the term *mukhodaka* is a compound formed by eliding the middle word (*majjhepadalopī-samāsa*).
