When giving this, one should bring both cold and warm water, and from that [mixture], whatever is used for three days, starting from the fourth day...

From that point on, water for rinsing the mouth of the same quality should be given. If he takes whatever is offered without making a distinction, then whatever kind he receives, that should be given.
If he uses both types, both should be brought forward.
"Having set aside the water for rinsing the mouth in the place designated for rinsing the mouth, the remaining areas should be swept."
"And while sweeping, one should sweep starting from the latrine. When that person has gone to the latrine, the courtyard should be swept;
in this way, the courtyard remains unvacant. It should be swept according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
To show what must be done beyond that, he said: "Of him, at the proper time," and so forth. "Of him" refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or the teacher (*ācariya*).
Or: "At the proper time" means at the time for drinking rice-gruel (*yāgu*). Here too, the remainder of the phrase is "a seat should be prepared. As it has been said:

"The seat should be prepared even before the elder has emerged from the restroom. Having performed his bodily functions and returned, one should perform the duty (*vatta*) prescribed for one who is seated there, beginning with the words: 'If there is rice-gruel... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "rice gruel should be brought to him," the words "having washed the vessel" are to be supplied as the remainder. As it has been said: "Having washed the vessel, the rice gruel should be brought.
"From the Saṅgha" means either obtained from the Saṅgha by means of voting tickets (*salākā*) and so forth;
or "from a family" means from a family such as that of lay devotees (*upāsaka*).

"The duty regarding the bowl must be performed"—this refers to the duty as it has been handed down: "After he has drunk the gruel, having given him water, and having received the vessel, he should wash it carefully without scraping it, keeping it low, and put it away;
when the preceptor has risen, the seat should be removed; if that place is dirty, that place should be swept."
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). By this, it is also shown that [the duties] must be performed even when one has already eaten during the day.

Regarding the duty [described] as "upon entering a village," he spoke with reference to the duties set forth in such a manner as: "If the preceptor wishes to enter a village, the inner robe (*nivāsana*) must be given [to him], and the outer robe (*paṭinivāsana*) must be received [from him]," and so forth. "[Must be performed]" (*kātabba*).
This should be applied to all the terms.

2474. Regarding "the duties concerning the robe": whatever duties were prescribed by the Great Seer (Mahesi) for one wishing to enter a village—namely, the giving of the robe, and upon returning, the taking up, folding, and putting away of the robe—all those must be performed.
"In the same way regarding the lodging" means: in whichever monastery...
The duty regarding lodgings (*senāsanavatta*) is also shown by the method stated in the passage beginning, "The preceptor dwells," etc., as something "to be done in the lodging.
The phrase "likewise" (*tathā*) should be applied to the footstool, the foot-scraper, and so forth.

Furthermore, the duty that has come down in the tradition—namely, "When the preceptor has returned from the village, and at the bathhouse, a foot-bath, a footstool, and a foot-scraper should be set out"—should also be observed.
It should be done. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the conduct beginning with "The preceptor (*upajjhāya*) should be asked for water" is included.

2475. Thus, when the rules of conduct (*vatta*) are being shown individually in all instances, [the author] says "such as these" (*evamādīni*) and so forth, desiring to show a count for the sake of easy comprehension, noting that there is prolixity (*papañca*) if they were shown separately. They range from [the rule regarding] illness up to the arrival [from a journey].
The periods for the teachers and preceptors begin from their recovery from illness and end with their arrival [at the monastery].

"There may be one hundred and thirty-three" means there are one hundred and thirty-three duties (*vatta*). Those duties, however, should be brought together according to the number already stated, following the sequence found in the Khandhaka-pāḷi:
the giving of tooth-sticks, the giving of water for rinsing the mouth, the arranging of the seat, and if there is rice-gruel, washing the vessel.
Bringing the rice gruel; after the teacher has drunk the gruel, giving him water, receiving the vessel, lowering it, and washing it carefully without scratching it, putting it away;
when the preceptor has risen, removing the seat;
if that place is dirty, sweeping it; and if the preceptor wishes to enter the village.
He should give him an undergarment, receive the inner robe in return, give him a waistband, and having made it with multiple layers, give him an upper robe;
having washed it, he should give him an alms bowl with water remaining in it.

If the preceptor desires an attendant monk, [the student], covering the three circles and wearing the lower garment evenly, having fastened the waistband and having made the upper robes with multiple layers...
Having put on the robes, having loosened the neck-tie, having washed the bowl, and having taken it, one should go as the attendant monk behind the preceptor;
one should walk neither too far behind nor too close; one should receive whatever is placed in the bowl;
and while the preceptor is speaking, one should not interject with talk in between, nor should one do so when the preceptor is speaking in connection with an offense.
Warding off [the sun or rain]; having returned earlier than [the guest], arranging a seat;

placing out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-wiping cloth; going out to meet [the guest] and receiving their bowl and robe; giving them a spare lower garment; receiving their own lower garment;
if the robe is damp, drying it for a short while in the warmth, but not leaving the robe in the heat; and so forth.
Folding the robe so that there is no break in the middle, one should extend the ear by four finger-widths;
then, making a fold for the waist-band. If there is almsfood and the preceptor wishes to eat, one should give water and present the almsfood.
One should ask the preceptor if he needs drinking water once he has finished eating.

Having given water and received the bowl, having lowered it and washed it thoroughly without scraping it, and having made it free of water, one should warm it for a short while in the heat, but not leave the bowl in the heat. The bowl and robe should be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand and the lower part of the bed or bench with the other hand.
Placing the bowl down after touching the lower part of the stand; not placing the bowl on ground that has not been cleared;

and when putting away the robe, holding the robe with one hand and wiping the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, then folding the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side of the robe—
Setting down [the bowl], rising from the seat once the preceptor has emerged, putting away the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-wiper;
if that place is dirty, sweeping it; if the preceptor wishes to bathe, preparing the bath;
if there is need of cold water, providing cold water; if there is need of warm water, [providing warm water].

Providing protection against heat; if the preceptor wishes to enter the sauna, [the student] should prepare the powder, moisten the clay, take the sauna-bench, follow closely behind the preceptor, give him the sauna-bench, receive his robe, and lay it aside to one side; he should then give the powder and the clay. If...
One should exert oneself to enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover the front and back [with a cloth], and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks, nor should one sit encroaching upon the junior monks.
Warding off [the sun] with a seat; performing services for the preceptor in the sauna;
when leaving the sauna, taking the sauna-bench and covering it from the front and back before exiting the sauna;
performing services for the preceptor even in the water; and having bathed, emerging first and [wiping] one's own limbs.
Having provided water for washing and having dressed himself, he should wipe the preceptor’s limbs with water, give him a lower robe, and give him an upper robe;
taking the sauna-bench, he should return first, prepare a seat, and set out the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-stand;
he should ask the preceptor if he wants drinking water, and if he wishes to have the recitation performed, he should arrange for the recitation.
If he wishes to inquire, he should inquire. If the dwelling where the preceptor resides is dirty, and if he is able, he should clean it.
While cleaning the dwelling, he should first take out the bowl and robes and set them aside, and then take out the sitting mat and spread.
Setting aside the mattress and pillow to one side after removing them;
setting aside the bed to one side after lowering it and carefully removing it through the door-sill without striking or knocking against it;
and setting aside the chair to one side after lowering it and carefully removing it through the door-sill without striking or knocking against it.
Removing [the bed] and placing it to one side; removing the bed-legs and placing them to one side;
removing the spittoon and placing it to one side; removing the leaning-board and placing it to one side;
and, having observed the floor-covering as it was arranged, removing it and placing it to one side.
If there is mold in the dwelling, first scrape it off from the ceiling; then wipe down the openings of the windows and the corners.
If the walls have been treated with red ochre and have become moldy, wipe them down after moistening and squeezing out a cloth.
If the floor has been treated with black pigment and has become moldy, wipe it down after moistening and squeezing out a cloth. If...
The ground is prepared by sprinkling it with water and sweeping it so that "the dwelling may not be covered in dust," by clearing away refuse and discarding it to one side,
by drying, cleaning, and shaking out the floor-covering and then bringing it back and spreading it down as arranged,
and by drying, wiping, and bringing back the bed-legs and placing them in their proper place.
The setting out [of the furniture] consists of: having dried the bed in the sun, cleaned it, dusted it, lowered it, and then carefully carrying it across the threshold without knocking or jarring it;

and having dried the stool in the sun, cleaned it, dusted it, lowered it, and then carefully carrying it across the threshold without knocking or jarring it, and finally placing them down according to their designated positions.
Having carried it back, he should arrange it according to its prescribed place;
having dried, cleaned, and beaten the mattress and pillow, he should carry them back and arrange them according to their prescribed places;
having dried, cleaned, and beaten the sitting mat and rug, he should carry them back and arrange them according to their prescribed places; and having dried and wiped the spittoon.
Having carried it back, one should place it in its proper place; having dried and wiped the leaning-board, one should carry it back and place it in its proper place;
the bowl and robe should be set down.
When setting down the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and [support] the lower part of the bed or bench with the other hand.
Either touching the lower seat before setting down the bowl, or not setting down the bowl on ground that is free from living beings;
and when putting away the robe, having grasped the robe with one hand and wiped the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand,
having made the edge far and the fold near, [of the robe]—
As for the closing [of windows]: if dusty winds blow from the east, one should close the eastern windows;
likewise for the western, likewise for the northern, and likewise for the southern windows.
If it is the cold season, one should open the windows during the day and close them at night; if it is the hot season, during the day...
The closing of the windows, the opening [of them] at night; if the courtyard is dirty, sweeping the courtyard;
if the storehouse is dirty, sweeping the storehouse; if the assembly hall is dirty, sweeping that; if the fire-hall is dirty, sweeping that. If...
The cowshed becomes dirty; its sweeping; if there is no drinking water, the providing of drinking water;

if there is no water for washing, the providing of water for washing; if there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, the pouring of water into the rinsing-pitcher; if the preceptor has a lack of interest...
If remorse arises in the preceptor, the student should dispel it or cause it to be dispelled, or provide a Dhamma talk for him;
if anxiety arises in the preceptor, the student should remove it or cause it to be removed, or provide a Dhamma talk for him; if a wrong view arises in the preceptor...

If the preceptor has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) and is deserving of probation (parivāsa), the student (saddhivihārika) should either separate himself from him or cause him to be separated, or he should give a discourse on the Dhamma to him; furthermore, the student should exert himself with the thought:
"How might the Saṅgha grant probation to my preceptor? If the preceptor is deserving of being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), [the same applies].
There is the exertion by the student (*saddhivihārika*) [thinking], "How might the Sangha send the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) back to the beginning?
If the preceptor is one who deserves the trial period (*mānatta*), there is the exertion by the student [thinking], "How might the Sangha grant the preceptor the trial period?
If the preceptor is one who deserves rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), [there is the exertion] by the student...
Making an effort means: "How indeed might the Saṅgha rehabilitate the preceptor?

If the Saṅgha intends to perform a formal act against the preceptor—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the co-resident disciple must make an effort, thinking: "How indeed might the Saṅgha [rehabilitate] the preceptor..."
“[The pupil] should ensure that the teacher does not perform an act, or that he transforms it into a minor one.

Furthermore, if a formal act (kamma) has been performed against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure (tajjanīya), a demotion (niyassa), a banishment (pabbājanīya), a reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya), or a suspension (ukkhepanīya)—the co-resident pupil must exert himself [to help], thinking:
“How might my preceptor behave properly, lower his pride, and conduct himself so as to be released from this?”

“May the Saṅgha suspend that legal procedure. If the preceptor’s robe needs washing, the student should either wash it himself or make an effort toward its being washed, thinking, “How can my preceptor’s robe be washed?
If the preceptor’s robe needs making, the student should either make it himself or make an effort toward its being made.

Or, [thinking] "How might I prepare a robe for my preceptor? if the preceptor's dye needs to be boiled, the student (saddhivihārika) should make an effort toward boiling it, thinking "How might I have the preceptor's dye boiled?
Or, if the preceptor's robe needs to be dyed, the student should [prepare] the dye...

Or making an effort, thinking, "How might my preceptor’s robe be dyed?"—when dyeing the robe, one should carefully turn it over repeatedly while applying the dye; one should not depart while the drips have not yet ceased;
and without having asked the preceptor for permission, one should not give an alms bowl to anyone, nor receive an alms bowl from anyone.
giving robes to some, but not accepting robes from others; giving requisites to some, but not accepting requisites from others;
cutting hair for some, but not having one’s hair cut by others;
performing services for some, but not having services performed by others; nor...
There is no performing of services for some, nor causing services to be performed by others; no going as an attendant for some, nor taking others along as attendants;
no carrying out of almsfood for some, nor having almsfood carried out by others;
no entering a village without asking permission from one's preceptor; and no going to a cemetery.

There is no departing for another region; if the preceptor is ill, there must be attendance for as long as life lasts, and upon his recovery, he must return—among these, some duties are specified in detail while others are not.
If the details of those not specified were to be stated, they would exceed the aforementioned number; however, without taking up that detailed classification...
It should be understood that this enumeration is shown by taking [the items] collectively.
Regarding the phrase "for one who does not perform," the word "duty" (*vatta*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

For a bhikkhu who, out of mere disrespect, does not perform his duty, there is—due to that breach of duty and that failure to perform it—the same number [of offenses] in every instance throughout the one hundred and thirty-seven categories of points.
The construction is: "the *dukkaṭa* offense has been declared.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the duties toward preceptors and teachers.

(2477) Having thus shown the duties toward preceptors and teachers in brief, [the text now addresses] the co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) and pupils (*antevāsika*) in relation to their preceptors and teachers.
To show the duties that are to be performed, he said, "The duties toward the preceptor," and so forth.

"The duties toward the preceptor" means that these are duties dependent upon the preceptor, because they are to be performed by the resident pupil (saddhivihārika) at the appropriate and fitting time.
Likewise, "toward the resident pupil" means that just as [duties] are to be performed by the resident pupil for the preceptor, so too [are duties] by the preceptor.
The duties toward a co-resident student (saddhivihārika) are as follows:
regarding the duties toward preceptors and teachers, when entering a village, one should follow behind as an attendant, neither going too far away nor too close;

one should not interrupt the conversation from time to time; one should prevent [the teacher] from speaking near a transgression; and one should receive whatever has been placed in the teacher’s alms-bowl.

Excluding the four *vattas* and the twenty prohibitions—beginning with the giving of the bowl and ending with departing without asking permission—there are one hundred and thirteen remaining *vattas*.

It is with reference to these that he says, "there are one hundred and thirteen," meaning that there are one hundred and thirteen *vattas*. [The same applies] when the teacher [speaks] regarding the resident pupil (*antevāsika*).
And the duties that ought to be performed are likewise exactly that many; such is the meaning.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the duties toward co-residents and pupils.
2478. [The method for] the cessation of dependence for co-residents and pupils by means of preceptors and teachers.
To demonstrate this, he said: “Or when [the preceptor] has departed,” and so forth. The construction is as follows:

in five ways—whether the preceptor has departed, or has gone away, or has joined another faction, or has died, or by means of an instruction—the dependence (*nissaya*) accepted by the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) from the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is extinguished.
“Departed” (*pakkanta*) means having gone in some direction with no intention of returning on that very day. “Gone away” (*vibbhanta*) means having entered the state of a householder (*gihibhāva*).

*Patte*: gone over to another faction; *pakkhasaṅkantake*: having gone to the sphere of the heretics; *mate*: deceased; *āṇattiya*: by means of the dismissal from formal dependence (*nissaya*). 2479–80.
The application is that the breaking of the formal dependence taken from a teacher by a pupil occurs in six ways, in six manners.
How so? He says: "And when he has departed," and so forth. That is exactly according to the method already stated regarding the breaking of dependence from a preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
However, he will himself explain the distinction with the words beginning "by an instruction" (*āṇattiya*).

In the phrase "by an instruction," the particle *pana* is used here as an indicator of a specific meaning, though it has been elided in the grammatical expression. Regarding the phrase "also when both have laid down their burden":

when the teacher dismisses the formal dependence (*nissaya*), if both the teacher and the pupil are indeed without mutual reliance upon one another, there occurs a dissolution of the dependence (*nissayabhedo*).
The meaning is "not for one alone. He strengthens that same point through contrast with the words "for each one," and so forth.
The construction is: "If there is attachment (ālaya) for either one or both, it is not severed. As it has been said:
"But in the case of an instruction, even if the teacher, being desirous of releasing [the pupil], dismisses him by means of the dismissal from dependence (nissayapaṇāmanā), the resident pupil..."
Even if [the pupil] thinks, "Although my teacher dismisses me, he is nevertheless soft-hearted," he remains full of longing, and the formal dependence (nissaya) is not lifted.

Even if the teacher is full of longing while the resident pupil is free from longing and, thinking, "I will no longer live under his dependence," lays down his burden, even so it is not lifted. When both are full of longing—
"But it does not subside; it subsides only through the relinquishing of responsibility by both.

This distinction, however, is shown only in the case of the breaking of dependence (*nissaya-bheda*) by the teacher's command (*ācariya-āṇatti*), and not by the preceptor's command (*upajjhāya-āṇatti*).

In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, however, it says: "Even if the teacher, being desirous of releasing [the pupil], dismisses him by means of the dismissal from dependence (*nissaya-panāmanā*), all of this [applies] to the preceptor..."
“It should also be understood in the case of a command,” it is said.
Having thus shown the five common factors, he spoke in order to show the uncommon factor: “It is also broken for one who has gone into association with a preceptor.
Therein, he spoke to show the going into association both in its essential nature and its classifications: “Seeing...”
"And the *savana* (hearing)"; thus, "the summary is considered twofold. This is the brief account here;
however, the detailed exposition should be taken from the *Samantapāsādikā*. It has not been elaborated upon here for the benefit of those who fear excessive textual expansion.
2482–3. When a suitable donor is not present, [one may accept] from a traveler or a sick person [with the thought]: "The sick person is attending to me."
The construction is: "There is no fault in one who has been asked [to stay] and a caregiver for the sick living without formal dependence (nissaya).

In the phrase "of the caregiver for the sick" (*gilānupaṭṭhākassa*), the short vowel is used for the sake of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*). By this, it is indicated that when there is a suitable provider of dependence present, one does not receive the exemption even for a single day.
"Knowing the state of dwelling at ease in his own forest" refers to [knowing] the attainment of one's own serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Even for one who knows there is comfortable living in the forest. The phrase "in the absence of a suitable donor" is the word-division (*padaccheda*).

All this procedure is to be understood as applying to a time other than during the rains retreat. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Suspension of Formal Support (*nissaya*).

2484. One who has *kuṭṭha* (leprosy) is a *kuṭṭhī*; this refers to such a person. The same method applies to the terms "one with a boil" (*gaṇḍī*) and so forth. The meaning is: a body that has reached a state of discoloration due to some kind of leprosy, whether it be red, black, or otherwise. As it is said:
"Whether it be red leprosy or black leprosy, whatever there may be—whether distinguished as *kiṭibha*, *daddu*, *kacchu*, and so on—all of it is simply called 'leprosy' (*kuṭṭha*).
And if that [leprosy] is even the size of a fingernail or the back of a finger, and it remains in a state of increasing," [so it is said].

He should not be ordained. However, if—in the areas naturally covered by the lower and upper robes—the [growth] is no larger than the surface of a fingernail and remains in the non-growing state, it is permissible.

But as for the mouth or the backs of the hands and feet, even if it remains in the non-growing state, it is not permissible at all, even if it is smaller than the size of a fingernail; thus it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
It has been stated: "Even when one is to be ordained after having had [a disease] treated, he should be ordained only when his natural appearance has returned.
Regarding the phrase "the size of the back of a fingernail," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "the back of the fingernail of the little finger is intended here.
Regarding the term *gaṇḍi*, it refers to one who possesses various types of swellings such as fat-tumors (*medagaṇḍa*) and so forth; as it is said: "Whether it be a fat-tumor or any other..."
"Even if there is a goitre the size of a jujube stone (*kolaṭṭhi*) that is growing, he should not be ordained," and so forth.
"Jujube stone" (*kolaṭṭhi*) means the stone of a *badara* fruit. "Leper" (*kilāsi*) means one who has leprosy. As it is said:

"Leprosy (*kilāsa*) is a non-ulcerating, non-exuding form of leprosy with the color of a lotus or white lily leaf, by which the body becomes spotted like that of cattle. The word "and" (*ca*)... [text continues]
All [the terms] ending in *-vant* should be joined individually. *Sosin* means one who has the disease of consumption (*khaya-roga*).
As it is said: "Consumption means the disease of consumption; if that exists, he should not be ordained. *Apamārin* means one who has epilepsy (*apamāra*). As it is said:

"Epilepsy means either bilious insanity (*pittummāra*) or possession by a spirit (*yakkhummāra*). In that case, one seized by a non-human being (*amanussa*) with whom there is a prior enmity is difficult to cure."
“...he exists; however, if there is even a slight offense, he must not be ordained.
Regarding the term *rājabhaṭa*: it refers to a royal official hired for food and wages, whether he has attained a position of rank or not.
As it is said: “Whether he be a minister, a high official, a servant, or one who has attained some position or not...”
Or, anyone who is a soldier hired for food and wages by the king—all such come to be reckoned as "the king’s soldiers.
As for "a thief," this refers to a thief well known to people through acts such as plundering villages or attacking travelers on the road.
As for "one who has been written down," this refers to someone who, having committed a theft or some other grave offense against the king, has fled; and the king [records] him on a document...

Or on a manuscript, one who causes it to be written such as: "Wherever a person named so-and-so is seen, he is to be seized and killed," or "His hands, feet, and so forth are to be cut off," or "He is to be made to pay such-and-such a fine"—this is a written warrant (*likhitaka*).

In the phrase "breaker of the prison" (*kārabhedaka*), the vowel is shortened by virtue of its placement within a metrical verse (*gāthābandha*). "Breaker of the prison" refers to one who has committed a crime for which a penalty is to be imposed, or one who has performed a criminal act.
Or one who, having been cast into a prison for some reason, or being bound by shackles, fetters, and the like, escapes and flees from there—such a person is a "breaker of prisons.
As it is said: "Prison (kārā) is called a place of confinement;
here, however, it may be a binding with iron chains, or a binding with fetters, or a binding with ropes, or a binding to a village, or a binding to a town."
“Whether it be a city prison, a guard post for men, a provincial prison,
or a national prison— whosoever, having cut, broken, released, or opened any such bond among these,
flees while they are either watching or not watching him, he is reckoned as a ‘prison-breaker.’”

"Struck with a whip" refers to the blow administered with a whip or similar instrument by one who, having borrowed money and being unable to repay it, is told, "Let this very thing be your punishment. As it has been said:
"One who is beaten for failing to perform verbal commands or errands does not undergo the punishment for his [specific] deed.
But one who, having taken or consumed something by means of a loan or otherwise, and being unable to give it back, is beaten with whips with the words, 'Let this very thing be your punishment'—"

"This one has been struck with a whip; he has undergone punishment. Whether he has been struck with whips or with any other such thing as a half-staff, as long as he is still moist from it, he must not be ordained. Regarding "one struck with a mark":

having placed the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over one shoulder, it refers to one who possesses a mark on a part of the body that cannot be concealed by the robe—such as a burn from heated iron—as described thus: [he is] "one struck with a mark."
"But for one who has a mark branded on the forehead or on the chest and other such places with red-hot iron:

if he is a free man (*bhujissa*), he must not be ordained as long as the wound is still moist. Even if his wounds have healed and the skin has grown back level, if the mark is still visible when he wears the three circles [of robes]—that is, when the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is placed over the covered area—"
If he is such [a person], it is permissible to give him the going-forth. If he is in an unhidden place, it is not permissible.
Regarding the phrase “and one who is indebted”: this refers to one whose debt has been taken up by his mother, father, grandfather, and so forth, or by himself. As it is said:
“One who is indebted is one for whom a debt has been taken up by his father or grandfather, or by whom a debt has been taken up personally.”
"Or, one who has taken up whatever was seized by his parents on his behalf is a debtor; he bears that debt to others, thus he is a 'debtor' (iṇāyika).
But as for those other relatives who take something on his behalf, he is not a debtor, for they have no authority to bind him.
Therefore, it is permissible to ordain him."
"One who is a slave" refers to any one of the four types of slaves: one born in the house, one bought with wealth, one brought by way of debt, or one who has entered into slavery of his own accord.
Furthermore, the detailed analysis of slaves should be understood here from the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who ordains [such a person], it should be construed individually with each of the accusative nouns beginning with "one afflicted with leprosy" (*kuṭṭhin*).
"Hand-severed" means one whose hand has been cut off anywhere—whether at the palm, at the wrist, or at the forearm.
"Finger-severed" refers to one of such a kind where, just as a fingernail might not be visible, one or all of the four toes have been cut off.
"Foot-severed" refers to one whose [foot] has been cut off at the toes or at the ankles.

Or, where one or two feet have been cut off—whether at the shank or anywhere else. Since the case of one whose hands and feet have been cut off is also mentioned in the Canon, it too should be included here;
however, it should be understood that it was not explicitly stated because its status as a basis for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is already evident through the method already described.
Regarding the phrase *kaṇṇanāsaṅgulicchinnam*: here the construction is “one whose ear is cut, one whose nose is cut, one whose ear and nose are cut, or one whose finger is cut.
One whose ear is cut (*kaṇṇacchinnam*) is one for whom one or two ears have been cut either at the root of the ear or the earlobe.
However, if the ears have been cut at the helix and it is possible to join them together, he [is not included].
Having joined the ear, he should be ordained. "One with a cut nose" refers to one whose nose has been severed anywhere—whether at the nostril, at the tip, or in a single fold.
However, if his nose can be rejoined, he should be ordained after it has been restored to a functional state.
"One with both ears and nose cut" refers to one who has had both of those severed. "One with a severed finger" refers to...
One for whom one or several fingers have been severed without showing any remnant of the nail is [ineligible].
However, it is permissible to ordain one for whom even a mere thread of a fiber or a remnant of a nail is discernible.

And "only one whose tendons have been severed" means one for whom the large sinews called *kaṇḍara* have been severed either in front or behind; because even one of these has been severed, with the forefoot...
Or he walks with a limp, or he walks with a root-like gait, or he is unable to set his foot down firmly.
2487. "One-eyed" (kāṇa) refers to one who is blind from birth, or whose vision is impaired by flowers and the like;
whoever does not see with both eyes or with one eye is called one-eyed. "Lame" (kuṇi) refers to one who is lame in the hand, lame in the foot, or lame in the fingers.
One in whom some curvature is perceived in these parts, such as the hands and so forth, is *kuṇī*.
"And one who is hunchbacked" (*khujjañca*): one whose body is hunched because the chest, back, or side has protruded—that is a hunchback.
However, it is permissible to ordain one whose various limbs and members are only slightly curved. For only a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*) possesses a body straight like a Brahma.
There is no remaining being who is not called "crooked.
A "dwarf" (vāmana) refers to one who is a dwarf in the shanks, or a dwarf in the waist, or a dwarf in both.
Among these, for one who is a dwarf in the shanks, the lower body from the waist downwards is short, while the upper body is well-proportioned. For one who is a dwarf in the waist, from the waist...
From the waist upwards, the upper body is short while the lower body is well-proportioned; in one who is dwarfed in both parts, both bodies are short.
When, due to the shortness of the body, the physical frame is round like a living being or like a large pot-bellied jar, none of these three types are permitted to go forth.

"Fan-hand" refers to one whose fingers are joined together like the wings of a bat. One who desires to ordain such a person must have the spaces between the fingers slit open, remove all the skin from between them, and make it functional before ordaining him.
Likewise, one who desires to ordain someone who has six fingers must have the extra finger cut off, make it functional, and then ordain him.
One who is lame because his knees bend inward; or one with broken shanks; or one who is a "bowl-footed" person because his feet are contracted at the middle while walking;
or one who is a "bowl-footed" person because his feet are contracted at the tips while walking on the middle of the back of his feet; or one who is lame because he walks only on the tips of his toes;
or one who is lame because he walks on his heels; or one who is lame because of the outer edge of the foot.
One who is lame while walking, meaning one who limps with the inner part of the foot;
or one who is lame while walking because the ankles are broken so that he walks on the entire back of his foot—it is not permitted to ordain such a person.

In this context, "one with sunken knees" refers to one whose feet have sunk inward. "One with a withered arm" refers to one for whom either one hand, one foot, or half the body does not function properly.
"Sīpadin" means one whose feet are diseased. One whose foot is swollen, covered in boils, and rough should not be ordained.

However, one whose foot has not yet become rough may be ordained if it is possible to apply a bandage, place him in a water-pit, fill it with sand until the veins are visible and the shank resembles a tube of oil.
If it is possible to cause [the growth] to wither in this way, then it is permissible to ordain him after making his foot such as that.
If, however, it grows again, he must be ordained by the one conferring the higher ordination (*upasampadā*) only after having made it so.
"One afflicted with a foul disease" refers to one who is constantly ill from any of the diseases such as hemorrhoids, fistula, bile, phlegm, cough, or consumption, and whose disease is incurable.
That which is loathsome and unpleasant.
2488. "Weak through old age" refers to one who, being weak due to the state of being aged, is incapable even of performing his own tasks such as dyeing his robes;
whereas one who, though advanced in years, is strong and capable of looking after himself—him [one should attend to].
He should be ordained. "Blind" means one who is blind from birth. "And likewise deaf" refers to one who does not hear at all;

however, it is permissible to ordain one who hears loud sounds. "Dumb" refers to one whose vocal faculty functions but who is unable to recite the formula for going for refuge in its entirety; such a person, though dumb, may not be ordained.
However, it is permissible to ordain one who is able to recite the mere formula for going for refuge in its entirety.
Alternatively, "mammana" refers to faltering speech; this is a designation for one who utters even a single syllable four or five times.
"Pīṭhasappi" refers to one whose bodily postures are impaired. "Mūga" refers to one whose vocal expression does not function.
2489. To show those who defile the assembly by defiling it with their own ugliness, he said, beginning with “too tall,” etc.
“Too tall” means one whose height exceeds the measure of the heads of others up to the navel. “Too short” means one who, like both types of dwarfs mentioned, is excessively short.
“Or too black” means one whose complexion is excessively dark, like a tree stump in a burnt field. “Resembling polished copper” [refers to the color of his skin].

The connection is also with "extremely white" (*accodāto*); the meaning is that his body is exceedingly white, having been polished by curd, buttermilk, and so forth, and possessing the color of refined copper.

2490. "Not too fat" (*atithūlo*) means one whose flesh is heavy, who has a large belly, and resembles a great elemental being (*mahābhūta*). "Too thin" (*atikiso*) means one whose flesh and blood are meager, as if his body were merely bone, sinew, and skin.
The construction is "not too large-headed" (*atimahāsīso*). "Not too large-headed" (*atimahāsīso*) [refers to] the basket on the head...
It is as if he were standing [there]. The word-division is: “*atikhuddakasīsenasahitena*. *Asahitena* means “unsuitable for the body.
It is an epithet for “*atikhuddakasīsena*. The construction is: “endowed with an unsuitable, very small head. As it has been said:
“Either having a very small head, which is unsuitable for the body, or being very small...”
“Endowed with a head like a winnowing basket.
One endowed with a “head like a winnowing basket” is one who possesses a head resembling a cluster of palm fruits.
One with a “peak-like head” is one endowed with a head that tapers gradually toward the top; it is narrow at the crown and broad at the base.
The meaning is: having a head resembling the peak of a mountain that has been offered as a sacrificial oblation (*huta*). "Equal to a bamboo tube" means like the stalk of a large bamboo tree.
"With a head" means with a long head; as it is said: "One with a tube-like head, or one endowed with a head like the stalk of a large bamboo tree. 2492.
"Also one with a cleft head" means one whose head is split in two by a visible fissure in the middle, resembling the frontal globe of an elephant.
"Endowed with": "With a head tilted back" means endowed with a head that is inclined in any of the four directions.

"With a scarred head" means endowed with a head possessed of scars. "With matted hair" means endowed with hair that has grown here and there like crops in a field grazed by insects. "Or with coarse hair" means endowed with hair resembling the fibers of a palm tree.
"Pūtisīsa" means a head with a foul odor. "Nillomasīsa" means a head devoid of hair.
"Jātipaṇḍarakesa" means one whose hair is white, having turned white due to old age. "Jātiyā tambakesa" means one endowed with hair that is copper-colored, as if set ablaze.
"Āvaṭṭasīsa" means one endowed with upward-pointing curls of hair resembling the whorls found on the bodies of cattle.
"Endowed with eyebrows joined together by hair from the head" means he is possessed of eyebrows whose hairs are connected as one with the hair of the head.
"Or with joined eyebrows" means having both eyebrows joined as one; the meaning is that he is possessed of eyebrows in which hair has grown in the middle.
"Or even with hairless eyebrows" means devoid of eyebrow-hair. "Or even with hairless eyebrows" [is repeated for emphasis].
By the word *pi* (also/even), used in the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avuttasamuccaya*), the "monkey-faced" type is included.
Regarding the phrase "one with large or small eyes" (*mahantakhuddanetto*): here, the word *netta* (eye) should be construed individually with the words *mahanta* (large) and *khudda* (small);
thus, the meaning is "one with large eyes" or "one with small eyes. As for "one with large eyes," this refers to one whose eyes are exceedingly large.
"Endowed with": "having small eyes" means being endowed with eyes that are excessively small, like holes made by striking with the corner of a buffalo hide.
"Having deformed eyes" means being endowed with one large eye and one small eye.
Or "squinting" means looking sideways. Here, by the word *api* ("also"), one includes those whose eyes have fallen out.
"One whose eye-pupils have protruded like those of a crab. "Deep-eyed" means one whose eye-pupils appear like water-bubbles in a deep well.
Here, "water-bubbles" refers to bubbles on the surface of water; "eye-pupils" refers to the eyeballs.
"Uneven-eyed" means having eyes that are asymmetrical, with one turned upward and the other downward.
He was endowed with [deformed] eye-sockets.
2496. "Jatukaṇṇo" means he was endowed with excessively small earlobes.
"Mūsikakaṇṇo" means he was endowed with ears resembling those of mice. "Hatthikaṇṇo" also means [endowed with ears] that were large and disproportionate.
He is endowed with ear-rings resembling elephant ears. "One whose ears are merely perforated" means one who has only a hole in the ear without ear-rings.
"One with unperforated ears" means one who is endowed with ears that have not been pierced for the purpose of inserting ear-rings.
2497. *Ṭaṅkitakaṇṇo* means one who possesses ears resembling the tips of a cow’s fodder-tube;
the meaning is that he is endowed with ears shaped like the points of a cow’s jaw. *Pūtikaṇṇo* also means one who possesses ears from which pus constantly drips.
By the word “also” (*api*) in *pūtikaṇṇopi*, one suffering from ear-fistula (*kaṇṇabhagandarikā*) is included. A “one with ear-fistula” is so called because of constant discharge of pus.
"Endowed with pierced ears. It was said that one with unpierced ears is a defiler of the assembly;

therefore, he says "even among those of the Yona race and so forth, this is not a defiler of the assembly," meaning that while ear-piercing is the natural custom of the Yonas, this person of the Yona race and others is not a defiler of the assembly.
2498. *Atipiṅgalanetta* means one endowed with eyes that are excessively tawny.
However, it is appropriate to ordain one who is honey-tawny (*madhupiṅgala*). *Nippakhumakkhi* means one whose eyes are devoid of eyelashes;
for the word *pakhuma* is conventionally used in the world to refer to the eyelashes. *Assupaggharanetta* means one endowed with eyes from which tears flow.
"Pakkapupphitalocano" is to be construed as "one with ripe eyes" and "one with blossomed eyes. The meaning is: one whose eyes are fully matured and whose eyes have developed blossoms. 2499.
"Mahānāso" means endowed with a large nose that is disproportionate to the body.
"Atikhuddakanāsiko" means likewise endowed with an excessively small nose. "Cipiṭanāso vā" means one with a flat nose, or one with a nose that has been pressed inward.
He is endowed with a nose that is flattened. By the word "or" (*vā*), which implies an unstated alternative, one with a long nose is included.
Furthermore, he is endowed with a nose that can be licked by a tongue resembling a well-fashioned parrot-beak.
"Crooked-nosed" means having a nose that does not stand in the middle of the face but is situated on one side.
“With a nose that constantly drips mucus” means a nose from which nasal mucus (siṅghāṇika) flows perpetually.

“With a large mouth” refers to one whose facial feature alone is large like that of a *paṭaṅga* frog, while the actual opening of the mouth is extremely small, like that of a gourd. A *paṭaṅga* frog is a type of large-mouthed frog.
Regarding the phrase “or with a crooked or split mouth,” it should be read here as: “or with a crooked mouth, or with a split mouth.”
The commentary (*yojanā*): "Crooked-mouthed" (*vaṅkamukha*) means having one side of the face or the nose sloping, thus being crooked-mouthed.
"Or with a split mouth" (*bhinnamukho vā*) means having a split mouth like that of a monkey. "Or with large lips" (*mahāoṭṭhopi vā*) means being endowed with lips resembling the rim of a mortar.
"Or with thin lips" (*tanukaoṭṭho vā*) means being endowed with lips incapable of covering the teeth, like the hide of a drum.
"Like the hide of a kettle-drum" means like the hide covering the mouth of a kettle-drum.
Regarding the phrase "thin-lipped," the word "or" (*vā*) here includes three alternatives: either having large lower lips, or having thin upper lips, or having thin lower lips.
"One with broad upper lips" means one with large upper lips. "One with severed lips" refers to one whose one or both lips are cut off. "One with a protruding mouth" means...
"Rotten-mouthed": even one with a mouth that smells of pus, whose mouth is constantly dripping.
2502–3. "With deformed lips": endowed with lips that are white on the outside and excessively red on the inside.
"Foul-smelling mouth": a mouth smelling of putrid corpses. "With large teeth": endowed with teeth resembling those of a camel. "Excessively... [The text continues:]...extremely...
"Excessively. "Whether below or above, with teeth protruding outward"—this is the explanatory phrase (*atthapada*) for "one with asura-teeth.
An *asura* is a *dānava*. "One with lips covering the teeth" or "one with lips [concealing] the teeth" is written in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
However, that which can be covered by the lips, which is visible only while speaking and not when not speaking—[that is what is meant here].
It is permissible to grant him the going-forth (pabbājana). "Untamed" (adanta) means devoid of teeth. "With decayed teeth" (pūtidanta) means endowed with teeth that have become putrid.
Regarding the phrase "one whose teeth are too small," the passage beginning with "of whom" (yassa) and so forth is an exception (apavāda). The construction is as follows:

if, between his [other] teeth, there stands even a single tooth that resembles a black tooth, like the tooth of a *kalandaka* (a type of monkey), and is minute, it is permissible to grant him the going-forth.
Regarding the phrase "pabbājetumpī" (even to ordain): here the particle *pi* has the sense of the particle *tu*.
The connection is with the words "yo poso" (whatever person). "Mahāhanuko" means one who is endowed with a jaw like that of an ox.
"Yuto rassenahanunā" (endowed with a short jaw) is a synonym for "cipiṭahanuko vā" (or one with a flat jaw). As it is said: "Cipiṭahanuko... (one with a flat jaw).
"Or he is endowed with a jaw that is exceedingly short, as if by one who has sat inside [something].
Regarding the phrase "or with a flat jaw," the word *vā* (or) here includes two alternatives: "or with a broken jaw, or with a crooked jaw.
"Or with no beard and no teeth" means having a face like that of a bhikkhunī. "Or with an excessively long neck" means having a neck like that of a crane.
"Endowed with a drooping neck": endowed with a neck that hangs down excessively, as if it had entered inside.
"Or with a broken neck, or even with a goitrous neck"—this is the construction; the meaning is: either having a broken neck-bone, or having a neck possessed by a goitre (*gaṇḍa*).
"Or with collapsed shoulder-tops": endowed with collapsed shoulder-tops, like those of a woman. "Broken back... [and so forth].
The construction is: "or even with arms broken," or "with very long arms or very short arms. The meaning is: "with excessively long arms or excessively short arms.
By the word *vā* (or), those with no arms or one arm are included. The construction is: "or afflicted with itch (*kacchu*) or afflicted with scab (*kaṇḍu*).
By the word *vā*, these two—"having a body with ringworm (*daddu*) or having limbs like a lizard (*godhā*)"—are included.
He embraces [them]. In that context, "one whose limbs fall like a lizard" (*godhāgatta*) refers to one from whose limbs powder falls off like that of a lizard.
Regarding "one with great humpbacked flesh" (*mahānisadamansa*), its synonym is "endowed with the simile of the top of a stove. As it has been said:
"Or, one who possesses great humpbacked flesh that protrudes like the peak of a stove. One with great humpbacked flesh.
In this context, by the word "or" (*vā*), the *bhaṭṭhakaṭika* is included.
A *vātaṇḍika* is one who possesses a growth disease within the testicular sacs. A *mahāūrū* is one who possesses thighs that are excessively large and disproportionate to the body.
A *saṅghaṭṭanakajāṇuka* is one who possesses knees that strike against each other.
2509. *Bhinnajāṇu*: one whose one or both knees are deformed. *Mahājāṇu*: one endowed with large knees. *Dīghajaṅgha*: one with shanks like a staff. *Vikaṭo vā*:
one who moves sideways, whose knees protrude outward while walking. *Paṇho vā*: one whose feet turn backward as he walks.
When he walks, his kneecaps enter within [the calves]. "Panta" and "saṇha" are synonyms for this very same quality.
*Ubbaddhapiṇḍiko* means one who is endowed with large calf-muscles that extend either downward from above or upward from below.
*Yaṭṭhijaṅgho* means one who is endowed with shanks resembling a staff. *Mahājaṅgho* refers to the body’s...
"He is endowed with great shanks that are disproportionate" means he possesses large shanks that do not correspond to his body.
By the word "also" (*api*), one who has thick calves is included; the meaning is that he is endowed with thick calves resembling a bowl for food.
"One whose shank rises from the middle of the foot" means one whose shank emerges from the midpoint of the foot.
“*Mahāpaṇhi* (large-heel) means one endowed with heels that are disproportionate and excessively large.
*Vaṅkapāda* (crooked-foot) is of two kinds: by way of the foot being turned inward or turned outward.
*Gaṇṭhikaṅgulika* (knotted-fingered) means one endowed with fingers resembling the bulbs of *siṅgivera* (ginger). ‘*Andhanakho vāpi* (or with blind nails)’—the meaning of this term is as follows.”
“And also having black, putrid nails. As it is said: “One who has blind nails, or who is possessed of black-colored, putrid nails.

The phrase “*iccevaṃ*” (thus indeed) is a collection of particles used for the purpose of indicating the aforementioned statement. Because the types of deficiency in the limbs are manifold, he says “*iccevamādikaṃ*” (beginning with these) in order to include every mode of deficiency without exception.
This concludes the commentary on the talk that defiles the assembly.

2514. Regarding the phrase "the bowl and robes": here, the word "of the novice" (*sāmaṇerassa*) is understood by virtue of the context. "Placing inside" means placing them inside a room or similar enclosure. "In all applications" means in all applications such as touching the bowl and robes.
2515–6. "Having performed the disciplinary act" (*daṇḍakammaṃ katvā*): having applied the disciplinary act. It is called "discipline" (*daṇḍa*) because one punishes or trains by means of it;

that very thing is called an "act" (*kamma*) because it is to be performed, hence "disciplinary act" (*daṇḍakamma*), such as confinement (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth. [This refers to] a novice who is ill-behaved and difficult to speak with.

The construction is as follows: it is permissible for a bhikkhu who desires only the welfare [of others] to perform a punitive act (*daṇḍakamma*), to apply that punitive act, and then—by means of the word "or" (*vā*) indicating rice-gruel, a meal, or a bowl, or a robe—to say, "When the punitive act has been carried out, you shall receive this.
The particle *kira* is a nipāta used for the purpose of filling out the meter.
2517. To show the disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma) established by the Theras who compiled the Dhamma, he said, “in accordance with the offense,” and so forth.
That which is called “disciplinary action in accordance with the offense” should be understood as the making [the offender] fetch sand, water, and so on.
By the word “and so on” (ādi), the fetching of wood and other such items is included. And that is done out of compassion, thinking, “He will desist,” and not otherwise.
By an evil disposition proceeding in such a manner as “He will perish,” “He will disrobe,” and so forth.
To show the disciplinary action that should not be performed, he says “On the head,” etc.
Regarding “on the head,” the word “of the novice” is understood from the context. Regarding “stones, etc.,” the word “etc. includes bricks and so forth. [Regarding] the novice...
The construction is: "It is not permissible for a monk to have [the patient] lie down on a hot stone, or to have him lie down on hot ground, or to have water poured [over him].
He said "here," etc., in order to show the disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma) authorized by the Blessed One. "Here" means in this context concerning disciplinary acts.
“Mere obstruction” means merely a prohibition, such as “Do not enter here. “Announced” refers to what was said:
“Monks, I allow you to make an obstruction wherever one dwells or wherever one retreats.
Regarding the phrase “wherever one dwells or wherever one retreats”: it means wherever one dwells or enters; both cases are included.

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "One's own cell and the lodging obtained by seniority," as long as they are performing the penal labor assigned, one does not allow them to enter either one's own private cell or the lodging obtained by seniority;
this is what is meant by "prevention" or "obstruction. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the word "one's own" refers to those...
They create an obstruction; it is understood that this was said with reference to the teachers and preceptors.
However, some here, taking the word "of oneself" (*attano*) to mean that it was said with reference to the person against whom they create the obstruction, offer their own analysis on that point.
Still others, accepting the meaning in both ways, state that the obstruction should be created toward both. One should investigate this.
Whatever among these is most appropriate should be accepted. This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding prohibitions (nivāraṇakathā). 2520. The analysis (*viggaha*) is:
"a faction" (*pakko*), "arising from exertion" (*opakkamiko*), and "poured in" (*āsittō*). And herein, "on a non-observance day, the observance day..."

In such passages as "he performs [the act]," just as the ritual to be performed on the Uposatha day is called "Uposatha," so too one who enters into the state of a paṇḍaka during a fortnight (pakkha) of the month is called a "pakkha-paṇḍaka.
Alternatively, "pakkha-paṇḍaka" is formed by the elision of the final member of the compound, just as "Bhīmasena" is shortened to "Bhīma.
And this refers to one who, through the power of evil, enters the state of a paṇḍaka specifically during the dark fortnight (kaṇhapakkha).
This is a designation (*adhivacana*). As it is said: "Due to the experience of unwholesome karmic fruition, one becomes a paṇḍaka during the dark fortnight after dark fortnight;
however, during the bright fortnight, his fever subsides—this is a 'fortnightly paṇḍaka' (*pakkhapaṇḍaka*).
One whose seeds have been removed by means of an external intervention is an "instrumental paṇḍaka" (*opakkamikapaṇḍaka*). One [who has intercourse] with the sexual organ of others...
One whose fever is pacified by taking [the organ] into the mouth and sprinkling it with impurity is an *āsittapaṇḍaka*.
One who is called "jealous" (*usūyaka*) is one for whom the fever is pacified when jealousy arises upon seeing the transgressions of others; this is a *usūyapaṇḍaka*.
One who is born utterly devoid of [sexual function] even at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is a *napuṃsakapaṇḍaka*.
“Among them” means among those five types of paṇḍakas. Because it is stated in the *Kuruṇḍī* that “for a pakkhapaṇḍaka,

ordination is prohibited for whichever side he is a paṇḍaka on,” it should be understood that the statement “it is prohibited for three” refers specifically to the paṇḍaka-phase of that particular paṇḍaka.

2522. “He is to be expelled”: this is said with reference to the expulsion from the marks (liṅganāsana). As it is said: “He too is to be expelled by means of the very expulsion from the marks. This same method applies to similar instances further on.

The commentary on the discussion concerning the paṇḍaka. 2523. It deceives, thus it is a “deceiver” (theno); a deceiver of the marks—that is, the deceiver of the outward appearance of one who has gone forth—is a “deceiver of the marks” (liṅgatheno). Of the communal life, such as the counting of the years since ordination as a bhikkhu...
"Theno saṃvāsatheno": the connection is that "theno" (a thief) refers to both of these—the mark [of a monk] and the communal life.
The construction is: "This one, though threefold, is called a 'thief in communal life' (theyyasaṃvāsaka).
Regarding those three types of thieves in communal life, he who, having gone forth by himself, [counts] the years as a bhikkhu...

He does not accept [greetings]; he does not even accept prostrations according to seniority. By the word "api" (even/also), it is implied that he does not offer a seat, nor does he appear at the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies;
thus, because he fails to provide such hospitality, he performs neither of those two duties.
This is the construction: he is a "liṅgatthena" (one who steals the outward mark) because he deceives by means of the mere mark—the mere appearance of one who has gone forth—through theft or fraud.

And the construction of the sentence is as follows: he who, having gone forth, counts his years as a bhikkhu, is considered a "one who has abandoned the purpose of the community" (*saṃvāsatthenaka*) precisely because he consents to communal life such as paying respect according to seniority. As it is said:
"Indeed, every variety of activity, beginning with the counting of years as a bhikkhu, should be understood as 'communal life' (*saṃvāsa*) in this context."

"Exactly as stated before" means it is said by taking the individual characteristics previously stated for both [the one who ordains and the one being ordained] to be the characteristic of this [person living in communion by theft].
This threefold person living in communion by theft—whether unordained—is not to be ordained; if already ordained, he is to be expelled;
and even if he requests the going-forth again, he is not to be admitted. Thus, the characteristic of living in communion by theft is shown by way of its opposite.
In order to establish [the point], he says "and as it has been said," citing the two verses found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
The intention is that this meaning should be understood through contrast (*byatireka*) with the way the Master of the *Aṭṭhakathā* stated the two verses concerning the king, famine, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "from fear of kings, famine, wildernesses, disease, and enemies," the word "fear" (*bhaya*) should be construed with each [term] individually.
“Out of fear of kings, fear of famine,” and so forth. “For the purpose of bringing back robes” means for the purpose of bringing back to the monastery the robe he himself had relinquished.
“In this” means in this Dispensation. “He does not consent to co-residence”:
the meaning is that as long as he is of pure mind—that is, as long as he has not adopted the outward marks out of fear of kings and the like—he does not consent to co-residence.
For one who, without fear of the king or other such motives, takes the robe-ordination solely out of a desire to live together with monks by deceiving them,
becomes known as a "one living in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) precisely because of taking the signs with an impure mind. This person, however,
because he lacks the desire to deceive the monks with such an impure mind, does not become [a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*] as long as he does not consent to living in communion.
Therefore, one is not yet called a "one who dwells in communion through theft.

For this very reason, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* (commentarial notes) that: "Even though those who have taken the robes out of fear of the king and so forth possess a deceptive intention—thinking, 'May people know me as a monk rather than a householder'—no fault arises because there is an absence of the desire to deceive the monks."
Some, however, say that "here, purity of mind is the state of having fear allayed.

If this were the case, it would follow that as long as one who has had his fear allayed does not consent to living together, he is not called a "one who lives in communion by theft"; such is the meaning understood.
And when this meaning is understood, even if one consents to living together while his fear is not yet allayed, he is a "one who lives in communion by theft."

One would not fall into the offense [of living in communion with one who has not been rehabilitated] if it were not for the fact that the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) shows that "living in communion with one who is not to be lived with" (*atheyyasaṃvāsakatā*) refers to accepting co-residence with one whose fear has not subsided.
Furthermore, by the phrase "eating the food of all heretics," it is indicated that one must live only while refusing to accept co-residence even with one whose fear has not subsided.
For this very reason, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Because [one does not enter] the monastery..."
"For one who comes and takes up residence with the Saṅgha, it is difficult to maintain that communal life;

therefore, it was said: 'one who eats the food of all sectarians. Consequently, in this context, the mere assumption of the outward signs due to fear of kings and the like should be understood as a state of pure mind.

Thus, he is not yet called a 'thief-living-in-communion' (theyyasaṃvāsaka). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method presented in the Aṭṭhakathā, beginning with: "In this regard, this is the detailed method."
Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Lives in Communion by Theft (Theyyasaṃvāsaka). 2529–30.

The connection is as follows: a fully ordained bhikkhu who, thinking "I shall become a sectarian," goes to the dwelling place of sectarians while still wearing his own [monastic] robes—that is, in his very bhikkhu attire—is one who has gone over to the sectarians;
he is one who has entered among the sectarians, a "one who has gone over to the sectarians" (*titthiyapakkantaka*).
“Dependent on their marks” means having assumed the dress of those sectarians (titthiya).

2531. The construction is as follows: even one who, thinking “I shall become a sectarian,” puts on the *kusacīra* (grass-cloth) and so forth by himself, would be a “defector” (*pakkantaka*), a “defector to the sectarians. 2532–4. The construction is:
“having gone naked to the dwelling place (*upassaya*) of those [such as] the Ājīvakas and others. “Has his hair plucked out” refers to himself.
He has his hair plucked out. He adopts their vows—this is the construction. "He adopts their vows" means he adopts vows such as the practice of squatting (ukkuṭikappadhāna) and so forth.

Or, if he takes up the mark or sign of those sectarians, such as the peacock-feather fan and so on, or if he regards their renunciation or even their supernatural attainments as essential—that is, he approaches them with regard for them—this is the construction. "This is renunciation..."

"In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: 'He becomes a "seṭṭha" (superior) because he attains the state of a seṭṭha. This person is indeed one who has gone over to the faction of the heretics (*titthiya*), yet he is not liberated from the state of having gone over to the heretics.
"Of one going naked" means of one who, thinking "I shall become an Ājīvaka," approaches the Ājīvakas without taking up saffron robes and so forth, remaining naked.
2535. A "thievish co-resident" (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is spoken of by way of one who has not received full ordination (anupasampanna), not by way of one who has received it.

By this, he illustrates the determination found in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*): "Even if a fully ordained monk (*upasampanno bhikkhu*) accepts a false rainy-season residence (*kūṭavassa*), he does not cease to be a recluse (*assamaṇa*). Even if one, while still aspiring to the outward marks (*liṅge saussāho*), commits a defeat (*pārājika*) and counts his years as a monk and so forth, he does not become a thievish co-resident."
The construction is: "it is stated thus. By the phrase "by a bhikkhu who is fully ordained," one excludes those who are not fully ordained.

And by this, he shows the decision found in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā: "Even a novice who has gone to the sphere of other sects while still wearing his own robes obtains ordination and full admission again."
"What should be done with one who has gone over to another sect? He should not be ordained; even if already ordained, he should not be given full admission (*upasampadā*);

and if he has already been fully admitted, his saffron robes should be taken away, white clothes should be given to him, and he should be returned to the state of a layperson. This is the meaning of the rule:
"Monks, one who has gone over to another sect, if unordained, should not be given full admission; if already ordained, he should be expelled."
This should be understood from both the Pāli text and the commentary’s statement: “He is not only not to be ordained, but he is also not to be given the going-forth.
This concludes the explanation of the discussion on those who have gone over to other sects. 2536.
“Herein” means in this section concerning the going-forth and full ordination. “Other than one of human birth” refers specifically to one belonging to the animal realm.
In order to show that [the term] is included within [the category], he said, “Whether a yakkha or even a Sakka.
Regarding the phrase “an animal is mentioned,” the word *iti* is indicated here as being elided. Since it is stated in the scripture, “Bhikkhus, an unordained animal must not be ordained;
if already ordained, he is to be expelled,” it should be understood that even the going forth (*pabbajjā*) is thereby prohibited by implication; thus it was said, “to cause to go forth...”
"It is not permissible. Therefore, it was stated by the Aṭṭhakathā masters—who were cognizant of the Blessed One’s intention—that an animal must not be ordained.
This concludes the commentary on the "animal-talk" (tiracchānakathā).

2537. He supports five persons who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*): the matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an *arahant*, the shedder of [a Buddha’s] blood, and the schismatic.

In this context, one called a "matricide" is one by whom a biological mother, being a human female, has been intentionally deprived of life by him while he himself is likewise of human birth; such a person is a matricide by virtue of the deed of matricide that entails immediate retribution.

For him, both the going forth and the full ordination are prohibited. However, for one who has killed a human female—even if she is not his biological mother, but rather his foster mother, his stepmother, or his grandmother—or even if she is his biological mother but is not a human female, his going forth is not forbidden, nor does he incur an immediate offense (*ānantariya*).
For one who, being himself an animal, [kills] a human female...
If one kills one's mother, even that [act] does not constitute an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense; however, because she is an animal, his admission into the Order (*pabbajjā*) is indeed prohibited.

The same principle applies to the killing of a father. For even if he is the son of a courtesan and does not know, "This is my father," if he kills the man by whose seed he was born, he is reckoned as a "patricide."
And one incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
The killer of an *arahant* should also be understood as such only by way of a human *arahant*.

For even if he belongs to the human race, if one intentionally deprives of life—even if they have not gone forth—any child, whether boy or girl, whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), one becomes a killer of an *arahant*.
One incurs an immediate transgression (*ānantariya*) and one's admission into the order (*pabbajjā*) is barred if one kills an Arahant who is a non-human being;

however, having killed an Arahant who is human, or any other noble person (*ariyapuggala*), one does not incur an immediate transgression, nor is one's admission barred, yet the kamma remains powerful.
Even a beast, having killed a human Arahant, does not incur an immediate transgression, though the kamma is grave.

One who, with a wicked mind and a murderous intent like Devadatta, causes even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly to flow from the living body of a Tathāgata, is called a "shedder of blood";
for such a person, both the going forth and the full ordination are forbidden.
However, one who, for the sake of curing a disease, like Jīvaka, cuts [the flesh] with a knife and [removes] putrid flesh...
Having removed the blood, he makes [the community] at ease and generates much merit.

One who, like Devadatta, makes the teaching contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, and splits the Saṅgha by means of one of the four formal acts (kamma), is called a "schismatic" (saṅghabhedaka);
for such a person, both going forth and full ordination are forbidden.
"Monks, one who has killed his mother, if not yet ordained, is not to be ordained;

if already ordained, he is to be expelled"—since this passage from the Canon indicates the prohibition of ordination as a characteristic mark for the prohibition of going forth, it is said: "there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who allows [such a person] to go forth.
The connection is that there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who likewise allows someone who is both a hermaphrodite and a defiler of nuns to go forth.
"Ubhatobyañjana" is an expression formed by the elision of the letter *ka*.

One who possesses both sexual characteristics (*byañjana*)—due to the presence of the female characteristic-producing kamma and the male characteristic-producing kamma—is called an "ubhatobyañjanaka. He is of two kinds:
the female-ubhatobyañjanaka and the male-ubhatobyañjanaka.
In that regard, for a hermaphrodite woman (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*), the female characteristic (*itthinimitta*) is manifest while the male characteristic (*purisanimitta*) is concealed.
For a hermaphrodite man (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*), the male characteristic is manifest while the female characteristic is concealed.
When a hermaphrodite woman exerts masculinity toward women, her female characteristic remains concealed.

The male characteristic becomes manifest. When a person possessing both sets of characteristics (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) transitions from the male state to the female state, the male characteristic becomes concealed and the female characteristic becomes manifest.
A female *ubhatobyañjanaka* conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive a fetus. A male *ubhatobyañjanaka* himself...
"He does not take [it] himself, but causes another to take it"—this is the distinction between these two.

Furthermore, it should be understood that for this hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka) of both types, there is only admission into the order (pabbajjā), but no full ordination (upasampadā); this is the definitive conclusion here.
One who violates a regular bhikkhunī in any one of the three ways is a "defiler of bhikkhunīs" (bhikkhunidūsaka).

For him, both the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and the full ordination (*upasampadā*) are prohibited. However, for one who brings about the destruction of virtue through physical contact, neither the going-forth nor the full ordination is prohibited.
Yet, even one who defiles a woman against her will by forcibly making her wear white garments is indeed a defiler of a nun (*bhikkhunī-dūsaka*). Even by force, [making her] wear white garments...

One who defiles a woman with the intention of violating her does not become a "defiler of a bhikkhunī. Why? Because as soon as she has merely consented to the state of a householder, she ceases to be a bhikkhunī.
However, one who later defiles a woman who has already fallen away from virtue does not become a "defiler of a bhikkhunī," and she may even receive the going-forth and full ordination.
2538. To show the determination handed down through the lineage of teachers, which is independent of the Pāli commentaries, he said, "On one side," and so forth.
By the word "on one side," it might be understood that the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) is also included;
to avoid that, he said, "but in the presence of the nuns. By this, he indicates the fitness of that defiler of nuns. He is indeed a defiler of nuns.

One might think: "She indeed receives both the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), and she is not defeated. This [point] should be brought here and connected with the second verse.
It was stated solely with the intention that she is simply not one who has received full ordination within the community of nuns (*bhikkhunī-saṅgha*).
By the phrase "and she is not defeated," the possibility of her again undertaking the going-forth and full ordination is indicated.

It illuminates [this point]. This meaning is indeed stated in the *Aṭṭhakathāgaṇṭhipada*: “The legal determination is that one who defiles a woman who has received full ordination from only one side (on the bhikkhunī side) is not a ‘defiler of a bhikkhunī’;
he receives the going-forth and so forth, and she does not become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. 2539.
Furthermore, one who misconducts himself with a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) or a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*) is not at all a defiler of a bhikkhunī, nor does he lose his going-forth.
To show the determination found in the Aṭṭhakathā [commentary], he said: "If he is one who has violated a person not yet fully ordained.
The statement, "He indeed receives both full ordination and going-forth," should also be applied to its proper place.

Furthermore, as for the phrase "and she is neither defeated," this is because it is not mentioned in the Aṭṭhakathā and because there is no conceptualization of one who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained.

It should be applied. For if there were no alternative category for those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), the prohibition against including those who have been defeated (*parājita*) would be meaningless;

therefore, it should be understood that those two—going forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination—are indeed possible [for them]. However, these eleven types of persons, beginning with the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch), are excluded based on such statements as:
"Monks, one who is a *paṇḍaka*, if not yet ordained, should not be ordained; if already ordained, he should be expelled."
They are indeed incapable; neither their going forth nor their full ordination takes root, and therefore they should not be admitted to the going forth.

One who knowingly admits them to the going forth or grants them full ordination incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Even if they have been admitted to the going forth or ordained without [the teacher] knowing, once it is known, they must be expelled by the removal of their robes and insignia.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Eleven Persons Unworthy of Ordination.
2540. "Not to be ordained" means one who should not be admitted into the higher ordination (*upasampadā*).

"Without a preceptor" means either one whose preceptor is absent or one who has not formally accepted a preceptor. "One who does so" refers to one who performs the ordination for such a person. This constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"It becomes" means that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both the preceptor and the assembly.

"It does not become invalid if it has been performed" means that if the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadākamma*) were performed for one who lacks a preceptor, it does not become invalid because it was performed by a harmonious Saṅgha, which is irreversible and fit for its purpose. 2541.
"Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. It is stated [here] because it is firmly asserted in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "it must certainly not be accepted."

This is that statement. And here, it should be understood that even if the preceptor is not present and the formal act of designating him has not been performed, the proclamation of the preceptor has nonetheless been made within the *kammavācā*.

Otherwise, the ritual action (*kamma*) would be subject to invalidation due to the occurrence of a failure of the ritual (*kammavipatti*), as it is stated that "one does not point to the individual. For this very reason, [it says] "without proclaiming the preceptor."
It is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Without having approached [the preceptor], he did not have him take the preceptorship.

And just as at the time of full ordination for one whose bowl and robes are incomplete, even though the formal act (*kammavācā*) is performed by reciting the non-existent fact that "his bowl and robes are complete," the ordination is nonetheless valid;
