so too [in the case of] "this Buddharakkhita [approaches] the venerable Dhammarakkhita..."

It should be understood that even if one proclaims a person who does not actually exist as "desirous of full ordination," the full ordination is indeed valid once the formal act (*kammavācā*) has been performed by merely uttering the words for an existing person. For this very reason, it is said: "It is not frustrated if [the procedure] has been performed. And:
"Monks, one should not grant full ordination to one who is without a preceptor; whoever should grant it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."

Having said only this much, because it was not stated that "that person is unordained" (*anupasampanna*), and because the characteristic of a failure of the formal act (*kammavipatti*) is impossible [in those cases], it is said:
"That must certainly not be accepted. "In all the remaining cases" refers to those enumerated as:

the Saṅgha, the group (*gaṇa*), the paṇḍaka, the one who should not be questioned (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), the one who has gone over to another sect (*titthiyapakkantaka*), the animal, the matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an Arhat, the defiler of a bhikkhunī, the schismatic of the Saṅgha, the shedder of blood [from a Tathāgata's body], and the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*).
In all thirteen alternatives regarding those who have been ordained with a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), for it was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, one should not be ordained with the Saṅgha as the preceptor; whoever should ordain [in such a way], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so forth.

It is not only in these thirteen cases, but also in the following: "one without a bowl, one without a robe, one with a bowl but no robe, one who has asked for a bowl, one who has asked for a robe, one who has asked for both bowl and robe."
This method should be applied to these six alternatives. By the inclusion of the word "the rest" (*sesa*), these [other cases] are also subsumed.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, one who does not possess a bowl must not be ordained; whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so forth.
This method is the method stated as: "If it has been done, he is not disturbed."
2542. "Twenty-five" refers to the twenty-four *pārājika* offenses plus the one regarding a person less than twenty years of age, making twenty-five.
For it is said: "Monks, a person known to be less than twenty years of age must not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him is to be dealt with according to the rule.
"Admission" (*osāra*) means admission in the sense of full ordination (*upasampadā*). Therefore, in the *Campeyyakhandhaka*, it says: "If that..."

In the commentary on the passage beginning, "The Saṅgha reinstates; some are reinstated," it is stated: "'Reinstates' means he causes [the person] to enter by means of the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*).

By the phrase "one deserving of expulsion" (*nāsanāraho*), it is indicated that even for one who has already been ordained, his status as a layperson must be restored by giving him white robes, based on such statements as: "Monks, a paṇḍaka who has not been ordained should not be ordained."
2543. Regarding the thirty-two cases beginning with "one whose hand has been cut off," as stated in the Campeyya-khandhaka:
"Monks, one whose hand has been cut off has not reached the point of reinstatement; yet if the Saṅgha reinstates him, he is reinstated. One whose foot has been cut off...

[and so on] ...one whose hand and foot have been cut off... one whose ear has been cut off... one whose nose has been cut off... one whose ear and nose have been cut off... one whose finger has been cut off... one whose toe has been cut off..."
One with severed tendons... one with a hand like a hooded serpent... a hunchback... a dwarf... one with a goiter... one branded with marks... one whipped... one scarred...

one suffering from elephantiasis... one afflicted by a foul disease... one who corrupts the assembly... one who is blind in one eye... one with a crooked arm... one who is lame... one with a withered arm... one whose bodily postures are impaired... one weak with old age... one who is blind...
one who is mute... one who is deaf... one who is both blind and mute... one who is both blind and deaf... one who is both mute and deaf... one who is blind, mute, and deaf.
“Monks, one who has not yet reached rehabilitation—if the Saṅgha rehabilitates him, he is rehabilitated. Thus [there are] thirty-two.
And the thirteen beginning with the leper are mentioned in the Mahākhandhaka:
“The leper, the one with a boil, the one with consumption, the one with dropsy, and the one with epilepsy;”
Likewise, for one who ordains a royal official, a thief, one listed in the records,
a prison-breaker, a man struck with a whip, a man branded with a mark,
a debtor, or a slave, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The thirteen as previously stated;

thus these forty-five have been mentioned. Among them, since the three—those branded with a whip, those branded with a hammer, and those branded with a stylus—are included in both lists, they should be understood as forty-two by taking what was not already taken.
Regarding those persons mentioned as "the thirty-two such as those with severed hands, and the thirteen such as lepers," their exclusion is not applicable.
The meaning is "conformable to full ordination" (*upasampadānanurūpa*). And as for the phrase "if it were performed":

if the admission known as full ordination (*upasampadā*) were performed by monks who have failed to perceive the state of what ought not to be done, [the question arises] whether it "thrives" (*rūhati*), which means it succeeds;
the intention is that those persons are indeed fully ordained. However, the preceptor and others incur an offense. As it is said in the *Campeyyakhandhaka-ṭīkā*:
"But those thirty-two who have been 'well-admitted'—such as those whose hands have been cut off and so forth—even though they were admitted, they are not truly ordained;
nothing can be said against them. However, the preceptor, the teacher, and the Sangha that performed the act are guilty of an offense; no one is released from their transgression."
“Monks, I allow you to perform two or three *ekānussāvana* (single proclamations),
provided they are done by a single preceptor. Because of this statement, if three teachers are seated within the same boundary (*sīmā*) and, having taken the name of one preceptor,
simultaneously utter the ritual formula (*kammavācā*) for each of the three candidates for full ordination (*upasampadā*), they thereby ordain all three.
To show that it is permissible, he said, "He has one preceptor," and so forth.
The word "three" is stated because in the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*) it appears as "of many elders. "Together" means at one and the same moment.

"Announcement" refers to the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*). "Having recited" means having spoken. "The act" refers to the act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*). "And it does not become invalid" means...
It does not fail. "Is allowable" means that because it does not fail, it is permissible to do so.

From the statement, "Monks, I allow you to perform two or three [ordinations] with a single proclamation," if one preceptor says, "Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita are desirous of receiving full ordination from the Venerable Sāriputta,"...

Having stated the formal act (*kammavācā*) after taking the individual names of those seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkhā*), [the text] says "he has one preceptor" (*ekūpajjhāyako hoti*) and so forth, in order to show that it is permissible to ordain two or even three at once.
Those who seek full ordination are called "those seeking full ordination" (*upasampadāpekkhā*); their name is...
The names of those who are receiving full ordination as well as that of the preceptors. The construction is: "having announced them in due order.

This means having spoken at the appropriate place in the formal ritual (kammavācā) according to the method already stated, such as "Buddharakkhita," and so forth; thus it is said, "having announced. "By him" means by one teacher.
"Together" means having grouped two or three people together. "Having announced" means having recited the formal ritual. The act of full ordination has been performed.

2548. *Aññamaññānusāvetvā* means having announced each other’s names; the meaning is "having taken [the names]," for it is said that one should speak the formal act (*kammavācā*) after having taken each other’s names.
2549. To show that procedure, he says "Sumano," and so forth. *Sumano* is the teacher. Of the Elder Tissa, who was his preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
*Sissakaṃ* means the resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*). *Anusāveti* means he announces the formal act. *Tisso* refers first to him who was the preceptor.
"Acceptance. Regarding "of the Elder Sumanatthera": first, he refers to the teacher-elder (ācariyatthera).
These two, sitting within the same boundary (sīmā) at the same moment, recite the formal ritual (kammavācā) for each other’s resident pupils (saddhivihārika);

thus, in relation to their own respective resident pupils, they are both preceptors (upajjhāya), and in relation to their own respective students (antevāsika), they are both teachers (ācariya), while serving as mutual complements to the quorum (gaṇapūraka).
And it is said that they must be so. As it was stated:

"But if they have different teachers and different preceptors—such as when Elder Tissa makes the resident pupil of Elder Sumana announce [the invitation], and Elder Sumana makes the resident pupil of Elder Tissa announce it, and they each serve as the completer of the quorum for one another—it is permissible."
2550. *Idha* means in this section concerning full ordination (*upasampadā*). *Paṭikkhittā* means prohibited by the words, "But not [one] without a preceptor.
Regarding *Ādiccabandhunā*: he who is called the first king of men in the world, the son of Ādicca (the Sun), was born in his lineage;
thus, because the Blessed One has that as his kin, he is *Ādiccabandhu*. By him.
Commentary on the Mahākhandhaka.
Commentary on the Uposathakkhandhaka. 2551–2.

That [boundary] which is free from the eleven defects of boundaries (*sīmāvipatti*) and endowed with the three perfections (*sampatti*), having joined the boundary-mark to the boundary-mark by means of a sign (*nimitta*).
The construction is: "If it is formally authorized, this may be what is called a 'bound boundary' (*baddhasīmā*). In that regard, there are: one that is too small; one that is too large;
one with broken marks; one with shadow-marks; one without marks; one authorized while standing outside the boundary; one authorized over a river;
one authorized over the ocean; one authorized over a lake; one authorized by merging one boundary into another; and one authorized by covering one boundary with another.
Because of the statement, "By these eleven modes, formal acts fail due to the boundary," these are called the eleven "failed boundaries" (*vipattisīmā*);
that is to say, they are "defective boundaries.
Among them, one called "too small" is where twenty-one monks are unable to sit. One called "too large" is...
That which is designated as even by the mere breadth of a hair-tip extending three *yojanas* is called a "name.
A "broken sign" (*khaṇḍanimitta*) is said to be a sign that has not been joined together.

Having designated the sign in the eastern direction, and then in sequence in the southern, western, and northern directions, one then re-designates what was previously designated in the eastern direction.
It is proper to set it aside; in this way, the sign (nimitta) remains unbroken.
However, if one brings it along step by step, defines the sign in the northern direction, and then sets it down right there, it is called a "broken sign" (khaṇḍanimittā).
Furthermore, another kind of broken sign occurs when one uses a tree with no heartwood or a mere stump, or a heap of dust or sand, which are devoid of a sign.
It is authorized by making a certain sign (*nimitta*) within [the boundary].

That which is called "authorized by means of a shadow-sign" (*chāyānimittā*) is authorized by making any kind of shadow—such as the shadow of a mountain—as the sign. That which is called "authorized without signs" (*animittā*) is authorized without mentioning any signs whatsoever.
That which is called "authorized by one standing outside the boundary" (*bahisīme ṭhitasammatā*) is authorized by one who stands outside the signs after the signs have been proclaimed.

“Designated” means designated among these things such as rivers and so forth. For although it is thus designated, because of the statement, “Bhikkhus, every river is not a boundary; every ocean is not a boundary; every lake is not a boundary,” it is indeed not a [valid] boundary.
When one who is joining a boundary to a boundary [does so], it is called “designated” when one’s own boundary joins another person’s boundary.
It is considered valid by one who merges them. For if, in the eastern direction of an old monastery,
there are two trees— a mango tree and a rose-apple tree— whose branches are intertwined with one another,
and if the boundary of the monastery is fixed by including the rose-apple tree within it and designating the mango tree as its limit, then later...

When a monastery has been built in the eastern direction of a monastery, the monks who are binding the boundary (sīmā) include that mango tree within it and exclude the rose-apple tree (*jambu*), and thus they bind [the boundary].

In this way, one boundary becomes merged with another boundary. By "one boundary encompassing another boundary," it is meant that by one who has formally established his own boundary, he encompasses the boundary of others. For if [he does so] regarding those of others...
Having established a boundary for the whole area or having included a portion of it within one's own boundary, one formally designates that boundary;
this is what is meant by "one boundary being overlapped by another boundary. Thus, the meaning is: "avoided by these eleven defective boundaries.

"Endowed with the three perfections" refers to these three: perfection of the signs (*nimitta-sampatti*), perfection of the assembly (*parisā-sampatti*), and perfection of the formal act (*kammavācā-sampatti*).
They are endowed with excellences. In this context, "endowed with excellence of signs" means that among the eight signs mentioned—
namely, the mountain sign, the rock sign, the forest sign, the tree sign, the path sign, the anthill sign, the river sign, and the water sign—
one has acquired whichever signs are appropriate in their respective directions.

The boundary markers are properly designated by reciting them correctly according to the method beginning with, "What is the marker in the eastern direction? Venerable sir, that is a mountain; the mountain is the marker," and so forth.
What is called "endowed with the perfection of the assembly" means having gathered together with at least four monks as the minimum limit.

As many bhikkhus as are standing within that village boundary—whether it be a fixed boundary, or one established by a river, the ocean, or a lake—without having stepped outside, they are all considered duly appointed either by being within arm’s reach of one another or by bringing their consent (*chanda*). This is what is meant by "being endowed with the perfection of the formal act" (*kammavācā*), beginning with:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: as far as the boundaries have been proclaimed on all sides," and so forth.
She is ordained by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*), which has been stated according to the rule and is pure.

Thus, having transcended the eleven boundaries of failure and being endowed with the threefold success, a boundary that is ordained by joining one marker to another should be understood as a "bound boundary" (*baddhasīmā*).
2553–4. Those beginning with the "broken," "common residence," and "non-separation" are the primary ones; or rather, those boundaries among which these occur at the beginning...

"Khaṇḍasamānasaṃvāsādibhedato" means: the classification of those [boundaries] or by those [factors], such as the broken boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the common-residence boundary (samānasaṃvāsasīmā), and the non-separation boundary (avippavāsasīmā);
thus, it is said that this is by way of the distinction produced by these boundaries acting as instruments or as causes.
A boundary that is divided into sections within an area where there is common residence and non-separation, and which is not confused with others, is called a "section-boundary" (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
It is called "common residence" (*samānasaṃvāsa*) because monks who share common residence perform the Uposatha and other communal acts together in that place.
The characteristic of "non-separation" (*avippavāsa*) will be explained by the words beginning with "having bound" (*bandhitvā*). Thus, it is said that boundaries are of three kinds when bound.
Thus, the threefold classification of the bound boundary (baddhasīmā) has been stated.
In the term *udakukkhepā*, the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of cause. "Seven inner [distances]" (*sattabbhantarā*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of seven inner units;

it means "even from that. The connection is: "the unbound [boundary] (*abaddhā*) is also threefold. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*): it refers to those three types of unbound boundaries. "The delimitation of a village" (*gāmaparicchedo*)...
A village area is that portion of a village delimited by boundaries in all directions, defined by its extent as "this much is the produce of this place.

As it has been said: "In whatever area the lords of that village bring tribute, whether that area be small or large, it receives the designation 'village boundary' (gāmasīmā). Even within the field of a single village..."
If a king demarcates a single portion of land, thinking, "Let this be a separate village," and gives it to someone, that too indeed becomes a separate village boundary.
By the phrase "the delimitation of a village," the delimitation of a city is also included. As it has been said:

"In this context, by the mention of 'village,' the city is also certainly included. However, because the boundary of a market town (*nigama*) is mentioned separately, its inclusion here [is not intended].
It should not be said [that this is the same as the village boundary]. For it is stated in the Pāḷi:

"Whatever village or town one dwells in dependence upon—whatever is the village boundary of that village or the town boundary of that town—this constitutes a common community and a single Uposatha therein.
Because its specific characteristic has been stated separately, it is characterized precisely by the characteristic of the village boundary.
2555. Regarding the passage beginning with “*jātassara*,” the characteristics of natural ponds (*jātassara*) and so forth should be understood as follows:

A natural pond is a pool that is not man-made by anyone digging it out, but has arisen spontaneously; it remains filled with water flowing in from all sides, wherein water collects during the rainy season of the kind to be described later for rivers. Furthermore, [the same applies to...]
A pond dug by water that has emerged after breaking through a river or the ocean attains this characteristic;
this too is indeed a spring-water lake. The ocean is well known.
During the time of righteous kings, it does not exceed [its limits] every half-month, every ten days, or every five days.
When it rains and the clouds have just cleared away, the current ceases; such a stream does not count as a river.

However, that for which the current does not cease even during such a period of heavy rain—the four months of the rainy season—wherein, whether by a ford or a non-ford, one who has arrived at the time for training covers the three circles and [puts on] the inner robe...

If the inner robe of a nun who is crossing [a body of water] becomes wet even by as much as one or two finger-breadths without being lifted up, whether she enters the ocean or a pond, it is called a "river" starting from its source.
"On all sides" means all around. "Of a medium-sized person" refers to a man of medium strength. "A splash of water" is as will be explained below.
An internal area is delimited by the range of a throw according to one’s method, strength, and measure—whether of water or sand—at the spot where it falls.
Just as dice-players throw a wooden ball, so too, having taken water or sand in the hand, it should be thrown with all the strength of a man of medium build; therein, wherever it is thus thrown...
"Whether water or sand falls [within the boundary], this is called 'water-throw' (*udakukkhepa*). "Designated by the water-throw" means it is characterized as "water-throw.
2556. "In a forest devoid of villages" means in a great wilderness such as the Viñjhāṭavi, which is free from any village.
"Seven *abbhantara*s all around" refers to a boundary whose demarcation consists of seven *abbhantara*s surrounding the place where one stands. This...
The boundary called "within seven *nāḷi* [of space]" is so named.
2557. "By means of tossing a wooden ball" refers to the manner in which gamblers toss a wooden ball. "Water-tossing" is according to the analogy of tossing water. 2558.
To show the sequence for extending these two types of boundaries, he said: "The inner water-tossing, the standing place..."
"Beyond" means further than the place where the assembly is standing;
starting from the edge of the assembly, seven *abbhantara*s must be measured and the water-sprinkling (*udakukkhepa*) must be performed—this is the meaning.
Regarding "within the boundary": it refers to a space delimited either by the water-sprinkling or by the seven *abbhantara*s.
"Within": the construction is "standing having left the reach of the hand," or "standing without exceeding that same extent.
The meaning is: standing without exceeding one *udakukkhepa* (a splash of water) or seven *abbhantara*s (cubits) which must be placed for the purpose of marking the boundary.
"He disrupts the formal act" means that by standing inside [the boundary], he causes a division within the act;
or by standing outside without exceeding that specific area, yet becoming a completer of another Saṅgha's quorum, he disrupts the act by causing confusion within the boundary.
Thus, according to the method of the Aṭṭhakathā, he stands having left the handspan's reach inside the boundary.
It should be performed within arm’s reach, or outside the delimited space for the sake of the boundary line (*sīmanta*).

It should be understood that if one stands not exceeding that delimitation, then by remaining exactly as one is, one does not invalidate the ritual action (*kamma*) provided one does not become a member of the quorum for another ritual action.
2561–2. *Saṇṭhānaṃ* means a triangular shape. *Nimittaṃ* means a landmark such as a mountain and so forth.
*Disākittanaṃ* means the designation of directions, such as "What is the landmark in the eastern direction? and so forth. *Pamāṇaṃ* means the maximum extent of three yojanas.
*Sodhetvā* means having cleared out those fully ordained monks who reside within the village territory where the boundary is being established.
When residing in a monastery where a boundary has been established, one is not permitted to go outside the boundary;

when residing in a monastery where no boundary has been established, one must remain within arm’s reach of those who should be kept within arm’s reach, while placing the remainder outside the boundary and arranging for protection along all paths—this is what is meant.
"Boundary" (sīmā) here refers to a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīma).
He said, "What are they like? and replied, "Triangular," and so forth. "Resembling a *paṇava* drum" means having the shape of a *paṇava*, being narrow in the middle and broad at both ends.
Regarding the phrases "having the form of a canopy" and "having the form of a bow," the word *ākāra* (form) should be applied to each respectively.

"Having the form of a bow" means having the shape of a drawn bow; regarding the phrases "resembling a *mudiṅga* drum" and "resembling a cart," the word *upamā* (resemblance) should be applied to each respectively.
The *mudiṅga* is said to be a particular kind of musical instrument that is broad in the middle and thin at both ends;
such is the meaning. "One should mark the boundary" (*sīmaṃ bandheyya*) is the construction.
To show the signs consisting of mountains and so forth as well as the signs consisting of conventional marks, he says "mountain," etc. Thus, there are eight signs.
"Make it shine" is the construction. In this regard, the sign should be understood briefly as follows:
a mountain—whether consisting of pure earth, pure rock, or a mixture of both—is a "sign-possessor" when it is at least the size of an elephant;

anything smaller than that is not suitable. Or, a forest consisting of trees that have heartwood, or are mixed with heartwood, even if it is only the size of four or five trees, [is a sign-possessor].
It must be of the size of a "sign" (nimitta); anything smaller than that is not permitted. Even an iron ball on a stone sign is counted as a stone;

therefore, any stone whatsoever, at the maximum limit starting from the size of an elephant, and at the minimum limit being the measure of a lump of thirty-two *palas* of clay, qualifies as a "sign," but nothing smaller than that does. As for a flat stone (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*), however—

Even one that is very large is permissible. A tree that is still living, with internal heartwood firmly established in the ground—even if it is only eight finger-breadths in height or as thin as the handle of a needle—is a valid object for the meditation mark (*nimitta*); less than that is not permissible.
As for a path, whether it be a footpath or a cart-track, if it passes through and connects two or three village fields, it is suitable.
A termite mound that is traversed by carts drawn by oxen or by human porters is indeed a "sign" (nimitta); it is not permissible for it to be untraversed.
By way of the lower limit, even a termite mound eight finger-breadths high, no larger than a cow’s horn, if born on that very day, is a sign;
anything smaller than that is not permissible. As for water: that which does not flow, remaining in pits, lotus ponds, tanks, natural lakes, salt mines, the ocean, and so forth.

Taking that as the starting point, even water brought in jars and poured into a pit dug in the earth at that very moment is a "fixed sign" (nimittupaga) if it remains stable until the conclusion of the formal proclamation (kammavācā);
otherwise, it is "flowing" (sandamānaka). That which does not remain within the stated boundaries, or water contained in a vessel, is not permissible.
As for the river mentioned in the definition of the unbound boundary (abaddhasīmā), that is a fixed sign; any other is not permissible.
2564. *Tesu* is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). *Tīṇi* indicates that which is to be specified;
by this, he shows that one or two signs are not permissible. As it is said: "Having been thus appointed, if she is bound by one or two signs, she remains unbonded.
In the phrase *satenāpi*, the particle *api* should be understood as expressing possibility (*sambhāvanāyaṃ*).
This indicates that there is no need to speak of twenty or thirty signs.
Regarding the phrase *tiyojanaparā*: it means that three *yojanas* is its maximum limit.
Since the word "twenty" (*vīsati*) and so forth can function both as a number (*saṅkhyāna*) and as the object numbered (*saṅkhyeyya*), here the word "twenty" is taken in the sense of a number.

It should be understood that the phrase "twenty-one bhikkhus" is a designation for a formal act (*adhikaraṇa*) performed by a divided assembly. While one would normally say "twenty-one," the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) occurs due to the requirements of the verse meter;
the meaning is that they take twenty-one bhikkhus because a formal act of the Saṅgha requires a quorum of twenty members, plus the one who is eligible to perform the act.
Furthermore, this is stated with reference to those who are actually seated [in the assembly].
For at the very minimum, it is permissible to establish a boundary in an area where twenty-one monks are able to sit;
this is the lowest limit.

As for both the highest and the lowest [limits], if they exceed or fall short by even as much as a hair’s breadth, these two types of boundaries are declared "non-boundaries" by the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha); such is the construction of the meaning.

"Having described every sign on all sides" means: having described every sign encountered in all directions—surrounding the eastern direction, the intermediate directions, and so forth—as it was found, [the teacher says]:
"The holder of the Vinaya should ask: 'What is the sign in the eastern direction?
[The pupil replies: 'A mountain, venerable sir. Then the holder of the Vinaya [should say]: 'This mountain is the sign,' and so forth."

Having joined sign to sign and having proclaimed it according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The analysis of the compound *ñattidutiyā* is "that which has a motion as its second part" (*yassa ñatti dutiyā*);

the meaning is: by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation, as stated in the word-commentary beginning with, "Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs, for as far as the signs have been proclaimed all around.
The intended meaning of *vinayadhara* is that he is capable and competent [to perform this].
2568. "Having bound" means: first having bound the boundary of common communion (*samānasamvāsasīma*) according to the method of characteristics as previously stated.
"Immediately after" means: without intervening with other duties; that is to say, without causing a delay in time. The intention is:
without giving an opportunity for the individuals who wish to abolish the boundary [to do so]. "Afterwards" means: following the formal authorization (*sammuti*) for common communion.
"Later. The construction is as follows: "Having authorized the non-separation from the robe-clothing, that which is bound [by the boundary] is called 'non-separation' (*avippavāsa*).
In this context, "having authorized the non-separation from the robe-clothing, that which is bound" means: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me:
that boundary which has been authorized by the Saṅgha as a common residence for a single Uposatha... [etc. ...excluding the village and the vicinity of the village..."

"Since it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this"—in accordance with the method stated thus, having authorized the non-separation from the robe-cloth, that which is bound [by the boundary] is called "non-separation.
It is so called because for the monks dwelling therein, there is no offense caused by separation from the robe-cloth; thus it is meant to be called the "boundary of non-separation."

2569. To show the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā* regarding such passages as, “Any river that has attained the characteristics of a river—even if one establishes a boundary there after enumerating its signs, it remains a non-boundary,” he said: “A river... does not overflow.
The meaning is that it does not spread out; it does not become pervasive as a boundary. “For that very reason” means for the reason that it does not overflow.

For this reason, he said: “Bhikkhus, every river is without a boundary (asīma), every ocean is without a boundary, every natural lake is without a boundary. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of boundaries (sīmākathā).
Regarding the phrase “or nine”:

although there are more than eight Uposatha days because of the designation of the eighth day as an Uposatha, the word “nine” is used here referring specifically to the Uposatha days intended in this context. Thus he said, “or nine.”
2571-3. To show them according to their specific forms, he said: “On the fourteenth... [etc. ...the Uposatha by means of a formal act (kamma).
That which completes fourteen days is the fourteenth; that which completes fifteen days is the fifteenth.

However, when—as described in the Kosambakkaṇḍhaka—the Saṅgha has been split and that monk has been reintegrated, the Saṅgha, for the sake of settling that matter, [performs] the concord of the Saṅgha (saṅghasāmaggi).
When [the Saṅgha] performs it, then—based on the statement, "At that very time the Uposatha must be performed;
the Pātimokkha must be recited"—any day other than the fourteenth or the fifteenth is also called the "Uposatha of concord" (sāmaggī-uposatha). Here, the word *iti* is indicated by elision (*lutta*).
These three types of Uposatha—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the Uposatha of concord—are all designated by way of the day itself.
The construction is: "performed by day itself.
"Uposatha in the Saṅgha" means the uposatha to be performed by the Saṅgha. "Uposatha for a group or an individual"—here too the same principle applies.
Since a relationship characterized by the goal and the means is obtainable, there arises the possibility of the genitive case in "in the Saṅgha" and so forth.
This is the explanation of the locative case. The *uposatha* is the object to be accomplished because it is an action (*kamma*);

the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual are the means of accomplishment because they function as the agents. "Recitation of the Sutta" (*suttuddesa*) means the recitation of the Sutta; that which has "recitation of the Sutta" as its designation is called "designated by the recitation of the Sutta. "By means of the action" (*kammena*) refers to the sense of a duty or function.

Regarding the term "resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna*), because it depends on the gender of the word being expressed, the neuter form "designated" (*niddiṭṭha*) is used. For suffixes such as *-tabba* follow the gender of the word they qualify; thus, while "the Pātimokkha is designated" and "purity (*pārisuddhi*) is designated" are neuter, they should be construed with masculine and feminine genders respectively.
2575. *Vuttā* means taught by such passages as: "Bhikkhus, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha: having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should be announced by way of summary;
this is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha. He says "the Nidāna," etc., to show briefly both that [recitation] and their recitations themselves.
*Sāvetabbaṃ* (should be announced)—here the word "by way of summary" (*sutena*) is understood. *Sesakaṃ* refers to the portion not recited.

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs... [as before] ... for when it has been disclosed, there is ease for him. Having recited this introduction, one should say: “Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited;
therefore I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask... [as before] ... thus do I understand this. Then one should say:
“Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited. But the venerable ones have heard it...”

"The four rules involving defeat... [as above] ...should be trained in without dispute"—the remainder should be announced by means of recitation (*suta*) according to the method stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

"In the remaining cases as well" means: in the remaining cases such as the recitation of the rules involving defeat (*pārājika*), etc., with reference to what has been recited; "this same method is to be understood."

Although it was stated in general terms, because of the statement, "The fifth [category] is by way of detailed exposition," this method—namely, "But the remainder should be announced"—does not apply to the detailed summary (vitthāruddesa).

Because of the statement, "But the remainder should be announced," in the recitation of the Pārājikas and so forth, whatever portion has been interrupted when an obstacle arises, the remainder should be announced by means of what has already been heard. In the summary of the Nidānas:
However, there is no such thing as "announcing by means of what has been heard" regarding that which has not been formally recited.
Because the recitation of the *aniyata* (undetermined) rules has been omitted from the *Bhikkhunīpātimokkha*, it is stated:

"And for the bhikkhunīs, four. The meaning of the phrase "these nine recitations, moreover" is that these nine recitations have been taught for both the *Pātimokkhas*: five for the bhikkhus and four for the bhikkhunīs.
"Uposatha" refers to the Uposatha of the Saṅgha. "Obstacles" refers to the ten kinds of obstacles, beginning with the obstacle of kings;

as it is said: "The obstacle of kings, the obstacle of thieves, the obstacle of fire, the obstacle of water, the obstacle of humans, the obstacle of non-humans, the obstacle of beasts of prey, the obstacle of reptiles, the obstacle to life, and the obstacle to the holy life."
In that regard, if while the monks are seated, thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha," a king arrives, this is an obstruction caused by a king (*rājantarāya*).

If thieves arrive, this is an obstruction caused by thieves (*corantarāya*). If a forest fire approaches, or a fire breaks out within the monastery grounds, this is an obstruction caused by fire (*aggiantarāya*).
If a cloud arises, or a flood arrives, this is an obstruction caused by water (*udakantarāya*). Many people...
They come; this is an obstacle caused by humans (*manussantarāya*). A *yakkha* seizes a bhikkhu; this is an obstacle caused by non-humans (*amanussantarāya*).
Fierce wild animals such as tigers come; this is an obstacle caused by beasts (*vāḷantarāya*). Snakes and the like bite a bhikkhu;
this is an obstacle caused by reptiles (*sarīsapantarāya*). A bhikkhu becomes ill, or dies, or his enemies seize him to kill him; this is an obstacle to life (*jīvitantarāya*).
If people, desiring to cause a monk to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*), seize him—whether one or many—this is an obstacle to the holy life.

By the word "even" (*ceva*), it is indicated that there is no offense even when the detailed recitation has not been performed, provided one perceives it as an obstacle while it is indeed an obstacle.
"Recitation" (*uddesa*) means a detailed recitation. "Prohibited" (*nivārita*) refers to: "Monks, when there is no obstacle, [the teaching] should not be given in brief."

It is prohibited by such statements as, “The Pātimokkha should be recited,” and so forth. By this, it is also clarified that [the Buddha] said: “Monks, I allow you to recite the Pātimokkha in brief when there is an obstacle.
2578. *Tassa* means of the Pātimokkha. He states the reason for its being authoritative: “Because of the reading ‘to be upheld by the Elders’ (*therādheyya*). *Therādheyya* means...
"Dependent on the elders" means "subject to the elders. "From the recitation" means from the words of the Pāḷi.
Because of the statement, "The Pātimokkha is to be entrusted to whichever monk there is who is competent and capable," he says, "by one who has not been appointed," and so forth.
"By one who has not been appointed" means by one unable to recite even the two summaries (uddesa). "Whoever was requested by the elder"—thus for one who has been so requested...
"But for whichever elder, novice, or middle-ranking monk that Pātimokkha is current and familiar to him, he is the master"—this is the connection.
"Requested" means commanded with the words, "Friend, recite the Pātimokkha";

by this it is shown that even though one has the capacity to recite it without being commanded, there is still a state of not being the master. As it is said: "If for the elder [there are] five or four..."
Or, if three recitations of the Pātimokkha do not come forth, but two are unbroken, perfectly clear, and mastered by word of mouth,
then the Pātimokkha depends solely on the Elder. But if he is unable to make even this much clear,
then it depends on a learned monk.”
"Uddisanteti" means while the reciter of the Pātimokkha is reciting the Pātimokkha. "Samā vā" means equal in number to the resident monks; "appā vā" means fewer.
"Āgacchanti sace panāti" means if, however, visiting monks (āgantuka-bhikkhus) arrive.
"Sesakanti" refers to the portion that has not yet been recited.
"Uddiṭṭhamattā" means at the very moment it has been announced, that is, even before the commencement of the discourse.
The word "vā" (or) should also be construed here; by this, it includes the alternative not explicitly stated: "or when [the assembly] has not yet settled.
"When the assembly has not yet settled" means while the assembly of monks is still seated engaged in mutual pleasant conversation. "Of the assembly" (parisāya).
Here, the words “of some” (*ekaccāya*) and “of all” (*sabbāya*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
The construction is: “when some of the assembly of monks has departed, or when the entire assembly has departed. “Of them” (*tesaṃ*) refers to those resident monks previously mentioned.
“At the root” (*mūle*) means in their presence. “Purification (*pārisuddhi*) must be made” is the construction. “But here, monks... [they] arrive in greater numbers... etc.
To show the method stated in the words, “Those monks, bhikkhus, must again recite the Pātimokkha,” he said, “If there are many.

Here, the phrase “the Pātimokkha must again be recited” is to be supplied. The meaning is that after performing the preliminary duties in all the various cases, the Pātimokkha is to be recited again. This, however, is the further analysis of the remaining points here:
If there are fifteen-day residents and others, let the others follow the same rules as the former;
if there are more of the former, let the former follow [the majority];
this same principle applies to their remaining cases as well.
For those who dwell on the first day of the fortnight, for others there is the Uposatha;
for those who have settled a dispute, there is concord.
"Let the holders of the root [boundary] grant it according to their wish.
Having gone outside, the Uposatha should be performed; if they do not grant it, [the boundary remains]."
There is consensus when there is no desire to give,
or when many are outside or have departed.
This same principle applies to those who wish to go on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada).
If one intentionally causes [another] to hear what should not be heard, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the one who causes them to hear.
2581. Regarding the phrase "to one who has been instructed": this indicates that there is no offense for others [than the one being instructed].

Here, the word "one who is not ill" (agilānassa) is to be supplied. When the Elder instructs [another], he should consider whether the person is performing some task, or is always alone, or is one capable of carrying a burden.
Or, according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Either one of the reciters or preachers of the Dhamma, or someone else, should be appointed for the purpose of sweeping the Uposatha hall;
the rest, however, should be appointed by turns. Thus he should be appointed.
If, having been appointed, he does not even obtain a temporary broom, he should sweep using a branch-bundle after having it made *kappiya* (rendered permissible).
Even for one who does not obtain it, it is considered as having been obtained.
Regarding the instruction to prepare seats, he should be instructed in the same manner already described.
And when giving the instruction, if there are no seats in the Uposatha hall, they should be brought from the Saṅgha’s residence, prepared, and then returned. In the absence of seats...
It is permissible to arrange [a lamp] even on a wooden frame or a board; if there are no boards, branches should be broken off and made allowable (*kappiya*) before being arranged.
For one who cannot find someone to make them allowable, it becomes allowable once they have been made so by another.
Regarding the preparation of the lamp itself, he should be instructed in the same manner already described. And when instructing him, [he should say]: "In such-and-such a place, the oil..."
“If there is a wick or a bowl, take that and make it. If oil and such items are not available, they should be sought even by means of going for alms.
For one who has sought them but does not obtain them, what has been obtained is permissible.
Furthermore, a fire should also be kindled in a bowl.

2582. Here, the word “having kindled” (*jāletvā*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. Alternatively, it should be construed with the word “having performed” (*katvā*). “Having set aside the motion of the group” means having laid down the motion of the group in this way:
“Venerable sirs, listen to me; today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day.
If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us perform the Uposatha of mutual purity. Thus it should be done.
"Uposatha by three" means the Uposatha is to be performed by three bhikkhus.
Among the three, the elder should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position (ukkuṭika), raise his joined palms, and speak thus three times:
"Friends, I am pure; may you know me as 'pure'. By the second and the third, in due order, [the same should be said]: "I am pure..."
"Venerable sir, may you remember me as pure"—this must be said three times.
(2583) Having performed the preliminary duties and so forth, and having put forward the motion, the elder should say this three times to the junior:
"Friend, I am pure; may you remember me as pure. The junior should also say to the elder: "I am pure..."
“Venerable sir, may you consider me pure”—this must be said three times.
However, in this instance, the only differences are the formal motion (*ñatti*) for the establishment [of the Uposatha] and the singular expression “consider me”;
setting those aside, he says “having completed the preliminary duties, one should resolve” in order to show the procedure for the Uposatha to be performed by an individual.
"An individual" means: one should resolve, "Today is my Uposatha; it is the fifteenth," or "It is the fourteenth.
The singular number is used with reference to the person mentioned at the end.
Just as it was stated, if even the Saṅgha, or three, or two, do not perform their respective authorized Uposatha without an obstacle, in that very same way...
"One should understand that they are committing an offense.
Now, in order to show the fourfold set of formal acts (*kammacatukka*) stated in the manner beginning with, "Monks, there are these four Uposatha formal acts:

a Uposatha formal act that is contrary to the Dhamma and incomplete," he says, "By what is contrary to the Dhamma and by what is incomplete," and so forth. By what is contrary to the Dhamma and by what is incomplete...

The construction is as follows: "The Victor declared that these four are the formal acts (kamma) for the Uposatha: an act contrary to the Dhamma performed by a unanimous assembly; an act according to the Dhamma performed by a divided assembly; and an act according to the Dhamma performed by a unanimous assembly.
Regarding the phrase "in all these four," it refers to these four types of formal acts.
The "fourth" refers to the fourth Uposatha formal act mentioned as "by a unanimous assembly and according to the Dhamma."
“Dhamma-kamma” is what is intended. To analyze those kammās, he said, beginning with “By means of non-Dhamma...,” and so forth.
Here, in this teaching, and here among these four types of Uposatha, the question is asked out of a desire to explain how a factional Uposatha is performed by means of non-Dhamma. Where...
The construction is: “In whichever single boundary (*ekasīmā*) four monks reside.

Therein, if one person brings his own purity (*pārisuddhi*) and those other three people perform the Uposatha with that purity, then the Uposatha performed in this way is *adhamma* (unlawful) and is called a *vagguposatha* (a factional Uposatha); for [the Uposatha] of the Saṅgha must be performed by four [monks] residing within a single boundary.
The meaning is that because the *gaṇa-uposatha* has been performed when it ought not to be performed, it is "unlawful" (*adhamma*);
and because he did not go into the midst of the Saṅgha without [first going] into the midst of the *gaṇa*, and because he did not come within arm's reach of him, it is "incomplete" (*vagga*). 2588.
Regarding the phrase "unlawfully and complete," here the question "What kind of uposatha? should be supplied. "Of a single bhikkhu... [and so forth].

The word division is as follows: “*hoti adhammiko*” is the word division. When the Saṅgha’s Uposatha should be performed by four [monks] in concord, performing the Uposatha of a group (*gaṇa*) is contrary to the Dhamma;
it is “in concord” because they have come together within hand’s reach.
2589–90. The construction is: “That Uposatha which is contrary to the Dhamma and is incomplete—how is that performed? In whatever place, within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*),...

The construction is as follows: "If four monks are staying [in one place], and having brought the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) from one of them, those three persons recite the *Pātimokkha*, it is a legally valid *Uposatha* that is incomplete (*vagga*).
The meaning is: because the *Saṅgha Uposatha* has been performed by four who are within the same boundary, it is "legal" (*dhamma*);
yet, because they have not come within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) of one another, it is "incomplete" (*vagga*).

2591. The construction is: "That which is complete according to the Dhamma—that is what is called 'done'. Here, in this teaching, if four bhikkhus recite the Pātimokkha together, this is intended to be understood as the Uposatha that is "complete according to the Dhamma.
It is "according to the Dhamma" because the Uposatha of the Saṅgha has been performed by the four [bhikkhus], since not even one of them has left the reach of hand-contact (hatthapāsa).
The intended meaning is "united. 2592. The construction is as follows:

for one who perceives a divided Saṅgha as united, or who perceives a united Saṅgha as divided, or for one who is uncertain in both cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) if he performs the Uposatha. 2593.
"With the intention of causing a schism" means having the desire for division, thinking: "Let these perish, let these be destroyed; what use have you for them?"
The phrase “for one performing the *uposatha*” should be supplied and connected [to the preceding]. For that monk there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense);

and because of the strength of unwholesome states, there is a *thullaccaya*. As it has been said: “In the case of the fifteen [grounds] involving intent toward schism, a *thullaccaya* is stated due to the strength of unwholesome states.
There is no offense for one who performs the *uposatha* while perceiving the Saṅgha—whether it be a faction (*vagga*) or a complete assembly (*samagga*)—as being complete (*samagga*).

The construction (*yojanā*). Furthermore, the remaining analysis to be stated here was not mentioned by one who wished to state it together with the words beginning with “by the offering of purity” at the conclusion of the analysis of the invitation (*pavāraṇa*).
2594–5. The instrumental-case words beginning with “by one who has been suspended” (*ukkhitteṇa*) are to be construed with the word “together with” (*saha*) as [part of] the Uposatha.
The phrase “it should not be done” is to be connected with each [of the following]. “By one who has been suspended” (ukkhitte) means by one who has been suspended for three reasons:
one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not making amends for an offense, and one suspended for not relinquishing an evil view.
For when these three types of suspended persons are present, the Saṅgha incurs a *pācittiya* offense if it performs the Uposatha.
By the term “householder,” even a member of another sect (tīrthika) is included. By the phrase “with fellow practitioners (sahadhammika),” it refers to the four fellow practitioners:

a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), and a female novice (sāmaṇerī). Regarding the phrase “by those who have fallen away or laid aside the training,” the grammatical analysis here is:
*cuto* and *nikkhittasikkho*. One who has fallen away (*cuto*) is one who has committed an offense involving defeat (*antimavatthu*). One who has laid aside the training (*nikkhittasikkho*)...
One who has renounced the training is not [a monk]. "By eleven" means:

a paṇḍaka, one living in communion by theft, one who has gone over to another sect, an animal, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an arahant, a defiler of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic, one who sheds blood [of a Buddha], and one who is both-sexed.

With these eleven types of persons who are incapable [of participating], one should not perform the Uposatha together with one who has committed an offense similar to that of another; nor should the Uposatha be performed with consent (chanda) given by one who is excluded.

For one who does so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This is the construction of the meaning. Thus, in all the various permutations excluding those who have been suspended (ukkhitto), there is only an offense of wrong-doing.

It should be understood as follows: because of the statement, “When two people incur an offense through a common basis such as eating at an improper time, such a similarity of basis is called ‘common’ (sabhāga),” the term “common offense” (sabhāgāpatti) must be taken to mean an offense that is common by way of its basis.
If, on the day of the Uposatha, the entire Saṅgha has incurred a common offense, [the procedure is as follows].
“Furthermore, monks, in a certain residence on that very Uposatha day, the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense.
In that case, monks, those monks should immediately send one monk to a neighboring residence, saying:
‘Go, friend; having confessed that offense, come back; we shall confess that offense in your presence.’”
If this can be obtained, that is good. If it cannot be obtained, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This entire Saṅgha has fallen into a shared offense.
When it sees another monk who is pure and free from offense, then [it shall confess] that [offense] in his presence.”
And [if he says], "I will make amends for the offense";
and if he is doubtful, [he should say]:
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me: this entire Sangha is doubtful regarding a similar offense; when I become free from doubt, then I will make amends for that offense. And...
The Uposatha should be performed according to the method already stated.
And here, "recitation" (*sajjhuka*) means for the purpose of arriving on that very day. This same principle applies to the Uposatha of a group (*gaṇa*) and so forth.
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathāgaṇṭhipada*: "Just as when the Saṅgha, having committed a shared offense and not obtaining purification, [thinks] 'when..."
“Having said, ‘When he sees that [the other] is pure, then I will confess that offense in his presence,’ one is permitted to perform the Uposatha;
thus it is allowable for two to perform the Uposatha after announcing it to one another.

It is said (kirā) that even by one person, having made the mental resolve (ābhoga), ‘I shall confess it once I have obtained a pure [person],’ it is allowable to perform it. Regarding “it is said” (kirā):
And here, this should be understood according to tradition (*anussava*), not out of mere personal preference.

Regarding the phrase "by one whose desire has been purified": even if one has sat down to perform the ritual after bringing forth the desire (*chanda*), if that desire is abandoned—thinking, "I will not do it for some reason such as the perception of foulness (*asubhalakkhaṇatā*)"—and he then performs it again, he must once more [purify] his desire.

Having brought it back, it must be performed. As it is said: "In this case of being set aside (*pārivāsika*), it is not permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*) without first bringing back the consent and purification of mind.
2596. "Without having confessed an offense" means without having confessed an offense that has been committed. "Without having cleared away doubt" means "I..."
“Venerable sir, I am uncertain regarding many offenses; when I become free from uncertainty, I shall then atone for those offenses.
Having thus failed to report his doubt, the Andhakaṭṭhakathā states:

“Regarding the phrase ‘when he becomes free from uncertainty,’ if he is not actually free from uncertainty, it is permissible for him to confess after first specifying the basis (vatthu) [of the offense]. In this regard, the following is said:
The Procedure for Confession: If the sun is obscured by clouds and a monk eats while doubting whether it is the right time or not, that monk should state the basis of the offense as follows:
"Venerable sir, I ate while doubting. If it was the right time, I have committed several offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if it was not the right time, I have committed several offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*). Thus he should state the basis.

Having enumerated them, one should say: "Venerable sir, whatever numerous offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or offenses requiring expiation (*pācittiya*) I have incurred in this matter, I confess them in your presence. This same method applies to all offenses.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, the following analysis is stated: "Friend, I am in doubt regarding such-and-such an offense..."
Having said, "When I am free from doubt, then I shall make amends for that offense," the Uposatha should be performed and the Pātimokkha should be heard;
because of this statement, as long as one is not free from doubt, one is not permitted to accept a shared offense.
Furthermore, one is considered pure regarding other formal acts (kamma). "Once again, having become free from doubt, one must indeed confess it."

This is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Aṭṭhakathā; however, there is no fault in teaching it. The same method applies here as well to the phrase: "Having emerged from this [meditation], I shall make amends for that offense.
2597. Regarding the *Uposatha*: by way of the day, the duty to be performed, and the form, there is the fifteenth-day [Uposatha], the Saṅgha-Uposatha, and the recitation of the Sutta.

On an Uposatha day endowed with these three characteristics: "from a residence with bhikkhus" refers to those residences with bhikkhus of the types that will be explained hereafter by the passage beginning, "on whatever Uposatha there is business," and so forth. Here, the remainder is "a non-residence.

Regarding the phrase "whether it be a residence or a non-residence," this means that one should not go [to a place] that is either without bhikkhus or has bhikkhus belonging to a different communion (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*).
Here, the phrase "except by means of the Saṅgha, except due to obstacles" is to be understood as a supplement.

"Non-residence" refers to places such as sheds and the like. On the Uposatha day, a bhikkhu—whether from a residence that has bhikkhus or from a non-residence, or from a residence that has no bhikkhus, or from a residence that has bhikkhus belonging to a different communion—should never, at any time, go elsewhere except by means of the Saṅgha or except due to obstacles.
"One should not go" is the construction.
2598. However, that residence where the Uposatha ceremony is performed is designated as "one having monks";
this implies that if the Uposatha is not performed in a certain place, even though monks are present there...
He explains that it is called "without monks.
2599. Desiring to determine the purpose of the *uposatha* and, by extension, the *pavāraṇā*, he says, "For what purpose is the *uposatha*?

and so forth. 2600. "Should protest" means should prevent. Regarding the phrase "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for one who does not give," here the words "to invalidate a legitimate legal act (*dhammika-kamma*)" must be supplied and connected.

2601. “And that” refers to the Saṅgha, which is fivefold, distinguished by categories such as the group of four and so forth. This is illustrated by way of the formal acts (kamma) that must be performed according to the minimum quorum; it is not intended to show that groups of six or more are unfit to perform them. 2602.

To demonstrate the formal acts based on the divisions of the group of four and so forth, he says: “Pavāraṇā,” etc. The construction is as follows: apart from the Pavāraṇā, the Abbhāna, and the Upasampadā, there is no formal act that cannot be performed by a group of four.

2603. *Majjhadese upasampadā* means "ordination in the Middle Country" (*majjhadesūpasampadā*). The construction is as follows: even without the [formal] rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) and ordination in the Middle Country, it is permissible to perform all formal acts (*kamma*) with a quorum of five.
2604. The construction is: "not even a single formal act is not to be performed.

The meaning is that every formal act must indeed be performed. Two negations lead to the affirmation of the intended matter. With a Saṅgha of twenty members, [it is permissible] for all formal acts...
Regarding the question of why a group of more than twenty is mentioned when the requisite number is to be fulfilled, he says: "To make it known that there is a fault in deficiency, but not in excess.
This means that among the four kinds of Saṅghas mentioned, a fault exists when one is deficient in number, but no fault exists when one is in excess;
thus, the state of being "in excess" is shown so as to indicate that a Saṅgha consisting of a group of more than twenty is intended.
2605. The construction is as follows: it is shown that when a formal act (kamma) is to be performed by a group of four, only four regular monks (pakatatta) are eligible for the act.

The remainder are regular monks who are entitled to give their consent (chandāraha). By "regular monks," those who have not been suspended (anukkhitto) and who have not committed any of the ultimate offenses (antimavatthuṃ anajjhāpanno) are to be understood.
"In the remaining cases" refers to those involving groups of five and so forth.

2606. For one who performs a formal act (*kamma*) that must be carried out by a quorum of four or more, having included a person with whom one does not live in communion (*asaṃvāsa-puggala*) to complete the number, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The construction is: "Not only is there an offense of wrong-doing, but the act performed is also invalid.
2607. Regarding the phrase "parivāsa, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes [the acts of] sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya-paṭikassana*), and so forth.

"Tatrattha" means "one who stands within those [acts], such as parivāsa, etc. By the word "tathā" (so), this [phrase] "the act performed is invalid and there is an offense of wrong-doing" is carried over [from the previous rule].

"But the rest," however, refers to other formal acts such as the Uposatha and so forth, distinct from the formal act of *parivāsa* (probation) and the like. "It is permissible" means that it is permissible to perform those [acts] by including those individuals under probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth as the ones who complete the quorum.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the Uposatha Khandhaka.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Entrance for the Rains (Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka-kathāvaṇṇanā). 2608.

"The entrance for the rains has been stated"—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the phrase "and the latter," the word *iti* here functions as an indicator (*nidassana*). "Entrance for the rains" (*vassūpanāyikā*) means the entering upon the rains (*vassūpagamana*).
"One should make a dwelling (*ālaya*) or a verbal declaration (*vacībhedo*)"—by this, the manner of entering upon the rains is shown.
It has been explained. The connection is that one who approaches must either establish a dwelling-place (*ālaya*) or make a verbal declaration.
And for one who is approaching, if there is no lodging, he should merely form the mental intention, "I shall dwell here for the rains";

but if there is a lodging, the meaning is that he should either make the verbal declaration, "I enter upon the rains-residence for these three months in this monastery," or "I enter upon the rains-residence here."
2609. The construction is: "for one who, knowing [the time], does not enter the rains residence.

Regarding "three months," the words "either the first or the latter" are to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding "even for one wandering," the word "on a journey" (*cārikā*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

The construction is: "even for one wandering on a journey without having dwelt for either the first three months or the latter three months, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Three months" [is the phrase].
The locative case is used for immediate connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). As it is said:

“Monks, having entered the rains residence, one should not set out on a journey without having stayed for either the first three months or the last three months; whoever should set out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)” (Vin II 167).

Regarding the phrase “in the hollow of a tree,” the word “pure” (*suddhe*) is to be understood as the remainder. As it is said: “Regarding ‘in the hollow of a tree,’ here [the meaning is] in a pure [hollow]” (Vin IV 40).

"It is not permissible [to stay] in a hollow of a tree; however, it is permissible to approach after having constructed a small hut with a thatched roof inside a large tree-hollow and provided it with an entrance door. By the phrase "in a hollow of a tree," even a branch of the tree is included;
that too is not permissible unless it is cleared out. As it was said: "In a tree-branch... (rukkhaviṭabhiyā).

“In this case as well, it is not permitted [to stay] in a mere clean bough; however, if one builds a framework upon a large bough, constructs a small hut there with a thatched roof, and approaches it—that is permitted.
“Regarding ‘under a parasol’: in this case as well, having placed a parasol upon four pillars, having made it a shelter, and having fitted a door—”

"It is permissible to approach [the dwelling]; this is what is called a 'parasol-hut' (chattakuṭikā). Regarding 'a jar' (cāṭī): here too, one must construct a hut using a large pot-covering (kapalla) in the manner described for the parasol, and only then is it permissible to approach.
From this statement in the Aṭṭhakathā, it should be understood that there is a prohibition against approaching pure parasols or jars when they have not been so constructed.
"A skin-hut" (chavakuṭī) refers to things such as bedsteads with iron frames. As it is said:
“‘A corpse-hut (chavakuṭikā)’ refers to a hut of various kinds, such as one with a frame-bed;
it is not permitted to go there. However, it is permitted to go after building another hut on the charnel ground.

In the Andhaka-ṭīkā, the corpse-hut is described as follows: “The hut is built for the purpose of cremating a corpse, and for the sake of the ashes and the bones. Regarding the “frame-bed”: [text continues]
“*Kasikuṭikāpāsāṇaghara* means ‘a stone house’,” says the Elder Vajirabuddhi. A house built by placing a stone on top of four other stones is also called a *ṭaṅkitamañca*.
They construct a bed by drilling holes in the middle of long bed-legs and inserting cross-pieces;
thus, for such a bed, there is no distinction of “this is above” and “this is below,” as it can be turned over.
It remains exactly as it was; they place it in a charnel ground or a shrine for deities (*devatā*), and this too is called a "stake-bed" (*ṭaṅkitamañca*).

2611. Regarding the phrase "if there is a deficiency of requisites, or due to physical indisposition," since the remaining obstacles will be explained later, the term "obstacle" (*antarāya*) here should be understood as the tenfold [types] beginning with the obstacle of a king (*rājantarāya*). 2612–4.
"I allow you, monks, to go on account of seven kinds of business even if not invited, much less [if invited]."
In order to show the method stated as "for a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, a sāmaṇerī, and for one’s mother and father," he said "of mother and father" and so forth.
[This applies] when there is a need for seeing one's mother and father, or for seeing these five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
Or, having seen one among them who is ill, or for the sake of seeking food and so forth for those attending him,
or for the sake of seeking food and so forth for them, or likewise, thinking: "Having gone to one among these five fellow-practitioners who is dissatisfied or disenchanted,
I will either dispel [his distress] myself or cause it to be dispelled, and I will give him a discourse on the Dhamma."
Or, thinking: "I shall dispel, or cause another among those five who follow the same Dhamma to dispel, a view that has arisen and occurred to him;
or I shall deliver a discourse on the Dhamma to him"; or thinking: "I shall remove, or cause another to remove, a remorse that has thus arisen;
or I shall deliver a discourse on the Dhamma to him"—in this way, by a monk who knows the Vinaya.
The construction is: "One must go even when sent on a seven-day errand, much more so when specifically dispatched.
Regarding the phrase "food, etc.," the word "etc. includes the seeking of medicine and so forth. As it is said:
"I shall seek food for the sick, or I shall seek food for the attendant of the sick, or I shall seek medicine for the sick..."
“I shall question him, or I shall attend upon him. “They will cause him to depart” means that they will take him away from wherever dissatisfaction has arisen and go elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase “or we shall dispel it,” the word “or” (*vā*) here implies: “But in this case, monks, a monk [violates] a heavy rule (*garudhamma*).”

He has committed an offense entailing a formal act of probation and is deserving of probation. If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying, “I have indeed committed a grave offense and am deserving of probation;

let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks,” then, monks, one may go on account of a business matter lasting seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited, thinking: “I shall make an effort to grant him probation.”
This includes such modes as: "I shall recite [the Kammavācā]," "I shall cause it to be recited," or "I shall serve as the one who completes the quorum.
One going on a seven-day mission must go having made a formal mental resolve (*ābhoga*) while still standing within the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*), thinking: "I will return within seven days.
They say that if one crosses the precinct boundary without making this resolve, one's rains-residence (*vassa*) is considered broken.

2615. “This, however, is the determination regarding the breaking of the night (*ratticcheda*) outside the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*) in this context”—saying this, he stated “by one who has entered the rains residence here,” etc., in order to show the determination regarding the breaking of the night as found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
“In this” means in this section concerning the duties of the seven-day period. The meaning is that this determination outside the canonical text is to be understood.
“On such-and-such a day,” and so forth, he will state the manner of invitation. “Previously” means first.
“It is permissible” means it is permissible to go on account of a seven-day business. As it has been said:

“If, in one great dwelling, an agreement has already been made that ‘one must assemble on such-and-such a day,’ then one who has been invited is indeed considered as having been invited; it is permissible to go.”
"It is permissible. "Some say that even if an agreement has been made by the lay followers, such as 'On this day we shall perform acts of giving and so forth;
let everyone assemble,' it is permissible to go, for one is indeed considered to have been invited. 2617.
"Bhaṇḍaka" means one's own robe-property. "It is not permissible" means it is not permissible to go on account of the seven-day business.
“They send” means they send by means of tasks such as washing robes.
By this very statement it is indicated that it is permissible to go on a seven-day mission for some blameless duty at the command of one’s teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya).
“For the purpose of recitation and so forth” refers to the reading of the scriptures (pāḷi); by the word “and so forth” (ādi), he includes questioning and other such activities.
“*Garūnan*” refers to teachers and preceptors who are not ill. “*Labhati gantuṃ*” means he is permitted to go on account of some business lasting seven days.
“*Puggalo*” (the person) refers specifically to a bhikkhu, as determined by the context of this section. “*Ācariyo*” is mentioned merely as an illustration;
the same rule applies even when one is restrained by a preceptor (*upajjhāya*). “*Sace pana naṃ*... [if, however, him...]
The teacher says, "Do not go today"; this is permissible. To show the method of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), he said:
"In the case of a break in the night, there is no offense; thus it is explained. "Break in the night" means for the purpose of breaking the rains-retreat (*vassa*).
They say that in all instances, "break in the night" is determined to mean "breaking the rains-retreat. Thus it is regarding one who has gone on a seven-day mission.
If the teacher or preceptor says, "Do not go today," to one who is returning within seven days,
the intention is that there is no offense even after the seven days have passed; however, it should be understood that a break in the rains residence (*vassa*) does indeed occur,
because the seven-day period has been spent outside [the monastery].
“Of any relative whatsoever” means of any other group of relatives besides one’s mother and father.

By the phrase “for the sake of seeing [them] as they depart,” it is indicated that the remaining relatives should act as follows: “We are ill and wish for the venerable ones to come,” and likewise from the families of supporters:
“We shall give a gift, we shall hear the Dhamma, and we wish to see the bhikkhus. Thus should it be done.
It is stated that for one who goes on a seven-day mission after having informed [the Sangha] or sent a messenger, there is no violation of the night-limit and no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
As it was said: "But here, monks, if a monk has a relative who is ill...
[omission] ...monks, one may go on a seven-day mission when sent, but certainly not when not sent," and: "But here..."
“Monks, suppose a lay follower has had a dwelling built for the Saṅgha... [and so on] ...he says:
‘I wish to give a gift, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the monks. Monks, one may go for seven days’ business when one is sent for, but not when one is not sent for.”
2621. “If, while going with the thought, ‘I will go to the village and return this very day,’ one is unable to reach it upon returning, it is permissible”—this is the construction.

Regarding the phrase “it is permissible,” the intention is that for one who has gone with the thought, “I will return this very day,” if dawn breaks while on the road, there is neither a breach of the rains-retreat (vassa-cheda) nor the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for breaking the night’s limit.
*Vajeti* means at the place where cowherds reside. *Satthe* means at a location where a caravan of foot-soldiers (*jaṅghasattha*) or a caravan of carts (*sakaṭasattha*) has encamped.

Regarding these three places, it is said that for a bhikkhu there is no offense in interrupting the rains-retreat (*vassaccheda*). This means that for one who travels together with them, there is no offense;
however, if he travels after separating from them, there is indeed an offense, and he is not permitted to perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
Regarding the *vajja* and other such cases, on the day of entering the rains retreat, that bhikkhu who is about to enter the rains should say to the lay devotees, "It is necessary to obtain a hut.
If they provide one after it has been built, he should enter it and say three times, "I enter the rains here.
If they do not provide one, he should enter beneath a cart standing in the vicinity of a hall.

Even if one does not obtain [a dwelling], one should make a formal declaration of intent (*ālaya*). However, in a caravan where there is no hut or similar structure, it is not permissible to enter after making a verbal declaration such as, "I am entering the rains retreat here";
only the mere act of making the declaration of intent is permitted. A "declaration of intent" (*ālaya*) means merely the arising of the thought, "I will dwell here for the rains retreat."
If the day for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) falls while the caravan is still on the road, the invitation must be performed right there.

If, however, the caravan passes the destination intended by the monk even while staying within the boundary (*antovassa*), he should stay at that intended place and perform the invitation ceremony there together with the monks.
Furthermore, if the caravan stays within the boundary even while passing through a certain point along the way...
Whether he stays in a village or disperses [from it], he must perform the *pavāraṇā* after staying together with the monks in that very same village;
it is not permitted to go beyond that without having performed the *pavāraṇā*.
Even one who enters the rains residence on a boat must enter a hut (*kuṭī*). If, after searching, he does not find one, this is the basis for his attachment.
It should be done. If the ship remains at sea for the duration of the three months of the *temāsa*, the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) must be performed right there.
If the ship reaches a shore and one wishes to go further oneself, it is not permitted to go.
One must stay only in whatever village the ship has reached and perform the invitation together with the monks. Even if the ship travels elsewhere along the coast, [the same rule applies].
If a bhikkhu wishes to stay in the very village he first reached, let the boat go on;
the bhikkhu may stay right there and perform the *pavāraṇā* together with the other bhikkhus.
Thus, in these three cases—on a journey, in a caravan, and on a boat—there is no offense in interrupting the rains residence, and he is permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*.
"2623. When there is a deficiency of requisites" means when there is a lack of requisites such as alms-food and so forth.

"Or due to bodily indisposition" means when there is a physical ailment or illness. "He may depart even after breaking the rains retreat" means that he may go to a place where he is comfortable even after having broken the rains retreat.
By the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that he may do so even without breaking the rains retreat, provided there is a reason for breaking it.
This indicates that it is permissible to go for the sake of a matter requiring seven days.
