(2624) "By whatever obstacle" means by any obstacle whatsoever, such as those caused by kings and so forth. The construction is: even for a monk who has not entered the rains residence, whether his rains residence has been interrupted or not, he should enter for the second *vassūpanāyikā* (the beginning of the rains).
(2625–6) "Seven days" is used in the accusative case to denote duration (*accantasamyoga*). It is connected with the word "spends" (*vītināmeti*).
Or, even if he has gone outside, he spends seven days there. For that bhikkhu—both for him who goes and for him who spends the time—the previous [rain-retreat] does not exist.
Because it was not entered and because the rain-retreat was broken, the previous *vassūpanāyikā* (commencement of the rains) neither exists nor is obtained.
This occurs respectively for these two cases upon the transgression of the boundary and the transgression of the seven-day limit.
And the offense should be understood.

Regarding the promise made by a bhikkhu: when it is said, "Stay here for the rains retreat," and having replied, "Very well," he then fails to fulfill that promise—that is, does not remain there—there is an offense.
To the question "What [offense]? he says: "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is not...
An offense occurs only upon the breach of this very promise; however, it should be understood that an offense also occurs upon the breach of other promises.
As it is said: "And regarding a promise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Here, an offense does not arise only from the breach of the promise, "Stay here for these three months during the rains," but also from [the breach of others], such as "For these three months..."

"Receive alms; we both shall dwell here for the rains retreat; we will recite the Uddesa together"—by such means, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of each respective promise.
Furthermore, that [offense] occurs on account of a subsequent breach of faith by one whose mind was pure at the time of the promise.
However, if the mind was impure from the outset, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) at the moment of making the promise.
“By deception, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” means that the offense of wrong-doing is joined with the offense of expiation (pācittiya).

2627. According to the statement in the Commentary: “Furthermore, for one who has entered the rains residence but, without waiting for dawn, departs on that very day for a seven-day business and returns within the seven days, there is no offense,” how much more so for one who, having stayed [there], goes outside?

And because it is about to be explained, the reading “having not caused dawn to rise” (anuṭṭhāpetvā panāruṇaṃ) should be accepted. Although the reading “having caused dawn to rise” (uṭṭhāpetvā panāruṇaṃ) appears in some manuscripts, it is not to be accepted. 2628.
“Having stayed” means having stayed for two or three days. Just as, having stayed for the rains-retreat, one might [leave] without having caused dawn to rise, on account of a seven-day business...

There is no offense for one who departs; likewise, there is no offense for one who returns from the place where they stayed within seven days and again departs on business for seven days without waiting for the dawn to rise.

Regarding the commentarial statement, "The dawn must be made to rise by means of the seven-day interval," this refers to including the day connected with the seventh dawn within that very seventh dawn, [thereby ensuring it occurs] within the interval of the seventh dawn.
This should be understood as being intended to demonstrate the breaking of the night for one who causes [the bowl] to be set out outside before the eighth dawn has arrived,
rather than being intended to demonstrate that it must be set out there at the seventh dawn itself; for this is how it is determined in the *Sikkhābhājaniya-aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada*.

2629. The word-division is “*nopeti asatiyā*. “*Nopeti*” means that one does not approach [the rains residence] by means of verbal expression, such as saying, “I enter this rains residence for these three months in this monastery.
2630. To support this very point, he said: “No fault whatsoever exists. 2631.
Only when the statement, “I enter this rains residence for these three months in this monastery,” has been uttered three times...
The construction is: "He may have entered the rains residence. The statement, "Only when it has been uttered three times," is said by way of the maximum limit;
for even if it is uttered once or twice, one is indeed said to have entered the rains residence. As it is said:
"Having uttered the words 'I enter the rains residence for these three months in this monastery' either once or two or three times, one should enter the rains residence."
"From the ninth day onwards it is permissible to go, whether one returns or not; there is no offense. To show the method according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he said:
"But having made the ninth the beginning," and so forth. "Having made the ninth the beginning" means starting from the ninth; that is, "from the ninth day onwards.
"It is permissible to go" means it is permissible to go specifically for a seven-day business; therefore, even on the day of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), [it is permissible].
It is permissible for one who is going for the sake of the *pavāraṇā* to go by means of a seven-day business (*sattāhakaraṇīya*) that would otherwise make it impossible to return on that very day.
For Vajirabuddhi Thera says: "But it is permissible to go after having performed the *pavāraṇā*, because the *pavāraṇā* is dependent upon that very day.
The construction is: "Whether he returns later or not, no fault exists."
Commentary on the Discourse on the Chapter on Entering the Rains Retreat. Commentary on the Discourse on the Chapter on the Invitation Ceremony (Pavāraṇā). 2633.
Regarding the term “invitation ceremony” (*pavāraṇā*), it should be construed individually with each of the terms beginning with “the fourteenth day. On each of those respective days...

The invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) should be performed; it is spoken of in that way by way of figurative usage for non-distinction. Concord (sāmaggī) is of the very nature described in the commentary on the Uposatha-kkhandhaka.

And those performing the invitation ceremony of concord must first set aside the invitation ceremony and perform it from the first day of the month (pāṭipada) until the full moon of the Kattika four-month period; neither after nor before that time.
It is permissible. Regarding "threefold, twofold, or singlefold": having established the respective formal motions (*ñatti*)—namely, "Let the venerable ones hear me...
[etc.]... one should perform the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) threefold, one should perform it twofold, or one should perform it singlefold"—this is what is called the invitation to be performed.
2634. "Excluding the three formal acts, one should invite by means of the last alone" refers to: "Monks, there are these four formal acts of invitation..."
Having stated, "An invitation procedure that is contrary to the Dhamma and incomplete... [and so on] ...an invitation procedure that is according to the Dhamma and complete," he said:
"In this regard, monks, as for that which is an invitation procedure contrary to the Dhamma and incomplete, monks, such an invitation procedure should not be performed...
[and so on] ...in this regard, monks, as for that which is an invitation procedure according to the Dhamma and complete, such an [invitation procedure should be performed]."

The meaning is: "One should perform the *pavāraṇā* by means of the fourth *pavāraṇā*-act, which is permitted to be performed after setting aside the three *pavāraṇā*-acts that must not be performed," based on such statements as, "O monks, the *pavāraṇā*-act should be performed.
He will explain a portion of its classification with the words, "In whatever residence there are five... and so forth.
2635. Having completed the preliminary duties:
"The broom, the lamp, water, and the seat—these are called the 'preliminary preparations' for the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā)."
“Consent, purification, the announcement of the season, the counting of the monks, and the exhortation— these,
together with the invitation (pavāraṇā), are called the ‘prior duties.
Having thus concluded the ninefold prior duties as they have been stated.
“‘The formal act has been brought together’ means:
‘As many bhikkhus as are competent for the formal act have assembled,
and no common offenses exist.’”
"And when there are no persons to be avoided in that [assembly],
it is called 'the time has come'.
When this had been said, the fourfold "time has come" was brought together and concluded.
"Having laid down the motion (*ñatti*)": "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today is the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha invite. Thus, by way of a comprehensive summary, and [by saying] "let [the Saṅgha] invite with three statements," when the night has mostly passed through the performance of giving and so forth, or when there is an obstacle such as a king, one should act accordingly with "two statements."

Having laid down the motion: "One may perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) with a single utterance (*ekavācika*) and for those of the same seniority (*samānavassika*)," the distinction between these is already shown in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). As it says:
"When this has been said, it is permissible to perform the invitation ceremony with three utterances, two utterances, or one utterance, [and] for those of the same seniority."
It is not permissible. However, when it is said, “One should invite with three utterances,” then only the three-utterance method is permissible; another is not permissible.

When it is said, “One should invite with two utterances,” then both the two-utterance and the three-utterance methods are permissible, but the one-utterance and the simultaneous-year method are not permissible.
But when it is said, “One should invite with one utterance,” then the one-utterance, two-utterance, and three-utterance methods are all permissible.
It is not permissible [to invite] only those of the same year of seniority. When it is said, "those of the same year of seniority," everything is permissible.

"It should be done" means that the elder monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down in the kneeling posture (ukkuṭika), and having raised his joined palms, should address him thus:
"Friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen... [and so on] ...for the third time."
"Friends, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen... [as before] ...seeing it, I shall make amends"—this should be performed according to the method stated.
A newly ordained bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder... [as before] ...for the third time, venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen...
[as before] ...seeing it, I shall make amends—this should be performed according to the method stated.

2636. When they are performing the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), the junior one among them should remain squatting until he himself has completed the invitation; this is the construction [of the rule]. 2637.
If four or three, or even two, reside in a single dwelling within a single boundary, they should state a formal motion (*ñatti*) as follows:
"Listen, venerable sirs! Today is the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*). If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us invite one another."
The construction is: "Having established the formal motion (*gaṇañatti*), they should perform the invitation (*pavāreyyun*). Regarding the phrase "they should perform the invitation":

here, the elder monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture, and having extended his joined palms in reverence, should address those three or two monks as follows: "I, friends, [invite] the venerable ones..."
"I invite you, friends, regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion;
seeing [the fault], I will make amends. For a second time... For a third time, friends, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I will make amends."
The invitation should be performed. Even by a junior [monk] it should be said: "Venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected;
may the venerable ones speak to me out of compassion, and seeing [the fault], I shall make amends.
A second time... and a third time: "Venerable sirs, I invite the venerable ones regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected..."
"May the Venerable Ones speak to me out of compassion; seeing [the fault], I shall make amends"—thus should one invite for criticism.
2638. Two persons may invite one another without a formal motion (*ñatti*); among them, the elder should say:
"Friend, I invite you regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected. May the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion."
“Observing, I will make amends. A second time… [and] a third time, he should invite: “Friends, I invite the Venerable One… [and so on] …I will make amends.

Even a junior monk should say: “Venerable Sir, I invite the Venerable One… [and so on] …May the Venerable One speak to me out of compassion; observing, I will make amends. A second time… [and] a third time, I…”
"Venerable sir, I invite the Venerable one [to point out my faults]... [and so on] ...I shall make amends," thus should he perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
"He should determine it" means that, having completed his preliminary duties, he should say, "Today is my invitation day;
it is the fourteenth" or "it is the fifteenth," and then determine it by saying, "I determine it. As it is said: "Regarding 'today is my invitation day,' if here it is the fourteenth..."
It is said: "If it is the fourteenth day, one should resolve: 'Today is my Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth';

if it is the fifteenth day, one should resolve: 'Today is my Pavāraṇā on the fifteenth. By this, it is clearly indicated that on each respective day, the corresponding terminology must be employed in all the formal announcements (ñatti), such as the *sabbasaṅgāha*.
"The remaining *saṅgha-pavāraṇā*": the *pavāraṇā* to be performed by five or more monks is a *saṅgha-pavāraṇā*.
"Having already performed *pavāraṇā*" means having performed the first *pavāraṇā*.
"Not yet arrived" means not having entered the rains residence during either the earlier or later period due to some obstacle. "Not yet spent [the rains]" means having entered the later period.

For it is said in the *Khuddasikkhā-vaṇṇanā*: “One who has not entered [the rains residence] is called ‘one who has not entered’ because he has arrived during the later period and [his stay] is not yet completed.
The construction is: “He should perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*. Here, the words “in their presence” are to be supplied. 2640–1.

But in whatever monastery five, four, or three monks reside, if they, having brought the *pavāraṇā* of each individual there, perform the *pavāraṇā* with one another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is the construction.

They understand the legal determination beginning with “a unanimous assembly acting contrary to the Dhamma,” and so forth. “Here” means in this section concerning the *pavāraṇā*. “An awakened one” (*budha*) refers to one who is an expert in the Vinaya. “In the manner stated for the *uposatha*” means according to the sequence set forth in the legal determination of the *uposatha*.

“One should know” (*nayet*) means one should understand. 2642. “To accomplish purity for oneself” means one accomplishes one’s own *uposatha*. “He accomplishes everything” means he brings to completion all formal acts (*kamma*), such as the *uposatha* and others. “Not by oneself” means one does not accomplish one’s own *uposatha*.
2643. Therefore, because one does not accomplish purity for oneself, [the text says] "of both. This refers to both oneself and the Saṅgha.

"For the sake of accomplishing the task" (*kiccasiddhatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of the successful completion of formal acts such as the Uposatha; "here" (*idha*) means in this context of the Uposatha procedure and so forth.
Regarding the term *pārisuddhi* (purity): here, by the word *pi* ("also"), the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is included. For this very reason, he will later say: "Either consent (*chanda*) or purity..."
or, having taken [the consent], [one performs] the invitation (pavāraṇā).

When one who is giving the invitation of consent and purity is guilty of an offense, he should confess that offense, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position, raise his joined palms, and say to the monk who is conveying the consent and so forth: "Consent..."
“I give my consent; take my consent; announce my consent. “I give my purity; take my purity;
announce my purity. “I give my invitation; take my invitation; announce my invitation; invite on my behalf.”
2644. The word division is “*chando ekena*. Consent (*chanda*) may be brought by one person even for many; likewise, full purification (*pārisuddhi*) may be brought.
By the word “also” (*pi*), it is to be understood that the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) may also be brought—this is the construction.

“Consent brought through a succession” refers to consent, full purification, or an invitation that has been received by another in the interval from the hand of the one who brings the consent, etc., whether for many or for one.
It does not lead to purification and does not reach the state of blamelessness because, by not going into the midst of the Saṅgha,
it causes a schism through the desire for a "cat's chain" and so forth.
And here, just as the first ring of a cat's chain reaches the second ring but not the third, [so too does this desire].
Thus, these factors beginning with desire (*chanda*), once given by the donor to a recipient, do not go elsewhere;

because they are like a cat’s chain, they are called “the cat’s chain. And it should be understood that the mention of the “cat’s chain” here is merely an illustration for any kind of chain whatsoever.

2645–6. Having received consent (*chanda*), purity (*pārisuddhi*), or an invitation to the *pavāraṇā*, if the one who carries the consent and so forth, before reaching the Saṅgha, should declare himself to be a novice (*sāmaṇera*) or the like, or should become insane, or should die—all that constitutes the consent and so forth as not having been brought.
Only upon reaching the Saṅgha would it be so if he were to declare himself a novice and the like, or had become insane, or had passed away.
The construction is: "or whatever [status] it may be, all of that is considered taken away and brought back.
In this context, "or he might claim the status of a novice (sāmaṇera), etc. means he would speak of his actual status as a novice, etc., by saying "I am a novice," and so forth;
the meaning is that he would subsequently establish himself on the ground of a novice. By the word "etc.," one who has committed the final offense (antimavatthu) is included.
"Having reached the Saṅgha" means having come within arm's reach of the Saṅgha consisting of at least four members who have attained the respective formal act;
this is the meaning. "Negligent" means having fallen into negligence, which is the loss of mindfulness. "Asleep" means having fallen into sleep.

"With deranged mind" means one whose mind has been brought to distraction by spirits (yakkhas) and the like. "Does not inform" means [does not inform] even a single person of the fact that his own desire and so forth have been brought forward.
"He does not tell the bhikkhu. "Intentionally" means that having intended it, knowing [the offense], he fails to inform out of disrespect; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"Those who" refers to those bhikkhus who are elders, novices, or those of middle standing. "Insight" includes serenity (samatha) by way of association.
Here, both serenity and insight are intended only in their nascent stages; therefore, they are referred to as "engaged in insight."
The meaning here is: "endowed with mature serenity and insight. Regarding the term *rattindivaṃ*, the accusative case is used to express continuous duration.
Regarding the word *atanditā*, it means "unwearied" or "not lazy.
As for the phrase *rattindivaṃ*, one might ask: does the word *ratti* (night) here refer only to the night, or to a portion of it? To this he says: "the first watch and the last watch of the night."
“Pubbaratti” means the first watch of the night, being that which is the earlier part of the night; “apararatti” means the latter part of the night, being the final watch.
In the compound “pubbarattāpararattaṃ,” formed by combining the earlier and later parts of the night into a collective dvanda compound, the suffix -a is applied at the end of the compound.
Here too, the accusative case is used to express continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). [This refers to] the middle watch of the night.
It is stated [in the texts] that sleeping is permitted for the purpose of allaying physical fatigue;
however, this was said specifically to show that one should avoid it and instead apply oneself to uninterrupted cultivation during the first and last watches of the night.

Those for whom insight (*vipassanā*) is the supreme resort are "those whose supreme resort is insight" (*vipassanā-parāyana*); that is, those who are devotedly engaged in serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*).
"It is said that they 'are'.
(2649) Those by whom a comfortable dwelling (*phāsuvihāra*) has been obtained are "those who have obtained a comfortable dwelling"; [the word] refers to them.

And "comfortable dwelling" is intended here as the nascent stages of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), because these are the primary causes for a pleasant dwelling; thus, it means "of those who have acquired nascent serenity and insight."
The meaning is as follows: "There might be no loss" means that if this is done, there will be no such thing as loss. The construction is:

"In the month of Kattika," which is reckoned as the robe-month, the inclusion of the Pavāraṇā ceremony is stated. Due to the requirements of metrical composition, the word *saṅgāho* is written with a long vowel; the sense is that the inclusion of the Pavāraṇā is stated. As it has been said:
"And this so-called 'inclusion of the Pavāraṇā' [is for those] whose meditation subjects have been relinquished and whose serenity and insight have become firm..."
It should not be given to those who are stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and so forth.

However, it must certainly be given even to a single individual—whether they be all those who have attained the young stages of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), or half of them, or just one person. Once it has been given, there is an exemption during the rains retreat within the "inclusion of the invitation" (*pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*);
incoming monks are not permitted to take their lodgings. Those [who receive it] must also not be considered as having broken their rains retreat.
"Having performed the *pavāraṇā*, however, they are permitted to set out on a journey even during the interval.
The manner of giving the *pavāraṇā-saṅgaha* (the invitation for inclusion) should be understood from the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the *Pavāraṇakkhandhaka*.
Commentary on the Chapter on Leather (Cammakkhandhakakathāvaṇṇanā) 2650.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "goats, sheep, and deer. Because the dual number for animals is optionally treated as singular and neuter, there is an expression in the plural.
[It refers to] goats, sheep, deer, roe deer, antelopes, and kuruṅga deer. And the *pasadā* are the mothers of deer.
And regarding *pasadamigamātā*: although it should be said *pasadamigamātuyā*, the nasalization (*niggahitāgama*) as *pasada* occurs for the sake of metrical composition (*gāthābandhavasena*).
The construction is: “The hide of the mother of the *pasada* deer is permitted for a bhikkhu.

By the word “deer” (*migānaṃ*), those very animals already mentioned are here shown in their specific divisions, such as “the rohitā and the eṇī,” etc.; *rohitā* and the others are specific sub-divisions of deer.
2651. The meaning is that, setting aside the skins of these aforementioned beings, any other skin is the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
And as for "any other," it is said: "The monkey and the black lion, the sarabha and the kadalī-deer;
whatever wild beasts there may be, their skins are not permitted."
The Commentary excludes [the use of] hide. "Monkey" refers to the *sākha* deer. "Black lion" refers to a species of large-faced ape.
"Wild beasts" refers to lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, and so forth. As it is said: "In this context, 'wild beasts' means lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas;
and not only these, but excluding those whose hides are permitted, all the rest, even down to..."
"Cows, buffaloes, camels, and so forth—all these, in this context, should be understood as 'wild beasts' (vāḷamiga). "Thavikā" means a bag;
"upāhanā" means sandals. The construction is: "All hide that is non-human—that is, devoid of human skin—is permitted for bags and sandals.
Here, "thavikā" includes the pouches for sandals and other such items. As it has been said:
"Except for human skin, sandals made from any other kind of skin are permitted. The same rule applies to the cases for sandals, the cases for knives, and the cases for keys.

2652. Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow sandals with multiple layers (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*) in all border regions," it is said that [other types] are permitted in the Middle Country, but not sandals with multiple layers. Regarding the Middle Country: "In the eastern..."
In the Middle Country, within the boundaries described by such passages as, "In this direction is the market town named Gajaṅgala," and so forth;
"multi-layered sandals" (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*) refers to sandals having four or more layers. As it is said: "Multi-layered sandals are said to be those starting from four layers.
The construction is: "In the Middle Country, multi-layered sandals are not permitted. "Inside the monastery" (*antoārāme*).
Here, by way of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*), the term “of all” is obtained; the meaning is “of all,” both those who are ill and others.
“In all places” means both inside the monastery and outside. The construction is: “for the sick” means they are permitted for one who is ill. 2653.
“Bound in bundles” and “bound in bags”—these should be construed individually. However, the distinction between these is found in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) itself.
It is said: “‘Bound with a strap’ refers to Yavana sandals, which cover the entire foot up to the shins.
‘Bound with a heel-strap’ refers to those made by fastening a strap on the sole for the purpose of covering the heels.
And regarding “pāliguṇṭhimā,” the Commentary states: “Those made by wrapping around; they cover only the upper part of the foot, not the shins.”
[The word] *dassitāva* means "already shown. *Tūlapuṇṇā* means made by filling with cotton-wool (*tūlapicu*). *Sabbāva nīlā* means "all blue";

those for which "all blue" is the first are "those beginning with all-blue. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of [the colors] ending with "great name" (*mahānāma*) and "red" (*ratta*) is intended.
Their specific characteristics are stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself: "The *nīlikā* is the color of the flax flower (*umāpuppha*); the *pītikā*..."
The *kaṇikāra* flower-colored [robe] is reddish; the *jayasumana* flower-colored is red; the *mañjiṭṭhika* is exactly the color of madder; the black is the color of *addāriṭṭhaka*;
the one dyed with great dye is the color of the back of a centipede; the one dyed with *mahānāma* dye is of a variegated color, like the color of a withered leaf.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated that "it is the color of a lotus flower. This also applies to all those beginning with blue.
By the word *api* (“also”), those with growths like blue [spots] and so forth are included.
(2654) *Citrā* means variegated. *Meṇḍavisāṇūpamavaddhikā* means having growths resembling the horns of rams;
the meaning is that they were made by attaching growths shaped like ram’s horns in the place of the ear-ornaments (*kaṇṇika*). This term, “having growths resembling the horns of rams,”...

This is a characterization of those [sandals] that are like the horns of a goat or made of leather strips. "Stitched with peacock feathers" means they are sewn with peacock feathers—either on the soles or on the leather strips—in a manner resembling thread. The construction is: "sandals such as these are not permitted.
2655. *Majjārā* means cats. *Kāḷakā* refers to thorny trees. *Ūlūkā* means owl-bats (bird-cats). *Sīhā* refers to maned lions and the like.
Lions. "Uddā" refers to species of four-footed animals. "Dīpī" means leopard. "Ajinassa" means of one with such a name [as a skin].
"Parikkhaṭā" means made by attaching the aforementioned kind of hide along the edge of the robe, like a lining.
2656. If such sandals are obtained, he says "having removed the inner lining, etc. in order to show the manner of using them.
The construction is: "Sandals should be worn after having completely cut off or removed the lining and so forth.
For one who wears them without doing so, but according to whatever method has been obtained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). As it is said:

"If, having obtained any of these [sandals], they can be used after removing the lining and so forth, they should be used; but for one who uses them while those [parts] are still present, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
Regarding the phrase "having thus made a change in color" (*vaṇṇabhedaṃ tathā katvā*): here, the words "by a part" (*ekadesena*) are to be supplied.

Alternatively, supplying the words "or entirely" (*sabbaso vā*), the construction is: having made a change in color either entirely or by a part, sandals that are entirely blue and so forth may be worn.
For one who wears them without having done so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). As it is said: "Having obtained any of these [colors], and having rubbed the dye with a cloth..."
"It is permissible to wear [the robe] after changing its color. Even if it is changed by only a small amount, it is indeed permissible.
Blue-bordered robes and others should also be worn after changing their color.

2657. Regarding that, having set aside the three types of footwear—urination footwear, defecation footwear, and rinsing footwear—the construction [of the rule] is that it is not permissible to wear any other footwear whatsoever, including all varieties such as palm-leaf sandals, which are intended for walking about.
2658. The construction is as follows: for one who uses a high bed or seat exceeding the prescribed measure—namely, a *āsandi* and a *pallaṅka*—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
An *āsandi* is of the characteristics already described. A *pallaṅka* is made by placing carved animal figures on the legs;
it is constructed from a single piece of wood through carving, is non-detachable, and remains fixed in that very place.
The fact that such a couch is permitted, even though wild animals are present on its legs, is indicated by the very term "imported" (*āharima*).
For it is stated in the *Sārasamāsa*: "An improper bed or couch is one made from improper materials. 2659.
*Gonaka* refers to a large woolen rug with long hair. It is said that its hairs are more than four finger-breadths in length and are black in color.
[It] exists. They say: "A woolen rug (kojava) with hair measuring less than four finger-breadths is permissible.
A *kuttaka* is a woolen spread suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand upon and dance.
A *citta* is a woolen spread decorated with various patterns such as wall-paintings or lattice-work. A *paṭika* is a white woolen spread. A *paṭalika* is one with thick floral designs.
*Uṇṇāmaya-lohitattharaṇaṃ*: a woolen covering spread with red [wool], which is also called "the *āmalaka*-leaf [pattern].
*Ekantalomi*: a woolen covering with hair standing up on both sides. *Vikatī*: a woolen covering variegated with the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth.
According to the *Dīghanikāya*, "*Ekantalomi*" refers to a woolen covering with hair on one side. *Tūlikā*: a mattress.
A natural mattress filled with any one of three types of cotton—namely, tree-cotton (*rukkhatūla*), creeper-cotton (*latātūla*), or *poṭaki*-cotton (*poṭakitūla*).

"With the hair upward" (*uddalomika*) refers to a woolen coverlet with the fleece raised on one side. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: "‘With the hair upward’ (*uddalomi*) means a woolen coverlet with the fleece on both sides;
‘with the hair on one side’ (*ekantalomi*) means a woolen coverlet with the fleece on one side. This is also mentioned in the *Sārasamāsa*.
However, it is said: “*Uddalomī* means having flowers blooming on one side; *ekantalomī* means having flowers blooming on both sides.
(2660) *Kaṭṭissa* refers to a bedspread made of silk (*koseyya*) interwoven with jewels. The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated:
“*Koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ* means made of a woven silk cloth (*saṭa*); that is, made of a folded piece of spun silk.”
The meaning is as follows: *Koseyya* refers to a silk bedspread (*paccattharaṇa*) made of silk thread and sewn with jewels.
However, pure silk (*suddhakoseyya*) that is devoid of jewel embroidery is permitted.
In the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated here: "With the exception of stuffed mattresses (*tūlikā*), all [bedspreads] such as the *gonaka* and others may be sewn with jewels."
It is said, "They are not permitted. In this context, by the phrase "except for a mattress," it is indicated that even a mattress lacking the stitching of jewels is not permitted.

However, by the statement "those stitched with jewels are not permitted," it should be understood that those which are stitched with jewels are permitted to be used as floor coverings or, as appropriate, placed upon beds and other such furniture.
And here, having reached the method of the Vinaya, since one must stand firm regarding what is grave, the decision should be understood according to the very method stated here [in the Vinaya].
However, because this teaching in the Suttas is stated with reference to householders as well, others say that for the sake of including them, it is stated:
"Excepting a mattress... they are permitted."
"Elephant, horse, and chariot rugs": a rug spread upon the back of an elephant is called an "elephant rug.
The same method applies to horse and chariot rugs as well. "And also choice spreads made from the skins of kadali deer": there is such a thing as the skin of a kadali deer;
the meaning is that it is a choice spread made from that. It is said that this [is placed] over white cloth.
Having spread out the hide of a kadali deer, they sew it together and fashion [the bed]. By the word "and" (pi), the antelope-hide rug (*ajinappaveṇī*) is included.
An antelope-hide rug is a mat made by sewing together antelope hides to the size of a bed. It is said that those hides are very fine;
therefore, they sew them after making them into double or triple layers. Thus it is called an "antelope-hide rug."
"Under a red canopy" means under a red canopy dyed with safflower or similar substances; it refers to a bed or seat spread with allowable coverings.
However, under a dark-red (kasāva) canopy, it is permissible [to use] a bed or seat spread with allowable coverings.
For this very reason, he will later say: "If there is no allowable [covering] underneath," and so forth.
"Red pillow on both sides" means a bed or seat provided with red pillows on both sides—that is, at the head-side and the foot-side.
For one who uses any of these [items], it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because they are unallowable.
However, if there is only a single pillow that is red on both sides, or has the color of a lotus, or is variegated, and it is of the proper measure—
The explanation in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) states that [only one pillow] is permitted; by this very statement, it is expressed through contrast (*byatireka*) that two are not.
It is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "Even two pillows that are mostly red are not permitted. By that same principle, it is understood that even a canopy that is mostly red is not permitted.
And here, although it is stated without distinction in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even two [mats] that are not blood-red are permissible;

having obtained more than that, they should be given to others. If one is unable to give them away, one may even lie down after spreading them crosswise on a bed and placing a coverlet over them," yet in the commentary on the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, it says:
Since it has been stated, “For one who is not ill, only two things are permitted: a head-pillow and a foot-pillow;

however, for one who is ill, it is also permitted to lie down after spreading out bolsters and placing a coverlet over them,” it should be understood that only one who is ill is allowed to lie down by spreading [the bedding] crosswise upon a bed.
2662. The construction is: even if there is a canopy above, it is not permitted if there is an improper spread below. "In that" refers to that improper spread. 2663.
By the word "excepting," it is indicated that there is no way for the three types of couches (āsanda, etc.
to be permissible. "The rest all" means everything from the woolen rug (gonaka) up to the two-colored pillow-covers. "Belonging to householders" means belonging to laypeople; by those very people...
"Prepared" (paññattaṃ) indicates that it is not permissible for it to be prepared by any one of the five types of fellow practitioners, or by their command.
"He obtains" (labhati) means he obtains [permission] to sit.
To show the restriction of the location—asking "Where does he obtain it?"—it says "on the Dhamma-seat" (dhammāsane), and so forth. "On the Dhamma-seat" means...

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "If, on the Dhamma-seat, even a blanket (*gonaka*) belonging to the Saṅgha is prepared and removed by monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others of their own accord, without being instructed by the monks, this is called 'removal of what is provided by householders. By means of this 'removal of what is provided by householders,' it is permissible.
"In the dining hall" (*bhattagge*) means: having been seated in the monastery, either at the place where the food is distributed or in the refectory.
Or [the word] "also" (api) indicates that there is no offense for sitting on a woolen rug (gonaka) or similar item prepared by householders even within their own homes.

By the restriction to specific locations such as the "Dhamma-seat" (dhammāsana), it is understood through the method of exclusion (byatireka) that it is not permitted to sit on anything other than those, even if it has been prepared by householders.
Regarding the term *bhūmattharaṇaka*: the word “made” (*kate*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound]. “Therein” (*tattha*) means:

when a bedspread (*bhūmattharaṇa*) has been made by laypeople themselves—whether belonging to the Saṅgha or belonging to a householder—who are followers of the Dhamma but have not been instructed by those who are.

It is permissible to lie down upon it after having placed one’s own upper covering over it. By the word “even” (*api*), it is implied that one may also sit there. Thus ends the section on “the bedspread.”

By this, it is shown that it is not permissible for one to lie down or sit upon beds and such items spread out by householders for the purpose of sleeping, having placed one's own coverlet on top of them.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion in the Cammakkhandhaka.
Commentary on the Chapter on Medicines (Bhesajjakkhandhaka) 2665.

The construction is as follows: "The Blessed One has stated that there are four allowable grounds (kappiyabhūmi): the ground belonging to a householder, the ground by formal agreement, the ground by proclamation, and the ground where cattle rest.
2666. How is the allowable [ground] to be established? "I allow you, monks, these four allowable grounds [to be established] by proclamation..."

Having thus extracted the four grounds with the words, "the householder Gonisādika’s [dwelling] by formal authorization," he said, "of the Saṅgha," and so forth, in order to show their common characteristic. The construction is as follows:
either a dwelling made for the purpose of residence belonging to the Saṅgha, or a dwelling made for the purpose of residence belonging to a bhikkhu.
It is to be made "proper" (kappiya), meaning it is to be established as a proper place (kappiya-ṭṭhāna).
It should be made so. "Sufficient for sleeping together" means it is fit for sleeping together according to the characteristics of being entirely covered or partially covered, and so forth. 2667.
Now, in order to show the four types of grounds (*bhūmi*) according to their essential nature, he says "excepting," etc.

The construction is as follows: that house which is given for the purpose of a permissible ground (*kappiyabhūmi*) by others, or which belongs to them, excluding the monk—this alone is called a "householder’s ground" (*gahapatibhūmi*).

2668. However, a hut that has been authorized by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) is called "authorized" (*sammutikā*). The construction is as follows:

at the time of its authorization, it is indeed permissible either to recite the formal act (*kammavācā*) or to perform a mere notification (*apalokana*), provided the formal act has not yet been uttered. 2669–70. Regarding the laying of the first brick, the first stone, the first pillar, or—by the inclusion of the term "first"—the first foundation of a wall;
while other people are lifting and placing them on all sides...
Having surrounded [the site], while repeatedly saying, "We are building a *kappiyakuṭī*, we are building a *kappiyakuṭī*," one should place bricks by touching them or by lifting them oneself;
or one may place a stone, a pillar, or a foundation for a wall.
This is to be understood as "a hut whose completion is signaled by the proclamation" (*ussāvanantikā kuṭī*).
"2671. ‘The laying down of the bricks, etc. means the laying down of the first bricks, etc., upon the ground.
‘Of those who say’ means of those saying, ‘We are building a kitchen for allowable goods (kappiyakuṭi), we are building a kitchen for allowable goods.

‘But it is permissible at the same time’ means it is permissible at one and the same time; by this [it is implied]: ‘If, while the speech is not yet finished, a pillar is laid down, or if that speech has not been completed...’"
"The work is finished; the *kappiyakuṭī* (a building for allowable goods) is no longer under construction"—this is the determination indicated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
2672. An entire monastery (*ārāma*), whether entirely unfenced or mostly unfenced, is called a "cow-pen" (*gonisādī*) by wise experts in the Vinaya.
This is because, due to the absence of any barrier to entry, it is suitable for cows that have entered to sit down there.
The construction is: "it is spoken of in that way. (2673) To show the purpose, he says:

"In this regard, both what is cooked... and so forth. "Material goods" (*āmisa*) refers to the two previous periods of time. By the word "material goods," he indicates that the other two periods of time, being "non-material" (*nirāmisa*), are permissible even if they have been stored in an unallowable hut or have been cooked there.
(2674–5) He asks, "When do these allowable huts lose their status? and answers with: "That which ends with the proclamation... and so forth.

The construction is as follows: that which is established by formal proclamation (*ussāvanantikā*) upon certain pillars and so forth continues to exist upon those pillars and so forth even when they are removed, and it also exists upon other pillars and so forth.
The construction is that when all the pillars and so forth have been removed, it would be one whose physical basis has been abandoned. A hut such as the *gonisādika* is enclosed.
It may have its site abandoned by means of a fence or other such enclosures. Regarding "enclosed" (*parikkhittā*):

because it is stated in the *Kurundi*, *Mahāpaccarī*, and other texts that "an ārāma is indeed called 'enclosed' even if it is half-enclosed or mostly enclosed," one should understand that this includes not only those entirely enclosed, but also those half-enclosed or mostly enclosed.
"Known as" refers to huts authorized for householders. The construction is to be understood as: "they may become those whose structural basis has been abandoned due to the destruction of the roof.

Regarding the phrase "due to the destruction of the roof," the words "except for the rafters alone" are to be supplied here. If there is even a single eaves-circle above the rafters, it is permissible.
But where none of these four types of allowable grounds exist, what should be done?
Having given it to one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) and having made it his property, it may be used.

2676. With the exception of a monk, receiving from the hands of others, their storage, and what has been stored within their [residence]—all this is permissible for a monk; such is the construction [of the rule].
2677. Whether it is the property of a monk or that of the Saṅgha, if it is in an improper place or in a house large enough for cohabitation...
Food cooked inside [the monastery] and food prepared inside [the monastery] is not permitted for a bhikkhu.

Even if it belongs to a bhikkhunī or to the Saṅgha, food cooked inside and food prepared inside a house large enough for two people to lie down together on an unsuitable ground is not permitted for a bhikkhunī.
Thus, the construction is that it is not permitted for both the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī.

2678. *Akappakuṭiyā* means an improper hut; the meaning is "on an improper ground," as stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) with the words, "in a house large enough for two people to lie down together. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), butter, oil, honey, and molasses are included.

2679. The construction is as follows: it is indeed permissible for a monk to consume that life-long medicine (*yāvajīvika*), provided it is non-material (*nirāmisa*), together with those seven-day medicines such as ghee (*sappi*) and so forth, which have been stored inside [the hut].
2680. "Cooked" means cooked by oneself; that which is for life-long use, if one consumes it while mixed with foodstuffs (āmiṣa) and consumes what has been stored indoors—what more need be said?
The construction is: "and he consumes what is cooked by himself. Because that which is for life-long use is mixed with foodstuffs, it belongs to the category of foodstuffs;
therefore, it is stated as "stored indoors."
2682. Water is not "timely" (*kālika*) because it is not included among the four types of "timely" [medicines].
2683. There are three types of "timely" [medicines]: those that are "as-long-as-life" (*yāvakālika*), those "for a watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*), and those "for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*).

These three types of "timely" [medicines] become causes of fault when consumed after their respective times have passed, solely by virtue of the rules regarding acceptance (*paṭiggaha*); as for the third type, it becomes an object of an offense involving forfeiture and expiation (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) upon the passing of the seven-day period.
The construction is: "even if not eaten, it causes an offense.

By the phrase "eaten causes an offense," it is shown that for the first two types of allowable times, merely exceeding the time limit after having received them does not constitute the cause for an offense; rather, it is only when they have been *eaten* that there is an offense.
For the seven-day allowable [medicine], even if it has not been consumed due to the lapse of the time limit, it constitutes an offense.

He explains that this is the reason. Among those [types of medicine], he says "and even when not eaten on the third day" specifically to show the distinction regarding that which is for seven days (*sattāhakālika*).

The word *ca* has the sense of the word *tu*. However, that which is for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*), once accepted, does not cause any fault when used for the duration of one's life provided there is no contact with other types of medicine;
therefore, it was not included [in that specific context].
2684. Words such as *amba* and others, which are names for trees, are used here by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) to refer to the drinks derived from their respective fruits;
thus he says, "the drink is called [by that name]. *Coca* is the drink made from the seeds of the plantain (*kadalī*).
*Moca* is the drink made from other varieties of plantain. *Madhu* is the juice of grape fruits (*muddika*). *Muddikā* is the drink made from grape fruits crushed in cold water.
Regarding the phrase "sālūkapānaṃ" (lotus-root drink), the Pāḷi commentary states it is "a drink made by crushing the roots (*sālūka*) of red, blue, and other varieties of lotuses.
Furthermore, because the word *sālūka* is shown with a long vowel in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it was shortened to [the short vowel] for the sake of metrical composition in the verse "sālu phārusakañca.
*Sālūka* refers to the juice of the fruit of the white and blue lotuses. However, in the *Khuddasikkhā-vaṇṇanā*, it says: "Sālūkapānaṃ nāma... [and so on].
It is said: "It is made from the pollen-dust of red lotuses, blue lotuses, and so forth.
Regarding the terms "phārusaka" and others, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that these refer to a single type of tree; the juice of its fruit is called "phārusaka.
The juice of these eight fruits is permissible when mixed with water; it is also permissible when crushed in cold water, clarified, and free of sediment.
Furthermore, a juice that has not been mixed with water is "yāvakālika" (to be consumed during the day).
2685. *Phala* refers to fruits such as mangoes. *Savatthukapaṭiggaha* means the acceptance of fruits that have a physical basis (*vatthu*).

Here, the "basis" (*vatthu*) is that in which the drink resides; it is the fruit. Because it is permissible [to accept] together with the basis, it is "with-basis" (*savatthuka*), referring to the drink.
"Acceptance of that which has a physical basis" (*savatthuka*) means acceptance of a physical object;
having taken this as the meaning, it is said: "the acceptance of fruits that have drink as their physical basis.
Because it is stated "having finely grated," the term "raw mango fruit" (*ambapakka*) refers specifically to an unripe mango fruit. Regarding "in water":
In cold water. "Having strained" means having mixed it with honey and so forth. As it is said:

"It should be prepared by mixing it with honey, sugar, camphor, and so on, which were received on that very day. Regarding the statement "it is permissible to drink," the detailed explanation here is:
"What is prepared in this manner is allowable only before midday; however, having obtained what was prepared by those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna)..."
"However, what is received before the meal may be used with food even before the meal;
after the meal, it may be used without food until sunrise. This same principle applies to all drinks," so it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
"In other drinks as well" means in drinks such as jambu-juice and the like.
2688. *Ucchu-rasa* (sugarcane juice) is mentioned here because it is included [within the category of non-staple foods], but not because it is permitted for the duration of a watch of the night;
rather, it is permitted only for seven days. 2689. *Madhuka-rasa* means the juice of the *madhuka* flower.
In this case, whether the *madhuka* flower juice has been cooked by fire or ripened by the sun, it is not permitted after the meal. Even before the meal, whatever drink one takes—
If they produce intoxicants, it is not permitted from the very beginning. However, fresh or dried *madhuka* flowers,
or those that have been roasted, or the molasses (*phāṇita*) made from them— provided that they no longer produce intoxicants—
all of these are permitted before the midday meal.
The juice of cooked non-staple food (*pakkakhādaka-rasa*) is the juice of cooked food that is to be consumed during the day (*yāvakālika*).
The construction is: "All juice from [cooked] grain is said to be for the duration of a watch (*yāmakālika*). This was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* with reference specifically to this:

"For the juice of grains to be consumed during the day is permissible only before the meal. 2690. Having set aside the juice produced from the fruit of the seven types of grain together with their by-products (*sānuloma*), the construction is: "All juice produced from fruit is permitted to be consumed at an improper time (*vikāla*)—that is, during the watch (*yāma*)—in accordance with the rule of conformity (*anuloma*)."

2691. The construction is as follows: even a juice made by crushing *yāvakālika* (food for the day) in cold water is uncooked; however, even that which is cooked by the sun is permitted at an improper time (*vikāla*). 2692–3.

To show the seven types of grain-conformities (*sattadhaññānuloma*) according to their specific forms, he says: "The palmyra and the coconut," and so forth. "Other food" (*aparaṇṇa*) refers to mung beans and the like.

By the term "conforming to the seven grains" (*sattadhaññānulomika*), it is indicated that their juice is [permitted] at the improper time known as the "watch-period" (*yāmakāla*), whereas [the solid grain itself] is for the day-time period (*yāvakālika*).
This shows that it is not permitted to consume [them].

2695. The construction is as follows: the juice of such minor fruits as these, however, because it conforms to the eight drinks (*aṭṭhapāna*), is indicated and described as conforming to the "post-midday" (*anulomika*) and "within the watch" (*yāmakālika*) categories.

2696. The construction here is: in this world, apart from the juice produced from the fruit of grain that conforms [to the rules], there is no other fruit juice that is not "within the watch" (*ayāmakālika*); this demonstrates that all [such juice] is indeed "within the watch" (*yāmakālika*).
Exposition of the Discussion on the Chapter on Medicines.
Exposition of the Discussion on the Chapter on the Kathina Robe. 2697.

For those who have completed the rains residence, from the time they enter the rains retreat during the earlier period until the Mahāpavāraṇā ceremony, there is no interruption of the night [of the kathina].

Without having [formally] entered the rains-residence, for the sake of obtaining the five benefits to be mentioned— namely, the five benefits such as wandering unannounced and so forth— for one, two, three, four, five, or more than five monks who have completed their rains-residence,
the Bull among Sages, the Blessed One, the supreme among all sages including householders and others, by virtue of his entire multitude of qualities, [bestowed this].
Regarding the phrase "I allow, monks, the spreading of the *kathina* for monks who have completed the rains residence":
the construction is that he spoke [the words] "I allow" and then "spreads.
Herein, this is the analysis: "Who receives the spreading of the *kathina*, and who does not? By way of enumeration..."
"At most five people may receive it at the final limit, and even more than a hundred thousand; fewer than five do not receive it.
This was said with reference to the act of giving *kaṭhina*-cloth to the Saṅgha by a monk who has spread [the cloth] according to the commentary.
"By way of having completed the rains-residence, having entered the rains-retreat during the first period, at the first invitation..."
"Those who have been invited receive [the robe]; those whose rains-residence has been interrupted, or those who have entered for the later rains-residence, do not receive it;

nor do those who have completed their rains-residence in another monastery receive it—this is stated in the Mahāpaccarī. This was said with reference to the obtaining of the benefit as described in the commentary, not regarding the formal act (kamma).
Now he shows these two by way of analysis:
"But for those who have entered upon the earlier [Vassa], all are fulfillers of the quorum, yet they do not receive the benefit;
the benefit belongs only to the others. If there are four, or three, or two, or even one who has entered upon the earlier [Vassa]..."
The others, having acted as the quorum-filler, should spread the *kaṭhina*.
Now, if four monks have arrived—consisting of one fully ordained novice (*sāmaṇera*) who receives full ordination during the later period—he both serves as the quorum-filler and receives the benefit.
[Likewise] three monks and two novices, two monks and three novices, or one monk...
The same principle applies here regarding "four novices.

If those who arrived during the earlier period are not skilled in the spreading of the Kathina, then elders who are experts in the Khandhaka and skilled in the spreading should be sought out and brought.
Having had them recite the formal ritual (kammavācā) and having had the Kathina spread, they may depart after giving gifts and eating; however, the merit belongs only to the others.

By whom may the *kathina* be given so that it is valid? It is valid if given by anyone—whether a deva or a human—or by any one of the five who share the same Dhamma. There is a duty for the giver of the *kathina*.
If he asks, being unaware of it, "Venerable sir, how should the *kathina* be given? he should be instructed thus: "Of the three robes..."
“It is permissible to give a cloth sufficient for one person at the time of sunrise, saying, ‘We give this as a Kathina robe.
For the purpose of preparing it, it is permissible to give this many needles, this much thread, and this much dye;
and it is permissible to give rice porridge and alms-food to this many monks who are performing the preparation.”
One who spreads the *kathina* cloth, having acquired it through lawful and equitable means, must know the proper procedure (*vatta*).
For even a garment stained with grain-dust from a weaver’s house is not permitted, nor is a soiled garment permitted;
therefore, having obtained the *kathina*-spreading cloth, one should wash it clean and prepare the requisites for robe-making, such as needles and the like.
Having prepared it, on that very day, together with many bhikkhus, having finished the sewing, having dyed it,
and having applied the *kappa-bindu*, the *kaṭhina* should be spread. If, while it has not yet been spread,

another person brings a cloth suitable for spreading as *kaṭhina* and offers many materials conducive to the benefits of the *kaṭhina*, then [the *kaṭhina*] should be spread for him who offers the greater benefit.
It should be spread by one who is present. The other person should be exhorted and persuaded in whatever way is appropriate.
But by whom should the kaṭhina be spread? By the one to whom the Saṅgha gives the kaṭhina robe-cloth.
To whom, then, should it be given by the Saṅgha? To the one whose robes are worn out. If there are many whose robes are worn out, it should be given to the most senior.
Even among those who are senior, it should be given to one who has a large retinue and is able to make and spread the robe on that very day.
If a senior monk is unable, but a junior monk is able, it should be given to him. Furthermore, it is appropriate for the Saṅgha to show consideration for a great elder;
therefore, they should say: "Venerable sir, you please take it; we shall make it and give it to you."
Of the three robes, that which is worn out should be given for its purpose. For one who normally wears a double-layered robe, a double-layered one should be given.

Even if his single-layered robe is thick and his *kathina* cloak is thin, enough should be given to make it a double-layered robe for the sake of propriety—even for one who says, "I will wear a single-layered robe when I do not receive [another]."
It is proper to give a double-layered cloth (dupaṭṭa). However, it should not be given to one who is dominated by greed.
Even that person, having spread out the kaṭhina, should not take it with the thought, "Later, having unraveled it, I will make two robes.
But for the one to whom it is given—
“Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me: this cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this cloth for the kaṭhina to the monk named so-and-so to spread the kaṭhina;
this is the motion. ‘Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me: this cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha [gives] this cloth for the kaṭhina...’”
[The donor] gives this cloth for the Kathina to the monk named so-and-so in order to spread the Kathina.
Whichever venerable one approves of the giving of this Kathina-cloth to the monk named so-and-so in order to spread the Kathina, let him be silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak.
"This Kathina-cloth has been given by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so in order to spread the Kathina. It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it to be so."
"It should be given with a formal act consisting of one motion and a second proclamation"—thus it is given.
2698–99. "Excluding the twenty-four [cases] beginning with 'merely marked out'" means that it is excluded from the twenty-four modes mentioned in the Canon, such as:
"The kaṭhina is not considered spread merely by being marked out. "Robe-cloth" (cīvara).

"A robe that has been spread by means of an unsoiled cloth" refers to any one of the three robes that has been completed and given according to one of the sixteen modes mentioned in the Canon, and which possesses the "permissible mark" (*kappabindu*).
Those twenty-four modes and the sixteen modes should be understood from the Canon and the Commentaries; they are not stated here for fear of making the text too cumbersome.
When a bhikkhu is about to spread out [the robe], knowing the eight conditions, he should take up the old robe that he himself is wearing;
having removed the old robe to be spread out so that it shares the same name as the robe to be spread,
and having relinquished it, he should determine the new robe to be spread out, determining it by means of the name of the old robe that has been relinquished.
The construction is as follows: if it is that inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), one should say, "I spread the *kaṭhina* with this inner robe.
If there is an upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), one should say, "I spread the *kaṭhina* with this upper robe";
if there is an outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), one should say, "I spread the *kaṭhina* with this outer robe."
2700-1. The construction is as follows: when this has been said three times in this manner, the *kaṭhina* is considered spread.
Furthermore, that junior monk, taking the *kaṭhina* robe-cloth and approaching the Saṅgha, should say: "Venerable sirs, the *kaṭhina* of the Saṅgha has been spread;
the spreading of the *kaṭhina* is in accordance with the Dhamma; please give your formal expression of appreciation (*anumodana*). This is the construction.
2702. And among those elders who are to give their approval, they should say: "Friends, the *kaṭhina* has been spread for the Saṅgha; the spreading of the *kaṭhina* is in accordance with the Dhamma;
we approve. But the junior monk, however, should speak again, uttering: "Venerable sirs, the *kaṭhina* has been spread for the Saṅgha;
the spreading of the *kaṭhina* is in accordance with the Dhamma; I approve"—this is the construction [of the meaning]. As for the verse, it refers to the recitation of the formula of approval.

It should be understood that the statement, “It has been well spread out by you, venerable sir,” was made by way of showing the meaning (*attha*), and not by way of showing the sequence of the recitation (*pāṭhakkama*).
Furthermore, regarding those who perform the spreading (*atthāraka*) and those who offer the thanksgiving (*anumodaka*), the sequence of speech from the young toward the elders has been stated;

however, it should be understood that the sequence of speech from the elders toward the young was not mentioned in the verses because it must be formulated accordingly, following that same principle, as appropriate.

Whether the Elder who performs the spreading is senior or junior, it is possible—following the method already stated—to arrange the sequence of speech for the group and the individual, as well as the sequence of speech for the group and the individual toward the one who performs the spreading, according to what is appropriate; therefore, this has not been explicitly stated.
However, when the Kathina has been thus spread, if the donors [wish to] give the benefits brought along with the Kathina robe: "By whom..."
If they say, "Our *kathina* has been spread; we give it to him alone," and they give it, the Saṅgha of monks has no ownership over it.
But if they give it and depart without having investigated [the matter], the Saṅgha of monks does have ownership.
Therefore, if the remaining robes of the one who spread the *kathina* are also weak, cloth should be given for their sake as well, after obtaining the consent of the Saṅgha.

However, for the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), only one is permitted. Regarding the remaining benefits of the Kathina, those items designated as "strongly established" (*balavavatthāni*) should be given by means of a distribution schedule (*ṭhitikā*) based on the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsa*);
in the absence of such a schedule, they should be distributed starting from the seat of the Elder (*therāsana*). Valuable goods (*garubhaṇḍa*) must not be divided.
But if there are many monasteries within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*), all the monks should be assembled together and the Kathina should be performed in one place.
It must be spread out; it is not permissible to spread it out separately. 2703.
He himself will explain [the verses] beginning with “What is the root of the kaṭhina? and so forth. 2706.
In the verse enumerating the eight matters, the preliminary duty is expressed by the preceding words themselves through the elision of the latter member of the compound.

For this very reason, he will say: “It is called the ‘prior duty’ (*pubbakicca*)”; and where “paccuddhāra” should be said, it is shortened to “paccuddhara” by virtue of the requirements of metrical composition in the verse.
For this same reason, he will say: “The relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*). “Adhiṭṭhāna” means the act of determining (*adhiṭṭhahana*).
Both relinquishment and determination are “relinquishment-and-determination” (*paccuddharādhiṭṭhānā*). This is a *dvanda* compound formed by mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*).
Regarding the term *atthāra*: here, from the context of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*), it is understood as "the spreading of the *kathina*.

By the word "matrix" (*mātikā*), it is known from the context that these are "the eight matrices for the suspension of the *kathina*. As it is said: "Monks, there are these eight matrices for the suspension of the *kathina*.
"Matrix" (*mātikā*) means mothers, those who give birth; [it refers to] the suspension of the *kathina*.
The meaning is: "these eight [benefits] produce. "Lifting" (uddhāra) means the lifting of the *kaṭhina*. "Benefits" (*ānisaṃsa*):
here, the word "of the *kaṭhina*" is understood from the context. The construction is: "These eight qualities are the benefits of the *kaṭhina*. As it was said:
"For you, monks, who have spread the *kaṭhina*, five things will be permissible," and so forth. There is also a reading "by way of benefit" (*ānisaṃsena*). Together with the benefit, these...
The construction is: "eight things.

2707. Having shown the procedure for dealing with a robe that has been finished as a *kaṭhina* (formal robe) by means of the passage beginning, "if one obtains a robe that is not merely marked out [by the needle], etc., and is excluded from the twenty-four [defects]," [the text now] shows the procedure if it is merely a cloth for which the work of sewing and so forth has not yet been performed.
Having obtained [the cloth], he says "washing," and so forth, in order to show the procedure for dealing with it by way of the preliminary duties.
Therein, "washing" is the making of the kathina-cloth white. "Discernment" is the deliberation:
"Let it be fivefold, or sevenfold, or ninefold, or elevenfold. "Cutting" is the cutting of the cloth according to that deliberation.
“Binding” means the application of false thread. “Sewing” means all needlework. “Dyeing” means the work of dyeing. “Fringes” means the giving of fringe-knots.
All this is called “preliminary duty” because it must be performed first for the *kaṭhina*-spreading ceremony. Regarding the phrase “*antaravāsako*,” the word *iti* is indicated here as being elided.

The construction is as follows: “The outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and also the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*)—for these very same [robes], the relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*), the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), and the assignment of purpose (*atthāropa*) have been stated.”
2709. To show the eighth matrix (mātikā), he says: “And the departure,” and so forth. Since it means “that which has departure within it,” it should have been called *pakkamanantika*;
however, by eliding the latter member of the compound, it is stated as *pakkamana*. This same method applies everywhere.
Regarding the word *aṭṭhi*, the term *mātikā* is understood here from the context of the treatise. The construction is: “These eight matrices.”
2710. To explain according to the sequence of the summary, he says: “Having taken his finished robe,” and so forth.

By the phrase “having taken his finished robe,” the removal of the impediment regarding robes is shown. By the phrase “without regard for his dwelling,” the second removal of the impediment regarding the dwelling is shown.
Here, in all the sentences, the remainder is: “if a bhikkhu who has performed the kaṭhina ceremony should depart. When [the time] has passed...
“Beyond the boundary” means having crossed the monastery boundary (*vihārasīmā*). Regarding the phrase “it becomes an offense of departure,” the words “of that bhikkhu” are to be supplied;
the meaning is that for that bhikkhu, there is a formal rule (*mātikā*) known as the “offense of departure.

2711–2. “Benefit” (*ānisansa*) refers to a robe obtained by one who has completed the rains residence (*vutthavassa*), provided it is not a robe for which the needlework has already been done. For this very reason, he will say:
“*Karoti*,” etc. By the phrase “indifferent toward the monastery,” the first [of the obstacles], the impediment of the dwelling place (*āvāsa-palibodha*), is shown here.
One who has happiness as his purpose for dwelling is a “dweller in happiness” (*sukhavihārika*); this refers to the dwelling (*vihāra*).

While dwelling in that very monastery, if he makes that robe, then upon the completion of that robe—meaning immediately after its completion—is the “immediate-after-completion” (*niṭṭhānantika*) [period].
The construction is: "it is said. By the phrase "when the robe is finished," the severance of the impediment regarding the robe is shown.

"That same [person]" means that very one who has completed the rains residence (*vutthavassāvāsa*). "Lays down the burden" refers to the moment the mind arises through the laying down of both burdens.
"Resolution" (*sanniṭṭhāna*) is indeed the laying down of the burden. Here, at that very same moment, the two impediments [are severed].
The *Aṭṭhakathā* states that "the severance [of the obstacles] occurs in the case of one who has reached a firm decision:
'I shall neither have this robe made, nor shall I return'—at the mere thought of this, both obstacles are severed at once.
(2714) *Kathinacchādana* means the material for a robe that possesses the benefits of the *kathina*. "Na paccessaṃ" means "I will not return."
Regarding the phrase "for one who is making": here, "robe" (*cīvara*) is understood from the context of the section;
alternatively, it should be connected with "the covering of the kaṭhina. "For one who is making" is a genitive used in the sense of disregard.
"Lost" means lost either because it was stolen by thieves or because it was eaten by termites and the like. "Or burnt" means burnt by fire. "Destruction" refers to such [loss] of the robe.
The meaning is that this matrix (mātikā), which is obtainable when there is no end [to the robe season], is called "ending with non-abandonment" (nāsanantika).

Here, by the phrase "I shall not return," the first [condition], the severance of the obstacle of the residence (āvāsa-palibodha), is shown. By the phrase "while he is still making [the robe]," the second, the severance of the obstacle of the robe-material (cīvara-palibodha), is shown.

2715. "One who has obtained the benefit" means one who has obtained the robe that is the benefit of the kaṭhina; "one who has regard for the benefit" means one who has expectations regarding the robe.
The construction is as follows: "One who has gone outside the boundary" refers to one who, having completed the rains residence, has gone outside the boundary;
if, after that robe has been made, he hears of its suspension before the time for suspension, it is called "savanantika" (dependent on hearing).

By the phrase "one who has gone outside the boundary" and so forth, the cutting off of the second impediment is shown. Here, because the term "one who has made the robe" is used, the cutting off of the impediment regarding robes is indicated.

The former occurs first; however, the latter occurs later because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "the obstacle of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*) is severed simultaneously with hearing [the news]. 2716–7.
One who has spent the rains retreat with the hope of obtaining a robe, having departed from his residence, [is told by someone]: "I will give you a robe."
However, when one who has spoken [of giving] has gone outside the boundary, it flows away;

then, when told, "I am not able to give you your robe," at the mere cutting off of hope and the mere cessation of expectation for the robe, this is considered and known as the matrix (mātikā) called "the cutting off of hope.
In the suspension of the kaṭhina during the cutting off of hope, the obstacle of the residence is severed first, because of the hope for the robe.
When [the robe] has been cut off, the impediment of the robe is severed.

2718–20. If one who has gone from the monastery where he spent the rains retreat to another monastery should, while coming back, pass the time for the suspension of the *kaṭhina* on the way, that suspension of the *kaṭhina* for him is considered to have ended by crossing the boundary.
The construction [of the commentary]. In that regard, when the kaṭhina is suspended due to crossing the boundary (*sīmātikkantika*), the impediment of the robe (*cīvarapalibodha*) is severed first;
then, outside the boundary, the impediment of the residence (*āvāsapalibodha*) is severed.
And here, it has been stated by some that "crossing the boundary means crossing the boundary of the robe-season. Outside the boundary...
"It is called 'exceeding the boundary' because the time for the robe season has passed," so it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī*.

However, because it is stated, "If one is coming [from abroad], [the Kathina is suspended] upon crossing the path leading to its removal," then for one who is coming while the Sangha is performing an internal suspension (antarubbhāra), the Kathina suspension would have already occurred even before reaching the monastery boundary; therefore, he would not be able to avail himself of that [suspension].

Our view is that for one who has thus gone beyond the boundary and then returns, if the *kathina*-suspension occurs while he is on the road, it is a "boundary-transgressing" (*sīmātikkantika*) suspension.
If, having taken the robe which is the benefit of the *kathina*, he has gone away with lingering attachment to his residence, and upon returning he reaches the suspension of the *kathina*—
that is, the internal suspension of the *kathina*— then for him that is the suspension of the *kathina*.

The construction is: "He exists; he is called 'the simultaneous suspension' (*sahubbhāra*). In the case of the simultaneous suspension, two impediments (*palibodha*) are severed neither before nor after [the others].

Regarding the phrase "by one who has crossed the boundary" (*sīmātikkantikena*), although it should have been stated as such, it is expressed as "from the boundary" (*sīmato*) by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound.
Departure (*pakkamana*), completion (*niṭṭhāna*), and determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*), together with that which has crossed the boundary—these are the four types of suspension of the *kaṭhina*.

The construction is as follows: the "internal suspension" (*antarubbhāra*), which is defined as a collective suspension, depends on individuals and is contingent upon individuals; it is dependent on the Saṅgha. The term "internal suspension" (*antarubbhāra*) has its vowel shortened due to the requirements of metrical composition in verse.

"Nāsanā" refers to the "terminus of destruction" (*nāsanantika*). "Savana" refers to the "terminus of hearing" (*savanantika*). And "the cutting off of hope" (*āsāvacchedikā*)—these three are also modes of the suspension of the *kaṭhina*.
"But not from the Saṅgha, nor from a bhikkhu" means that it does not arise from the Saṅgha, nor does it arise from an individual; this is the meaning.

Since the destruction of the robe did not occur through the agency of either the Saṅgha or the owner of the robe, the *nāsanaka* (destruction) *kathina-ubbhāra* (suspension of the *kathina*) is said to be "neither.
Likewise, it is stated that the hearing [of the proclamation] did not occur through the agency of both. The same applies to the "cutting off of hope" (*āsāvacchedikā*).
"Āvāsoyeva palibodho" is the analysis [of the compound]. Regarding "palibodho ca cīvare":

here, in the phrase "cīvare," the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*) because there is a desire for a specific distinction; the meaning is "an obstacle caused by robes," which is to say, "an obstacle consisting of robes.
One who, by nature, speaks matters endowed with qualities such as truthfulness and free from faults such as lying is called "one who speaks what is fitting and excellent"; by him.
"By means of the eight headings (*mātikā*)," refers both to the seven headings beginning with "departure" (*pakkamanantika*),
