which are stated by way of those who have gone outside the boundary, and to the "simultaneous rising" (*sahubbhāra*), which is stated by way of one who goes outside the boundary and succeeds in having the robe-material raised within the boundary.
"Or even from within the boundary" means without going outside the boundary, but remaining right there.

The connection is as follows: since it is obtained by means of the formal act of the suspension of the Kathina through those whose Kathina has been suspended, two types of suspension of the Kathina were taught by the Great Sage:

namely, the "simultaneous suspension" (*sahubbhāra*) for one who returns after having gone outside the boundary, and the "internal suspension" (*antarubbhāra*) for those who have come from outside the boundary;
thus, although there is only one type of suspension, it is spoken of in two ways. Therefore, regarding the internal suspension...
It should be understood that eight headings (*mātikā*) are analyzed in the Canon (*pāḷi*), rather than being taken individually.

Regarding "going without having been invited" (*anāmantacāra*): by means of eliding the latter member of the compound, it is called "not having been invited" (*anāmantā*). The meaning is: as long as the *kaṭhina* robe-rag has not been removed, going without having been invited shall be permissible; there will be no offense according to the training rule on wandering (*cāritta-sikkhāpada*).

Regarding "going without undertaking" (*asamādānacāra*): by eliding the latter member of the compound, it is called "non-undertaking" (*asamādāna*). "Going without undertaking" means wandering without having undertaken [the formal possession of] the three robes; the meaning is that separation from one's robes (*cīvaravippavāsa*) shall be permissible.

By the phrase “from a group” (*gaṇato*), eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*) is indicated through the elision of the final member of the compound. Eating in a group shall be permitted; that [rule] is stated in its own form in the section on offenses involving a *pācittiya*.

By the phrase “as much as required” (*yāvadatthikaṃ*), robes as much as required (*yāvadatthacīvara*) are mentioned. “Robes as much as required” means that whatever amount of robe-cloth is needed, that much shall be permitted provided it has not been formally resolved upon (*anadhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned to another (*avikappita*).
By the phrase “whatever arises there as robe-cloth,” the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) previously stated as “and whatever arises there as robe-cloth” is shown.

"And whatever robe-offering arises there" means: whether it be a robe for the deceased, or what has been given specifically for the Saṅgha, or brought by means of resources belonging to the Saṅgha—whatever robe belonging to the Saṅgha arises in any manner whatsoever within that boundary where the kaṭhina has been spread, the meaning is that "it shall belong to them.
This is connected to the statement: "And these five benefits of the kaṭhina have been declared."
Commentary on the Kathina-khandhaka.
Commentary on the Cīvara-khandhaka (2726–7).
Because robes arise from these, they are called "sources" (*uppādā*); they are specifically referred to as the "generative causes," meaning the field for the acquisition of robe-material.
The meaning is as follows: As it was said, “In order to show the field for the acquisition of the robes already mentioned, he said:
‘Monks, there are these eight matrices (mātikā),’ and so forth. “Robe-matrices” (cīvaramātikā) means the mothers who are the causes for the arising of robes.
Therefore, it is said in the *Kathinakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā*: “‘Matrices’ (mātikā) means mothers; the sense is ‘progenitors. And here, by “matrices,” the giving of robes is intended. As it was said:
“Giving to a boundary is the first heading; giving by agreement is the second,” and so forth.

One gives to a boundary, one gives by agreement, one gives by the designation of alms, one gives to the Saṅgha, one gives to both Saṅghas, one gives to the Saṅgha that has spent the rains retreat, one gives specifically designated, and one gives to an individual. The statement, “These are the eight headings,” is stated as a conclusion.
2728. *Tattha* means "in those eight headings. *Sīmāya deti* means "he gives within the boundary"; this refers to one who gives while pointing to the boundary, saying, "I give within the boundary.
The construction is: what is given in this manner is to be shared by the monks who are inside the boundary, so it is described [thus].
In that context, *antosīmagatehi* (by those inside the boundary) refers to those belonging to whichever boundary the donor has in view when he speaks thus.
"By all those who have entered within. "It should be divided" means that robe-cloth should be distributed.

"By one of excellent complexion" means it was praised—that is, described—by one of excellent complexion, endowed with the preeminent qualities pervading the entire world as expressed in the passage beginning, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One, the Worthy One," and endowed with the excellence of supreme radiance by way of the fathom-wide aura and the six-colored rays. This is the meaning here.
The commentary on the words: as for this analysis—"gives within the boundary" (*sīmāya deti*)—here, first of all, fifteen kinds of boundaries are to be understood:

the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), the common-residence boundary (*samānasaṃvāsasīmā*), the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*), the gain boundary (*lābhasīmā*), the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), the town boundary (*nigamasīmā*), the city boundary (*nagarasīmā*), the inner boundary (*abbhantarasīmā*), the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), the province boundary (*janapadasīmā*), the kingdom boundary (*raṭṭhasīmā*), the realm boundary (*rajjasīmā*), the island boundary (*dīpasīmā*), and the world-system boundary (*cakkavāḷasīmā*).

In this regard, the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) has been explained in the discussion on boundaries (*sīmākathā*). The precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*) is delimited by the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or by the area suitable for an enclosure in the case of an unenclosed monastery.
Furthermore, it may be delimited from the place where monks regularly assemble, or from a dining hall situated at the edge, or from a residence where they habitually dwell.
Alternatively, the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) should be understood as the distance within two throws of a clod by a man of medium strength.

That [boundary] increases when the dwellings increase and decreases when they decrease. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "It also increases when the monks increase. Therefore, if in a monastery... [by the monks assembled]...
Being joined together as one, they sit filling even a hundred yojanas; even a hundred yojanas becomes a boundary for the common precinct (*upacārasīmā*), and the gains (*lābha*) reach all of them.
Both the boundary for common residence (*samānasaṃvāsa*) and the boundary for non-separation (*avippavāsa*) have already been explained.
What is called a "boundary for gains" (*lābhasīmā*) was neither authorized by the Perfectly Enlightened One nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma.
Furthermore, kings, royal ministers, or great officials, having had a monastery built, delimit an area of four *gāvutas*, half a *yojana*, or one *yojana* all around,
and having driven stakes inscribed with the name "This is the boundary for the acquisitions of our monastery" into the ground,
they establish the boundary, saying: "Whatever arises within this area, we give all that to our monastery."
They establish [it]; this is called the "boundary of gain" (*lābhasīmā*). The boundaries of villages, market towns, cities, interiors, and water-throwing (*udakukkhepa*) have already been explained.
As for the "boundary of a district" (*janapadasīmā*), within kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala there are many districts; herein, each individual district-limit is a boundary of a district.
A "boundary of a kingdom" (*raṭṭhasīmā*) is the limit of a kingdom such as Kāsi or Kosala. A "boundary of a realm" (*rajjasīmā*) is the great province of Mahācoḷa.

"Kerala-bhoga" refers to the extent of the jurisdiction of each individual king. A "continent boundary" (*dīpasīmā*) consists of great continents and intermediate islands, delimited by the edge of the ocean.
A "world-system boundary" (*cakkavāḷasīmā*) is delimited by the world-system mountain itself.
Thus, among these boundaries, regarding a "local boundary" (*khaṇḍasīmā*): having seen the Saṅgha assembled for some business, [one thinks], "Right here..."
When it is said, “I give to the Saṅgha within the boundary,” it should be divided by as many bhikkhus as have entered inside that section of the boundary.
For that [gift] accrues only to them; it does not accrue to others, even those standing in the intermediate boundary (sīmantarikā) or the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā).
However, for one standing on a tree or a mountain situated within the section boundary, or below [on] the earth...
It reaches those who have gone to the middle [of the boundary].

However, what is given with the words, “I give this to the Saṅgha within this precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā),” reaches even those standing in the gaps between the boundaries (khaṇḍasīmā) or in the intermediate spaces (sīmantarikā).

But what is given with the words, “I give this to the boundary of common affiliation (samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā),” does not reach those standing in the gaps between the boundaries or in the intermediate spaces.
It does not reach them. What is given within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) or the robe-keeping boundary (*lābha-sīmā*) reaches only those who are inside those boundaries.

What is given within village boundaries (*gāma-sīmā*) and so forth reaches even those standing within a boundary that has been formally tied off (*baddha-sīmā*) inside those [village] boundaries. What is given within an inner boundary (*abbhantara-sīmā*) or a water-splash boundary (*udakukkhepa-sīmā*) reaches only those who are inside therein.
This also applies to the boundaries of a district (*janapada*), a kingdom (*raṭṭha*), a realm (*rajja*), an island (*dīpa*), and the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
The legal determination regarding village boundaries and so forth is exactly as previously stated.
However, if one staying in Jambudīpa says, "I give this to the Saṅgha in Tambapaṇṇidīpa," even a single person from Tambapaṇṇidīpa may go and take it for the sake of all [the monks there].
If, moreover, a single bhikkhu of similar standing is right there [in Tambapaṇṇidīpa] for those of similar standing...
He takes a share; he should not be prevented. This, first of all, is how the decision regarding the gift of one who gives after touching the boundary should be understood.

However, as for one who does not know how to say "in such-and-such a boundary," but merely knows the word "boundary" and, having come to the monastery, says, "I give to the boundary," or "I give to the Saṅgha residing within the boundary"—he...
He should be asked: "There are many kinds of boundaries; which boundary do you have in mind?
If he says, "I do not know which specific boundary it is; let the Saṅgha residing within the boundary divide and take it," then within which boundary should it be divided?
The Elder Mahāsīva reportedly said, "Within the non-separation boundary. Thereupon, they said to him: "The non-separation boundary..."
It is called "three yojanas. This being so, those standing at three yojanas will receive alms;
standing at three yojanas, they must fulfill the duties for visitors and enter the monastery; a traveler who has gone three yojanas must ask leave regarding his lodging;
for one undergoing formal dependence (*nissaya*), the dependence is suspended upon exceeding three yojanas; and by one on probation...
"The dawn must be made to rise after having passed three yojanas; a bhikkhunī standing within three yojanas must obtain permission to enter the monastery.
All of this is permissible only by way of defining the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā).
Therefore, it should be divided only within the precinct boundary."

2729. Those monasteries which, by agreement (*katikā*), share a single gain and share equally—in these monasteries, what is given [with the words] "I give by agreement" must be divided among all the bhikkhus together. This is how it is to be construed:
"by agreement" refers to an agreement regarding equal sharing. In this regard, the agreement should be made as follows: in one...
When the monks have assembled in a monastery, those who wish to take charge of another monastery and desire to make it share the same gains should mention its name—
whether saying, "Such-and-such a monastery is ancient," or "It was inhabited by the Buddha," or "It has little gain"—
and state whatever reason there may be, [saying]: "The Saṅgha should make that monastery share the same gains as this monastery."
"It is pleasing" should be announced three times. Up to this point, even one sitting in that monastery is as if sitting here;
likewise, the Saṅgha in that monastery must act in exactly the same way. Up to this point, even one sitting here is as if sitting in that monastery.
When a portion of alms is being distributed, it is permissible for one standing in the other place to receive a share.
Thus, many monasteries may be made to share a single profit together with one monastery.

2730. Wherever the Sangha’s constant services—such as the provision of robes by a donor, permanent maintenance, and regular offerings—are performed or carried out, that monastery given to the Sangha by that same donor [should be understood] by way of the "designation of alms" (*bhikkhāpaññatti*).
The construction is: "It was said by the Great Seer, 'It has been given.

Herein, this is the detailed analysis: in whichever monastery the property belonging to this giver of robes is held as the Sangha’s regular offering (*pākavatta*), or in whichever monastery the monks, taking it upon themselves as their own responsibility, always feed him at his home; therein—

Or perhaps a dwelling was built by him, or meals on tickets and so forth were regularly provided; however, in the case of one who has established an entire monastery, there is simply nothing further to be said—these are called "permanent benefactors" (*dhuvakāra*).
Therefore, if he says, "I give it where my permanent benefactors are being worked," or "Give it there," even if his permanent benefactors are at many locations...
It is as if it has been given everywhere.
However, if there are more monks in one monastery, they should say, "In your permanent residence, the monks are numerous in one place and few in another.
If he says, "Take [the portion] according to the number of monks," then...
It is permissible to take [the items] after having divided them in that manner. In this regard, even small items such as cloth or medicine can be easily divided;

however, if there is only a single bed or stool, one should ask [the owner] and give it to whichever monastery or to whichever dwelling-place he manages, even if it is a solitary cell. If he says, "Let such-and-such a monk take it," it is permissible.
If, however, having said, "Give it to my permanent attendant," he departs without further consideration, it is permissible for the Saṅgha to investigate the matter.
It should be investigated in this way: one should say, "Give it to the dwelling place of the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
If the lodging there is already full, it should be given where there is space. If there is only one [monk],...
If a bhikkhu says, "There is no furniture for the use of lodgings in my dwelling place," it should be given there.

As for that which was given to the Saṅgha—whatever robe was given upon entering the monastery with the words, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha"—the term *sammukhībhūtena* (by one who is present) is used;
although it should be said *sammukhībhūtena*, it is shortened due to the constraints of metrical verse (*gāthābandha*). [The commentary explains: *sammukhībhūtena*.

And [it may be done] by one standing within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*). "It should be distributed" means that after striking the bell and announcing the time, it should be distributed.
This is merely a brief illustration here; the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) is to be understood from the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). For example:
when a robe-giver enters the monastery and gives robes, saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha," and they are being distributed, for one who is within the boundary...
Even one who takes a share before having arrived should not be stopped.

If the monastery is large and robes are being distributed starting from the seats of the senior elders (*thera*), and the indolent great elders arrive late, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, these are for those with twenty years of seniority;
your turn has passed. Rather, setting aside their designated turn, one should give them [the robes].
It should be given to those who have arrived later.
Having heard that "much robe-cloth has arisen in such-and-such a monastery," monks come even from monasteries a *yojana* away;

it should be given to each one as they arrive, starting from the place where they stop. It should also be given to those who have not yet arrived, within the boundary of their approach (*upacārasīma*).

When those who have entered [the boundary] are receiving [alms] from among the pupils and others, it must certainly be given. If they say, "Give to those standing outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*)," it should not be given.

However, if they are connected as one unit with those who have entered the precinct boundary and are located either at the door of their own monastery or within the monastery itself, the boundary is said to have been extended by way of inclusion; therefore, it should be given.
Even when it has been given to the newest member of the Saṅgha, it must still be given to those who arrive later.

However, if the second portion is given once the Elder’s seat has been ascended, the first portion does not reach those who have arrived; from that second portion, it should be given according to seniority (*vassaggena*).
Suppose there are ten bhikkhus in a single monastery and they give ten robes, saying, "We give these to the Saṅgha"; [they should be distributed] individually.
They should be distributed. If they take them all, thinking, "All of these fall to us," then they have both improperly assigned and improperly taken them;

wherever they go, the items remain the property of the Saṅgha. However, it is permissible to set aside one item, give it to the senior monk of the Saṅgha saying, "This falls to you," and then take the remainder, thinking, "These fall to us."
If they bring a single robe with the words, “We give this to the Saṅgha,” and then take it without dividing it, saying,

“It falls to us,” it is both improperly distributed and improperly received. However, if one makes a mark with a knife or with turmeric and the like, and having assigned one portion to the senior of the Saṅgha,
saying, “This place falls to you,” they then take the remainder, saying, “It falls to us”— [it is properly distributed].
It is permissible to take [the cloth]. However, it is not permissible to make a demarcation by means of a flower or a fold belonging to the cloth itself.

If, having removed a single thread and given that spot to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, saying, "This place belongs to you," they then take the remainder, saying, "This belongs to us," it is permissible.
It is likewise permissible to divide it by cutting it into pieces and then distributing them.

In a monastery with only one bhikkhu, when robes have arisen for the Saṅgha, if that bhikkhu takes them all according to the method previously described, thinking, "They all fall to me," they are properly taken, but the established order (*ṭhitikā*) does not remain.
If, however, he takes them one by one, setting each aside and thinking, "This falls to me," then the established order remains. In this regard, regarding the established order:
If it has not been established, and another robe-cloth arises, and a single monk arrives, both may take it after cutting it in half.
If it has been established, and while that establishment remains, another robe-cloth arises, if one who is junior arrives, the established portion descends;
if one who is senior arrives, the established portion ascends.
If there is no other way, one should take it back by making oneself guilty of an offense.

However, anything given by touching upon the Saṅgha in any manner whatsoever—such as saying, "We give it to the Saṅgha," or "We give it to the community of bhikkhus"—is not permitted for those who wear rag-robes (paṃsukūlikas).
[For they have declared: "I reject householder's robes; this is the practice of wearing rag-robes."

This is because it was stated, "I undertake [the practice]," and not because of its being unallowable (*akappiya*). Even if it is given by the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) after having been consulted, it should not be accepted.
However, that which a monk gives from his own possession is called "given by a monk" (*bhikkhudattiya*) and is permissible.
Yet, it does not constitute a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*). Even so, the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is not broken. "We give to the monks; to the elders..."
When it is said, "We give this to you," it is permissible even for those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*). It is also permissible if it is given with the words, "We give this cloth to the Saṅgha;
with this, make sandals, bags for bowls, waist-bands, shoulder-straps, and so forth.
Even if many [pieces of cloth] are given for the purpose of making bowl-bags and the like, they may suffice for the purpose of robes; from those, one may [use] a robe.

It is permissible to take them and wear them after having cut them down. However, if the Saṅgha distributes surplus robes that have already been apportioned for the purpose of making sandals, bags, and so forth, it is not permissible to take them from there.
For only what has been specifically assigned by the owners is permissible, not the other.
Even if it is said, "We give this for the sake of water-strainers, shoulder-strap bags, and so forth, for the Paṃsukūlika Saṅgha," it is still not permissible to take it.
It is permissible. What is called "requisite" (parikkhāra) is desired even by those who wear rag-robes (paṃsukūlika). Whatever surplus there is therein may be applied toward robes;
it is permissible. If they give thread to the Saṅgha, it may be accepted even by those who wear rag-robes.
This, then, is the decision regarding cases where, having entered a monastery, one gives [cloth] saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha."
But if, having seen monks traveling on the road outside the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīmā),
one announces, "I give this to the Saṅgha," to either the senior monk of the Saṅgha or the junior monk of the Saṅgha— even if the assembly stands covering a distance of a league—
if they are connected as a single unit, it reaches all of them. However, for those who have not reached the assembly within twelve cubits, it does not reach them.
2732. Now, explaining the matrix (mātikā) “he gives to both Saṅghas,” he said: “designating both Saṅghas,” and so forth.
“Designating both Saṅghas” means having designated both the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. “He gives” means he gives [thinking], “I give to both Saṅghas.
Regarding the phrase “or much,” where “bahū vā” should have been used, the shortening occurs for the sake of metrical composition (gāthābandha).

The construction is as follows: whether there be few or many monks for the nuns, it is permissible to make the distribution in equal shares based on the two Saṅghas combined, rather than by way of individual persons.
In this regard, the following is the detailed explanation: even when it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas," [it means] "I give to the twofold Saṅgha; to the two..."
Even if it is said, "I give to the Saṅghas; I give to both the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha," it is indeed given to both Saṅghas;
having divided it into two equal portions, one should be given [to each].
If it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas and to you," then if there are ten bhikkhus and ten bhikkhunīs...

There are twenty-one portions; having divided them into twenty-one parts, one should be given to an individual, ten to the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), and ten to the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*).
He by whom the portion for an individual has been received is permitted to take it for himself according to his own seniority even from within the community.
Why? Because it was included by means of the inclusion of both communities.

The same principle applies even when it is said, “I give to both Saṅghas and to the Cetiya. However, in this case, there is no separate portion for the Cetiya that is obtained from the Saṅgha; rather, the portion belongs to the Cetiya as if it were the share of a single individual.

But when it is said, “To both Saṅghas, to you, and to the Cetiya,” one should divide it into twenty-two portions and give ten to the monks, ten to the nuns, one to the individual, and one to the Cetiya. In that regard:
An individual, even when included within the Saṅgha, may receive [an offering] again according to his own seniority. For a cetiya, there is only one [recipient].

However, when it is said, "I give to the community of monks and to the nuns," it should not be given by dividing it in the middle; rather, it should be given after counting both the monks and the nuns.

But when it is said, "To the community of monks, to the nuns, and to you," the individual does not receive separately; he receives only one portion from the point of distribution. Why? Because he is already included by the mention of the "community of monks."
Even when it is said, “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for the bhikkhunīs, for you, and for the cetiya,” a separate share for the cetiya is obtained,
but no separate share for the individual is obtained. Therefore, having given one portion to the cetiya,
the remainder should be divided by counting the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs.
Even when it is said, “I give to the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs,” it should not be given by dividing them in the middle; rather, it should be distributed according to the number of individuals.

Even when it is said, “To the bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs, you, and the cetiya,” the cetiya receives one share for a single individual, while there is no separate share for that individual; rather, it should be divided after counting only the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs.
Just as the method has been set forth beginning with the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha), so too it should be applied beginning with the community of nuns (bhikkhunīsaṅgha).
When it is said, "For the community of monks and for you," an individual share is not obtained separately; it must be taken according to the seniority of the rains-residence (vassagga) alone.
However, when it is said, "For the community of monks and for the shrine (cetiya)," a separate individual share is obtained for the shrine.
Even when it is said, “For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and for you and for the cetiya,” it accrues only to the cetiya, not to the individual (puggala).
Even when it is said, “For the bhikkhus and for you,” it is not obtained separately [for the individual].
However, when it is said, “For the bhikkhus and for the cetiya,” it accrues to the cetiya.

Even when it is said, “For the bhikkhus, for you, and for the cetiya,” the offering is obtained separately only for the cetiya, not for the individual person. The same should be applied starting with the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.
Previously, they gave gifts to both Saṅghas headed by the Buddha; the Blessed One sat in the middle, the bhikkhus sat on the right, and the bhikkhunīs sat on the left.
At that time, the Blessed One was the senior elder (saṅghatthera) of both Saṅghas. Then the Blessed One...
He himself enjoys the requisites he has obtained and causes them to be given to the monks as well.
Nowadays, however, wise people, having established a statue containing relics or a cetiya, give alms to the Saṅgha of both sides headed by the Buddha;
or, having placed a bowl on a stand before the statue or the cetiya and having offered water for the donation, they give.
Regarding the question: "When they say, 'We give to the Buddhas,' and there they first offer fresh or cooked food;
or when, having brought it to the monastery, they say, 'We give this to the shrine (cetiya),' and they offer alms-food, garlands, perfumes, and so forth—how should one proceed in such cases?
First of all, the garlands, perfumes, and so forth should be offered upon the shrine. Banners should be made with cloths, and lamps should be prepared with oil.
As for alms-food, honey, molasses, and so forth, these should be given to whoever is the appointed caretaker of the cetiya, whether they be a monastic or a layperson.
In the absence of an appointed caretaker, it is permissible to place the bowl brought [with the food] down, perform the proper duties (vatta), and then consume it.
Even when the time is drawing near [for the meal], it is likewise permissible to eat first and perform the duties afterwards.
Regarding garlands, perfumes, and so forth, if it is said, "Take this and offer it as worship to the Cetiya," one should carry it even a great distance and offer it.
Even if it is said, "Carry almsfood to the Saṅgha," it may be carried. However, if it is said, "I am going for alms;
there are monks in the assembly hall, they will take it," [the response should be], "Venerable sir, [it is] for you alone."

If he says, "I give it," it is permissible for him to eat it. However, if one who is carrying [the robe] thinking, "I will give it to the Saṅgha of monks," finds that the time has already arrived while on his way, it is permissible for him to take possession of it himself and eat it.
Furthermore, regarding a robe given with the words, "I give it to the Saṅgha that has spent the rains retreat in this monastery," it belongs to that very [monastery].

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: it is praised and taught that the robe should be distributed by the Saṅgha, the Gaṇa, or the individual who has spent the rains retreat in that residence.
Herein, this is the detailed analysis: having entered the monastery, one should say, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha that has spent the rains retreat."
It should be shared among as many bhikkhus as have spent the rains residence in that monastery, and as many as have completed the preceding rains residence without interrupting it;
it does not accrue to others. Even for one who has gone abroad, as long as there is someone to receive it, the gift must be given until the dismantling of the *kaṭhina*.
However, when the *kaṭhina* has not been spread, if it is given after saying this within the winter season, it belongs even to those who have spent the subsequent rains residence.
Those who know the characteristics say that it reaches [the recipients]. However, this has not been examined in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
But if, while standing outside the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*), one says, "I give to the Saṅgha that has spent the rains retreat," it reaches all those who have assembled there.
If, however, one says, "To the Saṅgha that has spent the rains retreat at such-and-such monastery," it reaches only those who have spent the rains retreat there.

[The robe] reaches [the recipients] as far as the time when the Kathina ceremony is completed. However, if one speaks thus starting from the very first day of the summer months, it reaches all those who are present at that time. Why? Because it arose during the period of the retreat.

Even if one says within the same rainy season, "I give this to those dwelling for the rains," those whose rains-retreat has been interrupted do not receive it; only those who have actually dwelt for the rains receive it.

They receive [the robe]. However, regarding the robe-month, when it is said, "I give to those dwelling for the rains," it reaches only those who have entered the rains residence during the later period;
it does not reach those who entered during the earlier period nor those whose rains residence has been broken.
From the beginning of the robe-month until the last day of the winter season, if one says, "We give the *vassāvāsika* (rain-season gift)..."
Once it has been said, whether the kaṭhina has been spread or not, it pertains only to one who has completed residence for the past rains.
However, from the first day of the summer months onwards, when it has been said, the following summary should be presented:
"Five months of the past rains-residence have passed; with the lapse of four months yet to come, it will be [the time for the robe]; to which rains-residence does this belong?"
If he says, "I give this for those who have spent the rains residence in the past year," it accrues only to those who actually spent the rains residence within that year.
Even those who have gone away to other regions may receive it, provided they are members of the same community.
If he says, "I give this as the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence gift) for the future," it must be set aside and taken on the day of the formal entry into the rains residence (*vassūpanāyikā*).

Then, if it is said, "The dwelling is unprotected, there is danger from thieves, it cannot be left behind, nor can one carry it while wandering," and he says, "I give it to those who have arrived," it should be taken after being divided.
If he says, "Venerable sir, I did not give my *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe) for the third year from this point; I give that," [it belongs] to the monks who have resided during that rainy season.
[The property] accrues [to him]. If those who had departed for the various directions have been replaced by another person of trust, it must be given to him.

But if he alone remains and the others have passed away, everything accrues to that one person alone. If not even one remains, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha; it should be divided among those who are present. 2734.
Furthermore, if after the gruel has been drunk or the meal eaten, [the donor] specifically designates: "By whomsoever this gruel was drunk by me..."
Having made a distinction by saying, “I give it to him who ate my meal; I give it to him,” one gives the robe-cloth.
The application here is that the holder of the Vinaya must give the gift right there and then. This same method applies to hard food, robe-cloth, bedding, medicine, and so forth.
In this regard, the following is the detailed analysis: having invited monks for either today’s or tomorrow’s alms-gruel... [they] of them...
When she gives rice-gruel to those who have entered the house, and having given the gruel, after it has been drunk, she says,
"I give these robes to those by whom my gruel was drunk," then it accrues only to those who were invited and drank the gruel;
however, for those who pass by the door of the house while on their alms-round or who have already entered the house, if they [drink] the gruel...
[The alms] do not reach those for whom the bowl was brought from the assembly hall and carried away by people, or those who were sent by the elders.

However, if many others besides the invited bhikkhus arrive and sit filling both the interior and exterior of the house, and the donor says: "Whether they were invited or uninvited, to whomever I [gave it]..."
If he says, "The rice gruel has been given; let these robes belong to all," they reach everyone. However, those who received the rice gruel from the hands of the elders do not receive [the robes].
Then, if he says, "Let it belong to all those by whom the rice gruel was drunk from me," it reaches everyone.
This same principle applies to the solid food and soft food as well.
Regarding "in regard to robe-cloth": even if someone has previously provided robe-cloth for the monks after spending the rains retreat there,

if that person, having fed the monks, says, "Let this robe-cloth, or thread, or ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, belong only to those to whom I previously gave robe-cloth," then everything accrues to them alone.
Regarding "in the lodging": when it is said, "Let this belong to whoever dwells in the monastery or the cell built by me," it belongs to that person alone.
Regarding "in the medicine": when it is said, "We give ghee and other medicines to the elders from time to time; let this belong only to those by whom they were received," it belongs to them alone.

(2735) It is called a "gift" (*dāna*) because it is given (*diyate*); thus, by way of the object of the action (*kamma-sādhana*), the robe is expressed. Since the robe is referred to by the word *yaṃ*, it must also be referred to by the word *taṃ*.

In this regard, the analysis is as follows: if one gives by saying "I give this robe to so-and-so," whether in the recipient's absence or in their presence by saying "Venerable sir, I give this to you," or by placing it at the feet, it belongs to that person alone.
But if one says, "I give this to you and to your pupils," then [it belongs] to the Elder...
It also reaches those who are resident pupils (*antevāsika*). There are those who come to receive the recitation (*uddesa*) and depart after having received it; for them, too, it reaches.

When it is said, "I give this to the bhikkhus who travel in regular company with you," it reaches all those who, having performed the duties toward their recitation-pupils, travel about receiving the recitations, cross-examinations, and so forth.

2737. *Vadaticcevameva ce*: if he speaks in this very manner according to the method already stated. *Taṃ*: that requisite. *Tesam*: of those [people], such as the mother and others. The construction is: "It becomes the property of the Saṅgha alone. 2738. By the phrase "Of five...
it belongs," he shows, in brief, the very same meaning that was explained in detail by the preceding two stanzas.
"Of five": of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma (*sahadhammika*). "In passing away": at the time of death. "Gift": [the thought] "When I have passed away..."
The relinquishing [of the requisites] is expressed by such phrases as, “Let this requisite be yours; make it your own. “Even something” means even a tooth-stick.
As for the gift to householders, the construction is that it accrues to the householders themselves who are the donors upon the passing away of those [recipients]. 2739.
If a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera dies in a bhikkhunī’s residence, [the property belongs to] that bhikkhu or sāmaṇera...
The construction is: "the requisites belong to the bhikkhus alone" or "belong to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus alone.
They belong to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus alone because the deceased [person] was included within the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Regarding the phrase "or a sāmaṇerī," the word "or" (*vā*) here includes the term "or a sikkhamānā. In the monastery...

In the place where the bhikkhus reside. Regarding the word *tassa* (of her): the construction is that the requisites belonging to a bhikkhunī, a sāmaṇerī, or a sikkhamānā become the property of the bhikkhunīs.
As for the word *santakā* (property), here too the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated regarding the bhikkhus.
2741. Regarding the phrase *dehi netvā* (having taken this and given it): here, "this robe" is understood from the context. "Having taken this robe..."
Regarding the robe given with the words, "Give this to so-and-so," it belongs to that former owner.
Regarding the robe given with the words, "I give this robe to so-and-so," it belongs to that latter person to whom it is sent; such is the construction.
Having identified the owners according to the aforementioned manner of expression, or through trust in them, when they have died—
He said “Thus,” etc., in order to show that it is permissible to take even a robe belonging to the deceased. The word division is “of one who is dead or of one who is not dead.
“Or he might take it on trust” means he might take the property of one who is living as a loan on trust.
“He might take a robe belonging to the deceased” means he might take the robe of the deceased after having it brought over in the manner of removing the requisites of the dead.

2743. "It dyes by means of this" (*rajate anenāti*) refers to all [dyes] beginning with root-dyes (*mūla*). "By one who has vomited out faults" (*vantadosena*) means by one in whom lust and other defilements have been eradicated along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

"The Such-like One" (*tādinā*) means one who is uniform due to the non-arising of lust and so forth toward the six objects such as visible forms, and due to being unmoved by the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).

2744–5. In the phrases beginning with "in the root" (*mūle*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Having set aside turmeric among root-dyes, [the phrase refers to] all root-dyes.
It is permissible. Regarding dyes for robes: with the exception of madder and *tuṅgahāraka*, all dye for robes is permissible.
Regarding dyes for bowls: with the exception of lac-dye and blue-dye, all dye for bowls is permissible.
Regarding dyes for flowers: with the exception of safflower and *kiṃsuka*, all dye for flowers is permissible.
With the exception of *lodda* and *kaṇḍula*, all bark dyes are permissible. The construction is that all fruit dyes as well are permissible.
*Mañjeṭṭha* is a certain thorny tree and a particular kind of creeper; its dye is the color of the seed of the *mañjeṭṭha*.
[The word] *hoti* [is used]. The trunk of the mañjeṭṭha tree is white in color;
it should not be included here because the context concerns dyes. *Tuṅgahāraka* is the name of a certain thorny tree, the dye of which is the color of turmeric (*haritāla*).
*Allī* is the small *tāpiñcha* tree, the dye of whose leaves is the color of turmeric (*haliddi*). *Nīlī* is a specific kind of shrub, the dye of which is blue in color.
It exists. *Kiṃsuka* refers to the flower of the *vallikiṃsuka* creeper, the dye of which is red in color.
(2746) *Kiliṭṭhasāṭakaṃ* means a soiled garment. *Dhovituṃ* means to wash once. It is said that when washed while still damp, it properly receives the dye.

(2747) "The rest is a discourse on robes" refers here to the discourse not explicitly stated, such as the types of causes for schism and so forth. "Stated in the first *kathina*" is the remainder of the phrase. "By the *vibhāvī*" refers to the reciter of the *Khandhaka*.
The Explanation of the Discourse on the Chapter on Robes (*Cīvarakkhandhaka*).
Thus ends the Explanation of the Decision on the Great Section (*Mahāvagga*) within the *Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā*,
which is an elucidation of the essence of the meaning of the Vinaya.
The Explanation of the Discussion on the Chapter on Those Under Probation (Pārivāsikakkhandhaka) in the Cūḷavagga:
Having thus shown the determination of the Mahāvagga in brief, he spoke in order to show the determination contained in the Cūḷavagga.

“*Tajjanīya*” and so forth. *Tajjanīya* refers to the formal legal act (*kamma*) of censure consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), which has been authorized as a means of restraint for the purpose of making monks who engage in quarrels desist from such behavior.

*Niyassa* refers to the formal legal act of demotion, [authorized] as a means of restraint for a monk who is foolish, incompetent, prone to offenses, lacking in support, and who dwells in improper association with householders.

And the act of demotion (*niyassakamma*), which is authorized by a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha*) to be performed for the purpose of making [the offender] live in dependence [on others].

And the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*), which is authorized by a motion followed by a fourth proclamation as a means of restraint so that a monk who has corrupted families does not receive the right to dwell in the very place where he committed the corruption of families.
And "reconciliation" (*paṭisāraṇīya*) refers to [the act toward] one who has faith...

And there is the act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*), authorized as a means of restraint for the purpose of making a monk—who has reviled a donor, a builder, or an attendant of the Saṅgha by means of insults based on birth and so forth—admit his fault; it is carried out by a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatuttha*). The threefold suspension (*ukkhepana*) consists of:
[suspension] for not seeing an offense, for not making amends for an offense, and for not relinquishing a pernicious view.
And then there is the threefold *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension), which is permitted by way of restraint after one has failed to desist;
this is done by means of a motion followed by a fourth resolution (*ñatticatuttha*). "Dīpaye" means that one should explain it according to the method stated in the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā.

Although the acts beginning with the *tajjanīyakamma* (act of censure) are each twofold—by way of reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) and expulsion (*nissāraṇa*)—one should not take account of that division here.
It should be understood that they are called "the seven formal acts" (*kamma*) solely by way of their classification.

However, the distinction between them as it has been shown here should be seen as being for the purpose of giving rise to a specific topic (*atthuppatti*). A detailed exposition of these is to be known from the Kammakkhandhaka.
2749. In the Khandhaka—that is, in the section of the Vinaya known as the Khandhaka—there are forty-three rules of conduct (*vatta*) recorded. Immediately following that...
Immediately following that *Kammakkhandhaka*. Regarding the term "Khandhaka," it refers to the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*. Those which have nine added to them are "nine-added";
thus, there are thirty observances (*vatta*), meaning forty-nine observances.
First, in the *Kammakkhandhaka*—
“Monks, a monk against whom a formal act of suspension has been carried out for not seeing an offense must conduct himself properly.
Herein, this is proper conduct: he must not give full ordination; he must not grant dependence; he must not have a novice attend upon him;
he must not accept appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even if appointed, he must not instruct the bhikkhunīs. Whoever—”
When a formal act of suspension has been carried out by the Saṅgha against one for not seeing an offense, that offense must not be committed, nor any other similar or more serious offense;
the formal act must not be criticized, nor should the performers of the act be criticized.
Furthermore, there is no need to perform salutations, rising from one’s seat, joining of palms, respectful service, or offering of a seat for a monk who is in his normal status (*pakatatta*).
One should accept the offering of a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, the receiving of bowl and robes, assistance with bathing,
and massage of the back; however, a regular bhikkhu should not be accused of failure in virtue, failure in conduct, failure in view, or failure in livelihood.
A bhikkhu should not cause a schism among the bhikkhus; he should not bear the banner of householders; he should not bear the banner of other sectarians;
he should not associate with those of other sects; he should associate with bhikkhus; he should train in the training of bhikkhus;
he should not live in a covered dwelling together with a regular bhikkhu; nor should he live in an uncovered non-dwelling together with a regular bhikkhu.
One should not dwell in a residence, whether it be a formal dwelling or not, under the same roof as a regular (*pakatatta*) monk; upon seeing a regular monk, one must rise from one's seat;
one must not sit together with a regular monk, either inside or outside; one must not cancel the *uposatha* ceremony for a regular monk;
one must not cancel his invitation (*pavāraṇā*); one must not issue a command to him; nor should one initiate a formal censure against him.

"He should not be granted an opportunity [to speak], he should not be accused, he should not be reminded, and he should not be associated with by the monks"—it is with reference to these forty-three duties that it was said: "The forty-three duties, in the Khandhaka concerning formal acts.
In the Pārivāsika-khandhaka—
“Monks, a monk who is undergoing probation must conduct himself properly. In this regard, this is proper conduct: he must not confer full ordination;
he must not give formal support (nissaya); he must not have a novice attend upon him; he must not accept the appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs;
even if appointed, he must not instruct the bhikkhunīs; and regarding whichever offense for which the Saṅgha has granted him probation...”
It has been granted; that offense should not be committed, nor any other similar one, nor one more serious than that;

the legal procedure (*kamma*) should not be censured, nor the performers of the procedure (*kammika*); the Uposatha should not be suspended for a regular monk (*pakatatta*), nor should the Invitation (*pavāraṇā*) be suspended;
he should not be made subject to formal instructions, nor should a charge be brought against him, nor should an opportunity [to speak] be denied him.
He is to be made to perform [the penance], but he is not to be accused, nor reminded, nor associated with by the monks.
"Monks, a monk who is on probation must not walk in front of a regular monk, nor sit in front of him;
whatever constitutes the limit of the Saṅgha’s seating, the limit of the bedding, or the limit of the dwelling—[he must not occupy it]."
Thus it should be given to him, and he should accept it.
"Monks, a monk who is on probation should not approach families as a preceding or following attendant of a regular monk;
he should not undertake the forest-dweller's practice, nor should he undertake the alms-food-eater's practice."
Nor, for the sake of that [concealment], should almsfood be caused to be brought out [thinking], "Lest they should know me.

"Monks, a monk who is on probation must inform an incoming monk; he must inform an incoming monk; he must inform [the community] on the Uposatha day; he must inform [the community] at the Pavāraṇā ceremony. If he is ill, he must inform even by means of a messenger.

"Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a residence where monks are present to a residence where no monks are present, except with a regular (pakatatta) monk or except when there are obstacles."
“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks,
except together with one who is a regular (pakatatta) monk or except due to an obstacle. Monks,
a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence without monks, except together with one who is a regular monk or except due to an obstacle.”
“Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a non-residence that has monks to a residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk (pakatatta) or except when there are obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a non-residence that has monks to a non-residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles. Monks, ...”
A monk who is undergoing probation may go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence or non-residence that has no monks,
except with a regular monk or except due to obstacles.
“Monks, a monk who is undergoing probation [may not go] from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence that has no monks...”
A residence may be gone to, except for one who is a regular member (pakatatta) and except in the event of obstacles.

Monks, a monk who is on probation (pārivāsika) should not go from a residence or a non-residence containing other monks to a non-residence without monks, except for one who is a regular member and except in the event of obstacles. Monks, a monk who is on probation [should not go] from a residence or a non-residence containing other monks...
Or a residence without monks, or a non-residence, may be gone to, except for one who is a regular member (pakatatta) and except in the event of obstacles.

“Monks, a monk on probation must not go from a residence with monks to a residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except for one who is a regular member and except in the event of obstacles. Monks, [he must not go]... ” [The rest of the prohibition follows].
A monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) may go from a residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka),
except in the case of one who is fully ordained (pakatatta) or except due to obstacles. Monks,
a monk who is undergoing probation must not go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion.
Except with one who is a regular member (pakatatta) and except when there is an obstacle:

"Monks, a monk on probation must not go from a non-residence that has monks to a residence that has monks where the monks belong to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), except with one who is a regular member and except when there is an obstacle. Monks, [he must not go]..."

A monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) may go from a non-residence containing monks to another non-residence containing monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), except in the case of one who is a regular member (pakatatta) or except due to obstacles.

Monks, a monk who is undergoing probation must not go from a non-residence containing monks to either a residence or a non-residence containing monks where there are... [monks belonging to a different communion].
“Monks, monks who belong to a different communion— except for one who is a regular member and except when there is an obstacle—
[are not to be approached]. Monks, a monk on probation must not go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence that has monks who belong to a different communion,
except for one who is a regular member and except when there is an obstacle.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence or non-residence containing monks to a non-residence containing monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of one who is fully ordained (pakatatta) or except due to an obstacle.
Monks, a monk who is on probation should not [go] from a residence or non-residence containing monks...”

One may go to either an inhabited or uninhabited dwelling where there are monks belonging to a different community, except in the case of one who is fully ordained (pakatatta) or except due to obstacles.

“Monks, a monk on probation may go from an inhabited dwelling containing monks to another inhabited dwelling containing monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a non-residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation may go from a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks, or from a residence with monks to a non-residence with monks, where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk who is on probation may go from a residence with monks or a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

“Monks, a monk on probation should go from a residence or non-residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks who belong to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk on probation should go from a residence or non-residence with monks to a residence or non-residence with monks where there are monks who belong to the same community, provided he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”
“Monks, a monk who is on probation must not live under the same roof as a regular monk;
he must not live under the same roof in a non-residence; he must not live under the same roof in either a residence or a non-residence.
Upon seeing a regular monk, he must rise from his seat, and he must invite the regular monk to take a seat.”
A regular monk must not sit on the same seat as one who is not a regular monk; when the other is sitting on a low seat, he must not sit on a high seat;
when the other is sitting on the ground, he must not sit on a seat. He must not walk up and down on the same walking path as one who is not a regular monk;

when the other is walking up and down on a low walking path, he must not walk up and down on a high walking path; when the other is walking up and down on the ground, he must not walk up and down on a walking path.

“Monks, a monk who is on probation must not stay under one roof with a monk who is senior to him and also on probation… with a monk who deserves to be sent back to the beginning… with a monk who deserves the trial period (mānatta)… with a monk who is undergoing the trial period… nor with a monk who deserves rehabilitation.”

One should dwell in a residence; one should not dwell in a non-residence where there is no cover overhead; one should not dwell in either a residence or a non-residence where there is no cover overhead;
one should not sit on the same seat; one should not sit on a high seat while [the other] is sitting on a low seat;
one should not sit on a seat while [the other] is sitting on the ground; one should not walk on the same walking path; nor on a low walking path.
One should walk on a high walking path when those walking on a high walking path are walking, but one should not walk on a walking path when those walking on the ground are walking.

"Monks, if one who is a fourth member of a group consisting of probationers were to grant probation, send back to the beginning, grant the trial period (mānatta), or rehabilitate [the offender], it is an invalid act and is not to be carried out.
Thus there are ninety-four rules of conduct for those on probation.
And that number of ninety-four for them should be understood as follows: nine procedures beginning with the non-conferring of full ordination and ending with the censure;
then eight beginning with the establishment of the Uposatha by one who is in his natural state and ending with the appointment of monks;
then five beginning with not going in front; then four beginning with not going in front; and [finally] those beginning with the announcement by a visitor.
Forty-three: thirty [rules] concerning going from a residence with monks to a residence without monks and so forth, plus three sets of nine [rules] making fifty-seven;
then eleven [rules] concerning living under one roof and so forth together with those who have not performed *parivāsa*;

then [the rules] concerning one who is not a *pārivāsika*, one who is senior, one deserving of *mūlāya paṭikassanā*, one deserving of *mānatta*, one undergoing *mānatta*, and one deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
Having grouped together eleven rules each concerning such matters as living under the same roof or being covered by the same roof, there are fifty-five rules in total.

Among these, for the three types of persons—the one deserving of probation (*pārivāsika*), the one deserving of being sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*), and the one deserving of the trial period (*mānattāraha*)—there is one set of eleven rules common to them.
For the two types of persons—the one practicing the trial period (*mānattacārika*) and the one deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*)—there is one set of eleven rules common to them.

There are two sets of eleven; at the end, in the fourfold set regarding the granting of probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth by a Saṅgha where the one on probation is the fourth member, there are four each [of further duties] due to the exclusion of the fault of completing the quorum.
Thus, there are ninety-four observances (*vatta*). By including what was not previously included, these are called thirty-nine observances.

These consist of nine from the beginning, eight such as the suspension of the Uposatha, and four such as living under the same roof with a regular monk (*pakatatta*) while being subject to a single concealment (*ekacchanna-vāsa*), and so forth.
Since the twenty-one rules (vatta) beginning with [the first] are included in the Kammakkhandhaka, they are not counted here;

rather, among the remaining seventy-three rules, the twenty-two rules concerning living under one roof (*ekacchanna*) and so forth with those who are *pārivāsika* or senior, etc., are identical to those for a regular monk (*pakatatta*).
Furthermore, that group of nine beginning with "Monks, you should go," and likewise...
Regarding the phrase "for one going [to another residence], it is for the purpose of seeing no offense,

not for one leaving a residence for the purpose of seeing an offense," if that [case] is not included, then among the remaining forty-two observances (*vatta*), by treating the fourfold formal act involving those on probation as one—
due to the commonality of their purpose in completing the quorum for emerging from a grave offense— and by removing three, the total becomes thirty-nine.
It is said: “Thirty-nine in the immediately following Khandhaka.

(2750) These thirty-nine observances (*vatta*), together with the previous forty-three observances, total eighty-two; thus he says: “In this way, all... by way of inclusion and non-inclusion. The construction is as follows:

in this manner, the observances of the Khandhakas spoken by the Great Sage in the Kammakkhandhaka and Pārivāsikakkhandhaka amount to exactly eighty-two by way of inclusion and non-inclusion. Thus, the eighty-two observances of the Khandhakas have been shown here.
In the commentary on the *Āgamaṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated:
"Having begun with 'I shall prescribe the duties for monks who are on probation,' there are sixty-six rules ending with 'one must not ordain [a person]...
nor should one walk up and down on a walking-path while those walking on the ground are doing so'; beyond that..."
“Monks, a monk on probation must not live under one roof in a residence with another monk who is senior to him and is also on probation,

nor with a monk deserving of being sent back to the beginning, nor with a monk deserving of the trial period (mānatta), nor with a monk undergoing the trial period, nor with a monk deserving of rehabilitation”—
because these [monks] are not different from those who should behave as ordinary (pakatatta) monks, they are treated separately.

Not counting those [duties] that must be performed toward other individuals such as those on probation (*pārivāsika*) or those senior to oneself, but rather grouping them according to those [other duties] and calculating them one by one, there are seventy-one observances (*vatta*).
Regarding the observances for one who has undergone a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), it is stated under the heading of establishing the rules of conduct:
“One should not accept a prostration from a regular (*pakatatta*) monk... nor should one consent to having one’s back massaged while bathing.”
This non-acceptance of salutations and so forth is one; and there are ten others, such as “a regular bhikkhu must not be accused of failure in virtue,” and so on.
Thus, these total eighty-two. Among these very rules, some are the observances for acts of censure and so forth, while some are the observances for those undergoing probation and so forth;
thus, by including what has not yet been included, they remain exactly eighty-two.”

It has been stated. However, these duties (*vatta*) should be understood as the "minor duties" (*khuddakavatta*) to be observed at times such as when one has undergone a censure-act (*tajjanīyakamma*) or when one is on probation (*pārivāsika*), because the fourteen major duties, beginning with those for newcomers (*āgantuka*), will be explained later. 2751.
Now, in order to show the interruption of the night and the breach of duties for a monk who is on probation, he says: "Of one who has undertaken both the probation and the duties," and so forth.
"Of one who has undertaken both the probation and the duties" means of one who has undertaken the probation by saying, "I undertake the probation."

“I undertake the duties”: this refers to one who has undertaken the duties by sitting in the squatting posture (ukkuṭika) before a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu, raising his joined palms (añjali), and making a vocal declaration. “A bhikkhunī” refers to a bhikkhu who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika). 2752.

Regarding “co-residence” and so forth, he himself will explain later under the phrase “under one roof,” etc. The construction is as follows: through these three—co-residence, living apart, and failing to announce [one’s status]—there occurs both the breaking of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the bhikkhu undergoing probation.
2753. "By the falling of water" means by the place where water falls all around the rim of a vessel.

"In a single-roofed [dwelling]" refers to a residence that is either covered on one side or not covered at all. The construction is: "The dwelling together with a regular bhikkhu is forbidden for one who has been suspended.
By the word "forbidden," it is indicated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

2754. *Antoyeva* means "right within" the boundary of the dwelling that is covered by a single roof. By the phrase "it is not permitted," it is indicated that there is both a breach of the night-period (*ratticcheda*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

2755. In the phrase "in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā and others," the word "others" (*ādi*) includes the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā and so forth. The construction is: "of both" refers to those who have been suspended (*ukkhitaka*) and those on probation (*pārivāsika*); thus it is explained without distinction. 2756.
Having shown, through this co-residence, both the breach of the night-period and the offense of wrong-doing, he speaks in order to show them [the same consequences] through non-co-residence:
“However, in a residence devoid of monks”: “residence” (*āvāsa*) refers to a lodging constructed for the purpose of dwelling.

“Non-residence” (*anāvāsa*) refers to such places as a shrine-hall (*cetiyaghara*), a Bodhi-tree hall, a dust-sweeping platform, a wooden platform, a water-shed, a latrine, a gatehouse, or any other similar location where one has not been designated for the purpose of dwelling.
[In such a place], one is away from home (*vippavāsa*).

"Of one who dwells [during] the rains-retreat" means: of one who spends the retreat in the absence of a regular member (pakatatta). "And there is an offense of wrong-doing for interrupting the night" means that there is both the interruption of the night and the wrong-doing of breaking the rule of conduct.
Having thus shown the offenses of wrong-doing for interrupting the night through being separated, he said "of a bhikkhu who is on probation," etc., in order to show them through failure to announce.
"Having seen a bhikkhu" means having seen an incoming bhikkhu who belongs to the same community (samāna-saṃvāsaka), even if he is traveling through the air.

"At that very moment" means at the very instant he is seen. The word division is: "anārocentassa eva etassa. By the use of the particle *eva*, it is indicated that both the breaking of the night (*ratti-ccheda*) and the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) belong to him; for if he has not seen [the other], there is only the breaking of the night.

It makes known that [the offense] occurs. As it is said: “Even for him, it constitutes a breach of the night; however, because of his lack of recognition, there is no *dukkaṭa* for the breach of the formal act.

It is not permissible to perform a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) together with one who belongs to a different community (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*); even if one does not inform such a person, there is no breach of the night.

2758–9. The construction is as follows: it is permissible for a *pārivāsika* monk, remaining in the very place where he stands in the junior position within the Saṅgha, to perform the five duties according to seniority (*yathāvuḍḍha*) together with the regular monks (*pakatatta*), following the order of seniority.
To show these [duties] in their specific form, he says: "Uposatha, Pavāraṇā," and so forth. [These are] the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā according to seniority.
The construction is: "he is permitted to do. Regarding the word "giving," the phrase "having struck the bell" is to be supplied.
"Givers to the Saṅgha" is a *kammadhāraya* compound. Although the Saṅgha is a singular entity, the plural form is used because it refers to those who are venerable.

There is also a reading: "If the giver to the Saṅgha gives. In that case, if the Saṅgha—having struck the bell and having divided [the robe]—gives the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe), then one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*)...
The construction is: "one receives it in one's own allotted place according to seniority.

*Oṇojana* means distribution; having received from the Saṅgha two or three portions of *uddesabhatta* (specified food) or other meals for oneself out of an expectation of receiving personal alms-food, [thinking], "I have an expectation of alms-food today; tomorrow..."
Having said, "I shall take [it]," it is meant that he receives the authorization from the Saṅgha.
"Alms-food" (bhatta) refers to the four-row meal provided for the Saṅgha in the monastery, which must be taken by those who have arrived in order of seniority as they come.
The construction is: "In that same way, one on probation (pārivāsika) receives according to seniority. "These five" concludes the very point already stated.
In this regard, the analysis is as follows: first, during the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, it is permissible to sit within arm’s reach while the Pātimokkha is being recited.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Without sitting apart from the text, one should sit while not releasing the arm’s reach, even if leaving the text.
When the Uposatha of confession of purity (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*) is being performed, one should sit in the place of the most junior member of the Saṅgha.
Seated right there, one should perform the Uposatha of purity for oneself according to one’s own recitation.
At the Pavāraṇā ceremony as well, sitting in the place of the most junior member of the Saṅgha, one should perform the Pavāraṇā for oneself while seated right there.
It is also permissible to take for oneself the *vassikasāṭika* (rain-season robe) being distributed by the Saṅgha after the bell has been struck.

Regarding the distribution of food: if two or three portions of *uddesabhatta* (food designated for specific individuals) or similar meals fall to a monk on probation (*pārivāsika*), and he has an expectation of receiving a private meal (*puggalika-bhatta*) elsewhere, he should take those [designated meals] in order and say, "Venerable sir, please take them later;
I have an expectation of a meal today, so I shall take them tomorrow," and then relinquish them. In this way, he may take them on subsequent days.

"He receives it. Regarding this, the *Kurundi* states: "On the following day, this [food] must be given to him first of all. However, if he does not accept it or does not relinquish it, he does not receive it on the next day.
This so-called *oṇojana* (distribution of food) is specifically permitted for one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*). Why?
Because when he is seated in the place of the newest member of the Saṅgha in the dining hall, [he receives] rice gruel, solid foods, and so forth.
Whether they reach it or not, for that reason, thinking, "May he not be exhausted by the food obtained through alms," this was specifically permitted for the sake of supporting him.
At the meal, he receives the four-course meal according to seniority, but he is not permitted to walk or stand according to the formal sequence of the Pāḷi.
Therefore, withdrawing from the sequence of the Pāḷi and standing within arm's reach, he extends his hand so that—just as a hawk swoops down— (He receives the food. [End of section]
It should be accepted in this manner. One may not have it brought by monastery attendants or novice monks;
however, if they bring it themselves, it is permissible. The same rule applies even regarding the king’s meal from the great storage-vessel (*mahāpeḷa*).

But in the case of the meal from the four-hall (*catussāla*), if one intends to partake of the food, one may take a morsel set aside for oneself, thinking: "I have food today; I shall take it tomorrow."
It should be stated: "On the following day, he receives two alms-meals," as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.

Even items such as *uddesabhatta* (food designated for a specific person) must be understood by tracing them back from the Pāḷi. However, in a place where they serve food after having seated [the monks], there the novice should sit with the senior-most monk among the novices acting as the junior-most member of the Saṅgha of monks.
Commentary on the Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation (*Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*). Commentary on the Chapter on the Settlement of Disputes (*Samathakkhandhaka*) 2760.

Now, in order to demonstrate the determination of the methods for settling disputes (*samatha-vinicchaya*), [the text explains] those legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) which, when present, must be settled by means of the methods for settling disputes.

Demonstrating these [points], he said: “The state of being a basis for dispute,” and so forth. “The state of being a basis for dispute” (*vivādādhāratā*) means the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that is a dispute.

The same method applies here to “the state of being a basis for an offense” (*āpattādhāratā*). “State of being a basis” (*ādhāratā*) is a synonym for “legal issue” (*adhikaraṇa*). It is called a “basis” (*ādhāra*) because it is supported by, overcome by, or settled through the means of pacification (*samatha*).

Since it is both a dispute (*vivāda*) and a basis (*ādhāra*), it is a “dispute-basis” (*vivādādhāra*); that itself is the “state of being a dispute-basis” (*vivādādhāratā*). Thus [is explained] the term “basis-legal-issue” (*ādhārādhikaraṇa*).
The compound *kammadhāraya* should be understood as being formed with words such as *vivāda* (dispute) and so forth.

That which is "made the subject of" (*adhikarīyati*), "overcome," or "settled" by means of the methods of pacification (*samatha*) is called a *adhikaraṇa* (legal issue); only the fourfold [set] beginning with dispute is shown in the Canon.
This meaning is understood from what will be stated later: "But because these four are fully settled, they are considered 'methods of pacification' (*samatha*)."

2761. These four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*)—namely, "But here, monks, monks dispute, saying 'this is Dhamma' or 'this is non-Dhamma'"—and the eighteen grounds for causing schism were taught by the Great Seer.
Among those, within the four legal issues, dispute is designated as a legal issue; it is dependent upon these eighteen grounds for causing schism.
The construction is: "it proceeds by depending on [these].

(2762) "The four failures" refers to the four failures mentioned in the passage: "But here, monks, monks reprove a monk for failure in virtue, or failure in conduct, or failure in view, or failure in livelihood."
“Accusation” (*codanā*) is the act of speaking after having pursued [the matter] regarding what was seen and so forth, by means of such things as a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*).
“Having approached” (*upāgato*) means being dependent; the meaning is that the accusation proceeds by depending upon the four kinds of failure.

Regarding the word “therein” (*tattha*), since it has already been stated as a specific selection (*niddhāraṇa*) previously, no purpose for its repetition here is apparent; nor is there any particular significance in the expression “arising” (*sambhavā*).
It is seen [in the texts]. Therefore, the reading “the basis for offenses therein, because seven offenses arise” is not appropriate;

rather, the reading “what is called the basis for offenses: the seven offenses are recognized” is more suitable. The meaning is that what is called the basis for offenses—namely, the legal issue of offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa)—is recognized as the seven offenses;
it is precisely the seven offenses that are intended.

"2763. Based on the affairs of the Saṅgha": this refers to the designation "matter-dispute" (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) with reference to the four types of Saṅgha-proceedings, beginning with the procedure by way of formal announcement (*apalokanakamma*).
The meaning is that the "matter-dispute" consists of these four Saṅgha-proceedings. "Of these four" means of these four disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).

"Settlements" (*samatha*) are so called because they are the causes for the pacification [of disputes]. "The settlements are considered" refers to the methods such as resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*), and so forth.
The seven methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*) are intended here. They are called "settlers" (*samatha*) because they settle or bring to rest legal issues;
thus, by the phrase "settled, they are considered settlers," he illustrates the etymological meaning of the word *samatha*.
To show them according to their specific forms, he says "face-to-face" (*sammukhā*), and so forth. The term "discipline" (*vinaya*) refers to these words beginning with "face-to-face."
Each should be applied individually: "resolution face-to-face," "resolution through mindfulness," and "resolution for one who is no longer deluded.
"Resolution by admission" refers to acting upon what has been admitted. The seventh *vinaya* is intended as a method of settling disputes (*samatha*).
The construction is: "The 'covering over as with grass'—these seven methods of settling disputes were spoken by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun."
