2766. Having grouped together those methods of settlement by which each of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) is settled, he says "dispute" (*vivāda*), etc., to demonstrate them.
2767–9. Explaining the meaning indicated by the summary statement beginning with "dispute," he says "by the sixth," etc.
Here, among these four legal issues and the methods of settlement, if one asks what is settled by what: a dispute is a legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).

By means of the sixth [method], *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority), and by means of the first method of settlement, *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of), it is settled by these two methods of settlement.
*Yebhuyyasikā* is that procedure in which those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority.

Regarding the four—namely, the presence of the Saṅgha, the presence of the Dhamma, the presence of the Vinaya, and the presence of the individuals—as stated [in the texts]: the presence of the Saṅgha and so forth...

It is stated that a legal dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) being settled by a group or an individual through their presence is resolved either in the presence of the Saṅgha, or otherwise by the other three [methods] with formal authorization (*sammati*).

In this context, "presence of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasammukhatā*) refers to the manifestation of the Saṅgha as the performing body through its communal concord (*saṅghasāmaggī*); [this applies to] that which is to be settled...
The reality of the subject matter (*vatthu*) is the presence of the *dhamma*; its being settled exactly as it ought to be settled is the presence of the *vinaya*.
And the presence of both parties—the one who disputes and the one with whom he disputes—being adversaries in the matter, is the presence of the person (*puggala*).
Having stated, "A formal charge (*anuvāda*) may be by four [means]," he says "in the presence" (*sammukhā*), etc., while explaining it. "In due order" (*anupubbenā*) means according to the sequence.
“By all three, beginning with *sammukhāvinaya*”: by all three, namely *sammukhāvinaya*, *sativinaya*, and *amūḷhavinaya*.
“In the same way” means that just as [the accusation] is settled by those three, so too is it settled by the fifth, the *tassapāpiyasikā* method of settling; how much more so by four.
Because it is to be performed against a person who is worse (*pāpiyo*) due to the prevalence of evil, the formal act is called “*tassapāpiyasikā*.”
An unfounded charge of failure in virtue made against the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who had attained fullness of mindfulness and whose taints were exhausted,

is settled by face-to-face settlement (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by the settlement through recollection (*sativinaya*) granted by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthā kammavācā*).
Likewise, a charge of an offense made against a monk who is insane is settled by face-to-face settlement in the same manner.
It is settled by the *dinna* (bestowal) and the *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who was not deluded). It is said that when a wicked bhikkhu, being accused of an offense in the midst of the Saṅgha,

denies it and then makes a confession and so forth, the accusation regarding his many offenses is settled by the *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence [of the parties]) and likewise by the formal act of *tassapāpiyasikā* (reproof for the worse).
“‘But an offense is settled by three [methods]’—this states the explanation for the summary. ‘By way of presence,’ and so forth. The construction is as follows:

that offense, which is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), reaches its settlement through these three methods of settling alone: by way of presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), by way of acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*), or by way of covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
Herein, ‘acting according to what has been admitted’ refers to the one who accepts the offense..."

When it is said, “Do you see [the offense]? the acceptance by the one confessing the offense is: “Yes, I see it. As for the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass), however, he will explain it himself.

Regarding the phrase “by three means of settling,” here a grave offense is settled by two means: by *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and by *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what has been admitted).
Having committed a light offense, it is to be confessed before the Saṅgha, a group,

or an individual through face-to-face reconciliation (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*). If there are various kinds of offenses committed while engaging in a great dispute similar to that of the Kosambakas,
then among those, setting aside the grave offenses (*thullavajja*) and so forth whose nature will be explained later, all the remaining ones—
The meaning is that offenses are settled by means of *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass).
As for the phrase "a legal matter (*kicca*) is a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)," the construction is that it is settled by one [method] alone, namely *sammukhāvinaya*.

Regarding the expression "in the act of majority decision (*yebhuyyasikakamma*)," the locative case here has the sense of a cause or occasion. "Have them take voting tickets (*salāka*)" refers to those who carry out the formal decision.
To determine whether those who speak according to the Dhamma in the Saṅgha are numerous or few, one should have voting sticks distributed according to the method that will be explained.

The term "Buddha" indicates a person endowed with five attributes, as stated: "He does not proceed by way of favoritism... [etc. ...and he knows what has been accepted and what has not been accepted. The phrase beginning with "in secret" describes the manner of distributing the voting sticks.
It has been explained. Regarding the term *kaṇṇajappa*: here the analysis (*viggaha*) is "that method of taking voting tickets (*salākaggāha*) in which whispering occurs at the ear.

Here, what is called a "secret voting ticket" (*gūḷhasalākaggāha*) is as follows: having placed the voting tickets of those who speak according to the Dhamma and the voting tickets of those who speak against the Dhamma separately into the corners of their robes (*cīvarakaṇṇa*), and having approached each individual separately and shown them the voting tickets individually...
“Take from here what pleases you”—this refers to causing [the gift] to be taken while standing in private.
“Openly” (vivaṭakaṃ) means knowing that there are many who speak according to the Dhamma, one causes it to be taken in the presence of individuals while everyone knows.
“Whispering in the ear” (kaṇṇajappanaṃ) means causing it to be taken by standing right at the root of the ear in private.

2771. Regarding the phrase *alajjussadeti*, the word “in the Saṅgha” (*saṅghe*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the phrase *lajjisu bālesu*, the word “among those who are shameless” (*ussadesu*) should also be supplied.
2772. Regarding the phrase *sakena kammunāyeva*, it means “by that very action which is one’s own duty.
2773–5. The passage beginning with “*āpajjatī*” is a demonstration of the karma that serves as the cause for knowing [who is] “shameless,” “conscientious,” or “foolish.”
"Evil-thinker" means one who thinks badly by way of the threefold mental misconduct, such as covetousness and so forth.

"Ill-speaker" means one whose habit is to speak badly by way of the fourfold verbal misconduct, such as false speech and so forth, and by way of the transgression of the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed for the door of speech.

"Doer of what is wrong" means [one who acts wrongly] by way of the threefold bodily misconduct, such as the destruction of life and so forth, and by way of the transgression of the training rules prescribed for the door of the body.

"One who is habitually inclined to perform despicable deeds. Thus, by means of the characteristic itself, he concludes the previously mentioned characteristics of the shameless, the modest, and the fool.
With the verse beginning "A majority decision" (*yebhuyyasikā*), he says "in three ways," etc., in order to conclude the very meaning already demonstrated.
"In three ways by the taking of voting sticks" (*tidhāsalākagāhena*) means by one or another of the three types of taking voting sticks. If there are many who speak according to the Dhamma...

The construction is: "it may be. Regarding the word "to be performed" (*kātabba*), the phrase "the settling of a legal issue arising from a dispute" (*vivādādhikaraṇavūpasamana*) is to be supplied here.

2777. That person who is shameless (*alajjī*) and subject to reproach (*sānuvāda*)—meaning impure in his actions of body and speech, and loathsome to the Fully Enlightened One—is such a wicked person for that *pāpiyasika* (act of further penalty).
The connection is "there is a *yoga*. Regarding the term *sānuvāda*: here, *anuvāda* means an accusation (*codanā*);
it is called *sānuvāda* because it occurs together with an accusation, meaning it is appropriate for an accusation to be made by persons who are free from fault. 2778–9.
*Bhaṇḍana* refers to the preliminary stage of a quarrel (*kalaha*). *Kalaha* refers to [actions] such as physical assault, which proceed through the doors of body and speech.
"And in quarrels": when various kinds of disputes have arisen, meaning not a few. "And having practiced much that is un-monk-like" (*bahu-assāmaṇe ciṇṇe*):
having committed various kinds of bodily and verbal transgressions that are unworthy of monks. "Inexhaustible" (*anagge*): endless. "Having practiced base talk" (*bhassake ciṇṇe*):
the construction is "having practiced base, unpleasant speech"; the meaning is "having spoken. "Seeking" (*gavesantaṃ*): that which is being sought.
"Legal issue arising from an offense" (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is the remainder [of the phrase]. "Fierce" (*vāḷa*) means violent. "Harsh" (*kakkhala*) means aggressive.
"Should be done" (*kātabba*) means it should be settled. The connection is: "In whatever way it is settled, by means of the 'covering over as with grass' (*tiṇavatthāraka*), one becomes pure.
"Gross offense" (*thullavajja*) refers to both a *pārājika* and a *saṅghādisesa*. "Connected with householders" (*gihīhi paṭisaṃyuta*) means [connected] with the birth and so forth of householders.

One commits an offense on account of reviling and disparaging by means of the ten grounds for abuse found in the Canon (Pāḷi) and other grounds for abuse found in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), as well as on account of not fulfilling a legitimate promise.

Indeed, this very same offense is called "connected with householders" in the Parivāra, where it says: "There is that which is connected with householders; there is that which is not connected with householders."

Having set aside the dyad, it is because of the statement: "Those connected with householders are the offense of the Elder Sudhamma, and the offense incurred by the non-fulfillment of a lawful promise; the remainder are not connected with householders.
Regarding "the offense of the Elder Sudhamma," this refers to the offense arising from censuring and reviling the householder Citta on account of his birth.

The offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) incurred by one who has fallen into [the transgression] classified under the training rule regarding abusive speech (*omasavāda-sikkhāpada*) should be understood here.

This, however, is merely an illustration; therefore, it should be known that when others revile or disparage a layperson by means of other grounds for abuse, that offense is likewise connected with a layperson.
When one who has fallen into such an offense is making confession, [he must remain within] the range of sight...

Without having her leave the vicinity of hearing, without having her leave [the assembly], having had her arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, having had her sit in the *ukkuṭika* posture, and having had her raise her joined palms, that offense must be confessed. Regarding the term *diṭṭhāvikammika*:
it is called *diṭṭhāvikammika* because it is connected with the disclosure of what has been seen (*diṭṭhāvikamme niyutto*). In the Commentary, it says: "Those who..."
However, regarding those individuals who were shown as saying, "This is not acceptable to me," and thus engaging in mutual disclosure of their views— it is the inclusion of one or another of them.
As for "he" (yo), it refers to one who,
having engaged in a great dispute with monks who are quarrelsome, has committed numerous offenses.

"A bhikkhu who has fallen [into an offense]" refers to the monk who has committed an offense. "Therein" means in that assembly of bhikkhus who perform the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass) method of settling a dispute.
"Is not present" means that because he did not come to that assembly of bhikkhus after having given his consent (*chanda*), he is not found there. The construction is: "and excluding him.

When the *tiṇavatthāraka* has been performed, from the moment of the ordination hall onwards, one becomes pure, being free from the remaining offenses committed; such is the construction: "the Saṅgha is pure."
Commentary on the Samathakkhandhaka.
Commentary on the Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka. 2783. *Kuṭṭeti*:
in one of the various types of walls made of brick, stone, or wood. *Aṭṭāne*: here, "aṭṭāna" refers to a tree.
Having cut that [wood] like a plank and incised lines in the pattern of a checkerboard, they bury it in a bathing place;
there, having scattered powders, people rub their bodies.
"With a gandhabba-hand" means with a wooden hand placed at the bathing place. It is said that by means of it, the powders—

Having taken it, people rub the body with it. "With a kuruvindakasutti" refers to a bundle of small pills made by binding together the powder of kuruvindaka stones with lac; taking hold of that at both ends, they rub the body.
"With a mallaka" means with a bowl made in the shape of the base of a makara-tooth after the tooth itself has been cut away. This...
It is not permitted even for one who is ill. "And [touching] each other with the body" means that they should rub against one another with their bodies.
2785. What is called an "unmade bowl" is one made by cutting off the teeth of a *makara* fish; this is not permitted for one who is not ill. 2786.
"Fragments of skull and brick" refers to pieces of skull and pieces of brick. "For all" means for both the ill and the non-ill.
It is permissible to rub [the body] with it after having rubbed it on one's own body. "A broad palm" refers to hand-massage;
therefore, it is permissible for anyone to perform back-massage with their hand. "A cloth roll" refers to the alternative mentioned in the Pāḷi regarding one who uses an upper garment;
therefore, it is permissible for anyone bathing to rub themselves with a roll of a bathing cloth as well.
2787. *Pheṇakaṃ* means sea-foam. *Kathalaṃ* means a fragment of a skull. These were mentioned and permitted for the purpose of rubbing the feet.
*Katakaṃ* means something shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, made by setting up thorns for the purpose of rubbing the feet;
it is not permissible to accept this, nor is it permissible to use it.
2788. “Any ornament whatsoever” means any kind of ornament among those such as hand-ornaments and so forth.
2789. “Should bend” means she should bend it while fashioning it for the purpose of an ornament.
“With the hand-fan” means they bend it with their fingers, performing the function of a fan with the hand itself. “With a fan” means with anything made of ivory and so forth. “With leather” means...
With a brush made of *usira* grass or with a brush made of *muñja* or *pabbaja* grass.
"With beeswax-oil and water-oil" is the analysis (*viggaha*): namely, beeswax-oil and water-oil; by these [two].
Therein, "beeswax-oil" refers to anything sticky, such as honey-beeswax, resin, and so forth. "Sticky" refers to resin. "Water-oil" [is explained as follows:]...
“Oil mixed with water” means oil mixed with water. In some manuscripts, the reading is “siṭṭhā,” which has the same meaning.

“For the purpose of applying it toward the forehead” means for the purpose of applying it in a downward direction toward the forehead. “With hair standing upward” means with hair that stands with its tips pointing upward. 2791.

“Having moistened the hand with oil” means having smeared the palm of the hand with oil. “Siroruha” means hair. “Of one distressed by heat” means of one whose head is covered in dust and distressed by heat. The construction is: “It is proper to wipe the hair with a dry cloth.”
2792. Regarding "when a mirror has arisen": here, even bronze plates and the like—in which the reflection of the face is discerned—all are included under the designation of "mirror" (ādāsa);

and sour gruel and so forth are also included under the designation of "water-vessel" (udapatta). Therefore, for one who looks at anything whatsoever [in such a vessel], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
2793. To show the reason why there is no offense for one looking at the face, he said, “with the skin intact,” and so forth.
The construction is as follows: it is permissible to look at the face on account of illness, thinking, “Is there a wound on my face, or is the skin intact?
and it is also permissible to look at the face for the purpose of knowing the conditions of one’s own life-span, thinking, “Am I old, or am I not?”
2794. "Dancing" (*nacca*) means any kind of dancing whatsoever, even including the dancing of peacocks.

"Singing" (*gīta*) means any kind of singing, whether the singing of actors or the singing of virtuous singers—even including the "tooth-singing" (a form of rhythmic clapping) which they perform by making grunting sounds in the preliminary stage with the thought, "We shall sing.
This, too, is not permitted. "Instrumental music" (*vādita*) means any kind of instrumental performance. "To see or to hear" refers to [dancing]... [the text continues].
"To see" or "to hear singing or instrumental music.

2795. Regarding the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who dances or causes another to dance, sings or causes another to sing, plays an instrument or causes another to play an instrument—whether doing so oneself or having others do so—the author says "even to see, at the very least," etc., in order to show a portion of that [explanation].
2796. *Suṇāti* means he hears either singing or instrumental music. *Passati* means he sees a dance. 2797.

Regarding the phrase *passissāmi*, the word *suṇissāmi* (I will hear) is understood as the remainder. The construction is: for one who goes from one monastery to another thinking, "I will see a dance," or "I will hear singing or instrumental music," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
2798. *Uṭṭhahitvāna gacchato*: [this refers to] one who goes thinking, "I will see a dance," or "I will hear singing or instrumental music."
The construction is as follows: having risen from the place where one was sitting, there is an offense even for one who goes toward various directions within the monastery.
The construction is also as follows: there is an offense even for one who stands in the path and looks by stretching out the neck.
2799. "Long" means longer than two finger-breadths. "One should not wear" means it should not be worn. [This refers to] two finger-breadths or two months.
"Two-fingered" (*dvaṅgula*) means that its measure here is two finger-breadths; thus it refers to the hair. "Two-monthly" (*dumāsa*) means that its maximum limit is two months.
One maintaining [the length of] hair should maintain it at either two finger-breadths or for two months.
"Beyond that is not permitted" means that it is not permitted to maintain hair longer than those two finger-breadths or two months.
Alternatively, two finger-breadths joined together are "two-finger-breadths" (*dvaṅgula*); two months joined together are "two-months" (*dumāsa*).

In both cases, the accusative case is used because of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*). The meaning is: while wearing hair, one may wear it for the measure of two finger-breadths or for the measure of two months;
beyond that limit of time, it is not permitted to wear the hair. If [the hair] is [cut] within two months...
If they reach two finger-breadths [in length], they must be cut off within two months. It is not permitted for them to exceed two finger-breadths.
Even if they are not long, one is not allowed to let them exceed two months by even a single day.
Thus, this is stated as the maximum limit in both respects; beyond that, there is no such thing as being "new" (or "unused").
2800. The construction is: "He should not maintain long nails, nor long nose-hairs"; that is, he should not keep them;
the meaning is that he should cut them off. "Polishing twenty" means it is not permissible for a bhikkhu to polish—that is, to make smooth—the surface of twenty fingernails.
Having scraped them with a knife and rubbed them with powder so that they are like crystal gems...

“Brightening” refers to what is called polishing after shaving. Because it was permitted by the statement, “Bhikkhus, I allow you to remove the mere dirt,” it is permissible to remove nail-dirt with things such as the husk of a mung bean. 2801.
“One should have the beard shaved separately”: this means that one who has had his hair cut should have the beard shaved separately. “The mustache” (dāṭhikaṃ).

"Should set aside" means: having had the hair cut and not having had the beard trimmed, one should set it aside separately. "In the private parts" refers to the private area consisting of the armpits and the genitals.
"Should have the hair removed" means: one should have it cut by another person—whether with a knife, tweezers, or any other instrument—or one should remove it oneself.
[The Buddha said: "Monks, I allow [the removal of hair] in the private parts on account of illness."

Because it was permitted [by the Buddha] that "one may have the hair removed," it is allowable to have the hair removed when there is an affliction such as the aforementioned abscesses, boils, or wounds in a congested area. 2802.

It is stated that for one who cuts [the hair] while not ill, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). The connection is that it is also stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who causes another person to cut it with scissors in that manner.

2803. "Cutting off the remaining limbs" (*sesaṅgacchedana*) refers to the cutting off of the remaining parts of the body, such as the fingers and so forth. "Taking one's own life" (*attavadha*) refers to the destruction of one's own life through one's own effort, or through an effort prompted by a command.
2804. "A limb" (*aṅga*) refers to a part of the body other than the sexual organ. There is no fault for one who cuts off a limb as a remedy for a bite by a snake, a worm, or the like;
there is no fault for one who cuts off a limb as a remedy for such an affliction.
The construction is: "Even for one who discharges blood, there is no fault.
(2805) If a monk who does not possess a water-strainer goes along a road, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

For one who asks for that strainer on the road during the journey and does not give it, for him who does not give—*adadato*, meaning "not giving"—there is likewise a *dukkaṭa* offense; such is the construction.
Furthermore, if someone asks for [a filter] even though a strainer is already in their own hand, one should not give it to them against one's will.
2806. The word "naked" (*nagga*) should be construed individually with each of the verbal phrases such as "does not eat" (*na bhuñje*).
"Does not eat" means he would not eat food and so forth that ought to be eaten. "Does not drink" means he would not drink rice-gruel and so forth that ought to be drunk. And...
One should not eat hard food such as roots and the like;
one should not consume what is to be consumed, such as molasses and the like, nor should one lick it. One should not give anything, such as alms-food, to another;
likewise, being naked oneself, one should not receive anything. *Añjasam* means the direct path.

2807. "One should not perform *parikamma* (massage/attendance)" means that one should not perform services such as massaging the back and so forth. "One should not have [it] performed" means that, being naked oneself, one should not have another person perform services such as massaging the back and so forth.
2808. Regarding services such as massaging the back, three types of coverings are prescribed:
"I allow you, monks, three kinds of coverings: a sauna-covering, a water-covering, and a cloth-covering. (Vinaya II 139)
The construction is: "it is permitted. That which covers shame is a "cover" (*paṭicchādi*); a bathhouse itself as a cover is a "bathhouse-cover" (*jantāgharapaṭicchādi*).
Water itself as a cover is a "water-cover" (*udakapaṭicchādi*). Cloth itself as a cover is a "cloth-cover" (*vatthapaṭicchādi*).
By the phrase "it is permissible in all cases," the other two types of covers are indicated as being for preparatory purposes only.
It indicates that it is permissible. "In all cases" means in all activities such as eating and so forth. 2809.

"Anywhere" refers to any kind of box—whether made of copper, brass, bronze, iron, gold, silver, or the like, or made of wood—in which [the bowl] is placed when used as a stand for a filled vessel. It is not permissible to eat from such a vessel.
It is not permitted to eat using a vessel as a stand. As it is said:
"A 'liquid-dripping base' (*āsittakūpadhāna*) is a designation for a box made of copper or silver;

however, because it is prohibited in general terms by the rule, 'Monks, one must not eat from a liquid-dripping base,' even one made of wood is not permitted. [The Buddha said: "I allow, monks, a *maḷorikā* (a wooden stand)."
Because it has been permitted, it is allowable to set down a *maḷorikā* and eat from it. "Maḷorikā" refers to a staff-stand;
that which people make into a stand by binding three, four, or many sticks together, making them wide at the top and bottom and narrow in the middle.
This also includes stands for poles, leaf-stands, baskets, back-rests, water-jars, door-bolts, vessels, and mortars.
These are included right here. "A support on a stick" means a support that has been tied after placing the stick itself upright.
Since it is possible for food to be served separately in a single vessel, if only "while eating from a single vessel" were stated, that case might also be included;
therefore, to exclude that, he says "together. The term "while eating" is an illustration (upalakkhaṇa).
It is not permitted to drink even gruel or other drinks from a single vessel together with another; as it is said: "Monks, one must not drink from the same bowl.
Alternatively, it should be understood that by the general term "eating" (*bhuñjanto*), drinking is also included because it shares the common characteristic of being swallowed.
This is the analysis here: if a single monk goes along taking fruit or a cake from a vessel, [he may do so].
When he has departed, it is permissible for the other to eat the remainder. For the other as well, it is permissible to take it up again at that moment. 2810. The construction is as follows:

for those two or three bhikkhus who lie down with a single upper robe, or a single bedspread, or both a single bedspread and a single upper robe; and for those who lie down together on even a single couch—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
2811. Regarding the phrase "having folded the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) into a bundle": here, "outer robe" refers to a robe formally determined (adhiṭṭhita-cīvara) by the name "saṅghāṭi."

The meaning is: having become intent upon entering with the *saṅghāṭi* wrapped around [the knees]. "He should not sit" means he should not sit anywhere—whether in a monastery (*vihāra*) or within a house (*antaraghara*).
There is no doubt that what is called "the *saṅghāṭi*" refers to a robe that has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) and has attained the conventional designation by the name "saṅghāṭi";
for this is also stated in the commentary on the *Khuddaka-sikkhā*: "He does not wrap [his knees] with the *saṅghāṭi*..."
It is stated: "One who has determined his robe [as his formal possession] must not sit with his legs crossed (pallatthika) either in a monastery or within a village.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is said: "For one who has entered a village for the purpose of staying there, it is permissible to sit with legs crossed without the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), provided he is apart from the other robes that have been determined [as his]."

"Should not play any game whatsoever" means he should not engage in any physical or verbal play, such as gambling with dice and the like. "Nor should he cause [others] to take" means he should neither cause them to take nor cause them to carry away;

this is the meaning. 2812. "Even on the beard" refers to the facial hair (*massu*). Regarding "grown," the word "frightful" (*bībhaccha*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Another" means one that is not grey. "Such" means frightful. 2813.
By the term "one who is not ill," he indicates that for one who is ill there is no offense. By the term "should wear," he provides a designation of the agent in its pure form.
It should be understood that there is no offense for having another apply [ointment] even when one is not ill, or for consenting to another applying it.
The construction is: "It is permissible for the sake of protecting oneself, and for the sake of protecting one's robes and so forth. In this regard, the following is the detailed analysis:
for one who has a burning sensation in the body, or an excess of bile, or weak eyesight, or any other ailment, without...
If one goes out with an umbrella, it is permissible for that person to have an umbrella whether in the village or in the forest.
It is permitted for the sake of protecting oneself from the fear of wild beasts and thieves; furthermore, during the rainy season, it is also permitted for the sake of protecting one’s robes.
However, a single-leaf umbrella is permitted in all circumstances. For it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "A 'single-leaf umbrella' means a palm leaf."

2814. By way of figurative usage (*abhedopacāra*), that which has the shape of an elephant’s trunk is called “elephant-trunk. The same applies to the following cases as well. “Clothing” (*vasana*) is a name for a robe (*cīvara*).
The two phrases, “an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who wears [it],” are each to be joined individually with all the preceding terms beginning with “elephant-trunk.
In the word *velliya*, the syllable *saṃ* is elided due to the requirements of the metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
"Wrap around" (saṃvelliyanti) means:
here, "elephant-trunk" (hatthisoṇḍa) refers to a lower garment worn by women in Coḷa, which is fastened from the base of the navel and hangs down in the shape of an elephant's trunk.
"Four-cornered" (catukkaṇṇa) means: two above and two below, thus four.
*Kaṇṇe dassetvā nivatthaṃ*: worn by showing the ear [of the cloth]. *Macchavāḷakaṃ*: so-called because it is worn by hanging it down, biting it on one side and letting it hang on the other.
*Saṃvelliyaṃ*: the lower garment worn by tying up the waist, like wrestlers, laborers, and so forth.
*Tālavaṇṭakaṃ*: so-called because the robe is worn hanging down in the shape of a palm-leaf fan. By the word "and" (*ca*), the *satavalika* is included.
A *satavalika* is a long robe (*dīghasāṭaka*) worn after being pleated many times and tucked into the waistband, or worn so that folds appear continuously on the left and right sides.
However, it is permissible if only one or two folds are visible starting from the knee. It is not permitted for one who is ill or traveling on a journey to wear it in this manner.

Furthermore, when walking on a path, it is not permissible to lift one or two corners [of the inner robe] and hang them over the upper robe (*antaravāsaka*), or to wear one saffron robe (*kāṣāya*) inside in that manner and then put another robe over it outside.
However, one who is ill is permitted to show the tucked-in fold of the inner robe and then put another robe over it. One who is not ill may not do so. Two...
While wearing it, one should wear the lower robe having made it well-adjusted.

Thus, avoiding everything that is prohibited here as well as what was mentioned in the commentary on the Sekhiyas, one should wear it in a circular manner, covering the three circles without any alteration.
One who makes any alteration whatsoever is not freed from an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"Householder’s attire" refers to anything worn other than that which possesses the characteristic of being properly circular (parimaṇḍala), such as:

"the white-cloth attire of a wanderer, the single-robe attire, the intoxicated man’s attire, the harem attendant’s attire, the great elder’s attire, the hut-enterer’s attire, the brahmin’s attire, or the scroll-maker’s attire.
All such [attire] is called "householder’s attire. Therefore...
Just as the Śvetapaṭas and the Aḍḍhapāla Nigaṇṭhas wear their robes; and just as some wanderers (paribbājaka) expose their chests and place the cloak over both shoulders;

and just as people wearing a single garment (ekasāṭaka) cover their backs with one end of the wrapped garment and place both ends over both shoulders; and just as those addicted to liquor and the like [do].
Wrapping the neck with a cloth, they let both ends hang down over the belly, or they throw them over the back;
just as women of the inner apartments put on a veil after showing only the pupils of their eyes,
or just as the Mahājeṭṭhas, having put on a long robe, cover their entire body with one end of it, or just as farmers do.
When entering the field-hut, they wrap the cloth around it, tuck it under both armpits,
and then cover their bodies with one end of it; and just as Brahmins insert the cloth between both armpits and tuck it over the tops of their shoulders,
and just as a monk who is a reciter of the scriptures covers his left arm with the single-shoulder-draping.
Having opened the robe, he places it over the shoulder;
thus, having avoided all these faults of wearing the robe improperly, as well as other such defects in donning it, one should wear it evenly all around without agitation.

Likewise, for one who, having worn it improperly, acts with negligence or displays any agitation while in the monastery or within a house, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). From being even all around...

The meaning is that, having avoided the faults of wearing and draping [robes] with the characteristics of one who is "liberated," it is precisely the state of being "even all around" (*parimaṇḍala*) that is intended as the stated characteristic. 2816.

"One should not recite *Lokāyata*" refers to the treatises of the non-Buddhist sects associated with pointless reasoning, such as: "Everything is impure; everything is pure; a crow is white; a crane is black—for this and that reason."
One should not teach it to others. Nor should one master that Lokāyata; one should neither master nor learn it.
"Animal sciences" refers to elephant-lore, horse-lore, archery, and so forth—sciences that cause harm to others.
The construction is: these should not be mastered by a bhikkhu, nor should they be taught.
2817. "A yak-tail fan of all kinds" means a fan made from all the hair-tufts of yaks, whether white or of any other color.

"One should not set fire to a forest" means that one should not burn a forest with fire, except for the purpose of giving a counter-fire which has been permitted as a means of preventing calamities such as forest conflagrations.
However, when a forest fire approaches and there is no one who is not ordained (anupasampanna) present to give the counter-fire, [one may do so].
One may provide protection by clearing away [grass] or digging a trench; one may also extinguish a fire—whether it has reached or not yet reached the lodging—by breaking off green branches.
However, this must be done only with water that is *kappiya* (permissible), and not otherwise.
But if there is a person who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it should be caused to be done using that very same *kappiya* terminology. [The mouth... is not...
"And he shall not smear his face with red arsenic (manosilā) and the like, nor shall he apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) to his body"—this is the meaning.
2818. *Ubhatokāja*: a yoke for carrying loads by both ends. *Antarakāja*: a yoke for carrying a load in the middle, to be borne by carriers standing at both ends.
Loads carried on the head, shoulders, or waist, etc., have the characteristics already described below.

2819. The construction is as follows: "If a bhikkhu chews a tooth-stick that exceeds eight finger-breadths by that same measure, or is less than four finger-breadths by that same measure, for one who chews in this way, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

2820. "Even when there is a necessity" means even when there is a necessity for taking dry sticks and so forth. "A man's height" (porisa) means the measure of a person; it is said to be the length of a fathom (byāma).
"In cases of distress" (āpadāsu) refers to seeing wild beasts and the like, or being lost on the road and wishing to look toward the directions.
Having offered an oblation, or upon seeing a forest fire or a flood approaching, or in such calamities as these—it is indeed permissible to climb even a very tall tree. 2821.
If one were not unwell or ill, [one should avoid] raw garlic, Māgadha garlic, and Bhaṇḍika garlic.
The construction is: "one may eat and indeed consume. That which is called *bhaṇḍika-lasuṇa* (cluster garlic) is that which has many seeds starting from the fourth seed onward.
Regarding onions (*palāṇḍuka*), leeks (*bhañjanaka*), and other types of garlic, there is no fault even if they were grown in Magadha. The classification of garlic has already been shown below.
However, it is permissible for one who is ill to eat garlic. As it was said: "I allow you, monks, [to eat] on account of illness."
"Garlic should be eaten. "On account of illness" means for the sake of that specific illness for which garlic is the medicine;

this is the meaning. "The word of the Buddha" refers to the Pāli of the Three Piṭakas as recorded in the three councils. "Otherwise" means it should not be planted on the path of recitation consisting of the corrupted speech of the Sakas and others;
thus it is said that it should not be established in such a manner.
"Thrown" means thrown by anyone whatsoever. The construction is: "it should not be said, 'Live!
When a monk has thrown [the stone], it is permissible for a householder who says "Live! to further say "Live long!"—this is the construction.
Even though the word "long" (*ciraṃ*) is present, it is permissible.
2823. *Ākoṭentassa*: of one who strikes with the body or with things connected to the body, etc. *Pupphasaṃkiṇṇe*: strewn with flowers; that is, covered with a bed of flowers. 2824. *Nhāpitapubbaka*:
one for whom barbering was formerly done; the meaning is "one of the barber caste. *Khurabhaṇḍaṃ*: the equipment of a barber.
*Na gaṇheyya*: he should not take up; that is, he should not carry it about. If there is one who belongs to the barber caste, he...
The meaning is that one should not take away a saddle-bag after having taken it. It is permissible to cut hair and so forth after taking [an item] from another’s hand.
Regarding the term *uṇṇī*, this refers to a type of woolen cloak (*pāvuraṇa*) made of wool, excluding a hair-blanket (*kesakambala*).

He said “all” because they possess the various distinctions mentioned in the passage beginning with “the *gonaka*, the *kuttaka*, the *cittaka*,” and so on. He stated that it is permissible to wear [it] after having placed a woolen cloth inside.
“With the hair on the outside”: as it is said, “Monks, wool with the hair on the outside must not be worn. In the commentary on the training rule (*sikkhāpada-aṭṭhakathā*), it says:
“They put on a woolen cloak having placed the woolly hairs on the outside; for one who wears it in that manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
It is permissible to put it on having placed the hairs on the inside.”

2825. *Aṅgarāga* means saffron and so forth. "While making" means while anointing. The construction is: "Even for one who enters a village without having fastened the waistband, a *dukkaṭa* offense is declared.
And here, if one has departed without fastening it due to forgetfulness, one must fasten it at the place where one remembers.
It is permissible to go with the thought, "I will fasten it in the assembly hall. Having remembered...
As long as it has not been tied [to the waist], one must not go for alms.

2826. Apart from all weapons, all items made of iron or consisting of iron—namely the bowl, sandals suitable for walking, and the couch with the aforementioned characteristics, as well as the chair—and apart from all items made of wood or consisting of wood that have the aforementioned characteristics:
The *kataka* (water-wheel), the potter’s [wheel], and likewise the hut made entirely of clay for Dhaniya, as well as all articles made entirely of clay—these are allowable;
such is the construction of the sense.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the Minor Section on Requisites (*Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka*).
Commentary on the Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka) 2827.
*Āsandika* means a square chair. *Atikkantapamāṇa* means having legs that exceed the measure of one cubit (*vaḍḍhakihattha*) from the bottom of the frame.
However, it is not permitted for a chair to have long legs that are high on only one side. As it is said: "Even a high [chair]..."
"Because of the word *āsandikā*, a long bench with legs exceeding eight finger-breadths is indeed not permitted on one side;
however, a square chair (*caturassa-āsandika*), even if it exceeds the [standard] measure, is permitted.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), this refers back to the phrase "exceeding the measure. A five-limbed chair (*pañcaṅga-pīṭha*) consists of four legs...
“With supports” means a bedstead equipped with these five parts. “Seven-part” means one made by attaching supports on three sides;
for it is called a “seven-part bedstead” because it is equipped with four legs and three supports.
This same method applies to the couch as well, as it was said: “A ‘seven-part’ [couch] is a couch made by providing supports on three sides.”
“This too is permissible as it exceeds the [prescribed] measure.
(2828) “Covered with cotton” means bound after having placed cotton on top. “Only in a house” is connected with the phrase “it is permissible to sit” in the houses of householders.
By the word “to sit,” lying down is already excluded. “A pillow of *sīsa*-wood.”
"A pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *pi* (also); it should be brought back and connected with the phrase "for one who is not ill" (*agilānassa*).
By this, it is shown that it is permissible even for one who is not ill, let alone for one who is ill. 2829.
To show that it is not only the *sīsa-pādūpadhāna* (head-and-feet pillow) that is permissible for one who is ill, but also this [other type], he says:
“Having spread out,” and so forth. “Having spread out the cushions” means having laid down many cushions.
“And there” means on that spread of cushions. “Having placed a coverlet” means having spread a coverlet over it. 2830. “Horizontally” means in width.
“A fist-cubit” (*muṭṭhiratana*) refers to a natural cubit measured by the fist; however, for carpenters...
"A span's measure" (*vidatthimattaṃ*). The construction is: "Measured" (*mitaṃ*) means it is manifestly endowed with the proper proportion.
In some manuscripts, the reading "mataṃ" is seen; that is not to be accepted. "In length" (*dīghato*) means from the length of the pillow. The connection is:
"One and a half" (*diyaḍḍhaṃ*) means it is either one and a half cubits or two cubits, as stated in the *Kurundi*. For this very [is what is meant].
“Cushion the size of the head” is what is intended. As it is said:

“The size of the head means that when measured across the three corners, the distance between two corners is one span and four finger-breadths, while the middle part is one fist-span in length. Furthermore, as for the length...
“Or one and a half ratanas, or two ratanas,” so it is stated in the *Kurundi*. This is the maximum limit for the size of the head;
more than this is not permitted, but less than this is allowed.
2831. *Coḷa* means a rag (*pilotikā*). *Paṇṇa* means the leaf of trees or creepers. *Uṇṇā* means the wool of sheep and the like. *Tiṇa* means...
"Any grass such as *dabba* grass, etc. refers to grasses. "Bamboo" (*vāka*) refers to plantain, *akkama*, *kacivāka*, and so forth.

The construction is as follows: "Cushions filled with these five [materials]"; because they are the end of the enumeration of cottons, they are said to be five by way of the enumeration of the cores of these five types of cores.

2832. To show the interior of the bolster (*bimbohana*), he said "cotton wool" (*bhisī*), and so forth. "The five" refers to the five [materials] previously mentioned, such as cloth (*coḷa*) and the rest.
Likewise, "the three cotton wools" refers to the three types of cotton wool permitted by the rule: "Monks, I allow three types of cotton wool: tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and *poṭaki*-cotton.
In this context, "tree-cotton" refers to that of any [trees] such as the *simbali* tree.
The cotton of trees. "Cotton of creepers" refers to the cotton of any kind of creeper, such as the milk-creepers (*khīravalli*) and so forth.
"Cotton of grasses" refers to the cotton of any kind of grass, such as *poṭaki* grass and so forth, including even sugar cane, reeds, and the like.

"The fur of beasts and birds" refers to the fur of four-footed animals such as lions and so forth, and the feathers of birds such as peacocks and so forth. These are the inner cores of lotus roots and so forth.
"These are the ten types of stuffing for a bolster (bimbohana)"—this is the connection.
Having thus shown the allowable (kappiya) stuffing for a mattress or bolster, he now says "human hair," etc., in order to show what is not allowable (akappiya).
Among hairs, human hair; among flowers, all flowers such as the *bakula* and *piyaṅgu*; and among leaves... [the rest of the sentence continues].

And the construction is: "pure, absolute, and *tamāla* leaf alone is not permitted. By the word "pure" (*suddha*), it is indicated by contrast that the *tamāla* leaf is permitted when mixed with other fillers.
2834. *Masūraka*: a bolster for the skin of a hide.
2835. By the word "pure" (*suddha*), the meaning already shown through contrast is now explained in its own form; thus he says "mixed" (*missa*), and so forth. 2836.
"Of an animal" (*tiracchānagatassa*) means even down to a gadfly. "Having it done" (*kārentassa*) means either having it made by means of painting, woodwork, and so on, or doing it oneself.

2837. "Birth stories" (*jātaka*) refers to the *Jātaka* collection, such as the *Apaṇṇaka-jātaka* and others. "Subjects" (*vatthu*) refers to the *Vimānavatthu* and other such works that inspire serene confidence.

Or a subject that produces a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), such as the *Petavatthu* and so forth. By the word "or" (*vā*), it includes the works presented here that have come down in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding the phrase "or by others," the word "or" (*vā*) here functions as a restriction;

it indicates that it is permissible only to have it made by others, and not to do it oneself. Regarding the phrase "even to do it oneself," the word "even" (*api*) indicates that it goes without saying that one may have it made by others.
2838. However, whichever monk—whether he is senior or junior—is two years or one year senior to another monk, he is said to be a "fellow-seated" (samānāsani) with that monk;
such is the construction of the rule. 2839. “A five-year monk [is a fellow-seated] with a seven-year monk”: this is an example of those who are senior by two years being fellow-seated.
“A five-year monk [is a fellow-seated] with a six-year monk”: this is an example of those who are senior by one year being fellow-seated.
2840. The construction is as follows: that which is capable of supporting three people sitting upon it is called a "long seat" (*dīghāsana*) for those below.

Regarding the case cited where "those sharing a seat sat on a couch and broke the couch, and sat on a chair and broke the chair," because it was authorized by the rule, "Bhikkhus, I allow a couch for two persons and a chair for two persons," the term "two" is used.
This was stated with reference to two [cases] involving a shared seat.

2841. The construction is as follows: except for one who possesses both sexual organs (*ubhatobyañjana*), a woman, and a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), it is permitted for one to sit on a long seat together with all men, whether they be householders or those gone forth (*pabbajita*). However, in some manuscripts...
The reading “sabbesan” is seen as ending in the genitive case; however, the reading “sabbehipi,” ending in the instrumental case, is more appropriate.
Or rather, it should be understood that this is a designation in the genitive case occurring within the context of the instrumental case. As it is said:
“Whatever is sufficient for three people—whether it be portable or non-portable—even such a fragment of a wooden plank may [be used] by one who is not fully ordained.”
“It is proper to sit together. 2842.

Regarding the term *purimikā* (the earlier [Kathina] period): on the day of entering the rains retreat (*vassa*), one should sit with a monk who has been appointed by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and who is endowed with the five qualities stated as: “He should not fall into partiality through favoritism... [etc. ...and he should know what has been accepted and what has not been accepted.”
“Monks, I allow you first to count the monks; having first counted the monks, to count the lodgings;

having counted the lodgings, to assign them by way of the lodgings. According to this method of what has been thus authorized, the assignment of lodgings is called the *purimika* (first) assignment of lodgings.
In the same way, the assignment of lodgings on the day of the later (*pacchimikā*) entry into the rains retreat [is the *pacchimika* assignment].

This is called the "later" (pacchimika). In the same way, on the day immediately following the Mahāpavāraṇā day, if one says, "Venerable sirs, please take up lodgings that have been released in the interim," and causes the lodgings to be taken according to seniority, this is called the "interim-release" (antarāmuttaka). It is stated:
"When Āsāḷhī has passed by one day, the 'earlier' (purimika) should be caused to be taken; when Āsāḷhī has passed by one month, the 'later' (pacchimika)."
"It should be taken; on the following day when the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) has passed, the *antarāmuttaka* [robe] should be taken for the purpose of the upcoming rains residence (*vassāvāsa*).
Having stated this, he spoke "the dawn of the first day of the month," etc., in order to demonstrate that very meaning by way of restriction.

Here, "the first day of the month" (*pāṭipada*) refers both to the two days of entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*) and the day immediately following the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*). Of these three days of the first of the month...
*Aruṇa* (dawn) is called *pubbāruṇa* (first dawn). When that day has passed, the dawn connected with the second lunar date is called *punāruṇa* (subsequent dawn).
The word *idam* (this) refers to what follows immediately after both types of dawn. Regarding the term *senāsanagāhakassa* (of the receiver of lodgings):

here the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of the base itself; thus, it means "of the one who takes up lodgings. As it is said: "For this is the field for the taking up of lodgings. Regarding *vassūpagate*: when the entering of the rains (*vassūpagama*) is to be performed.

When "sati" (being) is present, the locative case is used in the sense of a purpose to be accomplished. Alternatively, in the phrase "vassūpagate" (when the rains-residence has been entered), the locative case is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*).
For the taking of lodgings on that very day is the sign for entering the rains-residence during both the earlier and the later periods;
however, the "one released in the interval" is the sign for the future entry into the rains-residence. Thus, all three types of taking lodgings serve as signs for the entry into the rains-residence.

2844. When the dawn has already risen on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada) and the lodgings have been assigned, if another bhikkhu arrives and requests a lodging from the assigner of lodgings, that bhikkhu should be told by the assigner of lodgings: "The lodging has already been taken.
This is the construction [of the sentence].

2845. This is the *vassāvāsika* (the robe belonging to the rainy-season residence); it is the robe to be given to those who have completed the rains-retreat. By way of metrical composition, the word *vassāvāsika* has its vowel shortened to *vassavāsika*. The construction is as follows:

if the *vassāvāsika* robe taken after obtaining the consent of the Sangha is "born there" (*tatraja*) or "arisen there" (*tatruppāda*), then even one who has left the order during the rains-retreat receives it. Regarding the phrase "if born there": [it refers to what was produced within that specific monastery].
This indicates that he does not receive what was taken by the donors on account of the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) requisites.
As it is said: "But they say that what was taken on account of the requisites is not received.
2846–8. If a monk who has completed the rains-residence [receives] any suitable article, such as the three robes, from the hand of a resident [monk]...
Having taken it for himself and said, "Take this *vassāvāsika* robe-cloth which was received by me from such-and-such a family," he gives it to that resident monk and departs for another region.

If, having gone there, he renounces the order or becomes a layman, then that *vassāvāsika* cloth— which had reached him while he was away and which he had given away in that manner— [remains his property].
The resident monk does not receive [the robe]; the connection is that the *vassāvāsika* robe assigned to him remains the property of the Saṅgha.
As it is said: “In this case, monks, if a monk who has completed the rains retreat disrobes, this [robe] belongs to the Saṅgha alone.

(2849) If he causes it to be accepted in the presence of the people who are the donors for that family, then the resident monk receives the *vassāvāsika* robe that has arrived for him while he is away on a journey; such is the connection.
2850. Therein, "grove" (ārāma) means either a grove of flowers or a grove of fruit. "Monastery" (vihāra) means any kind of lodging such as a palace and so forth.
"Sites for both" means the sites for both types, namely, the site for a grove and the site for a monastery.
"Site for a grove" (ārāmavatthu) means a piece of land set aside and demarcated for the purpose of those very groves, or [the land] when those groves have fallen into ruin.
Their ancient site is the location where the monastery stands. A "monastery site" (*vihāravatthu*) is the place established for it.
A "cushion" (*bhisi*) is any one of the five types, such as a woolen cushion and so forth. A "pillow" (*bimbohana*) is any one of the types of pillows previously mentioned.
A "bed" (*mañca*) refers to the four types previously mentioned: the *masāraka*, the *bundikābaddha*, the *kuḷīrapādaka*, and the *āhaccapādaka*.
"One of the beds" refers to any one of them. "A stool" (*pīṭha*) means any one of the four types of stools, such as the *masāraka* and so forth.
"An iron pot" (*lohakumbhī*) is a pot made of any kind of metal, whether black iron or copper. A "cauldron" (*kaṭāha*) is well known.
"A water-jar" (*bhāṇaka*) is what is called an *alañjara*; an *alañjara* is a vessel that holds a large quantity of water.
A *mahācāṭi* is a large bowl; an *alanti-alanjaro* is a water-jar used for holding water. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*:
“It is made like a round bowl, somewhat elongated at the mouth, with a constriction shown in the middle. A *vāraka* is a water-pot (*ghaṭa*). *Ku* refers to the earth;
because it breaks (*dālanato*) or tears it open (*vidāraṇato*), the specific iron tool is called a *kudāla*.
2852. Regarding "valli, veḷu, etc.": *veḷu* refers to the great bamboo. *Tiṇa* refers to grass used for roofing a house. *Paṇṇa* refers to palm leaves and the like.
*Muñja* refers to muñja-grass. *Pabbaja* refers to pabbaja-grass. *Matti* (clay) refers either to natural clay or to clay of five colors such as red ochre (*geruka*) and so forth.
And the Master of the Commentary said:
2853. *Dve*: these are the first and second heavy articles (*garubhaṇḍa*). They are comprised of two because it is stated: "A grove and the site of a grove—this is the first;

a monastery and the site of a monastery—this is the second. *Catusaṅgaha*: the analysis is "that which has a collection (*saṅgaha*) consisting of four things, such as mattresses (*bhisi*) and so forth.
*Navakoṭṭhāsa*: the analysis is "that which has nine sections (*koṭṭhāsa*), such as the iron cauldrons (*lohakumbhi*) and so forth."
"In eight ways" means by way of the eight types beginning with creepers (*valli*).

"Thus" (*iti*) is used in the sense of illustration. The construction is as follows: the Lord, whose eyes are the fivefold stainless vision, has revealed the twenty-five kinds of heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*)—which, according to the method already stated, consist of the enumerations of heavy goods specified within the five groups—by way of their collective total.

The analysis of the compound is: "one whose five eyes are stainless. The meaning is: one whose five kinds of eyes are purified by way of the flesh-eye, the divine eye, the Dhamma-eye, the Buddha-eye, and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).
2855. *Vissajjento*: giving away because of his lordship over another. *Vibhājento*: having brought [the recipient] to the appropriate age for receiving.
"Dividing. For all this heavy property is stated in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* as "not to be disposed of," and in the *Kiṭāgirivatthu* as "not to be shared out.
By way of showing the difference in terminology found in both places, and demonstrating the offense for one who acts contrary to those rules there, he said:
"The bhikkhu incurs a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). However, in the *Parivāra*—
"Five things are declared by the Great Seer as not to be given away and not to be shared;
there is no offense for one who gives them away or uses them.
This question was conceived by those skilled in wisdom."

It has arrived. Therefore, because it would result in the cutting off of the root, it is not to be given away nor is it to be shared; however, for one who exchanges it or uses it by way of bartering, there is no offense—this is the intended meaning here. 2856.

Whether by an individual monk, or by a *saṅgha*, or by a *gaṇa*, heavy property that has been given away remains ungiven, and what has been divided remains undivided—this is the construction [of the sentence].
2857. Herein, among these five types of heavy property, there is nothing whatsoever that is not heavy property in the first three.
The application [of the term]. In the fourth [case], regarding "precious goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*), he says "iron pot," etc., in order to show the method stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"These three—iron pot, iron vessel, and iron cauldron—whether they be large or small, even those that hold as little as a *pasata* of water, are indeed precious goods."
2858. This connects with the phrase "it is threefold. Regarding the term *pādagaṇhanaka*: here, a *pāda* is a specific vessel that holds exactly five *nāḷi*s of Magadha-measure.
When determining the capacity of vessels, people in the island of Sīhaḷa mostly measure by means of that very *pāda*.
Therefore, it is stated in the commentary: "In the island of Sīhaḷa, the *pādagaṇhanaka* [measure] should be divided. *Lohavāraka* means...
[An object] made from any one of black iron, copper, brass, bronze, or bell-metal. "To be distributed" means it must be divided.
2859. "One who takes more than that" refers to one who takes more than the vessel used for receiving a quarter-share.

Having thus shown the determination of those terms as they appear in the Canon (Pāḷi), he says "the water-pot and so forth" etc., in order to show those appearing in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). The *bhiṅgāra*...
The *nāma* is a specific type of large water vessel with a high neck and a wide mouth, from which water flows out through a spout shaped like the tip of an elephant’s trunk.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes those small or large items mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) such as "the bowl, the *uḷuṅka* scoop, the wooden ladle, the *kaṭacchu* spoon, the *pātita*, the *taṭṭaka* plate, the *sarakasa* cup, the box, the charcoal pan, the incense burner, the *kaṭacchu* spoon, and so forth.
"All" means whether they are small or large.
2860. The construction is: "The tambathālaka and ayathālaka vessels are to be divided. By the word *ca* (and), it is included as stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:

"Except for articles made from vessels, in other allowable metal utensils as well—such as a collyrium box, a collyrium stick, an ear-wick, a needle, a leaf-needle, a small pair of forceps, a small metal thorn, a key, a drum, a walking staff, and a piercing instrument—"

The phrase "one may trade" includes such items as a natthu-dāna (nose-bottle), a bhindi-vāla (bellows), a *lohakūṭa* (iron hammer), a *lohakuṭṭi* (iron chisel), a *lohaguḷa* (iron ball), a *lohapiṇḍi* (lump of iron), an *loharaṇī* (iron fire-drill), a *cakkalikaṃ* (wheel), and any other unfinished metalware.
"Smoke-pipe" (*dhūmanetta*) means a smoke-tube. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the following are included]:
sickles, lamps, tree-lamps, hanging lamps, wall-lamps, and images of women, men, and animals.

Furthermore, this includes all other items to be affixed to walls, ceilings, doors, and so forth—even down to a metal peg—as well as all metal articles, which are indeed "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*); thus it is said. 2861.
Regarding the phrase *attanā paṭiladdhaṃ*: here the particle *pi* is indicated by elision, meaning "even what has been obtained by oneself."
The meaning is as follows: the construction is that even that metal vessel which has been obtained by a bhikkhu himself must not be used in any way for personal consumption.
(2862) The construction is that vessels made of copper, brass, iron, or alloys thereof are also entirely forbidden from being used for personal consumption.
"By this same method" refers to the method shown by the passage beginning with "not for personal use. The construction is as follows:
there is no fault in using, for the purpose of consumption, items belonging to the Saṅgha or items belonging to householders, provided they are of the kind already mentioned. [It is said:

"Even if a vessel made of bronze, copper, or other materials has been given to the Saṅgha, it is not permitted to keep it as one's own personal property (*pārihārika*); it must be used only through the medium of a lay steward (*gihivikatanihārena*)."
This is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. And here, "borrowed" (pārihāriya) is not permitted; it is not allowed to take and consume it as if it were one's own property.

By the phrase "it should be consumed only by way of a householder’s gift," it is shown that if monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others have set it aside and returned it, it is permissible to consume it.
2864. *Khīrapāsāṇa* (milk-stone) refers to a soft species of stone. For it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā-gaṇṭhipada*:
“A milk-stone is a soft stone. *Garuka* means heavy goods. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), items such as *sarakas* (cups) are included.
A *ghaṭaka* is a vessel made specifically of milk-stone. By the phrase “above the ankle-height,” the [measure for] the ankle-grasper is indicated.
"He explains [the term] as 'agallochum merchandise.

He says this to show the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: 'Even vessels made of gold, silver, brass, bronze, or crystal that have been fashioned for household use are not permitted, let alone those used for the community (saṅgha) or for personal use.'"
“Siṅgī,” and so forth. *Siṅgī* means gold. *Sajjhu* means silver. *Hārakūṭa* is a type of metal that has the color of gold.
*Phalika-ubbhava* means produced from crystal; the meaning is a vessel made of crystal.

By the word “even” (*api*) in the phrase “even those belonging to householders,” it is indicated that these are not permitted even for use as articles of personal property belonging to householders, let alone for use by the Saṅgha or for individual private use.
He fans it or lights it. Regarding the use of lodgings, however, everything is permissible, whether it has been formally authorized (*āmāsa*) or not.
2866. "Small" refers to a small adze such that, having set it aside, one is unable to perform any other major work except for cutting tooth-sticks or stripping sugarcane;
such a small adze is to be shared. "Larger" refers to one of the dimensions previously described.
A chisel (*vāsi*) that is larger than [the standard] or made of any material whatsoever is a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*).
The phrase "and likewise the axe (*pharasu*) used by physicians for bloodletting is a heavy object" is how it should be construed.
Regarding the *kuṭhārī* (adze), the determination here is the same as for the *pharasu*. However, that which is fashioned as part of a weapon is [also considered a heavy object].
This is the *anāmāsā*. A pickaxe (*kudāla*) is even as small as four finger-breadths.
A *sikharaṇī* is a thorn for piercing wood and such materials, bent from a bowstring. "By that very [means]" means by the digging-in itself.
In order to show the various types of digging-in by dividing them up because they possess different forms, he said: "square-faced" and "scoop-mouthed."
*Doṇimukhaṃ* means having a mouth bent on both sides like a wooden trough (*doṇi*). *Vaṅkaṃ* means a toothpick made by bending it at the tip.
By the word *pi* (also), a straight one is included. *Tattha ca* means "and in that case," referring to that toothpick. The construction is:
"Every toothpick, whether with a handle or small, is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*). By these two qualifying terms, "with a handle" and "small," [the distinction is made].
A handleless fruit-spoon, a small box suitable for carrying, a broom-handle, a peg, and a small chisel are light articles;
however, it is shown that a large chisel, even if handleless, is a heavy article.
If those people by whom axes and such tools were given to the monastery have their houses burned or [plundered] by thieves...
If they say, "Venerable sir, give us back our requisites; we will restore them to their original state," they should be given.
If they bring them back, one should not prevent them; nor should those who do not bring them back be reproached.
[The following items belong to] smiths, weavers, coppersmiths, reed-workers, jewelers, bowl-binders, and the like: anvils, hammers, tongs, scales, and so forth.
All iron implements become "heavy goods" (garubhaṇḍa) from the moment they are given to the Saṅgha. The same principle applies to the tools of the tin-smelter, the goldsmith, and the leather-worker.
However, there is this distinction: among the tools of the tin-smelter, it is the knife for cutting tin;
among the tools of the goldsmith, it is the knife for cutting gold; and among the tools of the leather-worker, it is the small knife used for cutting prepared leather.

"These are articles that may be shared," he said, beginning with "a pair of tongs" (*muṭṭhika*) and so forth, in order to show a portion of the legal determination found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding the phrase "scales and so forth" (*tulādikam*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here includes instruments such as the large knife (*kattarī*) and other tools.
2870. "Even among the tools of barbers and tailors, setting aside the large knife, the large pair of scissors, and the large pincers..."
"Everything is subject to distribution. The large scissors and so forth are heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).

To show the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), he said "of the barber," and so forth. The construction is as follows: among the implements of a barber, the tweezers and the large scissors;
and among the implements of tailors, the large scissors and the large thimble-block (*mahāpipphalaka*) are heavy goods.
2871. Having thus shown the determination regarding the fourth heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*), he now says “creeper,” etc., in order to show the determination regarding the fifth heavy article.

The construction is as follows: a creeper such as a rattan vine (*vettalatā*) given to the Saṅgha in a place where it is difficult to obtain, or one grown there on the Saṅgha’s land, being protected or guarded, becomes a heavy article when it reaches the measure of half an arm-span.
"In 'half-arms' (aḍḍhabāhu), it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that it means from the elbow down to the shoulder blade.

Others say that 'half-arm' refers to a span of four finger-breadths. If that creeper remains after work has been done for the Saṅgha or for a shrine, it is permissible to use it for individual purposes.
However, if it is not protected [by being formally assigned], it does not constitute "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).

In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "Ropes or cords made of thread, cotton, coconut husk, or hide—whether made by twisting together thread, cotton, coconut husk, and hide into a single strand or a double strand—are considered heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*) from the time they are given to the Saṅgha.
However, if the thread is given without being twisted, and the cotton, cotton cloth, coconut husk, and hide are given [separately], they are common property (*bhājanīya*)."

To demonstrate the determination regarding what has been brought [to the monastery], he said: “Produced from bark-fiber, etc. By the word “etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of *makaci*-fiber, coconut-husk fiber, and leather.
A rope that is not too long is permissible; a cord that is excessively long is not. (2873) The construction is as follows:

even a single-strand cord made by winding it around coconut-husk fiber or *makaci*-fiber is considered heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*). However, those who have given these ropes, cords, and so forth, should not be prevented from taking them away for their own business.

2874. A bamboo eight finger-breadths long by the carpenter’s finger-measure, in circumference like the handle of a needle—measured by the handle of the writing-needle used by scribes in the island of Sīhaḷa—whether it has been given to the Saṅgha or is produced there, should be protected and guarded as a heavy article.
This is the construction [of the sentence]. "That which is the size of the tip of the little finger of a man of medium stature; this, in the island of Sīhaḷa..."

They say that this is the measure for the pens and needles of scribes. And when it has been used for the business of the Saṅgha or for work on a cetiya, it is permissible to give what remains as personal property. 2875.
*Daṇḍa* (staff) and *salākā* (slip) form the compound *daṇḍasalākā*; the analysis is "the staff and slips of an umbrella. Thus, *chattadaṇḍo*.
The name is *chattapiṇḍi*. "Umbrella ribs" refers to the ribs of the umbrella frame. "Staff" refers to the staff for sandals.

Although "staff" is stated as a general term, since it is not explicitly mentioned here among those items found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the staff for sandals alone must be understood through this general term by means of the method of elimination (*pārisesato*).
People who have taken goods from a house that has been burned and are leaving should not be stopped.

2876. Regarding "among *muñja* grass and so forth, which are suitable for roofing a house": any amount of grass even as small as a handful, or even a single palm leaf and such, that is suitable for roofing a house—if it has been given to the Saṅgha, or if it grows on land belonging to the Saṅgha—it should be understood as a "heavy article" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
In this context, "a handful" (*muṭṭhimatta*) means the measure of a *karaḷa*. And this [measure] is made by those who cover [the ground] using a *karaḷa*.

It should be understood by way of its function as a roof-covering. Regarding the phrase "palm leaves, etc.," the word "etc. includes the leaves of coconut trees and other such leaves used for house roofing.

Even that [material], when there is a surplus after it has been used for communal works (*saṅghakamma*) or work for a shrine (*cetiyakamma*), is permitted to be given for personal work (*puggalikakamma*).
When people take away [materials] from a burnt house, they should not be stopped.
"Measuring eight finger-breadths" means measuring exactly eight finger-breadths in length; some say it refers to the width.
"An empty book" means a book devoid of writing lines, that is to say, one that has not been written upon.

By the phrase "measuring eight finger-breadths," it is indicated that what is smaller than eight finger-breadths must be shared; by the phrase "an empty book," it is indicated that even what exceeds eight finger-breadths [is permissible].
This shows that the written manuscript is to be shared.
As for the clay— it may be natural clay, or five-colored clay, or lime, or whatever is difficult to obtain brought from elsewhere,
or given there, or produced locally, or protected and guarded— even if it is only as large as a ripe palm fruit.
To show the determination found in the commentaries regarding the phrase "it becomes a heavy object," he said "clay," and so forth.
The construction is: "clay" refers either to natural clay or to clay of five colors, such as white or ochre. "Resin" (sileso) refers to the resin of the *kapiṭṭha* tree and others;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *sajju*, *rasaka*, *kaṅguṭṭha*, and others is intended. "The size of a palm fruit" means even the size of a single-stone palm fruit. That too—
When work for the Saṅgha, such as with clay, or work for a cetiya has been completed, it is permissible to give what remains for personal work.

2879–80. The word division is “veḷuādikaṃ. The construction is as follows: by one taking what is protected or guarded, whether equal or more than that, it should be taken after giving something stable—even if only sand—of equivalent value.
However, in the Aṭṭhakathā it says: “By one taking a protected or guarded bamboo, [it should be taken] after giving something stable, whether equal or more...”
"At the very least, it must be accepted after performing an act of service (phātikamma) worth even a single grain of sand.
One who accepts it without performing an act of service should use it right there; when departing, he should leave it in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.

However, if one has departed having accepted it through forgetfulness, he must send someone back to give it [to the Saṅgha]. If he has gone to another country, he should leave it in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha upon reaching that residence."

This specific determination was stated regarding bamboo alone; however, since here it is said "any kind such as creepers or bamboo," and because creepers and so forth are mentioned collectively, it should be understood that this is merely an illustration, and the rule applies accordingly to creepers and other such materials as well. 2881.
*Añjana* means made of stone. The same applies to yellow orpiment (*harītāla*) and realgar (*manosilā*).

2882. This is the determination regarding wooden articles: any wooden article whatsoever, eight finger-breadths in length and having the circumference of the aforementioned needle-handle, which has been given to the Saṅgha in a place where wood is scarce, or which is produced there, and is protected and guarded, constitutes a "heavy article"—this is the construction [of the meaning].
2883. Having thus shown the determination as it appears in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, he says “the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*,” etc., in order to show what appears in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Therein, the seven components of the *āsandi* have the characteristics already stated.
“*Bhaddapīṭha*” refers to a seat made of cane. A “*pīṭhikā*” is simply a seat bound with strips of cloth.
2884. *Eḷakapādapīṭha* (the sheep’s-foot stool) refers to a stool made like a dining couch by placing the feet upon a wooden plank.
Regarding the term *āmalakavaṭṭakapīṭha*, *āmaṇḍakavaṭṭaka* is a synonym;
therefore, by either term, it refers to a multi-legged stool constructed in the shape of an *āmalaka* fruit. In some manuscripts—
The reading is “*tathā maṇḍaka-pīṭhakan*. The use of the word *maṇḍaka* is for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse.
A *koccha* (wicker stool) is of the form described in the fourth training rule (*sikkhāpada*) of the Bhūtagāma-vagga. A *palāla-pīṭha* is a straw mattress made for the purpose of lying down;
by this, stools made of plantain leaves and so forth are also indicated by way of illustration. As it has been said: “By means of a *palāla-pīṭha*...”
"And here, even seats made of plantain leaves and the like are included. Regarding "a board for washing," this refers to a board for washing robes;
there is an elision of the case-ending in words such as *dhovana* (washing) and so forth.

Among these items, whether they be small or large, anything given to the Saṅgha constitutes "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*). This includes even that which is covered with a tiger skin or adorned with the forms of predatory beasts.
A mat woven with jewels is indeed a valuable commodity. 2885.
*Bhaṇḍikā* refers to a bundle for cutting sticks and wood. *Muggara* means a staff-mallet.
A staff-mallet is that by which one beats dyed robes. *Vatthaghaṭṭanamuggara* is a mallet for smoothing or beating clothes.
By which they strike against the wind and so forth. *Ambaṇa* is a water vessel made with wooden planks, resembling a lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*).
A *mañjūsā* is a wooden box. A *nāvā* is a boat. A *rajanadoṇikā* is a dye-vat where one dyes robes or pours in liquid dye. 2886.
An *uḷuṅka* is a scoop made from coconut shells, wood, or similar materials. Both [types] are called *samugga* when they have a lid. "Small..."
They say that a *karaṇḍa* is a basket. Here, a *karaṇḍa* is intended as one larger than the size of a foot.
A *kaṭacchu* is a spoon. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of water-cups, water-strainers, and so forth.
