"Household requisites" (*gehasambhāra*) refers to household equipment. This includes wooden items such as pillars, beams, stair-rungs, and planks, as well as those made of stone.
This is already included by that [previous rule]. "Permissible hide" refers to the permissible hides shown below, such as those of sheep, goats, and deer;

by contrast, the opposite is impermissible. It is not to be shared because it is a heavy article (garubhaṇḍa). It is allowable to use it after having made it into a floor-covering. In the Commentary, it says:
"But a sheepskin falls under the category of a bed-covering, and that too is indeed a heavy article."
Because it has been so stated, he says: "The *eḷa*-skin is declared heavy. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is said: "Any skin the size of a bed is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*).
And here, by the phrase "it falls under the same category as a bedspread," he indicates that it is also permissible to spread it over beds and chairs.
Some say, "A bedspread such as a woolen rug (*pāvāra*) is also heavy property," while others say, "No"; one should investigate this.
It should be accepted. "The size of a bed" refers to a bed of appropriate proportions.
A bed of appropriate proportions is one that is nine spans (*vidatthi*) in length and half of that in width. "A mortar with a lid" means a mortar together with its cover.
By the word "etcetera," the pestle, winnowing basket, grindstone, small grindstone, stone trough, and stone basin are included. "Weavers and so forth..."
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of leather-workers and others is intended. The construction is as follows:

the weaver’s tools such as the spinning wheel and loom, the tanner’s tools such as the bellows, the farmer’s tools such as the yoke and plough, and so forth—when belonging to the Saṅgha, that is, owned by the Saṅgha, they constitute "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
(2889) By the phrase "in the same way," the term "belonging to the Saṅgha" (*saṅghika*) is referred back. A "stand" (*ādhāraka*) is a bowl-stand. A "palmyra fan" (*tālavaṇṭa*)...
It is made with palm-leaf fans (*tālavaṇṭa*). Even those made with bamboo, ivory, or reeds, or with peacock feathers, leatherwork, or similar materials, are likewise called "palm-leaf fans.

Since round fans are included within the category of palm-leaf fans, there are also square fans and fans made of *ketaka* shoots, *kuntāla* leaves, and so forth, as well as ivory fans with handles made of ivory, horn, or other materials.
And it is so called. A *pacchi* is well known. A small vessel made of palm leaves and the like used for cooking is a *caṅkoṭaka*.
"All brooms" refers to two kinds of brooms for sweeping the precincts and courtyards: the staff-broom bound with coconut husks and the like, and the hand-broom;
likewise, there are two kinds of house-sweeping brooms bound with dates, coconut leaves, and so forth.
And thus, all brooms are considered heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).
2890. "A vehicle equipped with wheels" refers to vehicles such as hand-pushed carts and so forth.
2891. "An umbrella" is of three kinds: made of leaves, made of *kilañja* grass, or a white umbrella. "A palm-leaf fan" refers to a fan made of *tāla* palm leaves.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is: "a horn vessel and a gourd vessel" (*visāṇabhājanañca tumbabhājanañca*);

it is a single-remainder compound (*ekadesasarūpekaseso*), and the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) occurs by virtue of the metrical structure of the verse. The meaning is: "a vessel made of horn and a vessel made of gourd. Here, the remainder is:
"exceeding the measure of what is taken for a foot-meal" (*pādagaṇhanakato atirittappamāṇaṃ*). "Araṇī" means a fire-drill together with its companion stick. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi-saddena*),...
It includes a vessel for *āmalaka* fruit and a staff permitted for use. "Light" refers to light articles; the meaning is that they are "to be shared.
Heavy articles are those exceeding the measure of what is permissible for holding in the hand.
2892. "Horn" refers to any horn whatsoever, such as a cow's horn and so forth. If it is untrimmed, it is to be shared exactly as it was received.
The construction is: "Whatever has not been finished, such as bed-legs and so forth, is 'to be shared' (*bhājanīya*). As it was said:

"Bed-legs, bed-frames, chair-legs, chair-frames, and the handles of axes, hatchets, and so forth—among these, anything for which the planing work is unfinished is indeed 'not finished' and must be shared;
however, once planed and polished, it becomes 'heavy property' (*garubhaṇḍa*)."
2893. "Finished" (*niṭṭhita*) or "carved" (*tacchita*): this refers also to what is finished by being carved. "Straps" (*vidha*) refers to the straps permitted for binding the waist.
"Chest for asafoetida" (*hiṅgukaraṇḍaka*) means a chest made of asafoetida or a chest used as its container. "Ointment box" (*añjanī*) refers both to the tube for ointment and the box for ointment.
"Stick" (*salākā*) refers to the applicator stick for ointment. "Water-wiper" (*udapuñchanī*) refers to a water-wiping cloth made from elephant tusks, horns, and so forth.
All of this is indeed subject to distribution.
"Fit for use" means suitable for the enjoyment and utilization of human beings. "Pottery" refers even to the wares of a potter, such as jars, cooking pots, and the like.
"A bowl, a charcoal pan, and a brazier" refers to a bowl-pan and a charcoal-pan. "Smoke-vessel" is a tube. "Shell" refers to a lamp-shell.
2895. *Thūpikā* refers to the spires of palaces and the like. *Dīparukkha* means a lamp-stand.
*Cayanacchadaniṭṭhakā* refers both to the bricks for the construction of ramparts, shrines, and so forth, and to the roof-tiles for houses and the like.
*Sabbampi* means all the aforementioned requisites without exception.
2896. *Kañcanakoti-sarako*: A *ghaṭaka* (water-pot) that is not larger than the size of one who can grasp it with both hands is a *ghaṭakoti*.
To include the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, which states, "Just as with earthenware vessels, so too with metal vessels, the *kuṇḍikā* belongs to the category of those that may be shared," he said:
"And among metal vessels, the *kuṇḍikā* is also to be shared."
2897. "Heavy" refers to the latter three heavy articles. "Stable" refers to the first two. "Of the Saṅgha" means by the Saṅgha.
"Having exchanged" means having exchanged with those [articles] belonging to individuals and so forth that are of a similar nature. In this regard, the method of exchange is as follows:
the Saṅgha’s coconut grove is located at a distance; the attendants (kappiyakārakas) consume most of it; therefore, [one may exchange it for] the price of a cart.

Having given it, they bring back only a small portion. However, if there is a monastery near a village inhabited by people belonging to another [monastery], and those people approach the Saṅgha and request that monastery using their own monastery as the basis for the gift, it should be accepted by the Saṅgha after obtaining the formal consent with the words, “It is pleasing to the Saṅgha.
Even if there are a thousand trees belonging to the monks...
There are five hundred people; therefore, it should not be said, "Is your monastery not small?
For although this one is small, it nevertheless yields more income than the other.
Even if it yields exactly the same amount, it must still be accepted, because it is possible to enjoy it whenever one desires.
But if there are more trees belonging to the people, one should say, "Are not your trees more numerous?
If they say, "May our merit be greater; we give them to the Saṅgha," it is permissible to accept them after making this known.
The trees belonging to the bhikkhus bear fruit, whereas the trees belonging to the people have not yet taken fruit.
Even if they do not take [the fruit] now, one must certainly accept it with the thought: "In no long time they will take it.
Trees bear fruit for human beings, yet the bhikkhus have not yet taken the fruit. One should say: "Do your trees not bear fruit?
If they say, "Take them, venerable sir; it will be a merit for us," then having made them understand, [one may take them].
It is permissible to accept [the exchange]. In this way, a monastery (ārāma) may be exchanged for a monastery.

By this same method, a monastery site (ārāmavatthu), a monastery building (vihāra), or a monastery site for a monastery building may be exchanged for a monastery. And by means of a large or small monastery site, [one may exchange] monasteries, monastery sites, monastery buildings, or monastery sites for monastery buildings.
How should one dwelling be exchanged for another dwelling? Suppose the Saṅgha has a house within a village, while people have a palace in the middle of the monastery;
if both are equal in value, and the people request that house in exchange for the palace, it is permissible to accept.
If the monks' house is of greater value, [they should say]: "It is of greater value..."
When they say, "It is our house," and [the monks] reply, "Even though it is more costly, it is unsuitable for those who have gone forth;
it is not possible for renunciants to live there, but this one is suitable, so please take it," it is permissible to accept it even in that way.
However, if it is very expensive for people, [one should say], "Is it not your own house?"...
"It should be said, 'It is very costly. But when it is said, 'Let it be so, venerable sir; let there be merit for us; please accept it,' then it is permissible to accept it.
In this way, one monastery should be exchanged for another monastery.
By this same method, a monastery site, a park, or a park site should also be exchanged for a monastery. And by means of a monastery site..."
Whether of great value or small value, [one may exchange] dwellings, dwelling sites, monasteries, or monastery sites. Thus, first, the exchange of durable goods for durable goods is to be understood.
Furthermore, regarding the exchange of heavy goods for heavy goods, as for a bed or a chair, whether it be large or small—
Even if it is as small as a four-finger-high footstool made by village children playing with sand-houses, from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha, it becomes "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).

Even if kings, royal ministers, and others should offer a hundred or a thousand beds all at once, all the allowable beds (kappiyamañca) should be accepted; having accepted them, [they should be distributed].
They should be given according to seniority with the instruction, "Use them for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha," and not on an individual basis.
It is also permissible to arrange extra beds in storehouses and such places and deposit one's bowl and robes there.
A bed given outside the monastery boundary with the words, "We give this to the Saṅgha," should be placed in the residence of the senior monk of the Saṅgha. Therein...

If there are many beds, but no work to be done with the bed, then it should be given [to someone] where there is work in their place of residence, saying, "Use this as the Sangha’s property for consumption.
If one obtains another hundred beds in exchange for a single bed worth a high price—whether worth a hundred [coins] or a thousand—one may take them after bartering. This applies not only to a bed.
A bed itself, as well as a garden or its site, a monastery or its site, a bench, a couch, and a pillow, may be exchanged.
This same method applies to benches, couches, and pillows; for among these, what is allowable and what is unallowable is exactly as stated in the previous rule.
Among them, that which is unallowable must not be used, while that which is allowable may be used through communal ownership by the Saṅgha.
Having exchanged what is improper or of great value for what is proper, the aforementioned items are to be taken;
however, there is no such thing as a mattress or pillow made of non-weighty materials.
2898. The connection is that a bhikkhu should not approach a lodging with an unwashed foot or a wet foot. They lie down...
Here, "and there is sitting" refers to the bed and seat (*sayanāsana*), such as a rug spread upon a prepared floor.
"Or with wet feet" means with such drenched feet by which water is visible at the place where one has stepped. As it is said:
"With wet feet means with such feet by which water is visible at the place where one has stepped; [this applies to] a floor that has been plastered or a lodging."
"Or it should not be stepped upon. But if only the moisture of the water is visible, and no water itself, it is permissible.
Regarding the phrase "one with sandals," one should say "one who has washed his feet. The construction is as follows:
a bhikkhu wearing sandals fastened to his feet does not step upon a place where he ought to step with washed feet—that is, a place designated for washing the feet—in that same manner.
"2899. 'By one who has prepared [the surface]' means by one who has prepared it with plaster and so forth. 'Of one who spits' means of one who lets saliva fall.
'A wall that has been prepared' means a white-plastered wall or a wall decorated with painting. And it is not only a wall;
it also includes a door, a window, a wooden ledge, a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar."
If one has not covered [the bed] with a robe or anything else, it is certainly not permitted to lie down upon it.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "Furthermore, doorways, windows, and so forth—even if they have not been finished—must not be used as a support for lying down if they are not covered.

(2901) The construction is as follows: if, while someone is sleeping, any part of their body suddenly touches the bed because the bedding has become compressed, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

2902. When the bedding touches the body, it is permissible to step upon it with the palms of the hands and feet; this is the construction [of the rule]. If the bed or chair strikes against the body of one who is removing it, there is no offense.

Regarding the statement in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Sīhaḷagaṇṭhipada*: "There is no fault for one who uses a lodging place or a bed, chair, and so forth, given by donors with the instruction, 'Use it at your pleasure after touching it with your body,' in accordance with the conditions specified by the donor."
Because it has been so stated, there is no offense for one who uses it in that manner.
When it is said, "I give this bed, chair, and so forth to the Saṅgha," it becomes a heavy article (garubhaṇḍa) and must not be distributed, because it has been dedicated to the Saṅgha as a whole.
When it is said, "I give this bed, chair, and so forth for the Vassa-portion of the venerable ones to take," although it remains a heavy article, it is a permissible object (kappiyavatthu).
It is permissible to take [an item] after it has been distributed; however, one may not take an unallowable article (akappiya-bhaṇḍa) even after it has been distributed.
When it is said, "I give this bed and chair to the Saṅgha to be taken according to seniority (vassaggena)," it should be taken after being distributed by seniority.
This is because the distribution by seniority was mentioned first, whereas the gift to the Saṅgha was mentioned afterwards. [When it is said: "I give this to the Saṅgha..."

However, when it is said, "I give this bed and chair to be taken according to the *vassa* [rain-retreat] seniority," it becomes a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*) because it was first handled by the Saṅgha;
this distinction is also stated only in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentary on the *Mātikā*.
To show one part of the analysis regarding the distribution of meals (*uddesabhatta*), he says, "worth a thousand," and so forth. Worth a thousand...
If almsfood together with robes has been received by a bhikkhu who has passed sixty years, and it has also been recorded and kept in that monastery with the inscription,
"Such almsfood together with robes has been received by a bhikkhu who has passed sixty years," then, after the lapse of sixty years,
if any such almsfood worth a thousand [pieces] together with robes should arise, that almsfood—
The construction is as follows: "A wise monk skilled in legal decisions, instead of giving [the robe] with a sixty-year standing, should give it with a ten-year standing.
(2905) "Having eaten the designated meal" means having consumed the designated meal obtained according to one's own seniority at the time of full ordination.
"If he has become a novice" means if, by way of renouncing the training or other such causes, he has become a novice.

"Those" refers specifically to that *uddesabhatta* (food for recitation) received at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*). "In the sequence of the novices" means he is permitted to take his own bowl later, following the order of the novices.
2906. That novice who is twenty years of age and is to be told, "Tomorrow you will receive the recitation," today...

The construction is: "He has received full ordination (*upasampanna*), and the period of standing [as a novice] may have passed. The meaning is that because he was ordained today, the period of standing as a novice (*sāmaṇera-ṭhitikā*)—which was to be completed tomorrow—has been exceeded;
thus it is said that he does not receive that meal. 2907. Immediately after the meal by distribution (*uddesabhatta*), he says "But if...
and so forth, in order to show the meal by tickets (*salākabhatta*). If the ticket...

The construction is as follows: having received [food] on that day, if no meal was obtained, one must take his meal on the following day; there is no doubt—no such doubt as "should it be taken or should it not be taken? should be entertained. (2908) *Uttaribhaṅga*:

that which has a further (*uttara*) or additional (*atireka*) solid food (*bhaṅga*) or curry (*byañjana*) is *uttaribhaṅga*; the meaning is "of that additional curry. *Ekacarassa*: of one who goes alone (*ekacārika*). *Salākikā*: just like a voting-stick (*salākā*).
2909. *Uttaribhaṅgameva* means simply *uttaribhaṅgaka*. 2910. *Yena yena hi*:

by whichever [monk] means by whichever monk who has taken a voting stick (*salāka*). *Yaṃ yaṃ*: among the food and the curry, whichever food or whichever curry. 2911. *Saṅghuddesādikam*: such as the meal for the Saṅgha, the designated meal (*uddesabhatta*), and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the five types of meals are included: the invitation meal (*nimantana*), the voting-stick meal (*salāka*), the fortnightly meal (*pakkhika*), the Uposatha meal (*uposathika*), and the meal on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipadika*).
Therein, that which is given to the entire Saṅgha is called *saṅghabhatta* (food for the Saṅgha).
That which is given after saying, "Designate so many bhikkhus from the Saṅgha and give [it] to them," and so forth, is *uddesabhatta* (designated food).

That which is given after saying, "Take food for so many bhikkhus from the Saṅgha," and so forth, is called *nimantana* (an invitation). [This applies to] those who distribute voting tickets by their respective names.
What is given to the bhikkhus is called *salākabhatta*. What is given on the fourteenth day is *pakkhika* (fortnightly).

What is given on the Uposatha day is *uposathika*. What is given on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*) is *pāṭipadika*. It is designated by whatever name it is given under that specific title.

The detailed explanation of these, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) beginning with the words, "In the case of those specifically designated," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "for guests, etc.": here, by the word "etc.," three types of meals are included—meals for those departing, meals for the sick, and meals for those attending the sick.
A meal given to guests is a "guest-meal" (*āgantuka-bhatta*). The same method applies to the remaining two.

(2912) "Monastery" (*vihāra*) refers to a "monastery-meal" (*vihāra-bhatta*) through the elision of the final member of the compound; this is a designation for a meal provided specifically for that purpose within the monastery.
*Vārabhatta* (turn-taking food) is that which, during a time of famine, is given starting from the primary household with the thought, "We shall take turns looking after the monks.
*Nicca* (regular) refers to regular food (*niccabhatta*), by dropping the final member of the compound; this too is given only after having spoken in that manner.
*Kuṭibhatta* (hut-food) is that which is given after a dwelling has been built for the Saṅgha, with the thought, "May those who reside in our lodging take our food."
All fifteen kinds of food have been pointed out and explained here in this section on lodgings (*senāsanakkhandhaka*).
Those who desire a detailed analysis should consult the *Samantapāsādikā*.

In order to instruct regarding the distribution of requisites, saying that one must practice with diligence because there is great danger in wrong conduct concerning the distribution of requisites, he said: "The text," and so forth.
Exposition of the Chapter on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka-kathāvaṇṇanā). Exposition of the Chapter on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka-kathāvaṇṇanā) 2914–5.
The newcomer, the resident, the alms-gatherer, the lodging, the forest-dweller, and the expression of appreciation.

The analysis [of the compound] is: *viggaho*, *tāsu vattāni*. Because the gender of a *itaretarayoga-dvanda* compound follows the gender of its final member (*uttarapada*), this is specified as feminine.

In the phrase *bhatte bhattagge*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final member. The word "duties" (*vattāni*) should be construed individually with each of the terms beginning with "in the meal" (*bhatte*). The analysis is:
"the duties of the teacher (*ācariya*), the preceptor (*upajjhāyaka*), the student (*sisso*), and the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihāriko*). Regarding the word "all" (*sabba*):

"By all the divisions of the parts. "Only fourteen" means that although the discourses (*vattāni*) are of many kinds due to the divisions of their parts, they are stated to be exactly fourteen according to the division of their subject matter (*visaya*).
"With a purified mind" means with a mental continuum that is utterly pure due to the abandonment of all defilements (*saṃkilesa*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

"By the Leader" (*vināyaka*): he is a leader because he leads beings; by virtue of being the unsurpassed charioteer of persons to be tamed, [he leads] the gods, Brahmas, *nāgas*, and so forth who are to be tamed.

The meaning is that he tames beings by means of various methods of discipline. Alternatively, *vināyaka* means one whose leader (*nāyaka*) has departed; [he tames them] by that means. 2916. Regarding the word *ārāma*:

here, the designation for the vicinity is applied to the object itself. As it is said: "Now, by the phrase 'I shall enter the monastery' (*ārāma*), he indicates the vicinity of the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*);
therefore, having reached the precinct boundary, all such acts as the removal of sandals must be performed."
The word division is: “*pana apanetabbaṃ*. “*Muñcitabbā*” means that the sandals must be removed from the feet. 2917.

“*Oguṇṭhanaṃ*” refers to covering oneself with a hood or wearing a robe over the head. The connection is: “one must not do so on the head,” or simply “the robe itself [must not be worn] on the head. “*Tenā*” means by the visiting monk. “*Pānīyavārinā*” means by the water to be drunk. 2918.
“*Pucchitvā*” means having asked about the calculation of the years of seniority (*vassa-gaṇanā*). By the visiting monk, [regarding] the elder monk in the monastery...
They must indeed be saluted. "At the proper time" means at the very early hour. The construction is: that incoming bhikkhu should ask regarding the lodging, "Which lodging falls to me?
(2919) The word "should be asked" is to be construed individually with each of the accusative-case nouns beginning with "the place for excrement."

It should be applied. "Only drinking water" means: according to the method found in the Aṭṭhakathā, [one should ask] whether they drink only the drinking water of this lotus pond, or whether they also utilize it for bathing and so forth; likewise for "water for use. "The agreement of the Saṅgha" means:
"In some places there are wild beasts or non-human beings; therefore, at what time should one enter, and at what..."
And the formal agreement (*katika*) made with the Saṅgha according to the method found in the Aṭṭhakathā, [to the effect that] "one must go out at the proper time.
Regarding "the alms-round and so forth": here, "the alms-round" refers to the manner described as: "The alms-round should be asked about: 'Is the village for alms near or far?
And should one go for alms early in the morning or not?'—thus the practice of begging for food should be asked about. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other matters are included].
“An improper resort (agocara) has been taken. Regarding “improper resort,” it refers to a village of those with wrong views, or a village where alms are restricted;
even a village where only one or two [persons] give alms must be questioned—this is according to the method stated.

Having thus shown the conduct for a guest, he now says “the elder,” etc., in order to show the conduct for a resident. The construction is: “having gone out to meet him, the bowl and the robe should be received. The word “and” (ca) is indicated as being elided.
“Of him” means of the guest. “And water for the feet”: by the word “and,” it is included that a footstool—whereon washed and unwashed feet may be placed—and a foot-scraper should be set out.
“And he should be asked for water”: when asking for drinking water, if he drinks all the water brought once, [the host should think], “I shall bring more.”
"He should be asked," according to the method stated, he should be asked for water. And here, by the word "and" (ca), it is implied:

"Furthermore, he may also be fanned with a fan; while fanning, having fanned once on the instep of the foot, once in the middle [of the body], and once on the head, when told 'Enough,' he should fan more gently than before. Again, when told 'Enough'..."
After he has spoken, one should fan him more gently than before. After he has spoken for the third time, the fan should be set aside.
His feet should also be washed; having washed them, if one has oil of one’s own, they should be anointed with it.
If not, they should be anointed with what belongs to him.”
He includes those who have completed their training and those who are still training. 2922–3. “One should pay homage”: a newly arrived senior monk should be paid homage.
“One should assign [a dwelling]”: when asked, “Where does my lodging fall? one should assign a lodging, saying, “This lodging falls to you.”

The meaning is: "It should be explained in this way. Regarding the word "to be told" (*vattabbo*), it should be applied individually by substituting each term—such as "inhabited" (*ajjhāvuttha*) and "uninhabited" (*avuttha*)—according to their respective gender and number.

"Inhabited" (*ajjhāvuttha*) refers to the state of a designated dwelling having been first occupied by monks. "Or uninhabited" (*avutthaṃ vā*) refers to the state of that [dwelling] not having been occupied by monks during the robe-season (*cīvarakāla*).
Or. The "proper and improper range" has already been explained.
"Families of those in training" refers to families that have received the designation (*sammuti*) of being for those in training (*sekha*).

"The time for entering and departing" has the same meaning as what was stated here under the heading "the Sangha’s agreement. "Water for drinking, etc."—by the word "etc.," items such as water for rinsing and walking sticks are included.
Explaining [the Dhamma] brings them together.
2924. "Sitting right where one is" means sitting in the very place where oneself is seated. "Of him" refers to the junior monk.
2925. "Place your bowl here; sit on this seat"—in this manner, everything [should be done].
The word *vattabbaṃ* (should be stated) is to be construed [with the following]. "And the lodging (*senāsana*) should also be given": the lodging must be provided.
By the word *ca* ("and"), it includes what was stated in the passage beginning with "it should be pointed out whether it is unoccupied or already occupied.
Even in a large monastery, it is not permissible for one who has arrived to fail to perform the duties toward a guest who has come into one's presence.
2926. Someone might think: "Should the observances (*vatta*) be performed according to the order indicated in the *mātikā*, or rather according to the order of their occurrence?

To show that there is no fixed rule that they must be performed according to the order of the *mātikā*—that they should instead be performed according to the order of their occurrence—the observance for those going on a journey (*gamika-vatta*) was begun without regard for the order of the *mātikā*.
Alternatively, it is because the desire to perform the observances follows a specific sequence.
It should be understood that this exposition has been made according to one’s own preference, without following the sequence of the matrix (mātikā) for the application of terms.
"Wooden articles and earthenware" refers to items such as beds and chairs, as well as dye-vessels. "Having put away" means having placed them in a secure location.
"Having bolted the dwelling" means having closed the doors and panels of the dwelling.
"Even after taking leave" means having handed over [the bedding] to a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or an ārāmika, saying, "Look after this.
"Even when there is no one to ask" (*pucchitabbe asante pi*): here the word *pi* has the sense of the word *pana*.
"Or even by guarding it well" means according to the method described in such passages as, "having prepared a bed on four stones, and having placed bed upon bed," and so forth.
The construction is: "Having properly put away [the bowl], one should go.
(2928) To show the conduct for one who goes for alms, he said "sahasā" and so forth. A bhikkhu going for alms, when entering among the houses, should not enter hastily;
he should not enter quickly. When departing, he should not depart hastily; he should not depart quickly.
He should not go out; he should enter and go out in a manner befitting a bhikkhu.
When a bhikkhu wandering for alms has arrived at the door of a house, he should not stand too far away, nor should he stand in a place too close to the threshold.
He should not stand too near, nor should he stand in a place closer than the threshold.
"Having held out" means having extended [the bowl]. "A vessel" means a bowl (*patta*). "Having inclined with the right hand" means having extended it with the right hand.
Regarding "one should receive alms-food," the remainder here is "having received it with both hands.
As it has been said: "The alms-food should be received by receiving the bowl with both hands."
2930. Whether she wishes to give soup or does not wish to give it, he should observe her for a moment and wait. "In between" means at the time of giving alms.
"Not [staring at] the giver of alms" means that whether it be a woman or a man, one must not look at their face at the time of receiving alms.

2931. Having shown the duties regarding alms-gathering (*piṇḍacārika-vatta*), he spoke the words beginning with "water and so forth" (*pānīyādi*) in order to show the duties regarding forest-dwelling (*āraññika-vatta*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the requisites for use (*paribhojanīya*), fire, a water-strainer, and a walking stick (*kattarayaṭṭhi*). Herein is the analysis:
"Water should be provided"—if there are not enough vessels, then the water itself [serves as] the requisites for use as well.
Having prepared it, one should maintain it. If one cannot obtain a vessel, one should maintain it even with a bamboo tube.
If even that is unavailable, one should act so that there is a small pit nearby. When fire-sticks are not available, it is also permissible not to make a fire.
And just as it is for a forest-dweller, so too for one traveling through a wilderness, [fire-sticks] should be maintained.
It should be desired. However, for one living in a community, it is permissible even without that [knowledge].
Regarding the phrase "the lunar mansion," the connection is that the twenty-seven kinds of lunar mansions, such as Assayuja and so forth, should be known. To the question "How should they be known?
he says, "And the conjunction with that," meaning that the conjunction of the moon with that lunar mansion should be known.
“And the directions should be known”: one dwelling in the forest should know even the eight directions without confusion.
To show another practice, he says: “The sites for excrement and urine,” and so forth. “They occur in succession” means they are to be used according to the order in which they are encountered.
As it is said: “In the latrine, at the place for urine, and at the bathing ford—in these three... [and so on].

"The measure is simply according to the order in which they arrived. "One who acts according to seniority" means one who acts according to the order of seniority rather than the order in which they arrived.
2933. One entering the restroom should not enter hastily. "Having lifted up" means having raised the robe.
2934. The construction is: "A monk should not defecate while sneezing. [This is said] because of the difficulty of escaping from the excrement.
"If one has been afflicted and then lets out a yawn, there is no fault," as stated in the *Sikkhābhājanavinicchaya*.
The construction is: "For a monk who defecates while chewing a wooden stick (*daṇḍakaṭṭha*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
2936. "With something harsh" means with something rough, or with a split piece of wood, or with a knot, or with a thorn, or with a hollow.
One should not scrape or wipe with a stick that is either dirty or putrid. "One should not throw a stick into the latrine pit" means one should not discard that stick in the latrine pit.
"One should not spit into the urine vessel" is the construction [of the rule].

2937. "In the sandals" means in the sandals used for defecation and urination. "At the time of departure" means at the moment of leaving. "Right there" means right there in the sandals used for defecation and urination. "One should cover oneself" means that having lowered the robe that was lifted up, one should cover the body.

2938. The construction is as follows: "If one, having defecated, does not rinse oneself when water is available, nor performs the necessary water-rite, for him a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) is declared.

By the Sage, the All-Knowing One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has eradicated by means of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*)—which abandons delusion together with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) and, along with that, all defilements that are to be abandoned simultaneously with it—the [taints] have been destroyed.
By the phrase “*sati udake*,” he demonstrates that there is no fault when [water] is absent. As it is said:
“Regarding ‘*sati udake*’: here, if water exists but there is no concealed place, one should rinse after having carried it out in a vessel.
If a vessel is not available, it should be carried out in a bowl. If even a bowl is not available, [and water is] absent...”

It is called "nāma. [The rule states: "If one goes thinking, 'This is too shallow; there will be another body of water ahead,' and the time for the alms-round arrives before finding water, one may go after wiping [the bowl] with a stick or something similar; it is permissible to eat and to give the blessing (anumodana).
2939. "With sound" means making a sound in the water. "If, having struck a place such as a rock, the water makes a sound..."
“There is no fault,” as stated in the *Sikkhābhājanavinicchaya*. The construction is: “Having made such an imitation sound as ‘capu capū ti ca,’ one should not rinse the mouth.

“Having rinsed” means having performed the water-rite. “One should not leave water remaining in the saucer, which is the vessel for rinsing the mouth”—this, however, is said with reference to a place common to all. As it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: [text follows].
“Regarding the phrase ‘at the place for rinsing water’ (ācamanasarāvake), this is said with reference to a place used in common by all. For there, various people come and go;

therefore, one must not leave any water remaining. However, it is permissible in a place that has been set aside within even a communal monastery (saṅghika-vihāra) for the purpose of being visited regularly, or in a private place (puggalika-ṭhāna). After drinking a purgative, again and again...”
"It is indeed permissible even for one entering [the village]. 2940.
"Even if it has been rubbed away" means a place defiled by impurity that has been rubbed away either by another or by oneself unintentionally.
"Without washing" means that if water is available, one should not wash; if water is not available, one should go after wiping it with wood or some other material. As it has been said:
“There is water but no vessel—this is called ‘non-existent. There is a vessel but no water—this too is non-existent.
When both are absent, it is simply non-existent; one should go after sweeping with a stick or something similar.
Regarding “if they are cluttered,” this means if the places for excrement and urine are strewn with refuse. “They must be cleared out completely” means...
This shows that the removal of some refuse from there does not constitute "cleansing"; rather, cleansing is defined as the removal of all refuse without exception.
2941. *Piṭhara* is a vessel for placing the scraping-stick. *Kumbhī ce rittā*: if the rinsing-pot (*ācamanakumbhī*) is empty. 2942.
Having thus shown the etiquette regarding the latrine, he says "unasked," etc., in order to show the etiquette regarding the lodging. *Anajjhiṭṭho*: unpermitted.

2943. The construction is: "having asked permission of an elder, while speaking. Regarding "if an even more senior one arrives": this refers to when there is the arrival of a monk who is even more senior than the one whom he had asked permission from before beginning to speak.
2944. "In a single dwelling" means in one house. The term "without asking permission" should be applied as appropriate to the rules that will be explained below. 2945.
First, the duty to be performed in the presence of elders, regardless of where they may be, has been indicated; now—

In order to show that this must be done even by one living in a solitary dwelling, he further said, "And the Dhamma should not be preached. By the phrase "with the eye of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhunā*), he means with the vision of the Dhamma and with reverence for the Dhamma;
by this, he indicates that an occasion provided by one who is not such as this would be fruitless. (2946) "It should be made" means it should be kindled.
"That" refers to the lamp. Since a "gate" (*dvāra*) is a place of great traffic, therefore, in that regard—
Since it is said, "there is no need for the duty of asking permission," he did not mention that, but spoke instead to show the field of offenses:
"Should he close or open the window shutters?

(2947). "He should turn away from the elder" means he should turn away from where the elder is; the meaning is that he should turn away facing the elder without showing his back. Nor should he touch that elder with the hem of his robe or with his body.

2948. Having thus shown the rules of conduct regarding lodgings (*senāsanavatta*), he spoke the words beginning with "in front" (*purato*) in order to show the rules of conduct regarding the bathhouse (*jantāgharavatta*).
One should not bathe in front of the elders; nor should one bathe upstream. As for those who are descending, one who is ascending should yield the path to the elders;
one should not strike them, whether with the body or with the robe—this is how the construction is to be understood.

Because the rules of conduct for the dining hall (*bhattagga-vatta*)—stated in the manner beginning with, “Having dressed in a circular robe so as to cover the three circles, and having fastened the waist-band,” etc.—are spoken of in the section on the training rules (*sekhiya-kathā*), and because the rules of conduct for the preceptor (*upajjhāya-vatta*) and others are spoken of in the *Mahākhandhaka*, [the Buddha said]:
“I allow you, monks, in the dining hall... [regarding the rules of thanksgiving].

Because they are included within the duties of the meal hall (*bhattagga-vatta*) by way of the method beginning with, "Let [the meal] be approached by four or five senior and junior monks," these are not mentioned in the *Niddesa*;
nevertheless, among those [duties], the duty of giving thanks (*anumodana-vatta*) should be understood as follows:
when the Sangha’s senior elder is seated for the purpose of giving thanks, the [other] four should sit in the row below him.
When the junior elder is seated, the three below him should sit; when the fifth is seated, the four above him should sit.
Even if the junior bhikkhu is requested by the senior of the Sangha to sit below, the four should still sit starting from the senior of the Sangha.
However, if the bhikkhu who offers the thanksgiving says, "Venerable sirs, you may go..."
If he says, "There is no business for me to wait for," it is permissible to go. If the Great Elder says, "Let us go, friend," and [the other] says, "Go," it is likewise permissible.

Even if one has made the intention, "We shall wait outside the village," and having gone outside the village, tells those dependent on him, "You should wait for his arrival," it is still permissible to go.

It is indeed permissible. However, if people have someone perform the thanksgiving (anumodanā) according to their own preference, there is no offense for the one performing the thanksgiving, nor does it become a burden for the Great Elder (mahāthera).
For while the people are conversing during the seated discussion itself, the Great Elder should be informed, and he should wait only when requested by the Great Elder to perform the thanksgiving.
"This is the characteristic here.

(2949) "They practice" means they perform the aforementioned conduct pertaining to higher morality (*ābhisamācārika-vatta*). As it is said: "It is impossible that one who has not fulfilled the conduct pertaining to higher morality will fulfill virtue (*sīla*).

"Does not find" means does not obtain. (2950) "One-pointedness" refers to a mind that is not concentrated precisely because of its distracted state. "And does not see" means he does not see with the eye of knowledge; the meaning is that he is not capable of seeing. "From suffering" means from the suffering of birth and so forth.

2951. Therefore, because one is not liberated from suffering [otherwise], for that reason it was said: "Having followed the instruction of the Best of Buddhas, one will go to Nibbāna. "Ehiti" means "will reach" or "will attain.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Khandhaka on the Rules of Conduct (Vatta-khandhaka). Commentary on the Discourse on the Khandhaka on the Nuns (Bhikkhunī-khandhaka).
2952. Having opened [the robe] means having uncovered it. 2953.

"Engaging in anything whatsoever" means performing any kind of improper conduct (*anācāra*). "From that" means by means of that which is termed improper conduct, namely, unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*). "Speaking" means speaking with words. 2954–6.
"Long" means long from one end to the other. "With *vilīva* beads and bands" means even with fine *vilīva* beads.
"By means of a bandage": by means of a leather bandage (*cammapaṭṭena*)—that is, a bandage made of hide. "By means of a cloth bandage" (*dussapaṭṭena*): by means of a white cloth.
"By means of a cloth-woven cord" (*dussaveṇiyā*): by means of a cord knotted with cloth. "By means of a cloth coil" (*dussavaṭṭiyā*): by means of a coil made of cloth.

"The sides should not be bent" means that, for the sake of thinning the middle part, they should not be bent like those of a village girl. "The hips" (*jaghana*) refers to the region of the urinary organ.
“With bones, etc. means with the knee-bones of an ox, and so forth. “Should not cause to be rubbed” means she should not cause it to be struck. This phrase “with bones, etc.
is to be connected both with the verb “should not cause to be rubbed” and with the verb “causes to be pounded.

2957. “Causes to be pounded” is to be construed individually with each of the accusative case endings beginning with “the hand,” and so forth. “The hand” means the upper arm. “The back of the hand” means the back of the hand. “The foot” means the lower leg.
2958. “One must not smear the face” means that one must not apply various kinds of smearing agents, such as ground sesame, mustard, or myrobalan, which serve to brighten the complexion.
“One must not powder it” means that one must not apply facial powder. The construction is:
“For one who smears her face with red arsenic (manosilā), there may be an offense.”
2959. "No bodily ointment should be applied" means that the natural color of the skin should not be altered with turmeric, saffron, or similar substances.
"And no mark on the face should be made" means that one should not apply collyrium by drawing lines outside the corners of the eyes.
"No decorative mark should be made" means that one should not draw a decorative mark (*visesaka*) in the form of various patterns on the cheeks.
"Olokanaka" means from a window. "Rāga" means by way of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Oloketaṃ" means to look out across the street; the construction is:
"one should not stand in a place where there is light. In a place with light, one should not stand opening the door and showing half the body. "Sanacca" refers to a theatrical performance.

2961. For one who ordains a *gaṇikā* (prostitute), for one who ordains a *vesī* (courtesan). The word "selling" (*vikiṇantiyā*) should be construed individually with each of the accusative-case words beginning with "liquor" (*sura*).
2963. "And he must not be made to serve" means that one must not cause him to perform personal service.
Even if he is an animal, whether a male or female slave, or even an animal, or a laborer—he must not be made to serve; nor indeed [must one make] oneself... [serve].
He should be made to perform services. By the word "api" (even), it is indicated that this applies all the more so when he is a human being.
2964. By the phrase "all-blue and so forth," [it refers to]:
"All-blue, best-maṅjeṭṭha, black, red, and yellow;"
"In the *Mahānāma-mahāraṅga-ratta-sutta*," thus it is said;
the unallowable robes (*akappiya-cīvara*) are included therein. Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "What is called a *namataka* is made from sheep's wool, not woven;
it should be used for the purpose of using a piece of hide," and because in the *Gaṇṭhipada* it says: "It is similar to a rug (*santharaṇa*)."
And because it is stated, "a specific requisite made from cloth-pieces," that which is to be used for reclining—a specific requisite called a *namataka*—[is prohibited]. 2965.
For one who looks with a mind of lust, thinking "it is here," at any of the six male sexual organs, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "All" means all of the aforementioned types. 2966.
Having seen a monk even from afar, [the meaning] is to be construed as: "having stepped aside from the path while that monk is still at a distance, the way must be yielded."

2967. But when a bhikkhunī, while wandering for alms, sees a bhikkhu, she should take out the bowl with which she is wandering for alms, remove her outer robe (saṅghāṭicīvara) which was standing there covering it, turn it upside down—meaning with the opening facing upward—and show it to the bhikkhu;
such is the construction of the sentence.

2968. The construction is as follows: "The Great Sage has permitted a waist-string (*kaṭisuttaka*) to be made and the waistband (*kaccha*) to be tied for bhikkhunīs who are menstruating, at the time of their period, when flowers have appeared.
By this, he indicates that it is not permissible to tie a waist-string at any other time. As it is said: "Monks, a bhikkhunī must not wear a waist-string at all times."
"It should not be worn; whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). I allow, monks, a waist-string for one who is menstruating. 2969.

"Connected with women's ornaments" means connected with women, or men, or both women and men. Or, "connected with women's ornaments" refers specifically to a hand-turned toy. "Pāṭaṅkī" means a small cloth pouch. 2970.

"A grave offense" (garudhamma) means an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa). "Probation" (mānatta) means the probation lasting for a fortnight. "Having appointed" means having appointed by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (ñattidutiyā kammavācā).

2971. If a woman who has gone forth gives birth while in the state of pregnancy, then for that mother of the child, as long as the boy has not reached the age of discretion—that is, as long as he is unable by his own nature to eat, to chew, and to bathe—the second bhikkhunī must be formally appointed and given [the child] to care for; such is the construction of the sentence.
2972. The construction is as follows: that mother nun is permitted to suckle her own son, feed him, adorn him, and lie down with him upon her breast.

2973. The construction is as follows: setting aside the rule regarding sleeping together with a child, she should behave toward that child in exactly the same manner as she would behave toward other men.
2974. "By means of renunciation alone" means by the mere act of voluntarily adopting white robes. As it has been said: "Because she..."
“Having gone forth by her own choice and inclination, she is clothed in white garments; for that very reason she is not a bhikkhunī, not because of having renounced the training.

Herein, “here” means in this Dispensation. Regarding the phrase “having gone,” the words “from her own residence” are to be supplied as the remainder. As it was said: “That bhikkhunī, monks, who [has left] from her own residence...”
“Having gone over to a different sectarian order (titthāyatana), she has returned; she should not be granted full ordination (upasampadā).

Not only should she not be granted full ordination, she does not even receive the going forth (pabbajjā). However, one who has left after taking the white robes [of a laywoman] may receive the mere going forth.
2976. ‘Vandana’ means bowing by massaging the feet. It is permissible to accept it; thus [the Buddha said]: ‘I allow you, monks...’”
Because it has been authorized by the words "it may be consumed," it is permissible.

Regarding this, some teachers say: "If [the parties] are lustful or infatuated, whether on one side or both, it is exactly according to the basis of the offense (*yathāvatthuka*). Other teachers say: "There is no offense here.
Having thus presented these views of the teachers, the commentaries state: "This is permitted as specifically authorized; therefore, it is permissible."
That which has been stated is authoritative. For by the very words, “I allow you, monks, to accept,” it is permissible. 2977.
One should not defecate in any kind of latrine where the bottom is open and the top is covered;

however, it is allowable to defecate where the bottom is open and the top is covered. Regarding the phrase “where the bottom is open and the top is covered,” the Commentary states: “If... [text continues]”
"It is said: 'A well has been dug, but only the wooden planks at the top are visible from all directions;
even in such a case, it is permissible. (2978) "In all places" means in all locations, such as the nuns' quarters, inside a house, and so forth.
"For one who is ill" refers to her for whom there is no comfort without a *pallaṅka* (couch). "Half-*pallaṅka*" means a *pallaṅka* made by folding one leg across. That one...
Placing one heel near the root of the thigh and the other further away is called the "contracted cross-legged posture" (*ābhujitapallaṅka*).
2979. Regarding "men's bathing places": this refers to bathing places for men. As it is said: "Monks, a nun must not bathe at a men's bathing place;
whoever should so bathe, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Monks, I allow [bathing]..."
"‘To bathe at Mahilātīrtha. 2980.

The construction is as follows: "If a female ascetic should bathe against the current with her body scented by either scented powder or scented clay, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for her.
By the specific qualification "scented," it is indicated that what is unscented is permissible.
As it is said: “I allow you, monks, ordinary clay.

(2981) “Without having eaten”: here the meaning is that one has not taken even a mere morsel of food, nor used the bowl and robes for even a few days. If it is unsuitable, it is permissible to discard everything.
(2982) When no non-ordained persons are present, all that has been received by the monks, whether formally accepted or not, may be stored.
The construction is: "It is permissible for bhikkhunīs to consume all kinds of food after having had it received by bhikkhus.
The phrase "it is permissible for bhikkhunīs" is stated by way of the specific context [of this rule].
It is likewise permissible for bhikkhus to consume such things after having had them received by bhikkhunīs. As it was said: "I allow you, bhikkhus..."
“Having had the monks’ store brought back by the nuns, one may consume it.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the nuns (*bhikkhunikkhandhaka*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya*, which is an elucidation of the essence of the Vinaya meaning.
The commentary on the Khandhaka section is concluded.
Commentary on the Fourfold Formal Acts (Kamma): 2983.

There is the formal act known as an act of notification (apalokana-kamma), an act consisting of a motion (ñatti-kamma), an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma), and an act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma).
The construction is: "these are the four kinds of actions. In this context, "four" is a numerical delimitation.

"These" is a term referring to what is proximate and evident, because they are about to be explained immediately hereafter. "Actions" is an indication of the specific actions being delimited. "By means of intimation" (*apalokana-saññāta*) and so forth is the demonstration of their essential nature.
In this regard, the summary of the analysis is as follows:

A *apalokana-kamma* (an act of seeking permission) is said to be a formal act that is to be performed after purifying the Saṅgha residing within the boundary, obtaining the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it, announcing the specific matter with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, and proclaiming three times, "Does it please the Saṅgha?
A *ñatti-kamma* (an act consisting of a motion) is as follows:
A formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by a single motion (*ñatti*) with the consent of a united Saṅgha is to be done in the manner already described.

A formal act with a motion as the second member (*ñattidutiyakamma*) is a formal act to be performed with one motion and one proclamation (*anussāvana*), with the consent of a united Saṅgha, in the manner already described.
A formal act with a motion as the fourth member (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is [to be performed] in the manner already described...

With the consent of a united Saṅgha, by means of one motion (*ñatti*) and three proclamations (*anussāvana*), such is the formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by means of three proclamations with a motion as the fourth.
That proclamation which has a motion as its second part is "motion-and-second" (*ñattidutiya*); the formal act to be performed by means of that is a "motion-and-second act" (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
[That] proclamation which has a motion as its fourth part... [is "motion-and-fourth" (*ñatticatuttha*)].
That which is to be performed by means of a motion followed by a fourth [proclamation] is a *ñatticatutthakamma*.
(2984–7) In order to show the classification according to their respective bases, he says: "The act of intimation" (*apalokanakamma*), and so forth. The collection of nine bases is "nine bases";
this is connected with the word "goes. The phrase "an act consisting of a motion" (*ñattikamma*) indicates the agent of the action of going.

“Nine grounds” (*navaṭṭhāna*) is a designation for types of formal acts (*kamma*). “Second” refers to a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). The construction is: “it goes to seven grounds.

Now, in order to show those divisions of grounds according to their specific forms, he says: “and expulsion,” and so forth. These are designations for specific types of formal acts, such as expulsion and the rest. The construction is:
it goes to these five grounds—namely, the formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*), which is “expulsion,” and so on, up to the fifth characteristic of a formal act.
Having thus shown the acts of expulsion and so forth by way of their names, he says, “And expulsion,” etc., in order to demonstrate them by analyzing their meaning.
The construction is: “From a novice” (*samaṇuddesa*) means from a thorn-like novice; [the text] speaks of both expulsion and reinstatement (*osāraṇa*).

In this context, the expulsion of a thorn-like novice is the removal [of one who is unfit], while the admission of those very same types [who have subsequently displayed] proper conduct should be understood as “reinstatement.”
The meaning is: "By one who has gone forth (*pabbajantena*), acting as the cause, one should state the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍuka*) and the inquiry regarding the shaving of the head.

"Shaving of the head" refers to the inquiry concerning the cutting of the hair for one seeking admission to the order. The construction is: "By one who has covered himself (*channena*), acting as the cause, one states the act of the *brahmadaṇḍa*.
"Of such a kind" means of one similar to Channa, a talkative person, by means of ill-spoken words toward the monks.

“Of one who harasses. It should be done as follows: “Venerable sirs, a certain monk named so-and-so is talkative and dwells harassing other monks with ill-spoken words; that monk may say whatever he wishes.
I ask the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, regarding this monk named so-and-so: [he] should not be addressed, nor exhorted, nor instructed by the monks.”
“The Saṅgha approves the imposition of the brahma-penalty upon the monk so-and-so. A second time I ask... a third time I ask:
“Venerable sirs, does the Saṅgha approve the imposition of the brahma-penalty upon the monk so-and-so?
In this way, the brahma-penalty is to be imposed.

Regarding the phrase “having asked for permission” (*āpucchitvāna*), the prior action is implied; regarding “having taken,” the subsequent action must be supplied. “According to one’s wish” (*ruciyā*) is an adjective qualifying that [taking].
Regarding the word “gives” (*deti*), the remainder of the phrase is “of robes and so forth that have not been lost.

Having the entire Saṅgha assembled and having asked for permission from all the monks present within the boundary (*sīmā*), whether they have arrived or not, [one gives] with such-and-such an article...
The construction is as follows: having asked three times for the consent of the monks who were selected after asking individually, "Is it proper?
Does he approve of this gift?", one gives requisites such as robes to those whose robes have been stolen;

that which is such a gift to the Saṅgha constitutes the characteristic of that *apalokana-kamma* (act of seeking permission). It is called a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized (*lakkhīyati*).
Kamma itself is the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), and not the act of expulsion and so forth; thus it is "the characteristic of kamma" (*kammalakkhaṇa*).

Having thus shown the five points regarding the *apalokana*-kamma by way of summary and exposition, he now says "expulsion," etc., in order to show first the characteristic of kamma regarding the *ñatti*-kamma. Thus, "nine points for the *ñatti*" is this summary.
This is clarified by the very description to be stated, beginning with the word “in adjudication” (*vinicchaye*).

2992. “In adjudication” (*vinicchaye*) means in a formal judicial inquiry (*ubbāhika-vinicchaye*). “Not having reached a conclusion” (*asampatte*) means not having arrived at a final decision. “Of the elder” (*therassa*) refers to the preacher of the Dhamma.
For this reason, he said, “one who does not know the discipline” (*avinayaññuno*). To him [the assembly] says: “Venerable sirs, listen to me; this monk named so-and-so is a preacher of the Dhamma.”
For him, neither the Sutta nor the Suttavibhaṅga is relevant; not having discerned the meaning, he misinterprets the meaning based on the mere shadow of the phrasing.

"Venerable sirs, if it seems appropriate to you, let us have the monk named so-and-so expelled and then settle this legal issue"—thus [should one address] the Dhamma-preacher in a formal judicial decision.

The construction is as follows: that which is called the "departure" (*nissaraṇā*) for a bhikkhu is here referred to as "sending away" (*nissāraṇā*) in the context of a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*).
2993–4. Regarding one who desires full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*): "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
So-and-so is desirous of full ordination from the Venerable so-and-so; he has been instructed by me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let so-and-so come."
"Come," this is the bringing [of the person] into the presence of the Saṅgha in connection with those words; that is called "restoration" (osāraṇā).
The word-division is "Come, restoration.
This applies both by way of the Uposatha and by way of the Pavāraṇā. Because it is established by a formal motion (ñatti): "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me..."
"Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth; if it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha," and "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: today is the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth;

if it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā"—because these two formal acts (*ñattikamma*) are established by means of a motion (*ñatti*) regarding the Uposatha and the Pavāraṇā, they are called "Uposatha" and "Pavāraṇā."
By the words, “‘And you should instruct the one seeking full ordination,’” this single motion is taken: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
So-and-so is seeking full ordination from the venerable so-and-so.
If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I shall instruct so-and-so.”

2995. By the statement, “I, the bhikkhu named so-and-so, would ask the bhikkhu named so-and-so about the Vinaya,” this single motion (*ñatti*) is taken up: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me;
if it is timely for the Saṅgha, I would ask the bhikkhu named so-and-so about the Vinaya.
By the word “and so forth” (*evamādi*), [the following is included]: “If it is timely for the Saṅgha, the bhikkhu named so-and-so [would ask] the bhikkhu named so-and-so...”
“...should instruct him,” “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, I shall question so-and-so regarding the obstructing factors,” “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha,
so-and-so shall question so-and-so regarding the obstructing factors,” “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha,
so-and-so shall question so-and-so regarding the Vinaya,” “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha...”
“If it is appropriate for me, being asked about the Vinaya by such-and-such a person, I would answer,” and “If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha,
let such-and-such a person, being asked about the Vinaya by such-and-such a person, answer”— these six motions (ñatti) have been taken up.
Thus, these two former ones and these six— these eight motions are called “formal appointments” (sammuti).
2996. Regarding "the giving away of robes and so forth that have been relinquished": "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This robe, which was to be relinquished by the monk so-and-so, has been relinquished to the Saṅgha.

If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe back to the monk so-and-so. In this way, the giving away of robes, bowls, and so forth that have been relinquished is what is meant by "giving."
It is said: "The receiver of offenses" refers to one who says: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so remembers an offense;
he reveals it, makes it clear, and confesses it. If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, I shall receive the offense of the monk named so-and-so.
And: "When it is appropriate for the venerable ones, I [shall receive the offense] of the monk named so-and-so..."
"One should receive a monk’s offense. He should be addressed with: "Do you see it? "Yes, I see it.
"You should exercise restraint in the future. Thus, the receiving of offenses is called "receiving" (*paṭiggāha*). 2997.
*Pavārukkaḍḍhanā* means the drawing forth of the invitation (*pavāraṇukkaḍḍhanā*). The letter *ṇa* is elided due to the requirements of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*). Alternatively...
The word *pavāra* is a synonym for the word *pavāraṇā*. By the phrase, "Having performed this Uposatha, I shall perform the *pavāraṇā* on the dark day," there is this motion (*ñatti*):
"Let the venerable residents listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha; we shall perform the *pavāraṇā* on the dark day."
It is shown by way of illustration. Thus, the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) that has been performed is considered a "postponement" (*paccukkaḍḍhanā*).

And here, "in the dark fortnight" (*kāḷe*) refers to the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pubbakattika; by this, the motion (*ñatti*)—"We shall invite when the moon is bright"—is also illustrated.
"In the bright fortnight" (*juṇhe*) refers to the Uposatha day of the bright fortnight of the latter Kattika month.
“*Tiṇavatthāraka*” refers to the settlement by covering over as with grass. “The motion first of all” refers to what is called the inclusive motion (*sabbasaṅgāhikā ñatti*).
“And the other two” refers to the two motions established separately for each of the two sides;

thus, this formal act consisting of a motion proceeding in three ways possesses the characteristic of a formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*). This is according to the method stated in the passage beginning with “in the determination,” and so forth.
The construction is: "Nine points are to be understood regarding the motion (*ñatti*). (2999–3000).

Having thus shown the nine points regarding a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), he now says, "And also the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second [announcement]," etc., in order to show the seven points regarding a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*). The summary verse beginning with "The formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second [announcement]" is of plain meaning.

In the detailed explanation (*niddesa*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the overturning of the bowl, and so forth" includes the righting of the bowl. "The expulsion of one who has been suspended" is considered [to be included].

It is understood as "expulsion" (*nissāraṇā*) and "reinstatement" (*osāraṇā*). In this context, expulsion should be understood as the overturning of the bowl (*pattanikkujjana*) by the Saṅgha for the purpose of depriving a lay follower—who is possessed of the eight factors such as striving against the acquisition of gains for monks—of communal participation;
and reinstatement is the turning upright of that very bowl when he conducts himself properly.
That [formal authorization] was explained in the section on the Minor Matters (*Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka*) within the account of the Licchavis of Vaḍḍha.
3001. Authorization (*sammuti*) refers to formal consent; it is considered to be of fifteen kinds:

authorization of boundaries (*sīmāsammuti*), authorization for not being separated from the three robes (*ticīvarena avippavāsasammuti*), authorization for the rug (*santhatasammuti*), the designator of meals (*bhattuddesaka*), the assigner of lodgings (*senāsanaggāhāpaka*), the storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*), the receiver of robes (*cīvarapaṭiggāhaka*), and the distributor of rice-gruel (*yāgubhājaka*).

The appointment for the distributor of fruit, the distributor of hard food, the dispenser of trifles, the provider of robes, the provider of bowls, the assigner of monastery attendants, and the assigner of novices—thus that appointment is considered to be of fifteen kinds;
such is the meaning. Regarding the phrase *matakacīvarassa*: it is the cloth for the Kathina ceremony;
that which is dead is *matika*; the clothing of the dead is *matakavāsa*; [the word] *tassa* refers to that clothing of the dead, i.e., the robe of the dead.

3002. Ubbhāra (lifting) that occurs within the five-month period itself, which constitutes the field of benefits, is called *antarubbhāra*. The construction is: "The instruction regarding the site for a hut (*kuṭi*) and the site for a monastery (*vihāra*) is what is called 'instruction' (*desanā*).
3003. In the case of the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass), there are three motions (*ñatti*):

the motion to be established by way of commonality for both factions, and subsequently, two separate motions to be established for each of the two factions; these constitute three motions because of the absence of formal proclamations (*kammavācā*).
In the case of a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), it is shown that "the characteristic of the act" (*kammalakkhaṇa*) applies;

subsequently, for each of the two separate groups, the two formal proclamations following the motion (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) in a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation are shown to be the "characteristic of the act. To demonstrate this, he says: "In the case of a formal act of covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
By the phrase "in cases such as the imposition of delusion (*mohāropanatādi*)," both the formal act of imposing delusion shown among the *pācittiya* offenses and...

It also includes acts such as speaking otherwise, causing harassment, and imposing [punishment]. "In this" means in this formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
"The characteristic of the act itself" is the state of having the characteristic of an act. 3004–5.

Thus, in the manner described above, these are the seven divisions of the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). Having thus shown the seven points regarding the *ñattidutiyakamma*, he says "likewise," etc., in order to show the division of points for the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*).
3006. Regarding the phrase "tajjanādīnaṃ," the word *ādi* (and so forth) includes *niyassa* and the others. It refers to the subsiding or pacification of those seven formal acts (*kamma*). 3007.
The expression "the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs" is stated by way of the result (*phalūpacāra*) for the formal authorization (*sammuti*) of one who exhorts the bhikkhunīs.
3008–9. *Mūlapaṭikkasso* means sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassanā*). Due to the requirements of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*), the letter *ka* has been doubled.

"Followers of one who has been suspended" (*ukkhitassānuvattikā*) refers to those who follow one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattikā*). There is one case that requires a formal act up to the third time (*yāvatatiyaka*), eight cases involving offenses entailing a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*), and two cases involving Ariṭṭha and Caṇḍakāḷī; these eleven constitute the cases requiring a formal act up to the third time.

"By means of these" (*imesaṃ vasā*) means by way of these formal acts of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) directed toward individuals such as those who follow one who has been suspended. "Ten and one" (*daseka*) means eleven.

3011. Having thus shown the classification of the bases for the four types of formal acts (*kamma*), he says, "And the *apalokana* act," etc., in order to show the manner in which they are to be performed through both positive and negative correlation (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*).
The construction is: "One should not have it done even by means of a motion (*ñatti*)," and "one should not have it done even by means of a motion followed by a second resolution (*ñattidutiya*).
3012. Since the manner in which the *ñatti*-act and the others are to be performed can be understood from the characteristics described for the *apalokana*-act, [the author] proceeds as follows.

Without showing that [the previous category], he says, "The formal acts consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma)," etc., in order to show the specific distinction found in the formal acts consisting of a motion and a second.
The construction is as follows: there are also light formal acts consisting of a motion and a second that are to be performed after having obtained permission (apaloketvā).

As to what those are, he says, "All formal permissions (sammuti) would be [such]. Here, excluding the formal permission for the boundary (sīmāsammuti), the others—beginning with the formal permission for not being separated from the three robes (ticīvarā-vippavāsa-sammuti)—are meant.
The meaning is "all conventional designations" (sammuti). 3013.
"The remaining ones" refers to the six formal acts (kamma) other than those already mentioned, such as the formal act for the designation of a boundary (sīmā-sammuti) and so forth.

"Are not permitted" means they are not allowed; the elision of the letter *na* is due to the requirements of metrical composition (gāthā-bandha). As it has been said: "The designation of a boundary, the removal of a boundary, the offering of the kaṭhina robe..."
“The lifting of the *kaṭhina*, the designation of the site for a hut, and the designation of the site for a monastery—these six formal acts (*kamma*) are weighty;

they are not permitted to be performed by merely seeking permission (*apaloketvā*); they must be performed only after proclaiming the motion and the second part of the formal act (*ñattidutiyakamma-vācanā*). However, the statement “it is not permitted to perform them by merely seeking permission” is merely an illustration;
they are also not permitted to be performed by way of a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*).

It continues in this very manner. Therefore he said: "In the same way as previously stated, one should have it made by that very [method]. The meaning is: "by whichever method was stated for performing whichever specific work, by that very method.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the fourfold types of work.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Failure of Kamma (Kammavipattikathāvaṇṇanā) 3014. Since success in kamma is understood through the contrast with its failure when the latter has been shown, he first explains the failure of kamma, saying “by way of the basis,” and so forth.
It is called a “basis” (*vatthu*) because the fruit, which is designated as kamma, dwells therein, being dependent upon it for its existence.

“From the basis (*vatthu*)” means from the primary cause of the formal act (*kamma*), that is, from the basis. “From the proclamation and the boundary (*anussāvana-sīmāto*)” means from the proclamation and from the boundary.
“Only five” indicates, by means of the particle *eva*, that this is the maximum number of faults in a formal act.
Having analyzed the failure of the formal act (*kamma-vipatti*) according to the sequence of the matrix (*mātikā*) of faults as they were set forth, he says “In the presence,” and so on.

An action that must be performed by applying the fourfold *sammukhāvinaya*—consisting of the presence of the Saṅgha, the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person—is called "to be done in their presence" (*sammukhākaraṇīya*).
In this regard, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act must have arrived; and the consent of those who are eligible to give their consent must have been brought forward.

When those who are present do not protest, this is "presence before the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasammukhatā*). When the Saṅgha performs that formal act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction, this is "presence of the Dhamma" (*dhammasammukhatā*) and "presence of the Vinaya" (*vinayasammukhatā*).
In this context, "Dhamma" means the factual basis; "Vinaya" means both the formal charge and the subsequent reminder; and "the Teacher’s instruction" means—

It consists of both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*). The presence of the person before whom the Saṅgha performs that legal act is "presence of the individual" (*puggalasammukhatā*).

Thus, regarding the Saṅgha-act described as "to be performed" by means of the fourfold *sammukhāvinaya*, if one performs it in the absence [of these conditions], omitting even one of the four characteristics, that—

The construction is as follows: an action (*kamma*) that has failed in its basis (*vatthu*) due to a deficiency in the basis known as *sammukhāvinaya* (decision in the presence) is called an "unlawful action" (*adhammakamma*).

Having thus shown the failure of an action in terms of its basis regarding what must be done in the presence (*sammukhākaraṇīya*), he said "not in the presence," etc., in order to show by way of classification what is not to be done in the presence.

This includes the act of disclosure (*pakāsanīyakamma*) performed against Devadatta. The construction is: the authorization for those in training (*sekkhasammuti*) and the authorization for the insane (*ummattakasammuti*). [And] the act of non-worship (*avandiyakamma*).

Under the heading of "individuals," it is stated that [he] is "not to be saluted. The "ordination by messenger" (dūtūpasampadā) is the ordination authorized for the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī by means of a messenger.
Thus, having set aside these eight formal acts (kamma), all remaining acts whatsoever are "to be performed in the presence" (sammukhākaraṇīya);
this is how the Teacher, the Sugata—so called because of his beautiful gait and other qualities—spoke. This is the construction of the sentence.
3019–20. Having thus shown the failure of the legal act (*kammavipatti*) by way of the subject matter (*vatthu*), he says “by way of the motion (*ñatti*), etc. to show it by way of the motion.

“The manner of failure” (*vipajjananaya*) means the sequence of the failure of the discipline (*vinaya*). “He does not touch upon the subject matter” means that he does not touch upon the person for whom he performs the legal act of ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth;
he does not take up his name. [As in: “Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs, this...”
