When it should be said, "Dhammarakkhita is seeking full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable Sir, let the Sangha hear me:
[Dhammarakkhita] is seeking full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita. In this way, he does not misrepresent the subject matter.
"He does not misrepresent the Sangha" means he does not misrepresent the name of the Sangha; he does not take its name [for himself]. "Let [the Sangha] hear..."
When it should be said, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this is Dhammarakkhita," he says, "Venerable sirs, let [the Saṅgha] hear this Dhammarakkhita.
In this way, he does not misrepresent the Saṅgha.
He does not misrepresent the individual means that he does not misrepresent the preceptor (upajjhāya) of the one seeking ordination.
He does not take the name [of the candidate]. When it should be said, "Venerable Saṅgha, let it hear me:
this Dhammarakkhita desires the full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita," he says instead, "Venerable Saṅgha, let it hear me: this Dhammarakkhita desires the full ordination.
In this way, he does not misrepresent the person.
"He does not violate the motion" means he does not violate the motion in every respect:
in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), he omits the motion and performs the act of proclamation with the formal statement (*kammavācā*) alone twice;

likewise, in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), he omits the motion and performs the act of proclamation with the formal statement alone four times. In this way, he does not violate the motion.

"Or he establishes the motion afterwards" means that after first performing the formal act of proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*) with the ritual words (*kammavācā*), he says, "This is the motion," and then says, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent; thus do I understand this.
In this way, he establishes the motion afterwards. "By five reasons" means by these five causes.

3021-2. Having thus shown the failure of the formal act (*kammavipatti*) by way of the motion (*ñatti*), he now says “by way of the proclamation (*anussāvana*)” and so forth to show it by way of that.
The construction is: “Five faults of the formal act are declared by way of the proclamation.

In such passages as “he does not touch the subject matter (*vatthu*) or [the rest],” the subject matter and so forth are to be understood according to the method already stated. However, their non-touching occurs as follows: “Let the Sangha listen... [and so on].

At the first proclamation, saying, “May the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me,” or at the second and third proclamations, saying, “For a second time I state this matter... for a third time I state this matter;

may the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me,” one should say, “This Dhammarakkhita desires the full ordination from the Venerable Buddharakkhita. Instead of that, one should say: “May the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me.”
When one says, "of the Venerable Buddharakkhita," one does not misrepresent the subject.
When one should say, "Venerable Saṅgha, let it be heard by me: this is Dhammarakkhita," if one says, "Venerable, let it be heard by me: this is Dhammarakkhita," one does not misrepresent the Saṅgha.
When one should say, "Venerable Saṅgha, let it be heard by me: this is Dhammarakkhita [acting] for the sake of the Venerable Buddharakkhita..."
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs: this Dhammarakkhita desires full ordination”—by speaking thus, one is said not to point out the person.
To omit the proclamation means: in every respect, one does not perform the formal proclamation (*anussāvana*) within the ritual formula;

in a procedure consisting of a motion and a second announcement (*ñattidutiyakamma*), one merely sets forth the motion twice; in a procedure consisting of a motion and a fourth announcement (*ñatticatutthakamma*), one merely sets forth the motion four times.
In this way, one omits the proclamation (*anussāvana*).

Even in a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*), if one, having set forth the motion, omits a syllable or mispronounces a phrase while reciting the formal act (*kammavācā*), this too constitutes omitting the proclamation.
However, in a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution (*ñatticatutthakamma*), after setting forth the motion, [if one recites] the formal act only once or twice...
It should be understood that even one who performs the proclamation (*anussāvana*), yet omits a syllable or a word, or utters it incorrectly, indeed fails in the proclamation.

Regarding the phrase "utters it incorrectly" (*duruttaṃ karoti*), this is the analysis: for if one says something other than what should be said in a particular syllable, this is called "uttering it incorrectly. Therefore, when a monk is performing the formal act (*kammavācā*), he— [The text continues: ...this [monk]... must ensure that the syllables and words are neither omitted nor uttered incorrectly. If he utters them incorrectly, the act is not accomplished; thus, the proclamation is considered failed. It should be understood that even if one recites the entire formula, if any part is omitted or uttered incorrectly, the proclamation is nonetheless deficient. As for the expression "utters it incorrectly," the following is the determination: if, when another syllable ought to be spoken, one speaks something else, this is indeed called "uttering it incorrectly. Consequently, the monk performing the formal act must—
“Loose and forceful, long and short;
heavy and light, and the nasal stop (niggahita);
connected, distinct, and released;”
"The division according to the perception of phonemes is tenfold"—this has been stated; it should be thoroughly observed.
For here, "soft" refers to the first and third [consonants] in each of the five groups, while "hard" refers to the second and fourth in those same groups.

*Dīgha* (long) refers to vowels such as *ā* and so forth that require a long duration of time to pronounce. *Rassa* (short) refers to vowels such as *a* and so forth that require half that duration of time. *Garuka* (heavy) is synonymous with long;
alternatively, it refers to what is pronounced followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), such as in the phrases "of the venerable Thera Buddharakkhita" or "to whom it does not please.
*Lahuka* (light) is synonymous with short; alternatively, it refers to [what is pronounced] as in "of the venerable Thera Buddharakkhita..."
"Of whom it is not acceptable"—thus it is spoken, making "asaṃyoga" (non-conjunction) the primary factor.
"Niggahita" (the nasal stop) is that which should be uttered by restraining the vocal organs, not releasing them, and producing a nasal sound with the mouth unclosed.
"Sambandha" (connection) is that which is connected with a subsequent word and is spoken as either "tuṇhassā" or "tuṇhissā. "Vavatthita" (determined) is that which [is fixed] by a subsequent word...
Having made it unconnected and having interrupted it, one says "tuṇhī assā" or "tuṇha assā.
"Vimutta" (released) refers to that which is spoken without restraining the articulatory organs, releasing them, with the mouth open, and without nasalization.

In that context, where "suṇātu me" (may he hear me) should be said, by changing the letter *ta* to the letter *tha*, the expression "suṇāthu me" occurs; this is [an example of] the relaxed [articulation].
The softening of a hard consonant (*dhanita*) is as follows: where one should say, "It is the proper time; this is the motion" (*pattakallaṃ, esā ñatti*), saying instead, "It is the desired time;

this is the purpose" (*patthakallaṃ, esā ñatthi*), and so forth. Furthermore, where one should say, "Venerable Saṅgha" (*bhante saṅgho*), changing the letters *bh* and *h* to *b* and *g*, and saying "bante saṃgo," is called the softening of a hard consonant.
[Also,] where one says "May it be heard by me" (*suṇātu me*) with an open [mouth]...
Furthermore, when one should say "suṇantu me" (let them hear me) with the mouth open, or when one should say "esā ñatti" (this is the motion),
saying "esaṃ ñatti" with the mouth closed and producing a nasal sound is called "speech with a suppressed *niggahīta*.
When one should say "pattakallaṃ" (it is the right time) with the mouth closed and producing a nasal sound, saying "pattakallā" with the mouth open and [producing] a nasal sound...
Not pronouncing [a letter] when it should be pronounced is called "releasing" (*vimutta-vacana*). Thus, if what is required is a soft consonant (*sithila*), one uses a hard one (*dhanita*);
if a hard one is required, a soft one; if a released one is required, a nasalized one (*niggahita*); and if a nasalized one is required, a released one.
These four types of phonemes (*byañjana*) vitiate the formal act (*kamma*) within the *kammavācā*. For one who speaks in such a manner regarding another syllable...
It should be said that one who speaks otherwise than what ought to be said is called "one who utters what is ill-spoken.
However, regarding the other six consonants— long, short, and so forth— one who speaks that very same syllable in its respective place,
such as a long vowel in the place of a long vowel and a short vowel in the place of a short vowel, thereby following the traditional lineage (paveṇi) arrived at in due order...

The formal proclamation (kammavācā) must be performed without error. However, if one fails to do so, and instead pronounces a short vowel where a long one should be spoken, or a long vowel where a short one should be spoken;
likewise, if one pronounces a heavy syllable where a light one should be spoken, or a light syllable where a heavy one should be spoken;
or if one pronounces a compound where a distinct term should be spoken, or a distinct term where a compound should be spoken—[the procedure is invalid].
He speaks; even when this is said, the formal act (*kammavācā*) is not invalidated. For these six phonetic substitutions do not invalidate the act:
namely, what the Sutta-reciting elders say—"the letter *da* becomes *ta*; the letter *ta* becomes *da*; the letter *ca* becomes *ja*;
the letter *ja* becomes *ca*; the letter *ya* becomes *ka*; the letter *ka* becomes *ya*."
Therefore, they say that when it is necessary to use words beginning with *da*, using words beginning with *ta* does not constitute a contradiction;
however, this is not permissible when it comes to the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*). Consequently, the Vinaya master must neither change a *da*-sound to a *ta*-sound...

[and so on] ... nor a *ka*-sound to a *ya*-sound. Having purified the phonology according to the canonical text, he should avoid the faults mentioned regarding the tenfold phonetic system of syllables.
The formal proclamation (kammavācā) must be performed. Otherwise, it is said that one omits the announcement.

"One announces at an improper time" means that at a time when there is no opportunity for an announcement, one performs the first act of non-proclamation (anussāvanakamma) without having established the motion (ñatti), and only afterwards establishes the motion.
Thus, by these five ways, formal acts fail because of [improper] proclamation.
Therefore he said: "But they fail in this way, even from the proclamation.
(3023) Having thus shown the failure of the *kamma* due to the proclamation, he said, "By eleven...

[as] by me," referring by extension to that very point, since the failure of the *kamma* due to the boundary (*sīma*) follows the method stated in the Uposatha Khandhaka. The state of being a fault in the *kamma* is simply "faultiness in the *kamma*. This is the first section.
3024–7. Having thus demonstrated the failure of the formal act (*kamma*) by way of its boundary, he now says, “by a quorum of four,” etc., to demonstrate it by way of the assembly (*parisa*).
Regarding the term *kammappattā* (those who have reached the formal act), the remainder is “four regular monks (*pakatattā*); as it is said:
“In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four, four monks who are regular are those who have reached the formal act. And here, “regular” means not suspended.
Four monks who have not been suspended and whose virtue is pure are those entitled to the formal act (*kamma*), worthy of it, and appropriate for it;
they are its masters. Without them, that formal act is not performed, nor does their consent (*chanda*) or purity (*pārisuddhi*) come [to the assembly].

"Not arrived" means not having come within hand's reach of the assembly. Regarding "consent," the phrase "of those entitled to give consent" (*chandārahānaṃ*) is to be supplied here, as it has been said: "The remainder..."
“Those who are regular members and entitled to give their consent. By this, the following meaning is illustrated:
“But as for the rest—if they number even a thousand, provided they belong to the same community (samānasaṃvāsaka)—they are all indeed entitled to give their consent;
whether they come after having given their consent and formal purity (chandapārisuddhi) or not, the legal act nevertheless stands. “In the presence” means being present.

"Threefold" means endowed with the three factors consisting of the failure of the motion (*kamma*), the failure of the arrival [of monks], and the failure of the announcement of consent (*chandānāharaṇa*) or the protest (*paṭikkosa*). "Fault" has the characteristic of the failure of the formal act (*kamma-vipatti*).

"It may be according to the assembly" means it occurs by way of the assembly. "Protesting" means they object. In the second case, regarding a formal act requiring a quorum of four, the construction is: "the fault is twofold and may be according to the assembly.
Here, in this third case of a formal act requiring a quorum of four, there is only the protest, and not the other two faults of the assembly; thus, it is "onefold."

The construction is: “The fault may be due to the influence of the assembly. Because the second [type] of fault of an assembly endowed with two factors has been taught, the fault of an assembly endowed with two factors is called “the second.
Likewise, because the third has been taught, the one endowed with a single factor should be understood as “the third.
Extending this same method to the threefold nature of the Saṅgha consisting of five groups and so forth, he said: “In the same way... even in the threefold [cases].”
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Sanghas of ten and twenty members is intended.
(3028) Thus, in order to show that there are twelve types of failure in the formal act (*kamma*) due to the assembly (*parisa*) among the four kinds of Sanghas by way of the four triads, he says:

"The fourth member" (*catutthikā*). By way of a restatement (*anuvāda*), it is prescribed that "there should be ten or two"; that is, the assembly is defined by its having the fourth member as its limit.
The construction is: "the faults may be ten, two, or twelve. "Therein" (*ettha*) refers to these five faults of action mentioned by way of "by way of the basis" (*vatthuto*) and so forth;

the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). "From among the assemblies" (*parisāvasā*)—this is what is to be selected. "Actions" (*kammāni*) refers to the four types of formal acts, beginning with the *apalokana* (motion).

And herein, regarding those formal acts to be performed by a quorum of four or more, it is only that which has been performed after the *kammavācā* (formal proclamation) has been announced by one who is a regular member (*pakatatta*) [of the Saṅgha].
The formal act (kamma) is performed by one who has attained the status of a participant in the act.

It should be understood that if, having set aside those who have attained the status of participants, it is performed by someone who has not so attained—even if they alone recite the formal proclamation (kammavācā)—it is defective due to the fault of non-proclamation, because it lacks the characteristic of being performed by one who has attained the status of a participant and because the formal proclamation was not recited [by such a person]. For this very reason, the Elder Theras who were ancient masters of the Vinaya...
To avoid the suspicion of a failure in the formal act (*kamma*), they cause the proclamation of the *kamma* to be heard by two or three together. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the Pāḷi at the end of the Parivāra or from the Commentary.
Explanation of the Discussion on Failure in the Formal Act.
Commentary on the Discussion of Miscellaneous Determinations (Pakiṇṇakavinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā) 3029.

“Any kind of leaf-parasol” means any parasol made of leaves, such as those made from palm leaves and so forth. “Outside” means above; “inside” means below. “To sew” means to perform needlework after displaying the form [of the parasol].
3030. “Leaf” refers to the covering leaf. “Half-moon” means having the shape of a half-moon. “Crocodile-tooth” means having the shape of a crocodile’s tooth.
That which is called a "mountain peak" (*girikūṭa*). The connection is that it is not permissible to cut [it].
They make mountain peaks and so forth by bending them over the rim of the mouth or by tying together the ends of leaves, or by using the tip of a skull-bowl;
by this, that is prohibited. "Staff" refers to a parasol-staff. "Jar-shape" means having the form of a jar. "Or a beast-form" means an image of beasts such as tigers and the like.
Or: "By drawing" means having engraved it, or having carved it, or having produced lines by way of painting.
3031. Or: having sewn the umbrella inside and out with a single-colored thread—such as blue—among the five-colored threads for the sake of firmness;
or having woven the handle-grip, the pins, and the lattice-work for the sake of firmness.

The construction is: “It is allowable. By the phrase “for the sake of strength with one color among five colors,” it is indicated that it is not allowable to sew or braid with threads of many colors for the sake of making the color smooth.
In the manuscripts, however, the reading “with five colors” (pañcavaṇṇena) is seen; regarding this, [the meaning is] either with one color or with five colors.
The construction should be understood as: "It is permissible to sew or tie it fast with a five-colored thread. This refers back to what was stated below:
"It is not permissible to sew with a five-colored thread," and also to the passage:
"Some people sew palm-leaf umbrellas, either on the inside or the outside, with a five-colored thread..."

To polish it for the sake of beauty is not permitted. However, it is permitted to sew it with a single-colored thread—whether blue, yellow, or any other color—either inside or out, or to bind a handle for the umbrella-staff or a lattice-work frame, provided it is for the purpose of making it durable and not for the purpose of beautifying it; such is the reading in the Aṭṭhakathā.
It is obstructed; therefore, it should not be accepted. 3032.

"Or else, a mere line" means a line made with a tally-stick (*salākā*) of the kind already described. "Having cut" means having cut what was made by carving. "Having engraved" means having engraved what was made by means of painting and so forth. 3033.
"In the handle-bundle" means in the split bundle intended for gripping the frame of a parasol-handle; "at the base."
This is the meaning. This is the method stated here without doubt. However, in the *Khuddasikkhā-gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "At the base of the umbrella-handle.
"In the shape of an *ahichattaka*" means having the appearance of a blooming *ahichattaka* flower.
Having had it grasped with cords, they tie it to the handle; at that place of binding, they carve and raise it like a ring for the purpose of tying. For the purpose of binding.
Just as it does not move due to the wind, so too [the umbrella] is bound to the handle with cords for the purpose of securing the cage. The construction is:

"A line drawn by scratching is appropriate. As it has been said: "In order to prevent movement caused by the force of the wind, they cause the circular frame of the umbrella to be grasped with cords and bind it to the handle;
at that point of binding, they establish a line by scratching it in the shape of a ring."
"It is permissible. "Even if they do not bind it, because it is a place where binding is required, it is permissible to carve out a ring," so it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.

3034. "Equal to a hundred-padded [seat] and so forth" means similar to a hundred-padded seat and so on; when there is the possibility of using the instrumental case in the sense of equality, the genitive case is used.
3035. "Or at the edge of the bowl" means at either edge of the wind (the rim). "Or also at the mouth of the bowl" refers to the two...
In the case of bowls that have reached full expansion, it is at the place where they are joined, or even at the rim;
or, for the purpose of filling a deficiency in a single bowl, it is also at the place where it is joined. "Veṇī" refers to a seam sewn in the shape of a *kudrūsa* (wild grain) ear;
some say it is in the shape of a *varaka* (a type of bean) ear. "Saṅkhalikā" refers to a seam like a cat’s collar; some say it is like a hundred-petalled flower.
3036. *Paṭṭanti* means even a cloth band (*paṭṭa*). That which has a method or manner such as eight corners, etc., is called "the method of eight corners, etc. (*aṭṭhakoṇādikavidhi*); that [method].
In the phrase "eight corners, etc.," the elision of the nasal consonant (*niggahita*) occurs for the sake of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*). This term "the method of eight corners, etc.
is either a coordinate adjective (*samānādhikaraṇa-visesana*) qualifying "cloth band" (*paṭṭa*), or an adverbial modifier (*kiriyāvisesana*) of the verb "they make" (*karonti*).
This is the connection. Alternatively, *paṭṭa* is used here in the accusative case in the sense of the locative;
thus, it means "on the band. In this alternative, *aṭṭhakoṇādikaṃ* is in the accusative case. It is a qualification of the word *vidhi*.
Here, "eight-cornered and so forth" refers to a name other than the four-cornered shape that will be described here. *Tattha* means "in those two bands."
“*Agghiyagadārūpaṃ*” means a sewing in the shape of a *agghiya* (auspicious symbol) and the shape of a mace (*gadā*). “*Muggaraṃ*” means a sewing in the shape of a club (*laguḷa*).
By the word “etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of shapes such as a *cetiya* (stupa) and so forth is intended.
“*Tattha*” means in that place, on the two strips of cloth. “*Kakkaṭakakkhīnī*” refers to variations in the sewing resembling the eyes of a crab (*kuḷīra*).
"Uṭṭhāpentī" means they make [it]. "Tattha" means in that cloth-strip with loops and fastenings.

"Suttā" refers both to the threads sewn from corner to corner and to the threads sewn across the four sides. "Piḷakā" refers to the ends of those same threads where they have been turned back and sewn.
"Duviññeyyāvā" means that at the time of dyeing, they are described as being of a non-coarse form that is difficult to discern. Thus it is permitted.
As it is said: “Threads and knots at the corners are permissible when the robe is dyed, as they are difficult to discern.
3038. Regarding the phrase *gaṇṭhipāsakapaṭṭakā*, the construction is: “knots and strips, and loops and strips.
As for “threads at the corners,” one should cut both the threads at the edges of the robe and the threads at the corners of the knots, loops, and strips. Herein—

And as for "thread at the edge" (*kaṇṇasutta*): when a robe has been sewn according to its length and width, and after being dyed, is hung out to dry in the wind by tying it with a rope to a line or a clothes-stand, the threads tied along the windward side are called "edge-threads.
As it is said: "An edge-thread on a robe is not permitted; it must be cut off at the time of dyeing."

"But that which was thus authorized by the statement, 'Monks, I allow ear-threads,' should be made into a loop and tied when there is a breeze, for the purpose of hanging [the robe] during the time of dyeing. 3039.
"Or a modification of needlework" means sewing with various threads in patterns such as the *satapadi* (centipede) for the sake of decorating the robe.
They place a visiting visitor’s cloth [banner], or such a kind of needlework;
or "anything else" means any other kind of sewing work, such as flower arrangements, embroidery of deer, birds, or footprints. "To make" means to make it oneself.
"To have made" means to have it made by another.

3040. The construction is as follows: for that bhikkhu who, desiring and longing for the highest, most excellent appearance and luster, places his robe in sour gruel, flour, dregs of oil, and so forth—for that bhikkhu there is no release from the *dukkaṭa* offense.
"Sour gruel" (*kañjī*) refers to thick sour gruel similar to the gruel used for lubricating weaving threads. "Flour" (*piṭṭha*) refers to rice-flour. By means of rice-flour...
"Pakkā" means boiled. "Khali" refers to a decoction. By the word "etc. (ādi), lac and other such substances are included.

3041. The construction is as follows: it is permissible to place [the robe] in boiled rice-water, flour-paste, *khalia*, *allika*, and so forth, for the purpose of washing the needle-threads, dye-residue, and the like that have arisen while making the robe at the time of its manufacture, and also for the purpose of washing it when it has become soiled.
3042. *Tattha* means: in that dye with which one dyes the robe—whether it be perfume for the sake of making the robe fragrant, oil for the sake of making it bright, or lac for the sake of its color.

*Kiñci* means: any such thing whatsoever. 3043. *Maṇinā* means: with a stone. *Aññenapi ca kenaci* means: by any other object whatsoever, such as a mallet or the like, by which [the dye] becomes bright.
*Doṇiyā* means: in the dye-tub. *Na ghaṃsitabbaṃ* means: having grasped it with the hand, it must not be rubbed or struck.
3044. The construction is: "It is permissible to strike a dyed robe with the hands even slightly.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "Where they throw the dye, that is the dye-vat; there it is permissible to let the shoulder-straps, waist-bands, and so forth, touch [the robe].
3045. "In a knot" means in a knot made of bamboo, ivory, horn, or similar materials. "Or lines" refers to lines of various kinds, such as circular ones and so forth.

"Pustules" (*piḷakā*) refers to small blisters resembling mustard seeds. "One who breaks the ear-ornaments" (*pāḷikaṇṇikabhedaka*) means one who destroys the form of the ear-ornaments, such as necklaces, strings of beads, or flower-shaped pendants.
The construction is: "or a change in the auspicious spots (*kappabindu*) is not permitted.

(3046) "With the point of an awl" (*āraggena*) means with the tip of an *āraka*-thorn or with the point of a needle. "Any line" (*kācipi lekha*) means any streak whatsoever, shaped like a circle, a cow’s urine drop, or the like.
3047. *Bhamaṃ āropetvā* means having caused it to lean against a wall. 3048. *Pattamaṇḍalake*:
on a bowl-rim (*pattamaṇḍalaka*), which is made of tin, lead, or similar materials for the purpose of protecting the bowl’s surface, and should be placed beneath the bowl, upon its supports.
*Bhittikammaṃ*: wall-painting, consisting of various forms and decorative designs created by dividing the surface into sections.
As it was said: “Monks, you should not carry bowls with variegated circular designs, covered with figures, or decorated with wall-paintings.
*Tattha* means “in that bowl-design. *Assa* means “of the monk. *Makaradantaka* means having the shape of a mountain peak.

3049. The construction is as follows: apart from that line which was permitted for the purpose of binding the strainer on the rim of the mouth, no line whatsoever is allowed either on the handle of the water-vessel (*dhammakaraṇa*) or on its belly.
3050. *Tahiṃ tahiṃ* means here and there with clay. *Taṃ* refers to the waistband made of double-thread that has been pounded in that manner. 3051.

For the sake of strength at the ends, they pound it after making it double at the edge of the fringe; the construction is "it is permissible. *Cittikaṃ pi* means even a waistband adorned with patterns such as floral or creeper designs.
3052. *Akkhīni* refers to elephant eyes. *Tattha*—what need is there to mention that it is permissible for a waistband? *Uṭṭhāpetuṃ* means to carve out.

3053. They join together in the shape of a jar (*ghaṭasaṇṭhāna*). "Like the head of a *deḍḍubha*" means having the shape of the head and mouth of a water-snake (*udakasappa*). The construction is: "Whatever deformed matter (*vikārarūpa*) is not suitable for the ten openings.
3054. "Like a fish-thorn" (*macchakaṇṭa*) means having the form of a fish-bone. "Having the shape of a date-palm leaf" (*khajjūripattakākāra*) means having the configuration of a date-palm leaf.
Alternatively, it refers to a smooth strip like a fish-thorn or a date-palm leaf that has been cut straight and polished.
"It is allowable" is the construction. Herein, on both sides, that which has a weaving like the back-fin of a fish, with its strips joined by fish-bones, is called a "fish-bone waist-band.
That which has a weaving shaped like a date-palm leaf is called "having the form of a date-palm leaf."
3055. A natural strip of cloth (*paṭṭikā*). A "pig's snout" (*sūkaranta*) is shaped like a key-case.
Of those two types of waist-bands (*kāyabandhana*), there the cord is in accordance with the pig's snout, while the cloth-strip is in accordance with the strip of cloth.
By the word "etcetera," the *muddikā* waist-band is included, and that too is in accordance with the pig's snout. As it is said: "A single-corded [waist-band]..."
"But the grape-shaped waistband conforms to the *sūkarantaka*. In this context, "single-stringed" means having a single loop.
He will later explain that a multi-stringed one is unallowable. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "'Grape-shaped waistband' means it is prepared without being made square."
The *muraja* is so named because it is made by wrapping [the frame] in the shape of a drum-head (*murajavaṭṭi*). "Wrapping" means wrapping with various threads.
However, in the *Sikkhābhājanavinicchaya*, it is stated: "The *muraja* is that which is wrapped with a single thread after many cords have been joined together.
The *maddavīṇā* is shaped like a *pāmaṅga* lute. The *deḍḍubhaka* is shaped like the head of a water-snake.
*Kalābukam* means having many cords. Regarding "cords": when many cords are not tied together at one end at both ends, but are tied in such a manner, it is called *kalābukam*.
"They are not permitted" means that all these, including the *muraja* drum and so forth, as waist-bands, are not permitted.
"The first two" refers to the *muraja* and the soft lute (*maddavīṇā*). [In the original Pali,] where it should have been said, "they may be on the fringes,"...
Due to the constraints of verse composition and the elision of syllables, it is stated that "there may be ten. As it has been said:
"The phrase 'murajaṃ maddavīṇaṃ' is permitted only within the [category of] ten.
3057. "Shaped like a pāmaṅga" means having a square shape, like a pāmaṅga necklace.
3058. *Ekarajjukamayam*: having wound together various twists (*vaṭṭa*), it is a waistband made from a single cord.
Regarding the phrase "the cord rolls," in that context [of the Vinaya], a single-twist cord such as a cloth-strip was intended;

however, here, only that which is made by winding various twists together into one is taken as a "single-cord" waistband. *Taṃ ca*: that too, namely, that single-cord waistband. It has the shape of a *pāmaṅga* (a type of ornamental belt).
“Even a single one is not permitted” means that even a solitary one is not permitted.
(3059) “Having joined many ropes together” is the construction. “It is permitted to tie [it]” means that there is no *muraja* or *kalābu* drum;
the intention is that it is merely a body-binding made of a collection of ropes. This, however, is the detailed analysis: “many ropes... [The text continues:]... “ropes.”
Having joined them together on one side and wrapped [the drum] continuously with a single [rope], it should not be called "many-rope" (*bahurajjuka*);

that is permissible. This is stated here exactly as it appears in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. As for what was said in the *Sikkhābhājanavinicchaya*—"a *muraja* drum is one made by joining many ropes together and wrapping it with a single rope"—that should not be accepted, as it contradicts this [explanation].

3060. By the word *danta*, elephant tusks are meant. *Jatu* means lac. *Saṅkhamayaṃ* means made from the navel of a conch shell. Regarding the phrase *vidhakā matā*, there is also a reading *veṭhakā*; here, *veṭha* is a synonym for *vidha*. 3061.
*Kāyabandhanavidha* refers to the decorative patterns (*vidha*) made of wood, ivory, and so forth, intended to provide stability to the fringes of a waistband.
*Vikāra* refers to the eight auspicious symbols (*aṭṭhamaṅgala*) and the like. *Tattha tattha* means in those respective places; *ubhayakoṭiyaṃ* means at both ends.
The meaning [of *tu*] is as follows: by the word *tu*, it is indicated that the form of a jar (*ghaṭākāra*) is also permissible.

3062. “Adorned with garlands... variegated”: it is variegated by means of garland-work (*mālākamma*), creeper-work (*latākamma*), and various forms such as the figures of animals and birds. “Delighting the people” (*janarañjanī*): it is that which entices foolish people. 3064. “A pond with eight corners”:
here, by the word *api*, the inclusion of ponds with sixteen corners and so forth is intended. “Smooth with color” (*vaṇṇamaṭṭhā*): smooth with the colors of garland-work and the like.
3065. The construction is: "Even an ointment-stick is not permitted for the sake of beauty.
The reading, "And for an ointment-box, a painted design with threads of various colors is not permitted," is appropriate.
Although the reading "And even a box" is seen, it should not be accepted.

3066. The construction is as follows: it is permissible for one who uses any kind of small box made of cloth, rags, or similar materials, having sewn it together with thread of any single color such as red and so forth.
3067. *Maṇika* means a large bubble; *piḷaka* means a small bubble. *Pipphala* refers to a cloth-cutting knife.
*Ārakaṇṭaka* refers to the prongs used for piercing the rings that support a bowl. *Ṭhapetuṃ* means to set up or raise. *Yaṃ kiñci* means "whatever."
The remainder is polished and variegated.
(3068) Regarding "in the handle" (*daṇḍake*): this refers to the handle of a water-strainer (*pipphaladaṇḍaka*). As it has been said:

"It is not permitted to cause anything to protrude on the strainer, whether it be a jewel, a knob, or anything else; however, a boundary line is permitted on the handle. "Merely a boundary line" means...
Having reached the place where the cord is fastened, a single line is sufficient for the purpose of marking the limit.

"Having made a fold" means having formed an opening at both ends and drawn the folds together in the middle. The construction is: "Since they perform the cutting of the nails, therefore it is permissible. 3069.

A staff that performs the function of the upper fire-stick when combined with the lower fire-stick is called the *uttarāraṇī*. By the word "or" (*vā*), the lower fire-stick (*adharāraṇī*) is included.
"Grasps" is a designation for the pestle-handle. "A bow" refers to a drawing-stick or a slingshot.
"A mallet" refers to a handle used for pressing the head [of a pestle] or a pushing-stick.
3070. "Pincers" they call fire-tongs. Likewise, with a wood-cutting axe or anything else used for polishing metal surfaces—
"It is not allowable" is the connection [of the sentence]. "On both sides" means on both sides of the adze. "With iron" means with allowable (kappiya) iron.
"It is allowable to bind" means it is allowable to bind it straight, either square or octagonal.
"Sandāsa" refers to a fire-tongs; this was stated without doubt. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), a needle-tongs is shown here.
3071. "From below" means from beneath the iron plate-rim. Regarding the phrase "above, as large as a mushroom," this is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. 3072.
"On a horn" refers to the horns of a cow, gayal, buffalo, or similar animals used for pouring oil. "In a tube" refers to a tube such as a bamboo pipe; by the word "api" (also), a gourd is included.
"In a jar of *āmaṇḍa* essence" refers to an oil-jar made of *āmalaka* powder. "In an oil vessel" [is explained as follows].

In a vessel for oil of the kind already described. "All decorative painting is permitted" means that all decorative painting—such as floral designs and the like—is permitted, provided it is devoid of male and female figures.
3073–5. "In a water-pitcher" means in a pitcher for drinking water. "Also in a dye-tub" means even in a tub for dye. "On a wooden bench" means...
"On a stool made of wood": this refers to a support for a ring and so forth; "and so forth" includes a support for a staff.
"A foot-wiper" means a foot-wiper made of cloth or similar materials. "A stool" refers to a foot-stool, and by association, also to a foot-stand.
"And all that is variegated is permissible" means that among the aforementioned requisites of a bhikkhu, anything that is devoid of the form of a woman [is allowed].
All the remaining decorative work (*cittakamma*), excluding the requisites for the bhikkhunīs and excluding male figures.
3076. "Various and those gems" means *nānāmaṇi*; these are the sapphire (*indanīla*) and so forth. Made from various gems is "made of various gems" (*nānāmaṇimaya*).
Pillars, door-panels, doors, and walls are "pillars, door-panels, doors, and walls" (*thambhakavāṭadvārabhittiyo*); [these] are made of various gems.

That [palace] is described as such because it possesses pillars, door-panels, gates, and walls. What need is there to mention its polished color? The meaning is that there is no need at all to speak of its polished colors, such as those resulting from floral designs, creeper patterns, or painted decorations.
Having shown the suitability of a stable palace made of jewels, [the text now addresses] the enjoyment of all palaces, even those made of gold and other materials.
To show its suitability, he said, "made of gold," and so forth. "Sovaṇṇayaṃ" means made of gold.
Since the door-panels were shown in the immediately preceding verse, by the phrase "the fastening of the door-panels," the door-joint (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa) consisting of the door-posts is included.
"Dvārakavāṭāni" refers to the door and the panels; "bandhaṃ" is the fastening of the door and panels.
"Door-panel-fastening" means a wooden frame (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa) known as the upper side-beam and the corner-posts. "Various gems" means various jewels;
gold and various gems are "gold-and-various-gems"; wall and floor are "wall-and-floor";
a wall-and-floor made of gold-and-various-gems is "gold-and-various-gem wall-and-floor. Thus, among these...
Regarding the components of the lodging: "Nothing at all is to be refused" means that not even a single article belonging to the lodging is to be refused;

the meaning is that even the lodging itself should not be rejected. "The entire lodging is permissible" means that the use of every single item belonging to the lodging is permissible. As it has been said:
“‘All the palace furnishings’: doors decorated with gold, silver, and so forth; couches and stools; palm-leaf fans;
water-jars and water-basins made of gold and silver; whatever is fashioned as decorative art—all this is permitted.
If they say, ‘We give the male and female slaves, the fields and lands, and the cattle and buffalo of the palace,’ it must be accepted separately.”

"There is no [fault], for once a palace has been accepted, it is already accepted. However, it is not permitted to use woolen blankets and such items after spreading them over beds and chairs in either a communal monastery or a private dwelling.
But as for Dhamma-seats, they may be obtained under the principle of 'householder-made,' yet even there, it is not permitted to lie down."
Alternatively, there is the reading “sovaṇṇadvārakavāṭabandhan,” which is a *bahubbīhi* compound. By this [phrase] and by the second line, the lodging (*senāsana*) is qualified.
3078. He does not engage in jesting, thinking: “Is the Buddha a ‘stone-Buddha’? Is the Dhamma the ‘Dhamma of cows’ or the ‘Dhamma of goats’?

Is the Saṅgha the ‘Saṅgha of cows,’ the ‘Saṅgha of goats,’ or the ‘Saṅgha of deer’? He does not practice the observances of the non-Buddhist sects, such as the vow of silence (*mūgabbata*), and so forth.
"One should not take" is the construction. 3079.
"Those bhikkhunīs should not even sprinkle with water, etc. is the construction. 3080.
"In another place," that is, having spent the rains-retreat in one monastery, [one should not take] a share in another place, that is, a share of the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence) property.
If he takes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The construction is: "If that robe is lost, torn, or worn out, the share must be given again.

(3081) *So* refers to the monk who was taking a share elsewhere. *Tehi* means by those owners of the robes. *Taṃ* refers to the share of the rainy-season robe thus taken. *Tesam* refers to the owners of the robes. (3082) *Karoto* means of one who causes [it] to be made.
*Davā sīlaṃ pavijjhanto* refers to those desiring to play at the game of *pantika*, [acting] by way of demonstrating their skill.
He rolls a pebble or pierces a stone by way of making it roll along a downward slope.
Not only a stone, but it is not permissible to pierce anything else whatsoever—be it a piece of wood or a fragment of brick—with either the hand or a mechanical device.
For the sake of cetiyas and the like, one may even roll or throw stones and such things with laughter.
They may even pick [fruit], as it is permissible during the time for the formal act (*kamma-samaya*).

3083. Regarding "the giving of what is guarded by householders": even when fruits and so forth from gardens and such places guarded by householders through gardeners and others are given to one's satisfaction, there is no fault whatsoever for the monk who accepts them. No fault at all for the receiver.
There is no offense. The method of delimitation regarding palm fruits and the like belonging to the Saṅgha or a shrine, when being given by gardeners and others, is explained as follows:
there is no offense in taking only those items that have been specifically assigned as wages for them. This is the construction [of the sentence].
(3084) "Connected with men" means being carried by men who are porters. "Hand-pushed" means a cart that must be pushed with the hand alone.
3085. The construction is: "One should neither engage in nor cause to be engaged in any improper conduct with a bhikkhunī.
There is also a reading as "kiñci" (anything); the meaning is that one should not engage anyone—whether a householder or one gone forth—with a bhikkhunī in any manner of improper conduct.
"Obhāsentassa" means of one who manifests an intention of sensual desire.
3086. *Hava* is a particle used in the sense of "having" (*ekaṃsatthe*).
3087. "Given for one's own use" refers to the three robes and so forth given while saying, "You yourselves should use them.
3088. "Unsuitable" means a cause of discomfort by way of provoking the humors such as bile (*pitta*) and the rest. It may also mean to be removed or abandoned.
The intended meaning is "to give it oneself. The phrase "or to give after taking the best portion" is said with reference to food and so forth that are worthy of being taken as the best portion;

the words "having eaten for a few days" are to be supplied. The meaning is that it is permissible to take the best portion from the alms-food and so forth, and having eaten [from] the bowl and such for a few days, to give it.
3089. Ordination by a group of five (*pañcavaggūpasampadā*) is ordination to be performed by a Saṅgha with a master of the Vinaya as the fifth member.
"New" means not used even once by others. "Layered sandals" (*guṇaṅguṇaupāhanā*) refers to sandals with many layers, starting from four layers.
"Leather spread" (*cammatthāra*) refers to a permissible leather mat. "Regular bathing" (*dhuvanhāna*) refers to ordinary bathing.

3090. "Of the narrow passage" (*sambādha*): the construction is that surgical treatment (*satthakamma*) or enema treatment (*vatthikamma*) within two finger-breadths of the two passages—the urinary tract and the anal tract—is prohibited.

Surgical treatment (*satthakamma*) by means of a blade—even down to a fingernail—by way of cutting, tearing, and so forth, as well as enema treatment (*vatthikamma*) to be performed by means of enema bags for the purpose of introducing medicinal oil internally, are both subject to the prescription of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
The meaning is "forbidden. It should be taken from two finger-breadths around the urinary passage, starting from the tip of the sexual organ. 3091.
By the word "pākattha" (exposed), he indicates that there is no fault in moving [the organ] while extinguishing [the fire]. 3092. "Upaḷāleti" means:
having said, "I give you requisites such as bowl and robes," one entices and takes [them].

*Tattha* means "in that person. *Ādīnavaṃ* means having shown the state of being shameless and so forth, [he shows] the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) such as falling into a state of shamelessness when engaging in social enjoyment and the like with such a person.
*Tassa* means "of him," referring to the one who is to be separated from that [person].
To show the manner of seeing the disadvantage, he said: "Smearing," and so forth. "By one who has gone to bathe with excrement and urine..."
The construction is as follows: "It is proper to speak of the danger there, saying, 'This was done by you who dwell in dependence upon one who is immoral, like [relying on] butter.
3094–5. *Bhattagge* means while eating in the dining hall (*bhojanasālā*). *Yāgupāne* means at the time of drinking rice-gruel (*yāgu*). *Antogāme* means within a house (*antaraghara*).
*Vīthiyaṃ* means in the street (*rathikā*) of a market town, city, village, or similar place. *Andhakāre* means while darkness is prevailing.

The meaning is "one who has gone into darkness. For if one were to bow to such a person, the forehead might strike even the legs of the bed or other furniture. "Inattentive" means not attending to the act of bowing because of being preoccupied with some task.
"One who is turned away" refers to an enemy, an adversary, or a hostile person standing on the side of an opponent;
for if one were to bow to such a person, they might even strike with their foot. "Engrossed" means occupied with another task, such as the work of sewing.
"Sutta" means one who has fallen asleep. "Khādanti" means while eating dry foods such as flour-cakes and the like.
"Bhuñjanti" means while eating boiled rice and the like. "Vaccaṃ vā muttaṃ vā karanti" means while performing defecation or urination.
The connection is that for these thirteen [cases], bowing is prohibited in the sense of being inappropriate.
3096–7. Regarding the three types of those who belong to different communities (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*):

because one belonging to a different community by way of *kamma* is included under the category of one who has been suspended (*ukkhitto*); because one who belongs to a different community by way of boundary (*sīmā*) is subject to veneration by one who is senior and regular;

and because, by the method of elimination (*pārisesa*), it is stated that "one belonging to a different community who is senior and speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be venerated"—therefore, here the term "one belonging to a different community" refers to one who differs in tenet (*laddhi*).
"He is one who has been taken up" is how it should be understood. "Suspended" means one who has been suspended by any of the three kinds of acts of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*).

"And the five heavy matters" refers to the five heavy matters known as: deserving probation, deserving to be sent back to the beginning, deserving the trial period (*mānatta*), deserving the further trial period (*mānatta-cārika*), and deserving rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
However, these [individuals] receive salutations and so forth from one another according to seniority, just like a regular monk (*pakatatta*).

The state of being unworthy of salutation is taken as referring to those who are unworthy of salutation. These twenty-two persons are those previously mentioned, beginning with the naked ascetics (nagga). 3098.

The term "one who speaks according to the Dhamma" (*dhammavādī*) is a qualification of "one who is senior by virtue of a different affiliation" (*nānāsaṃvāsavuḍḍhaka*). As it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three who are worthy of salutation:
one who was ordained earlier is worthy of salutation by one who was ordained later; one who belongs to a different affiliation and is senior..."

“O monks, one who speaks according to the Dhamma is worthy of veneration in the world with its devas, its Māras... [and so on]... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of veneration.

Because there was no fixed rule stating, “Only these are worthy of veneration, and no others,” he said, “such as censure, etc.,” in order to show that there are indeed others who are also worthy of veneration.
Here, by the word “etc.,” the formal acts of suspension (*niyassa*), banishment (*pabbājanīya*), and reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya*) are included.
He includes [this]. "In this" means in this section concerning those worthy of veneration. "Kamma" refers to the fourfold formal act, beginning with the *apalokana* (motion).
To show the procedure to be followed by one who is unable, or by those who are unable, to prevent an illegal (*adhamma*) kamma being performed by the Saṅgha, he says "resolution," and so forth.
The construction is: "the resolution, moreover, is assigned to a single person. [This refers to] an illegal kamma.
It is said that while sitting among the monks who were performing [the act], even though one monk knew it was "unlawful" (*adhamma*), he was unable to stop them;
thus, he made a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) in his mind, saying, "This is not acceptable to me.
Or, "of two or three" means that when two or three monks, being unable to stop those very [monks], [resolve] among themselves...
“‘This is not acceptable’—this is the declaration of one’s view (*diṭṭhāvikamma*), meaning the making known of one’s own respective view.
Beyond that, ‘beyond three,’ it is the protesting against four formal acts (*kamma*);
the meaning is that it is the rejection [of them], saying, ‘Do not perform this illegal act (*adhammakamma*).’”

3101. To show that the characteristic of seizing with confidence (*vissāsaggāhalakkhaṇa*) is fivefold by way of seizing what has not been seized, he said, "One who is a friend" (*sandiṭṭho*), and so forth.
The construction here should be understood as follows: one who is a friend and is living, and is pleased when [something] is seized;
one who is an intimate (*sambhatto*) and is living, and is pleased when [something] is seized; and one who has been addressed and is living.

And when he has taken [the robe], he is satisfied; thus, by assigning three characteristics of gaining confidence for each of these three types of persons—those who are seen, those who are associates, and those who have conversed—it should be understood that there are nine kinds.
Furthermore, the meaning of the words and the detailed analysis here have already been stated below.

3102. The construction is as follows: "The two failures arising from conduct and livelihood—namely, failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*)"—meaning that failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*) and failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*) are what is stated.

3103. "Therein" means among those four types of failure. The construction is as follows: "Two offenses—the *pārājika* which cannot be remedied, and the *saṅghādisesa* offense leading to rehabilitation—are declared to be 'failure in virtue'.
3104. "And that view which grasps at extremes, and that view which has ten bases—this twofold view is 'failure in view.'"

The construction is "it has been explained. In that context, "extreme-grasping view" (*antaggāhikā-diṭṭhi*) refers to a view that proceeds by way of grasping at the extremes of annihilationism (*ucchedanta*) or eternalism (*sassatanta*).
It is the ten-based view (*dasavatthukā diṭṭhi*) that proceeds in the manner of "there is no giving," and so forth.
As for the five offenses beginning with the grave offense (*thullaccaya*), which lead to confession (*desanāgāminī*): those were [established] by the Blessed One, who is skilled in conduct.
The construction is: "it is said to be a failure of conduct. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita* offenses.
"They" (*yā*) refers to the plurality in view of the five types of offenses. "It" (*sā*) refers to the singularity in view of the commonality of "failure of conduct.

3106. Regarding "deceit, etc.": by the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of flattery (*lapanā*), hinting (*nemittikatā*), belittling (*nippesikatā*), and seeking gain with gain (*lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā*).
"Taken up"—the detailed explanation of hypocrisy (*kuhana*) and so forth should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

The grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that offense for which livelihood is the condition and the cause. "Sixfold" means sixfold by way of the offenses of the fourth *pārājika*, *sañcaritta*, *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, and *dukkaṭa*. They have been "proclaimed":
“For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one who has evil desires and is overcome by desire speaks of a non-existent, unreal superhuman state;

this is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). For the sake of livelihood... [as before] ...he engages in matchmaking; this is an offense entailing formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa). For the sake of livelihood...
[as before] ...he says, ‘The monk who dwells in your monastery is an Arahant’; for one who makes such a claim, there is an offense.”

[Regarding] a grave offense (thullaccaya). For the sake of livelihood... [as before] ...if a monk, not being ill, solicits and eats fine foods for his own benefit, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
For the sake of livelihood... [as before] ...if a nun, not being ill, solicits and eats fine foods for her own benefit, there is an offense of confession (pāṭidesanīya).
For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, [soliciting] soup...
“Or if one who is not ill, having requested rice or boiled grain for his own sake, eats it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Thus it is taught. By this, failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*) is illustrated.

3107. “One who has been suspended,” and so forth, is the definition of those three types of persons living apart (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*), given in their respective order. Among them, the three kinds of those suspended have already been explained.

3108–9. “If one who sits on the side of those for whom the Saṅgha has performed an act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) and who speak contrary to the Dhamma, having heard the views of both them and the others, gives rise to the thought: ‘These are speakers of what is contrary to the Dhamma;
the others are speakers of the Dhamma’—then even while sitting in their midst, he belongs to a different communion from them and subverts the legal act.”
To show the determination of the commentary which states, "He incurs [the offense] because he has not come within arm's reach of the others," he said,
"In the faction of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma," and so forth.
"In the faction of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma" means in the faction of those speakers contrary to the Dhamma who have been expelled by a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
“Sitting” means sitting without having left the reach of the hand, acting as a completer of the quorum.
“Reflecting” means thinking in various ways, such as: “Are these indeed speakers of Dhamma, or are they not? One arouses the thought, “But these are speakers of Dhamma.
When that thought has thus arisen, while still sitting on the side of those who speak what is not Dhamma, in this way...
"This bhikkhu is one who gives rise to a [wrong] mental state. "By way of a view" means by way of a view consisting of such a mental state that has been produced.
It is thus explained that he becomes one of a different communion from those who speak what is not the Dhamma.
"But he remains right there" means he remains seated right within that faction of those who speak what is not the Dhamma; for the verbal root *sad* has the sense of obstructing movement.

Sitting there, he is called "one who stands there. "Of two" refers to the two Saṅghas consisting of the faction of those who speak according to the Dhamma and the faction of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma.

"An act" refers to an act to be performed by a Saṅgha of four members and so forth. "He causes division" means that because he belongs to the faction of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma, he becomes one who completes their number;
and because the others, while remaining within the same boundary, do not come within arm's reach [of him].

Because consent has not been given, he invalidates the legal act (*kamma*). However, one who sits on the side of those speaking contrary to the Dhamma and enters among them saying, "These are speakers of what is contrary to the Dhamma;

the others are speakers of the Dhamma," or whoever, sitting on whichever side, takes up [the position] that "these are speakers of the Dhamma"—it should be understood that such a person makes himself a member of the same community (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) with them by his own action.

3110. The construction is as follows: if a regular (pakatatta) monk who has gone outside the boundary is standing within arm’s reach, he is considered to be of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) from the boundary.

Even a formal act (kamma) performed by including him as a completer of the quorum is invalid. Thus, according to the method stated above, three types of those of a different communion have been taught by the Great Sage. This is the construction.

“*Cuto*” means one who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense; he is designated as “fallen” because of having fallen away from the Teaching (*sāsana*). The phrase “eleven kinds of bhikkhunīs are incapable” is the word-division (*padaccheda*).
These seventeen persons are mentioned collectively (*sāmaññena*) without regard for their specific distinctions. They are called “those with whom there is no communal living” (*asaṃvāsā*):

they are not to be lived with, or else, because there is no communal living—such as performing formal acts (*ekakamma*) and so forth—with them alongside those of normal status (*pakatatta*), they are known as “those with whom there is no communal living.”
"Of all forms of non-residence" (asaṃvāsassa sabbassa) means of all the seventeen kinds of non-residence as previously described.

"And likewise of one deserving an act" (tathā kammārahassa ca) refers to one who is "deserving an act" as stated in the Parivāra: "He for whom the Saṅgha performs an act is neither one who has reached the point of the act, nor one who is entitled to give consent;
rather, he is one deserving an act. "Of the insane and so forth"—by the word "so forth" (ādi),...

This refers to the inclusion of those whose minds are deranged (*khittacitta*) and so forth. When the Saṅgha is performing acts such as *tajjanīya* (censure) against them, "objection" (*paṭikkhepa*) means protestation (*paṭikkosanā*).
"It does not take root" means it does not remain in the place where the protest is made; the intended meaning is that it does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*).

3113. Regarding the phrase "one who lives in communion" (*sasaṃvāsaka*)... [and] "a monk" (*bhikkhu*), according to the method already stated, one who has attained the status of being "not in communion" (*asaṃvāsika*) either through a formal act or through a doctrinal conviction (*laddhi*).

Because he has not entered [into schism], being of the same communion, and because he has not entered into a state of non-communion within the boundary—remaining within a single boundary—he is a regular monk who has not committed the ultimate offense.

Even for one standing immediately next to him within arm’s reach, an objection raised by means of speech through vocal expression succeeds; it remains in the very place of objection and subverts the formal act (*kamma*). This is the intended meaning.

"By six modes" means: by way of shame, by way of ignorance, by way of being overcome by remorse, by way of forgetfulness, by way of perceiving the improper as proper, and by way of perceiving the proper as improper—by these six modes.
The construction is: "The five allowable things for a recluse have been stated, and the five purifications have been stated."
“I allow you, monks, to consume fruit by means of five ways in which it has been made allowable for ascetics (*samaṇakappa*):
that which is prepared by fire, that which is prepared by a knife, that which is prepared by the fingernail, seedless, and fifthly, that from which the seed has been removed.

These are the five things made allowable for ascetics authorized in the *Khuddakavatthuka*. Regarding the “five purifications,” they are mentioned in the *Ekuttara* of the *Parivāra* as “the five purifications.”

In its exposition (*niddesa*), the five purifications known as the recitations of the *Pātimokkha*—shown by way of the method beginning with, “Having recited the introduction (*nidāna*), the remainder should be proclaimed by means of hearing;

this is the first purification”—and the five purifications spoken of thus: “The recitation of the Sutta, the Uposatha of complete purity, the Uposatha of formal determination, the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), and the Uposatha of concord as the fifth.”
The two sets of five purifications (*visuddhi*) are included under a general term, as in the expressions “the two sets of five consciousnesses” (*dvipañcaviññāṇāni*) and so forth. 3115–7.
*Nidāna* (the origin) is that wherein the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is given—that is, it is fully explained or established.

It refers to places such as Vesālī, which served as the locus for the promulgation of various training rules. *Puṃ* refers to hell (*niraya*); it is so called because it swallows or crushes the suffering of those in hell.

One who experiences [the results of actions] is a "person" (puggala), a "being" (satta). Noble persons (ariya-puggala) are so called because they resemble that [original person], or because they were formerly in such a state of existence;

thus they should be understood as "persons. However, here these are intended as those who are beginners in the transgression of the training rules (sikkhāpada). Now he will explain the exposition of the person (puggala-niddesa).
It is here that the formal proclamation of the training rules—known as the Blessed One’s command—resides, and it proceeds in dependence upon that.
The *vatthu* (basis) is the transgression that serves as the cause for the formulation of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) for each respective individual.
*Vidhāna* means analysis, method, or classification. It is called *paññatti* because by it the Blessed One’s command (*āṇā*) is made known (*paññāpīyati*) in a specific manner (*pakārena*).

Regarding the phrase "the method of the formulation" (*paññattividhi*), although one should say "the method of the formulation" (*paññattiyā vidhi*), it is expressed as "the method of the formulation" (*vidhiṃ paññattiyā*).
This is an exposition by way of inability according to the composition of verses. Furthermore, that method of designation (*paññatti-vidhi*) is ninefold, by way of:

primary designation (*paññatti*), secondary designation (*anupaññatti*), designation for what has not yet arisen (*anuppanna-paññatti*), universal designation (*sabbattha-paññatti*), partial designation (*padesa-paññatti*), common designation (*sādhāraṇa-paññatti*), uncommon designation (*asādhāraṇa-paññatti*), designation on one side (*ekatopaññatti*), and designation on both sides (*ubhatopaññatti*).
The word-division is: “*vipatti*, *āpatti*, *anāpattī*. That by which virtue (*sīla*) and the rest fall away is *vipatti*.
It is fourfold according to virtue, conduct, view, and livelihood. That has already been shown above by way of enumeration.
That by which those who have become unwholesome or indeterminate commit a transgression of the Blessed One’s command is *āpatti*. It is [further classified] by way of preliminary effort and so forth.
An offense has many classifications. There is no offense when one does not transgress a command due to ignorance and so forth. "Origins" (samuṭṭhānāni) means those by which offenses arise;
they are the sixfold causes of offenses, consisting of body and so forth. The method regarding these origins is the "method of origins" (samuṭṭhānanaya);
that [is what is explained].

Fault (*vajja*), action (*kamma*), performance (*kiriyā*), perception (*saññā*), consciousness (*citta*), and command (*āṇatti*)—these are "fault, action, performance, perception, consciousness, and command" (*vajjakammakriyāsaññācittāṇattiyo*).

The method (*vidhi*) for these is thus stated; that [is what is meant]. Regarding "the method of fault" (*vajjavidhi*): it refers to the method of fault as it has been stated: "That which, on the side of the conscious, possesses only unwholesome consciousness, is a fault according to the world (*lokavajjā*);
the rest are faults according to the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajjā*). Regarding "the method of action" (*kammavidhi*): "All... [and so forth].
The method of action (*kammavidhi*) is shown as being threefold by way of bodily action, verbal action, and both together. The method of performance (*kriyāvidhi*) is shown by such a method as:

"There is an offense that originates from performance (*kiriyato*), there is one from non-performance (*akiriyato*), there is one from both performance and non-performance, and there is one that may be from performance or may be from non-performance.
The method of perception (*saññāvidhi*) is shown by such [passages] as "liberations through perception" (*saññāvimokkhā*).
The method for perception as demonstrated by way of principle;
the method for consciousness, which is stated as: "All [states] are twofold according to consciousness: those with consciousness and those without consciousness";
the method for instruction, which is stated as: "That which involves instruction and that which does not involve instruction"; and the arrangement of the factors.
The classification of factors for the offenses in all the training rules has been stated. The application is as follows:

the triad of feelings and the triad of the wholesome. That, moreover, has already been shown in various places as "unwholesome consciousness," "two consciousnesses," "three consciousnesses," "painful feeling," "two feelings," and "three feelings."

"This characteristic is seventeenfold" means that the common characteristic of all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) consists of the seventeen divisions previously mentioned, beginning with the "origin" (*nidāna*).
"Having shown" means having made manifest. "The Buddha, skilled in the Vinaya, should apply [it] appropriately to each respective training rule" is the syntactical connection.
3118. Regarding these seventeen characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), he first spoke the words beginning with “nidāna” in order to demonstrate the source (*nidāna*) and the person (*puggala*).

Therein, the locative case in “tattha” (therein) refers to those seventeen common characteristics; it is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). “Nidāna” indicates that which is to be selected.
The word “puraṃ” (the city) should be construed individually with each of the phrases beginning with “Vesālī. [The phrase] “Sakkabhagga” means...
By these words denoting regions, the city-dwellers residing in those places are to be understood.

And those [regions] have already been illustrated in the introductory accounts (nidāna) of the training rules (sikkhāpada) in various places, such as: "He dwells among the Sakyas in Kapilavatthu; he dwells among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira.
The detailed analysis of the meaning of phrases such as "Ten at Vesālī" will be made clear further on. Regarding Giribbaja:
In the city of Rājagaha. For it is called "Giribbaja" because it is surrounded on all sides by five mountains such as Isigili and others, which resemble a fence (vaja). 3121.
The connection is that twenty-three types of persons who are first-time offenders, such as Sudinna and Dhaniya, have been mentioned in the Pātimokkha for bhikkhus.
3122. The construction is as follows: all those persons who appear in both Pātimokkhas, when totaled together, become thirty.

Since the detailed analysis of the *vatthu* (offenses) and so forth will be explained later on, it is not stated here. [Objection: But will not the analysis of the *nidāna* (introductory narratives) and the persons also be explained there?
Why then is that stated here? [Response: This is no fault; because this is a manual (*pakaraṇa*), it must be stated here as well.
If it is asked: "In that case, the determination of the basis (*vatthu*) and so forth should also be stated here; why has it not been stated?"—the answer is:

since this [determination] is presented as a single conjunction (*ekayoga*), by the statement of this one, that too is effectively stated; thus it should be understood as being abbreviated by way of showing only a portion.
3123. The connection is: "He who knows this tree knows the designation (*paññatti*) without remainder. Here, "this... [refers to the following].

By the word "tree" (*taru*), he illustrates by means of a metaphor the collection of characteristics common to all training rules (*sikkhāpada*), which consists of seventeen types beginning with the "origin" (*nidāna*).
To the question, "Of what kind is this tree? he says: "having three roots," and so forth.

Therein, "having three roots" (*timūla*) means that which has three roots—namely, the origin (*nidāna*), the person (*puggala*), and the subject matter (*vatthu*)—is "three-rooted. "Having nine leaves" (*navapatta*)... [text continues]

That which has nine kinds of designations as its leaves is called *navapattaṃ*. That which has two sprouts—namely, those designated as world-transgressions (*lokavajja*) and rule-transgressions (*paṇṇattivajja*)—is called *dvayaṅkuraṃ*.
Although it should have been stated as *dviaṅkuraṃ*, the vowel *i* was replaced by *ay*, and thus it is expressed as *dvayaṅkuraṃ*.

That which has seven fruits—namely, those designated as command (*āṇatti*), offense (*āpatti*), non-offense (*anāpatti*), failure (*vipatti*), perception (*saññā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*)—is called *sattaphalaṃ*.
It has seven fruits, thus it is "seven-fruited" (*sattaphala*). It has six flowers, namely those reckoned as the six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), thus it is "six-flowered" (*chapuppha*).
It has two sources, namely those reckoned as the two types of mental action (*cittakamma*), thus it is "two-sourced" (*dvippabhava*).
It has two branches, namely those reckoned as the two factors of activity (*kiriyaaṅga*), thus it is "two-branched" (*dvisākha*). "Whoever knows this tree... [is the meaning].

The monk who knows the tree known as the determination of the collection of seventeen characteristics, which are stated together with their specific forms and common features—he is that monk. "Exposition" (paññatti) refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka. "In its entirety" means completely.
3124. Thus, whoever recites this supreme and most excellent determination, whose word-meanings are sweet and unconfused—
The construction is as follows: while reciting it aloud he masters it, he listens thoroughly in the presence of his teacher, and he asks about the meaning and inquires into its purpose;
that bhikkhu becomes equal to Upāli in the determination of the Vinaya, being like the Great Elder Upāli who was established in the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discussion of Miscellaneous Determinations within the *Vinayavinicchayavaṇṇanā*, which is an Elucidation of the Essence of the Meaning of the Vinaya.
Now begins the commentary on the Discussion of the Method for the Manifestation of Meditation Subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
3125. “One should show virtue at the beginning;
one should clarify the path in the middle;
and at the conclusion, Nibbāna.”
“This is the established method for a Dhamma-preacher.
Recalling this definition of a Dhamma-preacher as it has been stated, this teacher,

having shown the exposition illustrating the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha by way of neither too brief nor too detailed an approach, [proceeds] to [explain] the other three virtues rooted in that, and...
Having shown that very [Dhamma] by its mere sight, as well as the five purifications beginning with purification of mind (cittavisuddhi) which are rooted in purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi),
and the purification of knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi) known as the Noble Path which is rooted in those,

and the Nibbāna to be attained through that, he said "In the foremost," etc., desiring to bring to completion the discourse on discipline (vinaya) as it had been commenced. Therein, "in the foremost" (pāmokkhe):

It is supreme by virtue of being the foundation for blameless states such as concentration (*samādhi*). It is "for the entry into liberation" in the sense of being the sign for entering the great city of the Deathless Nibbāna.
It is the "mouth," serving as the unique gateway. As it has been said:
"How could there be another staircase for ascending to heaven equal to virtue (*sīla*)?"
"Or else, it is the gateway for entering the city of Nibbāna.

Regarding "the destruction of all suffering": because the Noble Path is the means for attaining the destruction of all sufferings, such as the suffering of birth, it is designated as "the destruction of all suffering" by way of figurative application (*phalūpacāra*).
Furthermore, "in the foremost" (*pāmokkhe*) means "at the mouth for entering liberation" (*mokkhappavesane mukhe*).

And the phrases “in the destruction of all suffering” and “in the Pātimokkha” are qualifiers of this [term]. “When it has been spoken” means when it has been explained in its various modes starting from the pārājikas.

The connection is that the other three [types of virtue] have indeed already been spoken of. The other triad of virtues—namely, the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, the virtue of purity of livelihood, and the virtue dependent on the requisites—is already included, just as when it is said, “The king has arrived,” the arrival of his retinue is implied; therefore...
The intention is: "I shall not speak of that. 3126.
This fourfold virtue refers to the fourfold purification of virtue, beginning with the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.

"Having known" means having understood it by way of its characteristics, its purification, and its various modes such as that which partakes of decline, that which partakes of stability, that which partakes of distinction, and that which partakes of penetration.
And having understood. "Therein" means in the fourfold virtue (*sīla*). "Established" means established by bringing about the state of being endowed with the factors such as being without breach.
"Concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to mundane concentration distinguished as access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*).

"Having developed" means having increased it through repeated application among the forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "By wisdom" (*paññā*) means by that which discerns the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*) and so forth.
"By means of supramundane wisdom" means by that which has become its cause and its instrument.

"Is liberated" means that, having severed all the bonds of the defilements, one is released from the prison of *saṃsāra* on every side; the intention is that one attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa*).
3127. Explaining this very meaning as it was stated in brief, he says: "The ten recollections," and so forth. The ten recollections.
The connection is that ten kasinas, ten foulness subjects (asubhas), four immeasurables (appamaññās), and likewise four formless attainments (āruppas) have been mentioned;
and furthermore, two other meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhānas) have been mentioned.
Therein, the "ten recollections" (anussatis) are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue (sīla),...

The ten recollections (anussati) spoken of as follows: "recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, mindfulness directed to the body, recollection of death, mindfulness of breathing, and recollection of peace.

The ten totalities (kasiṇa) are: the earth totality, the water totality, the fire totality, the air totality, the blue totality, [the yellow totality, the red totality, the white totality, the space totality, and the consciousness totality].
The ten *kasiṇas* are those stated as: the yellow *kasiṇa*, the red *kasiṇa*, the white *kasiṇa*, the light *kasiṇa*, and the limited-space *kasiṇa*.

The ten unattractive objects (*asubha*) are those stated as: the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut up, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the blood-stained, the worm-infested, and the skeleton. These are the ten unattractive objects.
The four illimitables (*appamaññā*) are those stated as “loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity.

The four formless attainments (*āruppa*) are those stated as “the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, there is another pair of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), namely “the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment” and “the analysis of the four elements.”
The "place" and "both" have been stated.
(3128) Thus, the construction is: "In this way, all forty kinds of meditation subjects for the mind have been fully pointed out.
A *kammaṭṭhāna* is a place (*ṭhāna*)—meaning a state of occurrence by way of being an object—for action (*kamma*) in the sense of application (*yoga*).
It is called a *ṭhāna* (base) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein, owing to its dependence upon that; it is thus a cause. A *kammaṭṭhāna* is the base or cause for insight into karma.
To the question "Of what?", he says: "of the mind-master" (*manobhuno*). It is a "mind-master" (*manobhū*) because it overcomes the mind;
the meaning is: of the deva of the sense-sphere who has acquired that name by obstructing the arising of wholesome consciousness.
By this, the section on the counting of meditation subjects has been shown.
