(3129–30) Now, in order to show the development of these meditation subjects by breaking it down into its constituent parts, he first presents the matrix, saying:
"From access and absorption," and so forth. Therein, "from access and absorption" means: "this many meditation subjects lead to access; this many lead to absorption."
“...so many lead to absorption”—thus it is by way of access and absorption. As for the "divisions of jhāna":
it refers to the divisions of jhāna such as, “so many belong to the first jhāna, so many to the threefold or fourfold jhāna, and so many to the fivefold jhāna,” and so forth.
As for "transcending": it is by transcending the factors and the objects. And as for "expansion and non-expansion": it is by way of [the range] of one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, and so on.

[The jhānas] are to be developed and not to be developed. "By way of object and plane" means by way of objects such as the sign (nimitta) and so forth, and also by way of the planes where they are obtainable and unobtainable.
"By way of apprehension" means because they are to be apprehended by way of seeing and so forth. "By way of conditions" means because of their being the causal conditions for their respective stages.

"Furthermore" has the sense of the word *puna* (again) and the sense of emphasis (*nīhāra*). "In accordance with temperament" means by way of being favorable to temperaments such as those dominated by lust (*rāga*) and so forth.
This is the distinction, this is the difference. Among these forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna).

Having thus demonstrated the matrix (mātikā), while demonstrating them in their proper order, [the author] first says "eight recollections" (aṭṭhānussatiyo) and so forth, in order to show those that bring about access concentration (upacāra) and the rest. Therein: in this matrix, or among those forty.

Among the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), there are ten: the eight recollections (*anussati*)—excluding both mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*)—namely, the recollection of the Buddha and so forth;
the perception of the repulsiveness of food (*āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā*); and the definition of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*).

These ten bring about access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) because the qualities of the Buddha and so forth exist as ultimate realities (*paramattha-bhāva*), and because they are manifold, even for a single [quality].

Furthermore, because it is impossible for concentration to become established through absorption (*appanā*) within these ten meditation subjects due to their profound nature, the concentration that has reached the development of absorption becomes established only at the level of access (*upacāra*); therefore, these are conducive to access.
But is it not the case here that the second and fourth immaterial-sphere concentrations, as well as supramundane concentration, do reach absorption regarding ultimate realities?

[One] attains [it]; therefore, why is it not stated that "by way of being the ultimate reality" (*paramatthabhāvato*) is the cause for the non-attainment of absorption (*appanā*), acting as the causal factor?

No; because the occurrence of ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*) is possible through a specific kind of cultivation (*bhāvanāvisesa*), and because this [state] is possible through a specific kind of fourth-jhāna cultivation belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
For indeed, the second and fourth immaterial-sphere absorptions (*ārūpāvacarasamādhi*) are the fourth jhānas of immaterial-sphere absorption that have reached the state of absorption (*appanā*).
By means of the development that consists merely in the surmounting of the object, one attains absorption even with respect to an object that possesses intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Through the power of the progressive sequence of purification in development, supramundane concentration (*lokuttara samādhi*) attains absorption.
3132. "Therein" refers to those thirty meditation subjects conducive to jhāna. "Foulnesses" (*asubha*) refers to the ten, beginning with the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*).
The foul (asubha) and mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati)—these eleven [meditative subjects] are associated with the first jhāna.

Because they have a repulsive object, and because a state of mind can only arise toward a repulsive object through the power of applied thought (vitakka)—just as a boat cannot remain steady on a river with a violent current except by the force of its rudder—the second jhāna and those above it, which are without applied thought, are impossible here; thus, these belong only to the first jhāna, which possesses applied thought.
According to possibility, they belong to the first jhāna. Both mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) and the kasiṇas—these eleven—are fourfold-jhāna factors;
they consist of the fourfold jhānas of the fine-material sphere according to the fourfold method, as well as the fivefold jhānas.
3133. "Only three immeasurables" means that the immeasurables are only three: loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and gladness (*muditā*). In the *Sāmaññaniddesa*:

How is it to be understood that only these [four] are included? It is understood through the method of elimination (*pārisesato*), because the state of the fourth immeasurable (*appamaññā*) as belonging to the fourth jhāna will be explained by the passage beginning with “Then the last,” etc. Regarding the phrase “three-jhāna”: this means those possessing three jhānas.

It should be understood that although one ought to say “three-jhāna” (*tikajjhānā*), it is stated thus by a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). As for loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the others, they are incompatible with ill-will accompanied by grief, cruelty, and lack of delight.
Because it is to be abandoned, its being accompanied by joy—which is the opposite of displeasure—is stated;
thus, according to the fourfold method, its possession of three jhānas is stated, and according to the fivefold method, its possession of four jhānas is stated.
The word "atha" (then) is for the purpose of precluding a connection with the preceding word "tisso" (three) via the term "pacchimā" (last).
The final two immeasurables and the four formless attainments are considered, according to the fourfold method, to possess four jhānas, as well as five jhānas.

Having abandoned the three types of activity that proceed through the various modes of loving-kindness and so forth—namely, “May all beings be happy,” “May they be freed from suffering,” and “May they not be deprived of the attainment of happiness”—one develops a state of mind toward beings that has reached the mode of equanimity through the vision of beings as the owners of their own karma (*kammassakatā*). From this development arises [the fifth jhāna].

In this context, because equanimity (*upekkhā*) is more powerful than neutrality, it is stated that the sublime abiding of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*), when reached in absorption (*appanā*), can be accompanied by happiness (*sukha*).
Thus, its being "accompanied by equanimity" is mentioned.
(3134) The phrase "the transcendence from the factors and the object is stated in two ways" is to be construed as follows: "in the fourfold and fivefold jhānas" refers to the ten kasiṇas.

"Mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānasati*) refers to those meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) consisting of the eleven sets of four jhānas, as well as the three sets of three jhānas comprised within the first of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), namely loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the others.
"Transcending the factors" (*aṅgātikkama*) means that while remaining on the very same object, one transcends the jhāna-factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*);
thus, because the second jhāna and the others arise upon the same object as the first jhāna and so forth, there is a "transcending of factors."
This is the intended meaning. "The state of transcending the factors" (*aṅgātikkamatā*) is simply the transcending of the factors.

(3135) "Transcending the factors" means by way of transcending the mental joy (*somanassa*) associated with the third jhāna. "Having transcended the object" refers to [the objects] consisting of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*), the kasiṇa, the space resulting from the removal [of the kasiṇa], the first formless-sphere consciousness whose domain is that space, and the absence of that [consciousness].

Having successively transcended the four objects—namely, the four immaterial-sphere jhānas (ārūpāvacara-jhāna) beginning with the base of infinite space, which arise and emerge as the four immaterial attainments (āruppa) having as their respective objects:

first, the consciousness of the first immaterial state whose object is the space remaining after the removal of the kasiṇa; and third, the consciousness of the third immaterial state whose object is the non-existence of that [consciousness]—these four arise and emerge.
"In these" means in these objects. "They should be expanded" means: "as much of a space as one pervades with the kasiṇa..."
Within that [attainment], one becomes capable of hearing sounds with the divine ear-element, seeing forms with the divine eye, and knowing the minds of other beings with one's own mind;

it is with reference to this stated purpose that, having delimited [the practice] by way of the counting of factors and so forth, one should extend it as much as one desires. The rest—all such practices as the foul (asubha) and so on—is the same.
The construction is: "The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should certainly not be developed because of the absence of a purpose. 3137.

Therein, among those meditation subjects, the construction is: "The twenty-two meditation subjects—namely, the ten kasiṇas, the ten foulness subjects (asubha), mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati)—have counterpart objects (paṭibhāgārammaṇa). Here, by the words "kasiṇas" and so forth, the jhānas that have those [bases] as their objects are included.
"Analysis of elements" (*dhātuvavatthāna*) means the analysis of the four elements; it is shortened due to the requirements of the verse meter.

"Infinite consciousness" (*viññāṇañca*) refers to the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). "Neither-perception" (*nevasaññā*) refers to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*). "Ten and two" means twelve.

"The sphere of existence" (*bhāvagocara*) means having phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) as their sphere; what is meant is that they have ultimate phenomena (*paramattha-dhamma*) as their object.
3139. "And two immaterial-sphere states of mind" refers to the two types of immaterial-sphere consciousness-arising known as the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness.

These six factors are explained as having an indeterminable range of objects (*navattabbagocara*). This is because they take as their objects: (1) the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*), which are a designation for beings (*sattapaññatti*);

(2) the first immaterial attainment, which is a designation for the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭimākāsapaññatti*); and (3) the third immaterial attainment, which is a designation for the absence of the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment.

3140. "Perception of repulsiveness" refers to the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment (*āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā*). Regarding "mindfulness directed to the body" (*kāyagatāsati*): from among the twelve [levels], it does not occur among the gods in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) because of the impossibility of corpses or of those who are fit for repulsiveness;

this is the construction. 3141. And those twelve. The word *bhiyyo* is a particle used in the sense of "more than"; more than that, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*)—making thirteen—does not arise at all in the fine-material and immaterial realms because of the absence of inhalation and exhalation; this is the construction.

3142. In the formless realm (arūpāvacara), within the formless existence (arūpabhava), with the exception of the four formless [attainments], the other thirty-six states do not arise because of the absence of the transcendence of form;
such is the construction. All forty-eight states arise in the human world among humans, as they are obtainable by all.
3143. "Excluding the fourth kasiṇa" means excluding the air-kasiṇa, because it must be grasped through what is seen and touched.

The construction is as follows: these nineteen things—the nine kasiṇas and the ten foul objects—must be apprehended at the preliminary stage during the time of preparation by the very visual consciousness that has seen them.
What is meant is that, having looked with the eye at the preliminary stage, the preparatory work is performed; thus, the sign acquired through that [vision] is what must be apprehended for them.

"By what is touched" means by way of what is touched at the tip of the nose or the upper lip. In the mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), the fivefold skin should be apprehended by what is seen.

"The breeze" (*māluto*)—that is, the wind-kasiṇa—should be apprehended by what is seen and touched, because it is to be apprehended both by way of perceiving the moving color on the leaves of sugarcane crops and so forth, and by the impact upon the bodily sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*). Here...
Regarding these meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), "the rest" refers to what remains after those already mentioned. The eight recollections beginning with the recollection of the Buddha,

the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the four formless attainments (*āruppa*), the perception of repulsiveness in food, the analysis of the four elements, and the five internal parts of the body such as the kidneys within mindfulness of the body—
all of this is said to be "to be grasped by hearing alone," because it must be acquired by hearing from another.

3145. Here, among these meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), with the exception of the space-kasiṇa, the nine kasiṇas arise as conditions—meaning they become the causal basis—for the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa*), which serves as the object for the first immaterial-sphere consciousness (*āruppacitta*);

such is the construction of the sentence. 3146. All ten kasiṇas become conditions for the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), such as the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) and so forth; such is the construction. "Of the fourth" refers to the fourth sublime abiding (*brahmavihāra*).
"Lower and lower immaterial [attainments]" refers to the base of infinite space and so forth. "Of each subsequent one" is to be construed as:

it is declared to be the condition for each successive higher jhāna, such as the base of infinite consciousness and so on. "Neither-perception" refers to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"Of cessation" refers to the cessation of perception and feeling, that is, by means of that attainment of cessation.

"3148. 'All' refers to the forty-four dhammas that serve as meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). 'For dwelling in happiness' means for dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).

And 'for the escape from existence' means for Nibbāna, which is to be attained through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) by way of taking insight (*vipassanā*) as its proximate cause, since it is the necessary support for the cessation of existence.
And 'for the pleasures of existence' refers to those [states] occurring during the stages of preliminary (*parikamma*) and access (*upacāra*) development."
It is explained that wholesome states of consciousness belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are conditions for the happiness of existence in the sense-sphere happy realms;

consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) occurring during the access stage (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*) are conditions for the happiness of existence in the fine-material sphere; and the others, which belong to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), are conditions for the happiness of existence in the immaterial sphere.

(3149) It should be understood that these eleven—namely, the ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*) and mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*)—are especially suitable for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).

The interpretation: By the word “specifically,” he indicates that [the practice] is stated because it is the direct opposite of greed and because it is highly conducive to it, while the others are not excluded.
For this has been said in the *Visuddhimagga*: “All of this is stated by way of being the direct opposite and by way of being highly conducive;
however, they do not suppress greed and the other [defilements], nor do they assist faith and the other [wholesome qualities].”
“There is no such thing as the development of the wholesome.

3150. “Together with the four colored kasiṇas”: this means they are accompanied by the four colored kasiṇas. “The four immeasurables”: these eight are explained as being conducive to those of a hateful temperament.
3151. “Of deluded nature”: this refers to one of a deluded temperament. The word division is: “Mindfulness of breathing alone.”

3152. *Maranūpasame*: death (*maraṇa*) and tranquility (*upasama*) together constitute "death-and-tranquility" (*maranūpasama*); [the practice] is in that death-and-tranquility. "Mindfulness" (*sati*) refers to mindfulness of death (*maraṇānussati*) and mindfulness of tranquility (*upasamānussati*); these are the four states. "Those whose nature is wisdom" (*paññāpakati*) refers to one of an intellectual temperament (*buddhicarita*). 3153.

"The sixfold set of recollections beginning with the Buddha" (*ādianussaticchakka*) refers to the group of six consisting of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and the deities.

"Described as suitable for those of faithful temperament" (*saddhācaritavaṇṇita*) means it is said to be conducive to one of a faithful temperament (*saddhācarita*). "The formless states" (*āruppa*) refers to the four formless attainments.
"The remaining kasiṇas" refers to the ten remaining states by way of the kasiṇas of the primary elements, light, and space.
"Suitable for all" means suitable for all six types of temperament.
Having thus explained the classification of meditation subjects according to the sequence of the matrix as it was set forth, now...

In order to show the method of development (*bhāvanānaya*), he says "Thus," and so forth. "Having thus known the meditation subjects according to their divisions" refers to the demonstration of the undertaking of development by way of the methods of classification as previously stated.
"The wise one" (*paṇḍita*) refers to a person capable [of attainment] who possesses wisdom through the wisdom of a three-rooted rebirth-linking (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi*).

"Among these" (*tesu*) is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). "The intelligent one" (*medhāvī*) is one endowed with the wisdom of mastery (*pārihāriya-paññā*). "Grasping firmly," and so on, [refers to] the beginning, middle, and end.
By one who observes well, having made it firm and having mastered it with care. A "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta) is one who is:
"Dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem;
one who gives counsel and is patient with what is said."
"One who delivers profound discourse and does not direct one toward what is improper"—
this refers to a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta) endowed with qualities such as virtue, learning, and wisdom, as defined by these characteristics.
The construction is: "Having first cut off the obstacles. "First" means right at the beginning of the development of meditation (*bhāvanā*). "Having cut off the obstacles" refers to the following:
"The dwelling, the family, gain, the group, and action as the fifth."
“Travel, relatives, illness, books,
and psychic powers— these are the ten.
Regarding these ten great impediments that have been mentioned, such as cutting long hair, nails, and body hair, dyeing robes, boiling bowls, and so forth:

"By cutting off both minor obstacles (*khuddaka-palibodha*)": this means either by bringing them to an end through their completion, or by cutting them off through the relinquishing of attachment (*ālaya*).
However, in this context, supernormal power (*iddhi*) is an obstacle to insight (*vipassanā*), not to the development of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*).
For this has been said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "Supernormal power refers to the supernormal power of worldlings (*pothujjanikā iddhi*). For that [power] is like a child lying on its back..."
Like a young plantain tree or like a tender crop, it is difficult to maintain and breaks with even the slightest [distraction].
Furthermore, that [restlessness] is an obstacle to insight (vipassanā), but not to concentration (samādhi), because concentration is to be attained after having reached concentration itself.
Thus, the construction is: "by one dwelling in a suitable dwelling free from defects. Regarding "free from defects":
“A large dwelling, a new dwelling, and a dilapidated dwelling; a roadside lodging;
a tavern, a leaf-hut, and a flower-house; a fruit-grove, and one specifically sought out.
A city, a forest, a field, and a port that is alien.”
“A border region where what is beneficial is lacking, and where no friend is to be found.
Having understood these eighteen states,
a wise person should avoid them from afar, just as one would a dangerous path.

“Dwelling in a suitable place” means: “In this case, monks, the lodging is not too far away, nor too close; it is well-served by roads for coming and going; by day... [and so forth, as stated in the commentaries regarding the eighteen faults].
It is not crowded, quiet at night, with little noise and little sound, and free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles.
Furthermore, for one dwelling in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick arise without difficulty.
Moreover, those monks who dwell in that lodging are learned, masters of the tradition, and bearers of the Dhamma.
Those who are holders of the Vinaya and holders of the Mātikā approach them from time to time and inquire and question them, saying:

"Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this? Those venerable ones then reveal what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that are grounds for uncertainty.
“Thus, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.”—The meaning is:
by dwelling in a suitable monastery that possesses the five qualities praised by the Blessed One and is conducive to the work of meditation.
“The first and so forth” refers to the fine-material-sphere jhānas, beginning with the first and second. Entirely...

“Having developed” means: having developed according to the detailed sequence set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* under the heading “It should be developed without omitting any of the methods of development”;
that is to say, having accomplished purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*). “Possessing wisdom” means:

by means of the wisdom of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) which is born of kamma and is root-conditioned, and by discerning those things conducive to the attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara) is endowed with the wisdom of application (pārihāriyapaññā), which consists in avoiding what is unsuitable and cultivating what is suitable. "From that" means:

having entered any one of the eight meditative absorptions (jhāna) that serve as a basis for insight (vipassanā)—excluding the formless attainments of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—and having emerged from that absorption, he [practices]. Thus it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“Excepting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having emerged from any one of the remaining fine-material or immaterial-sphere jhānas.

Regarding the phrase “having defined name-and-form”: this means that, having entered by whichever door one desires among the doors such as the five aggregates, etc., as described in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on Purification of View (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*), one defines name-and-form, [thinking]: “This is name; this is form.”
Having reached the conclusion that "there is nothing to be called a self or anything else apart from this name-and-form," purity of view is demonstrated by this.

"Having crossed over doubt" refers to the description of the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi*) regarding the phenomena of name-and-form as they have been seen, in the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*).

Having analyzed it in five ways according to the method already stated, one sees name-and-form as it truly is in its fivefold aspect, thinking: "This name-and-form is not without cause, nor does it have a self or similar [factors] as its cause.
Through this fivefold vision of name-and-form, one abandons the sixteenfold doubt that proceeds in the manner of: "Did I exist in the past time?
and so forth, as well as the eightfold doubt that proceeds in the manner of: "He doubts the Teacher," and so forth.
By crossing over and abandoning through energy, the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi*) is thus shown.

Having established himself in the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*) by accomplishing the purification by overcoming doubt in this way, the practitioner applies the three characteristics to the appropriate name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),

and [proceeds] with the knowledge of the subsiding of doubt (*kaṅkhā-vūpasama-ñāṇa*) as described in the section on the purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).

While comprehending formations in the manner described, when the ten imperfections— namely, illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and attachment— become manifest,
one regards those ten imperfections such as illumination that have thus appeared as "not the path," and regards only the insight-knowledge proceeding along the course of the path as "the path."

The meaning is that the wise one, the person of wisdom, the practitioner of yoga, knows; by this, the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*) has been shown in brief.

3159. Up to this point is the application regarding "the three determinations" (*tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vavatthānāni*). "Up to this point" refers to the method shown in brief by the passage beginning, "Having made the determination of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-vavatthānaṃ katvā*).
"Of those three" refers to the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*), the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*), and [the purification by knowledge and vision of the way].

"Purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path" refers to the three purifications: [the purification by knowledge and vision of] mentality-materiality and its conditions, and [the purification by knowledge and vision of] the path and the non-path, each according to their respective insight.

When these have been defined and determined, "the defining of the three truths" means that the defining of the three truths—namely, those designated as suffering, origin, and the path—has been accomplished by means of the mundane thorough knowledge consisting of knowing and scrutinizing.

The meaning is that a decision has been made by means of knowledge through the process of full comprehension. How so? The determination of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is accomplished by the knowledge of purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi-ñāṇa*), which is termed the "distinguishing of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*). The determination of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is accomplished by the knowledge of purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi-ñāṇa*), which is termed the "comprehension of conditions" (*paccaya-pariggaha*). [And] the determination of what is the path and what is not the path... by the knowledge of purification of view... is accomplished. By the knowledge of purification by overcoming doubt... is accomplished. By the knowledge of purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path... is accomplished. Thus, by means of these three knowledges, the four truths have been determined. Therefore, it is said: "A decision has been made by means of knowledge through the process of full comprehension. This is the meaning. How so? The determination of the truth of suffering is accomplished by the knowledge of purification of view, which is termed the "distinguishing of name-and-form"; the determination of the truth of the origin is accomplished by the knowledge of purification by overcoming doubt, which is termed the "comprehension of conditions"; [and] the determination of what is the path and what is not the path... by the knowledge of purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path... is accomplished. The definition of the truth of the path occurs through the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

Having thus briefly shown the two types of full understanding—namely, the full understanding of the known and the full understanding by scrutinization—he said, beginning with "arising and passing away," in order to show the nine knowledges that constitute the body of the full understanding of abandoning.
Therein, "arising and passing away" refers to that which proceeds by way of the contemplation of origination and dissolution.

By eliding the middle term, it is called "arising-and-falling" (*udayabbaya*). Therein, the contemplation of dissolution that occurs by setting aside arising and focusing on falling away is called "dissolution" (*bhaṅga*).

Fear, disadvantage, and disenchantment constitute "fear-disadvantage-disenchantment"; the contemplation of fear is that which proceeds by way of contemplating formations as fearful, and the contemplation of disadvantage is that which proceeds by way of regarding what has been seen as fearful from the perspective of its disadvantage.

The contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*) that occurs regarding those things already seen as dangerous, and the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*) that occurs by way of penetration (*nibbedava*), are described in that same manner.
Knowledge that occurs solely by way of the desire to be liberated from formations after having become disenchanted is "knowledge of the desire for liberation" (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*).
Furthermore, knowledge that occurs by way of undertaking the three types of formations for the purpose of applying the means to liberation is [the knowledge of the way].
Contemplation by way of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*).

Knowledge that proceeds after having looked on with equanimity toward the phenomena of formations (*saṅkhāra-dhamma*) by way of avoiding both fear and delight is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).

Because it is an absolute condition for the attainment of that [equanimity], it is called "conformity to the truths" (*saccānulomika*); and thus, among the knowledge of comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa*) and the others...

The ninth knowledge, called "conformity-knowledge" (anuloma-ñāṇa), is so termed because it conforms to the accomplishment of the functions of the preceding nine knowledges and to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that follow;

this is the application [of the meaning]: that which was shown as the full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā) under the heading of the nine successive stages of insight is here declared as "knowledge and vision of the way" (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana).
3162. Then, immediately after the consciousness termed "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū)—
which, having followed the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), serves as the preliminary adverting for the Path, takes Nibbāna as its object,
and so overcomes the lineage of the worldling while developing and increasing the lineage of the Noble Ones— the phrase "making peace the object" is used.

Having taken as its object Nibbāna—which is designated as "peace" because it is the sign for the subsiding of all the fevers of the defilements and the fire of the suffering of conditioned phenomena—one attains what is called "knowledge and vision.
In this context, "knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to knowing in the sense of full understanding through the realization of the Four Noble Truths;
"vision" (dassana) is so designated because it sees directly, as if with an eye.
The meaning is that the seventh purification-knowledge, known as the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*), is born; it arises.

(3163) "Ending with review" means having the conclusion of the reviewing impulsion (*paccavekkhaṇa-javana*). "Of that" refers to the path of stream-entry, which is designated as knowledge and vision. "Fruit" means the fruit-consciousness (*phala-citta*); it is born subsequently, following immediately after the path.
Here, the term "ending with review" is an adjective qualifying "fruit," specifically qualifying the action.
Or, the meaning is that the reviewing impulsion (paccavekkhaṇa-javana) acts as the limit.
After the path, when the fruit has arisen and ceased either twice or thrice, immediately thereafter the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs.
Having turned back from the life-continuum and taking the path as its object, mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) arises, followed by the reviewing impulsions.
Thus, the resultant consciousness extends only as far as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and does not extend to the stage of reviewing. Nevertheless,
in order to show that the reviewing-javana occurs immediately after the resultant-javanas— intervened by another javana—
the life-continuum and the adverting consciousnesses that arise immediately following the resultant-reviewing-javanas are mentioned.
It should be understood that it is stated: "Having made them [the path factors] the object of designation, the fruit arises, having review as its limit, following upon that [path].
And this review is fivefold, by way of reviewing the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements.
Among these, one reviews each one with a single impulsion-moment; thus, there are five impulsion-moments of review.
These are to be understood as shown collectively by the inclusion of "reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇa*). And "by that very same method":
the path was first attained through the methods of insight (*vipassanā*) such as the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-anupassanā*);
it is by that very same method. "That bhikkhu" refers to that practitioner of yoga, the bhikkhu. "Cultivating again and again" means repeatedly.
Having increased insight (*vipassanā*), just as he attained the first path and fruit, so too does he attain the remaining paths and fruits—that is, the second and subsequent paths and fruits. 3165.
Thus, by the method already stated, because he has transcended arising and passing away, he has directly realized the Dhamma that is absolutely deathless.
Having penetrated [the truth], having utterly destroyed all unwholesome states, and having abandoned them through their total eradication, he—
having specifically dried up the three existences (bhava) by means of the drying up of attachment within the three existences beginning with the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava)—

that monk who is a supreme recipient of offerings and whose taints are exhausted, first, in the parinibbāna of defilements, is devoid of the "residue of clinging" (upādi), which consists of the resultant aggregates and the matter produced by past karma.
The construction is: "He approaches" means he attains the Nibbāna-element without residue.
Thus, the method for the development of the meditation subject has been shown by the Teacher in brief;
therefore, for the sake of assisting those who fear prolixity, a detailed exposition has not been undertaken here, but only a word-by-word commentary has been made. As for its detailed exposition:
It should be understood from the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentary.
Or, "according to the sequence of understanding" means according to the sequence of the composition of the text consisting of letters, phrases, and sentences.

Or, "by way of the preceding and following" means by way of the succession of the specific meanings to be expressed. Or, "in the arrangement of letters" means by means of the application of the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), the science of poetics (*alaṅkārasattha*), and the science of prosody (*chandovicitisattha*).

The meaning is: in the arrangement of syllables and words that ought to be made, it refers to the composition of verses (*gāthābandha*). The construction is: "If it appears as if improper. *Taṃ* means that place which appears as "improper.
"It should not be taken in that way" means it should not be taken as improper merely because of the manner in which it appears.
To the question "How then should it be taken? he says: "It should be taken from the perspective of its faultlessness. He states the reason for this: "By me..."

"Having investigated thoroughly, because it has been completed in every respect. Whatever fault might be seen here—whether it be the fault of being disordered (*khittadosa*) or the fault of perverted apprehension (*vipallāsaggahaṇadosa*)—he indicates that there is no other [fault].

By this, he demonstrates that this treatise serves as a standard for all those elders who are learned in the various divisions of the scriptural tradition of the Three Piṭakas and who desire training. By indicating his own standard, he himself...

It should be understood that by demonstrating the authority of this *Vinayavinicchaya* which has been composed, [the author] encourages the audience of listeners to apply themselves to hearing, grasping, and retaining it.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya*, titled the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the method for the development of the meditation subject is finished.
Commentary on the concluding discourse (3168–78):
Thus, "The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint; restraint is for the purpose of non-regret; non-regret is for the purpose of gladness..."
Gladness is for the purpose of rapture; rapture is for the purpose of tranquility; tranquility is for the purpose of happiness; happiness is for the purpose of concentration;
concentration is for the purpose of knowing and seeing things as they truly are; knowing and seeing things as they truly are is for the purpose of disenchantment;

disenchantment is for the purpose of dispassion; dispassion is for the purpose of liberation; liberation is for the purpose of the knowledge and vision of liberation; and the knowledge and vision of liberation [is for the purpose of final Nibbāna].

Having expounded the discourse on the Vinaya— including its benefits— extending up to the element of Nirvana without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) by way of determining the succession of benefits shown in the phrase "for the sake of Nirvana through non-clinging," and having clarified its measure,

[the author], following the conduct of the Blessed One— who, because of his own wisdom born of learning, said, "Monks, I teach the Dhamma with its basis" (*sanidānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemi*)— [proceeds] with respect to that...
In order to show the causal occasion (*nidāna*) by way of place, time, and so forth, he said, "Of the excellent," and so on.

Therein, "of the excellent" means of one who is more praiseworthy due to the perfection of enjoyments and possessions such as wealth, grain, clothing, and ornaments, as well as the perfection of villages, royal capitals, fields, lands, rivers, ponds, lakes, and monasteries.
"Not surpassed" refers to that which is like a navel because it abides in the center. "Unconfused" [refers] precisely because it abides in the center.

[It is] free from the confusion of destruction and so forth, because of the presence of perfectly circular [trees] and the like. Furthermore, the connection is with the village called Bhūtamangala, which is even more delightful—as if all the loveliness of the entire world were gathered together.
Again, asking what further qualities it possesses, he says "plantain" and so forth: plantains, *sāla* trees, *tāla* palms, sugarcane, and coconut trees...
And plantains... [and so on] ...coconuts; their groves are groves of plantains... [and so on] ...groves of coconuts;
the meaning is that it is crowded and filled with them. *Kamalāni* (lotuses) and *uppālāni* (water-lilies) are *kamaluppalāni*;

covered by these is *kamaluppalasañchannā*. *Salilassa āsayā* means reservoirs of water; those which are both covered by lotuses and water-lilies and are reservoirs of water are *kamala...pe...* [as above].
It is beautiful with those bodies of water; it is beautified by those bodies of water covered with lotuses and water-lilies.
The water of the Kāverī is "kāverijala"; the flow or occurrence of that Kāverī water is "kāverijalasampāta";
that by which the surface of the earth is completely surrounded or pervaded on all sides is "kāverijalasampātaparibhūtamahītala. This [is the description] of him.
In that [place]. "Iddhi" means perfected with various prosperities. "Sabbanga-sampanne" means endowed with all requisites for happiness.
"Maṅgale" means being the cause for the prosperity and growth of people. "Bhūtamaṅgale" refers to the village of that name.

"Pavaro" (excellent) refers to the appearance of the ocean and so forth, with its central regions sinking under the weight of the circular range of world-encircling mountains (Kulācala-cakka), which are like the coils of a serpent, along with the groups of islands such as Tiratā.

These are of excellent form; "pākāra" means a wall and "parikhā" means a moat; thus, "pākāraparikhā" means a wall and a moat. Since they are of excellent form and are walls and moats, they are called "pavarākārapākāraparikhā.
Encircled by these is "pavarākārapākāraparikhāparivārito"; [it is] in that [place]. "Dassanīye" means worthy of being seen.
"Manorame" means that where the mind finds delight; [it is] in that [place].

The edge of a bank (*tīra*) is the interior of the bank (*tīranta*), or the bank itself is the edge, thus *tīranta*; the region of the slope of lotus ponds, pools, water-channels, moats, and so forth, is the bank.
Because they grow (*ruhiṃsu*) and are born (*jāyiṃsu*) on the edge of the bank, they are "growing-on-the-bank" (*tīrantarūha*);

and because those growing-on-the-bank are numerous, immeasurable, and boundless, they are "growing-on-the-bank-and-boundless" (*tīrantarūhavātīra*). The letter *v* is a euphonic junction (*sandhija*). Kings of trees are "tree-kings" (*tarurājāna*).
“*Tīrantaruhavātīratarurājāno*” means those trees growing on the banks and those kings of trees;

it is “resplendent with those,” that is, resplendent with the trees growing on the banks... [as before] ...resplendent. The meaning is: “adorned with great trees that bear flowers, bear fruit, and provide shade.
Alternatively, there is the reading “*tīrantaruhavānatarurājivirājite*,” which refers to the rows of trees (*vānatarū*)—that is, *vetara* or *uparukkha* trees—growing on the banks.
The meaning is "adorned with rows of streaks. "Flocks of birds" (*dijagaṇā*) refers to groups of birds; "various flocks of birds" (*nānādijagaṇā*) means those various flocks of birds.

It is a "pleasure grove for various flocks of birds" (*nānādijagaṇārāmo*) because they come from here and there and take delight therein; the meaning is that it is a place where birds such as parrots, cuckoos, and peacocks come and enjoy themselves.
"Delightful with various groves" (*nānārāmamanorame*) means various, that is, many, groves consisting of flowering and fruiting trees.
"Various gardens" means delightful with those [gardens]; thus it is "delightful with various gardens," and [the place] is in that.
"Beautiful lotuses" means beautiful lotuses (*cārupaṅkaja*), such as the *kamala*, *uppala*, *kumuda*, and so forth;
"strewn with beautiful lotuses" means covered or overspread by beautiful lotuses; and "pools strewn with beautiful lotuses" refers to pools that are strewn with beautiful lotuses.
Adorned and decorated by them, beautiful... [and so on] ...adorned, in that place. That which has a beautiful and sweet flavor is "surasam" (of excellent taste);
that which is both of excellent taste and water is "surasodakam" (water of excellent taste); that which is filled with water of excellent taste is "surasodakasampunnā";
those which are both excellent wells and filled with water of excellent taste are "surasodakasampunnavarakupā."
Adorned by those [trees], it was full of flavor... [and so on] ...adorned by that well. "Variegated" means especially variegated;
and since they were both variegated and vast, they are "variegated-and-vast"; and since they were variegated-and-vast pavilions, they are...
[and so on] ...pavilions. "Exceedingly lofty" means risen above all; and since they were exceedingly lofty and excellent pavilions... [and so on] ...pavilions.
"Vicitravipula-uccavara-maṇḍapa": there is an elision of the vowel due to the construction of the verse. "Vicitravipula" means diverse and vast; "uccavara" means lofty and excellent;

thus, "vicitravipula-uccavara-maṇḍapa" refers to those diverse, vast, lofty, and excellent pavilions. He who is adorned or decorated by them is "adorned... [etc. ...by those pavilions," and it is in that [place].

A "maṇḍapa" (pavilion) is so called because it protects (*pāti*) or guards the essence (*maṇḍa*) against the rays of the sun. It is also called such because people come from here and there and dwell therein.
“Dwelling” (*āvāsa*) refers to palaces, monasteries, pavilions, and so forth. “By many” (*anekehi*) means by numerous [beings].

“Exceedingly” (*accantaṃ*) means to an extreme degree. The construction is as follows: in a monastery adorned by a stupa that, as if having burst through the surface of the earth and risen up, or as if laughing while conquering the peak of Mount Kelāsa with its harsh and rugged [form].
“One who gives water” (*ambuṃ dadāti*) is an *ambuda*; an *ambuda* in autumn is a *saradambuda*. This is because of the commonality between the states of being abundant and being great.
"Resembling an autumn cloud" means like an autumn cloud; in that [place]. "Well-raised" means risen high; in that [place].
"Producing serenity" means it generates clarity of mind and joy for those looking upon it and for those dwelling there; in that [place].
At this point, he indicates the location where the discourse on the determination of the Vinaya took place by saying "by me," which denotes the agent, and "dwelling," which denotes the action.

Because he endures the offenses committed by Devadatta, Ciñcā-Māṇavikā, and others, as well as the perils of cold, heat, and so forth, and because he destroys the defilements and other such factors residing within his own continuum, he is like a lion;
thus he is a "Lion" (Sīha). He is both the Buddha and the Lion, hence "Buddha-Sīha. Alternatively, the word *sīha* is a synonym for "best";
the meaning is "by the best of Buddhas. "Of what was spoken" means of what was taught. "Of the Vinaya" means of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Vinicchaya" (the exposition) refers to the exposition found in the texts, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), and handed down through the lineage of teachers.
"Buddhasīha" refers to the Great Elder (Mahāthera) of that name. "Samuddissa" means having designated;
it is said to mean "in reliance upon the request made by him. By this, the external cause is shown.

The construction is as follows: "This exposition was composed in brief by me, while dwelling in the Varapāsāda, for the benefit of the monks and specifically with reference to my co-resident, Buddhasīha.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "For the sake of understanding the Vinaya, and easily and without delay.

This is because this treatise of the Vinaya Piṭaka—which has the attainment of Nibbāna without residue as its ultimate benefit—has been well-explained both by way of its textual compilation and by way of its meaning.

The meaning is that it is for the sake of awakening easily and without delay. The word "bhikkhūnaṃ" (of the monks) is an indication of the exertion, or it is a singular-inclusive expression (ekasesa-niddesa), as stated previously:
"For the benefit of both monks and nuns, I, being concentrated, shall speak."
"Because it has been undertaken. By this, the purpose is shown.
(3179) Having thus shown the place, the agent, the cause, and the purpose, he says "Accutā" and so forth in order to show the determination of time.
"Vikkanta" means stepping forward; the sense is "a stride. "Accuta" means unvanquished by anyone; and that which is both such [unvanquished] and a stride (vikkanta).
"Accutavikkanta" means one who possesses the heroic stride (*vikkanta*) of Accuta, which is like that of Nārāyaṇa;
thus he is "Accutaccutavikkanta. Who is he? The King. He is "Kalambhakulanandana," meaning he gladdens the Kalambha clan; in him [is this].
By this, his family lineage is indicated. [He was] a Coḷa king named Accutaccutavikkanta, born of the lineage of the Kalambha clan.
"While the Coḷa king was ruling and governing the land of Coḷarāṭṭha correctly, this legal exposition (vinicchaya) was both undertaken and completed by me.
By this, he indicates the time. Now, by composing this work on the legal exposition of the Vinaya, [the author] [dedicates] his own store of merit for the welfare of the entire world.
While transforming [the meaning], he said "yathā" and so forth. The construction is as follows:

just as this determination of the Vinaya attained success—that is, accomplishment—without obstacle, so may the intentions and mental arisings of beings associated with the Dhamma and based on the wholesome, or all intended objects, be accomplished and brought to fulfillment without obstacle.

3181. Desiring the long endurance of the Blessed One’s teaching—the sole cause for the welfare of the entire world—by virtue of that very fruit of merit, he said, “As long as it stands,” and so forth. A *mandara* is called a cool and moist king of mountains.
Water is called *kaṃ*; a place split open by that [water] where [water] issues forth is called a *kandara*. [It is characterized] by broad, cool, and moist sandy banks.
It is called Cārukandara because its lovely (*cāru*) caves (*kandarā*) possess waters that are flowing, sweet, cool, and clear;
where shoals of various kinds of fish sport; where groves of trees on both banks are adorned with flowers, fruits, and sprouts;

where the warbling of birds such as parrots, mynas, cuckoos, peacocks, and swans resounds; and which are filled with the delightful humming of bees wandering here and there. "Kali" refers to an offense; it is so called because it instructs (*sāsati*) or strikes (*hiṃsati*) one for that [offense].
It is called *kalisāsana* because it removes (*apaneti*) evil; alternatively, the reading is *kalusāsana*. "Kalusa" means evil;

that which scatters (*asati*), distracts, or drives far away (*dūramussārayati*) that evil is *kalusāsana*. It is the threefold teaching consisting of the study (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*paṭivedha*).
Thus, [he established] the long endurance of this teaching which, when encountered, accomplishes welfare in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal.
Having made this aspiration, and desiring for the sake of the world’s welfare in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), he said "At the proper time," and so forth.
"At the proper time" means at a time suitable for the abundance of crops.

"May they rain properly" means may the rains fall in such a manner—free from the faults of drought or excessive rain—that the crops and other things may flourish; that is the meaning. "The rain-clouds."

The rain-cloud deities are presided over by the divine son Pajjunna. "Protectors of the earth" refers to kings. "According to the Dhamma" means according to the ten duties of a king (*daśarājadharma*).
"The entire earth" refers to the whole body of people residing upon the ground. 3183.
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing both mundane and supramundane prosperity for the entire world, [he performed] the dedication of his own merit.
Having done so, now, while dedicating his merit specifically for the purpose of producing the attainment of the supramundane which has been understood, he said, "This," and so forth.

By this, he states the definitive exposition (vinicchaya) composed by himself as something directly perceived. "Essential" (*sārabhūta*) means that it is like the essence of a hand, because it reveals the threefold essence of training beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
"Beneficial" (*hita*) means [it leads] to the end of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*) for those who practice for its sake.
Because it brings about welfare and because it pacifies the suffering of saṃsāra, it is "beneficial" (hita), like the medicine of immortality (amatosadha).

"Appropriate to the goal" (atthayutta) means that it is appropriate to the goal because it is connected with the discipline (vinaya) and so forth regarding matters pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate truth (paramattha). "By me who was composing" (karontena) means by me while creating [this work].
"Whatever merit (puñña) has been obtained": it is called *puñña* because it purifies the doer; it is so named because it produces the fruit of a praiseworthy existence (*pujja-bhava*).

Or, that which has come to be designated as "merit" (*puñña*)—the wholesome karma that has flowed forth and been attained, extending to the limit of immeasurable existences—by means of that merit acting as the cause.
"This world" refers to this entire world of sentient beings.

"Attained by the Lord of Sages" means reached by the Lord of Sages, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). "Free from sorrow" means devoid of grief; [devoid] of sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, despair, and so forth.
Because they are free from [defilements] and because they are the sign for their departure, the suffering of saṃsāra, such as sorrow and so forth, has departed.

"May he reach the auspicious city"—that is, may he realize the city of Nibbāna; it is said that he should attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) and through the Nibbāna-element without residue (*anupādisesā nibbānadhātu*).

"Thus, by Tambapaṇṇiya," and so forth, is a statement placed by the author's disciple—desiring to inspire reverence for this treatise by way of the qualities of the author’s noble lineage, learning, and so on.
In this context: "Tambapaṇṇiya" means one born in Tambapaṇṇi, known there, or come from there; by him.
"Veyyākaraṇa" means one who has studied grammar (*byākaraṇa*) after having investigated it; and he is the supreme and most excellent grammarian.
...and thus he is one who possesses supreme analytical exposition. The three Piṭakas are brought together; or, the collection of the three Piṭakas is the Tipiṭaka.

They are called "methods" (nayā) because they lead or cause those seeking the goal to understand; or, they are called "methods" because by means of them one specifically leads to mundane and supramundane prosperity.

These include the method of the text (pāḷinaya), the method of the meaning (atthanaya), the method of unity (ekattanaya), and so forth. The methods contained within the Tipiṭaka are the "Tipiṭaka-methods."

*Vidhāna* means instruction or governance, or else *vidhi* means procedure; the procedure of the methods of the Three Piṭakas is the "Three-Piṭaka-Method-Procedure" (*tipiṭakanayavidhi*), and one who is skilled in that Three-Piṭaka-Method-Procedure is "skilled in the Three-Piṭaka-Method-Procedure" (*tipiṭakanayavidhikusala*).
Furthermore, those poets are supreme, thus they are "supreme poets" (*paramakavija*); the hearts of those supreme poets are "the hearts of supreme poets" (*paramakavijanahadayāni*).

"Puṇḍarīka forests" (padumavanāni) refers to lotus groves; and since these are both the hearts of the supreme poets and lotus groves, they are "the lotus groves that are the hearts of the supreme poets.
He causes their blossoming—that is, their awakening—just as the sun does; thus he is "the one who causes the lotus groves that are the hearts of the supreme poets to blossom," by which [he is meant].
They are both poets and excellent, thus "excellent poets" (kavivarā); or, they are the best among poets, thus "excellent poets" (kavivarā). He is the bull (vasabho) among those excellent poets.
The meaning is: "the most excellent bull among the best of poets," that is, by the king of the kings of poets.
Furthermore, it is "supreme delight" (*paramarati*) because it is both supreme and delight; "producing supreme delight" means they cause supreme delight to arise.

They are "excellent and sweet" (*varamadhura*) because they are both excellent and sweet; and they are "excellent and sweet words" (*varamadhuravacana*) because they are both excellent and sweet and are words.
"Extremely delightful and most sweet words" means those words which are both extremely delightful and most sweet;
"utterance" (*uggāra*) means speaking. That which has the utterance of extremely delightful and most sweet words is "extremely delightful...
word-utterance," by that. "Uragapura" means a village of the supreme lineage where he dwelt; by that. "By Buddhadatta."
"By the elder named thus" means by the elder Ācariya Buddhadatta. "This exposition of the Vinaya has been composed"—this is the syntactical connection.
And thus ends this commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya*, titled the *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*.
The Commentary on the Vinayavinicchaya is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Uttaravinicchaya.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work (Ka):
To the Sugata, the God beyond gods, who is worshipped by gods, Brahmās, and Indras;
Having understood the Dhamma that cuts off the cycle of existence and the assembly that has transcended the cycle,
(Kha) by means of the meritorious deed consisting of homage to the Triple Gem;
Having severed all calamities, I shall strive with a concentrated mind.
(Ga) This is a brief summary composed by the Elder Buddhadatta.
The commentary is unadulterated, according to the capacity of the successor.

1. Now, this teacher, for the purpose of generating various kinds of proficiency among the bhikkhus regarding the Vinaya he himself has composed and its underlying basis, the Vinaya Piṭaka, has here collected the determinations (vinicchaya) as they appear in the Parivāra-ṭīkā.

Desiring to explain the *Uttarapakaraṇa*, he first spoke the words beginning with "Sabbasattuttama," paying homage to the Triple Gem in order to accomplish his intended purpose by warding off obstacles.
Regarding the purpose of paying homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of a treatise,
it has been elaborated upon in many ways by various teachers in various places.
Since we have already presented this in brief in our *Vinayavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā*, we shall not elaborate upon it here.
The title, subject matter, means of composition, types [of content], and purpose should also be understood here according to the method shown therein.
Here, however, I shall provide an explanation of the words not [already] commented upon, by way of demonstrating the connections and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "Having paid homage to the Jina, the Dhamma, and the Gaṇa, I shall now compose the Uttara.
To the question, "To what kind of Jina, Dhamma, and Gaṇa does he pay homage?", he says: "To the Supreme among all beings," and so forth. Therein, "supreme among all beings" (*sabbasattuttama*):

those who are attached (*satta*), clinging (*āsatta*), and stuck (*visatta*) to the five strands of sensual pleasure are called "beings" (*sattā*). From the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), this refers to the designation of a being...

The aggregates that have become objects of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*) are designated as "beings" (*satta*) by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*), based upon the continuity of the aggregates from a linguistic standpoint (*vohārato*).

These, moreover, are of infinite variety according to such distinctions as the planes of existence—such as the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth—the locations—such as the hells and so forth—and the types of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)—such as those without root-cause (*ahetuka*) and so forth.
Among these, for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), the conventional designation "being" is used in the sense of the etymological derivation already mentioned.
It is not found. Nevertheless, because of their past state of existence or because they resemble it, they are called "beings" (*satta*).
And all those beings together are "all beings" (*sabba-satta*). He is supreme because he has been drawn up, because he has emerged, and because he is excellent;
he is supreme among all beings through mundane and supramundane qualities of form and formlessness, or else he is the most excellent among all beings.
"Best" (*seṭṭha*) means the supreme among all beings; it is an epithet for "Conqueror" (*jina*).

Furthermore, asking what more he is distinguished by, [the author] says "steadfast" (*dhīra*). Wisdom (*dhī*) is called *paññā*; one who moves or proceeds by means of that is steadfast (*dhīra*), and [the word refers to] him.

By virtue of his state of suchness (*tādibhāva*), like the threshold pillar (*indakhīla*) or Mount Sineru, he is [unshaken] by the violent wind known as the eight worldly conditions (*aṭṭhalokadhamma*).

In the sense of being unshakable, and in the sense of being incapable of being shaken by anyone in the world including the devas by virtue of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), he is "steadfast" (*dhīra*);
the meaning is that he is endowed with fortitude. This too is an epithet of him.
"Having paid homage" means having saluted through the doors of body, speech, and mind; that is, having praised him by proclaiming his qualities as they truly are.
"By the head"—that is, by means of the supreme limb consisting of the cultivation of devotion (*bhakti*). By this, physical prostration is specifically shown;
verbal prostration is indicated by the recitation of his qualities; and mental prostration is also implied, as it is inseparable from both of these forms of prostration.

"He conquers" (*jinati*)—by way of crushing their power, annihilating them, abandoning them, severing their causes, and transcending their objects—the fivefold Māras known as the Māra of the sons of gods (*devaputta-māra*), the Māra of defilements (*kilesa-māra*), the Māra of volitional formations (*abhisankhāra-māra*), the Māra of death (*maccu-māra*), and the Māra of the aggregates (*khandha-māra*).
He is the "Conqueror" (Jina) because he has conquered in five ways;
that [is the meaning]. The analysis of the meaning of the word "Dhamma," by way of its etymology and so forth, has already been shown below.

Regarding the phrase "the destroyer of non-Dhamma" (adhammavidhaṃsa): because it is the opposite of the wholesome state designated as "Dhamma," "non-Dhamma" refers to unwholesome states; that which is designated as unwholesome...

It destroys, ruins, and abandons non-Dhamma (*adhamma*) by means of abandonment through its own nature (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), subsidence (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*);
thus it is "the destruction of non-Dhamma" (*adhammaviddhaṃsa*). This refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma together with the scriptures (*pariyatti*).

For the scriptures are so called by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit, because they are the primary cause of the five kinds of abandonment; that is the "destruction of non-Dhamma. This is an epithet for the word "Dhamma."
They count it as a *gaṇa* because it is a collection (*samūha*) of the eight noble persons (*ariyapuggala*); such is the meaning of *saṅgha*. Regarding *aṅgaṇanāsana*:
they consider themselves to be "blemishes" (*aṅgaṇa*) because they rely on [defilements]; thus, *aṅgaṇā* refers to the defilements—namely, lust, hatred, and delusion.

One who destroys those blemishes by abandoning them through the appropriate methods of abandonment—namely, abandonment by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*)—is called an *aṅgaṇanāsana*.
"Taṃ" is an adjective qualifying "gaṇaṃ. 2.
The construction is: "of that exposition (vinicchaya) which is the essence of the Vinaya composed by me. It is "anuttara" because there is nothing superior to it;
that is, it is unsurpassed among all expositions, or it is the unsurpassed [work] of all expositions.
"Uttamo vinicchayo" means "the most excellent," that is, the unsurpassed. The construction is: "Now I shall compose this further treatise (pakaraṇa).
"Bhaṇato" means for one who speaks, making it fluent and mastered by recitation. "Paṭhato" means for one who reads or rehearses it until it is mastered.
"Payuñjato" means for one who applies oneself to it in the proper manner, or for one who teaches it to others.
"Listening" (*suṇato*) means for one who hears what is being spoken by others. "Reflecting" (*cintayato*) means for one who reflects upon the meaning and the words according to what has been heard.
In the phrase "the increase of wisdom for the non-awakened," the case ending is elided for the sake of metrical composition in the verse.
It refers to the increase of wisdom for the non-awakened—that is, for the foolish community of monks and nuns who lack knowledge of the discipline (*vinaya*). It is the increase of wisdom.

It produces an increase in wisdom regarding the determination of the Vinaya. Alternatively, because it has been thoroughly practiced in the determination of the Buddha’s [teachings], it increases the intelligence of a wise person;
by bringing about a state of sharpness and clarity in the intellect—that is, in wisdom—it accomplishes a further advancement.
This work, called the *Paramatthavinicchaya* (The Supreme Determination), is spoken by me as I explain it; from my presence, those who are devoted [to it]...
"In the Vinicchaya, or specifically in the three trainings—be attentive, know, and produce the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayañāṇa*).
Thus he exhorts the audience of listeners to listen.
[End of] the Commentary on the Exposition of the Compendium of the Mahāvibhaṅga.
4. Having thus directed the audience toward listening, he said, beginning with “sexual intercourse,” in order to demonstrate the further determination as promised.

“How many offenses?”—this is a question of five types: comparison with what has been seen, inquiry regarding what has not been seen, cutting off doubt, seeking permission, and inquiry out of a desire to speak; it is the inquiry out of a desire to speak. There are three offenses.
This is, in brief, the answer to that.

5. This is the demonstration by way of the actual form of the terms "in existence" (*bhave*) and so forth, which were previously shown by way of enumeration. "In a field" (*khette*) means in any place belonging to the three types of paths, even a spot as small as a sesame seed.
For one who engages in sexual intercourse [there], it is a *pārājika* offense; thus it is said, "it becomes [a *pārājika*]."

The connection [of the sentence] is: "It is stated as 'a grave offense' (thullaccaya). The phrase "when more than half is shown" is merely an illustration, because it has already been stated below that a grave offense occurs even when half is shown. The connection is:
for one who inserts the genitals without touching the mouth when it is turned like a ring, a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated.
6. “Taking what is not given,” and so forth, are also according to the method already stated.
7. “In the case of five māsakas or more”: this refers to five māsakas, which is the fourth part of an old blue kahāpaṇa, or to something of that value.
“Or more than”: this means either exceeding five māsakas or being of that value. Regarding the twenty-five [māsakas] of what is not given...
The meaning is that defeat occurs when something has been stolen by any one of the types of theft.

In the case of a month, or less than a month, or for an object of that value, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "In between from five māsakas" means within the range starting from five māsakas.

"Five māsakas" refers to five māsakas brought together, or the collection of five māsakas; thus it is *pañcamāsa*. That which is worth five māsakas is "worth five māsakas" (*pañcamāsagghana*); [the phrase] "five māsakas and that which is worth five māsakas" refers to both.

"worth five months": this is a partial *sarūpekaśeṣa* (retention of one member from among similar items). In that [compound], even in the case of "in a month" (*māse vā*), although one should have said "a month and what is worth a month" (*māsa-māsagghanaka*), the term "in a month" (*māse*) is a partial *sarūpekaśeṣa*, and the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be understood.
Even though it is stated generally as "worth five months" (*pañcamāsagghane*), it refers specifically to a fourth part of an ancient blue *kahāpaṇa*.

A five-month restriction must be observed. For it was in this way that when the Blessed One was enacting the second *pārājika* rule, he questioned the monk—who had formerly been a chief magistrate among those ordained—asking, "On what basis does King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha, having seized a thief, execute him, imprison him, or banish him? and [the monk] replied, "By a quarter..."
When it was said, "or by a quarter-pāda," this was prescribed for one who takes what has not been given according to that very measure.
And in the Commentary, having cited the Pāli text, "A quarter-pāda is five māsakas," it says: "At that time in Rājagaha, a kahāpaṇa was worth twenty māsakas;
therefore, five māsakas constitute a quarter-pāda. By this definition, in all provinces, one-fourth of a kahāpaṇa is called a 'quarter-pāda'."
This should be understood by way of the ancient blue kahāpaṇa coin, and not by way of others such as the *dudradāmaka* and so forth.
For it was on account of that [measure] that even the Buddhas of the past laid down the *pārājika* rule, and those of the future will likewise lay it down.
Indeed, there is no difference among all Buddhas regarding either the basis for a *pārājika* offense or the *pārājika* rule itself; these four bases for *pārājika* offenses are the same for all.
"These four *pārājikas* alone exist; there is nothing less than this, nor anything more.

Therefore, having rebuked Dhaniya, the Blessed One himself, while prescribing the second *pārājika*, spoke the words beginning with: 'Whatever bhikkhu, taking what is not given, by way of theft... Thus it is said.
And in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:

“It should be understood that ‘a quarter’ means a *pāda*”—by this very statement, it should be seen that it is already implied that in all regions a *māsaka* is indeed the twentieth part of a *kahāpaṇa*.
It should be understood that blue *kahāpaṇas* produced according to the ancient teachers' tradition are those endowed with the [proper] characteristics.
One produced by Dudradāma is called a *dudradāmaka*. It is said that he [produced] the blue *kahāpaṇa*...
Having said, "It is worth three parts," [he continued]: "In whatever place blue kahāpaṇas are not available, even there the valuation must be made by means of blue kahāpaṇas.

How so? Taking a commodity that circulates at a value equal to a blue kahāpaṇa—whether in a place where blue kahāpaṇas are in circulation or not—one should take a portion of it worth a fourth part of the value of that [blue kahāpaṇa]."
The meaning stated here is: "A legal decision should be made after determining that it is worth one-quarter of a blue kahāpaṇa.
In this context, those who mint coins do so using gold, silver, copper, or a mixture of gold, silver, and copper.
Among these, which coin is the "blue kahāpaṇa"? Some say it is the "gold kahāpaṇa," while others say it is the "mixed kahāpaṇa."
In this regard, the intention of those who say "golden kahāpaṇa" is as follows: with respect to the basis for a *pārājika* offense, there must be a single characteristic throughout;
however, there must be a difference in value according to factors such as time, place, and usage.

For the Blessed One has declared that in the case of taking what is not given, a *pārājika* offense occurs only in accordance with the punishment—killing, binding, or banishment—meted out by righteous kings.
It is so formulated, not otherwise. Therefore, since this [definition] is unerring at all times and in all places, it must be that [the coin] is made of gold by its fourth part.
However, for those who say it is a "mixed kahāpaṇa," the intended meaning is as follows:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“At that time, a kahāpaṇa in Rājagaha was worth twenty māsakas; therefore, a quarter (pāda) was five māsakas.
By this standard, it should be understood that in all provinces, a quarter of a kahāpaṇa is called a ‘pāda. And that indeed refers to the ancient [kahāpaṇa].”
Because it is stated [in the *Sāratthadīpanī*]: "By way of the blue kahāpaṇa, and not by way of others such as the dudradāmaka and so forth," and because it is said in the *Sāratthadīpanī*:
"It should be understood that 'blue kahāpaṇas' are those produced possessing the characteristics in accordance with the ancient teachers."
Because it has been so stated, and because of the statement, "Having reached the Vinayavinicchaya, one should stand firm regarding what is grave," the mixed kahāpaṇa alone is the blue kahāpaṇa.
For in that very place, the characteristic prescribed by the ancient teachers is seen. How so?
Having mixed together twenty māṣas—five māṣas of gold, likewise five of silver, and ten of copper—for the purpose of binding [them together]...

Having added a measure of rice-grain worth of copper and having fashioned it so as to display either letters or the image of an elephant or some other form, it is called a "blue kahāpaṇa" because it is faultless.
And in the *Sikkhābhājana-vinicchaya* and in certain manuscripts, it says: "A 'quarter' (pāda) is five māṣas of gold."
The reading has been recorded according to the opinion of the proponents of the first position.
In some manuscripts, however, the reading “five māṣas of gold” is recorded according to the opinion of the proponents of the second position.

Furthermore, in the *Sāmaṇerasikkhā* written by the ancients in the Sinhalese language, regarding the commentary statement “of an ancient blue kahāpaṇa,” and in the ancient sutta titled *Ratana-sutta*—
In accordance with the definition of a *kahaṇa* coin as it has been stated, one might ask: "Is a coin made by minting gold, silver, or copper after mixing them together called a *kahaṇa*?

and "What is the difference between novices (*sāmaṇera*) and those fully ordained (*upasampanna*) regarding the offense of stealing (*adinnādāna-pārājika*)? To which it is replied: "For novices, even taking [an object] as small as a thread for a curtain constitutes a *pārājika* offense; for those fully ordained..."
Furthermore, the distinction is shown by the phrase "even for twenty grains of rice worth of gold.
That gold amounts to two and a half māsakas in terms of gold coins; and for five māsakas, a pārājika offense was declared by the Blessed One.

It has been so prescribed. Therefore, since that kahāpaṇa with the aforementioned characteristics is not obtainable in all places, and since the offense of defeat (pārājika) is defined by means of gold alone—worth five māsaka quarters—which is common to all regions, it serves as a benefit for those dwelling in all regions;
thus, the delimitation of the offense of defeat is established by means of gold alone.
This is the conclusion. This very rule has been grasped as the essence from the traditions of the Sinhalese teachers.
Therefore, this very decision should be accepted as the essence by those who are diligent in the training, virtuous in all respects, and masters of the Vinaya.
And on this point there are these verses: "The characteristics of gold, silver, and copper as specified in the texts..."
A blue kahāpaṇa coin of twenty māṣas was made by not omitting [the required weight].
Indeed, having mixed gold for one foot, silver for one foot, and copper for two feet,
and having applied the alloy, it is shown in the treatises as how to make it.
‘Elā’ is said to be a fault; because it is free from fault, it is thus designated.
Its value is considered to be twenty *vīhi* grains of gold.
However, in that region where it is not current, the *kahāpaṇa* [is used].
"A sacrificial altar worth twenty measures of gold is worth only a quarter of that [robe].
Monks who wear such robes are losing their monastic virtues," so say those who know the Vinaya.
9. *Opātanti* means a pit. The construction is: "born into suffering. 10.

Regarding *uttariṃ dhammaṃ*: here, where one ought to say *uttarimanussadhammaṃ*, the term *uttariṃ dhammaṃ* is used by applying the rules of euphonic combination (*niruttinaya*), namely by eliding the middle word and inserting the nasal *niggahīta*.
It refers to those who possess a state superior to that of ordinary human beings, as well as to meditators.
And the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, which is a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*). "Applicable to oneself" (*attupanāyika*) means:
one who applies it to oneself, behaving [as if] saying, "It exists in me"; or one who applies oneself to that [state], behaving as if saying, "I am seen therein.
Thus, it is "applicable to oneself" (*attupanāyika*); the connection is: "speaking while having done so."

11. *Pariyāya*: In speaking by way of indirect methods, such as saying, "The monk who dwells in your monastery is an Arahant," and so forth. *Ñāte*: When the person for whose sake one speaks—a wise human being—is soon recognized. *No ce*: If he does not recognize [the speaker].
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the *Pārājika* offenses in the *Uttaravinicchaya*, the Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning.
13. When one intends, makes an effort, and there is emission—when these three factors are complete, it is said to be a grave offense (*garuka*).

If one intends and makes an effort, but there is no emission—when these two factors are present, the application is that it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*). Regarding "the preliminary action" (*payoga*):
