this refers to the preliminary action consisting of the movement of the sexual organ to make an effort, or the commanding of another; such are the cases of direct physical action (*sāhatthika*) and commanding action (*āṇattika*).

14. Since it is possible to understand the subsequent questions by the same method already stated, [the author], wishing not to repeat them, said: "From here onwards," and so forth. We too shall explain only that which has not been mentioned previously and whose meaning remains unelucidated.
15. "By the body" means by one's own body. "The body" refers to the body of a woman. This same method applies to the term "kāyabaddha" (body-bound) as well. 16. The construction is:
when that which is bound to one's own body touches that which is bound to a woman's body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
17. The construction is: “there may be three offenses. “Of two paths” means of the path for excrement and the path for urine.

18. “In speaking of color, etc. means in speaking by way of color and so forth. The construction is: “if one speaks of something connected to the body by way of color, etc., it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 19.
“By way of acting according to one’s own desire” means by way of performing service according to one’s own desire.

20. The construction is as follows: "of that monk who speaks in praise of serving one's own desires even in the presence of a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch). The same principle applies here to "even in the presence of an animal. 21. The construction is as follows:

"When a monk has entered into the state of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*)—the state of mediating—between a woman and a man, and when the triad of receiving, testing, and bringing back [the message] is completed, the Wise One (the Buddha) should designate that for him as a grave offense (*garuka*)."

22. *Dvaṅgasamāyoge*: in the combination of two of these three factors in any way whatsoever. *Aṅge sati panekasmiṃ*: when one factor is present; that is, when even one of the three factors is present. 24. *Payoge*:

in all the preliminary activities starting from the journey into the forest for the purpose of procuring materials, with the thought, "I shall have a hut built on an unassigned site and exceeding the proper dimensions, and a large monastery built on an unassigned site. *Ekapiṇḍe anāgate*: when not even a single morsel [of food] has been brought [to him].
This was said with reference to the very last morsel of alms-food.
25. Here the construction is: "whatever monk should accuse [another] with a groundless *pārājika* offense.
26. "Without having obtained leave" means: without having had that monk obtain leave by saying, "Venerable sir, please give me leave; I wish to speak to you."
28. *Aññabhāgiya* means a training rule characterized by a phrase belonging to another category. In this way, the meaning should be understood in other similar instances as well.
29. The word division is: “samanubhāsanāya eva” (only for the formal admonition). “Na paṭinissajjanti” means those who do not relinquish [the wrong view].

30. The construction is as follows: one may incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) through the motion (*ñatti*); one may incur a *thullaṃ* (grave offense) through two proclamations (*kammavācā*); and one may incur a heavy offense (*garuka*) at the conclusion of the proclamation. The term “*thullaṃ*” here is an indicative expression for the offense of *thullaccaya*.

31. Regarding the four [offenses] that involve a formal proposal up to three times: having shown the delimitation of the offense for the first, since the other three share the same delimitation, he says "those who follow the schism," etc., referring to them by way of the method already stated therein.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the *saṅghādisesa* rules in the *Uttara-līnatthapakāsinī*.

32. "Extraneous robe-cloth" (*atirekacīvara*) refers to a robe that has not been formally determined (*anadhiṭṭhita*), nor assigned to another (*avikappita*), which is of a size that would otherwise be subject to assignment (*vikappanupaga*).
Having obtained such a robe, if one lets ten days pass, one incurs one offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).

If one dwells even for a single night without the three robes (*ticīvara*), one incurs one offense of expiation involving forfeiture. This [offense] is considered a single unit based on its nature as a class.
This is because it must be delimited by the number of instances according to the enumeration of the underlying facts (*vatthugaṇanā*).
33. "Having received an out-of-season robe" means having accepted an out-of-season robe.

"For a month" means for the month permitted to be kept when there is an expectation [of receiving more]. "Transgressing" means transgressing even while there is an expectation, failing to determine [the robe] within the month.
"Or without making a formal determination" means that he lets thirty days pass; the meaning is that he causes the thirtieth dawn to rise starting from the dawn of the day the robe was received.
"He incurs one offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya-āpatti*)"—this is how the construction should be understood.
34. Regarding "to an unrelated nun": "any old robe whatsoever" refers to any robe, such as the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭī*) or others, that has been used even once.

35. Regarding the phrase "in the act" (*payogasmiṃ*): it refers to the act of a monk giving an order, such as "wash," and likewise to every act performed by the nun who has been so ordered, such as at the hearth and so forth.
The construction is: "it is both a *nissaggiya* and a *pācittiya* offense" means that it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
36. Regarding the phrase "accepts": here the construction is "except in exchange" (*aññatra pārivattakā*).
38. "In the act" means in the act of making known. "Made known" means when the robe that was made known has been obtained. 39.
"A monk" refers to a monk whose robe has been taken away or whose robe has been lost. "Beyond that" means beyond the limit of the inner and outer robes (santaruttara).
41. "In the act" means in the act of assigning or obtaining [the robe].
42. Regarding "two": it should be connected as follows—one incurs two offenses by way of a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) and a *pācittiya* (expiation).

44. Regarding "the undertaking" (*payoga*): this refers to the undertaking that results in a surplus beyond what is permitted. Regarding "the gain" (*lābha*): this refers to the acquisition of the robe-cloth.
This concludes the first commentary on the Kathina Chapter.

45. Regarding the five training rules at the beginning of the *Kosiya-vagga*, the construction is that there are two offenses for each [rule]. "In the application" (*payoge*) means in the application of performing [the act] oneself or causing it to be performed. "In the acquisition" (*lābhe*) means upon the completion [of the robe] after having had it made or caused to be made.
46. The word-division is: “having taken the sheep’s wool. “They exceed” (*atikkamanti*) means those who are exceeding. 47. “To one not related” (*aññāya*) means to a nun who is not a relative.

The word-division is: “she has it washed, the sheep’s wool” (*dhovāpeti eḷalomakaṃ*). “Sheep’s wool” (*eḷalomakaṃ*) means sheep’s wool (*eḷakaloma*). The change of the letter *ka* [to *ka*] is according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*). “In the application” (*payoge*) means in the application of having it washed.
48. *Payoga*: in the act of receiving. 49. *Nānākāraṃ*: in various ways. *Samāpajjanti*:
the monk who is entering [the attainment]. *Samāpanne*: when the transaction has been completed. *Payoga*: in the act of entering [the attainment]. 50. *Payoga*:
in the act of engaging in buying and selling. *Tasmiṃ kate*: when that commodity has been made one's own property.
The second commentary on the *Kosiya-vagga*. 51.

"Excessive" (*atireka*) means a bowl that has not been formally resolved upon (*anadhiṭṭhita*) or assigned (*avikappita*). For a monk who lets ten days pass [with such a bowl], there is a single offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiyāpatti*);

this is the construction of the sentence. 52–3. "Without five bands" (*apañcabandhana*) means one for which the five types of binding [mends] do not exist; the meaning is "in a bowl that has fewer than five bands. "In the application" (*payoge*) means in the application of making a request. "Upon the acquisition" (*lābhe*) means upon the obtaining of that bowl.
54. "Medicine" refers to ghee and so forth. 55.
"In the act of seeking" means in the act of searching for it. 56.
"In the act of taking" means in the act of seizing or causing it to be seized. "Seized" means taken after having been snatched away.

57. However, one incurs two offenses: there is a *dukkaṭa* for the act of causing [the weaving] to be done, and a *nissaggiya* offense when it has been finished according to the maximum size of a robe that does not require further determination (*vikappanupaga*). This is the meaning of "one incurs two offenses. 58–9.
As for the monk who, without being invited, approaches a weaver who is unrelated to him and makes a request regarding a robe:
"he" refers to that monk. The construction is: "He incurs two offenses; there is no doubt."
“Payogena” means by means of an undertaking or an act of formal determination (*vikappana*).
60. “Having received a robe designated as urgent” is the construction. “Time” means the time for robes. 61.
“Any one of the three requisites” means any one of the three robes. “In a house” means within a dwelling.

"Having deposited" means having set aside. The construction is as follows: if one stays elsewhere than in that forest monastery where the robe was deposited in the alms-village, for more than six days without that robe, one incurs an offense requiring relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). 62.
"Knowing it to be a gain dedicated to the Sangha" means knowing it as such while being aware of it.
63. *Payoge* means in the application of the dedication. *Sabbattha* means in all training rules (*sikkhāpada*), such as the *pārājika*s and so forth.
*Appanāvāraparihānī* means the omission of the section on the establishment of the offense (*katthapaññattivāra*) which was stated first in the *Parivāra*; the meaning here is its non-mention.
Although that section ought to have been stated first—since it is the very first in the *Parivāra*—it is nevertheless to be stated there [in this context].

The intention is that, for one who wishes to grasp [the sequence] later, I have first stated the section on offenses immediately following that, in order to show the confession of the first offense, having set that aside. This concludes the third commentary,
the Explanation of the Chapter on Attainment (Pattavagga).
Thus ends the commentary on the thirty *nissaggiya* rules in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*. 64.

Regarding "superhuman states" (*manussuttaridhamma*): this refers to superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*). When one falsely claims such superhuman qualities, there is defeat, which constitutes an offense of *pārājika*.
65. The construction is as follows: "If one accuses a bhikkhu with a groundless *pārājika* offense by means of a baseless final statement, it is a heavy *saṅghādisesa*.
Regarding "by way of indirect speech" (*pariyāyavacana*): this refers to speaking by way of an indirect expression, such as "He who dwells in your monastery," and so forth.
Regarding "when he is known": this means when the person to whom one speaks becomes aware [of the accusation] immediately after the words are spoken.
66. But if it does not cognize—this is stated by way of a figurative expression; immediately following that statement, if it does not know.

"Samudāhaṭaṃ" means spoken. 67. Two offenses are stated for a monk who reviles: for one who reviles a person who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), there may be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); for one who reviles the other, namely a person not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there may be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—such is the construction.
68. In the case of inciting dissension as well, there are two offenses.

69. Regarding *payogo*: from the commencement of the act of speaking while reciting the Dhamma word by word, up until the completion of the words and so forth—in this interval, for each instance of pronouncing a syllable, there is a *dukkaṭa*.

Upon the completion of the words, there is a *pācittiya*. 70. The analysis of the phrase is: *“tirattā anupasampannasahaseyyāyā”* (more than three nights’ co-sleeping with one not fully ordained). “Co-sleeping with one not fully ordained” (*anupasampannasahaseyyā*) means sleeping together with one who is not fully ordained;

[the offense is incurred] by that. The construction is: “more than three nights (*tirattā uttariṃ*) of co-sleeping with one not fully ordained. Regarding *payogo*: it refers to the preliminary application such as the mental volition (*kāyāvajjana*) involved in preparing the bedding for the purpose of lying down.
"Panneti" means lying down on a bed characterized by the stretching out of the body. 71.

As for the monk who makes a bed with a woman for even one night: "Dukkaṭa, etc."—the construction is that he incurs the two aforementioned offenses, namely, "there is a dukkaṭa for the preliminary effort (payoga), and a pācittiya when he has lain down.
72. "Payoge" refers to the preliminary effort characterized as previously described.

73. "Anupasampanne" (before one who is not fully ordained): this locative case is used here in the sense of proximity. The construction is: "if one should report a superhuman state that has occurred in the presence of one who is not fully ordained.
Regarding "dukkaṭa, etc.": if the person to whom it is reported does not understand, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
if they do understand, it is a *pācittiya*. Thus, two offenses accrue to him in this manner.

74. The construction is as follows: "When one who is fully ordained speaks of an offense committed by another who is fully ordained and is corrupt, to one who is not fully ordained, in the presence of one who is not fully ordained, he is one who speaks.
Regarding the "preliminary effort" (*payoga*): from the very beginning of the undertaking, for the prior effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
he incurs an offense of wrong-doing. "When it has been announced, it may be an offense entailing expiation (*pācitti*)"—this is the construction.
75. *Payoga*: All the efforts such as searching for a spade with the intention, "I will dig unallowable earth.
This concludes the first commentary, on the Chapter on False Speech (*Musāvādavagga*).
76. *Pātento*: Destroying. *Tassa*: Of that [living organism]. *Pāteti*: In the sense of destroying.

77. Since those who speak otherwise and those who cause vexation are presented as being joined together [in one category], and since it is possible to understand the case of those who cause vexation by the same method explained therein, no separate classification of offenses is stated for them there.
78. "Another" means another person who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), such as one appointed by the Saṅgha as a distributor of lodgings (*senāsanapaññāpaka*) and so forth.
"Grumbling" means desiring to bring disrepute upon him, causing the monks to despise him by saying: "Out of favoritism, such-and-such a person [is doing] this and that..."
Having said such things as "he does," and so forth, one looks upon [the other] with contempt or considers them as inferior.
"Application" refers to the preliminary acts for the purpose of reviling, such as speaking dispraise of that person. 83.
Knowing that a monk has already arrived at a monastery belonging to the Sangha, one knowingly intrudes and makes one's bed there.

The construction is: "of him who thus prepares a bed. Regarding the phrase "the preliminary effort (payoga) entails a dukkaṭa offense," etc., this is a compound without elision (aluttasamāsa). By the word "etc.," the *pācittiya* offense for preparing a bed is included. 84. Regarding "preliminary effort":

it refers to the preliminary effort of expulsion, whether by means of a command such as "Expel him! and so forth; or by speech such as "Go! Go! and so forth; or by bodily action performed by touching his limbs with the hand and so forth. "The rest" refers to the *pācittiya* offense.

85. “Above a gabled upper chamber” (*vehāsakuṭiyā upari*) is the word-division. Regarding the term “with a fixed footrest” (*āhaccapādake*), the words “on a bed or a chair” (*mañce vā pīṭhe vā*) are to be supplied.
“Sinking” means sitting down. “Offenses such as *dukkaṭa*,” etc., means that one incurs these offenses: a *dukkaṭa* for the preliminary action and a *pācittiya* for the act of lying down.
86. Regarding the first quarter of this *pajja*, it is stated in the *Chandoviciti* that it consists of ten syllables per quarter.

Since it is established as being in the *gāthā* meter by the definition of *Chandoviciti*—"the *gāthā* meter has two [syllables] in excess"—it should be understood that two syllables are stated here in excess of the *dvattipariyāya* (the "two-and-three" pattern).
In the phrase "in application" (*payoge*), it refers to the application of the established [meter]. It is "established" (*adhiṭṭhite*).
When the determination has been made after two or three repetitions:
87. *Payoge* means in the act of sprinkling or causing to sprinkle. *Sitte* means at the conclusion of the action of sprinkling.
This concludes the second commentary on the section on plants (*Bhūtagāmavagga*).
88. The construction is: "he incurs a *dukkaṭa*. The construction is: "if she has been exhorted, it may be a *pācittiya*. 89.
"Distinction" (*vibhāga*) is simply the state of being distinguished (*vibhāgatā*).
90. The construction is: "A monk giving a robe to an unrelated nun, except in exchange, incurs two offenses. "In the preliminary effort" (*payoge*) means in the preliminary effort of giving.

93. The word-division is “nāvaṃ ekaṃ. Regarding “in the act” (*payoge*), it refers to the act of boarding. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in “dukkaṭādayo,” the offense of *pācittiya* incurred once boarded is included.
94. The word-division is “duvidhaṃ āpattiṃ.
96. The construction is: a monk who engages in sitting in private with a nun incurs two offenses, beginning with *dukkaṭa*, during the course of the act (*payoge*).

The third commentary: the Ovādavagga (Chapter on Exhortation). 97. *Taduttarin* means beyond that; from the second day onwards, as opposed to the single day permitted for eating. *Anantarassa vaggassa* refers to the preceding chapter, the Ovādavagga. *Navamena* refers to the training rule concerning almsfood prepared by a bhikkhunī.
99. *Dvattipatte* means two or three bowlfuls. *Taduttarin* means beyond two or three bowlfuls. *Payoge* refers to the act of receiving.
101. *Abhihaṭṭhūnti* means having brought forward. 102.
*Tassā* means of him who is bringing it forward. *Piṭake* refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
103. Regarding *dasamepi*: here the word division is *dasame api*.

The fourth commentary on the Chapter on Food (Bhojanavagga). 104. Regarding the phrase "naked ascetics, etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), those mentioned as "a male wanderer (*paribbājaka*) or a female wanderer (*paribbājikā*)" are included. Regarding "food, etc.": by the word "etc.," edible food (*khādanīya*) is included. Regarding "the act" (*payoga*): it refers to the act of giving with one's own hand. 105.

"Having caused some material gift to be given, or not having caused it to be given"—regarding "the act": it refers to the act of inciting [another] to give. "In that case" means in regard to that monk. The construction is: "if he has been incited, there shall be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)."
109. "Transgressing the boundary" means transgressing the threshold of the city gate (indakhīla). 110.
"Beyond that" means beyond either the limit of the night as defined, or the limit of the medicine as defined.
111. The construction is: one who goes for the purpose of seeing an army would incur two offenses.
The fifth commentary on the Acelaka-vagga. 114. *Mereyya* means intoxicant (*meraya*).
According to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*), the letter *a* becomes *e*, and the letter *ya* is doubled. Alternatively, the word *mereyya* is a synonym for the word *meraya*.
*Munī* refers to a bhikkhu. 115. The phrase-break is: “*Bhikkhu aṅgulipatodena*. *Payoge* means in the act of causing laughter. *Tassa* means of him who is making [others] laugh.
116. If [the water] is below the ankle, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Above the ankle" means above the ankle, in the water; that is, in water exceeding the measure of the ankle. 117.
"Disrespect" means disrespect toward persons or disrespect toward the Dhamma. "In the undertaking" means in the bodily or verbal undertaking proceeding by way of disrespect.
"When disrespect has been committed. 118. "In the undertaking" means in the undertaking of frightening [others].
119. *Jotinti aggiṃ*: having kindled it means having made it blaze. By the term "blazing," the cause is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the effect.
For the act of blazing is the result of the act of kindling; thus, by the conventional expression "the act of blazing," it is actually the "act of kindling" that is meant.
Therefore, in the phrase "blazing," the meaning is "kindling. *Payoge*: in the application, that is, in the application of the acts of kindling and causing to be kindled.
"Visīviteti" means it has been concentrated according to the method already stated. 120.
"In the application" refers to all applications such as the preparation of powders, clay, and so forth. "The other" refers to the *pācittiya* offense. 121.

"Of the three ways of making discolored" refers to the three ways of making discolored: those consisting of bronze-blue, leaf-blue, and mud-blue. "Without taking one or another" means without having applied one or another [of these]. "Cīvara" refers to a new robe.

122. *Anuddhāra* means that there is no lifting up (*uddhāra*) of it; thus, while it should be called *anuddhāraṃ*, the shortening occurs by way of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*). The meaning is "that which has not been formally relinquished" (*akata-paccuddhāra*).
123. *Apanidhento*: removing and then placing down or depositing. *Pattādikam*: by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the robe, the sitting mat, the needle-case, and the waist-band.
*Payoge*: in the act of removing. In those five kinds of requisites, such as the bowl and so forth, when they have been removed.
The construction is: "the remaining [cases] may be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on Drinking Liquor (Surāpānavagga).
124. *Tapodhana*: one who possesses the wealth of asceticism (*tapodhana*)—that is, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha—is called a *tapodhana*; [this refers to] a bhikkhu.
125. In that pit. 126.
A human being means one with a human body; a non-human being means a nāga or a supaṇṇa. Of that person digging the pit.
127. With keen intelligence means by the Blessed One, through his subtle knowledge regarding all phenomena to be known.
128. *Payoga* refers to the application of effort, such as taking [something] for the purpose of use.

*Tassa* means "of that monk. 129. *Ukkoṭento* means moving [something], not allowing it to remain in its original place. *Payoge* refers to the application of the act of moving. The construction is: "If it has been moved, there may be an offense of *pācittiya*. 130.

*Duṭṭhullaṃ vajjaṃ* refers to a grave fault, such as an offense involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*). The construction is: "It is explained that one incurs one *pācittiya* offense."

131. *Payoge* means in the preliminary application, such as the search for a group (*gaṇa*) and so forth. *Dukkaṭaṃ patto siyā* means he would have incurred a *dukkaṭa* offense; this is the meaning. *Sesā* refers to the *pācittiya* offense, which may occur once [the person] has been ordained. The elision of the prefix (*upasagga*) is due to the requirements of the metrical composition (*gāthābandha*). 132–3. The construction is:

for one who, knowing [it is so], travels the road in company with a band of thieves after making an agreement, and likewise for one who travels the road in company with a woman after making an agreement.
*Payoge* refers to the preliminary application, such as making inquiries and so forth, in order to go after having made the agreement.
"Those who have entered upon the path" means those practicing the path. "Immediately after" means immediately after passing through the interval between two villages half a *yojana* apart.
134. The construction is: "one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the conclusion of the motion (*ñatti*).
135. "By one who has not performed the *anudhamma*"—here *anudhamma* refers to either the non-recognition of an offense or the non-remediation of a grave offense.

"Having seen that one who has been suspended according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction for not relinquishing a wrong view has performed the concordant duties (*anulomavatta*) and has been reinstated—this concordant practice (*anudhamma*) consisting of reinstatement has not been performed by him; such a person is called 'one by whom the concordant practice has not been performed'.
The meaning is: "with such a monk. "Sharing together" means a monk who engages in the sharing of material goods (*āmisa*).

*Payoga* refers to the means of receiving food and so forth for the purpose of eating. *Bhutta* means having consumed; the meaning is that it has been enjoyed by both together, or that one or the other has performed the act. 136.
*Upalāpento* means winning over by means of such things as offering alms bowls, robes, instruction, or questioning. *Payoga* here refers to the means of winning over.
The seventh commentary on the Sappāṇaka-vagga.

137. *Sahadhammikaṃ*: this is the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental. It refers to the training rule (sikkhāpada) proclaimed by the Buddha, which is known by the name "sahadhammika" because it is to be trained in by the five [classes of] fellow-followers of the Dhamma (*sahadhammika*), or because it belongs to them.
"Being spoken to" is the meaning. "Speaking" is in grammatical apposition with the word "of the bhikkhu.

"Deprecating" means censuring by saying, "What is the use of these minor and lesser training rules having been recited? and so forth. "In the application" refers to the verbal activity occurring through the mode of censure, such as "What is the use of these? and so on. "Deprecated" means censured.

139. *Mohento*: by saying, “Just now, friend, do I come to know,” and so forth, he indicates his state of having committed an offense through his own lack of knowledge; thus, the meaning is “deceiving” or “deluding” a bhikkhu. *Moheti* is used in the sense of the act of imposing delusion (*mohāropana*).
When it has been imposed, it is “done. 140. The construction is: “striking” means giving a blow to a bhikkhu while being angry.
*Payoge* refers to the preliminary application, such as the taking up of a staff and so forth. 141. *Payoge* refers to the application of vomiting. *Uggiriteti* means when it has been uttered.

142. *Amūleneva* means precisely by that which is devoid of the roots such as wrong view (*diṭṭhi*). *Yoge* refers to the application (*payoga*) such as creating an opportunity. *Uddhaṃsite* means having been reproached. 143.

*Kukkuccaṃ janayanto* means instilling remorse (*kukkucca*) by saying things such as, "I think you have been ordained for less than twenty years. *Yoge* refers to the application of producing remorse.

*Uppādite* means when remorse has been produced. 144. The word division is: *tiṭṭhanto upassutiṃ*. *Upassuti* is the vicinity of hearing (*sutiyā samīpaṃ*); the meaning is "within earshot" (*savanūpacāre*).
145. “Of legal acts” means of the four types of acts—such as the *apalokanakamma* and so forth—performed in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
“Thereafter” means after the giving of consent (*chandadāna*). “An act of censure” (*khīyanadhamma*) refers to a speech that makes manifest one’s own intended state of mind.

“Two offenses, such as *dukkaṭa*, would be incurred” means: an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is incurred in the process of undertaking the act of censure, and [another] when the act of censure has been committed.
*Pācittiyan* means that one would incur two offenses, such as *dukkaṭa* and so forth;

this is the meaning. 146. *Saṅghe* means in the midst of the Saṅgha. *Vinicchaye* means in the formal adjudication concerning the subject matter. *Niṭṭhaṃ agate* means when the subject matter has not been adjudicated, or when the motion (*ñatti*) has been proposed but the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) has not yet been completed.
148. *Samaggena saṅghena* means by a Saṅgha that is united, standing within the same boundary (*sīmā*) and belonging to the same community (*saṃvāsa*).
The eighth: The Explanation of the Chapter on Those of the Same Dhamma. 150.
“Without being known” means without his arrival being known to the king. 152.
“Jewel” refers to the ten kinds of jewels, beginning with pearls. “In the act of taking” means in the process of seizing the jewels.
153. "At the wrong time" means from the point of passing the midday meal until sunrise.
155. "Produced from bone, tooth, or horn" means made of bone, tooth, or horn. "In the act" refers to the act of having it made. 156. The construction is:
when that bed or similar object has been made, the remaining [offenses] may be offenses of expiation (pācittiya).
The ninth commentary on the Ratana-vagga is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Pācittiya-kathā within the Uttaravinicchaya Līnatthappakāsinī.
159. In the case of the four *pāṭidesanīya* [offenses] as well, the construction is that the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, has pointed out the offense in two ways without distinction.
160. "In all cases" means in all four.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the *pāṭidesanīya*.
161. The discussion on the training rules (*sekhiya*) is indeed of plain meaning. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the training rules. 162.
In the *Mahāvibhaṅga*, which is divided into sixteen sections as first shown in the *Parivāra*, [the first rule is] "the first *pārājika*."
The section on where [the rules] are laid down (*katthapaññattivāra*) consists of various classifications such as, "Where is it laid down?
The section on the offenses committed (*katāpattivāra*) consists of various classifications such as, "While engaging in sexual intercourse, how many offenses does one incur?

The section on failure (*vipattivāra*) consists of various classifications such as, "Of the four failures, how many failures do the offenses incurred by one engaging in sexual intercourse fall under? "Sexual..."

The section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*) consists of such classifications as: "Of the offenses for one who practices the Dhamma, how many of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) are they included in?

The section on origination (*samuṭṭhānavāra*) consists of such classifications as: "Of the offenses for one who practices sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*), by how many of the six origins of offenses (*āpattisamuṭṭhāna*) do they originate?"

The section on legal issues (*adhikaraṇavāra*) consists of such classifications as: “For one who engages in sexual intercourse, among the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), to which category does his offense belong?

The section on settlement (*samathavāra*) consists of such classifications as: “For one who engages in sexual intercourse, by how many of the seven methods of settling disputes (*samatha*) are his offenses settled?
The section that follows immediately after these is mixed with these seven sections.

Regarding the eighth section, the "Section on Compendium": among these eight sections, since the seventeen characteristics beginning with the *nidāna*—which are to be included in the "Section on Attainment" (*appanāvāra*) that constitutes the first part of the "Designation of the Categories of Offenses"—will be explained later as being common to both *Vibhaṅgas*, this section is set aside;

immediately following it is the "Section on the Occurrence of Offenses" (*katāpattivāra*), which is not common [to both], extending up to the end of the *Sekhiyas* in accordance with the sequence of the Canon.

Having shown [the first section], and considering that the six subsequent sections beginning with the "Section on Defeat" (vipattivāra) will be explained as common to both Vibhaṅgas, those too are set aside;
thus, there are eight sections shown by connecting them with the word *paccaya* (condition). Then, again, by connecting the word *paccaya*, [the text continues] with:
"Where was the Pārājika offense prescribed on account of engaging in sexual intercourse? and so forth.

It is said that eight other sections have been applied; therein, having made the section on the condition of having committed an offense (*katāpatti-paccaya-vāra*)—the second [section]—identical in its delimitation with this section on having committed an offense (*katāpatti-vāra*), he says "prescribed" (*paññattā*) and so forth to demonstrate it. "By reason of using" (*paṭisevana-paccayā*) means by way of the cause of using. 163.
"In entering an improper place" (*alokāsa-ppavesane*) means in entering an improper place within one of the three paths of a living body.

The connection is as follows: "Whether it is fully described or even by the word 'pi' (also) [meaning] mostly described, a bhikkhu who engages in sexual intercourse upon entering or for the purpose of entering incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Likewise, a bhikkhu who engages in sexual intercourse when it is mostly described or even half-described [incurs a *pārājika* offense].
The construction is: "one incurs a *thullaccaya*. The connection is: "if the mouth is made circular, a *dukkaṭa* is stated. The connection is:
"regarding 'with a dildo' (*jatumaṭṭhaka*), it is stated that when a dildo is given to a nun, there is a *pācittiya*.

166. "Of one who is lustful" (*avassutassa*) means of one who is moistened by the passion for physical contact. "Of a man" (*posassa*) is the genitive case used in connection with the action of grasping.
“Bhikkhunīyā” (by a bhikkhunī) is the genitive case used in relation to herself; “of herself” (*attano*) is the remainder [of the sense]. The construction is:
for a lustful bhikkhunī who consents to a lustful man’s grasping at her own area below the collarbone and so forth, it is a *pārājika*.

167. “With the body” (*kāyena*) means with her own body. “The body” (*kāyaṃ*) means the body of a woman. “Touches” (*phusanto*) means touching with the passion for bodily contact. The same principle applies here as well to the phrase “body-to-body” (*kāyena kāyabaddhaṃ*).

168. "With a body that is attached" means with a body attached to one's own [person]. "Attached" refers to touching what is attached to a woman’s body; for that monk, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Why is it said, "The compendium of the Mahāvibhaṅga is finished"? Is it not the case that in the *Mahāvibhaṅga* compendium of the sixteen sections, only the section on offenses committed has been stated here, and not the other sections?
True; however, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the whole is used for its part.

It has been stated. It should be understood that the section on the commission of offenses (*katāpattivāra*)—which serves as the introductory framework for showing all the various categories of offenses found in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*, both common and uncommon—has been presented; and by its presentation, the other sections, though secondary, are also shown by way of introduction, which is why it was stated thus.
Thus ends the commentary on the Compendium of the Mahāvibhaṅga within the *Līnatthappakāsinī*.
The Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.

170. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the monks' proficiency in the analysis of the Vinaya": this is stated by way of showing that the primary focus is on the monks, since the proficiency of the bhikkhunīs is also dependent upon that [analysis].

Alternatively, because it is desired that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) be common to both [monks and bhikkhunīs], the designation is given in the masculine or neuter gender according to the application of grammatical science; thus, it is expressed in the masculine as "of the monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ*).
171. "Nandantī" means consenting.
172. The construction is: she incurs three offenses. For her who consents to the grasping [of the hand] above the knee and below the collarbone, there is a *pārājika*; this is the construction. 173.
For her who consents to the grasping of something attached to the body, there is a *dukkaṭa*.
174. They declare another bhikkhunī to have committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
176. "That conviction" means: the construction is that she does not relinquish that conviction which she approves for herself, even though it has been suspended.
178. The word-division is: "Come here. The word-division is: "Having been told, she comes."
179. *Hatthapāsappavesane*: in the entering of hand’s reach; or the reading is *hatthagatappavesane*, which has the same meaning.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the Pārājika offenses in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, within the *Uttaralīnatthapakāsani*.
180. "Of one" (ekassa) means of oneself or of one's own legal opponent. "In the announcement" (ārocane) means in the reporting to the judges of what is to be said. 181.
"In the second announcement" (dutiyārocane) means for the second person, or in the announcing of the second [statement].
182. "By two" (dvīhi) means by two formal acts (kammavācā). "At the conclusion of the formal act" (kammavācosāne) means at the end of the formal act.

183. "When the enclosure has been crossed": for one who, having left her own village, enters another village, this means when the first foot has crossed the enclosure of that village; the sense is that once the first foot has crossed the enclosure, it has entered the interior of the village.

184. "By the second": by the second foot standing outside the village enclosure. "Crossed": when that village enclosure has been crossed; the sense is that when that foot has been brought inside the village. The remainder is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the discussion of the *saṅghādisesa* rules in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* within the *Uttaralīnatthappakāsinī*. 193.
Here, the construction is as follows: if a nun accumulates alms bowls, she incurs one *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense only.
194. "Distributing an out-of-season robe by treating it as an in-season robe" is the construction. "In the preparation" means in the act of preparing for distribution.
195. "Torn" means not torn. 196.
"Beyond that" means other than that first one.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the Nissaggiya offenses in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga of the *Līnatthappakāsinī*. 199.
If one eats garlic, two offenses are incurred; this is the construction of the sentence.
200. *Payogeti* means in the act of causing to be gathered. *Saṃhaṭeti* means when it has been gathered by oneself or caused to be gathered by another; there is an offense of *pācittiya*. 201.
*Kateti* means when the striking with the palm has been performed.
202. *Jatunā maṭṭhakan’ti* means a polished handle made of lacquer. The word-division is: “*dukkaṭaṃ ādinne*. (There is an offense of *dukkaṭa* when it has been taken.)
204. The construction is: “while a bhikkhu is eating within hand’s reach. Having left hand’s reach. 205.
“Having requested” means even having asked one’s own mother. The construction is: “for each swallow, it is declared a *pācittiya* offense. 206.
Regarding “excrement, etc.,” by the word “etc.,” there is the inclusion of food scraps, sweepings, and urine.
The first commentary on the Garlic Chapter. 209.

Here, in this "Chapter on Darkness at Night," the construction is as follows: the determination (vinicchaya) for the first, second, third, and fourth [rules] is equal to—that is, similar to—the sixth training rule (sikkhāpada) of the Garlic Chapter.
210. "On a seat" means on a couch or on that which serves as its space. "Without asking the owner" means without asking any person of understanding belonging to that family.
211. “Not leaking” refers to the space inside the threshold and outside the wall. “Crossing over the second” means when one’s second foot crosses the place where water falls at the threshold.
212. “Sitting down” means when she has sat down.
213. “In the act” means in the act of complaining.
214. "Cursing oneself or another with 'hell' and so forth," means making an oath; the construction is that one incurs two [offenses]. "Abhisappite" means having been cursed. 215.
"Having struck" means having struck with the hands or other [limbs]. The word division is "karoti ekaṃ.
This concludes the second commentary on the Chapter on Darkness at Night.
216. *Naggā* means naked, either unclothed or uncovered. *Payoga* refers to the preparation, such as the mixing of powder and clay. 217.
*Pamāṇātikkantaṃ* means exceeding the prescribed measure, which is stated as: "four spans long according to the Sugata-span, and two spans wide. *Payoga* refers to the act of having it made. 218.
*Visibbetvā* means having unpicked out poorly sewn seams for the purpose of sewing them again.
219. *Pañca ahāni* means five days; *pañcāham* means for five days; *pañcāhikam* means [an offense] occurring after five days.

*Saṅghāṭicāro*: the circulation of outer robes (*saṅghāṭī*). By way of usage or by way of wearing, it refers to the exchange of these five robes—namely, the triple robe (*ticīvara*), the water-bath cloth (*udakasāṭikā*), and the breast-cloth (*saṃkaccikā*)—which have received the name "outer robe" (*saṅghāṭī*) in the sense of being stitched together. A bhikkhunī who exceeds [this limit]... [commits an offense].
One would transgress. However, the construction is that only one *pācittiya* offense is indicated for her.
220. "Transferable" means that which ought to be transferred; it refers to any one of the five [types of robes] taken from another without asking permission, which must be returned again. 221.

"Of the acquisition of a robe for the community" means of a robe to be received by the community of nuns (*bhikkhunī-saṅgha*). "Creates an obstacle" means she exerts herself in such a way that those who wish to give do not give.

222. "Dhammikaṃ" means that which is being performed by a Saṅgha that has assembled in full concord. "Paṭibāhantī" means they are prohibiting it. "Paṭibāhite" means when it has been prohibited or forbidden.

223. "Agārikādino" (of householders, etc.): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes what is stated as "or for a male wanderer (*paribbājaka*) or a female wanderer (*paribbājikā*). "Samaṇacīvaraṃ" refers to a robe that has been made allowable and is suitable to be worn as an undergarment or upper garment.
"Payoge" refers to the act of giving. 224. "Cīvare dubbalāsāya" means with a weak expectation regarding the robe, merely thinking, "If we are able, we shall give."
The meaning is: "having heard [the news], hope has been generated. "Time" refers to the period for robes.

"Transgresses" means that while the robe-cloth is being distributed among the bhikkhunīs, she says, "Wait, noble ladies, there is an expectation of robe-cloth for the Saṅgha," and thereby transgresses that distribution of the robe-cloth.
225. A *dhammika* (lawful) *kathinuddhāra* is the suspension of the *kathina* robe-season performed by a unanimous Saṅgha. *Paṭibāhantiyā*: by one who prevents it.
This concludes the third commentary, on the section concerning bathing.
226. *Tuvaṭṭeyyuṃ*: they should lie down. The other [offense] is a *pācittiya*.
227. When an act is being performed that causes discomfort for the nun Payogā.
228. "Suffering" means one who is ill. "Or not attending to her" means either not having others attend to her, or not doing so oneself.
229. "Having given a dwelling place" means having given one's own private vihāra with its door fastened. "Dragged out" means expelled.
230. "Associated" means a nun who dwells in association with a householder or a householder’s son; she is being turned back from dwelling in such association by the Saṅgha.
"By the motion, she incurs a dukkaṭa" means she would commit a dukkaṭa offense regarding the formal motion for the act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma).
231. "Within the kingdom" means within the realm of the one whose domain she dwells in. "Has set out" means while she is making a journey. "The remainder" refers to the pācittiya offense.
The fourth commentary on the Tuvatta-vagga. 233.
Regarding the phrase "the royal palace, etc.," the word "etc. includes the pleasure pavilion and other such structures.

235. Regarding "in the process," this refers to all processes beginning with the carding of cotton. Regarding "rolling it back and forth," this refers to as much as has been pulled by hand and wrapped in a cloth.
237. *Payoga* refers to the act of giving hard food and other provisions with one’s own hand to a householder, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer.
238. The word-division is: “*Samaṃ āpattipabhedato*,” meaning “equal according to the classification of offenses.
239. *Tiracchānavijjā* refers to any kind of external science that is unbeneficial and causes harm to others.

*Hatthisikkhādisippaṃ* means the craft of elephant-training and so forth. *Paṭhantiyā* means by one who is learning. *Payoge* means in the application, such as the practice of making oneself difficult to approach.
*Pade pade* means for one who masters [the text] word by word, either by way of the words themselves or by way of the syllables within those words. 240.

In the ninth [case], the word is "pariyāpuṇāti" (he masters), and in the tenth, the word is "vāceti" (he causes to recite). Thus, in both instances, it is merely the difference between these two words that serves as the distinguishing feature.
The fifth commentary on the Chapter on the Painted Hall (Cittāgāravagga). 241.
"That is a grove" (tam ārāmaṃ) refers to that area containing monks, even if they are dwelling there at the foot of a tree. 243.

"He reviles" (akkosati) means he reviles him either face-to-face or behind his back by means of one of the ten grounds for reviling. "He scolds" (paribhāsati) means he threatens him by showing him fear. The word-division is: "There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) when reviled."

244. *Caṇḍikabhāvena* means with anger. *Gaṇaṃ* refers to the community of bhikkhunīs. *Paribhāsati* means she reviles them with such words as "these women are fools. *Payoge* means in the act of reviling. *Paribhaṭṭhe* means when she has been reviled. The other [offense] is a *pācittiya*. 245.
*Nimantitā* means invited in the manner described under the rule on eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*).

*Pavāritā* means restrained in the manner described under the training rule on *pavāraṇā*. *Khādanaṃ bhojanampi vā* refers to rice gruel, cakes, and snacks; or to food that may be eaten at the proper time, such as edible roots and other solid foods.
The construction is as follows: whichever nun is eating even food such as boiled rice, she incurs two offenses.
247. *Maccharāyantī* means being stingy; the meaning is that she cannot bear the sharing [of alms] with others by the family that provides her requisites.
*Payoge* refers to the corresponding bodily and verbal application. *Maccharite* means by way of stinginess.
When the preparatory undertaking has been completed. 248.
However, regarding "living in a residence devoid of monks": this refers to a residence where, within a distance of half a *yojana* from the nuns' quarters, no monks who give exhortation reside;
or where the path is unsafe and it is impossible to travel without obstruction—such a residence is meant.

Regarding the phrase "in the preliminary duties": the construction is that when the preliminary duties—such as preparing the lodgings and setting out drinking water—are being performed with the thought, "I shall spend the rains retreat," it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). 249.

"Those who have spent the rains retreat" means those who have completed either the first or the second three-month period. "In both Saṅghas" means in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. "By all three grounds" refers to the three reasons stated beginning with "by what has been seen."

250. "For the sake of exhortation" means for the sake of receiving the exhortation regarding the *garudhammas*. "For the sake of living together" means for the sake of both inquiring about the *uposatha* and for the sake of the *pavāraṇā*. "Does not go" means she does not approach a monk. 251.
"Nor do they ask for exhortation" means they neither request nor inquire of a monk regarding the approach for exhortation on the *uposatha* day and so forth.
"Uposatha" refers to the thirteenth or fourteenth day prior to the *uposatha* day.
or does not ask about the Uposatha.
252. "Without having asked the Saṅgha" means without having sought permission from either the Saṅgha or a group (gaṇa).
"'Causes to be split'—this is merely an illustration; [it includes] causing it to be ploughed, or caused to be washed, or caused to be smeared, or caused to be bound, or caused to be released."

The word “or” (*vā*) is used because these alternative modes of action (*kriyā-vikalpa*) are also to be included. *Pasākhaja* refers to a boil or a blood-clot that has arisen in the region below the navel and above the kneecaps.
*Payoga* refers to the application of means such as causing it to burst.
This concludes the sixth commentary, the *Ārāmavagga-vaṇṇanā*.

253. “A pregnant woman” (*gabbhini*) refers to a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) who has conceived a child. “Ordaining” (*vuṭṭhāpentī*) means conferring full admission (*upasampadā*) while acting as her preceptor (*upajjhāyā*). “In the undertaking” (*payoge*) refers to the undertaking of seeking a group of nuns and so forth. “Has been ordained” (*vuṭṭhāpite*) means she has been admitted;

the meaning is that this occurs at the conclusion of the formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*). 255. “A co-resident” (*sahajīvini*) refers to a student nun (*saddhivihārinī*). “Not supporting” (*nānuggaṇhantī*) means not caring for her by providing instruction and so forth.
The seventh commentary, on the section concerning pregnant women, is concluded.
258. "Enough with her being ordained"—being told this and being restrained by the bhikkhunīs.
"She censures" means that seeing the formal authorization for ordination being granted to other competent and modest women, she censures herself by saying, "Surely I alone am foolish," and so forth.
"In the act" means in the act of censuring. "Has censured" means when the act of censuring is completed.
The eighth: The Commentary on the Chapter on the Maidenhood (Kumāribhūtavagga). 260.
"An umbrella and sandals" refers to an umbrella and sandals possessing the characteristics already described. "In the act of using" means in the act of carrying them. 261.
"By vehicle" means by means of a cart or similar conveyance. "If she has gone by vehicle" means if she has traveled by means of a vehicle.
262. *Saṅghāṇi*: anything that serves as a waistband. *Dhārentiyā*: by one who fastens it around the waist. 263. *Gandhavaṇṇena*: with any kind of color and any kind of fragrance.

"Fragrance" (*gandha*) refers to things such as sandalwood ointment; "color" (*vaṇṇa*) refers to things such as saffron or turmeric. *Payoge*: in the application, meaning from the time of the preliminary preparation for the application of the fragrance and so forth.
266. *Anāpuccha*: without having asked permission, [saying] "I am sitting down, Venerable Lady. When she has sat down, even if the monk is merely sitting on the ground within his vicinity.
267. "Without having made an appointment" means not having made an appointment such as, "I will ask [about this] in such-and-such a place.
268. "Entering" should be explained by making it identical with the first training rule of the Ārāmavagga regarding the Vinicchaya; thus is the construction.
This concludes the ninth commentary, the Chattupāhanavagga.
Thus ends the commentary on the discussion of the *pācittiya* rules in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* within the *Uttaralīnatthappakāsanī*.

Regarding the eight *pāṭidesanīya* training rules as well, the application is that the offense occurs in two ways. "From that" means by way of taking hold [of the food]. "In all" refers to all the *pāṭidesanīya* training rules.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Pāṭidesanīya Offenses. 271–2.

A wise and discerning bhikkhu, having understood through its purpose this supreme, most excellent, unsurpassed, and faultless teaching—so named—that is devoid of any superior statement and is difficult to transcend with effort, [should apply it].
Since one crosses the great ocean of the Vinaya— which has been laid out— easily and with ease, therefore,
in this treatise (*uttarapakaraṇa*) which is like a sword for cutting through doubt and resolving uncertainty regarding the Vinaya,
a living bhikkhu— one endowed with heat, possessed of the fire-element of karma— is constantly and continuously [engaged].
The construction is: "A person who is constantly delighted [in the training] is fit and suitable to undertake application and constant exertion.
The *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* is concluded; here too, the origin story (*uppatti*) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
Thus ends the *Uttaralīnatthapakāsanī*.
The commentary on the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Four Failures (273).
Now, treating both [the monks’ and nuns’ rules] as common, he says “How many offenses? and so forth, in order to compile the specific sections beginning with the section on failures (*vipattivāra*).
274. If a bhikkhunī conceals [an offense], she has fallen [from her status]. If she conceals it while being in doubt, there may be a *thullaccaya*—this is the construction.
275. *Saṅghādisesa*: the *saṅghādisesa* offense of another.
276. The word-division is: “How many causes for failure in conduct?”
277. *Ācāravipattiṃ*: the failure of conduct, whether one's own or another's.
279. *Pāpikaṃ diṭṭhiṃ*: an evil view, such as the views of non-causality, non-action, and nihilism.
281. *Manussuttaridhammaṃ*: a state superior to that of ordinary human beings.
282. The construction is: “He engaged in matchmaking for the sake of livelihood. Regarding “figurative speech”:

this refers to deceptive statements such as, “The monk who dwells in your monastery is an arahant,” and so forth. Regarding “known”: it means that as soon as the words are spoken, the person to whom he speaks—who belongs to the human race—is known.
"Having spoken" means having requested for one's own sake when not ill. However, regarding the nun:
if it is so—that is, if the nun, being not ill, has requested exquisite food for her own sake and has eaten it—this is the intended meaning.
The construction is: "for her there may be an offense entailing confession."
284. By the phrase "having requested for one's own sake," it is shown that there is no offense for one who, having requested for the sake of another relative who has invited [him],
either consumes what is given by that person or consumes it through that person's trust,
provided that the relatives in question are not those who have invited him and his mind is pure.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discourse on the Four Failings in the *Uttaralīnatthappakāsinī*.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Conditions for Legal Issues (*adhikaraṇa*).

285. Regarding the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*): it refers to that which arises according to the method beginning with “one proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma,” and is based upon the eighteen grounds for schism.
286. The construction is: “For a monk who reviles one who is fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

287. “On account of the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*): the very legal issue of accusation—which has another name, “reproach”—is the condition; therefore, the meaning is “on account of the cause of the legal issue of accusation.”
289. By the word “likewise,” the absence of a basis is extended by analogy.

290. “On account of an offense” means on account of a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). 293. “On account of a legal issue concerning business” means due to a legal issue concerning business consisting of the fourfold formal acts, such as the motion for information (*apalokanakamma*), and so forth.
294. *Accajantīvā* means not relinquishing one's own view. 297. The construction is as follows:

for that nun who, when exhorted up to three times for the sake of relinquishing an evil view that has been formed, does not relinquish that view, there is a *pācittiya* offense; and for the monk who [does not] cause her to relinquish it, there is likewise a *pācittiya*.
Thus ends the *Uttare Līnatthapakāsanī*.
The commentary on the discussion of the condition of the subject (*adhikaraṇapaccaya*) is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the questions regarding the Khandhakas 300:
"In the remaining [cases]" refers to all the statements that indicate persons incapable [of realization].

302. “May these perish” (*nassantu ete*)—this is the word-division. Regarding *purakkhakā*: here the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive; thus the meaning is “of one who has precedence for schism,” or “by those who have precedence for schism. 303. “In the remaining cases” (*sesesu*):
this refers to the remaining prohibitory passages that indicate those who are not in communion (*asaṃvāsaka*), and so forth.

304. “Only one offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is stated”: this means that only one offense of wrong-doing is stated by way of its origin, arising from causes such as not entering the rains residence (*vassa*), and so on.
305. "Considered as having occurred on the Uposatha day" refers to those offenses considered as having occurred that are described in the Uposatha Khandhaka.
306. "In the Leather Khandhaka": the connection is that for the group of six (Chabbaggiyā) who, having seized a heifer, killed it, a *pācittiya* offense was stated.
"A heifer" (*vacchatariṃ*) means a young cow endowed with strength; for she [retains] the state of being a calf...
Because she stands having crossed over and transcended [the state of being a heifer], she is called a "vacchatarī" (a young cow).
"Touching the private parts" means touching the private parts of cows with one's own private parts from the outside.
"In the remaining cases" refers to seizing cows by their horns and so forth, as well as mounting them on their backs. As it was said: "The group-of-six bhikkhus..."
“...even seizing the horns of cows as they were crossing the river Aciravatī,” and so forth.
309. Regarding that, in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*: “Within two finger-breadths around” means within a space of two finger-breadths around the anus and the urinary passage.
The construction is: “For one performing surgical treatment [therein], a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is declared. As it has been said:
“Monks, surgical treatment or medicinal application with a cloth should not be performed within two fingerbreadths of the private parts.
Whoever should perform it, there is an offense of thullaccaya. And here, the phrase “within two fingerbreadths” is stated specifically with reference to surgical treatment;
however, medicinal application with a cloth is prohibited at the private parts themselves.
Because it was said: “Monks, one who has been invited elsewhere must not consume the rice-gruel of another;

whoever should so consume it is to be dealt with according to the rule,” he said: “In the case of rice-gruel for eating, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). And here, “rice-gruel for eating” (bhojjayāgu) means thick gruel.

In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: “Rice-gruel that is to be drunk after being rolled into balls. “An offense of expiation” (pācittiya) refers to [the offenses] under the training rules concerning eating in succession and the invitation to eat.
*Pācittiya*. "In the remaining cases" refers to [the offenses regarding] food stored overnight, food cooked inside [a monastery], food cooked by oneself, consumption, and so forth. As it is said:

"Monks, one must not consume food that has been stored overnight, cooked inside [a monastery], or cooked by oneself; whoever should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so on.
310. *Cīvarasaṃyutta*: in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka* (The Chapter on Robes).

313. In the cases of *Campeyyaka* and *Kosambī*, it refers to the *Campeyyaka-khandhaka* and the *Kosambaka-khandhaka*. The same principle applies to [the terms] such as “in a formal act” (*kammasmiṃ*). 317.
“Chewing the cud” (*romantha*) means the process of moving food back into the mouth from the stomach in order to soften it, so that what has been eaten may be digested quickly.
318. “In regard to lodgings” (*senāsanasmim*) refers to the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*. “A heavy thing” (*garuno*) refers to a heavy article.
320. Regarding "in the case of schism in the Saṅgha," this refers to the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
321. "Of those who follow the schism" means of those who side with the schism in the Saṅgha. "In a group meal" means in the eating together of a group. 322.
"This [offense]"—the remainder here is that it occurs through disrespect regarding all the rules of conduct. The rest is self-evident.
Thus ends the commentary on the discussion of questions regarding the Khandhakas within the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion concerning the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*).

325–6. I shall hereafter explain the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of those training rules (*sikkhāpada*), such as the *pārājika* and others, which were laid down by the Great Seer (*Mahesin*) in the two *vibhaṅgas* and recited on the Uposatha day, for the sake of the monks’ proficiency.
Listen with a concentrated mind—this is the construction (*yojanā*).
327. Body and speech—thus "body-speech"—refers to the three origins that are without consciousness;
when these very same [origins] are each joined with consciousness, they become the three origins that possess consciousness.
In this way, the origin is single-limbed by way of the first two, double-limbed by way of the third, fourth, and fifth, and [triple-limbed] by way of the sixth.
The construction is: "And [they] speak of the method of origination in six ways as 'threefold' (*tivaṅgika*). Body and speech constitute one twofold category;
body-and-speech, body-and-mind, and speech-and-mind constitute three twofold categories; and body-speech-and-mind constitutes one threefold category.
The intention is that they speak of this sixfold method of origination according to the distinctions of its constituent parts.
328. Among those six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), the connection is that various offenses arise by means of one origin, or two, or three, or four, or all six origins.
329. Regarding those various offenses: there exists no such offense as has five origins—that is, an analysis [of the compound] as "that which has five origins.
Nor does there exist any offense that has each and every one of the origins individually; this refers even to the last three origins.

Regarding "only with a conscious mind (sacittaka) and by three origins": the intention is that whichever offense has a single origin arises from any one of the three [factors] involving a conscious mind.
"From the third and the sixth as well" means from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind.
"And from the fourth and the sixth" means from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind. "Also from the fifth and the sixth" means from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
Namely: first, "from body and from body-and-mind," which has two origins; second, "from speech and from speech-and-mind";
third, "from body and speech and from body-speech-and-mind"; fourth, "from body-and-mind and from body-speech-and-mind";
and fifth, "from speech-and-mind and from body-speech-and-mind," which also has two origins. Thus, they exist in these five ways.
This offense arises from two origins; it originates from two origins.

It does not originate from anything else—that is, it does not originate from body alone or speech alone as one [origin], nor from speech and body as another; thus, it does not originate from other origins when applied in a manner contrary to the sequence already stated.
"By the first three" means by the three origins of non-conscious action (acittaka-samuṭṭhāna) previously specified as "from body, from speech, and from both body and speech.

"And by the last" means by the three origins of conscious action (sacittaka-samuṭṭhāna) stated subsequently as "from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from both body, speech, and mind. "Not otherwise" means [not] from body, from speech, or from body and mind... [etc.]
It does not originate from the other three origins—namely, from speech, from body and speech, and from body and mind—because it is excluded by the aforementioned inversions.
The first and third, as well as the fourth and sixth, originate from these four origins: from the body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
The second... [and so on] ...as well as the sixth, originates from speech.
An offense is of fourfold origination by way of these four: from body and speech, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
That very offense arises through these four origins established in two ways.
It does not, however, arise through the four origins joined by means of a transposed method, such as "from body, from speech, from body and speech, and from body and mind," and so forth.
It does not arise from anything else. That which has six origins is "six-origin. It arises from exactly six origins: from the three with mind and the three without mind.
Because there is no other mode [of origin], it is not stated here as "not from another.
And the Master of the Commentary said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:

335. It arises *from* this, thus it is a "source of origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*). There are six kinds, beginning with the body. That which has one source of origination as its cause is "single-originated.
Because there is no other mode, it is threefold. How so? It is threefold by way of the three sources of origination for those [beings] possessing consciousness.
That which has arisen from two sources of origination is "dual-originated," meaning an offense with two sources of origination.
The meaning is as follows: "In five ways" means of five kinds according to the method already stated. That which has three origins is "three-originated" (*tisamuṭṭhānā*);
that which has four origins is "four-originated" (*caturuṭṭhānā*). The compound *ticaturuṭṭhānā* is formed by the rule of *ekadesasarūpekaseso* (retaining one part of similar forms).
Those with three origins are divided into two types, and those with four origins are likewise divided into two types.
The meaning is as follows: "Arising from six" (*chasamuṭṭhitā*) means arising by way of six origins; the sense is "six origins.
"In one way" (*ekadhā*) means that because there is no other mode, they stand as only one; this is the intended meaning. 336.
All offenses, according to the distinctions of their origins, thus stand in thirteen ways among the various classifications of origins.
Because they were first formulated as the primary training rules (*sikkhāpada*) arising from those various [offenses], they receive thirteen names according to those [bases];
I shall explain them hereafter—this is the construction [of the sentence].
337. "The first and last subject" refers to that which originates from the first *pārājika*. "The second" refers to that which originates from taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
“Saṃcaritta-kā” means originating from matchmaking (saṃcaritta). “Samanubhāsana” means originating from formal admonition (samanubhāsana).
The phrase “kathinaṃ eḷakalomakaṃ” is to be analyzed as follows: it originates from the Kathina robe and originates from wool (eḷakaloma). 338.
“Padasodhamma” means originating from the training in the words (padasodhamma). “Addhānaṃ theyyasattha” means originating from traveling with a caravan of thieves (addhāna).

"Originating from a caravan of thieves" means originating from a caravan of thieves. "Teaching" means originating from the teaching of the Dhamma. "Announcing what has occurred" means originating from announcing what has occurred.
"Causing a thief to be ordained" means originating from causing a thief to be ordained.
339. "And that which is not permitted" means originating from that which is not permitted; these thirteen [offenses] arise from those respective origins.

Because they precede the other training rules that originate from those training rules which were first specified—namely, those originating from the first *pārājika* and so forth—they are called "heads.
As it is said in the *Parivāra-ṭīkā*: "The first *pārājika* is one head of origin; the rest are similar to it," and so on. These are the thirteen methods of origin.
These thirteen methods of origination have been shown by the wise, such as the Elder Upāli and others, according to their respective origins.
Regarding this, among the thirteen heads of origination: "Yā" means whichever offense; "ādipārājikuṭṭhānā" means originating from the first *pārājika*. The construction is:

"adinnādānapubbakā" means that for this offense, the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*) is the preceding [factor]; thus it is taught as "originating from the taking of what is not given. (340–341)
342. *Jātu* means "certainly" or "absolutely. 343. The construction is:
this [offense] is stated as "originating from formal admonition" (*samanubhāsanāsamuṭṭhānā*) by way of its origin. 344.

That offense which has the word *kathina* as its prefix (*upapada*) is "having *kathina* as its prefix"; it is considered and known as "originating from *kathina*" (*kathinasamuṭṭhānā*). The meaning is that this is known as "originating from *kathina*" by way of its origin.
345. That whose origin is the word *eḷakaloma* (sheep’s wool) and so forth is "originated by sheep’s wool and so forth"; this is the meaning. 349.
Here, regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*). 350.

That offense which has the word *bhūtārocana* (reporting what has occurred) as its prior part is "preceded by reporting what has occurred" (*bhūtārocanapubbakā*), meaning it is originated by reporting what has occurred (*bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānā*).

351. *Samuṭṭhānaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ*: that which has arisen from the instigation of inciting a theft is "arisen from the instigation of inciting a theft" (*corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhitā*); the meaning is "having the instigation of inciting a theft as its source" (*corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhānā*). 353. *Tattha*:

among these thirteen types of sources (*samuṭṭhāna*), the phrase "the source is with consciousness" (*samuṭṭhānaṃ sacittakaṃ*) should be connected individually with each of the terms beginning with "the first.
"The first source" refers to the source of the first offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*). "The second source" refers to... [and so on].
The fourth origin is that which originates from taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
The ninth origin is that which originates from a caravan of thieves (*theyyasattha*). The tenth origin is that which originates from teaching the Dhamma.
The twelfth origin is that which originates from causing a thief to leave the order (*corivuṭṭhāpana*).
354. *Samuṭṭhāneti* means "in the headings of the origins" (*samuṭṭhānasīse*). *Sadisā* means that the offenses originate according to their respective headings of origin.
*Idha* means in this determination of origins (*samuṭṭhānavinicchaye*). *Dissare* means they are seen; the sense is "they are seen.
Alternatively, *idha dissare* means that here, in both Vibhaṅgas, within each of these thirteen origins, there are also others.
The meaning is that their origins are seen to be similar. Now, in order to point them out according to their specific forms, he says, "And semen," and so forth.
Therein, "semen" refers to the training rule concerning the emission of semen. This same method applies to the [rules] beginning with "bodily contact.
Whatever among these is difficult to understand, that we shall explain.

355. "The ripening of what has been previously approached" refers to the training rule regarding a monk who knowingly approaches [a woman] (*pubbupagata*) and the training rule regarding almsfood prepared by a nun (*bhikkhuniparipācita*).
"In secret with a nun" refers to the training rule regarding sitting in secret together with a nun.

"In a family where food is being served, and two in secret" refers to the training rule regarding intruding upon a family where food is being served, and the two training rules regarding sitting in secret.
And: "Fingers in water" refers to the training rule on finger-snapping and the training rule on laughing in water.
356. "Striking and spitting" refers to the training rule on giving a blow and the training rule on spitting with the palm of the hand.
And the fifty-three *sekhiyas* refers to those among the seventy-five *sekhiyas* to be explained later, beginning with "laughing loudly," which originate from [the offense of] admonishing.
Excluding the ten [rules], the eleven origins of Dhamma-teachings such as *Chattapāṇi* and others, the origin concerning a caravan of thieves,
and the training rule regarding the request for soup and rice— setting these aside,

there are the remaining thirty-five training rules beginning with "wearing the lower robe all around" (*parimaṇḍala-nivāsana*), as well as the training rule for bhikkhunīs: "below the collarbone and above the knees" (*adhakkhakubbhajāṇu*).
“Lustful between villages” refers to the training rule regarding going between villages and the training rule regarding taking fresh food from the hand of one who is lustful (357–8).
“The palm, the *maṭṭha*, and purification by water” refers to striking with the palm, the *jatumaṭṭha* [massage], and traveling for the purpose of purification by water, etc.
“Those who have spent the rains” refers to the training rule beginning, “Having spent the rains... up to five or six *yojanas*” (359). “They do not go for exhortation” refers to the exhortation.
And the training rule on not following [a preceptor]. And the training rule: "One should not follow a *pavattinī* for two years after having had her ordained.
These seventy-five rules explained in both Vibhaṅgas should be connected as follows: they are originated by body and mind;
they are equal to sexual intercourse in their nature; and they are considered to have a single origin.
And here, in the Pāḷi, the numerical limit of "sixty-seven" is shown together with the originating training rule (*samuṭṭhāna-sikkhāpada*).

Here, however, the number is shown without that [specific rule], but only for those similar to it. For this very reason, the first heading of the originating rules was shown by way of number in the Pāḷi, but it is not shown here.
As for the heading of the originating rules appearing elsewhere above...

The mention here, however, is for the purpose of showing that those [factors] which will be explained later possess a similar nature, and for the purpose of showing that they are included within the enumeration that will be stated later.
For this very reason, even in that [later section], he will state the enumeration without including them.
Commentary on the Origin of the First Pārājika.

359. “Viggahanti” refers to the training rule on quarreling (*manussaviggaha-sikkhāpada*). “And furthermore, *uttari* [means]” refers to the training rule on superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma-sikkhāpada*).

“*Duṭṭhulla*” refers to the training rule on indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā-sikkhāpada*). “*Attakāmatā*” refers to the training rule on service for one’s own pleasure (*attakāmapāricariyā-sikkhāpada*).

“And two on *duṭṭhadosa*” refers to the two training rules on corrupt faults (*duṭṭhadosa-sikkhāpada*). “And also the second *aniyata*” refers to the second training rule on undetermined offenses (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*).
"360. And taking back [what was given]" means taking back a robe after having given it oneself.
"Misappropriation" means misappropriating for oneself a gain belonging to the Saṅgha. "False speech, abuse, and slander" means false speech, abusive speech, and slandering monks.
"And the announcement of a grave offense" refers to the training rule regarding the announcement of a grave offense (duṭṭhulla-āpatti). "And digging the earth" as well—
And the training rule on digging the earth. 361.
"A living plant and speaking otherwise" refers to the training rule on living plants and the training rule on speaking otherwise.
"And even reviling" refers to the training rule on reviling. "Ejecting and pouring" refers to ejecting from the monastery and [pouring] water.
And sprinkling grass, etc.; and "for the sake of material gain" refers to the training rule on exhorting nuns for the sake of material gain.
362. "Having eaten" refers to the training rule on inviting [others] with non-leftover food, such as hard foods, etc.;
and "not showing respect" refers to the training rule stated as "Come, friend, to the village," and the training rule on disrespect. And "frightening" alone...

"And the frightening of bhikkhus" refers to the training rule concerning the frightening of bhikkhus. "Should set aside" refers to the training rule concerning setting aside bowls and other requisites.

"Intentionally a living being" refers to intentionally depriving a living being of life. "And even with water containing living beings" refers to the training rule concerning knowingly using water containing living beings.

363. "And reopening" refers to reopening a formal act for the sake of a renewed proceeding. "Deficient" refers to the training rule concerning those less than twenty years of age. "Communion" refers to...

The training rule concerning living together with one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*); and "in expulsion" (*nāsane*), which refers to the training rule concerning social interaction with a novice who has been expelled (*nāsitaka-sāmaṇera-sambhoga-sikkhāpada*);

"legitimate" (*sahadhammika*), which refers to the training rule concerning what is said to be legitimate; and "distress" (*vilekhā*), which refers to the training rule that comes down as "leading to distress";
"delusion" (*mohana*), which refers to the training rule concerning delusion; and "without ground" (*amūlakena*), which refers to [accusing someone] of a *saṅghādisesa* offense without grounds.
And the training rule on reviling. 364.
