“Having given cause for remorse and having given a vote of censure” means: causing remorse, giving a vote of censure regarding formal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma, and giving a vote of censure after having given a robe. “He should divert it to an individual” means: [he should divert] communal gain to an individual.
The training rule on diverting [a gift] to a specific person; the training rule regarding [the robe] that has arrived at an improper time, namely, “What will this man do for you, Noble Lady?”;
the training rule on designating an out-of-season robe as an in-season robe;
the training rule on taking back a robe after having exchanged it with a nun; and the training rule on taking back [a robe] after exchanging it with a nun.

"By means of a bad grasp" (*duggaha-nirayena*) refers both to the training rule concerning the reviling of another based on what was wrongly grasped or wrongly maintained, and to the training rule concerning the cursing of either the holy life (*brahmacariya*) or hell (*niraya*). 365.
"Of a group" (*gaṇassa*) refers to the training rule stating, "One should create an obstacle to the acquisition of robes for a group."
“And the distribution” refers to the training rule stated as: “One should obstruct the legitimate distribution of robes.
“And likewise the weak expectation” refers to the training rule stated as: “One should let the robe-season period pass because of a weak expectation for a robe.
“A legitimate suspension of the kaṭhina” refers to the training rule stated as: “One should obstruct a legitimate suspension of the kaṭhina.”
"And intentionally causing discomfort" refers to the training rule stated: "If one intentionally causes discomfort to a bhikkhunī.
(366) "Having given a dwelling oneself" refers to the training rule stated: "Having given a dwelling to a bhikkhunī, if one, being angry and displeased, should drive her out.
"And reviles" refers to the training rule stated: "If one should revile or abuse a bhikkhu."
“Caṇḍikā” refers to the training rule stated as: “If she is fierce, she should not revile the group. “Kulamaccharinī assā” refers to the training rule stated as:
“She should not be one who is stingy regarding families. “Gabbhiniṃ vuṭṭhāpeyya ca” refers to the training rule stated as: “She should not give full admission to a pregnant woman.”
367. "One who is nursing" refers to the training rule stated: "One should not ordain a woman who is nursing. "Two years" refers to the training rule stated:
"One should not ordain a trainee (sikkhamānā) who has not trained for two years in the six rules. "Not authorized by the Sangha" refers to the training rule stated:
"One should not ordain a trainee who has completed her training but has not been authorized by the Sangha."

And the training rules concerning those who have gone to live as a householder. Three types of women who have gone to live as householders are mentioned: namely, the training rules stated as "a girl less than twelve years old who has gone to live as a householder;
a girl of full twelve years who has gone to live as a householder but has not trained for two years in the six rules;
and one who has trained for two years but has not been approved by the Saṅgha. And three types of unmarried girls are mentioned: "one less than twenty years..."
And the three [rules] stated by way of the method beginning with "one who has become a maiden" (kumāribhūtā), etc.;

and the two training rules stated as: "If one should give the full admission to one less than twelve years old," and "If one should give the full admission to one who is twelve years old but not authorized by the Saṅgha. And "Enough for you now": "Enough for you now..."
And the training rule stated as: "Venerable lady, [you have] ordained one who has already been ordained.
And the training rule stated as: "One should ordain a trainee who is fierce and a dwelling place of grief. And the training rule stated as:
"One should ordain a trainee by means of giving consent while being on probation."
369. Regarding the two [rules] for each year: there are sixty-nine training rules (sikkhāpada), including the two stated as “He should ordain one every year” and “In one year he may ordain two.
Because they are equal to taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*): this is because they share the same origination (*samuṭṭhāna*) as taking what is not given.
How are they said to have three origins? They are said to originate from the three origins associated with volition (*sacittaka*).
Commentary on the Origin of the Second Pārājika Offense. 370.
“Acting as a go-between, building a hut, and building a large dwelling,” refers to acting as a matchmaker, building a hut by means of begging, and building a large monastery.
“Washing and receiving” refers to having an unrelated nun wash one’s old robes and the receiving of robes.
"And the requesting of robe-cloth" refers to the training rule concerning the solicitation of robe-cloth from an unrelated householder or housewife.
"And the taking of what exceeds that" refers to the training rule concerning the acceptance of what exceeds that [allowance].
"And the two regarding what has been set aside" refers to the two training rules that have come down beginning with, "A means for purchasing robe-cloth has been set aside."
Likewise, "by messenger" refers to the training rule concerning cloth sent by messenger for the purpose of purchasing robes; "silk" refers to the training rule concerning [cloth] mixed with silk;
"pure black" refers to the training rule beginning with "pure black [wool]"; and "taking two parts only" refers to the training rule stating that "two parts are to be taken."
372. "Six years" refers to the training rule concerning the storage [of robes] for six years. "Of old" refers to the training rule stated as "of an old rug.
"And the washing of wool" refers to the training rule concerning the washing of sheep's wool. "The acceptance of money" refers to the training rule concerning the acceptance of money.
"Both in various ways" refers to the training rules concerning trading with money and buying and selling.
373. “The bowl with fewer than five mends” refers to the training rule concerning a bowl with fewer than five mends.
“The cloth for the rainy season” refers to the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe and the training rule concerning having robes made after requesting the thread.

“Making a formal assignment” refers to approaching a weaver and making a formal assignment regarding the robe. “As far as the giving of the door and the sewing” means “as far as... [the text continues].

The training rule stated as: "A door-bolt for the purpose of fixing a bolt"; and the two training rules stated as: "One should give a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī" and "One should sew a robe [for an unrelated bhikkhunī]";
and the training rule regarding the invitation to receive gifts, stated as: "With cakes or with flour-cakes"; and the term "requisite."
And the training rule on the invitation regarding requisites for the four-month period; "fire" refers to the training rule on kindling a fire;
"jewel" refers to the training rule on jewels; "needle... up to... of the Sugata" refers to the seven training rules beginning with the needle-case;
and "the training rule on requesting another" refers to the training rule stated as "one should request another," as well as the exchange of goods for something else.
And there is the training rule stated as: “Having exchanged one thing, she should exchange for another. Two are stated regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha:

the two training rules stated as “She should exchange with what belongs to the Saṅgha for something else,” and “She should exchange by means of a request with what belongs to the Saṅgha for something else.
Two are regarding what belongs to a group: “She should exchange with what belongs to a group for something else,” and “She should exchange by means of a request with what belongs to a group...”
And the two training rules stated as: "If one should have another [article] bartered for. 376. Likewise, the single training rule stated as:
"If one should have another [article] bartered for using what belongs to an individual obtained through begging," namely:
"the training rule on bartering for a heavy cloak" (*garupāvuraṇa*) and "the training rule on bartering for a light cloak" (*lahu*).
The word division is: “vighāsā udasāṭi cā. There are two *vighāsa* rules: the two training rules on *vighāsa* stated thus:
“If one should throw away or cause to be thrown away excrement, urine, rubbish, or *vighāsa*, either beyond a wall or beyond a fence;
or if one should throw away or cause to be thrown away [these things] upon green crops. And “udasāṭi cā” means the training rule on the water-spread (*udakasāṭika*).
Likewise, "the ascetic’s robe" refers to the training rule stated as, "one should give an ascetic’s robe.

Thus, these forty-nine rules were established by the Blessed One, who sees the end of suffering; they have six origins, and exactly like the rule on matchmaking (*sañcaritta*), they are made identical with and permitted by the rule on matchmaking—this is the construction.
This concludes the commentary on the origin of the rule on matchmaking.

378. "Schism in the Saṅgha" refers to the training rule on schism in the Saṅgha. "Following the schism, abusive speech, and corrupting families" refers to the training rules on following a schism, abusive speech, and corrupting families.
"Concealing a grave offense" refers to the training rule on concealing a grave offense. "Wrong view" refers to the training rule on not relinquishing wrong view.
"The two regarding giving consent and loud laughter" refers to the training rule on going [to a meal] without having given consent, and [the rule on] laughing loudly within an inhabited area.
And the two training rules concerning walking and sitting (379).
"Speaking softly, two have been stated" refers to the two training rules stated as: "I shall walk with soft voice in inhabited areas" and "I shall sit with soft voice.
"Not speaking" refers to the training rule stated as: "I shall not speak with food in my mouth."

“On the ground,” “on a low seat,” and “standing” refer to the training rule stated as: “having sat on the ground, having sat on a low seat, [one should not preach] while standing to one who is seated.
And “from behind along a by-path” refers to the two training rules stated as: “walking behind one who is walking in front, and walking along a by-path to one who is walking on the main path.”

380. "Concealing a fault" refers to the training rule concerning the concealment of a fault (*vajjacchādana*). "And following [one who has been suspended]" refers to the training rule concerning following one who has been suspended (*ukkhittānuvattana*).
"Taking hold" refers to the training rule stating, "or should consent to taking hold of the hand.

"And should reinstate" refers to the training rule stating, "should reinstate [the person] without having obtained the permission of the Sangha that performed the act and without knowing the will of the group. "I renounce" means...
"And the training" refers to the training rule stated as: "I renounce the Buddha. Likewise, "in some particular matter" refers to the training rule stated as:
"having been censured in some particular legal issue.
381. "And two on intimate association" refers to: "if nuns indeed live in intimate association," and "whichever nun..."
The two training rules stated in reference to the words beginning with, "Venerable lady, you should dwell in association," and so forth;
and the training rule stated as, "Having struck [herself]," meaning "she should weep, having struck herself again and again";
and the training rule stated as, "Having unfastened a bhikkhunī’s robe, or having had it unfastened"; and "afflicted."
And the training rule stated as: “A co-resident who is suffering”; and again, the training rule on socializing stated as:
“She should live in social association with a householder or a householder’s son”;
and “nor should she settle it,” meaning: when being addressed thus, “Come, Venerable One, settle this legal issue,” she says, “Very well.”
And the training rule stated: "Having given her consent, if she subsequently encounters no obstacle, she must not fail to settle [the matter].
(382) And the training rule stated: "Knowing that a monastery has monks, one should not enter it without having asked permission.
Likewise, the training rule stated: "One should not invite [criticism] from both Saṅghas in three ways."
Likewise, "every half-month" refers to the training rule stated thus: "Every half-month, two matters must be expected by a bhikkhunī from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

"Two co-residents" refers to the two training rules stated thus: "Having ordained a co-resident, one should not fail to support her for two years," and "Having ordained a co-resident, one should not fail to have her dismissed."
383–4. And the training rule stated thus: "If you, noble lady, will give me a robe, I will ordain you";
and the training rule stated thus: "If you, noble lady, will follow me for two years, I will ordain you. These were proclaimed by the peerless Buddha.
The construction is as follows: all thirty-seven factors, beginning with body and speech—that is, from body, speech, and mind—are made to have a single origin;
they may be "formulated by admonition" (*samanubhāsana*), meaning they may be similar to the training rule on admonition (*samanubhāsana-sikkhāpada*) in terms of their origin (*samuṭṭhāna*).
This concludes the commentary on the origin of the rule on admonition.
385. "And the three *kathina* [cases]" refers to the first three training rules stated as: "When a robe has been finished and the *kathina* has been removed by a monk.
"The bowl" refers to the training rule stated as: "An extra bowl may be kept for at most ten days. "And medicine itself" refers to the training rule stated as:
"Medicines that are to be taken within a day. "And the urgent [case] also" refers to...
And the training rule on haste (*accekasikkhāpada*). "With apprehension" refers to the training rule on apprehension immediately following that.
"The two rules on departing" refers to the two training rules stated in the Chapter on Plants (*Bhūtagāmavagga*) beginning with: "While departing, one should not lift it [the bowl]. 386.
"Having likewise gone to the dwelling place" refers to: "Having approached the nuns' dwelling place, one should exhort the nuns."
And the training rule concerning eating in succession: this refers to the training rule stated as, "In eating in succession, there is an offense of expiation.
And the training rule concerning what is not left over: this refers to the training rule stated as, "If one eats fresh or cooked food that is not left over...

And the training rule concerning being invited with a meal: this refers to the training rule stated as, "Being invited and having accepted a meal... And likewise regarding the assignment [of robes]: this refers to the robe...
And the training rule stated as “having assigned [the robe]”; 387.
And the training rule stated as “of a king,” namely “of a kṣatriya king”; and the training rule stated as “at an improper time,” namely “one should enter a village at an improper time”;
and the training rule stated as “instructing,” namely “standing in a manner that is instructive”; and [the training rule] regarding “in the forest.”
The word division is: *ussayavādikā*. Regarding *āraññake*: it refers to the training rule stated as, "In such forest dwellings (*āraññaka* seats), without having previously made an announcement.
Regarding *ussayavādikā*: it refers to the training rule stated as, "One should not live as a litigant (*ussayavādikā*). Regarding *pattasannicayañceva*:
it refers to the training rule stated as, "One should not make a hoard of bowls (*pattasannicaya*). [The words] *pure*, *pacchā*,...

“Vikāla” refers to the triad of training rules stated as: “Whatever bhikkhunī, having approached families before the meal,” “having approached families after the meal,” and “having approached families at an improper time.
(388–9) “Pañcāhika” refers to the training rule stated as: “Should she exceed the five-day limit for the distribution of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).”

"Saṅkamanī" refers to the training rule stated as: "One should wear [a robe] that is to be exchanged. Likewise, "the two rules concerning lodgings" refers to the two training rules stated together with the lodging:
"One should not use a lodging-robe without having relinquished it," and "One should not set out on a journey without having relinquished the lodging.
"Pasākha" refers to a boil born in the groin...

And the training rule stated as "or" [is also included]. Regarding "on a seat," this refers to the training rule stated as "she should sit on a seat in front of a bhikkhu without having asked permission.
Now, these twenty-nine rules arise from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; thus, all of them have two origins.
Consequently, because they arise from the *kathina* (formal robe-making ceremony), they are "originated by *kathina*"; such is the construction of the meaning.
Commentary on the Origin of the Kathina Rules. 390.
“Two on beds” refers to the two training rules concerning sleeping together. “And with feet crossed” refers to the training rule concerning having the feet crossed.
“And alms” refers to the training rule concerning eating at a public rest-house. “Eating in a group” refers to the training rule concerning eating in a group.

“Improper time” refers to the training rule concerning eating at improper times (*vikālabhojana-sikkhāpada*). “And stored food” refers to the training rule concerning the storage of food (*sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada*).
“Tooth-sticks” refers to the training rule concerning tooth-sticks (*dantapona-sikkhāpada*). “Naked ascetics” refers to the training rule concerning naked ascetics (*acelaka-sikkhāpada*).
391. “And an army” refers to the training rule stated as: “One should not go to see an army on campaign. “Should stay…” [and so forth].
The word division is *uyyodhiṃ*. “*Vase*” refers to the training rule stated as: “One should not stay with an army. “*Uyyodhin*” refers to the training rule stated as:
“One should not go to a battle... or to see a military review. “*Surā*” refers to the training rule concerning the drinking of fermented liquor.
“*Orena nhāyanan*” refers to the training rule concerning bathing more than once every half-month. “*Dubbaṇṇakaraṇañceva*” [refers to] the three... [of robes].

And the training rule stated as "for making [oneself] ugly. And the two *pāṭidesanīya*s means the remaining two *pāṭidesanīya* rules that have been stated. 392. "Garlic" refers to the training rule concerning garlic.
"Should wait upon" refers to the training rule stated as "one should wait upon a bhikkhu while he is eating with water or a fan. And "the seeing of dancing" alone... [refers to] "dancing..."
And the training rule stated: "One should not go to see singing, dancing, or instrumental music.
And the training rule stated: "One should not bathe naked. And the training rule stated: "They should not lie down on the same covering or cloak.
And the training rule stated: "They should not lie down on the same bed. And within the kingdom...

And the training rule stated as: “In a region within the kingdom that is considered dangerous”; likewise, “outside” refers to the training rule stated as: “In a region outside the kingdom that is considered dangerous.
(393) “During the rains” refers to the training rule stated as: “One should not go on a journey during the rains. “A palace” refers to the training rule stated as:
“One should not go to see a royal palace or a pleasure house... or a lotus pond. “A high couch” refers to... [the training rule].
And the training rule stated as: “One should use a high couch or a long chair.
And the training rule stated as: “One should spin thread. And the training rule stated as: “One should perform services for householders. And with one’s own hand:
“To a householder, or a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, [one should give] fresh food with one’s own hand...”
And the training rule stated as: “or one should give solid food or soft food”; and the training rule stated as:
“one should spend the rains residence in a monastery where no bhikkhus are present.
394. And the training rule stated as: “one should carry a sunshade and sandals”; and the training rule stated as: “one should travel by means of a vehicle.”
And the training rule concerning the waist-band: "She shall not wear a waist-band"—this is the training rule so stated. And the training rule concerning ornaments:
"She shall not wear female ornaments"—this is the training rule so stated. And the two training rules concerning perfumes and scents:
"She shall not bathe with perfumes and cosmetics" and "She shall not bathe with scented oil"—these are the two training rules so stated. "A bhikkhunī... [down to] ...a householder woman."
By this [phrase], the four training rules beginning with "she should have herself massaged by a bhikkhunī" are stated.
Likewise, there is the training rule stated as "she should enter a village without a saṃkaccikā.
These forty-three rules, however, all originate from both body and mind (dvisamuṭṭhānika). They originate from wool (*eḷakaloma*).
The construction is: "they are equal.
This concludes the commentary on the origin of the offense regarding sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma). 396–7.
Regarding the phrase "except" (*aññatra*): "If one should teach the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words, except in the presence of a person who understands..."
And the training rule stated as: "By means of a male form. And "If not authorized" refers to the training rule stated as: "A bhikkhu who is not authorized should exhort bhikkhunīs.
Likewise, "and when [the sun] has set" refers to the training rule stated as: "He should exhort bhikkhunīs when the sun has set.
Two types of "animal sciences" (tiracchānavijjā) have been mentioned: "He should master an animal science..."

And the two training rules stated as "he should recite [the Dhamma]," and the training rule stated as "he should ask a question of a monk who has not given leave"—these six rules have two origins: they originate from speech and from speech-mind.
This is their similarity to the *padasodhamma* (recitation of words).

The construction is: "the state of similarity by way of the rule concerning traveling together" (*padasodhamma-sadisa-bhāvo*). This concludes the commentary on the origin of the rule concerning traveling together (*padasodhamma-samutthāna-vaṇṇanā*). 398–9.
"One" refers to the training rule stated as: "If one should set out on a journey together with a bhikkhunī after making an appointment."
And [the offense of] a boat: the training rule stated as, "One should not board a single boat. And "delicacies":
the training rule stated as, "If one who is not ill should, for one's own sake, request and eat delicacies. And "arrangement":
the training rule regarding traveling in arrangement with a woman. "Has removed": "one should have hair removed from a private part."
And the training rule concerning what has been spoken of. "Grain" refers to the training rule stating, "Having requested raw grain.
"And being invited" refers to the training rule stating, "If one who has been invited or has been offered food should eat or consume fresh or cooked food.
The "eight offenses entailing confession" (pāṭidesanīya) are the eight offenses entailing confession prescribed for bhikkhunīs.
And these fourteen training rules (sikkhā) prescribed by the Best of Buddhas arise from four origins—namely, from body, from body and speech, from body and mind, and from speech and mind.
The construction [of the sentence] is: "It is considered that, according to their origin, they are equal to the training rule concerning the journey (addhāna-sikkhāpada) by way of the journey."

Commentary on the Origin by Way of Traveling (Addhānasamuṭṭhāna). 400–1. "Eavesdropping" refers to the training rule concerning standing to eavesdrop. "Requesting rice soup, etc. refers to the training rule concerning requesting rice soup and boiled rice.
"In the dark" refers to the training rule stated as "in the darkness of night without a lamp. And likewise, "in a concealed place" [refers to the same].
The training rule stated as “in a concealed place”; the training rule stated as “in the open air with a man”;

and the training rule that follows immediately after that, which comes down as “on a carriage road, or in a street, or at a crossroads, with a man”—all these six were taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.

The construction is as follows: mental factors arising from the fourth and sixth [bases], or from body and mind, or from body, speech, and mind, may have the same origin as those originating from a caravan of thieves, according to the training rule concerning caravans of thieves (*theyyasattha-sikkhāpada*).
This concludes the commentary on the origin of caravans of thieves.

402. "With a sunshade, with a staff, or even with a sword" refers to the two training rules stated as: "Not [to eat] while holding a sunshade in one's hand" and "not while holding a staff in one's hand.
"With a weapon or with arms" refers to the two training rules stated as: "Not [to eat] while holding a weapon in one's hand" and "not while holding arms in one's hand.
"Shoes, sandals, or a vehicle" refers to the three training rules stated as: "Not [to eat] while wearing shoes," "not while wearing sandals," and "not while riding in a vehicle."
“Lying down” and “sitting cross-legged” refer to the two training rules stated as: “not [to eat] while lying down” and “not [to eat] while sitting cross-legged.
403. “With head wrapped” and “with head covered” refer to the two training rules stated as: “not [to eat] with the head wrapped” and “not [to eat] with the head covered.
Thus, all eleven rules indicated here arise from a single origin, namely, that which is designated as speech and mind.
The construction is: "perceived as arising from the teaching of the Dhamma" and "observed.
This concludes the commentary on arising from the teaching of the Dhamma. 404.
Thus, first, mixed arising should be understood; fixed arising is threefold, and that belongs to a single [type] alone.
Regarding the phrase "it pertains to a training rule," he says "and that which concerns the reporting of what has occurred" and so forth, in order to show it separately.

"And that which concerns the reporting of what has occurred" refers to the training rule on reporting what has occurred, which arises from three types of offenses originating unintentionally (*acittaka*).
"And also that which concerns the instigating of thieves" refers to the training rule on instigating thieves, which arises from two types: from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

"Merely unpermitted" means simply that which is not permitted. "Merely unpermitted" refers to the training rule on what is unpermitted as it arises from four origins: from speech, from body and speech, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
"These three" refers to this triad of training rules. "Unmixed" means having an origin that is not commingled with any other training rule.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the origins [of offenses], the first part of the *Līnatthappakāsinī* sub-commentary.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Origins of Offenses.
405. It incurs [offenses] by means of the first originative factor, which is reckoned as bodily action.
406–7. Regarding the phrase "dukkaṭa, etc.," the word "etc. includes thullaccaya and saṅghādisesa. As it has been said: "In the preliminary effort there is dukkaṭa;
when even a single morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya; when that morsel has arrived, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa."
"But at the wrong time, it is an offense of expiation" means: an offense of expiation for eating at the wrong time. "From the hand of one not related" means:

from the hand of a nun who has entered among the houses of the laity and is not a blood relative. "Having taken" means: having received with one's own hand either solid food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*).
The word-division is: "These five are offenses."
408. "By the second" means by the origination consisting of speech.
409–10. "If he commands or speaks": "in every way ruined" means a place that has been ruined in all its aspects, such as by not having the site formally designated (*adesitavatthuka*) and so forth.
"A hut" means a hut built by personal solicitation (*saññācikā*). As it is said in the *Parivāra*: "They build a hut for him..."
“[A hut] whose site has not been approved, which exceeds the proper measure, where harm is likely to arise, and which lacks space on all sides.
It is stated thus because it is the root source from which that *pācittiya* offense originates; and here, the instrumental case (*mūlena*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*).
411. "By the third origination" means by the origination consisting of body and speech.
412. "Having made an agreement" means having deliberated together; the meaning is: having consulted with others, [thinking] "let us build a hut. 413.
"Having spoken" means having requested it for one's own sake. "A bhikkhunī" refers to one who stands in the place where the bhikkhus eat.
“Having told the lay followers, ‘Give soup here, give rice there,’ [and] causing them to give while she is being complacent—‘not having restrained’ means:
the construction is that she eats without having dissuaded them by saying, ‘Sister, step back for as long as the monks are eating. 414.
The construction is: how many offenses might there be through the fourth [offense], which originates from body and mind?”
417. "By the fifth" means by that which originates from speech and mind. "They speak" means speaking while engaging in discourse. 418. "A hut" (*kuṭi*) is mentioned merely as an illustration;

it should be understood that even a dwelling place (*senāsana*)—one where no site has been formally designated, which exceeds the proper dimensions, involves harm to living beings, and lacks space for circumambulation—is included in this prohibition.

419. Regarding the phrase "recites the Dhamma word by word," the term "one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*) is to be supplied as the object. As it is said: "A bhikkhu, perceiving something as improper..."

“He teaches the Dhamma word by word to one who is not fully ordained. Regarding “speaking out of a desire for sport”: this refers to speaking with the intention of playing using grounds for abuse such as birth and so forth.
The term *davakamyatā* is an expression formed by the elision of the letter *ya*, as in the case of [phrases like] “having reflected thoroughly” (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*).
420. By the sixth [factor], which originates from body, speech, and mind. “Having made an appointment” (*saṃvidahitvāna*) means having arranged it, [thinking] “you and I...”
Having made an agreement, saying, "We shall take [it] from one side," if he says, "You take one heavy load, I will take this," and then causes him to move from that place, [he is guilty]. 423.

Herein, in this teaching (*sāsane*). Regarding the phrase "the supreme resolution of doubt" (*vimatūparamaṃ paramaṃ*), it refers to [the inquiry]: "Is this allowable (*kappiya*) or not allowable (*akappiya*)?"
Or, doubt (*vimati*) is the wavering that occurs in various ways, such as the manner of "Is this an offense or not an offense? or "Is this the Dhamma or not the Dhamma?
It is called "the cessation of doubt" (*vimatūparamaṃ*) because it brings doubt to rest and destroys it.

It is "supreme" (*paramaṃ*), meaning most excellent. It is "superior" (*uttaraṃ*) by virtue of its status as the answer to the questions concerning the determinations of the introductions (*nidāna*) and so forth found in the *Vibhaṅga* and *Khandhaka*.

Because it is established, it is "superior" (*uttara*). This treatise called "The Superior" (*Uttara*) is that which one "crosses over" (*uttarati*) by means of wisdom, having plunged into it and brought it to completion.
Here, in the two-word phrase "the superior, the superior," one should be understood as indicating a quality and the other as indicating a weapon.
The connection is: "That person, endowed with a good method (*sunaya*), crosses over the Vinaya Piṭaka. To show what kind [of person], he says:

“*Sunaya*,” etc. It is *sunaya* because it contains herein the methods of formal rule (*paññatti*) and non-rule (*anupaññatti*), as well as the distinctions of strengthening or loosening the observance of what is permitted and what is prohibited;
that [is *sunaya*]. Or, it is *sunaya* because by means of it the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) is properly led forth; thus it is the higher determination (*uttaravinicchaya*).

One who is “connected with” (*saṃyutta*) or endowed with that is one possessed of the understanding of the legal determination. It is “difficult to cross” (*duttara*) because it is crossed over with difficulty. This is due to its being an illuminator of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
Because it serves as the foundation for attaining the "higher" (uttara), which consists of concentration, wisdom, and Nibbāna, one "crosses over the higher" (uttarati);
the meaning is that, having plunged in, one reaches the ultimate end.
Here, one who crosses over this treatise called *Vimativinodanī*, the supreme and highest "Higher" (*Uttara*), is one who is endowed with the excellent method (*sunaya*).
The construction is: "That person crosses over the difficult-to-cross, excellent Vinaya, which is a good method.
By the word *ca* (and), in the sense of including other teachers' views, he illuminates this meaning as follows:

namely, here, whoever crosses over the difficult-to-cross, excellent Vinaya, which is a good method—that person, being endowed with the good method, crosses over the treatise named *Uttara*, which is the supreme, excellent crossing that brings an end to doubt.

By this it should be understood that the extreme utility of the *Uttarapakaraṇa* for knowing the Vinaya Piṭaka has been demonstrated: "He who knows the *Uttara* knows the Vinaya; he who knows the Vinaya knows the *Uttara*.
Thus ends the *Līnatthapakāsanī* on the *Uttara*.
The commentary on the discussion of the origins of offenses is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the method of single-increment (ekuttara): 424.

"From here onwards" means after the discussion on the determination of origins. "Onwards" (para) means further. "Single-increment method" (ekuttara-naya) refers to the method beginning with the ones, twos, and so forth, which is designated as "single-increment" because each successive category exceeds the previous by one factor.
425–7. *Ke āpattikarā dhammā*... *kā cādesanagāminī*: the meaning is already clear by way of each individual question. 428. *Samuṭṭhānāni*:

this refers to the subsequent discourse consisting of the answers, beginning with that term. Therein, regarding *samuṭṭhānāni*... they are "explained" because it is by means of these that a person commits (*karoti*) and incurs (*āpajjati*) an offense;
therefore, they are called "offense-makers" (*āpattikarā*). 429. *Tattha*: in those offenses. *Lahukā*: they are "light" because they are purified by a light disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*).
An offense of *saṅghādisesa* is called a "grave offense" because it is purified by a formal act of the Saṅgha (*vinayakamma*) that is grave;
likewise, an offense of *pārājika* is called grave because it is impossible to bring it to the state of being non-offensive in any way.
However, since those [grave offenses] can be understood by implication when the light offenses are stated, they are not mentioned separately in the response.

431. It is called *duṭṭhulla* because it goes toward (*ulati*) a state that is corrupt (*duṭṭha*), vile, extremely disgusting, and censurable; that is, the offenses of *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*. Therefore he said:

"The offense is twofold from the beginning. 432. "Connected with the five deeds of immediate retribution" refers to the *pārājika* offense involving a human being committed by those who have killed their mother, father, or an arahant, as well as the unwholesome volition—consisting of activity through the doors of body and speech—which is the cause for the incapacity of those who shed blood [of an arahant] or cause a schism in the Saṅgha.
Because they are the cause for rebirth in the states of misery immediately after [death], these five are called "connected with the immediate" (*anantara-saṃyutta*).
Furthermore, because they are included among those fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), they are described as "fixed" (*niyata*).
In the *Parivāra*, however, many other single-item groups are shown, such as the "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) and so forth; these were presented for the benefit of people who fear voluminous texts.
These have not been shown here by the Teacher; they should be understood by those who seek [the truth] through the very fact that they are surrounded [by these offenses].
And herein, even the seven classes of offenses, when intentionally transgressed, create obstacles to heaven and obstacles to liberation; thus they are called "obstructive.
However, an offense that is a violation of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajjāpatti*), when transgressed unknowingly, creates neither an obstacle to heaven nor an obstacle to liberation.

It is unobstructive. Even for one who has committed an obstructive offense, once they have confessed it so that it leads to confession, and having emerged from it so that it leads to emergence, and has attained purity—whether remaining on the level of a novice (sāmaṇera) or otherwise—the path to heaven and the path to liberation are not barred.
This concludes the commentary on the section on the single [offense].
435. One "deficient in age" is one less than twenty years old. One "deficient in limbs" refers to those such as those with severed hands and so forth.
One "deficient in subject matter" refers to a paṇḍaka, an animal, and a hermaphrodite.

The remaining eight, beginning with those living in communion through theft, have reached a state of incapacity and are called "doers of wrong-doing"; by their own action of wrong-doing within this very existence—
The meaning is: one who has reached an impossible state. "Incomplete" means one whose bowl and robes are incomplete. "Does not ask" means he does not ask for full ordination (*upasampadā*).
"Prohibited" means forbidden by such statements as, "Two persons should not be ordained," and so forth.

436. *Hava* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis. The construction is as follows: "For a monk who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), there is indeed an offense described; for one who has not attained absorption, there is likewise an offense described. Thus, it is applied.

437. *Bhūtassa* means of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) existing within oneself. *Abhūtārocanāpatti* means an offense of the fourth *pārājika*. The construction is: "one points out [it] to one who has not attained [that state]. 438.
In such passages as “*Atthi saddhammasaṃyuttā*,” the word *atthi* (is) should be construed individually with each of the singular case endings. 439.
Regarding the phrase “*padasodhammamūlādī*,” by the word *ādi* (etcetera), there is the inclusion of offenses such as “teaching the Dhamma in more than five or six words.”
"Enjoyment" (bhogeti) means using for one's own personal use. The phrase "connected with one's own requisites" is merely an illustration.

Improper uses, such as "the relinquishing of bowl and robe," "the washing of soiled robes," and "the cleaning of a bowl stained by grime," and so forth, as well as the offenses associated with them, are likewise connected with one's own requisites.

441. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "beds, chairs, etc.," items such as cushions (*bhisi*) and so forth are included. "And also when spread out in the open air" means when it has been spread out or caused to be spread out in the open air.
"Going without asking permission" means going without having asked permission;
by the word "or" (*vā*), going without having had [the items] removed or caused to be removed is also included. "Connected with what belongs to others" means being tied to the requisites of another.
443. Regarding the phrase “sikharaṇīsī”: the construction is that for one who speaks a true statement [of this kind], it may constitute a Saṅghādisesa offense of grave and indecent speech. 445.

“A grave offense” refers to an offense of defeat (pārājika) concerning a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma). “In the case of reporting what is real” means in the case of reporting to one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) a superhuman state that is real.
“Speaking the truth” means speaking a true statement. “Light” refers to an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

447. "To disturb" means to disturb by means of acting in a faction. "Leaving the hand’s reach" means leaving the hand’s reach within the boundary itself; the meaning is that having left the hand’s reach, one sits to one side. "Touches" means one who has gone to the ground would touch. 448. The construction is:
"One who sits down upon a bed or a bench with legs that strike [the floor] while above a lofted hut (vehāsakuṭi) incurs an offense while situated in the air (vehāsagata).
If one were to sit down after having arranged it on the ground, one would not incur an offense. Therefore it is said: "not from the ground."
449. "Entering" means entering the monastery (*ārāma*). "Going out" means going out from that very place. "That" refers to the monastery. 450.

"Without fulfilling the proper conduct" means without performing the duty of removing the sunshade from the head and the duty of taking off the sandals from the feet. Even if one goes out while carrying the sunshade and sandals, one does not incur an offense.
451. "Going out" is a synonym for the word "departing. "And not entering" means that one would not incur an offense while entering the same monastery toward which one had previously gone.
453. The construction is: "Whatever nun undertakes an excessively deep water-cleansing [bath] incurs an offense.
457. Regarding "but his own duty": the construction is that he is said to incur [an offense] even while not undertaking that duty of final liberation prescribed for himself. 460.
Of the other teacher, and likewise of the student (saddhivihārika).
462. "Giving" means giving without exchange.
463. "Soft" means having soft buttocks. The phrase is "lambī-ādino"; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), it includes:
"for one who, having exerted himself with the hand, emits semen; for one who thrusts the penis with the thigh; for one who, while weeping, strikes himself again and again..."
This includes such statements as, “It is an offense for a bhikkhunī,” and so forth. Regarding the term *atta* (self):

here, it should be understood according to the rules of Pali grammar (*niruttilakkhaṇa*) that the words *nissita* (dependent) and the case ending have been elided. *Sesa* (the rest) refers to the offenses mentioned in connection with sexual intercourse, bodily contact, giving blows, and so on.
*Paranissita* (dependent on another) means that which is to be committed in dependence upon another.
465. Because of the statement, “Monks, the exhortation (ovāda) must not be disregarded,” one who does not accept or receive the exhortation incurs an offense of wrong-doing (vajja).
470. *Aruṇugga* means at the rising of the sun. *Naaruṇuggama* means at a time other than the rising of the sun. 471. The construction is as follows:
“exceeding one night,” “exceeding six nights,” “exceeding seven days,” and “exceeding ten days. By the word *ādi* (and so forth),...
This is the summary of the [offenses] beginning with the month. Regarding the phrase "the offense stated": in all cases, this refers to the offense of *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
The word-division is: “he incurs [it] at the rising of the dawn. 473.

For one who cuts trees, creepers, and so forth belonging to another with intent to steal, there is a *pārājika* offense; for one who cuts them [without such intent], there is merely a *pācittiya*. Therefore, it is said: “One who cuts living plants (*bhūtagāma*) incurs both a *pārājika* and a *pācittiya*.”
475. Regarding the phrase "but while concealing," the words "what offense? are to be supplied. To this he says: "A man who conceals an offense incurs [an offense].

"One whose [robe] has been taken away" means one whose robe has been snatched away. "Not concealing" means not covering his own sense of shame and modesty with anything whatsoever—such as grass, leaves, or a broken branch. As it is said: "Having covered [it] with grass or leaves..."
“One should come, but one must not come naked. Whoever should come [naked], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). 476.

Regarding the phrase “grass-cloth and so forth,” by the word “and so forth” (ādi), the inclusion of the sectarian banners such as bark-cloth, wooden-plate clothing, and others is intended. The ellipsis is “someone who wears [them] incurs [an offense]. In this regard, it says: “One who wears grass-cloth and so forth, for every instance of wearing them, incurs [an offense]. 477.
As for the bowl that has been relinquished and given back with the words, “This bowl, monk, is to be kept by you until it breaks,”...

If one does not handle it with care, one becomes full of hatred and incurs an offense. Regarding the pair on "with mind" and "without mind," the pair on "perception" and "liberation" follows in sequence;
thus he said, "the pair on with mind," and so forth. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the pairs.
478. The offense that exists while the Lord is still present, but not when he has attained final nibbāna—that offense exists.

The offense that exists when the Lord has attained final nibbāna, but not while he is still present—that offense also exists. The construction is: the offense that exists both while the Lord is still present and when he has attained final nibbāna—that offense exists.

479. "What is that? he asked, and replied: "The offense of causing the shedding of blood," and so forth. Regarding this, concerning the addressing of an elder with the term "friend" (*āyuṣmān*) when he has attained final Nibbāna, [the Buddha said]:

"Ānanda, just as monks nowadays address one another with the term 'friend,' it should not be addressed in such a manner after my passing... [and so on]... a junior monk [should not address] a more senior monk..."

"Because of the statement, 'He should be addressed as "Venerable Sir" (bhante) or "Venerable" (āyasmā),' one incurs an offense for addressing a Thera with the term 'friend' (āvuso) only after the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, not while he is still present; this is the meaning. 481. [The following concerns] the questions:

How can there be an offense only at the proper time (kāla), and not at the improper time (vikāla)? How can there be an offense only at the improper time, and not at the proper time? How can there be an offense in both cases—both at the proper time and at the improper time?
482. Answering in due order, he says “while eating,” and so forth.
483. The construction is as follows: one incurs all the remaining offenses both at the proper time and at the improper time, and there is no doubt in that regard.

484. To show the triad mentioned as: “There is an offense incurred at night, not by day; there is an offense incurred by day, not at night; there is an offense incurred both at night and by day,” he says “only at night,” and so forth.

486. There is an offense that one who has ten years of seniority incurs, but not one who has less than ten years; how can that be? There is an offense that one who has less than ten years incurs, but not one who has ten years;
how does that come about? There is an offense that both one who has ten years and one who has less than ten years incur;
how does the offense come about in both cases? This is the construction [of the meaning].
487. Regarding this, he states the answer beginning with “he establishes,” and so forth. For the explanatory word for “a fool” (bāla) is “one who is incompetent” (abyatta). 488.
One who is less than ten years [of standing] thus gathers a following, thinking, “I am wise”; such is the construction, meaning that he likewise incurs an offense.

The phrase is to be analyzed as “less than ten years” (dasavasso ūno). Both of these—the one who is ten years [of standing] and the one who is less than ten years—[are subject to the offense] from the act of establishing a following.
The construction is: "one incurs another offense. And here, although one should say "āpajjante," the letter *na* has been elided for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse. 489.

How does one incur an offense during the dark fortnight (*kāḷa*) and not during the bright fortnight (*juṇha*), how does one incur an offense during the bright fortnight and not during the dark fortnight, and how does one incur it in both—the dark and the bright?

Such is the construction. 490. He states the answer beginning with "vassaṃ" and so forth. The word division is: "āpajjate appavārento" (one who incurs [it] while not inviting [the rains retreat]). "Juṇhe" refers to the first half of the month; "kāḷake" refers to the second half of the month.

491. "By one who is without failure" means it was prescribed by the Blessed One because he is free from the four kinds of failure. "The remainder" refers to all other offenses remaining after those arising from not entering the rains residence and those arising from the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).

492. Entering the rains residence is permissible during the dark fortnight (*kāḷa*), but not permissible during the bright fortnight (*juṇha*); the invitation ceremony is permissible during the bright fortnight, but not permissible during the dark fortnight. The application is as follows: all other permitted business of the Saṅgha is permissible both during the dark fortnight and the bright fortnight; thus, it is permissible in both cases.
493. There is an offense in the winter season; there is no offense in the other two seasons reckoned as summer and the rainy season.

There is an offense only in the summer season, not in the remaining ones reckoned as the rainy and winter seasons. There is an offense in the rainy season, but not in the other two reckoned as winter and summer—this is the construction [of the meaning].
Regarding the question, "What are those three kinds of offenses?", it says: "On the day when the first of the month has been declared," and so forth.

Therein, the construction is as follows: if one wears that *vassasāṭika* robe—which was set aside and assigned on the first day of the dark fortnight following the full moon of the later *Kattika*—during the winter, one incurs an offense in the winter. Thus it should be understood.
Regarding the word *pacchima* (last): here, although the context calls for a genitive case, the locative is used.

On whichever full-moon day of the last month of Kattika the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*) is to be relinquished, if one does not relinquish it on that very day but instead lets the dawn rise on the first day of the new moon (*pāṭipada*), one incurs an offense due to non-relinquishment only during the winter season; as for the others...
The construction is as follows: “It is not an offense during the two seasons of summer and the rains,” as indicated in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*.
Because this statement from the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* does not contradict the canonical text which says, “I allow you, monks, to determine the use of a rain-cloak for four months of the rainy season;
beyond that, it must be assigned [to another],” the *Samantapāsādikā* states, “That too is well-said.”
Because it has been stated thus, it should be understood that both meanings apply to the expression "he incurs [the offense] in the winter.

497. In the summer season (*gimhika-utu*) connected with the months of summer. Since "exceeding by a month" means "more than a month," it should be said that the remaining time is "exceeding by a month" (*atirekamāsa*).
"Seeking" means from a place where one is not related or not invited, by means of causing the thought [of the offense] to arise.
One who seeks a rain-bathing robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) while there is still more than one month remaining [of the rainy season], and one who wears it during the summer, incurs an offense.
The phrase “but not so in the other two seasons” (*na tu eva itarautudvaye*) is the word-division. One who seeks it during the summer incurs [the offense] by making it three months prior;
one who wears it incurs [the offense] by making it the three months of summer plus an additional half-month. Without doubt, [this applies to] “of the summers” (*gimhānaṃ*).
As for the statement, "In the seven months prior to the last month," that is incorrect,
because it is shown that the offense occurs only in the summer season (*gimhāna*), and because it is prohibited [from occurring] in the other two seasons. And here,
having taken the mention of the offense regarding seeking [robes] in the verse as merely illustrative, the offense regarding wearing [robes] is also shown, since it can only arise in the summer.

498. Furthermore, in this teaching, the construction is as follows: if a bhikkhu, while possessing a rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*), lets his body be rained upon while naked, he certainly incurs an offense during the rains, that is, in the rainy season. 499. Regarding the triad stated thus:
“There is an offense incurred by the Saṅgha, not by a group (*gaṇa*) nor by an individual (*puggala*); there is an offense incurred by a group, not by the Saṅgha nor by an individual;
there is an offense incurred by an individual, not by the Saṅgha nor by a group.”
To demonstrate this, he said: "For the Saṅgha incurs [an offense]," and so forth.
To explain how it is incurred, he said: "The formal act (adhiṭṭhāna)," and so forth. The connection is: "performing the *adhiṭṭhāna*-uposatha or the *pārisuddhi*-uposatha.
Here, it refers to performing the uposatha without having first performed one's own uposatha according to the specific offense incurred.

Because the intention here is to show the offenses that are to be incurred, and because the faults of acting for oneself will be explained individually later on, the application of the phrase "neither a group nor an individual" should be understood according to what is appropriate:
namely, that neither does an individual who makes a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) incur [the offense], nor does a group who performs the *pārisuddhi* ceremony.
This is an alternative interpretation based on reversing the sequence, as in: "I shall apply the connection according to the order."
It should not be done. In this way, for the subsequent sections as well, one should apply the appropriate connection according to what is available, having established the opposite of the reverse.
501. The term "Uposatha" should be construed individually with each of the phrases "recitation of the Sutta" and "formal undertaking.
502. Regarding the phrase "or while performing the recitation of the Sutta," the word "or" (vā) here includes "confession of purity" (pārisuddhi). [The recitation of the Sutta...]

The construction is as follows: "When an individual performing the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) or the *uposatha* commits an offense, but the Saṅgha performing the recitation of the Sutta does not commit one, nor does the Gaṇa performing the *pārisuddhi* commit one.

Furthermore, how is it that only one who is ill commits an offense, and not one who is not ill; how is it that only one who is not ill commits an offense, and not one who is ill; and how is it that both—the one who is ill and the one who is not ill—commit an offense? This is the construction.

504. However, the construction is as follows: if one who is not ill but is sick, when another medicine is available, requests a different medicine from that [prescribed] one, he incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya). 505.

Even when no other medicine is available, if one requests medicine while not being ill, one incurs an offense on account of the request, just like one who is not ill. As for the remaining offenses, both the one who is ill and the one who is not ill incur them.

506. There is an offense committed internally, not externally; likewise, there is an offense committed only externally, not internally; and there is an offense committed both internally and externally—this is the construction [of the meaning].
507. The construction is that it is committed only internally.
508. "Beds, etc. refers to beds belonging to the Saṅgha, and so forth.
509. The analysis of the phrase is: “An offense [is committed] only within the boundary.

How does one commit an offense only within the boundary and not commit an offense outside the boundary? How does one commit an offense only outside the boundary and not commit an offense within the boundary?
And how does one commit an offense in both places—both within the boundary and outside the boundary? Such is the construction.

510. "A monk with a sunshade and sandals" refers to a visiting monk who is accompanied by a sunshade and sandals. "Entering while possessing ascetic wealth" refers to one entering the monastery of the Saṅgha without having performed the duties of a visitor (*āgantuka-vatta*).
511. The word-division is: "at the crossing of the precincts" (*upacārassa atikkame*).
512. The construction is as follows: "The remainder of all [the offenses] are incurred both within the boundary (*sīmā*) and outside the boundary. And herein:

Although one incurs the offense of interrupting the rains-residence upon going outside the boundary, and the offense of entering a nunnery’s park while inside the boundary, it should be understood that both of these are included within the same delimitation as the offenses regarding the duties of visitors and those departing;
thus, they are not mentioned separately because they are implied by this very [category]. This should be understood to apply in all such instances everywhere.
The detailed exposition (vinicchaya) should be understood.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Triads (Tikakathāvaṇṇanā). 515.

An offense committed through the door of speech (*vacīdvārika-āpatti*) refers to an offense that is to be incurred through the door of speech by means of lying, slander, backbiting, and so forth. "One is purified by the speech of another" means one is purified by a single formal act of covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka-kamma-vācā*) performed in the midst of the Saṅgha.
516. "A fault is indeed a fault"; the meaning is that it is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*).

518–9. "Having confessed that, one is purified" means being purified after having confessed that. "But up to the third time" refers to an offense of formal meeting (*saṅghādisesa*) committed through the formal act of admonition up to the third time.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "probation and so forth,"...
The procedures of *mānatta*, *mūlāya-paṭikassana*, and *abbhāna* are included.
522. "An offense committed through the door of the body" refers to an offense such as dealing a blow that must be committed by means of the bodily door. 523.
"One is purified by the body alone" means that one is purified by going to a *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over with grass) and restoring bodily harmony.

526. The construction is as follows: "How does one who, while asleep, incurs an offense, become purified once awakened? And how does one who, while already awakened, has incurred an offense, become purified while asleep?
528. "One who lies down with a woman" refers to an offense such as lying down in the same bed with a woman.
529. "While watching" means being awake, dispelling sleep.
531. *Paṭibuddho*: not sleeping. 532. *Acitto*:
"I shall transgress the training rule"—one who lacks such an intention is "without [transgressive] mind. 535. *Sacittakāpattiṃ*:

an offense committed with intentional mind, such as the offense of eating at an improper time. While lying down on a grass mat during a *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering-over-as-if-with-grass) legal procedure, one may fall asleep.
When performing [the act], one who emerges from the offense while devoid of the thought, "By this action I emerge from the offense," is purified without conscious intent (*acittaka*).
Regarding the final two lines:
"Having committed [an offense], being without conscious intent, one is purified while being without conscious intent."
“Having committed [an offense], one who possesses a mind is purified by that very mind.”—these are two lines of verse.

“Without mixing” means without making a mixture in this very way with the terms “without mind” and “with mind. “In this case” refers to the preceding pair of lines. “According to what was stated” means according to the method stated.
“As an official act” means as an act of formal admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*).
540. "Having committed [an offense] without a formal act" means having committed it even without a formal act of censure (*samanubhāsanakamma*).
541. Regarding the phrase "in the censure," he refers to the *saṅghādisesa* offense that is to be committed during the censure by way of figurative designation (*kāraṇūpacāra*).
542. "The remainder" refers to the *pācittiya* offenses for false speech and so forth.
543. "He is purified in the absence" means he is purified in the absence of the Saṅgha.

And this is said with reference to a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) that is settled by both the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) and the *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what has been admitted).

In that case, although there is the presence of the individual, it is called "in the absence" because purification occurs due to the absence of the Saṅgha; thus, one either incurs or is purified [of the offense] in the absence of the Saṅgha.
551. “The tetrad of the mindless” and “the tetrad of the unknowing” are stated by way of the initial term, just like the designations “wholesome triad,” “contact pentad,” and so forth. 552–3.
There is an offense committed by a visitor, but not by the other, the resident; there is an offense committed by the resident alone, but not by the other, the visitor;
there is an offense committed by both the visitor and the resident.
The construction is as follows: "Both incur [the offense], while for the remainder they do not incur it.

(555) "The other" refers to the resident monk (*āvāsika*). "The duty of the residence" (*āvāsavatta*) is the duty that must be performed by the resident toward the guest. "The residents" refers to the resident monks.
(556) "Nor does the guest" means that the guest who fails to perform that duty of the residence does not incur [the offense]; as for the remainder...
An offense pertaining to the doors of body and speech. Both the visitor and the resident [monk] do not incur an offense that is not common to both monks and nuns.
557. "Diversity of the basis" means diversity of transgression. "Diversity of offenses" means the mutual diversity among the seven classes of offenses, beginning with the *pārājika*.

563. “Of the *pārājika* offenses... [etc. ...there is no difference” (*nānabhāvo*)—this is merely an illustration, because for the *saṅghādisesa* offenses and those beginning with the *aniyata*, a difference in the subject matter (*vatthu*) and a difference in the offense (*āpatti*) are both possible.

565. “This is the very same determination” (*vinicchaya*)—it is not only in the case of *pārājika* offenses that this aforementioned determination applies to those who incur common offenses both collectively and individually; rather, it applies by the same method to the remaining common offenses as well.
This is the very same method of analysis that should be applied here.
577. *Ādiyanto* means taking up; *payojento* means causing to take up. 579.
Regarding the phrase "less than a foot... touches lightly," this is said with reference to a *thullaccaya* and a *dukkaṭa*.
580. By this very same method, regarding the remaining three lines as well—following the procedure already explained in the first analysis—one incurs a light offense by taking fewer than four lines;
one incurs a heavy offense of defeat (pārājika) by commanding someone to take four lines or more for the purpose of acquisition; and one [incurs an offense] by actually taking four lines or more.
If one instructs another to take [the robe] for the purpose of taking it, one stands guilty of a grave offense, a *pārājika*;

if one takes less than a quarter [of the robe], or instructs another to take it for the purpose of taking it, one stands guilty of a light offense, a *thullaccaya*, or a *dukkaṭa*. In this way, the remaining three terms [should be understood].
"Precisely because of the possibility of the meaning" means precisely by virtue of the occurrence of the meaning as previously stated.

581–2. How can there be an offense only during the proper time (*kāla*) and not during the improper time (*vikāla*), or an offense only during the improper time and not during the proper time? There is an offense manifested both during the proper time and during the improper time; there is an offense manifested neither during the proper time nor during the improper time—this is the application (*yojanā*). 586–7.

What that is received during the proper time which is allowable during the proper time but not allowable during the improper time? What that is taken during the improper time which is allowable during the improper time but not allowable during the proper time?
What indeed is that which is received both during the proper time and during the improper time [and is allowable] during the proper time...?

The construction is as follows: "It is allowable at an improper time, and it is allowable both at a proper time and at an improper time; what indeed is not allowable both at a proper time and at an improper time?
Speak, O gentle-faced one. (589) The construction is:
"It is allowable only at an improper time, and even on the following day at a proper time, it is not allowable."

592. Regarding the phrase "acts that defile a family" (*kuladūsanakamma*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes such things as making false claims, trading in goods for money, and hypocrisy (*kuhana*). 593–4.
Which offense is committed in border regions (*paccantima*) and not in the Middle Country (*majjhima*)?
Which offense is committed in the Middle Country but not in border regions? Which offense is committed both in border regions and... [and so forth].

[The construction is as follows: "He incurs [an offense] in the Middle [Countries], and he does not incur it in the Border [Countries]; which offense does he neither incur in the Border Countries nor in the Middle [Countries]?
596. The word-division for “so guṇaṅguṇupāhanaṃ” is “so guṇaṃ guṇaṃ upāhanaṃ. The meaning is: “that monk. 599.

Having thus shown the tetrad of the Border [Countries] by way of the phrases “he incurs” and “he does not incur,” he said “in the Border [Countries],” etc., in order to show it by way of the phrases “it is not allowable” and “it is not allowable.”
601. "Vuttaṃ" (stated) refers to what was stated previously in the verse beginning with "by a group of five," and so forth.
603. "Evaṃ vattuṃ" means to say, "it is not allowable. "Pañcaloṇādikaṃ" refers to [the passage] beginning with, "Monks, I allow salts," and so forth.
608. The construction is: one does not enter within the scope of what has been permitted; rather, by transgressing that [limit], one enters into what is outside [of it].
612. "Layings down for those in training" (sekkhapaññatti) refers to the layings down concerning the rules of training (sekhiyapaññatti).
613. "Not in a group" (agaṇā) means not with a companion; for in this context, even a single person is called a "group.
614. In both cases, it should be understood that the offense is unique (asādhāraṇa), being a rule specifically prescribed for bhikkhunīs.

616. “The one who is ill does not incur [the offense], and the one who is not ill does not incur it”—thus the construction is that both do not incur it. This refers to the repeated taking up of the terms shown in the *tikas* (triads) and so forth by way of showing them in *catukkās* (tetrads) and beyond.
618. The word-division is: “Either the one who is not ill incurs [the offense]. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the *catukkās*.
620. Where it should have been said “*garudullaccayan*,” [the form] “*garun*” occurs due to the elision of the *niggahīta*.
621. The five benefits of the *kaṭhina* robe have already been stated above. 626.

“*Aggisatthanakhakkantan*” means struck or touched by fire, weapons, or nails; the sense is that it has been hit. “*Abījan*” means not containing seed. “*Ubbaṭṭabījakan*” means having the seeds removed.
628. *Pavāraṇā* also includes the *pavāraṇā* by way of refusal. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "rice and so forth," there is the inclusion of *sattu*, *kummāsa*, fish, and meat.
By the phrase "by means of taking with the body and so forth," it means by taking [the food] with the body or with what is connected to the body.
Having taken one of those two together with these four factors—namely, "the request of one who wishes to give" and "being within reach of the hand"—...
There are exactly five ways of receiving [alms]. 629–30.
"In one who knows the Vinaya" means in a person who is a holder of the Vinaya. "And his own virtue" refers to his own virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
"It is well-guarded" means that by virtue of knowing what is an offense and what is not, and what is allowable and what is unallowable, he has abandoned that which should not be practiced.
That which ought to be practiced is well protected by way of its practice.
"He dispels the remorse of another" means he prevents the remorse that has arisen in another fellow-celibate regarding what is permissible and what is impermissible.

"He speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha" means that when a discussion concerning the determination of what is permissible and impermissible arises, he is without hesitation and free from fear.
He speaks thus. "Hostile monks" refers to persons who are one's adversaries. "For the stability and continuation of the Dhamma":
because of the statement, "The Vinaya is called the life-span of the Dispensation; when the Vinaya stands, the Dispensation stands," he is practicing for the sake of the stability of the True Dhamma.
For that reason—in that regard, concerning the state of being an expert in the Vinaya—a wise monk is one possessed of discernment.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Fivefold Group. 631–2.
*Chaḷabhiññena*: one who possesses six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) is called "one with the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñña*);
by him [it was said]. A bed and chair that exceed the prescribed measure, a sitting mat that exceeds the measure, and likewise a itch-covering cloth, a rain-cloak, and a robe that exceed the measure.
"Measuring robe" refers to the robe of the Sugata; there are six such types.

(633–4) "Ignorance and remorse" means ignorance-and-remorse (*aññāṇa-kukkuccā*); by these, it is meant both through ignorance and through being overcome by remorse. "By perverted perception" means by the perception of what is allowable as unallowable, and the perception of what is unallowable as allowable.

In this regard, how does one incur [an offense] through lack of shame? One who knows full well that something is unallowable nevertheless crushes [the precept] and transgresses it. And this has also been said:
“He intentionally commits an offense;
he conceals the offense;
and he goes upon a wrong path.”
“Such a person is called one who is shameless.

How does one commit an offense through ignorance? An ignorant person—dull and utterly deluded, not knowing what should and should not be done—does what should not be done and fails in what should be done. Thus one commits an offense through ignorance.
How does one commit an offense through being overcome by remorse? When remorse has arisen concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable, [one consults] a master of the Vinaya...
Having asked whether something is allowable (*kappiya*), if it is allowable, it may be done; if it is unallowable (*akappiya*), it must not be done.
Yet, this person, having crushed [the truth] with the thought “this is permissible,” simply transgresses. Thus, one falls into an offense through being overcome by remorse (*kukkucca*).

How does one fall into an offense through the perception of the unallowable regarding what is allowable? One eats pork thinking it is “deer meat,” or one eats at the wrong time with the perception that it is the right time. In this way, one falls into an offense through the perception of the unallowable regarding what is allowable.

How does one commit an offense through the perception of what is allowable regarding what is unallowable? One eats the flesh of a deer, perceiving it as "pig's meat," or one eats at an improper time, perceiving it as the proper time. In this way, one commits an offense through the perception of what is allowable regarding what is unallowable. How does one commit an offense through forgetfulness?
One commits offenses such as sleeping in the same room [with a woman] or being separated from one's robe through forgetfulness.
635–8. The phrase is to be analyzed as: "It should be attended to by a bhikkhu. By the "Dhamma-eye" means by that which is comprised of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.

The "Dhamma-eye" (dhammacakkhu) is that which has the Dhamma of practice as its eye; by means of this Dhamma-eye, endowed with six factors, a bhikkhu should perform the full ordination (upasampadā), grant dependence (nissaya), and have a novice (sāmaṇera) attend upon him—this is the construction [of the meaning].
He knows what is an offense, he knows what is not an offense, he knows a grave offense, and he knows a light offense.
The application [of the rule] is as follows: both Pātimokkhas of that bhikkhu are well-mastered in detail, well-analyzed in meaning, and well-determined in both the rules and their phrasing;
he is either ten years senior or more than ten years senior—this is the application.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Six Sets. 639.
It is said that there are seven modes of proper conduct (*sāmīci*): "That monk is not censured, and those monks are worthy of praise;
this is the proper conduct therein. 'Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to your own task; let not your own task perish'—this is the proper conduct therein."
"This almsbowl of yours, O bhikkhu, should be kept until it breaks"—this is the proper course therein.
Having taken it out from there, it should be shared with the bhikkhus—this is the proper course therein.
It should be understood, inquired about, and investigated—this is the proper course therein. "Whoever shall have need of it, he shall take it"—this is the proper course therein.
“Proper conduct” (*sāmīcī*): six types of proper conduct are stated in the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*;

together with that which is stated in the *Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha*—namely, “That bhikkhunī is not reproved, and those bhikkhunīs are to be censured; this is the proper conduct therein”—seven types of proper conduct are stated.

“And likewise seven methods for settling disputes” (*samatha*): the seven methods for settling disputes, beginning with resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhā-vinaya*), are also stated as being seven. “The offenses that have been formulated.”
"Sattā" refers to the seven offenses prescribed, beginning with the *pārājika*.

"By the Seer of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment" means by the Blessed One who perceives the seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*), as they truly are. This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the sevens.

640-1. Herein, the construction is as follows: "A monk who corrupts families, for the sake of his livelihood alone, corrupts families by means of these eight modes: flowers, fruits, scented powder, clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, medical treatment, and running errands on foot.
By the phrase "with flowers" and so forth, he shows that the giving of flowers and the rest is merely illustrative (*upalakkhaṇa*). "With flowers": [and so on].
The meaning to be understood here is "by the gift of flowers. The giving of flowers and so forth are mentioned in the section on corrupting families.

Regarding the two sets of eight [verses] beginning with “Even when there are eight things left over, and even when there are eight things not left over,” he says “and that which has been made unallowable,” etc., in order to show first the eight things that are not left over.
These eight are specified as “that which is left over by one who is ill.”

The construction is: "they are to be known as *anatiritta* (not left over). Improper acts and so forth have been explained in the commentary on the *Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*. 646. Regarding "known *ñatti*" (*ñātañatti*):

this refers to the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for what is known, and the offense of wrong-doing for the motion (*ñatti*). Regarding "counter-proclamation" (*paṭisāvana*): this means in response. The determination of the eight offenses of wrong-doing has been stated in the commentary on the second *pārājika*.
648–9. Ordination by "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*): this refers to the Blessed One’s address of "Come, monk" to the son of a noble family named Yasa and others.
"Ordination by granting" (*dinna-upasampadā*). "And by going for refuge" refers to the ordination authorized by means of the threefold going for refuge during the First Enlightenment.

"Ordination by answering questions and giving instruction" refers to Sopāka’s ordination through the answering of questions, and the ordination of the Elder Mahākassapa through the acceptance of instruction.
"Ordination by accepting the heavy rules" refers to the ordination of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī through the acceptance of the eight heavy rules (*garudhamma*) as authorized.

"By a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*)," this refers now to the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of monks. "Eightfold proclamation" (*aṭṭhavācikā*) means that the full ordination of nuns is called "eightfold proclamation" because it consists of eight formal utterances (*kammavācā*): by means of a formal act of one motion and three proclamations in the presence of the nuns, and by means of a formal act of one motion and three proclamations in the presence of the monks.
"By a messenger for nuns" refers to [the case of] Aḍḍhakāsī, the courtesan.
The ordination of bhikkhunīs by means of a messenger was authorized.

650. "One of pure vision" (suddhadiṭṭhi): because his vision, known as the "all-seeing eye," is completely purified through the abandonment of the defilements together with their latent tendencies, he is one of pure vision; [this refers] to that Perfectly Enlightened One, the All-Seeing Eye. 651.
"One of evil desires" (pāpicchā) means one who has the desire for the recognition of qualities that do not exist.
