652–3. "And one should not be a drinker of intoxicants": one should not be a drinker of intoxicants; one should not become a drinker of intoxicants, meaning one should not drink intoxicants.
"From unchaste conduct": one should abstain from sexual intercourse, which is the practice of the ignoble. "One should not eat at night, [which is] eating at the wrong time":
having observed the Uposatha, one should not eat either a meal at night or food during the daytime at an improper time.
"And one should not use perfumes" means that one should not smear oneself with scents.

"One should lie on a bed or on the ground, having spread out a mat" means that one should lie either on a permissible bed or on a mat made by spreading grass, leaves, straw, and so forth upon the ground that has been prepared with plaster and the like.
For this is called the eightfold Uposatha; it [abstains from] killing living beings and the other [offenses].
The Uposatha observed by one who practices it without deficiency is called "eightfold" because it is endowed with eight factors.

The phrase "by the Buddha who has gone to the end of suffering" is to be construed as: by the Buddha who has reached and attained the end of the suffering of saṃsāra, namely, the Great Nibbāna of the Deathless, and who has proclaimed [this teaching].
The eight factors for a monk who exhorts the nuns are already shown in the commentary on the discourse concerning the exhortation of nuns.

Commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathā*. 655. Regarding the phrase "nine excellent foods are mentioned": these are indeed those spoken of in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) concerning excellent foods. The construction is as follows: for one who eats the nine types of meat from among the ten kinds of forbidden meat, excluding human flesh, a *dukkaṭa* offense is specified.
656. Regarding the passage beginning with "the *Pātimokkha*... is elucidated": there are five recitations for the monks, and for the nuns, [they are elucidated] by means of the *aniyata* recitation.

"Without four" refers to nine headings that have been explained. "Nine Uposathas" means there are nine Uposathas by way of day, three by way of the performer, and three by way of the act—thus nine Uposathas.
"In this" means in this Dispensation. "The Sangha is split by nine" is to be construed as:
the Sangha is split by nine persons. As it has been said:
“Upāli, on one side there are four, on the other side there are four, and a ninth proclaims:
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve this.
In this way too, Upāli, there is both a schism in the Saṅgha and a breaking of the Saṅgha. Or, Upāli, with nine, or more than nine...”
“There is both a fracture in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha.
This concludes the commentary on the Discourse on the Novice.

657. He will speak of the ten grounds for abuse. The ten training rules (sikkhāpada) are well known. The ten kinds of unallowable meat, such as human flesh and so forth, have already been mentioned above. “The ten bright ones” refers to the ten bright colors, beginning with blue.
659. There are ten dangers in entering the king’s inner palace; these should be understood according to the recitation of the text:
“Monks, there are these ten dangers in entering the king’s inner palace. What are the ten?
Here, monks, the king is seated together with his chief queen, and a monk enters there; or the chief queen, upon seeing the monk...”
He breaks into a smile; or, seeing a monk or a great seer, he breaks into a smile. Then the king thinks:
"Surely they have done something, or they will do something. This, monks, is the first danger in entering the royal harem.
"Furthermore, monks, the king has many duties and many tasks; having gone to a certain woman, he does not [return]."
It wanders; it conceives a womb there. Then the king thinks:
"No one else enters here except a renunciant; could this be the work of a renunciant? Monks, this is the second danger in entering a royal palace.
“Furthermore, monks, suppose some jewel is lost in the king’s inner palace.
Then it occurs to the king: ‘No one else enters here except a renunciant;
could this be the work of a renunciant? This, monks, is the third danger in entering the king’s inner palace.
“Furthermore, monks, secret counsels within the king’s inner palace are leaked to the outside.
Then the king thinks: ‘No one else enters here except a renunciant;
could this be the work of a renunciant? This, monks, is the fourth danger in entering the king’s inner palace.
“Furthermore, monks, in the royal palace a father may long for his son, or a son may long for his father, and they think:
‘No one else enters here except a renunciant;
could it be that a renunciant might perform some service? Monks, this is the fifth danger in entering a royal palace.”
“Furthermore, monks, a king appoints someone of low status to a high position. Those who find this disagreeable think:
‘The king is indeed associating with a renunciant; could there not be some action on the part of that renunciant?
This, monks, is the sixth danger in entering the royal palace.
“Furthermore, monks, a king may appoint one of high station to a low position. Those for whom this is displeasing think:
‘The king is indeed associating with a renunciant; could this be the work of the renunciant?
This, monks, is the seventh disadvantage in entering the royal palace.
“Furthermore, monks, a king dispatches his army at an improper time. Those who find this disagreeable think:
‘The king is indeed associating with a renunciant; could this be the work of the renunciant?
Monks, this is the eighth disadvantage in entering a royal palace.
“Furthermore, monks, when a king has dispatched his army at the proper time and then recalls it from midway on the road, those who find this unpleasant think:
‘The king is indeed associating with a renunciant; could there perhaps be some action involving the renunciant?
This, monks, is the ninth danger in entering a royal palace.
“Furthermore, monks, the royal palace is crowded with elephants, crowded with horses, and crowded with chariots;
it contains forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects that are seductive and unsuitable for one who has gone forth.
This, monks, is the tenth danger in entering a royal palace. These, monks, are the ten dangers.”
“...and entering the royal palace.
In that context, “the father desires the son” means he wishes to kill the son; the same method applies to “the son desires the father.
“Elephant-tread” (*hatthisammadda*) means a place where there is the treading, the trampling, of elephants.
The same applies to [the terms] "assasammadda" and so forth.
Regarding "by ten aspects":
"An offense that has not been suspended, nor obstructed..."
Multiplicity and the perception of suchness;
desiring to conceal and then the concealing;
"concealed" [is said] when the sun has risen over the ten factors.
By means of the ten factors that have been grasped.
660. "Ten paths of merit" refers to the ten wholesome courses of action, beginning with abstaining from taking life.
"Ten [paths] of demerit likewise" refers to the same ten unwholesome courses of action, beginning with taking life. He will later speak of the ten bases of giving.
And those same seven treasures are:
“Pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells,
crystal, coral, silver, and gold.”
“Red gems and also emeralds;
the wise one displays these jewels—one should know them.
Thus are the ten jewels specified.
662. The construction is: "Ten persons who are not to be saluted have been explained by the Lord of Sages. How so? "Monks, these ten are not to be saluted:
one who was ordained later is not to be saluted by one who was ordained earlier; one who is not fully ordained is not to be saluted;
one of a different communion who is senior but speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be saluted; a woman is not to be saluted; a paṇḍaka is not to be saluted."
"One who is undergoing probation is not to be saluted; one deserving to be sent back to the beginning is not to be saluted; one deserving the *mānatta* penance is not to be saluted;
one practicing the *mānatta* penance is not to be saluted; one deserving rehabilitation is not to be saluted. These, monks, are the ten who are not to be saluted. 663–4.
"Cemetery-dweller" means that which has been discarded in a cemetery. "Market-stall discard" means that which has been discarded at the door of a shop. "Rat-guarded" means...
"Scavenged by rats" refers to a rag that has been abandoned after being gnawed by them. The same principle applies to those gnawed by cattle and so forth.
"Stūpa-cloth" refers to cloth abandoned after being wrapped around an anthill as an offering. "Consecration-cloth" refers to cloth abandoned in the consecration pavilion of kings.
"Gone-and-returning" refers to a rag discarded by people who have returned from the cemetery after bathing.
665. All the [colors] beginning with blue have been mentioned; regarding the phrase "wearing ten robes," the *Kurundi* states:
"It is said that 'they wear robes that are entirely blue,' and by way of this statement, there are ten.
Herein, in this group of ten, nine robes—namely, the three robes together with either the *saṃkaccikā* or the *udakasāṭikā*—which are determined by name, are called "the wearing of ten robes."
As it is said: "It is stated that 'ten' is said by including either a water-bath robe or a waist-cloth among the nine allowable robes.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the ten. 666.
As for the eleven types of persons incapable [of ordination], such as eunuchs and others, the application is that even if they have been ordained, they are not truly ordained.
667. The construction is: "Those declared 'unallowable' (akappiya) consist of eleven kinds of bowls. By "a bowl made of wood" is meant a bowl consisting of wood.
"Arising from gems" means that ten bowls made of gems, together with [the wooden one], constitute the eleven; this is the construction.
In the phrase "and by a wooden one," the word "and" (ca) includes a bowl made of copper. As it is said: "The eleven bowls [include] one made of copper..."
"Or together with one made of wood, or [together] with those made of the ten gems. Here, "gem" (*ratana*) refers to the ten gems beginning with pearl.
668. The construction is: "There are eleven kinds of improper sandals. As it is said: "Eleven kinds of sandals: ten made of gems and one wooden sandal.
However, sandals made of grass, *muñja* grass, *pabbaja* grass, and so forth, are included within the category of wooden sandals."
669–70. "Too small" and "too large" are to be construed [with the preceding]. "Based on a broken landmark" and "based on a shadow landmark" are to be construed [with the preceding].
"Validated by one standing outside" means validated by one standing outside the boundary. "In a river, a lake, or the ocean, it is likewise validated" is to be construed [with the preceding].
"Intersected with the boundary" and "encompassed by the boundary" are to be construed [with the preceding]. These are the eleven [types of invalid boundaries].
The construction is: "there may be no boundaries.
671. The construction is: "eleven types of earth are allowable (kappiya), and eleven types of earth are unallowable (akappiya).
In that context, the eleven types of allowable earth are: pure stone, pure gravel, pure potsherds, and pure sand; [and so forth].
Pure sand; mostly stones; mostly gravel; mostly potsherds; mostly pebbles;
mostly sand—these ten, together with either the burnt earth or the mound of dust from four months of rain or a mound of clay, make eleven.
“With little dust, with very little dust”—these are further types of earth.
Those [types of earth] mentioned are for the most part included within five categories, such as stone and so forth.
The eleven kinds of "unallowable earth" (akappiyapathavī) are defined as follows: pure soil, pure clay, with little stone, little gravel, little pebble, little sand, and little grit;
that which consists mostly of soil and mostly of clay; and even that which is not burnt is called "arisen."
“Earth”: even a heap of dust or a heap of clay that has been lying for more than four months is called “earth that has come into being.
Thus eleven [types] have been stated.

Regarding the statement, “The allowable (kappiya) knots have been stated, and eleven types of tubes (vīdhaka),” the construction here is: “eleven allowable knots and tubes have been stated. These, moreover—
“Those made of bamboo, ivory, horn, bone, wood, lac, fruit, conch-shell,
navel [of a shell], thread, reed, and even metal;
these various kinds are allowable, as are knots made of those same materials.”
It should be understood that [these] are included by this verse.

674–5. The nun who follows one who has been suspended (ukkhitto), depending on both the monks and the nuns, is declared as one of these eleven matters to be dealt with "up to the third time" (*yāvatatiyaka*) among the offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
676. The ten grounds for the cessation of formal dependence (*nissaya*) have been stated as exactly eleven. They are said to be "sixfold according to the teacher."
“When [the teacher] has gone away, when he has changed sides, when he has departed, and also when [the pupil] has lost his dependence;
through death, through a formal act of instruction, and through the meeting with the preceptor—thus is it authorized.

Thus, six ways for the cessation of dependence from a teacher have been stated. But as for the preceptor, there are five ways; among those, excluding the meeting with the preceptor, the remaining five ways for the cessation of dependence on a preceptor have been stated. These make eleven.
Commentary on the Elevenfold Discourse. 677.
"There are thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)" means that the ascetic practices, beginning with the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga), are exactly thirteen.
"And fourteen are supreme" refers to: "An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days; for a month at most by one... [and so forth].
That robe must be deposited by the bhikkhu; that bhikkhu may accept that robe only as a maximum of one inner and one upper garment;
he may stand silently waiting for it for a maximum of six times; furthermore, having had a new rug made, a bhikkhu must use it for six years;
it may be used for a maximum of six years; [and] it may be carried for a maximum of three *yojanas*.
They must be carried by hand; an extra bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days; food stored as an accumulation may be consumed for a maximum of seven days;
that monk may be separated from his robe for a maximum of six nights;
[the dye] may be taken up to a maximum of four *kaṃsa*, a maximum of two and a half *kaṃsa*, or a maximum of two finger-joints; [the length] may be up to eight finger-breadths.
"A bed-leg support" and "a tooth-stick no more than eight finger-breadths long"—these are the fourteen limits.
As for the sixteen prescribed as "knowing," they are prescribed after saying "knowing"; they should be understood as follows:
knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been dedicated to oneself; knowing that [a guest] has already arrived first...
If he should spread out a bed intruding upon a bhikkhu; or if, knowing it contains living beings, he should sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled water, grass, or clay;
or if, knowing it has been prepared by a bhikkhunī, he should consume almsfood; or if, knowing it is for the purpose of causing offense, he should eat when [the meal] is finished;
or if, knowing it contains living beings, he should consume water—[in each case], there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya). Knowing... [and so on].
If one should reopen for a formal legal act a case that has been settled according to the Dhamma; if one should knowingly conceal a grave offense;
if one should knowingly ordain a person who is less than twenty years of age; if one should knowingly set out on a journey together with a caravan of thieves by prior arrangement;
if one [should associate] with a monk who speaks thus and has not made amends according to the Dhamma, knowing him to be such...
Likewise: if one knowingly diverts to an individual a gain intended for the Saṅgha that has been assigned to it;
if one knowingly fails to personally admonish a nun who has committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika);

if one knowingly enters a monastery containing monks without having obtained permission from a thief known to be condemned to death; or if one knowingly enters a monastery containing monks without having asked for leave.
678. Here, in this teaching, that bhikkhu who understands the entire *vinayavinicchaya*—which is unsurpassed, yet accompanied by what is surpassed, together with its supplementary sections;

and which pertains to the most eminent, vast, unsurpassed, peerless, and supreme methods of discipline (*vinayanaya*) derived from the Vinaya—including the determination of offenses and non-offenses, heavy and light matters, and what is permissible and impermissible.

Alternatively, according to the method of training (*vinayanaya*), that monk who acts in accordance with the *Vinayapiṭaka* becomes "unsurpassed" (*niruttara*), meaning he stands having transcended any further reply to be uttered by his adversaries;
or he becomes "supreme" (*seṭṭha*), meaning that neither he nor others should entertain any doubt—this is the construction.
In the word "knowing" (*jānatī*), the vowel is shortened due to the requirements of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the method of single enumerations (*ekuttaranaya*) within the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning.
Now begins the commentary on the discourse on the breaking of perspiration (*sedamocana*).
679. These verses, which produce proficiency in monks who hear them as they listen, and which perfect skill in wisdom regarding the determination of the Vinaya, are therefore excellent and supreme.
Regarding the phrase "Sedamocanagāthāyo" (Verses that cause perspiration):

they are called "Sedamocanā" because, while one is contemplating the fact that those who are enemies of the meaning and enemies of the Dispensation are unable to refute [the teaching], the body becomes exhausted and breaks out in sweat. Thus, they are "Sedamocanā."

The construction is as follows: "I shall hereafter explain the verses of questions followed by their meanings (*atthānugatapañhā*) established by the Elder Upāli, as well as the verses of answers connected therewith.

681. *Kabandha* means a headless trunk, a body upon which eyes and a mouth have appeared on the chest. As it is said: "A headless trunk (*kabandha*) is that which has eyes and a mouth upon its chest. By means of the "mouth," acting as the instrument. "Having done" (*katvā*) means having practiced or cultivated.
682. How could that bhikkhu be one who has committed a *pārājika* offense? How could there be a *pārājika* dhamma? 684.

"Something" (*kiñci*) refers to the property of another, whether it be a foot-measure of land or what is worth a foot-measure. "And does not incite another" means he does not command another, saying, "Steal such-and-such an item belonging to so-and-so.

685. The connection is: "not taking anything belonging to another. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and an order" (*āṇattiñca*), both "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*) and "signal" (*saṅketa*) are included.

686. *Garukaṃ bhaṇḍanti*: "Precious goods" refers to the state of being worth one *pāda* [in value]; it is an adjective for the term "requisites" (*parikkhāra*). "The requisites of another" means any kind of requisite belonging to another.
692. *Manussuttarike dhamme*: Regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). *Katikaṃ katvāna*:

Having made a pact such as, "When he is sitting thus, standing thus, or walking thus, he reveals the goal," and so forth. *Sambhāvanādhippāyo*: With the intention of being esteemed, thinking, "He is an Arahant."
The intention is that he acts with great honor after having accepted [the invitation]. "And if he transgresses" means:
if he transgresses the agreement thus made, the meaning is that he performs such a sitting, standing, or walking. "Having fallen away" means:
when someone of human kind, upon seeing such a sitting and so forth, recognizes at that very moment that "he is an Arahant," that person incurs a *pārājika* offense.
693. The construction is: "How could there be [these] having a single basis?
694. "A woman" means one particular woman. "One who acts" means that at a single moment, after having spoken the message uttered by another man, she accepts it with this [man];
this indicates that two factors have already been established previously for the purpose of "examining. Of this...
And [the offense] committed by taking back [the robe]. Having engaged in physical contact and spoken lewd words, he speaks in praise of serving his own desires. 695.
"Without having performed the aforementioned duties" means without having performed the duties such as probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, as stated by the Blessed One.
696. Because these training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are not shared with the nuns, it is said: "There is no status of a *saṅghādisesa* offense."
697. Regarding the phrase *yena kuddho pasaṃsito* (“by whom [he] was praised when angry”), the word *nindito ca* (“and when censured”) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
698. The construction is: he who becomes angry while the praise of the sectarians (*titthiya*) is being recited is the one who succeeds (*ārādhaka*).

The intended meaning is that he is satisfied and praised. This refers to one who was formerly a follower of a sect, but having obtained ordination in this teaching, [remains attached to] the sectarians...
If, upon hearing the praise being spoken, one becomes angry and displeased, one is not one who pleases the Saṅgha, nor one who gladdens the Saṅgha.
If one becomes angry when the praise of the Fully Awakened One (Sambuddha) is being spoken, the construction is "he is censured.
Here, "of the Fully Awakened One" is an illustrative designation (upalakkhaṇa).
701. *Gahetvā* means having accepted. 751.
By the phrase beginning with “not with a lustful mind,” he demonstrates the absence of even the mere arising of a transgressive thought regarding the three preceding *pārājika* offenses.
Regarding the term *maraṇāya*, here the phrase “of one belonging to the human species” is understood from the context of the *pārājika* section itself.
“Of him” means of one who is giving something. “That” refers to what is being given in that manner. 752.

The term “defeat” is stated here because the schismatic is included among those persons incapable [of rehabilitation]. One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha even by the casting of voting tickets is indeed a schismatic. 753.
Regarding the phrase “having deposited one robe, whichever of the three robes it may be, at a distance of half a yojana,” this is the construction.

754. The construction is: having laid down the three robes at the foot of a tree resembling a well-established banyan tree, how does one incur [offenses] while causing the dawn to rise at half a *yojana*?
755. The construction is: how does one simultaneously, neither before nor after, incur numerous bodily offenses of various bases?
757. The construction is: how does one simultaneously, neither before nor after, incur numerous verbal offenses of various bases, which are not bodily?
758. *Vinaya-nasattha* means in the *Vinayapiṭaka*. [The phrase] "of that bhikkhu" refers to him. 759.

In the expressions beginning with "by a woman," the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*). The construction is: "not practicing, not engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman, or a man, or a paṇḍaka, or a *nimittaka*, he passes away on account of sexual intercourse.
760. *Kāyasaṃsagga-tā* is simply bodily contact; they have fallen into that. The Pārājika offense known by the name "the eightfold cutting" (*aṭṭhavatthukaṃ chejjaṃ*).

762. "At the time designated as 'the back'" means during the period designated as the "back," which lasts for seven months from the first day of the last month of summer until the first day of winter.

Regarding the phrase "and even his mother," although it should have been stated as "and also his mother" (*mātarampi ca*), it was stated as "and even his mother" (*mātarampi ca*). Or rather, that very reading is the correct one.
764. By the phrase “having taken alms from the hand of one who is lustful,” the basis for a *saṅghādisesa* offense is stated;
by “garlic,” the basis for a *pācittiya* offense; by “human flesh,” the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense; and by “any other unallowable thing,” the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the term “unallowable thing,” the word “flesh” (*maṃsa*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the context]. The word division is “sabbe ekato. Here, after “ekato,” the word “having crushed” (*madditvā*) is to be supplied.
The remainder means that she eats it after having crushed it together with unallowable meats.
All of this—“having taken,” “having crushed,” and “eats”—is the object of those actions. In the phrase “and human flesh,” the particle *ca* (and) must be construed with each individual term.
“Her” refers to the bhikkhunī. At a single moment, there are the offenses of *saṅghādisesa*, *pācittiya*, *dukkaṭa*, *pāṭidesanīya*, and *thullaccaya*.
765. The phrase is to be divided as “puggalo eko. “Two who have completed their years” refers to two novices who have both reached twenty years of age.

“But for them there was only one formal act” means that for both of those novices, the formal act of ordination (*upasampadā-kammavācā*) was performed by a single preceptor. “Of one” means of even a single novice. “The formal act” refers to the formal act of ordination.
"It does not grow" means it does not succeed; "tell me, O gentle-faced one, what is the reason for this?"—this is the intended meaning.

(766) Regarding "among those with great psychic power": among the two novices. However, if even one of them is as much as a hair’s breadth above the earth, situated in the air, then that formal act of full ordination performed for the one situated in the air neither grows nor succeeds; whereas for the one on the ground, it does grow—this is the construction.
767. A formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) must not be performed for a novice (*sāmaṇera*) standing on the ground by a Saṅgha situated in the air through supernormal power (*iddhi*).
If one performs it, it is invalid—this is the construction. And this is a characteristic common to all formal acts. As it has been said:
"Even by a Saṅgha sitting in the air, a formal act must not be performed for one standing on the ground. If one performs it, it is invalid."
768. It is not a cloth that has been made allowable (*kappakata*), nor is it dyed; it is an unallowable thing such as a woolen blanket made of hair (*kesakambala*).
For one who wears it, there is an offense—that is, for the monk who wears it, there is an offense. "How might there be no offense?
Speak, O fair-faced one!"—this is the construction [of the verse].
769. Here, regarding this wearing of unallowable things for that purpose:
the construction is "there may be no offense for a bhikkhu whose robe has been stolen. By the words "even a little," etc., he confirms the very meaning already stated.
For that bhikkhu whose robe has been stolen, there exists not even the slightest robe that is unallowable; therefore, the intention is that there is no offense.

770. Furthermore, if a person does not take anything from the hand of another for food, nor gives anything from his own food to anyone else, yet nevertheless incurs and falls into a grave offense of *saṅghādisesa*, how does he incur it?
If you are skilled in the Vinaya, tell me this reason.
“Tell me,” is the construction. *Hava* is merely a particle.

771. But whichever nun, having been urged by another nun in the manner stated in the Saṅghādisesa matrix—beginning with, “Come, noble lady, eat whatever solid food this man gives you”—and so forth, [if she] has not tasted it...
If a person, having taken and received whatever food, eats it, then regarding her who eats thus—
having been incited by another— the wise, masters of the Vinaya, and learned ones declare that there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the one who incited her;
they say there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the one who incited her at the conclusion of the meal of the one who was incited.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: “For, O venerable ones, at the conclusion of that meal, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for the instigator.
(772) The construction is: “If you understand—that is, if you know—then speak well; explain it thoroughly. (773) “When used”:
the meaning is that when the tooth-stick has been accepted from the hand of that person by the nun who was instigated and has been used, the instigator incurs a light offense (*lahuvajja*).

775. By the term “one who has been suspended” (*ukkhitto*), he refers to the fault of an offense (*āpatti-vajja*). As it is said: “In that case, there is no formal act of the Vinaya (*vinaya-kamma*) together with him; therefore, having committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense and concealing it, he does not touch the fault. 776.

“Born with or without life” (*sappāṇa-appāṇaja*) means born among those possessing life and those lacking life. “Neither moving on foot” (*neva jaṅgama*) means not moving upon the ground by means of feet.
“Nor flying through the air” (*na vihaṅgama*) means not moving through the sky by spreading wings. “Twice-born” (*dvija*) [means] by two...
Because it is born from conditions, or because it is born twice, it is called *dvija*. *Kanta* means charming; *akanta* means uncharming. 777.

Sound born of living beings (*sappāṇaja*) is said to be mind-born (*cittaja*); sound not born of living beings (*appāṇaja*) is said to be temperature-born (*utu-ja*). That [latter] is considered *dvija* because it is born from two conditions—this is the construction.
778. The verse beginning with “In the Vinaya” has its meaning already explained.
Thus ends the commentary on the "Discourse on the Shedding of Sweat" from the *Uttaralīnatthappakāsinī*.
[Now begins] the commentary on the "Discourse on the Common and the Uncommon."
779–80. “Of all training rules” means of all the training rules found in both Vibhaṅgas.
“By monks and by nuns” is an instrumental construction used in both instances to denote the agent.
This refers to those rules prescribed as non-common for both—namely, those prescribed for monks and for nuns [by monks], and likewise those prescribed for nuns and for monks [by nuns].
The construction is as follows: "I shall speak of the training rule (sikkhāpada) common to both [monks and nuns] regarding 'bhikkhunīhi bhikkhūnañca'.

"Samāhitā" means those whose minds are one-pointed. "Tañ" refers to that method beginning with the introduction (nidāna) which is being spoken by me. "Suṇātha" (Listen! directs the audience toward attentive hearing. 781.
The verse beginning with "Nidānan" has its meaning already explained.
782–3. The interrogative verses beginning with “How many at Vesālī? have their meaning already explained. 786.
Regarding the explanatory verses beginning with “Ten at Vesālī,” the terms such as “sexual intercourse” are stated by way of definition.

“Human being” (viggaho) refers to the offense of defeat (pārājika) involving a human being. “The fourth final matter” refers to the offense of defeat concerning superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).
"An extra robe" refers to the first *kathina* rule. "Pure black wool" refers to the second rule in the section on wool. 787.
"A living being" refers to the eighth rule in the first section on false speech. "And from one to another" refers to the training rule on eating in succession.
"The mouth-door" refers to the tenth rule in the fourth section on eating. "And reviling nuns" refers to the *Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha*.
The second [offense] in the sixth section on Monasteries (*ārāmavagga*). 788.
"Two kinds of reviling" refers to the eighth and ninth *saṅghādisesa* rules. "Acceptance of a robe" is the fifth [rule] in the section on Robes (*cīvaravagga*).
789. "Money" is the eighth [rule] in the section on Wool (*eḷakalomavagga*). "Requesting thread" is the sixth [rule] in the section on Bowls (*pattavagga*). "Slandering" [is the seventh rule].
The third [offense] in the second section on inhabited places (*bhūtagāma*); the ninth in the third section on instruction (*ovāda*), concerning "fully cooked alms-food" (*paripācita-piṇḍa*);
likewise, the second in the fourth section on food (*bhojana*), concerning "eating in a group" (*gaṇabhojana*);
the seventh in that same [section], concerning "eating at the wrong time" (*vikālabhojana*); and the sixth in the fifth section on naked ascetics (*acelaka*), concerning "wandering" (*cāritta*).
"Bathing" is the sixth [offense] in the sixth section on drinking liquor. "Less than twenty years old" is the fifth [offense] in the seventh section on containing living beings.
"Having given a robe by the Saṅgha" is the ninth [offense] in the eighth section on those who share the same Dhamma. 791.
"Attending upon" is the second *pāṭidesanīya* for monks. "Dancing or singing" is the first [offense] in the first section on garlic.
The tenth [offense]. Regarding the "two walking tours," these are the seventh and eighth [rules] in the fourth section on the *tuvaṭṭa* (reclining).

Regarding "giving of consent," this is the eleventh in the eighth section on young girls (*kumāribhūta*). Alternatively, the reading is "chanda-dāne ti"; the word-division is "chanda-dānaṃ iti ime. 792.
"Cottage" (*kuṭī*) is the sixth *saṅghādisesa*. "Silk" (*kosiya*) is the first in the second section on wool (*eḷakaloma*) among the *nissaggiya* [pācittiya] offenses.
"Seyyanti" is the fifth in the Chapter on False Speech. "Pathavī" is the tenth in the Chapter on False Speech.
"Bhūtagāmaṃ" is the first in the second [section] of the Chapter on Plant Life. "Sappāṇakañca siñcantī" is the tenth in the Chapter on Plant Life.
800. "Three hundred less six" means three hundred less six; that is to say, two hundred and ninety-four. "With even minds"—
"Regarding Vadhaka, Devadatta, the thief Aṅgulimāla,
Dhanapāla, and Rāhula— the Tathāgata was even-minded in all these cases," according to this statement,
the Tathāgata possessed an equal mind through his lack of agitation toward all things beneficial and harmful, as well as the eight worldly conditions such as gain and loss.

"Those remaining after what has been stated" means those left over from what was stated in the six cities beginning with Vesālī. The meaning is that all these rules of training (*sikkhāpada*) were enacted and laid down in Sāvatthī.
Regarding "the four *pārājika* offenses": there is sexual intercourse with a human being in Vesālī, and the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) in Vesālī;
and theft in Rājagaha—thus there are four. Regarding "the seven *saṅghādisesa* offenses": there are two cases of false accusation (*anuddhaṃsana*) mentioned in Rājagaha.
And there are two schisms: the hut-builder at Āḷavī and the large monastery at Kosambī; and the seven on difficult speech.

There are eight offenses entailing relinquishment: the extra robe at Vesālī, black wool, the acceptance of robes at Rājagaha, the acceptance of money, the solicitation for thread, the mixture of silk at Āḷavī, and the washing of wool at Kapilavatthu.
"Less than five bonds" refers to eight [offenses].

"And thirty-two minor rules" refers to: the reporting of a ghost at Vesālī, eating in succession, not receiving [food), the naked ascetic, the five beginning with "Whatever bhikkhunī should abuse a bhikkhu," and the complaining at Rājagaha.

[The offenses for] food prepared by a nun, eating in a group, eating at the wrong time, and the rule beginning with "Whatever monk, having been invited," and so forth; bathing more than once every half-month;

[ordaining] one under twenty years of age; and the eight [rules] for monks beginning with "Having given a robe by a unanimous Saṅgha," while for nuns, those beginning with "Dancing or singing," and so forth, and the rule beginning with "Whatever nun..."

The two [rules] beginning with “within the rains” and “any bhikkhunī who, having completed the rains residence,” the four [rules] beginning with “any bhikkhunī who, by giving her consent while on probation,” [the rule] regarding staying more than two or three nights with one not fully ordained at Āḷavī,
[the rules] beginning with “should dig the earth,” [the rule] regarding the destruction of plant life, and [the rule] regarding knowing [water] to contain living beings.

There are four [offenses] regarding water at Kosambī: addressing others with irrelevant speech, harassing others, placing a bolt on a door as far as the door-chamber, drinking fermented liquor and spirits, and showing disrespect—these five;
and at Kapilavatthu, the offense beginning with "having gone to the nuns' quarters," and the offense beginning with "a monk who is not ill [may stay for] four months"—and so forth.
“Made of bone or made of ivory,” and so forth, constitute three offenses for monks; for nuns, however, there are two:

“But [the offense of] purification by water,” and so forth, and “For the sake of exhortation,” and so forth; and in the Bhagga country, there is one: “One who is not ill and desires to warm himself,” and so forth—these together amount to exactly thirty-two *pācittiya* offenses.

802. "Two offenses entailing acknowledgment" refers to the two *pāṭidesanīya* rules: beginning with "If a monk [should eat] among families... and beginning with "Those which are forest-dwelling [dwellings]...
"Three trainings" refers to the three *sekhiya* rules: at Kosambī, not making a slurping sound;
in the Bhagga country, not holding a water vessel for drinking with a hand soiled by food; and not rinsing the bowl with rice grains still in it. Fifty-six...
The construction is as follows: the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were promulgated collectively in the six cities beginning with Vesālī. 803.
Furthermore, all these training rules promulgated in the seven cities amount to exactly two hundred and fifty.
Together with the two hundred and ninety-four training rules promulgated in Sāvatthī, [the total is] in the six...
The meaning is that there are three hundred and fifty-six training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed in the cities.
Those for which there is a "fourth by half" are "three and a half.
Having thus shown the city by way of its origin (nidāna), [the author] now, without omitting any other origins, [will treat] those found in the two Vibhaṅgas.
In order to show the enumeration of all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) solely by way of their total number, he said: “The training rules for the bhikkhus,” and so forth.
(811) Having thus shown the origin and the enumeration of all the training rules, he now said:

“Forty-six,” and so forth, in order to show those that are not shared (*asādhāraṇa*), namely, the training rules brought forth by the Great Sage (*Mahesi*) which are not shared by the bhikkhus with the bhikkhunīs.
The construction is: "there are exactly forty-six. By this, he states the enumeration (*uddesa*).
Having shown the exposition (*niddesa*) by means of the two verses beginning with "And six *saṅghādisesas*," he provides the detailed exposition (*paṭiniddesa*) with the words "the *vissaṭṭhī*," etc.

815. The word-division for "In the *Nissaggiya*, in the first chapter" is as follows: "washing" (*dhovana*) refers to the washing of a robe by a nun who is not a relative; "receiving" (*paṭiggaha*) refers to the receiving of the robe from her very hand.
816. *Ārañña* (the forest) refers to the twenty-ninth training rule (*sikkhāpada*). 817.
The construction is as follows: all the *pācittiya* offenses prescribed for both monks and nuns amount to eight hundred and eighty in total.
Regarding "eight hundred and eighty," this refers to the six hundred and sixty *pācittiya* rules found in the *Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha*.
Together with the twenty-two *pācittiya* rules for bhikkhunīs that are about to be explained, there are one hundred and eighty-eight.
The construction is as follows: "From these one hundred and eighty-eight *pācittiyas*, these twenty-two minor rules are extracted and constitute the *pātimokkha* for bhikkhus."

818. *Bhikkhunivaggo* means the section on the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs. A training rule (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed regarding eating in succession is "eating in succession" (*paramparabhojana*). That which exists together with eating in succession is "with eating in succession" (*saparamparabhojana*).

822. The passage beginning with “But those prescribed for one [group]” is the conclusion. The construction is as follows: these training rules, which have reached a state of non-commonality with the bhikkhunīs and are thus prescribed for one [group] alone, when combined, amount to forty-six.
823. The construction is as follows: the training rules for bhikkhunīs, which were rendered unique by the Great Sage (Mahesin) and have been collected together, amount to one hundred and thirty.

824. He states the detailed exposition (*niddesa*) of those thus enumerated with the words beginning “the *pārājikas*. There are four *pārājikas*, namely: those concerning [sexual intercourse] above the knees, concealing an offense, following one who has been suspended (*ukkhitānuvattikā*), and the eight grounds (*aṭṭhavatthuka*).
826. The sub-exposition (*paṭiniddesa*) of those explained in two stanzas begins with “but for the bhikkhunīs, by means of the *saṅghādisesas*,” and so forth.
Because the four *pārājika* offenses are already evident by way of their recitation (*uddesa*), they are not included in the detailed exposition (*paṭiniddesa*).

"Six from the beginning" refers to the six *saṅghādisesa* offenses beginning with false accusation (*ussayavādikā*). This term "from the beginning" should also be construed with the phrase "up to the third time" (*yāvatatiyaka*);
thus, it is stated that among the eight offenses involving a limit of three admonitions, these are the first four training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

827. Regarding the phrase "the seven beginning with *aññadatthika*," by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the four rules following the *aññadatthika* training rule are included, as well as the two preceding ones:
"should request one thing" and "should have another bartered. The phrase "and a bowl" refers to the first training rule concerning the accumulation of bowls.
In the second chapter, the first two training rules are included by the expression "heavy and light."
828. Here, in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha, the construction is: these twelve Nissaggiya rules were laid down by the Teacher specifically for the bhikkhunīs alone.

829–30. “All together, at the end of the count,” and so forth, is the conclusion. The construction is: those rules laid down specifically for the bhikkhunīs that are not shared with the bhikkhus amount to one hundred and thirty.
831–3. The word division is: “Not shared by both. There are one hundred and [thirty] training rules not shared by both.
There are seventy-six [offenses]. The exposition of those thus enumerated begins with "the four *pārājikas*," and so forth.
There are four *pārājika* offenses for bhikkhunīs that are not shared with bhikkhus.
"Ten and six" refers to the ten *saṅghādisesa* offenses for bhikkhunīs that are not shared with bhikkhus, and the [six] beginning with *vissaṭṭhi* for bhikkhus that are not shared with bhikkhunīs.
"Six *saṅghādisesas*": thus there are sixteen *saṅghādisesas*.
"And two *aniyatās*": these two *aniyatās* are not shared with the nuns; they belong to the monks alone. "Twenty-four *nissaggas*":
twelve are not shared with the nuns [belonging to the monks], and [twelve] are not shared with the monks [belonging to the nuns].
“There are twelve for bhikkhunīs”—thus there are twenty-four *nissaggiya* rules. “One hundred and eighteen minor rules”:

these are the one hundred and eighteen minor rules that are not shared by bhikkhunīs, namely, twenty-two that are not shared with bhikkhunīs and ninety-six that are not shared with bhikkhus. “In this” means in this compendium of non-shared rules.
"And twelve indeed are censurable" means that there are four *pāṭidesanīya* rules not shared by monks with nuns, and eight not shared by nuns with monks;
thus, these one hundred and seventy-six training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are not shared by either [the two orders].
This is the construction.
834. The construction is as follows: it is declared that there are one hundred and seventy-four training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Teacher that are common to both [monks and nuns].

835–836. Regarding "the four pārājikas": these are the four pārājikas consisting of sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, physical contact with a human being, and claiming superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).

"The seven saṅghādisesas" refers to the following: the seven cases of acting as a go-between, the unfounded accusation, the groundless charge of a different offense, and the four offenses involving a third admonition (yāvatatiyaka).
And seven Saṅghādisesa rules. And eighteen Nissaggiya rules: in the first section on robes (*cīvaravagga*), eight [rules] excluding the two training rules on washing and accepting;
in the section on wool (*eḷakalomavagga*), three—namely the eighth, ninth, and tenth;
and in the section on bowls (*pattavagga*), seven, excluding the triad of training rules concerning the bowl, the rainy-season robe, and the forest-dweller's robe.
And these eighteen rules on forfeiture (*nissaggiya-sikkhāpada*). Regarding the "seventy minor rules" (*khuddaka*):

excluding the twenty-two *pācittiya* rules that were stated as being specific to monks and not shared with nuns—namely, those beginning from "The entire Bhikkhunī-vagga... down to the twenty-two"—the remainder [constitute the seventy].
Seventy *pācittiya* rules have been prescribed by way of being common to both [orders]. As for the seventy-five *sekhiya* rules as well— thus,
the application is that there are one hundred and seventy-four training rules (*sikkhāpada*) in total, which constitute the common training shared equally by both monks and nuns.
Thus ends the commentary on the discussion of common and uncommon [characteristics] in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
837. *Itoti*: regarding the discourse on the common and uncommon [rules]. *Sabbagan ti*: that which is common to all training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
*Vadato me ti*: "of me who speaks"—listen to my words. *Nibodhathā ti*: "understand"; the meaning is: "be attentive with one-pointed minds and listen respectfully.
838–9. The word-division is: *vipatti*, *āpatti*, *anāpatti*. The word-division is: *āṇatti*, *aṅgaṃ*. [The term] *vajjakamma-pabhedakaṃ*...

"Breaking the Vajjis" means breaking the [monastic] rules. "The two triads" refers to the two triads of the wholesome (*kusala*) and the feeling (*vedanā*) categories. "In all instances" (*sabbattha*) refers here to the characteristics common to all seventeen types.
"In all places" (*sabbattha*) means in all training rules (*sikkhāpada*). 840. The construction is as follows:

"Having excluded here—in these seventeen types—all those characteristics previously mentioned according to the stated method, as well as those that are obvious, I shall provide an elucidation of the meaning, an exposition of the meaning."
841. *Nidāna* refers to the seven cities, such as Rājagaha, which served as the locations for the promulgation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
Since that has already been shown previously, he says "the person," etc., in order to show what remains. What is called "the person"?
It is whichever nun or monk with reference to whom a training rule was promulgated; this nun and this monk [are the persons] regarding the promulgation of the training rule.
The construction is: "he is called a person who is a beginner.

Regarding "Dhaniya and the others," by the word "and others" (ādi), there are included many bhikkhus, the bhikkhus from the banks of the Vaggumudā River, Seyyasaka, Udāyī, the bhikkhus of Āḷavī, Channa, Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, Devadatta, and the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu.
The group of six bhikkhus, Upananda the Sakyan-son, a certain bhikkhu, Hatthaka the Sakyan-son, Anuruddha,
the seventeen bhikkhus of the group of seventeen, Cūḷapanthaka, Belaṭṭhasīsa, the Venerable Ānanda,
the Elder Sāgata, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, and the Venerable Ānanda— these twenty-one are included here.

843. Regarding "Thullanandā and others": by the word "others," Sundarīnandā, the group of six bhikkhunīs, a certain bhikkhunī, Caṇḍakāḷī, several bhikkhunīs, and two bhikkhunīs—these six are included.
"All" refers to all individuals who are first offenders (ādikammika) in respect of both Pātimokkhas.

844. Regarding "basis" (*vatthu*): the construction is as follows—"the transgression and violation in every way of that very person, such as Sudinna, and of the basis [of the offense], such as sexual intercourse, is called 'basis'. 845–6.
The "sole" (*kevalā*) is the fundamental formulation (*mūla-paññatti*). "Anu," "anuppanna," "sabbattha," and "padesa"—these are the "anu-anuppanna-sabbattha-padesa";
these very words are the "anu-anuppanna-sabbattha-padesa-words," which are the preceding terms of those formulations (*paññatti*).

These [rules] are preceded by the categories of *sabbattha* (universal) and *padesa* (partial), as well as by the terms *anuppanna* (unoriginated) and *pada* (term). The construction is: "In that very same way, that is a *paññatti* (formal rule).
A subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) is an unoriginated rule (*anuppannapaññatti*), and it is either a universal rule (*sabbatthapaññatti*) or a partial rule (*padesapaññatti*).

The construction is: "How is that *paññatti* preceded by both? That which has both the single-term and the double-term preceding it is "preceded by both" (*ekatoubhatopubbā*), namely, a single-term rule (*ekatopaññatti*).
It is said that these are "prohibitions prescribed for both.
Regarding this, among the ninefold prescriptions, one asks: "What is called a prescription? To which it is replied:
"That which is sexual intercourse," and so forth. Namely: "Whosoever, as a bhikkhu, should engage in sexual intercourse," and "Whosoever, as a bhikkhu, should take what is not given."
The construction is: "This and such as this is the formal promulgation (*paññatti*) that constitutes the root of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

(848) Regarding the phrase "this and such as this," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes such statements as "without having renounced the training or disclosed one's weakness" and "from a village or from the wilderness.
(849) A formal promulgation made even before an offense has arisen is an "unarisen promulgation" (*anuppanna-paññatti*); that is what is meant by an arisen promulgation.

The construction is as follows: it is stated that this fourfold formal rule (*paññatti*)—namely, the training rule on leather rugs together with the training rule on sandals with double soles, the training rule on frequent bathing, the training rule on frequent bathing, and the training rule on ordination by a group of five—is called a "local formal rule" (*padesapaññatti*).
"It occurs only in the Middle Country" means that it constitutes an offense only within the Middle Country.
"Na aññato" means not elsewhere, that is, not in another place apart from the border regions.
"Ito" means from the fourfold designation of locations. "Ettha" means in this particular classification of designations.
"Sādhāraṇadukādikaṃ" refers to the pair of dyads consisting of common designation and uncommon designation, and designation on one side and designation on both sides.

"In meaning, it is one and the same" means that in meaning they are entirely identical to one another. The detailed determination of failure, offense, and non-offense has already been explained extensively and is not shown here.
However, this is the summary: "Failure" (vipatti) refers to any one of the failures of virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood.
"Offense" (āpatti) refers to the classification of offenses by way of preliminary action and so forth. "Non-offense" (anāpatti) refers to non-offense by way of ignorance and so forth.

853. The construction is: "An offense (āpatti), moreover, may be with a formal injunction (sāṇattikā) or it may be without a formal injunction (anāṇattikā). By the statement, "And this so-called 'injunction' (āṇatti) is an ordering," I have here indicated that the word *āṇatti* possesses a common essential nature [with *āṇāpanā*].
854. The construction is: "In all training rules (sikkhāpada), however, every classification of factors (aṅgabhedo) for all offenses must be understood by one who discerns."

856. The phrase “and that arises from non-action” (*akriyasamuṭṭhānā*) is the word-division. Because there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) due to not formally determining (*anadhiṭṭhāna*) an extra robe within ten days—whether by body or by speech—the example “as in the first *kaṭhina* [period]” is given.
857. “It arises from both action and non-action” means it arises from both *kiriyā* (action) and *akiriyā* (non-action). Regarding this, he states the example: “as in the taking of a robe.
Taking a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun is an action (*kiriyā*), while not giving it in exchange is non-action (*akiriyā*).
"Non-action" (*akiriya*) refers to falling into this [offense] through both action (*kiriya*) and non-action.

858. "But it may be for one who acts or one who does not act": as for that offense which may be for one who acts and may be for one who does not act, this arises sometimes from action and sometimes from non-action. The word *siyā* is a particle used in the sense of the adverb *kadāci* (sometimes).
Regarding this, he states the illustration: "In the case of taking silver. In the taking of silver, or in causing it to be taken, it may sometimes arise from an act (*kiriya*).
In the case of consenting to what has been deposited, it may sometimes belong to one who does not perform what ought to be done by body or speech;

thus it belongs to one who does not act. That offense which belongs to one who acts, to one who does not act, and sometimes to one who acts, may be an offense arising from both act and non-act (*kiriya-akiriya*).
The construction is: "It may also arise from action (kiriyato). One should say, "Like the offense of having a hut built.

For that [offense] arises from action when one has the site pointed out and then builds it exceeding the prescribed dimensions; it arises from both action and non-action (kiriyākiriyato) when one builds it exceeding the dimensions or even building it within the proper dimensions without having had the site pointed out.

861. From whichever offense [it arises]. This is the offense. It is called "liberation through perception" (*saññāvimokkha*) because liberation occurs by means of this perception acting as the instrument.
And here, even though the perception of transgression is non-existent, it is included in the sense of being the most effective factor for liberation from the offense.
Just as a famine resulting from the absence of rain is called "caused by rain," so too is this case.
This should be understood as an offense committed with consciousness (*sacittakāpatti*).

On the other hand, the other is an offense without consciousness (*acittakāpatti*). Because there is no liberation from it due to the absence of the perception of transgression, it is called "not liberation through perception" (*nosaññāvimokkhā*).

[It is so called] because of the abandonment of defilements along with their latent tendencies by means of pure consciousness, and through association with all mundane and supramundane wholesome states.
The construction is as follows: all offenses proclaimed by the Blessed One with a beautiful mind may be twofold according to the state of the mind.

As for the phrase "but by way of origination from a conscious state," it means precisely by way of origination from a conscious state. The word *pana* (but) is stated in the sense of the particle *eva* (precisely), for the purpose of excluding those that are mixed with the conscious state.
That which arises either by means of those with consciousness or by way of origination mixed with those without consciousness is "without consciousness" (*acittaka*). 865.
"By the Well-Vidant" (*suvijjena*) means by one endowed with the three or eight vidyās that shine forth;

"by the Blameless One" (*anavajjena*) means by the Blessed One who is free from the blame of defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā-kilesa*). From the perspective of worldly convention regarding what is blameworthy...
The construction is as follows: all offenses, by way of being blameworthy according to worldly convention, are stated in pairs as being twofold by way of their blameworthiness.
866. "In whichever case involving a conscious state, the mind may be unwholesome":
in whichever offense—such as drinking liquor—which originates from both conscious and unconscious states, in the case of its originating from a conscious state, the mind is indeed unwholesome.

The meaning is: "This is what is called 'worldly transgression' (lokavajja). However, for those offenses such as the first *pārājika* which originate with a conscious mind (*sacittaka-samuṭṭhāna*) and where the mind is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*), there is no need to state their status as worldly transgressions.

Or rather, even in the case of an offense that is unconscious (*acittaka*), once its status as a worldly transgression is established when it occurs on the side of a conscious mind accompanied by a wholesome mind (*kusala-citta*), it remains a worldly transgression even on the side of an unconscious mind.
Since it is a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*) that must be committed with an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*), why then would it not be mentioned separately?

However, because a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*) may be either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*) depending on the violation of the objective basis (*vatthu*), there is no fixed rule that the mind must be exclusively wholesome in the case of its being associated with consciousness; therefore, he said, "The remaining ones are transgressions of the formal rule."
By this characteristic, "those involving a transgression of the rules," when there is a mind that discerns the object on the side of consciousness,
the mind may be wholesome, it may be unwholesome, or it may be indeterminate; therefore, he said that there is no such fixed rule that on the side of consciousness it must necessarily be unwholesome.
867. That which is to be committed by way of the body-door is bodily action (*kāyakamma*). That which is to be committed in both [doors] is both bodily and verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
Mental action (*manokamma*) was not mentioned because there is no such thing as an "offense" in the mind-door.

Furthermore, the statement that "there is no offense in the mind-door" is made by way of general rule; for in cases such as consenting to what has been placed near one, there is indeed an offense even in the mind-door.
"The teachers [say] 'because of the possibility of an offense.

(868–9) "The pair of triads beginning with the wholesome" refers to both the triad of the wholesome (*kusala-ttika*) and the triad of feeling (*vedanā-ttika*). The construction is as follows: one who commits an offense does so having a wholesome or unwholesome mind, or likewise having an indeterminate (*abyākata*) mind.
"Associated with suffering, etc."—by the word "etc.," those possessing the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhā-vedanā*) are included. Even though this is so, in all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*)...
By way of unwholesome consciousness, there is one consciousness; by way of wholesome and indeterminate, two consciousnesses;
and by way of all, three consciousnesses. By way of painful feeling, there is one feeling; by way of pleasant and equanimous, two; and by way of all, three feelings.
Only this division is obtained, and no other division.
Even if the triad of wholesome states (*kusalattika*) is included, it is not obtained by way of all consciousnesses;
rather, it is obtained only by way of the thirty-two consciousnesses that originate offenses (*āpatti*). For only these thirty-two consciousnesses originate offenses:
the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, and the ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses.

From the wholesome, from the functional, and from the two types of superknowledge-consciousness—thus, even though an offense arises from thirty-two types of consciousness, it is either unwholesome or indeterminate; there is no offense that is wholesome. As it is said in the *Samathakkhandhaka*:
"A legal issue concerning offenses may be unwholesome or it may be indeterminate; there is no legal issue concerning offenses that is wholesome. This, however, is the reading...
This was said with reference only to what is prohibited by the rules (paṇṇattivajja), not to what is prohibited by the world (lokavajja).

For in cases such as digging the earth or destroying plant life—which are legal issues involving offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa)—a wholesome mind (kusalacitta) is a factor; and since that exists, it cannot be said that "there is no legal issue involving an offense that is wholesome.
Therefore, this was not said with reference to a mind capable of being a factor [for the offense]. As for that legal issue involving an offense...
That which is a world-transgression (*lokavajja*) is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*). In that regard, there is no alternative possibility such as "it might be unwholesome.
However, as for that which is a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), it is unwholesome only when one intentionally transgresses it with the thought, "I am violating this offense";
but because it may be committed unintentionally by one who is unaware of it—such as through sleeping in the same bed—it is indeterminate (*abyākata*).
Therefore, with reference to this state of differentiation based on whether an offense was committed intentionally or unintentionally, it was said therein:
"An offense-dispute may be unwholesome or indeterminate; there is no offense-dispute that is wholesome.
However, if one were to say, "That which a person with a wholesome mind commits is called a wholesome offense-dispute," [it would be incorrect].
Even for those who are without consciousness (*acittaka*), such as when the offenses of *eḷakaloma*, *pada*, *sodhamma*, and so forth arise, a wholesome mind (*kusalacitta*) might occur;

yet, even if a wholesome mind exists there, it is not a factor (*aṅga*) for the offense. Rather, the factor is either body or speech, which have moved or proceeded by way of bodily or vocal intimation (*viññatti*).
And since these are included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), they are indeterminate (*abyākata*).
870. "This, however, is the characteristic" (*idaṃ tu lakkhaṇaṃ*): this refers to the characteristic of the general determination [of offenses] beginning with the *nidāna*.
871. The verse beginning with "A sprout" (*taruṃ*) has already had its meaning explained previously. However, this is the distinction:
there it was called "a two-sprout," whereas here it is "four-crested. There, "two-sprout" includes both what is forbidden by the world and what is forbidden by the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*).
Here, "four peaks" (*catussikhā*) refers to the four failures (*vipatti*). The grammatical analysis (*viggha*) is: that which has four peaks as its sprouts.
In that context, "failure" (*vipatti*) is included among the seven fruits (*sattaphala*); here, taking the fault (*vajja*) in the sense of failure, there are seven fruits. 872.
It has reached unsurpassedness (*anuttaratam*) because no one superior or higher than itself exists; thus it is "unsurpassed" (*uttara*).
Regarding the treatise named *Uttara*: whichever among the elders, novices, or those of middle standing masters it—
meaning he studies it by making the text familiar through fluent recitation, inquires into it, and having heard both the meaning and the commentary on the meaning,
learns it thoroughly, examines it with the mind, penetrates it well with wisdom, and retains it— that monk, by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), likewise [masters] the *Vinayavinicchaya*.

The monk who is devoted to the discipline of body and speech—that is, to the restraint and subduing of transgressions of body and speech—attains unsurpassedness in the Vinaya, the Basket of Discipline;
he reaches a state where no one superior to himself is found. Regarding this, the reason is stated: "from the superior" (*uttarato*).
This refers to having mastered the recitation through proficiency and memorization, and having heard the commentary on the meaning of what has been studied.
The meaning is: "by means of this supplementary section (uttarapakaraṇa), which has become the cause through being well-retained by means of memorization.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discussion of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā) in the *Uttaralīnatthappakāsinī*.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Method of All Calculations (Sabbasaṅkalananayakathāvaṇṇanā): 873.
In the *Parivāra*, there are eight sections beginning with the "Where-Formulation" (*kattha-paññatti-vāra*) that appear explicitly;

when these same eight sections are joined with the word "condition" (*paccaya*), they are stated as the "Eight Condition Sections. These are presented individually in each of the two *Vibhaṅgas*, making sixteen *parivāras* in total.
"Of the horse" means of that which has a retinue of sixteen; "of that [retinue] of sixteen.
They lead all the methods of enumeration because all the stated methods of enumeration are to be included; thus, "the method of enumerating all the divisions.
875. "Bodily offenses are sixfold": the offense of the first *pārājika*, the offense of *dukkaṭa* regarding the preliminary effort (*payoga*) in building a hut, and one...

There are six kinds [of offenses]: when the alms-food has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya; when it has arrived, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa; regarding eating at the improper time, there is an offense of pācittiya;

and the first offense of pāṭidesanīya—thus they are sixfold. Likewise, there are also six verbal [offenses]: the fourth pārājika, the preliminary stages of having a hut built, the pācittiya for reciting the Dhamma step-by-step, disparaging someone out of a desire for sport, and the dubbhāsita for that [act]—thus they are likewise sixfold.

Regarding "three for one who conceals": there is a *pārājika* offense for a nun who conceals a fault; a *pācittiya* for a monk who conceals a *saṅghādisesa*; and a *dukkaṭa* for concealing one's own grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*)—thus there are three. "Five conditions regarding physical contact":
there is a *pārājika* for a nun in the case of bodily contact; a *saṅghādisesa* for a monk;

a *thullaccaya* for bodily contact with something attached to the body; a *dukkaṭa* for bodily contact with something that must be relinquished (*nissaggiya*); and [the same] for tickling with fingers...
“Pācittiya” refers to five offenses based on physical contact. 877.

For a nun who conceals a fault (vajja) there is a pārājika offense; for a monk who conceals a saṅghādisesa offense there is a pācittiya; thus there are two [offenses] regarding the concealing of a grave matter (duṭṭhulla).
879. This is understood from the explanatory restatement beginning with “Four within a village,” and so forth.
881. *Vajantiyā* means “of one who is going. 885.

If, however, a bhikkhunī, in the darkness of night and without a lamp, should converse with a man while within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*), there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for her. If she stands at a distance, having left the range of arm’s reach, and should speak [to him], the application of the rule is that it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) only.
886. If, however, a bhikkhunī, during the day, should be with a man in a concealed place, a hidden spot... [of that man].

If she should speak or converse while standing within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*), it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). If she should speak after having left arm’s reach, it is simply an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
such is the application. 891.

“And an offense of expiation together with relinquishment” means that it is an offense of expiation accompanied precisely by a formal act of discipline involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya-vinaya-kamma*).
893. Here, in this teaching.
896. "Of two" means of two [persons]. 898.
"The ground of common affiliation" refers to a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu who shares the same views as another within a single boundary (ekasīmā).
The state of being established (*ṭhitabhāva*). That which has "various grounds" as its prior member is *nānāpadapubbikā*; the meaning is "the ground of various affiliations" (*nānāsaṃvāsakabhūmi*).
Those who have been suspended (*ukkhitto*), those with various gains (*nānāladdhiko*), and those who have gone to various boundaries (*nānāsīmagato*) constitute the ground of various affiliations.
For it is these two grounds of affiliation alone that were spoken by the Great Sage, the Compassionate One—this is the construction [of the sentence].
899. *Duvinnaṃ* means of two persons: one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) and one who is practicing the *mānatta* penance.
*Dvayātītena* means by one who has transcended the two extremes—namely, the pursuit of sensual pleasure and the pursuit of self-mortification—and stands in the Middle Way;

or alternatively, by one who has transcended the two views of eternalism and annihilationism. 900. Regarding the expressions “only two finger-joints may be taken” and likewise “two finger-joints or two months,” the construction is that two [rules] concerning two finger-joints have been laid down.
905. “By command, the killing of a human being; by command, the taking of what is not given”—this is the construction.
907. “Three manifestations of lust”: these are the three ways of manifesting an intention for sexual intercourse.
908. It is a *saṅghādisesa* precisely because it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
910. *Vanappati* refers to species of trees such as the *nigrodha*, *udumbara*, *assattha*, and *pilakkha* that bear fruit without flowers;

however, here the intended meaning is "the lord of the forest," referring to a protected and guarded sacred tree (*cetiyarukkha*). *Thullatā* means a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). 912. *Vissaṭṭhi*: the verbal root *sṛj* (to emit) with the prefix *vi-*;

it means "in discarding" (*chaḍḍane*), that is, in the act of releasing [excrement] after having made an effort. The phrase "discarding excrement and urine on green [grass]" (*harite uccāraṃ passāvaṃ chaḍḍane*) is the word division.
913. What is their measure? How many are there? 915.

Regarding the phrase "a bhikkhu together with a bhikkhunī": here, although the context suggests a genitive case (*sāmivacana*), it is used in the nominative (*paccatta*), meaning "a bhikkhu. Alternatively, due to the requirements of the metrical composition (*gāthābandha*), there is an elision of the vowel.
918. Within arm’s reach of a second person.
Regarding the phrase “there are three offenses for the third time,” in its commentary they read: “there may be a thullaccaya for one who follows the schismatic of the Saṅgha.
However, because it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that “for the three followers of the schism, such as Kokālika and others, there is a saṅghādisesa,” that reading should not be accepted.

923. *Yāvatatiyaka* means the third [vocal] completion of three; it is the formal act (*kammavācā*). An offense that must be incurred at the conclusion of the third formal act is called a *yāvatatiyaka*.

926. “To one who is lustful... even something” (*avassutassa... kiñci*)—this shows the basis for a grave offense (*garukāpatti*). “All meat is unallowable” (*sabbaṃ maṃsaṃ akappiyaṃ*)—this shows the basis for a serious offense (*thullaccaya*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

927. “Having requested... and even food”—this shows the basis for an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*). “And even garlic”—this shows the basis for an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*). The word-division is: “for one who swallows [them] together. 930. The construction is:
for one who looks at a woman’s private parts with a lustful mind, a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated.

931. “Those of right conduct” (*sammāvattakā*) means those whose conduct is right. The forty-three rules of conduct are shown in the section on the fulfillment of the seventy-two rules of conduct in the Khandhaka.

932. There are two persons who have committed an offense regarding non-confession; one person who has committed an offense regarding the non-renunciation of a wicked view—these three are persons suspended (*ukkhitto*).
934. A "defiler" (*dūsako*) is one who defiles a nun. A "thorn" (*kaṇṭako*) is the novice Kaṇṭaka. 937. "One should give in this manner, etc.
refers to the formal motion (*ñatti*), such as "the Saṅgha should grant," which constitutes the application of the motion and the performance of the motion.

The meaning [is as follows]: "The Saṅgha gives," "the Saṅgha performs," and so forth—at the time of the formal proclamation (kammavācā), because the verbal action has not yet been completed due to such distinctions as "the Saṅgha gives" or "the Saṅgha performs," it may be called the "present-incomplete" (vippakata-paccuppanna). 938.

"Given," "performed," and so forth—when the formal proclamation has been concluded, statements such as "it has been given by the Saṅgha" or "it has been performed by the Saṅgha" are called the "past-performed" (atīta-karaṇa).
“939. ‘In the Saṅgha’ means in the midst of the Saṅgha.
Why was it said, ‘The Saṅgha is split by two causes, and not otherwise,’ when it is stated that, ‘Upāli, the Saṅgha is split in five ways.
Which five? By formal act (kamma), by recitation (uddesa), by speaking (voharanta), by proclamation (anussāvana)...’?”

Since it was stated [in the Sutta] by way of "taking a voting stick" (*salākaggāha*), and since the Commentary states "by five reasons," is it not improper here to speak of a schism in the Saṅgha by means of these two reasons alone?
It is said: It is not improper, because it was stated with reference to the one who performs the preliminary effort (*pubbapayogakāraka*).
For thus it is said in the Commentary:
“By means of a formal act” means by one of the four formal acts, such as the act of seeking permission (*apalokana-kamma*).

“By means of a recitation” means by one of the five recitations of the *Pātimokkha*. “Speaking” means conversing; that is, pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as “what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma,” according to various rebirths.
“By means of a proclamation” means [saying], “Do you not know my high birth? and so forth.

It is appropriate for you to instill in his mind the thought: "One such as I—possessing the status of a renunciant and being so learned—would never act contrary to the Dhamma or contrary to the Vinaya in the Teacher’s instruction.

By whispering words into his ear in this manner, one should provide the formal proclamation, saying: "Is Avīci cool to me like a grove of blue lotuses? Do I not fear the states of misery? and so forth.

"By means of taking voting tickets (*salākaggāha*)," means: having thus announced it, having steadied their minds, and having made them firm in their resolve so that they would not turn back, [the monk says], "Take this voting ticket.

In this context, the formal act (*kamma*) itself, or the proclamation (*uddesa*), is the authority; however, the preliminary stage consists of the formal procedure, the announcement, and the taking of the voting tickets.
For when they speak by way of illustrating eighteen grounds, even if a voting ticket has been taken after making an announcement for the purpose of generating approval therein,
the Saṅgha remains undivided. But when, having thus caused four or more to take a voting ticket,
he performs an exclusive formal act (kamma) or a recitation (uddesa), then the Saṅgha is said to be split.”
Because it has been stated that "the two primary causes for the acts of taking voting tickets (*salākaggāha*) are [the proclamation and the act of voting]," only those two are shown here.
But is it not the case that the taking of voting tickets was also said to be a preliminary stage to a schism in the Saṅgha, while only the acts of proclamation were stated to be the primary factors?
Therefore, how can this taking of voting tickets be considered a primary cause? It is replied: even the acts of proclamation...
Since they necessarily arise once the taking of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*) has been accomplished, they remain unaccomplished without the application that effects the purpose;

therefore, it is taken here as being primary. However, the proclamation (*uddesa*)—because it is preceded by the formal act (*kamma*) as it has been prescribed—is included within the "formal act" itself, and thus it should be understood that it is not mentioned separately here.

941. *Payuttāyuttavācāyā* means: it is "employed and improper" (*payuttāyuttā*) because it is employed for the purpose of procuring requisites and is improper—that is, unsuitable—for the state of being a follower of the Sakyan (a Buddhist monk). That very speech is "employed and improper speech" (*payuttāyuttavācā*);
[the offense occurs] by means of that. 944. The construction is: "Whatever nun eats after having requested [food], for her there may be an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
945. *Anāmaya* means one who is not ill, i.e., one who is not sick.

946. Regarding the verse beginning with “*Dasasatāni*,” the word “hundred” (*sata*) is understood as the remainder for the term “nights” (*rattīnaṃ*). The accusative case is used due to the absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*) with the action of concealing.
The construction is: “having concealed one hundred offenses for a hundred nights. Thus, when the construction is made in this way:
“Having concealed ten hundreds—that is, a hundred offenses—for a hundred nights;”
"Having stayed for ten nights, one who is on probation (pārivāsika) would be released"—this is the measure of the verses in the Parivāra.

The meaning is: having committed one hundred saṅghādisesa offenses on a single day, and having concealed one thousand saṅghādisesa offenses over the course of ten days by way of concealment on the hundredth day. This is the point here.

The summary meaning is as follows: if one commits one hundred *saṅghādisesa* offenses over ten days and conceals them for ten days, then a hundred nights’ concealment amounts to a concealment of one thousand offenses.
Regarding the phrase "having lived for ten nights":
the meaning is that, having requested probation on the grounds that "all those offenses were concealed for ten days," one has lived for ten nights.
