“‘One who is released while on probation’ means that a monk living his probationary period would be released from the probation he was required to live out;
the meaning is that he would be freed.
‘Eight pārājikas’ is stated by way of including what has not been previously mentioned. ‘Twenty-three grave offenses’ refers to those not shared with other monks.”
There are ten for bhikkhunīs, six not shared with bhikkhunīs that apply to bhikkhus, and seven shared by both;
thus, there are twenty-three *saṅghādisesa* rules.
948. "Those spoken" refers to the *nissaggiya* rules as previously mentioned. "They amount to forty-two" refers to those included in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga.
There are thirty [offenses] not shared with the monks, and twelve from the beginning for the nuns; thus, there are forty-two *nissaggiya* offenses.
The eight hundred and eighty *pācittiya* offenses have already been shown previously. 949.
"By the Well-Trained One" means by the Blessed One who was well-trained in the threefold training, such as higher virtue (*adhisīla*).

950. *Supaññena*: He is "possessed of excellent wisdom" (*supañña*) because he possesses that wisdom which is beautiful—consisting of the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the six unique qualities, and so forth.

*Yasassinā*: He is "renowned" (*yasassin*) because he is endowed with both fame (*yasa*), consisting of a retinue comprising the assembly of the eight types of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), and glory (*kitti*), consisting of the report of his virtues that pervades the entire world.
*Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni satāni bhavanti*: "There are three hundred and fifty" according to the calculation shown above.
The meaning is that, by way of counting the groups (*piṇḍa*), there are three hundred and fifty.
The construction is: all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed by the renowned Gotama of great wisdom amount to three hundred and fifty.
951. The construction is: the entire essential exposition (*vinicchaya*) to be stated regarding these training rules has been spoken by me in brief, in its entirety and in every aspect.
952. This is the treatise named *Uttara*.

953. Therefore, it is because I have spoken [this] after having investigated it. Or, "in meaning" (*atthe*) refers to meanings distinguished as the literal meaning (*vacanattha*), the essential meaning (*bhāvattha*), and so forth.

Or, "in the arrangement of syllables" (*akkharabandhe*) refers to the arrangement of words consisting of syllables. Or, "even in the sequence for one desiring understanding" (*viññāsassa kamepi*) refers to [the sequence] by way of enumeration (*uddesa*).
Regarding the laying down of the bonds (*ganthanikkhepa*), there should be no doubt. One should not entertain such doubts as:
"Does this express what is intended, or does it not? or "Is this inappropriate, or appropriate? or "Is this redundant, or deficient?
or "Is this a confused sequence, or a coherent sequence? or "Does this contradict established doctrine, or..."

One should not harbor any doubt or uncertainty regarding anything—whether thinking, "Is this not contrary to the established doctrine? or "Was this poorly spoken, or was it well spoken? or "Is this purposeful, or is it useless?

"Great esteem" means that because it is the fundamental cause for the succession of purposes pointed out in such passages as "The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint," one should accord it great honor; this is the meaning.

954. That bhikkhu who knows the treatise called *Vinayavinicchaya*—which is "with a superior" (*sauttara*), being accompanied by the *Uttarapakaraṇa*—and understands it in every respect according to the letter, the meaning, and the analysis;
that bhikkhu, because he has fully mastered the training to be trained in, is able to train even without a teacher who instructs him in the training.
"Capable. "Having released the dependence" means having released the residence under the tutelage of a teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya).
"He may go wherever he wishes" means he would be fit to go to whatever places he himself intends to go; this is the meaning. 955. "By one wishing to grant dependence":
"with the analysis" means together with the detailed explanation (vibhaṅga); "with the matrix" means together with the summary outline (mātikā). This...

Having thoroughly mastered this *Vinayavinicchayapakaraṇa* together with its commentary (*sauttara*), having made it well-versed by tongue through the text, and having correctly understood it in terms of both meaning and legal decision (*vinicchaya*), [the conclusion is] that it should be given in this manner. 956–7.
Whatever monk recites this *Vinayavinicchayapakaraṇa* together with its commentary verbally and mentally...
He reflects; he hears what is being said by others; he questions the meaning; he causes another to recite it; he constantly examines the meaning;

having approached the meaning as questioned through the application of reasons and examples, he surveys it from all sides, determines it with wisdom, and defines it. For that bhikkhu, all [these qualities] are dependent upon training.

The construction is as follows: all meanings—the distinctions between what constitutes an offense and what does not, what is permissible and what is impermissible, and so forth—appear clearly and become manifest, like an *āmalaka* fruit in the hand or like a stainless jewel in the palm.
"Amala" means that which has no stain (*mala*); thus, "āmalaka" refers to a stainless jewel.
958. "Abuddhi" means those who possess no intelligence. "Abuddhijana" refers to those people who lack such intelligence.
One who gives, takes away, or effects the destruction of the essence of these unintelligent people is called "abuddhijanasāradaṃ"—that which is bottomless and profound for those devoid of wisdom.

It is the ocean of the Deathless (amata-sāgara), in which they find no foothold, and which possesses the flavor of the essence of the meaning of the Truth (saddattha-rasa), namely, the Deathless of Nibbāna.
Or, because it is the cause for obtaining [the goal], this supreme and most excellent "Uttara-sāgara" (Ocean Beyond)—
which is like the ocean, immediate and perceptible, and known as the *Uttarapakaraṇa*—

having become its very essence, the person who is a bhikkhu, crossing over and reaching the end, is indeed one who has gone to the further shore (*pārago*), having reached the limit of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The construction is: "He might go, he would go, to Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the further shore of saṃsāra.
(Verse 959) Because of that very reason—"from" (*orato*) meaning "away from" (*ava-pūrato*), "from" (*orato*) meaning "out of" (*nir-āsaṅkatāya*);
a person who has turned back from evil and is fearful of evil, having shaken off darkness—precisely because of that fear of evil, [darkness] which arises by way of the obsession of the mind...

Having dispelled the darkness of delusion by means of its specific abandonment (*tadaṅgappahāna*), it bestows—that is, brings about—the "bestowing of the work of all stains" (*sabbaṅgaṇakammada*), which is the work of all stains such as lust and so forth, namely their abandonment through specific abandonment and other methods; thus it receives the name "bestower of the work of all stains.
It is the "footing of happiness," the cause of mundane and supramundane happiness, endowed with qualities (*guṇasaṃhita*) consisting of the benefits such as virtue (*sīla*) and the rest.

One should diligently and constantly study this treatise called the *Uttara*, which is endowed with virtues, joined with virtues, and clarifies virtues; which is beneficial like the ambrosial medicine because it is free from all faults and all diseases, and because it brings about qualities such as agelessness and immortality;
thinking, "I shall practice until I am thoroughly familiar with it," one should apply oneself single-mindedly so as to be capable of accomplishing the aforementioned purpose.
The construction is as follows: having performed [these duties], one should indeed train by means of study and so forth;

one should not remain indifferent. 960. Regarding those who bear themselves with modesty (*lajjipuggala*), it produces proficiency, skill, and intrepidity in making oneself proficient in fulfilling the morality of the Pātimokkha restraint and in overcoming the enemies of the Dispensation—thus, "in making oneself proficient" refers to the supreme [task].
Therefore, by a keen ascetic who desires proficiency, skill, and wisdom in the supreme Piṭaka, the Vinaya Piṭaka,
this treatise on the determination of the Vinaya— which is surpassed by nothing—

should be mastered constantly and continuously through the methods of learning, memorizing, interrogation, reflection, and so forth, by means of a keen, stainless practice, and an expert, essential procedure.
The construction is: "it is to be trained in.
Thus ends the commentary on the Discourse on the Method of Total Computation (*Sabbasaṅkalanayanakathā*) within the *Uttaralīnatthappakāsinī*.
Commentary on the Conclusion (Nigamanakathāvaṇṇanā) 961–3.
By one who desires the very long endurance of the threefold teaching of the Great Sage, who wishes for its persistence over an exceedingly long period of time,
who is wise, possessed of highly praised knowledge, pure in heart, and whose inner disposition is purified by being free from regard for gain and honor.
It was composed by the eminent teacher named Buddhadatta.
In terms of its phrasing and its meaning, it is the most supreme and excellent exposition;
it has reached completion and attained perfection without any internal or external obstacles.
Likewise, may the intentions and aspirations of beings connected with the Dhamma and conducive to the wholesome succeed without obstacle and reach fulfillment;
by this great arising of merit consisting in the composition of this superior exposition, he delights the people through the four bases of sympathy,
and thus the protector of the earth, who has attained the designation "King," [delights] the mass of people dependent upon the earth.

May he protect [the kingdom] by the right method, without violating the ten duties of a king. May the god Pajjunna rain down properly at the right time, when it is fit for the use of both the stationary and the moving beings;
may he rain properly, avoiding both drought and excessive rain. 964.
As long as Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, stands firm, and as long as the world endures, may the moon remain the delight to the eyes of all people.

As long as it shines and as long as it illuminates its own intrinsic nature, may the True Dhamma of the illustrious Gotama, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—this True Dhamma which is threefold by way of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*paṭivedha*)—endure and prevail.
965. Having endured, withstood, and overcome external and internal dangers such as lions and burning fevers...
*Pavattanaṃ* means patience (*khanti*). *Soraccaṃ*: one who delights (*rato*) in what is beautiful (*sobhane*) is *surato*; the state of being *surato* is *soraccaṃ*.
One who possesses beautiful virtue (*sīla*) characterized by qualities such as being unbroken is *susīlo*; the state of being *susīlo* is [the meaning of *soraccaṃ*].
The commentary on the concluding statement is finished.
The *Uttaravinicchayaṭīkā* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Vinayavinicchaya* titled *Vinayatthasārasandīpanī*,
and the commentary on the *Uttaravinicchaya* titled *Līnatthapakāsanī*.
[The work is] completed.
These verses were later composed by the Elder of steadfast mind, who desired to illuminate the Teaching.
Virtuous, wise, and ethical, a good friend, gentle likewise— Among the Sīhaḷa and Ari-madda [peoples],
the Elder Sīvali was as manifest As the moon and the sun,
possessed of great majesty and great fame.
The Sinhalese [commentary] which was brought here by that wise one has been well-written with the Sinhalese script.
It was composed by the Elder named Revata, whose mind was steadfast.
Having carefully revised it while residing in Arimaddana,
this commentary was caused to be written for the benefit of the monks in Arimaddana.
This excellent exposition has now reached its conclusion.
In that same way, may all things be successful for all sentient beings.
